title: The Boy Who Lived
text: /nMr. and Mrs. Dursley, of number four, Privet Drive,/nwere proud to say that they were perfectly normal,/nthank you very much. They were the last people you'd/nexpect to be involved in anything strange or/nmysterious, because they just didn't hold with such/nnonsense./n/nMr. Dursley was the director of a firm called/nGrunnings, which made drills. He was a big, beefy/nman with hardly any neck, although he did have a/nvery large mustache. Mrs. Dursley was thin and/nblonde and had nearly twice the usual amount of/nneck, which came in very useful as she spent so/nmuch of her time craning over garden fences, spying/non the neighbors. The Dursley s had a small son/ncalled Dudley and in their opinion there was no finer/nboy anywhere./n/nThe Dursleys had everything they wanted, but they/nalso had a secret, and their greatest fear was that/nsomebody would discover it. They didn't think they/ncould bear it if anyone found out about the Potters./nMrs. Potter was Mrs. Dursley's sister, but they hadn't/n/n/n/n/nmet for several years; in fact, Mrs. Dursley pretended/nshe didn't have a sister, because her sister and her/ngood-for-nothing husband were as unDursleyish as it/nwas possible to be. The Dursleys shuddered to think/nwhat the neighbors would say if the Potters arrived in/nthe street. The Dursleys knew that the Potters had a/nsmall son, too, but they had never even seen him./n/nThis boy was another good reason for keeping the/nPotters away; they didn't want Dudley mixing with a/nchild like that./n/nWhen Mr. and Mrs. Dursley woke up on the dull, gray/nTuesday our story starts, there was nothing about the/ncloudy sky outside to suggest that strange and/nmysterious things would soon be happening all over/nthe country. Mr. Dursley hummed as he picked out/nhis most boring tie for work, and Mrs. Dursley/ngossiped away happily as she wrestled a screaming/nDudley into his high chair./n/nNone of them noticed a large, tawny owl flutter past/nthe window./n/nAt half past eight, Mr. Dursley picked up his/nbriefcase, pecked Mrs. Dursley on the cheek, and/ntried to kiss Dudley good-bye but missed, because/nDudley was now having a tantrum and throwing his/ncereal at the walls. "Little tyke," chortled Mr. Dursley/nas he left the house. He got into his car and backed/nout of number four's drive./n/nIt was on the corner of the street that he noticed the/nfirst sign of something peculiar — a cat reading a/nmap. For a second, Mr. Dursley didn't realize what he/nhad seen — then he jerked his head around to look/nagain. There was a tabby cat standing on the corner/nof Privet Drive, but there wasn't a map in sight. What/ncould he have been thinking of? It must have been a/ntrick of the light. Mr. Dursley blinked and stared at/n/n/n/n/nthe cat. It stared back. As Mr. Dursley drove around/nthe corner and up the road, he watched the cat in his/nmirror. It was now reading the sign that said Privet/nDrive — no, looking at the sign; cats couldn't read/nmaps or signs. Mr. Dursley gave himself a little shake/nand put the cat out of his mind. As he drove toward/ntown he thought of nothing except a large order of/ndrills he was hoping to get that day./n/nBut on the edge of town, drills were driven out of his/nmind by something else. As he sat in the usual/nmorning traffic jam, he couldn't help noticing that/nthere seemed to be a lot of strangely dressed people/nabout. People in cloaks. Mr. Dursley couldn't bear/npeople who dressed in funny clothes — the getups/nyou saw on young people! He supposed this was some/nstupid new fashion. He drummed his fingers on the/nsteering wheel and his eyes fell on a huddle of these/nweirdos standing quite close by. They were whispering/nexcitedly together. Mr. Dursley was enraged to see/nthat a couple of them weren't young at all; why, that/nman had to be older than he was, and wearing an/nemerald-green cloak! The nerve of him! But then it/nstruck Mr. Dursley that this was probably some silly/nstunt — these people were obviously collecting for/nsomething ... yes, that would be it. The traffic moved/non and a few minutes later, Mr. Dursley arrived in the/nGrunnings parking lot, his mind back on drills./n/nMr. Dursley always sat with his back to the window in/nhis office on the ninth floor. If he hadn't, he might/nhave found it harder to concentrate on drills that/nmorning. He didn't see the owls swooping past in/nbroad daylight, though people down in the street did;/nthey pointed and gazed open-mouthed as owl after/nowl sped overhead. Most of them had never seen an/nowl even at nighttime. Mr. Dursley, however, had a/nperfectly normal, owl-free morning. He yelled at five/ndifferent people. He made several important telephone/n/n/n/n/ncalls and shouted a bit more. He was in a very good/nmood until lunchtime, when he thought he'd stretch/nhis legs and walk across the road to buy himself a/nbun from the bakery./n/nHe'd forgotten all about the people in cloaks until he/npassed a group of them next to the baker's. He eyed/nthem angrily as he passed. He didn't know why, but/nthey made him uneasy. This bunch were whispering/nexcitedly, too, and he couldn't see a single collecting/ntin. It was on his way back past them, clutching a/nlarge doughnut in a bag, that he caught a few words/nof what they were saying./n/n"The Potters, that's right, that's what I heard — "/n/n" — yes, their son, Harry — "/n/nMr. Dursley stopped dead. Fear flooded him. He/nlooked back at the whisperers as if he wanted to say/nsomething to them, but thought better of it./n/nHe dashed back across the road, hurried up to his/noffice, snapped at his secretary not to disturb him,/nseized his telephone, and had almost finished dialing/nhis home number when he changed his mind. He put/nthe receiver back down and stroked his mustache,/nthinking ... no, he was being stupid. Potter wasn't/nsuch an unusual name. He was sure there were lots/nof people called Potter who had a son called Harry./nCome to think of it, he wasn't even sure his nephew/nwas called Harry. He'd never even seen the boy. It/nmight have been Harvey. Or Harold. There was no/npoint in worrying Mrs. Dursley; she always got so/nupset at any mention of her sister. He didn't blame/nher — if he'd had a sister like that ... but all the/nsame, those people in cloaks .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe found it a lot harder to concentrate on drills that/nafternoon and when he left the building at five o'clock,/nhe was still so worried that he walked straight into/nsomeone just outside the door./n/n"Sorry," he grunted, as the tiny old man stumbled/nand almost fell. It was a few seconds before Mr./nDursley realized that the man was wearing a violet/ncloak. He didn't seem at all upset at being almost/nknocked to the ground. On the contrary, his face split/ninto a wide smile and he said in a squeaky voice that/nmade passersby stare, "Don't be sorry, my dear sir,/nfor nothing could upset me today! Rejoice, for You-/nKnow-Who has gone at last! Even Muggles like/nyourself should be celebrating, this happy, happy/nday!"/n/nAnd the old man hugged Mr. Dursley around the/nmiddle and walked off./n/nMr. Dursley stood rooted to the spot. He had been/nhugged by a complete stranger. He also thought he/nhad been called a Muggle, whatever that was. He was/nrattled. He hurried to his car and set off for home,/nhoping he was imagining things, which he had never/nhoped before, because he didn't approve of/nimagination./n/nAs he pulled into the driveway of number four, the/nfirst thing he saw — and it didn't improve his mood —/nwas the tabby cat he'd spotted that morning. It was/nnow sitting on his garden wall. He was sure it was the/nsame one; it had the same markings around its eyes./n/n"Shoo!" said Mr. Dursley loudly./n/nThe cat didn't move. It just gave him a stern look./n/nWas this normal cat behavior? Mr. Dursley wondered./nTrying to pull himself together, he let himself into the/n/n/n/n/n/nhouse. He was still determined not to mention/nanything to his wife./n/nMrs. Dursley had had a nice, normal day. She told/nhim over dinner all about Mrs. Next Door's problems/nwith her daughter and how Dudley had learned a new/nword ("Won't!"). Mr. Dursley tried to act normally./nWhen Dudley had been put to bed, he went into the/nliving room in time to catch the last report on the/nevening news:/n/n"And finally, bird-watchers everywhere have reported/nthat the nation's owls have been behaving very/nunusually today. Although owls normally hunt at/nnight and are hardly ever seen in daylight, there have/nbeen hundreds of sightings of these birds flying in/nevery direction since sunrise. Experts are unable to/nexplain why the owls have suddenly changed their/nsleeping pattern." The newscaster allowed himself a/ngrin. "Most mysterious. And now, over to Jim/nMcGuffin with the weather. Going to be any more/nshowers of owls tonight, Jim?"/n/n"Well, Ted," said the weatherman, "I don't know about/nthat, but it's not only the owls that have been acting/noddly today. Viewers as far apart as Kent, Yorkshire,/nand Dundee have been phoning in to tell me that/ninstead of the rain I promised yesterday, they've had a/ndownpour of shooting stars! Perhaps people have/nbeen celebrating Bonfire Night early — it's not until/nnext week, folks! But I can promise a wet night/ntonight."/n/nMr. Dursley sat frozen in his armchair. Shooting stars/nall over Britain? Owls flying by daylight? Mysterious/npeople in cloaks all over the place? And a whisper, a/nwhisper about the Potters . . ./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Dursley came into the living room carrying two/ncups of tea. It was no good. He'd have to say/nsomething to her. He cleared his throat nervously. "Er/n— Petunia, dear — you haven't heard from your sister/nlately, have you?"/n/nAs he had expected, Mrs. Dursley looked shocked and/nangry. After all, they normally pretended she didn't/nhave a sister./n/n"No," she said sharply. "Why?"/n/n"Funny stuff on the news," Mr. Dursley mumbled./n"Owls . . . shooting stars . . . and there were a lot of/nfunny-looking people in town today ..."/n/n"So?" snapped Mrs. Dursley./n/n"Well, I just thought ... maybe ... it was something to/ndo with ... you know ... her crowd."/n/nMrs. Dursley sipped her tea through pursed lips. Mr./nDursley wondered whether he dared tell her he'd/nheard the name "Potter." He decided he didn't dare./nInstead he said, as casually as he could, "Their son —/nhe'd be about Dudley's age now, wouldn't he?"/n/n"I suppose so," said Mrs. Dursley stiffly./n/n"What's his name again? Howard, isn't it?"/n/n"Harry. Nasty, common name, if you ask me."/n/n"Oh, yes," said Mr. Dursley, his heart sinking/nhorribly. "Yes, I quite agree."/n/nHe didn't say another word on the subject as they/nwent upstairs to bed. While Mrs. Dursley was in the/nbathroom, Mr. Dursley crept to the bedroom window/n/n/n/n/n/nand peered down into the front garden. The cat was/nstill there. It was staring down Privet Drive as though/nit were waiting for something./n/nWas he imagining things? Could all this have/nanything to do with the Potters? If it did ... if it got out/nthat they were related to a pair of — well, he didn't/nthink he could bear it./n/nThe Dursleys got into bed. Mrs. Dursley fell asleep/nquickly but Mr. Dursley lay awake, turning it all over/nin his mind. His last, comforting thought before he fell/nasleep was that even if the Potters were involved,/nthere was no reason for them to come near him and/nMrs. Dursley. The Potters knew very well what he and/nPetunia thought about them and their kind. ... He/ncouldn't see how he and Petunia could get mixed up/nin anything that might be going on — he yawned and/nturned over — it couldn't affect them. .../n/nHow very wrong he was./n/nMr. Dursley might have been drifting into an uneasy/nsleep, but the cat on the wall outside was showing no/nsign of sleepiness. It was sitting as still as a statue,/nits eyes fixed unblinkingly on the far corner of Privet/nDrive. It didn't so much as quiver when a car door/nslammed on the next street, nor when two owls/nswooped overhead. In fact, it was nearly midnight/nbefore the cat moved at all./n/nA man appeared on the corner the cat had been/nwatching, appeared so suddenly and silently you'd/nhave thought he'd just popped out of the ground. The/ncat's tail twitched and its eyes narrowed./n/nNothing like this man had ever been seen on Privet/nDrive. He was tall, thin, and very old, judging by the/nsilver of his hair and beard, which were both long/n/n/n/n/n/nenough to tuck into his belt. He was wearing long/nrobes, a purple cloak that swept the ground, and/nhigh-heeled, buckled boots. His blue eyes were light,/nbright, and sparkling behind half-moon spectacles/nand his nose was very long and crooked, as though it/nhad been broken at least twice. This man's name was/nAlbus Dumbledore./n/nAlbus Dumbledore didn't seem to realize that he had/njust arrived in a street where everything from his/nname to his boots was unwelcome. He was busy/nrummaging in his cloak, looking for something. But/nhe did seem to realize he was being watched, because/nhe looked up suddenly at the cat, which was still/nstaring at him from the other end of the street. For/nsome reason, the sight of the cat seemed to amuse/nhim. He chuckled and muttered, "I should have/nknown."/n/nHe found what he was looking for in his inside/npocket. It seemed to be a silver cigarette lighter. He/nflicked it open, held it up in the air, and clicked it./nThe nearest street lamp went out with a little pop. He/nclicked it again — the next lamp flickered into/ndarkness. Twelve times he clicked the Put-Outer,/nuntil the only lights left on the whole street were two/ntiny pinpricks in the distance, which were the eyes of/nthe cat watching him. If anyone looked out of their/nwindow now, even beady-eyed Mrs. Dursley, they/nwouldn't be able to see anything that was happening/ndown on the pavement. Dumbledore slipped the Put-/nOuter back inside his cloak and set off down the/nstreet toward number four, where he sat down on the/nwall next to the cat. He didn't look at it, but after a/nmoment he spoke to it./n/n"Fancy seeing you here, Professor McGonagall."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe turned to smile at the tabby, but it had gone./nInstead he was smiling at a rather severe-looking/nwoman who was wearing square glasses exactly the/nshape of the markings the cat had had around its/neyes. She, too, was wearing a cloak, an emerald one./nHer black hair was drawn into a tight bun. She/nlooked distinctly ruffled./n/n"How did you know it was me?" she asked./n/n"My dear Professor, I've never seen a cat sit so stiffly."/n/n"You'd be stiff if you'd been sitting on a brick wall all/nday," said Professor McGonagall./n/n"All day? When you could have been celebrating? I/nmust have passed a dozen feasts and parties on my/nway here."/n/nProfessor McGonagall sniffed angrily./n/n"Oh yes, everyone's celebrating, all right," she said/nimpatiently. "You'd think they'd be a bit more careful,/nbut no — even the Muggles have noticed something's/ngoing on. It was on their news." She jerked her head/nback at the Dursleys' dark living-room window. "I/nheard it. Flocks of owls ... shooting stars. ... Well,/nthey're not completely stupid. They were bound to/nnotice something. Shooting stars down in Kent — I'll/nbet that was Dedalus Diggle. He never had much/nsense."/n/n"You can't blame them," said Dumbledore gently./n"We've had precious little to celebrate for eleven/nyears."/n/n"I know that," said Professor McGonagall irritably./n/n"But that's no reason to lose our heads. People are/nbeing downright careless, out on the streets in broad/n/n/n/n/n/ndaylight, not even dressed in Muggle clothes,/nswapping rumors."/n/nShe threw a sharp, sideways glance at Dumbledore/nhere, as though hoping he was going to tell her/nsomething, but he didn't, so she went on. "A fine/nthing it would be if, on the very day You-Know-Who/nseems to have disappeared at last, the Muggles found/nout about us all. I suppose he really has gone,/nDumbledore?"/n/n"It certainly seems so," said Dumbledore. "We have/nmuch to be thankful for. Would you care for a lemon/ndrop?"/n/n"A what?"/n/n"A lemon drop. They're a kind of Muggle sweet I'm/nrather fond of."/n/n"No, thank you," said Professor McGonagall coldly, as/nthough she didn't think this was the moment for/nlemon drops. "As I say, even if You-Know-Who has/ngone — "/n/n"My dear Professor, surely a sensible person like/nyourself can call him by his name? All this You-/nKnow-Who' nonsense — for eleven years I have been/ntrying to persuade people to call him by his proper/nname: Voldemort." Professor McGonagall flinched, but/nDumbledore, who was unsticking two lemon drops,/nseemed not to notice. "It all gets so confusing if we/nkeep saying You-Know-Who.' I have never seen any/nreason to be frightened of saying Voldemort's name."/n/n"I know you haven't," said Professor McGonagall,/nsounding half exasperated, half admiring. "But you're/ndifferent. Everyone knows you're the only one You-/nKnow- oh, all right, Voldemort, was frightened of."/n/n/n/n/n/n"You flatter me," said Dumbledore calmly. "Voldemort/nhad powers I will never have."/n/n/n/n"Only because you're too — well — noble to use/nthem."/n/n"It's lucky it's dark. I haven't blushed so much since/nMadam Pomfrey told me she liked my new earmuffs."/n/nProfessor McGonagall shot a sharp look at/nDumbledore and said, "The owls are nothing next to/nthe rumors that are flying around. You know what/neveryone's saying? About why he's disappeared?/n/nAbout what finally stopped him?"/n/nIt seemed that Professor McGonagall had reached the/npoint she was most anxious to discuss, the real/nreason she had been waiting on a cold, hard wall all/nday, for neither as a cat nor as a woman had she/nfixed Dumbledore with such a piercing stare as she/ndid now. It was plain that whatever "everyone" was/nsaying, she was not going to believe it until/nDumbledore told her it was true. Dumbledore,/nhowever, was choosing another lemon drop and did/nnot answer./n/n"What they're saying," she pressed on, "is that last/nnight Voldemort turned up in Godric's Hollow. He/nwent to find the Potters. The rumor is that Lily and/nJames Potter are — are — that they're — dead."/n/nDumbledore bowed his head. Professor McGonagall/ngasped./n/n"Lily and James ... I can't believe it ... I didn't want to/nbelieve it ... Oh, Albus ..."/n/nDumbledore reached out and patted her on the/nshoulder. "I know ... I know ..." he said heavily./n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor McGonagall's voice trembled as she went/non. "That's not all. They're saying he tried to kill the/nPotters' son, Harry. But — he couldn't. He couldn't/nkill that little boy. No one knows why, or how, but/nthey're saying that when he couldn't kill Harry Potter,/nVoldemort's power somehow broke — and that's why/nhe's gone."/n/nDumbledore nodded glumly./n/n"It's — it's true?" faltered Professor McGonagall. "After/nall he's done ... all the people he's killed ... he couldn't/nkill a little boy? It's just astounding ... of all the/nthings to stop him . . . but how in the name of heaven/ndid Harry survive?"/n/n"We can only guess," said Dumbledore. "We may/nnever know."/n/nProfessor McGonagall pulled out a lace handkerchief/nand dabbed at her eyes beneath her spectacles./nDumbledore gave a great sniff as he took a golden/nwatch from his pocket and examined it. It was a very/nodd watch. It had twelve hands but no numbers;/ninstead, little planets were moving around the edge. It/nmust have made sense to Dumbledore, though,/nbecause he put it back in his pocket and said,/n"Hagrid's late. I suppose it was he who told you I'd be/nhere, by the way?"/n/n"Yes," said Professor McGonagall. "And I don't/nsuppose you're going to tell me why you're here, of all/nplaces?"/n/n"I've come to bring Harry to his aunt and uncle./nThey're the only family he has left now."/n/n"You don't mean — you can't mean the people who/nlive here?" cried Professor McGonagall, jumping to her/n/n/n/n/n/nfeet and pointing at number four. "Dumbledore — you/ncan't. I've been watching them all day. You couldn't/nfind two people who are less like us. And they've got/nthis son — I saw him kicking his mother all the way/nup the street, screaming for sweets. Harry Potter/ncome and live here!"/n/n"It's the best place for him," said Dumbledore firmly./n"His aunt and uncle will be able to explain everything/nto him when he's older. I've written them a letter."/n/n"A letter?" repeated Professor McGonagall faintly,/nsitting back down on the wall. "Really, Dumbledore,/nyou think you can explain all this in a letter? These/npeople will never understand him! He'll be famous —/na legend — I wouldn't be surprised if today was/nknown as Harry Potter Day in the future — there will/nbe books written about Harry — every child in our/nworld will know his name!"/n/n"Exactly," said Dumbledore, looking very seriously/nover the top of his half-moon glasses. "It would be/nenough to turn any boy's head. Famous before he can/nwalk and talk! Famous for something he won't even/nremember! Can't you see how much better off he'll be,/ngrowing up away from all that until he's ready to take/nit?"/n/n/n/nProfessor McGonagall opened her mouth, changed her/nmind, swallowed, and then said, "Yes — yes, you're/nright, of course. But how is the boy getting here,/nDumbledore?" She eyed his cloak suddenly as though/nshe thought he might be hiding Harry underneath it./n/n"Hagrid's bringing him."/n/n"You think it — wise — to trust Hagrid with/nsomething as important as this?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I would trust Hagrid with my life," said Dumbledore./n/n"I'm not saying his heart isn't in the right place," said/nProfessor McGonagall grudgingly, "but you can't/npretend he's not careless. He does tend to — what/nwas that?"/n/nA low rumbling sound had broken the silence around/nthem. It grew steadily louder as they looked up and/ndown the street for some sign of a headlight; it/nswelled to a roar as they both looked up at the sky —/nand a huge motorcycle fell out of the air and landed/non the road in front of them./n/nIf the motorcycle was huge, it was nothing to the man/nsitting astride it. He was almost twice as tall as a/nnormal man and at least five times as wide. He looked/nsimply too big to be allowed, and so wild — long/ntangles of bushy black hair and beard hid most of his/nface, he had hands the size of trash can lids, and his/nfeet in their leather boots were like baby dolphins. In/nhis vast, muscular arms he was holding a bundle of/nblankets./n/n"Hagrid," said Dumbledore, sounding relieved. "At/nlast. And where did you get that motorcycle?"/n/n"Borrowed it, Professor Dumbledore, sir," said the/ngiant, climbing carefully off the motorcycle as he/nspoke. "Young Sirius Black lent it to me. I've got him,/nsir."/n/n"No problems, were there?"/n/n"No, sir — house was almost destroyed, but I got him/nout all right before the Muggles started swarmin'/naround. He fell asleep as we was flyin' over Bristol."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore and Professor McGonagall bent forward/nover the bundle of blankets. Inside, just visible, was a/nbaby boy, fast asleep. Under a tuft of jet-black hair/nover his forehead they could see a curiously shaped/ncut, like a bolt of lightning./n/n"Is that where — ?" whispered Professor McGonagall./n/n"Yes," said Dumbledore. "Hell have that scar forever."/n/n"Couldn't you do something about it, Dumbledore?"/n/n"Even if I could, I wouldn't. Scars can come in handy./n/nI have one myself above my left knee that is a perfect/nmap of the London Underground. Well — give him/nhere, Hagrid — we'd better get this over with."/n/nDumbledore took Harry in his arms and turned/ntoward the Dursleys' house./n/n"Could I — could I say good-bye to him, sir?" asked/nHagrid. He bent his great, shaggy head over Harry/nand gave him what must have been a very scratchy,/nwhiskery kiss. Then, suddenly, Hagrid let out a howl/nlike a wounded dog./n/n"Shhh!" hissed Professor McGonagall, "you'll wake the/nMuggles!"/n/n"S-s-sorry," sobbed Hagrid, taking out a large, spotted/nhandkerchief and burying his face in it. "But I c-c-/ncan't stand it — Lily an' James dead — an' poor little/nHarry off ter live with Muggles — "/n/n"Yes, yes, it's all very sad, but get a grip on yourself,/nHagrid, or we'll be found," Professor McGonagall/nwhispered, patting Hagrid gingerly on the arm as/nDumbledore stepped over the low garden wall and/nwalked to the front door. He laid Harry gently on the/n/n/n/n/ndoorstep, took a letter out of his cloak, tucked it/ninside Harry's blankets, and then came back to the/nother two. For a full minute the three of them stood/nand looked at the little bundle; Hagrid's shoulders/nshook, Professor McGonagall blinked furiously, and/nthe twinkling light that usually shone from/nDumbledore's eyes seemed to have gone out./n/n"Well," said Dumbledore finally, "that's that. We've no/nbusiness staying here. We may as well go and join the/ncelebrations."/n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid in a very muffled voice, "I'd best/nget this bike away. G 'night, Professor McGonagall —/nProfessor Dumbledore, sir."/n/nWiping his streaming eyes on his jacket sleeve, Hagrid/nswung himself onto the motorcycle and kicked the/nengine into life; with a roar it rose into the air and off/ninto the night./n/n"I shall see you soon, I expect, Professor McGonagall,"/nsaid Dumbledore, nodding to her. Professor/nMcGonagall blew her nose in reply./n/nDumbledore turned and walked back down the street./nOn the corner he stopped and took out the silver Put-/nOuter. He clicked it once, and twelve balls of light/nsped back to their street lamps so that Privet Drive/nglowed suddenly orange and he could make out a/ntabby cat slinking around the corner at the other end/nof the street. He could just see the bundle of blankets/non the step of number four./n/n"Good luck, Harry," he murmured. He turned on his/nheel and with a swish of his cloak, he was gone./n/nA breeze ruffled the neat hedges of Privet Drive, which/nlay silent and tidy under the inky sky, the very last/n/n/n/n/n/nplace you would expect astonishing things to happen./nHarry Potter rolled over inside his blankets without/nwaking up. One small hand closed on the letter/nbeside him and he slept on, not knowing he was/nspecial, not knowing he was famous, not knowing he/nwould be woken in a few hours' time by Mrs./n/nDursley's scream as she opened the front door to put/nout the milk bottles, nor that he would spend the next/nfew weeks being prodded and pinched by his cousin/nDudley. ... He couldn't know that at this very/nmoment, people meeting in secret all over the country/nwere holding up their glasses and saying in hushed/nvoices: "To Harry Potter — the boy who lived!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Vanishing Glass
text: /nNearly ten years had passed since the Dursleys had/nwoken up to find their nephew on the front step, but/nPrivet Drive had hardly changed at all. The sun rose/non the same tidy front gardens and lit up the brass/nnumber four on the Dursleys' front door; it crept into/ntheir living room, which was almost exactly the same/nas it had been on the night when Mr. Dursley had/nseen that fateful news report about the owls. Only the/nphotographs on the mantelpiece really showed how/nmuch time had passed. Ten years ago, there had been/nlots of pictures of what looked like a large pink beach/nball wearing different-colored bonnets — but Dudley/nDursley was no longer a baby, and now the/nphotographs showed a large blond boy riding his first/nbicycle, on a carousel at the fair, playing a computer/ngame with his father, being hugged and kissed by his/nmother. The room held no sign at all that another boy/nlived in the house, too./n/nYet Harry Potter was still there, asleep at the moment,/nbut not for long. His Aunt Petunia was awake and it/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwas her shrill voice that made the first noise of the/nday./n/n"Up! Get up! Now!"/n/nHarry woke with a start. His aunt rapped on the door/nagain./n/n"Up!" she screeched. Harry heard her walking toward/nthe kitchen and then the sound of the frying pan/nbeing put on the stove. He rolled onto his back and/ntried to remember the dream he had been having. It/nhad been a good one. There had been a flying/nmotorcycle in it. He had a funny feeling he'd had the/nsame dream before./n/nHis aunt was back outside the door./n/n"Are you up yet?" she demanded./n/n"Nearly," said Harry./n/n"Well, get a move on, I want you to look after the/nbacon. And don't you dare let it burn, I want/neverything perfect on Duddy's birthday."/n/nHarry groaned./n/n"What did you say?" his aunt snapped through the/ndoor./n/n"Nothing, nothing ..."/n/nDudley's birthday — how could he have forgotten?/nHarry got slowly out of bed and started looking for/nsocks. He found a pair under his bed and, after/npulling a spider off one of them, put them on. Harry/nwas used to spiders, because the cupboard under the/nstairs was full of them, and that was where he slept./n/n/n/n/nWhen he was dressed he went down the hall into the/nkitchen. The table was almost hidden beneath all/nDudley's birthday presents. It looked as though/nDudley had gotten the new computer he wanted, not/nto mention the second television and the racing bike./nExactly why Dudley wanted a racing bike was a/nmystery to Harry, as Dudley was very fat and hated/nexercise — unless of course it involved punching/nsomebody. Dudley's favorite punching bag was Harry,/nbut he couldn't often catch him. Harry didn't look it,/nbut he was very fast./n/nPerhaps it had something to do with living in a dark/ncupboard, but Harry had always been small and/nskinny for his age. He looked even smaller and/nskinnier than he really was because all he had to/nwear were old clothes of Dudley's, and Dudley was/nabout four times bigger than he was. Harry had a thin/nface, knobbly knees, black hair, and bright green/neyes. He wore round glasses held together with a lot/nof Scotch tape because of all the times Dudley had/npunched him on the nose. The only thing Harry liked/nabout his own appearance was a very thin scar on his/nforehead that was shaped like a bolt of lightning. He/nhad had it as long as he could remember, and the/nfirst question he could ever remember asking his/nAunt Petunia was how he had gotten it./n/n"In the car crash when your parents died," she had/nsaid. "And don't ask questions."/n/nDon't ask questions — that was the first rule for a/nquiet life with the Dursleys./n/nUncle Vernon entered the kitchen as Harry was/nturning over the bacon./n/n"Comb your hair!" he barked, by way of a morning/ngreeting./n/n/n/n/n/nAbout once a week, Uncle Vernon looked over the top/nof his newspaper and shouted that Harry needed a/nhaircut. Harry must have had more haircuts than the/nrest of the boys in his class put together, but it made/nno difference, his hair simply grew that way — all over/nthe place./n/nHarry was frying eggs by the time Dudley arrived in/nthe kitchen with his mother. Dudley looked a lot like/nUncle Vernon. He had a large pink face, not much/nneck, small, watery blue eyes, and thick blond hair/nthat lay smoothly on his thick, fat head. Aunt Petunia/noften said that Dudley looked like a baby angel —/nHarry often said that Dudley looked like a pig in a/nwig./n/nHarry put the plates of egg and bacon on the table,/nwhich was difficult as there wasn't much room./nDudley, meanwhile, was counting his presents. His/nface fell./n/n"Thirty-six," he said, looking up at his mother and/nfather. "That's two less than last year."/n/n"Darling, you haven't counted Auntie Marge's present,/nsee, it's here under this big one from Mommy and/nDaddy."/n/n"All right, thirty-seven then," said Dudley, going red/nin the face. Harry, who could see a huge Dudley/ntantrum coming on, began wolfing down his bacon as/nfast as possible in case Dudley turned the table over./n/nAunt Petunia obviously scented danger, too, because/nshe said quickly, "And we'll buy you another two/npresents while we're out today. How's that, popkin?/nTwo more presents. Is that all right?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDudley thought for a moment. It looked like hard/nwork. Finally he said slowly, "So I'll have thirty .../nthirty ..."/n/n"Thirty-nine, sweetums," said Aunt Petunia./n/n"Oh." Dudley sat down heavily and grabbed the/nnearest parcel. "All right then."/n/nUncle Vernon chuckled./n/n"Little tyke wants his money's worth, just like his/nfather. 'Atta boy, Dudley!" He ruffled Dudley's hair./n/nAt that moment the telephone rang and Aunt Petunia/nwent to answer it while Harry and Uncle Vernon/nwatched Dudley unwrap the racing bike, a video/ncamera, a remote control airplane, sixteen new/ncomputer games, and a VCR. He was ripping the/npaper off a gold wristwatch when Aunt Petunia came/nback from the telephone looking both angry and/nworried./n/n"Bad news, Vernon," she said. "Mrs. Figg's broken her/nleg. She can't take him." She jerked her head in/nHarry's direction./n/nDudley's mouth fell open in horror, but Harry's heart/ngave a leap. Every year on Dudley's birthday, his/nparents took him and a friend out for the day, to/nadventure parks, hamburger restaurants, or the/nmovies. Every year, Harry was left behind with Mrs./nFigg, a mad old lady who lived two streets away./n/nHarry hated it there. The whole house smelled of/ncabbage and Mrs. Figg made him look at photographs/nof all the cats she'd ever owned./n/n"Now what?" said Aunt Petunia, looking furiously at/nHarry as though he'd planned this. Harry knew he/n/n/n/n/n/nought to feel sorry that Mrs. Figg had broken her leg,/nbut it wasn't easy when he reminded himself it would/nbe a whole year before he had to look at Tibbies,/nSnowy, Mr. Paws, and Tufty again./n/n"We could phone Marge," Uncle Vernon suggested./n/n"Don't be silly, Vernon, she hates the boy."/n/nThe Dursleys often spoke about Harry like this, as/nthough he wasn't there — or rather, as though he was/nsomething very nasty that couldn't understand them,/nlike a slug./n/n"What about what's-her-name, your friend —/nYvonne?"/n/n"On vacation in Majorca," snapped Aunt Petunia./n/n"You could just leave me here," Harry put in hopefully/n(he'd be able to watch what he wanted on television/nfor a change and maybe even have a go on Dudley's/ncomputer) ./n/nAunt Petunia looked as though she'd just swallowed a/nlemon./n/n"And come back and find the house in ruins?" she/nsnarled./n/n"I won't blow up the house," said Harry, but they/nweren't listening./n/n"I suppose we could take him to the zoo," said Aunt/nPetunia slowly, "... and leave him in the car. ..."/n/n"That cars new, he's not sitting in it alone. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDudley began to cry loudly. In fact, he wasn't really/ncrying — it had been years since he'd really cried —/nbut he knew that if he screwed up his face and/nwailed, his mother would give him anything he/nwanted./n/n"Dinky Duddydums, don't cry, Mummy won't let him/nspoil your special day!" she cried, flinging her arms/naround him./n/n"I ... don't ... want ... him ... t-t-to come!" Dudley/nyelled between huge, pretend sobs. "He always sp-/nspoils everything!" He shot Harry a nasty grin through/nthe gap in his mothers arms./n/nJust then, the doorbell rang — "Oh, good Lord,/nthey're here!" said Aunt Petunia frantically — and a/nmoment later, Dudley's best friend, Piers Polkiss,/nwalked in with his mother. Piers was a scrawny boy/nwith a face like a rat. He was usually the one who/nheld people's arms behind their backs while Dudley/nhit them. Dudley stopped pretending to cry at once./n/nHalf an hour later, Harry, who couldn't believe his/nluck, was sitting in the back of the Dursleys' car with/nPiers and Dudley, on the way to the zoo for the first/ntime in his life. His aunt and uncle hadn't been able/nto think of anything else to do with him, but before/nthey'd left, Uncle Vernon had taken Harry aside./n/n"I'm warning you," he had said, putting his large/npurple face right up close to Harry's, "I'm warning you/nnow, boy — any funny business, anything at all —/nand you'll be in that cupboard from now until/nChristmas."/n/nI'm not going to do anything," said Harry, "honestly/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Uncle Vernon didn't believe him. No one ever did./n/n/n/nThe problem was, strange things often happened/naround Harry and it was just no good telling the/nDursleys he didn't make them happen./n/nOnce, Aunt Petunia, tired of Harry coming back from/nthe barbers looking as though he hadn't been at all,/nhad taken a pair of kitchen scissors and cut his hair/nso short he was almost bald except for his bangs,/nwhich she left "to hide that horrible scar." Dudley had/nlaughed himself silly at Harry, who spent a sleepless/nnight imagining school the next day, where he was/nalready laughed at for his baggy clothes and taped/nglasses. Next morning, however, he had gotten up to/nfind his hair exactly as it had been before Aunt/nPetunia had sheared it off. He had been given a week/nin his cupboard for this, even though he had tried to/nexplain that he couldn't explain how it had grown/nback so quickly./n/nAnother time, Aunt Petunia had been trying to force/nhim into a revolting old sweater of Dudley's (brown/nwith orange puff balls). The harder she tried to pull it/nover his head, the smaller it seemed to become, until/nfinally it might have fitted a hand puppet, but/ncertainly wouldn't fit Harry. Aunt Petunia had decided/nit must have shrunk in the wash and, to his great/nrelief, Harry wasn't punished./n/nOn the other hand, he'd gotten into terrible trouble/nfor being found on the roof of the school kitchens./nDudley's gang had been chasing him as usual when,/nas much to Harry's surprise as anyone else's, there he/nwas sitting on the chimney. The Dursleys had/nreceived a very angry letter from Harry's headmistress/ntelling them Harry had been climbing school/nbuildings. But all he'd tried to do (as he shouted at/nUncle Vernon through the locked door of his/n/n/n/n/ncupboard) was jump behind the big trash cans/noutside the kitchen doors. Harry supposed that the/nwind must have caught him in mid-jump./n/nBut today, nothing was going to go wrong. It was even/nworth being with Dudley and Piers to be spending the/nday somewhere that wasn't school, his cupboard, or/nMrs. Figg's cabbage-smelling living room./n/nWhile he drove, Uncle Vernon complained to Aunt/nPetunia. He liked to complain about things: people at/nwork, Harry, the council, Harry, the bank, and Harry/nwere just a few of his favorite subjects. This morning,/nit was motorcycles./n/n"... roaring along like maniacs, the young hoodlums,"/nhe said, as a motorcycle overtook them./n/n"I had a dream about a motorcycle," said Harry,/nremembering suddenly. "It was flying."/n/nUncle Vernon nearly crashed into the car in front. He/nturned right around in his seat and yelled at Harry,/nhis face like a gigantic beet with a mustache:/n"MOTORCYCLES DONT FLY!"/n/nDudley and Piers sniggered./n/n"I know they don't," said Harry. "It was only a dream."/n/nBut he wished he hadn't said anything. If there was/none thing the Dursleys hated even more than his/nasking questions, it was his talking about anything/nacting in a way it shouldn't, no matter if it was in a/ndream or even a cartoon — they seemed to think he/nmight get dangerous ideas./n/nIt was a very sunny Saturday and the zoo was/ncrowded with families. The Dursleys bought Dudley/n/n/n/n/n/nand Piers large chocolate ice creams at the entrance/nand then, because the smiling lady in the van had/nasked Harry what he wanted before they could hurry/nhim away, they bought him a cheap lemon ice pop. It/nwasn't bad, either, Harry thought, licking it as they/nwatched a gorilla scratching its head who looked/nremarkably like Dudley, except that it wasn't blond./n/nHarry had the best morning he'd had in a long time./nHe was careful to walk a little way apart from the/nDursleys so that Dudley and Piers, who were starting/nto get bored with the animals by lunchtime, wouldn't/nfall back on their favorite hobby of hitting him. They/nate in the zoo restaurant, and when Dudley had a/ntantrum because his knickerbocker glory didn't have/nenough ice cream on top, Uncle Vernon bought him/nanother one and Harry was allowed to finish the first./n/nHarry felt, afterward, that he should have known it/nwas all too good to last./n/nAfter lunch they went to the reptile house. It was cool/nand dark in there, with lit windows all along the/nwalls. Behind the glass, all sorts of lizards and snakes/nwere crawling and slithering over bits of wood and/nstone. Dudley and Piers wanted to see huge,/npoisonous cobras and thick, man-crushing pythons./nDudley quickly found the largest snake in the place. It/ncould have wrapped its body twice around Uncle/nVernon's car and crushed it into a trash can — but at/nthe moment it didn't look in the mood. In fact, it was/nfast asleep./n/nDudley stood with his nose pressed against the glass,/nstaring at the glistening brown coils./n/n"Make it move," he whined at his father. Uncle Vernon/ntapped on the glass, but the snake didn't budge./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Do it again," Dudley ordered. Uncle Vernon rapped/nthe glass smartly with his knuckles, but the snake/njust snoozed on./n/n"This is boring," Dudley moaned. He shuffled away./n/nHarry moved in front of the tank and looked intently/nat the snake. He wouldn't have been surprised if it/nhad died of boredom itself — no company except/nstupid people drumming their fingers on the glass/ntrying to disturb it all day long. It was worse than/nhaving a cupboard as a bedroom, where the only/nvisitor was Aunt Petunia hammering on the door to/nwake you up; at least he got to visit the rest of the/nhouse./n/nThe snake suddenly opened its beady eyes. Slowly,/nvery slowly, it raised its head until its eyes were on a/nlevel with Harry's./n/nIt winked./n/nHarry stared. Then he looked quickly around to see if/nanyone was watching. They weren't. He looked back/nat the snake and winked, too./n/nThe snake jerked its head toward Uncle Vernon and/nDudley, then raised its eyes to the ceiling. It gave/nHarry a look that said quite plainly:/n/n"I get that all the time."/n/n"I know," Harry murmured through the glass, though/nhe wasn't sure the snake could hear him. "It must be/nreally annoying."/n/nThe snake nodded vigorously./n/n"Where do you come from, anyway?" Harry asked./n/n/n/n/n/nThe snake jabbed its tail at a little sign next to the/nglass. Harry peered at it./n/nBoa Constrictor, Brazil./n/n"Was it nice there?"/n/nThe boa constrictor jabbed its tail at the sign again/nand Harry read on: This specimen was bred in the/nzoo. "Oh, I see — so you've never been to Brazil?"/n/nAs the snake shook its head, a deafening shout/nbehind Harry made both of them jump. "DUDLEY!/nMR. DURSLEY! COME AND LOOK AT THIS SNAKE!/nYOU WONT BELIEVE WHAT IT'S DOING!"/n/nDudley came waddling toward them as fast as he/ncould./n/n"Out of the way, you," he said, punching Harry in the/nribs. Caught by surprise, Harry fell hard on the/nconcrete floor. What came next happened so fast no/none saw how it happened — one second, Piers and/nDudley were leaning right up close to the glass, the/nnext, they had leapt back with howls of horror./n/nHarry sat up and gasped; the glass front of the boa/nconstrictor's tank had vanished. The great snake was/nuncoiling itself rapidly, slithering out onto the floor./nPeople throughout the reptile house screamed and/nstarted running for the exits./n/nAs the snake slid swiftly past him, Harry could have/nsworn a low, hissing voice said, "Brazil, here I come./n... Thanksss, amigo."/n/nThe keeper of the reptile house was in shock./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But the glass," he kept saying, "where did the glass/ngo?" "/n/nThe zoo director himself made Aunt Petunia a cup of/nstrong, sweet tea while he apologized over and over/nagain. Piers and Dudley could only gibber. As far as/nHarry had seen, the snake hadn't done anything/nexcept snap playfully at their heels as it passed, but/nby the time they were all back in Uncle Vernon's car,/nDudley was telling them how it had nearly bitten off/nhis leg, while Piers was swearing it had tried to/nsqueeze him to death. But worst of all, for Harry at/nleast, was Piers calming down enough to say, "Harry/nwas talking to it, weren't you, Harry?"/n/nUncle Vernon waited until Piers was safely out of the/nhouse before starting on Harry. He was so angry he/ncould hardly speak. He managed to say, "Go —/ncupboard — stay — no meals," before he collapsed/ninto a chair, and Aunt Petunia had to run and get/nhim a large brandy./n/nHarry lay in his dark cupboard much later, wishing/nhe had a watch. He didn't know what time it was and/nhe couldn't be sure the Dursleys were asleep yet./n/nUntil they were, he couldn't risk sneaking to the/nkitchen for some food./n/nHe'd lived with the Dursleys almost ten years, ten/nmiserable years, as long as he could remember, ever/nsince he'd been a baby and his parents had died in/nthat car crash. He couldn't remember being in the car/nwhen his parents had died. Sometimes, when he/nstrained his memory during long hours in his/ncupboard, he came up with a strange vision: a/nblinding flash of green light and a burning pain on his/nforehead. This, he supposed, was the crash, though/nhe couldn't imagine where all the green light came/nfrom. He couldn't remember his parents at all. His/n/n/n/n/naunt and uncle never spoke about them, and of/ncourse he was forbidden to ask questions. There were/nno photographs of them in the house./n/nWhen he had been younger, Harry had dreamed and/ndreamed of some unknown relation coming to take/nhim away, but it had never happened; the Dursleys/nwere his only family. Yet sometimes he thought (or/nmaybe hoped) that strangers in the street seemed to/nknow him. Very strange strangers they were, too. A/ntiny man in a violet top hat had bowed to him once/nwhile out shopping with Aunt Petunia and Dudley./nAfter asking Harry furiously if he knew the man, Aunt/nPetunia had rushed them out of the shop without/nbuying anything. A wild-looking old woman dressed/nall in green had waved merrily at him once on a bus./n/nA bald man in a very long purple coat had actually/nshaken his hand in the street the other day and then/nwalked away without a word. The weirdest thing/nabout all these people was the way they seemed to/nvanish the second Harry tried to get a closer look./n/nAt school, Harry had no one. Everybody knew that/nDudley's gang hated that odd Harry Potter in his/nbaggy old clothes and broken glasses, and nobody/nliked to disagree with Dudley's gang./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n3/n/n/n/n

title: The Letters From No One
text: /nThe escape of the Brazilian boa constrictor earned/nHarry his longest-ever punishment. By the time he/nwas allowed out of his cupboard again, the summer/nholidays had started and Dudley had already broken/nhis new video camera, crashed his remote control/nairplane, and, first time out on his racing bike,/nknocked down old Mrs. Figg as she crossed Privet/nDrive on her crutches./n/nHarry was glad school was over, but there was no/nescaping Dudley's gang, who visited the house every/nsingle day. Piers, Dennis, Malcolm, and Gordon were/nall big and stupid, but as Dudley was the biggest and/nstupidest of the lot, he was the leader. The rest of/nthem were all quite happy to join in Dudley's favorite/nsport: Harry Hunting./n/nThis was why Harry spent as much time as possible/nout of the house, wandering around and thinking/nabout the end of the holidays, where he could see a/ntiny ray of hope. When September came he would be/ngoing off to secondary school and, for the first time in/n/n/n/nhis life, he wouldn't be with Dudley. Dudley had been/naccepted at Uncle Vernon's old private school,/nSmeltings. Piers Polkiss was going there too. Harry,/non the other hand, was going to Stonewall High, the/nlocal public school. Dudley thought this was very/nfunny./n/n"They stuff people's heads down the toilet the first day/nat Stonewall," he told Harry. "Want to come upstairs/nand practice?"/n/n"No, thanks," said Harry. "The poor toilet's never had/nanything as horrible as your head down it — it might/nbe sick." Then he ran, before Dudley could work out/nwhat he'd said./n/nOne day in July, Aunt Petunia took Dudley to London/nto buy his Smeltings uniform, leaving Harry at Mrs./nFigg's. Mrs. Figg wasn't as bad as usual. It turned out/nshe'd broken her leg tripping over one of her cats, and/nshe didn't seem quite as fond of them as before. She/nlet Harry watch television and gave him a bit of/nchocolate cake that tasted as though she'd had it for/nseveral years./n/nThat evening, Dudley paraded around the living room/nfor the family in his brand-new uniform. Smeltings/nboys wore maroon tailcoats, orange knickerbockers,/nand flat straw hats called boaters. They also carried/nknobbly sticks, used for hitting each other while the/nteachers weren't looking. This was supposed to be/ngood training for later life./n/nAs he looked at Dudley in his new knickerbockers,/nUncle Vernon said gruffly that it was the proudest/nmoment of his life. Aunt Petunia burst into tears and/nsaid she couldn't believe it was her Ickle Dudleykins,/nhe looked so handsome and grown-up. Harry didn't/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ntrust himself to speak. He thought two of his ribs/nmight already have cracked from trying not to laugh./n/n/n/nk k k/n/n/n/nThere was a horrible smell in the kitchen the next/nmorning when Harry went in for breakfast. It seemed/nto be coming from a large metal tub in the sink. He/nwent to have a look. The tub was full of what looked/nlike dirty rags swimming in gray water./n/n"What's this?" he asked Aunt Petunia. Her lips/ntightened as they always did if he dared to ask a/nquestion./n/n"Your new school uniform," she said./n/nHarry looked in the bowl again./n/n"Oh," he said, "I didn't realize it had to be so wet."/n/n"Don't be stupid," snapped Aunt Petunia. "I'm dyeing/nsome of Dudley's old things gray for you. It'll look just/nlike everyone else's when I've finished."/n/nHarry seriously doubted this, but thought it best not/nto argue. He sat down at the table and tried not to/nthink about how he was going to look on his first day/nat Stonewall High — like he was wearing bits of old/nelephant skin, probably./n/nDudley and Uncle Vernon came in, both with/nwrinkled noses because of the smell from Harry's new/nuniform. Uncle Vernon opened his newspaper as/nusual and Dudley banged his Smelting stick, which/nhe carried everywhere, on the table./n/nThey heard the click of the mail slot and flop of letters/non the doormat./n/n/n/n/n/n"Get the mail, Dudley," said Uncle Vernon from/nbehind his paper./n/n"Make Harry get it."/n/n"Get the mail, Harry."/n/n"Make Dudley get it."/n/n"Poke him with your Smelting stick, Dudley."/n/nHarry dodged the Smelting stick and went to get the/nmail. Three things lay on the doormat: a postcard/nfrom Uncle Vernon's sister Marge, who was/nvacationing on the Isle of Wight, a brown envelope/nthat looked like a bill, and — a letter for Harry./n/nHarry picked it up and stared at it, his heart twanging/nlike a giant elastic band. No one, ever, in his whole/nlife, had written to him. Who would? He had no/nfriends, no other relatives — he didn't belong to the/nlibrary, so he'd never even got rude notes asking for/nbooks back. Yet here it was, a letter, addressed so/nplainly there could be no mistake:/n/nMr. H. Potter/n/nThe Cupboard under the Stairs/n4 Privet Drive/nLittle Whinging/nSurrey/n/nThe envelope was thick and heavy, made of yellowish/nparchment, and the address was written in emerald-/ngreen ink. There was no stamp./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nTurning the envelope over, his hand trembling, Harry/nsaw a purple wax seal bearing a coat of arms; a lion,/nan eagle, a badger, and a snake surrounding a large/nletter H./n/n"Hurry up, boy!" shouted Uncle Vernon from the/nkitchen. "What are you doing, checking for letter/nbombs?" He chuckled at his own joke./n/nHarry went back to the kitchen, still staring at his/nletter. He handed Uncle Vernon the bill and the/npostcard, sat down, and slowly began to open the/nyellow envelope./n/nUncle Vernon ripped open the bill, snorted in disgust,/nand flipped over the postcard./n/n"Marge's ill," he informed Aunt Petunia. "Ate a funny/nwhelk ..."/n/n"Dad!" said Dudley suddenly. "Dad, Harry's got/nsomething!"/n/nHarry was on the point of unfolding his letter, which/nwas written on the same heavy parchment as the/nenvelope, when it was jerked sharply out of his hand/nby Uncle Vernon./n/n"That's mine\" said Harry, trying to snatch it back./n/n"Who'd be writing to you?" sneered Uncle Vernon,/nshaking the letter open with one hand and glancing at/nit. His face went from red to green faster than a set of/ntraffic lights. And it didn't stop there. Within seconds/nit was the grayish white of old porridge./n/n"P-P-Petunia!" he gasped./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDudley tried to grab the letter to read it, but Uncle/nVernon held it high out of his reach. Aunt Petunia/ntook it curiously and read the first line. For a moment/nit looked as though she might faint. She clutched her/nthroat and made a choking noise./n/n"Vernon! Oh my goodness — Vernon!"/n/nThey stared at each other, seeming to have forgotten/nthat Harry and Dudley were still in the room. Dudley/nwasn't used to being ignored. He gave his father a/nsharp tap on the head with his Smelting stick./n/n"I want to read that letter," he said loudly./n/n"I want to read it," said Harry furiously, "as it's mine."/n/n"Get out, both of you," croaked Uncle Vernon, stuffing/nthe letter back inside its envelope./n/nHarry didn't move./n/n"I WANT MY LETTER!" he shouted./n/n"Let me see it!" demanded Dudley./n/n"OUT!" roared Uncle Vernon, and he took both Harry/nand Dudley by the scruffs of their necks and threw/nthem into the hall, slamming the kitchen door behind/nthem. Harry and Dudley promptly had a furious but/nsilent fight over who would listen at the keyhole;/nDudley won, so Harry, his glasses dangling from one/near, lay flat on his stomach to listen at the crack/nbetween door and floor./n/n"Vernon," Aunt Petunia was saying in a quivering/nvoice, "look at the address — how could they possibly/nknow where he sleeps? You don't think they're/nwatching the house?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Watching — spying — might be following us,"/nmuttered Uncle Vernon wildly./n/n"But what should we do, Vernon? Should we write/nback? Tell them we don't want — "/n/nHarry could see Uncle Vernon's shiny black shoes/npacing up and down the kitchen./n/n"No," he said finally. "No, we'll ignore it. If they don't/nget an answer. ... Yes, that's best ... we won't do/nanything. ..."/n/n"But — "/n/n"I'm not having one in the house, Petunia! Didn't we/nswear when we took him in we'd stamp out that/ndangerous nonsense?"/n/nThat evening when he got back from work, Uncle/nVernon did something he'd never done before; he/nvisited Harry in his cupboard./n/n"Where's my letter?" said Harry, the moment Uncle/nVernon had squeezed through the door. "Who's/nwriting to me?"/n/n"No one. It was addressed to you by mistake," said/nUncle Vernon shortly. "I have burned it."/n/n"It was not a mistake," said Harry angrily, "it had my/ncupboard on it."/n/n"SILENCE!" yelled Uncle Vernon, and a couple of/nspiders fell from the ceiling. He took a few deep/nbreaths and then forced his face into a smile, which/nlooked quite painful./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Er — yes, Harry — about this cupboard. Your aunt/nand I have been thinking ... you're really getting a bit/nbig for it . . . we think it might be nice if you moved/ninto Dudley's second bedroom."/n/n"Why?" said Harry./n/n"Don't ask questions!" snapped his uncle. "Take this/nstuff upstairs, now."/n/nThe Dursleys' house had four bedrooms: one for/nUncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia, one for visitors/n(usually Uncle Vernon's sister, Marge), one where/nDudley slept, and one where Dudley kept all the toys/nand things that wouldn't fit into his first bedroom. It/nonly took Harry one trip upstairs to move everything/nhe owned from the cupboard to this room. He sat/ndown on the bed and stared around him. Nearly/neverything in here was broken. The month-old video/ncamera was lying on top of a small, working tank/nDudley had once driven over the next door neighbor's/ndog; in the corner was Dudley's first-ever television/nset, which he'd put his foot through when his favorite/nprogram had been canceled; there was a large/nbirdcage, which had once held a parrot that Dudley/nhad swapped at school for a real air rifle, which was/nup on a shelf with the end all bent because Dudley/nhad sat on it. Other shelves were full of books. They/nwere the only things in the room that looked as/nthough they'd never been touched./n/nFrom downstairs came the sound of Dudley bawling/nat his mother, "I don't want him in there ... I need/nthat room ... make him get out. ..."/n/nHarry sighed and stretched out on the bed. Yesterday/nhe'd have given anything to be up here. Today he'd/nrather be back in his cupboard with that letter than/nup here without it./n/n/n/n/n/nNext morning at breakfast, everyone was rather quiet./nDudley was in shock. He'd screamed, whacked his/nfather with his Smelting stick, been sick on purpose,/nkicked his mother, and thrown his tortoise through/nthe greenhouse roof, and he still didn't have his room/nback. Harry was thinking about this time yesterday/nand bitterly wishing he'd opened the letter in the hall./nUncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia kept looking at each/nother darkly./n/nWhen the mail arrived, Uncle Vernon, who seemed to/nbe trying to be nice to Harry, made Dudley go and get/nit. They heard him banging things with his Smelting/nstick all the way down the hall. Then he shouted,/n"There's another one! 'Mr. H. Potter, The Smallest/nBedroom, 4 Privet Drive — ' "/n/nWith a strangled cry, Uncle Vernon leapt from his/nseat and ran down the hall, Harry right behind him./nUncle Vernon had to wrestle Dudley to the ground to/nget the letter from him, which was made difficult by/nthe fact that Harry had grabbed Uncle Vernon around/nthe neck from behind. After a minute of confused/nfighting, in which everyone got hit a lot by the/nSmelting stick, Uncle Vernon straightened up,/ngasping for breath, with Harry's letter clutched in his/nhand./n/n"Go to your cupboard — I mean, your bedroom," he/nwheezed at Harry. "Dudley — go — just go."/n/nHarry walked round and round his new room./nSomeone knew he had moved out of his cupboard and/nthey seemed to know he hadn't received his first/nletter. Surely that meant they'd try again? And this/ntime he'd make sure they didn't fail. He had a plan./n/nThe repaired alarm clock rang at six o'clock the next/nmorning. Harry turned it off quickly and dressed/n/n/n/n/n/nsilently. He mustn't wake the Dursleys. He stole/ndownstairs without turning on any of the lights./n/nHe was going to wait for the postman on the corner of/nPrivet Drive and get the letters for number four first./nHis heart hammered as he crept across the dark hall/ntoward the front door —/n/n"AAAAARRRGH ! "/n/nHarry leapt into the air; he'd trodden on something/nbig and squashy on the doormat — something alive\/n/nLights clicked on upstairs and to his horror Harry/nrealized that the big, squashy something had been his/nuncle's face. Uncle Vernon had been lying at the foot/nof the front door in a sleeping bag, clearly making/nsure that Harry didn't do exactly what he'd been/ntrying to do. He shouted at Harry for about half an/nhour and then told him to go and make a cup of tea./nHarry shuffled miserably off into the kitchen and by/nthe time he got back, the mail had arrived, right into/nUncle Vernon's lap. Harry could see three letters/naddressed in green ink./n/n"I want — " he began, but Uncle Vernon was tearing/nthe letters into pieces before his eyes./n/nUncle Vernon didn't go to work that day. He stayed at/nhome and nailed up the mail slot./n/n"See," he explained to Aunt Petunia through a/nmouthful of nails, "if they can't deliver them they'll/njust give up."/n/n"I'm not sure that'll work, Vernon."/n/n"Oh, these peoples minds work in strange ways,/nPetunia, they're not like you and me," said Uncle/n/n/n/n/n/nVernon, trying to knock in a nail with the piece of/nfruitcake Aunt Petunia had just brought him./n/nOn Friday, no less than twelve letters arrived for/nHarry. As they couldn't go through the mail slot they/nhad been pushed under the door, slotted through the/nsides, and a few even forced through the small/nwindow in the downstairs bathroom./n/nUncle Vernon stayed at home again. After burning all/nthe letters, he got out a hammer and nails and/nboarded up the cracks around the front and back/ndoors so no one could go out. He hummed "Tiptoe/nThrough the Tulips" as he worked, and jumped at/nsmall noises./n/nOn Saturday, things began to get out of hand./nTwenty-four letters to Harry found their way into the/nhouse, rolled up and hidden inside each of the two/ndozen eggs that their very confused milkman had/nhanded Aunt Petunia through the living room/nwindow. While Uncle Vernon made furious telephone/ncalls to the post office and the dairy trying to find/nsomeone to complain to, Aunt Petunia shredded the/nletters in her food processor./n/n"Who on earth wants to talk to you this badly?"/nDudley asked Harry in amazement./n/n/n/n•k k k/n/n/n/nOn Sunday morning, Uncle Vernon sat down at the/nbreakfast table looking tired and rather ill, but happy./n/n"No post on Sundays," he reminded them cheerfully/nas he spread marmalade on his newspapers, "no/ndamn letters today — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSomething came whizzing down the kitchen chimney/nas he spoke and caught him sharply on the back of/nthe head. Next moment, thirty or forty letters came/npelting out of the fireplace like bullets. The Dursleys/nducked, but Harry leapt into the air trying to catch/none —/n/n"Out! OUT!"/n/nUncle Vernon seized Harry around the waist and/nthrew him into the hall. When Aunt Petunia and/nDudley had run out with their arms over their faces,/nUncle Vernon slammed the door shut. They could/nhear the letters still streaming into the room,/nbouncing off the walls and floor./n/n"That does it," said Uncle Vernon, trying to speak/ncalmly but pulling great tufts out of his mustache at/nthe same time. "I want you all back here in five/nminutes ready to leave. We're going away. Just pack/nsome clothes. No arguments!"/n/nHe looked so dangerous with half his mustache/nmissing that no one dared argue. Ten minutes later/nthey had wrenched their way through the boarded-up/ndoors and were in the car, speeding toward the/nhighway. Dudley was sniffling in the back seat; his/nfather had hit him round the head for holding them/nup while he tried to pack his television, VCR, and/ncomputer in his sports bag./n/nThey drove. And they drove. Even Aunt Petunia didn't/ndare ask where they were going. Every now and then/nUncle Vernon would take a sharp turn and drive in/nthe opposite direction for a while./n/n"Shake 'em off ... shake 'em off," he would mutter/nwhenever he did this./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey didn't stop to eat or drink all day. By nightfall/nDudley was howling. He'd never had such a bad day/nin his life. He was hungry, he'd missed five television/nprograms he'd wanted to see, and he'd never gone so/nlong without blowing up an alien on his computer./n/nUncle Vernon stopped at last outside a gloomy-/nlooking hotel on the outskirts of a big city. Dudley/nand Harry shared a room with twin beds and damp,/nmusty sheets. Dudley snored but Harry stayed awake,/nsitting on the windowsill, staring down at the lights of/npassing cars and wondering.../n/nThey ate stale cornflakes and cold tinned tomatoes on/ntoast for breakfast the next day. They had just/nfinished when the owner of the hotel came over to/ntheir table./n/n" 'Scuse me, but is one of you Mr. H. Potter? Only I/ngot about an 'undred of these at the front desk."/n/nShe held up a letter so they could read the green ink/naddress:/n/nMr. H. Potter/n/nRoom 1 7/n/nRailview Hotel/n/nCokeworth/n/nHarry made a grab for the letter but Uncle Vernon/nknocked his hand out of the way. The woman stared./n/n"I'll take them," said Uncle Vernon, standing up/nquickly and following her from the dining room./n/n•k k k/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wouldn't it be better just to go home, dear?" Aunt/nPetunia suggested timidly, hours later, but Uncle/nVernon didn't seem to hear her. Exactly what he was/nlooking for, none of them knew. He drove them into/nthe middle of a forest, got out, looked around, shook/nhis head, got back in the car, and off they went again./nThe same thing happened in the middle of a plowed/nfield, halfway across a suspension bridge, and at the/ntop of a multilevel parking garage./n/n"Daddy's gone mad, hasn't he?" Dudley asked Aunt/nPetunia dully late that afternoon. Uncle Vernon had/nparked at the coast, locked them all inside the car,/nand disappeared./n/nIt started to rain. Great drops beat on the roof of the/ncar. Dudley sniveled./n/n"It's Monday," he told his mother. "The Great/nHumberto's on tonight. I want to stay somewhere with/na television."/n/nMonday. This reminded Harry of something. If it was/nMonday — and you could usually count on Dudley to/nknow the days of the week, because of television —/nthen tomorrow, Tuesday, was Harry's eleventh/nbirthday. Of course, his birthdays were never exactly/nfun — last year, the Dursleys had given him a coat/nhanger and a pair of Uncle Vernon's old socks. Still,/nyou weren't eleven every day./n/nUncle Vernon was back and he was smiling. He was/nalso carrying a long, thin package and didn't answer/nAunt Petunia when she asked what he'd bought./n/n"Found the perfect place!" he said. "Come on!/n/nEveryone out!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was very cold outside the car. Uncle Vernon was/npointing at what looked like a large rock way out at/nsea. Perched on top of the rock was the most/nmiserable little shack you could imagine. One thing/nwas certain, there was no television in there./n/n"Storm forecast for tonight!" said Uncle Vernon/ngleefully, clapping his hands together. "And this/ngentleman's kindly agreed to lend us his boat!"/n/nA toothless old man came ambling up to them,/npointing, with a rather wicked grin, at an old rowboat/nbobbing in the iron-gray water below them./n/n"I've already got us some rations," said Uncle Vernon,/n"so all aboard!"/n/nIt was freezing in the boat. Icy sea spray and rain/ncrept down their necks and a chilly wind whipped/ntheir faces. After what seemed like hours they/nreached the rock, where Uncle Vernon, slipping and/nsliding, led the way to the broken-down house./n/nThe inside was horrible; it smelled strongly of/nseaweed, the wind whistled through the gaps in the/nwooden walls, and the fireplace was damp and empty./nThere were only two rooms./n/nUncle Vernon's rations turned out to be a bag of chips/neach and four bananas. He tried to start a fire but the/nempty chip bags just smoked and shriveled up./n/n"Could do with some of those letters now, eh?" he said/ncheerfully./n/nHe was in a very good mood. Obviously he thought/nnobody stood a chance of reaching them here in a/nstorm to deliver mail. Harry privately agreed, though/nthe thought didn't cheer him up at all./n/n/n/n/n/nAs night fell, the promised storm blew up around/nthem. Spray from the high waves splattered the walls/nof the hut and a fierce wind rattled the filthy/nwindows. Aunt Petunia found a few moldy blankets in/nthe second room and made up a bed for Dudley on/nthe moth-eaten sofa. She and Uncle Vernon went off/nto the lumpy bed next door, and Harry was left to find/nthe softest bit of floor he could and to curl up under/nthe thinnest, most ragged blanket./n/nThe storm raged more and more ferociously as the/nnight went on. Harry couldn't sleep. He shivered and/nturned over, trying to get comfortable, his stomach/nrumbling with hunger. Dudley's snores were drowned/nby the low rolls of thunder that started near midnight./nThe lighted dial of Dudley's watch, which was/ndangling over the edge of the sofa on his fat wrist, told/nHarry he'd be eleven in ten minutes' time. He lay and/nwatched his birthday tick nearer, wondering if the/nDursleys would remember at all, wondering where the/nletter writer was now./n/nFive minutes to go. Harry heard something creak/noutside. He hoped the roof wasn't going to fall in,/nalthough he might be warmer if it did. Four minutes/nto go. Maybe the house in Privet Drive would be so/nfull of letters when they got back that he'd be able to/nsteal one somehow./n/nThree minutes to go. Was that the sea, slapping hard/non the rock like that? And (two minutes to go) what/nwas that funny crunching noise? Was the rock/ncrumbling into the sea?/n/nOne minute to go and he'd be eleven. Thirty seconds/n... twenty ... ten ... nine — maybe he'd wake Dudley/nup, just to annoy him — three ... two ... one .../n/nBOOM./n/n/n/n/n/nThe whole shack shivered and Harry sat bolt upright,/nstaring at the door. Someone was outside, knocking/nto come in./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Keeper Of The Keys
text: /nBOOM. They knocked again. Dudley jerked awake./n/n"Where's the cannon?" he said stupidly./n/nThere was a crash behind them and Uncle Vernon/ncame skidding into the room. He was holding a rifle in/nhis hands — now they knew what had been in the/nlong, thin package he had brought with them./n/n"Who's there?" he shouted. "I warn you — I'm armed!"/n/nThere was a pause. Then —/n/nSMASH!/n/nThe door was hit with such force that it swung clean/noff its hinges and with a deafening crash landed flat/non the floor./n/nA giant of a man was standing in the doorway. His/nface was almost completely hidden by a long, shaggy/nmane of hair and a wild, tangled beard, but you could/n/n/n/n/nmake out his eyes, glinting like black beetles under/nall the hair./n/nThe giant squeezed his way into the hut, stooping so/nthat his head just brushed the ceiling. He bent down,/npicked up the door, and fitted it easily back into its/nframe. The noise of the storm outside dropped a little./nHe turned to look at them all./n/n"Couldn't make us a cup o' tea, could yeh? It's not/nbeen an easy journey. ..."/n/nHe strode over to the sofa where Dudley sat frozen/nwith fear./n/n"Budge up, yeh great lump," said the stranger./n/nDudley squeaked and ran to hide behind his mother,/nwho was crouching, terrified, behind Uncle Vernon./n/n"An' here's Harry!" said the giant./n/nHarry looked up into the fierce, wild, shadowy face/nand saw that the beetle eyes were crinkled in a smile./n/n"Las' time I saw you, you was only a baby," said the/ngiant. "Yeh look a lot like yer dad, but yeh've got yer/nmom's eyes."/n/nUncle Vernon made a funny rasping noise./n/n"I demand that you leave at once, sir!" he said. "You/nare breaking and entering!"/n/n"Ah, shut up, Dursley, yeh great prune," said the/ngiant; he reached over the back of the sofa, jerked the/ngun out of Uncle Vernon's hands, bent it into a knot/nas easily as if it had been made of rubber, and threw/nit into a corner of the room./n/n/n/n/n/nUncle Vernon made another funny noise, like a/nmouse being trodden on./n/n"Anyway — Harry," said the giant, turning his back/non the Dursleys, "a very happy birthday to yeh. Got/nsummat fer yeh here — I mighta sat on it at some/npoint, but it'll taste all right."/n/nFrom an inside pocket of his black overcoat he pulled/na slightly squashed box. Harry opened it with/ntrembling fingers. Inside was a large, sticky chocolate/ncake with Happy Birthday Harry written on it in green/nicing./n/nHarry looked up at the giant. He meant to say thank/nyou, but the words got lost on the way to his mouth,/nand what he said instead was, "Who are you?"/n/nThe giant chuckled./n/n"True, I haven't introduced meself. Rubeus Hagrid,/nKeeper of Keys and Grounds at Hogwarts."/n/nHe held out an enormous hand and shook Harry's/nwhole arm./n/n"What about that tea then, eh?" he said, rubbing his/nhands together. "I'd not say no ter summat stronger if/nyeh've got it, mind."/n/nHis eyes fell on the empty grate with the shriveled/nchip bags in it and he snorted. He bent down over the/nfireplace; they couldn't see what he was doing but/nwhen he drew back a second later, there was a/nroaring fire there. It filled the whole damp hut with/nflickering light and Harry felt the warmth wash over/nhim as though he'd sunk into a hot bath./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe giant sat back down on the sofa, which sagged/nunder his weight, and began taking all sorts of things/nout of the pockets of his coat: a copper kettle, a/nsquashy package of sausages, a poker, a teapot,/nseveral chipped mugs, and a bottle of some amber/nliquid that he took a swig from before starting to/nmake tea. Soon the hut was full of the sound and/nsmell of sizzling sausage. Nobody said a thing while/nthe giant was working, but as he slid the first six fat,/njuicy, slightly burnt sausages from the poker, Dudley/nfidgeted a little. Uncle Vernon said sharply, "Don't/ntouch anything he gives you, Dudley."/n/nThe giant chuckled darkly./n/n"Yer great puddin' of a son don' need fattenin'/nanymore, Dursley, don' worry."/n/nHe passed the sausages to Harry, who was so hungry/nhe had never tasted anything so wonderful, but he/nstill couldn't take his eyes off the giant. Finally, as/nnobody seemed about to explain anything, he said,/n"I'm sorry, but I still don't really know who you are."/n/nThe giant took a gulp of tea and wiped his mouth with/nthe back of his hand./n/n"Call me Hagrid," he said, "everyone does. An' like I/ntold yeh, I'm Keeper of Keys at Hogwarts — yeh'll/nknow all about Hogwarts, o' course."/n/n"Er — no," said Harry./n/nHagrid looked shocked./n/n"Sorry," Harry said quickly./n/n"Sorry?" barked Hagrid, turning to stare at the/nDursleys, who shrank back into the shadows. "It's/n/n/n/n/n/nthem as should be sorry! I knew yeh weren't gettin'/nyer letters but I never thought yeh wouldn't even/nknow abou' Hogwarts, fer cryin' out loud! Did yeh/nnever wonder where yer parents learned it all?"/n/n"All what?" asked Harry./n/n"ALL WHAT?" Hagrid thundered. "Now wait jus' one/nsecond!"/n/nHe had leapt to his feet. In his anger he seemed to fill/nthe whole hut. The Dursleys were cowering against/nthe wall./n/n"Do you mean ter tell me," he growled at the Dursleys,/n"that this boy — this boy! — knows nothin' abou' —/nabout ANYTHING?"/n/nHarry thought this was going a bit far. He had been to/nschool, after all, and his marks weren't bad./n/n"I know some things," he said. "I can, you know, do/nmath and stuff."/n/nBut Hagrid simply waved his hand and said, "About/nour world, I mean. Your world. My world. Yer parents'/nworld."/n/n"What world?"/n/nHagrid looked as if he was about to explode./n"DURSLEY!" he boomed./n/nUncle Vernon, who had gone very pale, whispered/nsomething that sounded like "Mimblewimble." Hagrid/nstared wildly at Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But yeh must know about yer mom and dad," he/nsaid. "I mean, they're famous. You're famous."/n/n"What? My — my mom and dad weren't famous, were/nthey?"/n/n"Yeh don' know ... yeh don' know ..." Hagrid ran his/nfingers through his hair, fixing Harry with a/nbewildered stare./n/n"Yeh don' know what yeh are?" he said finally./n/nUncle Vernon suddenly found his voice./n/n"Stop!" he commanded. "Stop right there, sir! I forbid/nyou to tell the boy anything!"/n/nA braver man than Vernon Dursley would have/nquailed under the furious look Hagrid now gave him;/nwhen Hagrid spoke, his every syllable trembled with/nrage./n/n"You never told him? Never told him what was in the/nletter Dumbledore left fer him? I was there! I saw/nDumbledore leave it, Dursley! An' you've kept it from/nhim all these years?"/n/n"Kept what from me?" said Harry eagerly./n/n"STOP! I FORBID YOU!" yelled Uncle Vernon in panic./n/nAunt Petunia gave a gasp of horror./n/n"Ah, go boil yer heads, both of yeh," said Hagrid./n"Harry — yer a wizard."/n/nThere was silence inside the hut. Only the sea and/nthe whistling wind could be heard./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'm a what?" gasped Harry./n/n/n/n"A wizard, o' course," said Hagrid, sitting back down/non the sofa, which groaned and sank even lower, "an'/na thumpin' good'un, I'd say, once yeh've been trained/nup a bit. With a mum an' dad like yours, what else/nwould yeh be? An' I reckon it's abou' time yeh read/nyer letter."/n/nHarry stretched out his hand at last to take the/nyellowish envelope, addressed in emerald green to Mr./nH. Potter, The Floor, Hut-on-the-Rock, The Sea. He/npulled out the letter and read:/n/nHOGWARTS SCHOOL/no/WITCHCRAFT and WIZARDRY/n/nHeadmaster: ALBUS DUMBLEDORE/n/n(Order of Merlin, First Class, Grand Sore., Chf./n/nWarlock, Supreme Mugwump, International Confed. of/nWizards)/n/nDear Mr. Potter,/n/nWe are pleased to inform you that you have been/naccepted at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and/nWizardry. Please find enclosed a list of all necessary/nbooks and equipment./n/nTerm begins on September 1. We await your owl by no/nlater than July 31./n/nYours sincerely,/n/nMinerva McGonagall,/n/nDeputy Headmistress/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nQuestions exploded inside Harry's head like fireworks/nand he couldn't decide which to ask first. After a few/nminutes he stammered, "What does it mean, they/nawait my owl?"/n/n"Gallopin' Gorgons, that reminds me," said Hagrid,/nclapping a hand to his forehead with enough force to/nknock over a cart horse, and from yet another pocket/ninside his overcoat he pulled an owl — a real, live,/nrather ruffled-looking owl — a long quill, and a roll of/nparchment. With his tongue between his teeth he/nscribbled a note that Harry could read upside down:/n/nDear Professor Dumbledore,/n/nGiven Harry his letter./n/nTaking him to buy his things tomorrow./n/nWeather's horrible. Hope you're well./n/nHagrid/n/nHagrid rolled up the note, gave it to the owl, which/nclamped it in its beak, went to the door, and threw/nthe owl out into the storm. Then he came back and/nsat down as though this was as normal as talking on/nthe telephone./n/nHarry realized his mouth was open and closed it/nquickly./n/n"Where was I?" said Hagrid, but at that moment,/n/nUncle Vernon, still ashen-faced but looking very/nangry, moved into the firelight./n/n"He's not going," he said./n/nHagrid grunted./n/n/n/n/n/n"I'd like ter see a great Muggle like you stop him," he/nsaid./n/n/n/n"A what?" said Harry, interested./n/n"A Muggle," said Hagrid, "it's what we call nonmagic/nfolk like them. An' it's your bad luck you grew up in a/nfamily o' the biggest Muggles I ever laid eyes on."/n/n"We swore when we took him in we'd put a stop to/nthat rubbish," said Uncle Vernon, "swore we'd stamp/nit out of him! Wizard indeed!"/n/n"You knew?" said Harry. "You knew I'm a — a/nwizard?"/n/n"Knew!" shrieked Aunt Petunia suddenly. "Knew\ Of/ncourse we knew! How could you not be, my dratted/nsister being what she was? Oh, she got a letter just/nlike that and disappeared off to that — that school —/nand came home every vacation with her pockets full/nof frog spawn, turning teacups into rats. I was the/nonly one who saw her for what she was — a freak!/n/nBut for my mother and father, oh no, it was Lily this/nand Lily that, they were proud of having a witch in/nthe family!"/n/nShe stopped to draw a deep breath and then went/nranting on. It seemed she had been wanting to say all/nthis for years./n/n"Then she met that Potter at school and they left and/ngot married and had you, and of course I knew you'd/nbe just the same, just as strange, just as — as —/nabnormal — and then, if you please, she went and got/nherself blown up and we got landed with you!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry had gone very white. As soon as he found his/nvoice he said, "Blown up? You told me they died in a/ncar crash!"/n/n"CAR CRASH!" roared Hagrid, jumping up so angrily/nthat the Dursleys scuttled back to their corner.
