"How/ncould a car crash kill Lily an' James Potter? It's an/noutrage! A scandal! Harry Potter not knowin' his own/nstory when every kid in our world knows his name!"/n/n"But why? What happened?" Harry asked urgently./n/nThe anger faded from Hagrid's face. He looked/nsuddenly anxious./n/n"I never expected this," he said, in a low, worried/nvoice. "I had no idea, when Dumbledore told me there/nmight be trouble gettin' hold of yeh, how much yeh/ndidn't know. Ah, Harry, I don' know if I'm the right/nperson ter tell yeh — but someone's gotta — yeh can't/ngo off ter Hogwarts not knowin'."/n/nHe threw a dirty look at the Dursleys./n/n"Well, it's best yeh know as much as I can tell yeh —/nmind, I can't tell yeh everythin', it's a great myst'ry,/nparts of it. ..."/n/nHe sat down, stared into the fire for a few seconds,/nand then said, "It begins, I suppose, with — with a/nperson called — but it's incredible yeh don't know his/nname, everyone in our world knows — "/n/n"Who?"/n/n"Well — I don' like sayin' the name if I can help it. No/none does."/n/n"Why not?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Gulpin' gargoyles, Harry, people are still scared./nBlimey, this is difficult. See, there was this wizard/nwho went ... bad. As bad as you could go. Worse./nWorse than worse. His name was ..."/n/nHagrid gulped, but no words came out./n/n"Could you write it down?" Harry suggested./n/n"Nah — can't spell it. All right — Voldemort." Hagrid/nshuddered. "Don' make me say it again. Anyway, this/n— this wizard, about twenty years ago now, started/nlookin' fer followers. Got 'em, too — some were afraid,/nsome just wanted a bit o' his power, 'cause he was/ngettin' himself power, all right. Dark days, Harry./nDidn't know who ter trust, didn't dare get friendly/nwith strange wizards or witches . . . terrible things/nhappened. He was takin' over. 'Course, some stood up/nto him — an' he killed 'em. Horribly. One o' the only/nsafe places left was Hogwarts. Reckon Dumbledore's/nthe only one You-Know-Who was afraid of. Didn't dare/ntry takin' the school, not jus' then, anyway./n/n"Now, yer mum an' dad were as good a witch an'/nwizard as I ever knew. Head boy an' girl at Hogwarts/nin their day! Suppose the myst'ry is why You-Know-/nWho never tried to get 'em on his side before . . ./nprobably knew they were too close ter Dumbledore ter/nwant anythin' ter do with the Dark Side./n/n"Maybe he thought he could persuade 'em ... maybe/nhe just wanted 'em outta the way. All anyone knows/nis, he turned up in the village where you was all/nliving, on Halloween ten years ago. You was just a/nyear old. He came ter yer house an' — an' — "/n/nHagrid suddenly pulled out a very dirty, spotted/nhandkerchief and blew his nose with a sound like a/nfoghorn./n/n/n/n/n/n"Sorry," he said. "But it's that sad — knew yer mum/nan' dad, an' nicer people yeh couldn't find — anyway/n/n/n/n"You-Know-Who killed 'em. An' then — an' this is the/nreal myst'ry of the thing — he tried to kill you, too./nWanted ter make a clean job of it, I suppose, or/nmaybe he just liked killin' by then. But he couldn't do/nit. Never wondered how you got that mark on yer/nforehead? That was no ordinary cut. That's what yeh/nget when a powerful, evil curse touches yeh — took/ncare of yer mum an' dad an' yer house, even — but it/ndidn't work on you, an' that's why yer famous, Harry./nNo one ever lived after he decided ter kill 'em, no one/nexcept you, an' he'd killed some o' the best witches/nan' wizards of the age — the McKinnons, the Bones,/nthe Prewetts — an' you was only a baby, an' you/nlived."/n/nSomething very painful was going on in Harry's mind./nAs Hagrid's story came to a close, he saw again the/nblinding flash of green light, more clearly than he had/never remembered it before — and he remembered/nsomething else, for the first time in his life: a high,/ncold, cruel laugh./n/nHagrid was watching him sadly./n/n"Took yeh from the ruined house myself, on/nDumbledore's orders. Brought yeh ter this lot ..."/n/n"Load of old tosh," said Uncle Vernon. Harry jumped;/nhe had almost forgotten that the Dursleys were there./nUncle Vernon certainly seemed to have got back his/ncourage. He was glaring at Hagrid and his fists were/nclenched./n/n"Now, you listen here, boy," he snarled, "I accept/nthere's something strange about you, probably/n/n/n/n/n/nnothing a good beating wouldn't have cured — and as/nfor all this about your parents, well, they were/nweirdos, no denying it, and the world's better off/nwithout them in my opinion — asked for all they got,/ngetting mixed up with these wizarding types — just/nwhat I expected, always knew they'd come to a sticky/nend — "/n/nBut at that moment, Hagrid leapt from the sofa and/ndrew a battered pink umbrella from inside his coat./nPointing this at Uncle Vernon like a sword, he said,/n"I'm warning you, Dursley — I'm warning you — one/nmore word ..."/n/nIn danger of being speared on the end of an umbrella/nby a bearded giant, Uncle Vernon's courage failed/nagain; he flattened himself against the wall and fell/nsilent./n/n"That's better," said Hagrid, breathing heavily and/nsitting back down on the sofa, which this time sagged/nright down to the floor./n/nHarry, meanwhile, still had questions to ask,/nhundreds of them./n/n"But what happened to Vol-, sorry — I mean, You-/nKnow-Who?"/n/n"Good question, Harry. Disappeared. Vanished. Same/nnight he tried ter kill you. Makes yeh even more/nfamous. That's the biggest myst'ry, see ... he was/ngettin' more an' more powerful — why'd he go?/n/n"Some say he died. Codswallop, in my opinion. Dunno/nif he had enough human left in him to die. Some say/nhe's still out there, bidin' his time, like, but I don'/nbelieve it. People who was on his side came back ter/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nours. Some of 'em came outta kinda trances. Don'/nreckon they could've done if he was cornin' back./n/n"Most of us reckon he's still out there somewhere but/nlost his powers. Too weak to carry on. 'Cause/nsomethin' about you finished him, Harry. There was/nsomethin' goin' on that night he hadn't counted on —/n/ dunno what it was, no one does — but somethin'/nabout you stumped him, all right."/n/nHagrid looked at Harry with warmth and respect/nblazing in his eyes, but Harry, instead of feeling/npleased and proud, felt quite sure there had been a/nhorrible mistake. A wizard? Him? How could he/npossibly be? He'd spent his life being clouted by/nDudley, and bullied by Aunt Petunia and Uncle/nVernon; if he was really a wizard, why hadn't they/nbeen turned into warty toads every time they'd tried/nto lock him in his cupboard? If he'd once defeated the/ngreatest sorcerer in the world, how come Dudley had/nalways been able to kick him around like a football?/n/n"Hagrid," he said quietly, "I think you must have/nmade a mistake. I don't think I can be a wizard."/n/nTo his surprise, Hagrid chuckled./n/n"Not a wizard, eh? Never made things happen when/nyou was scared or angry?"/n/nHarry looked into the fire. Now he came to think/nabout it . . . every odd thing that had ever made his/naunt and uncle furious with him had happened when/nhe, Harry, had been upset or angry ... chased by/nDudley's gang, he had somehow found himself out of/ntheir reach . . . dreading going to school with that/nridiculous haircut, he'd managed to make it grow/nback . . . and the very last time Dudley had hit him,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhadn't he got his revenge, without even realizing he/nwas doing it? Hadn't he set a boa constrictor on him?/n/n/n/nHarry looked back at Hagrid, smiling, and saw that/nHagrid was positively beaming at him./n/n"See?" said Hagrid. "Harry Potter, not a wizard — you/nwait, you'll be right famous at Hogwarts."/n/nBut Uncle Vernon wasn't going to give in without a/nfight./n/n"Haven't I told you he's not going?" he hissed. "He's/ngoing to Stonewall High and he'll be grateful for it. I've/nread those letters and he needs all sorts of rubbish —/nspell books and wands and — "/n/n"If he wants ter go, a great Muggle like you won't stop/nhim," growled Hagrid. "Stop Lily an' James Potter's/nson goin' ter Hogwarts! Yer mad. His name's been/ndown ever since he was born. He's off ter the finest/nschool of witchcraft and wizardry in the world. Seven/nyears there and he won't know himself. He'll be with/nyoungsters of his own sort, fer a change, an' he'll be/nunder the greatest headmaster Hogwarts ever had,/nAlbus Dumbled — "/n/n"I AM NOT PAYING FOR SOME CRACKPOT OLD/nFOOL TO TEACH HIM MAGIC TRICKS!" yelled Uncle/nVernon./n/nBut he had finally gone too far. Hagrid seized his/numbrella and whirled it over his head, "NEVER — " he/nthundered, "— INSULT — ALBUS — DUMBLEDORE/n— IN — FRONT — OF — ME!"/n/nHe brought the umbrella swishing down through the/nair to point at Dudley — there was a flash of violet/nlight, a sound like a firecracker, a sharp squeal, and/n/n/n/n/n/nthe next second, Dudley was dancing on the spot with/nhis hands clasped over his fat bottom, howling in/npain. When he turned his back on them, Harry saw a/ncurly pig's tail poking through a hole in his trousers./n/nUncle Vernon roared. Pulling Aunt Petunia and/nDudley into the other room, he cast one last terrified/nlook at Hagrid and slammed the door behind them./n/nHagrid looked down at his umbrella and stroked his/nbeard./n/n"Shouldn'ta lost me temper," he said ruefully, "but it/ndidn't work anyway. Meant ter turn him into a pig,/nbut I suppose he was so much like a pig anyway there/nwasn't much left ter do."/n/nHe cast a sideways look at Harry under his bushy/neyebrows./n/n"Be grateful if yeh didn't mention that ter anyone at/nHogwarts," he said. "I'm — er — not supposed ter do/nmagic, strictly speakin'. I was allowed ter do a bit ter/nfollow yeh an' get yer letters to yeh an' stuff — one o'/nthe reasons I was so keen ter take on the job — "/n/n"Why aren't you supposed to do magic?" asked Harry./n/n"Oh, well — I was at Hogwarts meself but I — er —/ngot expelled, ter tell yeh the truth. In me third year./nThey snapped me wand in half an' everything. But/nDumbledore let me stay on as gamekeeper. Great/nman, Dumbledore."/n/n"Why were you expelled?"/n/n"It's gettin' late and we've got lots ter do tomorrow,"/nsaid Hagrid loudly. "Gotta get up ter town, get all yer/nbooks an' that."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe took off his thick black coat and threw it to Harry./n/n/n/n"You can kip under that," he said. "Don' mind if it/nwriggles a bit, I think I still got a couple o' dormice in/none o' the pockets."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Diagon Alley
text: /nHarry woke early the next morning. Although he/ncould tell it was daylight, he kept his eyes shut tight./n/n"It was a dream," he told himself firmly. "I dreamed a/ngiant called Hagrid came to tell me I was going to a/nschool for wizards. When I open my eyes I'll be at/nhome in my cupboard."/n/nThere was suddenly a loud tapping noise./n/nAnd there's Aunt Petunia knocking on the door, Harry/nthought, his heart sinking. But he still didn't open his/neyes. It had been such a good dream./n/nTap. Tap. Tap./n/n"All right," Harry mumbled, "I'm getting up."/n/nHe sat up and Hagrid 's heavy coat fell off him. The/nhut was full of sunlight, the storm was over, Hagrid/nhimself was asleep on the collapsed sofa, and there/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwas an owl rapping its claw on the window, a/nnewspaper held in its beak./n/nHarry scrambled to his feet, so happy he felt as/nthough a large balloon was swelling inside him. He/nwent straight to the window and jerked it open. The/nowl swooped in and dropped the newspaper on top of/nHagrid, who didn't wake up. The owl then fluttered/nonto the floor and began to attack Hagrid 's coat./n/n"Don't do that."/n/nHarry tried to wave the owl out of the way, but it/nsnapped its beak fiercely at him and carried on/nsavaging the coat./n/n"Hagrid!" said Harry loudly. "There's an owl — "/n/n"Pay him," Hagrid grunted into the sofa./n/n"What?"/n/n"He wants payin' fer deliverin' the paper. Look in the/npockets."/n/nHagrid 's coat seemed to be made of nothing but/npockets — bunches of keys, slug pellets, balls of/nstring, peppermint humbugs, teabags ... finally, Harry/npulled out a handful of strange-looking coins./n/n"Give him five Knuts," said Hagrid sleepily./n/n"Knuts?"/n/n"The little bronze ones."/n/nHarry counted out five little bronze coins, and the owl/nheld out his leg so Harry could put the money into a/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nsmall leather pouch tied to it. Then he flew off/nthrough the open window./n/nHagrid yawned loudly, sat up, and stretched./n/n"Best be off, Harry, lots ter do today, gotta get up ter/nLondon an' buy all yer stuff fer school."/n/nHarry was turning over the wizard coins and looking/nat them. He had just thought of something that made/nhim feel as though the happy balloon inside him had/ngot a puncture./n/n"Urn — Hagrid?"/n/n"Mm?" said Hagrid, who was pulling on his huge/nboots./n/n"I haven't got any money — and you heard Uncle/nVernon last night ... he won't pay for me to go and/nlearn magic."/n/n"Don't worry about that," said Hagrid, standing up/nand scratching his head. "D'yeh think yer parents/ndidn't leave yeh anything?"/n/n"But if their house was destroyed — "/n/n"They didn' keep their gold in the house, boy! Nah,/nfirst stop fer us is Gringotts. Wizards' bank. Have a/nsausage, they're not bad cold — an' I wouldn' say no/nteh a bit o' yer birthday cake, neither."/n/n"Wizards have banks?"/n/n"Just the one. Gringotts. Run by goblins."/n/nHarry dropped the bit of sausage he was holding./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Goblins?"/n/n/n/n"Yeah — so yeh'd be mad ter try an' rob it, I'll tell yeh/nthat. Never mess with goblins, Harry. Gringotts is the/nsafest place in the world fer anything yeh want ter/nkeep safe — 'cept maybe Hogwarts. As a matter o'/nfact, I gotta visit Gringotts anyway Fer Dumbledore./nHogwarts business." Hagrid drew himself up proudly./n"He usually gets me ter do important stuff fer him./nFetchin' you — gettin' things from Gringotts — knows/nhe can trust me, see./n/n"Got everythin'? Come on, then."/n/nHarry followed Hagrid out onto the rock. The sky was/nquite clear now and the sea gleamed in the sunlight./nThe boat Uncle Vernon had hired was still there, with/na lot of water in the bottom after the storm./n/n"How did you get here?" Harry asked, looking around/nfor another boat./n/n"Flew," said Hagrid./n/n"Flew?"/n/n"Yeah — but we'll go back in this. Not s'pposed ter/nuse magic now I've got yeh."/n/nThey settled down in the boat, Harry still staring at/nHagrid, trying to imagine him flying./n/n"Seems a shame ter row, though," said Hagrid, giving/nHarry another of his sideways looks. "If I was ter — er/n— speed things up a bit, would yeh mind not/nmentionin' it at Hogwarts?"/n/n"Of course not," said Harry, eager to see more magic./nHagrid pulled out the pink umbrella again, tapped it/n/n/n/n/n/ntwice on the side of the boat, and they sped off toward/nland./n/n"Why would you be mad to try and rob Gringotts?"/nHarry asked./n/n"Spells — enchantments," said Hagrid, unfolding his/nnewspaper as he spoke. "They say there's dragons/nguardin' the high-security vaults. And then yeh gotta/nfind yer way — Gringotts is hundreds of miles under/nLondon, see. Deep under the Underground. Yeh'd die/nof hunger tryin' ter get out, even if yeh did manage ter/nget yer hands on summat."/n/nHarry sat and thought about this while Hagrid read/nhis newspaper, the Daily Prophet Harry had learned/nfrom Uncle Vernon that people liked to be left alone/nwhile they did this, but it was very difficult, he'd/nnever had so many questions in his life./n/n"Ministry o' Magic messin' things up as usual," Hagrid/nmuttered, turning the page./n/n"There's a Ministry of Magic?" Harry asked, before he/ncould stop himself./n/n" 'Course," said Hagrid. "They wanted Dumbledore fer/nMinister, o' course, but he'd never leave Hogwarts, so/nold Cornelius Fudge got the job. Bungler if ever there/nwas one. So he pelts Dumbledore with owls every/nmorning, askin' fer advice."/n/n"But what does a Ministry of Magic do?"/n/n"Well, their main job is to keep it from the Muggles/nthat there's still witches an' wizards up an' down the/ncountry."/n/n"Why?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Why? Blimey, Harry, everyone 'd be wantin' magic/nsolutions to their problems. Nah, we're best left/nalone."/n/nAt this moment the boat bumped gently into the/nharbor wall. Hagrid folded up his newspaper, and/nthey clambered up the stone steps onto the street./n/nPassersby stared a lot at Hagrid as they walked/nthrough the little town to the station. Harry couldn't/nblame them. Not only was Hagrid twice as tall as/nanyone else, he kept pointing at perfectly ordinary/nthings like parking meters and saying loudly, "See/nthat, Harry? Things these Muggles dream up, eh?"/n/n"Hagrid," said Harry, panting a bit as he ran to keep/nup, "did you say there are dragons at Gringotts?"/n/n"Well, so they say," said Hagrid. "Crikey, I'd like a/ndragon."/n/n"You'd like one?"/n/n"Wanted one ever since I was a kid — here we go."/n/nThey had reached the station. There was a train to/nLondon in five minutes' time. Hagrid, who didn't/nunderstand "Muggle money," as he called it, gave the/nbills to Harry so he could buy their tickets./n/nPeople stared more than ever on the train. Hagrid/ntook up two seats and sat knitting what looked like a/ncanary-yellow circus tent./n/n"Still got yer letter, Harry?" he asked as he counted/nstitches./n/nHarry took the parchment envelope out of his pocket./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Good," said Hagrid. "There's a list there of everything/nyeh need."/n/n/n/nHarry unfolded a second piece of paper he hadn't/nnoticed the night before, and read:/n/nHOGWARTS SCHOOL/no/WITCHCRAFT and WIZARDRY/n/nUNIFORM/n/n/n/nFirst-year students will require:/n/n1 . Three sets of plain work robes (black)/n/n2. One plain pointed hat (black) for day wear/n/n3. One pair of protective gloves (dragon hide or/nsimilar)/n/n4. One winter cloak (black, silver fastenings)/n/nPlease note that all pupils' clothes should carry name/ntags/n/n/n/nCOURSE BOOKS/n/n/n/nAll students should have a copy of each of the/nfollowing:/n/nThe Standard Book of Spells (Grade 1) by Miranda/nGoshawk/n/nA History of Magic by Bathilda Bagshot/n/nMagical Theory by Adalbert Waffling/n/nA Beginners' Guide to Transfiguration by Emeric/nSwitch/n/n/n/n/n/nOne Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi by Phyllida/nSpore/n/nMagical Drafts and Potions by Arsenius Jigger/n/nFantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them by Newt/nScamander/n/nThe Dark Forces: A Guide to Self-Protection by Quentin/nTrimble/n/n/n/nOTHER EQUIPMENT/n/n/n/n1 wand/n/n1 cauldron (pewter, standard size 2)/n/n1 set glass or crystal phials/n1 telescope/n1 set brass scales/n/nStudents may also bring an owl OR a cat OR a toad/n/nPARENTS ARE REMINDED THAT FIRST YEARS ARE/nNOT ALLOWED THEIR OWN BROOMSTICKS/n/n"Can we buy all this in London?" Harry wondered/naloud./n/n"If yeh know where to go," said Hagrid./n/nHarry had never been to London before. Although/nHagrid seemed to know where he was going, he was/nobviously not used to getting there in an ordinary/nway. He got stuck in the ticket barrier on the/nUnderground, and complained loudly that the seats/nwere too small and the trains too slow./n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't know how the Muggles manage without/nmagic," he said as they climbed a broken-down/nescalator that led up to a bustling road lined with/nshops./n/nHagrid was so huge that he parted the crowd easily;/nall Harry had to do was keep close behind him. They/npassed book shops and music stores, hamburger/nrestaurants and cinemas, but nowhere that looked as/nif it could sell you a magic wand. This was just an/nordinary street full of ordinary people. Could there/nreally be piles of wizard gold buried miles beneath/nthem? Were there really shops that sold spell books/nand broomsticks? Might this not all be some huge/njoke that the Dursleys had cooked up? If Harry hadn't/nknown that the Dursleys had no sense of humor, he/nmight have thought so; yet somehow, even though/neverything Hagrid had told him so far was/nunbelievable, Harry couldn't help trusting him./n/n"This is it," said Hagrid, coming to a halt, "the Leaky/nCauldron. It's a famous place."/n/nIt was a tiny, grubby-looking pub. If Hagrid hadn't/npointed it out, Harry wouldn't have noticed it was/nthere. The people hurrying by didn't glance at it. Their/neyes slid from the big book shop on one side to the/nrecord shop on the other as if they couldn't see the/nLeaky Cauldron at all. In fact, Harry had the most/npeculiar feeling that only he and Hagrid could see it./nBefore he could mention this, Hagrid had steered him/ninside./n/nFor a famous place, it was very dark and shabby. A/nfew old women were sitting in a corner, drinking tiny/nglasses of sherry. One of them was smoking a long/npipe. A little man in a top hat was talking to the old/nbartender, who was quite bald and looked like a/ntoothless walnut. The low buzz of chatter stopped/n/n/n/n/nwhen they walked in. Everyone seemed to know/nHagrid; they waved and smiled at him, and the/nbartender reached for a glass, saying, "The usual,/nHagrid?"/n/n"Can't, Tom, I'm on Hogwarts business," said Hagrid,/nclapping his great hand on Harry's shoulder and/nmaking Harry's knees buckle./n/n"Good Lord," said the bartender, peering at Harry, "is/nthis — can this be — ?"/n/nThe Leaky Cauldron had suddenly gone completely/nstill and silent./n/n"Bless my soul," whispered the old bartender, "Harry/nPotter ... what an honor."/n/nHe hurried out from behind the bar, rushed toward/nHarry and seized his hand, tears in his eyes./n/n"Welcome back, Mr. Potter, welcome back."/n/nHarry didn't know what to say. Everyone was looking/nat him. The old woman with the pipe was puffing on it/nwithout realizing it had gone out. Hagrid was/nbeaming./n/nThen there was a great scraping of chairs and the/nnext moment, Harry found himself shaking hands/nwith everyone in the Leaky Cauldron./n/n"Doris Crockford, Mr. Potter, can't believe I'm meeting/nyou at last."/n/n"So proud, Mr. Potter, I'm just so proud."/n/n"Always wanted to shake your hand — I'm all of a/nflutter."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Delighted, Mr. Potter, just can't tell you, Diggle's the/nname, Dedalus Diggle."/n/n"I've seen you before!" said Harry, as Dedalus Diggle's/ntop hat fell off in his excitement. "You bowed to me/nonce in a shop."/n/n"He remembers!" cried Dedalus Diggle, looking/naround at everyone. "Did you hear that? He/nremembers me!"/n/nHarry shook hands again and again — Doris/nCrockford kept coming back for more./n/nA pale young man made his way forward, very/nnervously. One of his eyes was twitching./n/n"Professor Quirrell!" said Hagrid. "Harry, Professor/nQuirrell will be one of your teachers at Hogwarts."/n/n"P-P-Potter," stammered Professor Quirrell, grasping/nHarry's hand, "c-can't t-tell you how p-pleased I am to/nmeet you."/n/n"What sort of magic do you teach, Professor Quirrell?"/n/n"D-Defense Against the D-D-Dark Arts," muttered/nProfessor Quirrell, as though he'd rather not think/nabout it. "N-not that you n-need it, eh, P-P-Potter?"/n/nHe laughed nervously. "You'll be g-getting all your/nequipment, I suppose? I've g-got to p-pick up a new b-/nbook on vampires, m-myself." He looked terrified at/nthe very thought./n/nBut the others wouldn't let Professor Quirrell keep/nHarry to himself. It took almost ten minutes to get/naway from them all. At last, Hagrid managed to make/nhimself heard over the babble./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Must get on — lots ter buy. Come on, Harry."/n/nDoris Crockford shook Harry's hand one last time,/nand Hagrid led them through the bar and out into a/nsmall, walled courtyard, where there was nothing but/na trash can and a few weeds./n/nHagrid grinned at Harry./n/n"Told yeh, didn't I? Told yeh you was famous. Even/nProfessor Quirrell was tremblin' ter meet yeh — mind/nyou, he's usually tremblin'."/n/n"Is he always that nervous?"/n/n"Oh, yeah. Poor bloke. Brilliant mind. He was fine/nwhile he was studyin' outta books but then he took a/nyear off ter get some firsthand experience. ... They say/nhe met vampires in the Black Forest, and there was a/nnasty bit o' trouble with a hag — never been the same/nsince. Scared of the students, scared of his own/nsubject — now, where's me umbrella?"/n/nVampires? Hags? Harry's head was swimming./n/nHagrid, meanwhile, was counting bricks in the wall/nabove the trash can./n/n"Three up ... two across ..." he muttered. "Right,/nstand back, Harry."/n/nHe tapped the wall three times with the point of his/numbrella./n/nThe brick he had touched quivered — it wriggled — in/nthe middle, a small hole appeared — it grew wider/nand wider — a second later they were facing an/narchway large enough even for Hagrid, an archway/nonto a cobbled street that twisted and turned out of/nsight./n/n/n/n/n/n"Welcome," said Hagrid, "to Diagon Alley."/n/nHe grinned at Harry's amazement. They stepped/nthrough the archway. Harry looked quickly over his/nshoulder and saw the archway shrink instantly back/ninto solid wall./n/nThe sun shone brightly on a stack of cauldrons/noutside the nearest shop. Cauldrons — All Sizes —/nCopper, Brass, Pewter, Silver — Self-Stirring —/nCollapsible, said a sign hanging over them./n/n"Yeah, you'll be needin' one," said Hagrid, "but we/ngotta get yer money first."/n/nHarry wished he had about eight more eyes. He/nturned his head in every direction as they walked up/nthe street, trying to look at everything at once: the/nshops, the things outside them, the people doing their/nshopping. A plump woman outside an Apothecary/nwas shaking her head as they passed, saying,/n/n"Dragon liver, sixteen Sickles an ounce, they're mad."/n/nA low, soft hooting came from a dark shop with a sign/nsaying Eeylops Owl Emporium — Tawny, Screech,/nBarn, Brown, and Snowy. Several boys of about/nHarry's age had their noses pressed against a window/nwith broomsticks in it. "Look," Harry heard one of/nthem say, "the new Nimbus Two Thousand — fastest/never — " There were shops selling robes, shops selling/ntelescopes and strange silver instruments Harry had/nnever seen before, windows stacked with barrels of/nbat spleens and eels' eyes, tottering piles of spell/nbooks, quills, and rolls of parchment, potion bottles,/nglobes of the moon. .../n/n"Gringotts," said Hagrid./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey had reached a snowy white building that/ntowered over the other little shops. Standing beside/nits burnished bronze doors, wearing a uniform of/nscarlet and gold, was —/n/n"Yeah, that's a goblin," said Hagrid quietly as they/nwalked up the white stone steps toward him. The/ngoblin was about a head shorter than Harry. He had a/nswarthy, clever face, a pointed beard and, Harry/nnoticed, very long fingers and feet. He bowed as they/nwalked inside. Now they were facing a second pair of/ndoors, silver this time, with words engraved upon/nthem:/n/nEnter, stranger, but take heed/n/nOf what awaits the sin of greed,/n/nFor those who take, but do not earn,/n/nMust pay most dearly in their turn./n/nSo if you seek beneath our floors/n/nA treasure that was never yours,/n/nThief, you have been warned, beware/n/nOf finding more than treasure there./n/n"Like I said, yeh'd be mad ter try an' rob it," said/nHagrid./n/nA pair of goblins bowed them through the silver doors/nand they were in a vast marble hall. About a hundred/nmore goblins were sitting on high stools behind a long/ncounter, scribbling in large ledgers, weighing coins in/nbrass scales, examining precious stones through/neyeglasses. There were too many doors to count/n/n/n/n/nleading off the hall, and yet more goblins were/nshowing people in and out of these. Hagrid and Harry/nmade for the counter./n/n"Morning," said Hagrid to a free goblin. "We've come/nter take some money outta Mr. Harry Potter's safe."/n/n"You have his key, sir?"/n/n"Got it here somewhere," said Hagrid, and he started/nemptying his pockets onto the counter, scattering a/nhandful of moldy dog biscuits over the goblins book of/nnumbers. The goblin wrinkled his nose. Harry/nwatched the goblin on their right weighing a pile of/nrubies as big as glowing coals./n/n"Got it," said Hagrid at last, holding up a tiny golden/nkey./n/nThe goblin looked at it closely./n/n"That seems to be in order."/n/n"An' I've also got a letter here from Professor/nDumbledore," said Hagrid importantly, throwing out/nhis chest. "It's about the You-Know-What in vault/nseven hundred and thirteen."/n/nThe goblin read the letter carefully./n/n"Very well," he said, handing it back to Hagrid, "I will/nhave someone take you down to both vaults./nGriphook!"/n/nGriphook was yet another goblin. Once Hagrid had/ncrammed all the dog biscuits back inside his pockets,/nhe and Harry followed Griphook toward one of the/ndoors leading off the hall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's the You-Know-What in vault seven hundred/nand thirteen?" Harry asked./n/n"Can't tell yeh that," said Hagrid mysteriously. "Very/nsecret. Hogwarts business. Dumbledore's trusted me./nMore'n my job's worth ter tell yeh that."/n/nGriphook held the door open for them. Harry, who/nhad expected more marble, was surprised. They were/nin a narrow stone passageway lit with flaming/ntorches. It sloped steeply downward and there were/nlittle railway tracks on the floor. Griphook whistled/nand a small cart came hurtling up the tracks toward/nthem. They climbed in — Hagrid with some difficulty/n— and were off./n/nAt first they just hurtled through a maze of twisting/npassages. Harry tried to remember, left, right, right,/nleft, middle fork, right, left, but it was impossible. The/nrattling cart seemed to know its own way, because/nGriphook wasn't steering./n/nHarry's eyes stung as the cold air rushed past them,/nbut he kept them wide open. Once, he thought he saw/na burst of fire at the end of a passage and twisted/naround to see if it was a dragon, but too late — they/nplunged even deeper, passing an underground lake/nwhere huge stalactites and stalagmites grew from the/nceiling and floor./n/n"I never know," Harry called to Hagrid over the noise/nof the cart, "what's the difference between a/nstalagmite and a stalactite?"/n/n"Stalagmite's got an 'm' in it," said Hagrid. "An' don'/nask me questions just now, I think I'm gonna be/nsick."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe did look very green, and when the cart stopped at/nlast beside a small door in the passage wall, Hagrid/ngot out and had to lean against the wall to stop his/nknees from trembling./n/nGriphook unlocked the door. A lot of green smoke/ncame billowing out, and as it cleared, Harry gasped./nInside were mounds of gold coins. Columns of silver./nHeaps of little bronze Knuts./n/n"All yours," smiled Hagrid./n/nAll Harry's — it was incredible. The Dursleys couldn't/nhave known about this or they'd have had it from him/nfaster than blinking. How often had they complained/nhow much Harry cost them to keep? And all the time/nthere had been a small fortune belonging to him,/nburied deep under London./n/nHagrid helped Harry pile some of it into a bag./n/n"The gold ones are Galleons," he explained./n/n"Seventeen silver Sickles to a Galleon and twenty-nine/nKnuts to a Sickle, it's easy enough. Right, that should/nbe enough fer a couple o' terms, we'll keep the rest/nsafe for yeh." He turned to Griphook. "Vault seven/nhundred and thirteen now, please, and can we go/nmore slowly?"/n/n"One speed only," said Griphook./n/nThey were going even deeper now and gathering/nspeed. The air became colder and colder as they/nhurtled round tight corners. They went rattling over/nan underground ravine, and Harry leaned over the/nside to try to see what was down at the dark bottom,/nbut Hagrid groaned and pulled him back by the scruff/nof his neck./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nVault seven hundred and thirteen had no keyhole./n/n"Stand back," said Griphook importantly. He stroked/nthe door gently with one of his long fingers and it/nsimply melted away./n/n"If anyone but a Gringotts goblin tried that, they'd be/nsucked through the door and trapped in there," said/nGriphook./n/n"How often do you check to see if anyone's inside?"/nHarry asked./n/n"About once every ten years," said Griphook with a/nrather nasty grin./n/nSomething really extraordinary had to be inside this/ntop security vault, Harry was sure, and he leaned/nforward eagerly, expecting to see fabulous jewels at/nthe very least — but at first he thought it was empty./nThen he noticed a grubby little package wrapped up/nin brown paper lying on the floor. Hagrid picked it up/nand tucked it deep inside his coat. Harry longed to/nknow what it was, but knew better than to ask./n/n"Come on, back in this infernal cart, and don't talk to/nme on the way back, it's best if I keep me mouth/nshut," said Hagrid./n/n/n/nOne wild cart ride later they stood blinking in the/nsunlight outside Gringotts. Harry didn't know where/nto run first now that he had a bag full of money. He/ndidn't have to know how many Galleons there were to/na pound to know that he was holding more money/nthan he'd had in his whole life — more money than/neven Dudley had ever had./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Might as well get yer uniform," said Hagrid, nodding/ntoward Madam Malkin's Robes for All Occasions./n"Listen, Harry, would yeh mind if I slipped off fer a/npick-me-up in the Leaky Cauldron? I hate them/nGringotts carts." He did still look a bit sick, so Harry/nentered Madam Malkin's shop alone, feeling nervous./n/nMadam Malkin was a squat, smiling witch dressed all/nin mauve./n/n"Hogwarts, dear?" she said, when Harry started to/nspeak. "Got the lot here — another young man being/nfitted up just now, in fact."/n/nIn the back of the shop, a boy with a pale, pointed/nface was standing on a footstool while a second witch/npinned up his long black robes. Madam Malkin stood/nHarry on a stool next to him, slipped a long robe over/nhis head, and began to pin it to the right length./n/n"Hello," said the boy, "Hogwarts, too?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n"My father's next door buying my books and mother's/nup the street looking at wands," said the boy. He had/na bored, drawling voice. "Then I'm going to drag them/noff to look at racing brooms. I don't see why first years/ncan't have their own. I think I'll bully father into/ngetting me one and I'll smuggle it in somehow."/n/nHarry was strongly reminded of Dudley./n/n"Have you got your own broom?" the boy went on./n/n"No," said Harry./n/n"Play Quidditch at all?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," Harry said again, wondering what on earth/nQuidditch could be./n/n" I do — Father says it's a crime if I'm not picked to/nplay for my House, and I must say, I agree. Know/nwhat House you 11 be in yet?"/n/n"No," said Harry, feeling more stupid by the minute./n/n"Well, no one really knows until they get there, do/nthey, but I know I'll be in Slytherin, all our family/nhave been — imagine being in Hufflepuff, I think I'd/nleave, wouldn't you?"/n/n"Mmm," said Harry, wishing he could say something a/nbit more interesting./n/n"I say, look at that man!" said the boy suddenly,/nnodding toward the front window. Hagrid was/nstanding there, grinning at Harry and pointing at two/nlarge ice creams to show he couldn't come in./n/n"That's Hagrid," said Harry, pleased to know/nsomething the boy didn't. "He works at Hogwarts."/n/n"Oh," said the boy, "I've heard of him. He's a sort of/nservant, isn't he?"/n/n"He's the gamekeeper," said Harry. He was liking the/nboy less and less every second./n/n"Yes, exactly. I heard he's a sort of savage — lives in a/nhut on the school grounds and every now and then he/ngets drunk, tries to do magic, and ends up setting fire/nto his bed."/n/n"I think he's brilliant," said Harry coldly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Do you?" said the boy, with a slight sneer. "Why is he/nwith you? Where are your parents?"/n/n"They're dead," said Harry shortly. He didn't feel/nmuch like going into the matter with this boy./n/n"Oh, sorry," said the other, not sounding sorry at all./n"But they were our kind, weren't they?"/n/n"They were a witch and wizard, if that's what you/nmean."/n/n"I really don't think they should let the other sort in,/ndo you? They're just not the same, they've never been/nbrought up to know our ways. Some of them have/nnever even heard of Hogwarts until they get the letter,/nimagine. I think they should keep it in the old/nwizarding families. What's your surname, anyway?"/n/nBut before Harry could answer, Madam Malkin said,/n"That's you done, my dear," and Harry, not sorry for/nan excuse to stop talking to the boy, hopped down/nfrom the footstool./n/n"Well, I'll see you at Hogwarts, I suppose," said the/ndrawling boy./n/nHarry was rather quiet as he ate the ice cream Hagrid/nhad bought him (chocolate and raspberry with/nchopped nuts)./n/n"What's up?" said Hagrid./n/n"Nothing," Harry lied. They stopped to buy parchment/nand quills. Harry cheered up a bit when he found a/nbottle of ink that changed color as you wrote. When/nthey had left the shop, he said, "Hagrid, what's/nQuidditch?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Blimey, Harry, I keep forgettin' how little yeh know —/nnot knowin' about Quidditch!"/n/n"Don't make me feel worse," said Harry. He told/nHagrid about the pale boy in Madam Malkin's./n/n" — and he said people from Muggle families shouldn't/neven be allowed in — "/n/n"Yer not from a Muggle family. If he'd known who yeh/nwere — he's grown up knowin' yer name if his/nparents are wizardin' folk. You saw what everyone in/nthe Leaky Cauldron was like when they saw yeh./nAnyway, what does he know about it, some o' the best/nI ever saw were the only ones with magic in 'em in a/nlong line o' Muggles — look at yer mum! Look what/nshe had fer a sister!"/n/n"So what is Quidditch?"/n/n"It's our sport. Wizard sport. It's like — like soccer in/nthe Muggle world — everyone follows Quidditch —/nplayed up in the air on broomsticks and there's four/nballs — sorta hard ter explain the rules."/n/n"And what are Slytherin and Hufflepuff?"/n/n"School Houses. There's four. Everyone says/nHufflepuff are a lot o' duffers, but — "/n/n"I bet I'm in Hufflepuff," said Harry gloomily./n/n"Better Hufflepuff than Slytherin," said Hagrid darkly./n"There's not a single witch or wizard who went bad/nwho wasn't in Slytherin. You-Know-Who was one."/n/n"Vol-, sorry — You-Know-Who was at Hogwarts?"/n/n"Years an' years ago," said Hagrid./n/n/n/n/n/nThey bought Harry's school books in a shop called/nFlourish and Blotts where the shelves were stacked to/nthe ceiling with books as large as paving stones/nbound in leather; books the size of postage stamps in/ncovers of silk; books full of peculiar symbols and a/nfew books with nothing in them at all. Even Dudley,/nwho never read anything, would have been wild to get/nhis hands on some of these. Hagrid almost had to/ndrag Harry away from Curses and Counter-curses/n(Bewitch Your Friends and Befuddle Your Enemies/nwith the Latest Revenges: Hair Loss, Jelly-Legs,/nTongue-Tying and Much, Much More) by Professor/nVindictus Viridian./n/n"I was trying to find out how to curse Dudley."/n/n"I'm not sayin' that's not a good idea, but yer not ter/nuse magic in the Muggle world except in very special/ncircumstances," said Hagrid. "An' anyway, yeh/ncouldn' work any of them curses yet, yeh'll need a lot/nmore study before yeh get ter that level."/n/nHagrid wouldn't let Harry buy a solid gold cauldron,/neither ("It says pewter on yer list"), but they got a nice/nset of scales for weighing potion ingredients and a/ncollapsible brass telescope. Then they visited the/nApothecary, which was fascinating enough to make/nup for its horrible smell, a mixture of bad eggs and/nrotted cabbages. Barrels of slimy stuff stood on the/nfloor; jars of herbs, dried roots, and bright powders/nlined the walls; bundles of feathers, strings of fangs,/nand snarled claws hung from the ceiling. While/nHagrid asked the man behind the counter for a/nsupply of some basic potion ingredients for Harry,/nHarry himself examined silver unicorn horns at/ntwenty-one Galleons each and minuscule, glittery-/nblack beetle eyes (five Knuts a scoop)./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nOutside the Apothecary, Hagrid checked Harry's list/nagain./n/n"Just yer wand left — oh yeah, an' I still haven't got/nyeh a birthday present."/n/nHarry felt himself go red./n/n"You don't have to — "/n/n"I know I don't have to. Tell yeh what, I'll get yer/nanimal. Not a toad, toads went outta fashion years/nago, yeh'd be laughed at — an' I don' like cats, they/nmake me sneeze. I'll get yer an owl. All the kids want/nowls, they're dead useful, carry yer mail an'/neverythin'."/n/nTwenty minutes later, they left Eeylops Owl/nEmporium, which had been dark and full of rustling/nand flickering, jewel-bright eyes. Harry now carried a/nlarge cage that held a beautiful snowy owl, fast asleep/nwith her head under her wing. He couldn't stop/nstammering his thanks, sounding just like Professor/nQuirrell./n/n"Don' mention it," said Hagrid gruffly. "Don' expect/nyou've had a lotta presents from them Dursleys. Just/nOllivanders left now — only place fer wands,/nOllivanders, and yeh gotta have the best wand."/n/nA magic wand . . . this was what Harry had been really/nlooking forward to./n/nThe last shop was narrow and shabby. Peeling gold/nletters over the door read Ollivanders: Makers of Fine/nWands since 382b. c. A single wand lay on a faded/npurple cushion in the dusty window./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA tinkling bell rang somewhere in the depths of the/nshop as they stepped inside. It was a tiny place,/nempty except for a single, spindly chair that Hagrid/nsat on to wait. Harry felt strangely as though he had/nentered a very strict library; he swallowed a lot of new/nquestions that had just occurred to him and looked/ninstead at the thousands of narrow boxes piled neatly/nright up to the ceiling. For some reason, the back of/nhis neck prickled. The very dust and silence in here/nseemed to tingle with some secret magic./n/n"Good afternoon," said a soft voice. Harry jumped./nHagrid must have jumped, too, because there was a/nloud crunching noise and he got quickly off the/nspindly chair./n/nAn old man was standing before them, his wide, pale/neyes shining like moons through the gloom of the/nshop./n/n"Hello," said Harry awkwardly./n/n"Ah yes," said the man. "Yes, yes. I thought I'd be/nseeing you soon. Harry Potter." It wasn't a question./n"You have your mother's eyes. It seems only yesterday/nshe was in here herself, buying her first wand. Ten/nand a quarter inches long, swishy, made of willow./nNice wand for charm work."/n/nMr. Ollivander moved closer to Harry. Harry wished/nhe would blink. Those silvery eyes were a bit creepy./n/n"Your father, on the other hand, favored a mahogany/nwand. Eleven inches. Pliable. A little more power and/nexcellent for transfiguration. Well, I say your father/nfavored it — it's really the wand that chooses the/nwizard, of course."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMr. Ollivander had come so close that he and Harry/nwere almost nose to nose. Harry could see himself/nreflected in those misty eyes./n/n"And that's where ..."/n/nMr. Ollivander touched the lightning scar on Harry's/nforehead with a long, white finger./n/n"I'm sorry to say I sold the wand that did it," he said/nsoftly. "Thirteen-and-a-half inches. Yew. Powerful/nwand, very powerful, and in the wrong hands ... well,/nif I'd known what that wand was going out into the/nworld to do. ..."/n/nHe shook his head and then, to Harry's relief, spotted/nHagrid./n/n"Rubeus! Rubeus Hagrid! How nice to see you again./n/n... Oak, sixteen inches, rather bendy, wasn't it?"/n/n"It was, sir, yes," said Hagrid./n/n"Good wand, that one. But I suppose they snapped it/nin half when you got expelled?" said Mr. Ollivander,/nsuddenly stern./n/n"Er — yes, they did, yes," said Hagrid, shuffling his/nfeet. "I've still got the pieces, though," he added/nbrightly./n/n"But you don't use them?" said Mr. Ollivander/nsharply./n/n"Oh, no, sir," said Hagrid quickly. Harry noticed he/ngripped his pink umbrella very tightly as he spoke./n/n"Hmmm," said Mr. Ollivander, giving Hagrid a/npiercing look. "Well, now — Mr. Potter. Let me see."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe pulled a long tape measure with silver markings/nout of his pocket. "Which is your wand arm?"/n/n"Er — well, I'm right-handed," said Harry./n/n"Hold out your arm. That's it." He measured Harry/nfrom shoulder to finger, then wrist to elbow, shoulder/nto floor, knee to armpit and round his head. As he/nmeasured, he said, "Every Ollivander wand has a core/nof a powerful magical substance, Mr. Potter. We use/nunicorn hairs, phoenix tail feathers, and the/nheartstrings of dragons. No two Ollivander wands are/nthe same, just as no two unicorns, dragons, or/nphoenixes are quite the same. And of course, you will/nnever get such good results with another wizard's/nwand."/n/nHarry suddenly realized that the tape measure, which/nwas measuring between his nostrils, was doing this/non its own. Mr. Ollivander was flitting around the/nshelves, taking down boxes./n/n"That will do," he said, and the tape measure/ncrumpled into a heap on the floor. "Right then, Mr./nPotter. Try this one. Beech-wood and dragon/nheartstring. Nine inches. Nice and flexible. Just take/nit and give it a wave."/n/nHarry took the wand and (feeling foolish) waved it/naround a bit, but Mr. Ollivander snatched it out of his/nhand almost at once./n/n"Maple and phoenix feather. Seven inches. Quite/nwhippy. Try — "/n/nHarry tried — but he had hardly raised the wand/nwhen it, too, was snatched back by Mr. Ollivander./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No, no — here, ebony and unicorn hair, eight and a/nhalf inches, springy. Go on, go on, try it out."/n/nHarry tried. And tried. He had no idea what Mr./nOllivander was waiting for. The pile of tried wands/nwas mounting higher and higher on the spindly chair,/nbut the more wands Mr. Ollivander pulled from the/nshelves, the happier he seemed to become./n/n"Tricky customer, eh? Not to worry, well find the/nperfect match here somewhere — I wonder, now —/nyes, why not — unusual combination — holly and/nphoenix feather, eleven inches, nice and supple."/n/nHarry took the wand. He felt a sudden warmth in his/nfingers. He raised the wand above his head, brought it/nswishing down through the dusty air and a stream of/nred and gold sparks shot from the end like a firework,/nthrowing dancing spots of light on to the walls. Hagrid/nwhooped and clapped and Mr. Ollivander cried, "Oh,/nbravo! Yes, indeed, oh, very good. Well, well, well .../nhow curious ... how very curious ..."/n/nHe put Harry's wand back into its box and wrapped it/nin brown paper, still muttering, "Curious . . . curious/n/n/n/n"Sorry," said Harry, "but what's curious?"/n/nMr. Ollivander fixed Harry with his pale stare./n/n"I remember every wand I've ever sold, Mr. Potter./nEvery single wand. It so happens that the phoenix/nwhose tail feather is in your wand, gave another/nfeather — just one other. It is very curious indeed/nthat you should be destined for this wand when its/nbrother — why, its brother gave you that scar."/n/n/n/nHarry swallowed./n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, thirteen-and-a-half inches. Yew. Curious indeed/nhow these things happen. The wand chooses the/nwizard, remember. ... I think we must expect great/nthings from you, Mr. Potter. ... After all, He-Who-/nMust-Not-Be-Named did great things — terrible, yes,/nbut great."/n/nHarry shivered. He wasn't sure he liked Mr./n/nOllivander too much. He paid seven gold Galleons for/nhis wand, and Mr. Ollivander bowed them from his/nshop./n/nThe late afternoon sun hung low in the sky as Harry/nand Hagrid made their way back down Diagon Alley,/nback through the wall, back through the Leaky/nCauldron, now empty. Harry didn't speak at all as/nthey walked down the road; he didn't even notice how/nmuch people were gawking at them on the/nUnderground, laden as they were with all their funny-/nshaped packages, with the snowy owl asleep in its/ncage on Harry's lap. Up another escalator, out into/nPaddington station; Harry only realized where they/nwere when Hagrid tapped him on the shoulder./n/n"Got time fer a bite to eat before yer train leaves," he/nsaid./n/nHe bought Harry a hamburger and they sat down on/nplastic seats to eat them. Harry kept looking around./nEverything looked so strange, somehow./n/n"You all right, Harry? Yer very quiet," said Hagrid./n/nHarry wasn't sure he could explain. He'd just had the/nbest birthday of his life — and yet — he chewed his/nhamburger, trying to find the words./n/n"Everyone thinks I'm special," he said at last. "All/nthose people in the Leaky Cauldron, Professor/n/n/n/n/n/nQuirrell, Mr. Ollivander ... but I don't know anything/nabout magic at all. How can they expect great things?/nI'm famous and I can't even remember what I'm/nfamous for. I don't know what happened when Vol-,/nsorry — I mean, the night my parents died."/n/nHagrid leaned across the table. Behind the wild beard/nand eyebrows he wore a very kind smile./n/n"Don' you worry, Harry. You'll learn fast enough./nEveryone starts at the beginning at Hogwarts, you'll/nbe just fine. Just be yerself. I know it's hard. Yeh've/nbeen singled out, an' that's always hard. But yeh'll/nhave a great time at Hogwarts — I did — still do,/n'smatter of fact."/n/nHagrid helped Harry on to the train that would take/nhim back to the Dursleys, then handed him an/nenvelope./n/n"Yer ticket fer Hogwarts," he said. "First o' September/n— King's Cross — it's all on yer ticket. Any problems/nwith the Dursleys, send me a letter with yer owl, she'll/nknow where to find me. ... See yeh soon, Harry."/n/nThe train pulled out of the station. Harry wanted to/nwatch Hagrid until he was out of sight; he rose in his/nseat and pressed his nose against the window, but he/nblinked and Hagrid had gone./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Journey From Platform Nine And Three-Quarters
text: /nHarry's last month with the Dursleys wasn't fun./nTrue, Dudley was now so scared of Harry he wouldn't/nstay in the same room, while Aunt Petunia and Uncle/nVernon didn't shut Harry in his cupboard, force him/nto do anything, or shout at him — in fact, they didn't/nspeak to him at all. Half terrified, half furious, they/nacted as though any chair with Harry in it were/nempty. Although this was an improvement in many/nways, it did become a bit depressing after a while./n/nHarry kept to his room, with his new owl for/ncompany. He had decided to call her Hedwig, a name/nhe had found in A History of Magic. His school books/nwere very interesting. He lay on his bed reading late/ninto the night, Hedwig swooping in and out of the/nopen window as she pleased. It was lucky that Aunt/nPetunia didn't come in to vacuum anymore, because/nHedwig kept bringing back dead mice. Every night/nbefore he went to sleep, Harry ticked off another day/n/n/n/n/n/n/non the piece of paper he had pinned to the wall,/ncounting down to September the first./n/nOn the last day of August he thought he'd better/nspeak to his aunt and uncle about getting to King's/nCross station the next day, so he went down to the/nliving room where they were watching a quiz show on/ntelevision. He cleared his throat to let them know he/nwas there, and Dudley screamed and ran from the/nroom./n/n"Er — Uncle Vernon?"/n/nUncle Vernon grunted to show he was listening./n/n"Er — I need to be at King's Cross tomorrow to — to/ngo to Hogwarts."/n/nUncle Vernon grunted again./n/n"Would it be all right if you gave me a lift?"/n/nGrunt. Harry supposed that meant yes./n/n"Thank you."/n/nHe was about to go back upstairs when Uncle Vernon/nactually spoke./n/n"Funny way to get to a wizards' school, the train./nMagic carpets all got punctures, have they?"/n/nHarry didn't say anything./n/n"Where is this school, anyway?"/n/n"I don't know," said Harry, realizing this for the first/ntime. He pulled the ticket Hagrid had given him out of/nhis pocket./n/n/n/n/n/n"I just take the train from platform nine and three-/nquarters at eleven o'clock," he read./n/nHis aunt and uncle stared./n/n"Platform what?"/n/n"Nine and three-quarters."/n/n"Don't talk rubbish," said Uncle Vernon. "There is no/nplatform nine and three-quarters."/n/n"It's on my ticket."/n/n"Barking," said Uncle Vernon, "howling mad, the lot of/nthem. You 11 see. You just wait. All right, we'll take/nyou to King's Cross. We're going up to London/ntomorrow anyway, or I wouldn't bother."/n/n"Why are you going to London?" Harry asked, trying/nto keep things friendly./n/n"Taking Dudley to the hospital," growled Uncle/nVernon. "Got to have that ruddy tail removed before/nhe goes to Smeltings."/n/nHarry woke at five o'clock the next morning and was/ntoo excited and nervous to go back to sleep. He got up/nand pulled on his jeans because he didn't want to/nwalk into the station in his wizard's robes — he'd/nchange on the train. He checked his Hogwarts list yet/nagain to make sure he had everything he needed, saw/nthat Hedwig was shut safely in her cage, and then/npaced the room, waiting for the Dursleys to get up./nTwo hours later, Harry's huge, heavy trunk had been/nloaded into the Dursleys' car, Aunt Petunia had/ntalked Dudley into sitting next to Harry, and they had/nset off./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey reached King's Cross at half past ten. Uncle/nVernon dumped Harry's trunk onto a cart and/nwheeled it into the station for him. Harry thought this/nwas strangely kind until Uncle Vernon stopped dead,/nfacing the platforms with a nasty grin on his face./n/n"Well, there you are, boy. Platform nine — platform/nten. Your platform should be somewhere in the/nmiddle, but they don't seem to have built it yet, do/nthey?"/n/nHe was quite right, of course. There was a big plastic/nnumber nine over one platform and a big plastic/nnumber ten over the one next to it, and in the middle,/nnothing at all./n/n"Have a good term," said Uncle Vernon with an even/nnastier smile. He left without another word. Harry/nturned and saw the Dursleys drive away. All three of/nthem were laughing. Harry's mouth went rather dry./nWhat on earth was he going to do? He was starting to/nattract a lot of funny looks, because of Hedwig. He'd/nhave to ask someone./n/nHe stopped a passing guard, but didn't dare mention/nplatform nine and three-quarters. The guard had/nnever heard of Hogwarts and when Harry couldn't/neven tell him what part of the country it was in, he/nstarted to get annoyed, as though Harry was being/nstupid on purpose. Getting desperate, Harry asked for/nthe train that left at eleven o'clock, but the guard said/nthere wasn't one. In the end the guard strode away,/nmuttering about time wasters. Harry was now trying/nhard not to panic. According to the large clock over/nthe arrivals board, he had ten minutes left to get on/nthe train to Hogwarts and he had no idea how to do it;/nhe was stranded in the middle of a station with a/ntrunk he could hardly lift, a pocket full of wizard/nmoney, and a large owl./n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid must have forgotten to tell him something you/nhad to do, like tapping the third brick on the left to/nget into Diagon Alley. He wondered if he should get/nout his wand and start tapping the ticket inspector's/nstand between platforms nine and ten./n/nAt that moment a group of people passed just behind/nhim and he caught a few words of what they were/nsaying./n/n" — packed with Muggles, of course — "/n/nHarry swung round. The speaker was a plump/nwoman who was talking to four boys, all with flaming/nred hair. Each of them was pushing a trunk like/nHarry's in front of him — and they had an owl./n/nHeart hammering, Harry pushed his cart after them./nThey stopped and so did he, just near enough to hear/nwhat they were saying./n/n"Now, what's the platform number?" said the boys'/nmother./n/n"Nine and three-quarters!" piped a small girl, also red-/nheaded, who was holding her hand, "Mom, can't I go/n/n/n/n"You're not old enough, Ginny, now be quiet. All right,/nPercy, you go first."/n/nWhat looked like the oldest boy marched toward/nplatforms nine and ten. Harry watched, careful not to/nblink in case he missed it — but just as the boy/nreached the dividing barrier between the two/nplatforms, a large crowd of tourists came swarming in/nfront of him and by the time the last backpack had/ncleared away, the boy had vanished./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Fred, you next," the plump woman said./n/n/n/n"I'm not Fred, I'm George," said the boy. "Honestly,/nwoman, you call yourself our mother? Can't you tell/nI'm George?"/n/n"Sorry, George, dear."/n/n"Only joking, I am Fred," said the boy, and off he/nwent. His twin called after him to hurry up, and he/nmust have done so, because a second later, he had/ngone — but how had he done it?/n/nNow the third brother was walking briskly toward the/nbarrier — he was almost there — and then, quite/nsuddenly, he wasn't anywhere./n/nThere was nothing else for it./n/n"Excuse me," Harry said to the plump woman./n/n"Hello, dear," she said. "First time at Hogwarts? Ron's/nnew, too."/n/nShe pointed at the last and youngest of her sons. He/nwas tall, thin, and gangling, with freckles, big hands/nand feet, and a long nose./n/n"Yes," said Harry. "The thing is — the thing is, I don't/nknow how to — "/n/n"How to get onto the platform?" she said kindly, and/nHarry nodded./n/n"Not to worry," she said. "All you have to do is walk/nstraight at the barrier between platforms nine and/nten. Don't stop and don't be scared you'll crash into/nit, that's very important. Best do it at a bit of a run if/nyou're nervous. Go on, go now before Ron."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Er — okay," said Harry./n/nHe pushed his trolley around and stared at the/nbarrier. It looked very solid./n/nHe started to walk toward it. People jostled him on/ntheir way to platforms nine and ten. Harry walked/nmore quickly. He was going to smash right into that/nbarrier and then he'd be in trouble — leaning forward/non his cart, he broke into a heavy run — the barrier/nwas coming nearer and nearer — he wouldn't be able/nto stop — the cart was out of control — he was a foot/naway — he closed his eyes ready for the crash —/n/nIt didn't come ... he kept on running ... he opened his/neyes./n/nA scarlet steam engine was waiting next to a platform/npacked with people. A sign overhead said Hogwarts/nExpress, eleven o'clock. Harry looked behind him and/nsaw a wrought-iron archway where the barrier had/nbeen, with the words Platform Nine and Three-/nQuarters on it. He had done it./n/nSmoke from the engine drifted over the heads of the/nchattering crowd, while cats of every color wound/nhere and there between their legs. Owls hooted to one/nanother in a disgruntled sort of way over the babble/nand the scraping of heavy trunks./n/nThe first few carriages were already packed with/nstudents, some hanging out of the window to talk to/ntheir families, some fighting over seats. Harry pushed/nhis cart off down the platform in search of an empty/nseat. He passed a round-faced boy who was saying,/n"Gran, I've lost my toad again."/n/n"Oh, Neville," he heard the old woman sigh./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA boy with dreadlocks was surrounded by a small/ncrowd./n/n/n/n"Give us a look, Lee, go on."/n/nThe boy lifted the lid of a box in his arms, and the/npeople around him shrieked and yelled as something/ninside poked out a long, hairy leg./n/nHarry pressed on through the crowd until he found/nan empty compartment near the end of the train. He/nput Hedwig inside first and then started to shove and/nheave his trunk toward the train door. He tried to lift/nit up the steps but could hardly raise one end and/ntwice he dropped it painfully on his foot./n/n"Want a hand?" It was one of the red-haired twins/nhe'd followed through the barrier./n/n"Yes, please," Harry panted./n/n"Oy, Fred! C'mere and help!"/n/nWith the twins' help, Harry's trunk was at last tucked/naway in a corner of the compartment./n/n"Thanks," said Harry, pushing his sweaty hair out of/nhis eyes./n/n"What's that?" said one of the twins suddenly,/npointing at Harry's lightning scar./n/n"Blimey," said the other twin. "Are you — ?"/n/n"He is," said the first twin. "Aren't you?" he added to/nHarry./n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n" Harry Potter," chorused the twins./n/n"Oh, him," said Harry. "I mean, yes, I am."/n/nThe two boys gawked at him, and Harry felt himself/nturning red. Then, to his relief, a voice came floating/nin through the train's open door./n/n"Fred? George? Are you there?"/n/n"Coming, Mom."/n/nWith a last look at Harry, the twins hopped off the/ntrain./n/nHarry sat down next to the window where, half/nhidden, he could watch the red-haired family on the/nplatform and hear what they were saying. Their/nmother had just taken out her handkerchief./n/n"Ron, you've got something on your nose."/n/nThe youngest boy tried to jerk out of the way, but she/ngrabbed him and began rubbing the end of his nose./n/n"Mom — geroff." He wriggled free./n/n"Aaah, has ickle Ronnie got somefink on his nosie?"/nsaid one of the twins./n/n"Shut up," said Ron./n/n"Where's Percy?" said their mother./n/n"He's coming now."/n/nThe oldest boy came striding into sight. He had/nalready changed into his billowing black Hogwarts/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nrobes, and Harry noticed a shiny red and gold badge/non his chest with the letter P on it./n/n"Can't stay long, Mother," he said. "I'm up front, the/nprefects have got two compartments to themselves — "/n/n"Oh, are you a prefect, Percy?" said one of the twins,/nwith an air of great surprise. "You should have said/nsomething, we had no idea."/n/n"Hang on, I think I remember him saying something/nabout it," said the other twin. "Once — "/n/n"Or twice — "/n/n"A minute — "/n/n"All summer — "/n/n"Oh, shut up," said Percy the Prefect./n/n"How come Percy gets new robes, anyway?" said one/nof the twins./n/n"Because he's a prefect," said their mother fondly. "All/nright, dear, well, have a good term — send me an owl/nwhen you get there."/n/nShe kissed Percy on the cheek and he left. Then she/nturned to the twins./n/n"Now, you two — this year, you behave yourselves. If I/nget one more owl telling me you've — you've blown up/na toilet or — "/n/n"Blown up a toilet? We've never blown up a toilet."/n"Great idea though, thanks, Mom."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's not funny. And look after Ron."/n/n"Don't worry, ickle Ronniekins is safe with us."/n/n"Shut up," said Ron again. He was almost as tall as/nthe twins already and his nose was still pink where/nhis mother had rubbed it./n/n"Hey, Mom, guess what? Guess who we just met on/nthe train?"/n/nHarry leaned back quickly so they couldn't see him/nlooking./n/n"You know that black-haired boy who was near us in/nthe station? Know who he is?"/n/n"Who?"/n/n" Harry Potted"/n/nHarry heard the little girl's voice./n/n"Oh, Mom, can I go on the train and see him, Mom,/noh please. ..."/n/n"You've already seen him, Ginny, and the poor boy/nisn't something you goggle at in a zoo. Is he really,/nFred? How do you know?"/n/n"Asked him. Saw his scar. It's really there — like/nlightning."/n/n"Poor dear — no wonder he was alone, I wondered. He/nwas ever so polite when he asked how to get onto the/nplatform."/n/n"Never mind that, do you think he remembers what/nYou-Know-Who looks like?"/n/n/n/n/n/nTheir mother suddenly became very stern./n/n/n/n"I forbid you to ask him, Fred. No, don't you dare. As/nthough he needs reminding of that on his first day at/nschool."/n/n"All right, keep your hair on."/n/nA whistle sounded./n/n"Hurry up!" their mother said, and the three boys/nclambered onto the train. They leaned out of the/nwindow for her to kiss them good-bye, and their/nyounger sister began to cry./n/n"Don't, Ginny, we'll send you loads of owls."/n/n"Well send you a Hogwarts toilet seat."/n/n" Georg e\"/n/n"Only joking, Mom."/n/nThe train began to move. Harry saw the boys' mother/nwaving and their sister, half laughing, half crying,/nrunning to keep up with the train until it gathered too/nmuch speed, then she fell back and waved./n/nHarry watched the girl and her mother disappear as/nthe train rounded the corner. Houses flashed past the/nwindow. Harry felt a great leap of excitement. He/ndidn't know what he was going to — but it had to be/nbetter than what he was leaving behind./n/nThe door of the compartment slid open and the/nyoungest redheaded boy came in./n/n"Anyone sitting there?" he asked, pointing at the seat/nopposite Harry. "Everywhere else is full."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry shook his head and the boy sat down. He/nglanced at Harry and then looked quickly out of the/nwindow, pretending he hadn't looked. Harry saw he/nstill had a black mark on his nose./n/n"Hey, Ron."/n/nThe twins were back./n/n"Listen, we're going down the middle of the train —/n/nLee Jordan's got a giant tarantula down there."/n/n"Right," mumbled Ron./n/n"Harry," said the other twin, "did we introduce/nourselves? Fred and George Weasley. And this is Ron,/nour brother. See you later, then."/n/n"Bye," said Harry and Ron. The twins slid the/ncompartment door shut behind them./n/n"Are you really Harry Potter?" Ron blurted out./n/nHarry nodded./n/n"Oh — well, I thought it might be one of Fred and/nGeorge's jokes," said Ron. "And have you really got —/nyou know ..."/n/nHe pointed at Harry's forehead./n/nHarry pulled back his bangs to show the lightning/nscar. Ron stared./n/n"So that's where You-Know-Who — ?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry, "but I can't remember it."/n/n"Nothing?" said Ron eagerly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Well — I remember a lot of green light, but nothing/nelse."/n/n/n/n"Wow," said Ron. He sat and stared at Harry for a few/nmoments, then, as though he had suddenly realized/nwhat he was doing, he looked quickly out of the/nwindow again./n/n"Are all your family wizards?" asked Harry, who found/nRon just as interesting as Ron found him./n/n"Er — yes, I think so," said Ron. "I think Mom's got a/nsecond cousin who's an accountant, but we never talk/nabout him."/n/n"So you must know loads of magic already."/n/nThe Weasleys were clearly one of those old wizarding/nfamilies the pale boy in Diagon Alley had talked/nabout./n/n"I heard you went to live with Muggles," said Ron./n"What are they like?"/n/n"Horrible — well, not all of them. My aunt and uncle/nand cousin are, though. Wish I'd had three wizard/nbrothers."/n/n"Five," said Ron. For some reason, he was looking/ngloomy. "I'm the sixth in our family to go to Hogwarts./nYou could say I've got a lot to live up to. Bill and/nCharlie have already left — Bill was head boy and/nCharlie was captain of Quidditch. Now Percy's a/nprefect. Fred and George mess around a lot, but they/nstill get really good marks and everyone thinks they're/nreally funny. Everyone expects me to do as well as the/nothers, but if I do, it's no big deal, because they did it/nfirst. You never get anything new, either, with five/n/n/n/n/n/nbrothers. I've got Bill's old robes, Charlie's old wand,/nand Percy's old rat."/n/nRon reached inside his jacket and pulled out a fat/ngray rat, which was asleep./n/n"His name's Scabbers and he's useless, he hardly ever/nwakes up. Percy got an owl from my dad for being/nmade a prefect, but they couldn't aff — I mean, I got/nScabbers instead."/n/nRon's ears went pink. He seemed to think he'd said/ntoo much, because he went back to staring out of the/nwindow./n/nHarry didn't think there was anything wrong with not/nbeing able to afford an owl. After all, he'd never had/nany money in his life until a month ago, and he told/nRon so, all about having to wear Dudley's old clothes/nand never getting proper birthday presents. This/nseemed to cheer Ron up./n/n"... and until Hagrid told me, I didn't know anything/nabout being a wizard or about my parents or/nVoldemort — "/n/nRon gasped./n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n" You said You-Know-Who's name\" said Ron, sounding/nboth shocked and impressed. "I'd have thought you,/nof all people — "/n/n"I'm not trying to be brave or anything, saying the/nname," said Harry, "I just never knew you shouldn't./nSee what I mean? I've got loads to learn. ... I bet," he/nadded, voicing for the first time something that had/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbeen worrying him a lot lately, "I bet I'm the worst in/nthe class."/n/n"You won't be. There's loads of people who come from/nMuggle families and they learn quick enough."/n/nWhile they had been talking, the train had carried/nthem out of London. Now they were speeding past/nfields full of cows and sheep. They were quiet for a/ntime, watching the fields and lanes flick past./n/nAround half past twelve there was a great clattering/noutside in the corridor and a smiling, dimpled woman/nslid back their door and said, "Anything off the cart,/ndears?"/n/nHarry, who hadn't had any breakfast, leapt to his feet,/nbut Ron's ears went pink again and he muttered that/nhe'd brought sandwiches. Harry went out into the/ncorridor./n/nHe had never had any money for candy with the/nDursleys, and now that he had pockets rattling with/ngold and silver he was ready to buy as many Mars/nBars as he could carry — but the woman didn't have/nMars Bars. What she did have were Bertie Bott's/nEvery Flavor Beans, Drooble's Best Blowing Gum,/nChocolate Frogs, Pumpkin Pasties, Cauldron Cakes,/nLicorice Wands, and a number of other strange things/nHarry had never seen in his life. Not wanting to miss/nanything, he got some of everything and paid the/nwoman eleven silver Sickles and seven bronze Knuts./n/nRon stared as Harry brought it all back in to the/ncompartment and tipped it onto an empty seat./n/n"Hungry, are you?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Starving," said Harry, taking a large bite out of a/npumpkin pasty./n/nRon had taken out a lumpy package and unwrapped/nit. There were four sandwiches inside. He pulled one/nof them apart and said, "She always forgets I don't/nlike corned beef."/n/n"Swap you for one of these," said Harry, holding up a/npasty. "Go on — "/n/n"You don't want this, it's all dry," said Ron. "She/nhasn't got much time," he added quickly, "you know,/nwith five of us."/n/n"Go on, have a pasty," said Harry, who had never had/nanything to share before or, indeed, anyone to share/nit with. It was a nice feeling, sitting there with Ron,/neating their way through all Harry's pasties, cakes,/nand candies (the sandwiches lay forgotten)./n/n"What are these?" Harry asked Ron, holding up a/npack of Chocolate Frogs. "They're not really frogs, are/nthey?" He was starting to feel that nothing would/nsurprise him./n/n"No," said Ron. "But see what the card is. I'm missing/nAgrippa."/n/n"What?"/n/n"Oh, of course, you wouldn't know — Chocolate Frogs/nhave cards inside them, you know, to collect —/nfamous witches and wizards. I've got about five/nhundred, but I haven't got Agrippa or Ptolemy."/n/nHarry unwrapped his Chocolate Frog and picked up/nthe card. It showed a man's face. He wore half-moon/nglasses, had a long, crooked nose, and flowing silver/n/n/n/n/n/nhair, beard, and mustache. Underneath the picture/nwas the name Albus Dumbledore./n/n/n/n"So this is Dumbledore!" said Harry./n/n"Don't tell me you'd never heard of Dumbledore!" said/nRon. "Can I have a frog? I might get Agrippa — thanks/n/n/n/nHarry turned over his card and read:/n/nALBUS DUMBLEDORE/n/nCURRENTLY HEADMASTER OF HOGWARTS/n/nConsidered by many the greatest wizard of modern/ntimes, Dumbledore is particularly famous for his/ndefeat of the Dark wizard Grindelwald in 1945, for the/ndiscovery of the twelve uses of dragon's blood, and his/nwork on alchemy with his partner, Nicolas Flamel./nProfessor Dumbledore enjoys chamber music and ten/npin bowling./n/nHarry turned the card back over and saw, to his/nastonishment, that Dumbledore 's face had/ndisappeared./n/n"He's gone!"/n/n"Well, you can't expect him to hang around all day,"/nsaid Ron. "He'll be back. No, I've got Morgana again/nand I've got about six of her ... do you want it? You/ncan start collecting."/n/nRon's eyes strayed to the pile of Chocolate Frogs/nwaiting to be unwrapped./n/n"Help yourself," said Harry. "But in, you know, the/nMuggle world, people just stay put in photos."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Do they? What, they don't move at all?" Ron sounded/namazed. "Weird)."/n/n/n/nHarry stared as Dumbledore sidled back into the/npicture on his card and gave him a small smile. Ron/nwas more interested in eating the frogs than looking/nat the Famous Witches and Wizards cards, but Harry/ncouldn't keep his eyes off them. Soon he had not only/nDumbledore and Morgana, but Hengist of Woodcraft,/nAlberic Grunnion, Circe, Paracelsus, and Merlin. He/nfinally tore his eyes away from the druidess Cliodna,/nwho was scratching her nose, to open a bag of Bertie/nBott's Every Flavor Beans./n/n"You want to be careful with those," Ron warned/nHarry. "When they say every flavor, they mean every/nflavor — you know, you get all the ordinary ones like/nchocolate and peppermint and marmalade, but then/nyou can get spinach and liver and tripe. George/nreckons he had a booger-flavored one once."/n/nRon picked up a green bean, looked at it carefully,/nand bit into a corner./n/n"Bleaaargh — see? Sprouts."/n/nThey had a good time eating the Every Flavor Beans./nHarry got toast, coconut, baked bean, strawberry,/ncurry, grass, coffee, sardine, and was even brave/nenough to nibble the end off a funny gray one Ron/nwouldn't touch, which turned out to be pepper./n/nThe countryside now flying past the window was/nbecoming wilder. The neat fields had gone. Now there/nwere woods, twisting rivers, and dark green hills./n/nThere was a knock on the door of their compartment/nand the round-faced boy Harry had passed on/n/n/n/n/n/nplatform nine and three-quarters came in. He looked/ntearful./n/n/n/n"Sorry," he said, "but have you seen a toad at all?"/n/nWhen they shook their heads, he wailed, "I've lost/nhim! He keeps getting away from me!"/n/n"Hell turn up," said Harry./n/n"Yes," said the boy miserably. "Well, if you see him ..."/nHe left./n/n"Don't know why he's so bothered," said Ron. "If I'd/nbrought a toad I'd lose it as quick as I could. Mind/nyou, I brought Scabbers, so I can't talk."/n/nThe rat was still snoozing on Ron's lap./n/n"He might have died and you wouldn't know the/ndifference," said Ron in disgust. "I tried to turn him/nyellow yesterday to make him more interesting, but/nthe spell didn't work. I'll show you, look ..."/n/nHe rummaged around in his trunk and pulled out a/nvery battered-looking wand. It was chipped in places/nand something white was glinting at the end./n/n"Unicorn hair's nearly poking out. Anyway — "/n/nHe had just raised his wand when the compartment/ndoor slid open again. The toadless boy was back, but/nthis time he had a girl with him. She was already/nwearing her new Hogwarts robes./n/n"Has anyone seen a toad? Neville's lost one," she said./nShe had a bossy sort of voice, lots of bushy brown/nhair, and rather large front teeth./n/n/n/n/n/n"We've already told him we haven't seen it," said Ron,/nbut the girl wasn't listening, she was looking at the/nwand in his hand./n/n"Oh, are you doing magic? Let's see it, then."/n/nShe sat down. Ron looked taken aback./n/n"Er — all right."/n/nHe cleared his throat./n/n" Sunshine , daisies, butter mellow,/n/nTurn this stupid, fat rat yellow."/n/nHe waved his wand, but nothing happened. Scabbers/nstayed gray and fast asleep./n/n"Are you sure that's a real spell?" said the girl. "Well,/nit's not very good, is it? I've tried a few simple spells/njust for practice and it's all worked for me. Nobody in/nmy family's magic at all, it was ever such a surprise/nwhen I got my letter, but I was ever so pleased, of/ncourse, I mean, it's the very best school of witchcraft/nthere is, I've heard — I've learned all our course books/nby heart, of course, I just hope it will be enough — I'm/nHermione Granger, by the way, who are you?"/n/nShe said all this very fast./n/nHarry looked at Ron, and was relieved to see by his/nstunned face that he hadn't learned all the course/nbooks by heart either./n/n"I'm Ron Weasley," Ron muttered./n/n"Harry Potter," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Are you really?" said Hermione. "I know all about/nyou, of course — I got a few extra books for/nbackground reading, and you're in Modern Magical/nHistory and The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts and/nGreat Wizarding Events of the Twentieth Century."/n/n"Am I?" said Harry, feeling dazed./n/n"Goodness, didn't you know, I'd have found out/neverything I could if it was me," said Hermione. "Do/neither of you know what House you'll be in? I've been/nasking around, and I hope I'm in Gryffindor, it sounds/nby far the best; I hear Dumbledore himself was in it,/nbut I suppose Ravenclaw wouldn't be too bad. .../nAnyway, we'd better go and look for Neville's toad./n/nYou two had better change, you know, I expect we'll/nbe there soon."/n/nAnd she left, taking the toadless boy with her./n/n"Whatever House I'm in, I hope she's not in it," said/nRon. He threw his wand back into his trunk. "Stupid/nspell — George gave it to me, bet he knew it was a/ndud."/n/n"What House are your brothers in?" asked Harry./n/n"Gryffindor," said Ron. Gloom seemed to be settling/non him again. "Mom and Dad were in it, too. I don't/nknow what they'll say if I'm not. I don't suppose/nRavenclaw would be too bad, but imagine if they put/nme in Slytherin."/n/n"That's the House Vol-, I mean, You-Know-Who was/nin?"/n/n/n/n"Yeah," said Ron. He flopped back into his seat,/nlooking depressed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You know, I think the ends of Scabbers' whiskers are/na bit lighter," said Harry, trying to take Ron's mind off/nHouses. "So what do your oldest brothers do now that/nthey've left, anyway?"/n/nHarry was wondering what a wizard did once he'd/nfinished school./n/n"Charlie's in Romania studying dragons, and Bill's in/nAfrica doing something for Gringotts," said Ron. "Did/nyou hear about Gringotts? It's been all over the Daily/nProphet, but I don't suppose you get that with the/nMuggles — someone tried to rob a high security/nvault."/n/nHarry stared./n/n"Really? What happened to them?"/n/n"Nothing, that's why it's such big news. They haven't/nbeen caught. My dad says it must've been a powerful/nDark wizard to get round Gringotts, but they don't/nthink they took anything, that's what's odd. 'Course,/neveryone gets scared when something like this/nhappens in case You-Know-Who's behind it."/n/nHarry turned this news over in his mind. He was/nstarting to get a prickle of fear every time You-Know-/nWho was mentioned. He supposed this was all part of/nentering the magical world, but it had been a lot more/ncomfortable saying "Voldemort" without worrying./n/n"What's your Quidditch team?" Ron asked./n/n"Er — I don't know any," Harry confessed./n/n"What!" Ron looked dumbfounded. "Oh, you wait, it's/nthe best game in the world — " And he was off,/nexplaining all about the four balls and the positions of/n/n/n/n/n/nthe seven players, describing famous games he'd been/nto with his brothers and the broomstick he'd like to/nget if he had the money. He was just taking Harry/nthrough the finer points of the game when the/ncompartment door slid open yet again, but it wasn't/nNeville the toadless boy, or Hermione Granger this/ntime./n/nThree boys entered, and Harry recognized the middle/none at once: It was the pale boy from Madam Malkin's/nrobe shop. He was looking at Harry with a lot more/ninterest than he'd shown back in Diagon Alley./n/n"Is it true?" he said. "They're saying all down the train/nthat Harry Potter's in this compartment. So it's you, is/nit?"/n/n/n/n"Yes," said Harry. He was looking at the other boys./nBoth of them were thickset and looked extremely/nmean. Standing on either side of the pale boy, they/nlooked like bodyguards./n/n"Oh, this is Crabbe and this is Goyle," said the pale/nboy carelessly, noticing where Harry was looking./n/n"And my names Malfoy, Draco Malfoy."/n/nRon gave a slight cough, which might have been/nhiding a snigger. Draco Malfoy looked at him./n/n"Think my name's funny, do you? No need to ask who/nyou are. My father told me all the Weasleys have red/nhair, freckles, and more children than they can/nafford."/n/nHe turned back to Harry.
