"You'll soon find out some/nwizarding families are much better than others,/n/nPotter. You don't want to go making friends with the/nwrong sort. I can help you there."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe held out his hand to shake Harry's, but Harry/ndidn't take it./n/n"I think I can tell who the wrong sort are for myself,/nthanks," he said coolly./n/nDraco Malfoy didn't go red, but a pink tinge appeared/nin his pale cheeks./n/n"I'd be careful if I were you, Potter," he said slowly./n"Unless you're a bit politer you'll go the same way as/nyour parents. They didn't know what was good for/nthem, either. You hang around with riffraff like the/nWeasleys and that Hagrid, and it'll rub off on you."/n/nBoth Harry and Ron stood up./n/n"Say that again," Ron said, his face as red as his hair./n/n"Oh, you're going to fight us, are you?" Malfoy/nsneered./n/n"Unless you get out now," said Harry, more bravely/nthan he felt, because Crabbe and Goyle were a lot/nbigger than him or Ron./n/n"But we don't feel like leaving, do we, boys? We've/neaten all our food and you still seem to have some."/n/nGoyle reached toward the Chocolate Frogs next to/nRon — Ron leapt forward, but before he'd so much as/ntouched Goyle, Goyle let out a horrible yell./n/nScabbers the rat was hanging off his finger, sharp/nlittle teeth sunk deep into Goyle 's knuckle — Crabbe/nand Malfoy backed away as Goyle swung Scabbers/nround and round, howling, and when Scabbers finally/nflew off and hit the window, all three of them/ndisappeared at once. Perhaps they thought there were/n/n/n/n/nmore rats lurking among the sweets, or perhaps/nthey'd heard footsteps, because a second later,/nHermione Granger had come in./n/n"What has been going on?" she said, looking at the/nsweets all over the floor and Ron picking up Scabbers/nby his tail./n/n"I think he's been knocked out," Ron said to Harry./n/nHe looked closer at Scabbers. "No — I don't believe it/n— he's gone back to sleep."/n/nAnd so he had./n/n"You've met Malfoy before?"/n/nHarry explained about their meeting in Diagon Alley./n/n"I've heard of his family," said Ron darkly. "They were/nsome of the first to come back to our side after You-/nKnow-Who disappeared. Said they'd been bewitched./nMy dad doesn't believe it. He says Malfoy's father/ndidn't need an excuse to go over to the Dark Side." He/nturned to Hermione. "Can we help you with/nsomething?"/n/n"You'd better hurry up and put your robes on, I've/njust been up to the front to ask the conductor, and he/nsays we're nearly there. You haven't been fighting,/nhave you? You'll be in trouble before we even get/nthere!"/n/n"Scabbers has been fighting, not us," said Ron,/nscowling at her. "Would you mind leaving while we/nchange?"/n/n"All right — I only came in here because people/noutside are behaving very childishly, racing up and/ndown the corridors," said Hermione in a sniffy voice./n/n/n/n/n/n"And you've got dirt on your nose, by the way, did you/nknow?"/n/n/n/nRon glared at her as she left. Harry peered out of the/nwindow. It was getting dark. He could see mountains/nand forests under a deep purple sky. The train did/nseem to be slowing down./n/nHe and Ron took off their jackets and pulled on their/nlong black robes. Ron's were a bit short for him, you/ncould see his sneakers underneath them./n/nA voice echoed through the train: "We will be reaching/nHogwarts in five minutes' time. Please leave your/nluggage on the train, it will be taken to the school/nseparately."/n/nHarry's stomach lurched with nerves and Ron, he/nsaw, looked pale under his freckles. They crammed/ntheir pockets with the last of the sweets and joined/nthe crowd thronging the corridor./n/nThe train slowed right down and finally stopped./nPeople pushed their way toward the door and out on/nto a tiny, dark platform. Harry shivered in the cold/nnight air. Then a lamp came bobbing over the heads/nof the students, and Harry heard a familiar voice:/n"Firs' years! Firs' years over here! All right there,/nHarry?"/n/nHagrid's big hairy face beamed over the sea of heads./n/n"C'mon, follow me — any more firs' years? Mind yer/nstep, now! Firs' years follow me!"/n/nSlipping and stumbling, they followed Hagrid down/nwhat seemed to be a steep, narrow path. It was so/ndark on either side of them that Harry thought there/nmust be thick trees there. Nobody spoke much./n/n/n/n/n/nNeville, the boy who kept losing his toad, sniffed once/nor twice./n/n/n/n"Yeh'll get yer firs' sight o' Hogwarts in a sec," Hagrid/ncalled over his shoulder, "jus' round this bend here."/n/nThere was a loud "Oooooh!"/n/nThe narrow path had opened suddenly onto the edge/nof a great black lake. Perched atop a high mountain/non the other side, its windows sparkling in the starry/nsky, was a vast castle with many turrets and towers./n/n"No more'n four to a boat!" Hagrid called, pointing to/na fleet of little boats sitting in the water by the shore./nHarry and Ron were followed into their boat by Neville/nand Hermione./n/n"Everyone in?" shouted Hagrid, who had a boat to/nhimself. "Right then — FORWARD!"/n/nAnd the fleet of little boats moved off all at once,/ngliding across the lake, which was as smooth as/nglass. Everyone was silent, staring up at the great/ncastle overhead. It towered over them as they sailed/nnearer and nearer to the cliff on which it stood./n/n"Heads down!" yelled Hagrid as the first boats reached/nthe cliff; they all bent their heads and the little boats/ncarried them through a curtain of ivy that hid a wide/nopening in the cliff face. They were carried along a/ndark tunnel, which seemed to be taking them right/nunderneath the castle, until they reached a kind of/nunderground harbor, where they clambered out onto/nrocks and pebbles./n/n"Oy, you there! Is this your toad?" said Hagrid, who/nwas checking the boats as people climbed out of/nthem./n/n/n/n/n/n"Trevor!" cried Neville blissfully, holding out his/nhands. Then they clambered up a passageway in the/nrock after Hagrid's lamp, coming out at last onto/nsmooth, damp grass right in the shadow of the castle./n/nThey walked up a flight of stone steps and crowded/naround the huge, oak front door./n/n"Everyone here? You there, still got yer toad?"/n/nHagrid raised a gigantic fist and knocked three times/non the castle door./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n7/n/n/n/n

title: The Sorting Hat
text: /nThe door swung open at once. A tall, black-haired/nwitch in emerald-green robes stood there. She had a/nvery stern face and Harry's first thought was that this/nwas not someone to cross./n/n"The firs' years, Professor McGonagall," said Hagrid./n/n"Thank you, Hagrid. I will take them from here."/n/nShe pulled the door wide. The entrance hall was so/nbig you could have fit the whole of the Dursleys'/nhouse in it. The stone walls were lit with flaming/ntorches like the ones at Gringotts, the ceiling was too/nhigh to make out, and a magnificent marble staircase/nfacing them led to the upper floors./n/nThey followed Professor McGonagall across the/nflagged stone floor. Harry could hear the drone of/nhundreds of voices from a doorway to the right — the/nrest of the school must already be here — but/nProfessor McGonagall showed the first years into a/nsmall, empty chamber off the hall. They crowded in,/n/n/n/nstanding rather closer together than they would/nusually have done, peering about nervously./n/n"Welcome to Hogwarts," said Professor McGonagall./n"The start-of-term banquet will begin shortly, but/nbefore you take your seats in the Great Hall, you will/nbe sorted into your Houses. The Sorting is a very/nimportant ceremony because, while you are here,/nyour House will be something like your family within/nHogwarts. You will have classes with the rest of your/nHouse, sleep in your House dormitory, and spend free/ntime in your House common room./n/n"The four Houses are called Gryffindor, Hufflepuff,/nRavenclaw, and Slytherin. Each House has its own/nnoble history and each has produced outstanding/nwitches and wizards. While you are at Hogwarts, your/ntriumphs will earn your House points, while any rule-/nbreaking will lose House points. At the end of the/nyear, the House with the most points is awarded the/nHouse cup, a great honor. I hope each of you will be a/ncredit to whichever House becomes yours./n/n"The Sorting Ceremony will take place in a few/nminutes in front of the rest of the school. I suggest/nyou all smarten yourselves up as much as you can/nwhile you are waiting."/n/nHer eyes lingered for a moment on Neville's cloak,/nwhich was fastened under his left ear, and on Ron's/nsmudged nose. Harry nervously tried to flatten his/nhair./n/n"I shall return when we are ready for you," said/nProfessor McGonagall. "Please wait quietly."/n/nShe left the chamber. Harry swallowed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"How exactly do they sort us into Houses?" he asked/nRon./n/n/n/n"Some sort of test, I think. Fred said it hurts a lot, but/nI think he was joking."/n/nHarry's heart gave a horrible jolt. A test? In front of/nthe whole school? But he didn't know any magic yet/n— what on earth would he have to do? He hadn't/nexpected something like this the moment they/narrived. He looked around anxiously and saw that/neveryone else looked terrified, too. No one was talking/nmuch except Hermione Granger, who was whispering/nvery fast about all the spells she'd learned and/nwondering which one she'd need. Harry tried hard not/nto listen to her. He'd never been more nervous, never,/nnot even when he'd had to take a school report home/nto the Dursleys saying that he'd somehow turned his/nteachers wig blue. He kept his eyes fixed on the door./nAny second now, Professor McGonagall would come/nback and lead him to his doom./n/nThen something happened that made him jump about/na foot in the air — several people behind him/nscreamed./n/n"What the — ?"/n/nHe gasped. So did the people around him. About/ntwenty ghosts had just streamed through the back/nwall. Pearly-white and slightly transparent, they/nglided across the room talking to one another and/nhardly glancing at the first years. They seemed to be/narguing. What looked like a fat little monk was/nsaying: "Forgive and forget, I say, we ought to give/nhim a second chance — "/n/n"My dear Friar, haven't we given Peeves all the/nchances he deserves? He gives us all a bad name and/n/n/n/n/n/nyou know, he's not really even a ghost — I say, what/nare you all doing here?"/n/n/n/nA ghost wearing a ruff and tights had suddenly/nnoticed the first years./n/nNobody answered./n/n"New students!" said the Fat Friar, smiling around at/nthem. "About to be Sorted, I suppose?"/n/nA few people nodded mutely./n/n"Hope to see you in Hufflepuff!" said the Friar. "My old/nHouse, you know."/n/n"Move along now," said a sharp voice. "The Sorting/nCeremony's about to start."/n/nProfessor McGonagall had returned. One by one, the/nghosts floated away through the opposite wall./n/n"Now, form a line," Professor McGonagall told the first/nyears, "and follow me."/n/nFeeling oddly as though his legs had turned to lead,/nHarry got into line behind a boy with sandy hair, with/nRon behind him, and they walked out of the chamber,/nback across the hall, and through a pair of double/ndoors into the Great Hall./n/nHarry had never even imagined such a strange and/nsplendid place. It was lit by thousands and thousands/nof candles that were floating in midair over four long/ntables, where the rest of the students were sitting./nThese tables were laid with glittering golden plates/nand goblets. At the top of the hall was another long/ntable where the teachers were sitting. Professor/nMcGonagall led the first years up here, so that they/n/n/n/n/ncame to a halt in a line facing the other students,/nwith the teachers behind them. The hundreds of faces/nstaring at them looked like pale lanterns in the/nflickering candlelight. Dotted here and there among/nthe students, the ghosts shone misty silver. Mainly to/navoid all the staring eyes, Harry looked upward and/nsaw a velvety black ceiling dotted with stars. He heard/nHermione whisper, "It's bewitched to look like the sky/noutside. I read about it in Hogwarts, A History."/n/nIt was hard to believe there was a ceiling there at all,/nand that the Great Hall didn't simply open on to the/nheavens./n/nHarry quickly looked down again as Professor/nMcGonagall silently placed a four-legged stool in front/nof the first years. On top of the stool she put a pointed/nwizard's hat. This hat was patched and frayed and/nextremely dirty. Aunt Petunia wouldn't have let it in/nthe house./n/nMaybe they had to try and get a rabbit out of it, Harry/nthought wildly, that seemed the sort of thing —/nnoticing that everyone in the hall was now staring at/nthe hat, he stared at it, too. For a few seconds, there/nwas complete silence. Then the hat twitched. A rip/nnear the brim opened wide like a mouth — and the/nhat began to sing:/n/n"Oh, you may not think I'm pretty,/n/nBut don't judge on what you see,/n/nI'll eat myself if you can find/n/nA smarter hat than me./n/nYou can keep your bowlers black,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nYour top hats sleek and tall,/n/nFor I'm the Hogwarts Sorting Hat/nAnd I can cap them all./n/nThere's nothing hidden in your head/nThe Sorting Hat can't see,/n/nSo try me on and I will tell you/nWhere you ought to be./n/nYou might belong in Gryffindor,/n/nWhere dwell the brave at heart,/n/nTheir daring, nerve, and chivalry/nSet Gryffindors apart;/n/nYou might belong in Hufflepuff,/n/nWhere they are just and loyal,/n/nThose patient Hufflepuffs are true/nAnd unafraid of toil;/n/nOr yet in wise old Ravenclaw,/n/nIf you've a ready mind,/n/nWhere those of wit and learning,/n/nWill always find their kind;/n/nOr perhaps in Slytherin/n/n/n/n/n/nYou'll make your real friends,/n/nThose cunning folk use any means/nTo achieve their ends./n/nSo put me on! Don't be afraid l\/n/nAnd don't get in a flap\/n/nYou're in safe hands (though I have none)/n/nFor I'm a Thinking Cap\"/n/nThe whole hall burst into applause as the hat finished/nits song. It bowed to each of the four tables and then/nbecame quite still again./n/n"So we've just got to try on the hat!" Ron whispered to/nHarry. "I'll kill Fred, he was going on about wrestling/na troll."/n/nHarry smiled weakly. Yes, trying on the hat was a lot/nbetter than having to do a spell, but he did wish they/ncould have tried it on without everyone watching. The/nhat seemed to be asking rather a lot; Harry didn't feel/nbrave or quick-witted or any of it at the moment. If/nonly the hat had mentioned a House for people who/nfelt a bit queasy, that would have been the one for/nhim./n/nProfessor McGonagall now stepped forward holding a/nlong roll of parchment./n/n"When I call your name, you will put on the hat and/nsit on the stool to be sorted," she said. "Abbott,/nHannah!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA pink-faced girl with blonde pigtails stumbled out of/nline, put on the hat, which fell right down over her/neyes, and sat down. A moment's pause —/n/n"HUFFLEPUFF!" shouted the hat./n/nThe table on the right cheered and clapped as/nHannah went to sit down at the Hufflepuff table./n/nHarry saw the ghost of the Fat Friar waving merrily at/nher./n/n"Bones, Susan!"/n/n"HUFFLEPUFF!" shouted the hat again, and Susan/nscuttled off to sit next to Hannah./n/n"Boot, Terry!"/n/n"RAVENCLAW!"/n/nThe table second from the left clapped this time;/nseveral Ravenclaws stood up to shake hands with/nTerry as he joined them./n/n"Brocklehurst, Mandy" went to Ravenclaw too, but/n"Brown, Lavender" became the first new Gryffindor,/nand the table on the far left exploded with cheers;/nHarry could see Ron's twin brothers catcalling./n/n"Bulstrode, Millicent" then became a Slytherin./nPerhaps it was Harry's imagination, after all he'd/nheard about Slytherin, but he thought they looked/nlike an unpleasant lot./n/nHe was starting to feel definitely sick now. He/nremembered being picked for teams during gym at his/nold school. He had always been last to be chosen, not/nbecause he was no good, but because no one wanted/nDudley to think they liked him./n/n/n/n/n/n"Finch-Fletchley, Justin!"/n/n/n/n"HUFFLEPUFF!"/n/nSometimes, Harry noticed, the hat shouted out the/nHouse at once, but at others it took a little while to/ndecide. "Finnigan, Seamus," the sandy-haired boy/nnext to Harry in the line, sat on the stool for almost a/nwhole minute before the hat declared him a/nGryffindor./n/n"Granger, Hermione!"/n/nHermione almost ran to the stool and jammed the hat/neagerly on her head./n/n"GRYFFINDOR!" shouted the hat. Ron groaned./n/nA horrible thought struck Harry, as horrible thoughts/nalways do when you're very nervous. What if he/nwasn't chosen at all? What if he just sat there with/nthe hat over his eyes for ages, until Professor/nMcGonagall jerked it off his head and said there had/nobviously been a mistake and he'd better get back on/nthe train?/n/nWhen Neville Longbottom, the boy who kept losing his/ntoad, was called, he fell over on his way to the stool./nThe hat took a long time to decide with Neville. When/nit finally shouted, "GRYFFINDOR," Neville ran off still/nwearing it, and had to jog back amid gales of laughter/nto give it to "MacDougal, Morag."/n/nMalfoy swaggered forward when his name was called/nand got his wish at once: the hat had barely touched/nhis head when it screamed, "SLYTHERIN!"/n/nMalfoy went to join his friends Crabbe and Goyle,/nlooking pleased with himself./n/n/n/n/n/nThere weren't many people left now./n/n/n/n"Moon" , "Nott" ... , "Parkinson" ... , then a pair of/ntwin girls, "Path" and "Path" ... , then "Perks, Sally-/nAnne" . . . , and then, at last —/n/n"Potter, Harry!"/n/nAs Harry stepped forward, whispers suddenly broke/nout like little hissing fires all over the hall./n/n" Potter , did she say?"/n/n" The Harry Potter?"/n/nThe last thing Harry saw before the hat dropped over/nhis eyes was the hall full of people craning to get a/ngood look at him. Next second he was looking at the/nblack inside of the hat. He waited./n/n"Hmm," said a small voice in his ear. "Difficult. Very/ndifficult. Plenty of courage, I see. Not a bad mind/neither. There's talent, oh my goodness, yes — and a/nnice thirst to prove yourself, now that's interesting. .../nSo where shall I put you?"/n/nHarry gripped the edges of the stool and thought, Not/nSlytherin, not Slytherin./n/n"Not Slytherin, eh?" said the small voice. "Are you/nsure? You could be great, you know, it's all here in/nyour head, and Slytherin will help you on the way to/ngreatness, no doubt about that — no? Well, if you're/nsure — better be GRYFFINDOR!"/n/nHarry heard the hat shout the last word to the whole/nhall. He took off the hat and walked shakily toward/nthe Gryffindor table. He was so relieved to have been/nchosen and not put in Slytherin, he hardly noticed/n/n/n/n/n/nthat he was getting the loudest cheer yet. Percy the/nPrefect got up and shook his hand vigorously, while/nthe Weasley twins yelled, "We got Potter! We got/nPotter!" Harry sat down opposite the ghost in the ruff/nhe'd seen earlier. The ghost patted his arm, giving/nHarry the sudden, horrible feeling he'd just plunged it/ninto a bucket of ice-cold water./n/nHe could see the High Table properly now. At the end/nnearest him sat Hagrid, who caught his eye and gave/nhim the thumbs up. Harry grinned back. And there,/nin the center of the High Table, in a large gold chair,/nsat Albus Dumbledore. Harry recognized him at once/nfrom the card he'd gotten out of the Chocolate Frog on/nthe train. Dumbledore's silver hair was the only thing/nin the whole hall that shone as brightly as the ghosts./nHarry spotted Professor Quirrell, too, the nervous/nyoung man from the Leaky Cauldron. He was looking/nvery peculiar in a large purple turban./n/nAnd now there were only four people left to be sorted./n"Thomas, Dean," a Black boy even taller than Ron,/njoined Harry at the Gryffindor table. "Turpin, Lisa,"/nbecame a Ravenclaw and then it was Ron's turn. He/nwas pale green by now. Harry crossed his fingers/nunder the table and a second later the hat had/nshouted, "GRYFFINDOR!"/n/nHarry clapped loudly with the rest as Ron collapsed/ninto the chair next to him./n/n"Well done, Ron, excellent," said Percy Weasley/npompously across Harry as "Zabini, Blaise," was/nmade a Slytherin. Professor McGonagall rolled up her/nscroll and took the Sorting Hat away./n/nHarry looked down at his empty gold plate. He had/nonly just realized how hungry he was. The pumpkin/npasties seemed ages ago./n/n/n/n/n/nAlbus Dumbledore had gotten to his feet. He was/nbeaming at the students, his arms opened wide, as if/nnothing could have pleased him more than to see/nthem all there./n/n"Welcome!" he said. "Welcome to a new year at/nHogwarts! Before we begin our banquet, I would like/nto say a few words. And here they are: Nitwit!/n/nBlubber! Oddment! Tweak!/n/n"Thank you!"/n/nHe sat back down. Everybody clapped and cheered./nHarry didn't know whether to laugh or not./n/n"Is he — a bit mad?" he asked Percy uncertainly./n/n"Mad?" said Percy airily. "He's a genius! Best wizard/nin the world! But he is a bit mad, yes. Potatoes,/nHarry?"/n/nHarry's mouth fell open. The dishes in front of him/nwere now piled with food. He had never seen so many/nthings he liked to eat on one table: roast beef, roast/nchicken, pork chops and lamb chops, sausages,/nbacon and steak, boiled potatoes, roast potatoes,/nfries, Yorkshire pudding, peas, carrots, gravy,/nketchup, and, for some strange reason, peppermint/nhumbugs./n/nThe Dursleys had never exactly starved Harry, but/nhe'd never been allowed to eat as much as he liked./nDudley had always taken anything that Harry really/nwanted, even if it made him sick. Harry piled his plate/nwith a bit of everything except the peppermints and/nbegan to eat. It was all delicious./n/n"That does look good," said the ghost in the ruff sadly,/nwatching Harry cut up his steak./n/n/n/n/n/n"Can't you — ?"/n/n/n/n"I haven't eaten for nearly five hundred years," said/nthe ghost. "I don't need to, of course, but one does/nmiss it. I don't think I've introduced myself? Sir/nNicholas de Mimsy-Porpington at your service./nResident ghost of Gryffindor Tower."/n/n"I know who you are!" said Ron suddenly. "My/nbrothers told me about you — you're Nearly Headless/nNick!"/n/n"I would prefer you to call me Sir Nicholas de Mimsy/n— " the ghost began stiffly, but sandy-haired Seamus/nFinnigan interrupted./n/n"Nearly Headless? How can you be nearly headless?"/n/nSir Nicholas looked extremely miffed, as if their little/nchat wasn't going at all the way he wanted./n/n"Like this," he said irritably. He seized his left ear and/npulled. His whole head swung off his neck and fell/nonto his shoulder as if it was on a hinge. Someone/nhad obviously tried to behead him, but not done it/nproperly. Looking pleased at the stunned looks on/ntheir faces, Nearly Headless Nick flipped his head/nback onto his neck, coughed, and said, "So — new/nGryffindors! I hope you're going to help us win the/nHouse Championship this year? Gryffindors have/nnever gone so long without winning. Slytherins have/ngot the cup six years in a row! The Bloody Baron's/nbecoming almost unbearable — he's the Slytherin/nghost."/n/nHarry looked over at the Slytherin table and saw a/nhorrible ghost sitting there, with blank staring eyes, a/ngaunt face, and robes stained with silver blood. He/nwas right next to Malfoy who, Harry was pleased to/n/n/n/n/n/nsee, didn't look too pleased with the seating/narrangements./n/n"How did he get covered in blood?" asked Seamus/nwith great interest./n/n"I've never asked," said Nearly Headless Nick/ndelicately./n/nWhen everyone had eaten as much as they could, the/nremains of the food faded from the plates, leaving/nthem sparkling clean as before. A moment later the/ndesserts appeared. Blocks of ice cream in every flavor/nyou could think of, apple pies, treacle tarts, chocolate/neclairs and jam doughnuts, trifle, strawberries, Jell-/n0, rice pudding .../n/nAs Harry helped himself to a treacle tart, the talk/nturned to their families./n/n"I'm half-and-half," said Seamus. "Me dad's a Muggle./nMom didn't tell him she was a witch 'til after they/nwere married. Bit of a nasty shock for him."/n/nThe others laughed./n/n"What about you, Neville?" said Ron./n/n"Well, my gran brought me up and she's a witch,"/nsaid Neville, "but the family thought I was all- Muggle/nfor ages. My Great Uncle Algie kept trying to catch me/noff my guard and force some magic out of me — he/npushed me off the end of Blackpool pier once, I nearly/ndrowned — but nothing happened until I was eight./nGreat Uncle Algie came round for dinner, and he was/nhanging me out of an upstairs window by the ankles/nwhen my Great Auntie Enid offered him a meringue/nand he accidentally let go. But I bounced — all the/nway down the garden and into the road. They were all/n/n/n/n/nreally pleased, Gran was crying, she was so happy./nAnd you should have seen their faces when I got in/nhere — they thought I might not be magic enough to/ncome, you see. Great Uncle Algie was so pleased he/nbought me my toad."/n/nOn Harry's other side, Percy Weasley and Hermione/nwere talking about lessons ("I do hope they start right/naway, there's so much to learn, I'm particularly/ninterested in Transfiguration, you know, turning/nsomething into something else, of course, it's/nsupposed to be very difficult — "You'll be starting/nsmall, just matches into needles and that sort of/nthing — ")./n/n/n/nHarry, who was starting to feel warm and sleepy,/nlooked up at the High Table again. Hagrid was/ndrinking deeply from his goblet. Professor McGonagall/nwas talking to Professor Dumbledore. Professor/nQuirrell, in his absurd turban, was talking to a/nteacher with greasy black hair, a hooked nose, and/nsallow skin./n/nIt happened very suddenly. The hook-nosed teacher/nlooked past Quirrell's turban straight into Harry's/neyes — and a sharp, hot pain shot across the scar on/nHarry's forehead./n/n"Ouch!" Harry clapped a hand to his head./n/n"What is it?" asked Percy./n/n"N-nothing."/n/nThe pain had gone as quickly as it had come. Harder/nto shake off was the feeling Harry had gotten from the/nteacher's look — a feeling that he didn't like Harry at/nall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Who's that teacher talking to Professor Quirrell?" he/nasked Percy./n/n"Oh, you know Quirrell already, do you? No wonder/nhe's looking so nervous, that's Professor Snape. He/nteaches Potions, but he doesn't want to — everyone/nknows he's after Quirrell's job. Knows an awful lot/nabout the Dark Arts, Snape."/n/nHarry watched Snape for a while, but Snape didn't/nlook at him again./n/nAt last, the desserts too disappeared, and Professor/nDumbledore got to his feet again. The hall fell silent./n/n"Ahem — just a few more words now that we are all/nfed and watered. I have a few start-of-term notices to/ngive you./n/n"First years should note that the forest on the/ngrounds is forbidden to all pupils. And a few of our/nolder students would do well to remember that as/nwell."/n/nDumbledore 's twinkling eyes flashed in the direction/nof the Weasley twins./n/n"I have also been asked by Mr. Filch, the caretaker, to/nremind you all that no magic should be used between/nclasses in the corridors./n/n"Quidditch trials will be held in the second week of/nthe term. Anyone interested in playing for their House/nteams should contact Madam Hooch./n/n"And finally, I must tell you that this year, the third-/nfloor corridor on the right-hand side is out of bounds/nto everyone who does not wish to die a very painful/ndeath."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry laughed, but he was one of the few who did./n/n/n/n"He's not serious?" he muttered to Percy./n/n"Must be," said Percy, frowning at Dumbledore. "It's/nodd, because he usually gives us a reason why we're/nnot allowed to go somewhere — the forest's full of/ndangerous beasts, everyone knows that. I do think he/nmight have told us prefects, at least."/n/n"And now, before we go to bed, let us sing the school/nsong!" cried Dumbledore. Harry noticed that the other/nteachers' smiles had become rather fixed./n/nDumbledore gave his wand a little flick, as if he was/ntrying to get a fly off the end, and a long golden/nribbon flew out of it, which rose high above the tables/nand twisted itself, snakelike, into words./n/n"Everyone pick their favorite tune," said Dumbledore,/n"and off we go!"/n/nAnd the school bellowed:/n/n"Hogwarts, Hogwarts, Hoggy Warty Hogwarts,/n/nTeach us something please,/n/nWhether we be old and bald/nOr young with scabby knees,/n/nOur heads could do with filling/nWith some interesting stuff,/n/nFor now they're bare and full of air,/n/nDead flies and bits of fluff,/n/n/n/n/n/nSo teach us things worth knowing,/n/nBring back what we've forgot,/n/nJust do your best, we'll do the rest,/n/nAnd learn until our brains all rot."/n/nEverybody finished the song at different times. At last,/nonly the Weasley twins were left singing along to a/nvery slow funeral march. Dumbledore conducted their/nlast few lines with his wand and when they had/nfinished, he was one of those who clapped loudest./n/n"Ah, music," he said, wiping his eyes. "A magic/nbeyond all we do here! And now, bedtime. Off you/ntrot!"/n/nThe Gryffindor first years followed Percy through the/nchattering crowds, out of the Great Hall, and up the/nmarble staircase. Harry's legs were like lead again,/nbut only because he was so tired and full of food. He/nwas too sleepy even to be surprised that the people in/nthe portraits along the corridors whispered and/npointed as they passed, or that twice Percy led them/nthrough doorways hidden behind sliding panels and/nhanging tapestries. They climbed more staircases,/nyawning and dragging their feet, and Harry was just/nwondering how much farther they had to go when/nthey came to a sudden halt./n/nA bundle of walking sticks was floating in midair/nahead of them, and as Percy took a step toward them/nthey started throwing themselves at him./n/n"Peeves," Percy whispered to the first years. "A/npoltergeist." He raised his voice, "Peeves — show/nyourself."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA loud, rude sound, like the air being let out of a/nballoon, answered./n/n"Do you want me to go to the Bloody Baron?"/n/nThere was a pop, and a little man with wicked, dark/neyes and a wide mouth appeared, floating cross-/nlegged in the air, clutching the walking sticks./n/n"Oooooooh!" he said, with an evil cackle. "Ickle/nFirsties! What fun!"/n/nHe swooped suddenly at them. They all ducked./n/n"Go away, Peeves, or the Baron'll hear about this, I/nmean it!" barked Percy./n/nPeeves stuck out his tongue and vanished, dropping/nthe walking sticks on Neville's head. They heard him/nzooming away, rattling coats of armor as he passed./n/n"You want to watch out for Peeves," said Percy, as/nthey set off again. "The Bloody Baron's the only one/nwho can control him, he won't even listen to us/nprefects. Here we are."/n/nAt the very end of the corridor hung a portrait of a/nvery fat woman in a pink silk dress./n/n"Password?" she said./n/n"Caput Draconis," said Percy, and the portrait swung/nforward to reveal a round hole in the wall. They all/nscrambled through it — Neville needed a leg up —/nand found themselves in the Gryffindor common/nroom, a cozy, round room full of squashy armchairs./n/nPercy directed the girls through one door to their/ndormitory and the boys through another. At the top of/n/n/n/n/n/na spiral staircase — they were obviously in one of the/ntowers — they found their beds at last: five four-/nposters hung with deep red, velvet curtains. Their/ntrunks had already been brought up. Too tired to talk/nmuch, they pulled on their pajamas and fell into bed./n/n"Great food, isn't it?" Ron muttered to Harry through/nthe hangings. "Get off Scabbers! He's chewing my/nsheets."/n/nHarry was going to ask Ron if he'd had any of the/ntreacle tart, but he fell asleep almost at once./n/nPerhaps Harry had eaten a bit too much, because he/nhad a very strange dream. He was wearing Professor/nQuirrell's turban, which kept talking to him, telling/nhim he must transfer to Slytherin at once, because it/nwas his destiny. Harry told the turban he didn't want/nto be in Slytherin; it got heavier and heavier; he tried/nto pull it off but it tightened painfully — and there/nwas Malfoy, laughing at him as he struggled with it —/nthen Malfoy turned into the hook-nosed teacher,/nSnape, whose laugh became high and cold — there/nwas a burst of green light and Harry woke, sweating/nand shaking./n/nHe rolled over and fell asleep again, and when he/nwoke next day, he didn't remember the dream at all./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Potions Master
text: /n"There, look."/n/n"Where?"/n/n"Next to the tall kid with the red hair."/n/n"Wearing the glasses?"/n/n"Did you see his face?"/n/n"Did you see his scar?"/n/nWhispers followed Harry from the moment he left his/ndormitory the next day. People lining up outside/nclassrooms stood on tiptoe to get a look at him, or/ndoubled back to pass him in the corridors again,/nstaring. Harry wished they wouldn't, because he was/ntrying to concentrate on finding his way to classes./n/nThere were a hundred and forty-two staircases at/nHogwarts: wide, sweeping ones; narrow, rickety ones;/nsome that led somewhere different on a Friday; some/n/n/n/n/nwith a vanishing step halfway up that you had to/nremember to jump. Then there were doors that/nwouldn't open unless you asked politely, or tickled/nthem in exactly the right place, and doors that weren't/nreally doors at all, but solid walls just pretending. It/nwas also very hard to remember where anything was,/nbecause it all seemed to move around a lot. The/npeople in the portraits kept going to visit each other,/nand Harry was sure the coats of armor could walk./n/nThe ghosts didn't help, either. It was always a nasty/nshock when one of them glided suddenly through a/ndoor you were trying to open. Nearly Headless Nick/nwas always happy to point new Gryffindors in the/nright direction, but Peeves the Poltergeist was worth/ntwo locked doors and a trick staircase if you met him/nwhen you were late for class. He would drop/nwastepaper baskets on your head, pull rugs from/nunder your feet, pelt you with bits of chalk, or sneak/nup behind you, invisible, grab your nose, and screech,/n"GOT YOUR CONK!"/n/nEven worse than Peeves, if that was possible, was the/ncaretaker, Argus Filch. Harry and Ron managed to get/non the wrong side of him on their very first morning./nFilch found them trying to force their way through a/ndoor that unluckily turned out to be the entrance to/nthe out-of-bounds corridor on the third floor. He/nwouldn't believe they were lost, was sure they were/ntrying to break into it on purpose, and was/nthreatening to lock them in the dungeons when they/nwere rescued by Professor Quirrell, who was passing./n/nFilch owned a cat called Mrs. Norris, a scrawny, dust-/ncolored creature with bulging, lamplike eyes just like/nFilch's. She patrolled the corridors alone. Break a rule/nin front of her, put just one toe out of line, and she'd/nwhisk off for Filch, who'd appear, wheezing, two/nseconds later. Filch knew the secret passageways of/n/n/n/n/nthe school better than anyone (except perhaps the/nWeasley twins) and could pop up as suddenly as any/nof the ghosts. The students all hated him, and it was/nthe dearest ambition of many to give Mrs. Norris a/ngood kick./n/nAnd then, once you had managed to find them, there/nwere the classes themselves. There was a lot more to/nmagic, as Harry quickly found out, than waving your/nwand and saying a few funny words./n/nThey had to study the night skies through their/ntelescopes every Wednesday at midnight and learn/nthe names of different stars and the movements of the/nplanets. Three times a week they went out to the/ngreenhouses behind the castle to study Herbology,/nwith a dumpy little witch called Professor Sprout,/nwhere they learned how to take care of all the strange/nplants and fungi, and found out what they were used/nfor./n/nEasily the most boring class was History of Magic,/nwhich was the only one taught by a ghost. Professor/nBinns had been very old indeed when he had fallen/nasleep in front of the staff room fire and got up next/nmorning to teach, leaving his body behind him. Binns/ndroned on and on while they scribbled down names/nand dates, and got Emeric the Evil and Uric the/nOddball mixed up./n/nProfessor Flitwick, the Charms teacher, was a tiny/nlittle wizard who had to stand on a pile of books to/nsee over his desk. At the start of their first class he/ntook the roll call, and when he reached Harry's name/nhe gave an excited squeak and toppled out of sight./n/nProfessor McGonagall was again different. Harry had/nbeen quite right to think she wasn't a teacher to/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncross. Strict and clever, she gave them a talking- to/nthe moment they sat down in her first class./n/n"Transfiguration is some of the most complex and/ndangerous magic you will learn at Hogwarts," she/nsaid. "Anyone messing around in my class will leave/nand not come back. You have been warned."/n/nThen she changed her desk into a pig and back again./nThey were all very impressed and couldn't wait to get/nstarted, but soon realized they weren't going to be/nchanging the furniture into animals for a long time./nAfter taking a lot of complicated notes, they were each/ngiven a match and started trying to turn it into a/nneedle. By the end of the lesson, only Hermione/nGranger had made any difference to her match;/nProfessor McGonagall showed the class how it had/ngone all silver and pointy and gave Hermione a rare/nsmile./n/nThe class everyone had really been looking forward to/nwas Defense Against the Dark Arts, but Quirrell's/nlessons turned out to be a bit of a joke. His classroom/nsmelled strongly of garlic, which everyone said was to/nward off a vampire he'd met in Romania and was/nafraid would be coming back to get him one of these/ndays. His turban, he told them, had been given to him/nby an African prince as a thank-you for getting rid of/na troublesome zombie, but they weren't sure they/nbelieved this story. For one thing, when Seamus/nFinnigan asked eagerly to hear how Quirrell had/nfought off the zombie, Quirrell went pink and started/ntalking about the weather; for another, they had/nnoticed that a funny smell hung around the turban,/nand the Weasley twins insisted that it was stuffed full/nof garlic as well, so that Quirrell was protected/nwherever he went./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry was very relieved to find out that he wasn't/nmiles behind everyone else. Lots of people had come/nfrom Muggle families and, like him, hadn't had any/nidea that they were witches and wizards. There was so/nmuch to learn that even people like Ron didn't have/nmuch of a head start./n/nFriday was an important day for Harry and Ron. They/nfinally managed to find their way down to the Great/nHall for breakfast without getting lost once./n/n"What have we got today?" Harry asked Ron as he/npoured sugar on his porridge./n/n"Double Potions with the Slytherins," said Ron./n"Snape's Head of Slytherin House. They say he always/nfavors them — we'll be able to see if it's true."/n/n"Wish McGonagall favored us," said Harry. Professor/nMcGonagall was head of Gryffindor House, but it/nhadn't stopped her from giving them a huge pile of/nhomework the day before./n/nJust then, the mail arrived. Harry had gotten used to/nthis by now, but it had given him a bit of a shock on/nthe first morning, when about a hundred owls had/nsuddenly streamed into the Great Hall during/nbreakfast, circling the tables until they saw their/nowners, and dropping letters and packages onto their/nlaps./n/nHedwig hadn't brought Harry anything so far. She/nsometimes flew in to nibble his ear and have a bit of/ntoast before going off to sleep in the owlery with the/nother school owls. This morning, however, she/nfluttered down between the marmalade and the sugar/nbowl and dropped a note onto Harry's plate. Harry/ntore it open at once. It said, in a very untidy scrawl:/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDear Harry,/n/n/n/nI know you get Friday afternoons off so would you like/nto come and have a cup of tea with me around three?/n/nI want to hear all about your first week. Send us an/nanswer back with Hedwig./n/nHagrid/n/nHarry borrowed Ron's quill, scribbled Yes, please, see/nyou later on the back of the note, and sent Hedwig off/nagain./n/nIt was lucky that Harry had tea with Hagrid to look/nforward to, because the Potions lesson turned out to/nbe the worst thing that had happened to him so far./n/nAt the start-of-term banquet, Harry had gotten the/nidea that Professor Snape disliked him. By the end of/nthe first Potions lesson, he knew he'd been wrong./nSnape didn't dislike Harry — he hated him./n/nPotions lessons took place down in one of the/ndungeons. It was colder here than up in the main/ncastle, and would have been quite creepy enough/nwithout the pickled animals floating in glass jars all/naround the walls./n/nSnape, like Flitwick, started the class by taking the/nroll call, and like Flitwick, he paused at Harry's name./n/n"Ah, yes," he said softly, "Harry Potter. Our new —/ncelebrity."/n/nDraco Malfoy and his friends Crabbe and Goyle/nsniggered behind their hands. Snape finished calling/nthe names and looked up at the class. His eyes were/nblack like Hagrid 's, but they had none of Hagrid 's/n/n/n/n/n/nwarmth. They were cold and empty and made you/nthink of dark tunnels./n/n"You are here to learn the subtle science and exact art/nof potion-making," he began. He spoke in barely more/nthan a whisper, but they caught every word — like/nProfessor McGonagall, Snape had the gift of keeping a/nclass silent without effort. "As there is little foolish/nwand- waving here, many of you will hardly believe/nthis is magic. I don't expect you will really understand/nthe beauty of the softly simmering cauldron with its/nshimmering fumes, the delicate power of liquids that/ncreep through human veins, bewitching the mind,/nensnaring the senses. ... I can teach you how to bottle/nfame, brew glory, even stopper death — if you aren't/nas big a bunch of dunderheads as I usually have to/nteach."/n/nMore silence followed this little speech. Harry and/nRon exchanged looks with raised eyebrows. Hermione/nGranger was on the edge of her seat and looked/ndesperate to start proving that she wasn't a/ndunderhead./n/n"Potter!" said Snape suddenly. "What would I get if I/nadded powdered root of asphodel to an infusion of/nwormwood?"/n/nPowdered root of what to an infusion of what? Harry/nglanced at Ron, who looked as stumped as he was;/nHermione 's hand had shot into the air./n/n"I don't know, sir," said Harry./n/nSnape 's lips curled into a sneer./n/n"Tut, tut — fame clearly isn't everything."/n/nHe ignored Hermione 's hand./n/n/n/n/n/n"Let's try again. Potter, where would you look if I told/nyou to find me a bezoar?"/n/nHermione stretched her hand as high into the air as it/nwould go without her leaving her seat, but Harry/ndidn't have the faintest idea what a bezoar was. He/ntried not to look at Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle, who/nwere shaking with laughter./n/n"I don't know, sir."/n/n"Thought you wouldn't open a book before coming,/neh, Potter?"/n/nHarry forced himself to keep looking straight into/nthose cold eyes. He had looked through his books at/nthe Dursleys', but did Snape expect him to remember/neverything in One Thousand Magical Herbs and/nFungi ?/n/nSnape was still ignoring Hermione's quivering hand./n/n"What is the difference, Potter, between monkshood/nand wolfsbane?"/n/nAt this, Hermione stood up, her hand stretching/ntoward the dungeon ceiling./n/n"I don't know," said Harry quietly. "I think Hermione/ndoes, though, why don't you try her?"/n/nA few people laughed; Harry caught Seamus's eye,/nand Seamus winked. Snape, however, was not/npleased./n/n"Sit down," he snapped at Hermione. "For your/ninformation, Potter, asphodel and wormwood make a/nsleeping potion so powerful it is known as the/nDraught of Living Death. A bezoar is a stone taken/n/n/n/n/n/nfrom the stomach of a goat and it will save you from/nmost poisons. As for monkshood and wolfsbane, they/nare the same plant, which also goes by the name of/naconite. Well? Why aren't you all copying that down?"/n/nThere was a sudden rummaging for quills and/nparchment. Over the noise, Snape said, "And a point/nwill be taken from Gryffindor House for your cheek,/nPotter."/n/nThings didn't improve for the Gryffindors as the/nPotions lesson continued. Snape put them all into/npairs and set them to mixing up a simple potion to/ncure boils. He swept around in his long black cloak,/nwatching them weigh dried nettles and crush snake/nfangs, criticizing almost everyone except Malfoy,/nwhom he seemed to like. He was just telling everyone/nto look at the perfect way Malfoy had stewed his/nhorned slugs when clouds of acid green smoke and a/nloud hissing filled the dungeon. Neville had somehow/nmanaged to melt Seamus's cauldron into a twisted/nblob, and their potion was seeping across the stone/nfloor, burning holes in people's shoes. Within/nseconds, the whole class was standing on their stools/nwhile Neville, who had been drenched in the potion/nwhen the cauldron collapsed, moaned in pain as/nangry red boils sprang up all over his arms and legs./n/n"Idiot boy!" snarled Snape, clearing the spilled potion/naway with one wave of his wand. "I suppose you/nadded the porcupine quills before taking the cauldron/noff the fire?"/n/nNeville whimpered as boils started to pop up all over/nhis nose./n/n"Take him up to the hospital wing," Snape spat at/nSeamus. Then he rounded on Harry and Ron, who/nhad been working next to Neville./n/n/n/n/n/n"You — Potter — why didn't you tell him not to add/nthe quills? Thought he'd make you look good if he got/nit wrong, did you? That's another point you've lost for/nGryffindor."/n/nThis was so unfair that Harry opened his mouth to/nargue, but Ron kicked him behind their cauldron./n/n"Don't push it," he muttered, "I've heard Snape can/nturn very nasty."/n/nAs they climbed the steps out of the dungeon an hour/nlater, Harry's mind was racing and his spirits were/nlow. He'd lost two points for Gryffindor in his very/nfirst week — why did Snape hate him so much?/n/n"Cheer up," said Ron, "Snape's always taking points/noff Fred and George. Can I come and meet Hagrid/nwith you?"/n/nAt five to three they left the castle and made their way/nacross the grounds. Hagrid lived in a small wooden/nhouse on the edge of the forbidden forest. A crossbow/nand a pair of galoshes were outside the front door./n/nWhen Harry knocked they heard a frantic scrabbling/nfrom inside and several booming barks. Then Hagrid 's/nvoice rang out, saying, "Back, Fang — back."/n/nHagrid 's big, hairy face appeared in the crack as he/npulled the door open./n/n"Hang on," he said. "Back, Fang."/n/nHe let them in, struggling to keep a hold on the collar/nof an enormous black boarhound./n/nThere was only one room inside. Hams and pheasants/nwere hanging from the ceiling, a copper kettle was/n/n/n/n/n/nboiling on the open fire, and in the corner stood a/nmassive bed with a patchwork quilt over it./n/n"Make yerselves at home," said Hagrid, letting go of/nFang, who bounded straight at Ron and started/nlicking his ears. Like Hagrid, Fang was clearly not as/nfierce as he looked./n/n"This is Ron," Harry told Hagrid, who was pouring/nboiling water into a large teapot and putting rock/ncakes onto a plate./n/n"Another Weasley, eh?" said Hagrid, glancing at Ron's/nfreckles. "I spent half me life chasin' yer twin brothers/naway from the forest."/n/nThe rock cakes were shapeless lumps with raisins/nthat almost broke their teeth, but Harry and Ron/npretended to be enjoying them as they told Hagrid all/nabout their first lessons. Fang rested his head on/nHarry's knee and drooled all over his robes./n/nHarry and Ron were delighted to hear Hagrid call/nFilch "that old git."/n/n"An' as fer that cat, Mrs. Norris, I'd like ter introduce/nher to Fang sometime. D'yeh know, every time I go up/nter the school, she follows me everywhere? Can't get/nrid of her — Filch puts her up to it."/n/nHarry told Hagrid about Snape's lesson. Hagrid, like/nRon, told Harry not to worry about it, that Snape/nliked hardly any of the students./n/n"But he seemed to really hate me."/n/n"Rubbish!" said Hagrid. "Why should he?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nYet Harry couldn't help thinking that Hagrid didn't/nquite meet his eyes when he said that./n/n"How's yer brother Charlie?" Hagrid asked Ron. "I/nliked him a lot — great with animals."/n/nHarry wondered if Hagrid had changed the subject on/npurpose. While Ron told Hagrid all about Charlie's/nwork with dragons, Harry picked up a piece of paper/nthat was lying on the table under the tea cozy. It was/na cutting from the Daily Prophet :/n/nGRINGOTTS BREAK-IN LATEST/n/nInvestigations continue into the break-in at Gringotts/non 3 1 July, widely believed to be the work of Dark/nwizards or witches unknown./n/nGringotts goblins today insisted that nothing had/nbeen taken. The vault that was searched had in fact/nbeen emptied the same day./n/n"But we're not telling you what was in there, so keep/nyour noses out if you know what's good for you," said/na Gringotts spokesgoblin this afternoon./n/nHarry remembered Ron telling him on the train that/nsomeone had tried to rob Gringotts, but Ron hadn't/nmentioned the date./n/n"Hagrid!" said Harry, "that Gringotts break-in/nhappened on my birthday! It might've been happening/nwhile we were there!"/n/nThere was no doubt about it, Hagrid definitely didn't/nmeet Harry's eyes this time. He grunted and offered/nhim another rock cake. Harry read the story again./n/nThe vault that was searched had in fact been emptied/nearlier that same day. Hagrid had emptied vault seven/n/n/n/n/nhundred and thirteen, if you could call it emptying,/ntaking out that grubby little package. Had that been/nwhat the thieves were looking for?/n/nAs Harry and Ron walked back to the castle for/ndinner, their pockets weighed down with rock cakes/nthey'd been too polite to refuse, Harry thought that/nnone of the lessons he'd had so far had given him as/nmuch to think about as tea with Hagrid. Had Hagrid/ncollected that package just in time? Where was it/nnow? And did Hagrid know something about Snape/nthat he didn't want to tell Harry?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n9/n/n/n/n

title: The Midnight Duel
text: /nHarry had never believed he would meet a boy he/nhated more than Dudley, but that was before he met/nDraco Malfoy. Still, first-year Gryffindors only had/nPotions with the Slytherins, so they didn't have to put/nup with Malfoy much. Or at least, they didn't until/nthey spotted a notice pinned up in the Gryffindor/ncommon room that made them all groan. Flying/nlessons would be starting on Thursday — and/nGryffindor and Slytherin would be learning together./n/n"Typical," said Harry darkly. "Just what I always/nwanted. To make a fool of myself on a broomstick in/nfront of Malfoy."/n/nHe had been looking forward to learning to fly more/nthan anything else./n/n"You don't know that you'll make a fool of yourself,"/nsaid Ron reasonably. "Anyway, I know Malfoy's always/ngoing on about how good he is at Quidditch, but I bet/nthat's all talk."/n/n/n/n/nMalfoy certainly did talk about flying a lot. He/ncomplained loudly about first years never getting on/nthe House Quidditch teams and told long, boastful/nstories that always seemed to end with him narrowly/nescaping Muggles in helicopters. He wasn't the only/none, though: the way Seamus Finnigan told it, he'd/nspent most of his childhood zooming around the/ncountryside on his broomstick. Even Ron would tell/nanyone who'd listen about the time he'd almost hit a/nhang glider on Charlie's old broom. Everyone from/nwizarding families talked about Quidditch constantly./nRon had already had a big argument with Dean/nThomas, who shared their dormitory, about soccer./nRon couldn't see what was exciting about a game with/nonly one ball where no one was allowed to fly. Harry/nhad caught Ron prodding Dean's poster of West Ham/nsoccer team, trying to make the players move./n/nNeville had never been on a broomstick in his life,/nbecause his grandmother had never let him near one./nPrivately, Harry felt she'd had good reason, because/nNeville managed to have an extraordinary number of/naccidents even with both feet on the ground./n/nHermione Granger was almost as nervous about/nflying as Neville was. This was something you couldn't/nlearn by heart out of a book — not that she hadn't/ntried. At breakfast on Thursday she bored them all/nstupid with flying tips she'd gotten out of a library/nbook called Quidditch Through the Ages. Neville was/nhanging on to her every word, desperate for anything/nthat might help him hang on to his broomstick later,/nbut everybody else was very pleased when Hermione 's/nlecture was interrupted by the arrival of the mail./n/nHarry hadn't had a single letter since Hagrid's note,/nsomething that Malfoy had been quick to notice, of/ncourse. Malfoy 's eagle owl was always bringing him/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/npackages of sweets from home, which he opened/ngloatingly at the Slytherin table./n/nA barn owl brought Neville a small package from his/ngrandmother. He opened it excitedly and showed/nthem a glass ball the size of a large marble, which/nseemed to be full of white smoke./n/n"It's a Remembrall!" he explained. "Gran knows I/nforget things — this tells you if there's something/nyou've forgotten to do. Look, you hold it tight like this/nand if it turns red — oh ..." His face fell, because the/nRemembrall had suddenly glowed scarlet, "... you've/nforgotten something ..."/n/nNeville was trying to remember what he'd forgotten/nwhen Draco Malfoy, who was passing the Gryffindor/ntable, snatched the Remembrall out of his hand./n/nHarry and Ron jumped to their feet. They were half/nhoping for a reason to fight Malfoy, but Professor/nMcGonagall, who could spot trouble quicker than any/nteacher in the school, was there in a flash./n/n"What's going on?"/n/n"Malfoy's got my Remembrall, Professor."/n/nScowling, Malfoy quickly dropped the Remembrall/nback on the table./n/n"Just looking," he said, and he sloped away with/nCrabbe and Goyle behind him./n/nAt three-thirty that afternoon, Harry, Ron, and the/nother Gryffindors hurried down the front steps onto/nthe grounds for their first flying lesson. It was a clear,/nbreezy day, and the grass rippled under their feet as/nthey marched down the sloping lawns toward a/n/n/n/n/nsmooth, flat lawn on the opposite side of the grounds/nto the forbidden forest, whose trees were swaying/ndarkly in the distance./n/nThe Slytherins were already there, and so were twenty/nbroomsticks lying in neat lines on the ground. Harry/nhad heard Fred and George Weasley complain about/nthe school brooms, saying that some of them started/nto vibrate if you flew too high, or always flew slightly/nto the left./n/nTheir teacher, Madam Hooch, arrived. She had short,/ngray hair, and yellow eyes like a hawk./n/n"Well, what are you all waiting for?" she barked./n"Everyone stand by a broomstick. Come on, hurry/nup." "/n/nHarry glanced down at his broom. It was old and/nsome of the twigs stuck out at odd angles./n/n"Stick out your right hand over your broom," called/nMadam Hooch at the front, "and say 'Up!' "/n/n"UP!" everyone shouted./n/nHarry's broom jumped into his hand at once, but it/nwas one of the few that did. Hermione Granger's had/nsimply rolled over on the ground, and Neville's hadn't/nmoved at all. Perhaps brooms, like horses, could tell/nwhen you were afraid, thought Harry; there was a/nquaver in Neville's voice that said only too clearly that/nhe wanted to keep his feet on the ground./n/nMadam Hooch then showed them how to mount their/nbrooms without sliding off the end, and walked up/nand down the rows correcting their grips. Harry and/nRon were delighted when she told Malfoy he'd been/ndoing it wrong for years./n/n/n/n/n/n"Now, when I blow my whistle, you kick off from the/nground, hard," said Madam Hooch. "Keep your/nbrooms steady, rise a few feet, and then come straight/nback down by leaning forward slightly. On my whistle/n— three — two — "/n/nBut Neville, nervous and jumpy and frightened of/nbeing left on the ground, pushed off hard before the/nwhistle had touched Madam Hooch's lips./n/n"Come back, boy!" she shouted, but Neville was rising/nstraight up like a cork shot out of a bottle — twelve/nfeet — twenty feet. Harry saw his scared white face/nlook down at the ground falling away, saw him gasp,/nslip sideways off the broom and —/n/nWHAM — a thud and a nasty crack and Neville lay/nfacedown on the grass in a heap. His broomstick was/nstill rising higher and higher, and started to drift/nlazily toward the forbidden forest and out of sight./n/nMadam Hooch was bending over Neville, her face as/nwhite as his./n/n"Broken wrist," Harry heard her mutter. "Come on,/nboy — it's all right, up you get."/n/nShe turned to the rest of the class./n/n"None of you is to move while I take this boy to the/nhospital wing! You leave those brooms where they are/nor you'll be out of Hogwarts before you can say/n'Quidditch.' Come on, dear."/n/nNeville, his face tear-streaked, clutching his wrist,/nhobbled off with Madam Hooch, who had her arm/naround him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNo sooner were they out of earshot than Malfoy burst/ninto laughter./n/n"Did you see his face, the great lump?"/n/nThe other Slytherins joined in./n/n"Shut up, Malfoy," snapped Parvati Patil./n/n"Ooh, sticking up for Longbottom?" said Pansy/nParkinson, a hard-faced Slytherin girl. "Never thought/nyou'd like fat little crybabies, Parvati."/n/n"Look!" said Malfoy, darting forward and snatching/nsomething out of the grass. "It's that stupid thing/nLongbottom's gran sent him."/n/nThe Remembrall glittered in the sun as he held it up./n/n"Give that here, Malfoy," said Harry quietly. Everyone/nstopped talking to watch./n/nMalfoy smiled nastily./n/n"I think I'll leave it somewhere for Longbottom to find/n— how about — up a tree?"/n/n"Give it here!" Harry yelled, but Malfoy had leapt onto/nhis broomstick and taken off. He hadn't been lying, he/ncould fly well. Hovering level with the topmost/nbranches of an oak he called, "Come and get it,/nPotter!"/n/nHarry grabbed his broom./n/n"iVo!" shouted Hermione Granger. "Madam Hooch told/nus not to move — you'll get us all into trouble."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry ignored her. Blood was pounding in his ears./n/nHe mounted the broom and kicked hard against the/nground and up, up he soared; air rushed through his/nhair, and his robes whipped out behind him — and in/na rush of fierce joy he realized he'd found something/nhe could do without being taught — this was easy,/nthis was wonderful. He pulled his broomstick up a/nlittle to take it even higher, and heard screams and/ngasps of girls back on the ground and an admiring/nwhoop from Ron./n/nHe turned his broomstick sharply to face Malfoy in/nmidair. Malfoy looked stunned./n/n"Give it here," Harry called, "or I'll knock you off that/nbroom!"/n/n"Oh, yeah?" said Malfoy, trying to sneer, but looking/nworried./n/nHarry knew, somehow, what to do. He leaned forward/nand grasped the broom tightly in both hands, and it/nshot toward Malfoy like a javelin. Malfoy only just got/nout of the way in time; Harry made a sharp about-/nface and held the broom steady. A few people below/nwere clapping./n/n"No Crabbe and Goyle up here to save your neck,/nMalfoy," Harry called./n/nThe same thought seemed to have struck Malfoy./n/n"Catch it if you can, then!" he shouted, and he threw/nthe glass ball high into the air and streaked back/ntoward the ground./n/nHarry saw, as though in slow motion, the ball rise up/nin the air and then start to fall. He leaned forward/nand pointed his broom handle down — next second/n/n/n/n/n/nhe was gathering speed in a steep dive, racing the ball/n— wind whistled in his ears, mingled with the/nscreams of people watching — he stretched out his/nhand — a foot from the ground he caught it, just in/ntime to pull his broom straight, and he toppled gently/nonto the grass with the Remembrall clutched safely in/nhis fist./n/n"HARRY POTTER!"/n/nHis heart sank faster than he'd just dived. Professor/nMcGonagall was running toward them. He got to his/nfeet, trembling./n/n"Never — in all my time at Hogwarts — "/n/nProfessor McGonagall was almost speechless with/nshock, and her glasses flashed furiously, " — how dare/nyou — might have broken your neck — "/n/n"It wasn't his fault, Professor — "/n/n"Be quiet, Miss Patil — "/n/n"But Malfoy — "/n/n"That's enough, Mr. Weasley. Potter, follow me, now."/n/nHarry caught sight of Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle's/ntriumphant faces as he left, walking numbly in/nProfessor McGonagall's wake as she strode toward the/ncastle. He was going to be expelled, he just knew it./n/nHe wanted to say something to defend himself, but/nthere seemed to be something wrong with his voice./nProfessor McGonagall was sweeping along without/neven looking at him; he had to jog to keep up. Now/nhe'd done it. He hadn't even lasted two weeks. He'd be/npacking his bags in ten minutes. What would the/nDursleys say when he turned up on the doorstep?/n/n/n/n/nUp the front steps, up the marble staircase inside,/nand still Professor McGonagall didn't say a word to/nhim. She wrenched open doors and marched along/ncorridors with Harry trotting miserably behind her./nMaybe she was taking him to Dumbledore. He/nthought of Hagrid, expelled but allowed to stay on as/ngamekeeper. Perhaps he could be Hagrid's assistant./nHis stomach twisted as he imagined it, watching Ron/nand the others becoming wizards while he stumped/naround the grounds carrying Hagrid's bag./n/nProfessor McGonagall stopped outside a classroom./nShe opened the door and poked her head inside./n/n"Excuse me, Professor Flitwick, could I borrow Wood/nfor a moment?"/n/nWood? thought Harry, bewildered; was Wood a cane/nshe was going to use on him?/n/nBut Wood turned out to be a person, a burly fifth-year/nboy who came out of Flitwick's class looking/nconfused./n/n"Follow me, you two," said Professor McGonagall, and/nthey marched on up the corridor, Wood looking/ncuriously at Harry./n/n"In here."/n/nProfessor McGonagall pointed them into a classroom/nthat was empty except for Peeves, who was busy/nwriting rude words on the blackboard./n/n"Out, Peeves!" she barked. Peeves threw the chalk/ninto a bin, which clanged loudly, and he swooped out/ncursing. Professor McGonagall slammed the door/nbehind him and turned to face the two boys./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Potter, this is Oliver Wood. Wood — I've found you a/nSeeker."/n/nWood's expression changed from puzzlement to/ndelight./n/n"Are you serious, Professor?"/n/n"Absolutely," said Professor McGonagall crisply. "The/nboy's a natural. I've never seen anything like it. Was/nthat your first time on a broomstick, Potter?"/n/nHarry nodded silently. He didn't have a clue what was/ngoing on, but he didn't seem to be being expelled, and/nsome of the feeling started coming back to his legs./n/n"He caught that thing in his hand after a fifty-foot/ndive," Professor McGonagall told Wood. "Didn't even/nscratch himself. Charlie Weasley couldn't have done/nit."/n/nWood was now looking as though all his dreams had/ncome true at once./n/n"Ever seen a game of Quidditch, Potter?" he asked/nexcitedly./n/n"Wood's captain of the Gryffindor team," Professor/nMcGonagall explained./n/n"He's just the build for a Seeker, too," said Wood, now/nwalking around Harry and staring at him. "Light —/nspeedy — we'll have to get him a decent broom,/nProfessor — a Nimbus Two Thousand or a/nCleansweep Seven, I'd say."/n/n"I shall speak to Professor Dumbledore and see if we/ncan't bend the first-year rule. Heaven knows, we need/na better team than last year. Flattened in that last/n/n/n/n/n/nmatch by Slytherin, I couldn't look Severus Snape in/nthe face for weeks. ..."/n/nProfessor McGonagall peered sternly over her glasses/nat Harry./n/n"I want to hear you're training hard, Potter, or I may/nchange my mind about punishing you."/n/nThen she suddenly smiled./n/n"Your father would have been proud," she said. "He/nwas an excellent Quidditch player himself."/n/n"You're joking."/n/nIt was dinnertime. Harry had just finished telling Ron/nwhat had happened when he'd left the grounds with/nProfessor McGonagall. Ron had a piece of steak and/nkidney pie halfway to his mouth, but he'd forgotten all/nabout it./n/n"Seeker?" he said. "But first years never — you must/nbe the youngest House player in about — "/n/n" — a century," said Harry, shoveling pie into his/nmouth. He felt particularly hungry after the/nexcitement of the afternoon. "Wood told me."/n/nRon was so amazed, so impressed, he just sat and/ngaped at Harry./n/n"I start training next week," said Harry. "Only don't/ntell anyone, Wood wants to keep it a secret."/n/nFred and George Weasley now came into the hall,/nspotted Harry, and hurried over./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well done," said George in a low voice. "Wood told us./nWe're on the team too — Beaters."/n/n"I tell you, we're going to win that Quidditch Cup for/nsure this year," said Fred. "We haven't won since/nCharlie left, but this year's team is going to be/nbrilliant. You must be good, Harry, Wood was almost/nskipping when he told us."/n/n"Anyway, we've got to go, Lee Jordan reckons he's/nfound a new secret passageway out of the school."/n/n"Bet it's that one behind the statue of Gregory the/nSmarmy that we found in our first week. See you."/n/nFred and George had hardly disappeared when/nsomeone far less welcome turned up: Malfoy, flanked/nby Crabbe and Goyle./n/n"Having a last meal, Potter? When are you getting the/ntrain back to the Muggles?"/n/n"You're a lot braver now that you're back on the/nground and you've got your little friends with you,"/nsaid Harry coolly. There was of course nothing at all/nlittle about Crabbe and Goyle, but as the High Table/nwas full of teachers, neither of them could do more/nthan crack their knuckles and scowl./n/n"I'd take you on anytime on my own," said Malfoy./n"Tonight, if you want. Wizard's duel. Wands only —/nno contact. What's the matter? Never heard of a/nwizard's duel before, I suppose?"/n/n"Of course he has," said Ron, wheeling around. "I'm/nhis second, who's yours?"/n/nMalfoy looked at Crabbe and Goyle, sizing them up./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Crabbe," he said. "Midnight all right? Well meet you/nin the trophy room; that's always unlocked."/n/nWhen Malfoy had gone, Ron and Harry looked at each/nother./n/n"What is a wizard's duel?" said Harry. "And what do/nyou mean, you're my second?"/n/n"Well, a second's there to take over if you die," said/nRon casually, getting started at last on his cold pie./nCatching the look on Harry's face, he added quickly,/n"But people only die in proper duels, you know, with/nreal wizards. The most you and Malfoy'll be able to do/nis send sparks at each other. Neither of you knows/nenough magic to do any real damage. I bet he/nexpected you to refuse, anyway."/n/n"And what if I wave my wand and nothing happens?"/n/n"Throw it away and punch him on the nose," Ron/nsuggested./n/n"Excuse me."/n/nThey both looked up. It was Hermione Granger./n/n"Can't a person eat in peace in this place?" said Ron./n/nHermione ignored him and spoke to Harry./n/n"I couldn't help overhearing what you and Malfoy/nwere saying — "/n/n"Bet you could," Ron muttered./n/n" — and you mustn't go wandering around the school/nat night, think of the points you'll lose Gryffindor if/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nyou're caught, and you're bound to be. It's really very/nselfish of you."/n/n"And it's really none of your business," said Harry./n"Good-bye," said Ron./n/nAll the same, it wasn't what you'd call the perfect end/nto the day, Harry thought, as he lay awake much later/nlistening to Dean and Seamus falling asleep (Neville/nwasn't back from the hospital wing). Ron had spent/nall evening giving him advice such as "If he tries to/ncurse you, you'd better dodge it, because I can't/nremember how to block them." There was a very good/nchance they were going to get caught by Filch or Mrs./nNorris, and Harry felt he was pushing his luck,/nbreaking another school rule today. On the other/nhand, Malfoy's sneering face kept looming up out of/nthe darkness — this was his big chance to beat/nMalfoy face-to-face. He couldn't miss it./n/n"Half-past eleven," Ron muttered at last, "we'd better/ngo."/n/nThey pulled on their bathrobes, picked up their/nwands, and crept across the tower room, down the/nspiral staircase, and into the Gryffindor common/nroom. A few embers were still glowing in the fireplace,/nturning all the armchairs into hunched black/nshadows. They had almost reached the portrait hole/nwhen a voice spoke from the chair nearest them, "I/ncan't believe you're going to do this, Harry."/n/nA lamp flickered on. It was Hermione Granger,/nwearing a pink bathrobe and a frown./n/n"You!" said Ron furiously. "Go back to bed!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I almost told your brother," Hermione snapped,/n/n"Percy — he's a prefect, he'd put a stop to this."/n/nHarry couldn't believe anyone could be so interfering./n/n"Come on," he said to Ron. He pushed open the/nportrait of the Fat Lady and climbed through the hole./n/nHermione wasn't going to give up that easily. She/nfollowed Ron through the portrait hole, hissing at/nthem like an angry goose./n/n"Don't you care about Gryffindor, do you only care/nabout yourselves, / don't want Slytherin to win the/nHouse Cup, and you'll lose all the points I got from/nProfessor McGonagall for knowing about Switching/nSpells."/n/n"Go away."/n/n"All right, but I warned you, you just remember what/nI said when you're on the train home tomorrow,/nyou're so — "/n/nBut what they were, they didn't find out. Hermione/nhad turned to the portrait of the Fat Lady to get back/ninside and found herself facing an empty painting./n/nThe Fat Lady had gone on a nighttime visit and/nHermione was locked out of Gryffindor Tower./n/n"Now what am I going to do?" she asked shrilly./n/n"That's your problem," said Ron. "We've got to go,/nwe're going to be late."/n/nThey hadn't even reached the end of the corridor/nwhen Hermione caught up with them./n/n"I'm coming with you," she said./n/n/n/n/n/n"You are not."/n/n/n/n"D'you think I'm going to stand out here and wait for/nFilch to catch me? If he finds all three of us I'll tell/nhim the truth, that I was trying to stop you, and you/ncan back me up."/n/n"You've got some nerve — " said Ron loudly./n/n"Shut up, both of you!" said Harry sharply. "I heard/nsomething."/n/nIt was a sort of snuffling./n/n"Mrs. Norris?" breathed Ron, squinting through the/ndark./n/nIt wasn't Mrs. Norris. It was Neville. He was curled up/non the floor, fast asleep, but jerked suddenly awake/nas they crept nearer./n/n"Thank goodness you found me! I've been out here for/nhours, I couldn't remember the new password to get/nin to bed."/n/n"Keep your voice down, Neville. The password's 'Pig/nsnout' but it won't help you now, the Fat Lady's gone/noff somewhere."/n/n"How's your arm?" said Harry./n/n"Fine," said Neville, showing them. "Madam Pomfrey/nmended it in about a minute."/n/n"Good — well, look, Neville, we've got to be/nsomewhere, we'll see you later — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't leave me!" said Neville, scrambling to his feet,/n/n"I don't want to stay here alone, the Bloody Baron's/nbeen past twice already."/n/nRon looked at his watch and then glared furiously at/nHermione and Neville./n/n"If either of you get us caught, I'll never rest until I've/nlearned that Curse of the Bogies Quirrell told us/nabout, and used it on you."/n/nHermione opened her mouth, perhaps to tell Ron/nexactly how to use the Curse of the Bogies, but Harry/nhissed at her to be quiet and beckoned them all/nforward./n/nThey flitted along corridors striped with bars of/nmoonlight from the high windows. At every turn Harry/nexpected to run into Filch or Mrs. Norris, but they/nwere lucky. They sped up a staircase to the third floor/nand tiptoed toward the trophy room./n/nMalfoy and Crabbe weren't there yet. The crystal/ntrophy cases glimmered where the moonlight caught/nthem. Cups, shields, plates, and statues winked silver/nand gold in the darkness. They edged along the walls,/nkeeping their eyes on the doors at either end of the/nroom. Harry took out his wand in case Malfoy leapt in/nand started at once. The minutes crept by./n/n"He's late, maybe he's chickened out," Ron whispered./n/nThen a noise in the next room made them jump./n/nHarry had only just raised his wand when they heard/nsomeone speak — and it wasn't Malfoy./n/n"Sniff around, my sweet, they might be lurking in a/ncorner."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was Filch speaking to Mrs. Norris. Horror-struck,/nHarry waved madly at the other three to follow him as/nquickly as possible; they scurried silently toward the/ndoor, away from Filch's voice. Neville's robes had/nbarely whipped round the corner when they heard/nFilch enter the trophy room./n/n"They're in here somewhere," they heard him mutter,/n"probably hiding."/n/n"This way!" Harry mouthed to the others and,/npetrified, they began to creep down a long gallery full/nof suits of armor. They could hear Filch getting/nnearer. Neville suddenly let out a frightened squeak/nand broke into a run — he tripped, grabbed Ron/naround the waist, and the pair of them toppled right/ninto a suit of armor./n/nThe clanging and crashing were enough to wake the/nwhole castle./n/n"RUN!" Harry yelled, and the four of them sprinted/ndown the gallery, not looking back to see whether/nFilch was following — they swung around the/ndoorpost and galloped down one corridor then/nanother, Harry in the lead, without any idea where/nthey were or where they were going — they ripped/nthrough a tapestry and found themselves in a hidden/npassageway, hurtled along it and came out near their/nCharms classroom, which they knew was miles from/nthe trophy room./n/n"I think we've lost him," Harry panted, leaning against/nthe cold wall and wiping his forehead. Neville was/nbent double, wheezing and spluttering./n/n"I — told — you," Hermione gasped, clutching at the/nstitch in her chest, "I — told — you."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We've got to get back to Gryffindor Tower," said Ron,/n"quickly as possible."/n/n"Malfoy tricked you," Hermione said to Harry. "You/nrealize that, don't you? He was never going to meet/nyou — Filch knew someone was going to be in the/ntrophy room, Malfoy must have tipped him off."/n/nHarry thought she was probably right, but he wasn't/ngoing to tell her that./n/n"Let's go."/n/nIt wasn't going to be that simple. They hadn't gone/nmore than a dozen paces when a doorknob rattled/nand something came shooting out of a classroom in/nfront of them./n/nIt was Peeves. He caught sight of them and gave a/nsqueal of delight./n/n"Shut up, Peeves — please — you'll get us thrown/nout."/n/nPeeves cackled./n/n"Wandering around at midnight, Ickle Firsties? Tut,/ntut, tut. Naughty, naughty, you'll get caughty."/n/n"Not if you don't give us away, Peeves, please."/n/n"Should tell Filch, I should," said Peeves in a sanity/nvoice, but his eyes glittered wickedly. "It's for your/nown good, you know."/n/n"Get out of the way," snapped Ron, taking a swipe at/nPeeves — this was a big mistake./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"STUDENTS OUT OF BED!" Peeves bellowed,/n"STUDENTS OUT OF BED DOWN THE CHARMS/nCORRIDOR!"/n/nDucking under Peeves, they ran for their lives, right/nto the end of the corridor where they slammed into a/ndoor — and it was locked./n/n"This is it!" Ron moaned, as they pushed helplessly at/nthe door, "We're done for! This is the end!"/n/nThey could hear footsteps, Filch running as fast as he/ncould toward Peeves 's shouts./n/n"Oh, move over," Hermione snarled. She grabbed/nHarry's wand, tapped the lock, and whispered,/n"Alohomora\"/n/nThe lock clicked and the door swung open — they/npiled through it, shut it quickly, and pressed their/nears against it, listening./n/n"Which way did they go, Peeves?" Filch was saying./n"Quick, tell me."/n/n"Say 'please.' "/n/n"Don't mess with me, Peeves, now where did they go?"/n/n"Shan't say nothing if you don't say please," said/nPeeves in his annoying singsong voice./n/n"All right — please."/n/n"NOTHING! Ha haaa! Told you I wouldn't say nothing/nif you didn't say please! Ha ha! Haaaaaa!" And they/nheard the sound of Peeves whooshing away and Filch/ncursing in rage./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He thinks this door is locked," Harry whispered. "I/nthink well be okay — get off Neville!" For Neville had/nbeen tugging on the sleeve of Harry's bathrobe for the/nlast minute. "What?"/n/nHarry turned around — and saw, quite clearly, what./nFor a moment, he was sure he'd walked into a/nnightmare — this was too much, on top of everything/nthat had happened so far./n/nThey weren't in a room, as he had supposed. They/nwere in a corridor. The forbidden corridor on the third/nfloor. And now they knew why it was forbidden./n/nThey were looking straight into the eyes of a/nmonstrous dog, a dog that filled the whole space/nbetween ceiling and floor. It had three heads. Three/npairs of rolling, mad eyes; three noses, twitching and/nquivering in their direction; three drooling mouths,/nsaliva hanging in slippery ropes from yellowish fangs./n/nIt was standing quite still, all six eyes staring at them,/nand Harry knew that the only reason they weren't/nalready dead was that their sudden appearance had/ntaken it by surprise, but it was quickly getting over/nthat, there was no mistaking what those thunderous/ngrowls meant./n/nHarry groped for the doorknob — between Filch and/ndeath, he'd take Filch./n/nThey fell backward — Harry slammed the door shut,/nand they ran, they almost flew, back down the/ncorridor. Filch must have hurried off to look for them/nsomewhere else, because they didn't see him/nanywhere, but they hardly cared — all they wanted to/ndo was put as much space as possible between them/nand that monster. They didn't stop running until they/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nreached the portrait of the Fat Lady on the seventh/nfloor./n/n"Where on earth have you all been?" she asked,/nlooking at their bathrobes hanging off their shoulders/nand their flushed, sweaty faces./n/n"Never mind that — pig snout, pig snout," panted/nHarry, and the portrait swung forward. They/nscrambled into the common room and collapsed,/ntrembling, into armchairs./n/nIt was a while before any of them said anything./nNeville, indeed, looked as if he'd never speak again./n/n"What do they think they're doing, keeping a thing/nlike that locked up in a school?" said Ron finally. "If/nany dog needs exercise, that one does."/n/nHermione had got both her breath and her bad/ntemper back again./n/n"You don't use your eyes, any of you, do you?" she/nsnapped. "Didn't you see what it was standing on?"/n/n"The floor?" Harry suggested. "I wasn't looking at its/nfeet, I was too busy with its heads."/n/n"No, not the floor. It was standing on a trapdoor. It's/nobviously guarding something."/n/nShe stood up, glaring at them./n/n"I hope you're pleased with yourselves. We could all/nhave been killed — or worse, expelled. Now, if you/ndon't mind, I'm going to bed."/n/nRon stared after her, his mouth open./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No, we don't mind," he said. "You'd think we dragged/nher along, wouldn't you?"/n/nBut Hermione had given Harry something else to/nthink about as he climbed back into bed. The dog was/nguarding something. . . . What had Hagrid said?/nGringotts was the safest place in the world for/nsomething you wanted to hide — except perhaps/nHogwarts./n/nIt looked as though Harry had found out where the/ngrubby little package from vault seven hundred and/nthirteen was./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n10/n/n/n/n

title: Halloween
