They hadn't realized how loudly they/nhad been talking./n/n"Quick!"/n/nRon threw the cloak back over them as the luminous/neyes of Mrs. Norris came round the door. Ron and/nHarry stood quite still, both thinking the same thing/n— did the cloak work on cats? After what seemed an/nage, she turned and left./n/n"This isn't safe — she might have gone for Filch, I bet/nshe heard us. Come on."/n/nAnd Ron pulled Harry out of the room./n/nThe snow still hadn't melted the next morning./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Want to play chess, Harry?" said Ron./n/n/n/n"No."/n/n"Why don't we go down and visit Hagrid?"/n/n"No ... you go ..."/n/n"I know what you're thinking about, Harry, that/nmirror. Don't go back tonight."/n/n"Why not?"/n/n"I dunno, I've just got a bad feeling about it — and/nanyway, you've had too many close shaves already./nFilch, Snape, and Mrs. Norris are wandering around./nSo what if they can't see you? What if they walk into/nyou? What if you knock something over?"/n/n"You sound like Hermione."/n/n"I'm serious, Harry, don't go."/n/nBut Harry only had one thought in his head, which/nwas to get back in front of the mirror, and Ron wasn't/ngoing to stop him./n/nThat third night he found his way more quickly than/nbefore. He was walking so fast he knew he was/nmaking more noise than was wise, but he didn't meet/nanyone./n/nAnd there were his mother and father smiling at him/nagain, and one of his grandfathers nodding happily./nHarry sank down to sit on the floor in front of the/nmirror. There was nothing to stop him from staying/nhere all night with his family. Nothing at all./n/nExcept —/n/n/n/n/n/n"So — back again, Harry?"/n/nHarry felt as though his insides had turned to ice. He/nlooked behind him. Sitting on one of the desks by the/nwall was none other than Albus Dumbledore. Harry/nmust have walked straight past him, so desperate to/nget to the mirror he hadn't noticed him./n/n"I — I didn't see you, sir."/n/n"Strange how nearsighted being invisible can make/nyou," said Dumbledore, and Harry was relieved to see/nthat he was smiling./n/n"So," said Dumbledore, slipping off the desk to sit on/nthe floor with Harry, "you, like hundreds before you,/nhave discovered the delights of the Mirror of Erised."/n/n"I didn't know it was called that, sir."/n/n"But I expect you've realized by now what it does?"/n/n"It — well — it shows me my family — "/n/n"And it showed your friend Ron himself as Head Boy."/n/n"How did you know — ?"/n/n"I don't need a cloak to become invisible," said/nDumbledore gently. "Now, can you think what the/nMirror of Erised shows us all?"/n/nHarry shook his head./n/n"Let me explain. The happiest man on earth would be/nable to use the Mirror of Erised like a normal mirror,/nthat is, he would look into it and see himself exactly/nas he is. Does that help?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry thought. Then he said slowly, "It shows us/nwhat we want ... whatever we want ..."/n/n"Yes and no," said Dumbledore quietly. "It shows us/nnothing more or less than the deepest, most/ndesperate desire of our hearts. You, who have never/nknown your family, see them standing around you./nRonald Weasley, who has always been overshadowed/nby his brothers, sees himself standing alone, the best/nof all of them. However, this mirror will give us/nneither knowledge or truth. Men have wasted away/nbefore it, entranced by what they have seen, or been/ndriven mad, not knowing if what it shows is real or/neven possible./n/n"The Mirror will be moved to a new home tomorrow,/nHarry, and I ask you not to go looking for it again. If/nyou ever do run across it, you will now be prepared. It/ndoes not do to dwell on dreams and forget to live,/nremember that. Now, why don't you put that/nadmirable cloak back on and get off to bed?"/n/nHarry stood up./n/n"Sir — Professor Dumbledore? Can I ask you/nsomething?"/n/n"Obviously, you've just done so," Dumbledore smiled./n"You may ask me one more thing, however."/n/n"What do you see when you look in the mirror?"/n/n"I? I see myself holding a pair of thick, woolen socks."/n/nHarry stared./n/n"One can never have enough socks," said/nDumbledore. "Another Christmas has come and gone/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nand I didn't get a single pair. People will insist on/ngiving me books."/n/nIt was only when he was back in bed that it struck/nHarry that Dumbledore might not have been quite/ntruthful. But then, he thought, as he shoved/nScabbers off his pillow, it had been quite a personal/nquestion./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Nicholas Flamel
text: /nDumbledore had convinced Harry not to go looking/nfor the Mirror of Erised again, and for the rest of the/nChristmas holidays the Invisibility Cloak stayed/nfolded at the bottom of his trunk. Harry wished he/ncould forget what he'd seen in the mirror as easily,/nbut he couldn't. He started having nightmares. Over/nand over again he dreamed about his parents/ndisappearing in a flash of green light, while a high/nvoice cackled with laughter./n/n"You see, Dumbledore was right, that mirror could/ndrive you mad," said Ron, when Harry told him about/nthese dreams./n/nHermione, who came back the day before term/nstarted, took a different view of things. She was torn/nbetween horror at the idea of Harry being out of bed,/nroaming the school three nights in a row ("If Filch had/ncaught you!"), and disappointment that he hadn't at/nleast found out who Nicolas Flamel was./n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey had almost given up hope of ever finding Flamel/nin a library book, even though Harry was still sure/nhe'd read the name somewhere. Once term had/nstarted, they were back to skimming through books/nfor ten minutes during their breaks. Harry had even/nless time than the other two, because Quidditch/npractice had started again./n/nWood was working the team harder than ever. Even/nthe endless rain that had replaced the snow couldn't/ndampen his spirits. The Weasleys complained that/nWood was becoming a fanatic, but Harry was on/nWood's side. If they won their next match, against/nHufflepuff, they would overtake Slytherin in the/nHouse Championship for the first time in seven years./nQuite apart from wanting to win, Harry found that he/nhad fewer nightmares when he was tired out after/ntraining./n/nThen, during one particularly wet and muddy practice/nsession, Wood gave the team a bit of bad news. He'd/njust gotten very angry with the Weasleys, who kept/ndive-bombing each other and pretending to fall off/ntheir brooms./n/n"Will you stop messing around!" he yelled. "That's/nexactly the sort of thing that'll lose us the match!/nSnape's refereeing this time, and he'll be looking for/nany excuse to knock points off Gryffindor!"/n/nGeorge Weasley really did fall off his broom at these/nwords./n/n" Snape's refereeing?" he spluttered through a/nmouthful of mud. "When's he ever refereed a/nQuidditch match? He's not going to be fair if we might/novertake Slytherin."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe rest of the team landed next to George to/ncomplain, too./n/n"It's not my fault," said Wood. "We've just got to make/nsure we play a clean game, so Snape hasn't got an/nexcuse to pick on us."/n/nWhich was all very well, thought Harry, but he had/nanother reason for not wanting Snape near him while/nhe was playing Quidditch. .../n/nThe rest of the team hung back to talk to one another/nas usual at the end of practice, but Harry headed/nstraight back to the Gryffindor common room, where/nhe found Ron and Hermione playing chess. Chess was/nthe only thing Hermione ever lost at, something Harry/nand Ron thought was very good for her./n/n"Don't talk to me for a moment," said Ron when Harry/nsat down next to him, "I need to concern" He caught/nsight of Harry's face. "What's the matter with you?/n/nYou look terrible."/n/nSpeaking quietly so that no one else would hear,/n/nHarry told the other two about Snape 's sudden,/nsinister desire to be a Quidditch referee./n/n"Don't play," said Hermione at once./n/n"Say you're ill," said Ron./n/n"Pretend to break your leg," Hermione suggested./n/n" Really break your leg," said Ron./n/n"I can't," said Harry. "There isn't a reserve Seeker. If I/nback out, Gryffindor can't play at all."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAt that moment Neville toppled into the common/nroom. How he had managed to climb through the/nportrait hole was anyone's guess, because his legs/nhad been stuck together with what they recognized at/nonce as the Leg-Locker Curse. He must have had to/nbunny hop all the way up to Gryffindor Tower./n/nEveryone fell over laughing except Hermione, who/nleapt up and performed the countercurse. Neville's/nlegs sprang apart and he got to his feet, trembling./n/n"What happened?" Hermione asked him, leading him/nover to sit with Harry and Ron./n/n"Malfoy," said Neville shakily. "I met him outside the/nlibrary. He said he'd been looking for someone to/npractice that on."/n/n"Go to Professor McGonagall!" Hermione urged/nNeville. "Report him!"/n/nNeville shook his head./n/n"I don't want more trouble," he mumbled./n/n"You've got to stand up to him, Neville!" said Ron./n"He's used to walking all over people, but that's no/nreason to lie down in front of him and make it easier."/n/n"There's no need to tell me I'm not brave enough to be/nin Gryffindor, Malfoy's already done that," Neville/nchoked out./n/nHarry felt in the pocket of his robes and pulled out a/nChocolate Frog, the very last one from the box/nHermione had given him for Christmas. He gave it to/nNeville, who looked as though he might cry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're worth twelve of Malfoy," Harry said. "The/nSorting Hat chose you for Gryffindor, didn't it? And/nwhere's Malfoy? In stinking Slytherin."/n/nNeville's lips twitched in a weak smile as he/nunwrapped the frog./n/n"Thanks, Harry ... I think I'll go to bed. ... D'you want/nthe card, you collect them, don't you?"/n/nAs Neville walked away, Harry looked at the Famous/nWizard card./n/n"Dumbledore again," he said, "He was the first one I/never — "/n/nHe gasped. He stared at the back of the card. Then he/nlooked up at Ron and Hermione./n/n"I've found him\" he whispered. "I've found Flamel! I/ntold you I'd read the name somewhere before, I read it/non the train coming here — listen to this:/n/n'Dumbledore is particularly famous for his defeat of/nthe Dark wizard Grindelwald in 1945, for the/ndiscovery of the twelve uses of dragon's blood, and his/nwork on alchemy with his partner, Nicolas Flamel'V'/n/nHermione jumped to her feet. She hadn't looked so/nexcited since they'd gotten back the marks for their/nvery first piece of homework./n/n"Stay there!" she said, and she sprinted up the stairs/nto the girls' dormitories. Harry and Ron barely had/ntime to exchange mystified looks before she was/ndashing back, an enormous old book in her arms./n/n"I never thought to look in here!" she whispered/nexcitedly. "I got this out of the library weeks ago for a/nbit of light reading."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Light?" said Ron, but Hermione told him to be quiet/nuntil she'd looked something up, and started flicking/nfrantically through the pages, muttering to herself./n/nAt last she found what she was looking for./n/n"I knew it! I knew it!"/n/n"Are we allowed to speak yet?" said Ron grumpily./nHermione ignored him./n/n"Nicolas Flamel," she whispered dramatically, "is the/nonly known maker of the Sorcerer's Stone\"/n/nThis didn't have quite the effect she'd expected./n/n"The what?" said Harry and Ron./n/n"Oh, honestly , don't you two read? Look — read that,/nthere."/n/nShe pushed the book toward them, and Harry and/nRon read:/n/nThe ancient study of alchemy is concerned with/nmaking the Sorcerer's Stone, a legendary substance/nwith astonishing powers. The Stone will transform/nany metal into pure gold. It also produces the Elixir of/nLife, which will make the drinker immortal./n/nThere have been many reports of the Sorcerer's Stone/nover the centuries, but the only Stone currently in/nexistence belongs to Mr. Nicolas Flamel, the noted/nalchemist and opera lover. Mr. Flamel, who celebrated/nhis six hundred and sixty-fifth birthday last year,/nenjoys a quiet life in Devon with his wife, Perenelle/n(six hundred and fifty-eight)./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"See?" said Hermione, when Harry and Ron had/nfinished. "The dog must be guarding Flamel's/nSorcerer's Stone! I bet he asked Dumbledore to keep/nit safe for him, because they're friends and he knew/nsomeone was after it, that's why he wanted the Stone/nmoved out of Gringotts!"/n/n"A stone that makes gold and stops you from ever/ndying!" said Harry. "No wonder Snape's after it!/n/nAnyone would want it."/n/n"And no wonder we couldn't find Flamel in that Study/nof Recent Developments in Wizardry," said Ron. "He's/nnot exactly recent if he's six hundred and sixty-five, is/nhe?"/n/nThe next morning in Defense Against the Dark Arts,/nwhile copying down different ways of treating werewolf/nbites, Harry and Ron were still discussing what they'd/ndo with a Sorcerer's Stone if they had one. It wasn't/nuntil Ron said he'd buy his own Quidditch team that/nHarry remembered about Snape and the coming/nmatch./n/n"I'm going to play," he told Ron and Hermione. "If I/ndon't, all the Slytherins will think I'm just too scared/nto face Snape. I'll show them ... it'll really wipe the/nsmiles off their faces if we win."/n/n"Just as long as we're not wiping you off the field,"/nsaid Hermione./n/nAs the match drew nearer, however, Harry became/nmore and more nervous, whatever he told Ron and/nHermione. The rest of the team wasn't too calm,/neither. The idea of overtaking Slytherin in the House/nChampionship was wonderful, no one had done it for/nseven years, but would they be allowed to, with such/na biased referee?/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry didn't know whether he was imagining it or not,/nbut he seemed to keep running into Snape wherever/nhe went. At times, he even wondered whether Snape/nwas following him, trying to catch him on his own./nPotions lessons were turning into a sort of weekly/ntorture, Snape was so horrible to Harry. Could Snape/npossibly know they'd found out about the Sorcerer's/nStone? Harry didn't see how he could — yet he/nsometimes had the horrible feeling that Snape could/nread minds./n/nHarry knew, when they wished him good luck/noutside the locker rooms the next afternoon, that Ron/nand Hermione were wondering whether they'd ever/nsee him alive again. This wasn't what you'd call/ncomforting. Harry hardly heard a word of Wood's pep/ntalk as he pulled on his Quidditch robes and picked/nup his Nimbus Two Thousand./n/nRon and Hermione, meanwhile, had found a place in/nthe stands next to Neville, who couldn't understand/nwhy they looked so grim and worried, or why they had/nboth brought their wands to the match. Little did/nHarry know that Ron and Hermione had been secretly/npracticing the Leg-Locker Curse. They'd gotten the/nidea from Malfoy using it on Neville, and were ready/nto use it on Snape if he showed any sign of wanting to/nhurt Harry./n/n"Now, don't forget, it's Locomotor Mortis," Hermione/nmuttered as Ron slipped his wand up his sleeve./n/n"I know," Ron snapped. "Don't nag."/n/nBack in the locker room, Wood had taken Harry/naside./n/n"Don't want to pressure you, Potter, but if we ever/nneed an early capture of the Snitch it's now. Finish/n/n/n/n/n/nthe game before Snape can favor Hufflepuff too/nmuch."/n/n"The whole school's out there!" said Fred Weasley,/npeering out of the door. "Even — blimey —/nDumbledore's come to watch!"/n/nHarry's heart did a somersault./n/n"Dumbledore?" he said, dashing to the door to make/nsure. Fred was right. There was no mistaking that/nsilver beard./n/nHarry could have laughed out loud with relief. He was/nsafe. There was simply no way that Snape would dare/nto try to hurt him if Dumbledore was watching./n/nPerhaps that was why Snape was looking so angry as/nthe teams marched onto the field, something that Ron/nnoticed, too./n/n"I've never seen Snape look so mean," he told/nHermione. "Look — they're off. Ouch!"/n/nSomeone had poked Ron in the back of the head. It/nwas Malfoy./n/n"Oh, sorry, Weasley, didn't see you there."/n/nMalfoy grinned broadly at Crabbe and Goyle./n/n"Wonder how long Potter's going to stay on his broom/nthis time? Anyone want a bet? What about you,/nWeasley?"/n/nRon didn't answer; Snape had just awarded/nHufflepuff a penalty because George Weasley had hit/na Bludger at him. Hermione, who had all her fingers/ncrossed in her lap, was squinting fixedly at Harry,/n/n/n/n/n/nwho was circling the game like a hawk, looking for the/nSnitch./n/n"You know how I think they choose people for the/nGryffindor team?" said Malfoy loudly a few minutes/nlater, as Snape awarded Hufflepuff another penalty/nfor no reason at all. "It's people they feel sorry for./n/nSee, there's Potter, who's got no parents, then there's/nthe Weasleys, who've got no money — you should be/non the team, Longbottom, you've got no brains."/n/nNeville went bright red but turned in his seat to face/nMalfoy./n/n"I'm worth twelve of you, Malfoy," he stammered./n/nMalfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle howled with laughter, but/nRon, still not daring to take his eyes from the game,/nsaid, "You tell him, Neville."/n/n"Longbottom, if brains were gold you'd be poorer than/nWeasley, and that's saying something."/n/nRon's nerves were already stretched to the breaking/npoint with anxiety about Harry./n/n"I'm warning you, Malfoy — one more word — "/n/n"Ron!" said Hermione suddenly, "Harry — !"/n/n"What? Where?"/n/nHarry had suddenly gone into a spectacular dive,/nwhich drew gasps and cheers from the crowd./nHermione stood up, her crossed fingers in her mouth,/nas Harry streaked toward the ground like a bullet./n/n"You're in luck, Weasley, Potter's obviously spotted/nsome money on the ground!" said Malfoy./n/n/n/n/n/nRon snapped. Before Malfoy knew what was/nhappening, Ron was on top of him, wrestling him to/nthe ground. Neville hesitated, then clambered over the/nback of his seat to help./n/n"Come on, Harry!" Hermione screamed, leaping onto/nher seat to watch as Harry sped straight at Snape —/nshe didn't even notice Malfoy and Ron rolling around/nunder her seat, or the scuffles and yelps coming from/nthe whirl of fists that was Neville, Crabbe, and Goyle./n/nUp in the air, Snape turned on his broomstick just in/ntime to see something scarlet shoot past him, missing/nhim by inches — the next second, Harry had pulled/nout of the dive, his arm raised in triumph, the Snitch/nclasped in his hand./n/nThe stands erupted; it had to be a record, no one/ncould ever remember the Snitch being caught so/nquickly./n/n"Ron! Ron! Where are you? The game's over! Harry's/nwon! We've won! Gryffindor is in the lead!" shrieked/nHermione, dancing up and down on her seat and/nhugging Parvati Patil in the row in front./n/nHarry jumped off his broom, a foot from the ground./nHe couldn't believe it. He'd done it — the game was/nover; it had barely lasted five minutes. As Gryffindors/ncame spilling onto the field, he saw Snape land/nnearby, white-faced and tight-lipped — then Harry felt/na hand on his shoulder and looked up into/nDumbledore's smiling face./n/n"Well done," said Dumbledore quietly, so that only/nHarry could hear. "Nice to see you haven't been/nbrooding about that mirror . . . been keeping busy . . ./nexcellent ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSnape spat bitterly on the ground./n/n/n/nJc Jc Jc/n/n/n/nHarry left the locker room alone some time later, to/ntake his Nimbus Two Thousand back to the/nbroomshed. He couldn't ever remember feeling/nhappier. He'd really done something to be proud of/nnow — no one could say he was just a famous name/nany more. The evening air had never smelled so/nsweet. He walked over the damp grass, reliving the/nlast hour in his head, which was a happy blur:/nGryffindors running to lift him onto their shoulders;/nRon and Hermione in the distance, jumping up and/ndown, Ron cheering through a heavy nosebleed./n/nHarry had reached the shed. He leaned against the/nwooden door and looked up at Hogwarts, with its/nwindows glowing red in the setting sun. Gryffindor in/nthe lead. He'd done it, he'd shown Snape. .../n/nAnd speaking of Snape . . ./n/nA hooded figure came swiftly down the front steps of/nthe castle. Clearly not wanting to be seen, it walked/nas fast as possible toward the forbidden forest./nHarry's victory faded from his mind as he watched./nHe recognized the figure's prowling walk. Snape,/nsneaking into the forest while everyone else was at/ndinner — what was going on?/n/nHarry jumped back on his Nimbus Two Thousand/nand took off. Gliding silently over the castle he saw/nSnape enter the forest at a run. He followed./n/nThe trees were so thick he couldn't see where Snape/nhad gone. He flew in circles, lower and lower,/nbrushing the top branches of trees until he heard/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nvoices. He glided toward them and landed noiselessly/nin a towering beech tree./n/nHe climbed carefully along one of the branches,/nholding tight to his broomstick, trying to see through/nthe leaves./n/nBelow, in a shadowy clearing, stood Snape, but he/nwasn't alone. Quirrell was there, too. Harry couldn't/nmake out the look on his face, but he was stuttering/nworse than ever. Harry strained to catch what they/nwere saying./n/n"... d-don't know why you wanted t-t-to meet here of/nall p-places, Severus ..."/n/n"Oh, I thought we'd keep this private," said Snape, his/nvoice icy. "Students aren't supposed to know about/nthe Sorcerer's Stone, after all."/n/nHarry leaned forward. Quirrell was mumbling/nsomething. Snape interrupted him./n/n"Have you found out how to get past that beast of/nHagrid's yet?"/n/n"B-b-but Severus, I — "/n/n"You don't want me as your enemy, Quirrell," said/nSnape, taking a step toward him./n/n"I-I don't know what you — "/n/n"You know perfectly well what I mean."/n/nAn owl hooted loudly, and Harry nearly fell out of the/ntree. He steadied himself in time to hear Snape say,/n/n" — your little bit of hocus-pocus. I'm waiting."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"B-but I d-d-don't — "/n/n/n/n"Very well," Snape cut in. "Well have another little/nchat soon, when you've had time to think things over/nand decided where your loyalties lie."/n/nHe threw his cloak over his head and strode out of the/nclearing. It was almost dark now, but Harry could see/nQuirrell, standing quite still as though he was/npetrified./n/n/n/nJc Jc Jc/n/n/n/n"Harry, where have you been?" Hermione squeaked./n/n"We won! You won! We won!" shouted Ron, thumping/nHarry on the back. "And I gave Malfoy a black eye,/nand Neville tried to take on Crabbe and Goyle single-/nhanded! He's still out cold but Madam Pomfrey says/nhe'll be all right — talk about showing Slytherin!/nEveryone's waiting for you in the common room, we're/nhaving a party, Fred and George stole some cakes and/nstuff from the kitchens."/n/n"Never mind that now," said Harry breathlessly. "Let's/nfind an empty room, you wait 'til you hear this. ..."/n/nHe made sure Peeves wasn't inside before shutting/nthe door behind them, then he told them what he'd/nseen and heard./n/n"So we were right, it is the Sorcerer's Stone, and/nSnape's trying to force Quirrell to help him get it. He/nasked if he knew how to get past Fluffy — and he said/nsomething about Quirrell's 'hocus-pocus' — I reckon/nthere are other things guarding the stone apart from/nFluffy, loads of enchantments, probably, and Quirrell/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwould have done some anti-Dark Arts spell that/nSnape needs to break through — "/n/n"So you mean the Stone's only safe as long as Quirrell/nstands up to Snape?" said Hermione in alarm./n/n"It'll be gone by next Tuesday," said Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Norbert The Norwegian Ridgeback
text: /nQuirrell, however, must have been braver than they'd/nthought. In the weeks that followed he did seem to be/ngetting paler and thinner, but it didn't look as though/nhe'd cracked yet./n/nEvery time they passed the third-floor corridor, Harry,/nRon, and Hermione would press their ears to the door/nto check that Fluffy was still growling inside. Snape/nwas sweeping about in his usual bad temper, which/nsurely meant that the Stone was still safe. Whenever/nHarry passed Quirrell these days he gave him an/nencouraging sort of smile, and Ron had started telling/npeople off for laughing at Quirrell's stutter./n/nHermione, however, had more on her mind than the/nSorcerer's Stone. She had started drawing up study/nschedules and color-coding all her notes. Harry and/nRon wouldn't have minded, but she kept nagging/nthem to do the same./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Hermione, the exams are ages away."/n/n"Ten weeks," Hermione snapped. "That's not ages,/nthat's like a second to Nicolas Flamel."/n/n"But we're not six hundred years old," Ron reminded/nher. "Anyway, what are you studying for, you already/nknow it all."/n/n"What am I studying for? Are you crazy? You realize/nwe need to pass these exams to get into the second/nyear? They're very important, I should have started/nstudying a month ago, I don't know what's gotten into/nme."/n/nUnfortunately, the teachers seemed to be thinking/nalong the same lines as Hermione. They piled so/nmuch homework on them that the Easter holidays/nweren't nearly as much fun as the Christmas ones. It/nwas hard to relax with Hermione next to you reciting/nthe twelve uses of dragon's blood or practicing wand/nmovements. Moaning and yawning, Harry and Ron/nspent most of their free time in the library with her,/ntrying to get through all their extra work./n/n"I'll never remember this," Ron burst out one/nafternoon, throwing down his quill and looking/nlongingly out of the library window. It was the first/nreally fine day they'd had in months. The sky was a/nclear, forget-me-not blue, and there was a feeling in/nthe air of summer coming./n/nHarry, who was looking up "Dittany" in One Thousand/nMagical Herbs and Fungi, didn't look up until he/nheard Ron say, "Hagrid! What are you doing in the/nlibrary?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid shuffled into view, hiding something behind/nhis back. He looked very out of place in his moleskin/novercoat./n/n"Jus' lookin'," he said, in a shifty voice that got their/ninterest at once. "An' what're you lot up ter?" He/nlooked suddenly suspicious. "Yer not still lookin' fer/nNicolas Flamel, are yeh?"/n/n"Oh, we found out who he is ages ago," said Ron/nimpressively. "And we know what that dog's guarding,/nit's a Sorcerer's St — "/n/n"Shhhh\" Hagrid looked around quickly to see if/nanyone was listening. "Don' go shoutin' about it,/nwhat's the matter with yeh?"/n/n"There are a few things we wanted to ask you, as a/nmatter of fact," said Harry, "about what's guarding/nthe Stone apart from Fluffy — "/n/n"SHHHH!" said Hagrid again. "Listen — come an' see/nme later, I'm not promisin' I'll tell yeh anythin', mind,/nbut don' go rabbitin' about it in here, students aren'/ns'pposed ter know. They'll think I've told yeh — "/n/n"See you later, then," said Harry./n/nHagrid shuffled off./n/n"What was he hiding behind his back?" said/nHermione thoughtfully./n/n"Do you think it had anything to do with the Stone?"/n/n"I'm going to see what section he was in," said Ron,/nwho'd had enough of working. He came back a/nminute later with a pile of books in his arms and/nslammed them down on the table./n/n/n/n/n/n"Dragons'." he whispered. "Hagrid was looking up stuff/nabout dragons! Look at these: Dragon Species of Great/nBritain and Ireland; From Egg to Inferno, A Dragon/nKeeper's Guide."/n/n"Hagrid 's always wanted a dragon, he told me so the/nfirst time I ever met him," said Harry./n/n"But it's against our laws," said Ron. "Dragon/nbreeding was outlawed by the Warlocks' Convention/nof 1709, everyone knows that. It's hard to stop/nMuggles from noticing us if we're keeping dragons in/nthe back garden — anyway, you can't tame dragons,/nit's dangerous. You should see the burns Charlie's got/noff wild ones in Romania."/n/n"But there aren't wild dragons in Britain?" said Harry./n/n"Of course there are," said Ron. "Common Welsh/nGreen and Hebridean Blacks. The Ministry of Magic/nhas a job hushing them up, I can tell you. Our kind/nhave to keep putting spells on Muggles who've spotted/nthem, to make them forget."/n/n"So what on earth's Hagrid up to?" said Hermione./n/nWhen they knocked on the door of the gamekeeper's/nhut an hour later, they were surprised to see that all/nthe curtains were closed. Hagrid called "Who is it?"/nbefore he let them in, and then shut the door quickly/nbehind them./n/nIt was stifling hot inside. Even though it was such a/nwarm day, there was a blazing fire in the grate./n/nHagrid made them tea and offered them stoat/nsandwiches, which they refused./n/n"So — yeh wanted to ask me somethin'?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes," said Harry. There was no point beating around/nthe bush. "We were wondering if you could tell us/nwhat's guarding the Sorcerer's Stone apart from/nFluffy."/n/nHagrid frowned at him./n/n"O' course I can't," he said. "Number one, I don' know/nmeself. Number two, yeh know too much already, so I/nwouldn' tell yeh if I could. That Stone's here fer a good/nreason. It was almost stolen outta Gringotts — I/ns'ppose yeh've worked that out an' all? Beats me how/nyeh even know abou' Fluffy."/n/n"Oh, come on, Hagrid, you might not want to tell us,/nbut you do know, you know everything that goes on/nround here," said Hermione in a warm, flattering/nvoice. Hagrid 's beard twitched and they could tell he/nwas smiling. "We only wondered who had done the/nguarding, really." Hermione went on. "We wondered/nwho Dumbledore had trusted enough to help him,/napart from you."/n/nHagrid 's chest swelled at these last words. Harry and/nRon beamed at Hermione./n/n"Well, I don' s'pose it could hurt ter tell yeh that .../nlet's see ... he borrowed Fluffy from me ... then some/no' the teachers did enchantments ... Professor Sprout/n— Professor Flitwick — Professor McGonagall — " he/nticked them off on his fingers, "Professor Quirrell —/nan' Dumbledore himself did somethin', o' course./n/nHang on, I've forgotten someone. Oh yeah, Professor/nSnape."/n/n"Snape?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah — yer not still on abou' that, are yeh? Look,/nSnape helped protect the Stone, he's not about ter/nsteal it."/n/nHarry knew Ron and Hermione were thinking the/nsame as he was. If Snape had been in on protecting/nthe Stone, it must have been easy to find out how the/nother teachers had guarded it. He probably knew/neverything — except, it seemed, Quirrell's spell and/nhow to get past Fluffy./n/n"You're the only one who knows how to get past/nFluffy, aren't you, Hagrid?" said Harry anxiously./n/n"And you wouldn't tell anyone, would you? Not even/none of the teachers?"/n/n"Not a soul knows except me an' Dumbledore," said/nHagrid proudly./n/n"Well, that's something," Harry muttered to the/nothers. "Hagrid, can we have a window open? I'm/nboiling."/n/n"Can't, Harry, sorry," said Hagrid. Harry noticed him/nglance at the fire. Harry looked at it, too./n/n"Hagrid — what's that?"/n/nBut he already knew what it was. In the very heart of/nthe fire, underneath the kettle, was a huge, black egg./n/n"Ah," said Hagrid, fiddling nervously with his beard,/n"That's — er ..."/n/n"Where did you get it, Hagrid?" said Ron, crouching/nover the fire to get a closer look at the egg. "It must've/ncost you a fortune."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Won it," said Hagrid. "Las' night. I was down in the/nvillage havin' a few drinks an' got into a game o' cards/nwith a stranger. Think he was quite glad ter get rid of/nit, ter be honest."/n/n"But what are you going to do with it when it's/nhatched?" said Hermione./n/n"Well, I've bin doin' some readin'," said Hagrid, pulling/na large book from under his pillow. "Got this outta the/nlibrary — Dragon Breeding for Pleasure and Profit —/nit's a bit outta date, o' course, but it's all in here. Keep/nthe egg in the fire, 'cause their mothers breathe on/n'em, see, an' when it hatches, feed it on a bucket o'/nbrandy mixed with chicken blood every half hour. An'/nsee here — how ter recognize diff'rent eggs — what I/ngot there's a Norwegian Ridge-back. They're rare,/nthem."/n/nHe looked very pleased with himself, but Hermione/ndidn't./n/n"Hagrid, you live in a wooden house," she said./n/nBut Hagrid wasn't listening. He was humming merrily/nas he stoked the fire./n/nSo now they had something else to worry about: what/nmight happen to Hagrid if anyone found out he was/nhiding an illegal dragon in his hut./n/n"Wonder what it's like to have a peaceful life," Ron/nsighed, as evening after evening they struggled/nthrough all the extra homework they were getting./nHermione had now started making study schedules/nfor Harry and Ron, too. It was driving them nuts./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThen, one breakfast time, Hedwig brought Harry/nanother note from Hagrid. He had written only two/nwords: It's hatching./n/nRon wanted to skip Herbology and go straight down to/nthe hut. Hermione wouldn't hear of it./n/n"Hermione, how many times in our lives are we going/nto see a dragon hatching?"/n/n"We've got lessons, we'll get into trouble, and that's/nnothing to what Hagrid 's going to be in when someone/nfinds out what he's doing — "/n/n"Shut up!" Harry whispered./n/nMalfoy was only a few feet away and he had stopped/ndead to listen. How much had he heard? Harry didn't/nlike the look on Malfoy's face at all./n/nRon and Hermione argued all the way to Herbology/nand in the end, Hermione agreed to run down to/nHagrid's with the other two during morning break./nWhen the bell sounded from the castle at the end of/ntheir lesson, the three of them dropped their trowels/nat once and hurried through the grounds to the edge/nof the forest. Hagrid greeted them, looking flushed/nand excited./n/n"It's nearly out." He ushered them inside./n/nThe egg was lying on the table. There were deep/ncracks in it. Something was moving inside; a funny/nclicking noise was coming from it./n/nThey all drew their chairs up to the table and watched/nwith bated breath./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAll at once there was a scraping noise and the egg/nsplit open. The baby dragon flopped onto the table. It/nwasn't exactly pretty; Harry thought it looked like a/ncrumpled, black umbrella. Its spiny wings were huge/ncompared to its skinny jet body, it had a long snout/nwith wide nostrils, the stubs of horns and bulging,/norange eyes./n/nIt sneezed. A couple of sparks flew out of its snout./n/n"Isn't he beautiful?" Hagrid murmured. He reached/nout a hand to stroke the dragon's head. It snapped at/nhis fingers, showing pointed fangs./n/n"Bless him, look, he knows his mommy!" said Hagrid./n/n"Hagrid," said Hermione, "how fast do Norwegian/nRidgebacks grow, exactly?"/n/nHagrid was about to answer when the color suddenly/ndrained from his face — he leapt to his feet and ran to/nthe window./n/n"What's the matter?"/n/n"Someone was lookin' through the gap in the curtains/n— it's a kid — he's runnin' back up ter the school."/n/nHarry bolted to the door and looked out. Even at a/ndistance there was no mistaking him./n/nMalfoy had seen the dragon./n/nSomething about the smile lurking on Malfoy's face/nduring the next week made Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nvery nervous. They spent most of their free time in/nHagrid 's darkened hut, trying to reason with him./n/n"Just let him go," Harry urged. "Set him free."/n/n/n/n/n/n"I can't," said Hagrid. "He's too little. He'd die."/n/n/n/nThey looked at the dragon. It had grown three times/nin length in just a week. Smoke kept furling out of its/nnostrils. Hagrid hadn't been doing his gamekeeping/nduties because the dragon was keeping him so busy./nThere were empty brandy bottles and chicken/nfeathers all over the floor./n/n"I've decided to call him Norbert," said Hagrid, looking/nat the dragon with misty eyes. "He really knows me/nnow, watch. Norbert! Norbert! Where's Mommy?"/n/n"He's lost his marbles," Ron muttered in Harry's ear./n/n"Hagrid," said Harry loudly, "give it two weeks and/nNorbert's going to be as long as your house. Malfoy/ncould go to Dumbledore at any moment."/n/nHagrid bit his lip./n/n"I — I know I can't keep him forever, but I can't jus'/ndump him, can't."/n/nHarry suddenly turned to Ron./n/n"Charlie," he said./n/n"You're losing it, too," said Ron. "I'm Ron, remember?"/n/n"No — Charlie — your brother, Charlie. In Romania./nStudying dragons. We could send Norbert to him./nCharlie can take care of him and then put him back/nin the wild!"/n/n"Brilliant!" said Ron. "How about it, Hagrid?"/n/nAnd in the end, Hagrid agreed that they could send/nan owl to Charlie to ask him./n/n/n/n/n/nThe following week dragged by. Wednesday night/nfound Hermione and Harry sitting alone in the/ncommon room, long after everyone else had gone to/nbed. The clock on the wall had just chimed midnight/nwhen the portrait hole burst open. Ron appeared out/nof nowhere as he pulled off Harry's Invisibility Cloak./nHe had been down at Hagrid's hut, helping him feed/nNorbert, who was now eating dead rats by the crate./n/n"It bit me!" he said, showing them his hand, which/nwas wrapped in a bloody handkerchief. "I'm not going/nto be able to hold a quill for a week. I tell you, that/ndragon's the most horrible animal I've ever met, but/nthe way Hagrid goes on about it, you'd think it was a/nfluffy little bunny rabbit. When it bit me he told me off/nfor frightening it. And when I left, he was singing it a/nlullaby."/n/nThere was a tap on the dark window./n/n"It's Hedwig!" said Harry, hurrying to let her in. "She'll/nhave Charlie's answer!"/n/nThe three of them put their heads together to read the/nnote./n/nDear Ron,/n/nHow are you? Thanks for the letter — I'd be glad to/ntake the Norwegian Ridgeback, but it won't be easy/ngetting him here. I think the best thing will be to send/nhim over with some friends of mine who are coming to/nvisit me next week. Trouble is, they mustn't be seen/ncarrying an illegal dragon./n/nCould you get the Ridgeback up the tallest tower at/nmidnight on Saturday? They can meet you there and/ntake him away while it's still dark./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSend me an answer as soon as possible./n/n/n/nLove,/n/nCharlie/n/nThey looked at one another./n/n"We've got the Invisibility Cloak," said Harry. "It/nshouldn't be too difficult — I think the cloak's big/nenough to cover two of us and Norbert."/n/nIt was a mark of how bad the last week had been that/nthe other two agreed with him. Anything to get rid of/nNorbert — and Malfoy./n/nThere was a hitch. By the next morning, Ron's bitten/nhand had swollen to twice its usual size. He didn't/nknow whether it was safe to go to Madam Pomfrey —/nwould she recognize a dragon bite? By the afternoon,/nthough, he had no choice. The cut had turned a nasty/nshade of green. It looked as if Norbert's fangs were/npoisonous./n/nHarry and Hermione rushed up to the hospital wing/nat the end of the day to find Ron in a terrible state in/nbed./n/n"It's not just my hand," he whispered, "although that/nfeels like it's about to fall off. Malfoy told Madam/nPomfrey he wanted to borrow one of my books so he/ncould come and have a good laugh at me. He kept/nthreatening to tell her what really bit me — I've told/nher it was a dog, but I don't think she believes me — I/nshouldn't have hit him at the Quidditch match, that's/nwhy he's doing this."/n/nHarry and Hermione tried to calm Ron down./n/n/n/n/n/n"It'll all be over at midnight on Saturday," said/nHermione, but this didn't soothe Ron at all. On the/ncontrary, he sat bolt upright and broke into a sweat./n/n"Midnight on Saturday!" he said in a hoarse voice./n/n"Oh no — oh no — I've just remembered — Charlie's/nletter was in that book Malfoy took, he's going to/nknow we're getting rid of Norbert."/n/nHarry and Hermione didn't get a chance to answer./nMadam Pomfrey came over at that moment and made/nthem leave, saying Ron needed sleep./n/n"It's too late to change the plan now," Harry told/nHermione. "We haven't got time to send Charlie/nanother owl, and this could be our only chance to get/nrid of Norbert. We'll have to risk it. And we have got/nthe Invisibility Cloak, Malfoy doesn't know about/nthat."/n/nThey found Fang the boarhound sitting outside with a/nbandaged tail when they went to tell Hagrid, who/nopened a window to talk to them./n/n"I won't let you in," he puffed. "Norbert's at a tricky/nstage — nothin' I can't handle."/n/nWhen they told him about Charlie's letter, his eyes/nfilled with tears, although that might have been/nbecause Norbert had just bitten him on the leg./n/n"Aargh! It's all right, he only got my boot — jus'/nplayin' — he's only a baby, after all."/n/nThe baby banged its tail on the wall, making the/nwindows rattle. Harry and Hermione walked back to/nthe castle feeling Saturday couldn't come quickly/nenough./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey would have felt sorry for Hagrid when the time/ncame for him to say good-bye to Norbert if they hadn't/nbeen so worried about what they had to do. It was a/nvery dark, cloudy night, and they were a bit late/narriving at Hagrid 's hut because they'd had to wait for/nPeeves to get out of their way in the entrance hall,/nwhere he'd been playing tennis against the wall./n/nHagrid had Norbert packed and ready in a large crate./n/n"He's got lots o' rats an' some brandy fer the journey,"/nsaid Hagrid in a muffled voice. "An' I've packed his/nteddy bear in case he gets lonely."/n/nFrom inside the crate came ripping noises that/nsounded to Harry as though the teddy was having his/nhead torn off./n/n"Bye-bye, Norbert!" Hagrid sobbed, as Harry and/nHermione covered the crate with the Invisibility Cloak/nand stepped underneath it themselves. "Mommy will/nnever forget you!"/n/nHow they managed to get the crate back up to the/ncastle, they never knew. Midnight ticked nearer as/nthey heaved Norbert up the marble staircase in the/nentrance hall and along the dark corridors. Up/nanother staircase, then another — even one of Harry's/nshortcuts didn't make the work much easier./n/n"Nearly there!" Harry panted as they reached the/ncorridor beneath the tallest tower./n/nThen a sudden movement ahead of them made them/nalmost drop the crate. Forgetting that they were/nalready invisible, they shrank into the shadows,/nstaring at the dark outlines of two people grappling/nwith each other ten feet away. A lamp flared./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor McGonagall, in a tartan bathrobe and a hair/nnet, had Malfoy by the ear./n/n/n/n"Detention!" she shouted. "And twenty points from/nSlytherin! Wandering around in the middle of the/nnight, how dare you — "/n/n"You don't understand, Professor. Harry Potter's/ncoming — he's got a dragon!"/n/n"What utter rubbish! How dare you tell such lies!/nCome on — I shall see Professor Snape about you,/nMalfoy!"/n/nThe steep spiral staircase up to the top of the tower/nseemed the easiest thing in the world after that. Not/nuntil they'd stepped out into the cold night air did/nthey throw off the cloak, glad to be able to breathe/nproperly again. Hermione did a sort of jig./n/n"Malfoy's got detention! I could sing!"/n/n"Don't," Harry advised her./n/nChuckling about Malfoy, they waited, Norbert/nthrashing about in his crate. About ten minutes later,/nfour broomsticks came swooping down out of the/ndarkness./n/nCharlie's friends were a cheery lot. They showed/nHarry and Hermione the harness they'd rigged up, so/nthey could suspend Norbert between them. They all/nhelped buckle Norbert safely into it and then Harry/nand Hermione shook hands with the others and/nthanked them very much./n/nAt last, Norbert was going ... going ... gone./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey slipped back down the spiral staircase, their/nhearts as light as their hands, now that Norbert was/noff them. No more dragon — Malfoy in detention —/nwhat could spoil their happiness?/n/nThe answer to that was waiting at the foot of the/nstairs. As they stepped into the corridor, Filch's face/nloomed suddenly out of the darkness./n/n"Well, well, well," he whispered, "we are in trouble."/n/nThey'd left the Invisibility Cloak on top of the tower./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Forbidden Forest
text: /nThings couldn't have been worse./n/nFilch took them down to Professor McGonagall's/nstudy on the first floor, where they sat and waited/nwithout saying a word to each other. Hermione was/ntrembling. Excuses, alibis, and wild cover-up stories/nchased each other around Harry's brain, each more/nfeeble than the last. He couldn't see how they were/ngoing to get out of trouble this time. They were/ncornered. How could they have been so stupid as to/nforget the cloak? There was no reason on earth that/nProfessor McGonagall would accept for their being out/nof bed and creeping around the school in the dead of/nnight, let alone being up the tallest Astronomy Tower,/nwhich was out-of-bounds except for classes. Add/nNorbert and the Invisibility Cloak, and they might as/nwell be packing their bags already./n/nHad Harry thought that things couldn't have been/nworse? He was wrong. When Professor McGonagall/nappeared, she was leading Neville./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry!" Neville burst out, the moment he saw the/nother two. "I was trying to find you to warn you, I/nheard Malfoy saying he was going to catch you, he/nsaid you had a drag — "/n/nHarry shook his head violently to shut Neville up, but/nProfessor McGonagall had seen. She looked more/nlikely to breathe fire than Norbert as she towered over/nthe three of them./n/n"I would never have believed it of any of you. Mr. Filch/nsays you were up in the Astronomy Tower. It's one/no'clock in the morning. Explain yourselves."/n/nIt was the first time Hermione had ever failed to/nanswer a teacher's question. She was staring at her/nslippers, as still as a statue./n/n"I think I've got a good idea of what's been going on,"/nsaid Professor McGonagall. "It doesn't take a genius/nto work it out. You fed Draco Malfoy some cock-and-/nbull story about a dragon, trying to get him out of bed/nand into trouble. I've already caught him. I suppose/nyou think it's funny that Longbottom here heard the/nstory and believed it, too?"/n/nHarry caught Neville's eye and tried to tell him/nwithout words that this wasn't true, because Neville/nwas looking stunned and hurt. Poor, blundering/nNeville — Harry knew what it must have cost him to/ntry and find them in the dark, to warn them./n/n"I'm disgusted," said Professor McGonagall. "Four/nstudents out of bed in one night! I've never heard of/nsuch a thing before! You, Miss Granger, I thought you/nhad more sense. As for you, Mr. Potter, I thought/nGryffindor meant more to you than this. All three of/nyou will receive detentions — yes, you too, Mr./nLongbottom, nothing gives you the right to walk/n/n/n/n/naround school at night, especially these days, it's very/ndangerous — and fifty points will be taken from/nGryffindor."/n/n"Fifty?" Harry gasped — they would lose the lead, the/nlead he'd won in the last Quidditch match./n/n"Fifty points each," said Professor McGonagall,/nbreathing heavily through her long, pointed nose./n/n"Professor — please — "/n/n"You can't—"/n/n"Don't tell me what I can and can't do, Potter. Now get/nback to bed, all of you. I've never been more ashamed/nof Gryffindor students."/n/nA hundred and fifty points lost. That put Gryffindor in/nlast place. In one night, they'd ruined any chance/nGryffindor had had for the House Cup. Harry felt as/nthough the bottom had dropped out of his stomach./nHow could they ever make up for this?/n/nHarry didn't sleep all night. He could hear Neville/nsobbing into his pillow for what seemed like hours./nHarry couldn't think of anything to say to comfort/nhim. He knew Neville, like himself, was dreading the/ndawn. What would happen when the rest of/nGryffindor found out what they'd done?/n/nAt first, Gryffindors passing the giant hourglasses/nthat recorded the House points the next day thought/nthere 'd been a mistake. How could they suddenly/nhave a hundred and fifty points fewer than yesterday?/nAnd then the story started to spread: Harry Potter,/nthe famous Harry Potter, their hero of two Quidditch/nmatches, had lost them all those points, him and a/ncouple of other stupid first years./n/n/n/n/n/nFrom being one of the most popular and admired/npeople at the school, Harry was suddenly the most/nhated. Even Ravenclaws and Hufflepuffs turned on/nhim, because everyone had been longing to see/nSlytherin lose the House Cup. Everywhere Harry/nwent, people pointed and didn't trouble to lower their/nvoices as they insulted him. Slytherins, on the other/nhand, clapped as he walked past them, whistling and/ncheering, "Thanks Potter, we owe you one!"/n/nOnly Ron stood by him./n/n"They'll all forget this in a few weeks. Fred and George/nhave lost loads of points in all the time they've been/nhere, and people still like them."/n/n"They've never lost a hundred and fifty points in one/ngo, though, have they?" said Harry miserably./n/n"Well — no," Ron admitted./n/nIt was a bit late to repair the damage, but Harry/nswore to himself not to meddle in things that weren't/nhis business from now on. He'd had it with sneaking/naround and spying. He felt so ashamed of himself that/nhe went to Wood and offered to resign from the/nQuidditch team./n/n"Resign?" Wood thundered. "What good'll that do?/n/nHow are we going to get any points back if we can't/nwin at Quidditch?"/n/nBut even Quidditch had lost its fun. The rest of the/nteam wouldn't speak to Harry during practice, and if/nthey had to speak about him, they called him "the/nSeeker."/n/nHermione and Neville were suffering, too. They didn't/nhave as bad a time as Harry, because they weren't as/n/n/n/n/n/nwell-known, but nobody would speak to them, either./nHermione had stopped drawing attention to herself in/nclass, keeping her head down and working in silence./n/nHarry was almost glad that the exams weren't far/naway. All the studying he had to do kept his mind off/nhis misery. He, Ron, and Hermione kept to/nthemselves, working late into the night, trying to/nremember the ingredients in complicated potions,/nlearn charms and spells by heart, memorize the dates/nof magical discoveries and goblin rebellions. .../n/nThen, about a week before the exams were due to/nstart, Harry's new resolution not to interfere in/nanything that didn't concern him was put to an/nunexpected test. Walking back from the library on his/nown one afternoon, he heard somebody whimpering/nfrom a classroom up ahead. As he drew closer, he/nheard Quirrell's voice./n/n"No — no — not again, please — "/n/nIt sounded as though someone was threatening him./nHarry moved closer./n/n"All right — all right — " he heard Quirrell sob./n/nNext second, Quirrell came hurrying out of the/nclassroom straightening his turban. He was pale and/nlooked as though he was about to cry. He strode out/nof sight; Harry didn't think Quirrell had even noticed/nhim. He waited until Quirrell's footsteps had/ndisappeared, then peered into the classroom. It was/nempty, but a door stood ajar at the other end. Harry/nwas halfway toward it before he remembered what/nhe'd promised himself about not meddling./n/nAll the same, he'd have gambled twelve Sorcerer's/nStones that Snape had just left the room, and from/n/n/n/n/n/nwhat Harry had just heard, Snape would be walking/nwith a new spring in his step — Quirrell seemed to/nhave given in at last./n/nHarry went back to the library, where Hermione was/ntesting Ron on Astronomy. Harry told them what he'd/nheard./n/n"Snape's done it, then!" said Ron. "If Quirrell's told/nhim how to break his Anti-Dark Force spell — "/n/n"There's still Fluffy, though," said Hermione./n/n"Maybe Snape's found out how to get past him/nwithout asking Hagrid," said Ron, looking up at the/nthousands of books surrounding them. "I bet there's a/nbook somewhere in here telling you how to get past a/ngiant three-headed dog. So what do we do, Harry?"/n/nThe light of adventure was kindling again in Ron's/neyes, but Hermione answered before Harry could./n/n"Go to Dumbledore. That's what we should have done/nages ago. If we try anything ourselves we'll be thrown/nout for sure."/n/n"But we've got no proof." said Harry. "Quirrell's too/nscared to back us up. Snape's only got to say he/ndoesn't know how the troll got in at Halloween and/nthat he was nowhere near the third floor — who do/nyou think they'll believe, him or us? It's not exactly a/nsecret we hate him, Dumbledore 'll think we made it/nup to get him sacked. Filch wouldn't help us if his life/ndepended on it, he's too friendly with Snape, and the/nmore students get thrown out, the better, he'll think./nAnd don't forget, we're not supposed to know about/nthe Stone or Fluffy. That'll take a lot of explaining."/n/nHermione looked convinced, but Ron didn't./n/n/n/n/n/n"If we just do a bit of poking around — "/n/n/n/n"No," said Harry flatly, "we've done enough poking/naround."/n/nHe pulled a map of Jupiter toward him and started to/nlearn the names of its moons./n/nThe following morning, notes were delivered to Harry,/nHermione, and Neville at the breakfast table. They/nwere all the same:/n/nYour detention will take place at eleven o'clock/ntonight./n/nMeet Mr. Filch in the entrance hall./n/nProfessor M. McGonagall/n/nHarry had forgotten they still had detentions to do in/nthe furor over the points they'd lost. He half expected/nHermione to complain that this was a whole night of/nstudying lost, but she didn't say a word. Like Harry,/nshe felt they deserved what they'd got./n/nAt eleven o'clock that night, they said good-bye to Ron/nin the common room and went down to the entrance/nhall with Neville. Filch was already there — and so/nwas Malfoy. Harry had also forgotten that Malfoy had/ngotten a detention, too./n/n"Follow me," said Filch, lighting a lamp and leading/nthem outside./n/n"I bet you'll think twice about breaking a school rule/nagain, won't you, eh?" he said, leering at them. "Oh/nyes . . . hard work and pain are the best teachers if you/nask me. ... It's just a pity they let the old/npunishments die out . . . hang you by your wrists from/n/n/n/n/nthe ceiling for a few days, I've got the chains still in/nmy office, keep 'em well oiled in case they're ever/nneeded. ... Right, off we go, and don't think of running/noff, now, it'll be worse for you if you do."/n/nThey marched off across the dark grounds. Neville/nkept sniffing. Harry wondered what their punishment/nwas going to be. It must be something really horrible,/nor Filch wouldn't be sounding so delighted./n/nThe moon was bright, but clouds scudding across it/nkept throwing them into darkness. Ahead, Harry/ncould see the lighted windows of Hagrid's hut. Then/nthey heard a distant shout./n/n"Is that you, Filch? Hurry up, I want ter get started."/n/nHarry's heart rose; if they were going to be working/nwith Hagrid it wouldn't be so bad. His relief must/nhave showed in his face, because Filch said, "I/nsuppose you think you'll be enjoying yourself with/nthat oaf? Well, think again, boy — it's into the forest/nyou're going and I'm much mistaken if you'll all come/nout in one piece."/n/nAt this, Neville let out a little moan, and Malfoy/nstopped dead in his tracks./n/n"The forest?" he repeated, and he didn't sound quite/nas cool as usual. "We can't go in there at night —/nthere's all sorts of things in there — werewolves, I/nheard."/n/nNeville clutched the sleeve of Harry's robe and made a/nchoking noise./n/n"That's your problem, isn't it?" said Filch, his voice/ncracking with glee. "Should've thought of them/nwerewolves before you got in trouble, shouldn't you?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid came striding toward them out of the dark,/nFang at his heel. He was carrying his large crossbow,/nand a quiver of arrows hung over his shoulder./n/n"Abou' time," he said. "I bin waitin' fer half an hour/nalready. All right, Harry, Hermione?"/n/n"I shouldn't be too friendly to them, Hagrid," said/nFilch coldly, "they're here to be punished, after all."/n/n"That's why yer late, is it?" said Hagrid, frowning at/nFilch. "Bin lecturin' them, eh? 'Snot your place ter do/nthat. Yeh've done yer bit, I'll take over from here."/n/n"I'll be back at dawn," said Filch, "for what's left of/nthem," he added nastily, and he turned and started/nback toward the castle, his lamp bobbing away in the/ndarkness./n/nMalfoy now turned to Hagrid./n/n"I'm not going in that forest," he said, and Harry was/npleased to hear the note of panic in his voice./n/n"Yeh are if yeh want ter stay at Hogwarts," said/nHagrid fiercely. "Yeh've done wrong an' now yeh've got/nter pay fer it."/n/n"But this is servant stuff, it's not for students to do. I/nthought we'd be copying lines or something, if my/nfather knew I was doing this, he'd — "/n/n" — tell yer that's how it is at Hogwarts," Hagrid/ngrowled. "Copyin' lines! What good's that ter anyone?/nYeh'll do summat useful or yeh'll get out. If yeh think/nyer father'd rather you were expelled, then get back/noff ter the castle an' pack. Go on!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMalfoy didn't move. He looked at Hagrid furiously, but/nthen dropped his gaze./n/n"Right then," said Hagrid, "now, listen carefully,/n/n'cause it's dangerous what we're gonna do tonight, an'/nI don' want no one takin' risks. Follow me over here a/nmoment."/n/nHe led them to the very edge of the forest. Holding his/nlamp up high, he pointed down a narrow, winding/nearth track that disappeared into the thick black/ntrees. A light breeze lifted their hair as they looked/ninto the forest./n/n"Look there," said Hagrid, "see that stuff shinin' on/nthe ground? Silvery stuff? That's unicorn blood./nThere's a unicorn in there bin hurt badly by summat./nThis is the second time in a week. I found one dead/nlast Wednesday. We're gonna try an' find the poor/nthing. We might have ter put it out of its misery."/n/n"And what if whatever hurt the unicorn finds us/nfirst?" said Malfoy, unable to keep the fear out of his/nvoice./n/n"There's nothin' that lives in the forest that'll hurt yeh/nif yer with me or Fang," said Hagrid. "An' keep ter the/npath. Right, now, we're gonna split inter two parties/nan' follow the trail in diff'rent directions. There's blood/nall over the place, it must've bin staggerin' around/nsince last night at least."/n/n"I want Fang," said Malfoy quickly, looking at Fang's/nlong teeth./n/n"All right, but I warn yeh, he's a coward," said Hagrid./n"So me, Harry, an' Hermione'll go one way an' Draco,/nNeville, an' Fang'll go the other. Now, if any of us/nfinds the unicorn, we'll send up green sparks, right?/n/n/n/n/n/nGet yer wands out an' practice now — that's it — an'/nif anyone gets in trouble, send up red sparks, an' we'll/nall come an' find yeh — so, be careful — let's go."/n/nThe forest was black and silent. A little way into it/nthey reached a fork in the earth path, and Harry,/nHermione, and Hagrid took the left path while Malfoy,/nNeville, and Fang took the right./n/nThey walked in silence, their eyes on the ground./nEvery now and then a ray of moonlight through the/nbranches above lit a spot of silver-blue blood on the/nfallen leaves./n/nHarry saw that Hagrid looked very worried./n/n" Could a werewolf be killing the unicorns?" Harry/nasked./n/n"Not fast enough," said Hagrid. "It's not easy ter catch/na unicorn, they're powerful magic creatures. I never/nknew one ter be hurt before."/n/nThey walked past a mossy tree stump. Harry could/nhear running water; there must be a stream/nsomewhere close by. There were still spots of unicorn/nblood here and there along the winding path./n/n"You all right, Hermione?" Hagrid whispered. "Don'/nworry, it can't've gone far if it's this badly hurt, an'/nthen well be able ter — GET BEHIND THAT TREE!"/n/nHagrid seized Harry and Hermione and hoisted them/noff the path behind a towering oak. He pulled out an/narrow and fitted it into his crossbow, raising it, ready/nto fire. The three of them listened. Something was/nslithering over dead leaves nearby: it sounded like a/ncloak trailing along the ground. Hagrid was squinting/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nup the dark path, but after a few seconds, the sound/nfaded away./n/n"I knew it," he murmured. "There's summat in here/nthat shouldn' be."/n/n"A werewolf?" Harry suggested./n/n"That wasn' no werewolf an' it wasn' no unicorn,/nneither," said Hagrid grimly. "Right, follow me, but/ncareful, now."/n/nThey walked more slowly, ears straining for the/nfaintest sound. Suddenly, in a clearing ahead,/nsomething definitely moved./n/n"Who's there?" Hagrid called. "Show yerself — I'm/narmed!"/n/nAnd into the clearing came — was it a man, or a/nhorse? To the waist, a man, with red hair and beard,/nbut below that was a horse's gleaming chestnut body/nwith a long, reddish tail. Harry and Hermione's jaws/ndropped./n/n"Oh, it's you, Ronan," said Hagrid in relief. "How are/nyeh?"/n/nHe walked forward and shook the centaur's hand./n/n"Good evening to you, Hagrid," said Ronan. He had a/ndeep, sorrowful voice. "Were you going to shoot me?"/n/n"Can't be too careful, Ronan," said Hagrid, patting his/ncrossbow. "There's summat bad loose in this forest./nThis is Harry Potter an' Hermione Granger, by the/nway. Students up at the school. An' this is Ronan,/nyou two. He's a centaur."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We'd noticed," said Hermione faintly./n/n/n/n"Good evening," said Ronan. "Students, are you? And/ndo you learn much, up at the school?"/n/n"Erm — "/n/n"A bit," said Hermione timidly./n/n"A bit. Well, that's something." Ronan sighed. He/nflung back his head and stared at the sky. "Mars is/nbright tonight."/n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid, glancing up, too. "Listen, I'm glad/nwe've run inter yeh, Ronan, 'cause there's a unicorn/nbin hurt — you seen anythin'?"/n/nRonan didn't answer immediately. He stared/nunblinkingly upward, then sighed again./n/n"Always the innocent are the first victims," he said./n/n"So it has been for ages past, so it is now."/n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid, "but have yeh seen anythin',/nRonan? Anythin' unusual?"/n/n"Mars is bright tonight," Ronan repeated, while/nHagrid watched him impatiently. "Unusually bright."/n/n"Yeah, but I was meanin' anythin' unusual a bit/nnearer home," said Hagrid. "So yeh haven't noticed/nanythin' strange?"/n/nYet again, Ronan took a while to answer. At last, he/nsaid, "The forest hides many secrets."/n/nA movement in the trees behind Ronan made Hagrid/nraise his bow again, but it was only a second centaur,/n/n/n/n/n/nblack-haired and -bodied and wilder-looking than/nRonan./n/n/n/n"Hullo, Bane," said Hagrid. "All right?"/n/n"Good evening, Hagrid, I hope you are well?"/n/n"Well enough. Look, I've jus' bin askin' Ronan, you/nseen anythin' odd in here lately? There's a unicorn/nbin injured — would yeh know anythin' about it?"/n/nBane walked over to stand next to Ronan. He looked/nskyward./n/n"Mars is bright tonight," he said simply./n/n"We've heard," said Hagrid grumpily. "Well, if either of/nyou do see anythin', let me know, won't yeh? We'll be/noff, then."/n/nHarry and Hermione followed him out of the clearing,/nstaring over their shoulders at Ronan and Bane until/nthe trees blocked their view./n/n"Never," said Hagrid irritably, "try an' get a straight/nanswer out of a centaur. Ruddy stargazers. Not/ninterested in anythin' closer'n the moon."/n/n"Are there many of them in here?" asked Hermione./n/n"Oh, a fair few. . . . Keep themselves to themselves/nmostly, but they're good enough about turnin' up if/never I want a word. They're deep, mind, centaurs .../nthey know things ... jus' don' let on much."/n/n"D'you think that was a centaur we heard earlier?"/nsaid Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Did that sound like hooves to you? Nah, if yeh ask/nme, that was what's bin killin' the unicorns — never/nheard anythin' like it before."/n/nThey walked on through the dense, dark trees. Harry/nkept looking nervously over his shoulder. He had the/nnasty feeling they were being watched. He was very/nglad they had Hagrid and his crossbow with them./nThey had just passed a bend in the path when/nHermione grabbed Hagrid 's arm./n/n"Hagrid! Look! Red sparks, the others are in trouble!"/n/n"You two wait here!" Hagrid shouted. "Stay on the/npath, I'll come back for yeh!"/n/nThey heard him crashing away through the/nundergrowth and stood looking at each other, very/nscared, until they couldn't hear anything but the/nrustling of leaves around them./n/n"You don't think they've been hurt, do you?"/nwhispered Hermione./n/n"I don't care if Malfoy has, but if something's got/nNeville ... it's our fault he's here in the first place."/n/nThe minutes dragged by. Their ears seemed sharper/nthan usual. Harry's seemed to be picking up every/nsigh of the wind, every cracking twig. What was going/non? Where were the others?/n/nAt last, a great crunching noise announced Hagrid's/nreturn. Malfoy, Neville, and Fang were with him./nHagrid was fuming. Malfoy, it seemed, had sneaked/nup behind Neville and grabbed him as a joke. Neville/nhad panicked and sent up the sparks./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well be lucky ter catch anythin' now, with the racket/nyou two were makin'. Right, we're changin' groups —/nNeville, you stay with me an' Hermione, Harry, you go/nwith Fang an' this idiot. I'm sorry," Hagrid added in a/nwhisper to Harry, "but he'll have a harder time/nfrightenin' you, an' we've gotta get this done."/n/nSo Harry set off into the heart of the forest with/nMalfoy and Fang. They walked for nearly half an/nhour, deeper and deeper into the forest, until the path/nbecame almost impossible to follow because the trees/nwere so thick. Harry thought the blood seemed to be/ngetting thicker. There were splashes on the roots of a/ntree, as though the poor creature had been thrashing/naround in pain close by. Harry could see a clearing/nahead, through the tangled branches of an ancient/noak./n/n"Look — " he murmured, holding out his arm to stop/nMalfoy./n/nSomething bright white was gleaming on the ground./nThey inched closer./n/nIt was the unicorn all right, and it was dead. Harry/nhad never seen anything so beautiful and sad. Its/nlong, slender legs were stuck out at odd angles where/nit had fallen and its mane was spread pearly-white on/nthe dark leaves./n/nHarry had taken one step toward it when a slithering/nsound made him freeze where he stood. A bush on/nthe edge of the clearing quivered. ... Then, out of the/nshadows, a hooded figure came crawling across the/nground like some stalking beast. Harry, Malfoy, and/nFang stood transfixed. The cloaked figure reached the/nunicorn, lowered its head over the wound in the/nanimals side, and began to drink its blood./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"AAAAAAAAAAARGH ! "/n/n/n/nMalfoy let out a terrible scream and bolted — so did/nFang. The hooded figure raised its head and looked/nright at Harry — unicorn blood was dribbling down its/nfront. It got to its feet and came swiftly toward Harry/n— he couldn't move for fear./n/nThen a pain like he'd never felt before pierced his/nhead; it was as though his scar were on fire. Half/nblinded, he staggered backward. He heard hooves/nbehind him, galloping, and something jumped clean/nover Harry, charging at the figure./n/nThe pain in Harry's head was so bad he fell to his/nknees. It took a minute or two to pass. When he/nlooked up, the figure had gone. A centaur was/nstanding over him, not Ronan or Bane; this one/nlooked younger; he had white-blond hair and a/npalomino body./n/n"Are you all right?" said the centaur, pulling Harry to/nhis feet./n/n"Yes — thank you — what was that?"/n/nThe centaur didn't answer. He had astonishingly blue/neyes, like pale sapphires. He looked carefully at/nHarry, his eyes lingering on the scar that stood out,/nlivid, on Harry's forehead./n/n"You are the Potter boy," he said. "You had better get/nback to Hagrid. The forest is not safe at this time —/nespecially for you. Can you ride? It will be quicker/nthis way./n/n"My name is Firenze," he added, as he lowered/nhimself on to his front legs so that Harry could/nclamber onto his back./n/n/n/n/n/nThere was suddenly a sound of more galloping from/nthe other side of the clearing. Ronan and Bane came/nbursting through the trees, their flanks heaving and/nsweaty./n/n"Firenze!" Bane thundered. "What are you doing? You/nhave a human on your back! Have you no shame? Are/nyou a common mule?"/n/n"Do you realize who this is?" said Firenze. "This is the/nPotter boy. The quicker he leaves this forest, the/nbetter."/n/n"What have you been telling him?" growled Bane./n"Remember, Firenze, we are sworn not to set/nourselves against the heavens. Have we not read what/nis to come in the movements of the planets?"/n/nRonan pawed the ground nervously. "I'm sure Firenze/nthought he was acting for the best," he said in his/ngloomy voice./n/nBane kicked his back legs in anger./n/n"For the best! What is that to do with us? Centaurs/nare concerned with what has been foretold! It is not/nour business to run around like donkeys after stray/nhumans in our forest!"/n/nFirenze suddenly reared on to his hind legs in anger,/nso that Harry had to grab his shoulders to stay on./n/n"Do you not see that unicorn?" Firenze bellowed at/nBane. "Do you not understand why it was killed? Or/nhave the planets not let you in on that secret? I set/nmyself against what is lurking in this forest, Bane,/nyes, with humans alongside me if I must."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd Firenze whisked around; with Harry clutching on/nas best he could, they plunged off into the trees,/nleaving Ronan and Bane behind them./n/nHarry didn't have a clue what was going on./n/n"Why's Bane so angry?" he asked. "What was that/nthing you saved me from, anyway?"/n/nFirenze slowed to a walk, warned Harry to keep his/nhead bowed in case of low-hanging branches, but did/nnot answer Harry's question. They made their way/nthrough the trees in silence for so long that Harry/nthought Firenze didn't want to talk to him anymore./nThey were passing through a particularly dense patch/nof trees, however, when Firenze suddenly stopped./n/n"Harry Potter, do you know what unicorn blood is/nused for?"/n/n"No," said Harry, startled by the odd question. "We've/nonly used the horn and tail hair in Potions."/n/n"That is because it is a monstrous thing, to slay a/nunicorn," said Firenze. "Only one who has nothing to/nlose, and everything to gain, would commit such a/ncrime. The blood of a unicorn will keep you alive, even/nif you are an inch from death, but at a terrible price./nYou have slain something pure and defenseless to/nsave yourself, and you will have but a half-life, a/ncursed life, from the moment the blood touches your/nlips."/n/nHarry stared at the back of Firenze's head, which was/ndappled silver in the moonlight./n/n"But who'd be that desperate?" he wondered aloud. "If/nyou're going to be cursed forever, death's better, isn't/nit?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"It is," Firenze agreed, "unless all you need is to stay/nalive long enough to drink something else —/nsomething that will bring you back to full strength/nand power — something that will mean you can never/ndie. Mr. Potter, do you know what is hidden in the/nschool at this very moment?"/n/n"The Sorcerer's Stone! Of course — the Elixir of Life!/nBut I don't understand who — "/n/n"Can you think of nobody who has waited many years/nto return to power, who has clung to life, awaiting/ntheir chance?"/n/nIt was as though an iron fist had clenched suddenly/naround Harry's heart. Over the rustling of the trees,/nhe seemed to hear once more what Hagrid had told/nhim on the night they had met: "Some say he died./nCodswallop, in my opinion. Dunno if he had enough/nhuman left in him to die."/n/n"Do you mean," Harry croaked, "that was VoZ — "/n/n"Harry! Harry, are you all right?"/n/nHermione was running toward them down the path,/nHagrid puffing along behind her./n/n"I'm fine," said Harry, hardly knowing what he was/nsaying. "The unicorn's dead, Hagrid, it's in that/nclearing back there."/n/n"This is where I leave you," Firenze murmured as/nHagrid hurried off to examine the unicorn. "You are/nsafe now."/n/nHarry slid off his back./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Good luck, Harry Potter," said Firenze. "The planets/nhave been read wrongly before now, even by centaurs./nI hope this is one of those times."/n/nHe turned and cantered back into the depths of the/nforest, leaving Harry shivering behind him./n/nRon had fallen asleep in the dark common room,/nwaiting for them to return. He shouted something/nabout Quidditch fouls when Harry roughly shook him/nawake. In a matter of seconds, though, he was wide-/neyed as Harry began to tell him and Hermione what/nhad happened in the forest./n/nHarry couldn't sit down. He paced up and down in/nfront of the fire. He was still shaking./n/n"Snape wants the Stone for Voldemort ... and/nVoldemort's waiting in the forest ... and all this time/nwe thought Snape just wanted to get rich. ..."/n/n"Stop saying the name!" said Ron in a terrified/nwhisper, as if he thought Voldemort could hear them./n/nHarry wasn't listening./n/n"Firenze saved me, but he shouldn't have done so. .../nBane was furious ... he was talking about interfering/nwith what the planets say is going to happen. ... They/nmust show that Voldemort's coming back. ... Bane/nthinks Firenze should have let Voldemort kill me. ... I/nsuppose that's written in the stars as well."/n/n"Will you stop saying the name\" Ron hissed./n/n"So all I've got to wait for now is Snape to steal the/nStone," Harry went on feverishly, "then Voldemort will/nbe able to come and finish me off. ... Well, I suppose/nBane 11 be happy."/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione looked very frightened, but she had a word/nof comfort./n/n"Harry, everyone says Dumbledore's the only one/nYou-Know-Who was ever afraid of. With Dumbledore/naround, You-Know-Who won't touch you. Anyway,/nwho says the centaurs are right? It sounds like/nfortune-telling to me, and Professor McGonagall says/nthat's a very imprecise branch of magic."/n/nThe sky had turned light before they stopped talking./nThey went to bed exhausted, their throats sore. But/nthe night's surprises weren't over./n/nWhen Harry pulled back his sheets, he found his/nInvisibility Cloak folded neatly underneath them./nThere was a note pinned to it:/n/nJust in case./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Through The Trapdoor
text: /nIn years to come, Harry would never quite remember/nhow he had managed to get through his exams when/nhe half expected Voldemort to come bursting through/nthe door at any moment. Yet the days crept by, and/nthere could be no doubt that Fluffy was still alive and/nwell behind the locked door./n/nIt was sweltering hot, especially in the large/nclassroom where they did their written papers. They/nhad been given special, new quills for the exams,/nwhich had been bewitched with an Anti-Cheating/nspell./n/nThey had practical exams as well. Professor Flitwick/ncalled them one by one into his class to see if they/ncould make a pineapple tap-dance across a desk./nProfessor McGonagall watched them turn a mouse/ninto a snuffbox — points were given for how pretty the/nsnuffbox was, but taken away if it had whiskers./nSnape made them all nervous, breathing down their/nnecks while they tried to remember how to make a/nForgetfulness potion./n/n/n/n/nHarry did the best he could, trying to ignore the/nstabbing pains in his forehead, which had been/nbothering him ever since his trip into the forest./nNeville thought Harry had a bad case of exam nerves/nbecause Harry couldn't sleep, but the truth was that/nHarry kept being woken by his old nightmare, except/nthat it was now worse than ever because there was a/nhooded figure dripping blood in it./n/nMaybe it was because they hadn't seen what Harry/nhad seen in the forest, or because they didn't have/nscars burning on their foreheads, but Ron and/nHermione didn't seem as worried about the Stone as/nHarry. The idea of Voldemort certainly scared them,/nbut he didn't keep visiting them in dreams, and they/nwere so busy with their studying they didn't have/nmuch time to fret about what Snape or anyone else/nmight be up to./n/nTheir very last exam was History of Magic. One hour/nof answering questions about batty old wizards who'd/ninvented self-stirring cauldrons and they'd be free,/nfree for a whole wonderful week until their exam/nresults came out. When the ghost of Professor Binns/ntold them to put down their quills and roll up their/nparchment, Harry couldn't help cheering with the/nrest./n/n"That was far easier than I thought it would be," said/nHermione as they joined the crowds flocking out onto/nthe sunny grounds. "I needn't have learned about the/n1637 Werewolf Code of Conduct or the uprising of/nElfric the Eager."/n/nHermione always liked to go through their exam/npapers afterward, but Ron said this made him feel ill,/nso they wandered down to the lake and flopped under/na tree. The Weasley twins and Lee Jordan were/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ntickling the tentacles of a giant squid, which was/nbasking in the warm shallows./n/n/n/n"No more studying," Ron sighed happily, stretching/nout on the grass. But as they stepped into it, light/nsuddenly flooded the room to reveal an astonishing/nsight./n/nThey were standing on the edge of a huge chessboard,/nbehind the black chessmen, which were all taller than/nthey were and carved from what looked like black/nstone. Facing them, way across the chamber, were/nthe white pieces. Harry, Ron and Hermione shivered/nslightly — the towering white chessmen had no faces./n/n"Now what do we do?" Harry whispered./n/n/n/n/n/n"It's obvious, isn't it?" said Ron. "We've got to play our/nway across the room."/n/n/n/nBehind the white pieces they could see another door./n/n"How?" said Hermione nervously./n/n"I think," said Ron, "we're going to have to be/nchessmen."/n/nHe walked up to a black knight and put his hand out/nto touch the knights horse. At once, the stone sprang/nto life. The horse pawed the ground and the knight/nturned his helmeted head to look down at Ron./n/n"Do we — er — have to join you to get across?"/n/nThe black knight nodded. Ron turned to the other/ntwo./n/n"This needs thinking about. ..." he said. "I suppose/nwe've got to take the place of three of the black pieces./n/n/n/nHarry and Hermione stayed quiet, watching Ron/nthink. Finally he said, "Now, don't be offended or/nanything, but neither of you are that good at chess —/n/n/n/n"We're not offended," said Harry quickly. "Just tell us/nwhat to do."/n/n"Well, Harry, you take the place of that bishop, and/nHermione, you go there instead of that castle."/n/n"What about you?"/n/n"I'm going to be a knight," said Ron./n/n/n/n/n/nThe chessmen seemed to have been listening, because/nat these words a knight, a bishop, and a castle turned/ntheir backs on the white pieces and walked off the/nboard, leaving three empty squares that Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione took./n/n"White always plays first in chess," said Ron, peering/nacross the board. "Yes ... look ..."/n/nA white pawn had moved forward two squares./n/nRon started to direct the black pieces. They moved/nsilently wherever he sent them. Harry's knees were/ntrembling. What if they lost?/n/n"Harry — move diagonally four squares to the right."/n/nTheir first real shock came when their other knight/nwas taken. The white queen smashed him to the floor/nand dragged him off the board, where he lay quite/nstill, facedown./n/n"Had to let that happen," said Ron, looking shaken./n"Leaves you free to take that bishop, Hermione, go/non."/n/nEvery time one of their men was lost, the white pieces/nshowed no mercy. Soon there was a huddle of limp/nblack players slumped along the wall. Twice, Ron only/njust noticed in time that Harry and Hermione were in/ndanger. He himself darted around the board, taking/nalmost as many white pieces as they had lost black/nones./n/n"We're nearly there," he muttered suddenly. "Let me/nthink — let me think ..."/n/nThe white queen turned her blank face toward him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes ..." said Ron softly, "it's the only way ... I've got/nto be taken."/n/n/n/n"NO!" Harry and Hermione shouted./n/n"That's chess!" snapped Ron. "You've got to make/nsome sacrifices!
