He leaned on/nthe sill, the cool night air pleasant on his face after a/nlong time under the blankets. Hedwig had been/nabsent for two nights now. Harry wasn't worried/nabout her: she'd been gone this long before. But he/nhoped she'd be back soon — she was the only living/ncreature in this house who didn't flinch at the sight of/nhim./n/nHarry, though still rather small and skinny for his/nage, had grown a few inches over the last year. His/njet-black hair, however, was just as it always had/nbeen — stubbornly untidy, whatever he did to it. The/neyes behind his glasses were bright green, and on his/nforehead, clearly visible through his hair, was a thin/nscar, shaped like a bolt of lightning./n/nOf all the unusual things about Harry, this scar was/nthe most extraordinary of all. It was not, as the/nDursleys had pretended for ten years, a souvenir of/nthe car crash that had killed Harry's parents, because/nLily and James Potter had not died in a car crash./nThey had been murdered, murdered by the most/nfeared Dark wizard for a hundred years, Lord/nVoldemort. Harry had escaped from the same attack/nwith nothing more than a scar on his forehead, where/nVoldemort's curse, instead of killing him, had/nrebounded upon its originator. Barely alive,/n/nVoldemort had fled. .../n/nBut Harry had come face-to-face with him at/nHogwarts. Remembering their last meeting as he/nstood at the dark window, Harry had to admit he was/nlucky even to have reached his thirteenth birthday./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe scanned the starry sky for a sign of Hedwig,/nperhaps soaring back to him with a dead mouse/ndangling from her beak, expecting praise. Gazing/nabsently over the rooftops, it was a few seconds before/nHarry realized what he was seeing./n/nSilhouetted against the golden moon, and growing/nlarger every moment, was a large, strangely lopsided/ncreature, and it was flapping in Harry's direction. He/nstood quite still, watching it sink lower and lower. For/na split second he hesitated, his hand on the window/nlatch, wondering whether to slam it shut. But then/nthe bizarre creature soared over one of the street/nlamps of Privet Drive, and Harry, realizing what it/nwas, leapt aside./n/nThrough the window soared three owls, two of them/nholding up the third, which appeared to be/nunconscious. They landed with a soft flump on/nHarry's bed, and the middle owl, which was large and/ngray, keeled right over and lay motionless. There was/na large package tied to its legs./n/nHarry recognized the unconscious owl at once — his/nname was Errol, and he belonged to the Weasley/nfamily. Harry dashed to the bed, untied the cords/naround Errol's legs, took off the parcel, and then/ncarried Errol to Hedwig's cage. Errol opened one/nbleary eye, gave a feeble hoot of thanks, and began to/ngulp some water./n/nHarry turned back to the remaining owls. One of/nthem, the large snowy female, was his own Hedwig./nShe, too, was carrying a parcel and looked extremely/npleased with herself. She gave Harry an affectionate/nnip with her beak as he removed her burden, then/nflew across the room to join Errol./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry didn't recognize the third owl, a handsome/ntawny one, but he knew at once where it had come/nfrom, because in addition to a third package, it was/ncarrying a letter bearing the Hogwarts crest. When/nHarry relieved this owl of its burden, it ruffled its/nfeathers importantly, stretched its wings, and took off/nthrough the window into the night./n/nHarry sat down on his bed and grabbed Errol's/npackage, ripped off the brown paper, and discovered a/npresent wrapped in gold, and his first ever birthday/ncard. Fingers trembling slightly, he opened the/nenvelope. Two pieces of paper fell out — a letter and a/nnewspaper clipping./n/nThe clipping had clearly come out of the wizarding/nnewspaper, the Daily Prophet, because the people in/nthe black-and-white picture were moving. Harry/npicked up the clipping, smoothed it out, and read:/n/nMINISTRY OF MAGIC EMPLOYEE/n/nSCOOPS GRAND PRIZE/n/nArthur Weasley, Head of the Misuse of Muggle Artifacts/nOffice at the Ministry of Magic, has won the annual/nDaily Prophet Grand Prize Galleon Draw./n/nA delighted Mr. Weasley told the Daily Prophet, "We/nwill be spending the gold on a summer holiday in/nEgypt, where our eldest son, Bill, works as a curse/nbreaker for Gringotts Wizarding Bank. "/n/nThe Weasley family will be spending a month in/nEgypt, returning for the start of the new school year/nat Hogwarts, which five of the Weasley children/ncurrently attend./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry scanned the moving photograph, and a grin/nspread across his face as he saw all nine of the/nWeasleys waving furiously at him, standing in front of/na large pyramid. Plump little Mrs. Weasley; tall,/nbalding Mr. Weasley; six sons; and one daughter, all/n(though the black-and-white picture didn't show it)/nwith flaming-red hair. Right in the middle of the/npicture was Ron, tall and gangling, with his pet rat,/nScabbers, on his shoulder and his arm around his/nlittle sister, Ginny./n/nHarry couldn't think of anyone who deserved to win a/nlarge pile of gold more than the Weasleys, who were/nvery nice and extremely poor. He picked up Ron's/nletter and unfolded it./n/nDear Harry,/n/nHappy birthday!/n/nLook, I'm really sorry about that telephone call. I hope/nthe Muggles didn't give you a hard time. I asked Dad,/nand he reckons I shouldn't have shouted./n/nIt's amazing here in Egypt. Bill's taken us around all/nthe tombs and you wouldn't believe the curses those/nold Egyptian wizards put on them. Mum wouldn't let/nGinny come in the last one. There were all these/nmutant skeletons in there, of Muggles who'd broken in/nand grown extra heads and stuff./n/nI couldn't believe it when Dad won the Daily Prophet/nDraw. Seven hundred galleons! Most of it's gone on/nthis trip, but they're going to buy me a new wand for/nnext year./n/nHarry remembered only too well the occasion when/nRon's old wand had snapped. It had happened when/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe car the two of them had been flying to Hogwarts/nhad crashed into a tree on the school grounds./n/nWe'll be back about a week before term starts and/nwe'll be going up to London to get my wand and our/nnew books. Any chance of meeting you there?/n/nDon't let the Muggles get you down!/n/nTry and come to London,/n/nRon/n/nPS. Percy's Head Boy. He got the letter last week./n/nHarry glanced back at the photograph. Percy, who/nwas in his seventh and final year at Hogwarts, was/nlooking particularly smug. He had pinned his Head/nBoy badge to the fez perched jauntily on top of his/nneat hair, his horn-rimmed glasses flashing in the/nEgyptian sun./n/nHarry now turned to his present and unwrapped it./nInside was what looked like a miniature glass/nspinning top. There was another note from Ron/nbeneath it./n/nHarry — this is a Pocket Sneakoscope. If there's/nsomeone untrustworthy around, it's supposed to light/nup and spin. Bill says it's rubbish sold for wizard/ntourists and isn't reliable, because it kept lighting up at/ndinner last night. But he didn't realize Fred and George/nhad put beetles in his soup./n/nBye —/n/nRon/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry put the Pocket Sneakoscope on his bedside/ntable, where it stood quite still, balanced on its point,/nreflecting the luminous hands of his clock. He looked/nat it happily for a few seconds, then picked up the/nparcel Hedwig had brought./n/nInside this, too, there was a wrapped present, a card,/nand a letter, this time from Hermione./n/nDear Harry,/n/nRon wrote to me and told me about his phone call to/nyour Uncle Vernon. I do hope you're all right./n/nI'm on holiday in France at the moment and I didn't/nknow how I was going to send this to you — what if/nthey'd opened it at customs? — but then Hedwig/nturned up! I think she wanted to make sure you got/nsomething for your birthday for a change. I bought your/npresent by owl-order; there was an advertisement in/nthe Daily Prophet (I've been getting it delivered; it's so/ngood to keep up with what's going on in the wizarding/nworld). Did you see that picture of Ron and his family a/nweek ago? I bet he's learning loads. I'm really jealous/n— the ancient Egyptian wizards were fascinating./n/nThere's some interesting local history of witchcraft/nhere, too. I've rewritten my whole History of Magic/nessay to include some of the things I've found out. I/nhope it's not too long — it's two rolls of parchment more/nthan Professor Binns asked for./n/nRon says he's going to be in London in the last week of/nthe holidays. Can you make it? Will your aunt and/nuncle let you come? I really hope you can. If not, I'll see/nyou on the Hogwarts Express on September first!/n/nLove from/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione/n/n/n/nPS. Ron says Percy's Head Boy. I'll bet Percy's really/npleased./n/nRon doesn't seem too happy about it./n/nHarry laughed as he put Hermione 's letter aside and/npicked up her present. It was very heavy. Knowing/nHermione, he was sure it would be a large book full of/nvery difficult spells — but it wasn't. His heart gave a/nhuge bound as he ripped back the paper and saw a/nsleek black leather case, with silver words stamped/nacross it, reading Broomstick Servicing Kit./n/n"Wow, Hermione!" Harry whispered, unzipping the/ncase to look inside./n/nThere was a large jar of Fleetwood's High-Finish/nHandle Polish, a pair of gleaming silver Tail-Twig/nClippers, a tiny brass compass to clip on your broom/nfor long journeys, and a Handbook of Do-It-Yourself/nBroomcare./n/nApart from his friends, the thing that Harry missed/nmost about Hogwarts was Quidditch, the most/npopular sport in the magical world — highly/ndangerous, very exciting, and played on broomsticks./nHarry happened to be a very good Quidditch player;/nhe had been the youngest person in a century to be/npicked for one of the Hogwarts House teams. One of/nHarry's most prized possessions was his Nimbus Two/nThousand racing broom./n/nHarry put the leather case aside and picked up his/nlast parcel. He recognized the untidy scrawl on the/nbrown paper at once: this was from Hagrid, the/nHogwarts gamekeeper. He tore off the top layer of/npaper and glimpsed something green and leathery,/n/n/n/n/nbut before he could unwrap it properly, the parcel/ngave a strange quiver, and whatever was inside it/nsnapped loudly — as though it had jaws./n/nHarry froze. He knew that Hagrid would never send/nhim anything dangerous on purpose, but then,/n/nHagrid didn't have a normal person's view of what/nwas dangerous. Hagrid had been known to befriend/ngiant spiders, buy vicious, three-headed dogs from/nmen in pubs, and sneak illegal dragon eggs into his/ncabin./n/nHarry poked the parcel nervously. It snapped loudly/nagain. Harry reached for the lamp on his bedside/ntable, gripped it firmly in one hand, and raised it over/nhis head, ready to strike. Then he seized the rest of/nthe wrapping paper in his other hand and pulled./n/nAnd out fell — a book. Harry just had time to register/nits handsome green cover, emblazoned with the/ngolden title The Monster Book of Monsters, before it/nflipped onto its edge and scuttled sideways along the/nbed like some weird crab./n/n"Uh-oh," Harry muttered./n/nThe book toppled off the bed with a loud clunk and/nshuffled rapidly across the room. Harry followed it/nstealthily. The book was hiding in the dark space/nunder his desk. Praying that the Dursleys were still/nfast asleep, Harry got down on his hands and knees/nand reached toward it./n/n"Ouch!"/n/nThe book snapped shut on his hand and then flapped/npast him, still scuttling on its covers. Harry/nscrambled around, threw himself forward, and/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmanaged to flatten it. Uncle Vernon gave a loud,/nsleepy grunt in the room next door./n/nHedwig and Errol watched interestedly as Harry/nclamped the struggling book tightly in his arms,/nhurried to his chest of drawers, and pulled out a belt,/nwhich he buckled tightly around it. The Monster Book/nshuddered angrily, but could no longer flap and snap,/nso Harry threw it down on the bed and reached for/nHagrid's card./n/nDear Harry,/n/nHappy birthday!/n/nThink you might find this useful for next year./n/nWon't say no more here. Tell you when I see you./n/nHope the Muggles are treating you right./n/nAll the best,/n/nHagrid/n/nIt struck Harry as ominous that Hagrid thought a/nbiting book would come in useful, but he put Hagrid's/ncard up next to Ron's and Hermione's, grinning more/nbroadly than ever. Now there was only the letter from/nHogwarts left./n/nNoticing that it was rather thicker than usual, Harry/nslit open the envelope, pulled out the first page of/nparchment within, and read:/n/nDear Mr. Potter,/n/nPlease note that the new school year will begin on/nSeptember the first. The Hogwarts Express will leave/n/n/n/n/n/nfrom King's Cross station, platform nine and three-/nquarters, at eleven o'clock./n/nThird years are permitted to visit the village of/nHogsmeade on certain weekends. Please give the/nenclosed permission form to your parent or guardian to/nsign./n/nA list of books for next year is enclosed./n/nYours sincerely,/n/nProfessor M. McGonagall/nDeputy Headmistress/n/nHarry pulled out the Hogsmeade permission form and/nlooked at it, no longer grinning. It would be wonderful/nto visit Hogsmeade on weekends; he knew it was an/nentirely wizarding village, and he had never set foot/nthere. But how on earth was he going to persuade/nUncle Vernon or Aunt Petunia to sign the form?/n/nHe looked over at the alarm clock. It was now two/no'clock in the morning./n/nDeciding that he'd worry about the Hogsmeade form/nwhen he woke up, Harry got back into bed and/nreached up to cross off another day on the chart he'd/nmade for himself, counting down the days left until/nhis return to Hogwarts. Then he took off his glasses/nand lay down, eyes open, facing his three birthday/ncards./n/nExtremely unusual though he was, at that moment/nHarry Potter felt just like everyone else — glad, for the/nfirst time in his life, that it was his birthday./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Aunt Marge's Big Mistake
text: /nHarry went down to breakfast the next morning to/nfind the three Dursleys already sitting around the/nkitchen table. They were watching a brand-new/ntelevision, a welcome-home-for-the-summer present/nfor Dudley, who had been complaining loudly about/nthe long walk between the fridge and the television in/nthe living room. Dudley had spent most of the/nsummer in the kitchen, his piggy little eyes fixed on/nthe screen and his five chins wobbling as he ate/ncontinually./n/nHarry sat down between Dudley and Uncle Vernon, a/nlarge, beefy man with very little neck and a lot of/nmustache. Far from wishing Harry a happy birthday,/nnone of the Dursleys made any sign that they had/nnoticed Harry enter the room, but Harry was far too/nused to this to care. He helped himself to a piece of/ntoast and then looked up at the reporter on the/ntelevision, who was halfway through a report on an/nescaped convict:/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"... The public is warned that Black is armed and/nextremely dangerous. A special hot line has been set/nup, and any sighting of Black should be reported/nimmediately."/n/n"No need to tell us he's no good," snorted Uncle/nVernon, staring over the top of his newspaper at the/nprisoner. "Look at the state of him, the filthy/nlayabout! Look at his hair!"/n/nHe shot a nasty look sideways at Harry, whose untidy/nhair had always been a source of great annoyance to/nUncle Vernon. Compared to the man on the/ntelevision, however, whose gaunt face was/nsurrounded by a matted, elbow-length tangle, Harry/nfelt very well groomed indeed./n/nThe reporter had reappeared./n/n"The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries will/nannounce today — "/n/n"Hang on!" barked Uncle Vernon, staring furiously at/nthe reporter. "You didn't tell us where that maniac's/nescaped from! What use is that? Lunatic could be/ncoming up the street right now!"/n/nAunt Petunia, who was bony and horse-faced,/nwhipped around and peered intently out of the/nkitchen window. Harry knew Aunt Petunia would/nsimply love to be the one to call the hot line number./nShe was the nosiest woman in the world and spent/nmost of her life spying on the boring, law-abiding/nneighbors./n/n"When will they learn," said Uncle Vernon, pounding/nthe table with his large purple fist, "that hanging's the/nonly way to deal with these people?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Very true," said Aunt Petunia, who was still/nsquinting into next door's runner beans./n/nUncle Vernon drained his teacup, glanced at his/nwatch, and added, "I'd better be off in a minute,/nPetunia. Marge's train gets in at ten."/n/nHarry, whose thoughts had been upstairs with the/nBroomstick Servicing Kit, was brought back to earth/nwith an unpleasant bump./n/n"Aunt Marge?" he blurted out. "Sh — she's not/ncoming here, is she?"/n/nAunt Marge was Uncle Vernon's sister. Even though/nshe was not a blood relative of Harry's (whose mother/nhad been Aunt Petunia's sister), he had been forced to/ncall her "Aunt" all his life. Aunt Marge lived in the/ncountry, in a house with a large garden, where she/nbred bulldogs. She didn't often stay at Privet Drive,/nbecause she couldn't bear to leave her precious dogs,/nbut each of her visits stood out horribly vividly in/nHarry's mind./n/nAt Dudley's fifth birthday party, Aunt Marge had/nwhacked Harry around the shins with her walking/nstick to stop him from beating Dudley at musical/nstatues. A few years later, she had turned up at/nChristmas with a computerized robot for Dudley and/na box of dog biscuits for Harry. On her last visit, the/nyear before Harry started at Hogwarts, Harry had/naccidentally trodden on the tail of her favorite dog./nRipper had chased Harry out into the garden and up/na tree, and Aunt Marge had refused to call him off/nuntil past midnight. The memory of this incident still/nbrought tears of laughter to Dudley's eyes./n/n"Marge'll be here for a week," Uncle Vernon snarled,/n"and while we're on the subject" — he pointed a fat/n/n/n/n/n/nfinger threateningly at Harry — "we need to get a few/nthings straight before I go and collect her."/n/nDudley smirked and withdrew his gaze from the/ntelevision. Watching Harry being bullied by Uncle/nVernon was Dudley's favorite form of entertainment./n/n"Firstly," growled Uncle Vernon, "you'll keep a civil/ntongue in your head when you're talking to Marge."/n/n"All right," said Harry bitterly, "if she does when she's/ntalking to me."/n/n"Secondly," said Uncle Vernon, acting as though he/nhad not heard Harry's reply, "as Marge doesn't know/nanything about your abnormality, I don't want any —/nany funny stuff while she's here. You behave yourself,/ngot me?"/n/n"I will if she does," said Harry through gritted teeth./n/n"And thirdly," said Uncle Vernon, his mean little eyes/nnow slits in his great purple face, "we've told Marge/nyou attend St. Brutus's Secure Center for Incurably/nCriminal Boys."/n/n"What?" Harry yelled./n/n"And you'll be sticking to that story, boy, or there'll be/ntrouble," spat Uncle Vernon./n/nHarry sat there, white-faced and furious, staring at/nUncle Vernon, hardly able to believe it. Aunt Marge/ncoming for a week-long visit — it was the worst/nbirthday present the Dursleys had ever given him,/nincluding that pair of Uncle Vernon's old socks./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, Petunia," said Uncle Vernon, getting heavily to/nhis feet, "111 be off to the station, then. Want to come/nalong for the ride, Dudders?"/n/n"No," said Dudley, whose attention had returned to/nthe television now that Uncle Vernon had finished/nthreatening Harry./n/n"Duddy's got to make himself smart for his auntie,"/nsaid Aunt Petunia, smoothing Dudley's thick blond/nhair. "Mummy's bought him a lovely new bow tie."/n/nUncle Vernon clapped Dudley on his porky shoulder./n/n"See you in a bit, then," he said, and he left the/nkitchen./n/nHarry, who had been sitting in a kind of horrified/ntrance, had a sudden idea. Abandoning his toast, he/ngot quickly to his feet and followed Uncle Vernon to/nthe front door./n/nUncle Vernon was pulling on his car coat./n/n"I'm not taking you," he snarled as he turned to see/nHarry watching him./n/n"Like I wanted to come," said Harry coldly. "I want to/nask you something."/n/nUncle Vernon eyed him suspiciously./n/n"Third years at Hog — at my school are allowed to/nvisit the village sometimes," said Harry./n/n"So?" snapped Uncle Vernon, taking his car keys from/na hook next to the door./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I need you to sign the permission form," said Harry/nin a rush./n/n"And why should I do that?" sneered Uncle Vernon./n/n"Well," said Harry, choosing his words carefully, "it'll/nbe hard work, pretending to Aunt Marge I go to that/nSt. Whatsits — "/n/n"St. Brutus's Secure Center for Incurably Criminal/nBoys!" bellowed Uncle Vernon, and Harry was pleased/nto hear a definite note of panic in Uncle Vernon's/nvoice./n/n"Exactly," said Harry, looking calmly up into Uncle/nVernon's large, purple face. "It's a lot to remember. I'll/nhave to make it sound convincing, won't I? What if I/naccidentally let something slip?"/n/n" You'll get the stuffing knocked out of you, won't you?"/nroared Uncle Vernon, advancing on Harry with his fist/nraised. But Harry stood his ground./n/n"Knocking the stuffing out of me won't make Aunt/nMarge forget what I could tell her," he said grimly./n/nUncle Vernon stopped, his fist still raised, his face an/nugly puce./n/n"But if you sign my permission form," Harry went on/nquickly, "I swear I'll remember where I'm supposed to/ngo to school, and I'll act like a Mug — like I'm normal/nand everything."/n/nHarry could tell that Uncle Vernon was thinking it/nover, even if his teeth were bared and a vein was/nthrobbing in his temple./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Right," he snapped finally. "I shall monitor your/nbehavior carefully during Marge's visit. If, at the end/nof it, you've toed the line and kept to the story, I'll/nsign your ruddy form."/n/nHe wheeled around, pulled open the front door, and/nslammed it so hard that one of the little panes of/nglass at the top fell out./n/nHarry didn't return to the kitchen. He went back/nupstairs to his bedroom. If he was going to act like a/nreal Muggle, he'd better start now. Slowly and sadly/nhe gathered up all his presents and his birthday/ncards and hid them under the loose floorboard with/nhis homework. Then he went to Hedwig's cage. Errol/nseemed to have recovered; he and Hedwig were both/nasleep, heads under their wings. Harry sighed, then/npoked them both awake./n/n"Hedwig," he said gloomily, "you're going to have to/nclear off for a week. Go with Errol. Ron'll look after/nyou. I'll write him a note, explaining. And don't look at/nme like that" — Hedwig's large amber eyes were/nreproachful — "it's not my fault. It's the only way I'll/nbe allowed to visit Hogsmeade with Ron and/nHermione."/n/nTen minutes later, Errol and Hedwig (who had a note/nto Ron bound to her leg) soared out of the window/nand out of sight. Harry, now feeling thoroughly/nmiserable, put the empty cage away inside the/nwardrobe./n/nBut Harry didn't have long to brood. In next to no/ntime, Aunt Petunia was shrieking up the stairs for/nHarry to come down and get ready to welcome their/nguest./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Do something about your hair!" Aunt Petunia/nsnapped as he reached the hall./n/nHarry couldn't see the point of trying to make his hair/nlie flat. Aunt Marge loved criticizing him, so the/nuntidier he looked, the happier she would be./n/nAll too soon, there was a crunch of gravel outside as/nUncle Vernon's car pulled back into the driveway,/nthen the clunk of the car doors and footsteps on the/ngarden path./n/n"Get the door!" Aunt Petunia hissed at Harry./n/nA feeling of great gloom in his stomach, Harry pulled/nthe door open./n/nOn the threshold stood Aunt Marge. She was very like/nUncle Vernon: large, beefy, and purple-faced, she/neven had a mustache, though not as bushy as his. In/none hand she held an enormous suitcase, and tucked/nunder the other was an old and evil-tempered/nbulldog./n/n"Where's my Dudders?" roared Aunt Marge. "Where's/nmy neffy-poo?"/n/nDudley came waddling down the hall, his blond hair/nplastered flat to his fat head, a bow tie just visible/nunder his many chins. Aunt Marge thrust the/nsuitcase into Harry's stomach, knocking the wind out/nof him, seized Dudley in a tight one-armed hug, and/nplanted a large kiss on his cheek./n/nHarry knew perfectly well that Dudley only put up/nwith Aunt Marge's hugs because he was well paid for/nit, and sure enough, when they broke apart, Dudley/nhad a crisp twenty-pound note clutched in his fat fist./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Petunia!" shouted Aunt Marge, striding past Harry as/nthough he was a hat stand. Aunt Marge and Aunt/nPetunia kissed, or rather, Aunt Marge bumped her/nlarge jaw against Aunt Petunia's bony cheekbone./n/nUncle Vernon now came in, smiling jovially as he shut/nthe door./n/n"Tea, Marge?" he said. "And what will Ripper take?"/n/n"Ripper can have some tea out of my saucer," said/nAunt Marge as they all proceeded into the kitchen,/nleaving Harry alone in the hall with the suitcase. But/nHarry wasn't complaining; any excuse not to be with/nAunt Marge was fine by him, so he began to heave the/ncase upstairs into the spare bedroom, taking as long/nas he could./n/nBy the time he got back to the kitchen, Aunt Marge/nhad been supplied with tea and fruitcake, and Ripper/nwas lapping noisily in the corner. Harry saw Aunt/nPetunia wince slightly as specks of tea and drool/nflecked her clean floor. Aunt Petunia hated animals./n/n"Who's looking after the other dogs, Marge?" Uncle/nVernon asked./n/n"Oh, I've got Colonel Fubster managing them,"/nboomed Aunt Marge. "He's retired now, good for him/nto have something to do. But I couldn't leave poor old/nRipper. He pines if he's away from me."/n/nRipper began to growl again as Harry sat down. This/ndirected Aunt Marge's attention to Harry for the first/ntime./n/n"So!" she barked. "Still here, are you?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't you say 'yes' in that ungrateful tone," Aunt/nMarge growled. "It's damn good of Vernon and/nPetunia to keep you. Wouldn't have done it myself./nYou'd have gone straight to an orphanage if you'd/nbeen dumped on my doorstep."/n/nHarry was bursting to say that he'd rather live in an/norphanage than with the Dursleys, but the thought of/nthe Hogsmeade form stopped him. He forced his face/ninto a painful smile./n/n"Don't you smirk at me!" boomed Aunt Marge. "I can/nsee you haven't improved since I last saw you. I hoped/nschool would knock some manners into you." She/ntook a large gulp of tea, wiped her mustache, and/nsaid, "Where is it that you send him, again, Vernon?"/n/n"St. Brutus's," said Uncle Vernon promptly. "It's a/nfirst-rate institution for hopeless cases."/n/n"I see," said Aunt Marge. "Do they use the cane at St./nBrutus's, boy?" she barked across the table./n/n"Er — "/n/n/n/nUncle Vernon nodded curtly behind Aunt Marge's/nback./n/n"Yes," said Harry. Then, feeling he might as well do/nthe thing properly, he added, "all the time."/n/n"Excellent," said Aunt Marge. "I won't have this/nnamby-pamby, wishy-washy nonsense about not/nhitting people who deserve it. A good thrashing is/nwhat's needed in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred./nHave you been beaten often?"/n/n"Oh, yeah," said Harry, "loads of times."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAunt Marge narrowed her eyes./n/n/n/n"I still don't like your tone, boy," she said. "If you can/nspeak of your beatings in that casual way, they/nclearly aren't hitting you hard enough. Petunia, I'd/nwrite if I were you. Make it clear that you approve the/nuse of extreme force in this boy's case."/n/nPerhaps Uncle Vernon was worried that Harry might/nforget their bargain; in any case, he changed the/nsubject abruptly./n/n"Heard the news this morning, Marge? What about/nthat escaped prisoner, eh?"/n/nAs Aunt Marge started to make herself at home, Harry/ncaught himself thinking almost longingly of life at/nnumber four without her. Uncle Vernon and Aunt/nPetunia usually encouraged Harry to stay out of their/nway, which Harry was only too happy to do. Aunt/nMarge, on the other hand, wanted Harry under her/neye at all times, so that she could boom out/nsuggestions for his improvement. She delighted in/ncomparing Harry with Dudley, and took huge/npleasure in buying Dudley expensive presents while/nglaring at Harry, as though daring him to ask why he/nhadn't got a present too. She also kept throwing out/ndark hints about what made Harry such an/nunsatisfactory person./n/n"You mustn't blame yourself for the way the boy's/nturned out, Vernon," she said over lunch on the third/nday. "If there's something rotten on the inside, there's/nnothing anyone can do about it."/n/nHarry tried to concentrate on his food, but his hands/nshook and his face was starting to burn with anger./nRemember the form, he told himself. Think about/nHogsmeade. Don't say anything. Don't rise —/n/n/n/n/n/nAunt Marge reached for her glass of wine./n/n/n/n"It's one of the basic rules of breeding," she said. "You/nsee it all the time with dogs. If there's something/nwrong with the bitch, there'll be something wrong/nwith the pup — "/n/nAt that moment, the wineglass Aunt Marge was/nholding exploded in her hand. Shards of glass flew in/nevery direction and Aunt Marge sputtered and/nblinked, her great ruddy face dripping./n/n"Marge!" squealed Aunt Petunia. "Marge, are you all/nright?"/n/n"Not to worry," grunted Aunt Marge, mopping her face/nwith her napkin. "Must have squeezed it too hard. Did/nthe same thing at Colonel Fubster's the other day. No/nneed to fuss, Petunia, I have a very firm grip ..."/n/nBut Aunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon were both/nlooking at Harry suspiciously, so he decided he'd/nbetter skip dessert and escape from the table as soon/nas he could./n/nOutside in the hall, he leaned against the wall,/nbreathing deeply. It had been a long time since he'd/nlost control and made something explode. He couldn't/nafford to let it happen again. The Hogsmeade form/nwasn't the only thing at stake — if he carried on like/nthat, he'd be in trouble with the Ministry of Magic./n/nHarry was still an underage wizard, and he was/nforbidden by wizard law to do magic outside school./nHis record wasn't exactly clean either. Only last/nsummer he'd gotten an official warning that had/nstated quite clearly that if the Ministry got wind of/nany more magic in Privet Drive, Harry would face/nexpulsion from Hogwarts./n/n/n/n/n/nHe heard the Dursleys leaving the table and hurried/nupstairs out of the way./n/nHarry got through the next three days by forcing/nhimself to think about his Handbook of Do-It-Yourself/nBroomcare whenever Aunt Marge started on him. This/nworked quite well, though it seemed to give him a/nglazed look, because Aunt Marge started voicing the/nopinion that he was mentally subnormal./n/nAt last, at long last, the final evening of Marge's stay/narrived. Aunt Petunia cooked a fancy dinner and/nUncle Vernon uncorked several bottles of wine. They/ngot all the way through the soup and the salmon/nwithout a single mention of Harry's faults; during the/nlemon meringue pie, Uncle Vernon bored them all/nwith a long talk about Grunnings, his drill-making/ncompany; then Aunt Petunia made coffee and Uncle/nVernon brought out a bottle of brandy./n/n"Can I tempt you, Marge?"/n/nAunt Marge had already had quite a lot of wine. Her/nhuge face was very red./n/n"Just a small one, then," she chuckled. "A bit more/nthan that ... and a bit more ... that's the ticket."/n/nDudley was eating his fourth slice of pie. Aunt/nPetunia was sipping coffee with her little finger/nsticking out. Harry really wanted to disappear into his/nbedroom, but he met Uncle Vernon's angry little eyes/nand knew he would have to sit it out./n/n"Aah," said Aunt Marge, smacking her lips and/nputting the empty brandy glass back down. "Excellent/nnosh, Petunia. It's normally just a fry-up for me of an/nevening, with twelve dogs to look after. ..." She/nburped richly and patted her great tweed stomach./n/n/n/n/n"Pardon me. But I do like to see a healthy-sized boy,"/nshe went on, winking at Dudley. "You'll be a proper-/nsized man, Dudders, like your father. Yes, I'll have a/nspot more brandy, Vernon. ..."/n/n"Now, this one here — "/n/nShe jerked her head at Harry, who felt his stomach/nclench. The Handbook, he thought quickly./n/n"This one's got a mean, runty look about him. You get/nthat with dogs. I had Colonel Fubster drown one last/nyear. Ratty little thing it was. Weak. Underbred."/n/nHarry was trying to remember page twelve of his/nbook: A Charm to Cure Reluctant Reversers./n/n"It all comes down to blood, as I was saying the other/nday. Bad blood will out. Now, I'm saying nothing/nagainst your family, Petunia" — she patted Aunt/nPetunia's bony hand with her shovellike one — "but/nyour sister was a bad egg. They turn up in the best/nfamilies. Then she ran off with a wastrel and here's/nthe result right in front of us."/n/nHarry was staring at his plate, a funny ringing in his/nears. Grasp your broom firmly by the tail, he thought./nBut he couldn't remember what came next. Aunt/nMarge's voice seemed to be boring into him like one of/nUncle Vernon's drills./n/n"This Potter," said Aunt Marge loudly, seizing the/nbrandy bottle and splashing more into her glass and/nover the tablecloth, "you never told me what he did?"/n/nUncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia were looking/nextremely tense. Dudley had even looked up from his/npie to gape at his parents./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He — didn't work," said Uncle Vernon, with half a/nglance at Harry. "Unemployed."/n/n/n/n"As I expected!" said Aunt Marge, taking a huge swig/nof brandy and wiping her chin on her sleeve. "A no-/naccount, good-for-nothing, lazy scrounger who — "/n/n"He was not," said Harry suddenly. The table went/nvery quiet. Harry was shaking all over. He had never/nfelt so angry in his life./n/n"MORE BRANDY!" yelled Uncle Vernon, who had gone/nvery white. He emptied the bottle into Aunt Marge's/nglass. "You, boy," he snarled at Harry. "Go to bed, go/non — "/n/n/n/n"No, Vernon," hiccuped Aunt Marge, holding up a/nhand, her tiny bloodshot eyes fixed on Harry's. "Go/non, boy, go on. Proud of your parents, are you? They/ngo and get themselves killed in a car crash (drunk, I/nexpect) — "/n/n"They didn't die in a car crash!" said Harry, who/nfound himself on his feet./n/n"They died in a car crash, you nasty little liar, and left/nyou to be a burden on their decent, hardworking/nrelatives!" screamed Aunt Marge, swelling with fury./n"You are an insolent, ungrateful little — "/n/nBut Aunt Marge suddenly stopped speaking. For a/nmoment, it looked as though words had failed her./n/nShe seemed to be swelling with inexpressible anger —/nbut the swelling didn't stop. Her great red face started/nto expand, her tiny eyes bulged, and her mouth/nstretched too tightly for speech — next second,/nseveral buttons had just burst from her tweed jacket/nand pinged off the walls — she was inflating like a/nmonstrous balloon, her stomach bursting free of her/n/n/n/n/ntweed waistband, each of her fingers blowing up like a/nsalami —/n/n"MARGE!" yelled Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia/ntogether as Aunt Marge's whole body began to rise off/nher chair toward the ceiling. She was entirely round,/nnow, like a vast life buoy with piggy eyes, and her/nhands and feet stuck out weirdly as she drifted up/ninto the air, making apoplectic popping noises. Ripper/ncame skidding into the room, barking madly./n/n"NOOOOOOO!"/n/nUncle Vernon seized one of Marge's feet and tried to/npull her down again, but was almost lifted from the/nfloor himself. A second later, Ripper leapt forward and/nsank his teeth into Uncle Vernon's leg./n/nHarry tore from the dining room before anyone could/nstop him, heading for the cupboard under the stairs./nThe cupboard door burst magically open as he/nreached it. In seconds, he had heaved his trunk to the/nfront door. He sprinted upstairs and threw himself/nunder the bed, wrenching up the loose floorboard,/nand grabbed the pillowcase full of his books and/nbirthday presents. He wriggled out, seized Hedwig's/nempty cage, and dashed back downstairs to his/ntrunk, just as Uncle Vernon burst out of the dining/nroom, his trouser leg in bloody tatters./n/n"COME BACK IN HERE!" he bellowed. "COME BACK/nAND PUT HER RIGHT!"/n/nBut a reckless rage had come over Harry. He kicked/nhis trunk open, pulled out his wand, and pointed it at/nUncle Vernon./n/n"She deserved it," Harry said, breathing very fast./n/n"She deserved what she got. You keep away from me."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe fumbled behind him for the latch on the door./n/n/n/n"I'm going," Harry said. "I've had enough."/n/nAnd in the next moment, he was out in the dark,/nquiet street, heaving his heavy trunk behind him,/nHedwig's cage under his arm./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n3/n/n/n/n

title: The Knight Bus
text: /nHarry was several streets away before he collapsed/nonto a low wall in Magnolia Crescent, panting from/nthe effort of dragging his trunk. He sat quite still,/nanger still surging through him, listening to the/nfrantic thumping of his heart./n/nBut after ten minutes alone in the dark street, a new/nemotion overtook him: panic. Whichever way he/nlooked at it, he had never been in a worse fix. He was/nstranded, quite alone, in the dark Muggle world, with/nabsolutely nowhere to go. And the worst of it was, he/nhad just done serious magic, which meant that he/nwas almost certainly expelled from Hogwarts. He had/nbroken the Decree for the Restriction of Underage/nWizardry so badly, he was surprised Ministry of Magic/nrepresentatives weren't swooping down on him where/nhe sat./n/nHarry shivered and looked up and down Magnolia/nCrescent. What was going to happen to him? Would/nhe be arrested, or would he simply be outlawed from/nthe wizarding world? He thought of Ron and/n/n/n/n/nHermione, and his heart sank even lower. Harry was/nsure that, criminal or not, Ron and Hermione would/nwant to help him now, but they were both abroad,/nand with Hedwig gone, he had no means of contacting/nthem./n/nHe didn't have any Muggle money, either. There was a/nlittle wizard gold in the money bag at the bottom of/nhis trunk, but the rest of the fortune his parents had/nleft him was stored in a vault at Gringotts Wizarding/nBank in London. He'd never be able to drag his trunk/nall the way to London. Unless .../n/nHe looked down at his wand, which he was still/nclutching in his hand. If he was already expelled (his/nheart was now thumping painfully fast), a bit more/nmagic couldn't hurt. He had the Invisibility Cloak he/nhad inherited from his father — what if he bewitched/nthe trunk to make it feather-light, tied it to his/nbroomstick, covered himself in the cloak, and flew to/nLondon? Then he could get the rest of his money out/nof his vault and ... begin his life as an outcast. It was/na horrible prospect, but he couldn't sit on this wall/nforever, or he'd find himself trying to explain to/nMuggle police why he was out in the dead of night/nwith a trunkful of spellbooks and a broomstick./n/nHarry opened his trunk again and pushed the/ncontents aside, looking for the Invisibility Cloak —/nbut before he had found it, he straightened up/nsuddenly, looking around him once more./n/nA funny prickling on the back of his neck had made/nHarry feel he was being watched, but the street/nappeared to be deserted, and no lights shone from/nany of the large square houses./n/nHe bent over his trunk again, but almost immediately/nstood up once more, his hand clenched on his wand./n/n/n/n/n/nHe had sensed rather than heard it: someone or/nsomething was standing in the narrow gap between/nthe garage and the fence behind him. Harry squinted/nat the black alleyway. If only it would move, then he'd/nknow whether it was just a stray cat or — something/nelse./n/n"Lumos," Harry muttered, and a light appeared at the/nend of his wand, almost dazzling him. He held it high/nover his head, and the pebble-dashed walls of number/ntwo suddenly sparkled; the garage door gleamed, and/nbetween them Harry saw, quite distinctly, the hulking/noutline of something very big, with wide, gleaming/neyes./n/nHarry stepped backward. His legs hit his trunk and/nhe tripped. His wand flew out of his hand as he flung/nout an arm to break his fall, and he landed, hard, in/nthe gutter —/n/nThere was a deafening BANG, and Harry threw up his/nhands to shield his eyes against a sudden blinding/nlight —/n/nWith a yell, he rolled back onto the pavement, just in/ntime. A second later, a gigantic pair of wheels and/nheadlights screeched to a halt exactly where Harry/nhad just been lying. They belonged, as Harry saw/nwhen he raised his head, to a triple-decker, violently/npurple bus, which had appeared out of thin air. Gold/nlettering over the windshield spelled The Knight Bus./n/nFor a split second, Harry wondered if he had been/nknocked silly by his fall. Then a conductor in a purple/nuniform leapt out of the bus and began to speak/nloudly to the night./n/n"Welcome to the Knight Bus, emergency transport for/nthe stranded witch or wizard. Just stick out your/n/n/n/n/n/nwand hand, step on board, and we can take you/nanywhere you want to go. My name is Stan Shunpike,/nand I will be your conductor this eve — "/n/nThe conductor stopped abruptly. He had just caught/nsight of Harry, who was still sitting on the ground./nHarry snatched up his wand again and scrambled to/nhis feet. Close up, he saw that Stan Shunpike was/nonly a few years older than he was, eighteen or/nnineteen at most, with large, protruding ears and/nquite a few pimples./n/n"What were you doin' down there?" said Stan,/ndropping his professional manner./n/n"Fell over," said Harry./n/n" 'Choo fall over for?" sniggered Stan./n/n"I didn't do it on purpose," said Harry, annoyed. One/nof the knees in his jeans was torn, and the hand he/nhad thrown out to break his fall was bleeding. He/nsuddenly remembered why he had fallen over and/nturned around quickly to stare at the alleyway/nbetween the garage and fence. The Knight Bus's/nheadlamps were flooding it with light, and it was/nempty./n/n" 'Choo lookin' at?" said Stan./n/n"There was a big black thing," said Harry, pointing/nuncertainly into the gap. "Like a dog ... but massive/n/n/n/nHe looked around at Stan, whose mouth was slightly/nopen. With a feeling of unease, Harry saw Stan's eyes/nmove to the scar on Harry's forehead./n/n"Woss that on your 'ead?" said Stan abruptly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Nothing," said Harry quickly, flattening his hair over/nhis scar. If the Ministry of Magic was looking for him,/nhe didn't want to make it too easy for them./n/n"Woss your name?" Stan persisted./n/n"Neville Longbottom," said Harry, saying the first/nname that came into his head. "So — so this bus," he/nwent on quickly, hoping to distract Stan, "did you say/nit goes anywhere?"/n/n"Yep," said Stan proudly, "anywhere you like, long's/nit's on land. Can't do nuffink underwater. 'Ere," he/nsaid, looking suspicious again, "you did flag us down,/ndincha? Stuck out your wand 'and, dincha?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry quickly. "Listen, how much would it/nbe to get to London?"/n/n"Eleven Sickles," said Stan, "but for firteen you get 'ot/nchocolate, and for fifteen you get an 'ot water bottle/nan' a toofbrush in the color of your choice."/n/nHarry rummaged once more in his trunk, extracted/nhis money bag, and shoved some gold into Stan's/nhand. He and Stan then lifted his trunk, with/nHedwig's cage balanced on top, up the steps of the/nbus./n/nThere were no seats; instead, half a dozen brass/nbedsteads stood beside the curtained windows./nCandles were burning in brackets beside each bed,/nilluminating the wood-paneled walls. A tiny wizard in/na nightcap at the rear of the bus muttered, "Not now,/nthanks, I'm pickling some slugs" and rolled over in his/nsleep./n/n"You 'ave this one," Stan whispered, shoving Harry's/ntrunk under the bed right behind the driver, who was/n/n/n/n/n/nsitting in an armchair in front of the steering wheel./n"This is our driver, Ernie Prang. This is Neville/nLongbottom, Ern."/n/nErnie Prang, an elderly wizard wearing very thick/nglasses, nodded to Harry, who nervously flattened his/nbangs again and sat down on his bed./n/n"Take 'er away, Ern," said Stan, sitting down in the/narmchair next to Ernie's./n/nThere was another tremendous BANG, and the next/nmoment Harry found himself flat on his bed, thrown/nbackward by the speed of the Knight Bus. Pulling/nhimself up, Harry stared out of the dark window and/nsaw that they were now bowling along a completely/ndifferent street. Stan was watching Harry's stunned/nface with great enjoyment./n/n"This is where we was before you flagged us down," he/nsaid. "Where are we, Ern? Somewhere in Wales?"/n/n"Ar," said Ernie./n/n"How come the Muggles don't hear the bus?" said/nHarry./n/n"Them!" said Stan contemptuously. "Don' listen/nproperly, do they? Don' look properly either. Never/nnotice nuffink, they don'."/n/n"Best go wake up Madam Marsh, Stan," said Ern./n"Well be in Abergavenny in a minute."/n/nStan passed Harry's bed and disappeared up a/nnarrow wooden staircase. Harry was still looking out/nof the window, feeling increasingly nervous. Ernie/ndidn't seem to have mastered the use of a steering/nwheel. The Knight Bus kept mounting the pavement,/n/n/n/n/nbut it didn't hit anything; lines of lampposts,/nmailboxes, and trash cans jumped out of its way as it/napproached and back into position once it had/npassed./n/nStan came back downstairs, followed by a faintly/ngreen witch wrapped in a traveling cloak./n/n" 'Ere you go, Madam Marsh," said Stan happily as/nErn stamped on the brake and the beds slid a foot or/nso toward the front of the bus. Madam Marsh/nclamped a handkerchief to her mouth and tottered/ndown the steps. Stan threw her bag out after her and/nrammed the doors shut; there was another loud/nBANG, and they were thundering down a narrow/ncountry lane, trees leaping out of the way./n/nHarry wouldn't have been able to sleep even if he had/nbeen traveling on a bus that didn't keep banging/nloudly and jumping a hundred miles at a time. His/nstomach churned as he fell back to wondering what/nwas going to happen to him, and whether the/nDursleys had managed to get Aunt Marge off the/nceiling yet./n/nStan had unfurled a copy of the Daily Prophet and/nwas now reading with his tongue between his teeth. A/nlarge photograph of a sunken-faced man with long,/nmatted hair blinked slowly at Harry from the front/npage. He looked strangely familiar./n/n"That man!" Harry said, forgetting his troubles for a/nmoment. "He was on the Muggle news!"/n/nStanley turned to the front page and chuckled./n/n"Sirius Black," he said, nodding. " 'Course 'e was on/nthe Muggle news, Neville, where you been?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe gave a superior sort of chuckle at the blank look/non Harry's face, removed the front page, and handed/nit to Harry./n/n"You oughta read the papers more, Neville."/n/nHarry held the paper up to the candlelight and read:/nBLACK STILL AT LARGE/n/nSirius Black, possibly the most infamous prisoner/never to be held in Azkaban fortress, is still eluding/ncapture, the Ministry of Magic confirmed today./n/n"We are doing all we can to recapture Black," said the/nMinister of Magic, Cornelius Fudge, this morning,/n/n"and we beg the magical community to remain calm."/n/nFudge has been criticized by some members of the/nInternational Federation of Warlocks for informing the/nMuggle Prime Minister of the crisis./n/n"Well, really, I had to, don't you know," said an/nirritable Fudge. "Black is mad. He's a danger to/nanyone who crosses him, magic or Muggle. I have the/nPrime Minister's assurance that he will not breathe a/nword of Black's true identity to anyone. And let's face/nit — who'd believe him if he did?"/n/nWhile Muggles have been told that Black is carrying a/ngun (a kind of metal wand that Muggles use to kill/neach other), the magical community lives in fear of a/nmassacre like that of twelve years ago, when Black/nmurdered thirteen people with a single curse./n/n/n/nHarry looked into the shadowed eyes of Sirius Black,/nthe only part of the sunken face that seemed alive./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry had never met a vampire, but he had seen/npictures of them in his Defense Against the Dark Arts/nclasses, and Black, with his waxy white skin, looked/njust like one./n/n"Scary-lookin' fing, inee?" said Stan, who had been/nwatching Harry read./n/n"He murdered thirteen people?" said Harry, handing/nthe page back to Stan, "with one curse?"/n/n"Yep," said Stan, "in front of witnesses an' all. Broad/ndaylight. Big trouble it caused, dinnit, Ern?"/n/n"Ar," said Ern darkly./n/nStan swiveled in his armchair, his hands on the back,/nthe better to look at Harry./n/n"Black woz a big supporter of You-Know-'Oo," he said./n/n"What, Voldemort?" said Harry, without thinking./n/nEven Stan's pimples went white; Ern jerked the/nsteering wheel so hard that a whole farmhouse had to/njump aside to avoid the bus./n/n"You outta your tree?" yelped Stan. " 'Choo say 'is/nname for?"/n/n"Sorry," said Harry hastily. "Sorry, I — I forgot — "/n/n"Forgot!" said Stan weakly. "Blimey, my 'eart's goin'/nthat fast..."/n/n"So — so Black was a supporter of You-Know-Who?"/nHarry prompted apologetically./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah," said Stan, still rubbing his chest. "Yeah,/nthat's right. Very close to You-Know-'Oo, they say./nAnyway, when little 'Arry Potter got the better of You-/nKnow-'Oo — "/n/nHarry nervously flattened his bangs down again./n/n" — all You-Know-'Oo's supporters was tracked down,/nwasn't they, Ern? Most of 'em knew it was all over,/nwiv You-Know-'Oo gone, and they came quiet. But not/nSirius Black. I 'eard he thought 'e'd be second-in-/ncommand once You-Know-'Oo 'ad taken over./n/n"Anyway, they cornered Black in the middle of a street/nfull of Muggles an' Black took out 'is wand and 'e/nblasted 'alf the street apart, an' a wizard got it, an' so/ndid a dozen Muggles what got in the way. 'Orrible, eh?/nAn' you know what Black did then?" Stan continued/nin a dramatic whisper./n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"Laughed," said Stan. "Jus' stood there an' laughed./nAn' when reinforcements from the Ministry of Magic/ngot there, 'e went wiv 'em quiet as anyfink, still/nlaughing 'is 'ead off. 'Cos 'e's mad, inee, Ern? Inee/nmad?"/n/n"If he weren't when he went to Azkaban, he will be/nnow," said Ern in his slow voice. "I'd blow meself up/nbefore I set foot in that place. Serves him right, mind/nyou ... after what he did. ..."/n/n"They 'ad a job coverin' it up, din' they, Ern?" Stan/nsaid. " 'Ole street blown up an' all them Muggles/ndead. What was it they said 'ad 'appened, Ern?"/n/n"Gas explosion," grunted Ernie./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"An' now 'e's out," said Stan, examining the/nnewspaper picture of Black's gaunt face again. "Never/nbeen a breakout from Azkaban before, 'as there, Ern?/nBeats me 'ow 'e did it. Frightenin', eh? Mind, I don't/nfancy 'is chances against them Azkaban guards, eh,/nErn?"/n/nErnie suddenly shivered./n/n"Talk about summat else, Stan, there's a good lad./nThem Azkaban guards give me the collywobbles."/n/nStan put the paper away reluctantly, and Harry/nleaned against the window of the Knight Bus, feeling/nworse than ever. He couldn't help imagining what/nStan might be telling his passengers in a few nights'/ntime./n/n" 'Ear about that 'Arry Potter? Blew up 'is aunt! We/n'ad 'im 'ere on the Knight Bus, di'n't we, Ern? 'E was/ntryin' to run for it. ..."/n/nHe, Harry, had broken wizard law just like Sirius/nBlack. Was inflating Aunt Marge bad enough to land/nhim in Azkaban? Harry didn't know anything about/nthe wizard prison, though everyone he'd ever heard/nspeak of it did so in the same fearful tone. Hagrid, the/nHogwarts gamekeeper, had spent two months there/nonly last year. Harry wouldn't soon forget the look of/nterror on Hagrid 's face when he had been told where/nhe was going, and Hagrid was one of the bravest/npeople Harry knew./n/nThe Knight Bus rolled through the darkness,/nscattering bushes and wastebaskets, telephone/nbooths and trees, and Harry lay, restless and/nmiserable, on his feather bed. After a while, Stan/nremembered that Harry had paid for hot chocolate,/nbut poured it all over Harry's pillow when the bus/n/n/n/n/nmoved abruptly from Anglesey to Aberdeen. One by/none, wizards and witches in dressing gowns and/nslippers descended from the upper floors to leave the/nbus. They all looked very pleased to go./n/nFinally, Harry was the only passenger left./n/n"Right then, Neville," said Stan, clapping his hands,/n"whereabouts in London?"/n/n"Diagon Alley," said Harry./n/n"Righto," said Stan. " 'Old tight, then ..."/n/nBANG!/n/nThey were thundering along Charing Cross Road./nHarry sat up and watched buildings and benches/nsqueezing themselves out of the Knight Bus's way./n/nThe sky was getting a little lighter. He would lie low/nfor a couple of hours, go to Gringotts the moment it/nopened, then set off — where, he didn't know./n/nErn slammed on the brakes and the Knight Bus/nskidded to a halt in front of a small and shabby-/nlooking pub, the Leaky Cauldron, behind which lay/nthe magical entrance to Diagon Alley./n/n"Thanks," Harry said to Ern./n/nHe jumped down the steps and helped Stan lower his/ntrunk and Hedwig's cage onto the pavement./n/n"Well," said Harry. " 'Bye then!"/n/nBut Stan wasn't paying attention. Still standing in the/ndoorway to the bus, he was goggling at the shadowy/nentrance to the Leaky Cauldron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" There you are, Harry," said a voice./n/n/n/nBefore Harry could turn, he felt a hand on his/nshoulder. At the same time, Stan shouted, "Blimey!/nErn, come 'ere! Come 'ere!"/n/nHarry looked up at the owner of the hand on his/nshoulder and felt a bucketful of ice cascade into his/nstomach — he had walked right into Cornelius Fudge,/nthe Minister of Magic himself./n/nStan leapt onto the pavement beside them./n/n"What didja call Neville, Minister?" he said excitedly./n/nFudge, a portly little man in a long, pinstriped cloak,/nlooked cold and exhausted./n/n"Neville?" he repeated, frowning. "This is Harry/nPotter."/n/n"I knew it!" Stan shouted gleefully. "Ern! Ern! Guess/n'oo Neville is, Ern! 'E's 'Arry Potter! I can see 'is scar!"/n/n"Yes," said Fudge testily, "well, I'm very glad the/nKnight Bus picked Harry up, but he and I need to/nstep inside the Leaky Cauldron now ..."/n/nFudge increased the pressure on Harry's shoulder,/nand Harry found himself being steered inside the pub./nA stooping figure bearing a lantern appeared through/nthe door behind the bar. It was Tom, the wizened,/ntoothless landlord./n/n"You've got him, Minister!" said Tom. "Will you be/nwanting anything? Beer? Brandy?"/n/n"Perhaps a pot of tea," said Fudge, who still hadn't let/ngo of Harry./n/n/n/n/n/nThere was a loud scraping and puffing from behind/nthem, and Stan and Ern appeared, carrying Harry's/ntrunk and Hedwig's cage and looking around/nexcitedly./n/n" 'Ow come you di'n't tell us 'oo you are, eh, Neville?"/nsaid Stan, beaming at Harry, while Ernie's owlish face/npeered interestedly over Stan's shoulder./n/n"And a private parlor, please, Tom," said Fudge/npointedly./n/n" 'Bye," Harry said miserably to Stan and Ern as Tom/nbeckoned Fudge toward the passage that led from the/nbar./n/n" 'Bye, Neville!" called Stan./n/nFudge marched Harry along the narrow passage after/nTom's lantern, and then into a small parlor. Tom/nclicked his fingers, a fire burst into life in the grate,/nand he bowed himself out of the room./n/n"Sit down, Harry," said Fudge, indicating a chair by/nthe fire./n/nHarry sat down, feeling goose bumps rising up his/narms despite the glow of the fire. Fudge took off his/npinstriped cloak and tossed it aside, then hitched up/nthe trousers of his bottle-green suit and sat down/nopposite Harry./n/n"I am Cornelius Fudge, Harry. The Minister of Magic."/n/nHarry already knew this, of course; he had seen/nFudge once before, but as he had been wearing his/nfather's Invisibility Cloak at the time, Fudge wasn't to/nknow that./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nTom the innkeeper reappeared, wearing an apron over/nhis nightshirt and bearing a tray of tea and crumpets./nHe placed the tray on a table between Fudge and/nHarry and left the parlor, closing the door behind/nhim./n/n"Well, Harry," said Fudge, pouring out tea, "you've/nhad us all in a right flap, I don't mind telling you./nRunning away from your aunt and uncle's house like/nthat! I'd started to think ... but you're safe, and that's/nwhat matters."/n/nFudge buttered himself a crumpet and pushed the/nplate toward Harry./n/n"Eat, Harry, you look dead on your feet. Now then .../nYou will be pleased to hear that we have dealt with/nthe unfortunate blowing-up of Miss Marjorie Dursley./nTwo members of the Accidental Magic Reversal Squad/nwere dispatched to Privet Drive a few hours ago. Miss/nDursley has been punctured and her memory has/nbeen modified. She has no recollection of the incident/nat all. So that's that, and no harm done."/n/nFudge smiled at Harry over the rim of his teacup,/nrather like an uncle surveying a favorite nephew./nHarry, who couldn't believe his ears, opened his/nmouth to speak, couldn't think of anything to say,/nand closed it again./n/n"Ah, you're worrying about the reaction of your aunt/nand uncle?" said Fudge. "Well, I won't deny that they/nare extremely angry, Harry, but they are prepared to/ntake you back next summer as long as you stay at/nHogwarts for the Christmas and Easter holidays."/n/nHarry unstuck his throat./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I always stay at Hogwarts for the Christmas and/nEaster holidays," he said, "and I don't ever want to go/nback to Privet Drive."/n/n"Now, now, I'm sure you'll feel differently once you've/ncalmed down," said Fudge in a worried tone. "They/nare your family, after all, and I'm sure you are fond of/neach other — er — very deep down."/n/nIt didn't occur to Harry to put Fudge right. He was/nstill waiting to hear what was going to happen to him/nnow./n/n"So all that remains," said Fudge, now buttering/nhimself a second crumpet, "is to decide where you're/ngoing to spend the last three weeks of your vacation. I/nsuggest you take a room here at the Leaky Cauldron/nand — "/n/n"Hang on," blurted Harry. "What about my/npunishment?"/n/nFudge blinked./n/n"Punishment?"/n/n"I broke the law!" Harry said. "The Decree for the/nRestriction of Underage Wizardry!"/n/n"Oh, my dear boy, we're not going to punish you for a/nlittle thing like that!" cried Fudge, waving his crumpet/nimpatiently. "It was an accident! We don't send people/nto Azkaban just for blowing up their aunts!"/n/nBut this didn't tally at all with Harry's past dealings/nwith the Ministry of Magic./n/n"Last year, I got an official warning just because a/nhouse-elf smashed a pudding in my uncle's house!"/n/n/n/n/n/nhe told Fudge, frowning. "The Ministry of Magic said/nI'd be expelled from Hogwarts if there was any more/nmagic there!"/n/nUnless Harry's eyes were deceiving him, Fudge was/nsuddenly looking awkward./n/n"Circumstances change, Harry. ... We have to take/ninto account ... in the present climate . . . Surely you/ndon't want to be expelled?"/n/n"Of course I don't," said Harry./n/n"Well then, what's all the fuss about?" laughed Fudge./n"Now, have a crumpet, Harry, while I go and see if/nTom's got a room for you."/n/nFudge strode out of the parlor and Harry stared after/nhim. There was something extremely odd going on./nWhy had Fudge been waiting for him at the Leaky/nCauldron, if not to punish him for what he'd done?/nAnd now Harry came to think of it, surely it wasn't/nusual for the Minister of Magic himself to get involved/nin matters of underage magic?/n/nFudge came back, accompanied by Tom the/ninnkeeper./n/n"Room eleven's free, Harry," said Fudge. "I think you'll/nbe very comfortable. Just one thing, and I'm sure/nyou'll understand ... I don't want you wandering off/ninto Muggle London, all right? Keep to Diagon Alley./nAnd you're to be back here before dark each night./nSure you'll understand. Tom will be keeping an eye on/nyou for me."/n/n"Okay," said Harry slowly, "but why — ?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't want to lose you again, do we?" said Fudge/nwith a hearty laugh. "No, no ... best we know where/nyou are. ... I mean ..."/n/nFudge cleared his throat loudly and picked up his/npinstriped cloak./n/n"Well, I'll be off, plenty to do, you know. ..."/n/n"Have you had any luck with Black yet?" Harry asked./n/nFudge's finger slipped on the silver fastenings of his/ncloak./n/n"What's that? Oh, you've heard — well, no, not yet,/nbut it's only a matter of time. The Azkaban guards/nhave never yet failed ... and they are angrier than I've/never seen them."/n/nFudge shuddered slightly./n/n"So, I'll say good-bye."/n/nHe held out his hand and Harry, shaking it, had a/nsudden idea./n/n"Er — Minister? Can I ask you something?"/n/n"Certainly," said Fudge with a smile./n/n"Well, third years at Hogwarts are allowed to visit/nHogsmeade, but my aunt and uncle didn't sign the/npermission form. D'you think you could — ?"/n/nFudge was looking uncomfortable./n/n"Ah," he said. "No, no, I'm very sorry, Harry, but as/nI'm not your parent or guardian — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But you're the Minister of Magic," said Harry eagerly./n"If you gave me permission — "/n/n"No, I'm sorry, Harry, but rules are rules," said Fudge/nflatly. "Perhaps you'll be able to visit Hogsmeade next/nyear. In fact, I think it's best if you don't ... yes .../nwell, I'll be off. Enjoy your stay, Harry."/n/nAnd with a last smile and shake of Harry's hand,/nFudge left the room. Tom now moved forward,/nbeaming at Harry./n/n"If you'll follow me, Mr. Potter," he said, "I've already/ntaken your things up. ..."/n/nHarry followed Tom up a handsome wooden staircase/nto a door with a brass number eleven on it, which/nTom unlocked and opened for him./n/nInside was a very comfortable-looking bed, some/nhighly polished oak furniture, a cheerfully crackling/nfire and, perched on top of the wardrobe —/n/n"Hedwig!" Harry gasped./n/nThe snowy owl clicked her beak and fluttered down/nonto Harry's arm./n/n"Very smart owl you've got there," chuckled Tom./n"Arrived about five minutes after you did. If there's/nanything you need, Mr. Potter, don't hesitate to ask."/n/nHe gave another bow and left./n/nHarry sat on his bed for a long time, absentmindedly/nstroking Hedwig. The sky outside the window was/nchanging rapidly from deep, velvety blue to cold,/nsteely gray and then, slowly, to pink shot with gold./nHarry could hardly believe that he'd left Privet Drive/n/n/n/n/nonly a few hours ago, that he wasn't expelled, and/nthat he was now facing three Dursley-free weeks./n/n/n/n"It's been a very weird night, Hedwig," he yawned./n/nAnd without even removing his glasses, he slumped/nback onto his pillows and fell asleep./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Leaky Cauldron
text: /nIt took Harry several days to get used to his strange/nnew freedom. Never before had he been able to get up/nwhenever he wanted or eat whatever he fancied. He/ncould even go wherever he pleased, as long as it was/nin Diagon Alley, and as this long cobbled street was/npacked with the most fascinating wizarding shops in/nthe world, Harry felt no desire to break his word to/nFudge and stray back into the Muggle world./n/nHarry ate breakfast each morning in the Leaky/nCauldron, where he liked watching the other guests:/nfunny little witches from the country, up for a day's/nshopping; venerable-looking wizards arguing over the/nlatest article in Transfiguration Today; wild-looking/nwarlocks; raucous dwarfs; and once, what looked/nsuspiciously like a hag, who ordered a plate of raw/nliver from behind a thick woollen balaclava./n/nAfter breakfast Harry would go out into the backyard,/ntake out his wand, tap the third brick from the left/nabove the trash bin, and stand back as the archway/ninto Diagon Alley opened in the wall./n/n/n/n/nHarry spent the long sunny days exploring the shops/nand eating under the brightly colored umbrellas/noutside cafes, where his fellow diners were showing/none another their purchases ("it's a lunascope, old/nboy — no more messing around with moon charts,/nsee?") or else discussing the case of Sirius Black/n("personally, I won't let any of the children out alone/nuntil he's back in Azkaban"). Harry didn't have to do/nhis homework under the blankets by flashlight/nanymore; now he could sit in the bright sunshine/noutside Florean Fortescue's Ice Cream Parlor,/nfinishing all his essays with occasional help from/nFlorean Fortescue himself, who, apart from knowing a/ngreat deal about medieval witch burnings, gave Harry/nfree sundaes every half an hour./n/nOnce Harry had refilled his money bag with gold/nGalleons, silver Sickles, and bronze Knuts from his/nvault at Gringotts, he had to exercise a lot of self-/ncontrol not to spend the whole lot at once. He had to/nkeep reminding himself that he had five years to go at/nHogwarts, and how it would feel to ask the Dursleys/nfor money for spellbooks, to stop himself from buying/na handsome set of solid gold Gobstones (a wizarding/ngame rather like marbles, in which the stones squirt a/nnasty-smelling liquid into the other player's face when/nthey lose a point). He was sorely tempted, too, by the/nperfect, moving model of the galaxy in a large glass/nball, which would have meant he never had to take/nanother Astronomy lesson. But the thing that tested/nHarry's resolution most appeared in his favorite shop,/nQuality Quidditch Supplies, a week after he'd arrived/nat the Leaky Cauldron./n/nCurious to know what the crowd in the shop was/nstaring at, Harry edged his way inside and squeezed/nin among the excited witches and wizards until he/nglimpsed a newly erected podium, on which was/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmounted the most magnificent broom he had ever/nseen in his life./n/n"Just come out — prototype — " a square-jawed/nwizard was telling his companion./n/n"It's the fastest broom in the world, isn't it, Dad?"/nsqueaked a boy younger than Harry, who was/nswinging off his father's arm./n/n"Irish International Side's just put in an order for/nseven of these beauties!" the proprietor of the shop/ntold the crowd. "And they're favorites for the World/nCup!"/n/nA large witch in front of Harry moved, and he was/nable to read the sign next to the broom:/n/nTHE FIREBOLT/n/nThis state-of-the-art racing broom sports a stream-/nlined, superfine handle of ash, treated with a/ndiamond-hard polish and hand-numbered with its/nown registration number. Each individually selected/nbirch twig in the broomtail has been honed to/naerodynamic perfection, giving the Firebolt/nunsurpassable balance and pinpoint precision. The/nFirebolt has an acceleration of 150 miles an hour in/nten seconds and incorporates an unbreakable/nBraking Charm. Price on request./n/nPrice on request ... Harry didn't like to think how/nmuch gold the Firebolt would cost. He had never/nwanted anything as much in his whole life — but he/nhad never lost a Quidditch match on his Nimbus Two/nThousand, and what was the point in emptying his/nGringotts vault for the Firebolt, when he had a very/ngood broom already? Harry didn't ask for the price,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbut he returned, almost every day after that, just to/nlook at the Firebolt./n/nThere were, however, things that Harry needed to/nbuy. He went to the Apothecary to replenish his store/nof potions ingredients, and as his school robes were/nnow several inches too short in the arm and leg, he/nvisited Madam Malkin's Robes for All Occasions and/nbought new ones. Most important of all, he had to/nbuy his new schoolbooks, which would include those/nfor his two new subjects, Care of Magical Creatures/nand Divination./n/nHarry got a surprise as he looked in at the bookshop/nwindow. Instead of the usual display of gold-/nembossed spellbooks the size of paving slabs, there/nwas a large iron cage behind the glass that held about/na hundred copies of The Monster Book of Monsters./nTorn pages were flying everywhere as the books/ngrappled with each other, locked together in furious/nwrestling matches and snapping aggressively./n/nHarry pulled his booklist out of his pocket and/nconsulted it for the first time. The Monster Book of/nMonsters was listed as the required book for Care of/nMagical Creatures. Now Harry understood why Hagrid/nhad said it would come in useful. He felt relieved; he/nhad been wondering whether Hagrid wanted help with/nsome terrifying new pet./n/nAs Harry entered Flourish and Blotts, the manager/ncame hurrying toward him./n/n"Hogwarts?" he said abruptly. "Come to get your new/nbooks?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry, "I need — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Get out of the way," said the manager impatiently,/nbrushing Harry aside. He drew on a pair of very thick/ngloves, picked up a large, knobbly walking stick, and/nproceeded toward the door of the Monster Books' cage./n/n"Hang on," said Harry quickly, "I've already got one of/nthose."/n/n"Have you?" A look of enormous relief spread over the/nmanager's face. "Thank heavens for that. I've been/nbitten five times already this morning — "/n/nA loud ripping noise rent the air; two of the Monster/nBooks had seized a third and were pulling it apart./n/n"Stop it! Stop it!" cried the manager, poking the/nwalking stick through the bars and knocking the/nbooks apart. "I'm never stocking them again, never!/n/nIt's been bedlam! I thought we'd seen the worst when/nwe bought two hundred copies of the Invisible Book of/nInvisibility — cost a fortune, and we never found/nthem. ... Well ... is there anything else I can help you/nwith?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry, looking down his booklist, "I need/nUnfogging the Future by Cassandra Vablatsky."/n/n"Ah, starting Divination, are you?" said the manager,/nstripping off his gloves and leading Harry into the/nback of the shop, where there was a corner devoted to/nfortune-telling. A small table was stacked with/nvolumes such as Predicting the Unpredictable: Insulate/nYourself Against Shocks and Broken Balls: When/nFortunes Turn Foul./n/n"Here you are," said the manager, who had climbed a/nset of steps to take down a thick, black-bound book./n"Unfogging the Future. Very good guide to all your/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbasic fortune-telling methods — palmistry, crystal/nballs, bird entrails — "/n/nBut Harry wasn't listening. His eyes had fallen on/nanother book, which was among a display on a small/ntable: Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the/nWorst Is Coming./n/n"Oh, I wouldn't read that if I were you," said the/nmanager lightly, looking to see what Harry was/nstaring at. "You'll start seeing death omens/neverywhere. It's enough to frighten anyone to death."/n/nBut Harry continued to stare at the front cover of the/nbook; it showed a black dog large as a bear, with/ngleaming eyes. It looked oddly familiar. .../n/nThe manager pressed Unfogging the Future into/nHarry's hands./n/n"Anything else?" he said./n/n"Yes," said Harry, tearing his eyes away from the/ndog's and dazedly consulting his booklist. "Er — I/nneed Intermediate Transfiguration and The Standard/nBook of Spells, Grade Three."/n/nHarry emerged from Flourish and Blotts ten minutes/nlater with his new books under his arms and made/nhis way back to the Leaky Cauldron, hardly noticing/nwhere he was going and bumping into several people./n/nHe tramped up the stairs to his room, went inside,/nand tipped his books onto his bed. Somebody had/nbeen in to tidy; the windows were open and sun was/npouring inside. Harry could hear the buses rolling by/nin the unseen Muggle street behind him and the/nsound of the invisible crowd below in Diagon Alley. He/ncaught sight of himself in the mirror over the basin./n/n/n/n/n"It can't have been a death omen," he told his/nreflection defiantly. "I was panicking when I saw that/nthing in Magnolia Crescent. ... It was probably just a/nstray dog. ..."/n/nHe raised his hand automatically and tried to make/nhis hair lie flat./n/n"You're fighting a losing battle there, dear," said his/nmirror in a wheezy voice./n/nAs the days slipped by, Harry started looking/nwherever he went for a sign of Ron or Hermione./n/nPlenty of Hogwarts students were arriving in Diagon/nAlley now, with the start of term so near. Harry met/nSeamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas, his fellow/nGryffindors, in Quality Quidditch Supplies, where/nthey too were ogling the Firebolt; he also ran into the/nreal Neville Longbottom, a round-faced, forgetful boy,/noutside Flourish and Blotts. Harry didn't stop to chat;/nNeville appeared to have mislaid his booklist and was/nbeing told off by his very formidable-looking/ngrandmother. Harry hoped she never found out that/nhe'd pretended to be Neville while on the run from the/nMinistry of Magic./n/nHarry woke on the last day of the holidays, thinking/nthat he would at least meet Ron and Hermione/ntomorrow, on the Hogwarts Express. He got up,/ndressed, went for a last look at the Firebolt, and was/njust wondering where he'd have lunch, when someone/nyelled his name and he turned./n/n"Harry! HARRY!"/n/nThey were there, both of them, sitting outside Florean/nFortescue's Ice Cream Parlor — Ron looking/nincredibly freckly, Hermione very brown, both waving/nfrantically at him./n/n/n/n/n/n"Finally!" said Ron, grinning at Harry as he sat down./n"We went to the Leaky Cauldron, but they said you'd/nleft, and we went to Flourish and Blotts, and Madam/nMalkin's, and — "/n/n"I got all my school stuff last week," Harry explained./n"And how come you knew I'm staying at the Leaky/nCauldron?"/n/n"Dad," said Ron simply./n/nMr. Weasley, who worked at the Ministry of Magic,/nwould of course have heard the whole story of what/nhad happened to Aunt Marge./n/n"Did you really blow up your aunt, Harry?" said/nHermione in a very serious voice./n/n"I didn't mean to," said Harry while Ron roared with/nlaughter. "I just — lost control."/n/n"It's not funny, Ron," said Hermione sharply./n"Honestly, I'm amazed Harry wasn't expelled."/n/n"So am I," admitted Harry. "Forget expelled, I thought/nI was going to be arrested." He looked at Ron. "Your/ndad doesn't know why Fudge let me off, does he?"/n/n"Probably 'cause it's you, isn't it?" shrugged Ron, still/nchuckling. "Famous Harry Potter and all that. I'd hate/nto see what the Ministry'd do to me if I blew up an/naunt. Mind you, they'd have to dig me up first,/nbecause Mum would've killed me. Anyway, you can/nask Dad yourself this evening. We're staying at the/nLeaky Cauldron tonight too! So you can come to/nKing's Cross with us tomorrow! Hermione's there as/nwell!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione nodded, beaming. "Mum and Dad dropped/nme off this morning with all my Hogwarts things."/n/n"Excellent!" said Harry happily. "So, have you got all/nyour new books and stuff?"/n/n"Look at this," said Ron, pulling a long thin box out of/na bag and opening it. "Brand-new wand. Fourteen/ninches, willow, containing one unicorn tail-hair. And/nwe've got all our books — " He pointed at a large bag/nunder his chair. "What about those Monster Books,/neh? The assistant nearly cried when we said we/nwanted two."/n/n"What's all that, Hermione?" Harry asked, pointing at/nnot one but three bulging bags in the chair next to/nher./n/n"Well, I'm taking more new subjects than you, aren't/nI?" said Hermione. "Those are my books for/nArithmancy, Care of Magical Creatures, Divination,/nStudy of Ancient Runes, Muggle Studies — "/n/n"What are you doing Muggle Studies for?" said Ron,/nrolling his eyes at Harry. "You're Muggle-born! Your/nmum and dad are Muggles! You already know all/nabout Muggles!"/n/n"But it'll be fascinating to study them from the/nwizarding point of view," said Hermione earnestly./n/n"Are you planning to eat or sleep at all this year,/nHermione?" asked Harry, while Ron sniggered./nHermione ignored them./n/n"I've still got ten Galleons," she said, checking her/npurse. "It's my birthday in September, and Mum and/nDad gave me some money to get myself an early/nbirthday present."/n/n/n/n/n/n"How about a nice book?" said Ron innocently./n/n"No, I don't think so," said Hermione composedly. "I/nreally want an owl. I mean, Harry's got Hedwig and/nyou've got Errol — "/n/n"I haven't," said Ron. "Errol's a family owl. All I've got/nis Scabbers." He pulled his pet rat out of his pocket./n"And I want to get him checked over," he added,/nplacing Scabbers on the table in front of them. "I/ndon't think Egypt agreed with him."/n/nScabbers was looking thinner than usual, and there/nwas a definite droop to his whiskers./n/n"There's a magical creature shop just over there," said/nHarry, who knew Diagon Alley very well by now. "You/ncould see if they've got anything for Scabbers, and/nHermione can get her owl."/n/nSo they paid for their ice cream and crossed the street/nto the Magical Menagerie./n/nThere wasn't much room inside. Every inch of wall/nwas hidden by cages. It was smelly and very noisy/nbecause the occupants of these cages were all/nsqueaking, squawking, jabbering, or hissing. The/nwitch behind the counter was already advising a/nwizard on the care of double-ended newts, so Harry,/nRon, and Hermione waited, examining the cages./n/nA pair of enormous purple toads sat gulping wetly/nand feasting on dead blowflies. A gigantic tortoise/nwith a jewel-encrusted shell was glittering near the/nwindow. Poisonous orange snails were oozing slowly/nup the side of their glass tank, and a fat white rabbit/nkept changing into a silk top hat and back again with/na loud popping noise. Then there were cats of every/ncolor, a noisy cage of ravens, a basket of funny/n/n/n/n/ncustard-colored furballs that were humming loudly,/nand on the counter, a vast cage of sleek black rats/nthat were playing some sort of skipping game using/ntheir long, bald tails./n/nThe double-ended newt wizard left, and Ron/napproached the counter./n/n"It's my rat," he told the witch. "He been a bit off-color/never since I brought him back from Egypt."/n/n"Bang him on the counter," said the witch, pulling a/npair of heavy black spectacles out of her pocket./n/nRon lifted Scabbers out of his inside pocket and/nplaced him next to the cage of his fellow rats, who/nstopped their skipping tricks and scuffled to the wire/nfor a better look./n/nLike nearly everything Ron owned, Scabbers the rat/nwas secondhand (he had once belonged to Ron's/nbrother Percy) and a bit battered. Next to the glossy/nrats in the cage, he looked especially woebegone./n/n"Hm," said the witch, picking up Scabbers. "How old/nis this rat?"/n/n"Dunno," said Ron. "Quite old. He used to belong to/nmy brother."/n/n"What powers does he have?" said the witch,/nexamining Scabbers closely./n/n"Er — " The truth was that Scabbers had never shown/nthe faintest trace of interesting powers. The witch's/neyes moved from Scabbers 's tattered left ear to his/nfront paw, which had a toe missing, and tutted/nloudly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He's been through the mill, this one," she said./n/n/n/n"He was like that when Percy gave him to me," said/nRon defensively./n/n"An ordinary common or garden rat like this can't be/nexpected to live longer than three years or so," said/nthe witch. "Now, if you were looking for something a/nbit more hard-wearing, you might like one of these — "/n/nShe indicated the black rats, who promptly started/nskipping again. Ron muttered, "Show-offs."/n/n"Well, if you don't want a replacement, you can try/nthis rat tonic," said the witch, reaching under the/ncounter and bringing out a small red bottle./n/n"Okay," said Ron.
