"How much — OUCH!"/n/nRon buckled as something huge and orange came/nsoaring from the top of the highest cage, landed on/nhis head, and then propelled itself, spitting madly, at/nScabbers./n/n"NO, CROOKSHANKS, NO!" cried the witch, but/nScabbers shot from between her hands like a bar of/nsoap, landed splay-legged on the floor, and then/nscampered for the door./n/n"Scabbers!" Ron shouted, racing out of the shop after/nhim; Harry followed./n/nIt took them nearly ten minutes to catch Scabbers,/nwho had taken refuge under a wastepaper bin outside/nQuality Quidditch Supplies. Ron stuffed the trembling/nrat back into his pocket and straightened up,/nmassaging his head./n/n"What was that?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"It was either a very big cat or quite a small tiger,"/nsaid Harry./n/n"Where's Hermione?"/n/n"Probably getting her owl — "/n/nThey made their way back up the crowded street to/nthe Magical Menagerie. As they reached it, Hermione/ncame out, but she wasn't carrying an owl. Her arms/nwere clamped tightly around the enormous ginger cat./n/n"You bought that monster?" said Ron, his mouth/nhanging open./n/n"He's gorgeous, isn't he?" said Hermione, glowing./n/nThat was a matter of opinion, thought Harry. The/ncat's ginger fur was thick and fluffy, but it was/ndefinitely a bit bowlegged and its face looked grumpy/nand oddly squashed, as though it had run headlong/ninto a brick wall. Now that Scabbers was out of sight,/nhowever, the cat was purring contentedly in/nHermione 's arms./n/n"Hermione, that thing nearly scalped me!" said Ron./n/n"He didn't mean to, did you, Crookshanks?" said/nHermione./n/n"And what about Scabbers?" said Ron, pointing at the/nlump in his chest pocket. "He needs rest and/nrelaxation! How's he going to get it with that thing/naround?"/n/n"That reminds me, you forgot your rat tonic," said/nHermione, slapping the small red bottle into Ron's/nhand. "And stop worrying, Crookshanks will be/nsleeping in my dormitory and Scabbers in yours,/n/n/n/n/n/nwhat's the problem? Poor Crookshanks, that witch/nsaid he'd been in there for ages; no one wanted him."/n/n"I wonder why," said Ron sarcastically as they set off/ntoward the Leaky Cauldron./n/nThey found Mr. Weasley sitting in the bar, reading the/nDaily Prophet./n/n"Harry!" he said, smiling as he looked up. "How are/nyou?"/n/n"Fine, thanks," said Harry as he, Ron, and Hermione/njoined Mr. Weasley with all their shopping./n/nMr. Weasley put down his paper, and Harry saw the/nnow familiar picture of Sirius Black staring up at him./n/n"They still haven't caught him, then?" he asked./n/n"No," said Mr. Weasley, looking extremely grave./n"They've pulled us all off our regular jobs at the/nMinistry to try and find him, but no luck so far."/n/n"Would we get a reward if we caught him?" asked/nRon. "It'd be good to get some more money — "/n/n"Don't be ridiculous, Ron," said Mr. Weasley, who on/ncloser inspection looked very strained. "Black's not/ngoing to be caught by a thirteen-year-old wizard. It's/nthe Azkaban guards who'll get him back, you mark/nmy words."/n/nAt that moment Mrs. Weasley entered the bar, laden/nwith shopping bags and followed by the twins, Fred/nand George, who were about to start their fifth year at/nHogwarts; the newly elected Head Boy, Percy; and the/nWeasleys' youngest child and only girl, Ginny./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGinny, who had always been very taken with Harry,/nseemed even more heartily embarrassed than usual/nwhen she saw him, perhaps because he had saved/nher life during their previous year at Hogwarts. She/nwent very red and muttered "hello" without looking at/nhim. Percy, however, held out his hand solemnly as/nthough he and Harry had never met and said, "Harry./nHow nice to see you."/n/n"Hello, Percy," said Harry, trying not to laugh./n/n"I hope you're well?" said Percy pompously, shaking/nhands. It was rather like being introduced to the/nmayor./n/n"Very well, thanks — "/n/n"Harry!" said Fred, elbowing Percy out of the way and/nbowing deeply. "Simply splendid to see you, old boy —/n/n/n/n"Marvelous," said George, pushing Fred aside and/nseizing Harry's hand in turn. "Absolutely spiffing."/n/nPercy scowled./n/n"That's enough, now," said Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Mum!" said Fred as though he'd only just spotted her/nand seizing her hand too. "How really corking to see/nyou — "/n/n"I said, that's enough," said Mrs. Weasley, depositing/nher shopping in an empty chair. "Hello, Harry, dear. I/nsuppose you've heard our exciting news?" She pointed/nto the brand-new silver badge on Percy's chest./n"Second Head Boy in the family!" she said, swelling/nwith pride./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And last," Fred muttered under his breath./n/n/n/n"I don't doubt that," said Mrs. Weasley, frowning/nsuddenly. "I notice they haven't made you two/nprefects."/n/n"What do we want to be prefects for?" said George,/nlooking revolted at the very idea. "It'd take all the fun/nout of life."/n/nGinny giggled./n/n"You want to set a better example for your sister!"/nsnapped Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Ginny's got other brothers to set her an example,/nMother," said Percy loftily. "I'm going up to change for/ndinner. ..."/n/nHe disappeared and George heaved a sigh./n/n"We tried to shut him in a pyramid," he told Harry./n"But Mum spotted us."/n/nDinner that night was a very enjoyable affair. Tom the/ninnkeeper put three tables together in the parlor, and/nthe seven Weasleys, Harry, and Hermione ate their/nway through five delicious courses./n/n"How're we getting to King's Cross tomorrow, Dad?"/nasked Fred as they dug into a sumptuous chocolate/npudding./n/n"The Ministry's providing a couple of cars," said Mr./nWeasley./n/nEveryone looked up at him./n/n"Why?" said Percy curiously./n/n/n/n/n/n"It's because of you, Perce," said George seriously./n"And there'll be little flags on the hoods, with HB on/nthem — "/n/n" — for Humongous Bighead," said Fred./n/nEveryone except Percy and Mrs. Weasley snorted into/ntheir pudding./n/n"Why are the Ministry providing cars, Father?" Percy/nasked again, in a dignified voice./n/n"Well, as we haven't got one anymore," said Mr./nWeasley, " — and as I work there, they're doing me a/nfavor — "/n/nHis voice was casual, but Harry couldn't help noticing/nthat Mr. Weasley's ears had gone red, just like Ron's/ndid when he was under pressure./n/n"Good thing, too," said Mrs. Weasley briskly. "Do you/nrealize how much luggage you've all got between you?/nA nice sight you'd be on the Muggle Underground. .../nYou are all packed, aren't you?"/n/n"Ron hasn't put all his new things in his trunk yet,"/nsaid Percy, in a long-suffering voice. "He's dumped/nthem on my bed."/n/n"You'd better go and pack properly, Ron, because we/nwon't have much time in the morning," Mrs. Weasley/ncalled down the table. Ron scowled at Percy./n/nAfter dinner everyone felt very full and sleepy. One by/none they made their way upstairs to their rooms to/ncheck their things for the next day. Ron and Percy/nwere next door to Harry. He had just closed and/nlocked his own trunk when he heard angry voices/nthrough the wall, and went to see what was going on./n/n/n/n/nThe door of number twelve was ajar and Percy was/nshouting./n/n"It was here, on the bedside table, I took it off for/npolishing — "/n/n"I haven't touched it, all right?" Ron roared back./n"What's up?" said Harry./n/n"My Head Boy badge is gone," said Percy, rounding on/nHarry./n/n"So's Scabbers's rat tonic," said Ron, throwing things/nout of his trunk to look. "I think I might've left it in/nthe bar — "/n/n"You're not going anywhere till you've found my/nbadge!" yelled Percy./n/n"I'll get Scabbers's stuff, I'm packed," Harry said to/nRon, and he went downstairs./n/nHarry was halfway along the passage to the bar,/nwhich was now very dark, when he heard another/npair of angry voices coming from the parlor. A second/nlater, he recognized them as Mr. and Mrs. Weasleys'./nHe hesitated, not wanting them to know he'd heard/nthem arguing, when the sound of his own name made/nhim stop, then move closer to the parlor door./n/n"... makes no sense not to tell him," Mr. Weasley was/nsaying heatedly. "Harry's got a right to know. I've tried/nto tell Fudge, but he insists on treating Harry like a/nchild. He's thirteen years old and — "/n/n"Arthur, the truth would terrify him!" said Mrs./nWeasley shrilly. "Do you really want to send Harry/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nback to school with that hanging over him? For/nheaven's sake, he's happy not knowing!"/n/n"I don't want to make him miserable, I want to put/nhim on his guard!" retorted Mr. Weasley. "You know/nwhat Harry and Ron are like, wandering off by/nthemselves — they've even ended up in the Forbidden/nForest! But Harry mustn't do that this year! When I/nthink what could have happened to him that night he/nran away from home! If the Knight Bus hadn't picked/nhim up, I'm prepared to bet he would have been dead/nbefore the Ministry found him."/n/n"But he's not dead, he's fine, so what's the point — "/n/n"Molly, they say Sirius Black's mad, and maybe he is,/nbut he was clever enough to escape from Azkaban,/nand that's supposed to be impossible. It's been a/nmonth, and no one's seen hide nor hair of him, and I/ndon't care what Fudge keeps telling the Daily Prophet,/nwe're no nearer catching Black than inventing self-/nspelling wands. The only thing we know for sure is/nwhat Black's after — "/n/n"But Harry will be perfectly safe at Hogwarts."/n/n"We thought Azkaban was perfectly safe. If Black can/nbreak out of Azkaban, he can break into Hogwarts."/n/n"But no one's really sure that Black's after Harry — "/n/nThere was a thud on wood, and Harry was sure Mr./nWeasley had banged his fist on the table./n/n"Molly, how many times do I have to tell you? They/ndidn't report it in the press because Fudge wanted it/nkept quiet, but Fudge went out to Azkaban the night/nBlack escaped. The guards told Fudge that Black's/nbeen talking in his sleep for a while now. Always the/n/n/n/n/nsame words: 'He's at Hogwarts ... he's at Hogwarts.'/nBlack is deranged, Molly, and he wants Harry dead. If/nyou ask me, he thinks murdering Harry will bring/nYou-Know-Who back to power. Black lost everything/nthe night Harry stopped You-Know-Who, and he's had/ntwelve years alone in Azkaban to brood on that. ..."/n/nThere was a silence. Harry leaned still closer to the/ndoor, desperate to hear more./n/n"Well, Arthur, you must do what you think is right./nBut you're forgetting Albus Dumbledore. I don't think/nanything could hurt Harry at Hogwarts while/nDumbledore 's headmaster. I suppose he knows about/nall this?"/n/n"Of course he knows. We had to ask him if he minds/nthe Azkaban guards stationing themselves around the/nentrances to the school grounds. He wasn't happy/nabout it, but he agreed."/n/n"Not happy? Why shouldn't he be happy, if they're/nthere to catch Black?"/n/n"Dumbledore isn't fond of the Azkaban guards," said/nMr. Weasley heavily. "Nor am I, if it comes to that .../nbut when you're dealing with a wizard like Black, you/nsometimes have to join forces with those you'd rather/navoid."/n/n"If they save Harry — "/n/n" — then I will never say another word against them,"/nsaid Mr. Weasley wearily. "It's late, Molly, we'd better/ngo up. ..."/n/nHarry heard chairs move. As quietly as he could, he/nhurried down the passage to the bar and out of sight./nThe parlor door opened, and a few seconds later/n/n/n/n/n/nfootsteps told him that Mr. and Mrs. Weasley were/nclimbing the stairs./n/n/n/nThe bottle of rat tonic was lying under the table they/nhad sat at earlier. Harry waited until he heard Mr./nand Mrs. Weasley's bedroom door close, then headed/nback upstairs with the bottle./n/nFred and George were crouching in the shadows on/nthe landing, heaving with laughter as they listened to/nPercy dismantling his and Ron's room in search of his/nbadge./n/n"We've got it," Fred whispered to Harry. "We've been/nimproving it."/n/nThe badge now read BigheacL Boy./n/nHarry forced a laugh, went to give Ron the rat tonic,/nthen shut himself in his room and lay down on his/nbed./n/nSo Sirius Black was after him. This explained/neverything. Fudge had been lenient with him because/nhe was so relieved to find him alive. He'd made Harry/npromise to stay in Diagon Alley where there were/nplenty of wizards to keep an eye on him. And he was/nsending two Ministry cars to take them all to the/nstation tomorrow, so that the Weasleys could look/nafter Harry until he was on the train./n/nHarry lay listening to the muffled shouting next door/nand wondered why he didn't feel more scared. Sirius/nBlack had murdered thirteen people with one curse;/nMr. and Mrs. Weasley obviously thought Harry would/nbe panic-stricken if he knew the truth. But Harry/nhappened to agree wholeheartedly with Mrs. Weasley/nthat the safest place on earth was wherever Albus/nDumbledore happened to be. Didn't people always say/n/n/n/n/nthat Dumbledore was the only person Lord Voldemort/nhad ever been afraid of? Surely Black, as Voldemort's/nright-hand man, would be just as frightened of him?/n/nAnd then there were these Azkaban guards everyone/nkept talking about. They seemed to scare most people/nsenseless, and if they were stationed all around the/nschool, Black's chances of getting inside seemed very/nremote./n/nNo, all in all, the thing that bothered Harry most was/nthe fact that his chances of visiting Hogsmeade now/nlooked like zero. Nobody would want Harry to leave/nthe safety of the castle until Black was caught; in/nfact, Harry suspected his every move would be/ncarefully watched until the danger had passed./n/nHe scowled at the dark ceiling. Did they think he/ncouldn't look after himself? He'd escaped Lord/nVoldemort three times; he wasn't completely useless./n/n/n/nUnbidden, the image of the beast in the shadows of/nMagnolia Crescent crossed his mind. What to do when/nyou know the worst is coming. . . ./n/n"I'm not going to be murdered," Harry said out loud./n/n"That's the spirit, dear," said his mirror sleepily./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n5/n/n/n/n

title: The Dementor
text: /nTom woke Harry the next morning with his usual/ntoothless grin and a cup of tea. They waved at him, but had no chance to/nspeak to him because the mass of people around/nthem was shunting them away along the platform./nHarry, Ron, and Hermione followed the rest of the/nschool along the platform and out onto a rough mud/ntrack, where at least a hundred stagecoaches awaited/nthe remaining students, each pulled, Harry could only/nassume, by an invisible horse, because when they/nclimbed inside and shut the door, the coach set off all/nby itself, bumping and swaying in procession./n/nThe coach smelled faintly of mold and straw. Harry/nfelt better since the chocolate, but still weak. Ron and/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione kept looking at him sideways, as though/nfrightened he might collapse again./n/nAs the carriage trundled toward a pair of magnificent/nwrought iron gates, flanked with stone columns/ntopped with winged boars, Harry saw two more/ntowering, hooded dementors, standing guard on/neither side. A wave of cold sickness threatened to/nengulf him again; he leaned back into the lumpy seat/nand closed his eyes until they had passed the gates./nThe carriage picked up speed on the long, sloping/ndrive up to the castle; Hermione was leaning out of/nthe tiny window, watching the many turrets and/ntowers draw nearer. At last, the carriage swayed to a/nhalt, and Hermione and Ron got out./n/nAs Harry stepped down, a drawling, delighted voice/nsounded in his ear./n/n"You fainted, Potter? Is Longbottom telling the truth?/nYou actually fainted?"/n/nMalfoy elbowed past Hermione to block Harry's way/nup the stone steps to the castle, his face gleeful and/nhis pale eyes glinting maliciously./n/n"Shove off, Malfoy," said Ron, whose jaw was/nclenched./n/n"Did you faint as well, Weasley?" said Malfoy loudly./n"Did the scary old dementor frighten you too,/nWeasley?"/n/n"Is there a problem?" said a mild voice. Professor/nLupin had just gotten out of the next carriage./n/nMalfoy gave Professor Lupin an insolent stare, which/ntook in the patches on his robes and the delapidated/nsuitcase. With a tiny hint of sarcasm in his voice, he/n/n/n/n/n/nsaid, "Oh, no — er — Professor," then he smirked at/nCrabbe and Goyle and led them up the steps into the/ncastle./n/nHermione prodded Ron in the back to make him/nhurry, and the three of them joined the crowd/nswarming up the steps, through the giant oak front/ndoors, into the cavernous entrance hall, which was lit/nwith flaming torches, and housed a magnificent/nmarble staircase that led to the upper floors./n/nThe door into the Great Hall stood open at the right;/nHarry followed the crowd toward it, but had barely/nglimpsed the enchanted ceiling, which was black and/ncloudy tonight, when a voice called, "Potter! Granger!/n/nI want to see you both!"/n/nHarry and Hermione turned around, surprised./nProfessor McGonagall, Transfiguration teacher and/nhead of Gryffindor House, was calling over the heads/nof the crowd. She was a stern-looking witch who wore/nher hair in a tight bun; her sharp eyes were framed/nwith square spectacles. Harry fought his way over to/nher with a feeling of foreboding: Professor McGonagall/nhad a way of making him feel he must have done/nsomething wrong./n/n"There's no need to look so worried — I just want a/nword in my office," she told them. "Move along there,/nWeasley."/n/nRon stared as Professor McGonagall ushered/nHarry and Hermione away from the chattering crowd;/nthey accompanied her across the entrance hall, up/nthe marble staircase, and along a corridor./n/nOnce they were in her office, a small room with a/nlarge, welcoming fire, Professor McGonagall motioned/nHarry and Hermione to sit down. She settled herself/n/n/n/n/n/nbehind her desk and said abruptly, "Professor Lupin/nsent an owl ahead to say that you were taken ill on/nthe train, Potter."/n/nBefore Harry could reply, there was a soft knock on/nthe door and Madam Pomfrey, the nurse, came/nbustling in./n/nHarry felt himself going red in the face. It was bad/nenough that he'd passed out, or whatever he had/ndone, without everyone making all this fuss./n/n"I'm fine," he said, "I don't need anything — "/n/n"Oh, it's you, is it?" said Madam Pomfrey, ignoring/nthis and bending down to stare closely at him. "I/nsuppose you've been doing something dangerous/nagain?"/n/n"It was a dementor, Poppy," said Professor/nMcGonagall./n/nThey exchanged a dark look, and Madam Pomfrey/nclucked disapprovingly./n/n"Setting dementors around a school," she muttered,/npushing back Harry's hair and feeling his forehead./n"He won't be the last one who collapses. Yes, he's all/nclammy. Terrible things, they are, and the effect they/nhave on people who are already delicate — "/n/n"I'm not delicate!" said Harry crossly./n/n"Of course you're not," said Madam Pomfrey/nabsentmindedly, now taking his pulse./n/n"What does he need?" said Professor McGonagall/ncrisply. "Bed rest? Should he perhaps spend tonight/nin the hospital wing?"/n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm /ine!" said Harry, jumping up. The thought of/nwhat Draco Malfoy would say if he had to go to the/nhospital wing was torture./n/n"Well, he should have some chocolate, at the very/nleast," said Madam Pomfrey, who was now trying to/npeer into Harry's eyes./n/n"I've already had some," said Harry. "Professor Lupin/ngave me some. He gave it to all of us."/n/n"Did he, now?" said Madam Pomfrey approvingly. "So/nwe've finally got a Defense Against the Dark Arts/nteacher who knows his remedies?"/n/n"Are you sure you feel all right, Potter?" Professor/nMcGonagall said sharply./n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n"Very well. Kindly wait outside while I have a quick/nword with Miss Granger about her course schedule,/nthen we can go down to the feast together."/n/nHarry went back into the corridor with Madam/nPomfrey, who left for the hospital wing, muttering to/nherself. He had to wait only a few minutes; then/nHermione emerged looking very happy about/nsomething, followed by Professor McGonagall, and the/nthree of them made their way back down the marble/nstaircase to the Great Hall./n/nIt was a sea of pointed black hats; each of the long/nHouse tables was lined with students, their faces/nglimmering by the light of thousands of candles,/nwhich were floating over the tables in midair./n/nProfessor Flitwick, who was a tiny little wizard with a/nshock of white hair, was carrying an ancient hat and/na three-legged stool out of the hall./n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh," said Hermione softly, "we've missed the/nSorting!"/n/nNew students at Hogwarts were sorted into Houses by/ntrying on the Sorting Hat, which shouted out the/nHouse they were best suited to (Gryffindor,/n/nRavenclaw, Hufflepuff, or Slytherin). Professor/nMcGonagall strode off toward her empty seat at the/nstaff table, and Harry and Hermione set off in the/nother direction, as quietly as possible, toward the/nGryffindor table. People looked around at them as/nthey passed along the back of the hall, and a few of/nthem pointed at Harry. Had the story of his collapsing/nin front of the dementor traveled that fast?/n/nHe and Hermione sat down on either side of Ron, who/nhad saved them seats./n/n"What was all that about?" he muttered to Harry./n/nHarry started to explain in a whisper, but at that/nmoment the headmaster stood up to speak, and he/nbroke off./n/nProfessor Dumbledore, though very old, always gave/nan impression of great energy. He had several feet of/nlong silver hair and beard, half-moon spectacles, and/nan extremely crooked nose. He was often described as/nthe greatest wizard of the age, but that wasn't why/nHarry respected him. You couldn't help trusting Albus/nDumbledore, and as Harry watched him beaming/naround at the students, he felt really calm for the first/ntime since the dementor had entered the train/ncompartment./n/n"Welcome!" said Dumbledore, the candlelight/nshimmering on his beard. "Welcome to another year/nat Hogwarts! I have a few things to say to you all, and/nas one of them is very serious, I think it best to get it/n/n/n/n/n/nout of the way before you become befuddled by our/nexcellent feast. ..."/n/nDumbledore cleared his throat and continued, "As/nyou will all be aware after their search of the/nHogwarts Express, our school is presently playing/nhost to some of the dementors of Azkaban, who are/nhere on Ministry of Magic business."/n/nHe paused, and Harry remembered what Mr. Weasley/nhad said about Dumbledore not being happy with the/ndementors guarding the school./n/n"They are stationed at every entrance to the grounds,"/nDumbledore continued, "and while they are with us, I/nmust make it plain that nobody is to leave school/nwithout permission. Dementors are not to be fooled/nby tricks or disguises — or even Invisibility Cloaks,"/nhe added blandly, and Harry and Ron glanced at each/nother. "It is not in the nature of a dementor to/nunderstand pleading or excuses. I therefore warn/neach and every one of you to give them no reason to/nharm you. I look to the prefects, and our new Head/nBoy and Girl, to make sure that no student runs afoul/nof the dementors," he said./n/nPercy, who was sitting a few seats down from Harry,/npuffed out his chest again and stared around/nimpressively. Dumbledore paused again; he looked/nvery seriously around the hall, and nobody moved or/nmade a sound./n/n"On a happier note," he continued, "I am pleased to/nwelcome two new teachers to our ranks this year./n/n"First, Professor Lupin, who has kindly consented to/nfill the post of Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was some scattered, rather unenthusiastic/napplause. Only those who had been in the/ncompartment on the train with Professor Lupin/nclapped hard, Harry among them. Professor Lupin/nlooked particularly shabby next to all the other/nteachers in their best robes./n/n"Look at Snape!" Ron hissed in Harry's ear./n/nProfessor Snape, the Potions master, was staring/nalong the staff table at Professor Lupin. It was/ncommon knowledge that Snape wanted the Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts job, but even Harry, who hated/nSnape, was startled at the expression twisting his/nthin, sallow face. It was beyond anger: it was loathing./nHarry knew that expression only too well; it was the/nlook Snape wore every time he set eyes on Harry./n/n"As to our second new appointment," Dumbledore/ncontinued as the lukewarm applause for Professor/nLupin died away. "Well, I am sorry to tell you that/nProfessor Kettleburn, our Care of Magical Creatures/nteacher, retired at the end of last year in order to/nenjoy more time with his remaining limbs. However, I/nam delighted to say that his place will be filled by/nnone other than Rubeus Hagrid, who has agreed to/ntake on this teaching job in addition to his/ngamekeeping duties."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione stared at one another,/nstunned. Then they joined in with the applause,/nwhich was tumultuous at the Gryffindor table in/nparticular. Harry leaned forward to see Hagrid, who/nwas ruby-red in the face and staring down at his/nenormous hands, his wide grin hidden in the tangle of/nhis black beard./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We should've known!" Ron roared, pounding the/ntable. "Who else would have assigned us a biting/nbook?"/n/n/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione were the last to stop/nclapping, and as Professor Dumbledore started/nspeaking again, they saw that Hagrid was wiping his/neyes on the tablecloth./n/n"Well, I think that's everything of importance," said/nDumbledore. "Let the feast begin!"/n/nThe golden plates and goblets before them filled/nsuddenly with food and drink. Harry, suddenly/nravenous, helped himself to everything he could reach/nand began to eat./n/nIt was a delicious feast; the hall echoed with talk,/nlaughter, and the clatter of knives and forks. Harry,/nRon, and Hermione, however, were eager for it to/nfinish so that they could talk to Hagrid. They knew/nhow much being made a teacher would mean to him./nHagrid wasn't a fully qualified wizard; he had been/nexpelled from Hogwarts in his third year for a crime/nhe had not committed. It had been Harry, Ron, and/nHermione who had cleared Hagrid 's name last year./n/nAt long last, when the last morsels of pumpkin tart/nhad melted from the golden platters, Dumbledore/ngave the word that it was time for them all to go to/nbed, and they got their chance./n/n"Congratulations, Hagrid!" Hermione squealed as they/nreached the teachers' table./n/n"All down ter you three," said Hagrid, wiping his/nshining face on his napkin as he looked up at them./n"Can' believe it ... great man, Dumbledore ... came/nstraight down to me hut after Professor Kettleburn/n/n/n/n/n/nsaid he'd had enough. ... It's what I always wanted./n/n/n/nOvercome with emotion, he buried his face in his/nnapkin, and Professor McGonagall shooed them away./n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione joined the Gryffindors/nstreaming up the marble staircase and, very tired/nnow, along more corridors, up more and more stairs,/nto the hidden entrance to Gryffindor Tower. A large/nportrait of a fat lady in a pink dress asked them,/n"Password?"/n/n"Coming through, coming through!" Percy called from/nbehind the crowd. "The new password's 'Fortuna/nMajor'!"/n/n"Oh no," said Neville Longbottom sadly. He always/nhad trouble remembering the passwords./n/nThrough the portrait hole and across the common/nroom, the girls and boys divided toward their separate/nstaircases. Harry climbed the spiral stair with no/nthought in his head except how glad he was to be/nback. They reached their familiar, circular dormitory/nwith its five four-poster beds, and Harry, looking/naround, felt he was home at last./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Talons And Tea Leaves
text: /nWhen Harry, Ron, and Hermione entered the Great/nHall for breakfast the next day, the first thing they/nsaw was Draco Malfoy, who seemed to be entertaining/na large group of Slytherins with a very funny story. As/nthey passed, Malfoy did a ridiculous impression of a/nswooning fit and there was a roar of laughter./n/n"Ignore him," said Hermione, who was right behind/nHarry. "Just ignore him, it's not worth it. ..."/n/n"Hey, Potter!" shrieked Pansy Parkinson, a Slytherin/ngirl with a face like a pug. "Potter! The dementors are/ncoming, Potter! Woooooooo!"/n/nHarry dropped into a seat at the Gryffindor table, next/nto George Weasley./n/n"New third-year course schedules," said George,/npassing them over. "What's up with you, Harry?"/n/n"Malfoy," said Ron, sitting down on George's other/nside and glaring over at the Slytherin table./n/n/n/n/nGeorge looked up in time to see Malfoy pretending to/nfaint with terror again./n/n"That little git," he said calmly. "He wasn't so cocky/nlast night when the dementors were down at our end/nof the train. Came running into our compartment,/ndidn't he, Fred?"/n/n"Nearly wet himself," said Fred, with a contemptuous/nglance at Malfoy./n/n"I wasn't too happy myself," said George. "They're/nhorrible things, those dementors. ..."/n/n"Sort of freeze your insides, don't they?" said Fred./n/n"You didn't pass out, though, did you?" said Harry in/na low voice./n/n"Forget it, Harry," said George bracingly. "Dad had to/ngo out to Azkaban one time, remember, Fred? And he/nsaid it was the worst place he'd ever been, he came/nback all weak and shaking. . . . They suck the/nhappiness out of a place, dementors. Most of the/nprisoners go mad in there."/n/n"Anyway, we'll see how happy Malfoy looks after our/nfirst Quidditch match," said Fred. "Gryffindor versus/nSlytherin, first game of the season, remember?"/n/nThe only time Harry and Malfoy had faced each other/nin a Quidditch match, Malfoy had definitely come off/nworse. Feeling slightly more cheerful, Harry helped/nhimself to sausages and fried tomatoes./n/nHermione was examining her new schedule./n/n"Ooh, good, we're starting some new subjects today,"/nshe said happily./n/n/n/n/n/n"Hermione," said Ron, frowning as he looked over her/nshoulder, "they've messed up your schedule. Look —/nthey've got you down for about ten subjects a day./nThere isn't enough time."/n/n"I'll manage. I've fixed it all with Professor/nMcGonagall."/n/n"But look," said Ron, laughing, "see this morning?/nNine o'clock, Divination. And underneath, nine/no'clock, Muggle Studies. And" — Ron leaned closer to/nthe schedule, disbelieving — " look — underneath/nthat, Arithmancy, nine o'clock. I mean, I know you're/ngood, Hermione, but no one's that good. How're you/nsupposed to be in three classes at once?"/n/n"Don't be silly," said Hermione shortly. "Of course I/nwon't be in three classes at once."/n/n"Well, then — "/n/n"Pass the marmalade," said Hermione./n/n"But — "/n/n"Oh, Ron, what's it to you if my schedule's a bit full?"/nHermione snapped. "I told you, I've fixed it all with/nProfessor McGonagall."/n/nJust then, Hagrid entered the Great Hall. He was/nwearing his long moleskin overcoat and was/nabsentmindedly swinging a dead polecat from one/nenormous hand./n/n"All righ'?" he said eagerly, pausing on the way to the/nstaff table. "Yer in my firs' ever lesson! Right after/nlunch! Bin up since five gettin' everythin' ready. .../nHope it's okay. ... Me, a teacher ... hones'ly. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe grinned broadly at them and headed off to the/nstaff table, still swinging the polecat./n/n"Wonder what he's been getting ready?" said Ron, a/nnote of anxiety in his voice./n/nThe hall was starting to empty as people headed off/ntoward their first lesson. Ron checked his course/nschedule./n/n"We'd better go, look, Divination's at the top of North/nTower. It'll take us ten minutes to get there. ..."/n/nThey finished their breakfasts hastily, said good-bye/nto Fred and George, and walked back through the/nhall. As they passed the Slytherin table, Malfoy did/nyet another impression of a fainting fit. The shouts of/nlaughter followed Harry into the entrance hall./n/nThe journey through the castle to North Tower was a/nlong one. Two years at Hogwarts hadn't taught them/neverything about the castle, and they had never been/ninside North Tower before./n/n"There's — got — to — be — a — shortcut," Ron/npanted as they climbed their seventh long staircase/nand emerged on an unfamiliar landing, where there/nwas nothing but a large painting of a bare stretch of/ngrass hanging on the stone wall./n/n"I think it's this way," said Hermione, peering down/nthe empty passage to the right./n/n"Can't be," said Ron. "That's south, look, you can see/na bit of the lake out of the window ..."/n/nHarry was watching the painting. A fat, dapple-gray/npony had just ambled onto the grass and was grazing/nnonchalantly. Harry was used to the subjects of/n/n/n/n/n/nHogwarts paintings moving around and leaving their/nframes to visit one another, but he always enjoyed/nwatching it. A moment later, a short, squat knight in/na suit of armor clanked into the picture after his/npony. By the look of the grass stains on his metal/nknees, he had just fallen off./n/n"Aha!" he yelled, seeing Harry, Ron, and Hermione./n"What villains are these, that trespass upon my/nprivate lands! Come to scorn at my fall, perchance?/nDraw, you knaves, you dogs!"/n/nThey watched in astonishment as the little knight/ntugged his sword out of its scabbard and began/nbrandishing it violently, hopping up and down in/nrage. But the sword was too long for him; a/nparticularly wild swing made him overbalance, and he/nlanded facedown in the grass./n/n"Are you all right?" said Harry, moving closer to the/npicture./n/n"Get back, you scurvy braggart! Back, you rogue!"/n/nThe knight seized his sword again and used it to push/nhimself back up, but the blade sank deeply into the/ngrass and, though he pulled with all his might, he/ncouldn't get it out again. Finally, he had to flop back/ndown onto the grass and push up his visor to mop his/nsweating face./n/n"Listen," said Harry, taking advantage of the knight's/nexhaustion, "we're looking for the North Tower. You/ndon't know the way, do you?"/n/n"A quest!" The knight's rage seemed to vanish/ninstantly. He clanked to his feet and shouted, "Come/nfollow me, dear friends, and we shall find our goal, or/nelse shall perish bravely in the charge!"/n/n/n/n/n/nHe gave the sword another fruitless tug, tried and/nfailed to mount the fat pony, gave up, and cried, "On/nfoot then, good sirs and gentle lady! On! On!"/n/nAnd he ran, clanking loudly, into the left side of the/nframe and out of sight./n/nThey hurried after him along the corridor, following/nthe sound of his armor. Every now and then they/nspotted him running through a picture ahead./n/n"Be of stout heart, the worst is yet to come!" yelled the/nknight, and they saw him reappear in front of an/nalarmed group of women in crinolines, whose picture/nhung on the wall of a narrow spiral staircase./n/nPuffing loudly, Harry, Ron, and Hermione climbed the/ntightly spiraling steps, getting dizzier and dizzier,/nuntil at last they heard the murmur of voices above/nthem and knew they had reached the classroom./n/n"Farewell!" cried the knight, popping his head into a/npainting of some sinister-looking monks. "Farewell,/nmy comrades-in-arms! If ever you have need of noble/nheart and steely sinew, call upon Sir Cadogan!"/n/n"Yeah, well call you," muttered Ron as the knight/ndisappeared, "if we ever need someone mental."/n/nThey climbed the last few steps and emerged onto a/ntiny landing, where most of the class was already/nassembled. There were no doors off this landing, but/nRon nudged Harry and pointed at the ceiling, where/nthere was a circular trapdoor with a brass plaque on/nit./n/n" 'Sibyll Trelawney, Divination teacher,' " Harry read./n"How're we supposed to get up there?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAs though in answer to his question, the trapdoor/nsuddenly opened, and a silvery ladder descended/nright at Harry's feet. Everyone got quiet./n/n"After you," said Ron, grinning, so Harry climbed the/nladder first./n/nHe emerged into the strangest-looking classroom he/nhad ever seen. In fact, it didn't look like a classroom/nat all, more like a cross between someone's attic and/nan old-fashioned tea shop. At least twenty small,/ncircular tables were crammed inside it, all/nsurrounded by chintz armchairs and fat little poufs./nEverything was lit with a dim, crimson light; the/ncurtains at the windows were all closed, and the/nmany lamps were draped with dark red scarves. It/nwas stiflingly warm, and the fire that was burning/nunder the crowded mantelpiece was giving off a/nheavy, sickly sort of perfume as it heated a large/ncopper kettle. The shelves running around the/ncircular walls were crammed with dusty-looking/nfeathers, stubs of candles, many packs of tattered/nplaying cards, countless silvery crystal balls, and a/nhuge array of teacups./n/nRon appeared at Harry's shoulder as the class/nassembled around them, all talking in whispers./n/n"Where is she?" Ron said./n/nA voice came suddenly out of the shadows, a soft,/nmisty sort of voice./n/n"Welcome," it said. "How nice to see you in the/nphysical world at last."/n/nHarry's immediate impression was of a large,/nglittering insect. Professor Trelawney moved into the/nfirelight, and they saw that she was very thin; her/n/n/n/n/n/nlarge glasses magnified her eyes to several times their/nnatural size, and she was draped in a gauzy spangled/nshawl. Innumerable chains and beads hung around/nher spindly neck, and her arms and hands were/nencrusted with bangles and rings./n/n"Sit, my children, sit," she said, and they all climbed/nawkwardly into armchairs or sank onto poufs. Harry,/nRon, and Hermione sat themselves around the same/nround table./n/n"Welcome to Divination," said Professor Trelawney,/nwho had seated herself in a winged armchair in front/nof the fire. "My name is Professor Trelawney. You may/nnot have seen me before. I find that descending too/noften into the hustle and bustle of the main school/nclouds my Inner Eye."/n/nNobody said anything to this extraordinary/npronouncement. Professor Trelawney delicately/nrearranged her shawl and continued, "So you have/nchosen to study Divination, the most difficult of all/nmagical arts. I must warn you at the outset that if/nyou do not have the Sight, there is very little I will be/nable to teach you. Books can take you only so far in/nthis field. ..."/n/nAt these words, both Harry and Ron glanced,/ngrinning, at Hermione, who looked startled at the/nnews that books wouldn't be much help in this/nsubject./n/n"Many witches and wizards, talented though they are/nin the area of loud bangs and smells and sudden/ndisappearings, are yet unable to penetrate the veiled/nmysteries of the future," Professor Trelawney went on,/nher enormous, gleaming eyes moving from face to/nnervous face. "It is a Gift granted to few. You, boy,"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nshe said suddenly to Neville, who almost toppled off/nhis pouf. "Is your grandmother well?"/n/n/n/n"I think so," said Neville tremulously./n/n"I wouldn't be so sure if I were you, dear," said/nProfessor Trelawney, the firelight glinting on her long/nemerald earrings. Neville gulped. Professor Trelawney/ncontinued placidly. "We will be covering the basic/nmethods of Divination this year. The first term will be/ndevoted to reading the tea leaves. Next term we shall/nprogress to palmistry. By the way, my dear," she shot/nsuddenly at Parvati Patil, "beware a red-haired man."/n/nParvati gave a startled look at Ron, who was right/nbehind her, and edged her chair away from him./n/n"In the second term," Professor Trelawney went on,/n/n"we shall progress to the crystal ball — if we have/nfinished with fire omens, that is. Unfortunately,/nclasses will be disrupted in February by a nasty bout/nof flu. I myself will lose my voice. And around Easter,/none of our number will leave us forever."/n/nA very tense silence followed this pronouncement, but/nProfessor Trelawney seemed unaware of it./n/n"I wonder, dear," she said to Lavender Brown, who/nwas nearest and shrank back in her chair, "if you/ncould pass me the largest silver teapot?"/n/nLavender, looking relieved, stood up, took an/nenormous teapot from the shelf, and put it down on/nthe table in front of Professor Trelawney./n/n"Thank you, my dear. Incidentally, that thing you are/ndreading — it will happen on Friday the sixteenth of/nOctober."/n/n/n/n/n/nLavender trembled./n/n/n/n"Now, I want you all to divide into pairs. Collect a/nteacup from the shelf, come to me, and I will fill it./nThen sit down and drink, drink until only the dregs/nremain. Swill these around the cup three times with/nthe left hand, then turn the cup upside down on its/nsaucer, wait for the last of the tea to drain away, then/ngive your cup to your partner to read. He grabbed both Harry and Ron/nand pulled them into a bone-breaking hug./n/n"I think you've had enough to drink, Hagrid," said/nHermione firmly. She took the tankard from the table/nand went outside to empty it./n/n"Ar, maybe she's right," said Hagrid, letting go of/nHarry and Ron, who both staggered away, rubbing/ntheir ribs. Hagrid heaved himself out of his chair and/nfollowed Hermione unsteadily outside. They heard a/nloud splash./n/n"What's he done?" said Harry nervously as Hermione/ncame back in with the empty tankard./n/n"Stuck his head in the water barrel," said Hermione,/nputting the tankard away./n/nHagrid came back, his long hair and beard sopping/nwet, wiping the water out of his eyes./n/n"Tha's better," he said, shaking his head like a dog/nand drenching them all. "Listen, it was good of yeh ter/ncome an' see me, I really — "/n/nHagrid stopped dead, staring at Harry as though he'd/nonly just realized he was there./n/n"WHAT DYEH THINK YOU'RE DOIN', EH?" he roared,/nso suddenly that they jumped a foot in the air./n/n"YEH 'RE NOT TO GO WANDERIN' AROUND AFTER/nDARK, HARRY! AN' YOU TWO! LETTIN' HIM!"/n/nHagrid strode over to Harry, grabbed his arm, and/npulled him to the door./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"C'mon!" Hagrid said angrily. "I'm takin'yer all back/nup ter school, an' don' let me catch yeh walkin' down/nter see me after dark again. I'm not worth that!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n7/n/n/n/n

title: The Boggart In The Wardrobe
text: /nMalfoy didn't reappear in classes until late on/nThursday morning, when the Slytherins and/nGryffindors were halfway through double Potions. He/nswaggered into the dungeon, his right arm covered in/nbandages and bound up in a sling, acting, in Harry's/nopinion, as though he were the heroic survivor of/nsome dreadful battle./n/n"How is it, Draco?" simpered Pansy Parkinson. "Does/nit hurt much?"/n/n"Yeah," said Malfoy, putting on a brave sort of/ngrimace. But Harry saw him wink at Crabbe and/nGoyle when Pansy had looked away./n/n"Settle down, settle down," said Professor Snape idly./n/nHarry and Ron scowled at each other; Snape wouldn't/nhave said "settle down" if they'd walked in late, he'd/nhave given them detention. But Malfoy had always/nbeen able to get away with anything in Snape 's/n/n/n/n/nclasses; Snape was head of Slytherin House, and/ngenerally favored his own students above all others./n/n/n/nThey were making a new potion today, a Shrinking/nSolution. Malfoy set up his cauldron right next to/nHarry and Ron, so that they were preparing their/ningredients on the same table./n/n"Sir," Malfoy called, "sir, I'll need help cutting up/nthese daisy roots, because of my arm — "/n/n"Weasley, cut up Malfoy's roots for him," said Snape/nwithout looking up./n/nRon went brick red./n/n"There's nothing wrong with your arm," he hissed at/nMalfoy./n/nMalfoy smirked across the table./n/n"Weasley, you heard Professor Snape; cut up these/nroots."/n/nRon seized his knife, pulled Malfoy's roots toward/nhim, and began to chop them roughly, so that they/nwere all different sizes./n/n"Professor," drawled Malfoy, "Weasley's mutilating my/nroots, sir."/n/nSnape approached their table, stared down his/nhooked nose at the roots, then gave Ron an/nunpleasant smile from beneath his long, greasy black/nhair./n/n"Change roots with Malfoy, Weasley."/n/n"But, sir — !"/n/n/n/n/n/nRon had spent the last quarter of an hour carefully/nshredding his own roots into exactly equal pieces./n/n"Now," said Snape in his most dangerous voice./n/nRon shoved his own beautifully cut roots across the/ntable at Malfoy, then took up the knife again./n/n"And, sir, 111 need this shrivelfig skinned," said/nMalfoy, his voice full of malicious laughter./n/n"Potter, you can skin Malfoy's shrivelfig," said Snape,/ngiving Harry the look of loathing he always reserved/njust for him./n/nHarry took Malfoy's shrivelfig as Ron began trying to/nrepair the damage to the roots he now had to use./nHarry skinned the shrivelfig as fast as he could and/nflung it back across the table at Malfoy without/nspeaking. Malfoy was smirking more broadly than/never./n/n"Seen your pal Hagrid lately?" he asked them quietly./n/n"None of your business," said Ron jerkily, without/nlooking up./n/n"I'm afraid he won't be a teacher much longer," said/nMalfoy in a tone of mock sorrow. "Father's not very/nhappy about my injury — "/n/n"Keep talking, Malfoy, and I'll give you a real injury,"/nsnarled Ron./n/n" — he's complained to the school governors. And to/nthe Ministry of Magic. Father's got a lot of influence,/nyou know. And a lasting injury like this" — he gave a/nhuge, fake sigh — "who knows if my arm'll ever be the/nsame again?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"So that's why you're putting it on," said Harry,/naccidentally beheading a dead caterpillar because his/nhand was shaking in anger. "To try to get Hagrid/nfired."/n/n"Well," said Malfoy, lowering his voice to a whisper,/n/n" partly , Potter. But there are other benefits too./nWeasley, slice my caterpillars for me."/n/nA few cauldrons away, Neville was in trouble. Neville/nregularly went to pieces in Potions lessons; it was his/nworst subject, and his great fear of Professor Snape/nmade things ten times worse. His potion, which was/nsupposed to be a bright, acid green, had turned —/n/n"Orange, Longbottom," said Snape, ladling some up/nand allowing it to splash back into the cauldron, so/nthat everyone could see. "Orange. Tell me, boy, does/nanything penetrate that thick skull of yours? Didn't/nyou hear me say, quite clearly, that only one rat/nspleen was needed? Didn't I state plainly that a dash/nof leech juice would suffice? What do I have to do to/nmake you understand, Longbottom?"/n/nNeville was pink and trembling. He looked as though/nhe was on the verge of tears./n/n"Please, sir," said Hermione, "please, I could help/nNeville put it right — "/n/n"I don't remember asking you to show off, Miss/nGranger," said Snape coldly, and Hermione went as/npink as Neville. "Longbottom, at the end of this lesson/nwe will feed a few drops of this potion to your toad/nand see what happens. Perhaps that will encourage/nyou to do it properly."/n/nSnape moved away, leaving Neville breathless with/nfear./n/n/n/n/n/n"Help me!" he moaned to Hermione./n/n/n/n"Hey, Harry," said Seamus Finnigan, leaning over to/nborrow Harry's brass scales, "have you heard? Daily/nProphet this morning — they reckon Sirius Black's/nbeen sighted."/n/n"Where?" said Harry and Ron quickly. On the other/nside of the table, Malfoy looked up, listening closely./n/n"Not too far from here," said Seamus, who looked/nexcited. "It was a Muggle who saw him. 'Course, she/ndidn't really understand. The Muggles think he's just/nan ordinary criminal, don't they? So she phoned the/ntelephone hot line. By the time the Ministry of Magic/ngot there, he was gone."/n/n"Not too far from here ... ," Ron repeated, looking/nsignificantly at Harry. He turned around and saw/nMalfoy watching closely. "What, Malfoy? Need/nsomething else skinned?"/n/nBut Malfoy's eyes were shining malevolently, and they/nwere fixed on Harry. He leaned across the table./n/n"Thinking of trying to catch Black single-handed,/nPotter?"/n/n"Yeah, that's right," said Harry offhandedly./n/nMalfoy's thin mouth was curving in a mean smile./n/n"Of course, if it was me," he said quietly, "I'd have/ndone something before now. I wouldn't be staying in/nschool like a good boy, I'd be out there looking for/nhim."/n/n"What are you talking about, Malfoy?" said Ron/nroughly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't you know, Potter?" breathed Malfoy, his pale/neyes narrowed./n/n/n/n"Know what?"/n/nMalfoy let out a low, sneering laugh./n/n"Maybe you'd rather not risk your neck," he said./n"Want to leave it to the dementors, do you? But if it/nwas me, I'd want revenge. I'd hunt him down myself."/n/n" What are you talking about?" said Harry angrily, but/nat that moment Snape called, "You should have/nfinished adding your ingredients by now; this potion/nneeds to stew before it can be drunk, so clear away/nwhile it simmers and then we'll test Longbottom's. ..."/n/nCrabbe and Goyle laughed openly, watching Neville/nsweat as he stirred his potion feverishly. Hermione/nwas muttering instructions to him out of the corner of/nher mouth, so that Snape wouldn't see. Harry and/nRon packed away their unused ingredients and went/nto wash their hands and ladles in the stone basin in/nthe corner./n/n"What did Malfoy mean?" Harry muttered to Ron as/nhe stuck his hands under the icy jet that poured from/nthe gargoyle's mouth. "Why would I want revenge on/nBlack? He hasn't done anything to me — yet."/n/n"He's making it up," said Ron savagely. "He's trying to/nmake you do something stupid. ..."/n/nThe end of the lesson in sight, Snape strode over to/nNeville, who was cowering by his cauldron./n/n"Everyone gather 'round," said Snape, his black eyes/nglittering, "and watch what happens to Longbottom's/ntoad. If he has managed to produce a Shrinking/n/n/n/n/n/nSolution, it will shrink to a tadpole. If, as I don't/ndoubt, he has done it wrong, his toad is likely to be/npoisoned."/n/nThe Gryffindors watched fearfully. The Slytherins/nlooked excited. Snape picked up Trevor the toad in/nhis left hand and dipped a small spoon into Neville's/npotion, which was now green. He trickled a few drops/ndown Trevor's throat./n/nThere was a moment of hushed silence, in which/nTrevor gulped; then there was a small pop, and Trevor/nthe tadpole was wriggling in Snape 's palm./n/nThe Gryffindors burst into applause. Snape, looking/nsour, pulled a small bottle from the pocket of his/nrobe, poured a few drops on top of Trevor, and he/nreappeared suddenly, fully grown./n/n"Five points from Gryffindor," said Snape, which/nwiped the smiles from every face. "I told you not to/nhelp him, Miss Granger. Class dismissed."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione climbed the steps to the/nentrance hall. Harry was still thinking about what/nMalfoy had said, while Ron was seething about/nSnape./n/n"Five points from Gryffindor because the potion was/nall right! Why didn't you lie, Hermione? You should've/nsaid Neville did it all by himself!"/n/nHermione didn't answer. Ron looked around./n/n"Where is she?"/n/nHarry turned too. They were at the top of the steps/nnow, watching the rest of the class pass them,/nheading for the Great Hall and lunch./n/n/n/n/n/n"She was right behind us," said Ron, frowning./n/nMalfoy passed them, walking between Crabbe and/nGoyle. He smirked at Harry and disappeared./n/n"There she is," said Harry./n/nHermione was panting slightly, hurrying up the/nstairs; one hand clutched her bag, the other seemed/nto be tucking something down the front of her robes./n/n"How did you do that?" said Ron./n/n"What?" said Hermione, joining them./n/n"One minute you were right behind us, the next/nmoment, you were back at the bottom of the stairs/nagain."/n/n"What?" Hermione looked slightly confused. "Oh — I/nhad to go back for something. Oh no — "/n/nA seam had split on Hermione's bag. Harry wasn't/nsurprised; he could see that it was crammed with at/nleast a dozen large and heavy books./n/n"Why are you carrying all these around with you?"/nRon asked her./n/n"You know how many subjects I'm taking," said/nHermione breathlessly. "Couldn't hold these for me,/ncould you?"/n/n"But — " Ron was turning over the books she had/nhanded him, looking at the covers. "You haven't got/nany of these subjects today. It's only Defense Against/nthe Dark Arts this afternoon."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh yes," said Hermione vaguely, but she packed all/nthe books back into her bag just the same. "I hope/nthere's something good for lunch, I'm starving," she/nadded, and she marched off toward the Great Hall./n/n"D'you get the feeling Hermione 's not telling us/nsomething?" Ron asked Harry./n/n/n/nProfessor Lupin wasn't there when they arrived at his/nfirst Defense Against the Dark Arts lesson. They all/nsat down, took out their books, quills, and/nparchment, and were talking when he finally entered/nthe room. Lupin smiled vaguely and placed his tatty/nold briefcase on the teacher's desk. He was as shabby/nas ever but looked healthier than he had on the train,/nas though he had had a few square meals./n/n"Good afternoon," he said. "Would you please put all/nyour books back in your bags. Today's will be a/npractical lesson. You will need only your wands."/n/nA few curious looks were exchanged as the class put/naway their books. They had never had a practical/nDefense Against the Dark Arts before, unless you/ncounted the memorable class last year when their old/nteacher had brought a cageful of pixies to class and/nset them loose./n/n"Right then," said Professor Lupin, when everyone/nwas ready. "If you'd follow me."/n/nPuzzled but interested, the class got to its feet and/nfollowed Professor Lupin out of the classroom. He led/nthem along the deserted corridor and around a/ncorner, where the first thing they saw was Peeves the/nPoltergeist, who was floating upside down in midair/nand stuffing the nearest keyhole with chewing gum./n/n/n/n/nPeeves didn't look up until Professor Lupin was two/nfeet away; then he wiggled his curly-toed feet and/nbroke into song./n/n"Loony, loopy Lupin," Peeves sang. "Loony, loopy/nLupin, loony, loopy Lupin — "/n/nRude and unmanageable as he almost always was,/nPeeves usually showed some respect toward the/nteachers. Everyone looked quickly at Professor Lupin/nto see how he would take this; to their surprise, he/nwas still smiling./n/n"I'd take that gum out of the keyhole if I were you,/nPeeves," he said pleasantly. "Mr. Filch won't be able to/nget in to his brooms."/n/nFilch was the Hogwarts caretaker, a bad-tempered,/nfailed wizard who waged a constant war against the/nstudents and, indeed, Peeves. However, Peeves paid/nno attention to Professor Lupin's words, except to/nblow a loud wet raspberry./n/nProfessor Lupin gave a small sigh and took out his/nwand./n/n"This is a useful little spell," he told the class over his/nshoulder. "Please watch closely."/n/nHe raised the wand to shoulder height, said,/n/n" Waddiwasil " and pointed it at Peeves./n/nWith the force of a bullet, the wad of chewing gum/nshot out of the keyhole and straight down Peeves 's left/nnostril; he whirled upright and zoomed away, cursing./n/n"Cool, sir!" said Dean Thomas in amazement./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Thank you, Dean," said Professor Lupin, putting his/nwand away again. "Shall we proceed?"/n/nThey set off again, the class looking at shabby/nProfessor Lupin with increased respect. He led them/ndown a second corridor and stopped, right outside the/nstaffroom door./n/n"Inside, please," said Professor Lupin, opening it and/nstanding back./n/nThe staffroom, a long, paneled room full of old,/nmismatched chairs, was empty except for one teacher./nProfessor Snape was sitting in a low armchair, and he/nlooked around as the class filed in. His eyes were/nglittering and there was a nasty sneer playing around/nhis mouth. As Professor Lupin came in and made to/nclose the door behind him, Snape said, "Leave it open,/nLupin. Td rather not witness this."/n/nHe got to his feet and strode past the class, his black/nrobes billowing behind him. At the doorway he turned/non his heel and said, "Possibly no one's warned you,/nLupin, but this class contains Neville Longbottom. I/nwould advise you not to entrust him with anything/ndifficult. Not unless Miss Granger is hissing/ninstructions in his ear."/n/nNeville went scarlet. Harry glared at Snape; it was bad/nenough that he bullied Neville in his own classes, let/nalone doing it in front of other teachers./n/nProfessor Lupin had raised his eyebrows./n/n"I was hoping that Neville would assist me with the/nfirst stage of the operation," he said, "and I am sure/nhe will perform it admirably."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNeville's face went, if possible, even redder. Snape's/nlip curled, but he left, shutting the door with a snap./n/n"Now, then," said Professor Lupin, beckoning the/nclass toward the end of the room, where there was/nnothing but an old wardrobe where the teachers kept/ntheir spare robes. As Professor Lupin went to stand/nnext to it, the wardrobe gave a sudden wobble,/nbanging off the wall./n/n"Nothing to worry about," said Professor Lupin calmly/nbecause a few people had jumped backward in alarm./n"There's a boggart in there."/n/nMost people seemed to feel that this was something to/nworry about. Neville gave Professor Lupin a look of/npure terror, and Seamus Finnigan eyed the now/nrattling doorknob apprehensively./n/n"Boggarts like dark, enclosed spaces," said Professor/nLupin. "Wardrobes, the gap beneath beds, the/ncupboards under sinks — I've even met one that had/nlodged itself in a grandfather clock. This one moved in/nyesterday afternoon, and I asked the headmaster if/nthe staff would leave it to give my third years some/npractice./n/n"So, the first question we must ask ourselves is, what/nis a boggart?"/n/nHermione put up her hand./n/n"It's a shape-shifter," she said. "It can take the shape/nof whatever it thinks will frighten us most."/n/n"Couldn't have put it better myself," said Professor/nLupin, and Hermione glowed. "So the boggart sitting/nin the darkness within has not yet assumed a form./n/nHe does not yet know what will frighten the person on/n/n/n/n/n/nthe other side of the door. Nobody knows what a/nboggart looks like when he is alone, but when I let/nhim out, he will immediately become whatever each of/nus most fears./n/n"This means," said Professor Lupin, choosing to/nignore Neville's small sputter of terror, "that we have a/nhuge advantage over the boggart before we begin./n/nHave you spotted it, Harry?"/n/nTrying to answer a question with Hermione next to/nhim, bobbing up and down on the balls of her feet/nwith her hand in the air, was very off-putting, but/nHarry had a go./n/n"Er — because there are so many of us, it won't know/nwhat shape it should be?"/n/n"Precisely," said Professor Lupin, and Hermione put/nher hand down, looking a little disappointed. "It's/nalways best to have company when you're dealing/nwith a boggart. He becomes confused. Which should/nhe become, a headless corpse or a flesh-eating slug? I/nonce saw a boggart make that very mistake — tried to/nfrighten two people at once and turned himself into/nhalf a slug. Not remotely frightening./n/n"The charm that repels a boggart is simple, yet it/nrequires force of mind. You see, the thing that really/nfinishes a boggart is laughter. What you need to do is/nforce it to assume a shape that you find amusing./n/n"We will practice the charm without wands first. After/nme, please ... riddikulusV'/n/n" RiddikulusV' said the class together./n/n"Good," said Professor Lupin. "Very good. But that/nwas the easy part, I'm afraid. You see, the word alone/n/n/n/n/n/nis not enough. And this is where you come in,/nNeville."/n/n/n/nThe wardrobe shook again, though not as much as/nNeville, who walked forward as though he were/nheading for the gallows./n/n"Right, Neville," said Professor Lupin. "First things/nfirst: what would you say is the thing that frightens/nyou most in the world?"/n/nNeville's lips moved, but no noise came out./n/n"Didn't catch that, Neville, sorry," said Professor/nLupin cheerfully./n/nNeville looked around rather wildly, as though/nbegging someone to help him, then said, in barely/nmore than a whisper, "Professor Snape."/n/nNearly everyone laughed. Even Neville grinned/napologetically. Professor Lupin, however, looked/nthoughtful./n/n"Professor Snape ... hmmm ... Neville, I believe you/nlive with your grandmother?"/n/n"Er — yes," said Neville nervously. "But — I don't/nwant the boggart to turn into her either."/n/n"No, no, you misunderstand me," said Professor/nLupin, now smiling. "I wonder, could you tell us what/nsort of clothes your grandmother usually wears?"/n/nNeville looked startled, but said, "Well ... always the/nsame hat. A tall one with a stuffed vulture on top./n/nAnd a long dress ... green, normally ... and sometimes/na fox-fur scarf."/n/n/n/n/n/n"And a handbag?" prompted Professor Lupin./n/n"A big red one," said Neville./n/n"Right then," said Professor Lupin. "Can you picture/nthose clothes very clearly, Neville? Can you see them/nin your mind's eye?"/n/n"Yes," said Neville uncertainly, plainly wondering/nwhat was coming next./n/n"When the boggart bursts out of this wardrobe,/n/nNeville, and sees you, it will assume the form of/nProfessor Snape," said Lupin. "And you will raise your/nwand — thus — and cry 'Riddikulus' — and/nconcentrate hard on your grandmother's clothes. If all/ngoes well, Professor Boggart Snape will be forced into/nthat vulture-topped hat, and that green dress, with/nthat big red handbag."/n/nThere was a great shout of laughter. The wardrobe/nwobbled more violently./n/n"If Neville is successful, the boggart is likely to shift/nhis attention to each of us in turn," said Professor/nLupin. "I would like all of you to take a moment now/nto think of the thing that scares you most, and/nimagine how you might force it to look comical. ..."/n/nThe room went quiet. Harry thought ... What scared/nhim most in the world?/n/nHis first thought was Lord Voldemort — a Voldemort/nreturned to full strength. But before he had even/nstarted to plan a possible counterattack on a boggart -/nVoldemort, a horrible image came floating to the/nsurface of his mind. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA rotting, glistening hand, slithering back beneath a/nblack cloak ... a long, rattling breath from an unseen/nmouth . . . then a cold so penetrating it felt like/ndrowning. .../n/nHarry shivered, then looked around, hoping no one/nhad noticed. Many people had their eyes shut tight./nRon was muttering to himself, "Take its legs off."/nHarry was sure he knew what that was about. Ron's/ngreatest fear was spiders./n/n"Everyone ready?" said Professor Lupin./n/nHarry felt a lurch of fear. He wasn't ready. How could/nyou make a dementor less frightening? But he didn't/nwant to ask for more time; everyone else was nodding/nand rolling up their sleeves./n/n"Neville, we're going to back away," said Professor/nLupin. "Let you have a clear field, all right? I'll call the/nnext person forward. ... Everyone back, now, so/nNeville can get a clear shot — "/n/nThey all retreated, backed against the walls, leaving/nNeville alone beside the wardrobe. He looked pale and/nfrightened, but he had pushed up the sleeves of his/nrobes and was holding his wand ready./n/n"On the count of three, Neville," said Professor Lupin,/nwho was pointing his own wand at the handle of the/nwardrobe. "One — two — three — now\"/n/nA jet of sparks shot from the end of Professor Lupin's/nwand and hit the doorknob. The wardrobe burst/nopen. Hook-nosed and menacing, Professor Snape/nstepped out, his eyes flashing at Neville./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNeville backed away, his wand up, mouthing/nwordlessly. Snape was bearing down upon him,/nreaching inside his robes./n/n"R — r — riddikulusV' squeaked Neville./n/nThere was a noise like a whip crack. Snape stumbled;/nhe was wearing a long, lace-trimmed dress and a/ntowering hat topped with a moth-eaten vulture, and/nhe was swinging a huge crimson handbag./n/nThere was a roar of laughter; the boggart paused,/nconfused, and Professor Lupin shouted, "Parvati!/nForward!"/n/nParvati walked forward, her face set. Snape rounded/non her. There was another crack, and where he had/nstood was a bloodstained, bandaged mummy; its/nsightless face was turned to Parvati and it began to/nwalk toward her very slowly, dragging its feet, its stiff/narms rising —/n/n"RiddikulusV' cried Parvati./n/nA bandage unraveled at the mummy's feet; it became/nentangled, fell face forward, and its head rolled off./n/n"Seamus!" roared Professor Lupin./n/nSeamus darted past Parvati./n/nCrack ! Where the mummy had been was a woman/nwith floor-length black hair and a skeletal, green-/ntinged face — a banshee. She opened her mouth wide/nand an unearthly sound filled the room, a long,/nwailing shriek that made the hair on Harry's head/nstand on end —/n/n"RiddikulusV' shouted Seamus./n/n/n/n/n/nThe banshee made a rasping noise and clutched her/nthroat; her voice was gone./n/nCrack). The banshee turned into a rat, which chased/nits tail in a circle, then — crack). — became a/nrattlesnake, which slithered and writhed before —/ncrack ! — becoming a single, bloody eyeball./n/n"It's confused!" shouted Lupin. "We're getting there!/nDean!"/n/nDean hurried forward./n/nCrack) The eyeball became a severed hand, which/nflipped over and began to creep along the floor like a/ncrab./n/n"RiddikulusV' yelled Dean./n/nThere was a snap, and the hand was trapped in a/nmousetrap./n/n"Excellent! Ron, you next!"/n/nRon leapt forward./n/nCrack)/n/nQuite a few people screamed. A giant spider, six feet/ntall and covered in hair, was advancing on Ron,/nclicking its pincers menacingly. For a moment, Harry/nthought Ron had frozen. Then —/n/n"RiddikulusV' bellowed Ron, and the spider's legs/nvanished; it rolled over and over; Lavender Brown/nsquealed and ran out of its way and it came to a halt/nat Harry's feet. He raised his wand, ready, but —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Here!" shouted Professor Lupin suddenly, hurrying/nforward./n/nCrack)./n/nThe legless spider had vanished. For a second,/neveryone looked wildly around to see where it was./nThen they saw a silvery-white orb hanging in the air/nin front of Lupin, who said, "RiddikulusV' almost/nlazily./n/nCrack !/n/n"Forward, Neville, and finish him off!" said Lupin as/nthe boggart landed on the floor as a cockroach. Crack)./nSnape was back. This time Neville charged forward/nlooking determined./n/n"RiddikulusV' he shouted, and they had a split/nsecond's view of Snape in his lacy dress before Neville/nlet out a great "Ha!" of laughter, and the boggart/nexploded, burst into a thousand tiny wisps of smoke,/nand was gone./n/n"Excellent!" cried Professor Lupin as the class broke/ninto applause. "Excellent, Neville. Well done,/neveryone. ... Let me see ... five points to Gryffindor for/nevery person to tackle the boggart — ten for Neville/nbecause he did it twice . . . and five each to Hermione/nand Harry."/n/n"But I didn't do anything," said Harry./n/n"You and Hermione answered my questions correctly/nat the start of the class, Harry," Lupin said lightly./n"Very well, everyone, an excellent lesson. Homework,/nkindly read the chapter on boggarts and summarize it/nfor me ... to be handed in on Monday. That will be/nall."/n/n/n/n/n/nTalking excitedly, the class left the staffroom. Harry,/nhowever, wasn't feeling cheerful. Professor Lupin had/ndeliberately stopped him from tackling the boggart./nWhy? Was it because he'd seen Harry collapse on the/ntrain, and thought he wasn't up to much? Had he/nthought Harry would pass out again?/n/nBut no one else seemed to have noticed anything./n/n"Did you see me take that banshee?" shouted/nSeamus./n/n"And the hand!" said Dean, waving his own around./n"And Snape in that hat!"/n/n"And my mummy!"/n/n"I wonder why Professor Lupin's frightened of crystal/nballs?" said Lavender thoughtfully./n/n"That was the best Defense Against the Dark Arts/nlesson we've ever had, wasn't it?" said Ron excitedly/nas they made their way back to the classroom to get/ntheir bags./n/n"He seems like a very good teacher," said Hermione/napprovingly. "But I wish I could have had a turn with/nthe boggart — "/n/n"What would it have been for you?" said Ron,/nsniggering. "A piece of homework that only got nine/nout of ten?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nd/n/n/n/n

title: Flight Of The Fat Lady
text: /nIn no time at all, Defense Against the Dark Arts had/nbecome most people's favorite class. Only Draco/nMalfoy and his gang of Slytherins had anything bad to/nsay about Professor Lupin./n/n"Look at the state of his robes," Malfoy would say in a/nloud whisper as Professor Lupin passed. "He dresses/nlike our old house-elf."/n/nBut no one else cared that Professor Lupin's robes/nwere patched and frayed. His next few lessons were/njust as interesting as the first. After boggarts, they/nstudied Red Caps, nasty little goblinlike creatures/nthat lurked wherever there had been bloodshed: in/nthe dungeons of castles and the potholes of deserted/nbattlefields, waiting to bludgeon those who had gotten/nlost. From Red Caps they moved on to kappas, creepy/nwater-dwellers that looked like scaly monkeys, with/nwebbed hands itching to strangle unwitting waders in/ntheir ponds./n/nHarry only wished he was as happy with some of his/nother classes. Worst of all was Potions. Snape was in/n/n/n/n/na particularly vindictive mood these days, and no one/nwas in any doubt why. The story of the boggart/nassuming Snape's shape, and the way that Neville/nhad dressed it in his grandmother's clothes, had/ntraveled through the school like wildfire. Snape didn't/nseem to find it funny. His eyes flashed menacingly at/nthe very mention of Professor Lupin's name, and he/nwas bullying Neville worse than ever./n/nHarry was also growing to dread the hours he spent/nin Professor Trelawney's stifling tower room,/ndeciphering lopsided shapes and symbols, trying to/nignore the way Professor Trelawney's enormous eyes/nfilled with tears every time she looked at him. He/ncouldn't like Professor Trelawney, even though she/nwas treated with respect bordering on reverence by/nmany of the class. Parvati Patil and Lavender Brown/nhad taken to haunting Professor Trelawney's tower/nroom at lunchtimes, and always returned with/nannoyingly superior looks on their faces, as though/nthey knew things the others didn't. They had also/nstarted using hushed voices whenever they spoke to/nHarry, as though he were on his deathbed./n/nNobody really liked Care of Magical Creatures, which,/nafter the action-packed first class, had become/nextremely dull. Hagrid seemed to have lost his/nconfidence. They were now spending lesson after/nlesson learning how to look after flobberworms, which/nhad to be some of the most boring creatures in/nexistence./n/n"Why would anyone bother looking after them?" said/nRon, after yet another hour of poking shredded/nlettuce down the flobberworms' slimy throats./n/nAt the start of October, however, Harry had/nsomething else to occupy him, something so enjoyable/nit more than made up for his unsatisfactory classes./n/n/n/n/n/nThe Quidditch season was approaching, and Oliver/nWood, Captain of the Gryffindor team, called a/nmeeting one Thursday evening to discuss tactics for/nthe new season./n/nThere were seven people on a Quidditch team: three/nChasers, whose job it was to score goals by putting/nthe Quaffle (a red, soccer-sized ball) through one of/nthe fifty-foot-high hoops at each end of the field; two/nBeaters, who were equipped with heavy bats to repel/nthe Bludgers (two heavy black balls that zoomed/naround trying to attack the players); a Keeper, who/ndefended the goal posts, and the Seeker, who had the/nhardest job of all, that of catching the Golden Snitch,/na tiny, winged, walnut-sized ball, whose capture/nended the game and earned the Seeker's team an/nextra one hundred and fifty points./n/nOliver Wood was a burly seventeen-year-old, now in/nhis seventh and final year at Hogwarts. There was a/nquiet sort of desperation in his voice as he addressed/nhis six fellow team members in the chilly locker rooms/non the edge of the darkening Quidditch field./n/n"This is our last chance — my last chance — to win/nthe Quidditch Cup," he told them, striding up and/ndown in front of them. "I'll be leaving at the end of/nthis year. I'll never get another shot at it./n/n"Gryffindor hasn't won for seven years now. Okay, so/nwe've had the worst luck in the world — injuries —/nthen the tournament getting called off last year. ..."/nWood swallowed, as though the memory still brought/na lump to his throat. "But we also know we've got the/nbest — ruddy — team — in — the — school," he said,/npunching a fist into his other hand, the old manic/nglint back in his eye./n/n"We've got three superb Chasers."/n/n/n/n/n/nWood pointed at Alicia Spinnet, Angelina Johnson,/nand Katie Bell./n/n"We've got two unbeatable Beaters."/n/n"Stop it, Oliver, you're embarrassing us," said Fred/nand George Weasley together, pretending to blush./n/n"And we've got a Seeker who has never failed to win/nus a match)." Wood rumbled, glaring at Harry with a/nkind of furious pride. "And me," he added as an/nafterthought./n/n"We think you're very good too, Oliver," said George./n/n"Spanking good Keeper," said Fred./n/n"The point is," Wood went on, resuming his pacing,/n"the Quidditch Cup should have had our name on it/nthese last two years. Ever since Harry joined the/nteam, I've thought the thing was in the bag. But we/nhaven't got it, and this year's the last chance we'll get/nto finally see our name on the thing. ..."/n/nWood spoke so dejectedly that even Fred and George/nlooked sympathetic./n/n"Oliver, this year's our year," said Fred./n/n"Well do it, Oliver!" said Angelina./n/n"Definitely," said Harry./n/nFull of determination, the team started training/nsessions, three evenings a week. The weather was/ngetting colder and wetter, the nights darker, but no/namount of mud, wind, or rain could tarnish Harry's/nwonderful vision of finally winning the huge, silver/nQuidditch Cup./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry returned to the Gryffindor common room one/nevening after training, cold and stiff but pleased with/nthe way practice had gone, to find the room buzzing/nexcitedly./n/n"What's happened?" he asked Ron and Hermione,/nwho were sitting in two of the best chairs by the/nfireside and completing some star charts for/nAstronomy./n/n"First Hogsmeade weekend," said Ron, pointing at a/nnotice that had appeared on the battered old bulletin/nboard. "End of October. Halloween."/n/n"Excellent," said Fred, who had followed Harry/nthrough the portrait hole. "I need to visit Zonko's. I'm/nnearly out of Stink Pellets."/n/nHarry threw himself into a chair beside Ron, his high/nspirits ebbing away. Hermione seemed to read his/nmind./n/n"Harry, I'm sure you'll be able to go next time," she/nsaid. "They're bound to catch Black soon. He's been/nsighted once already"/n/n"Black's not fool enough to try anything in/nHogsmeade," said Ron. "Ask McGonagall if you can go/nthis time, Harry. The next one might not be for ages/n/n/n/n"Ron\" said Hermione. "Harry's supposed to stay in/nschool — "/n/n"He can't be the only third year left behind," said Ron./n"Ask McGonagall, go on, Harry — "/n/n"Yeah, I think I will," said Harry, making up his mind./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione opened her mouth to argue, but at that/nmoment Crookshanks leapt lightly onto her lap. A/nlarge, dead spider was dangling from his mouth./n/n"Does he have to eat that in front of us?" said Ron,/nscowling./n/n"Clever Crookshanks, did you catch that all by/nyourself?" said Hermione./n/nCrookshanks slowly chewed up the spider, his yellow/neyes fixed insolently on Ron./n/n"Just keep him over there, that's all," said Ron/nirritably, turning back to his star chart. "I've got/nScabbers asleep in my bag."/n/nHarry yawned. He really wanted to go to bed, but he/nstill had his own star chart to complete. He pulled his/nbag toward him, took out parchment, ink, and quill,/nand started work./n/n"You can copy mine, if you like," said Ron, labeling/nhis last star with a flourish and shoving the chart/ntoward Harry./n/nHermione, who disapproved of copying, pursed her/nlips but didn't say anything. Crookshanks was still/nstaring unblinkingly at Ron, flicking the end of his/nbushy tail. Then, without warning, he pounced./n/n"OY!" Ron roared, seizing his bag as Crookshanks/nsank four sets of claws deep inside it and began/ntearing ferociously. "GET OFF, YOU STUPID ANIMAL!"/n/nRon tried to pull the bag away from Crookshanks, but/nCrookshanks clung on, spitting and slashing./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ron, don't hurt him!" squealed Hermione; the whole/ncommon room was watching; Ron whirled the bag/naround, Crookshanks still clinging to it, and Scabbers/ncame flying out of the top —/n/n"CATCH THAT CAT!" Ron yelled as Crookshanks freed/nhimself from the remnants of the bag, sprang over the/ntable, and chased after the terrified Scabbers./n/nGeorge Weasley made a lunge for Crookshanks but/nmissed; Scabbers streaked through twenty pairs of/nlegs and shot beneath an old chest of drawers./nCrookshanks skidded to a halt, crouched low on his/nbandy legs, and started making furious swipes/nbeneath it with his front paw./n/nRon and Hermione hurried over; Hermione grabbed/nCrookshanks around the middle and heaved him/naway; Ron threw himself onto his stomach and, with/ngreat difficulty, pulled Scabbers out by the tail./n/n"Look at him!" he said furiously to Hermione,/ndangling Scabbers in front of her. "He's skin and/nbone! You keep that cat away from him!"/n/n"Crookshanks doesn't understand it's wrong!" said/nHermione, her voice shaking. "All cats chase rats,/nRon!"/n/n"There's something funny about that animal!" said/nRon, who was trying to persuade a frantically wiggling/nScabbers back into his pocket. "It heard me say that/nScabbers was in my bag!"/n/n"Oh, what rubbish," said Hermione impatiently./n"Crookshanks could smell him, Ron, how else d'you/nthink — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"That cat's got it in for Scabbers!" said Ron, ignoring/nthe people around him, who were starting to giggle./n"And Scabbers was here first, and he's ill!"/n/nRon marched through the common room and out of/nsight up the stairs to the boys' dormitories./n/nRon was still in a bad mood with Hermione next day./nHe barely talked to her all through Herbology, even/nthough he, Harry, and Hermione were working/ntogether on the same puffapod./n/n"How's Scabbers?" Hermione asked timidly as they/nstripped fat pink pods from the plants and emptied/nthe shining beans into a wooden pail./n/n"He's hiding at the bottom of my bed, shaking," said/nRon angrily, missing the pail and scattering beans/nover the greenhouse floor./n/n"Careful, Weasley, careful!" cried Professor Sprout as/nthe beans burst into bloom before their very eyes./n/nThey had Transfiguration next. Harry, who had/nresolved to ask Professor McGonagall after the lesson/nwhether he could go into Hogsmeade with the rest,/njoined the line outside the class trying to decide how/nhe was going to argue his case. He was distracted,/nhowever, by a disturbance at the front of the line./n/nLavender Brown seemed to be crying. Parvati had her/narm around her and was explaining something to/nSeamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas, who were/nlooking very serious./n/n"What's the matter, Lavender?" said Hermione/nanxiously as she, Harry, and Ron went to join the/ngroup./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"She got a letter from home this morning," Parvati/nwhispered. "It's her rabbit, Binky. He's been killed by/na fox."/n/n"Oh," said Hermione, "I'm sorry, Lavender."/n/n"I should have known!" said Lavender tragically. "You/nknow what day it is?"/n/n"Er — "/n/n/n/n"The sixteenth of October! That thing you're dreading,/nit will happen on the sixteenth of October!'/nRemember? She was right, she was right!"/n/nThe whole class was gathered around Lavender now./nSeamus shook his head seriously.
