Hermione/nhesitated; then she said, "You — you were dreading/nBinky being killed by a fox?"/n/n"Well, not necessarily by a fox," said Lavender,/nlooking up at Hermione with streaming eyes, "but I/nwas obviously dreading him dying, wasn't I?"/n/n"Oh," said Hermione. She paused again. Then —/n/n"Was Binky an old rabbit?"/n/n"N — no!" sobbed Lavender. "H — he was only a/nbaby!"/n/nParvati tightened her arm around Lavender's/nshoulders./n/n"But then, why would you dread him dying?" said/nHermione./n/nParvati glared at her./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, look at it logically," said Hermione, turning to/nthe rest of the group. "I mean, Binky didn't even die/ntoday, did he? Lavender just got the news today — "/nLavender wailed loudly. " — and she can't have been/ndreading it, because it's come as a real shock — "/n/n"Don't mind Hermione, Lavender," said Ron loudly,/n"she doesn't think other people's pets matter very/nmuch."/n/nProfessor McGonagall opened the classroom door at/nthat moment, which was perhaps lucky; Hermione/nand Ron were looking daggers at each other, and/nwhen they got into class, they seated themselves on/neither side of Harry and didn't talk to each other for/nthe whole class./n/nHarry still hadn't decided what he was going to say to/nProfessor McGonagall when the bell rang at the end of/nthe lesson, but it was she who brought up the subject/nof Hogsmeade first./n/n"One moment, please!" she called as the class made/nto leave. "As you're all in my House, you should hand/nHogsmeade permission forms to me before Halloween./nNo form, no visiting the village, so don't forget!"/n/nNeville put up his hand./n/n"Please, Professor, I — I think I've lost — "/n/n"Your grandmother sent yours to me directly,/nLongbottom," said Professor McGonagall. "She/nseemed to think it was safer. Well, that's all, you may/nleave."/n/n"Ask her now," Ron hissed at Harry./n/n"Oh, but — " Hermione began./n/n/n/n/n/n"Go for it, Harry," said Ron stubbornly./n/nHarry waited for the rest of the class to disappear,/nthen headed nervously for Professor McGonagall's/ndesk./n/n"Yes, Potter?"/n/nHarry took a deep breath./n/n"Professor, my aunt and uncle — er — forgot to sign/nmy form," he said./n/nProfessor McGonagall looked over her square/nspectacles at him but didn't say anything./n/n"So — er — d'you think it would be all right — I/nmean, will it be okay if I — if I go to Hogsmeade?"/n/nProfessor McGonagall looked down and began/nshuffling papers on her desk./n/n"I'm afraid not, Potter," she said. "You heard what I/nsaid. No form, no visiting the village. That's the rule."/n/n"But — Professor, my aunt and uncle — you know,/nthey're Muggles, they don't really understand about/n— about Hogwarts forms and stuff," Harry said, while/nRon egged him on with vigorous nods. "If you said I/ncould go — "/n/n"But I don't say so," said Professor McGonagall,/nstanding up and piling her papers neatly into a/ndrawer. "The form clearly states that the parent or/nguardian must give permission." She turned to look at/nhim, with an odd expression on her face. Was it pity?/n"I'm sorry, Potter, but that's my final word. You had/nbetter hurry, or you'll be late for your next lesson."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was nothing to be done. Ron called Professor/nMcGonagall a lot of names that greatly annoyed/nHermione; Hermione assumed an "all-for-the-best"/nexpression that made Ron even angrier, and Harry/nhad to endure everyone in the class talking loudly/nand happily about what they were going to do first,/nonce they got into Hogsmeade./n/n"There's always the feast," said Ron, in an effort to/ncheer Harry up. "You know, the Halloween feast, in/nthe evening."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry gloomily, "great."/n/nThe Halloween feast was always good, but it would/ntaste a lot better if he was coming to it after a day in/nHogsmeade with everyone else. Nothing anyone said/nmade him feel any better about being left behind./nDean Thomas, who was good with a quill, had offered/nto forge Uncle Vernon's signature on the form, but as/nHarry had already told Professor McGonagall he/nhadn't had it signed, that was no good. Ron/nhalfheartedly suggested the Invisibility Cloak, but/nHermione stamped on that one, reminding Ron what/nDumbledore had told them about the dementors/nbeing able to see through them. Percy had what were/npossibly the least helpful words of comfort./n/n"They make a fuss about Hogsmeade, but I assure/nyou, Harry, it's not all it's cracked up to be," he said/nseriously. "All right, the sweetshop's rather good, and/nZonko's Joke Shop's frankly dangerous, and yes, the/nShrieking Shack's always worth a visit, but really,/nHarry, apart from that, you're not missing anything."/n/nOn Halloween morning, Harry awoke with the rest/nand went down to breakfast, feeling thoroughly/ndepressed, though doing his best to act normally./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well bring you lots of sweets back from/nHoneydukes," said Hermione, looking desperately/nsorry for him./n/n"Yeah, loads," said Ron. He and Hermione had finally/nforgotten their squabble about Crookshanks in the/nface of Harry's difficulties./n/n"Don't worry about me," said Harry, in what he hoped/nwas an offhand voice, "I'll see you at the feast. Have a/ngood time."/n/nHe accompanied them to the entrance hall, where/nFilch, the caretaker, was standing inside the front/ndoors, checking off names against a long list, peering/nsuspiciously into every face, and making sure that no/none was sneaking out who shouldn't be going./n/n"Staying here, Potter?" shouted Malfoy, who was/nstanding in line with Crabbe and Goyle. "Scared of/npassing the dementors?"/n/nHarry ignored him and made his solitary way up the/nmarble staircase, through the deserted corridors, and/nback to Gryffindor Tower./n/n"Password?" said the Fat Lady, jerking out of a doze./n/n"Fortuna Major," said Harry listlessly./n/nThe portrait swung open and he climbed through the/nhole into the common room. It was full of chattering/nfirst and second years, and a few older students, who/nhad obviously visited Hogsmeade so often the novelty/nhad worn off./n/n"Harry! Harry! Hi, Harry!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was Colin Creevey, a second year who was deeply in/nawe of Harry and never missed an opportunity to/nspeak to him./n/n"Aren't you going to Hogsmeade, Harry? Why not?/nHey" — Colin looked eagerly around at his friends —/n"you can come and sit with us, if you like, Harry!"/n/n"Er — no, thanks, Colin," said Harry, who wasn't in/nthe mood to have a lot of people staring avidly at the/nscar on his forehead. "I — I've got to go to the library,/ngot to get some work done."/n/nAfter that, he had no choice but to turn right around/nand head back out of the portrait hole again./n/n"What was the point waking me up?" the Fat Lady/ncalled grumpily after him as he walked away./n/nHarry wandered dispiritedly toward the library, but/nhalfway there he changed his mind; he didn't feel like/nworking. He turned around and came face-to-face/nwith Filch, who had obviously just seen off the last of/nthe Hogsmeade visitors./n/n"What are you doing?" Filch snarled suspiciously./n/n"Nothing," said Harry truthfully./n/n"Nothing!" spat Filch, his jowls quivering/nunpleasantly. "A likely story! Sneaking around on/nyour own — why aren't you in Hogsmeade buying/nStink Pellets and Belch Powder and Whizzing Worms/nlike the rest of your nasty little friends?"/n/nHarry shrugged./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, get back to your common room where you/nbelong!" snapped Filch, and he stood glaring until/nHarry had passed out of sight./n/nBut Harry didn't go back to the common room; he/nclimbed a staircase, thinking vaguely of visiting the/nOwlery to see Hedwig, and was walking along another/ncorridor when a voice from inside one of the rooms/nsaid, "Harry?"/n/nHarry doubled back to see who had spoken and met/nProfessor Lupin, looking around his office door./n/n"What are you doing?" said Lupin, though in a very/ndifferent voice from Filch. "Where are Ron and/nHermione?"/n/n"Hogsmeade," said Harry, in a would-be casual voice./n/n"Ah," said Lupin. He considered Harry for a moment./n"Why don't you come in? I've just taken delivery of a/ngrindylow for our next lesson."/n/n"A what?" said Harry./n/nHe followed Lupin into his office. In the corner stood a/nvery large tank of water. A sickly green creature with/nsharp little horns had its face pressed against the/nglass, pulling faces and flexing its long, spindly/nfingers./n/n"Water demon," said Lupin, surveying the grindylow/nthoughtfully. "We shouldn't have much difficulty with/nhim, not after the kappas. The trick is to break his/ngrip. You notice the abnormally long fingers? Strong,/nbut very brittle."/n/nThe grindylow bared its green teeth and then buried/nitself in a tangle of weeds in a corner./n/n/n/n/n/n"Cup of tea?" Lupin said, looking around for his/nkettle. "I was just thinking of making one."/n/n"All right," said Harry awkwardly./n/nLupin tapped the kettle with his wand and a blast of/nsteam issued suddenly from the spout./n/n"Sit down," said Lupin, taking the lid off a dusty tin./n"I've only got teabags, I'm afraid — but I daresay/nyou've had enough of tea leaves?"/n/nHarry looked at him. Lupin's eyes were twinkling./n/n"How did you know about that?" Harry asked./n/n"Professor McGonagall told me," said Lupin, passing/nHarry a chipped mug of tea. "You're not worried, are/nyou?"/n/n"No," said Harry./n/nHe thought for a moment of telling Lupin about the/ndog he'd seen in Magnolia Crescent but decided not/nto. He didn't want Lupin to think he was a coward,/nespecially since Lupin already seemed to think he/ncouldn't cope with a boggart./n/nSomething of Harry's thoughts seemed to have shown/non his face, because Lupin said, "Anything worrying/nyou, Harry?"/n/n"No," Harry lied. He drank a bit of tea and watched/nthe grindylow brandishing a fist at him. "Yes," he said/nsuddenly, putting his tea down on Lupin's desk. "You/nknow that day we fought the boggart?/n/n"Yes," said Lupin slowly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Why didn't you let me fight it?" said Harry abruptly./nLupin raised his eyebrows./n/n"I would have thought that was obvious, Harry," he/nsaid, sounding surprised./n/nHarry, who had expected Lupin to deny that he'd/ndone any such thing, was taken aback./n/n"Why?" he said again./n/n"Well," said Lupin, frowning slightly, "I assumed that/nif the boggart faced you, it would assume the shape of/nLord Voldemort."/n/nHarry stared. Not only was this the last answer he'd/nexpected, but Lupin had said Voldemort 's name. The/nonly person Harry had ever heard say the name aloud/n(apart from himself) was Professor Dumbledore./n/n"Clearly, I was wrong," said Lupin, still frowning at/nHarry. "But I didn't think it a good idea for Lord/nVoldemort to materialize in the staffroom. I imagined/nthat people would panic."/n/n"I didn't think of Voldemort," said Harry honestly. "I/n— I remembered those dementors."/n/n"I see," said Lupin thoughtfully. "Well, well ... I'm/nimpressed." He smiled slightly at the look of surprise/non Harry's face. "That suggests that what you fear/nmost of all is — fear. Very wise, Harry."/n/nHarry didn't know what to say to that, so he drank/nsome more tea./n/n"So you've been thinking that I didn't believe you/ncapable of fighting the boggart?" said Lupin shrewdly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Well ... yeah," said Harry. He was suddenly feeling a/nlot happier. "Professor Lupin, you know the/ndementors — "/n/nHe was interrupted by a knock on the door./n/n"Come in," called Lupin./n/nThe door opened, and in came Snape. He was/ncarrying a goblet, which was smoking faintly, and/nstopped at the sight of Harry, his black eyes/nnarrowing./n/n"Ah, Severus," said Lupin, smiling. "Thanks very/nmuch. Could you leave it here on the desk for me?"/n/nSnape set down the smoking goblet, his eyes/nwandering between Harry and Lupin./n/n"I was just showing Harry my grindylow," said Lupin/npleasantly, pointing at the tank./n/n"Fascinating," said Snape, without looking at it. "You/nshould drink that directly, Lupin."/n/n"Yes, yes, I will," said Lupin./n/n"I made an entire cauldronful," Snape continued. "If/nyou need more."/n/n"I should probably take some again tomorrow. Thanks/nvery much, Severus."/n/n"Not at all," said Snape, but there was a look in his/neye Harry didn't like. He backed out of the room,/nunsmiling and watchful./n/nHarry looked curiously at the goblet. Lupin smiled./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Professor Snape has very kindly concocted a potion/nfor me," he said. "I have never been much of a potion-/nbrewer and this one is particularly complex." He/npicked up the goblet and sniffed it. "Pity sugar makes/nit useless," he added, taking a sip and shuddering./n/n"Why — ?" Harry began. Lupin looked at him and/nanswered the unfinished question./n/n"I've been feeling a bit off-color," he said. "This potion/nis the only thing that helps. I am very lucky to be/nworking alongside Professor Snape; there aren't many/nwizards who are up to making it."/n/nProfessor Lupin took another sip and Harry had a/ncrazy urge to knock the goblet out of his hands./n/n"Professor Snape's very interested in the Dark Arts,"/nhe blurted out./n/n"Really?" said Lupin, looking only mildly interested as/nhe took another gulp of potion./n/n"Some people reckon — " Harry hesitated, then/nplunged recklessly on, "some people reckon he'd do/nanything to get the Defense Against the Dark Arts/njob."/n/nLupin drained the goblet and pulled a face./n/n"Disgusting," he said. "Well, Harry, I'd better get back/nto work. I'll see you at the feast later."/n/n"Right," said Harry, putting down his empty teacup./n/nThe empty goblet was still smoking./n/n"There you go," said Ron. "We got as much as we/ncould carry."/n/n/n/n/n/nA shower of brilliantly colored sweets fell into Harry's/nlap. It was dusk, and Ron and Hermione had just/nturned up in the common room, pink-faced from the/ncold wind and looking as though they'd had the time/nof their lives./n/n"Thanks," said Harry, picking up a packet of tiny/nblack Pepper Imps. "What's Hogsmeade like? Where/ndid you go?"/n/nBy the sound of it — everywhere. Dervish and/nBanges, the wizarding equipment shop, Zonko's Joke/nShop, into the Three Broomsticks for foaming mugs of/nhot butterbeer, and many places besides./n/n"The post office, Harry! About two hundred owls, all/nsitting on shelves, all color-coded depending on how/nfast you want your letter to get there!"/n/n"Honeydukes has got a new kind of fudge; they were/ngiving out free samples, there's a bit, look — "/n/n"We think we saw an ogre, honestly, they get all sorts/nat the Three Broomsticks — "/n/n"Wish we could have brought you some butterbeer,/nreally warms you up — "/n/n"What did you do?" said Hermione, looking anxious./n"Did you get any work done?"/n/n"No," said Harry. "Lupin made me a cup of tea in his/noffice. And then Snape came in. ..."/n/nHe told them all about the goblet. Ron's mouth fell/nopen./n/n" Lupin drank it?" he gasped. "Is he mad?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione checked her watch./n/n/n/n"We'd better go down, you know, the feast'll be/nstarting in five minutes. ..." They hurried through the/nportrait hole and into the crowd, still discussing/nSnape./n/n"But if he — you know" — Hermione dropped her/nvoice, glancing nervously around — "if he was trying/nto — to poison Lupin — he wouldn't have done it in/nfront of Harry."/n/n"Yeah, maybe," said Harry as they reached the/nentrance hall and crossed into the Great Hall. It had/nbeen decorated with hundreds and hundreds of/ncandle-filled pumpkins, a cloud of fluttering live bats,/nand many flaming orange streamers, which were/nswimming lazily across the stormy ceiling like brilliant/nwatersnakes./n/nThe food was delicious; even Hermione and Ron, who/nwere full to bursting with Honeydukes sweets,/nmanaged second helpings of everything. Harry kept/nglancing at the staff table. Professor Lupin looked/ncheerful and as well as he ever did; he was talking/nanimatedly to tiny little Professor Flitwick, the/nCharms teacher. Harry moved his eyes along the/ntable, to the place where Snape sat. Was he imagining/nit, or were Snape 's eyes flickering toward Lupin more/noften than was natural?/n/nThe feast finished with an entertainment provided by/nthe Hogwarts ghosts. They popped out of the walls/nand tables to do a bit of formation gliding; Nearly/nHeadless Nick, the Gryffindor ghost, had a great/nsuccess with a reenactment of his own botched/nbeheading./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt had been such a pleasant evening that Harry's good/nmood couldn't even be spoiled by Malfoy, who/nshouted through the crowd as they all left the hall,/n"The dementors send their love, Potter!"/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione followed the rest of the/nGryffindors along the usual path to Gryffindor Tower,/nbut when they reached the corridor that ended with/nthe portrait of the Fat Lady, they found it jammed/nwith students./n/n"Why isn't anyone going in?" said Ron curiously./n/nHarry peered over the heads in front of him. The/nportrait seemed to be closed./n/n"Let me through, please," came Percy's voice, and he/ncame bustling importantly through the crowd./n/n"What's the holdup here? You can't all have forgotten/nthe password — excuse me, I'm Head Boy — "/n/nAnd then a silence fell over the crowd, from the front/nfirst, so that a chill seemed to spread down the/ncorridor. They heard Percy say, in a suddenly sharp/nvoice, "Somebody get Professor Dumbledore. Quick."/n/nPeople's heads turned; those at the back were/nstanding on tiptoe./n/n"What's going on?" said Ginny, who had just arrived./n/nA moment later, Professor Dumbledore was there,/nsweeping toward the portrait; the Gryffindors/nsqueezed together to let him through, and Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione moved closer to see what the trouble/nwas./n/n"Oh, my — " Hermione grabbed Harry's arm./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe Fat Lady had vanished from her portrait, which/nhad been slashed so viciously that strips of canvas/nlittered the floor; great chunks of it had been torn/naway completely./n/nDumbledore took one quick look at the ruined/npainting and turned, his eyes somber, to see/nProfessors McGonagall, Lupin, and Snape hurrying/ntoward him./n/n"We need to find her," said Dumbledore. "Professor/nMcGonagall, please go to Mr. Filch at once and tell/nhim to search every painting in the castle for the Fat/nLady."/n/n"You'll be lucky!" said a cackling voice./n/nIt was Peeves the Poltergeist, bobbing over the crowd/nand looking delighted, as he always did, at the sight/nof wreckage or worry./n/n"What do you mean, Peeves?" said Dumbledore/ncalmly, and Peeves's grin faded a little. He didn't dare/ntaunt Dumbledore. Instead he adopted an oily voice/nthat was no better than his cackle./n/n"Ashamed, Your Headship, sir. Doesn't want to be/nseen. She's a horrible mess. Saw her running through/nthe landscape up on the fourth floor, sir, dodging/nbetween the trees. Crying something dreadful," he/nsaid happily. "Poor thing," he added unconvincingly./n/n"Did she say who did it?" said Dumbledore quietly./n/n"Oh yes, Professorhead," said Peeves, with the air of/none cradling a large bombshell in his arms. "He got/nvery angry when she wouldn't let him in, you see."/nPeeves flipped over and grinned at Dumbledore from/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbetween his own legs. "Nasty temper he's got, that/nSirius Black."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n9/n/n/n/n

title: Grim Defeat
text: /nProfessor Dumbledore sent all the Gryffindors back to/nthe Great Hall, where they were joined ten minutes/nlater by the students from Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, and/nSlytherin, who all looked extremely confused./n/n"The teachers and I need to conduct a thorough/nsearch of the castle," Professor Dumbledore told them/nas Professors McGonagall and Flitwick closed all/ndoors into the hall. "I'm afraid that, for your own/nsafety, you will have to spend the night here. I want/nthe prefects to stand guard over the entrances to the/nhall and I am leaving the Head Boy and Girl in/ncharge. Any disturbance should be reported to me/nimmediately," he added to Percy, who was looking/nimmensely proud and important. "Send word with one/nof the ghosts."/n/nProfessor Dumbledore paused, about to leave the hall,/nand said, "Oh, yes, you'll be needing ..."/n/nOne casual wave of his wand and the long tables flew/nto the edges of the hall and stood themselves against/n/n/n/n/nthe walls; another wave, and the floor was covered/nwith hundreds of squashy purple sleeping bags./n/n"Sleep well," said Professor Dumbledore, closing the/ndoor behind him./n/nThe hall immediately began to buzz excitedly; the/nGryffindors were telling the rest of the school what/nhad just happened./n/n"Everyone into their sleeping bags!" shouted Percy./n"Come on, now, no more talking! Lights out in ten/nminutes!"/n/n"C'mon," Ron said to Harry and Hermione; they seized/nthree sleeping bags and dragged them into a corner./n/n"Do you think Black's still in the castle?" Hermione/nwhispered anxiously./n/n"Dumbledore obviously thinks he might be," said Ron./n/n"It's very lucky he picked tonight, you know," said/nHermione as they climbed fully dressed into their/nsleeping bags and propped themselves on their elbows/nto talk. "The one night we weren't in the tower. ..."/n/n"I reckon he's lost track of time, being on the run,"/nsaid Ron. "Didn't realize it was Halloween. Otherwise/nhe'd have come bursting in here."/n/nHermione shuddered./n/nAll around them, people were asking one another the/nsame question: "How did he get in?"/n/n"Maybe he knows how to Apparate," said a Ravenclaw/na few feet away. "Just appear out of thin air, you/nknow."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Disguised himself, probably," said a Hufflepuff fifth/nyear./n/n"He could've flown in," suggested Dean Thomas./n/n"Honestly, am I the only person who's ever bothered/nto read Hogwarts, A History?" said Hermione crossly/nto Harry and Ron./n/n"Probably," said Ron. "Why?"/n/n"Because the castle's protected by more than walls,/nyou know," said Hermione. "There are all sorts of/nenchantments on it, to stop people entering by/nstealth. You can't just Apparate in here. And I'd like/nto see the disguise that could fool those dementors./nThey're guarding every single entrance to the/ngrounds. They'd have seen him fly in too. And Filch/nknows all the secret passages, they'll have them/ncovered. ..."/n/n"The lights are going out now!" Percy shouted. "I want/neveryone in their sleeping bags and no more talking!"/n/nThe candles all went out at once. The only light now/ncame from the silvery ghosts, who were drifting about/ntalking seriously to the prefects, and the enchanted/nceiling, which, like the sky outside, was scattered/nwith stars. What with that, and the whispering that/nstill filled the hall, Harry felt as though he were/nsleeping outdoors in a light wind./n/nOnce every hour, a teacher would reappear in the hall/nto check that everything was quiet. Around three in/nthe morning, when many students had finally fallen/nasleep, Professor Dumbledore came in. Harry watched/nhim looking around for Percy, who had been prowling/nbetween the sleeping bags, telling people off for/ntalking. Percy was only a short way away from Harry,/n/n/n/n/nRon, and Hermione, who quickly pretended to be/nasleep as Dumbledore's footsteps drew nearer./n/n"Any sign of him, Professor?" asked Percy in a/nwhisper./n/n"No. All well here?"/n/n"Everything under control, sir."/n/n"Good. There's no point moving them all now. I've/nfound a temporary guardian for the Gryffindor/nportrait hole. You'll be able to move them back in/ntomorrow."/n/n"And the Fat Lady, sir?"/n/n"Hiding in a map of Argyllshire on the second floor./nApparently she refused to let Black in without the/npassword, so he attacked. She's still very distressed,/nbut once she's calmed down, I'll have Mr. Filch/nrestore her."/n/nHarry heard the door of the hall creak open again,/nand more footsteps./n/n"Headmaster?" It was Snape. Harry kept quite still,/nlistening hard. "The whole of the third floor has been/nsearched. He's not there. And Filch has done the/ndungeons; nothing there either."/n/n"What about the Astronomy tower? Professor/nTrelawney's room? The Owlery?"/n/n"All searched ..."/n/n"Very well, Severus. I didn't really expect Black to/nlinger."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Have you any theory as to how he got in, Professor?"/nasked Snape./n/nHarry raised his head very slightly off his arms to free/nhis other ear./n/n"Many, Severus, each of them as unlikely as the/nnext."/n/nHarry opened his eyes a fraction and squinted up to/nwhere they stood; Dumbledore 's back was to him, but/nhe could see Percy's face, rapt with attention, and/nSnape 's profile, which looked angry./n/n"You remember the conversation we had,/n/nHeadmaster, just before — ah — the start of term?"/nsaid Snape, who was barely opening his lips, as/nthough trying to block Percy out of the conversation./n/n"I do, Severus," said Dumbledore, and there was/nsomething like warning in his voice./n/n"It seems — almost impossible — that Black could/nhave entered the school without inside help. I did/nexpress my concerns when you appointed — "/n/n"I do not believe a single person inside this castle/nwould have helped Black enter it," said Dumbledore,/nand his tone made it so clear that the subject was/nclosed that Snape didn't reply. "I must go down to the/ndementors," said Dumbledore. "I said I would inform/nthem when our search was complete."/n/n"Didn't they want to help, sir?" said Percy./n/n"Oh yes," said Dumbledore coldly. "But I'm afraid no/ndementor will cross the threshold of this castle while I/nam headmaster."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nPercy looked slightly abashed. Dumbledore left the/nhall, walking quickly and quietly. Snape stood for a/nmoment, watching the headmaster with an expression/nof deep resentment on his face; then he too left./n/nHarry glanced sideways at Ron and Hermione. Both of/nthem had their eyes open too, reflecting the starry/nceiling./n/n"What was all that about?" Ron mouthed./n/nThe school talked of nothing but Sirius Black for the/nnext few days. The theories about how he had entered/nthe castle became wilder and wilder; Hannah Abbott,/nfrom Hufflepuff, spent much of their next Herbology/nclass telling anyone who'd listen that Black could/nturn into a flowering shrub./n/nThe Fat Lady's ripped canvas had been taken off the/nwall and replaced with the portrait of Sir Cadogan/nand his fat gray pony. Nobody was very happy about/nthis. Sir Cadogan spent half his time challenging/npeople to duels, and the rest thinking up ridiculously/ncomplicated passwords, which he changed at least/ntwice a day./n/n"He's a complete lunatic," said Seamus Finnigan/nangrily to Percy. "Can't we get anyone else?"/n/n"None of the other pictures wanted the job," said/nPercy. "Frightened of what happened to the Fat Lady./nSir Cadogan was the only one brave enough to/nvolunteer."/n/nSir Cadogan, however, was the least of Harry's/nworries. He was now being closely watched. Teachers/nfound excuses to walk along corridors with him, and/nPercy Weasley (acting, Harry suspected, on his/nmother's orders) was tailing him everywhere like an/n/n/n/n/nextremely pompous guard dog. To cap it all, Professor/nMcGonagall summoned Harry into her office, with/nsuch a somber expression on her face Harry thought/nsomeone must have died./n/n"There's no point hiding it from you any longer,/nPotter," she said in a very serious voice. "I know this/nwill come as a shock to you, but Sirius Black — "/n/n"I know he's after me," said Harry wearily. "I heard/nRon's dad telling his mum. Mr. Weasley works for the/nMinistry of Magic."/n/nProfessor McGonagall seemed very taken aback. She/nstared at Harry for a moment or two, then said, "I see!/nWell, in that case, Potter, you'll understand why I/ndon't think it's a good idea for you to be practicing/nQuidditch in the evenings. Out on the field with only/nyour team members, it's very exposed, Potter — "/n/n"We've got our first match on Saturday!" said Harry,/noutraged. "I've got to train, Professor!"/n/nProfessor McGonagall considered him intently. Harry/nknew she was deeply interested in the Gryffindor/nteam's prospects; it had been she, after all, who'd/nsuggested him as Seeker in the first place. He waited,/nholding his breath./n/n"Hmm ..." Professor McGonagall stood up and stared/nout of the window at the Quidditch field, just visible/nthrough the rain. "Well ... goodness knows, I'd like to/nsee us win the Cup at last ... but all the same, Potter/n... I'd be happier if a teacher were present. I'll ask/nMadam Hooch to oversee your training sessions."/n/nThe weather worsened steadily as the first Quidditch/nmatch drew nearer. Undaunted, the Gryffindor team/nwas training harder than ever under the eye of/n/n/n/n/n/nMadam Hooch. Then, at their final training session/nbefore Saturday's match, Oliver Wood gave his team/nsome unwelcome news./n/n"We're not playing Slytherin!" he told them, looking/nvery angry. "Flint's just been to see me. We're playing/nHufflepuff instead."/n/n"Why?" chorused the rest of the team./n/n"Flint's excuse is that their Seeker's arm's still/ninjured," said Wood, grinding his teeth furiously. "But/nit's obvious why they're doing it. Don't want to play in/nthis weather. Think it'll damage their chances. ..."/n/nThere had been strong winds and heavy rain all day,/nand as Wood spoke, they heard a distant rumble of/nthunder./n/n"There's nothing wrong with Malfoy's arm!" said Harry/nfuriously. "He's faking it!"/n/n"I know that, but we can't prove it," said Wood/nbitterly. "And we've been practicing all those moves/nassuming we're playing Slytherin, and instead it's/nHufflepuff, and their style's quite different. They've got/na new Captain and Seeker, Cedric Diggory — "/n/nAngelina, Alicia, and Katie suddenly giggled./n/n"What?" said Wood, frowning at this lighthearted/nbehavior./n/n"He's that tall, good-looking one, isn't he?" said/nAngelina./n/n"Strong and silent," said Katie, and they started to/ngiggle again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He's only silent because he's too thick to string two/nwords together," said Fred impatiently. "I don't know/nwhy you're worried, Oliver, Hufflepuff is a pushover./nLast time we played them, Harry caught the Snitch in/nabout five minutes, remember?"/n/n"We were playing in completely different conditions!"/nWood shouted, his eyes bulging slightly. "Diggory's/nput a very strong side together! He's an excellent/nSeeker! I was afraid you'd take it like this! We mustn't/nrelax! We must keep our focus! Slytherin is trying to/nwrong-foot us! We must win!"/n/n"Oliver, calm down!" said Fred, looking slightly/nalarmed. "We're taking Hufflepuff very seriously./nSeriously."/n/nThe day before the match, the winds reached howling/npoint and the rain fell harder than ever. It was so/ndark inside the corridors and classrooms that extra/ntorches and lanterns were lit. The Slytherin team was/nlooking very smug indeed, and none more so than/nMalfoy./n/n"Ah, if only my arm was feeling a bit better!" he sighed/nas the gale outside pounded the windows./n/nHarry had no room in his head to worry about/nanything except the match tomorrow. Oliver Wood/nkept hurrying up to him between classes and giving/nhim tips. The third time this happened, Wood talked/nfor so long that Harry suddenly realized he was ten/nminutes late for Defense Against the Dark Arts, and/nset off at a run with Wood shouting after him,/n"Diggory's got a very fast swerve, Harry, so you might/nwant to try looping him — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry skidded to a halt outside the Defense Against/nthe Dark Arts classroom, pulled the door open, and/ndashed inside./n/n"Sorry I'm late, Professor Lupin, I — "/n/nBut it wasn't Professor Lupin who looked up at him/nfrom the teacher's desk; it was Snape./n/n"This lesson began ten minutes ago, Potter, so I think/nwe'll make it ten points from Gryffindor. Sit down."/n/nBut Harry didn't move./n/n"Where's Professor Lupin?" he said./n/n"He says he is feeling too ill to teach today," said/nSnape with a twisted smile. "I believe I told you to sit/ndown?"/n/nBut Harry stayed where he was./n/n"What's wrong with him?"/n/nSnape 's black eyes glittered./n/n"Nothing life-threatening," he said, looking as though/nhe wished it were. "Five more points from Gryffindor,/nand if I have to ask you to sit down again, it will be/nfifty."/n/nHarry walked slowly to his seat and sat down. Snape/nlooked around at the class./n/n"As I was saying before Potter interrupted, Professor/nLupin has not left any record of the topics you have/ncovered so far — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Please, sir, we've done boggarts, Red Caps, kappas,/nand grindylows," said Hermione quickly, "and we're/njust about to start — "/n/n"Be quiet," said Snape coldly. "I did not ask for/ninformation. I was merely commenting on Professor/nLupin's lack of organization."/n/n"He's the best Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher/nwe've ever had," said Dean Thomas boldly, and there/nwas a murmur of agreement from the rest of the/nclass. Snape looked more menacing than ever./n/n"You are easily satisfied. Lupin is hardly overtaxing/nyou — I would expect first years to be able to deal/nwith Red Caps and grindylows. Today we shall/ndiscuss — "/n/nHarry watched him flick through the textbook, to the/nvery back chapter, which he must know they hadn't/ncovered./n/n" — werewolves," said Snape./n/n"But, sir," said Hermione, seemingly unable to/nrestrain herself, "we're not supposed to do werewolves/nyet, we're due to start hinkypunks — "/n/n"Miss Granger," said Snape in a voice of deadly calm,/n"I was under the impression that I am teaching this/nlesson, not you. And I am telling you all to turn to/npage 394." He glanced around again. "All of you!/n/nNow\"/n/nWith many bitter sidelong looks and some sullen/nmuttering, the class opened their books./n/n"Which of you can tell me how we distinguish between/nthe werewolf and the true wolf?" said Snape./n/n/n/n/n/nEveryone sat in motionless silence; everyone except/nHermione, whose hand, as it so often did, had shot/nstraight into the air./n/n"Anyone?" Snape said, ignoring Hermione. His twisted/nsmile was back. "Are you telling me that Professor/nLupin hasn't even taught you the basic distinction/nbetween — "/n/n"We told you," said Parvati suddenly, "we haven't got/nas far as werewolves yet, we're still on — "/n/n"Silencel" snarled Snape. "Well, well, well, I never/nthought I'd meet a third -year class who wouldn't even/nrecognize a werewolf when they saw one. I shall make/na point of informing Professor Dumbledore how very/nbehind you all are. ..."/n/n"Please, sir," said Hermione, whose hand was still in/nthe air, "the werewolf differs from the true wolf in/nseveral small ways. The snout of the werewolf — "/n/n"That is the second time you have spoken out of turn,/nMiss Granger," said Snape coolly. "Five more points/nfrom Gryffindor for being an insufferable know-it-all."/n/nHermione went very red, put down her hand, and/nstared at the floor with her eyes full of tears. It was a/nmark of how much the class loathed Snape that they/nwere all glaring at him, because every one of them/nhad called Hermione a know-it-all at least once, and/nRon, who told Hermione she was a know-it-all at least/ntwice a week, said loudly, "You asked us a question/nand she knows the answer! Why ask if you don't want/nto be told?"/n/nThe class knew instantly he'd gone too far. Snape/nadvanced on Ron slowly, and the room held its/nbreath./n/n/n/n/n/n"Detention, Weasley," Snape said silkily, his face very/nclose to Ron's. "And if I ever hear you criticize the way/nI teach a class again, you will be very sorry indeed."/n/nNo one made a sound throughout the rest of the/nlesson. They sat and made notes on werewolves from/nthe textbook, while Snape prowled up and down the/nrows of desks, examining the work they had been/ndoing with Professor Lupin./n/n"Very poorly explained . . . That is incorrect, the kappa/nis more commonly found in Mongolia. . . . Professor/nLupin gave this eight out of ten? I wouldn't have given/nit three. ..."/n/nWhen the bell rang at last, Snape held them back./n/n"You will each write an essay, to be handed in to me,/non the ways you recognize and kill werewolves. I want/ntwo rolls of parchment on the subject, and I want/nthem by Monday morning. It is time somebody took/nthis class in hand. Weasley, stay behind, we need to/narrange your detention."/n/nHarry and Hermione left the room with the rest of the/nclass, who waited until they were well out of earshot,/nthen burst into a furious tirade about Snape./n/n"Snape 's never been like this with any of our other/nDefense Against the Dark Arts teachers, even if he did/nwant the job," Harry said to Hermione. "Why's he got/nit in for Lupin? D'you think this is all because of the/nboggart?"/n/n"I don't know," said Hermione pensively. "But I really/nhope Professor Lupin gets better soon. ..."/n/nRon caught up with them five minutes later, in a/ntowering rage./n/n/n/n/n/n"D'you know what that — " (he called Snape/nsomething that made Hermione say "Ron\") " — is/nmaking me do? I've got to scrub out the bedpans in/nthe hospital wing. Without magid" He was breathing/ndeeply, his fists clenched. "Why couldn't Black have/nhidden in Snape's office, eh? He could have finished/nhim off for us!"/n/nHarry woke extremely early the next morning; so early/nthat it was still dark. For a moment he thought the/nroaring of the wind had woken him. Then he felt a/ncold breeze on the back of his neck and sat bolt/nupright — Peeves the Poltergeist had been floating/nnext to him, blowing hard in his ear./n/n"What did you do that for?" said Harry furiously./n/nPeeves puffed out his cheeks, blew hard, and zoomed/nbackward out of the room, cackling./n/nHarry fumbled for his alarm clock and looked at it. It/nwas half past four. Cursing Peeves, he rolled over and/ntried to get back to sleep, but it was very difficult, now/nthat he was awake, to ignore the sounds of the/nthunder rumbling overhead, the pounding of the wind/nagainst the castle walls, and the distant creaking of/nthe trees in the Forbidden Forest. In a few hours he/nwould be out on the Quidditch field, battling through/nthat gale. Finally, he gave up any thought of more/nsleep, got up, dressed, picked up his Nimbus Two/nThousand, and walked quietly out of the dormitory./n/nAs Harry opened the door, something brushed against/nhis leg. He bent down just in time to grab/nCrookshanks by the end of his bushy tail and drag/nhim outside./n/n"You know, I reckon Ron was right about you," Harry/ntold Crookshanks suspiciously. "There are plenty of/n/n/n/n/n/nmice around this place — go and chase them. Go on,"/nhe added, nudging Crookshanks down the spiral/nstaircase with his foot. "Leave Scabbers alone."/n/nThe noise of the storm was even louder in the/ncommon room. Harry knew better than to think the/nmatch would be canceled; Quidditch matches weren't/ncalled off for trifles like thunderstorms. Nevertheless,/nhe was starting to feel very apprehensive. Wood had/npointed out Cedric Diggory to him in the corridor;/nDiggory was a fifth year and a lot bigger than Harry./nSeekers were usually light and speedy, but Diggory's/nweight would be an advantage in this weather/nbecause he was less likely to be blown off course./n/nHarry whiled away the hours until dawn in front of/nthe fire, getting up every now and then to stop/nCrookshanks from sneaking up the boys' staircase/nagain. At long last Harry thought it must be time for/nbreakfast, so he headed through the portrait hole/nalone./n/n"Stand and fight, you mangy cur!" yelled Sir Cadogan./n"Oh, shut up," Harry yawned./n/nHe revived a bit over a large bowl of porridge, and by/nthe time he'd started on toast, the rest of the team/nhad turned up./n/n"It's going to be a tough one," said Wood, who wasn't/neating anything./n/n"Stop worrying, Oliver," said Alicia soothingly, "we/ndon't mind a bit of rain."/n/nBut it was considerably more than a bit of rain. Such/nwas the popularity of Quidditch that the whole school/nturned out to watch the match as usual, but they ran/n/n/n/n/n/ndown the lawns toward the Quidditch field, heads/nbowed against the ferocious wind, umbrellas being/nwhipped out of their hands as they went. Just before/nhe entered the locker room, Harry saw Malfoy,/n/nCrabbe, and Goyle, laughing and pointing at him from/nunder an enormous umbrella on their way to the/nstadium./n/nThe team changed into their scarlet robes and waited/nfor Wood's usual pre-match pep talk, but it didn't/ncome. He tried to speak several times, made an odd/ngulping noise, then shook his head hopelessly and/nbeckoned them to follow him./n/nThe wind was so strong that they staggered sideways/nas they walked out onto the field. If the crowd was/ncheering, they couldn't hear it over the fresh rolls of/nthunder. Rain was splattering over Harry's glasses./nHow on earth was he going to see the Snitch in this?/n/nThe Hufflepuffs were approaching from the opposite/nside of the field, wearing canary -yellow robes. The/nCaptains walked up to each other and shook hands;/nDiggory smiled at Wood but Wood now looked as/nthough he had lockjaw and merely nodded. Harry saw/nMadam Hooch's mouth form the words, "Mount your/nbrooms." He pulled his right foot out of the mud with/na squelch and swung it over his Nimbus Two/nThousand. Madam Hooch put her whistle to her lips/nand gave it a blast that sounded shrill and distant —/nthey were off./n/nHarry rose fast, but his Nimbus was swerving slightly/nwith the wind. He held it as steady as he could and/nturned, squinting into the rain./n/nWithin five minutes Harry was soaked to his skin and/nfrozen, hardly able to see his teammates, let alone the/ntiny Snitch. He flew backward and forward across the/n/n/n/n/n/nfield past blurred red and yellow shapes, with no idea/nof what was happening in the rest of the game. He/ncouldn't hear the commentary over the wind. The/ncrowd was hidden beneath a sea of cloaks and/nbattered umbrellas. Twice Harry came very close to/nbeing unseated by a Bludger; his vision was so/nclouded by the rain on his glasses he hadn't seen/nthem coming./n/nHe lost track of time. It was getting harder and harder/nto hold his broom straight. The sky was getting/ndarker, as though night had decided to come early./nTwice Harry nearly hit another player, without/nknowing whether it was a teammate or opponent;/neveryone was now so wet, and the rain so thick, he/ncould hardly tell them apart. .../n/nWith the first flash of lightning came the sound of/nMadam Hooch's whistle; Harry could just see the/noutline of Wood through the thick rain, gesturing him/nto the ground. The whole team splashed down into/nthe mud./n/n"I called for time-out!" Wood roared at his team./n/n"Come on, under here — "/n/nThey huddled at the edge of the field under a large/numbrella; Harry took off his glasses and wiped them/nhurriedly on his robes./n/n"What's the score?"/n/n"We're fifty points up," said Wood, "but unless we get/nthe Snitch soon, we'll be playing into the night."/n/n"I've got no chance with these on," Harry said/nexasperatedly, waving his glasses./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAt that very moment, Hermione appeared at his/nshoulder; she was holding her cloak over her head/nand was, inexplicably, beaming./n/n"I've had an idea, Harry! Give me your glasses, quick!"/n/nHe handed them to her, and as the team watched in/namazement, Hermione tapped them with her wand/nand said, "Imperviusl"/n/n"There!" she said, handing them back to Harry./n"They'll repel water!"/n/nWood looked as though he could have kissed her./n/n"Brilliant!" he called hoarsely after her as she/ndisappeared into the crowd. "Okay, team, let's go for/nit!"/n/n/n/nHermione 's spell had done the trick. Harry was still/nnumb with cold, still wetter than he'd ever been in his/nlife, but he could see. Full of fresh determination, he/nurged his broom through the turbulent air, staring in/nevery direction for the Snitch, avoiding a Bludger,/nducking beneath Diggory, who was streaking in the/nopposite direction. .../n/nThere was another clap of thunder, followed/nimmediately by forked lightning. This was getting/nmore and more dangerous. Harry needed to get the/nSnitch quickly —/n/nHe turned, intending to head back toward the middle/nof the field, but at that moment, another flash of/nlightning illuminated the stands, and Harry saw/nsomething that distracted him completely — the/nsilhouette of an enormous shaggy black dog, clearly/nimprinted against the sky, motionless in the topmost,/nempty row of seats./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's numb hands slipped on the broom handle/nand his Nimbus dropped a few feet. Shaking his/nsodden bangs out of his eyes, he squinted back into/nthe stands. The dog had vanished./n/n"Harry!" came Wood's anguished yell from the/nGryffindor goal posts. "Harry, behind you!"/n/nHarry looked wildly around. Cedric Diggory was/npelting up the field, and a tiny speck of gold was/nshimmering in the rain-filled air between them —/n/nWith a jolt of panic, Harry threw himself flat to the/nbroom-handle and zoomed toward the Snitch./n/n"Come on!" he growled at his Nimbus as the rain/nwhipped his face. "Fasteri"/n/nBut something odd was happening. An eerie silence/nwas falling across the stadium. The wind, though as/nstrong as ever, was forgetting to roar. It was as/nthough someone had turned off the sound, as though/nHarry had gone suddenly deaf — what was going on?/n/nAnd then a horribly familiar wave of cold swept over/nhim, inside him, just as he became aware of/nsomething moving on the field below. . . ./n/nBefore he'd had time to think, Harry had taken his/neyes off the Snitch and looked down./n/nAt least a hundred dementors, their hidden faces/npointing up at him, were standing beneath him. It/nwas as though freezing water were rising in his chest,/ncutting at his insides. And then he heard it again. .../nSomeone was screaming, screaming inside his head/n... a woman . . ./n/n"Not Harry, not Harry, please not Harry\"/n/n/n/n/n/n" Stand aside, you silly girl ... stand aside, now. ..."/n/n/n/n" Not Harry, please no, take me, kill me instead — "/n/nNumbing, swirling white mist was filling Harry's/nbrain. . . . What was he doing? Why was he flying? He/nneeded to help her. ... She was going to die. ... She/nwas going to be murdered. .../n/nHe was falling, falling through the icy mist./n/n"Not Harry\ Please ... have mercy ... have mercy. ..."/n/nA shrill voice was laughing, the woman was/nscreaming, and Harry knew no more./n/n"Lucky the ground was so soft."/n/n"I thought he was dead for sure."/n/n"But he didn't even break his glasses."/n/nHarry could hear the voices whispering, but they/nmade no sense whatsoever. He didn't have a clue/nwhere he was, or how he'd got there, or what he'd/nbeen doing before he got there. All he knew was that/nevery inch of him was aching as though it had been/nbeaten./n/n"That was the scariest thing I've ever seen in my life."/n/nScariest . . . the scariest thing . . . hooded black figures/n... cold ... screaming .../n/nHarry's eyes snapped open. He was lying in the/nhospital wing. The Gryffindor Quidditch team,/nspattered with mud from head to foot, was gathered/naround his bed. Ron and Hermione were also there,/n/n/n/n/n/nlooking as though they'd just climbed out of a/nswimming pool./n/n"Harry!" said Fred, who looked extremely white/nunderneath the mud. "How're you feeling?"/n/nIt was as though Harry's memory was on fast forward./nThe lightning — the Grim — the Snitch — and the/ndementors .../n/n"What happened?" he said, sitting up so suddenly/nthey all gasped./n/n"You fell off," said Fred. "Must've been — what — fifty/nfeet?"/n/n"We thought you'd died," said Alicia, who was/nshaking./n/nHermione made a small, squeaky noise. Her eyes were/nextremely bloodshot./n/n"But the match," said Harry. "What happened? Are we/ndoing a replay?"/n/nNo one said anything. The horrible truth sank into/nHarry like a stone./n/n"We didn't — lose?"/n/n"Diggory got the Snitch," said George. "Just after you/nfell. He didn't realize what had happened. When he/nlooked back and saw you on the ground, he tried to/ncall it off. Wanted a rematch. But they won fair and/nsquare ... even Wood admits it."/n/n"Where is Wood?" said Harry, suddenly realizing he/nwasn't there./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Still in the showers," said Fred. "We think he's trying/nto drown himself."/n/nHarry put his face to his knees, his hands gripping/nhis hair. Fred grabbed his shoulder and shook it/nroughly./n/n"C'mon, Harry, you've never missed the Snitch/nbefore."/n/n"There had to be one time you didn't get it," said/nGeorge./n/n"It's not over yet," said Fred. "We lost by a hundred/npoints, right? So if Hufflepuff loses to Ravenclaw and/nwe beat Ravenclaw and Slytherin ..."/n/n"Hufflepuff'll have to lose by at least two hundred/npoints," said George./n/n"But if they beat Ravenclaw ..."/n/n"No way, Ravenclaw is too good. But if Slytherin loses/nagainst Hufflepuff ..."/n/n"It all depends on the points — a margin of a hundred/neither way — "/n/nHarry lay there, not saying a word. They had lost .../nfor the first time ever, he had lost a Quidditch match./n/nAfter ten minutes or so, Madam Pomfrey came over to/ntell the team to leave him in peace./n/n"Well come and see you later," Fred told him. "Don't/nbeat yourself up, Harry, you're still the best Seeker/nwe've ever had."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe team trooped out, trailing mud behind them./nMadam Pomfrey shut the door behind them, looking/ndisapproving. Ron and Hermione moved nearer to/nHarry's bed./n/n"Dumbledore was really angry," Hermione said in a/nquaking voice. "I've never seen him like that before./n/nHe ran onto the field as you fell, waved his wand, and/nyou sort of slowed down before you hit the ground./nThen he whirled his wand at the dementors. Shot/nsilver stuff at them. They left the stadium right away./n... He was furious they'd come onto the grounds. We/nheard him — "/n/n"Then he magicked you onto a stretcher," said Ron./n"And walked up to school with you floating on it./nEveryone thought you were ..."/n/nHis voice faded, but Harry hardly noticed. He was/nthinking about what the dementors had done to him/n... about the screaming voice. He looked up and saw/nRon and Hermione looking at him so anxiously that/nhe quickly cast around for something matter-of-fact to/nsay./n/n"Did someone get my Nimbus?"/n/nRon and Hermione looked quickly at each other./n/n"Er — "/n/n/n/n"What?" said Harry, looking from one to the other./n/n"Well ... when you fell off, it got blown away," said/nHermione hesitantly./n/n"And?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And it hit — it hit — oh, Harry — it hit the/nWhomping Willow."/n/nHarry's insides lurched. The Whomping Willow was a/nvery violent tree that stood alone in the middle of the/ngrounds./n/n"And?" he said, dreading the answer./n/n"Well, you know the Whomping Willow," said Ron. "It/n— it doesn't like being hit."/n/n"Professor Flitwick brought it back just before you/ncame around," said Hermione in a very small voice./n/nSlowly, she reached down for a bag at her feet, turned/nit upside down, and tipped a dozen bits of splintered/nwood and twig onto the bed, the only remains of/nHarry's faithful, finally beaten broomstick./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n10/n/n/n/n

title: The Marauder's Map
text: /nMadam Pomfrey insisted on keeping Harry in the/nhospital wing for the rest of the weekend. He didn't/nargue or complain, but he wouldn't let her throw/naway the shattered remnants of his Nimbus Two/nThousand. He knew he was being stupid, knew that/nthe Nimbus was beyond repair, but Harry couldn't/nhelp it; he felt as though he'd lost one of his best/nfriends./n/nHe had a stream of visitors, all intent on cheering him/nup. Hagrid sent him a bunch of earwiggy flowers that/nlooked like yellow cabbages, and Ginny Weasley,/nblushing furiously, turned up with a get-well card she/nhad made herself, which sang shrilly unless Harry/nkept it shut under his bowl of fruit. The Gryffindor/nteam visited again on Sunday morning, this time/naccompanied by Wood, who told Harry (in a hollow,/ndead sort of voice) that he didn't blame him in the/nslightest. Ron and Hermione left Harry's bedside only/nat night. But nothing anyone said or did could make/nHarry feel any better, because they knew only half of/nwhat was troubling him./n/n/n/n/nHe hadn't told anyone about the Grim, not even Ron/nand Hermione, because he knew Ron would panic/nand Hermione would scoff. The fact remained,/nhowever, that it had now appeared twice, and both/nappearances had been followed by near-fatal/naccidents; the first time, he had nearly been run over/nby the Knight Bus; the second, fallen fifty feet from/nhis broomstick. Was the Grim going to haunt him/nuntil he actually died? Was he going to spend the rest/nof his life looking over his shoulder for the beast?/n/nAnd then there were the dementors. Harry felt sick/nand humiliated every time he thought of them./nEveryone said the dementors were horrible, but no/none else collapsed every time they went near one. No/none else heard echoes in their head of their dying/nparents./n/nBecause Harry knew who that screaming voice/nbelonged to now. He had heard her words, heard/nthem over and over again during the night hours in/nthe hospital wing while he lay awake, staring at the/nstrips of moonlight on the ceiling. When the/ndementors approached him, he heard the last/nmoments of his mother's life, her attempts to protect/nhim, Harry, from Lord Voldemort, and Voldemort's/nlaughter before he murdered her. . . . Harry dozed/nfitfully, sinking into dreams full of clammy, rotted/nhands and petrified pleading, jerking awake to dwell/nagain on his mother's voice./n/nIt was a relief to return to the noise and bustle of the/nmain school on Monday, where he was forced to think/nabout other things, even if he had to endure Draco/nMalfoy's taunting. Malfoy was almost beside himself/nwith glee at Gryffindor's defeat. He had finally taken/noff his bandages, and celebrated having the full use of/nboth arms again by doing spirited imitations of Harry/nfalling off his broom. Malfoy spent much of their next/n/n/n/n/nPotions class doing dementor imitations across the/ndungeon; Ron finally cracked and flung a large,/nslippery crocodile heart at Malfoy, which hit him in/nthe face and caused Snape to take fifty points from/nGryffindor./n/n"If Snape's teaching Defense Against the Dark Arts/nagain, I'm skiving off," said Ron as they headed/ntoward Lupin's classroom after lunch. "Check who's/nin there, Hermione."/n/nHermione peered around the classroom door./n/n"It's okay!"/n/nProfessor Lupin was back at work. It certainly looked/nas though he had been ill. His old robes were hanging/nmore loosely on him and there were dark shadows/nbeneath his eyes; nevertheless, he smiled at the class/nas they took their seats, and they burst at once into/nan explosion of complaints about Snape's behavior/nwhile Lupin had been ill./n/n"It's not fair, he was only filling in, why should he give/nus homework?"/n/n"We don't know anything about werewolves — "/n/n" — two rolls of parchment!"/n/n"Did you tell Professor Snape we haven't covered them/nyet?" Lupin asked, frowning slightly./n/nThe babble broke out again./n/n"Yes, but he said we were really behind — "/n/n" — he wouldn't listen — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" — two rolls of parchmenti"/n/n/n/nProfessor Lupin smiled at the look of indignation on/nevery face./n/n"Don't worry. I'll speak to Professor Snape. You don't/nhave to do the essay."/n/n"Oh no," said Hermione, looking very disappointed./n"I've already finished it!"/n/nThey had a very enjoyable lesson. Professor Lupin/nhad brought along a glass box containing a/nhinkypunk, a little one-legged creature who looked as/nthough he were made of wisps of smoke, rather frail/nand harmless-looking./n/n"Lures travelers into bogs," said Professor Lupin as/nthey took notes. "You notice the lantern dangling from/nhis hand? Hops ahead — people follow the light —/nthen — ' "/n/nThe hinkypunk made a horrible squelching noise/nagainst the glass./n/nWhen the bell rang, everyone gathered up their things/nand headed for the door, Harry among them, but —/n/n"Wait a moment, Harry," Lupin called. "I'd like a/nword."/n/nHarry doubled back and watched Professor Lupin/ncovering the hinkypunk's box with a cloth./n/n"I heard about the match," said Lupin, turning back/nto his desk and starting to pile books into his/nbriefcase, "and I'm sorry about your broomstick. Is/nthere any chance of fixing it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Harry. "The tree smashed it to bits."/n/nLupin sighed./n/n"They planted the Whomping Willow the same year/nthat I arrived at Hogwarts. People used to play a/ngame, trying to get near enough to touch the trunk. In/nthe end, a boy called Davey Gudgeon nearly lost an/neye, and we were forbidden to go near it. No/nbroomstick would have a chance./n/n"Did you hear about the dementors too?" said Harry/nwith difficulty./n/nLupin looked at him quickly./n/n"Yes, I did. I don't think any of us have seen Professor/nDumbledore that angry. They have been growing/nrestless for some time ... furious at his refusal to let/nthem inside the grounds. ... I suppose they were the/nreason you fell?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry. He hesitated, and then the question/nhe had to ask burst from him before he could stop/nhimself. " Why? Why do they affect me like that? Am I/njust — ?"/n/n/n/n"It has nothing to do with weakness," said Professor/nLupin sharply, as though he had read Harry's mind./n"The dementors affect you worse than the others/nbecause there are horrors in your past that the others/ndon't have."/n/nA ray of wintery sunlight fell across the classroom,/nilluminating Lupin's gray hairs and the lines on his/nyoung face./n/n"Dementors are among the foulest creatures that walk/nthis earth. They infest the darkest, filthiest places,/n/n/n/n/n/nthey glory in decay and despair, they drain peace,/nhope, and happiness out of the air around them./n/nEven Muggles feel their presence, though they can't/nsee them. Get too near a dementor and every good/nfeeling, every happy memory will be sucked out of/nyou. If it can, the dementor will feed on you long/nenough to reduce you to something like itself . . . soul-/nless and evil. You'll be left with nothing but the worst/nexperiences of your life. And the worst that happened/nto you, Harry, is enough to make anyone fall off their/nbroom. You have nothing to feel ashamed of."/n/n"When they get near me — " Harry stared at Lupin's/ndesk, his throat tight. "I can hear Voldemort/nmurdering my mum."/n/nLupin made a sudden motion with his arm as though/nto grip Harry's shoulder, but thought better of it./n/nThere was a moment's silence, then —/n/n"Why did they have to come to the match?" said Harry/nbitterly./n/n"They're getting hungry," said Lupin coolly, shutting/nhis briefcase with a snap. "Dumbledore won't let them/ninto the school, so their supply of human prey has/ndried up. ... I don't think they could resist the large/ncrowd around the Quidditch field. All that excitement/n. . . emotions running high ... it was their idea of a/nfeast."/n/n"Azkaban must be terrible," Harry muttered. Lupin/nnodded grimly./n/n"The fortress is set on a tiny island, way out to sea,/nbut they don't need walls and water to keep the/nprisoners in, not when they're all trapped inside their/nown heads, incapable of a single cheerful thought./nMost of them go mad within weeks."/n/n/n/n/n/n"But Sirius Black escaped from them," Harry said/nslowly. "He got away. ..."/n/n/n/nLupin's briefcase slipped from the desk; he had to/nstoop quickly to catch it./n/n"Yes," he said, straightening up, "Black must have/nfound a way to fight them. I wouldn't have believed it/npossible. ... Dementors are supposed to drain a/nwizard of his powers if he is left with them too long./n/n/n/n"You made that dementor on the train back off," said/nHarry suddenly./n/n"There are — certain defenses one can use," said/nLupin. "But there was only one dementor on the train./nThe more there are, the more difficult it becomes to/nresist."/n/n"What defenses?" said Harry at once. "Can you teach/nme?"/n/n"I don't pretend to be an expert at fighting dementors,/nHarry ... quite the contrary. ..."/n/n"But if the dementors come to another Quidditch/nmatch, I need to be able to fight them — "/n/nLupin looked into Harry's determined face, hesitated,/nthen said, "Well ... all right. I'll try and help. But it'll/nhave to wait until next term, I'm afraid. I have a lot to/ndo before the holidays. I chose a very inconvenient/ntime to fall ill."/n/nWhat with the promise of anti-dementor lessons from/nLupin, the thought that he might never have to hear/nhis mother's death again, and the fact that Ravenclaw/nflattened Hufflepuff in their Quidditch match at the/n/n/n/n/n/nend of November, Harry's mood took a definite/nupturn. Gryffindor were not out of the running after/nall, although they could not afford to lose another/nmatch. Wood became repossessed of his manic/nenergy, and worked his team as hard as ever in the/nchilly haze of rain that persisted into December./n/nHarry saw no hint of a dementor within the grounds./nDumbledore's anger seemed to be keeping them at/ntheir stations at the entrances./n/nTwo weeks before the end of the term, the sky/nlightened suddenly to a dazzling, opaline white and/nthe muddy grounds were revealed one morning/ncovered in glittering frost. Inside the castle, there was/na buzz of Christmas in the air. Professor Flitwick, the/nCharms teacher, had already decorated his classroom/nwith shimmering lights that turned out to be real,/nfluttering fairies. The students were all happily/ndiscussing their plans for the holidays. Both Ron and/nHermione had decided to remain at Hogwarts, and/nthough Ron said it was because he couldn't stand two/nweeks with Percy, and Hermione insisted she needed/nto use the library, Harry wasn't fooled; they were/ndoing it to keep him company, and he was very/ngrateful./n/nTo everyone's delight except Harry's, there was to be/nanother Hogsmeade trip on the very last weekend of/nthe term./n/n"We can do all our Christmas shopping there!" said/nHermione. "Mum and Dad would really love those/nToothflossing Stringmints from Honeydukes!"/n/nResigned to the fact that he would be the only third/nyear staying behind again, Harry borrowed a copy of/nWhich Broomstick from Wood, and decided to spend/nthe day reading up on the different makes. He had/nbeen riding one of the school brooms at team/n/n/n/n/npractice, an ancient Shooting Star, which was very/nslow and jerky; he definitely needed a new broom of/nhis own./n/n/n/nOn the Saturday morning of the Hogsmeade trip,/nHarry bid good-bye to Ron and Hermione, who were/nwrapped in cloaks and scarves, then turned up the/nmarble staircase alone, and headed back toward/nGryffindor Tower. Snow had started to fall outside the/nwindows, and the castle was very still and quiet./n/n"Psst — Harry!"/n/nHe turned, halfway along the third-floor corridor, to/nsee Fred and George peering out at him from behind a/nstatue of a humpbacked, one-eyed witch./n/n"What are you doing?" said Harry curiously. "How/ncome you're not going to Hogsmeade?"/n/n"We've come to give you a bit of festive cheer before/nwe go," said Fred, with a mysterious wink. "Come in/nhere. ..."/n/nHe nodded toward an empty classroom to the left of/nthe one-eyed statue. Harry followed Fred and George/ninside. George closed the door quietly and then/nturned, beaming, to look at Harry./n/n"Early Christmas present for you, Harry," he said./n/nFred pulled something from inside his cloak with a/nflourish and laid it on one of the desks. It was a large,/nsquare, very worn piece of parchment with nothing/nwritten on it. Harry, suspecting one of Fred and/nGeorge's jokes, stared at it./n/n"What's that supposed to be?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"This, Harry, is the secret of our success," said/nGeorge, patting the parchment fondly./n/n"It's a wrench, giving it to you," said Fred, "but we/ndecided last night, your need's greater than ours."/n/n"Anyway, we know it by heart," said George. "We/nbequeath it to you. We don't really need it anymore."/n/n"And what do I need with a bit of old parchment?"/nsaid Harry./n/n"A bit of old parchment!" said Fred, closing his eyes/nwith a grimace as though Harry had mortally offended/nhim. Well, of course, Black was quicker./nBlew Pettigrew to smithereens. ..."/n/nProfessor McGonagall blew her nose and said thickly,/n"Stupid boy . . . foolish boy ... he was always hopeless/nat dueling ... should have left it to the Ministry. ..."/n/n"I tell yeh, if I'd got ter Black before little Pettigrew/ndid, I wouldn't've messed around with wands — I'd've/nripped him limb — from — limb," Hagrid growled./n/n"You don't know what you're talking about, Hagrid,"/nsaid Fudge sharply. "Nobody but trained Hit Wizards/n/n/n/n/n/nfrom the Magical Law Enforcement Squad would have/nstood a chance against Black once he was cornered. I/nwas Junior Minister in the Department of Magical/nCatastrophes at the time, and I was one of the first on/nthe scene after Black murdered all those people. I — I/nwill never forget it. I still dream about it sometimes. A/ncrater in the middle of the street, so deep it had/ncracked the sewer below. Bodies everywhere. Muggles/nscreaming. And Black standing there laughing, with/nwhat was left of Pettigrew in front of him ... a heap of/nbloodstained robes and a few — a few fragments — "/n/nFudge's voice stopped abruptly. There was the sound/nof five noses being blown./n/n"Well, there you have it, Rosmerta," said Fudge/nthickly. "Black was taken away by twenty members of/nthe Magical Law Enforcement Squad and Pettigrew/nreceived the Order of Merlin, First Class, which I/nthink was some comfort to his poor mother. Black's/nbeen in Azkaban ever since."/n/nMadam Rosmerta let out a long sigh./n/n"Is it true he's mad, Minister?"/n/n"I wish I could say that he was," said Fudge slowly. "I/ncertainly believe his master's defeat unhinged him for/na while. The murder of Pettigrew and all those/nMuggles was the action of a cornered and desperate/nman — cruel ... pointless. Yet I met Black on my last/ninspection of Azkaban. You know, most of the/nprisoners in there sit muttering to themselves in the/ndark; there's no sense in them ... but I was shocked/nat how normal Black seemed. He spoke quite/nrationally to me. It was unnerving. You'd have/nthought he was merely bored — asked if I'd finished/nwith my newspaper, cool as you please, said he/nmissed doing the crossword. Yes, I was astounded at/n/n/n/n/nhow little effect the dementors seemed to be having on/nhim — and he was one of the most heavily guarded in/nthe place, you know. Dementors outside his door day/nand night."/n/n"But what do you think he's broken out to do?" said/nMadam Rosmerta. "Good gracious, Minister, he isn't/ntrying to rejoin You-Know-Who, is he?"/n/n"I daresay that is his — er — eventual plan," said/nFudge evasively. "But we hope to catch Black long/nbefore that. I must say, You-Know-Who alone and/nfriendless is one thing . . . but give him back his most/ndevoted servant, and I shudder to think how quickly/nhe'll rise again. ..."/n/nThere was a small chink of glass on wood. Someone/nhad set down their glass./n/n"You know, Cornelius, if you're dining with the/nheadmaster, we'd better head back up to the castle,"/nsaid Professor McGonagall./n/nOne by one, the pairs of feet in front of Harry took the/nweight of their owners once more; hems of cloaks/nswung into sight, and Madam Rosemerta's glittering/nheels disappeared behind the bar. The door of the/nThree Broomsticks opened again, there was another/nflurry of snow, and the teachers had disappeared./n/n"Harry?"/n/nRon's and Hermione's faces appeared under the table./nThey were both staring at him, lost for words./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Firebolt
text: /nHarry didn't have a very clear idea of how he had/nmanaged to get back into the Honeydukes cellar,/nthrough the tunnel, and into the castle once more. All/nhe knew was that the return trip seemed to take no/ntime at all, and that he hardly noticed what he was/ndoing, because his head was still pounding with the/nconversation he had just heard./n/nWhy had nobody ever told him? Dumbledore, Hagrid,/nMr. Weasley, Cornelius Fudge ... why hadn't anyone/never mentioned the fact that Harry's parents had died/nbecause their best friend had betrayed them?/n/nRon and Hermione watched Harry nervously all/nthrough dinner, not daring to talk about what they'd/noverheard, because Percy was sitting close by them./nWhen they went upstairs to the crowded common/nroom, it was to find Fred and George had set off half a/ndozen Dungbombs in a fit of end-of-term high spirits./nHarry, who didn't want Fred and George asking him/nwhether he'd reached Hogsmeade or not, sneaked/nquietly up to the empty dormitory and headed/n/n/n/nstraight for his bedside cabinet. He pushed his books/naside and quickly found what he was looking for —/nthe leather-bound photo album Hagrid had given him/ntwo years ago, which was full of wizard pictures of his/nmother and father. He sat down on his bed, drew the/nhangings around him, and started turning the pages,/nsearching, until .../n/nHe stopped on a picture of his parents' wedding day./nThere was his father waving up at him, beaming, the/nuntidy black hair Harry had inherited standing up in/nall directions. There was his mother, alight with/nhappiness, arm in arm with his dad. And there .../nthat must be him. Their best man ... Harry had never/ngiven him a thought before./n/nIf he hadn't known it was the same person, he would/nnever have guessed it was Black in this old/nphotograph. His face wasn't sunken and waxy, but/nhandsome, full of laughter. Had he already been/nworking for Voldemort when this picture had been/ntaken? Was he already planning the deaths of the two/npeople next to him? Did he realize he was facing/ntwelve years in Azkaban, twelve years that would/nmake him unrecognizable?/n/nBut the dementors don't affect him, Harry thought,/nstaring into the handsome, laughing face. He doesn't/nhave to hear my mum screaming if they get too close —/n/nHarry slammed the album shut, reached over and/nstuffed it back into his cabinet, took off his robe and/nglasses and got into bed, making sure the hangings/nwere hiding him from view./n/nThe dormitory door opened./n/n"Harry?" said Ron's voice uncertainly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Harry lay still, pretending to be asleep. He heard/nRon leave again, and rolled over on his back, his eyes/nwide open./n/nA hatred such as he had never known before was/ncoursing through Harry like poison. He could see/nBlack laughing at him through the darkness, as/nthough somebody had pasted the picture from the/nalbum over his eyes. He watched, as though/nsomebody was playing him a piece of film, Sirius/nBlack blasting Peter Pettigrew (who resembled Neville/nLongbottom) into a thousand pieces. He could hear/n(though having no idea what Black's voice might/nsound like) a low, excited mutter. "It has happened,/nMy Lord . . . the Potters have made me their Secret-/nKeeper. ..." And then came another voice, laughing/nshrilly, the same laugh that Harry heard inside his/nhead whenever the dementors drew near. . . ./n/n"Harry, you — you look terrible."/n/nHarry hadn't gotten to sleep until daybreak. He had/nawoken to find the dormitory deserted, dressed, and/ngone down the spiral staircase to a common room/nthat was completely empty except for Ron, who was/neating a Peppermint Toad and massaging his/nstomach, and Hermione, who had spread her/nhomework over three tables./n/n"Where is everyone?" said Harry./n/n"Gone! It's the first day of the holidays, remember?"/nsaid Ron, watching Harry closely. "It's nearly/nlunchtime; I was going to come and wake you up in a/nminute."/n/nHarry slumped into a chair next to the fire. Snow was/nstill falling outside the windows. Crookshanks was/nspread out in front of the fire like a large, ginger rug./n/n/n/n/n/n"You really don't look well, you know," Hermione said,/npeering anxiously into his face./n/n"I'm fine," said Harry./n/n"Harry, listen," said Hermione, exchanging a look with/nRon, "you must be really upset about what we heard/nyesterday. But the thing is, you mustn't go doing/nanything stupid."/n/n"Like what?" said Harry./n/n"Like trying to go after Black," said Ron sharply./n/nHarry could tell they had rehearsed this conversation/nwhile he had been asleep. He didn't say anything./n/n"You won't, will you, Harry?" said Hermione./n/n"Because Black's not worth dying for," said Ron./n/nHarry looked at them. They didn't seem to/nunderstand at all./n/n"D'you know what I see and hear every time a/ndementor gets too near me?" Ron and Hermione/nshook their heads, looking apprehensive. "I can hear/nmy mum screaming and pleading with Voldemort./n/nAnd if you'd heard your mum screaming like that,/njust about to be killed, you wouldn't forget it in a/nhurry. And if you found out someone who was/nsupposed to be a friend of hers betrayed her and sent/nVoldemort after her — "/n/n"There's nothing you can do!" said Hermione, looking/nstricken. "The dementors will catch Black and he'll go/nback to Azkaban and — and serve him right!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You heard what Fudge said. Black isn't affected by/nAzkaban like normal people are. It's not a/npunishment for him like it is for the others."/n/n"So what are you saying?" said Ron, looking very/ntense. "You want to — to kill Black or something?"/n/n"Don't be silly," said Hermione in a panicky voice./n"Harry doesn't want to kill anyone, do you, Harry?"/n/nAgain, Harry didn't answer. He didn't know what he/nwanted to do. All he knew was that the idea of doing/nnothing, while Black was at liberty, was almost more/nthan he could stand./n/n"Malfoy knows," he said abruptly. "Remember what/nhe said to me in Potions? 'If it was me, I'd hunt him/ndown myself. ... I'd want revenge.' "/n/n"You're going to take Malfoy 's advice instead of ours?"/nsaid Ron furiously. "Listen ... you know what/nPettigrew's mother got back after Black had finished/nwith him? Dad told me — the Order of Merlin, First/nClass, and Pettigrew's finger in a box. That was the/nbiggest bit of him they could find. Black's a madman,/nHarry, and he's dangerous — "/n/n"Malfoy's dad must have told him," said Harry,/nignoring Ron. "He was right in Voldemort's inner/ncircle — "/n/n" Say You-Knotu-Who, will you?" interjected Ron/nangrily./n/n" — so obviously, the Malfoys knew Black was working/nfor Voldemort — "/n/n" — and Malfoy'd love to see you blown into about a/nmillion pieces, like Pettigrew! Get a grip. Malfoy's just/n/n/n/n/n/nhoping you 11 get yourself killed before he has to play/nyou at Quidditch."/n/n"Harry, please," said Hermione, her eyes now shining/nwith tears, "please be sensible. Black did a terrible,/nterrible thing, but d-don't put yourself in danger, it's/nwhat Black wants. ... Oh, Harry, you'd be playing/nright into Black's hands if you went looking for him./nYour mum and dad wouldn't want you to get hurt,/nwould they? They'd never want you to go looking for/nBlack!"/n/n"I'll never know what they'd have wanted, because/nthanks to Black, I've never spoken to them," said/nHarry shortly./n/nThere was a silence in which Crookshanks stretched/nluxuriously, flexing his claws. Ron's pocket quivered./n/n"Look," said Ron, obviously casting around for a/nchange of subject, "it's the holidays! It's nearly/nChristmas! Let's — let's go down and see Hagrid. We/nhaven't visited him for ages!"/n/n"No!" said Hermione quickly. "Harry isn't supposed to/nleave the castle, Ron — "/n/n"Yeah, let's go," said Harry, sitting up, "and I can ask/nhim how come he never mentioned Black when he/ntold me all about my parents!"/n/nFurther discussion of Sirius Black plainly wasn't/nwhat Ron had had in mind./n/n"Or we could have a game of chess," he said hastily,/n"or Gobstones. Percy left a set — "/n/n"No, let's visit Hagrid," said Harry firmly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSo they got their cloaks from their dormitories and set/noff through the portrait hole ("Stand and fight, you/nyellow-bellied mongrels!"), down through the empty/ncastle and out through the oak front doors./n/nThey made their way slowly down the lawn, making a/nshallow trench in the glittering, powdery snow, their/nsocks and the hems of their cloaks soaked and/nfreezing. The Forbidden Forest looked as though it/nhad been enchanted, each tree smattered with silver,/nand Hagrid's cabin looked like an iced cake./n/nRon knocked, but there was no answer./n/n"He's not out, is he?" said Hermione, who was/nshivering under her cloak./n/nRon had his ear to the door./n/n"There's a weird noise," he said. "Listen — is that/nFang?"/n/nHarry and Hermione put their ears to the door too./nFrom inside the cabin came a series of low, throbbing/nmoans./n/n"Think we'd better go and get someone?" said Ron/nnervously./n/n"Hagrid!" called Harry, thumping the door. "Hagrid,/nare you in there?"/n/nThere was a sound of heavy footsteps, then the door/ncreaked open. Hagrid stood there with his eyes red/nand swollen, tears splashing down the front of his/nleather vest./n/n"Yeh've heard?" he bellowed, and he flung himself/nonto Harry's neck./n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid being at least twice the size of a normal man,/nthis was no laughing matter. Harry, about to collapse/nunder Hagrid's weight, was rescued by Ron and/nHermione, who each seized Hagrid under an arm and/nheaved him back into the cabin. Hagrid allowed/nhimself to be steered into a chair and slumped over/nthe table, sobbing uncontrollably, his face glazed with/ntears that dripped down into his tangled beard./n/n"Hagrid, what is it?" said Hermione, aghast./n/nHarry spotted an official-looking letter lying open on/nthe table./n/n"What's this, Hagrid?"/n/nHagrid's sobs redoubled, but he shoved the letter/ntoward Harry, who picked it up and read aloud:/n/nDear Mr. Hagrid,/n/nFurther to our inquiry into the attack by a hippogriff on/na student in your class, we have accepted the/nassurances of Professor Dumbledore that you bear no/nresponsibility for the regrettable incident./n/n"Well, that's okay then, Hagrid!" said Ron, clapping/nHagrid on the shoulder. But Hagrid continued to sob,/nand waved one of his gigantic hands, inviting Harry to/nread on./n/nHowever, we must register our concern about the/nhippogriff in question. We have decided to uphold the/nofficial complaint of Mr. Lucius Malfoy, and this matter/nwill therefore be taken to the Committee for the/nDisposal of Dangerous Creatures. The hearing will take/nplace on April 20th, and we ask you to present/nyourself and your hippogriff at the Committee's offices/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nin London on that date. In the meantime, the hippogriff/nshould be kept tethered and isolated./n/nYours in fellowship .../n/nThere followed a list of the school governors./n/n"Oh," said Ron. "But you said Buckbeak isn't a bad/nhippogriff, Hagrid. I bet he'll get off — "/n/n"Yeh don' know them gargoyles at the Committee fer/nthe Disposal o' Dangerous Creatures!" choked Hagrid,/nwiping his eyes on his sleeve. "They've got it in fer/ninterestin' creatures!"/n/nA sudden sound from the corner of Hagrid 's cabin/nmade Harry, Ron, and Hermione whip around./nBuckbeak the hippogriff was lying in the corner,/nchomping on something that was oozing blood all over/nthe floor./n/n"I couldn' leave him tied up out there in the snow!"/nchoked Hagrid. "All on his own! At Christmas."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione looked at one another./n/nThey had never seen eye to eye with Hagrid about/nwhat he called "interesting creatures" and other/npeople called "terrifying monsters." On the other/nhand, there didn't seem to be any particular harm in/nBuckbeak.
