In fact, by Hagrid's usual standards, he/nwas positively cute./n/n"You'll have to put up a good strong defense, Hagrid,"/nsaid Hermione, sitting down and laying a hand on/nHagrid's massive forearm. "I'm sure you can prove/nBuckbeak is safe."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Won't make no difference!" sobbed Hagrid. "Them/nDisposal devils, they're all in Lucius Malfoy's pocket!/nScared o' him! An' if I lose the case, Buckbeak — "/n/nHagrid drew his finger swiftly across his throat, then/ngave a great wail and lurched forward, his face in his/narms./n/n"What about Dumbledore, Hagrid?" said Harry./n/n"He's done more'n enough fer me already," groaned/nHagrid. "Got enough on his plate what with keepin'/nthem dementors outta the castle, an' Sirius Black/nlurkin' around — "/n/nRon and Hermione looked quickly at Harry, as though/nexpecting him to start berating Hagrid for not telling/nhim the truth about Black. But Harry couldn't bring/nhimself to do it, not now that he saw Hagrid so/nmiserable and scared./n/n"Listen, Hagrid," he said, "you can't give up./nHermione's right, you just need a good defense. You/ncan call us as witnesses — "/n/n"I'm sure I've read about a case of hippogriff-baiting,"/nsaid Hermione thoughtfully, "where the hippogriff got/noff. I'll look it up for you, Hagrid, and see exactly what/nhappened."/n/nHagrid howled still more loudly. Harry and Hermione/nlooked at Ron to help them./n/n"Er — shall I make a cup of tea?" said Ron./n/nHarry stared at him./n/n"It's what my mum does whenever someone's upset,"/nRon muttered, shrugging./n/n/n/n/n/nAt last, after many more assurances of help, with a/nsteaming mug of tea in front of him, Hagrid blew his/nnose on a handkerchief the size of a tablecloth and/nsaid, "Yer right. I can' afford to go ter pieces. Gotta/npull meself together. ..."/n/nFang the boarhound came timidly out from under the/ntable and laid his head on Hagrid 's knee./n/n"I've not bin meself lately," said Hagrid, stroking Fang/nwith one hand and mopping his face with the other./n"Worried abou' Buckbeak, an' no one likin' me classes/n/n/n/n"We do like them!" lied Hermione at once./n/n"Yeah, they're great!" said Ron, crossing his fingers/nunder the table. "Er — how are the flobberworms?"/n/n"Dead," said Hagrid gloomily. "Too much lettuce."/n/n"Oh no!" said Ron, his lip twitching./n/n"An' them dementors make me feel ruddy terrible an'/nall," said Hagrid, with a sudden shudder. "Gotta walk/npast 'em ev'ry time I want a drink in the Three/nBroomsticks. 'S like bein' back in Azkaban — "/n/nHe fell silent, gulping his tea. Harry, Ron, and/nHermione watched him breathlessly. They had never/nheard Hagrid talk about his brief spell in Azkaban/nbefore. After a pause, Hermione said timidly, "Is it/nawful in there, Hagrid?"/n/n"Yeh've no idea," said Hagrid quietly. "Never bin/nanywhere like it. Thought I was goin' mad. Kep' goin'/nover horrible stuff in me mind . . . the day I got/nexpelled from Hogwarts . . . day me dad died . . . day I/nhad ter let Norbert go. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHis eyes filled with tears. Norbert was the baby/ndragon Hagrid had once won in a game of cards./n/n/n/n"Yeh can' really remember who yeh are after a while./nAn' yeh can' see the point o' livin' at all. I used ter/nhope I'd jus' die in me sleep. ... When they let me out,/nit was like bein' born again, ev'rythin' came floodin'/nback, it was the bes' feelin' in the world. Mind, the/ndementors weren't keen on lettin' me go."/n/n"But you were innocent!" said Hermione./n/nHagrid snorted./n/n"Think that matters to them? They don' care. Long as/nthey've got a couple o' hundred humans stuck there/nwith 'em, so they can leech all the happiness out of/n'em, they don' give a damn who's guilty an' who's/nnot."/n/nHagrid went quiet for a moment, staring into his tea./nThen he said quietly, "Thought o' jus' letting/nBuckbeak go ... tryin' ter make him fly away ... but/nhow d'yeh explain ter a hippogriff it's gotta go inter/nhidin'? An' — an' I'm scared o' breakin' the law. ..." He/nlooked up at them, tears leaking down his face again./n"I don' ever want ter go back ter Azkaban."/n/nThe trip to Hagrid's, though far from fun, had/nnevertheless had the effect Ron and Hermione had/nhoped. Though Harry had by no means forgotten/nabout Black, he couldn't brood constantly on revenge/nif he wanted to help Hagrid win his case against the/nCommittee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures./nHe, Ron, and Hermione went to the library the next/nday and returned to the empty common room laden/nwith books that might help prepare a defense for/nBuckbeak. The three of them sat in front of the/nroaring fire, slowly turning the pages of dusty/n/n/n/n/nvolumes about famous cases of marauding beasts,/nspeaking occasionally when they ran across/nsomething relevant./n/n"Here's something ... there was a case in 1722 ... but/nthe hippogriff was convicted — ugh, look what they/ndid to it, that's disgusting — "/n/n"This might help, look — a manticore savaged/nsomeone in 1296, and they let the manticore off — oh/n— no, that was only because everyone was too scared/nto go near it. ..."/n/nMeanwhile, in the rest of the castle, the usual/nmagnificent Christmas decorations had been put up,/ndespite the fact that hardly any of the students/nremained to enjoy them. Thick streamers of holly and/nmistletoe were strung along the corridors, mysterious/nlights shone from inside every suit of armor, and the/nGreat Hall was filled with its usual twelve Christmas/ntrees, glittering with golden stars. A powerful and/ndelicious smell of cooking pervaded the corridors, and/nby Christmas Eve, it had grown so strong that even/nScabbers poked his nose out of the shelter of Ron's/npocket to sniff hopefully at the air./n/nOn Christmas morning, Harry was woken by Ron/nthrowing his pillow at him./n/n"Oy! Presents!"/n/nHarry reached for his glasses and put them on,/nsquinting through the semi-darkness to the foot of his/nbed, where a small heap of parcels had appeared. Ron/nwas already ripping the paper off his own presents./n/n"Another sweater from Mum . . . maroon again . . . see if/nyou've got one."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry had. Mrs. Weasley had sent him a scarlet/nsweater with the Gryffindor lion knitted on the front,/nalso a dozen home-baked mince pies, some Christmas/ncake, and a box of nut brittle. As he moved all these/nthings aside, he saw a long, thin package lying/nunderneath./n/n"What's that?" said Ron, looking over, a freshly/nunwrapped pair of maroon socks in his hand./n/n"Dunno ..."/n/nHarry ripped the parcel open and gasped as a/nmagnificent, gleaming broomstick rolled out onto his/nbedspread. Ron dropped his socks and jumped off his/nbed for a closer look./n/n"I don't believe it," he said hoarsely./n/nIt was a Firebolt, identical to the dream broom Harry/nhad gone to see every day in Diagon Alley. Its handle/nglittered as he picked it up. He could feel it vibrating/nand let go; it hung in midair, unsupported, at exactly/nthe right height for him to mount it. His eyes moved/nfrom the golden registration number at the top of the/nhandle, right down to the perfectly smooth,/nstreamlined birch twigs that made up the tail./n/n"Who sent it to you?" said Ron in a hushed voice./n/n"Look and see if there's a card," said Harry./n/nRon ripped apart the Firebolt's wrappings./n/n"Nothing! Blimey, who'd spend that much on you?"/n/n"Well," said Harry, feeling stunned, "I'm betting it/nwasn't the Dursleys."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I bet it was Dumbledore," said Ron, now walking/naround and around the Firebolt, taking in every/nglorious inch. "He sent you the Invisibility Cloak/nanonymously. ..."/n/n"That was my dad's, though," said Harry./n"Dumbledore was just passing it on to me. He/nwouldn't spend hundreds of Galleons on me. He can't/ngo giving students stuff like this — "/n/n"That's why he wouldn't say it was from him!" said/nRon. "In case some git like Malfoy said it was/nfavoritism. Hey, Harry" — Ron gave a great whoop of/nlaughter — "Malfoyl Wait till he sees you on this! He'll/nbe sick as a pig! This is an international standard/nbroom, this is!"/n/n"I can't believe this," Harry muttered, running a hand/nalong the Firebolt, while Ron sank onto Harry's bed,/nlaughing his head off at the thought of Malfoy. " Who/n— ?"/n/n"I know," said Ron, controlling himself, "I know who it/ncould've been — Lupin!"/n/n"What?" said Harry, now starting to laugh himself./n"Lupin? Listen, if he had this much gold, he'd be able/nto buy himself some new robes."/n/n"Yeah, but he likes you," said Ron. "And he was away/nwhen your Nimbus got smashed, and he might've/nheard about it and decided to visit Diagon Alley and/nget this for you — "/n/n"What d'you mean, he was away?" said Harry. "He/nwas ill when I was playing in that match."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, he wasn't in the hospital wing," said Ron. "I/nwas there, cleaning out the bedpans on that detention/nfrom Snape, remember?"/n/nHarry frowned at Ron./n/n"I can't see Lupin affording something like this."/n/n"What 're you two laughing about?"/n/nHermione had just come in, wearing her dressing/ngown and carrying Crookshanks, who was looking/nvery grumpy, with a string of tinsel tied around his/nneck./n/n"Don't bring him in here!" said Ron, hurriedly/nsnatching Scabbers from the depths of his bed and/nstowing him in his pajama pocket. But Hermione/nwasn't listening. She dropped Crookshanks onto/nSeamus's empty bed and stared, open-mouthed, at/nthe Firebolt./n/n"Oh, Harry\ Who sent you that?"/n/n"No idea," said Harry. "There wasn't a card or/nanything with it."/n/nTo his great surprise, Hermione did not appear either/nexcited or intrigued by the news. On the contrary, her/nface fell, and she bit her lip./n/n"What's the matter with you?" said Ron./n/n"I don't know," said Hermione slowly, "but it's a bit/nodd, isn't it? I mean, this is supposed to be quite a/ngood broom, isn't it?"/n/nRon sighed exasperatedly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's the best broom there is, Hermione," he said./n/n"So it must've been really expensive. ..."/n/n"Probably cost more than all the Slytherins' brooms/nput together," said Ron happily./n/n"Well ... who'd send Harry something as expensive as/nthat, and not even tell him they'd sent it?" said/nHermione./n/n"Who cares?" said Ron impatiently. "Listen, Harry,/ncan I have a go on it? Can I?"/n/n"I don't think anyone should ride that broom just yet!"/nsaid Hermione shrilly./n/nHarry and Ron looked at her./n/n"What d'you think Harry's going to do with it — sweep/nthe floor?" said Ron./n/nBut before Hermione could answer, Crookshanks/nsprang from Seamus's bed, right at Ron's chest./n/n"GET — HIM — OUT — OF — HERE!" Ron bellowed/nas Crookshanks 's claws ripped his pajamas and/nScabbers attempted a wild escape over his shoulder./nRon seized Scabbers by the tail and aimed a/nmisjudged kick at Crookshanks that hit the trunk at/nthe end of Harry's bed, knocking it over and causing/nRon to hop up and down, howling with pain./n/nCrookshanks 's fur suddenly stood on end. A shrill,/ntinny whistling was filling the room. The Pocket/nSneakoscope had become dislodged from Uncle/nVernon's old socks and was whirling and gleaming on/nthe floor./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I forgot about that!" Harry said, bending down and/npicking up the Sneakoscope. "I never wear those/nsocks if I can help it. ..."/n/nThe Sneakoscope whirled and whistled in his palm./nCrookshanks was hissing and spitting at it./n/n"You'd better take that cat out of here, Hermione,"/nsaid Ron furiously, sitting on Harry's bed nursing his/ntoe. "Can't you shut that thing up?" he added to/nHarry as Hermione strode out of the room,/nCrookshanks 's yellow eyes still fixed maliciously on/nRon./n/nHarry stuffed the Sneakoscope back inside the socks/nand threw it back into his trunk. All that could be/nheard now were Ron's stifled moans of pain and rage./nScabbers was huddled in Ron's hands. It had been a/nwhile since Harry had seen him out of Ron's pocket,/nand he was unpleasantly surprised to see that/nScabbers, once so fat, was now very skinny; patches/nof fur seemed to have fallen out too./n/n"He's not looking too good, is he?" Harry said./n/n"It's stress!" said Ron. "He'd be fine if that big stupid/nfurball left him alone!"/n/nBut Harry, remembering what the woman at the/nMagical Menagerie had said about rats living only/nthree years, couldn't help feeling that unless Scabbers/nhad powers he had never revealed, he was reaching/nthe end of his life. And despite Ron's frequent/ncomplaints that Scabbers was both boring and/nuseless, he was sure Ron would be very miserable if/nScabbers died./n/nChristmas spirit was definitely thin on the ground in/nthe Gryffindor common room that morning. Hermione/n/n/n/n/n/nhad shut Crookshanks in her dormitory, but was/nfurious with Ron for trying to kick him; Ron was still/nfuming about Crookshanks 's fresh attempt to eat/nScabbers. Harry gave up trying to make them talk to/neach other and devoted himself to examining the/nFirebolt, which he had brought down to the common/nroom with him. For some reason this seemed to/nannoy Hermione as well; she didn't say anything, but/nshe kept looking darkly at the broom as though it too/nhad been criticizing her cat./n/nAt lunchtime they went down to the Great Hall, to/nfind that the House tables had been moved against/nthe walls again, and that a single table, set for twelve,/nstood in the middle of the room. Professors/nDumbledore, McGonagall, Snape, Sprout, and/nFlitwick were there, along with Filch, the caretaker,/nwho had taken off his usual brown coat and was/nwearing a very old and rather moldy-looking tailcoat./nThere were only three other students, two extremely/nnervous-looking first years and a sullen-faced/nSlytherin fifth year./n/n"Merry Christmas!" said Dumbledore as Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione approached the table. "As there are so/nfew of us, it seemed foolish to use the House tables./n/n... Sit down, sit down!"/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione sat down side by side at/nthe end of the table./n/n"Crackers!" said Dumbledore enthusiastically, offering/nthe end of a large silver noisemaker to Snape, who/ntook it reluctantly and tugged. With a bang like a/ngunshot, the cracker flew apart to reveal a large,/npointed witch's hat topped with a stuffed vulture./n/nHarry, remembering the boggart, caught Ron's eye/nand they both grinned; Snape 's mouth thinned and/n/n/n/n/n/nhe pushed the hat toward Dumbledore, who swapped/nit for his wizard's hat at once./n/n/n/n"Dig in!" he advised the table, beaming around./n/nAs Harry was helping himself to roast potatoes, the/ndoors of the Great Hall opened again. It was Professor/nTrelawney, gliding toward them as though on wheels./nShe had put on a green sequined dress in honor of/nthe occasion, making her look more than ever like a/nglittering, oversized dragonfly./n/n"Sibyll, this is a pleasant surprise!" said Dumbledore,/nstanding up./n/n"I have been crystal gazing, Headmaster," said/nProfessor Trelawney in her mistiest, most faraway/nvoice, "and to my astonishment, I saw myself/nabandoning my solitary luncheon and coming to join/nyou. Who am I to refuse the promptings of fate? I at/nonce hastened from my tower, and I do beg you to/nforgive my lateness. ..."/n/n"Certainly, certainly," said Dumbledore, his eyes/ntwinkling. "Let me draw you up a chair — "/n/nAnd he did indeed draw a chair in midair with his/nwand, which revolved for a few seconds before falling/nwith a thud between Professors Snape and/nMcGonagall. Professor Trelawney, however, did not sit/ndown; her enormous eyes had been roving around the/ntable, and she suddenly uttered a kind of soft scream./n/n"I dare not, Headmaster! If I join the table, we shall be/nthirteen! Nothing could be more unlucky! Never forget/nthat when thirteen dine together, the first to rise will/nbe the first to die!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well risk it, Sibyll," said Professor McGonagall/nimpatiently. "Do sit down, the turkey's getting stone/ncold."/n/n/n/nProfessor Trelawney hesitated, then lowered herself/ninto the empty chair, eyes shut and mouth clenched/ntight, as though expecting a thunderbolt to hit the/ntable. Professor McGonagall poked a large spoon into/nthe nearest tureen./n/n"Tripe, Sibyll?"/n/nProfessor Trelawney ignored her. Eyes open again,/nshe looked around once more and said, "But where is/ndear Professor Lupin?"/n/n"I'm afraid the poor fellow is ill again," said/nDumbledore, indicating that everybody should start/nserving themselves. "Most unfortunate that it should/nhappen on Christmas Day."/n/n"But surely you already knew that, Sibyll?" said/nProfessor McGonagall, her eyebrows raised./n/nProfessor Trelawney gave Professor McGonagall a very/ncold look./n/n"Certainly I knew, Minerva," she said quietly. "But/none does not parade the fact that one is All-Knowing./n/nI frequently act as though I am not possessed of the/nInner Eye, so as not to make others nervous."/n/n"That explains a great deal," said Professor/nMcGonagall tartly./n/nProfessor Trelawney's voice suddenly became a good/ndeal less misty./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"If you must know, Minerva, I have seen that poor/nProfessor Lupin will not be with us for very long. He/nseems aware, himself, that his time is short. He/npositively fled when I offered to crystal gaze for him —/n/n/n/n"Imagine that," said Professor McGonagall dryly./n/n"I doubt," said Dumbledore, in a cheerful but slightly/nraised voice, which put an end to Professor/nMcGonagall and Professor Trelawney's conversation,/n"that Professor Lupin is in any immediate danger./nSeverus, you've made the potion for him again?"/n/n"Yes, Headmaster," said Snape./n/n"Good," said Dumbledore. "Then he should be up and/nabout in no time. ... Derek, have you had any of these/nchipolatas? They're excellent."/n/nThe first-year boy went furiously red on being/naddressed directly by Dumbledore, and took the/nplatter of sausages with trembling hands./n/nProfessor Trelawney behaved almost normally until/nthe very end of Christmas dinner, two hours later./n/nFull to bursting with Christmas dinner and still/nwearing their party hats, Harry and Ron got up first/nfrom the table and she shrieked loudly./n/n"My dears! Which of you left his seat first? Which?"/n/n"Dunno," said Ron, looking uneasily at Harry./n/n"I doubt it will make much difference," said Professor/nMcGonagall coldly, "unless a mad axe-man is waiting/noutside the doors to slaughter the first into the/nentrance hall."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nEven Ron laughed. Professor Trelawney looked highly/naffronted./n/n"Coming?" Harry said to Hermione./n/n"No," Hermione muttered, "I want a quick word with/nProfessor McGonagall."/n/n"Probably trying to see if she can take any more/nclasses," yawned Ron as they made their way into the/nentrance hall, which was completely devoid of mad/naxe-men./n/nWhen they reached the portrait hole, they found Sir/nCadogan enjoying a Christmas party with a couple of/nmonks, several previous headmasters of Hogwarts,/nand his fat pony. He pushed up his visor and toasted/nthem with a flagon of mead./n/n"Merry — hie — Christmas! Password?"/n/n"Scurvy cur," said Ron./n/n"And the same to you, sir!" roared Sir Cadogan as the/npainting swung forward to admit them./n/nHarry went straight up to the dormitory, collected the/nFirebolt and the Broomstick Servicing Kit Hermione/nhad given him for his birthday, brought them/ndownstairs, and tried to find something to do to the/nFirebolt; however, there were no bent twigs to clip,/nand the handle was so shiny already it seemed/npointless to polish it. He and Ron simply sat admiring/nit from every angle until the portrait hole opened, and/nHermione came in, accompanied by Professor/nMcGonagall./n/nThough Professor McGonagall was head of Gryffindor/nHouse, Harry had seen her in the common room only/n/n/n/n/n/nonce before, and that had been to make a very grave/nannouncement. He and Ron stared at her, both/nholding the Firebolt. Hermione walked around them,/nsat down, picked up the nearest book, and hid her/nface behind it./n/n"So that's it, is it?" said Professor McGonagall beadily,/nwalking over to the fireside and staring at the/nFirebolt. "Miss Granger has just informed me that you/nhave been sent a broomstick, Potter."/n/nHarry and Ron looked around at Hermione. They/ncould see her forehead reddening over the top of her/nbook, which was upside down./n/n"May I?" said Professor McGonagall, but she didn't/nwait for an answer before pulling the Firebolt out of/ntheir hands. She examined it carefully from handle to/ntwig-ends. "Hmm. And there was no note at all,/n/nPotter? No card? No message of any kind?"/n/n"No," said Harry blankly./n/n"I see ... ," said Professor McGonagall. "Well, I'm/nafraid I will have to take this, Potter."/n/n"W — what?" said Harry, scrambling to his feet./n"Why?"/n/n"It will need to be checked for jinxes," said Professor/nMcGonagall. "Of course, I'm no expert, but I daresay/nMadam Hooch and Professor Flitwick will strip it/ndown — "/n/n"Strip it down?" repeated Ron, as though Professor/nMcGonagall was mad./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It shouldn't take more than a few weeks," said/nProfessor McGonagall. "You will have it back if we are/nsure it is jinx-free."/n/n"There's nothing wrong with it!" said Harry, his voice/nshaking slightly. "Honestly, Professor — "/n/n"You can't know that, Potter," said Professor/nMcGonagall, quite kindly, "not until you've flown it, at/nany rate, and I'm afraid that is out of the question/nuntil we are certain that it has not been tampered/nwith. I shall keep you informed."/n/nProfessor McGonagall turned on her heel and carried/nthe Firebolt out of the portrait hole, which closed/nbehind her. Harry stood staring after her, the tin of/nHigh-Finish Polish still clutched in his hands. Ron,/nhowever, rounded on Hermione./n/n"What did you go running to McGonagall for?"/n/nHermione threw her book aside. She was still pink in/nthe face, but stood up and faced Ron defiantly./n/n"Because I thought — and Professor McGonagall/nagrees with me — that that broom was probably sent/nto Harry by Sirius Black!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Patronus
text: /nHarry knew that Hermione had meant well, but that/ndidn't stop him from being angry with her. He had/nbeen the owner of the best broom in the world for a/nfew short hours, and now, because of her/ninterference, he didn't know whether he would ever/nsee it again. He was positive that there was nothing/nwrong with the Firebolt now, but what sort of state/nwould it be in once it had been subjected to all sorts/nof anti-jinx tests?/n/nRon was furious with Hermione too. As far as he was/nconcerned, the stripping-down of a brand-new/nFirebolt was nothing less than criminal damage./nHermione, who remained convinced that she had/nacted for the best, started avoiding the common room./nHarry and Ron supposed she had taken refuge in the/nlibrary and didn't try to persuade her to come back./nAll in all, they were glad when the rest of the school/nreturned shortly after New Year, and Gryffindor Tower/nbecame crowded and noisy again./n/n/n/n/n/n/nWood sought Harry out on the night before term/nstarted./n/n/n/n"Had a good Christmas?" he said, and then, without/nwaiting for an answer, he sat down, lowered his voice,/nand said, "I've been doing some thinking over/nChristmas, Harry. After the last match, you know. If/nthe dementors come to the next one ... I mean . . . we/ncan't afford you to — well — "/n/nWood broke off, looking awkward./n/n"I'm working on it," said Harry quickly. "Professor/nLupin said he'd train me to ward off the dementors./nWe should be starting this week. He said he'd have/ntime after Christmas."/n/n"Ah," said Wood, his expression clearing. "Well, in/nthat case — I really didn't want to lose you as Seeker,/nHarry. And have you ordered a new broom yet?"/n/n"No," said Harry./n/n"What! You'd better get a move on, you know — you/ncan't ride that Shooting Star against Ravenclaw!"/n/n"He got a Firebolt for Christmas," said Ron./n/n"A Firebolt? No! Seriously? A — a real Firebolt?"/n/n"Don't get excited, Oliver," said Harry gloomily. "I/nhaven't got it anymore. It was confiscated." And he/nexplained all about how the Firebolt was now being/nchecked for jinxes./n/n"Jinxed? How could it be jinxed?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Sirius Black," Harry said wearily. "He's supposed to/nbe after me. So McGonagall reckons he might have/nsent it."/n/nWaving aside the information that a famous murderer/nwas after his Seeker, Wood said, "But Black couldn't/nhave bought a Firebolt! He's on the run! The whole/ncountry's on the lookout for him! How could he just/nwalk into Quality Quidditch Supplies and buy a/nbroomstick?"/n/n"I know," said Harry, "but McGonagall still wants to/nstrip it down — "/n/nWood went pale./n/n"I'll go and talk to her, Harry," he promised. "I'll make/nher see reason. ... A Firebolt ... a real Firebolt, on our/nteam . . . She wants Gryffindor to win as much as we/ndo. ... I'll make her see sense. A Firebolt ..."/n/nClasses started again the next day. The last thing/nanyone felt like doing was spending two hours on the/ngrounds on a raw January morning, but Hagrid had/nprovided a bonfire full of salamanders for their/nenjoyment, and they spent an unusually good lesson/ncollecting dry wood and leaves to keep the fire blazing/nwhile the flame-loving lizards scampered up and/ndown the crumbling, white-hot logs. The first/nDivination lesson of the new term was much less fun;/nProfessor Trelawney was now teaching them/npalmistry, and she lost no time in informing Harry/nthat he had the shortest life line she had ever seen./n/nIt was Defense Against the Dark Arts that Harry was/nkeen to get to; after his conversation with Wood, he/nwanted to get started on his anti-dementor lessons as/nsoon as possible./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah yes," said Lupin, when Harry reminded him of his/npromise at the end of class. "Let me see ... how about/neight o'clock on Thursday evening? The History of/nMagic classroom should be large enough. ... I'll have/nto think carefully about how we're going to do this. .../nWe can't bring a real dementor into the castle to/npractice on. ..."/n/n"Still looks ill, doesn't he?" said Ron as they walked/ndown the corridor, heading to dinner. "What d'you/nreckon 's the matter with him?"/n/nThere was a loud and impatient "tuh" from behind/nthem. It was Hermione, who had been sitting at the/nfeet of a suit of armor, repacking her bag, which was/nso full of books it wouldn't close./n/n"And what are you tutting at us for?" said Ron/nirritably./n/n"Nothing," said Hermione in a lofty voice, heaving her/nbag back over her shoulder./n/n"Yes, you were," said Ron. "I said I wonder what's/nwrong with Lupin, and you — "/n/n"Well, isn't it obvious?" said Hermione, with a look of/nmaddening superiority./n/n"If you don't want to tell us, don't," snapped Ron./n/n"Fine," said Hermione haughtily, and she marched off./n/n"She doesn't know," said Ron, staring resentfully after/nHermione. "She's just trying to get us to talk to her/nagain."/n/nAt eight o'clock on Thursday evening, Harry left/nGryffindor Tower for the History of Magic classroom./n/n/n/n/n/nIt was dark and empty when he arrived, but he lit the/nlamps with his wand and had waited only five/nminutes when Professor Lupin turned up, carrying a/nlarge packing case, which he heaved onto Professor/nBinns' desk./n/n"What's that?" said Harry./n/n"Another boggart," said Lupin, stripping off his cloak./n"I've been combing the castle ever since Tuesday, and/nvery luckily, I found this one lurking inside Mr. Filch's/nfiling cabinet. It's the nearest we'll get to a real/ndementor. The boggart will turn into a dementor when/nhe sees you, so we'll be able to practice on him. I can/nstore him in my office when we're not using him;/nthere's a cupboard under my desk he'll like."/n/n"Okay," said Harry, trying to sound as though he/nwasn't apprehensive at all and merely glad that Lupin/nhad found such a good substitute for a real dementor./n/n"So ..." Professor Lupin had taken out his own wand,/nand indicated that Harry should do the same. "The/nspell I am going to try and teach you is highly/nadvanced magic, Harry — well beyond Ordinary/nWizarding Level. It is called the Patronus Charm."/n/n"How does it work?" said Harry nervously./n/n"Well, when it works correctly, it conjures up a/nPatronus," said Lupin, "which is a kind of anti-/ndementor — a guardian that acts as a shield between/nyou and the dementor."/n/nHarry had a sudden vision of himself crouching/nbehind a Hagrid-sized figure holding a large club./nProfessor Lupin continued, "The Patronus is a kind of/npositive force, a projection of the very things that the/ndementor feeds upon — hope, happiness, the desire/n/n/n/n/nto survive — but it cannot feel despair, as real/nhumans can, so the dementors can't hurt it. But I/nmust warn you, Harry, that the charm might be too/nadvanced for you. Many qualified wizards have/ndifficulty with it."/n/n"What does a Patronus look like?" said Harry/ncuriously./n/n"Each one is unique to the wizard who conjures it."/n"And how do you conjure it?"/n/n"With an incantation, which will work only if you are/nconcentrating, with all your might, on a single, very/nhappy memory."/n/nHarry cast his mind about for a happy memory./nCertainly, nothing that had happened to him at the/nDursleys' was going to do. Finally, he settled on the/nmoment when he had first ridden a broomstick./n/n"Right," he said, trying to recall as exactly as possible/nthe wonderful, soaring sensation of his stomach./n/n"The incantation is this — " Lupin cleared his throat./n"Expecto patronum)."/n/n"Expecto patronum," Harry repeated under his breath,/n"expecto patronum."/n/n"Concentrating hard on your happy memory?"/n/n"Oh — yeah — " said Harry, quickly forcing his/nthoughts back to that first broom ride. "Expecto/npatrono — no, patronum — sorry — expecto patronum,/nexpecto patronum — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSomething whooshed suddenly out of the end of his/nwand; it looked like a wisp of silvery gas./n/n/n/n"Did you see that?" said Harry excitedly. "Something/nhappened!"/n/n"Very good," said Lupin, smiling. "Right, then — ready/nto try it on a dementor?"/n/n"Yes," Harry said, gripping his wand very tightly, and/nmoving into the middle of the deserted classroom. He/ntried to keep his mind on flying, but something else/nkept intruding. . . . Any second now, he might hear his/nmother again . . . but he shouldn't think that, or he/nwould hear her again, and he didn't want to ... or did/nhe?/n/nLupin grasped the lid of the packing case and pulled./n/nA dementor rose slowly from the box, its hooded face/nturned toward Harry, one glistening, scabbed hand/ngripping its cloak. The lamps around the classroom/nflickered and went out. The dementor stepped from/nthe box and started to sweep silently toward Harry,/ndrawing a deep, rattling breath. A wave of piercing/ncold broke over him —/n/n"Expecto patronurrd" Harry yelled. "Expecto patronum)./nExpecto — "/n/nBut the classroom and the dementor were dissolving./n/n. . . Harry was falling again through thick white fog,/nand his mother's voice was louder than ever, echoing/ninside his head — " Not Harry\ Not Harry\ Please — I'll/ndo anything — "/n/n"Stand aside. Stand aside, girl\"/n/n"Harry!"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry jerked back to life. He was lying flat on his back/non the floor. The classroom lamps were alight again./nHe didn't have to ask what had happened./n/n"Sorry," he muttered, sitting up and feeling cold sweat/ntrickling down behind his glasses./n/n"Are you all right?" said Lupin./n/n"Yes ..." Harry pulled himself up on one of the desks/nand leaned against it./n/n"Here — " Lupin handed him a Chocolate Frog. "Eat/nthis before we try again. I didn't expect you to do it/nyour first time; in fact, I would have been astounded if/nyou had."/n/n"It's getting worse," Harry muttered, biting off the/nFrog's head. "I could hear her louder that time — and/nhim — Voldemort — "/n/nLupin looked paler than usual./n/n"Harry, if you don't want to continue, I will more than/nunderstand — "/n/n"I do!" said Harry fiercely, stuffing the rest of the/nChocolate Frog into his mouth. "I've got to! What if/nthe dementors turn up at our match against/nRavenclaw? I can't afford to fall off again. If we lose/nthis game we've lost the Quidditch Cup!"/n/n"All right then ... ," said Lupin. "You might want to/nselect another memory, a happy memory, I mean, to/nconcentrate on. ... That one doesn't seem to have/nbeen strong enough. ..."/n/nHarry thought hard and decided his feelings when/nGryffindor had won the House Championship last/n/n/n/n/n/nyear had definitely qualified as very happy. He/ngripped his wand tightly again and took up his/nposition in the middle of the classroom./n/n"Ready?" said Lupin, gripping the box lid./n/n"Ready," said Harry, trying hard to fill his head with/nhappy thoughts about Gryffindor winning, and not/ndark thoughts about what was going to happen when/nthe box opened./n/n"Go!" said Lupin, pulling off the lid. The room went/nicily cold and dark once more. The dementor glided/nforward, drawing its breath; one rotting hand was/nextending toward Harry —/n/n"Expecto patronum)." Harry yelled. "Expecto patronuml/nExpecto pat — "/n/nWhite fog obscured his senses . . . big, blurred shapes/nwere moving around him ... then came a new voice, a/nman's voice, shouting, panicking —/n/n"Lily, take Harry and go\ It's him\ Go! Run\ I'll hold him/n/noff~/n/nThe sounds of someone stumbling from a room — a/ndoor bursting open — a cackle of high-pitched/nlaughter —/n/n"Harry! Harry ... wake up. ..."/n/nLupin was tapping Harry hard on the face. This time/nit was a minute before Harry understood why he was/nlying on a dusty classroom floor./n/n"I heard my dad," Harry mumbled. "That's the first/ntime I've ever heard him — he tried to take on/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nVoldemort himself, to give my mum time to run for it./n/n/n/nHarry suddenly realized that there were tears on his/nface mingling with the sweat. He bent his face as low/nas possible, wiping them off on his robes, pretending/nto do up his shoelace, so that Lupin wouldn't see./n/n"You heard James?" said Lupin in a strange voice./n/n"Yeah ..." Face dry, Harry looked up. "Why — you/ndidn't know my dad, did you?"/n/n"I — I did, as a matter of fact," said Lupin. "We were/nfriends at Hogwarts. Listen, Harry — perhaps we/nshould leave it here for tonight. This charm is/nridiculously advanced. ... I shouldn't have suggested/nputting you through this. ..."/n/n"No!" said Harry. He got up again. "I'll have one more/ngo! I'm not thinking of happy enough things, that's/nwhat it is. ... Hang on. ..."/n/nHe racked his brains. A really, really happy memory/n. . . one that he could turn into a good, strong/nPatronus .../n/nThe moment when he'd first found out he was a/nwizard, and would be leaving the Dursleys for/nHogwarts! If that wasn't a happy memory, he didn't/nknow what was. ... Concentrating very hard on how/nhe had felt when he'd realized he'd be leaving Privet/nDrive, Harry got to his feet and faced the packing case/nonce more./n/n"Ready?" said Lupin, who looked as though he were/ndoing this against his better judgment./n/n"Concentrating hard? All right — go!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe pulled off the lid of the case for the third time, and/nthe dementor rose out of it; the room fell cold and/ndark —/n/n"EXPECTO PATRONUM " Harry bellowed. " EXPECTO/nPATRONUM EXPECTO PATRONUM "/n/nThe screaming inside Harry's head had started again/n— except this time, it sounded as though it were/ncoming from a badly tuned radio — softer and louder/nand softer again — and he could still see the/ndementor — it had halted — and then a huge, silver/nshadow came bursting out of the end of Harry's wand,/nto hover between him and the dementor, and though/nHarry's legs felt like water, he was still on his feet —/nthough for how much longer, he wasn't sure —/n/n" RiddikulusV' roared Lupin, springing forward./n/nThere was a loud crack, and Harry's cloudy Patronus/nvanished along with the dementor; he sank into a/nchair, feeling as exhausted as if he'd just run a mile,/nand felt his legs shaking. Out of the corner of his eye,/nhe saw Professor Lupin forcing the boggart back into/nthe packing case with his wand; it had turned into a/nsilvery orb again./n/n"Excellent!" Lupin said, striding over to where Harry/nsat. "Excellent, Harry! That was definitely a start!"/n/n"Can we have another go? Just one more go?"/n/n"Not now," said Lupin firmly. "You've had enough for/none night. Here — "/n/nHe handed Harry a large bar of Honeydukes' best/nchocolate./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Eat the lot, or Madam Pomfrey will be after my blood./nSame time next week?"/n/n"Okay," said Harry. He took a bite of the chocolate/nand watched Lupin extinguishing the lamps that had/nrekindled with the disappearance of the dementor. A/nthought had just occurred to him./n/n"Professor Lupin?" he said. "If you knew my dad, you/nmust've known Sirius Black as well."/n/nLupin turned very quickly./n/n"What gives you that idea?" he said sharply./n/n"Nothing — I mean, I just knew they were friends at/nHogwarts too. ..."/n/nLupin's face relaxed./n/n"Yes, I knew him," he said shortly. "Or I thought I did./nYou'd better be off, Harry, it's getting late."/n/nHarry left the classroom, walking along the corridor/nand around a corner, then took a detour behind a/nsuit of armor and sank down on its plinth to finish/nhis chocolate, wishing he hadn't mentioned Black, as/nLupin was obviously not keen on the subject. Then/nHarry's thoughts wandered back to his mother and/nfather. .../n/nHe felt drained and strangely empty, even though he/nwas so full of chocolate. Terrible though it was to hear/nhis parents' last moments replayed inside his head,/nthese were the only times Harry had heard their/nvoices since he was a very small child. But he'd never/nbe able to produce a proper Patronus if he half/nwanted to hear his parents again. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They're dead," he told himself sternly. "They're dead/nand listening to echoes of them won't bring them/nback. You'd better get a grip on yourself if you want/nthat Quidditch Cup."/n/nHe stood up, crammed the last bit of chocolate into/nhis mouth, and headed back to Gryffindor Tower./n/nRavenclaw played Slytherin a week after the start of/nterm. Slytherin won, though narrowly. According to/nWood, this was good news for Gryffindor, who would/ntake second place if they beat Ravenclaw too. He/ntherefore increased the number of team practices to/nfive a week. This meant that with Lupin's anti-/ndementor classes, which in themselves were more/ndraining than six Quidditch practices, Harry had just/none night a week to do all his homework. Even so, he/nwasn't showing the strain nearly as much as/nHermione, whose immense workload finally seemed to/nbe getting to her. Every night, without fail, Hermione/nwas to be seen in a corner of the common room,/nseveral tables spread with books, Arithmancy charts,/nrune dictionaries, diagrams of Muggles lifting heavy/nobjects, and file upon file of extensive notes; she/nbarely spoke to anybody and snapped when she was/ninterrupted./n/n"How's she doing it?" Ron muttered to Harry one/nevening as Harry sat finishing a nasty essay on/nUndetectable Poisons for Snape. Harry looked up./nHermione was barely visible behind a tottering pile of/nbooks./n/n"Doing what?"/n/n"Getting to all her classes!" Ron said. "I heard her/ntalking to Professor Vector, that Arithmancy witch,/nthis morning. They were going on about yesterday's/nlesson, but Hermione can't've been there, because she/n/n/n/n/n/nwas with us in Care of Magical Creatures! And Ernie/nMcMillan told me she's never missed a Muggle/nStudies class, but half of them are at the same time/nas Divination, and she's never missed one of them/neither!"/n/nHarry didn't have time to fathom the mystery of/nHermione's impossible schedule at the moment; he/nreally needed to get on with Snape's essay. Two/nseconds later, however, he was interrupted again, this/ntime by Wood./n/n"Bad news, Harry. I've just been to see Professor/nMcGonagall about the Firebolt. She — er — got a bit/nshirty with me. Told me I'd got my priorities wrong./nSeemed to think I cared more about winning the Cup/nthan I do about you staying alive. Just because I told/nher I didn't care if it threw you off, as long as you/ncaught the Snitch first." Wood shook his head in/ndisbelief. "Honestly, the way she was yelling at me . . ./nyou'd think I'd said something terrible. ... Then I/nasked her how much longer she was going to keep it./n..." He screwed up his face and imitated Professor/nMcGonagall's severe voice. " 'As long as necessary,/nWood' ... I reckon it's time you ordered a new broom,/nHarry. There's an order form at the back of Which/nBroomstick ... you could get a Nimbus Two Thousand/nand One, like Malfoy's got."/n/n"I'm not buying anything Malfoy thinks is good," said/nHarry flatly./n/nJanuary faded imperceptibly into February, with no/nchange in the bitterly cold weather. The match/nagainst Ravenclaw was drawing nearer and nearer,/nbut Harry still hadn't ordered a new broom. He was/nnow asking Professor McGonagall for news of the/nFirebolt after every Transfiguration lesson, Ron/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nstanding hopefully at his shoulder, Hermione rushing/npast with her face averted./n/n"No, Potter, you can't have it back yet," Professor/nMcGonagall told him the twelfth time this happened,/nbefore he'd even opened his mouth. "We've checked/nfor most of the usual curses, but Professor Flitwick/nbelieves the broom might be carrying a Hurling Hex. I/nshall tell you once we've finished checking it. Now,/nplease stop badgering me."/n/nTo make matters even worse, Harry's anti-dementor/nlessons were not going nearly as well as he had/nhoped. Several sessions on, he was able to produce/nan indistinct, silvery shadow every time the boggart-/ndementor approached him, but his Patronus was too/nfeeble to drive the dementor away. All it did was/nhover, like a semi-transparent cloud, draining Harry/nof energy as he fought to keep it there. Harry felt/nangry with himself, guilty about his secret desire to/nhear his parents' voices again./n/n"You're expecting too much of yourself," said/nProfessor Lupin sternly in their fourth week of/npractice. "For a thirteen-year-old wizard, even an/nindistinct Patronus is a huge achievement. You aren't/npassing out anymore, are you?"/n/n"I thought a Patronus would — charge the dementors/ndown or something," said Harry dispiritedly. "Make/nthem disappear — "/n/n"The true Patronus does do that," said Lupin. "But/nyou've achieved a great deal in a very short space of/ntime. If the dementors put in an appearance at your/nnext Quidditch match, you will be able to keep them/nat bay long enough to get back to the ground."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You said it's harder if there are loads of them," said/nHarry./n/n"I have complete confidence in you," said Lupin,/nsmiling. "Here — you've earned a drink — something/nfrom the Three Broomsticks. You won't have tried it/nbefore — "/n/nHe pulled two bottles out of his briefcase./n/n"Butterbeer!" said Harry, without thinking. "Yeah, I/nlike that stuff!"/n/nLupin raised an eyebrow./n/n"Oh — Ron and Hermione brought me some back/nfrom Hogsmeade," Harry lied quickly./n/n"I see," said Lupin, though he still looked slightly/nsuspicious. "Well — let's drink to a Gryffindor victory/nagainst Ravenclaw! Not that I'm supposed to take/nsides, as a teacher ... ," he added hastily./n/nThey drank the butterbeer in silence, until Harry/nvoiced something he'd been wondering for a while./n/n"What's under a dementor's hood?"/n/nProfessor Lupin lowered his bottle thoughtfully./n/n"Hmmm ... well, the only people who really know are/nin no condition to tell us. You see, the dementor/nlowers its hood only to use its last and worst/nweapon."/n/n"What's that?"/n/n"They call it the Dementor's Kiss," said Lupin, with a/nslightly twisted smile. "It's what dementors do to/n/n/n/n/n/nthose they wish to destroy utterly. I suppose there/nmust be some kind of mouth under there, because/nthey clamp their jaws upon the mouth of the victim/nand — and suck out his soul."/n/nHarry accidentally spat out a bit of butterbeer./n/n"What — they kill — ?"/n/n"Oh no," said Lupin. "Much worse than that. You can/nexist without your soul, you know, as long as your/nbrain and heart are still working. But you 11 have no/nsense of self anymore, no memory, no ... anything./nThere's no chance at all of recovery. You'll just —/nexist. As an empty shell. And your soul is gone forever/n... lost."/n/nLupin drank a little more butterbeer, then said, "It's/nthe fate that awaits Sirius Black. It was in the Daily/nProphet this morning. The Ministry have given the/ndementors permission to perform it if they find him."/n/nHarry sat stunned for a moment at the idea of/nsomeone having their soul sucked out through their/nmouth. But then he thought of Black./n/n"He deserves it," he said suddenly./n/n"You think so?" said Lupin lightly. "Do you really/nthink anyone deserves that?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry defiantly. "For ... for some things ..."/n/nHe would have liked to have told Lupin about the/nconversation he'd overheard about Black in the Three/nBroomsticks, about Black betraying his mother and/nfather, but it would have involved revealing that he'd/ngone to Hogsmeade without permission, and he knew/nLupin wouldn't be very impressed by that. So he/n/n/n/n/nfinished his butterbeer, thanked Lupin, and left the/nHistory of Magic classroom./n/nHarry half wished that he hadn't asked what was/nunder a dementor's hood, the answer had been so/nhorrible, and he was so lost in unpleasant thoughts of/nwhat it would feel like to have your soul sucked out of/nyou that he walked headlong into Professor/nMcGonagall halfway up the stairs./n/n"Do watch where you're going, Potter!"/n/n"Sorry, Professor — "/n/n"I've just been looking for you in the Gryffindor/ncommon room. Well, here it is, we've done everything/nwe could think of, and there doesn't seem to be/nanything wrong with it at all. You've got a very good/nfriend somewhere, Potter. ..."/n/nHarry's jaw dropped. She was holding out his/nFirebolt, and it looked as magnificent as ever./n/n"I can have it back?" Harry said weakly. "Seriously?"/n/n"Seriously," said Professor McGonagall, and she was/nactually smiling. "I daresay you'll need to get the feel/nof it before Saturday's match, won't you? And Potter/n— do try and win, won't you? Or we'll be out of the/nrunning for the eighth year in a row, as Professor/nSnape was kind enough to remind me only last night./n/n/n/nSpeechless, Harry carried the Firebolt back upstairs/ntoward Gryffindor Tower. As he turned a corner, he/nsaw Ron dashing toward him, grinning from ear to/near./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"She gave it to you? Excellent! Listen, can I still have/na go on it? Tomorrow?"/n/n"Yeah ... anything ... said Harry, his heart lighter/nthan it had been in a month. "You know what — we/nshould make up with Hermione. ... She was only/ntrying to help. ..."/n/n"Yeah, all right," said Ron. "She's in the common/nroom now — working, for a change — "/n/nThey turned into the corridor to Gryffindor Tower and/nsaw Neville Longbottom, pleading with Sir Cadogan,/nwho seemed to be refusing him entrance./n/n"I wrote them down!" Neville was saying tearfully./n/n"But I must've dropped them somewhere!"/n/n"A likely tale!" roared Sir Cadogan. Then, spotting/nHarry and Ron: "Good even, my fine young yeomen!/nCome clap this loon in irons. He is trying to force/nentry to the chambers within!"/n/n"Oh, shut up," said Ron as he and Harry drew level/nwith Neville./n/n"I've lost the passwords!" Neville told them miserably./n"I made him tell me what passwords he was going to/nuse this week, because he keeps changing them, and/nnow I don't know what I've done with them!"/n/n"Oddsbodikins," said Harry to Sir Cadogan, who/nlooked extremely disappointed and reluctantly swung/nforward to let them into the common room. There was/na sudden, excited murmur as every head turned and/nthe next moment, Harry was surrounded by people/nexclaiming over his Firebolt./n/n"Where 'd you get it, Harry?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Will you let me have a go?"/n/n"Have you ridden it yet, Harry?"/n/n"Ravenclaw'll have no chance, they're all on/nCleansweep Sevens!"/n/n"Can I just hold it, Harry?"/n/nAfter ten minutes or so, during which the Firebolt was/npassed around and admired from every angle, the/ncrowd dispersed and Harry and Ron had a clear view/nof Hermione, the only person who hadn't rushed over/nto them, bent over her work and carefully avoiding/ntheir eyes. Harry and Ron approached her table and/nat last, she looked up./n/n"I got it back," said Harry, grinning at her and holding/nup the Firebolt./n/n"See, Hermione? There wasn't anything wrong with/nit!" said Ron./n/n"Well — there might have been!" said Hermione. "I/nmean, at least you know now that it's safe!"/n/n"Yeah, I suppose so," said Harry. "I'd better put it/nupstairs — "/n/n"I'll take it!" said Ron eagerly. "I've got to give/nScabbers his rat tonic."/n/nHe took the Firebolt and, holding it as if it were made/nof glass, carried it away up the boys' staircase./n/n"Can I sit down, then?" Harry asked Hermione./n/n"I suppose so," said Hermione, moving a great stack/nof parchment off a chair./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry looked around at the cluttered table, at the/nlong Arithmancy essay on which the ink was still/nglistening, at the even longer Muggle Studies essay/n("Explain Why Muggles Need Electricity") and at the/nrune translation Hermione was now poring over./n/n"How are you getting through all this stuff?" Harry/nasked her./n/n"Oh, well — you know — working hard," said/nHermione. Close-up, Harry saw that she looked/nalmost as tired as Lupin./n/n"Why don't you just drop a couple of subjects?" Harry/nasked, watching her lifting books as she searched for/nher rune dictionary./n/n"I couldn't do that!" said Hermione, looking/nscandalized./n/n"Arithmancy looks terrible," said Harry, picking up a/nvery complicated-looking number chart./n/n"Oh no, it's wonderful!" said Hermione earnestly. "It's/nmy favorite subject! It's — "/n/nBut exactly what was wonderful about Arithmancy,/nHarry never found out. At that precise moment, a/nstrangled yell echoed down the boys' staircase. The/nwhole common room fell silent, staring, petrified, at/nthe entrance. Then came hurried footsteps, growing/nlouder and louder — and then Ron came leaping into/nview, dragging with him a bedsheet./n/n"LOOK!" he bellowed, striding over to Hermione's/ntable. "LOOK!" he yelled, shaking the sheets in her/nface./n/n"Ron, what — ?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"SCABBERS! LOOK! SCABBERS!"/n/n/n/nHermione was leaning away from Ron, looking utterly/nbewildered. Harry looked down at the sheet Ron was/nholding. There was something red on it. Something/nthat looked horribly like —/n/n"BLOOD!" Ron yelled into the stunned silence. "HE'S/nGONE! AND YOU KNOW WHAT WAS ON THE/nFLOOR?"/n/n"N — no," said Hermione in a trembling voice./n/nRon threw something down onto Hermione 's rune/ntranslation. Hermione and Harry leaned forward./nLying on top of the weird, spiky shapes were several/nlong, ginger cat hairs./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Gryffindor Versus Ravenclaw
text: /nIt looked like the end of Ron and Hermione's/nfriendship. Each was so angry with the other that/nHarry couldn't see how they'd ever make up./n/nRon was enraged that Hermione had never taken/nCrookshanks's attempts to eat Scabbers seriously,/nhadn't bothered to keep a close enough watch on him,/nand was still trying to pretend that Crookshanks was/ninnocent by suggesting that Ron look for Scabbers/nunder all the boys' beds. Hermione, meanwhile,/nmaintained fiercely that Ron had no proof that/nCrookshanks had eaten Scabbers, that the ginger/nhairs might have been there since Christmas, and/nthat Ron had been prejudiced against her cat ever/nsince Crookshanks had landed on Ron's head in the/nMagical Menagerie./n/nPersonally, Harry was sure that Crookshanks had/neaten Scabbers, and when he tried to point out to/nHermione that the evidence all pointed that way, she/nlost her temper with Harry too./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Okay, side with Ron, I knew you would!" she said/nshrilly. "First the Firebolt, now Scabbers, everything's/nmy fault, isn't it! Just leave me alone, Harry, I've got a/nlot of work to do!"/n/nRon had taken the loss of his rat very hard indeed./n/n"Come on, Ron, you were always saying how boring/nScabbers was," said Fred bracingly "And he's been/noff-color for ages, he was wasting away. It was/nprobably better for him to snuff it quickly — one/nswallow — he probably didn't feel a thing."/n/n"Fred\" said Ginny indignantly./n/n"All he did was eat and sleep, Ron, you said it/nyourself," said George./n/n"He bit Goyle for us once!" Ron said miserably./n"Remember, Harry?"/n/n"Yeah, that's true," said Harry./n/n"His finest hour," said Fred, unable to keep a straight/nface. "Let the scar on Goyle 's finger stand as a lasting/ntribute to his memory. Oh, come on, Ron, get yourself/ndown to Hogsmeade and buy a new rat, what's the/npoint of moaning?"/n/nIn a last-ditch attempt to cheer Ron up, Harry/npersuaded him to come along to the Gryffindor team's/nfinal practice before the Ravenclaw match, so that he/ncould have a ride on the Firebolt after they'd finished./nThis did seem to take Ron's mind off Scabbers for a/nmoment ("Great! Can I try and shoot a few goals on/nit?") so they set off for the Quidditch field together./n/nMadam Hooch, who was still overseeing Gryffindor/npractices to keep an eye on Harry, was just as/n/n/n/n/n/nimpressed with the Firebolt as everyone else had/nbeen. She took it in her hands before takeoff and gave/nthem the benefit of her professional opinion./n/n"Look at the balance on it! If the Nimbus series has a/nfault, it's a slight list to the tail end — you often find/nthey develop a drag after a few years. They've updated/nthe handle too, a bit slimmer than the Cleansweeps,/nreminds me of the old Silver Arrows — a pity they've/nstopped making them. I learned to fly on one, and a/nvery fine old broom it was too. ..."/n/nShe continued in this vein for some time, until Wood/nsaid, "Er — Madam Hooch? Is it okay if Harry has the/nFirebolt back? We need to practice. ..."/n/n"Oh — right — here you are, then, Potter," said/nMadam Hooch. "I'll sit over here with Weasley ..."/n/nShe and Ron left the field to sit in the stadium, and/nthe Gryffindor team gathered around Wood for his/nfinal instructions for tomorrow's match./n/n"Harry, I've just found out who Ravenclaw is playing/nas Seeker. It's Cho Chang. She's a fourth year, and/nshe's pretty good. ... I really hoped she wouldn't be fit,/nshe's had some problems with injuries. ..." Wood/nscowled his displeasure that Cho Chang had made a/nfull recovery, then said, "On the other hand, she rides/na Comet Two Sixty, which is going to look like a joke/nnext to the Firebolt." He gave Harry's broom a look of/nfervent admiration, then said, "Okay, everyone, let's/ngo/n/n/n/nAnd at long last, Harry mounted his Firebolt, and/nkicked off from the ground./n/nIt was better than he'd ever dreamed. The Firebolt/nturned with the lightest touch; it seemed to obey his/n/n/n/n/n/nthoughts rather than his grip; it sped across the field/nat such speed that the stadium turned into a green-/nand-gray blur; Harry turned it so sharply that Alicia/nSpinnet screamed, then he went into a perfectly/ncontrolled dive, brushing the grassy field with his toes/nbefore rising thirty, forty, fifty feet into the air again —/n/n"Harry, I'm letting the Snitch out!" Wood called./n/nHarry turned and raced a Bludger toward the goal/nposts; he outstripped it easily, saw the Snitch dart/nout from behind Wood, and within ten seconds had/ncaught it tightly in his hand./n/nThe team cheered madly. Harry let the Snitch go/nagain, gave it a minute's head start, then tore after it,/nweaving in and out of the others; he spotted it lurking/nnear Katie Bell's knee, looped her easily, and caught/nit again./n/nIt was the best practice ever; the team, inspired by/nthe presence of the Firebolt in their midst, performed/ntheir best moves faultlessly, and by the time they hit/nthe ground again, Wood didn't have a single criticism/nto make, which, as George Weasley pointed out, was a/nfirst./n/n"I can't see what's going to stop us tomorrow!" said/nWood. "Not unless — Harry, you've sorted out your/ndementor problem, haven't you?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, thinking of his feeble Patronus/nand wishing it were stronger./n/n"The dementors won't turn up again, Oliver./nDumbledore'd go ballistic," said Fred confidently./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, let's hope not," said Wood. "Anyway — good/nwork, everyone. Let's get back to the tower ... turn in/nearly — "/n/n"I'm staying out for a bit; Ron wants a go on the/nFirebolt," Harry told Wood, and while the rest of the/nteam headed off to the locker rooms, Harry strode/nover to Ron, who vaulted the barrier to the stands/nand came to meet him. Madam Hooch had fallen/nasleep in her seat./n/n"Here you go," said Harry, handing Ron the Firebolt./n/nRon, an expression of ecstasy on his face, mounted/nthe broom and zoomed off into the gathering darkness/nwhile Harry walked around the edge of the field,/nwatching him. Night had fallen before Madam Hooch/nawoke with a start, told Harry and Ron off for not/nwaking her, and insisted that they go back to the/ncastle./n/nHarry shouldered the Firebolt and he and Ron walked/nout of the shadowy stadium, discussing the Firebolt's/nsuperbly smooth action, its phenomenal acceleration,/nand its pinpoint turning. They were halfway toward/nthe castle when Harry, glancing to his left, saw/nsomething that made his heart turn over — a pair of/neyes, gleaming out of the darkness./n/nHarry stopped dead, his heart banging against his/nribs./n/n"What's the matter?" said Ron./n/nHarry pointed. Ron pulled out his wand and/nmuttered, "Lumos\"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA beam of light fell across the grass, hit the bottom of/na tree, and illuminated its branches; there, crouching/namong the budding leaves, was Crookshanks./n/n"Get out of here!" Ron roared, and he stooped down/nand seized a stone lying on the grass, but before he/ncould do anything else, Crookshanks had vanished/nwith one swish of his long ginger tail./n/n"See?" Ron said furiously, chucking the stone down/nagain. "She's still letting him wander about wherever/nhe wants — probably washing down Scabbers with a/ncouple of birds now. ..."/n/nHarry didn't say anything. He took a deep breath as/nrelief seeped through him; he had been sure for a/nmoment that those eyes had belonged to the Grim./nThey set off for the castle once more. Slightly/nashamed of his moment of panic, Harry didn't say/nanything to Ron — nor did he look left or right until/nthey had reached the well-lit entrance hall./n/nHarry went down to breakfast the next morning with/nthe rest of the boys in his dormitory, all of whom/nseemed to think the Firebolt deserved a sort of guard/nof honor. As Harry entered the Great Hall, heads/nturned in the direction of the Firebolt, and there was/na good deal of excited muttering. Harry saw, with/nenormous satisfaction, that the Slytherin team were/nall looking thunderstruck./n/n"Did you see his face?" said Ron gleefully, looking/nback at Malfoy. "He can't believe it! This is brilliant!"/n/nWood, too, was basking in the reflected glory of the/nFirebolt./n/n"Put it here, Harry," he said, laying the broom in the/nmiddle of the table and carefully turning it so that its/n/n/n/n/n/nname faced upward. People from the Ravenclaw and/nHufflepuff tables were soon coming over to look./nCedric Diggory came over to congratulate Harry on/nhaving acquired such a superb replacement for his/nNimbus, and Percy's Ravenclaw girlfriend, Penelope/nClearwater, asked if she could actually hold the/nFirebolt./n/n"Now, now, Penny, no sabotage!" said Percy heartily/nas she examined the Firebolt closely "Penelope and I/nhave got a bet on," he told the team. "Ten Galleons on/nthe outcome of the match!"/n/nPenelope put the Firebolt down again, thanked Harry,/nand went back to her table./n/n"Harry — make sure you win," said Percy, in an/nurgent whisper. "I haven't got ten Galleons. Yes, I'm/ncoming, Penny!" And he bustled off to join her in a/npiece of toast./n/n"Sure you can manage that broom, Potter?" said a/ncold, drawling voice./n/nDraco Malfoy had arrived for a closer look, Crabbe/nand Goyle right behind him./n/n"Yeah, reckon so," said Harry casually./n/n"Got plenty of special features, hasn't it?" said Malfoy,/neyes glittering maliciously. "Shame it doesn't come/nwith a parachute — in case you get too near a/ndementor."/n/nCrabbe and Goyle sniggered./n/n"Pity you can't attach an extra arm to yours, Malfoy,"/nsaid Harry. "Then it could catch the Snitch for you."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe Gryffindor team laughed loudly. Malfoy's pale/neyes narrowed, and he stalked away. They watched/nhim rejoin the rest of the Slytherin team, who put/ntheir heads together, no doubt asking Malfoy whether/nHarry's broom really was a Firebolt./n/nAt a quarter to eleven, the Gryffindor team set off for/nthe locker rooms. The weather couldn't have been/nmore different from their match against Hufflepuff. It/nwas a clear, cool day with a very light breeze; there/nwould be no visibility problems this time, and Harry,/nthough nervous, was starting to feel the excitement/nonly a Quidditch match could bring. They could hear/nthe rest of the school moving into the stadium/nbeyond. Harry took off his black school robes,/nremoved his wand from his pocket, and stuck it/ninside the T-shirt he was going to wear under his/nQuidditch robes. He only hoped he wouldn't need it./nHe wondered suddenly whether Professor Lupin was/nin the crowd, watching./n/n"You know what we've got to do," said Wood as they/nprepared to leave the locker rooms. "If we lose this/nmatch, we're out of the running. Just — just fly like/nyou did in practice yesterday, and we'll be okay!"/n/nThey walked out onto the field to tumultuous/napplause. The Ravenclaw team, dressed in blue, were/nalready standing in the middle of the field. Their/nSeeker, Cho Chang, was the only girl on their team./nShe was shorter than Harry by about a head, and/nHarry couldn't help noticing, nervous as he was, that/nshe was extremely pretty. She smiled at Harry as the/nteams faced each other behind their captains, and he/nfelt a slight lurch in the region of his stomach that he/ndidn't think had anything to do with nerves./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wood, Davies, shake hands," Madam Hooch said/nbriskly, and Wood shook hands with the Ravenclaw/nCaptain./n/n"Mount your brooms ... on my whistle . . . three — two/n— one — "/n/nHarry kicked off into the air and the Firebolt zoomed/nhigher and faster than any other broom; he soared/naround the stadium and began squinting around for/nthe Snitch, listening all the while to the commentary,/nwhich was being provided by the Weasley twins'/nfriend Lee Jordan./n/n"They're off, and the big excitement this match is the/nFirebolt that Harry Potter is flying for Gryffindor./nAccording to Which Broomstick, the Firebolt's going to/nbe the broom of choice for the national teams at this/nyear's World Championship — "/n/n"Jordan, would you mind telling us what's going on in/nthe match?" interrupted Professor McGonagall's voice./n/n"Right you are, Professor — just giving a bit of/nbackground information — the Firebolt, incidentally,/nhas a built-in auto-brake and — "/n/n"Jordan!"/n/n"Okay, okay, Gryffindor in possession, Katie Bell of/nGryffindor heading for goal ..."/n/nHarry streaked past Katie in the opposite direction,/ngazing around for a glint of gold and noticing that Cho/nChang was tailing him closely. She was undoubtedly/na very good flier — she kept cutting across him,/nforcing him to change direction./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Show her your acceleration, Harry!" Fred yelled as he/nwhooshed past in pursuit of a Bludger that was/naiming for Alicia./n/nHarry urged the Firebolt forward as they rounded the/nRavenclaw goal posts and Cho fell behind. Just as/nKatie succeeded in scoring the first goal of the match,/nand the Gryffindor end of the field went wild, he saw/nit — the Snitch was close to the ground, flitting near/none of the barriers./n/nHarry dived; Cho saw what he was doing and tore/nafter him — Harry was speeding up, excitement/nflooding him; dives were his speciality, he was ten feet/naway —/n/nThen a Bludger, hit by one of the Ravenclaw Beaters,/ncame pelting out of nowhere; Harry veered off course,/navoiding it by an inch, and in those few, crucial/nseconds, the Snitch had vanished./n/nThere was a great "Ooooooh" of disappointment from/nthe Gryffindor supporters, but much applause for/ntheir Beater from the Ravenclaw end. George Weasley/nvented his feelings by hitting the second Bludger/ndirectly at the offending Beater, who was forced to roll/nright over in midair to avoid it./n/n"Gryffindor leads by eighty points to zero, and look at/nthat Firebolt go! Potter's really putting it through its/npaces now, see it turn — Chang's Comet is just no/nmatch for it, the Firebolt's precision-balance is really/nnoticeable in these long — "/n/n"JORDAN! ARE YOU BEING PAID TO ADVERTISE/nFIREBOLTS? GET ON WITH THE COMMENTARY!"/n/nRavenclaw was pulling back; they had now scored/nthree goals, which put Gryffindor only fifty points/n/n/n/n/n/nahead — if Cho got the Snitch before him, Ravenclaw/nwould win. Harry dropped lower, narrowly avoiding a/nRavenclaw Chaser, scanning the field frantically — a/nglint of gold, a flutter of tiny wings — the Snitch was/ncircling the Gryffindor goal post —/n/nHarry accelerated, eyes fixed on the speck of gold/nahead — but just then, Cho appeared out of thin air,/nblocking him —/n/n"HARRY, THIS IS NO TIME TO BE A GENTLEMAN!"/nWood roared as Harry swerved to avoid a collision./n"KNOCK HER OFF HER BROOM IF YOU HAVE TO!"/n/nHarry turned and caught sight of Cho; she was/ngrinning. The Snitch had vanished again. Harry/nturned his Firebolt upward and was soon twenty feet/nabove the game. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw/nCho following him. ... She'd decided to mark him/nrather than search for the Snitch herself. . . . All right,/nthen ... if she wanted to tail him, she'd have to take/nthe consequences. .../n/nHe dived again, and Cho, thinking he'd seen the/nSnitch, tried to follow; Harry pulled out of the dive/nvery sharply; she hurtled downward; he rose fast as a/nbullet once more, and then saw it, for the third time/n— the Snitch was glittering way above the field at the/nRavenclaw end./n/nHe accelerated; so, many feet below, did Cho. He was/nwinning, gaining on the Snitch with every second —/nthen —/n/n"Oh!" screamed Cho, pointing./n/nDistracted, Harry looked down./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThree dementors, three tall, black, hooded dementors,/nwere looking up at him./n/nHe didn't stop to think. Plunging a hand down the/nneck of his robes, he whipped out his wand and/nroared, "Expecto patronum)."/n/nSomething silver-white, something enormous, erupted/nfrom the end of his wand. He knew it had shot/ndirectly at the dementors but didn't pause to watch;/nhis mind still miraculously clear, he looked ahead —/nhe was nearly there. He stretched out the hand still/ngrasping his wand and just managed to close his/nfingers over the small, struggling Snitch./n/nMadam Hooch's whistle sounded. Harry turned/naround in midair and saw six scarlet blurs bearing/ndown on him; next moment, the whole team was/nhugging him so hard he was nearly pulled off his/nbroom. Down below he could hear the roars of the/nGryffindors in the crowd./n/n"That's my boy!" Wood kept yelling. Alicia, Angelina,/nand Katie had all kissed Harry; Fred had him in a grip/nso tight Harry felt as though his head would come off./nIn complete disarray, the team managed to make its/nway back to the ground. Harry got off his broom and/nlooked up to see a gaggle of Gryffindor supporters/nsprinting onto the field, Ron in the lead. Before he/nknew it, he had been engulfed by the cheering crowd./n/n"Yes!" Ron yelled, yanking Harry's arm into the air./n"Yes! Yes!"/n/n"Well done, Harry!" said Percy, looking delighted. "Ten/nGalleons to me! Must find Penelope, excuse me — "/n/n"Good for you, Harry!" roared Seamus Finnigan./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ruddy brilliant!" boomed Hagrid over the heads of/nthe milling Gryffindors./n/n"That was quite some Patronus," said a voice in/nHarry's ear./n/nHarry turned around to see Professor Lupin, who/nlooked both shaken and pleased./n/n"The dementors didn't affect me at all!" Harry said/nexcitedly. "I didn't feel a thing!"/n/n"That would be because they — er — weren't/ndementors," said Professor Lupin. "Come and see — "/n/nHe led Harry out of the crowd until they were able to/nsee the edge of the field./n/n"You gave Mr. Malfoy quite a fright," said Lupin./n/nHarry stared. Lying in a crumpled heap on the ground/nwere Malfoy, Crabbe, Goyle, and Marcus Flint, the/nSlytherin team Captain, all struggling to remove/nthemselves from long, black, hooded robes. It looked/nas though Malfoy had been standing on Goyle 's/nshoulders. Standing over them, with an expression of/nthe utmost fury on her face, was Professor/nMcGonagall./n/n"An unworthy trick!" she was shouting. "A low and/ncowardly attempt to sabotage the Gryffindor Seeker!/nDetention for all of you, and fifty points from/nSlytherin! I shall be speaking to Professor/nDumbledore about this, make no mistake! Ah, here/nhe comes now!"/n/nIf anything could have set the seal on Gryffindor's/nvictory, it was this. Ron, who had fought his way/nthrough to Harry's side, doubled up with laughter as/n/n/n/n/n/nthey watched Malfoy fighting to extricate himself from/nthe robe, Goyle's head still stuck inside it./n/n/n/n"Come on, Harry!" said George, fighting his way over./n"Party! Gryffindor common room, now!"/n/n"Right," said Harry, and feeling happier than he had/nin ages, he and the rest of the team led the way, still/nin their scarlet robes, out of the stadium and back up/nto the castle./n/n/n/nIt felt as though they had already won the Quidditch/nCup; the party went on all day and well into the night./nFred and George Weasley disappeared for a couple of/nhours and returned with armfuls of bottles of/nbutterbeer, pumpkin fizz, and several bags full of/nHoneydukes sweets./n/n"How did you do that?" squealed Angelina Johnson as/nGeorge started throwing Peppermint Toads into the/ncrowd./n/n"With a little help from Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot, and/nProngs," Fred muttered in Harry's ear./n/nOnly one person wasn't joining in the festivities./nHermione, incredibly, was sitting in a corner,/nattempting to read an enormous book entitled Home/nLife and Social Habits of British Muggles. Harry broke/naway from the table where Fred and George had/nstarted juggling butterbeer bottles and went over to/nher./n/n"Did you even come to the match?" he asked her./n/n"Of course I did," said Hermione in a strangely high-/npitched voice, not looking up. "And I'm very glad we/n/n/n/n/n/nwon, and I think you did really well, but I need to/nread this by Monday."/n/n"Come on, Hermione, come and have some food,"/nHarry said, looking over at Ron and wondering/nwhether he was in a good enough mood to bury the/nhatchet./n/n"I can't, Harry. I've still got four hundred and twenty-/ntwo pages to read!" said Hermione, now sounding/nslightly hysterical. "Anyway ..." She glanced over at/nRon too. "He doesn't want me to join in."/n/nThere was no arguing with this, as Ron chose that/nmoment to say loudly, "If Scabbers hadn't just been/neaten, he could have had some of those Fudge Flies./nHe used to really like them — "/n/nHermione burst into tears. Before Harry could say or/ndo anything, she tucked the enormous book under/nher arm, and, still sobbing, ran toward the staircase/nto the girls' dormitories and out of sight./n/n"Can't you give her a break?" Harry asked Ron/nquietly./n/n"No," said Ron flatly. "If she just acted like she was/nsorry — but she'll never admit she's wrong, Hermione./nShe's still acting like Scabbers has gone on vacation/nor something."/n/nThe Gryffindor party ended only when Professor/nMcGonagall turned up in her tartan dressing gown/nand hair net at one in the morning, to insist that they/nall go to bed. Harry and Ron climbed the stairs to/ntheir dormitory, still discussing the match. At last,/nexhausted, Harry climbed into bed, twitched the/nhangings of his four-poster shut to block out a ray of/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmoonlight, lay back, and felt himself almost instantly/ndrifting off to sleep. .../n/nHe had a very strange dream. He was walking/nthrough a forest, his Firebolt over his shoulder,/nfollowing something silvery- white. It was winding its/nway through the trees ahead, and he could only catch/nglimpses of it between the leaves. Anxious to catch up/nwith it, he sped up, but as he moved faster, so did his/nquarry. Harry broke into a run, and ahead he heard/nhooves gathering speed. Now he was running flat out,/nand ahead he could hear galloping. Then he turned a/ncorner into a clearing and —/n/n"AAAAAAAAAAAAAARRRRRRRRRRRRGGGGGHHHHH/n! NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!"/n/nHarry woke as suddenly as though he'd been hit in/nthe face. Disoriented in the total darkness, he/nfumbled with his hangings — he could hear/nmovements around him, and Seamus Finnigan's voice/nfrom the other side of the room: "What's going on?"/n/nHarry thought he heard the dormitory door slam. At/nlast finding the divide in his curtains, he ripped them/nback, and at the same moment, Dean Thomas lit his/nlamp./n/nRon was sitting up in bed, the hangings torn from one/nside, a look of utmost terror on his face./n/n"Black! Sirius Black! With a knife!"/n/n"What?"/n/n"Here! Just now! Slashed the curtains! Woke me up!"/n"You sure you weren't dreaming, Ron?" said Dean./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Look at the curtains! I tell you, he was here!"/n/nThey all scrambled out of bed; Harry reached the/ndormitory door first, and they sprinted back down the/nstaircase. Doors opened behind them, and sleepy/nvoices called after them./n/n"Who shouted?"/n/n"What 're you doing?"/n/nThe common room was lit with the glow of the dying/nfire, still littered with the debris from the party. It was/ndeserted./n/n"Are you sure you weren't dreaming, Ron?"/n/n"I'm telling you, I saw him!"/n/n"What's all the noise?"/n/n"Professor McGonagall told us to go to bed!"/n/nA few of the girls had come down their staircase,/npulling on dressing gowns and yawning. Boys, too,/nwere reappearing./n/n"Excellent, are we carrying on?" said Fred Weasley/nbrightly./n/n"Everyone back upstairs!" said Percy,/nhurrying into the common room and pinning his/nHead Boy badge to his pajamas as he spoke./n/n"Perce — Sirius Black!" said Ron faintly. "In our/ndormitory! With a knife! Woke me up!"/n/nThe common room went very still./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Nonsense!" said Percy, looking startled. "You had too/nmuch to eat, Ron — had a nightmare — "/n/n/n/n"I'm telling you — "/n/n"Now, really, enough's enough!"/n/nProfessor McGonagall was back. She slammed the/nportrait behind her as she entered the common room/nand stared furiously around./n/n"I am delighted that Gryffindor won the match, but/nthis is getting ridiculous! Percy, I expected better of/nyou!"/n/n"I certainly didn't authorize this, Professor!" said/nPercy, puffing himself up indignantly. "I was just/ntelling them all to get back to bed! My brother Ron/nhere had a nightmare — "/n/n"IT WASNT A NIGHTMARE!" Ron yelled./n/n"PROFESSOR, I WOKE UP, AND SIRIUS BLACK WAS/nSTANDING OVER ME, HOLDING A KNIFE!"/n/nProfessor McGonagall stared at him./n/n"Don't be ridiculous, Weasley, how could he possibly/nhave gotten through the portrait hole?"/n/n"Ask him!" said Ron, pointing a shaking finger at the/nback of Sir Cadogan's picture. "Ask him if he saw — "/n/nGlaring suspiciously at Ron, Professor McGonagall/npushed the portrait back open and went outside. The/nwhole common room listened with bated breath./n/n"Sir Cadogan, did you just let a man enter Gryffindor/nTower?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Certainly, good lady!" cried Sir Cadogan./n/nThere was a stunned silence, both inside and outside/nthe common room./n/n"You — you did?" said Professor McGonagall. "But —/nbut the password!"/n/n"He had 'em!" said Sir Cadogan proudly. "Had the/nwhole week's, my lady! Read 'em off a little piece of/npaper!"/n/nProfessor McGonagall pulled herself back through the/nportrait hole to face the stunned crowd. She was/nwhite as chalk./n/n"Which person," she said, her voice shaking, "which/nabysmally foolish person wrote down this week's/npasswords and left them lying around?"/n/nThere was utter silence, broken by the smallest of/nterrified squeaks. Neville Longbottom, trembling from/nhead to fluffy-slippered toes, raised his hand slowly/ninto the air./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Snape's Grudge
text: /nNo one in Gryffindor Tower slept that night. They/nknew that the castle was being searched again, and/nthe whole House stayed awake in the common room,/nwaiting to hear whether Black had been caught./nProfessor McGonagall came back at dawn, to tell/nthem that he had again escaped./n/nThroughout the day, everywhere they went they saw/nsigns of tighter security; Professor Flitwick could be/nseen teaching the front doors to recognize a large/npicture of Sirius Black; Filch was suddenly bustling/nup and down the corridors, boarding up everything/nfrom tiny cracks in the walls to mouse holes. Sir/nCadogan had been fired. His portrait had been taken/nback to its lonely landing on the seventh floor, and/nthe Fat Lady was back. She had been expertly/nrestored, but was still extremely nervous, and had/nagreed to return to her job only on condition that she/nwas given extra protection. A bunch of surly security/ntrolls had been hired to guard her. They paced the/ncorridor in a menacing group, talking in grunts and/ncomparing the size of their clubs./n/n/n/n/nHarry couldn't help noticing that the statue of the/none-eyed witch on the third floor remained unguarded/nand unblocked. It seemed that Fred and George had/nbeen right in thinking that they — and now Harry,/nRon, and Hermione — were the only ones who knew/nabout the hidden passageway within it./n/n"D'you reckon we should tell someone?" Harry asked/nRon./n/n"We know he's not coming in through Honey duke's,"/nsaid Ron dismissively "We'd've heard if the shop had/nbeen broken into."/n/nHarry was glad Ron took this view. If the one-eyed/nwitch was boarded up too, he would never be able to/ngo into Hogsmeade again./n/nRon had become an instant celebrity. For the first/ntime in his life, people were paying more attention to/nhim than to Harry, and it was clear that Ron was/nrather enjoying the experience. Though still severely/nshaken by the night's events, he was happy to tell/nanyone who asked what had happened, with a wealth/nof detail./n/n"... I was asleep, and I heard this ripping noise, and I/nthought it was in my dream, you know? But then/nthere was this draft ... I woke up and one side of the/nhangings on my bed had been pulled down. ... I rolled/nover . . . and I saw him standing over me . . . like a/nskeleton, with loads of filthy hair . . . holding this great/nlong knife, must've been twelve inches ... and he/nlooked at me, and I looked at him, and then I yelled,/nand he scampered./n/n"Why, though?" Ron added to Harry as the group of/nsecond-year girls who had been listening to his/nchilling tale departed. "Why did he run?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry had been wondering the same thing. Why had/nBlack, having got the wrong bed, not silenced Ron/nand proceeded to Harry?
