Black had proved twelve/nyears ago that he didn't mind murdering innocent/npeople, and this time he had been facing five/nunarmed boys, four of whom were asleep./n/n"He must've known he'd have a job getting back out of/nthe castle once you'd yelled and woken people up,"/nsaid Harry thoughtfully. "He'd've had to kill the whole/nHouse to get back through the portrait hole . . . then/nhe would've met the teachers. ..."/n/nNeville was in total disgrace. Professor McGonagall/nwas so furious with him she had banned him from all/nfuture Hogsmeade visits, given him a detention, and/nforbidden anyone to give him the password into the/ntower. Poor Neville was forced to wait outside the/ncommon room every night for somebody to let him in,/nwhile the security trolls leered unpleasantly at him./nNone of these punishments, however, came close to/nmatching the one his grandmother had in store for/nhim. Two days after Black's break-in, she sent Neville/nthe very worst thing a Hogwarts student could receive/nover breakfast — a Howler./n/nThe school owls swooped into the Great Hall carrying/nthe mail as usual, and Neville choked as a huge barn/nowl landed in front of him, a scarlet envelope clutched/nin its beak. Harry and Ron, who were sitting opposite/nhim, recognized the letter as a Howler at once — Ron/nhad got one from his mother the year before./n/n"Run for it, Neville," Ron advised./n/nNeville didn't need telling twice. He seized the/nenvelope, and holding it before him like a bomb,/nsprinted out of the hall, while the Slytherin table/nexploded with laughter at the sight of him. They/n/n/n/n/n/nheard the Howler go off in the entrance hall —/nNeville's grandmother's voice, magically magnified to/na hundred times its usual volume, shrieking about/nhow he had brought shame on the whole family./n/nHarry was too busy feeling sorry for Neville to notice/nimmediately that he had a letter too. Hedwig got his/nattention by nipping him sharply on the wrist./n/n"Ouch! Oh — thanks, Hedwig."/n/nHarry tore open the envelope while Hedwig helped/nherself to some of Neville's cornflakes. The note inside/nsaid:/n/nDear Harry and Ron,/n/nHow about having tea with me this afternoon 'round/nsix?/n/n/n/nI'll come and collect you from the castle./n/nWAIT FOR ME IN THE ENTRANCE HALL;/n/nYOU'RE NOT ALLOWED OUT ON YOUR OWN/nCheers,/n/nHagrid/n/n"He probably wants to hear all about Black!" said/nRon./n/nSo at six o'clock that afternoon, Harry and Ron left/nGryffindor Tower, passed the security trolls at a run,/nand headed down to the entrance hall./n/nHagrid was already waiting for them./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"All right, Hagrid!" said Ron. "S'pose you want to hear/nabout Saturday night, do you?"/n/n"I've already heard all abou' it," said Hagrid, opening/nthe front doors and leading them outside./n/n"Oh," said Ron, looking slightly put out./n/nThe first thing they saw on entering Hagrid's cabin/nwas Buckbeak, who was stretched out on top of/nHagrid's patchwork quilt, his enormous wings folded/ntight to his body, enjoying a large plate of dead/nferrets. Averting his eyes from this unpleasant sight,/nHarry saw a gigantic, hairy brown suit and a very/nhorrible yellow-and-orange tie hanging from the top of/nHagrid's wardrobe door./n/n"What are they for, Hagrid?" said Harry./n/n"Buckbeak's case against the Committee fer the/nDisposal o' Dangerous Creatures," said Hagrid. "This/nFriday. Him an' me'll be goin' down ter London/ntogether. I've booked two beds on the Knight Bus. ..."/n/nHarry felt a nasty pang of guilt. He had completely/nforgotten that Buckbeak's trial was so near, and/njudging by the uneasy look on Ron's face, he had too./nThey had also forgotten their promise about helping/nhim prepare Buckbeak's defense; the arrival of the/nFirebolt had driven it clean out of their minds./n/nHagrid poured them tea and offered them a plate of/nBath buns, but they knew better than to accept; they/nhad had too much experience with Hagrid's cooking./n/n"I got somethin' ter discuss with you two," said/nHagrid, sitting himself between them and looking/nuncharacteristically serious./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"Hermione," said Hagrid./n/n"What about her?" said Ron./n/n"She's in a righ' state, that's what. She's bin cornin'/ndown ter visit me a lot since Chris 'mas. Bin feelin'/nlonely. Firs' yeh weren' talking to her because o' the/nFirebolt, now yer not talkin' to her because her cat — "/n/n" — ate Scabbers!" Ron interjected angrily./n/n"Because her cat acted like all cats do," Hagrid/ncontinued doggedly. "She's cried a fair few times, yeh/nknow. Goin' through a rough time at the moment./nBitten off more'n she can chew, if yeh ask me, all the/nwork she's tryin' ter do. Still found time ter help me/nwith Buckbeak's case, mind. ... She's found some/nreally good stuff fer me ... reckon he'll stand a good/nchance now. ..."/n/n"Hagrid, we should've helped as well — sorry — "/n/nHarry began awkwardly./n/n"I'm not blamin' yeh!" said Hagrid, waving Harry's/napology aside. "Gawd knows yeh've had enough ter be/ngettin' on with. I've seen yeh practicin' Quidditch ev'ry/nhour o' the day an' night — but I gotta tell yeh, I/nthought you two'd value yer friend more'n/nbroomsticks or rats. Tha's all."/n/nHarry and Ron exchanged uncomfortable looks./n/n"Really upset, she was, when Black nearly stabbed/nyeh, Ron. She's got her heart in the right place,/nHermione has, an' you two not talkin' to her — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"If she'd just get rid of that cat, I'd speak to her/nagain!" Ron said angrily. "But she's still sticking up/nfor it! It's a maniac, and she won't hear a word/nagainst it!"/n/n"Ah, well, people can be a bit stupid abou' their pets,"/nsaid Hagrid wisely. Behind him, Buckbeak spat a few/nferret bones onto Hagrid's pillow./n/nThey spent the rest of their visit discussing/nGryffindor's improved chances for the Quidditch Cup./nAt nine o'clock, Hagrid walked them back up to the/ncastle./n/nA large group of people was bunched around the/nbulletin board when they returned to the common/nroom./n/n"Hogsmeade, next weekend!" said Ron, craning over/nthe heads to read the new notice. "What d'you/nreckon?" he added quietly to Harry as they went to sit/ndown./n/n"Well, Filch hasn't done anything about the passage/ninto Honeydukes. ..." Harry said, even more quietly./n/n"Harry!" said a voice in his right ear. Harry started/nand looked around at Hermione, who was sitting at/nthe table right behind them and clearing a space in/nthe wall of books that had been hiding her./n/n"Harry, if you go into Hogsmeade again ... I'll tell/nProfessor McGonagall about that map!" said/nHermione./n/n"Can you hear someone talking, Harry?" growled Ron,/nnot looking at Hermione./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ron, how can you let him go with you? After what/nSirius Black nearly did to youl I mean it, I'll tell — "/n/n"So now you're trying to get Harry expelled!" said Ron/nfuriously. "Haven't you done enough damage this/nyear?"/n/nHermione opened her mouth to respond, but with a/nsoft hiss, Crookshanks leapt onto her lap. Hermione/ntook one frightened look at the expression on Ron's/nface, gathered up Crookshanks, and hurried away/ntoward the girls' dormitories./n/n"So how about it?" Ron said to Harry as though there/nhad been no interruption. "Come on, last time we/nwent you didn't see anything. You haven't even been/ninside Zonko's yet!"/n/nHarry looked around to check that Hermione was well/nout of earshot./n/n"Okay," he said. "But I'm taking the Invisibility Cloak/nthis time."/n/nOn Saturday morning, Harry packed his Invisibility/nCloak in his bag, slipped the Marauder's Map into his/npocket, and went down to breakfast with everyone/nelse. Hermione kept shooting suspicious looks down/nthe table at him, but he avoided her eye and was/ncareful to let her see him walking back up the marble/nstaircase in the entrance hall as everybody else/nproceeded to the front doors./n/n" 'Bye!" Harry called to Ron. "See you when you get/nback!"/n/nRon grinned and winked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry hurried up to the third floor, slipping the/nMarauder's Map out of his pocket as he went./nCrouching behind the one-eyed witch, he smoothed it/nout. A tiny dot was moving in his direction. Harry/nsquinted at it. The minuscule writing next to it read/nNeville Longbottom./n/nHarry quickly pulled out his wand, muttered,/n/n" Dissendium)." and shoved his bag into the statue, but/nbefore he could climb in himself, Neville came around/nthe corner./n/n"Harry! I forgot you weren't going to Hogsmeade/neither!"/n/n"Hi, Neville," said Harry, moving swiftly away from the/nstatue and pushing the map back into his pocket./n"What are you up to?"/n/n"Nothing," shrugged Neville. "Want a game of/nExploding Snap?"/n/n"Er — not now — I was going to go to the library and/ndo that vampire essay for Lupin — "/n/n"I'll come with you!" said Neville brightly. "I haven't/ndone it either!"/n/n"Er — hang on — yeah, I forgot, I finished it last/nnight!"/n/n"Great, you can help me!" said Neville, his round face/nanxious. "I don't understand that thing about the/ngarlic at all — do they have to eat it, or — "/n/nHe broke off with a small gasp, looking over Harry's/nshoulder./n/nIt was Snape. Neville took a quick step behind Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n"And what are you two doing here?" said Snape,/ncoming to a halt and looking from one to the other./n"An odd place to meet — "/n/nTo Harry's immense disquiet, Snape's black eyes/nflicked to the doorways on either side of them, and/nthen to the one-eyed witch./n/n"We're not — meeting here," said Harry. "We just —/nmet here."/n/n"Indeed?" said Snape. "You have a habit of turning up/nin unexpected places, Potter, and you are very rarely/nthere for no good reason. ... I suggest the pair of you/nreturn to Gryffindor Tower, where you belong."/n/nHarry and Neville set off without another word. As/nthey turned the corner, Harry looked back. Snape was/nrunning one of his hands over the one-eyed witch's/nhead, examining it closely./n/nHarry managed to shake Neville off at the Fat Lady by/ntelling him the password, then pretending he'd left his/nvampire essay in the library and doubling back. Once/nout of sight of the security trolls, he pulled out the/nmap again and held it close to his nose./n/nThe third floor corridor seemed to be deserted. Harry/nscanned the map carefully and saw, with a leap of/nrelief, that the tiny dot labeled Severus Snape was/nnow back in its office./n/nHe sprinted back to the one-eyed witch, opened her/nhump, heaved himself inside, and slid down to meet/nhis bag at the bottom of the stone chute. He wiped/nthe Marauder's Map blank again, then set off at a/nrun./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry, completely hidden beneath the Invisibility/nCloak, emerged into the sunlight outside Honeydukes/nand prodded Ron in the back./n/n"It's me," he muttered./n/n"What kept you?" Ron hissed./n/n"Snape was hanging around. ..."/n/nThey set off up the High Street./n/n"Where are you?" Ron kept muttering out of the/ncorner of his mouth. "Are you still there? This feels/nweird. ..."/n/nThey went to the post office; Ron pretended to be/nchecking the price of an owl to Bill in Egypt so that/nHarry could have a good look around. The owls sat/nhooting softly down at him, at least three hundred of/nthem; from Great Grays right down to tiny little Scops/nowls ("Local Deliveries Only"), which were so small/nthey could have sat in the palm of Harry's hand./n/nThen they visited Zonko's, which was so packed with/nstudents Harry had to exercise great care not to tread/non anyone and cause a panic. There were jokes and/ntricks to fulfill even Fred's and George's wildest/ndreams; Harry gave Ron whispered orders and passed/nhim some gold from under the cloak. They left/nZonko's with their money bags considerably lighter/nthan they had been on entering, but their pockets/nbulging with Dungbombs, Hiccup Sweets, Frog Spawn/nSoap, and a Nose-Biting Teacup apiece./n/nThe day was fine and breezy, and neither of them felt/nlike staying indoors, so they walked past the Three/nBroomsticks and climbed a slope to visit the/nShrieking Shack, the most haunted dwelling in/n/n/n/n/n/nBritain. It stood a little way above the rest of the/nvillage, and even in daylight was slightly creepy, with/nits boarded windows and dank overgrown garden./n/n"Even the Hogwarts ghosts avoid it," said Ron as they/nleaned on the fence, looking up at it. "I asked Nearly/nHeadless Nick ... he says he's heard a very rough/ncrowd lives here. No one can get in. Fred and George/ntried, obviously, but all the entrances are sealed shut./n/n/n/nHarry, feeling hot from their climb, was just/nconsidering taking off the cloak for a few minutes/nwhen they heard voices nearby. Someone was/nclimbing toward the house from the other side of the/nhill; moments later, Malfoy had appeared, followed/nclosely by Crabbe and Goyle. Malfoy was speaking./n/n"... should have an owl from Father any time now. He/nhad to go to the hearing to tell them about my arm . . ./nabout how I couldn't use it for three months. ..."/n/nCrabbe and Goyle sniggered./n/n"I really wish I could hear that great hairy moron/ntrying to defend himself ... There's no 'arm in 'im,/n'onest — ' . . . that hippogriff's as good as dead — "/n/nMalfoy suddenly caught sight of Ron. His pale face/nsplit in a malevolent grin./n/n"What are you doing, Weasley?"/n/nMalfoy looked up at the crumbling house behind Ron./n/n"Suppose you'd love to live here, wouldn't you,/nWeasley? Dreaming about having your own bedroom?/n/nI heard your family all sleep in one room — is that/ntrue?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry seized the back of Ron's robes to stop him from/nleaping on Malfoy./n/n"Leave him to me," he hissed in Ron's ear./n/nThe opportunity was too perfect to miss. Harry crept/nsilently around behind Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle,/nbent down, and scooped a large handful of mud out of/nthe path./n/n"We were just discussing your friend Hagrid," Malfoy/nsaid to Ron. "Just trying to imagine what he's saying/nto the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous/nCreatures. D'you think he'll cry when they cut off his/nhippogriff's — "/n/nSPLAT./n/nMalfoy's head jerked forward as the mud hit him; his/nsilver-blond hair was suddenly dripping in muck./n/n"What the — ?"/n/nRon had to hold onto the fence to keep himself/nstanding, he was laughing so hard. Malfoy, Crabbe,/nand Goyle spun stupidly on the spot, staring wildly/naround, Malfoy trying to wipe his hair clean./n/n"What was that? Who did that?"/n/n"Very haunted up here, isn't it?" said Ron, with the/nair of one commenting on the weather./n/nCrabbe and Goyle were looking scared. Their bulging/nmuscles were no use against ghosts. Malfoy was/nstaring madly around at the deserted landscape./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry sneaked along the path, where a particularly/nsloppy puddle yielded some foul-smelling, green/nsludge./n/nSPLATTER./n/nCrabbe and Goyle caught some this time. Goyle/nhopped furiously on the spot, trying to rub it out of/nhis small, dull eyes./n/n"It came from over there!" said Malfoy, wiping his/nface, and staring at a spot some six feet to the left of/nHarry./n/nCrabbe blundered forward, his long arms/noutstretched like a zombie. Harry dodged around him,/npicked up a stick, and lobbed it at Crabbe 's back./nHarry doubled up with silent laughter as Crabbe did a/nkind of pirouette in midair, trying to see who had/nthrown it. As Ron was the only person Crabbe could/nsee, it was Ron he started toward, but Harry stuck/nout his leg. Crabbe stumbled — and his huge, flat foot/ncaught the hem of Harry's cloak. Harry felt a great/ntug, then the cloak slid off his face./n/nFor a split second, Malfoy stared at him./n/n"AAARGH!" he yelled, pointing at Harry's head. Then/nhe turned tail and ran, at breakneck speed, back/ndown the hill, Crabbe and Goyle behind him./n/nHarry tugged the cloak up again, but the damage was/ndone./n/n"Harry!" Ron said, stumbling forward and staring/nhopelessly at the point where Harry had disappeared,/n"you'd better run for it! If Malfoy tells anyone — you'd/nbetter get back to the castle, quick — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"See you later," said Harry, and without another/nword, he tore back down the path toward Hogsmeade./n/n/n/nWould Malfoy believe what he had seen? Would/nanyone believe Malfoy? Nobody knew about the/nInvisibility Cloak — nobody except Dumbledore./nHarry's stomach turned over — Dumbledore would/nknow exactly what had happened, if Malfoy said/nanything —/n/nBack into Honeydukes, back down the cellar steps,/nacross the stone floor, through the trapdoor — Harry/npulled off the cloak, tucked it under his arm, and ran,/nflat out, along the passage. ... Malfoy would get back/nfirst . . . how long would it take him to find a teacher?/nPanting, a sharp pain in his side, Harry didn't slow/ndown until he reached the stone slide. He would have/nto leave the cloak where it was, it was too much of a/ngiveaway in case Malfoy had tipped off a teacher — he/nhid it in a shadowy corner, then started to climb, fast/nas he could, his sweaty hands slipping on the sides of/nthe chute. He reached the inside of the witch's hump,/ntapped it with his wand, stuck his head through, and/nhoisted himself out; the hump closed, and just as/nHarry jumped out from behind the statue, he heard/nquick footsteps approaching./n/nIt was Snape. He approached Harry at a swift walk,/nhis black robes swishing, then stopped in front of/nhim./n/n"So," he said./n/nThere was a look of suppressed triumph about him./nHarry tried to look innocent, all too aware of his/nsweaty face and his muddy hands, which he quickly/nhid in his pockets./n/n"Come with me, Potter," said Snape./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry followed him downstairs, trying to wipe his/nhands clean on the inside of his robes without Snape/nnoticing. They walked down the stairs to the/ndungeons and then into Snape's office./n/nHarry had been in here only once before, and he had/nbeen in very serious trouble then too. Snape had/nacquired a few more slimy horrible things in jars/nsince last time, all standing on shelves behind his/ndesk, glinting in the firelight and adding to the/nthreatening atmosphere./n/n"Sit," said Snape./n/nHarry sat. Snape, however, remained standing./n/n"Mr. Malfoy has just been to see me with a strange/nstory, Potter," said Snape./n/nHarry didn't say anything./n/n"He tells me that he was up by the Shrieking Shack/nwhen he ran into Weasley — apparently alone."/n/nStill, Harry didn't speak./n/n"Mr. Malfoy states that he was standing talking to/nWeasley, when a large amount of mud hit him in the/nback of the head. How do you think that could have/nhappened?"/n/nHarry tried to look mildly surprised./n/n"I don't know, Professor."/n/nSnape's eyes were boring into Harry's. It was exactly/nlike trying to stare down a hippogriff. Harry tried hard/nnot to blink./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mr. Malfoy then saw an extraordinary apparition./n/nCan you imagine what it might have been, Potter?"/n/n"No," said Harry, now trying to sound innocently/ncurious./n/n"It was your head, Potter. Floating in midair."/n/nThere was a long silence./n/n"Maybe he'd better go to Madam Pomfrey," said Harry./n"If he's seeing things like — "/n/n"What would your head have been doing in/nHogsmeade, Potter?" said Snape softly. "Your head is/nnot allowed in Hogsmeade. No part of your body has/npermission to be in Hogsmeade."/n/n"I know that," said Harry, striving to keep his face free/nof guilt or fear. "It sounds like Malfoy's having/nhallucin — "/n/n"Malfoy is not having hallucinations," snarled Snape,/nand he bent down, a hand on each arm of Harry's/nchair, so that their faces were a foot apart. "If your/nhead was in Hogsmeade, so was the rest of you."/n/n"I've been up in Gryffindor Tower," said Harry. "Like/nyou told — "/n/n"Can anyone confirm that?"/n/nHarry didn't say anything. Snape's thin mouth curled/ninto a horrible smile./n/n"So," he said, straightening up again. "Everyone from/nthe Minister of Magic downward has been trying to/nkeep famous Harry Potter safe from Sirius Black. But/nfamous Harry Potter is a law unto himself. Let the/n/n/n/n/n/nordinary people worry about his safety! Famous Harry/nPotter goes where he wants to, with no thought for/nthe consequences."/n/nHarry stayed silent. Snape was trying to provoke him/ninto telling the truth. He wasn't going to do it. Snape/nhad no proof — yet./n/n"How extraordinarily like your father you are, Potter,"/nSnape said suddenly, his eyes glinting. "He too was/nexceedingly arrogant. A small amount of talent on the/nQuidditch field made him think he was a cut above/nthe rest of us too. Strutting around the place with his/nfriends and admirers . . . The resemblance between you/nis uncanny."/n/n"My dad didn't strut," said Harry, before he could stop/nhimself. "And neither do I."/n/n"Your father didn't set much store by rules either,"/nSnape went on, pressing his advantage, his thin face/nfull of malice. "Rules were for lesser mortals, not/nQuidditch Cup-winners. His head was so swollen — "/n/n"SHUT UP!"/n/nHarry was suddenly on his feet. Rage such as he had/nnot felt since his last night in Privet Drive was/ncoursing through him. He didn't care that Snape's/nface had gone rigid, the black eyes flashing/ndangerously./n/n" What did you say to me, Potter?"/n/n"I told you to shut up about my dad!" Harry yelled. "I/nknow the truth, all right? He saved your life!/nDumbledore told me! You wouldn't even be here if it/nwasn't for my dad!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSnape's sallow skin had gone the color of sour milk./n/n"And did the headmaster tell you the circumstances/nin which your father saved my life?" he whispered./n/n"Or did he consider the details too unpleasant for/nprecious Potter's delicate ears?"/n/nHarry bit his lip. He didn't know what had happened/nand didn't want to admit it — but Snape seemed to/nhave guessed the truth./n/n"I would hate for you to run away with a false idea of/nyour father, Potter," he said, a terrible grin twisting/nhis face. "Have you been imagining some act of/nglorious heroism? Then let me correct you — your/nsaintly father and his friends played a highly amusing/njoke on me that would have resulted in my death if/nyour father hadn't got cold feet at the last moment./nThere was nothing brave about what he did. He was/nsaving his own skin as much as mine. Had their joke/nsucceeded, he would have been expelled from/nHogwarts."/n/nSnape's uneven, yellowish teeth were bared./n/n"Turn out your pockets, Potter!" he spat suddenly./n/nHarry didn't move. There was a pounding in his ears./n/n"Turn out your pockets, or we go straight to the/nheadmaster! Pull them out, Potter!"/n/nCold with dread, Harry slowly pulled out the bag of/nZonko's tricks and the Marauder's Map./n/nSnape picked up the Zonko's bag./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ron gave them to me," said Harry, praying he'd get a/nchance to tip Ron off before Snape saw him. "He —/nbrought them back from Hogsmeade last time — "/n/n"Indeed? And you've been carrying them around ever/nsince? How very touching . . . and what is this?"/n/nSnape had picked up the map. Harry tried with all his/nmight to keep his face impassive./n/n"Spare bit of parchment," he said with a shrug./n/nSnape turned it over, his eyes on Harry./n/n"Surely you don't need such a very old piece of/nparchment?" he said. "Why don't I just — throw this/naway?"/n/nHis hand moved toward the fire./n/n"No!" Harry said quickly./n/n"So!" said Snape, his long nostrils quivering. "Is this/nanother treasured gift from Mr. Weasley? Or is it —/nsomething else? A letter, perhaps, written in invisible/nink? Or — instructions to get into Hogsmeade without/npassing the dementors?"/n/nHarry blinked. Snape 's eyes gleamed./n/n"Let me see, let me see ... ," he muttered, taking out/nhis wand and smoothing the map out on his desk./n"Reveal your secret!" he said, touching the wand to/nthe parchment./n/nNothing happened. Harry clenched his hands to stop/nthem from shaking./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Show yourself!" Snape said, tapping the map/nsharply./n/nIt stayed blank. Harry was taking deep, calming/nbreaths./n/n"Professor Severus Snape, master of this school,/ncommands you to yield the information you conceal!"/nSnape said, hitting the map with his wand./n/nAs though an invisible hand were writing upon it,/nwords appeared on the smooth surface of the map./n/n"Mr. Moony presents his compliments to Professor/nSnape, and begs him to keep his abnormally large/nnose out of other people's business."/n/nSnape froze. Harry stared, dumbstruck, at the/nmessage. But the map didn't stop there. More writing/nwas appearing beneath the first./n/n"Mr. Prongs agrees with Mr. Moony, and would like to/nadd that Professor Snape is an ugly git."/n/nIt would have been very funny if the situation hadn't/nbeen so serious. And there was more. .../n/n"Mr. Padfoot would like to register his astonishment/nthat an idiot like that ever became a professor."/n/nHarry closed his eyes in horror. When he'd opened/nthem, the map had had its last word./n/n"Mr. Wormtail bids Professor Snape good day, and/nadvises him to wash his hair, the slimeball."/n/nHarry waited for the blow to fall./n/n"So ... ," said Snape softly. "We'll see about this. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe strode across to his fire, seized a fistful of/nglittering powder from ajar on the fireplace, and/nthrew it into the flames./n/n"Lupin!" Snape called into the fire. "I want a word!"/n/nUtterly bewildered, Harry stared at the fire. A large/nshape had appeared in it, revolving very fast. Seconds/nlater, Professor Lupin was clambering out of the/nfireplace, brushing ash off his shabby robes./n/n"You called, Severus?" said Lupin mildly./n/n"I certainly did," said Snape, his face contorted with/nfury as he strode back to his desk. "I have just asked/nPotter to empty his pockets. He was carrying this."/n/nSnape pointed at the parchment, on which the words/nof Messrs. Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot, and Prongs/nwere still shining. An odd, closed expression appeared/non Lupin's face./n/n"Well?" said Snape./n/nLupin continued to stare at the map. Harry had the/nimpression that Lupin was doing some very quick/nthinking./n/n"Well?" said Snape again. "This parchment is plainly/nfull of Dark Magic. This is supposed to be your area of/nexpertise, Lupin. Where do you imagine Potter got/nsuch a thing?"/n/nLupin looked up and, by the merest half-glance in/nHarry's direction, warned him not to interrupt./n/n"Full of Dark Magic?" he repeated mildly. "Do you/nreally think so, Severus? It looks to me as though it is/nmerely a piece of parchment that insults anybody who/n/n/n/n/n/nreads it. Childish, but surely not dangerous? I/nimagine Harry got it from a joke shop — "/n/n"Indeed?" said Snape. His jaw had gone rigid with/nanger. "You think a joke shop could supply him with/nsuch a thing? You don't think it more likely that he/ngot it directly from the manufacturers?"/n/nHarry didn't understand what Snape was talking/nabout. Nor, apparently, did Lupin./n/n"You mean, by Mr. Wormtail or one of these people?"/nhe said. "Harry, do you know any of these men?"/n/n"No," said Harry quickly./n/n"You see, Severus?" said Lupin, turning back to/nSnape. "It looks like a Zonko product to me — "/n/nRight on cue, Ron came bursting into the office. He/nwas completely out of breath, and stopped just short/nof Snape 's desk, clutching the stitch in his chest and/ntrying to speak./n/n"I — gave — Harry — that — stuff," he choked./n"Bought — it ... in Zonko 's ... ages — ago ..."/n/n"Well!" said Lupin, clapping his hands together and/nlooking around cheerfully. "That seems to clear that/nup! Severus, I'll take this back, shall I?" He folded the/nmap and tucked it inside his robes. "Harry, Ron,/ncome with me, I need a word about my vampire essay/n— excuse us, Severus — "/n/nHarry didn't dare look at Snape as they left his office./nHe, Ron, and Lupin walked all the way back into the/nentrance hall before speaking. Then Harry turned to/nLupin./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Professor, I — "/n/n/n/n"I don't want to hear explanations," said Lupin/nshortly. He glanced around the empty entrance hall/nand lowered his voice. "I happen to know that this/nmap was confiscated by Mr. Filch many years ago./n/nYes, I know it's a map," he said as Harry and Ron/nlooked amazed. "I don't want to know how it fell into/nyour possession. I am, however, astounded that you/ndidn't hand it in. Particularly after what happened the/nlast time a student left information about the castle/nlying around. And I can't let you have it back, Harry."/n/nHarry had expected that, and was too keen for/nexplanations to protest./n/n"Why did Snape think I'd got it from the/nmanufacturers?"/n/n"Because ... ," Lupin hesitated, "because these/nmapmakers would have wanted to lure you out of/nschool. They'd think it extremely entertaining."/n/n"Do you know them?" said Harry, impressed./n/n"We've met," he said shortly. He was looking at Harry/nmore seriously than ever before./n/n"Don't expect me to cover up for you again, Harry. I/ncannot make you take Sirius Black seriously. But I/nwould have thought that what you have heard when/nthe dementors draw near you would have had more of/nan effect on you. Your parents gave their lives to keep/nyou alive, Harry. A poor way to repay them —/ngambling their sacrifice for a bag of magic tricks."/n/nHe walked away, leaving Harry feeling worse by far/nthan he had at any point in Snape 's office. Slowly, he/nand Ron mounted the marble staircase. As Harry/n/n/n/n/n/npassed the one-eyed witch, he remembered the/nInvisibility Cloak — it was still down there, but he/ndidn't dare go and get it./n/n/n/n"It's my fault," said Ron abruptly. "I persuaded you to/ngo. Lupin's right, it was stupid, we shouldn't've done/n/n/n/nit — "/n/n/n/nHe broke off; they reached the corridor where the/nsecurity trolls were pacing, and Hermione was/nwalking toward them. One look at her face convinced/nHarry that she had heard what had happened. His/nheart plummeted — had she told Professor/nMcGonagall?/n/n"Come to have a good gloat?" said Ron savagely as/nshe stopped in front of them. "Or have you just been/nto tell on us?"/n/n"No," said Hermione. She was holding a letter in her/nhands and her lip was trembling. "I just thought you/nought to know ... Hagrid lost his case. Buckbeak is/ngoing to be executed."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Quidditch Final
text: /n"He — he sent me this," Hermione said, holding out/nthe letter./n/nHarry took it. The parchment was damp, and/nenormous teardrops had smudged the ink so badly in/nplaces that it was very difficult to read./n/nDear Hermione,/n/nWe lost I'm allowed to bring him back to Hogwarts./nExecution date to be fixed./n/nBeaky has enjoyed London./n/nI won't forget all the help you gave us./n/nHagrid/n/n"They can't do this," said Harry. "They can't./nBuckbeak isn't dangerous."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Malfoy's dad's frightened the Committee into it," said/nHermione, wiping her eyes. "You know what he's like./nThey're a bunch of doddery old fools, and they were/nscared. There'll be an appeal, though, there always is./nOnly I can't see any hope. ... Nothing will have/nchanged."/n/n"Yeah, it will," said Ron fiercely. "You won't have to do/nall the work alone this time, Hermione. I'll help."/n/n"Oh, Ron!"/n/nHermione flung her arms around Ron's neck and/nbroke down completely. Ron, looking quite terrified,/npatted her very awkwardly on the top of the head./nFinally, Hermione drew away./n/n"Ron, I'm really, really sorry about Scabbers ... ," she/nsobbed./n/n"Oh — well — he was old," said Ron, looking/nthoroughly relieved that she had let go of him. "And/nhe was a bit useless. You never know, Mum and Dad/nmight get me an owl now."/n/nThe safety measures imposed on the students since/nBlack's second break-in made it impossible for Harry,/nRon, and Hermione to go and visit Hagrid in the/nevenings. Their only chance of talking to him was/nduring Care of Magical Creatures lessons./n/nHe seemed numb with shock at the verdict./n/n"S'all my fault. Got all tongue-tied. They was all sittin'/nthere in black robes an' I kep' droppin' me notes and/nforgettin' all them dates yeh looked up fer me,/nHermione. An' then Lucius Malfoy stood up an' said/nhis bit, and the Committee jus' did exac'ly what he/ntold 'em. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"There's still the appeal!" said Ron fiercely. "Don't give/nup yet, we're working on it!"/n/nThey were walking back up to the castle with the rest/nof the class. Ahead they could see Malfoy, who was/nwalking with Crabbe and Goyle, and kept looking/nback, laughing derisively./n/n"S'no good, Ron," said Hagrid sadly as they reached/nthe castle steps. "That Committee's in Lucius Malfoy 's/npocket. I'm jus' gonna make sure the rest o' Beaky's/ntime is the happiest he's ever had. I owe him that. ..."/n/nHagrid turned around and hurried back toward his/ncabin, his face buried in his handkerchief./n/n"Look at him blubber!"/n/nMalfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle had been standing just/ninside the castle doors, listening./n/n"Have you ever seen anything quite as pathetic?" said/nMalfoy. "And he's supposed to be our teacher!"/n/nHarry and Ron both made furious moves toward/nMalfoy, but Hermione got there first — SMACK!/n/nShe had slapped Malfoy across the face with all the/nstrength she could muster. Malfoy staggered. Harry,/nRon, Crabbe, and Goyle stood flabbergasted as/nHermione raised her hand again./n/n"Don't you dare call Hagrid pathetic, you foul — you/nevil — "/n/n"Hermione!" said Ron weakly, and he tried to grab her/nhand as she swung it back./n/n"Get off, Ron!"/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione pulled out her wand. Malfoy stepped/nbackward. Crabbe and Goyle looked at him for/ninstructions, thoroughly bewildered./n/n"C'mon," Malfoy muttered, and in a moment, all three/nof them had disappeared into the passageway to the/ndungeons./n/n"Hermionel" Ron said again, sounding both stunned/nand impressed./n/n"Harry, you'd better beat him in the Quidditch final!"/nHermione said shrilly. Lee Jordan was howling/ninto the megaphone, dancing out of Professor/nMcGonagall's reach. "YOU FILTHY, CHEATING B — "/n/nProfessor McGonagall didn't even bother to tell him/noff. She was actually shaking her finger in Malfoy's/ndirection, her hat had fallen off, and she too was/nshouting furiously./n/nAlicia took Gryffindor's penalty, but she was so angry/nshe missed by several feet. The Gryffindor team was/nlosing concentration and the Slytherins, delighted by/nMalfoy's foul on Harry, were being spurred on to/ngreater heights./n/n"Slytherin in possession, Slytherin heading for goal —/nMontague scores — " Lee groaned. "Seventy-twenty to/nGryffindor. ..."/n/nHarry was now marking Malfoy so closely their knees/nkept hitting each other. Harry wasn't going to let/nMalfoy anywhere near the Snitch. .../n/n/n/n/n/n"Get out of it, Potter!" Malfoy yelled in frustration as/nhe tried to turn and found Harry blocking him./n/n"Angelina Johnson gets the Quaffle for Gryffindor,/ncome on, Angelina, COME ON!"/n/nHarry looked around. Every single Slytherin player/napart from Malfoy was streaking up the pitch toward/nAngelina, including the Slytherin Keeper — they were/nall going to block her —/n/nHarry wheeled the Firebolt around, bent so low he/nwas lying flat along the handle, and kicked it forward./nLike a bullet, he shot toward the Slytherins./n/n"AAAAAAARRRGH ! "/n/nThey scattered as the Firebolt zoomed toward them;/nAngelina's way was clear./n/n"SHE SCORES! SHE SCORES! Gryffindor leads by/neighty points to twenty!"/n/nHarry, who had almost pelted headlong into the/nstands, skidded to a halt in midair, reversed, and/nzoomed back into the middle of the field./n/nAnd then he saw something to make his heart stand/nstill. Malfoy was diving, a look of triumph on his face/n— there, a few feet above the grass below, was a tiny,/ngolden glimmer —/n/nHarry urged the Firebolt downward, but Malfoy was/nmiles ahead —/n/n"Go! Go! Go!" Harry urged his broom. He was gaining/non Malfoy — Harry flattened himself to the broom/nhandle as Bole sent a Bludger at him — he was at/nMalfoy's ankles — he was level —/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry threw himself forward, took both hands off his/nbroom. He knocked Malfoy's arm out of the way and/n/n/n/n"YES!"/n/nHe pulled out of his dive, his hand in the air, and the/nstadium exploded. Harry soared above the crowd, an/nodd ringing in his ears. The tiny golden ball was held/ntight in his fist, beating its wings hopelessly against/nhis fingers./n/nThen Wood was speeding toward him, half-blinded by/ntears; he seized Harry around the neck and sobbed/nunrestrainedly into his shoulder. Harry felt two large/nthumps as Fred and George hit them; then/nAngelina's, Alicia's, and Katie's voices, "We've won the/nCup\ We've won the Cup\" Tangled together in a/nmany-armed hug, the Gryffindor team sank, yelling/nhoarsely, back to earth./n/nWave upon wave of crimson supporters was pouring/nover the barriers onto the field. Hands were raining/ndown on their backs. Harry had a confused/nimpression of noise and bodies pressing in on him./nThen he, and the rest of the team, were hoisted onto/nthe shoulders of the crowd. Thrust into the light, he/nsaw Hagrid, plastered with crimson rosettes — "Yeh/nbeat 'em, Harry, yeh beat 'em! Wait till I tell/nBuckbeak!" There was Percy, jumping up and down/nlike a maniac, all dignity forgotten. Professor/nMcGonagall was sobbing harder even than Wood,/nwiping her eyes with an enormous Gryffindor flag;/nand there, fighting their way toward Harry, were Ron/nand Hermione. Words failed them. They simply/nbeamed as Harry was borne toward the stands, where/nDumbledore stood waiting with the enormous/nQuidditch Cup./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIf only there had been a dementor around. ... As a/nsobbing Wood passed Harry the Cup, as he lifted it/ninto the air, Harry felt he could have produced the/nworld's best Patronus./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Professor Trelawney's Prediction
text: /nHarry's euphoria at finally winning the Quidditch Cup/nlasted at least a week. Even the weather seemed to be/ncelebrating; as June approached, the days became/ncloudless and sultry, and all anybody felt like doing/nwas strolling onto the grounds and flopping down on/nthe grass with several pints of iced pumpkin juice,/nperhaps playing a casual game of Gobstones or/nwatching the giant squid propel itself dreamily across/nthe surface of the lake./n/nBut they couldn't. Exams were nearly upon them, and/ninstead of lazing around outside, the students were/nforced to remain inside the castle, trying to bully their/nbrains into concentrating while enticing wafts of/nsummer air drifted in through the windows. Even/nFred and George Weasley had been spotted working;/nthey were about to take their O.W.L.s (Ordinary/nWizarding Levels). Percy was getting ready to take his/nN.E.W.T.s (Nastily Exhausting Wizarding Tests), the/nhighest qualification Hogwarts offered. As Percy/n/n/n/n/nhoped to enter the Ministry of Magic, he needed top/ngrades. He was becoming increasingly edgy, and gave/nvery severe punishments to anybody who disturbed/nthe quiet of the common room in the evenings. In fact,/nthe only person who seemed more anxious than Percy/nwas Hermione./n/nHarry and Ron had given up asking her how she was/nmanaging to attend several classes at once, but they/ncouldn't restrain themselves when they saw the exam/nschedule she had drawn up for herself. The first/ncolumn read:/n/nMonday/n/n9 o'clock, Arithmancy/n9 o'clock, Transfiguration/nLunch/n/n1 o'clock, Charms/n1 o'clock, Ancient Runes/n/n"Hermione?" Ron said cautiously, because she was/nliable to explode when interrupted these days. "Er —/nare you sure you've copied down these times right?"/n/n"What?" snapped Hermione, picking up the exam/nschedule and examining it. "Yes, of course I have."/n/n"Is there any point asking how you're going to sit for/ntwo exams at once?" said Harry./n/n"No," said Hermione shortly. "Have either of you seen/nmy copy of Numerology and Gramatica?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh, yeah, I borrowed it for a bit of bedtime reading,"/nsaid Ron, but very quietly. Hermione started shifting/nheaps of parchment around on her table, looking for/nthe book. Just then, there was a rustle at the window/nand Hedwig fluttered through it, a note clutched tight/nin her beak./n/n"It's from Hagrid," said Harry, ripping the note open./n"Buckbeak's appeal — it's set for the sixth."/n/n"That's the day we finish our exams," said Hermione,/nstill looking everywhere for her Arithmancy book./n/n"And they're coming up here to do it," said Harry, still/nreading from the letter. "Someone from the Ministry of/nMagic and — and an executioner."/n/nHermione looked up, startled./n/n"They're bringing the executioner to the appeal! But/nthat sounds as though they've already decided!"/n/n"Yeah, it does," said Harry slowly./n/n"They can't!" Ron howled. "I've spent ages reading up/non stuff for him; they can't just ignore it all!"/n/nBut Harry had a horrible feeling that the Committee/nfor the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures had had its/nmind made up for it by Mr. Malfoy. Draco, who had/nbeen noticeably subdued since Gryffindor's triumph/nin the Quidditch final, seemed to regain some of his/nold swagger over the next few days. From sneering/ncomments Harry overheard, Malfoy was certain/nBuckbeak was going to be killed, and seemed/nthoroughly pleased with himself for bringing it about./nIt was all Harry could do to stop himself imitating/nHermione and hitting Malfoy in the face on these/noccasions. And the worst thing of all was that they/n/n/n/n/nhad no time or opportunity to go and see Hagrid,/nbecause the strict new security measures had not/nbeen lifted, and Harry didn't dare retrieve his/nInvisibility Cloak from below the one-eyed witch./n/nk k k/n/n/n/nExam week began and an unnatural hush fell over/nthe castle. The third years emerged from/nTransfiguration at lunchtime on Monday, limp and/nashen-faced, comparing results and bemoaning the/ndifficulty of the tasks they had been set, which had/nincluded turning a teapot into a tortoise. Hermione/nirritated the rest by fussing about how her tortoise/nhad looked more like a turtle, which was the least of/neveryone else's worries./n/n"Mine still had a spout for a tail, what a nightmare./n/n/n/n"Were the tortoises supposed to breathe steam?"/n/n"It still had a willow-patterned shell, d'you think/nthat 11 count against me?"/n/nThen, after a hasty lunch, it was straight back/nupstairs for the Charms exam. Hermione had been/nright; Professor Flitwick did indeed test them on/nCheering Charms. Harry slightly overdid his out of/nnerves and Ron, who was partnering him, ended up/nin fits of hysterical laughter and had to be led away to/na quiet room for an hour before he was ready to/nperform the charm himself. After dinner, the students/nhurried back to their common rooms, not to relax,/nbut to start studying for Care of Magical Creatures,/nPotions, and Astronomy./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid presided over the Care of Magical Creatures/nexam the following morning with a very preoccupied/nair indeed; his heart didn't seem to be in it at all. He/nhad provided a large tub of fresh flobberworms for the/nclass, and told them that to pass the test, their/nflobberworm had to still be alive at the end of one/nhour. As flobberworms flourished best if left to their/nown devices, it was the easiest exam any of them had/never taken, and also gave Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nplenty of opportunity to speak to Hagrid./n/n"Beaky's gettin' a bit depressed," Hagrid told them,/nbending low on the pretense of checking that Harry's/nflobberworm was still alive. "Bin cooped up too long./nBut still ... we'll know day after tomorrow — one way/nor the other — "/n/nThey had Potions that afternoon, which was an/nunqualified disaster. Try as Harry might, he couldn't/nget his Confusing Concoction to thicken, and Snape,/nstanding watch with an air of vindictive pleasure,/nscribbled something that looked suspiciously like a/nzero onto his notes before moving away./n/nThen came Astronomy at midnight, up on the tallest/ntower; History of Magic on Wednesday morning, in/nwhich Harry scribbled everything Florean Fortescue/nhad ever told him about medieval witch-hunts, while/nwishing he could have had one of Fortescue 's choco-/nnut sundaes with him in the stifling classroom./nWednesday afternoon meant Herbology, in the/ngreenhouses under a baking-hot sun; then back to/nthe common room once more, with sunburnt necks,/nthinking longingly of this time next day, when it/nwould all be over./n/nTheir second to last exam, on Thursday morning, was/nDefense Against the Dark Arts. Professor Lupin had/ncompiled the most unusual exam any of them had/n/n/n/n/n/never taken; a sort of obstacle course outside in the/nsun, where they had to wade across a deep paddling/npool containing a grindylow, cross a series of potholes/nfull of Red Caps, squish their way across a patch of/nmarsh while ignoring misleading directions from a/nhinkypunk, then climb into an old trunk and battle/nwith a new boggart./n/n"Excellent, Harry," Lupin muttered as Harry climbed/nout of the trunk, grinning. "Full marks."/n/nFlushed with his success, Harry hung around to/nwatch Ron and Hermione. Ron did very well until he/nreached the hinkypunk, which successfully confused/nhim into sinking waist-high into the quagmire./nHermione did everything perfectly until she reached/nthe trunk with the boggart in it. After about a minute/ninside it, she burst out again, screaming./n/n"Hermione!" said Lupin, startled. "What's the matter?"/n/n"P — P — Professor McGonagall!" Hermione gasped,/npointing into the trunk. "Sh — she said I'd failed/neverything!"/n/nIt took a little while to calm Hermione down. When at/nlast she had regained a grip on herself, she, Harry,/nand Ron went back to the castle. Ron was still slightly/ninclined to laugh at Hermione 's boggart, but an/nargument was averted by the sight that met them on/nthe top of the steps./n/nCornelius Fudge, sweating slightly in his pinstriped/ncloak, was standing there staring out at the grounds./nHe started at the sight of Harry./n/n"Hello there, Harry!" he said. "Just had an exam, I/nexpect? Nearly finished?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes," said Harry. Hermione and Ron, not being on/nspeaking terms with the Minister of Magic, hovered/nawkwardly in the background./n/n"Lovely day," said Fudge, casting an eye over the lake./n"Pity ... pity ..."/n/nHe sighed deeply and looked down at Harry./n/n"I'm here on an unpleasant mission, Harry. The/nCommittee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures/nrequired a witness to the execution of a mad/nhippogriff. As I needed to visit Hogwarts to check on/nthe Black situation, I was asked to step in."/n/n"Does that mean the appeal's already happened?" Ron/ninterrupted, stepping forward./n/n"No, no, it's scheduled for this afternoon," said Fudge,/nlooking curiously at Ron./n/n"Then you might not have to witness an execution at/nall!" said Ron stoutly. "The hippogriff might get off!"/n/nBefore Fudge could answer, two wizards came/nthrough the castle doors behind him. One was so/nancient he appeared to be withering before their very/neyes; the other was tall and strapping, with a thin/nblack mustache. Harry gathered that they were/nrepresentatives of the Committee for the Disposal of/nDangerous Creatures, because the very old wizard/nsquinted toward Hagrid's cabin and said in a feeble/nvoice, "Dear, dear, I'm getting too old for this. ... Two/no'clock, isn't it, Fudge?"/n/nThe black-mustached man was fingering something in/nhis belt; Harry looked and saw that he was running/none broad thumb along the blade of a shining axe./n/nRon opened his mouth to say something, but/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione nudged him hard in the ribs and jerked her/nhead toward the entrance hall./n/n"Why'd you stop me?" said Ron angrily as they/nentered the Great Hall for lunch. "Did you see them?/nThey've even got the axe ready! This isn't justice!"/n/n"Ron, your dad works for the Ministry, you can't go/nsaying things like that to his boss!" said Hermione,/nbut she too looked very upset. "As long as Hagrid/nkeeps his head this time, and argues his case/nproperly, they can't possibly execute Buckbeak. ..."/n/nBut Harry could tell Hermione didn't really believe/nwhat she was saying. All around them, people were/ntalking excitedly as they ate their lunch, happily/nanticipating the end of the exams that afternoon, but/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione, lost in worry about Hagrid/nand Buckbeak, didn't join in./n/nHarry's and Ron's last exam was Divination;/nHermione's, Muggle Studies. They walked up the/nmarble staircase together; Hermione left them on the/nfirst floor and Harry and Ron proceeded all the way/nup to the seventh, where many of their class were/nsitting on the spiral staircase to Professor Trelawney's/nclassroom, trying to cram in a bit of last-minute/nstudying./n/n"She's seeing us all separately," Neville informed them/nas they went to sit down next to him. He had his copy/nof Unfogging the Future open on his lap at the pages/ndevoted to crystal gazing. "Have either of you ever/nseen anything in a crystal ball?" he asked them/nunhappily./n/n"Nope," said Ron in an offhand voice. He kept/nchecking his watch; Harry knew that he was counting/ndown the time until Buckbeak's appeal started./n/n/n/n/n/nThe line of people outside the classroom shortened/nvery slowly. As each person climbed back down the/nsilver ladder, the rest of the class hissed, "What did/nshe ask? Was it okay?"/n/nBut they all refused to say./n/n"She says the crystal ball's told her that if I tell you,/n/nI'll have a horrible accident!" squeaked Neville as he/nclambered back down the ladder toward Harry and/nRon, who had now reached the landing./n/n"That's convenient," snorted Ron. "You know, I'm/nstarting to think Hermione was right about her" — he/njabbed his thumb toward the trapdoor overhead —/n"she's a right old fraud."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, looking at his own watch. It was/nnow two o'clock. "Wish she'd hurry up ..."/n/nParvati came back down the ladder glowing with/npride./n/n"She says I've got all the makings of a true Seer," she/ninformed Harry and Ron. "I saw loads of stuff. ... Well,/ngood luck!"/n/nShe hurried off down the spiral staircase toward/nLavender./n/n"Ronald Weasley," said the familiar, misty voice from/nover their heads. Ron grimaced at Harry and climbed/nthe silver ladder out of sight. Harry was now the only/nperson left to be tested. He settled himself on the floor/nwith his back against the wall, listening to a fly/nbuzzing in the sunny window, his mind across the/ngrounds with Hagrid./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nFinally, after about twenty minutes, Ron's large feet/nreappeared on the ladder./n/n"How'd it go?" Harry asked him, standing up./n/n"Rubbish," said Ron. "Couldn't see a thing, so I made/nsome stuff up. Don't think she was convinced,/nthough. ..."/n/n"Meet you in the common room," Harry muttered as/nProfessor Trelawney's voice called, "Harry Potter!"/n/nThe tower room was hotter than ever before; the/ncurtains were closed, the fire was alight, and the/nusual sickly scent made Harry cough as he stumbled/nthrough the clutter of chairs and tables to where/nProfessor Trelawney sat waiting for him before a large/ncrystal ball./n/n"Good day, my dear," she said softly. "If you would/nkindly gaze into the Orb. ... Take your time, now .../nthen tell me what you see within it. ..."/n/nHarry bent over the crystal ball and stared, stared as/nhard as he could, willing it to show him something/nother than swirling white fog, but nothing happened./n/n"Well?" Professor Trelawney prompted delicately./n"What do you see?"/n/nThe heat was overpowering and his nostrils were/nstinging with the perfumed smoke wafting from the/nfire beside them. He thought of what Ron had just/nsaid, and decided to pretend./n/n"Er — " said Harry, "a dark shape ... um ..."/n/n"What does it resemble?" whispered Professor/nTrelawney. "Think, now ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry cast his mind around and it landed on/nBuckbeak./n/n"A hippogriff," he said firmly./n/n"Indeed!" whispered Professor Trelawney, scribbling/nkeenly on the parchment perched upon her knees./n"My boy, you may well be seeing the outcome of poor/nHagrid's trouble with the Ministry of Magic! Look/ncloser. . . . Does the hippogriff appear to . . . have its/nhead?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry firmly./n/n"Are you sure?" Professor Trelawney urged him. "Are/nyou quite sure, dear? You don't see it writhing on the/nground, perhaps, and a shadowy figure raising an axe/nbehind it?"/n/n"No!" said Harry, starting to feel slightly sick./n/n"No blood? No weeping Hagrid?"/n/n"No!" said Harry again, wanting more than ever to/nleave the room and the heat. "It looks fine, it's —/nflying away. ..."/n/nProfessor Trelawney sighed./n/n"Well, dear, I think we'll leave it there. ... A little/ndisappointing ... but I'm sure you did your best."/n/nRelieved, Harry got up, picked up his bag and turned/nto go, but then a loud, harsh voice spoke behind him./n/n"It will happen tonight."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry wheeled around. Professor Trelawney had gone/nrigid in her armchair; her eyes were unfocused and/nher mouth sagging./n/n"S — sorry?" said Harry./n/nBut Professor Trelawney didn't seem to hear him. Her/neyes started to roll. Harry sat there in a panic. She/nlooked as though she was about to have some sort of/nseizure. He hesitated, thinking of running to the/nhospital wing — and then Professor Trelawney spoke/nagain, in the same harsh voice, quite unlike her own:/n/n"The Dark Lord lies alone and friendless, abandoned/nby his followers. His servant has been chained these/ntwelve years. Tonight, before midnight ... the servant/nwill break free and set out to rejoin his master. The/nDark Lord will rise again with his servant's aid,/ngreater and more terrible than ever he was. Tonight .../nbefore midnight . . . the servant . . . will set out ... to/nrejoin ... his master. ..."/n/nProfessor Trelawney's head fell forward onto her/nchest. She made a grunting sort of noise. Harry sat/nthere, staring at her. Then, quite suddenly, Professor/nTrelawney's head snapped up again./n/n"I'm so sorry, dear boy," she said dreamily, "the heat/nof the day, you know ... I drifted off for a moment. ..."/n/nHarry sat there, staring at her./n/n"Is there anything wrong, my dear?"/n/n"You — you just told me that the — the Dark Lord's/ngoing to rise again ... that his servant's going to go/nback to him. ..."/n/nProfessor Trelawney looked thoroughly startled./n/n/n/n/n/n"The Dark Lord? He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named? My/ndear boy, that's hardly something to joke about. .../nRise again, indeed — "/n/n"But you just said it! You said the Dark Lord — "/n/n"I think you must have dozed off too, dear!" said/nProfessor Trelawney. "I would certainly not presume/nto predict anything quite as far-fetched as that\"/n/nHarry climbed back down the ladder and the spiral/nstaircase, wondering ... had he just heard Professor/nTrelawney make a real prediction? Or had that been/nher idea of an impressive end to the test?/n/nFive minutes later he was dashing past the security/ntrolls outside the entrance to Gryffindor Tower,/nProfessor Trelawney's words still resounding in his/nhead. People were striding past him in the opposite/ndirection, laughing and joking, heading for the/ngrounds and a bit of long-awaited freedom; by the/ntime he had reached the portrait hole and entered the/ncommon room, it was almost deserted. Over in the/ncorner, however, sat Ron and Hermione./n/n"Professor Trelawney," Harry panted, "just told me — "/n/nBut he stopped abruptly at the sight of their faces./n/n"Buckbeak lost," said Ron weakly. "Hagrid's just sent/nthis."/n/nHagrid's note was dry this time, no tears had/nsplattered it, yet his hand seemed to have shaken so/nmuch as he wrote that it was hardly legible./n/nLost appeal. They're going to execute at sunset/n/n/n/nNothing you can do. Don't come down./n/n/n/n/n/nI don't want you to see it/nHagrid/n/n"We've got to go," said Harry at once. "He can't just sit/nthere on his own, waiting for the executioner!"/n/n"Sunset, though," said Ron, who was staring out the/nwindow in a glazed sort of way. "We'd never be/nallowed ... 'specially you, Harry. ..."/n/nHarry sank his head into his hands, thinking./n/n"If we only had the Invisibility Cloak. ..."/n/n"Where is it?" said Hermione./n/nHarry told her about leaving it in the passageway/nunder the one-eyed witch./n/n"... if Snape sees me anywhere near there again, I'm/nin serious trouble," he finished./n/n"That's true," said Hermione, getting to her feet. "If he/nsees you. ... How do you open the witch's hump/nagain?"/n/n"You — you tap it and say, 'Dissendium,' " said Harry./n"But — "/n/nHermione didn't wait for the rest of his sentence; she/nstrode across the room, pushed open the Fat Lady's/nportrait and vanished from sight./n/n"She hasn't gone to get it?" Ron said, staring after/nher./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe had. Hermione returned a quarter of an hour/nlater with the silvery cloak folded carefully under her/nrobes./n/n"Hermione, I don't know what's gotten into you/nlately!" said Ron, astounded. "First you hit Malfoy,/nthen you walk out on Professor Trelawney — "/n/nHermione looked rather flattered./n/nThey went down to dinner with everybody else, but/ndid not return to Gryffindor Tower afterward. Harry/nhad the cloak hidden down the front of his robes; he/nhad to keep his arms folded to hide the lump. They/nskulked in an empty chamber off the entrance hall,/nlistening, until they were sure it was deserted. They/nheard a last pair of people hurrying across the hall/nand a door slamming. Hermione poked her head/naround the door./n/n"Okay," she whispered, "no one there — cloak on — "/n/nWalking very close together so that nobody would see/nthem, they crossed the hall on tiptoe beneath the/ncloak, then walked down the stone front steps into/nthe grounds. The sun was already sinking behind the/nForbidden Forest, gilding the top branches of the/ntrees./n/nThey reached Hagrid's cabin and knocked. He was a/nminute in answering, and when he did, he looked all/naround for his visitor, pale-faced and trembling./n/n"It's us," Harry hissed. "We're wearing the Invisibility/nCloak. Let us in and we can take it off."/n/n"Yeh shouldn've come!" Hagrid whispered, but he/nstood back, and they stepped inside. Hagrid shut the/ndoor quickly and Harry pulled off the cloak./n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid was not crying, nor did he throw himself upon/ntheir necks. He looked like a man who did not know/nwhere he was or what to do. This helplessness was/nworse to watch than tears./n/n"Wan' some tea?" he said. His great hands were/nshaking as he reached for the kettle./n/n"Where's Buckbeak, Hagrid?" said Hermione/nhesitantly./n/n"I — I took him outside," said Hagrid, spilling milk all/nover the table as he filled up the jug. "He's tethered in/nme pumpkin patch. Thought he oughta see the trees/nan' — an' smell fresh air — before — "/n/nHagrid 's hand trembled so violently that the milk jug/nslipped from his grasp and shattered all over the/nfloor./n/n"I'll do it, Hagrid," said Hermione quickly, hurrying/nover and starting to clean up the mess./n/n"There's another one in the cupboard," Hagrid said,/nsitting down and wiping his forehead on his sleeve./nHarry glanced at Ron, who looked back hopelessly./n/n"Isn't there anything anyone can do, Hagrid?" Harry/nasked fiercely, sitting down next to him. "Dumbledore/n/n/n/n"He's tried," said Hagrid. "He's got no power ter/noverrule the Committee. He told 'em Buckbeak's all/nright, but they're scared. ... Yeh know what Lucius/nMalfoy's like ... threatened 'em, I expect ... an' the/nexecutioner, Macnair, he's an old pal o' Malfoy's .../nbut it'll be quick an' clean ... an' I'll be beside him. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid swallowed. His eyes were darting all over the/ncabin as though looking for some shred of hope or/ncomfort./n/n"Dumbledore 's gonna come down while it — while it/nhappens. Wrote me this mornin'. Said he wants ter —/nter be with me. Great man, Dumbledore. ..."/n/nHermione, who had been rummaging in Hagrid 's/ncupboard for another milk jug, let out a small, quickly/nstifled sob. She straightened up with the new jug in/nher hands, fighting back tears./n/n"Well stay with you too, Hagrid," she began, but/nHagrid shook his shaggy head./n/n"Yeh're ter go back up ter the castle. I told yeh, I don'/nwan' yeh watchin'. An' yeh shouldn' be down here/nanyway. ... If Fudge an' Dumbledore catch yeh out/nwithout permission, Harry, yehll be in big trouble."/n/nSilent tears were now streaming down Hermione 's/nface, but she hid them from Hagrid, bustling around/nmaking tea. Then, as she picked up the milk bottle to/npour some into the jug, she let out a shriek./n/n"Ron! I — I don't believe it — it's Scabbersl"/n/nRon gaped at her./n/n"What are you talking about?"/n/nHermione carried the milk jug over to the table and/nturned it upside down. With a frantic squeak, and/nmuch scrambling to get back inside, Scabbers the rat/ncame sliding out onto the table./n/n"Scabbers!" said Ron blankly. "Scabbers, what are/nyou doing here?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHe grabbed the struggling rat and held him up to the/nlight. Scabbers looked dreadful. He was thinner than/never, large tufts of hair had fallen out leaving wide/nbald patches, and he writhed in Ron's hands as/nthough desperate to free himself./n/n"It's okay, Scabbers!" said Ron. "No cats! There's/nnothing here to hurt you!"/n/nHagrid suddenly stood up, his eyes fixed on the/nwindow. His normally ruddy face had gone the color/nof parchment./n/n"They're cornin'. ..."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione whipped around. A group/nof men was walking down the distant castle steps. In/nfront was Albus Dumbledore, his silver beard/ngleaming in the dying sun. Next to him trotted/nCornelius Fudge. Behind them came the feeble old/nCommittee member and the executioner, Macnair./n/n"Yeh gotta go," said Hagrid. Every inch of him was/ntrembling. "They mustn' find yeh here. ... Go now. ..."/n/nRon stuffed Scabbers into his pocket and Hermione/npicked up the cloak./n/n"I'll let yeh out the back way," said Hagrid./n/nThey followed him to the door into his back garden./nHarry felt strangely unreal, and even more so when/nhe saw Buckbeak a few yards away, tethered to a tree/nbehind Hagrid's pumpkin patch. Buckbeak seemed to/nknow something was happening. He turned his sharp/nhead from side to side and pawed the ground/nnervously./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's okay, Beaky," said Hagrid softly. "It's okay ..." He/nturned to Harry, Ron, and Hermione. "Go on," he/nsaid. "Get goin'."/n/nBut they didn't move./n/n"Hagrid, we can't — "/n/n"Well tell them what really happened — "/n/n"They can't kill him — "/n/n"Go!" said Hagrid fiercely. "It's bad enough without/nyou lot in trouble an' all!"/n/nThey had no choice. As Hermione threw the cloak/nover Harry and Ron, they heard voices at the front of/nthe cabin. Hagrid looked at the place where they had/njust vanished from sight./n/n"Go quick," he said hoarsely. "Don' listen. ..."/n/nAnd he strode back into his cabin as someone/nknocked at the front door./n/nSlowly, in a kind of horrified trance, Harry, Ron, and/nHermione set off silently around Hagrid's house. As/nthey reached the other side, the front door closed with/na sharp snap./n/n"Please, let's hurry," Hermione whispered. "I can't/nstand it, I can't bear it. ..."/n/nThey started up the sloping lawn toward the castle./nThe sun was sinking fast now; the sky had turned to/na clear, purple-tinged grey, but to the west there was/na ruby-red glow./n/nRon stopped dead./n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh, please, Ron," Hermione began./n/n"It's Scabbers — he won't — stay put — "/n/nRon was bent over, trying to keep Scabbers in his/npocket, but the rat was going berserk; squeaking/nmadly, twisting and flailing, trying to sink his teeth/ninto Ron's hand./n/n"Scabbers, it's me, you idiot, it's Ron," Ron hissed./n/nThey heard a door open behind them and men's/nvoices./n/n"Oh, Ron, please let's move, they're going to do it!"/nHermione breathed./n/n"Okay — Scabbers, stay put — "/n/nThey walked forward; Harry, like Hermione, was/ntrying not to listen to the rumble of voices behind/nthem. Ron stopped again./n/n"I can't hold him — Scabbers, shut up, everyone'll/nhear us — "/n/nThe rat was squealing wildly, but not loudly enough/nto cover up the sounds drifting from Hagrid's garden./nThere was a jumble of indistinct male voices, a/nsilence, and then, without warning, the unmistakable/nswish and thud of an axe./n/nHermione swayed on the spot./n/n"They did it!" she whispered to Harry. "I d — don't/nbelieve it — they did it!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Cat, Rat, And Dog
text: /n/n/nHarry's mind had gone blank with shock. The three of/nthem stood transfixed with horror under the/nInvisibility Cloak. The very last rays of the setting sun/nwere casting a bloody light over the long-shadowed/ngrounds. Then, behind them, they heard a wild/nhowling./n/n"Hagrid," Harry muttered. Without thinking about/nwhat he was doing, he made to turn back, but both/nRon and Hermione seized his arms./n/n"We can't," said Ron, who was paper-white. "He'll be/nin worse trouble if they know we've been to see him./n/n/n/nHermione 's breathing was shallow and uneven./n/n"How — could — they?" she choked. "How could/nthey?"/n/n"Come on," said Ron, whose teeth seemed to be/nchattering./n/n/n/n/nThey set off back toward the castle, walking slowly to/nkeep themselves hidden under the cloak. The light/nwas fading fast now. By the time they reached open/nground, darkness was settling like a spell around/nthem./n/n"Scabbers, keep still," Ron hissed, clamping his hand/nover his chest. The rat was wriggling madly. Ron/ncame to a sudden halt, trying to force Scabbers/ndeeper into his pocket. "What's the matter with you,/nyou stupid rat? Stay still — OUCH! He bit me!"/n/n"Ron, be quiet!" Hermione whispered urgently./n"Fudge'll be out here in a minute — "/n/n"He won't — stay — put — "/n/nScabbers was plainly terrified. He was writhing with/nall his might, trying to break free of Ron's grip./n/n"What's the matter with him?"/n/nBut Harry had just seen — slinking toward them, his/nbody low to the ground, wide yellow eyes glinting/neerily in the darkness — Crookshanks. Whether he/ncould see them or was following the sound of/nScabbers's squeaks, Harry couldn't tell./n/n"Crookshanks!" Hermione moaned. "No, go away,/nCrookshanks! Go away!"/n/nBut the cat was getting nearer —/n/n"Scabbers — NO!"/n/nToo late — the rat had slipped between Ron's/nclutching fingers, hit the ground, and scampered/naway. In one bound, Crookshanks sprang after him,/nand before Harry or Hermione could stop him, Ron/n/n/n/n/n/nhad thrown the Invisibility Cloak off himself and/npelted away into the darkness./n/n/n/n"Ron\" Hermione moaned./n/nShe and Harry looked at each other, then followed at/na sprint; it was impossible to run full out under the/ncloak; they pulled it off and it streamed behind them/nlike a banner as they hurtled after Ron; they could/nhear his feet thundering along ahead and his shouts/nat Crookshanks./n/n"Get away from him — get away — Scabbers, come/nhere — "/n/nThere was a loud thud./n/n"Gotchal Get off, you stinking cat — "/n/nHarry and Hermione almost fell over Ron; they/nskidded to a stop right in front of him. He was/nsprawled on the ground, but Scabbers was back in/nhis pocket; he had both hands held tight over the/nquivering lump./n/n"Ron — come on — back under the cloak — "/n/nHermione panted. "Dumbledore — the Minister —/nthey'll be coming back out in a minute — "/n/nBut before they could cover themselves again, before/nthey could even catch their breath, they heard the/nsoft pounding of gigantic paws. ... Something was/nbounding toward them, quiet as a shadow — an/nenormous, pale-eyed, jet-black dog./n/nHarry reached for his wand, but too late — the dog/nhad made an enormous leap and the front paws hit/nhim on the chest; he keeled over backward in a whirl/nof hair; he felt its hot breath, saw inch-long teeth —/n/n/n/n/n/nBut the force of its leap had carried it too far; it rolled/noff him. Dazed, feeling as though his ribs were/nbroken, Harry tried to stand up; he could hear it/ngrowling as it skidded around for a new attack./n/nRon was on his feet. As the dog sprang back toward/nthem he pushed Harry aside; the dog's jaws fastened/ninstead around Ron's outstretched arm. Harry lunged/nforward, he seized a handful of the brute's hair, but it/nwas dragging Ron away as easily as though he were a/nrag doll —/n/nThen, out of nowhere, something hit Harry so hard/nacross the face he was knocked off his feet again. He/nheard Hermione shriek with pain and fall too./n/nHarry groped for his wand, blinking blood out of his/neyes —/n/n"Lumos\" he whispered./n/nThe wandlight showed him the trunk of a thick tree;/nthey had chased Scabbers into the shadow of the/nWhomping Willow and its branches were creaking as/nthough in a high wind, whipping backward and/nforward to stop them going nearer./n/nAnd there, at the base of the trunk, was the dog,/ndragging Ron backward into a large gap in the roots/n— Ron was fighting furiously, but his head and torso/nwere slipping out of sight —/n/n"Ron!" Harry shouted, trying to follow, but a heavy/nbranch whipped lethally through the air and he was/nforced backward again./n/nAll they could see now was one of Ron's legs, which/nhe had hooked around a root in an effort to stop the/ndog from pulling him farther underground — but a/n/n/n/n/n/nhorrible crack cut the air like a gunshot; Ron's leg/nhad broken, and a moment later, his foot vanished/nfrom sight./n/n"Harry — we've got to go for help — " Hermione/ngasped; she was bleeding too; the Willow had cut her/nacross the shoulder./n/n"No! That thing's big enough to eat him; we haven't/ngot time — "/n/n"Harry — we're never going to get through without/nhelp — "/n/nAnother branch whipped down at them, twigs/nclenched like knuckles./n/n"If that dog can get in, we can," Harry panted, darting/nhere and there, trying to find a way through the/nvicious, swishing branches, but he couldn't get an/ninch nearer to the tree roots without being in range of/nthe tree's blows./n/n"Oh, help, help," Hermione whispered frantically,/ndancing uncertainly on the spot, "please ..."/n/nCrookshanks darted forward. He slithered between/nthe battering branches like a snake and placed his/nfront paws upon a knot on the trunk./n/nAbruptly, as though the tree had been turned to/nmarble, it stopped moving. Not a leaf twitched or/nshook./n/n"Crookshanks!" Hermione whispered uncertainly. She/nnow grasped Harry's arm painfully hard. "How did he/nknow — ?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He's friends with that dog," said Harry grimly. "I've/nseen them together. Come on — and keep your wand/nout — "/n/nThey covered the distance to the trunk in seconds,/nbut before they had reached the gap in the roots,/nCrookshanks had slid into it with a flick of his/nbottlebrush tail. Harry went next; he crawled forward,/nheadfirst, and slid down an earthy slope to the/nbottom of a very low tunnel. Crookshanks was a little/nway along, his eyes flashing in the light from Harry's/nwand. Seconds later, Hermione slithered down beside/nhim./n/n"Where's Ron?" she whispered in a terrified voice./n/n"This way," said Harry, setting off, bent-backed, after/nCrookshanks./n/n"Where does this tunnel come out?" Hermione asked/nbreathlessly from behind him./n/n"I don't know. ... It's marked on the Marauder's Map/nbut Fred and George said no one's ever gotten into it./n...It goes off the edge of the map, but it looked like it/nwas heading for Hogsmeade. ..."/n/nThey moved as fast as they could, bent almost double;/nahead of them, Crookshanks 's tail bobbed in and out/nof view. On and on went the passage; it felt at least as/nlong as the one to Honeydukes. ... All Harry could/nthink of was Ron and what the enormous dog might/nbe doing to him. ... He was drawing breath in sharp,/npainful gasps, running at a crouch. .../n/nAnd then the tunnel began to rise; moments later it/ntwisted, and Crookshanks had gone. Instead, Harry/ncould see a patch of dim light through a small/nopening./n/n/n/n/n/nHe and Hermione paused, gasping for breath, edging/nforward. Both raised their wands to see what lay/nbeyond./n/nIt was a room, a very disordered, dusty room. Paper/nwas peeling from the walls; there were stains all over/nthe floor; every piece of furniture was broken as/nthough somebody had smashed it. The windows were/nall boarded up./n/nHarry glanced at Hermione, who looked very/nfrightened but nodded./n/nHarry pulled himself out of the hole, staring around./nThe room was deserted, but a door to their right stood/nopen, leading to a shadowy hallway. Hermione/nsuddenly grabbed Harry's arm again. Her wide eyes/nwere traveling around the boarded windows./n/n"Harry," she whispered, "I think we're in the Shrieking/nShack."/n/nHarry looked around. His eyes fell on a wooden chair/nnear them. Large chunks had been torn out of it; one/nof the legs had been ripped off entirely./n/n"Ghosts didn't do that," he said slowly./n/nAt that moment, there was a creak overhead./nSomething had moved upstairs. Both of them looked/nup at the ceiling. Hermione 's grip on Harry's arm was/nso tight he was losing feeling in his fingers. He raised/nhis eyebrows at her; she nodded again and let go./n/nQuietly as they could, they crept out into the hall and/nup the crumbling staircase. Everything was covered/nin a thick layer of dust except the floor, where a wide/nshiny stripe had been made by something being/ndragged upstairs./n/n/n/n/n/nThey reached the dark landing./n/n/n/n"Nox," they whispered together, and the lights at the/nend of their wands went out. Only one door was open./nAs they crept toward it, they heard movement from/nbehind it; a low moan, and then a deep, loud purring./nThey exchanged a last look, a last nod./n/nWand held tightly before him, Harry kicked the door/nwide open./n/nOn a magnificent four-poster bed with dusty hangings/nlay Crookshanks, purring loudly at the sight of them./nOn the floor beside him, clutching his leg, which/nstuck out at a strange angle, was Ron./n/nHarry and Hermione dashed across to him./n/n"Ron — are you okay?"/n/n"Where's the dog?"/n/n"Not a dog," Ron moaned. His teeth were gritted with/npain. "Harry, it's a trap — "/n/n"What — "/n/n"He's the dog ... he's an Animagus. ..."/n/nRon was staring over Harry's shoulder. Harry wheeled/naround. With a snap, the man in the shadows closed/nthe door behind them./n/nA mass of filthy, matted hair hung to his elbows. If/neyes hadn't been shining out of the deep, dark/nsockets, he might have been a corpse. The waxy skin/nwas stretched so tightly over the bones of his face, it/nlooked like a skull. His yellow teeth were bared in a/ngrin. It was Sirius Black./n/n/n/n/n/n" ExpelliarmusV' he croaked, pointing Ron's wand at/nthem./n/nHarry's and Hermione's wands shot out of their/nhands, high in the air, and Black caught them. Then/nhe took a step closer. His eyes were fixed on Harry./n/n"I thought you'd come and help your friend," he said/nhoarsely. His voice sounded as though he had long/nsince lost the habit of using it. "Your father would/nhave done the same for me. Brave of you, not to run/nfor a teacher. I'm grateful ... it will make everything/nmuch easier. ..."/n/nThe taunt about his father rang in Harry's ears as/nthough Black had bellowed it. A boiling hate erupted/nin Harry's chest, leaving no place for fear. For the first/ntime in his life, he wanted his wand back in his hand,/nnot to defend himself, but to attack ... to kill. Without/nknowing what he was doing, he started forward, but/nthere was a sudden movement on either side of him/nand two pairs of hands grabbed him and held him/nback. ... "No, Harry!" Hermione gasped in a petrified/nwhisper; Ron, however, spoke to Black./n/n"If you want to kill Harry, you'll have to kill us too!"/nhe said fiercely, though the effort of standing upright/nwas draining him of still more color, and he swayed/nslightly as he spoke./n/nSomething flickered in Black's shadowed eyes./n/n"Lie down," he said quietly to Ron. "You will damage/nthat leg even more."/n/n"Did you hear me?" Ron said weakly, though he was/nclinging painfully to Harry to stay upright. "You'll/nhave to kill all three of us!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"There'll be only one murder here tonight," said Black,/nand his grin widened./n/n/n/n"Why's that?" Harry spat, trying to wrench himself/nfree of Ron and Hermione. "Didn't care last time, did/nyou? Didn't mind slaughtering all those Muggles to/nget at Pettigrew. ... What's the matter, gone soft in/nAzkaban?"/n/n"Harry!" Hermione whimpered. "Be quiet!"/n/n"HE KILLED MY MUM AND DAD!" Harry roared, and/nwith a huge effort he broke free of Hermione 's and/nRon's restraint and lunged forward —/n/nHe had forgotten about magic — he had forgotten that/nhe was short and skinny and thirteen, whereas Black/nwas a tall, full-grown man — all Harry knew was that/nhe wanted to hurt Black as badly as he could and/nthat he didn't care how much he got hurt in return —/n/nPerhaps it was the shock of Harry doing something so/nstupid, but Black didn't raise the wands in time —/none of Harry's hands fastened over his wasted wrist,/nforcing the wand tips away; the knuckles of Harry's/nother hand collided with the side of Black's head and/nthey fell, backward, into the wall —/n/nHermione was screaming; Ron was yelling; there was/na blinding flash as the wands in Black's hand sent a/njet of sparks into the air that missed Harry's face by/ninches; Harry felt the shrunken arm under his fingers/ntwisting madly, but he clung on, his other hand/npunching every part of Black it could find./n/nBut Black's free hand had found Harry's throat —/n/n"No," he hissed, "I've waited too long — "/n/n/n/n/n/nThe fingers tightened, Harry choked, his glasses/naskew./n/nThen he saw Hermione 's foot swing out of nowhere./nBlack let go of Harry with a grunt of pain; Ron had/nthrown himself on Black's wand hand and Harry/nheard a faint clatter —/n/nHe fought free of the tangle of bodies and saw his own/nwand rolling across the floor; he threw himself toward/nit but —/n/n"Argh!"/n/nCrookshanks had joined the fray; both sets of front/nclaws had sunk themselves deep into Harry's arm;/nHarry threw him off, but Crookshanks now darted/ntoward Harry's wand —/n/n"NO YOU DONT!" roared Harry, and he aimed a kick/nat Crookshanks that made the cat leap aside,/nspitting; Harry snatched up his wand and turned —/n/n"Get out of the way!" he shouted at Ron and/nHermione./n/nThey didn't need telling twice. Hermione, gasping for/nbreath, her lip bleeding, scrambled aside, snatching/nup her and Ron's wands. Ron crawled to the four-/nposter and collapsed onto it, panting, his white face/nnow tinged with green, both hands clutching his/nbroken leg./n/nBlack was sprawled at the bottom of the wall. His thin/nchest rose and fell rapidly as he watched Harry/nwalking slowly nearer, his wand pointing straight at/nBlack's heart./n/n"Going to kill me, Harry?" he whispered./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry stopped right above him, his wand still pointing/nat Black's chest, looking down at him. A livid bruise/nwas rising around Black's left eye and his nose was/nbleeding./n/n"You killed my parents," said Harry, his voice shaking/nslightly, but his wand hand quite steady./n/nBlack stared up at him out of those sunken eyes./n/n"I don't deny it," he said very quietly. "But if you knew/nthe whole story."/n/n"The whole story?" Harry repeated, a furious/npounding in his ears. "You sold them to Voldemort./nThat's all I need to know."/n/n"You've got to listen to me," Black said, and there was/na note of urgency in his voice now. "You'll regret it if/nyou don't. ... You don't understand. ..."/n/n"I understand a lot better than you think," said Harry,/nand his voice shook more than ever. "You never heard/nher, did you?
