text: /n"Shocking business ... shocking ... miracle none of/nthem died . . . never heard the like ... by thunder, it/nwas lucky you were there, Snape. ..."/n/n"Thank you, Minister."/n/n"Order of Merlin, Second Class, I'd say. First Class, if/nI can wangle it!"/n/n"Thank you very much indeed, Minister."/n/n"Nasty cut you've got there. ... Black's work, I/nsuppose?"/n/n"As a matter of fact, it was Potter, Weasley, and/nGranger, Minister. ..."/n/n"iVo!"/n/n"Black had bewitched them, I saw it immediately. A/nConfundus Charm, to judge by their behavior. They/nseemed to think there was a possibility he was/n/n/n/n/ninnocent. They weren't responsible for their actions./nOn the other hand, their interference might have/npermitted Black to escape. ... They obviously thought/nthey were going to catch Black single-handed. They've/ngot away with a great deal before now. ... I'm afraid/nit's given them a rather high opinion of themselves .../nand of course Potter has always been allowed an/nextraordinary amount of license by the headmaster —/n/n/n/n"Ah, well, Snape ... Harry Potter, you know ... we've/nall got a bit of a blind spot where he's concerned."/n/n"And yet — is it good for him to be given so much/nspecial treatment? Personally, I try and treat him like/nany other student. And any other student would be/nsuspended — at the very least — for leading his/nfriends into such danger. Consider, Minister —/nagainst all school rules — after all the precautions/nput in place for his protection — out-of-bounds, at/nnight, consorting with a werewolf and a murderer —/nand I have reason to believe he has been visiting/nHogsmeade illegally too — "/n/n"Well, well ... we shall see, Snape, we shall see. ... The/nboy has undoubtedly been foolish. ..."/n/nHarry lay listening with his eyes tight shut. He felt/nvery groggy. The words he was hearing seemed to be/ntraveling very slowly from his ears to his brain, so/nthat it was difficult to understand. ... His limbs felt/nlike lead; his eyelids too heavy to lift. ... He wanted to/nlie here, on this comfortable bed, forever. .../n/n"What amazes me most is the behavior of the/ndementors ... you've really no idea what made them/nretreat, Snape?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No, Minister ... by the time I had come 'round they/nwere heading back to their positions at the entrances./n/n/n/n"Extraordinary. And yet Black, and Harry, and the girl/n/n/n/n"All unconscious by the time I reached them. I bound/nand gagged Black, naturally, conjured stretchers, and/nbrought them all straight back to the castle."/n/nThere was a pause. Harry's brain seemed to be/nmoving a little faster, and as it did, a gnawing/nsensation grew in the pit of his stomach. .../n/nHe opened his eyes./n/nEverything was slightly blurred. Somebody had/nremoved his glasses. He was lying in the dark hospital/nwing. At the very end of the ward, he could make out/nMadam Pomfrey with her back to him, bending over a/nbed. Harry squinted. Ron's red hair was visible/nbeneath Madam Pomfrey's arm./n/nHarry moved his head over on the pillow. In the bed/nto his right lay Hermione. Moonlight was falling/nacross her bed. Her eyes were open too. She looked/npetrified, and when she saw that Harry was awake,/npressed a finger to her lips, then pointed to the/nhospital wing door. It was ajar, and the voices of/nCornelius Fudge and Snape were coming through it/nfrom the corridor outside./n/nMadam Pomfrey now came walking briskly up the/ndark ward to Harry's bed. He turned to look at her./nShe was carrying the largest block of chocolate he/nhad ever seen in his life. It looked like a small/nboulder./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah, you're awake!" she said briskly. She placed the/nchocolate on Harry's bedside table and began/nbreaking it apart with a small hammer./n/n"How's Ron?" said Harry and Hermione together./n/n"He'll live," said Madam Pomfrey grimly. "As for you/ntwo ... you'll be staying here until I'm satisfied you're/n— Potter, what do you think you're doing?"/n/nHarry was sitting up, putting his glasses back on, and/npicking up his wand./n/n"I need to see the headmaster," he said./n/n"Potter," said Madam Pomfrey soothingly, "it's all/nright. They've got Black. He's locked away upstairs./nThe dementors will be performing the kiss any/nmoment now — "/n/n"WHAT?"/n/nHarry jumped up out of bed; Hermione had done the/nsame. But his shout had been heard in the corridor/noutside; next second, Cornelius Fudge and Snape had/nentered the ward./n/n"Harry, Harry, what's this?" said Fudge, looking/nagitated. "You should be in bed — has he had any/nchocolate?" he asked Madam Pomfrey anxiously./n/n"Minister, listen!" Harry said. "Sirius Black's innocent!/nPeter Pettigrew faked his own death! We saw him/ntonight! You can't let the dementors do that thing to/nSirius, he's — "/n/nBut Fudge was shaking his head with a small smile/non his face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, Harry, you're very confused, you've been/nthrough a dreadful ordeal, lie back down, now, we've/ngot everything under control. ..."/n/n"YOU HAVEN'T!" Harry yelled. "YOU VE GOT THE/nWRONG MAN!"/n/n"Minister, listen, please," Hermione said; she had/nhurried to Harry's side and was gazing imploringly/ninto Fudge's face. "I saw him too. It was Ron's rat,/nhe's an Animagus, Pettigrew, I mean, and — "/n/n"You see, Minister?" said Snape. "Confunded, both of/nthem. ... Black's done a very good job on them. ..."/n/n"WE'RE NOT CONFUNDED!" Harry roared./n/n"Minister! Professor!" said Madam Pomfrey angrily. "I/nmust insist that you leave. Potter is my patient, and/nhe should not be distressed!"/n/n"I'm not distressed, I'm trying to tell them what/nhappened!" Harry said furiously. "If they'd just listen/n/n/n/nBut Madam Pomfrey suddenly stuffed a large chunk/nof chocolate into Harry's mouth; he choked, and she/nseized the opportunity to force him back onto the bed./n/n"Now, please, Minister, these children need care./nPlease leave — "/n/nThe door opened again. It was Dumbledore. Harry/nswallowed his mouthful of chocolate with great/ndifficulty and got up again./n/n"Professor Dumbledore, Sirius Black — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"For heaven's sake!" said Madam Pomfrey/nhysterically. "Is this a hospital wing or not?/nHeadmaster, I must insist — "/n/n"My apologies, Poppy, but I need a word with Mr./nPotter and Miss Granger," said Dumbledore calmly. "I/nhave just been talking to Sirius Black — "/n/n"I suppose he's told you the same fairy tale he's/nplanted in Potter's mind?" spat Snape. "Something/nabout a rat, and Pettigrew being alive — "/n/n"That, indeed, is Black's story," said Dumbledore,/nsurveying Snape closely through his half-moon/nspectacles./n/n"And does my evidence count for nothing?" snarled/nSnape. "Peter Pettigrew was not in the Shrieking/nShack, nor did I see any sign of him on the grounds."/n/n"That was because you were knocked out, Professor!"/nsaid Hermione earnestly. "You didn't arrive in time to/nhear — "/n/n"Miss Granger, HOLD YOUR TONGUE!"/n/n"Now, Snape," said Fudge, startled, "the young lady is/ndisturbed in her mind, we must make allowances — "/n/n"I would like to speak to Harry and Hermione alone,"/nsaid Dumbledore abruptly. "Cornelius, Severus,/n/nPoppy — please leave us."/n/n"Headmaster!" sputtered Madam Pomfrey "They need/ntreatment, they need rest — "/n/n"This cannot wait," said Dumbledore. "I must insist."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMadam Pomfrey pursed her lips and strode away into/nher office at the end of the ward, slamming the door/nbehind her. Fudge consulted the large gold pocket/nwatch dangling from his waistcoat./n/n"The dementors should have arrived by now," he said./n"Ill go and meet them. Dumbledore, 111 see you/nupstairs."/n/nHe crossed to the door and held it open for Snape,/nbut Snape hadn't moved./n/n"You surely don't believe a word of Black's story?"/nSnape whispered, his eyes fixed on Dumbledore 's/nface./n/n"I wish to speak to Harry and Hermione alone,"/nDumbledore repeated./n/nSnape took a step toward Dumbledore./n/n"Sirius Black showed he was capable of murder at the/nage of sixteen," he breathed. "You haven't forgotten/nthat, Headmaster? You haven't forgotten that he once/ntried to kill me?"/n/n"My memory is as good as it ever was, Severus," said/nDumbledore quietly./n/nSnape turned on his heel and marched through the/ndoor Fudge was still holding. It closed behind them,/nand Dumbledore turned to Harry and Hermione. They/nboth burst into speech at the same time./n/n"Professor, Black's telling the truth — we saw/nPettigrew — "/n/n" — he escaped when Professor Lupin turned into a/nwerewolf — "/n/n/n/n/n/n" — he's a rat — "/n/n/n/n" — Pettigrew's front paw, I mean, finger, he cut it off/n/n/n/n" — Pettigrew attacked Ron, it wasn't Sirius — "/n/nBut Dumbledore held up his hand to stem the flood of/nexplanations./n/n"It is your turn to listen, and I beg you will not/ninterrupt me, because there is very little time," he/nsaid quietly. "There is not a shred of proof to support/nBlack's story, except your word — and the word of/ntwo thirteen-year-old wizards will not convince/nanybody. A street full of eyewitnesses swore they saw/nSirius murder Pettigrew. I myself gave evidence to the/nMinistry that Sirius had been the Potters' Secret-/nKeeper."/n/n"Professor Lupin can tell you — " Harry said, unable to/nstop himself./n/n"Professor Lupin is currently deep in the forest,/nunable to tell anyone anything. By the time he is/nhuman again, it will be too late, Sirius will be worse/nthan dead. I might add that werewolves are so/nmistrusted by most of our kind that his support will/ncount for very little — and the fact that he and Sirius/nare old friends — "/n/n"But — "/n/n" Listen to me, Harry. It is too late, you understand/nme? You must see that Professor Snape's version of/nevents is far more convincing than yours."/n/n"He hates Sirius," Hermione said desperately. "All/nbecause of some stupid trick Sirius played on him — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Sirius has not acted like an innocent man. The/nattack on the Fat Lady — entering Gryffindor Tower/nwith a knife — without Pettigrew, alive or dead, we/nhave no chance of overturning Sirius's sentence."/n/n"But you believe us."/n/n"Yes, I do," said Dumbledore quietly. "But I have no/npower to make other men see the truth, or to overrule/nthe Minister of Magic. ..."/n/nHarry stared up into the grave face and felt as though/nthe ground beneath him were falling sharply away. He/nhad grown used to the idea that Dumbledore could/nsolve anything. He had expected Dumbledore to pull/nsome amazing solution out of the air. But no . . . their/nlast hope was gone./n/n"What we need," said Dumbledore slowly, and his/nlight blue eyes moved from Harry to Hermione, "is/nmore time."/n/n"But — " Hermione began. And then her eyes became/nvery round. "OH!"/n/n"Now, pay attention," said Dumbledore, speaking very/nlow, and very clearly. "Sirius is locked in Professor/nFlitwick's office on the seventh floor. Thirteenth/nwindow from the right of the West Tower. If all goes/nwell, you will be able to save more than one innocent/nlife tonight. But remember this, both of you: you must/nnot be seen. Miss Granger, you know the law — you/nknow what is at stake. ... You — must — not — be —/nseen."/n/nHarry didn't have a clue what was going on./nDumbledore had turned on his heel and looked back/nas he reached the door./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I am going to lock you in. It is — " he consulted his/nwatch, "five minutes to midnight. Miss Granger, three/nturns should do it. Good luck."/n/n"Good luck?" Harry repeated as the door closed/nbehind Dumbledore. "Three turns? What's he talking/nabout? What are we supposed to do?"/n/nBut Hermione was fumbling with the neck of her/nrobes, pulling from beneath them a very long, very/nfine gold chain./n/n"Harry, come here," she said urgently. "Quick)."/n/nHarry moved toward her, completely bewildered. She/nwas holding the chain out. He saw a tiny, sparkling/nhourglass hanging from it./n/n"Here — "/n/nShe had thrown the chain around his neck too./n/n"Ready?" she said breathlessly./n/n"What are we doing?" Harry said, completely lost./n/nHermione turned the hourglass over three times./n/nThe dark ward dissolved. Harry had the sensation/nthat he was flying very fast, backward. A blur of/ncolors and shapes rushed past him, his ears were/npounding, he tried to yell but couldn't hear his own/nvoice —/n/nAnd then he felt solid ground beneath his feet, and/neverything came into focus again —/n/nHe was standing next to Hermione in the deserted/nentrance hall and a stream of golden sunlight was/n/n/n/n/n/nfalling across the paved floor from the open front/ndoors. He looked wildly around at Hermione, the/nchain of the hourglass cutting into his neck./n/n"Hermione, what — ?"/n/n"In here!" Hermione seized Harry's arm and dragged/nhim across the hall to the door of a broom closet; she/nopened it, pushed him inside among the buckets and/nmops, then slammed the door behind them./n/n"What — how — Hermione, what happened?"/n/n"We've gone back in time," Hermione whispered,/nlifting the chain off Harry's neck in the darkness./n"Three hours back ..."/n/nHarry found his own leg and gave it a very hard/npinch. It hurt a lot, which seemed to rule out the/npossibility that he was having a very bizarre dream./n/n"But — "/n/n"Shh! Listen! Someone's coming! I think — I think it/nmight be us!"/n/nHermione had her ear pressed against the cupboard/ndoor./n/n"Footsteps across the hall ... yes, I think it's us going/ndown to Hagrid's!"/n/n"Are you telling me," Harry whispered, "that we're/nhere in this cupboard and we're out there too?"/n/n"Yes," said Hermione, her ear still glued to the/ncupboard door. "I'm sure it's us. It doesn't sound like/nmore than three people ... and we're walking slowly/nbecause we're under the Invisibility Cloak — "/n/n/n/n/n/nShe broke off, still listening intently./n/n/n/n"We've gone down the front steps. ..."/n/nHermione sat down on an upturned bucket, looking/ndesperately anxious, but Harry wanted a few/nquestions answered./n/n"Where did you get that hourglass thing?"/n/n"It's called a Time-Turner," Hermione whispered, "and/nI got it from Professor McGonagall on our first day/nback. I've been using it all year to get to all my/nlessons. Professor McGonagall made me swear I/nwouldn't tell anyone. She had to write all sorts of/nletters to the Ministry of Magic so I could have one./nShe had to tell them that I was a model student, and/nthat I'd never, ever use it for anything except my/nstudies. ... I've been turning it back so I could do/nhours over again, that's how I've been doing several/nlessons at once, see? But .../n/n"Harry, I don't understand what Dumbledore wants us/nto do. Why did he tell us to go back three hours?/n/nHow's that going to help Sirius?"/n/nHarry stared at her shadowy face./n/n"There must be something that happened around now/nhe wants us to change," he said slowly. "What/nhappened? We were walking down to Hagrid's three/nhours ago. ..."/n/n"This is three hours ago, and we are walking down to/nHagrid's," said Hermione. "We just heard ourselves/nleaving. ..."/n/nHarry frowned; he felt as though he were screwing up/nhis whole brain in concentration./n/n/n/n/n/n"Dumbledore just said — just said we could save/nmore than one innocent life. ..." And then it hit him./n"Hermione, we're going to save Buckbeak!"/n/n"But — how will that help Sirius?"/n/n"Dumbledore said — he just told us where the/nwindow is — the window of Flitwick's office! Where/nthey've got Sirius locked up! We've got to fly/nBuckbeak up to the window and rescue Sirius! Sirius/ncan escape on Buckbeak — they can escape together!"/n/nFrom what Harry could see of Hermione's face, she/nlooked terrified./n/n"If we manage that without being seen, it'll be a/nmiracle!"/n/n"Well, we've got to try, haven't we?" said Harry. He/nstood up and pressed his ear against the door./n/n"Doesn't sound like anyone's there. ... Come on, let's/n/ngo. ..."/n/nHarry pushed open the closet door. The entrance hall/nwas deserted. As quietly and quickly as they could,/nthey darted out of the closet and down the stone/nsteps. "I have no hesitation in saying/n/n/n/n/n/nthat James would have been highly disappointed if/nhis son had never found any of the secret passages/nout of the castle."/n/nThere was a knock on the door. "It has/nbeen a real pleasure teaching you. I feel sure we'll/nmeet again sometime. Professor/nTrelawney's prediction!/n/n"Professor Dumbledore — yesterday, when I was/nhaving my Divination exam, Professor Trelawney went/nvery — very strange."/n/n"Indeed?" said Dumbledore. "He would have saved/nPettigrew too, I am sure of it."/n/nHarry looked up at him. Dumbledore wouldn't laugh/n— he could tell Dumbledore . . ./n/n/n/n/n/n"I thought it was my dad who'd conjured my/nPatronus. You found him inside/nyourself."/n/nAnd Dumbledore left the office, leaving Harry to his/nvery confused thoughts./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNobody at Hogwarts now knew the truth of what had/nhappened the night that Sirius, Buckbeak, and/nPettigrew had vanished except Harry, Ron, Hermione,/nand Professor Dumbledore. A muscle twitched/nunpleasantly at the corner of Snape's thin mouth/nevery time he looked at Harry, and he was constantly/nflexing his fingers, as though itching to place them/naround Harry's throat./n/nPercy had got his top-grade N.E.W.T.s; Fred and/nGeorge had scraped a handful of O.W.L.s each./nGryffindor House, meanwhile, largely thanks to their/nspectacular performance in the Quidditch Cup, had/nwon the House championship for the third year/nrunning. I know how/nto use a fellytone now — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"A telephone, Ron," said Hermione. "Honestly, you/nshould take Muggle Studies next year. ..."/n/nRon ignored her./n/n"It's the Quidditch World Cup this summer! How/nabout it, Harry? Come and stay, and we'll go and see/nit! Dad can usually get tickets from work."/n/nThis proposal had the effect of cheering Harry up a/ngreat deal./n/n"Yeah ... I bet the Dursleys'd be pleased to let me/ncome ... especially after what I did to Aunt Marge. ..."/n/nFeeling considerably more cheerful, Harry joined Ron/nand Hermione in several games of Exploding Snap,/nand when the witch with the tea cart arrived, he/nbought himself a very large lunch, though nothing/nwith chocolate in it./n/nBut it was late in the afternoon before the thing that/nmade him truly happy turned up. .../n/n"Harry," said Hermione suddenly, peering over his/nshoulder. "What's that thing outside your window?"/n/nHarry turned to look outside. Something very small/nand gray was bobbing in and out of sight beyond the/nglass. He stood up for a better look and saw that it/nwas a tiny owl, carrying a letter that was much too/nbig for it. The owl was so small, in fact, that it kept/ntumbling over in the air, buffeted this way and that in/nthe train's slipstream. Harry quickly pulled down the/nwindow, stretched out his arm, and caught it. It felt/nlike a very fluffy Snitch. He brought it carefully inside./nThe owl dropped its letter onto Harry's seat and began/nzooming around their compartment, apparently very/npleased with itself for accomplishing its task. Hedwig/n/n/n/n/nclicked her beak with a sort of dignified disapproval./nCrookshanks sat up in his seat, following the owl with/nhis great yellow eyes. Ron, noticing this, snatched the/nowl safely out of harm's way./n/nHarry picked up the letter. It was addressed to him./n/nHe ripped open the letter, and shouted, "It's from/nSirius!"/n/n"What?" said Ron and Hermione excitedly. "Read it/naloud!"/n/nDear Harry,/n/nI hope this finds you before you reach your aunt and/nuncle. I don't know whether they're used to owl post/n/nBuckbeak and I are in hiding. I won't tell you where, in/ncase this owl falls into the wrong hands. I have some/ndoubt about his reliability, but he is the best I could/nfind, and he did seem eager for the job./n/nI believe the dementors are still searching for me, but/nthey haven't a hope of finding me here. I am planning/nto allow some Muggles to glimpse me soon, a long way/nfrom Hogwarts, so that the security on the castle will/nbe lifted./n/nThere is something I never got around to telling you/nduring our brief meeting. It was I who sent you the/nFirebolt —/n/n"Ha!" said Hermione triumphantly. "See! I told you it/nwas from him!"/n/n"Yes, but he hadn't jinxed it, had he?" said Ron./n"Ouch!" The tiny owl, now hooting happily in his/nhand, had nibbled one of his fingers in what it/nseemed to think was an affectionate way./n/n/n/n/n/nCrookshanks took the order to the Owl Office for me. I/nused your name but told them to take the gold from my/nown Gringotts vault. Please consider it as thirteen/nbirthdays' worth of presents from your godfather./n/nI would also like to apologize for the fright I think I/ngave you that night last year when you left your/nuncle's house. I had only hoped to get a glimpse of you/nbefore starting my journey north, but I think the sight/nof me alarmed you./n/nI am enclosing something else for you, which I think/nwill make your next year at Hogwarts more enjoyable./n/nIf ever you need me, send word. Your owl will find me./n/nI'll write again soon./n/nSirius/n/nHarry looked eagerly inside the envelope. There was/nanother piece of parchment in there. He read it/nthrough quickly and felt suddenly as warm and/ncontented as though he'd swallowed a bottle of hot/nbutterbeer in one gulp./n/nI, Sirius Black, Harry Potter's godfather, hereby give/nhim permission to visit Hogsmeade on weekends./n/n"That'll be good enough for Dumbledore!" said Harry/nhappily. He looked back at Sirius's letter./n/n"Hang on, there's a P.S. ..."/n/nI thought your friend Ron might like to keep this owl,/nas it's my fault he no longer has a rat./n/nRon's eyes widened. The minute owl was still hooting/nexcitedly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Keep him?" he said uncertainly. He looked closely at/nthe owl for a moment; then, to Harry's and/nHermione's great surprise, he held him out for/nCrookshanks to sniff./n/n"What do'you reckon?" Ron asked the cat. "Definitely/nan owl?"/n/nCrookshanks purred./n/n"That's good enough for me," said Ron happily. "He's/nmine."/n/nHarry read and reread the letter from Sirius all the/nway back into King's Cross station. It was still/nclutched tightly in his hand as he, Ron, and/nHermione stepped back through the barrier of/nplatform nine and three-quarters. Harry spotted/nUncle Vernon at once. He was standing a good/ndistance from Mr. and Mrs. Weasley, eyeing them/nsuspiciously, and when Mrs. Weasley hugged Harry in/ngreeting, his worst suspicions about them seemed/nconfirmed./n/n"I'll call about the World Cup!" Ron yelled after Harry/nas Harry bid him and Hermione good-bye, then/nwheeled the trolley bearing his trunk and Hedwig's/ncage toward Uncle Vernon, who greeted him in his/nusual fashion./n/n"What's that?" he snarled, staring at the envelope/nHarry was still clutching in his hand. "If it's another/nform for me to sign, you've got another — "/n/n"It's not," said Harry cheerfully. "It's a letter from my/ngodfather."/n/n"Godfather?" sputtered Uncle Vernon. "You haven't/ngot a godfather!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, I have," said Harry brightly. "He was my mum/nand dad's best friend. He's a convicted murderer, but/nhe's broken out of wizard prison and he's on the run./nHe likes to keep in touch with me, though ... keep up/nwith my news ... check if I'm happy. ..."/n/nAnd, grinning broadly at the look of horror on Uncle/nVernon's face, Harry set off toward the station exit,/nHedwig rattling along in front of him, for what looked/nlike a much better summer than the last./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Riddle House
text: /nThe villagers of Little Hangleton still called it "the/nRiddle House," even though it had been many years/nsince the Riddle family had lived there. It stood on a/nhill overlooking the village, some of its windows/nboarded, tiles missing from its roof, and ivy spreading/nunchecked over its face. Once a fine-looking manor,/nand easily the largest and grandest building for miles/naround, the Riddle House was now damp, derelict,/nand unoccupied./n/nThe Little Hangletons all agreed that the old house/nwas "creepy." Half a century ago, something strange/nand horrible had happened there, something that the/nolder inhabitants of the village still liked to discuss/nwhen topics for gossip were scarce. The story had/nbeen picked over so many times, and had been/nembroidered in so many places, that nobody was/nquite sure what the truth was anymore. Every version/nof the tale, however, started in the same place: Fifty/nyears before, at daybreak on a fine summer's/nmorning, when the Riddle House had still been well/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nkept and impressive, a maid had entered the drawing/nroom to find all three Riddles dead./n/nThe maid had run screaming down the hill into the/nvillage and roused as many people as she could./n/n"Lying there with their eyes wide open! Cold as ice!/nStill in their dinner things!"/n/nThe police were summoned, and the whole of Little/nHangleton had seethed with shocked curiosity and ill-/ndisguised excitement. Nobody wasted their breath/npretending to feel very sad about the Riddles, for they/nhad been most unpopular. Elderly Mr. and Mrs./nRiddle had been rich, snobbish, and rude, and their/ngrown-up son, Tom, had been, if anything, worse. All/nthe villagers cared about was the identity of their/nmurderer — for plainly, three apparently healthy/npeople did not all drop dead of natural causes on the/nsame night./n/nThe Hanged Man, the village pub, did a roaring trade/nthat night; the whole village seemed to have turned/nout to discuss the murders. They were rewarded for/nleaving their firesides when the Riddles' cook arrived/ndramatically in their midst and announced to the/nsuddenly silent pub that a man called Frank Bryce/nhad just been arrested./n/n"Frank!" cried several people. "Never!"/n/nFrank Bryce was the Riddles' gardener. He lived alone/nin a rundown cottage on the grounds of the Riddle/nHouse. Frank had come back from the war with a/nvery stiff leg and a great dislike of crowds and loud/nnoises, and had been working for the Riddles ever/nsince./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was a rush to buy the cook drinks and hear/nmore details./n/n/n/n"Always thought he was odd," she told the eagerly/nlistening villagers, after her fourth sherry./n/n"Unfriendly, like. I'm sure if I've offered him a cuppa/nonce, I've offered it a hundred times. Never wanted to/nmix, he didn't."/n/n"Ah, now," said a woman at the bar, "he had a hard/nwar, Frank. He likes the quiet life. That's no reason to/n/n/n/n"Who else had a key to the back door, then?" barked/nthe cook. "There's been a spare key hanging in the/ngardener's cottage far back as I can remember!/nNobody forced the door last night! No broken/nwindows! All Frank had to do was creep up to the big/nhouse while we was all sleeping. ..."/n/nThe villagers exchanged dark looks./n/n"I always thought he had a nasty look about him,/nright enough," grunted a man at the bar./n/n"War turned him funny, if you ask me," said the/nlandlord./n/n"Told you I wouldn't like to get on the wrong side of/nFrank, didn't I, Dot?" said an excited woman in the/ncorner./n/n"Horrible temper," said Dot, nodding fervently. "I/nremember, when he was a kid ..."/n/nBy the following morning, hardly anyone in Little/nHangleton doubted that Frank Bryce had killed the/nRiddles./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut over in the neighboring town of Great Hangleton,/nin the dark and dingy police station, Frank was/nstubbornly repeating, again and again, that he was/ninnocent, and that the only person he had seen near/nthe house on the day of the Riddles' deaths had been/na teenage boy, a stranger, dark-haired and pale./nNobody else in the village had seen any such boy, and/nthe police were quite sure that Frank had invented/nhim./n/nThen, just when things were looking very serious for/nFrank, the report on the Riddles' bodies came back/nand changed everything./n/nThe police had never read an odder report. A team of/ndoctors had examined the bodies and had concluded/nthat none of the Riddles had been poisoned, stabbed,/nshot, strangled, suffocated, or (as far as they could/ntell) harmed at all. In fact (the report continued, in a/ntone of unmistakable bewilderment), the Riddles all/nappeared to be in perfect health — apart from the fact/nthat they were all dead. The doctors did note (as/nthough determined to find something wrong with the/nbodies) that each of the Riddles had a look of terror/nupon his or her face — but as the frustrated police/nsaid, whoever heard of three people being frightened/nto death?/n/nAs there was no proof that the Riddles had been/nmurdered at all, the police were forced to let Frank go./nThe Riddles were buried in the Little Hangleton/nchurchyard, and their graves remained objects of/ncuriosity for a while. To everyone's surprise, and amid/na cloud of suspicion, Frank Bryce returned to his/ncottage on the grounds of the Riddle House./n/n" 'S far as I'm concerned, he killed them, and I don't/ncare what the police say," said Dot in the Hanged/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMan. "And if he had any decency, he'd leave here,/nknowing as how we knows he did it."/n/nBut Frank did not leave. He stayed to tend the garden/nfor the next family who lived in the Riddle House, and/nthen the next — for neither family stayed long./n/nPerhaps it was partly because of Frank that the new/nowners said there was a nasty feeling about the place,/nwhich, in the absence of inhabitants, started to fall/ninto disrepair./n/nThe wealthy man who owned the Riddle House these/ndays neither lived there nor put it to any use; they/nsaid in the village that he kept it for "tax reasons,"/nthough nobody was very clear what these might be./nThe wealthy owner continued to pay Frank to do the/ngardening, however. Frank was nearing his seventy-/nseventh birthday now, very deaf, his bad leg stiffer/nthan ever, but could be seen pottering around the/nflower beds in fine weather, even though the weeds/nwere starting to creep up on him, try as he might to/nsuppress them./n/nWeeds were not the only things Frank had to contend/nwith either. Boys from the village made a habit of/nthrowing stones through the windows of the Riddle/nHouse. They rode their bicycles over the lawns Frank/nworked so hard to keep smooth. Once or twice, they/nbroke into the old house for a dare. They knew that/nold Frank's devotion to the house and grounds/namounted almost to an obsession, and it amused/nthem to see him limping across the garden,/nbrandishing his stick and yelling croakily at them./nFrank, for his part, believed the boys tormented him/nbecause they, like their parents and grandparents,/nthought him a murderer. So when Frank awoke one/nnight in August and saw something very odd up at/nthe old house, he merely assumed that the boys had/ngone one step further in their attempts to punish him./n/n/n/n/nIt was Frank's bad leg that woke him; it was paining/nhim worse than ever in his old age. He got up and/nlimped downstairs into the kitchen with the idea of/nrefilling his hot-water bottle to ease the stiffness in/nhis knee. Standing at the sink, filling the kettle, he/nlooked up at the Riddle House and saw lights/nglimmering in its upper windows. Frank knew at once/nwhat was going on. The boys had broken into the/nhouse again, and judging by the flickering quality of/nthe light, they had started a fire./n/nFrank had no telephone, and in any case, he had/ndeeply mistrusted the police ever since they had/ntaken him in for questioning about the Riddles'/ndeaths. He put down the kettle at once, hurried back/nupstairs as fast as his bad leg would allow, and was/nsoon back in his kitchen, fully dressed and removing/na rusty old key from its hook by the door. He picked/nup his walking stick, which was propped against the/nwall, and set off into the night./n/nThe front door of the Riddle House bore no sign of/nbeing forced, nor did any of the windows. Frank/nlimped around to the back of the house until he/nreached a door almost completely hidden by ivy, took/nout the old key, put it into the lock, and opened the/ndoor noiselessly./n/nHe let himself into the cavernous kitchen. Frank had/nnot entered it for many years; nevertheless, although/nit was very dark, he remembered where the door into/nthe hall was, and he groped his way toward it, his/nnostrils full of the smell of decay, ears pricked for any/nsound of footsteps or voices from overhead. He/nreached the hall, which was a little lighter owing to/nthe large mullioned windows on either side of the/nfront door, and started to climb the stairs, blessing/nthe dust that lay thick upon the stone, because it/nmuffled the sound of his feet and stick./n/n/n/n/n/nOn the landing, Frank turned right, and saw at once/nwhere the intruders were: At the very end of the/npassage a door stood ajar, and a flickering light shone/nthrough the gap, casting a long sliver of gold across/nthe black floor. Frank edged closer and closer,/ngrasping his walking stick firmly. Several feet from/nthe entrance, he was able to see a narrow slice of the/nroom beyond./n/nThe fire, he now saw, had been lit in the grate. This/nsurprised him. Then he stopped moving and listened/nintently, for a man's voice spoke within the room; it/nsounded timid and fearful./n/n"There is a little more in the bottle, My Lord, if you/nare still hungry."/n/n"Later," said a second voice. This too belonged to a/nman — but it was strangely high-pitched, and cold as/na sudden blast of icy wind. Something about that/nvoice made the sparse hairs on the back of Frank's/nneck stand up. "Move me closer to the fire, Wormtail."/n/nFrank turned his right ear toward the door, the better/nto hear. There came the clink of a bottle being put/ndown upon some hard surface, and then the dull/nscraping noise of a heavy chair being dragged across/nthe floor. Frank caught a glimpse of a small man, his/nback to the door, pushing the chair into place. He was/nwearing a long black cloak, and there was a bald/npatch at the back of his head. Then he went out of/nsight again./n/n"Where is Nagini?" said the cold voice./n/n"I — I don't know, My Lord," said the first voice/nnervously. "She set out to explore the house, I think./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You will milk her before we retire, Wormtail," said/nthe second voice. "I will need feeding in the night. The/njourney has tired me greatly."/n/nBrow furrowed, Frank inclined his good ear still closer/nto the door, listening very hard. There was a pause,/nand then the man called Wormtail spoke again./n/n"My Lord, may I ask how long we are going to stay/nhere?"/n/n"A week," said the cold voice. "Perhaps longer. The/nplace is moderately comfortable, and the plan cannot/nproceed yet. It would be foolish to act before the/nQuidditch World Cup is over."/n/nFrank inserted a gnarled finger into his ear and/nrotated it. Owing, no doubt, to a buildup of earwax,/nhe had heard the word "Quidditch," which was not a/nword at all./n/n"The — the Quidditch World Cup, My Lord?" said/nWormtail. (Frank dug his finger still more vigorously/ninto his ear.) "Forgive me, but — I do not understand/n— why should we wait until the World Cup is over?"/n/n"Because, fool, at this very moment wizards are/npouring into the country from all over the world, and/nevery meddler from the Ministry of Magic will be on/nduty, on the watch for signs of unusual activity,/nchecking and double-checking identities. They will be/nobsessed with security, lest the Muggles notice/nanything. So we wait."/n/nFrank stopped trying to clear out his ear. He had/ndistinctly heard the words "Ministry of Magic,"/n"wizards," and "Muggles." Plainly, each of these/nexpressions meant something secret, and Frank could/nthink of only two sorts of people who would speak in/n/n/n/n/ncode: spies and criminals. Frank tightened his hold/non his walking stick once more, and listened more/nclosely still./n/n"Your Lordship is still determined, then?" Wormtail/nsaid quietly./n/n"Certainly I am determined, Wormtail." There was a/nnote of menace in the cold voice now./n/nA slight pause followed — and then Wormtail spoke,/nthe words tumbling from him in a rush, as though he/nwas forcing himself to say this before he lost his/nnerve./n/n"It could be done without Harry Potter, My Lord."/n/nAnother pause, more protracted, and then —/n/n"Without Harry Potter?" breathed the second voice/nsoftly. "I see ..."/n/n"My Lord, I do not say this out of concern for the boy!"/nsaid Wormtail, his voice rising squeakily. "The boy is/nnothing to me, nothing at all! It is merely that if we/nwere to use another witch or wizard — any wizard —/nthe thing could be done so much more quickly! If you/nallowed me to leave you for a short while — you know/nthat I can disguise myself most effectively — I could/nbe back here in as little as two days with a suitable/nperson — "/n/n"I could use another wizard," said the cold voice/nsoftly, "that is true. ..."/n/n"My Lord, it makes sense," said Wormtail, sounding/nthoroughly relieved now. "Laying hands on Harry/nPotter would be so difficult, he is so well protected — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And so you volunteer to go and fetch me a/nsubstitute? I wonder . . . perhaps the task of nursing/nme has become wearisome for you, "Wormtail? Could/nthis suggestion of abandoning the plan be nothing/nmore than an attempt to desert me?"/n/n"My Lord! I — I have no wish to leave you, none at all/n/n/n/n"Do not lie to me!" hissed the second voice. "I can/nalways tell, Wormtail! You are regretting that you ever/nreturned to me. I revolt you. I see you flinch when you/nlook at me, feel you shudder when you touch me. ..."/n/n"No! My devotion to Your Lordship — "/n/n"Your devotion is nothing more than cowardice. You/nwould not be here if you had anywhere else to go./n/nHow am I to survive without you, when I need feeding/nevery few hours? Who is to milk Nagini?"/n/n"But you seem so much stronger, My Lord — "/n/n"Liar," breathed the second voice. "I am no stronger,/nand a few days alone would be enough to rob me of/nthe little health I have regained under your clumsy/ncare. Silencel"/n/nWormtail, who had been sputtering incoherently, fell/nsilent at once. For a few seconds, Frank could hear/nnothing but the fire crackling. Then the second man/nspoke once more, in a whisper that was almost a hiss./n/n"I have my reasons for using the boy, as I have/nalready explained to you, and I will use no other. I/nhave waited thirteen years. A few more months will/nmake no difference. As for the protection surrounding/nthe boy, I believe my plan will be effective. All that is/nneeded is a little courage from you, Wormtail —/n/n/n/n/n/ncourage you will find, unless you wish to feel the full/nextent of Lord Voldemort's wrath — "/n/n"My Lord, I must speak!" said Wormtail, panic in his/nvoice now. "All through our journey I have gone over/nthe plan in my head — My Lord, Bertha Jorkins's/ndisappearance will not go unnoticed for long, and if/nwe proceed, if I murder — "/n/n"IP" whispered the second voice. "If? If you follow the/nplan, Wormtail, the Ministry need never know that/nanyone else has died. You will do it quietly and/nwithout fuss; I only wish that I could do it myself, but/nin my present condition ... Come, Wormtail, one more/ndeath and our path to Harry Potter is clear. I am not/nasking you to do it alone. By that time, my faithful/nservant will have rejoined us — "/n/n"I am a faithful servant," said Wormtail, the merest/ntrace of sullenness in his voice./n/n"Wormtail, I need somebody with brains, somebody/nwhose loyalty has never wavered, and you,/nunfortunately, fulfill neither requirement."/n/n"I found you," said Wormtail, and there was definitely/na sulky edge to his voice now. "I was the one who/nfound you. I brought you Bertha Jorkins."/n/n"That is true," said the second man, sounding/namused. "A stroke of brilliance I would not have/nthought possible from you, Wormtail — though, if/ntruth be told, you were not aware how useful she/nwould be when you caught her, were you?"/n/n"I — I thought she might be useful, My Lord — "/n/n"Liar," said the second voice again, the cruel/namusement more pronounced than ever. "However, I/n/n/n/n/n/ndo not deny that her information was invaluable./nWithout it, I could never have formed our plan, and/nfor that, you will have your reward, Wormtail. I will/nallow you to perform an essential task for me, one/nthat many of my followers would give their right/nhands to perform. ..."/n/n"R-really, My Lord? What — ?" Wormtail sounded/nterrified again./n/n"Ah, Wormtail, you don't want me to spoil the/nsurprise? Your part will come at the very end ... but I/npromise you, you will have the honor of being just as/nuseful as Bertha Jorkins."/n/n"You ... you ..." Wormtail's voice suddenly sounded/nhoarse, as though his mouth had gone very dry. "You/n. . . are going ... to kill me too?"/n/n"Wormtail, Wormtail," said the cold voice silkily, "why/nwould I kill you? I killed Bertha because I had to. She/nwas fit for nothing after my questioning, quite/nuseless. In any case, awkward questions would have/nbeen asked if she had gone back to the Ministry with/nthe news that she had met you on her holidays./nWizards who are supposed to be dead would do well/nnot to run into Ministry of Magic witches at wayside/ninns. ..."/n/nWormtail muttered something so quietly that Frank/ncould not hear it, but it made the second man laugh/n— an entirely mirthless laugh, cold as his speech./n/n"We could have modified her memory? But Memory/nCharms can be broken by a powerful wizard, as I/nproved when I questioned her. It would be an insult to/nher memory not to use the information I extracted/nfrom her, Wormtail."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nOut in the corridor, Frank suddenly became aware/nthat the hand gripping his walking stick was slippery/nwith sweat. The man with the cold voice had killed a/nwoman. He was talking about it without any kind of/nremorse — with amusement. He was dangerous — a/nmadman. And he was planning more murders — this/nboy, Harry Potter, whoever he was — was in danger —/n/nFrank knew what he must do. Now, if ever, was the/ntime to go to the police. He would creep out of the/nhouse and head straight for the telephone box in the/nvillage . . . but the cold voice was speaking again, and/nFrank remained where he was, frozen to the spot,/nlistening with all his might./n/n"One more murder . . . my faithful servant at Hogwarts/n... Harry Potter is as good as mine, Wormtail. It is/ndecided. There will be no more argument. But quiet .../nI think I hear Nagini. ..."/n/nAnd the second man's voice changed. He started/nmaking noises such as Frank had never heard before;/nhe was hissing and spitting without drawing breath./nFrank thought he must be having some sort of fit or/nseizure./n/nAnd then Frank heard movement behind him in the/ndark passageway. He turned to look, and found/nhimself paralyzed with fright./n/nSomething was slithering toward him along the dark/ncorridor floor, and as it drew nearer to the sliver of/nfirelight, he realized with a thrill of terror that it was a/ngigantic snake, at least twelve feet long. Horrified,/ntransfixed, Frank stared as its undulating body cut a/nwide, curving track through the thick dust on the/nfloor, coming closer and closer — What was he to do?/nThe only means of escape was into the room where/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ntwo men sat plotting murder, yet if he stayed where/nhe was the snake would surely kill him —/n/nBut before he had made his decision, the snake was/nlevel with him, and then, incredibly, miraculously, it/nwas passing; it was following the spitting, hissing/nnoises made by the cold voice beyond the door, and in/nseconds, the tip of its diamond-patterned tail had/nvanished through the gap./n/nThere was sweat on Frank's forehead now, and the/nhand on the walking stick was trembling. Inside the/nroom, the cold voice was continuing to hiss, and/nFrank was visited by a strange idea, an impossible/nidea. . . . This man could talk to snakes./n/nFrank didn't understand what was going on. He/nwanted more than anything to be back in his bed with/nhis hot-water bottle. The problem was that his legs/ndidn't seem to want to move. As he stood there/nshaking and trying to master himself, the cold voice/nswitched abruptly to English again./n/n"Nagini has interesting news, Wormtail," it said./n/n"In-indeed, My Lord?" said Wormtail./n/n"Indeed, yes," said the voice. "According to Nagini,/nthere is an old Muggle standing right outside this/nroom, listening to every word we say."/n/nFrank didn't have a chance to hide himself. There/nwere footsteps, and then the door of the room was/nflung wide open./n/nA short, balding man with graying hair, a pointed/nnose, and small, watery eyes stood before Frank, a/nmixture of fear and alarm in his face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Invite him inside, Wormtail. Where are your/nmanners?"/n/nThe cold voice was coming from the ancient armchair/nbefore the fire, but Frank couldn't see the speaker./nThe snake, on the other hand, was curled up on the/nrotting hearth rug, like some horrible travesty of a pet/ndog./n/nWormtail beckoned Frank into the room. Though still/ndeeply shaken, Frank took a firmer grip upon his/nwalking stick and limped over the threshold./n/nThe fire was the only source of light in the room; it/ncast long, spidery shadows upon the walls. Frank/nstared at the back of the armchair; the man inside it/nseemed to be even smaller than his servant, for Frank/ncouldn't even see the back of his head./n/n"You heard everything, Muggle?" said the cold voice./n/n"What's that you're calling me?" said Frank defiantly,/nfor now that he was inside the room, now that the/ntime had come for some sort of action, he felt braver;/nit had always been so in the war./n/n"I am calling you a Muggle," said the voice coolly. "It/nmeans that you are not a wizard."/n/n"I don't know what you mean by wizard," said Frank,/nhis voice growing steadier. "All I know is I've heard/nenough to interest the police tonight, I have. You've/ndone murder and you're planning more! And I'll tell/nyou this too," he added, on a sudden inspiration, "my/nwife knows I'm up here, and if I don't come back — "/n/n"You have no wife," said the cold voice, very quietly./n"Nobody knows you are here. You told nobody that/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nyou were coming. Do not lie to Lord Voldemort,/nMuggle, for he knows ... he always knows. ..."/n/n"Is that right?" said Frank roughly. "Lord, is it? Well, I/ndon't think much of your manners, My Lord. Turn/n'round and face me like a man, why don't you?"/n/n"But I am not a man, Muggle," said the cold voice,/nbarely audible now over the crackling of the flames. "I/nam much, much more than a man. However ... why/nnot? I will face you. ... Wormtail, come turn my chair/naround."/n/nThe servant gave a whimper./n/n"You heard me, Wormtail."/n/nSlowly, with his face screwed up, as though he would/nrather have done anything than approach his master/nand the hearth rug where the snake lay, the small/nman walked forward and began to turn the chair. The/nsnake lifted its ugly triangular head and hissed/nslightly as the legs of the chair snagged on its rug./n/nAnd then the chair was facing Frank, and he saw/nwhat was sitting in it. His walking stick fell to the/nfloor with a clatter. He opened his mouth and let out/na scream. He was screaming so loudly that he never/nheard the words the thing in the chair spoke as it/nraised a wand. There was a flash of green light, a/nrushing sound, and Frank Bryce crumpled. He was/ndead before he hit the floor./n/nTwo hundred miles away, the boy called Harry Potter/nwoke with a start./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Scar
text: /nHarry lay flat on his back, breathing hard as though/nhe had been running. He had awoken from a vivid/ndream with his hands pressed over his face. The old/nscar on his forehead, which was shaped like a bolt of/nlightning, was burning beneath his fingers as though/nsomeone had just pressed a white-hot wire to his/nskin./n/nHe sat up, one hand still on his scar, the other/nreaching out in the darkness for his glasses, which/nwere on the bedside table. He put them on and his/nbedroom came into clearer focus, lit by a faint, misty/norange light that was filtering through the curtains/nfrom the street lamp outside the window./n/nHarry ran his fingers over the scar again. It was still/npainful. He turned on the lamp beside him, scrambled/nout of bed, crossed the room, opened his wardrobe,/nand peered into the mirror on the inside of the door. A/nskinny boy of fourteen looked back at him, his bright/ngreen eyes puzzled under his untidy black hair. He/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nexamined the lightning-bolt scar of his reflection more/nclosely. It looked normal, but it was still stinging./n/nHarry tried to recall what he had been dreaming/nabout before he had awoken. It had seemed so real. .../nThere had been two people he knew and one he/ndidn't. ... He concentrated hard, frowning, trying to/nremember. .../n/nThe dim picture of a darkened room came to him. .../nThere had been a snake on a hearth rug ... a small/nman called Peter, nicknamed Wormtail ... and a cold,/nhigh voice ... the voice of Lord Voldemort. Harry felt/nas though an ice cube had slipped down into his/nstomach at the very thought. .../n/nHe closed his eyes tightly and tried to remember what/nVoldemort had looked like, but it was impossible. .../nAll Harry knew was that at the moment when/nVoldemort's chair had swung around, and he, Harry,/nhad seen what was sitting in it, he had felt a spasm of/nhorror, which had awoken him ... or had that been/nthe pain in his scar?/n/nAnd who had the old man been? For there had/ndefinitely been an old man; Harry had watched him/nfall to the ground. It was all becoming confused./n/nHarry put his face into his hands, blocking out his/nbedroom, trying to hold on to the picture of that dimly/nlit room, but it was like trying to keep water in his/ncupped hands; the details were now trickling away as/nfast as he tried to hold on to them. ... Voldemort and/nWormtail had been talking about someone they had/nkilled, though Harry could not remember the name . . ./nand they had been plotting to kill someone else . . ./nhim)./n/nHarry took his face out of his hands, opened his eyes,/nand stared around his bedroom as though expecting/n/n/n/n/n/nto see something unusual there. As it happened,/nthere were an extraordinary number of unusual/nthings in this room. A large wooden trunk stood open/nat the foot of his bed, revealing a cauldron,/nbroomstick, black robes, and assorted spellbooks./nRolls of parchment littered that part of his desk that/nwas not taken up by the large, empty cage in which/nhis snowy owl, Hedwig, usually perched. On the floor/nbeside his bed a book lay open; Harry had been/nreading it before he fell asleep last night. The pictures/nin this book were all moving. Men in bright orange/nrobes were zooming in and out of sight on/nbroomsticks, throwing a red ball to one another./n/nHarry walked over to the book, picked it up, and/nwatched one of the wizards score a spectacular goal/nby putting the ball through a fifty-foot-high hoop./n/nThen he snapped the book shut. Even Quidditch — in/nHarry's opinion, the best sport in the world —/ncouldn't distract him at the moment. He placed Flying/nwith the Cannons on his bedside table, crossed to the/nwindow, and drew back the curtains to survey the/nstreet below./n/nPrivet Drive looked exactly as a respectable suburban/nstreet would be expected to look in the early hours of/nSaturday morning. All the curtains were closed. As far/nas Harry could see through the darkness, there/nwasn't a living creature in sight, not even a cat./n/nAnd yet . . . and yet . . . Harry went restlessly back to/nthe bed and sat down on it, running a finger over his/nscar again. It wasn't the pain that bothered him;/n/nHarry was no stranger to pain and injury. He had lost/nall the bones from his right arm once and had them/npainfully regrown in a night. The same arm had been/npierced by a venomous foot-long fang not long/nafterward. Only last year Harry had fallen fifty feet/nfrom an airborne broomstick. He was used to bizarre/n/n/n/n/naccidents and injuries; they were unavoidable if you/nattended Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry/nand had a knack for attracting a lot of trouble./n/nNo, the thing that was bothering Harry was that the/nlast time his scar had hurt him, it had been because/nVoldemort had been close by. ... But Voldemort/ncouldn't be here, now. ... The idea of Voldemort/nlurking in Privet Drive was absurd, impossible. .../n/nHarry listened closely to the silence around him. Was/nhe half-expecting to hear the creak of a stair or the/nswish of a cloak? And then he jumped slightly as he/nheard his cousin Dudley give a tremendous grunting/nsnore from the next room./n/nHarry shook himself mentally; he was being stupid./nThere was no one in the house with him except Uncle/nVernon, Aunt Petunia, and Dudley, and they were/nplainly still asleep, their dreams untroubled and/npainless./n/nAsleep was the way Harry liked the Dursleys best; it/nwasn't as though they were ever any help to him/nawake. Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia, and Dudley were/nHarry's only living relatives. They were Muggles who/nhated and despised magic in any form, which meant/nthat Harry was about as welcome in their house as/ndry rot. They had explained away Harry's long/nabsences at Hogwarts over the last three years by/ntelling everyone that he went to St. Brutus's Secure/nCenter for Incurably Criminal Boys. They knew/nperfectly well that, as an underage wizard, Harry/nwasn't allowed to use magic outside Hogwarts, but/nthey were still apt to blame him for anything that/nwent wrong about the house. Harry had never been/nable to confide in them or tell them anything about/nhis life in the wizarding world. The very idea of going/nto them when they awoke, and telling them about his/n/n/n/n/nscar hurting him, and about his worries about/nVoldemort, was laughable./n/nAnd yet it was because of Voldemort that Harry had/ncome to live with the Dursleys in the first place. If it/nhadn't been for Voldemort, Harry would not have had/nthe lightning scar on his forehead. If it hadn't been for/nVoldemort, Harry would still have had parents. .../n/nHarry had been a year old the night that Voldemort —/nthe most powerful Dark wizard for a century, a wizard/nwho had been gaining power steadily for eleven years/n— arrived at his house and killed his father and/nmother. Voldemort had then turned his wand on/nHarry; he had performed the curse that had disposed/nof many full-grown witches and wizards in his steady/nrise to power — and, incredibly, it had not worked./nInstead of killing the small boy, the curse had/nrebounded upon Voldemort. Harry had survived with/nnothing but a lightning-shaped cut on his forehead,/nand Voldemort had been reduced to something barely/nalive. His powers gone, his life almost extinguished,/nVoldemort had fled; the terror in which the secret/ncommunity of witches and wizards had lived for so/nlong had lifted, Voldemort's followers had disbanded,/nand Harry Potter had become famous./n/nIt had been enough of a shock for Harry to discover,/non his eleventh birthday, that he was a wizard; it had/nbeen even more disconcerting to find out that/neveryone in the hidden wizarding world knew his/nname. Harry had arrived at Hogwarts to find that/nheads turned and whispers followed him wherever he/nwent. But he was used to it now: At the end of this/nsummer, he would be starting his fourth year at/nHogwarts, and Harry was already counting the days/nuntil he would be back at the castle again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut there was still a fortnight to go before he went/nback to school. He looked hopelessly around his room/nagain, and his eye paused on the birthday cards his/ntwo best friends had sent him at the end of July./n/nWhat would they say if Harry wrote to them and told/nthem about his scar hurting?/n/nAt once, Hermione Granger's voice seemed to fill his/nhead, shrill and panicky./n/n" Your scar hurt? Harry, that's really serious. . . . Write/nto Professor Dumbledorel And I'll go and check/nCommon Magical Ailments and Afflictions. ... Maybe/nthere's something in there about curse scars. ..."/n/nYes, that would be Hermione's advice: Go straight to/nthe headmaster of Hogwarts, and in the meantime,/nconsult a book. Harry stared out of the window at the/ninky blue-black sky. He doubted very much whether a/nbook could help him now. As far as he knew, he was/nthe only living person to have survived a curse like/nVoldemort's; it was highly unlikely, therefore, that he/nwould find his symptoms listed in Common Magical/nAilments and Afflictions. As for informing the/nheadmaster, Harry had no idea where Dumbledore/nwent during the summer holidays. He amused himself/nfor a moment, picturing Dumbledore, with his long/nsilver beard, full-length wizard's robes, and pointed/nhat, stretched out on a beach somewhere, rubbing/nsuntan lotion onto his long crooked nose. Wherever/nDumbledore was, though, Harry was sure that/nHedwig would be able to find him; Harry's owl had/nnever yet failed to deliver a letter to anyone, even/nwithout an address. But what would he write?/n/nDear Professor Dumbledore, Sorry to bother you, but/nmy scar hurt this morning. Yours sincerely, Harry/nPotter./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nEven inside his head the words sounded stupid./n/nAnd so he tried to imagine his other best friend, Ron/nWeasley's, reaction, and in a moment, Ron's red hair/nand long-nosed, freckled face seemed to swim before/nHarry, wearing a bemused expression./n/n" Your scar hurt? But ... but You-Knotu-Who can't be/nnear you now, can he? I mean ... you'd know, wouldn't/nyou? He'd be trying to do you in again, wouldn't he? I/ndunno, Harry, maybe curse scars always twinge a bit/n... I'll ask Dad. ..."/n/nMr. Weasley was a fully qualified wizard who worked/nin the Misuse of Muggle Artifacts Office at the/nMinistry of Magic, but he didn't have any particular/nexpertise in the matter of curses, as far as Harry/nknew. In any case, Harry didn't like the idea of the/nwhole Weasley family knowing that he, Harry, was/ngetting jumpy about a few moments' pain. Mrs./nWeasley would fuss worse than Hermione, and Fred/nand George, Ron's sixteen-year-old twin brothers,/nmight think Harry was losing his nerve. The Weasleys/nwere Harry's favorite family in the world; he was/nhoping that they might invite him to stay any time/nnow (Ron had mentioned something about the/nQuidditch World Cup), and he somehow didn't want/nhis visit punctuated with anxious inquiries about his/nscar./n/nHarry kneaded his forehead with his knuckles. What/nhe really wanted (and it felt almost shameful to admit/nit to himself) was someone like — someone like a/nparent: an adult wizard whose advice he could ask/nwithout feeling stupid, someone who cared about/nhim, who had had experience with Dark Magic. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd then the solution came to him. It was so simple,/nand so obvious, that he couldn't believe it had taken/nso long — Sirius./n/nHarry leapt up from the bed, hurried across the room,/nand sat down at his desk; he pulled a piece of/nparchment toward him, loaded his eagle-feather quill/nwith ink, wrote Dear Sirius, then paused, wondering/nhow best to phrase his problem, still marveling at the/nfact that he hadn't thought of Sirius straight away./n/nBut then, perhaps it wasn't so surprising — after all,/nhe had only found out that Sirius was his godfather/ntwo months ago./n/nThere was a simple reason for Sirius's complete/nabsence from Harry's life until then — Sirius had/nbeen in Azkaban, the terrifying wizard jail guarded by/ncreatures called dementors, sightless, soul-sucking/nfiends who had come to search for Sirius at Hogwarts/nwhen he had escaped. Yet Sirius had been innocent/n— the murders for which he had been convicted had/nbeen committed by Wormtail, Voldemort's supporter,/nwhom nearly everybody now believed dead. Harry,/n/nRon, and Hermione knew otherwise, however; they/nhad come face-to-face with Wormtail only the/nprevious year, though only Professor Dumbledore had/nbelieved their story./n/nFor one glorious hour, Harry had believed that he was/nleaving the Dursleys at last, because Sirius had/noffered him a home once his name had been cleared./nBut the chance had been snatched away from him —/nWormtail had escaped before they could take him to/nthe Ministry of Magic, and Sirius had had to flee for/nhis life. Harry had helped him escape on the back of a/nhippogriff called Buckbeak, and since then, Sirius/nhad been on the run. The home Harry might have had/nif Wormtail had not escaped had been haunting him/nall summer. It had been doubly hard to return to the/n/n/n/n/nDursleys knowing that he had so nearly escaped them/nforever./n/nNevertheless, Sirius had been of some help to Harry,/neven if he couldn't be with him. It was due to Sirius/nthat Harry now had all his school things in his/nbedroom with him. The Dursleys had never allowed/nthis before; their general wish of keeping Harry as/nmiserable as possible, coupled with their fear of his/npowers, had led them to lock his school trunk in the/ncupboard under the stairs every summer prior to this./nBut their attitude had changed since they had found/nout that Harry had a dangerous murderer for a/ngodfather — for Harry had conveniently forgotten to/ntell them that Sirius was innocent./n/nHarry had received two letters from Sirius since he/nhad been back at Privet Drive. Both had been/ndelivered, not by owls (as was usual with wizards),/nbut by large, brightly colored tropical birds. Hedwig/nhad not approved of these flashy intruders; she had/nbeen most reluctant to allow them to drink from her/nwater tray before flying off again. Harry, on the other/nhand, had liked them; they put him in mind of palm/ntrees and white sand, and he hoped that, wherever/nSirius was (Sirius never said, in case the letters were/nintercepted), he was enjoying himself. Somehow,/n/nHarry found it hard to imagine dementors surviving/nfor long in bright sunlight; perhaps that was why/nSirius had gone south. Sirius's letters, which were/nnow hidden beneath the highly useful loose/nfloorboard under Harry's bed, sounded cheerful, and/nin both of them he had reminded Harry to call on him/nif ever Harry needed to. Well, he needed to now, all/nright. .../n/nHarry's lamp seemed to grow dimmer as the cold gray/nlight that precedes sunrise slowly crept into the room./nFinally, when the sun had risen, when his bedroom/n/n/n/n/n/nwalls had turned gold, and when sounds of movement/ncould be heard from Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia's/nroom, Harry cleared his desk of crumpled pieces of/nparchment and reread his finished letter./n/nDear Sirius,/n/nThanks for your last letter. That bird was enormous; it/ncould hardly get through my window./n/nThings are the same as usual here. Dudley's diet isn't/ngoing too well. My aunt found him smuggling/ndoughnuts into his room yesterday. They told him/nthey 'd have to cut his pocket money if he keeps doing/nit, so he got really angry and chucked his PlayStation/nout of the window. That's a sort of computer thing you/ncan play games on. Bit stupid really, now he hasn't/neven got Mega-Mutilation Part Three to take his mind/noff things./n/nI'm okay, mainly because the Dursleys are terrified/nyou might turn up and turn them all into bats if I ask/nyou to./n/nA weird thing happened this morning, though. My scar/nhurt again. Last time that happened it was because/nVoldemort was at Hogwarts. But I don't reckon he can/nbe anywhere near me now, can he? Do you know if/ncurse scars sometimes hurt years afterward?/n/nI'll send this with Hedwig when she gets back; she's/noffhunt-\ing at the moment. Say hello to Buckbeak for/nme./n/nHarry/n/nYes, thought Harry, that looked all right. There was/nno point putting in the dream; he didn't want it to/nlook as though he was too worried. He folded up the/n/n/n/n/n/nparchment and laid it aside on his desk, ready for/nwhen Hedwig returned. Then he got to his feet,/nstretched, and opened his wardrobe once more./nWithout glancing at his reflection, he started to get/ndressed before going down to breakfast./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n3/n/n/n/n

title: The Invitation
text: /nBy the time Harry arrived in the kitchen, the three/nDursleys were already seated around the table. None/nof them looked up as he entered or sat down. Uncle/nVernon's large red face was hidden behind the/nmorning's Daily Mail, and Aunt Petunia was cutting a/ngrapefruit into quarters, her lips pursed over her/nhorselike teeth./n/nDudley looked furious and sulky, and somehow/nseemed to be taking up even more space than usual./nThis was saying something, as he always took up an/nentire side of the square table by himself. When Aunt/nPetunia put a quarter of unsweetened grapefruit onto/nDudley's plate with a tremulous "There you are, Diddy/ndarling," Dudley glowered at her. His life had taken a/nmost unpleasant turn since he had come home for/nthe summer with his end-of-year report./n/nUncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia had managed to find/nexcuses for his bad marks as usual: Aunt Petunia/nalways insisted that Dudley was a very gifted boy/nwhose teachers didn't understand him, while Uncle/n/n/n/n/nVernon maintained that "he didn't want some swotty/nlittle nancy boy for a son anyway." They also skated/nover the accusations of bullying in the report — "He's/na boisterous little boy, but he wouldn't hurt a fly!"/nAunt Petunia had said tearfully./n/nHowever, at the bottom of the report there were a few/nwell-chosen comments from the school nurse that not/neven Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia could explain/naway. No matter how much Aunt Petunia wailed that/nDudley was big-boned, and that his poundage was/nreally puppy fat, and that he was a growing boy who/nneeded plenty of food, the fact remained that the/nschool outfitters didn't stock knickerbockers big/nenough for him anymore. The school nurse had seen/nwhat Aunt Petunia's eyes — so sharp when it came to/nspotting fingerprints on her gleaming walls, and in/nobserving the comings and goings of the neighbors —/nsimply refused to see: that far from needing extra/nnourishment, Dudley had reached roughly the size/nand weight of a young killer whale./n/nSo — after many tantrums, after arguments that/nshook Harry's bedroom floor, and many tears from/nAunt Petunia — the new regime had begun. The diet/nsheet that had been sent by the Smeltings school/nnurse had been taped to the fridge, which had been/nemptied of all Dudley's favorite things — fizzy drinks/nand cakes, chocolate bars and burgers — and filled/ninstead with fruit and vegetables and the sorts of/nthings that Uncle Vernon called "rabbit food." To/nmake Dudley feel better about it all, Aunt Petunia had/ninsisted that the whole family follow the diet too. She/nnow passed a grapefruit quarter to Harry. He noticed/nthat it was a lot smaller than Dudley's. Aunt Petunia/nseemed to feel that the best way to keep up Dudley's/nmorale was to make sure that he did, at least, get/nmore to eat than Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Aunt Petunia didn't know what was hidden under/nthe loose floorboard upstairs. She had no idea that/nHarry was not following the diet at all. The moment/nhe had got wind of the fact that he was expected to/nsurvive the summer on carrot sticks, Harry had sent/nHedwig to his friends with pleas for help, and they/nhad risen to the occasion magnificently. Hedwig had/nreturned from Hermione's house with a large box/nstuffed full of sugar-free snacks. (Hermione's parents/nwere dentists.) Hagrid, the Hogwarts gamekeeper, had/nobliged with a sack full of his own homemade rock/ncakes. (Harry hadn't touched these; he had had too/nmuch experience of Hagrid 's cooking.) Mrs. Weasley,/nhowever, had sent the family owl, Errol, with an/nenormous fruitcake and assorted meat pies. Poor/nErrol, who was elderly and feeble, had needed a full/nfive days to recover from the journey. And then on/nHarry's birthday (which the Dursleys had completely/nignored) he had received four superb birthday cakes,/none each from Ron, Hermione, Hagrid, and Sirius./nHarry still had two of them left, and so, looking/nforward to a real breakfast when he got back upstairs,/nhe ate his grapefruit without complaint./n/nUncle Vernon laid aside his paper with a deep sniff of/ndisapproval and looked down at his own grapefruit/nquarter./n/n"Is this it?" he said grumpily to Aunt Petunia./n/nAunt Petunia gave him a severe look, and then/nnodded pointedly at Dudley, who had already finished/nhis own grapefruit quarter and was eyeing Harry's/nwith a very sour look in his piggy little eyes./n/nUncle Vernon gave a great sigh, which ruffled his/nlarge, bushy mustache, and picked up his spoon./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe doorbell rang. Uncle Vernon heaved himself out/nof his chair and set off down the hall. Quick as a/nflash, while his mother was occupied with the kettle,/nDudley stole the rest of Uncle Vernon's grapefruit./n/nHarry heard talking at the door, and someone/nlaughing, and Uncle Vernon answering curtly. Then/nthe front door closed, and the sound of ripping paper/ncame from the hall./n/nAunt Petunia set the teapot down on the table and/nlooked curiously around to see where Uncle Vernon/nhad got to. She didn't have to wait long to find out;/nafter about a minute, he was back. He looked livid./n/n"You," he barked at Harry. "In the living room. Now."/n/nBewildered, wondering what on earth he was/nsupposed to have done this time, Harry got up and/nfollowed Uncle Vernon out of the kitchen and into the/nnext room. Uncle Vernon closed the door sharply/nbehind both of them./n/n"So," he said, marching over to the fireplace and/nturning to face Harry as though he were about to/npronounce him under arrest. "So."/n/nHarry would have dearly loved to have said, "So/nwhat?" but he didn't feel that Uncle Vernon's temper/nshould be tested this early in the morning, especially/nwhen it was already under severe strain from lack of/nfood. He therefore settled for looking politely puzzled./n/n"This just arrived," said Uncle Vernon. He brandished/na piece of purple writing paper at Harry. "A letter./nAbout you."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's confusion increased. Who would be writing to/nUncle Vernon about him? Who did he know who sent/nletters by the postman?/n/nUncle Vernon glared at Harry, then looked down at/nthe letter and began to read aloud:/n/nDear Mr. and Mrs. Dursley,/n/nWe have never been introduced, but I am sure you/nhave heard a great deal from Harry about my son Ron./n/nAs Harry might have told you, the final of the/nQuidditch World Cup takes place this Monday night,/nand my husband, Arthur, has just managed to get/nprime tickets through his connections at the/nDepartment of Magical Games and Sports./n/nI do hope you will allow us to take Harry to the match,/nas this really is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity; Britain/nhasn't hosted the cup for thirty years, and tickets are/nextremely hard to come by. We would of course be glad/nto have Harry stay for the remainder of the summer/nholidays, and to see him safely onto the train back to/nschool./n/nIt would be best for Harry to send us your answer as/nquickly as possible in the normal way, because the/nMuggle postman has never delivered to our house, and/nI am not sure he even knows where it is./n/nHoping to see Harry soon,/n/nYours sincerely,/n/nMolly Weasley/n/nP.S. I do hope we've put enough stamps on./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nUncle Vernon finished reading, put his hand back/ninto his breast pocket, and drew out something else./n/n"Look at this," he growled./n/nHe held up the envelope in which Mrs. Weasley's/nletter had come, and Harry had to fight down a laugh./nEvery bit of it was covered in stamps except for a/nsquare inch on the front, into which Mrs. Weasley/nhad squeezed the Dursleys' address in minute/nwriting./n/n"She did put enough stamps on, then," said Harry,/ntrying to sound as though Mrs. Weasley's was a/nmistake anyone could make. His uncle's eyes flashed./n/n"The postman noticed," he said through gritted teeth./n"Very interested to know where this letter came from,/nhe was. That's why he rang the doorbell. Seemed to/nthink it was funny."/n/nHarry didn't say anything. Other people might not/nunderstand why Uncle Vernon was making a fuss/nabout too many stamps, but Harry had lived with the/nDursleys too long not to know how touchy they were/nabout anything even slightly out of the ordinary. Their/nworst fear was that someone would find out that they/nwere connected (however distantly) with people like/nMrs. Weasley./n/nUncle Vernon was still glaring at Harry, who tried to/nkeep his expression neutral. If he didn't do or say/nanything stupid, he might just be in for the treat of a/nlifetime. He waited for Uncle Vernon to say/nsomething, but he merely continued to glare. Harry/ndecided to break the silence./n/n"So — can I go then?" he asked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA slight spasm crossed Uncle Vernon's large purple/nface. The mustache bristled. Harry thought he knew/nwhat was going on behind the mustache: a furious/nbattle as two of Uncle Vernon's most fundamental/ninstincts came into conflict. Allowing Harry to go/nwould make Harry happy, something Uncle Vernon/nhad struggled against for thirteen years. On the other/nhand, allowing Harry to disappear to the Weasleys' for/nthe rest of the summer would get rid of him two/nweeks earlier than anyone could have hoped, and/nUncle Vernon hated having Harry in the house. To/ngive himself thinking time, it seemed, he looked down/nat Mrs. Weasley's letter again./n/n"Who is this woman?" he said, staring at the/nsignature with distaste./n/n"You've seen her," said Harry. "She's my friend Ron's/nmother, she was meeting him off the Hog — off the/nschool train at the end of last term."/n/nHe had almost said "Hogwarts Express," and that was/na sure way to get his uncle's temper up. Nobody ever/nmentioned the name of Harry's school aloud in the/nDursley household./n/nUncle Vernon screwed up his enormous face as/nthough trying to remember something very/nunpleasant./n/n"Dumpy sort of woman?" he growled finally. "Load of/nchildren with red hair?"/n/nHarry frowned. He thought it was a bit rich of Uncle/nVernon to call anyone "dumpy," when his own son,/nDudley, had finally achieved what he'd been/nthreatening to do since the age of three, and become/nwider than he was tall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nUncle Vernon was perusing the letter again./n/n"Quidditch," he muttered under his breath./n/n"Quidditch — what is this rubbish?"/n/nHarry felt a second stab of annoyance./n/n"It's a sport," he said shortly. "Played on broom — "/n/n"All right, all right!" said Uncle Vernon loudly. Harry/nsaw, with some satisfaction, that his uncle looked/nvaguely panicky. Apparently his nerves couldn't stand/nthe sound of the word "broomsticks" in his living/nroom. He took refuge in perusing the letter again./nHarry saw his lips form the words "send us your/nanswer ... in the normal way." He scowled./n/n"What does she mean, 'the normal way'?" he spat./n/n"Normal for us," said Harry, and before his uncle/ncould stop him, he added, "you know, owl post. That's/nwhat's normal for wizards."/n/nUncle Vernon looked as outraged as if Harry had just/nuttered a disgusting swear word. Shaking with anger,/nhe shot a nervous look through the window, as/nthough expecting to see some of the neighbors with/ntheir ears pressed against the glass./n/n"How many times do I have to tell you not to mention/nthat unnaturalness under my roof?" he hissed, his/nface now a rich plum color. "You stand there, in the/nclothes Petunia and I have put on your ungrateful/nback — "/n/n"Only after Dudley finished with them," said Harry/ncoldly, and indeed, he was dressed in a sweatshirt so/nlarge for him that he had had to roll back the sleeves/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nfive times so as to be able to use his hands, and/nwhich fell past the knees of his extremely baggy jeans./n/n/n/n"I will not be spoken to like that!" said Uncle Vernon,/ntrembling with rage./n/nBut Harry wasn't going to stand for this. Gone were/nthe days when he had been forced to take every single/none of the Dursleys' stupid rules. He wasn't following/nDudley's diet, and he wasn't going to let Uncle Vernon/nstop him from going to the Quidditch World Cup, not/nif he could help it. Harry took a deep, steadying/nbreath and then said, "Okay, I can't see the World/nCup. Can I go now, then? Only I've got a letter to/nSirius I want to finish. You know — my godfather."/n/nHe had done it. He had said the magic words. Now he/nwatched the purple recede blotchily from Uncle/nVernon's face, making it look like badly mixed black/ncurrant ice cream./n/n"You're — you're writing to him, are you?" said Uncle/nVernon, in a would-be calm voice — but Harry had/nseen the pupils of his tiny eyes contract with sudden/nfear./n/n"Well — yeah," said Harry, casually. "It's been a while/nsince he heard from me, and, you know, if he doesn't,/nhe might start thinking something's wrong."/n/nHe stopped there to enjoy the effect of these words./n/nHe could almost see the cogs working under Uncle/nVernon's thick, dark, neatly parted hair. If he tried to/nstop Harry writing to Sirius, Sirius would think Harry/nwas being mistreated. If he told Harry he couldn't go/nto the Quidditch World Cup, Harry would write and/ntell Sirius, who would know Harry was being/nmistreated. There was only one thing for Uncle/nVernon to do. Harry could see the conclusion forming/n/n/n/n/nin his uncle's mind as though the great mustached/nface were transparent. Harry tried not to smile, to/nkeep his own face as blank as possible. And then —/n/n"Well, all right then. You can go to this ruddy ... this/nstupid ... this World Cup thing. You write and tell/nthese — these Weasleys they're to pick you up, mind./nI haven't got time to go dropping you off all over the/ncountry. And you can spend the rest of the summer/nthere. And you can tell your — your godfather ... tell/nhim ... tell him you're going."/n/n"Okay then," said Harry brightly./n/nHe turned and walked toward the living room door,/nfighting the urge to jump into the air and whoop. He/nwas going ... he was going to the Weasleys', he was/ngoing to watch the Quidditch World Cup!/n/nOutside in the hall he nearly ran into Dudley, who/nhad been lurking behind the door, clearly hoping to/noverhear Harry being told off. He looked shocked to/nsee the broad grin on Harry's face./n/n"That was an excellent breakfast, wasn't it?" said/nHarry. "I feel really full, don't you?"/n/nLaughing at the astonished look on Dudley's face,/nHarry took the stairs three at a time, and hurled/nhimself back into his bedroom./n/nThe first thing he saw was that Hedwig was back. She/nwas sitting in her cage, staring at Harry with her/nenormous amber eyes, and clicking her beak in the/nway that meant she was annoyed about something./nExactly what was annoying her became apparent/nalmost at once./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"OUCH!" said Harry as what appeared to be a small,/ngray, feathery tennis ball collided with the side of his/nhead. Harry massaged the spot furiously, looking up/nto see what had hit him, and saw a minute owl, small/nenough to fit into the palm of his hand, whizzing/nexcitedly around the room like a loose firework. Harry/nthen realized that the owl had dropped a letter at his/nfeet. Harry bent down, recognized Ron's handwriting,/nthen tore open the envelope. Inside was a hastily/nscribbled note./n/nHarry — DAD GOT THE TICKETS — Ireland versus/nBulgaria, Monday night. Mum's writing to the Muggles/nto ask you to stay. They might already have the letter,/n/nI don't know how fast Muggle post is.
