Thought I'd send/nthis with Pig anyway./n/nHarry stared at the word "Pig," then looked up at the/ntiny owl now zooming around the light fixture on the/nceiling. He had never seen anything that looked less/nlike a pig. Maybe he couldn't read Ron's writing. He/nwent back to the letter:/n/nWe're coming for you whether the Muggles like it or/nnot, you can't miss the World Cup, only Mum and Dad/nreckon it's better if we pretend to ask their permission/nfirst. If they say yes, send Pig back with your answer/npronto, and we'll come and get you at five o'clock on/nSunday. If they say no, send Pig back pronto and we'll/ncome and get you at five o'clock on Sunday anyway./n/nHermione's arriving this afternoon. Percy's started/nwork — the Department of International Magical/nCooperation. Don't mention anything about Abroad/nwhile you're here unless you want the pants bored off/nyou./n/nSee you soon —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRon/n/n/n/n"Calm down!" Harry said as the small owl flew low/nover his head, twittering madly with what Harry could/nonly assume was pride at having delivered the letter/nto the right person. "Come here, I need you to take my/nanswer back!"/n/nThe owl fluttered down on top of Hedwig's cage./nHedwig looked coldly up at it, as though daring it to/ntry and come any closer./n/nHarry seized his eagle-feather quill once more,/ngrabbed a fresh piece of parchment, and wrote:/n/nRon, it's all okay, the Muggles say I can come. See you/nfive o'clock tomorrow. Can't wait./n/nHarry/n/nHe folded this note up very small, and with immense/ndifficulty, tied it to the tiny owl's leg as it hopped on/nthe spot with excitement. The moment the note was/nsecure, the owl was off again; it zoomed out of the/nwindow and out of sight./n/nHarry turned to Hedwig./n/n"Feeling up to a long journey?" he asked her./n/nHedwig hooted in a dignified sort of a way./n/n"Can you take this to Sirius for me?" he said, picking/nup his letter. "Hang on ... I just want to finish it."/n/nHe unfolded the parchment and hastily added a/npostscript./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIf you want to contact me, I'll be at my friend Ron/nWeasley's for the rest of the summer. His dad's got us/ntickets for the Quidditch World Cup\/n/nThe letter finished, he tied it to Hedwig's leg; she kept/nunusually still, as though determined to show him/nhow a real post owl should behave./n/n"I'll be at Ron's when you get back, all right?" Harry/ntold her./n/nShe nipped his finger affectionately, then, with a soft/nswooshing noise, spread her enormous wings and/nsoared out of the open window./n/nHarry watched her out of sight, then crawled under/nhis bed, wrenched up the loose floorboard, and pulled/nout a large chunk of birthday cake. He sat there on/nthe floor eating it, savoring the happiness that was/nflooding through him. He had cake, and Dudley had/nnothing but grapefruit; it was a bright summer's day,/nhe would be leaving Privet Drive tomorrow, his scar/nfelt perfectly normal again, and he was going to watch/nthe Quidditch World Cup. It was hard, just now, to/nfeel worried about anything — even Lord Voldemort./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Back To The Burrow
text: /nBy twelve o'clock the next day, Harry's school trunk/nwas packed with his school things and all his most/nprized possessions — the Invisibility Cloak he had/ninherited from his father, the broomstick he had/ngotten from Sirius, the enchanted map of Hogwarts he/nhad been given by Fred and George Weasley last year./nHe had emptied his hiding place under the loose/nfloorboard of all food, double-checked every nook and/ncranny of his bedroom for forgotten spellbooks or/nquills, and taken down the chart on the wall counting/ndown the days to September the first, on which he/nliked to cross off the days remaining until his return/nto Hogwarts./n/nThe atmosphere inside number four, Privet Drive was/nextremely tense. The imminent arrival at their house/nof an assortment of wizards was making the Dursleys/nuptight and irritable. Uncle Vernon had looked/ndownright alarmed when Harry informed him that the/nWeasley s would be arriving at five o'clock the very/nnext day./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I hope you told them to dress properly, these people,"/nhe snarled at once. "I've seen the sort of stuff your lot/nwear. They'd better have the decency to put on/nnormal clothes, that's all."/n/nHarry felt a slight sense of foreboding. He had rarely/nseen Mr. or Mrs. Weasley wearing anything that the/nDursleys would call "normal." Their children might/ndon Muggle clothing during the holidays, but Mr. and/nMrs. Weasley usually wore long robes in varying/nstates of shabbiness. Harry wasn't bothered about/nwhat the neighbors would think, but he was anxious/nabout how rude the Dursleys might be to the/nWeasleys if they turned up looking like their worst/nidea of wizards./n/nUncle Vernon had put on his best suit. To some/npeople, this might have looked like a gesture of/nwelcome, but Harry knew it was because Uncle/nVernon wanted to look impressive and intimidating./nDudley, on the other hand, looked somehow/ndiminished. This was not because the diet was at last/ntaking effect, but due to fright. Dudley had emerged/nfrom his last encounter with a fully-grown wizard with/na curly pig's tail poking out of the seat of his trousers,/nand Aunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon had had to pay/nfor its removal at a private hospital in London. It/nwasn't altogether surprising, therefore, that Dudley/nkept running his hand nervously over his backside,/nand walking sideways from room to room, so as not to/npresent the same target to the enemy./n/nLunch was an almost silent meal. Dudley didn't even/nprotest at the food (cottage cheese and grated celery)./nAunt Petunia wasn't eating anything at all. Her arms/nwere folded, her lips were pursed, and she seemed to/nbe chewing her tongue, as though biting back the/nfurious diatribe she longed to throw at Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They'll be driving, of course?" Uncle Vernon barked/nacross the table./n/n"Er," said Harry./n/nHe hadn't thought of that. How were the Weasleys/ngoing to pick him up? They didn't have a car/nanymore; the old Ford Anglia they had once owned/nwas currently running wild in the Forbidden Forest at/nHogwarts. But Mr. Weasley had borrowed a Ministry/nof Magic car last year; possibly he would do the same/ntoday?/n/n"I think so," said Harry./n/nUncle Vernon snorted into his mustache. Normally,/nUncle Vernon would have asked what car Mr. Weasley/ndrove; he tended to judge other men by how big and/nexpensive their cars were. But Harry doubted whether/nUncle Vernon would have taken to Mr. Weasley even/nif he drove a Ferrari./n/nHarry spent most of the afternoon in his bedroom; he/ncouldn't stand watching Aunt Petunia peer out/nthrough the net curtains every few seconds, as/nthough there had been a warning about an escaped/nrhinoceros. Finally, at a quarter to five, Harry went/nback downstairs and into the living room./n/nAunt Petunia was compulsively straightening/ncushions. Uncle Vernon was pretending to read the/npaper, but his tiny eyes were not moving, and Harry/nwas sure he was really listening with all his might for/nthe sound of an approaching car. Dudley was/ncrammed into an armchair, his porky hands beneath/nhim, clamped firmly around his bottom. Harry/ncouldn't take the tension; he left the room and went/nand sat on the stairs in the hall, his eyes on his/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwatch and his heart pumping fast from excitement/nand nerves./n/nBut five o'clock came and then went. Uncle Vernon,/nperspiring slightly in his suit, opened the front door,/npeered up and down the street, then withdrew his/nhead quickly./n/n"They're late!" he snarled at Harry./n/n"I know," said Harry. "Maybe — er — the traffic's bad,/nor something."/n/nTen past five ... then a quarter past five ... Harry was/nstarting to feel anxious himself now. At half past, he/nheard Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia conversing in/nterse mutters in the living room./n/n"No consideration at all."/n/n"We might've had an engagement."/n/n"Maybe they think theyll get invited to dinner if/nthey're late."/n/n"Well, they most certainly won't be," said Uncle/nVernon, and Harry heard him stand up and start/npacing the living room. "They'll take the boy and go,/nthere 11 be no hanging around. That's if they're coming/nat all. Probably mistaken the day. I daresay their kind/ndon't set much store by punctuality. Either that or/nthey drive some tin-pot car that's broken d —/nAAAAAAAARRRRRGH ! "/n/nHarry jumped up. From the other side of the living/nroom door came the sounds of the three Dursleys/nscrambling, panic-stricken, across the room. Next/nmoment Dudley came flying into the hall, looking/nterrified./n/n/n/n/n/n"What happened?" said Harry. "What's the matter?"/n/nBut Dudley didn't seem able to speak. Hands still/nclamped over his buttocks, he waddled as fast as he/ncould into the kitchen. Harry hurried into the living/nroom./n/nLoud hangings and scrapings were coming from/nbehind the Dursleys' boarded-up fireplace, which had/na fake coal fire plugged in front of it./n/n"What is it?" gasped Aunt Petunia, who had backed/ninto the wall and was staring, terrified, toward the/nfire. "What is it, Vernon?"/n/nBut they were left in doubt barely a second longer./nVoices could be heard from inside the blocked/nfireplace./n/n"Ouch! Fred, no — go back, go back, there's been/nsome kind of mistake — tell George not to — OUCH!/nGeorge, no, there's no room, go back quickly and tell/nRon — "/n/n"Maybe Harry can hear us, Dad — maybe he'll be able/nto let us out — "/n/nThere was a loud hammering of fists on the boards/nbehind the electric fire./n/n"Harry? Harry, can you hear us?"/n/nThe Dursleys rounded on Harry like a pair of angry/nwolverines./n/n"What is this?" growled Uncle Vernon. "What's going/non?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They — they've tried to get here by Floo powder,"/nsaid Harry, fighting a mad desire to laugh. "They can/ntravel by fire — only you've blocked the fireplace —/nhang on — "/n/nHe approached the fireplace and called through the/nboards./n/n"Mr. Weasley? Can you hear me?"/n/nThe hammering stopped. Somebody inside the/nchimney piece said, "Shh!"/n/n"Mr. Weasley, it's Harry ... the fireplace has been/nblocked up. You won't be able to get through there."/n/n"Damn!" said Mr. Weasley's voice. "What on earth did/nthey want to block up the fireplace for?"/n/n"They've got an electric fire," Harry explained./n/n"Really?" said Mr. Weasley's voice excitedly. "Eclectic,/nyou say? With a plug? Gracious, I must see that. .../nLet's think ... ouch, Ron!"/n/nRon's voice now joined the others'./n/n"What are we doing here? Has something gone/nwrong?"/n/n"Oh no, Ron," came Fred's voice, very sarcastically./n"No, this is exactly where we wanted to end up."/n/n"Yeah, we're having the time of our lives here," said/nGeorge, whose voice sounded muffled, as though he/nwas squashed against the wall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Boys, boys ..." said Mr. Weasley vaguely. "I'm trying/nto think what to do. ... Yes ... only way ... Stand back,/nHarry."/n/nHarry retreated to the sofa. Uncle Vernon, however,/nmoved forward./n/n"Wait a moment!" he bellowed at the fire. "What/nexactly are you going to — "/n/nBANG./n/nThe electric fire shot across the room as the boarded-/nup fireplace burst outward, expelling Mr. Weasley,/nFred, George, and Ron in a cloud of rubble and loose/nchippings. Aunt Petunia shrieked and fell backward/nover the coffee table; Uncle Vernon caught her before/nshe hit the floor, and gaped, speechless, at the/nWeasleys, all of whom had bright red hair, including/nFred and George, who were identical to the last/nfreckle./n/n"That's better," panted Mr. Weasley, brushing dust/nfrom his long green robes and straightening his/nglasses. "Ah — you must be Harry's aunt and uncle!"/n/nTall, thin, and balding, he moved toward Uncle/nVernon, his hand outstretched, but Uncle Vernon/nbacked away several paces, dragging Aunt Petunia./nWords utterly failed Uncle Vernon. His best suit was/ncovered in white dust, which had settled in his hair/nand mustache and made him look as though he had/njust aged thirty years./n/n"Er — yes — sorry about that," said Mr. Weasley,/nlowering his hand and looking over his shoulder at/nthe blasted fireplace. "It's all my fault. It just didn't/noccur to me that we wouldn't be able to get out at the/nother end. I had your fireplace connected to the Floo/n/n/n/n/nNetwork, you see — just for an afternoon, you know,/nso we could get Harry. Muggle fireplaces aren't/nsupposed to be connected, strictly speaking — but/nI've got a useful contact at the Floo Regulation Panel/nand he fixed it for me. I can put it right in a jiffy,/nthough, don't worry. I'll light a fire to send the boys/nback, and then I can repair your fireplace before I/nDisapparate."/n/nHarry was ready to bet that the Dursleys hadn't/nunderstood a single word of this. They were still/ngaping at Mr. Weasley, thunderstruck. Aunt Petunia/nstaggered upright again and hid behind Uncle/nVernon./n/n"Hello, Harry!" said Mr. Weasley brightly. "Got your/ntrunk ready?"/n/n"It's upstairs," said Harry, grinning back./n/n"Well get it," said Fred at once. Winking at Harry, he/nand George left the room. They knew where Harry's/nbedroom was, having once rescued him from it in the/ndead of night. Harry suspected that Fred and George/nwere hoping for a glimpse of Dudley; they had heard a/nlot about him from Harry./n/n"Well," said Mr. Weasley, swinging his arms slightly,/nwhile he tried to find words to break the very nasty/nsilence. "Very — erm — very nice place you've got/nhere."/n/nAs the usually spotless living room was now covered/nin dust and bits of brick, this remark didn't go down/ntoo well with the Dursleys. Uncle Vernon's face/npurpled once more, and Aunt Petunia started chewing/nher tongue again. However, they seemed too scared to/nactually say anything./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMr. Weasley was looking around. He loved everything/nto do with Muggles. Harry could see him itching to go/nand examine the television and the video recorder./n/n"They run off eckeltricity, do they?" he said/nknowledgeably. "Ah yes, I can see the plugs. I collect/nplugs," he added to Uncle Vernon. "And batteries. Got/na very large collection of batteries. My wife thinks I'm/nmad, but there you are."/n/nUncle Vernon clearly thought Mr. Weasley was mad/ntoo. He moved ever so slightly to the right, screening/nAunt Petunia from view, as though he thought Mr./nWeasley might suddenly run at them and attack./n/nDudley suddenly reappeared in the room. Harry could/nhear the clunk of his trunk on the stairs, and knew/nthat the sounds had scared Dudley out of the kitchen./nDudley edged along the wall, gazing at Mr. Weasley/nwith terrified eyes, and attempted to conceal himself/nbehind his mother and father. Unfortunately, Uncle/nVernon's bulk, while sufficient to hide bony Aunt/nPetunia, was nowhere near enough to conceal Dudley./n/n"Ah, this is your cousin, is it, Harry?" said Mr./nWeasley, taking another brave stab at making/nconversation./n/n"Yep," said Harry, "that's Dudley."/n/nHe and Ron exchanged glances and then quickly/nlooked away from each other; the temptation to burst/nout laughing was almost overwhelming. Dudley was/nstill clutching his bottom as though afraid it might/nfall off. Mr. Weasley, however, seemed genuinely/nconcerned at Dudley's peculiar behavior. Indeed, from/nthe tone of his voice when he next spoke, Harry was/nquite sure that Mr. Weasley thought Dudley was quite/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nas mad as the Dursleys thought he was, except that/nMr. Weasley felt sympathy rather than fear./n/n"Having a good holiday, Dudley?" he said kindly./n/nDudley whimpered. Harry saw his hands tighten still/nharder over his massive backside./n/nFred and George came back into the room carrying/nHarry's school trunk. They glanced around as they/nentered and spotted Dudley. Their faces cracked into/nidentical evil grins./n/n"Ah, right," said Mr. Weasley. "Better get cracking/nthen."/n/nHe pushed up the sleeves of his robes and took out/nhis wand. Harry saw the Dursleys draw back against/nthe wall as one./n/n"Incendio\" said Mr. Weasley, pointing his wand at the/nhole in the wall behind him./n/nFlames rose at once in the fireplace, crackling merrily/nas though they had been burning for hours. Mr./nWeasley took a small drawstring bag from his pocket,/nuntied it, took a pinch of the powder inside, and/nthrew it onto the flames, which turned emerald green/nand roared higher than ever./n/n"Off you go then, Fred," said Mr. Weasley./n/n"Coming," said Fred. "Oh no — hang on — "/n/nA bag of sweets had spilled out of Fred's pocket and/nthe contents were now rolling in every direction —/nbig, fat toffees in brightly colored wrappers./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nFred scrambled around, cramming them back into his/npocket, then gave the Dursleys a cheery wave,/nstepped forward, and walked right into the fire, saying/n"the Burrow!" Aunt Petunia gave a little shuddering/ngasp. There was a whooshing sound, and Fred/nvanished./n/n"Right then, George," said Mr. Weasley, "you and the/ntrunk."/n/nHarry helped George carry the trunk forward into the/nflames and turn it onto its end so that he could hold/nit better. Then, with a second whoosh, George had/ncried "the Burrow!" and vanished too./n/n"Ron, you next," said Mr. Weasley./n/n"See you," said Ron brightly to the Dursleys. He/ngrinned broadly at Harry, then stepped into the fire,/nshouted "the Burrow!" and disappeared./n/nNow Harry and Mr. Weasley alone remained./n/n"Well ... T>ye then," Harry said to the Dursleys./n/nThey didn't say anything at all. Harry moved toward/nthe fire, but just as he reached the edge of the hearth,/nMr. Weasley put out a hand and held him back. He/nwas looking at the Dursleys in amazement./n/n"Harry said good-bye to you," he said. "Didn't you/nhear him?"/n/n"It doesn't matter," Harry muttered to Mr. Weasley./n"Honestly, I don't care."/n/nMr. Weasley did not remove his hand from Harry's/nshoulder./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You aren't going to see your nephew till next/nsummer," he said to Uncle Vernon in mild/nindignation. "Surely you're going to say good-bye?"/n/nUncle Vernon's face worked furiously. The idea of/nbeing taught consideration by a man who had just/nblasted away half his living room wall seemed to be/ncausing him intense suffering. But Mr. Weasley's/nwand was still in his hand, and Uncle Vernon's tiny/neyes darted to it once, before he said, very resentfully,/n"Good-bye, then."/n/n"See you," said Harry, putting one foot forward into/nthe green flames, which felt pleasantly like warm/nbreath. At that moment, however, a horrible gagging/nsound erupted behind him, and Aunt Petunia started/nto scream./n/nHarry wheeled around. Dudley was no longer/nstanding behind his parents. He was kneeling beside/nthe coffee table, and he was gagging and sputtering/non a foot-long, purple, slimy thing that was/nprotruding from his mouth. One bewildered second/nlater, Harry realized that the foot-long thing was/nDudley's tongue — and that a brightly colored toffee/nwrapper lay on the floor before him./n/nAunt Petunia hurled herself onto the ground beside/nDudley, seized the end of his swollen tongue, and/nattempted to wrench it out of his mouth;/nunsurprisingly, Dudley yelled and sputtered worse/nthan ever, trying to fight her off. Uncle Vernon was/nbellowing and waving his arms around, and Mr./nWeasley had to shout to make himself heard./n/n"Not to worry, I can sort him out!" he yelled,/nadvancing on Dudley with his wand outstretched, but/nAunt Petunia screamed worse than ever and threw/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nherself on top of Dudley, shielding him from Mr./nWeasley./n/n/n/n"No, really!" said Mr. Weasley desperately. "It's a/nsimple process — it was the toffee — my son Fred —/nreal practical joker — but it's only an Engorgement/nCharm — at least, I think it is — please, I can correct/n/n/n/nit — "/n/n/n/nBut far from being reassured, the Dursleys became/nmore panic-stricken; Aunt Petunia was sobbing/nhysterically, tugging Dudley's tongue as though/ndetermined to rip it out; Dudley appeared to be/nsuffocating under the combined pressure of his/nmother and his tongue; and Uncle Vernon, who had/nlost control completely, seized a china figure from on/ntop of the sideboard and threw it very hard at Mr./nWeasley, who ducked, causing the ornament to/nshatter in the blasted fireplace./n/n"Now really!" said Mr. Weasley angrily, brandishing/nhis wand. "I'm trying to help\"/n/nBellowing like a wounded hippo, Uncle Vernon/nsnatched up another ornament./n/n"Harry, go! Just go!" Mr. Weasley shouted, his wand/non Uncle Vernon. "I'll sort this out!"/n/nHarry didn't want to miss the fun, but Uncle Vernon's/nsecond ornament narrowly missed his left ear, and on/nbalance he thought it best to leave the situation to/nMr. Weasley. He stepped into the fire, looking over his/nshoulder as he said "the Burrow!" His last fleeting/nglimpse of the living room was of Mr. Weasley blasting/na third ornament out of Uncle Vernon's hand with his/nwand, Aunt Petunia screaming and lying on top of/nDudley, and Dudley's tongue lolling around like a/ngreat slimy python. But next moment Harry had/n/n/n/n/nbegun to spin very fast, and the Dursleys' living room/nwas whipped out of sight in a rush of emerald-green/nflames./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n5/n/n/n/n

title: Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes
text: /nHarry spun faster and faster, elbows tucked tightly to/nhis sides, blurred fireplaces flashing past him, until/nhe started to feel sick and closed his eyes. Then,/nwhen at last he felt himself slowing down, he threw/nout his hands and came to a halt in time to prevent/nhimself from falling face forward out of the Weasleys'/nkitchen fire./n/n"Did he eat it?" said Fred excitedly, holding out a/nhand to pull Harry to his feet./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, straightening up. "What was it?"/n/n"Ton-Tongue Toffee," said Fred brightly. "George and I/ninvented them, and we've been looking for someone to/ntest them on all summer. ..."/n/nThe tiny kitchen exploded with laughter; Harry looked/naround and saw that Ron and George were sitting at/nthe scrubbed wooden table with two red-haired people/nHarry had never seen before, though he knew/n/n/n/n/nimmediately who they must be: Bill and Charlie, the/ntwo eldest Weasley brothers./n/n/n/n"How're you doing, Harry?" said the nearer of the two,/ngrinning at him and holding out a large hand, which/nHarry shook, feeling calluses and blisters under his/nfingers. This had to be Charlie, who worked with/ndragons in Romania. Charlie was built like the twins,/nshorter and stockier than Percy and Ron, who were/nboth long and lanky. He had a broad, good-natured/nface, which was weather-beaten and so freckly that he/nlooked almost tanned; his arms were muscular, and/none of them had a large, shiny burn on it./n/nBill got to his feet, smiling, and also shook Harry's/nhand. Bill came as something of a surprise. Harry/nknew that he worked for the wizarding bank,/nGringotts, and that Bill had been Head Boy at/nHogwarts; Harry had always imagined Bill to be an/nolder version of Percy: fussy about rule-breaking and/nfond of bossing everyone around. However, Bill was —/nthere was no other word for it — cool. He was tall,/nwith long hair that he had tied back in a ponytail. He/nwas wearing an earring with what looked like a fang/ndangling from it. Bill's clothes would not have looked/nout of place at a rock concert, except that Harry/nrecognized his boots to be made, not of leather, but of/ndragon hide./n/nBefore any of them could say anything else, there was/na faint popping noise, and Mr. Weasley appeared out/nof thin air at George's shoulder. He was looking/nangrier than Harry had ever seen him./n/n"That wasn't funny, Fred!" he shouted. "What on/nearth did you give that Muggle boy?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I didn't give him anything," said Fred, with another/nevil grin. "I just dropped it. ... It was his fault he went/nand ate it, I never told him to."/n/n"You dropped it on purpose!" roared Mr. Weasley./n/n"You knew he'd eat it, you knew he was on a diet — "/n/n"How big did his tongue get?" George asked eagerly./n/n"It was four feet long before his parents would let me/nshrink it!"/n/nHarry and the Weasleys roared with laughter again./n/n"It isn't funny\" Mr. Weasley shouted. "That sort of/nbehavior seriously undermines wizard-Muggle/nrelations! I spend half my life campaigning against the/nmistreatment of Muggles, and my own sons — "/n/n"We didn't give it to him because he's a Muggle!" said/nFred indignantly./n/n"No, we gave it to him because he's a great bullying/ngit," said George. "Isn't he, Harry?"/n/n"Yeah, he is, Mr. Weasley," said Harry earnestly./n/n"That's not the point!" raged Mr. Weasley. "You wait/nuntil I tell your mother — "/n/n"Tell me what?" said a voice behind them./n/nMrs. Weasley had just entered the kitchen. She was a/nshort, plump woman with a very kind face, though/nher eyes were presently narrowed with suspicion./n/n"Oh hello, Harry, dear," she said, spotting him and/nsmiling. Then her eyes snapped back to her husband./n"Tell me what , Arthur?"/n/n/n/n/n/nMr. Weasley hesitated. Harry could tell that, however/nangry he was with Fred and George, he hadn't really/nintended to tell Mrs. Weasley what had happened./nThere was a silence, while Mr. Weasley eyed his wife/nnervously. Then two girls appeared in the kitchen/ndoorway behind Mrs. Weasley. One, with very bushy/nbrown hair and rather large front teeth, was Harry's/nand Ron's friend, Hermione Granger. The other, who/nwas small and red-haired, was Ron's younger sister,/nGinny. Both of them smiled at Harry, who grinned/nback, which made Ginny go scarlet — she had been/nvery taken with Harry ever since his first visit to the/nBurrow./n/n"Tell me what, Arthur?" Mrs. Weasley repeated, in a/ndangerous sort of voice./n/n"It's nothing, Molly," mumbled Mr. Weasley, "Fred and/nGeorge just — but I've had words with them — "/n/n"What have they done this time?" said Mrs. Weasley./n"If it's got anything to do with Weasleys' Wizard/nWheezes — "/n/n"Why don't you show Harry where he's sleeping,/n/nRon?" said Hermione from the doorway./n/n"He knows where he's sleeping," said Ron, "in my/nroom, he slept there last — "/n/n"We can all go," said Hermione pointedly./n/n"Oh," said Ron, cottoning on. "Right."/n/n"Yeah, we'll come too," said George./n/n"You stay where you are!" snarled Mrs. Weasley./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry and Ron edged out of the kitchen, and they,/nHermione, and Ginny set off along the narrow hallway/nand up the rickety staircase that zigzagged through/nthe house to the upper stories./n/n"What are Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes?" Harry asked/nas they climbed./n/nRon and Ginny both laughed, although Hermione/ndidn't./n/n"Mum found this stack of order forms when she was/ncleaning Fred and George's room," said Ron quietly./n"Great long price lists for stuff they've invented. Joke/nstuff, you know. Fake wands and trick sweets, loads/nof stuff. It was brilliant, I never knew they'd been/ninventing all that ..."/n/n"We've been hearing explosions out of their room for/nages, but we never thought they were actually making/nthings," said Ginny. "We thought they just liked the/nnoise."/n/n"Only, most of the stuff — well, all of it, really — was/na bit dangerous," said Ron, "and, you know, they were/nplanning to sell it at Hogwarts to make some money,/nand Mum went mad at them. Told them they weren't/nallowed to make any more of it, and burned all the/norder forms. ... She's furious at them anyway. They/ndidn't get as many O.W.L.s as she expected."/n/nO.W.L.s were Ordinary Wizarding Levels, the/nexaminations Hogwarts students took at the age of/nfifteen./n/n"And then there was this big row," Ginny said,/n"because Mum wants them to go into the Ministry of/nMagic like Dad, and they told her all they want to do/nis open a joke shop."/n/n/n/n/n/nJust then a door on the second landing opened, and a/nface poked out wearing horn-rimmed glasses and a/nvery annoyed expression./n/n"Hi, Percy," said Harry./n/n"Oh hello, Harry," said Percy. "I was wondering who/nwas making all the noise. I'm trying to work in here,/nyou know — I've got a report to finish for the office —/nand it's rather difficult to concentrate when people/nkeep thundering up and down the stairs."/n/n"We're not thundering," said Ron irritably. "We're/nwalking. Sorry if we've disturbed the top-secret/nworkings of the Ministry of Magic."/n/n"What are you working on?" said Harry./n/n"A report for the Department of International Magical/nCooperation," said Percy smugly. "We're trying to/nstandardize cauldron thickness. Some of these foreign/nimports are just a shade too thin — leakages have/nbeen increasing at a rate of almost three percent a/nyear — "/n/n"That'll change the world, that report will," said Ron./n"Front page of the Daily Prophet, I expect, cauldron/nleaks."/n/nPercy went slightly pink./n/n"You might sneer, Ron," he said heatedly, "but unless/nsome sort of international law is imposed we might/nwell find the market flooded with flimsy, shallow-/nbottomed products that seriously endanger — "/n/n"Yeah, yeah, all right," said Ron, and he started off/nupstairs again. Percy slammed his bedroom door/nshut. As Harry, Hermione, and Ginny followed Ron up/n/n/n/n/n/nthree more flights of stairs, shouts from the kitchen/nbelow echoed up to them. It sounded as though Mr./nWeasley had told Mrs. Weasley about the toffees./n/nThe room at the top of the house where Ron slept/nlooked much as it had the last time that Harry had/ncome to stay: the same posters of Ron's favorite/nQuidditch team, the Chudley Cannons, were whirling/nand waving on the walls and sloping ceiling, and the/nfish tank on the windowsill, which had previously/nheld frog spawn, now contained one extremely large/nfrog. Ron's old rat, Scabbers, was here no more, but/ninstead there was the tiny gray owl that had delivered/nRon's letter to Harry in Privet Drive. It was hopping/nup and down in a small cage and twittering madly./n/n"Shut up, Pig," said Ron, edging his way between two/nof the four beds that had been squeezed into the/nroom. "Fred and George are in here with us, because/nBill and Charlie are in their room," he told Harry./n"Percy gets to keep his room all to himself because/nhe's got to work."/n/n"Er — why are you calling that owl Pig?" Harry asked/nRon./n/n"Because he's being stupid," said Ginny. "Its proper/nname is Pigwidgeon."/n/n"Yeah, and that's not a stupid name at all," said Ron/nsarcastically. "Ginny named him," he explained to/nHarry. "She reckons it's sweet. And I tried to change/nit, but it was too late, he won't answer to anything/nelse. So now he's Pig. I've got to keep him up here/nbecause he annoys Errol and Hermes. He annoys me/ntoo, come to that."/n/nPigwidgeon zoomed happily around his cage, hooting/nshrilly. Harry knew Ron too well to take him/n/n/n/n/n/nseriously. He had moaned continually about his old/nrat, Scabbers, but had been most upset when/nHermione's cat, Crookshanks, appeared to have eaten/nhim./n/n"Where's Crookshanks?" Harry asked Hermione now./n/n"Out in the garden, I expect," she said. "He likes/nchasing gnomes. He's never seen any before."/n/n"Percy's enjoying work, then?" said Harry, sitting/ndown on one of the beds and watching the Chudley/nCannons zooming in and out of the posters on the/nceiling./n/n"Enjoying it?" said Ron darkly. "I don't reckon he'd/ncome home if Dad didn't make him. He's obsessed./nJust don't get him onto the subject of his boss./nAccording to Mr. Crouch ... as I was saying to Mr./nCrouch . . . Mr. Crouch is of the opinion . . . Mr. Crouch/nwas telling me ... They 11 be announcing their/nengagement any day now."/n/n"Have you had a good summer, Harry?" said/nHermione. "Did you get our food parcels and/neverything?"/n/n"Yeah, thanks a lot," said Harry. "They saved my life,/nthose cakes."/n/n"And have you heard from — ?" Ron began, but at a/nlook from Hermione he fell silent. Harry knew Ron/nhad been about to ask about Sirius. Ron and/nHermione had been so deeply involved in helping/nSirius escape from the Ministry of Magic that they/nwere almost as concerned about Harry's godfather as/nhe was. However, discussing him in front of Ginny/nwas a bad idea. Nobody but themselves and Professor/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore knew about how Sirius had escaped, or/nbelieved in his innocence./n/n"I think they've stopped arguing," said Hermione, to/ncover the awkward moment, because Ginny was/nlooking curiously from Ron to Harry. "Shall we go/ndown and help your mum with dinner?"/n/n"Yeah, all right," said Ron. The four of them left Ron's/nroom and went back downstairs to find Mrs. Weasley/nalone in the kitchen, looking extremely bad-tempered./n/n"We're eating out in the garden," she said when they/ncame in. "There's just not room for eleven people in/nhere. Could you take the plates outside, girls? Bill/nand Charlie are setting up the tables. Knives and/nforks, please, you two," she said to Ron and Harry,/npointing her wand a little more vigorously than she/nhad intended at a pile of potatoes in the sink, which/nshot out of their skins so fast that they ricocheted off/nthe walls and ceiling./n/n"Oh for heaven's sake," she snapped, now directing/nher wand at a dustpan, which hopped off the/nsideboard and started skating across the floor,/nscooping up the potatoes. "Those two!" she burst out/nsavagely, now pulling pots and pans out of a/ncupboard, and Harry knew she meant Fred and/nGeorge. "I don't know what's going to happen to them,/nI really don't. No ambition, unless you count making/nas much trouble as they possibly can. ..."/n/nMrs. Weasley slammed a large copper saucepan down/non the kitchen table and began to wave her wand/naround inside it. A creamy sauce poured from the/nwand tip as she stirred./n/n"It's not as though they haven't got brains," she/ncontinued irritably, taking the saucepan over to the/n/n/n/n/n/nstove and lighting it with a further poke of her wand,/n"but they're wasting them, and unless they pull/nthemselves together soon, they'll be in real trouble./nI've had more owls from Hogwarts about them than/nthe rest put together. If they carry on the way they're/ngoing, they'll end up in front of the Improper Use of/nMagic Office."/n/nMrs. Weasley jabbed her wand at the cutlery drawer,/nwhich shot open. Harry and Ron both jumped out of/nthe way as several knives soared out of it, flew across/nthe kitchen, and began chopping the potatoes, which/nhad just been tipped back into the sink by the/ndustpan./n/n"I don't know where we went wrong with them," said/nMrs. Weasley, putting down her wand and starting to/npull out still more saucepans. "It's been the same for/nyears, one thing after another, and they won't listen/nto — OH NOT AGAIN."/n/nShe had picked up her wand from the table, and it/nhad emitted a loud squeak and turned into a giant/nrubber mouse./n/n"One of their fake wands again!" she shouted. "How/nmany times have I told them not to leave them lying/naround?"/n/nShe grabbed her real wand and turned around to find/nthat the sauce on the stove was smoking./n/n"C'mon," Ron said hurriedly to Harry, seizing a/nhandful of cutlery from the open drawer, "let's go and/nhelp Bill and Charlie."/n/nThey left Mrs. Weasley and headed out the back door/ninto the yard./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey had only gone a few paces when Hermione's/nbandy-legged ginger cat, Crookshanks, came pelting/nout of the garden, bottle-brush tail held high in the/nair, chasing what looked like a muddy potato on legs./nHarry recognized it instantly as a gnome. Barely ten/ninches high, its horny little feet pattered very fast as it/nsprinted across the yard and dived headlong into one/nof the Wellington boots that lay scattered around the/ndoor. Harry could hear the gnome giggling madly as/nCrookshanks inserted a paw into the boot, trying to/nreach it. Meanwhile, a very loud crashing noise was/ncoming from the other side of the house. The source/nof the commotion was revealed as they entered the/ngarden, and saw that Bill and Charlie both had their/nwands out, and were making two battered old tables/nfly high above the lawn, smashing into each other,/neach attempting to knock the other's out of the air./nFred and George were cheering, Ginny was laughing,/nand Hermione was hovering near the hedge,/napparently torn between amusement and anxiety./n/nBill's table caught Charlie's with a huge bang and/nknocked one of its legs off. There was a clatter from/noverhead, and they all looked up to see Percy's head/npoking out of a window on the second floor./n/n"Will you keep it down?!" he bellowed./n/n"Sorry, Perce," said Bill, grinning. "How're the/ncauldron bottoms coming on?"/n/n"Very badly," said Percy peevishly, and he slammed/nthe window shut. Chuckling, Bill and Charlie directed/nthe tables safely onto the grass, end to end, and then,/nwith a flick of his wand, Bill reattached the table leg/nand conjured tablecloths from nowhere./n/nBy seven o'clock, the two tables were groaning under/ndishes and dishes of Mrs. Weasley's excellent cooking,/n/n/n/n/n/nand the nine Weasleys, Harry, and Hermione were/nsettling themselves down to eat beneath a clear, deep-/nblue sky. To somebody who had been living on meals/nof increasingly stale cake all summer, this was/nparadise, and at first, Harry listened rather than/ntalked as he helped himself to chicken and ham pie,/nboiled potatoes, and salad./n/nAt the far end of the table, Percy was telling his father/nall about his report on cauldron bottoms./n/n"I've told Mr. Crouch that I'll have it ready by/nTuesday," Percy was saying pompously. "That's a bit/nsooner than he expected it, but I like to keep on top of/nthings. I think he'll be grateful I've done it in good/ntime, I mean, it's extremely busy in our department/njust now, what with all the arrangements for the/nWorld Cup. We're just not getting the support we/nneed from the Department of Magical Games and/nSports. Ludo Bagman — "/n/n"I like Ludo," said Mr. Weasley mildly. "He was the/none who got us such good tickets for the Cup. I did/nhim a bit of a favor: His brother, Otto, got into a spot/nof trouble — a lawnmower with unnatural powers — I/nsmoothed the whole thing over."/n/n"Oh Bagman's likable enough, of course," said Percy/ndismissively, "but how he ever got to be Head of/nDepartment ... when I compare him to Mr. Crouch! I/ncan't see Mr. Crouch losing a member of our/ndepartment and not trying to find out what's/nhappened to them. You realize Bertha Jorkins has/nbeen missing for over a month now? Went on holiday/nto Albania and never came back?"/n/n"Yes, I was asking Ludo about that," said Mr./n/nWeasley, frowning. "He says Bertha's gotten lost/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nplenty of times before now — though I must say, if it/nwas someone in my department, I'd be worried. ..."/n/n"Oh Bertha's hopeless, all right," said Percy. "I hear/nshe's been shunted from department to department/nfor years, much more trouble than she's worth ... but/nall the same, Bagman ought to be trying to find her./nMr. Crouch has been taking a personal interest, she/nworked in our department at one time, you know, and/nI think Mr. Crouch was quite fond of her — but/nBagman just keeps laughing and saying she probably/nmisread the map and ended up in Australia instead of/nAlbania. However" — Percy heaved an impressive sigh/nand took a deep swig of elderflower wine — "we've got/nquite enough on our plates at the Department of/nInternational Magical Cooperation without trying to/nfind members of other departments too. As you know,/nwe've got another big event to organize right after the/nWorld Cup."/n/nPercy cleared his throat significantly and looked down/ntoward the end of the table where Harry, Ron, and/nHermione were sitting. " You know the one I'm talking/nabout, Father." He raised his voice slightly. "The top-/nsecret one."/n/nRon rolled his eyes and muttered to Harry and/nHermione, "He's been trying to get us to ask what that/nevent is ever since he started work. Probably an/nexhibition of thick-bottomed cauldrons."/n/nIn the middle of the table, Mrs. Weasley was arguing/nwith Bill about his earring, which seemed to be a/nrecent acquisition./n/n"... with a horrible great fang on it. Really, Bill, what/ndo they say at the bank?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mum, no one at the bank gives a damn how I dress/nas long as I bring home plenty of treasure," said Bill/npatiently./n/n"And your hair's getting silly, dear," said Mrs./n/nWeasley, fingering her wand lovingly. "I wish you'd let/nme give it a trim. ..."/n/n"I like it," said Ginny, who was sitting beside Bill./n"You're so old-fashioned, Mum. Anyway, it's nowhere/nnear as long as Professor Dumbledore's. ..."/n/nNext to Mrs. Weasley, Fred, George, and Charlie were/nall talking spiritedly about the World Cup./n/n"It's got to be Ireland," said Charlie thickly, through a/nmouthful of potato. "They flattened Peru in the/nsemifinals."/n/n"Bulgaria has got Viktor Krum, though," said Fred./n/n"Krum's one decent player, Ireland has got seven,"/nsaid Charlie shortly. "I wish England had got through./nThat was embarrassing, that was."/n/n"What happened?" said Harry eagerly, regretting more/nthan ever his isolation from the wizarding world when/nhe was stuck on Privet Drive./n/n"Went down to Transylvania, three hundred and/nninety to ten," said Charlie gloomily. "Shocking/nperformance. And Wales lost to Uganda, and Scotland/nwas slaughtered by Luxembourg."/n/nHarry had been on the Gryffindor House Quidditch/nteam ever since his first year at Hogwarts and owned/none of the best racing brooms in the world, a Firebolt./nFlying came more naturally to Harry than anything/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nelse in the magical world, and he played in the/nposition of Seeker on the Gryffindor House team./n/nMr. Weasley conjured up candles to light the/ndarkening garden before they had their homemade/nstrawberry ice cream, and by the time they had/nfinished, moths were fluttering low over the table, and/nthe warm air was perfumed with the smells of grass/nand honeysuckle. Harry was feeling extremely well fed/nand at peace with the world as he watched several/ngnomes sprinting through the rosebushes, laughing/nmadly and closely pursued by Crookshanks./n/nRon looked carefully up the table to check that the/nrest of the family were all busy talking, then he said/nvery quietly to Harry, "So — have you heard from/nSirius lately?"/n/nHermione looked around, listening closely./n/n"Yeah," said Harry softly, "twice. He sounds okay. I/nwrote to him yesterday. He might write back while I'm/nhere."/n/nHe suddenly remembered the reason he had written/nto Sirius, and for a moment was on the verge of telling/nRon and Hermione about his scar hurting again, and/nabout the dream that had awoken him . . . but he/nreally didn't want to worry them just now, not when/nhe himself was feeling so happy and peaceful./n/n"Look at the time," Mrs. Weasley said suddenly,/nchecking her wristwatch. "You really should be in/nbed, the whole lot of you — you'll be up at the crack/nof dawn to get to the Cup. Harry, if you leave your/nschool list out, I'll get your things for you tomorrow in/nDiagon Alley. I'm getting everyone else's. There might/nnot be time after the World Cup, the match went on/nfor five days last time."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wow — hope it does this time!" said Harry/nenthusiastically./n/n"Well, I certainly don't," said Percy sanctimoniously. "I/nshudder to think what the state of my in-tray would/nbe if I was away from work for five days."/n/n"Yeah, someone might slip dragon dung in it again,/neh, Perce?" said Fred./n/n"That was a sample of fertilizer from Norway!" said/nPercy, going very red in the face. "It was nothing/npersonall"/n/n"It was," Fred whispered to Harry as they got up from/nthe table. "We sent it."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Portkey
text: /nHarry felt as though he had barely lain down to sleep/nin Ron's room when he was being shaken awake by/nMrs. Weasley./n/n"Time to go, Harry, dear," she whispered, moving/naway to wake Ron./n/nHarry felt around for his glasses, put them on, and/nsat up. It was still dark outside. Ron muttered/nindistinctly as his mother roused him. At the foot of/nHarry's mattress he saw two large, disheveled shapes/nemerging from tangles of blankets./n/n" 'S' time already?" said Fred groggily./n/nThey dressed in silence, too sleepy to talk, then,/nyawning and stretching, the four of them headed/ndownstairs into the kitchen./n/nMrs. Weasley was stirring the contents of a large pot/non the stove, while Mr. Weasley was sitting at the/ntable, checking a sheaf of large parchment tickets. He/n/n/n/n/nlooked up as the boys entered and spread his arms so/nthat they could see his clothes more clearly. He was/nwearing what appeared to be a golfing sweater and a/nvery old pair of jeans, slightly too big for him and held/nup with a thick leather belt./n/n"What d'you think?" he asked anxiously. "We're/nsupposed to go incognito — do I look like a Muggle,/nHarry?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, smiling, "very good."/n/n"Where 're Bill and Charlie and Per-Per-Percy?" said/nGeorge, failing to stifle a huge yawn./n/n"Well, they're Apparating, aren't they?" said Mrs./nWeasley, heaving the large pot over to the table and/nstarting to ladle porridge into bowls. "So they can/nhave a bit of a lie-in."/n/nHarry knew that Apparating meant disappearing from/none place and reappearing almost instantly in/nanother, but had never known any Hogwarts student/nto do it, and understood that it was very difficult./n/n"So they're still in bed?" said Fred grumpily, pulling/nhis bowl of porridge toward him. "Why can't we/nApparate too?"/n/n"Because you're not of age and you haven't passed/nyour test," snapped Mrs. Weasley. "And where have/nthose girls got to?"/n/nShe bustled out of the kitchen and they heard her/nclimbing the stairs./n/n"You have to pass a test to Apparate?" Harry asked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh yes," said Mr. Weasley, tucking the tickets safely/ninto the back pocket of his jeans. "The Department of/nMagical Transportation had to fine a couple of people/nthe other day for Apparating without a license. It's not/neasy, Apparition, and when it's not done properly it/ncan lead to nasty complications. This pair I'm talking/nabout went and splinched themselves."/n/nEveryone around the table except Harry winced./n/n"Er — splinched?" said Harry./n/n"They left half of themselves behind," said Mr./n/nWeasley, now spooning large amounts of treacle onto/nhis porridge. "So, of course, they were stuck. Couldn't/nmove either way. Had to wait for the Accidental Magic/nReversal Squad to sort them out. Meant a fair old bit/nof paperwork, I can tell you, what with the Muggles/nwho spotted the body parts they'd left behind. ..."/n/nHarry had a sudden vision of a pair of legs and an/neyeball lying abandoned on the pavement of Privet/nDrive./n/n"Were they okay?" he asked, startled./n/n"Oh yes," said Mr. Weasley matter-of-factly. "But they/ngot a heavy fine, and I don't think they'll be trying it/nagain in a hurry. You don't mess around with/nApparition. There are plenty of adult wizards who/ndon't bother with it. Prefer brooms — slower, but/nsafer."/n/n"But Bill and Charlie and Percy can all do it?"/n/n"Charlie had to take the test twice," said Fred,/ngrinning. "He failed the first time, Apparated five/nmiles south of where he meant to, right on top of/nsome poor old dear doing her shopping, remember?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, well, he passed the second time," said Mrs./nWeasley, marching back into the kitchen amid hearty/nsniggers./n/n"Percy only passed two weeks ago," said George. "He's/nbeen Apparating downstairs every morning since, just/nto prove he can."/n/nThere were footsteps down the passageway and/nHermione and Ginny came into the kitchen, both/nlooking pale and drowsy./n/n"Why do we have to be up so early?" Ginny said,/nrubbing her eyes and sitting down at the table./n/n"We've got a bit of a walk," said Mr. Weasley./n/n"Walk?" said Harry. "What, are we walking to the/nWorld Cup?"/n/n"No, no, that's miles away," said Mr. Weasley, smiling./n"We only need to walk a short way. It's just that it's/nvery difficult for a large number of wizards to/ncongregate without attracting Muggle attention. We/nhave to be very careful about how we travel at the/nbest of times, and on a huge occasion like the/nQuidditch World Cup — "/n/n"George!" said Mrs. Weasley sharply, and they all/njumped./n/n"What?" said George, in an innocent tone that/ndeceived nobody./n/n"What is that in your pocket?"/n/n"Nothing!"/n/n"Don't you lie to me!"/n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley pointed her wand at George's pocket/nand said, "Acciol"/n/nSeveral small, brightly colored objects zoomed out of/nGeorge's pocket; he made a grab for them but missed,/nand they sped right into Mrs. Weasley 's outstretched/nhand./n/n"We told you to destroy them!" said Mrs. Weasley/nfuriously, holding up what were unmistakably more/nTon-Tongue Toffees. "We told you to get rid of the lot!/nEmpty your pockets, go on, both of you!"/n/nIt was an unpleasant scene; the twins had evidently/nbeen trying to smuggle as many toffees out of the/nhouse as possible, and it was only by using her/nSummoning Charm that Mrs. Weasley managed to/nfind them all./n/n"Acciol Acciol Acciol" she shouted, and toffees zoomed/nfrom all sorts of unlikely places, including the lining/nof George's jacket and the turn-ups of Fred's jeans./n/n"We spent six months developing those!" Fred/nshouted at his mother as she threw the toffees away./n/n"Oh a fine way to spend six months!" she shrieked./n/n"No wonder you didn't get more O.W.L.s!"/n/nAll in all, the atmosphere was not very friendly as/nthey took their departure. Mrs. Weasley was still/nglowering as she kissed Mr. Weasley on the cheek,/nthough not nearly as much as the twins, who had/neach hoisted their rucksacks onto their backs and/nwalked out without a word to her./n/n"Well, have a lovely time," said Mrs. Weasley, "and/nbehave yourselves," she called after the twins'/nretreating backs, but they did not look back or/n/n/n/n/n/nanswer. "I'll send Bill, Charlie, and Percy along/naround midday," Mrs. Weasley said to Mr. Weasley, as/nhe, Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Ginny set off across/nthe dark yard after Fred and George./n/nIt was chilly and the moon was still out. Only a dull,/ngreenish tinge along the horizon to their right showed/nthat daybreak was drawing closer. Harry, having been/nthinking about thousands of wizards speeding toward/nthe Quidditch World Cup, sped up to walk with Mr./nWeasley./n/n"So how does everyone get there without all the/nMuggles noticing?" he asked./n/n"It's been a massive organizational problem," sighed/nMr. Weasley. "The trouble is, about a hundred/nthousand wizards turn up at the World Cup, and of/ncourse, we just haven't got a magical site big enough/nto accommodate them all. There are places Muggles/ncan't penetrate, but imagine trying to pack a hundred/nthousand wizards into Diagon Alley or platform nine/nand three-quarters. So we had to find a nice deserted/nmoor, and set up as many anti-Muggle precautions as/npossible. The whole Ministry's been working on it for/nmonths. First, of course, we have to stagger the/narrivals. People with cheaper tickets have to arrive/ntwo weeks beforehand. A limited number use Muggle/ntransport, but we can't have too many clogging up/ntheir buses and trains — remember, wizards are/ncoming from all over the world. Some Apparate, of/ncourse, but we have to set up safe points for them to/nappear, well away from Muggles. I believe there's a/nhandy wood they're using as the Apparition point. For/nthose who don't want to Apparate, or can't, we use/nPortkeys. They're objects that are used to transport/nwizards from one spot to another at a prearranged/ntime. You can do large groups at a time if you need to./nThere have been two hundred Portkeys placed at/n/n/n/n/nstrategic points around Britain, and the nearest one/nto us is up at the top of Stoatshead Hill, so that's/nwhere we're headed."/n/nMr. Weasley pointed ahead of them, where a large/nblack mass rose beyond the village of Ottery St./nCatchpole./n/n"What sort of objects are Portkeys?" said Harry/ncuriously./n/n"Well, they can be anything," said Mr. Weasley./n"Unobtrusive things, obviously, so Muggles don't go/npicking them up and playing with them . . . stuff they'll/njust think is litter. ..."/n/nThey trudged down the dark, dank lane toward the/nvillage, the silence broken only by their footsteps. The/nsky lightened very slowly as they made their way/nthrough the village, its inky blackness diluting to/ndeepest blue. Harry's hands and feet were freezing./n/nMr. Weasley kept checking his watch./n/nThey didn't have breath to spare for talking as they/nbegan to climb Stoatshead Hill, stumbling/noccasionally in hidden rabbit holes, slipping on thick/nblack tuffets of grass. Each breath Harry took was/nsharp in his chest and his legs were starting to seize/nup when, at last, his feet found level ground./n/n"Whew," panted Mr. Weasley, taking off his glasses/nand wiping them on his sweater. "Well, we've made/ngood time — we've got ten minutes. ..."/n/nHermione came over the crest of the hill last,/nclutching a stitch in her side./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Now we just need the Portkey," said Mr. Weasley,/nreplacing his glasses and squinting around at the/nground. "It won't be big. ... Come on ..."/n/nThey spread out, searching. They had only been at it/nfor a couple of minutes, however, when a shout rent/nthe still air./n/n"Over here, Arthur! Over here, son, we've got it!"/n/nTwo tall figures were silhouetted against the starry/nsky on the other side of the hilltop./n/n"Amos!" said Mr. Weasley, smiling as he strode over to/nthe man who had shouted. The rest of them followed./n/nMr. Weasley was shaking hands with a ruddy-faced/nwizard with a scrubby brown beard, who was holding/na moldy-looking old boot in his other hand./n/n"This is Amos Diggory, everyone," said Mr. Weasley./n"He works for the Department for the Regulation and/nControl of Magical Creatures. And I think you know/nhis son, Cedric?"/n/nCedric Diggory was an extremely handsome boy of/naround seventeen. He was Captain and Seeker of the/nHufflepuff House Quidditch team at Hogwarts./n/n"Hi," said Cedric, looking around at them all./n/nEverybody said hi back except Fred and George, who/nmerely nodded. They had never quite forgiven Cedric/nfor beating their team, Gryffindor, in the first/nQuidditch match of the previous year./n/n"Long walk, Arthur?" Cedric's father asked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Not too bad," said Mr. Weasley. "We live just on the/nother side of the village there. You?"/n/n"Had to get up at two, didn't we, Ced? I tell you, I'll be/nglad when he's got his Apparition test. Still ... not/ncomplaining ... Quidditch World Cup, wouldn't miss it/nfor a sackful of Galleons — and the tickets cost about/nthat. Mind you, looks like I got off easy. ..." Amos/nDiggory peered good-naturedly around at the three/nWeasley boys, Harry, Hermione, and Ginny. "All these/nyours, Arthur?"/n/n"Oh no, only the redheads," said Mr. Weasley,/npointing out his children. "This is Hermione, friend of/nRon's — and Harry, another friend — "/n/n"Merlin's beard," said Amos Diggory, his eyes/nwidening. "Harry? Harry Potter?"/n/n"Er — yeah," said Harry./n/nHarry was used to people looking curiously at him/nwhen they met him, used to the way their eyes moved/nat once to the lightning scar on his forehead, but it/nalways made him feel uncomfortable./n/n"Ced's talked about you, of course," said Amos/nDiggory. "Told us all about playing against you last/nyear. ... I said to him, I said — Ced, that'll be/nsomething to tell your grandchildren, that will. ... You/nbeat Harry Potterl"/n/nHarry couldn't think of any reply to this, so he/nremained silent. Fred and George were both scowling/nagain. Cedric looked slightly embarrassed./n/n"Harry fell off his broom, Dad," he muttered. "I told/nyou ... it was an accident. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, but you didn't fall off, did you?" roared Amos/ngenially, slapping his son on his back. "Always/nmodest, our Ced, always the gentleman ... but the/nbest man won, I'm sure Harry'd say the same,/nwouldn't you, eh? One falls off his broom, one stays/non, you don't need to be a genius to tell which one's/nthe better flier!"/n/n"Must be nearly time," said Mr. Weasley quickly,/npulling out his watch again. "Do you know whether/nwe're waiting for any more, Amos?"/n/n"No, the Lovegoods have been there for a week already/nand the Fawcetts couldn't get tickets," said Mr./nDiggory. "There aren't any more of us in this area, are/nthere?"/n/n"Not that I know of," said Mr. Weasley. "Yes, it's a/nminute off. ... We'd better get ready. ..."/n/nHe looked around at Harry and Hermione./n/n"You just need to touch the Portkey, that's all, a/nfinger will do — "/n/nWith difficulty, owing to their bulky backpacks, the/nnine of them crowded around the old boot held out by/nAmos Diggory./n/nThey all stood there, in a tight circle, as a chill breeze/nswept over the hilltop. Nobody spoke. It suddenly/noccurred to Harry how odd this would look if a/nMuggle were to walk up here now ... nine people, two/nof them grown men, clutching this manky old boot in/nthe semidarkness, waiting. .../n/n"Three ..." muttered Mr. Weasley, one eye still on his/nwatch, "two ... one ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt happened immediately: Harry felt as though a hook/njust behind his navel had been suddenly jerked/nirresistibly forward. His feet left the ground; he could/nfeel Ron and Hermione on either side of him, their/nshoulders banging into his; they were all speeding/nforward in a howl of wind and swirling color; his/nforefinger was stuck to the boot as though it was/npulling him magnetically onward and then —/n/nHis feet slammed into the ground; Ron staggered into/nhim and he fell over; the Portkey hit the ground near/nhis head with a heavy thud./n/nHarry looked up. Mr. Weasley, Mr. Diggory, and/nCedric were still standing, though looking very/nwindswept; everybody else was on the ground./n/n"Seven past five from Stoatshead Hill," said a voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n7/n/n/n/n

title: Bagman And Crouch
text: /nHarry disentangled himself from Ron and got to his/nfeet. They had arrived on what appeared to be a/ndeserted stretch of misty moor. In front of them was a/npair of tired and grumpy-looking wizards, one of/nwhom was holding a large gold watch, the other a/nthick roll of parchment and a quill. Both were dressed/nas Muggles, though very inexpertly: The man with the/nwatch wore a tweed suit with thigh-length galoshes;/nhis colleague, a kilt and a poncho./n/n"Morning, Basil," said Mr. Weasley, picking up the/nboot and handing it to the kilted wizard, who threw it/ninto a large box of used Portkeys beside him; Harry/ncould see an old newspaper, an empty drinks can,/nand a punctured football./n/n"Hello there, Arthur," said Basil wearily. "Not on duty,/neh? It's all right for some. ... We've been here all/nnight. ... You'd better get out of the way, we've got a/nbig party coming in from the Black Forest at five-/nfifteen. Hang on, I'll find your campsite. ... Weasley .../nWeasley ..." He consulted his parchment list. "About a/n/n/n/nquarter of a mile's walk over there, first field you/ncome to. Site manager's called Mr. Roberts. Diggory .../nsecond field ... ask for Mr. Payne."/n/n"Thanks, Basil," said Mr. Weasley, and he beckoned/neveryone to follow him./n/nThey set off across the deserted moor, unable to make/nout much through the mist. After about twenty/nminutes, a small stone cottage next to a gate swam/ninto view. Beyond it, Harry could just make out the/nghostly shapes of hundreds and hundreds of tents,/nrising up the gentle slope of a large field toward a/ndark wood on the horizon. They said good-bye to the/nDiggorys and approached the cottage door./n/nA man was standing in the doorway, looking out at/nthe tents. Harry knew at a glance that this was the/nonly real Muggle for several acres. When he heard/ntheir footsteps, he turned his head to look at them./n/n"Morning!" said Mr. Weasley brightly./n/n"Morning," said the Muggle./n/n"Would you be Mr. Roberts?"/n/n"Aye, I would," said Mr. Roberts. "And who're you?"/n/n"Weasley — two tents, booked a couple of days ago?"/n/n"Aye," said Mr. Roberts, consulting a list tacked to the/ndoor. "You've got a space up by the wood there. Just/nthe one night?"/n/n"That's it," said Mr. Weasley./n/n"You'll be paying now, then?" said Mr. Roberts./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah — right — certainly — " said Mr. Weasley. He/nretreated a short distance from the cottage and/nbeckoned Harry toward him. "Help me, Harry," he/nmuttered, pulling a roll of Muggle money from his/npocket and starting to peel the notes apart. "This/none's a — a — a ten? Ah yes, I see the little number/non it now. ... So this is a five?"/n/n"A twenty," Harry corrected him in an undertone,/nuncomfortably aware of Mr. Roberts trying to catch/nevery word./n/n"Ah yes, so it is. ... I don't know, these little bits of/npaper ..."/n/n"You foreign?" said Mr. Roberts as Mr. Weasley/nreturned with the correct notes./n/n"Foreign?" repeated Mr. Weasley, puzzled./n/n"You're not the first one who's had trouble with/nmoney," said Mr. Roberts, scrutinizing Mr. Weasley/nclosely. "I had two try and pay me with great gold/ncoins the size of hubcaps ten minutes ago."/n/n"Did you really?" said Mr. Weasley nervously./n/nMr. Roberts rummaged around in a tin for some/nchange./n/n"Never been this crowded," he said suddenly, looking/nout over the misty field again. "Hundreds of pre-/nbookings. People usually just turn up. ..."/n/n"Is that right?" said Mr. Weasley, his hand held out/nfor his change, but Mr. Roberts didn't give it to him./n/n"Aye," he said thoughtfully. "People from all over./nLoads of foreigners. And not just foreigners. Weirdos,/n/n/n/n/n/nyou know? There's a bloke walking 'round in a kilt/nand a poncho."/n/n"Shouldn't he?" said Mr. Weasley anxiously./n/n"It's like some sort of ... I dunno ... like some sort of/nrally," said Mr. Roberts. "They all seem to know each/nother. Like a big party."/n/nAt that moment, a wizard in plus-fours appeared out/nof thin air next to Mr. Roberts's front door./n/n"Obliviate\" he said sharply, pointing his wand at Mr./nRoberts./n/nInstantly, Mr. Roberts's eyes slid out of focus, his/nbrows unknitted, and a look of dreamy unconcern fell/nover his face. Harry recognized the symptoms of one/nwho had just had his memory modified./n/n"A map of the campsite for you," Mr. Roberts said/nplacidly to Mr. Weasley. "And your change."/n/n"Thanks very much," said Mr. Weasley./n/nThe wizard in plus-fours accompanied them toward/nthe gate to the campsite. He looked exhausted: His/nchin was blue with stubble and there were deep/npurple shadows under his eyes. Once out of earshot/nof Mr. Roberts, he muttered to Mr. Weasley, "Been/nhaving a lot of trouble with him. Needs a Memory/nCharm ten times a day to keep him happy. And Ludo/nBagman's not helping. Trotting around talking about/nBludgers and Quaffles at the top of his voice, not a/nworry about anti-Muggle security. Blimey, I'll be glad/nwhen this is over. See you later, Arthur."/n/nHe Disapparated./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I thought Mr. Bagman was Head of Magical Games/nand Sports," said Ginny, looking surprised. "He/nshould know better than to talk about Bludgers near/nMuggles, shouldn't he?"/n/n"He should," said Mr. Weasley, smiling, and leading/nthem through the gates into the campsite, "but Ludo's/nalways been a bit ... well ... lax about security. You/ncouldn't wish for a more enthusiastic head of the/nsports department though. He played Quidditch for/nEngland himself, you know. And he was the best/nBeater the Wimbourne Wasps ever had."/n/nThey trudged up the misty field between long rows of/ntents. Most looked almost ordinary; their owners had/nclearly tried to make them as Muggle-like as possible,/nbut had slipped up by adding chimneys, or bellpulls,/nor weather vanes. However, here and there was a tent/nso obviously magical that Harry could hardly be/nsurprised that Mr. Roberts was getting suspicious./nHalfway up the field stood an extravagant confection/nof striped silk like a miniature palace, with several/nlive peacocks tethered at the entrance. A little farther/non they passed a tent that had three floors and/nseveral turrets; and a short way beyond that was a/ntent that had a front garden attached, complete with/nbirdbath, sundial, and fountain./n/n"Always the same," said Mr. Weasley, smiling. "We/ncan't resist showing off when we get together. Ah,/nhere we are, look, this is us."/n/nThey had reached the very edge of the wood at the top/nof the field, and here was an empty space, with a/nsmall sign hammered into the ground that read/nWEEZLY./n/n"Couldn't have a better spot!" said Mr. Weasley/nhappily. "The field is just on the other side of the/n/n/n/n/n/nwood there, we're as close as we could be." He hoisted/nhis backpack from his shoulders. "Right," he said/nexcitedly, "no magic allowed, strictly speaking, not/nwhen we're out in these numbers on Muggle land./nWe'll be putting these tents up by hand! Shouldn't be/ntoo difficult. ... Muggles do it all the time. ... Here,/nHarry, where do you reckon we should start?"/n/nHarry had never been camping in his life; the/nDursleys had never taken him on any kind of holiday,/npreferring to leave him with Mrs. Figg, an old/nneighbor. However, he and Hermione worked out/nwhere most of the poles and pegs should go, and/nthough Mr. Weasley was more of a hindrance than a/nhelp, because he got thoroughly overexcited when it/ncame to using the mallet, they finally managed to/nerect a pair of shabby two-man tents./n/nAll of them stood back to admire their handiwork./nNobody looking at these tents would guess they/nbelonged to wizards, Harry thought, but the trouble/nwas that once Bill, Charlie, and Percy arrived, they/nwould be a party of ten. Hermione seemed to have/nspotted this problem too; she gave Harry a quizzical/nlook as Mr. Weasley dropped to his hands and knees/nand entered the first tent./n/n"Well be a bit cramped," he called, "but I think we'll/nall squeeze in. Come and have a look."/n/nHarry bent down, ducked under the tent flap, and felt/nhis jaw drop. He had walked into what looked like an/nold-fashioned, three-room flat, complete with/nbathroom and kitchen. Oddly enough, it was/nfurnished in exactly the same sort of style as Mrs./nFigg's house: There were crocheted covers on the/nmismatched chairs and a strong smell of cats./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, it's not for long," said Mr. Weasley, mopping his/nbald patch with a handkerchief and peering in at the/nfour bunk beds that stood in the bedroom. "I/nborrowed this from Perkins at the office. Doesn't/ncamp much anymore, poor fellow, he's got lumbago."/n/nHe picked up the dusty kettle and peered inside it./n"Well need water. ..."/n/n"There's a tap marked on this map the Muggle gave/nus," said Ron, who had followed Harry inside the tent/nand seemed completely unimpressed by its/nextraordinary inner proportions. "It's on the other/nside of the field."/n/n"Well, why don't you, Harry, and Hermione go and get/nus some water then" — Mr. Weasley handed over the/nkettle and a couple of saucepans — "and the rest of/nus will get some wood for a fire?"/n/n"But we've got an oven," said Ron. "Why can't we just/n/n/n/n"Ron, anti-Muggle security!" said Mr. Weasley, his/nface shining with anticipation. "When real Muggles/ncamp, they cook on fires outdoors. I've seen them at/n/n/n/nit!/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAfter a quick tour of the girls' tent, which was slightly/nsmaller than the boys', though without the smell of/ncats, Harry, Ron, and Hermione set off across the/ncampsite with the kettle and saucepans./n/nNow, with the sun newly risen and the mist lifting,/nthey could see the city of tents that stretched in every/ndirection. They made their way slowly through the/nrows, staring eagerly around. It was only just/ndawning on Harry how many witches and wizards/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthere must be in the world; he had never really/nthought much about those in other countries./n/nTheir fellow campers were starting to wake up. First/nto stir were the families with small children; Harry/nhad never seen witches and wizards this young/nbefore. A tiny boy no older than two was crouched/noutside a large pyramid-shaped tent, holding a wand/nand poking happily at a slug in the grass, which was/nswelling slowly to the size of a salami. As they drew/nlevel with him, his mother came hurrying out of the/ntent./n/n" How ma.ny times, Kevin? You don't — touch —/nDaddy's — wand — yecchh!"/n/nShe had trodden on the giant slug, which burst. Her/nscolding carried after them on the still air, mingling/nwith the little boy's yells — "You bust slug! You bust/nslug!"/n/nA short way farther on, they saw two little witches,/nbarely older than Kevin, who were riding toy/nbroomsticks that rose only high enough for the girls'/ntoes to skim the dewy grass. A Ministry wizard had/nalready spotted them; as he hurried past Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione he muttered distractedly, "In broad/ndaylight! Parents having a lie-in, I suppose — "/n/nHere and there adult wizards and witches were/nemerging from their tents and starting to cook/nbreakfast. Some, with furtive looks around them,/nconjured fires with their wands; others were striking/nmatches with dubious looks on their faces, as though/nsure this couldn't work. Three African wizards sat in/nserious conversation, all of them wearing long white/nrobes and roasting what looked like a rabbit on a/nbright purple fire, while a group of middle-aged/nAmerican witches sat gossiping happily beneath a/n/n/n/n/nspangled banner stretched between their tents that/nread: THE SALEM WITCHES' INSTITUTE. Harry/ncaught snatches of conversation in strange languages/nfrom the inside of tents they passed, and though he/ncouldn't understand a word, the tone of every single/nvoice was excited./n/n"Er — is it my eyes, or has everything gone green?"/nsaid Ron./n/nIt wasn't just Ron's eyes. They had walked into a/npatch of tents that were all covered with a thick/ngrowth of shamrocks, so that it looked as though/nsmall, oddly shaped hillocks had sprouted out of the/nearth. Grinning faces could be seen under those that/nhad their flaps open. Then, from behind them, they/nheard their names./n/n"Harry! Ron! Hermione!"/n/nIt was Seamus Finnigan, their fellow Gryffindor fourth/nyear. He was sitting in front of his own shamrock-/ncovered tent, with a sandy-haired woman who had to/nbe his mother, and his best friend, Dean Thomas,/nalso of Gryffindor./n/n"Like the decorations?" said Seamus, grinning. "The/nMinistry's not too happy."/n/n"Ah, why shouldn't we show our colors?" said Mrs./nFinnigan. "You should see what the Bulgarians have/ngot dangling all over their tents. You'll be supporting/nIreland, of course?" she added, eyeing Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione beadily. When they had assured her/nthat they were indeed supporting Ireland, they set off/nagain, though, as Ron said, "Like we'd say anything/nelse surrounded by that lot."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I wonder what the Bulgarians have got dangling all/nover their tents?" said Hermione./n/n"Let's go and have a look," said Harry, pointing to a/nlarge patch of tents upheld, where the Bulgarian flag/n— white, green, and red — was fluttering in the/nbreeze./n/nThe tents here had not been bedecked with plant life,/nbut each and every one of them had the same poster/nattached to it, a poster of a very surly face with heavy/nblack eyebrows. The picture was, of course, moving,/nbut all it did was blink and scowl./n/n"Krum," said Ron quietly./n/n"What?" said Hermione./n/n"Krum!" said Ron. "Viktor Krum, the Bulgarian/nSeeker!"/n/n"He looks really grumpy," said Hermione, looking/naround at the many Krums blinking and scowling at/nthem./n/n" 'Really grumpy'?" Ron raised his eyes to the/nheavens. "Who cares what he looks like? He's/nunbelievable. He's really young too. Only just eighteen/nor something. He's a genius, you wait until tonight,/nyou'll see."/n/nThere was already a small queue for the tap in the/ncorner of the field. Harry, Ron, and Hermione joined/nit, right behind a pair of men who were having a/nheated argument. One of them was a very old wizard/nwho was wearing a long flowery nightgown. The other/nwas clearly a Ministry wizard; he was holding out a/npair of pinstriped trousers and almost crying with/nexasperation./n/n/n/n/n/n"Just put them on, Archie, there's a good chap. You/ncan't walk around like that, the Muggle at the gate's/nalready getting suspicious — "/n/n"I bought this in a Muggle shop," said the old wizard/nstubbornly. "Muggles wear them."/n/n"Muggle women wear them, Archie, not the men, they/nwear these," said the Ministry wizard, and he/nbrandished the pinstriped trousers./n/n"I'm not putting them on," said old Archie in/nindignation. "I like a healthy breeze 'round my/nprivates, thanks."/n/nHermione was overcome with such a strong fit of the/ngiggles at this point that she had to duck out of the/nqueue and only returned when Archie had collected/nhis water and moved away./n/nWalking more slowly now, because of the weight of/nthe water, they made their way back through the/ncampsite. Here and there, they saw more familiar/nfaces: other Hogwarts students with their families./nOliver Wood, the old captain of Harry's House/nQuidditch team, who had just left Hogwarts, dragged/nHarry over to his parents' tent to introduce him, and/ntold him excitedly that he had just been signed to the/nPuddlemere United reserve team. Next they were/nhailed by Ernie Macmillan, a Hufflepuff fourth year,/nand a little farther on they saw Cho Chang, a very/npretty girl who played Seeker on the Ravenclaw team./nShe waved and smiled at Harry, who slopped quite a/nlot of water down his front as he waved back. More to/nstop Ron from smirking than anything, Harry/nhurriedly pointed out a large group of teenagers/nwhom he had never seen before./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Who d'you reckon they are?" he said. "They don't go/nto Hogwarts, do they?"/n/n/n/n" 'Spect they go to some foreign school," said Ron. "I/nknow there are others. Never met anyone who went to/none, though. Bill had a penfriend at a school in Brazil/n. . . this was years and years ago . . . and he wanted to/ngo on an exchange trip but Mum and Dad couldn't/nafford it. His penfriend got all offended when he said/nhe wasn't going and sent him a cursed hat. It made/nhis ears shrivel up."/n/nHarry laughed but didn't voice the amazement he felt/nat hearing about other wizarding schools. He/nsupposed, now that he saw representatives of so/nmany nationalities in the campsite, that he had been/nstupid never to realize that Hogwarts couldn't be the/nonly one. He glanced at Hermione, who looked utterly/nunsurprised by the information. No doubt she had/nrun across the news about other wizarding schools in/nsome book or other./n/n"You've been ages," said George when they finally got/nback to the Weasleys' tents./n/n"Met a few people," said Ron, setting the water down./n"You not got that fire started yet?"/n/n"Dad's having fun with the matches," said Fred./n/nMr. Weasley was having no success at all in lighting/nthe fire, but it wasn't for lack of trying. Splintered/nmatches littered the ground around him, but he/nlooked as though he was having the time of his life./n/n"Oops!" he said as he managed to light a match and/npromptly dropped it in surprise./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Come here, Mr. Weasley," said Hermione kindly,/ntaking the box from him, and showing him how to do/nit properly./n/nAt last they got the fire lit, though it was at least/nanother hour before it was hot enough to cook/nanything. There was plenty to watch while they/nwaited, however. Their tent seemed to be pitched right/nalongside a kind of thoroughfare to the field, and/nMinistry members kept hurrying up and down it,/ngreeting Mr. Weasley cordially as they passed. Mr./nWeasley kept up a running commentary, mainly for/nHarry's and Hermione's benefit; his own children/nknew too much about the Ministry to be greatly/ninterested./n/n"That was Cuthbert Mockridge, Head of the Goblin/nLiaison Office. ... Here comes Gilbert Wimple; he's/nwith the Committee on Experimental Charms; he's/nhad those horns for awhile now. ... Hello, Arnie .../nArnold Peasegood, he's an Obliviator — member of the/nAccidental Magic Reversal Squad, you know. ... and/nthat's Bode and Croaker ... they're Unspeakables. ..."/n/n"They're what?"/n/n"From the Department of Mysteries, top secret, no/nidea what they get up to. ..."/n/nAt last, the fire was ready, and they had just started/ncooking eggs and sausages when Bill, Charlie, and/nPercy came strolling out of the woods toward them./n/n"Just Apparated, Dad," said Percy loudly. "Ah,/nexcellent, lunch!"/n/nThey were halfway through their plates of eggs and/nsausages when Mr. Weasley jumped to his feet,/nwaving and grinning at a man who was striding/n/n/n/n/n/ntoward them. "Aha!" he said. "The man of the/nmoment! Ludo!"/n/nLudo Bagman was easily the most noticeable person/nHarry had seen so far, even including old Archie in/nhis flowered nightdress. He was wearing long/nQuidditch robes in thick horizontal stripes of bright/nyellow and black. An enormous picture of a wasp was/nsplashed across his chest. He had the look of a/npowerfully built man gone slightly to seed; the robes/nwere stretched tightly across a large belly he surely/nhad not had in the days when he had played/nQuidditch for England. His nose was squashed/n(probably broken by a stray Bludger, Harry thought),/nbut his round blue eyes, short blond hair, and rosy/ncomplexion made him look like a very overgrown/nschoolboy./n/n"Ahoy there!" Bagman called happily. He was walking/nas though he had springs attached to the balls of his/nfeet and was plainly in a state of wild excitement./n/n"Arthur, old man," he puffed as he reached the/ncampfire, "what a day, eh? What a day! Could we/nhave asked for more perfect weather? A cloudless/nnight coming . . . and hardly a hiccough in the/narrangements. ... Not much for me to do!"/n/nBehind him, a group of haggard-looking Ministry/nwizards rushed past, pointing at the distant evidence/nof some sort of a magical fire that was sending violet/nsparks twenty feet into the air./n/nPercy hurried forward with his hand outstretched./nApparently his disapproval of the way Ludo Bagman/nran his department did not prevent him from wanting/nto make a good impression./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah — yes," said Mr. Weasley, grinning, "this is my/nson Percy. He's just started at the Ministry — and/nthis is Fred — no, George, sorry — that's Fred — Bill,/nCharlie, Ron — my daughter, Ginny — and Ron's/nfriends, Hermione Granger and Harry Potter."/n/nBagman did the smallest of double takes when he/nheard Harry's name, and his eyes performed the/nfamiliar flick upward to the scar on Harry's forehead./n/n"Everyone," Mr. Weasley continued, "this is Ludo/nBagman, you know who he is, it's thanks to him we've/ngot such good tickets — "/n/nBagman beamed and waved his hand as if to say it/nhad been nothing./n/n"Fancy a flutter on the match, Arthur?" he said/neagerly, jingling what seemed to be a large amount of/ngold in the pockets of his yellow-and-black robes. "I've/nalready got Roddy Pontner betting me Bulgaria will/nscore first — I offered him nice odds, considering/nIreland's front three are the strongest I've seen in/nyears — and little Agatha Timms has put up half/nshares in her eel farm on a week-long match."/n/n"Oh ... go on then," said Mr. Weasley.
