"Let's see ... a/nGalleon on Ireland to win?"/n/n"A Galleon?" Ludo Bagman looked slightly/ndisappointed, but recovered himself. "Very well, very/nwell . . . any other takers?"/n/n"They're a bit young to be gambling," said Mr./n/nWeasley. "Molly wouldn't like — "/n/n"Well bet thirty-seven Galleons, fifteen Sickles, three/nKnuts," said Fred as he and George quickly pooled all/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ntheir money, "that Ireland wins — but Viktor Krum/ngets the Snitch. Oh and we'll throw in a fake wand."/n/n/n/n"You don't want to go showing Mr. Bagman rubbish/nlike that — " Percy hissed, but Bagman didn't seem to/nthink the wand was rubbish at all; on the contrary,/nhis boyish face shone with excitement as he took it/nfrom Fred, and when the wand gave a loud squawk/nand turned into a rubber chicken, Bagman roared/nwith laughter./n/n"Excellent! I haven't seen one that convincing in/nyears! I'd pay five Galleons for that!"/n/nPercy froze in an attitude of stunned disapproval./n/n"Boys," said Mr. Weasley under his breath, "I don't/nwant you betting. ... That's all your savings. ... Your/nmother — "/n/n"Don't be a spoilsport, Arthur!" boomed Ludo/nBagman, rattling his pockets excitedly. "They're old/nenough to know what they want! You reckon Ireland/nwill win but Krum 'll get the Snitch? Not a chance,/nboys, not a chance. ... I'll give you excellent odds on/nthat one. ... We'll add five Galleons for the funny/nwand, then, shall we. ..."/n/nMr. Weasley looked on helplessly as Ludo Bagman/nwhipped out a notebook and quill and began jotting/ndown the twins' names./n/n"Cheers," said George, taking the slip of parchment/nBagman handed him and tucking it away carefully./nBagman turned most cheerfully back to Mr. Weasley./n/n"Couldn't do me a brew, I suppose? I'm keeping an/neye out for Barty Crouch. My Bulgarian opposite/nnumber's making difficulties, and I can't understand/n/n/n/n/n/na word he's saying. Barty'll be able to sort it out. He/nspeaks about a hundred and fifty languages."/n/n"Mr. Crouch?" said Percy, suddenly abandoning his/nlook of poker-stiff disapproval and positively writhing/nwith excitement. "He speaks over two hundred!/nMermish and Gobbledegook and Troll ..."/n/n"Anyone can speak Troll," said Fred dismissively. "All/nyou have to do is point and grunt."/n/nPercy threw Fred an extremely nasty look and stoked/nthe fire vigorously to bring the kettle back to the boil./n/n"Any news of Bertha Jorkins yet, Ludo?" Mr. Weasley/nasked as Bagman settled himself down on the grass/nbeside them all./n/n"Not a dicky bird," said Bagman comfortably. "But/nshe'll turn up. Poor old Bertha ... memory like a leaky/ncauldron and no sense of direction. Lost, you take my/nword for it. She'll wander back into the office/nsometime in October, thinking it's still July."/n/n"You don't think it might be time to send someone to/nlook for her?" Mr. Weasley suggested tentatively as/nPercy handed Bagman his tea./n/n"Barty Crouch keeps saying that," said Bagman, his/nround eyes widening innocently, "but we really can't/nspare anyone at the moment. Oh — talk of the devil!/nBarty!"/n/nA wizard had just Apparated at their fireside, and he/ncould not have made more of a contrast with Ludo/nBagman, sprawled on the grass in his old Wasp/nrobes. Barty Crouch was a stiff, upright, elderly man,/ndressed in an impeccably crisp suit and tie. The/nparting in his short gray hair was almost unnaturally/n/n/n/n/nstraight, and his narrow toothbrush mustache looked/nas though he trimmed it using a slide rule. His shoes/nwere very highly polished. Harry could see at once/nwhy Percy idolized him. Percy was a great believer in/nrigidly following rules, and Mr. Crouch had complied/nwith the rule about Muggle dressing so thoroughly/nthat he could have passed for a bank manager; Harry/ndoubted even Uncle Vernon would have spotted him/nfor what he really was./n/n"Pull up a bit of grass, Barty," said Ludo brightly,/npatting the ground beside him./n/n"No thank you, Ludo," said Crouch, and there was a/nbite of impatience in his voice. "I've been looking for/nyou everywhere. The Bulgarians are insisting we add/nanother twelve seats to the Top Box."/n/n"Oh is that what they're after?" said Bagman. "I/nthought the chap was asking to borrow a pair of/ntweezers. Bit of a strong accent."/n/n"Mr. Crouch!" said Percy breathlessly, sunk into a/nkind of half-bow that made him look like a/nhunchback. "Would you like a cup of tea?"/n/n"Oh," said Mr. Crouch, looking over at Percy in mild/nsurprise. "Yes — thank you, Weatherby."/n/nFred and George choked into their own cups. Percy,/nvery pink around the ears, busied himself with the/nkettle./n/n"Oh and I've been wanting a word with you too,/nArthur," said Mr. Crouch, his sharp eyes falling upon/nMr. Weasley. "Ali Bashir's on the warpath. He wants a/nword with you about your embargo on flying carpets."/n/nMr. Weasley heaved a deep sigh./n/n/n/n/n/n"I sent him an owl about that just last week. If I've/ntold him once I've told him a hundred times: Carpets/nare defined as a Muggle Artifact by the Registry of/nProscribed Charmable Objects, but will he listen?"/n/n"I doubt it," said Mr. Crouch, accepting a cup from/nPercy. "He's desperate to export here."/n/n"Well, they'll never replace brooms in Britain, will/nthey?" said Bagman./n/n"Ali thinks there's a niche in the market for a family/nvehicle," said Mr. Crouch. "I remember my/ngrandfather had an Axminster that could seat twelve/n— but that was before carpets were banned, of/ncourse."/n/nHe spoke as though he wanted to leave nobody in any/ndoubt that all his ancestors had abided strictly by the/nlaw./n/n"So, been keeping busy, Barty?" said Bagman/nbreezily./n/n"Fairly," said Mr. Crouch dryly. "Organizing Portkeys/nacross five continents is no mean feat, Ludo."/n/n"I expect you'll both be glad when this is over?" said/nMr. Weasley./n/nLudo Bagman looked shocked./n/n"Glad! Don't know when I've had more fun. ... Still,/nit's not as though we haven't got anything to look/nforward to, eh, Barty? Eh? Plenty left to organize, eh?"/n/nMr. Crouch raised his eyebrows at Bagman./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We agreed not to make the announcement until all/nthe details — "/n/n"Oh details!" said Bagman, waving the word away like/na cloud of midges. "They've signed, haven't they?/nThey've agreed, haven't they? I bet you anything these/nkids'll know soon enough anyway. I mean, it's/nhappening at Hogwarts — "/n/n"Ludo, we need to meet the Bulgarians, you know,"/nsaid Mr. Crouch sharply, cutting Bagman's remarks/nshort. "Thank you for the tea, Weatherby."/n/nHe pushed his undrunk tea back at Percy and waited/nfor Ludo to rise; Bagman struggled to his feet,/nswigging down the last of his tea, the gold in his/npockets chinking merrily./n/n"See you all later!" he said. "You'll be up in the Top/nBox with me — I'm commentating!" He waved, Barty/nCrouch nodded curtly, and both of them/nDisapparated./n/n"What's happening at Hogwarts, Dad?" said Fred at/nonce. "What were they talking about?"/n/n"You'll find out soon enough," said Mr.Weasley,/nsmiling./n/n"It's classified information, until such time as the/nMinistry decides to release it," said Percy stiffly. "Mr./nCrouch was quite right not to disclose it."/n/n"Oh shut up, Weatherby," said Fred./n/nA sense of excitement rose like a palpable cloud over/nthe campsite as the afternoon wore on. By dusk, the/nstill summer air itself seemed to be quivering with/nanticipation, and as darkness spread like a curtain/n/n/n/n/n/nover the thousands of waiting wizards, the last/nvestiges of pretence disappeared: the Ministry seemed/nto have bowed to the inevitable and stopped fighting/nthe signs of blatant magic now breaking out/neverywhere./n/nSalesmen were Apparating every few feet, carrying/ntrays and pushing carts full of extraordinary/nmerchandise. There were luminous rosettes — green/nfor Ireland, red for Bulgaria — which were squealing/nthe names of the players, pointed green hats/nbedecked with dancing shamrocks, Bulgarian scarves/nadorned with lions that really roared, flags from both/ncountries that played their national anthems as they/nwere waved; there were tiny models of Firebolts that/nreally flew, and collectible figures of famous players,/nwhich strolled across the palm of your hand, preening/nthemselves./n/n"Been saving my pocket money all summer for this,"/nRon told Harry as they and Hermione strolled through/nthe salesmen, buying souvenirs. Though Ron/npurchased a dancing shamrock hat and a large green/nrosette, he also bought a small figure of Viktor Krum,/nthe Bulgarian Seeker. The miniature Krum walked/nbackward and forward over Ron's hand, scowling up/nat the green rosette above him./n/n"Wow, look at these!" said Harry, hurrying over to a/ncart piled high with what looked like brass/nbinoculars, except that they were covered with all/nsorts of weird knobs and dials./n/n"Omnioculars," said the saleswizard eagerly. "You can/nreplay action . . . slow everything down . . . and they/nflash up a play-by-play breakdown if you need it./nBargain — ten Galleons each."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wish I hadn't bought this now," said Ron, gesturing/nat his dancing shamrock hat and gazing longingly at/nthe Omnioculars./n/n"Three pairs," said Harry firmly to the wizard./n/n"No — don't bother," said Ron, going red. He was/nalways touchy about the fact that Harry, who had/ninherited a small fortune from his parents, had much/nmore money than he did./n/n"You won't be getting anything for Christmas," Harry/ntold him, thrusting Omnioculars into his and/nHermione's hands. "For about ten years, mind."/n/n"Fair enough," said Ron, grinning./n/n"Oooh, thanks, Harry," said Hermione. "And I'll get us/nsome programs, look — "/n/nTheir money bags considerably lighter, they went/nback to the tents. Bill, Charlie, and Ginny were all/nsporting green rosettes too, and Mr. Weasley was/ncarrying an Irish flag. Fred and George had no/nsouvenirs as they had given Bagman all their gold./n/nAnd then a deep, booming gong sounded somewhere/nbeyond the woods, and at once, green and red/nlanterns blazed into life in the trees, lighting a path to/nthe field./n/n"It's time!" said Mr. Weasley, looking as excited as any/nof them. "Come on, let's go!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n-4/n/n/n

title: The Quidditch World Cup
text: /nClutching their purchases, Mr. Weasley in the lead,/nthey all hurried into the wood, following the lantern-/nlit trail. They could hear the sounds of thousands of/npeople moving around them, shouts and laughter,/nsnatches of singing. The atmosphere of feverish/nexcitement was highly infectious; Harry couldn't stop/ngrinning. They walked through the wood for twenty/nminutes, talking and joking loudly, until at last they/nemerged on the other side and found themselves in/nthe shadow of a gigantic stadium. Though Harry/ncould see only a fraction of the immense gold walls/nsurrounding the field, he could tell that ten/ncathedrals would fit comfortably inside it./n/n"Seats a hundred thousand," said Mr. Weasley,/nspotting the awestruck look on Harry's face. "Ministry/ntask force of five hundred have been working on it all/nyear. Muggle Repelling Charms on every inch of it./nEvery time Muggles have got anywhere near here all/nyear, they've suddenly remembered urgent/nappointments and had to dash away again . . . bless/nthem," he added fondly, leading the way toward the/n/n/n/n/nnearest entrance, which was already surrounded by a/nswarm of shouting witches and wizards./n/n"Prime seats!" said the Ministry witch at the entrance/nwhen she checked their tickets. "Top Box! Straight/nupstairs, Arthur, and as high as you can go."/n/nThe stairs into the stadium were carpeted in rich/npurple. They clambered upward with the rest of the/ncrowd, which slowly filtered away through doors into/nthe stands to their left and right. Mr. Weasley's party/nkept climbing, and at last they reached the top of the/nstaircase and found themselves in a small box, set at/nthe highest point of the stadium and situated exactly/nhalfway between the golden goal posts. About twenty/npurple-and-gilt chairs stood in two rows here, and/nHarry, filing into the front seats with the Weasleys,/nlooked down upon a scene the likes of which he could/nnever have imagined./n/nA hundred thousand witches and wizards were taking/ntheir places in the seats, which rose in levels around/nthe long oval field. Everything was suffused with a/nmysterious golden light, which seemed to come from/nthe stadium itself. The field looked smooth as velvet/nfrom their lofty position. At either end of the field/nstood three goal hoops, fifty feet high; right opposite/nthem, almost at Harry's eye level, was a gigantic/nblackboard. Gold writing kept dashing across it as/nthough an invisible giant's hand were scrawling upon/nthe blackboard and then wiping it off again; watching/nit, Harry saw that it was flashing advertisements/nacross the field./n/nThe Bluebottle: A Broom for All the Family — safe,/nreliable, and with Built-in Anti-Burglar Buzzer ... Mrs./nSkower's All-Purpose Magical Mess Remover: No Pain,/nNo Stain! ... Gladrags Wizardwear — London, Paris,/nHogsmeade .../n/n/n/n/n/nHarry tore his eyes away from the sign and looked/nover his shoulder to see who else was sharing the box/nwith them. So far it was empty, except for a tiny/ncreature sitting in the second from last seat at the/nend of the row behind them. The creature, whose legs/nwere so short they stuck out in front of it on the/nchair, was wearing a tea towel draped like a toga, and/nit had its face hidden in its hands. Yet those long,/nbatlike ears were oddly familiar. . . ./n/n" Dobby ?" said Harry incredulously./n/nThe tiny creature looked up and stretched its fingers,/nrevealing enormous brown eyes and a nose the exact/nsize and shape of a large tomato. It wasn't Dobby — it/nwas, however, unmistakably a house-elf, as Harry's/nfriend Dobby had been. Harry had set Dobby free/nfrom his old owners, the Malfoy family./n/n"Did sir just call me Dobby?" squeaked the elf/ncuriously from between its fingers. Its voice was/nhigher even than Dobby's had been, a teeny,/nquivering squeak of a voice, and Harry suspected —/nthough it was very hard to tell with a house-elf — that/nthis one might just be female. Ron and Hermione/nspun around in their seats to look. Though they had/nheard a lot about Dobby from Harry, they had never/nactually met him. Even Mr. Weasley looked around in/ninterest./n/n"Sorry," Harry told the elf, "I just thought you were/nsomeone I knew."/n/n"But I knows Dobby too, sir!" squeaked the elf. She/nwas shielding her face, as though blinded by light,/nthough the Top Box was not brightly lit. "My name is/nWinky, sir — and you, sir — " Her dark brown eyes/nwidened to the size of side plates as they rested upon/nHarry's scar. "You is surely Harry Potter!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, I am," said Harry./n/n/n/n"But Dobby talks of you all the time, sir!" she said,/nlowering her hands very slightly and looking/nawestruck./n/n"How is he?" said Harry. "How's freedom suiting/nhim?"/n/n"Ah, sir," said Winky, shaking her head, "ah sir,/nmeaning no disrespect, sir, but I is not sure you did/nDobby a favor, sir, when you is setting him free."/n/n"Why?" said Harry, taken aback. "What's wrong with/nhim?"/n/n"Freedom is going to Dobby's head, sir," said Winky/nsadly. "Ideas above his station, sir. Can't get another/nposition, sir."/n/n"Why not?" said Harry./n/nWinky lowered her voice by a half-octave and/nwhispered, "He is wanting paying for his work, sir."/n/n"Paying?" said Harry blankly. "Well — why shouldn't/nhe be paid?"/n/nWinky looked quite horrified at the idea and closed/nher fingers slightly so that her face was half-hidden/nagain./n/n"House-elves is not paid, sir!" she said in a muffled/nsqueak. "No, no, no. I says to Dobby, I says, go find/nyourself a nice family and settle down, Dobby. He is/ngetting up to all sorts of high jinks, sir, what is/nunbecoming to a house-elf. You goes racketing/naround like this, Dobby, I says, and next thing I hear/nyou's up in front of the Department for the Regulation/n/n/n/n/nand Control of Magical Creatures, like some common/ngoblin."/n/n"Well, it's about time he had a bit of fun," said Harry./n/n"House-elves is not supposed to have fun, Harry/nPotter," said Winky firmly, from behind her hands./n"House-elves does what they is told. I is not liking/nheights at all, Harry Potter" — she glanced toward the/nedge of the box and gulped — "but my master sends/nme to the Top Box and I comes, sir."/n/n"Why's he sent you up here, if he knows you don't like/nheights?" said Harry, frowning./n/n"Master — master wants me to save him a seat, Harry/nPotter. "And you've been letting me mime/neverything all day!"/n/n"Veil, it vos very funny," said the Bulgarian minister,/nshrugging./n/n"And as the Irish team performs a lap of honor,/nflanked by their mascots, the Quidditch World Cup/nitself is brought into the Top Box!" roared Bagman./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's eyes were suddenly dazzled by a blinding/nwhite light, as the Top Box was magically illuminated/nso that everyone in the stands could see the inside./nSquinting toward the entrance, he saw two panting/nwizards carrying a vast golden cup into the box,/nwhich they handed to Cornelius Fudge, who was still/nlooking very disgruntled that he'd been using sign/nlanguage all day for nothing./n/n"Let's have a really loud hand for the gallant losers —/nBulgaria!" Bagman shouted./n/nAnd up the stairs into the box came the seven/ndefeated Bulgarian players. The crowd below was/napplauding appreciatively; Harry could see thousands/nand thousands of Omniocular lenses flashing and/nwinking in their direction./n/nOne by one, the Bulgarians filed between the rows of/nseats in the box, and Bagman called out the name of/neach as they shook hands with their own minister/nand then with Fudge. Krum, who was last in line,/nlooked a real mess. Two black eyes were blooming/nspectacularly on his bloody face. He was still holding/nthe Snitch. Harry noticed that he seemed much less/ncoordinated on the ground. He was slightly duck-/nfooted and distinctly round-shouldered. But when/nKrum's name was announced, the whole stadium/ngave him a resounding, earsplitting roar./n/nAnd then came the Irish team. Aidan Lynch was being/nsupported by Moran and Connolly; the second crash/nseemed to have dazed him and his eyes looked/nstrangely unfocused. But he grinned happily as Troy/nand Quigley lifted the Cup into the air and the crowd/nbelow thundered its approval. Harry's hands were/nnumb with clapping./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAt last, when the Irish team had left the box to/nperform another lap of honor on their brooms (Aidan/nLynch on the back of Connolly's, clutching hard/naround his waist and still grinning in a bemused sort/nof way), Bagman pointed his wand at his throat and/nmuttered, "Quietus."/n/n"They'll be talking about this one for years," he said/nhoarsely, "a really unexpected twist, that. ... shame it/ncouldn't have lasted longer. ... Ah yes. ... yes, I owe/nyou . . . how much?"/n/nFor Fred and George had just scrambled over the/nbacks of their seats and were standing in front of/nLudo Bagman with broad grins on their faces, their/nhands outstretched./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n9/n/n/n/n

title: The Dark Mark
text: /n" Don't tell your mother you've been gambling," Mr./nWeasley implored Fred and George as they all made/ntheir way slowly down the purple-carpeted stairs./n/n"Don't worry, Dad," said Fred gleefully, "we've got big/nplans for this money. We don't want it confiscated."/n/nMr. Weasley looked for a moment as though he was/ngoing to ask what these big plans were, but seemed to/ndecide, upon reflection, that he didn't want to know./n/nThey were soon caught up in the crowds now flooding/nout of the stadium and back to their campsites./nRaucous singing was borne toward them on the night/nair as they retraced their steps along the lantern-lit/npath, and leprechauns kept shooting over their heads,/ncackling and waving their lanterns. When they finally/nreached the tents, nobody felt like sleeping at all, and/ngiven the level of noise around them, Mr. Weasley/nagreed that they could all have one last cup of cocoa/ntogether before turning in. They were soon arguing/nenjoyably about the match; Mr. Weasley got drawn/n/n/n/n/ninto a disagreement about cobbing with Charlie, and/nit was only when Ginny fell asleep right at the tiny/ntable and spilled hot chocolate all over the floor that/nMr. Weasley called a halt to the verbal replays and/ninsisted that everyone go to bed. Hermione and Ginny/nwent into the next tent, and Harry and the rest of the/nWeasleys changed into pajamas and clambered into/ntheir bunks. From the other side of the campsite they/ncould still hear much singing and the odd echoing/nbang./n/n"Oh I am glad I'm not on duty," muttered Mr. Weasley/nsleepily. "I wouldn't fancy having to go and tell the/nIrish they've got to stop celebrating."/n/nHarry, who was on a top bunk above Ron, lay staring/nup at the canvas ceiling of the tent, watching the glow/nof an occasional leprechaun lantern flying overhead,/nand picturing again some of Krum's more spectacular/nmoves. He was itching to get back on his own Firebolt/nand try out the Wronski Feint. ... Somehow Oliver/nWood had never managed to convey with all his/nwriggling diagrams what that move was supposed to/nlook like. ... Harry saw himself in robes that had his/nname on the back, and imagined the sensation of/nhearing a hundred-thousand-strong crowd roar, as/nLudo Bagman's voice echoed throughout the stadium,/n"I give you ... PotteA."/n/nHarry never knew whether or not he had actually/ndropped off to sleep — his fantasies of flying like/nKrum might well have slipped into actual dreams —/nall he knew was that, quite suddenly, Mr. Weasley/nwas shouting./n/n"Get up! Ron — Harry — come on now, get up, this is/nurgent!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry sat up quickly and the top of his head hit/ncanvas./n/n" 'S' matter?" he said./n/nDimly, he could tell that something was wrong. The/nnoises in the campsite had changed. The singing had/nstopped. He could hear screams, and the sound of/npeople running. He slipped down from the bunk and/nreached for his clothes, but Mr. Weasley, who had/npulled on his jeans over his own pajamas, said, "No/ntime, Harry — just grab a jacket and get outside —/nquickly!"/n/nHarry did as he was told and hurried out of the tent,/nRon at his heels./n/nBy the light of the few fires that were still burning, he/ncould see people running away into the woods, fleeing/nsomething that was moving across the field toward/nthem, something that was emitting odd flashes of/nlight and noises like gunfire. Loud jeering, roars of/nlaughter, and drunken yells were drifting toward/nthem; then came a burst of strong green light, which/nilluminated the scene./n/nA crowd of wizards, tightly packed and moving/ntogether with wands pointing straight upward, was/nmarching slowly across the field. Harry squinted at/nthem. ... They didn't seem to have faces. ... Then he/nrealized that their heads were hooded and their faces/nmasked. High above them, floating along in midair,/nfour struggling figures were being contorted into/ngrotesque shapes. It was as though the masked/nwizards on the ground were puppeteers, and the/npeople above them were marionettes operated by/ninvisible strings that rose from the wands into the air./nTwo of the figures were very small./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMore wizards were joining the marching group,/nlaughing and pointing up at the floating bodies. Tents/ncrumpled and fell as the marching crowd swelled./nOnce or twice Harry saw one of the marchers blast a/ntent out of his way with his wand. Several caught fire./nThe screaming grew louder./n/nThe floating people were suddenly illuminated as they/npassed over a burning tent and Harry recognized one/nof them: Mr. Roberts, the campsite manager. The/nother three looked as though they might be his wife/nand children. One of the marchers below flipped Mrs./nRoberts upside down with his wand; her nightdress/nfell down to reveal voluminous drawers and she/nstruggled to cover herself up as the crowd below her/nscreeched and hooted with glee./n/n"That's sick," Ron muttered, watching the smallest/nMuggle child, who had begun to spin like a top, sixty/nfeet above the ground, his head flopping limply from/nside to side. "That is really sick. ..."/n/nHermione and Ginny came hurrying toward them,/npulling coats over their nightdresses, with Mr./n/nWeasley right behind them. At the same moment, Bill,/nCharlie, and Percy emerged from the boys' tent, fully/ndressed, with their sleeves rolled up and their wands/nout./n/n"We're going to help the Ministry!" Mr. Weasley/nshouted over all the noise, rolling up his own sleeves./n"You lot — get into the woods, and stick together. I'll/ncome and fetch you when we've sorted this out!"/n/nBill, Charlie, and Percy were already sprinting away/ntoward the oncoming marchers; Mr. Weasley tore/nafter them. Ministry wizards were dashing from every/ndirection toward the source of the trouble. The crowd/nbeneath the Roberts family was coming ever closer./n/n/n/n/n"C'mon," said Fred, grabbing Ginny's hand and/nstarting to pull her toward the wood. Harry, Ron,/nHermione, and George followed. They all looked back/nas they reached the trees. The crowd beneath the/nRoberts family was larger than ever; they could see/nthe Ministry wizards trying to get through it to the/nhooded wizards in the center, but they were having/ngreat difficulty. It looked as though they were scared/nto perform any spell that might make the Roberts/nfamily fall./n/nThe colored lanterns that had lit the path to the/nstadium had been extinguished. Dark figures were/nblundering through the trees; children were crying;/nanxious shouts and panicked voices were/nreverberating around them in the cold night air./n/nHarry felt himself being pushed hither and thither by/npeople whose faces he could not see. Then he heard/nRon yell with pain./n/n"What happened?" said Hermione anxiously, stopping/nso abruptly that Harry walked into her. "Ron, where/nare you? Oh this is stupid — lumos\"/n/nShe illuminated her wand and directed its narrow/nbeam across the path. Ron was lying sprawled on the/nground./n/n"Tripped over a tree root," he said angrily, getting to/nhis feet again./n/n"Well, with feet that size, hard not to," said a drawling/nvoice from behind them./n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione turned sharply. Draco/nMalfoy was standing alone nearby, leaning against a/ntree, looking utterly relaxed. His arms folded, he/nseemed to have been watching the scene at the/ncampsite through a gap in the trees./n/n/n/n/n/nRon told Malfoy to do something that Harry knew he/nwould never have dared say in front of Mrs. Weasley/n/n"Language, Weasley," said Malfoy, his pale eyes/nglittering. "Hadn't you better be hurrying along, now?/nYou wouldn't like her spotted, would you?"/n/nHe nodded at Hermione, and at the same moment, a/nblast like a bomb sounded from the campsite, and a/nflash of green light momentarily lit the trees around/nthem./n/n"What's that supposed to mean?" said Hermione/ndefiantly./n/n"Granger, they're after Muggles," said Malfoy. "D'you/nwant to be showing off your knickers in midair?/nBecause if you do, hang around ... they're moving this/nway, and it would give us all a laugh."/n/n"Hermione's a witch," Harry snarled./n/n"Have it your own way, Potter," said Malfoy, grinning/nmaliciously. "If you think they can't spot a Mudblood,/nstay where you are."/n/n"You watch your mouth!" shouted Ron. Everybody/npresent knew that "Mudblood" was a very offensive/nterm for a witch or wizard of Muggle parentage./n/n"Never mind, Ron," said Hermione quickly, seizing/nRon's arm to restrain him as he took a step toward/nMalfoy./n/nThere came a bang from the other side of the trees/nthat was louder than anything they had heard./n/nSeveral people nearby screamed. Malfoy chuckled/nsoftly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Scare easily, don't they?" he said lazily. "I suppose/nyour daddy told you all to hide? What's he up to —/ntrying to rescue the Muggles?"/n/n"Where're your parents?" said Harry, his temper/nrising. "Out there wearing masks, are they?"/n/nMalfoy turned his face to Harry, still smiling./n/n"Well ... if they were, I wouldn't be likely to tell you,/nwould I, Potter?"/n/n"Oh come on," said Hermione, with a disgusted look/nat Malfoy, "let's go and find the others."/n/n"Keep that big bushy head down, Granger," sneered/nMalfoy./n/n"Come on," Hermione repeated, and she pulled Harry/nand Ron up the path again./n/n"I'll bet you anything his dad is one of that masked/nlot!" said Ron hotly./n/n"Well, with any luck, the Ministry will catch him!"/nsaid Hermione fervently. "Oh I can't believe this./n/nWhere have the others got to?"/n/nFred, George, and Ginny were nowhere to be seen,/nthough the path was packed with plenty of other/npeople, all looking nervously over their shoulders/ntoward the commotion back at the campsite. A huddle/nof teenagers in pajamas was arguing vociferously a/nlittle way along the path. When they saw Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione, a girl with thick curly hair turned and/nsaid quickly, " Ou est Madame Maxime? Nous Vavons/nperdue — "/n/n"Er — what?" said Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh ..." The girl who had spoken turned her back on/nhim, and as they walked on they distinctly heard her/nsay, " 'Ogwarts."/n/n"Beauxbatons," muttered Hermione./n/n"Sorry?" said Harry./n/n"They must go to Beauxbatons," said Hermione. "You/nknow . . . Beauxbatons Academy of Magic ... I read/nabout it in An Appraisal of Magical Education in/nEurope."/n/n"Oh ... yeah ... right," said Harry./n/n"Fred and George can't have gone that far," said Ron,/npulling out his wand, lighting it like Hermione's, and/nsquinting up the path. Harry dug in the pockets of his/njacket for his own wand — but it wasn't there. The/nonly thing he could find was his Omnioculars./n/n"Ah, no, I don't believe it ... I've lost my wand!"/n/n"You're kidding!"/n/nRon and Hermione raised their wands high enough to/nspread the narrow beams of light farther on the/nground; Harry looked all around him, but his wand/nwas nowhere to be seen./n/n"Maybe it's back in the tent," said Ron./n/n"Maybe it fell out of your pocket when we were/nrunning?" Hermione suggested anxiously./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "maybe ..."/n/nHe usually kept his wand with him at all times in the/nwizarding world, and finding himself without it in the/n/n/n/n/n/nmidst of a scene like this made him feel very/nvulnerable./n/n/n/nA rustling noise nearby made all three of them jump./nWinky the house-elf was fighting her way out of a/nclump of bushes nearby. She was moving in a most/npeculiar fashion, apparently with great difficulty; it/nwas as though someone invisible were trying to hold/nher back./n/n"There is bad wizards about!" she squeaked/ndistractedly as she leaned forward and labored to/nkeep running. "People high — high in the air! Winky/nis getting out of the way!"/n/nAnd she disappeared into the trees on the other side/nof the path, panting and squeaking as she fought the/nforce that was restraining her./n/n"What's up with her?" said Ron, looking curiously/nafter Winky. "Why can't she run properly?"/n/n"Bet she didn't ask permission to hide," said Harry./n/nHe was thinking of Dobby: Every time he had tried to/ndo something the Malfoys wouldn't like, the house-elf/nhad been forced to start beating himself up./n/n"You know, house-elves get a very raw deal!" said/nHermione indignantly. "It's slavery, that's what it is!/nThat Mr. Crouch made her go up to the top of the/nstadium, and she was terrified, and he's got her/nbewitched so she can't even run when they start/ntrampling tents! Why doesn't anyone do something/nabout it?"/n/n"Well, the elves are happy, aren't they?" Ron said./n/n"You heard old Winky back at the match ... 'House-/nelves is not supposed to have fun' ... that's what she/nlikes, being bossed around. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's people like you, Ron," Hermione began hotly,/n/n"who prop up rotten and unjust systems, just/nbecause they're too lazy to — "/n/nAnother loud bang echoed from the edge of the wood./n/n"Let's just keep moving, shall we?" said Ron, and/nHarry saw him glance edgily at Hermione. Perhaps/nthere was truth in what Malfoy had said; perhaps/nHermione was in more danger than they were. They/nset off again, Harry still searching his pockets, even/nthough he knew his wand wasn't there./n/nThey followed the dark path deeper into the wood,/nstill keeping an eye out for Fred, George, and Ginny./nThey passed a group of goblins who were cackling/nover a sack of gold that they had undoubtedly won/nbetting on the match, and who seemed quite/nunperturbed by the trouble at the campsite. Farther/nstill along the path, they walked into a patch of silvery/nlight, and when they looked through the trees, they/nsaw three tall and beautiful veela standing in a/nclearing, surrounded by a gaggle of young wizards, all/nof whom were talking very loudly./n/n"I pull down about a hundred sacks of Galleons a/nyear!" one of them shouted. "I'm a dragon killer for/nthe Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous/nCreatures."/n/n"No, you're not!" yelled his friend. "You're a/ndishwasher at the Leaky Cauldron. ... but I'm a/nvampire hunter, I've killed about ninety so far — "/n/nA third young wizard, whose pimples were visible even/nby the dim, silvery light of the veela, now cut in, "I'm/nabout to become the youngest ever Minister of Magic,/n/nI am."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry snorted with laughter. He recognized the/npimply wizard: His name was Stan Shunpike, and he/nwas in fact a conductor on the triple-decker Knight/nBus. He turned to tell Ron this, but Ron's face had/ngone oddly slack, and next second Ron was yelling,/n"Did I tell you I've invented a broomstick that'll reach/nJupiter?"/n/n"Honestly\" said Hermione, and she and Harry/ngrabbed Ron firmly by the arms, wheeled him around,/nand marched him away. By the time the sounds of/nthe veela and their admirers had faded completely,/nthey were in the very heart of the wood. They seemed/nto be alone now; everything was much quieter./n/nHarry looked around. "I reckon we can just wait here,/nyou know. Well hear anyone coming a mile off."/n/nThe words were hardly out of his mouth, when Ludo/nBagman emerged from behind a tree right ahead of/nthem./n/nEven by the feeble light of the two wands, Harry could/nsee that a great change had come over Bagman. He/nno longer looked buoyant and rosy-faced; there was/nno more spring in his step. He looked very white and/nstrained./n/n"Who's that?" he said, blinking down at them, trying/nto make out their faces. "What are you doing in here,/nall alone?"/n/nThey looked at one another, surprised./n/n"Well — there's a sort of riot going on," said Ron./nBagman stared at him./n/n"What?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"At the campsite . . . some people have got hold of a/nfamily of Muggles. ..."/n/nBagman swore loudly./n/n"Damn them!" he said, looking quite distracted, and/nwithout another word, he Disapparated with a small/npop\/n/n"Not exactly on top of things, Mr. Bagman, is he?"/nsaid Hermione, frowning./n/n"He was a great Beater, though," said Ron, leading/nthe way off the path into a small clearing, and sitting/ndown on a patch of dry grass at the foot of a tree./n/n"The Wimbourne Wasps won the league three times in/na row while he was with them."/n/nHe took his small figure of Krum out of his pocket, set/nit down on the ground, and watched it walk around./nLike the real Krum, the model was slightly duck-/nfooted and round-shouldered, much less impressive/non his splayed feet than on his broomstick. Harry was/nlistening for noise from the campsite. Everything/nseemed much quieter; perhaps the riot was over./n/n"I hope the others are okay," said Hermione after a/nwhile./n/n"They'll be fine," said Ron./n/n"Imagine if your dad catches Lucius Malfoy," said/nHarry, sitting down next to Ron and watching the/nsmall figure of Krum slouching over the fallen leaves./n"He's always said he'd like to get something on him."/n/n"That'd wipe the smirk off old Draco's face, all right,"/nsaid Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Those poor Muggles, though," said Hermione/nnervously. "What if they can't get them down?"/n/n"They will," said Ron reassuringly. "They'll find a/nway."/n/n"Mad, though, to do something like that when the/nwhole Ministry of Magic's out here tonight!" said/nHermione. "I mean, how do they expect to get away/nwith it? Do you think they've been drinking, or are/nthey just — "/n/nBut she broke off abruptly and looked over her/nshoulder. Harry and Ron looked quickly around too./n/nIt sounded as though someone was staggering toward/ntheir clearing. They waited, listening to the sounds of/nthe uneven steps behind the dark trees. But the/nfootsteps came to a sudden halt./n/n"Hello?" called Harry./n/nThere was silence. Harry got to his feet and peered/naround the tree. It was too dark to see very far, but he/ncould sense somebody standing just beyond the range/nof his vision./n/n"Who's there?" he said./n/nAnd then, without warning, the silence was rent by a/nvoice unlike any they had heard in the wood; and it/nuttered, not a panicked shout, but what sounded like/na spell./n/n"MORSMORDREl "/n/nAnd something vast, green, and glittering erupted/nfrom the patch of darkness Harry's eyes had been/nstruggling to penetrate; it flew up over the treetops/nand into the sky./n/n/n/n/n/n"What the — ?" gasped Ron as he sprang to his feet/nagain, staring up at the thing that had appeared./n/nFor a split second, Harry thought it was another/nleprechaun formation. Then he realized that it was a/ncolossal skull, comprised of what looked like emerald/nstars, with a serpent protruding from its mouth like a/ntongue. As they watched, it rose higher and higher,/nblazing in a haze of greenish smoke, etched against/nthe black sky like a new constellation./n/nSuddenly, the wood all around them erupted with/nscreams. Harry didn't understand why, but the only/npossible cause was the sudden appearance of the/nskull, which had now risen high enough to illuminate/nthe entire wood like some grisly neon sign. He/nscanned the darkness for the person who had/nconjured the skull, but he couldn't see anyone./n/n"Who's there?" he called again./n/n"Harry, come on, move\" Hermione had seized the/ncollar of his jacket and was tugging him backward./n/n"What's the matter?" Harry said, startled to see her/nface so white and terrified./n/n"It's the Dark Mark, Harry!" Hermione moaned,/npulling him as hard as she could. "You-Know-Who's/nsign!"/n/n"Voldemort's — ?"/n/n"Harry, come on!"/n/nHarry turned — Ron was hurriedly scooping up his/nminiature Krum — the three of them started across/nthe clearing — but before they had taken a few/nhurried steps, a series of popping noises announced/n/n/n/n/n/nthe arrival of twenty wizards, appearing from thin air,/nsurrounding them./n/nHarry whirled around, and in an instant, he/nregistered one fact: Each of these wizards had his/nwand out, and every wand was pointing right at/nhimself, Ron, and Hermione./n/nWithout pausing to think, he yelled, "DUCK!"/n/nHe seized the other two and pulled them down onto/nthe ground./n/n"STUPEFYl" roared twenty voices — there was a/nblinding series of flashes and Harry felt the hair on/nhis head ripple as though a powerful wind had swept/nthe clearing. Raising his head a fraction of an inch he/nsaw jets of fiery red light flying over them from the/nwizards' wands, crossing one another, bouncing off/ntree trunks, rebounding into the darkness —/n/n"Stop!" yelled a voice he recognized. "STOP! That's my/nson\"/n/nHarry's hair stopped blowing about. He raised his/nhead a little higher. The wizard in front of him had/nlowered his wand. He rolled over and saw Mr. Weasley/nstriding toward them, looking terrified./n/n"Ron — Harry" — his voice sounded shaky —/n"Hermione — are you all right?"/n/n"Out of the way, Arthur," said a cold, curt voice./n/nIt was Mr. Crouch. He and the other Ministry wizards/nwere closing in on them. Harry got to his feet to face/nthem. Mr. Crouch's face was taut with rage./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Which of you did it?" he snapped, his sharp eyes/ndarting between them. "Which of you conjured the/nDark Mark?"/n/n"We didn't do that!" said Harry, gesturing up at the/nskull./n/n"We didn't do anything!" said Ron, who was rubbing/nhis elbow and looking indignantly at his father. "What/ndid you want to attack us for?"/n/n"Do not lie, sir!" shouted Mr. Crouch. His wand was/nstill pointing directly at Ron, and his eyes were/npopping — he looked slightly mad. "You have been/ndiscovered at the scene of the crime!"/n/n"Barty," whispered a witch in a long woolen dressing/ngown, "they're kids, Barty, they'd never have been/nable to — "/n/n"Where did the Mark come from, you three?" said Mr./nWeasley quickly./n/n"Over there," said Hermione shakily, pointing at the/nplace where they had heard the voice. "There was/nsomeone behind the trees . . . they shouted words —/nan incantation — "/n/n"Oh, stood over there, did they?" said Mr. Crouch,/nturning his popping eyes on Hermione now, disbelief/netched all over his face. "Said an incantation, did/nthey? You seem very well informed about how that/nMark is summoned, missy — "/n/nBut none of the Ministry wizards apart from Mr./nCrouch seemed to think it remotely likely that Harry,/nRon, or Hermione had conjured the skull; on the/ncontrary, at Hermione's words, they had all raised/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ntheir wands again and were pointing in the direction/nshe had indicated, squinting through the dark trees./n/n"We're too late," said the witch in the woolen dressing/ngown, shaking her head. "They'll have Disapparated."/n/n"I don't think so," said a wizard with a scrubby brown/nbeard. It was Amos Diggory, Cedric's father. "Our/nStunners went right through those trees. ... There's a/ngood chance we got them. ..."/n/n"Amos, be careful!" said a few of the wizards/nwarningly as Mr. Diggory squared his shoulders,/nraised his wand, marched across the clearing, and/ndisappeared into the darkness. Hermione watched/nhim vanish with her hands over her mouth./n/nA few seconds later, they heard Mr. Diggory shout./n/n"Yes! We got them! There's someone here!/nUnconscious! It's — but — blimey ..."/n/n"You've got someone?" shouted Mr. Crouch, sounding/nhighly disbelieving. "Who? Who is it?"/n/nThey heard snapping twigs, the rustling of leaves, and/nthen crunching footsteps as Mr. Diggory reemerged/nfrom behind the trees. He was carrying a tiny, limp/nfigure in his arms. Harry recognized the tea towel at/nonce. It was Winky./n/nMr. Crouch did not move or speak as Mr. Diggory/ndeposited his elf on the ground at his feet. The other/nMinistry wizards were all staring at Mr. Crouch. For a/nfew seconds Crouch remained transfixed, his eyes/nblazing in his white face as he stared down at Winky./nThen he appeared to come to life again./n/n"This — cannot — be," he said jerkily. "No — "/n/n/n/n/n/nHe moved quickly around Mr. Diggory and strode off/ntoward the place where he had found Winky./n/n/n/n"No point, Mr. Crouch," Mr. Diggory called after him./n"There's no one else there."/n/nBut Mr. Crouch did not seem prepared to take his/nword for it. They could hear him moving around and/nthe rustling of leaves as he pushed the bushes aside,/nsearching./n/n"Bit embarrassing," Mr. Diggory said grimly, looking/ndown at Winky's unconscious form. "Barty Crouch's/nhouse-elf ... I mean to say ..."/n/n"Come off it, Amos," said Mr. Weasley quietly, "you/ndon't seriously think it was the elf? The Dark Mark's a/nwizard's sign. It requires a wand."/n/n"Yeah," said Mr. Diggory, "and she had a wand."/n/n"What?" said Mr. Weasley./n/n"Here, look." Mr. Diggory held up a wand and showed/nit to Mr. Weasley. "Had it in her hand. So that's/nclause three of the Code of Wand Use broken, for a/nstart. No non-human creature is permitted to carry or/nuse a wand."/n/nJust then there was another pop, and Ludo Bagman/nApparated right next to Mr. Weasley. Looking/nbreathless and disorientated, he spun on the spot,/ngoggling upward at the emerald-green skull./n/n"The Dark Mark!" he panted, almost trampling Winky/nas he turned inquiringly to his colleagues. "Who did/nit? Did you get them? Barty! What's going on?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMr. Crouch had returned empty-handed. His face was/nstill ghostly white, and his hands and his toothbrush/nmustache were both twitching./n/n"Where have you been, Barty?" said Bagman. "Why/nweren't you at the match? Your elf was saving you a/nseat too — gulping gargoyles!" Bagman had just/nnoticed Winky lying at his feet. "What happened to/nher?"/n/n"I have been busy, Ludo," said Mr. Crouch, still/ntalking in the same jerky fashion, barely moving his/nlips. "And my elf has been stunned."/n/n"Stunned? By you lot, you mean? But why — ?"/n/nComprehension dawned suddenly on Bagman's/nround, shiny face; he looked up at the skull, down at/nWinky, and then at Mr. Crouch./n/n"iVo!" he said. "Winky? Conjure the Dark Mark? She/nwouldn't know how! She'd need a wand, for a start!"/n/n"And she had one," said Mr. Diggory. "I found her/nholding one, Ludo. If it's all right with you, Mr./n/nCrouch, I think we should hear what she's got to say/nfor herself."/n/nCrouch gave no sign that he had heard Mr. Diggory,/nbut Mr. Diggory seemed to take his silence for assent./nHe raised his own wand, pointed it at Winky, and/nsaid, "Rennervatel"/n/nWinky stirred feebly. Her great brown eyes opened/nand she blinked several times in a bemused sort of/nway. Watched by the silent wizards, she raised herself/nshakily into a sitting position. She caught sight of Mr./nDiggory's feet, and slowly, tremulously, raised her/neyes to stare up into his face; then, more slowly still,/n/n/n/n/nshe looked up into the sky. Harry could see the/nfloating skull reflected twice in her enormous, glassy/neyes. She gave a gasp, looked wildly around the/ncrowded clearing, and burst into terrified sobs./n/n"Elf!" said Mr. Diggory sternly. "Do you know who I/nam? I'm a member of the Department for the/nRegulation and Control of Magical Creatures!"/n/nWinky began to rock backward and forward on the/nground, her breath coming in sharp bursts. Harry/nwas reminded forcibly of Dobby in his moments of/nterrified disobedience./n/n"As you see, elf, the Dark Mark was conjured here a/nshort while ago," said Mr. Diggory. "And you were/ndiscovered moments later, right beneath it! An/nexplanation, if you please!"/n/n"I — I — I is not doing it, sir!" Winky gasped. "I is not/nknowing how, sir!"/n/n"You were found with a wand in your hand!" barked/nMr. Diggory, brandishing it in front of her. And as the/nwand caught the green light that was filling the/nclearing from the skull above, Harry recognized it./n/n"Hey — that's mine!" he said./n/nEveryone in the clearing looked at him./n/n"Excuse me?" said Mr. Diggory, incredulously./n/n"That's my wand!" said Harry. "I dropped it!"/n/n"You dropped it?" repeated Mr. Diggory in disbelief./n/n"Is this a confession? You threw it aside after you/nconjured the Mark?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Amos, think who you're talking to!" said Mr. Weasley,/nvery angrily. "Is Harry Potter likely to conjure the/nDark Mark?"/n/n"Er — of course not," mumbled Mr. Diggory. "Sorry .../ncarried away ..."/n/n"I didn't drop it there, anyway," said Harry, jerking/nhis thumb toward the trees beneath the skull. "I/nmissed it right after we got into the wood."/n/n"So," said Mr. Diggory, his eyes hardening as he/nturned to look at Winky again, cowering at his feet./n"You found this wand, eh, elf? And you picked it up/nand thought you'd have some fun with it, did you?"/n/n"I is not doing magic with it, sir!" squealed Winky,/ntears streaming down the sides of her squashed and/nbulbous nose. "I is ... I is ... I is just picking it up, sir!/n/nI is not making the Dark Mark, sir, I is not knowing/nhow!"/n/n"It wasn't her!" said Hermione. She looked very/nnervous, speaking up in front of all these Ministry/nwizards, yet determined all the same. "Winky's got a/nsqueaky little voice, and the voice we heard doing the/nincantation was much deeper!" She looked around at/nHarry and Ron, appealing for their support. "It didn't/nsound anything like Winky, did it?"/n/n"No," said Harry, shaking his head. "It definitely didn't/nsound like an elf."/n/n"Yeah, it was a human voice," said Ron./n/n"Well, we'll soon see," growled Mr. Diggory, looking/nunimpressed. "There's a simple way of discovering the/nlast spell a wand performed, elf, did you know that?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWinky trembled and shook her head frantically, her/nears flapping, as Mr. Diggory raised his own wand/nagain and placed it tip to tip with Harry's./n/n" Prior Incantatol" roared Mr. Diggory./n/nHarry heard Hermione gasp, horrified, as a gigantic/nserpent-tongued skull erupted from the point where/nthe two wands met, but it was a mere shadow of the/ngreen skull high above them; it looked as though it/nwere made of thick gray smoke: the ghost of a spell./n/n"Deletrius\" Mr. Diggory shouted, and the smoky skull/nvanished in a wisp of smoke./n/n"So," said Mr. Diggory with a kind of savage triumph,/nlooking down upon Winky, who was still shaking/nconvulsively./n/n"I is not doing it!" she squealed, her eyes rolling in/nterror. "I is not, I is not, I is not knowing how! I is a/ngood elf, I isn't using wands, I isn't knowing how!"/n/n" You've been caught red-handed, elf." Mr. Diggory/nroared. "Caught with the guilty wand in your hand\"/n/n"Amos," said Mr. Weasley loudly, "think about it .../nprecious few wizards know how to do that spell. .../nWhere would she have learned it?"/n/n"Perhaps Amos is suggesting," said Mr. Crouch, cold/nanger in every syllable, "that I routinely teach my/nservants to conjure the Dark Mark?"/n/nThere was a deeply unpleasant silence. Amos Diggory/nlooked horrified. "Mr. Crouch ... not ... not at all ..."/n/n"You have now come very close to accusing the two/npeople in this clearing who are least likely to conjure/n/n/n/n/n/nthat Mark!" barked Mr. Crouch. "Harry Potter — and/nmyself! I suppose you are familiar with the boy's/nstory, Amos?"/n/n"Of course — everyone knows — " muttered Mr./nDiggory, looking highly discomforted./n/n"And I trust you remember the many proofs I have/ngiven, over a long career, that I despise and detest the/nDark Arts and those who practice them?" Mr. Crouch/nshouted, his eyes bulging again./n/n"Mr. Crouch, I — I never suggested you had anything/nto do with it!" Amos Diggory muttered again, now/nreddening behind his scrubby brown beard./n/n"If you accuse my elf, you accuse me, Diggory!"/nshouted Mr. Crouch. "Where else would she have/nlearned to conjure it?"/n/n"She — she might've picked it up anywhere — "/n/n"Precisely, Amos," said Mr. Weasley. " She might have/npicked it up anywhere. ... Winky?" he said kindly,/nturning to the elf, but she flinched as though he too/nwas shouting at her. "Where exactly did you find/nHarry's wand?"/n/nWinky was twisting the hem of her tea towel so/nviolently that it was fraying beneath her fingers./n/n"I — I is finding it ... finding it there, sir. ..." she/nwhispered, "there ... in the trees, sir. ..."/n/n"You see, Amos?" said Mr. Weasley. "Whoever/nconjured the Mark could have Disapparated right/nafter they'd done it, leaving Harry's wand behind. A/nclever thing to do, not using their own wand, which/ncould have betrayed them. And Winky here had the/n/n/n/n/nmisfortune to come across the wand moments later/nand pick it up."/n/n"But then, she'd have been only a few feet away from/nthe real culprit!" said Mr. Diggory impatiently. "Elf?/nDid you see anyone?"/n/nWinky began to tremble worse than ever. Her giant/neyes flickered from Mr. Diggory, to Ludo Bagman, and/nonto Mr. Crouch. Then she gulped and said, "I is/nseeing no one, sir ... no one ..."/n/n"Amos," said Mr. Crouch curtly, "I am fully aware/nthat, in the ordinary course of events, you would want/nto take Winky into your department for questioning. I/nask you, however, to allow me to deal with her."/n/nMr. Diggory looked as though he didn't think much of/nthis suggestion at all, but it was clear to Harry that/nMr. Crouch was such an important member of the/nMinistry that he did not dare refuse him./n/n"You may rest assured that she will be punished," Mr./nCrouch added coldly./n/n"M-m-master ..." Winky stammered, looking up at Mr./nCrouch, her eyes brimming with tears. "M-m-master,/np-p-please ..."/n/nMr. Crouch stared back, his face somehow/nsharpened, each line upon it more deeply etched./nThere was no pity in his gaze./n/n"Winky has behaved tonight in a manner I would not/nhave believed possible," he said slowly. "I told her to/nremain in the tent. I told her to stay there while I/nwent to sort out the trouble. And I find that she/ndisobeyed me. This means clothes."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No!" shrieked Winky, prostrating herself at Mr./nCrouch's feet. "No, master! Not clothes, not clothes!"/n/nHarry knew that the only way to turn a house-elf free/nwas to present it with proper garments. It was pitiful/nto see the way Winky clutched at her tea towel as she/nsobbed over Mr. Crouch's feet./n/n"But she was frightened!" Hermione burst out angrily,/nglaring at Mr. Crouch. "Your elf's scared of heights,/nand those wizards in masks were levitating people!/n/nYou can't blame her for wanting to get out of their/nway!"/n/nMr. Crouch took a step backward, freeing himself/nfrom contact with the elf, whom he was surveying as/nthough she were something filthy and rotten that was/ncontaminating his over-shined shoes./n/n"I have no use for a house-elf who disobeys me," he/nsaid coldly, looking over at Hermione. "I have no use/nfor a servant who forgets what is due to her master,/nand to her master's reputation."/n/nWinky was crying so hard that her sobs echoed/naround the clearing. There was a very nasty silence,/nwhich was ended by Mr. Weasley, who said quietly,/n"Well, I think I'll take my lot back to the tent, if/nnobody's got any objections. Amos, that wand's told/nus all it can — if Harry could have it back, please — "/n/nMr. Diggory handed Harry his wand and Harry/npocketed it./n/n"Come on, you three," Mr. Weasley said quietly. But/nHermione didn't seem to want to move; her eyes were/nstill upon the sobbing elf. "Hermione!" Mr. Weasley/nsaid, more urgently. She turned and followed Harry/nand Ron out of the clearing and off through the trees./n/n/n/n/n"What's going to happen to Winky?" said Hermione,/nthe moment they had left the clearing./n/n"I don't know," said Mr. Weasley./n/n"The way they were treating her!" said Hermione/nfuriously. "Mr. Diggory, calling her 'elf' all the time .../nand Mr. Crouch! He knows she didn't do it and he's/nstill going to sack her! He didn't care how frightened/nshe'd been, or how upset she was — it was like she/nwasn't even human!"/n/n"Well, she's not," said Ron./n/nHermione rounded on him./n/n"That doesn't mean she hasn't got feelings, Ron. It's/ndisgusting the way — "/n/n"Hermione, I agree with you," said Mr. Weasley/nquickly, beckoning her on, "but now is not the time to/ndiscuss elf rights. I want to get back to the tent as/nfast as we can. What happened to the others?"/n/n"We lost them in the dark," said Ron. "Dad, why was/neveryone so uptight about that skull thing?"/n/n"I'll explain everything back at the tent," said Mr./nWeasley tensely./n/nBut when they reached the edge of the wood, their/nprogress was impeded. A large crowd of frightened-/nlooking witches and wizards was congregated there,/nand when they saw Mr. Weasley coming toward them,/nmany of them surged forward./n/n"What's going on in there?"/n/n"Who conjured it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Arthur — it's not — Him?"/n/n/n/n"Of course it's not Him," said Mr. Weasley/nimpatiently. "We don't know who it was; it looks like/nthey Disapparated. Now excuse me, please, I want to/nget to bed."/n/nHe led Harry, Ron, and Hermione through the crowd/nand back into the campsite. All was quiet now; there/nwas no sign of the masked wizards, though several/nruined tents were still smoking./n/nCharlie's head was poking out of the boys' tent./n/n"Dad, what's going on?" he called through the dark./n"Fred, George, and Ginny got back okay, but the/nothers — "/n/n"I've got them here," said Mr. Weasley, bending down/nand entering the tent. Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nentered after him./n/nBill was sitting at the small kitchen table, holding a/nbedsheet to his arm, which was bleeding profusely./nCharlie had a large rip in his shirt, and Percy was/nsporting a bloody nose. Fred, George, and Ginny/nlooked unhurt, though shaken./n/n"Did you get them, Dad?" said Bill sharply. "The/nperson who conjured the Mark?"/n/n"No," said Mr. Weasley. "We found Barty Crouch's elf/nholding Harry's wand, but we're none the wiser about/nwho actually conjured the Mark."/n/n"What?" said Bill, Charlie, and Percy together./n/n"Harry's wand?" said Fred./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mr. Crouch's elf?" said Percy, sounding/nthunderstruck./n/nWith some assistance from Harry, Ron, and/nHermione, Mr. Weasley explained what had happened/nin the woods. When they had finished their story,/nPercy swelled indignantly./n/n"Well, Mr. Crouch is quite right to get rid of an elf like/nthat!" he said. "Running away when he'd expressly/ntold her not to ... embarrassing him in front of the/nwhole Ministry . . . how would that have looked, if/nshe'd been brought up in front of the Department for/nthe Regulation and Control — "/n/n"She didn't do anything — she was just in the wrong/nplace at the wrong time!" Hermione snapped at Percy,/nwho looked very taken aback. Hermione had always/ngot on fairly well with Percy — better, indeed, than/nany of the others./n/n"Hermione, a wizard in Mr. Crouch's position can't/nafford a house-elf who's going to run amok with a/nwand!" said Percy pompously, recovering himself./n/n"She didn't run amok!" shouted Hermione. "She just/npicked it up off the ground!"/n/n"Look, can someone just explain what that skull thing/nwas?" said Ron impatiently. "It wasn't hurting/nanyone. ... Why's it such a big deal?"/n/n"I told you, it's You-Know-Who's symbol, Ron," said/nHermione, before anyone else could answer. "I read/nabout it in The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts."/n/n"And it hasn't been seen for thirteen years," said Mr./nWeasley quietly. "Of course people panicked ... it was/nalmost like seeing You-Know-Who back again."/n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't get it," said Ron, frowning. "I mean ... it's still/nonly a shape in the sky. ..."/n/n"Ron, You-Know-Who and his followers sent the Dark/nMark into the air whenever they killed," said Mr./nWeasley. "The terror it inspired ... you have no idea,/nyou're too young. Just picture coming home and/nfinding the Dark Mark hovering over your house, and/nknowing what you're about to find inside. ..." Mr./nWeasley winced. "Everyone's worst fear ... the very/nworst ..."/n/nThere was silence for a moment. Then Bill, removing/nthe sheet from his arm to check on his cut, said,/n/n"Well, it didn't help us tonight, whoever conjured it. It/nscared the Death Eaters away the moment they saw/nit. They all Disapparated before we'd got near enough/nto unmask any of them. We caught the Robertses/nbefore they hit the ground, though. They're having/ntheir memories modified right now."/n/n"Death Eaters?" said Harry. "What are Death Eaters?"/n/n"It's what You-Know- Who's supporters called/nthemselves," said Bill. "I think we saw what's left of/nthem tonight — the ones who managed to keep/nthemselves out of Azkaban, anyway."/n/n"We can't prove it was them, Bill," said Mr. Weasley./n"Though it probably was," he added hopelessly./n/n"Yeah, I bet it was!" said Ron suddenly. "Dad, we met/nDraco Malfoy in the woods, and he as good as told us/nhis dad was one of those nutters in masks! And we all/nknow the Malfoys were right in with You-Know-Who!"/n/n"But what were Voldemort's supporters — " Harry/nbegan. Everybody flinched — like most of the/nwizarding world, the Weasleys always avoided saying/n/n/n/n/n/nVoldemort's name. "Sorry," said Harry quickly. "What/nwere You -Know- Who's supporters up to, levitating/nMuggles? I mean, what was the point?"/n/n"The point?" said Mr. Weasley with a hollow laugh./n"Harry, that's their idea of fun. Half the Muggle/nkillings back when You-Know-Who was in power were/ndone for fun. I suppose they had a few drinks tonight/nand couldn't resist reminding us all that lots of them/nare still at large. A nice little reunion for them," he/nfinished disgustedly./n/n"But if they were the Death Eaters, why did they/nDisapparate when they saw the Dark Mark?" said/nRon. "They'd have been pleased to see it, wouldn't/nthey?"/n/n"Use your brains, Ron," said Bill. "If they really were/nDeath Eaters, they worked very hard to keep out of/nAzkaban when You-Know-Who lost power, and told all/nsorts of lies about him forcing them to kill and torture/npeople. I bet they'd be even more frightened than the/nrest of us to see him come back. They denied they'd/never been involved with him when he lost his powers,/nand went back to their daily lives. ... I don't reckon/nhe'd be over-pleased with them, do you?"/n/n"So ... whoever conjured the Dark Mark ..." said/nHermione slowly, "were they doing it to show support/nfor the Death Eaters, or to scare them away?"/n/n"Your guess is as good as ours, Hermione," said Mr./nWeasley. "But I'll tell you this ... it was only the Death/nEaters who ever knew how to conjure it. I'd be very/nsurprised if the person who did it hadn't been a Death/nEater once, even if they're not now. ... Listen, it's very/nlate, and if your mother hears what's happened she'll/nbe worried sick. We'll get a few more hours sleep and/nthen try and get an early Portkey out of here."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry got back into his bunk with his head buzzing./nHe knew he ought to feel exhausted: It was nearly/nthree in the morning, but he felt wide-awake — wide-/nawake, and worried./n/nThree days ago — it felt like much longer, but it had/nonly been three days — he had awoken with his scar/nburning. And tonight, for the first time in thirteen/nyears, Lord Voldemort's mark had appeared in the/nsky. What did these things mean?/n/nHe thought of the letter he had written to Sirius/nbefore leaving Privet Drive. Would Sirius have gotten/nit yet? When would he reply? Harry lay looking up at/nthe canvas, but no flying fantasies came to him now/nto ease him to sleep, and it was a long time after/nCharlie's snores filled the tent that Harry finally dozed/noff./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n10/n/n/n/n

title: Mayhem At The Ministry
text: /nMr. Weasley woke them after only a few hours sleep./nHe used magic to pack up the tents, and they left the/ncampsite as quickly as possible, passing Mr. Roberts/nat the door of his cottage. Mr. Roberts had a strange,/ndazed look about him, and he waved them off with a/nvague "Merry Christmas."/n/n"Hell be all right," said Mr. Weasley quietly as they/nmarched off onto the moor. "Sometimes, when a/nperson's memory's modified, it makes him a bit/ndisorientated for a while . . . and that was a big thing/nthey had to make him forget."/n/nThey heard urgent voices as they approached the spot/nwhere the Portkeys lay, and when they reached it,/nthey found a great number of witches and wizards/ngathered around Basil, the keeper of the Portkeys, all/nclamoring to get away from the campsite as quickly as/npossible. Mr. Weasley had a hurried discussion with/nBasil; they joined the queue, and were able to take an/nold rubber tire back to Stoatshead Hill before the sun/nhad really risen. They walked back through Ottery St./n/n/n/nCatchpole and up the damp lane toward the Burrow/nin the dawn light, talking very little because they were/nso exhausted, and thinking longingly of their/nbreakfast. As they rounded the corner and the/nBurrow came into view, a cry echoed along the lane./n/n"Oh thank goodness, thank goodness!"/n/nMrs. Weasley, who had evidently been waiting for/nthem in the front yard, came running toward them,/nstill wearing her bedroom slippers, her face pale and/nstrained, a rolled-up copy of the Daily Prophet/nclutched in her hand./n/n"Arthur — I've been so worried — so worried — "/n/nShe flung her arms around Mr. Weasley's neck, and/nthe Daily Prophet fell out of her limp hand onto the/nground. Looking down, Harry saw the headline:/nSCENES OF TERROR AT THE QUIDDITCH WORLD/nCUP, complete with a twinkling black-and-white/nphotograph of the Dark Mark over the treetops./n/n"You're all right," Mrs. Weasley muttered distractedly,/nreleasing Mr. Weasley and staring around at them all/nwith red eyes, "you're alive. ... Oh boys ..."/n/nAnd to everybody's surprise, she seized Fred and/nGeorge and pulled them both into such a tight hug/nthat their heads banged together./n/n" Ouch\ Mum — you're strangling us — "/n/n"I shouted at you before you left!" Mrs. Weasley said,/nstarting to sob. "It's all I've been thinking about! What/nif You-Know-Who had got you, and the last thing I/never said to you was that you didn't get enough/nO.W.L.s? Oh Fred ... George ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Come on, now, Molly, we're all perfectly okay," said/nMr. Weasley soothingly, prising her off the twins and/nleading her back toward the house. "Bill," he added in/nan undertone, "pick up that paper, I want to see what/nit says. ..."/n/nWhen they were all crammed into the tiny kitchen,/nand Hermione had made Mrs. Weasley a cup of very/nstrong tea, into which Mr. Weasley insisted on/npouring a shot of Ogdens Old Firewhiskey, Bill/nhanded his father the newspaper. Mr. Weasley/nscanned the front page while Percy looked over his/nshoulder./n/n"I knew it," said Mr. Weasley heavily. "Ministry/nblunders ... culprits not apprehended ... lax security .../nDark wizards running unchecked . . . national disgrace/n... Who wrote this? Ah ... of course ... Rita Skeeter."/n/n"That woman's got it in for the Ministry of Magic!"/nsaid Percy furiously. "Last week she was saying we're/nwasting our time quibbling about cauldron thickness,/nwhen we should be stamping out vampires! As if it/nwasn't specifically stated in paragraph twelve of the/nGuidelines for the Treatment of Non-Wizard Part-/nHumans — "/n/n"Do us a favor, Perce," said Bill, yawning, "and shut/nup."/n/n"I'm mentioned," said Mr. Weasley, his eyes widening/nbehind his glasses as he reached the bottom of the/nDaily Prophet article./n/n"Where?" spluttered Mrs. Weasley, choking on her tea/nand whiskey. "If I'd seen that, I'd have known you/nwere alive!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Not by name," said Mr. Weasley. "Listen to this: 'If/nthe terrified wizards and witches who waited/nbreathlessly for news at the edge of the wood expected/nreassurance from the Ministry of Magic, they were/nsadly disappointed. A Ministry official emerged some/ntime after the appearance of the Dark Mark alleging/nthat nobody had been hurt, but refusing to give any/nmore information. Whether this statement will be/nenough to quash the rumors that several bodies were/nremoved from the woods an hour later, remains to be/nseen.' Oh really," said Mr. Weasley in exasperation,/nhanding the paper to Percy. "Nobody was hurt. What/nwas I supposed to say? Rumors that several bodies/nwere removed from the woods ... well, there certainly/nwill be rumors now she's printed that."/n/nHe heaved a deep sigh. "Molly, I'm going to have to go/ninto the office; this is going to take some smoothing/nover."/n/n"I'll come with you, Father," said Percy importantly./n"Mr. Crouch will need all hands on deck. And I can/ngive him my cauldron report in person."/n/nHe bustled out of the kitchen. Mrs. Weasley looked/nmost upset./n/n"Arthur, you're supposed to be on holiday! This hasn't/ngot anything to do with your office; surely they can/nhandle this without you?"/n/n"I've got to go, Molly," said Mr. Weasley. "I've made/nthings worse. I'll just change into my robes and I'll be/noff. ..."/n/n"Mrs. Weasley," said Harry suddenly, unable to/ncontain himself, "Hedwig hasn't arrived with a letter/nfor me, has she?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Hedwig, dear?" said Mrs. Weasley distractedly. "No .../nno, there hasn't been any post at all."/n/nRon and Hermione looked curiously at Harry. With a/nmeaningful look at both of them he said, "All right if I/ngo and dump my stuff in your room, Ron?"/n/n"Yeah ... think I will too," said Ron at once./n"Hermione?"/n/n"Yes," she said quickly, and the three of them/nmarched out of the kitchen and up the stairs./n/n"What's up, Harry?" said Ron, the moment they had/nclosed the door of the attic room behind them./n/n"There's something I haven't told you," Harry said./n/n"On Saturday morning, I woke up with my scar/nhurting again."/n/nRon's and Hermione's reactions were almost exactly/nas Harry had imagined them back in his bedroom on/nPrivet Drive. Hermione gasped and started making/nsuggestions at once, mentioning a number of/nreference books, and everybody from Albus/nDumbledore to Madam Pomfrey, the Hogwarts nurse./nRon simply looked dumbstruck./n/n"But — he wasn't there, was he? You-Know-Who? I/nmean — last time your scar kept hurting, he was at/nHogwarts, wasn't he?"/n/n"I'm sure he wasn't on Privet Drive," said Harry. "But I/nwas dreaming about him . . . him and Peter — you/nknow, Wormtail. I can't remember all of it now, but/nthey were plotting to kill ... someone."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe had teetered for a moment on the verge of saying/n"me," but couldn't bring himself to make Hermione/nlook any more horrified than she already did./n/n"It was only a dream," said Ron bracingly. "Just a/nnightmare."/n/n"Yeah, but was it, though?" said Harry, turning to/nlook out of the window at the brightening sky. "It's/nweird, isn't it? ... My scar hurts, and three days later/nthe Death Eaters are on the march, and Voldemort's/nsign's up in the sky again."/n/n"Don't — say — his — name!" Ron hissed through/ngritted teeth./n/n"And remember what Professor Trelawney said?"/n/nHarry went on, ignoring Ron. "At the end of last/nyear?"/n/nProfessor Trelawney was their Divination teacher at/nHogwarts. Hermione 's terrified look vanished as she/nlet out a derisive snort./n/n"Oh Harry, you aren't going to pay attention to/nanything that old fraud says?"/n/n"You weren't there," said Harry. "You didn't hear her./nThis time was different. I told you, she went into a/ntrance — a real one. And she said the Dark Lord/nwould rise again . . . greater and more terrible than ever/nbefore ... and he'd manage it because his servant was/ngoing to go back to him ... and that night Wormtail/nescaped."/n/nThere was a silence in which Ron fidgeted/nabsentmindedly with a hole in his Chudley Cannons/nbedspread./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Why were you asking if Hedwig had come, Harry?"/nHermione asked. "Are you expecting a letter?"/n/n"I told Sirius about my scar," said Harry, shrugging./n"I'm waiting for his answer."/n/n"Good thinking!" said Ron, his expression clearing. "I/nbet Sirius 'll know what to do!"/n/n"I hoped he'd get back to me quickly," said Harry./n/n"But we don't know where Sirius is ... he could be in/nAfrica or somewhere, couldn't he?" said Hermione/nreasonably. "Hedwig's not going to manage that/njourney in a few days."/n/n"Yeah, I know," said Harry, but there was a leaden/nfeeling in his stomach as he looked out of the window/nat the Hedwig-free sky./n/n"Come and have a game of Quidditch in the orchard,/nHarry," said Ron. "Come on — three on three, Bill and/nCharlie and Fred and George will play. ... You can try/nout the Wronski Feint. ..."/n/n"Ron," said Hermione, in an I-don't-think-you're-/nbeing- very- sensitive sort of voice, "Harry doesn't want/nto play Quidditch right now. ... He's worried, and he's/ntired. ... We all need to go to bed. ..."/n/n"Yeah, I want to play Quidditch," said Harry/nsuddenly. "Hang on, I'll get my Firebolt."/n/nHermione left the room, muttering something that/nsounded very much like "Boys."/n/nk k k/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNeither Mr. Weasley nor Percy was at home much/nover the following week. Both left the house each/nmorning before the rest of the family got up, and/nreturned well after dinner every night./n/n"It's been an absolute uproar," Percy told them/nimportantly the Sunday evening before they were due/nto return to Hogwarts. "I've been putting out fires all/nweek. People keep sending Howlers, and of course, if/nyou don't open a Howler straight away, it explodes./nScorch marks all over my desk and my best quill/nreduced to cinders."/n/n"Why are they all sending Howlers?" asked Ginny,/nwho was mending her copy of One Thousand Magical/nHerbs and Fungi with Spellotape on the rug in front of/nthe living room fire./n/n"Complaining about security at the World Cup," said/nPercy. "They want compensation for their ruined/nproperty. Mundungus Fletcher's put in a claim for a/ntwelve-bedroomed tent with en-suite Jacuzzi, but I've/ngot his number. I know for a fact he was sleeping/nunder a cloak propped on sticks."/n/nMrs. Weasley glanced at the grandfather clock in the/ncorner. Harry liked this clock. It was completely/nuseless if you wanted to know the time, but otherwise/nvery informative. It had nine golden hands, and each/nof them was engraved with one of the Weasley family's/nnames. There were no numerals around the face, but/ndescriptions of where each family member might be./n"Home," "school," and "work" were there, but there/nwas also "traveling," "lost," "hospital," "prison," and,/nin the position where the number twelve would be on/na normal clock, "mortal peril."/n/nEight of the hands were currently pointing to the/n"home" position, but Mr. Weasley's, which was the/n/n/n/n/n/nlongest, was still pointing to "work." Mrs. Weasley/nsighed./n/n/n/n"Your father hasn't had to go into the office on/nweekends since the days of You-Know-Who," she said./n"They're working him far too hard. His dinner's going/nto be mined if he doesn't come home soon."/n/n"Well, Father feels he's got to make up for his mistake/nat the match, doesn't he?" said Percy. "If truth be/ntold, he was a tad unwise to make a public statement/nwithout clearing it with his Head of Department first/n/n/n/n"Don't you dare blame your father for what that/nwretched Skeeter woman wrote!" said Mrs. Weasley,/nflaring up at once./n/n"If Dad hadn't said anything, old Rita would just have/nsaid it was disgraceful that nobody from the Ministry/nhad commented," said Bill, who was playing chess/nwith Ron. "Rita Skeeter never makes anyone look/ngood. Remember, she interviewed all the Gringotts'/nCharm Breakers once, and called me 'a long-haired/npillock'?"/n/n"Well, it is a bit long, dear," said Mrs. Weasley gently./n"If you'd just let me — "/n/n"No, Mum."/n/nRain lashed against the living room window./n/nHermione was immersed in The Standard Book of/nSpells, Grade 4, copies of which Mrs. Weasley had/nbought for her, Harry, and Ron in Diagon Alley./nCharlie was darning a fireproof balaclava. Harry was/npolishing his Firebolt, the broomstick servicing kit/nHermione had given him for his thirteenth birthday/nopen at his feet. Fred and George were sitting in a far/n/n/n/n/ncorner, quills out, talking in whispers, their heads/nbent over a piece of parchment./n/n"What are you two up to?" said Mrs. Weasley sharply,/nher eyes on the twins./n/n"Homework," said Fred vaguely./n/n"Don't be ridiculous, you're still on holiday," said Mrs./nWeasley./n/n"Yeah, we've left it a bit late," said George./n/n"You're not by any chance writing out a new order/nform, are you?" said Mrs. Weasley shrewdly. "You/nwouldn't be thinking of restarting Weasleys' Wizard/nWheezes, by any chance?"/n/n"Now, Mum," said Fred, looking up at her, a pained/nlook on his face. "If the Hogwarts Express crashed/ntomorrow, and George and I died, how would you feel/nto know that the last thing we ever heard from you/nwas an unfounded accusation?"/n/nEveryone laughed, even Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Oh your father's coming!" she said suddenly, looking/nup at the clock again./n/nMr. Weasley's hand had suddenly spun from "work"/nto "traveling"; a second later it had shuddered to a/nhalt on "home" with the others, and they heard him/ncalling from the kitchen./n/n"Coming, Arthur!" called Mrs. Weasley, hurrying out/nof the room./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA few moments later, Mr. Weasley came into the/nwarm living room carrying his dinner on a tray. He/nlooked completely exhausted./n/n"Well, the fat's really in the fire now," he told Mrs./nWeasley as he sat down in an armchair near the/nhearth and toyed unenthusiastically with his/nsomewhat shriveled cauliflower. "Rita Skeeter's been/nferreting around all week, looking for more Ministry/nmess-ups to report. And now she's found out about/npoor old Bertha going missing, so that'll be the/nheadline in the Prophet tomorrow. I told Bagman he/nshould have sent someone to look for her ages ago."/n/n"Mr. Crouch has been saying it for weeks and weeks,"/nsaid Percy swiftly./n/n"Crouch is very lucky Rita hasn't found out about/nWinky," said Mr. Weasley irritably. "There'd be a/nweek's worth of headlines in his house-elf being/ncaught holding the wand that conjured the Dark/nMark."/n/n"I thought we were all agreed that that elf, while/nirresponsible, did not conjure the Mark?" said Percy/nhotly./n/n"If you ask me, Mr. Crouch is very lucky no one at the/nDaily Prophet knows how mean he is to elves!" said/nHermione angrily./n/n"Now look here, Hermione!" said Percy. "A high-/nranking Ministry official like Mr. Crouch deserves/nunswerving obedience from his servants — "/n/n"His slave, you mean!" said Hermione, her voice rising/npassionately, "because he didn't pay Winky, did he?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I think you'd all better go upstairs and check that/nyou've packed properly!" said Mrs. Weasley, breaking/nup the argument. "Come on now, all of you. ..."/n/nHarry repacked his broomstick servicing kit, put his/nFirebolt over his shoulder, and went back upstairs/nwith Ron. The rain sounded even louder at the top of/nthe house, accompanied by loud whistlings and/nmoans from the wind, not to mention sporadic howls/nfrom the ghoul who lived in the attic. Pigwidgeon/nbegan twittering and zooming around his cage when/nthey entered. The sight of the half-packed trunks/nseemed to have sent him into a frenzy of excitement./n/n"Bung him some Owl Treats," said Ron, throwing a/npacket across to Harry. "It might shut him up."/n/nHarry poked a few Owl Treats through the bars of/nPigwidgeon's cage, then turned to his trunk. Hedwig's/ncage stood next to it, still empty./n/n"It's been over a week," Harry said, looking at/nHedwig's deserted perch. "Ron, you don't reckon/nSirius has been caught, do you?"/n/n"Nah, it would've been in the Daily Prophet," said Ron./n"The Ministry would want to show they'd caught/nsomeone, wouldn't they?"/n/n"Yeah, I suppose. ..."/n/n"Look, here's the stuff Mum got for you in Diagon/nAlley. And she's got some gold out of your vault for/nyou ... and she's washed all your socks."/n/nHe heaved a pile of parcels onto Harry's camp bed/nand dropped the money bag and a load of socks next/nto it. Harry started unwrapping the shopping. Apart/nfrom The Standard Book of Spells, Grade 4, by/n/n/n/n/n/nMiranda Goshawk, he had a handful of new quills, a/ndozen rolls of parchment, and refills for his potion-/nmaking kit — he had been running low on spine of/nlionfish and essence of belladonna. He was just piling/nunderwear into his cauldron when Ron made a loud/nnoise of disgust behind him./n/n"What is that supposed to be?"/n/nHe was holding up something that looked to Harry/nlike a long, maroon velvet dress.
