It had a moldy-/nlooking lace frill at the collar and matching lace cuffs./n/nThere was a knock on the door, and Mrs. Weasley/nentered, carrying an armful of freshly laundered/nHogwarts robes./n/n"Here you are," she said, sorting them into two piles./n"Now, mind you pack them properly so they don't/ncrease."/n/n"Mum, you've given me Ginny's new dress," said Ron,/nhanding it out to her./n/n"Of course I haven't," said Mrs. Weasley. "That's for/nyou. Dress robes."/n/n"What?" said Ron, looking horror-struck./n/n"Dress robes!" repeated Mrs. Weasley. "It says on your/nschool list that you're supposed to have dress robes/nthis year ... robes for formal occasions."/n/n"You've got to be kidding," said Ron in disbelief. "I'm/nnot wearing that, no way."/n/n"Everyone wears them, Ron!" said Mrs. Weasley/ncrossly. "They're all like that! Your father's got some/nfor smart parties!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'll go starkers before I put that on," said Ron/nstubbornly./n/n"Don't be so silly," said Mrs. Weasley. "You've got to/nhave dress robes, they're on your list! I got some for/nHarry too ... show him, Harry. ..."/n/nIn some trepidation, Harry opened the last parcel on/nhis camp bed. It wasn't as bad as he had expected,/nhowever; his dress robes didn't have any lace on them/nat all — in fact, they were more or less the same as/nhis school ones, except that they were bottle green/ninstead of black./n/n"I thought they'd bring out the color of your eyes,/ndear," said Mrs. Weasley fondly./n/n"Well, they're okay!" said Ron angrily, looking at/nHarry's robes. "Why couldn't I have some like that?"/n/n"Because ... well, I had to get yours secondhand, and/nthere wasn't a lot of choice!" said Mrs. Weasley,/nflushing./n/nHarry looked away. He would willingly have split all/nthe money in his Gringotts vault with the Weasleys,/nbut he knew they would never take it./n/n"I'm never wearing them," Ron was saying stubbornly./n"Never."/n/n"Fine," snapped Mrs. Weasley. "Go naked. And, Harry,/nmake sure you get a picture of him. Goodness knows/nI could do with a laugh."/n/nShe left the room, slamming the door behind her./nThere was a funny spluttering noise from behind/nthem. Pigwidgeon was choking on an overlarge Owl/nTreat./n/n/n/n/n/n"Why is everything I own rubbish?" said Ron/nfuriously, striding across the room to unstick/nPigwidgeon's beak./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Aboard The Hogwarts Express
text: /nThere was a definite end-of-the-holidays gloom in the/nair when Harry awoke next morning. Heavy rain was/nstill splattering against the window as he got dressed/nin jeans and a sweatshirt; they would change into/ntheir school robes on the Hogwarts Express./n/nHe, Ron, Fred, and George had just reached the first-/nfloor landing on their way down to breakfast, when/nMrs. Weasley appeared at the foot of the stairs,/nlooking harassed./n/n"Arthur!" she called up the staircase. "Arthur! Urgent/nmessage from the Ministry!"/n/nHarry flattened himself against the wall as Mr./nWeasley came clattering past with his robes on back-/nto-front and hurtled out of sight. When Harry and the/nothers entered the kitchen, they saw Mrs. Weasley/nrummaging anxiously in the drawers — "I've got a/nquill here somewhere!" — and Mr. Weasley bending/nover the fire, talking to —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry shut his eyes hard and opened them again to/nmake sure that they were working properly./n/nAmos Diggory's head was sitting in the middle of the/nflames like a large, bearded egg. It was talking very/nfast, completely unperturbed by the sparks flying/naround it and the flames licking its ears./n/n"... Muggle neighbors heard bangs and shouting, so/nthey went and called those what-d'you-call-'ems —/nplease-men. Arthur, you've got to get over there — "/n/n"Here!" said Mrs. Weasley breathlessly, pushing a/npiece of parchment, a bottle of ink, and a crumpled/nquill into Mr. Weasley's hands./n/n" — it's a real stroke of luck I heard about it," said Mr./nDiggory's head. "I had to come into the office early to/nsend a couple of owls, and I found the Improper Use/nof Magic lot all setting off — if Rita Skeeter gets hold/nof this one, Arthur — "/n/n"What does Mad-Eye say happened?" asked Mr./nWeasley, unscrewing the ink bottle, loading up his/nquill, and preparing to take notes./n/nMr. Diggory's head rolled its eyes. "Says he heard an/nintruder in his yard. Says he was creeping toward the/nhouse, but was ambushed by his dustbins."/n/n"What did the dustbins do?" asked Mr. Weasley,/nscribbling frantically./n/n"Made one hell of a noise and fired rubbish/neverywhere, as far as I can tell," said Mr. Diggory./n"Apparently one of them was still rocketing around/nwhen the please-men turned up — "/n/nMr. Weasley groaned./n/n/n/n/n/n"And what about the intruder?"/n/n/n/n"Arthur, you know Mad-Eye," said Mr. Diggory's head,/nrolling its eyes again. "Someone creeping into his yard/nin the dead of night? More likely there's a very shell-/nshocked cat wandering around somewhere, covered in/npotato peelings. But if the Improper Use of Magic lot/nget their hands on Mad-Eye, he's had it — think of/nhis record — we've got to get him off on a minor/ncharge, something in your department — what are/nexploding dustbins worth?"/n/n"Might be a caution," said Mr. Weasley, still writing/nvery fast, his brow furrowed. "Mad-Eye didn't use his/nwand? He didn't actually attack anyone?"/n/n"I'll bet he leapt out of bed and started jinxing/neverything he could reach through the window," said/nMr. Diggory, "but they'll have a job proving it, there/naren't any casualties."/n/n"All right, I'm off," Mr. Weasley said, and he stuffed/nthe parchment with his notes on it into his pocket/nand dashed out of the kitchen again./n/nMr. Diggory's head looked around at Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Sorry about this, Molly," it said, more calmly,/n"bothering you so early and everything . . . but Arthur's/nthe only one who can get Mad-Eye off, and Mad-Eye's/nsupposed to be starting his new job today. Why he/nhad to choose last night ..."/n/n"Never mind, Amos," said Mrs. Weasley. "Sure you/nwon't have a bit of toast or anything before you go?"/n/n"Oh go on, then," said Mr. Diggory./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley took a piece of buttered toast from a/nstack on the kitchen table, put it into the fire tongs,/nand transferred it into Mr. Diggory's mouth./n/n"Fanks," he said in a muffled voice, and then, with a/nsmall pop, vanished./n/nHarry could hear Mr. Weasley calling hurried good-/nbyes to Bill, Charlie, Percy, and the girls. Within five/nminutes, he was back in the kitchen, his robes on the/nright way now, dragging a comb through his hair./n/n"I'd better hurry — you have a good term, boys," said/nMr. Weasley to Harry, Ron, and the twins, fastening a/ncloak over his shoulders and preparing to/nDisapparate. "Molly, are you going to be all right/ntaking the kids to King's Cross?"/n/n"Of course I will," she said. "You just look after Mad-/nEye, we'll be fine."/n/nAs Mr. Weasley vanished, Bill and Charlie entered the/nkitchen./n/n"Did someone say Mad-Eye?" Bill asked. "What's he/nbeen up to now?/n/n"He says someone tried to break into his house last/nnight," said Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Mad-Eye Moody?" said George thoughtfully,/nspreading marmalade on his toast. "Isn't he that/nnutter — "/n/n"Your father thinks very highly of Mad-Eye Moody,"/nsaid Mrs. Weasley sternly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, well, Dad collects plugs, doesn't he?" said Fred/nquietly as Mrs. Weasley left the room. "Birds of a/nfeather ..."/n/n"Moody was a great wizard in his time," said Bill./n/n"He's an old friend of Dumbledore's, isn't he?" said/nCharlie./n/n"Dumbledore's not what you'd call normal, though, is/nhe?" said Fred. "I mean, I know he's a genius and/neverything ..."/n/n"Who is Mad-Eye?" asked Harry./n/n"He's retired, used to work at the Ministry," said/nCharlie. "I met him once when Dad took me into work/nwith him. He was an Auror — one of the best ... a/nDark wizard catcher," he added, seeing Harry's blank/nlook. "Half the cells in Azkaban are full because of/nhim. He made himself loads of enemies, though ... the/nfamilies of people he caught, mainly . . . and I heard/nhe's been getting really paranoid in his old age./nDoesn't trust anyone anymore. Sees Dark wizards/neverywhere."/n/nBill and Charlie decided to come and see everyone off/nat King's Cross station, but Percy, apologizing most/nprofusely, said that he really needed to get to work./n/n"I just can't justify taking more time off at the/nmoment," he told them. "Mr. Crouch is really starting/nto rely on me."/n/n"Yeah, you know what, Percy?" said George seriously./n"I reckon he'll know your name soon."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley had braved the telephone in the village/npost office to order three ordinary Muggle taxis to take/nthem into London./n/n/n/n"Arthur tried to borrow Ministry cars for us," Mrs./nWeasley whispered to Harry as they stood in the rain-/nwashed yard, watching the taxi drivers heaving six/nheavy Hogwarts trunks into their cars. "But there/nweren't any to spare. ... Oh dear, they don't look/nhappy, do they?"/n/nHarry didn't like to tell Mrs. Weasley that Muggle taxi/ndrivers rarely transported overexcited owls, and/nPigwidgeon was making an earsplitting racket. Nor/ndid it help that a number of Filibuster's Fabulous/nWet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks went off unexpectedly/nwhen Fred's trunk sprang open, causing the driver/ncarrying it to yell with fright and pain as Crookshanks/nclawed his way up the man's leg./n/nThe journey was uncomfortable, owing to the fact that/nthey were jammed in the back of the taxis with their/ntrunks. Crookshanks took quite a while to recover/nfrom the fireworks, and by the time they entered/nLondon, Harry, Ron, and Hermione were all severely/nscratched. They were very relieved to get out at King's/nCross, even though the rain was coming down harder/nthan ever, and they got soaked carrying their trunks/nacross the busy road and into the station./n/nHarry was used to getting onto platform nine and/nthree-quarters by now. It was a simple matter of/nwalking straight through the apparently solid barrier/ndividing platforms nine and ten. The only tricky part/nwas doing this in an unobtrusive way, so as to avoid/nattracting Muggle attention. They did it in groups/ntoday; Harry, Ron, and Hermione (the most/nconspicuous, since they were accompanied by/nPigwidgeon and Crookshanks) went first; they leaned/n/n/n/n/ncasually against the barrier, chatting unconcernedly,/nand slid sideways through it ... and as they did so,/nplatform nine and three-quarters materialized in front/nof them./n/nThe Hogwarts Express, a gleaming scarlet steam/nengine, was already there, clouds of steam billowing/nfrom it, through which the many Hogwarts students/nand parents on the platform appeared like dark/nghosts. Pigwidgeon became noisier than ever in/nresponse to the hooting of many owls through the/nmist. Harry, Ron, and Hermione set off to find seats,/nand were soon stowing their luggage in a/ncompartment halfway along the train. They then/nhopped back down onto the platform to say good-bye/nto Mrs. Weasley, Bill, and Charlie./n/n"I might be seeing you all sooner than you think,"/nsaid Charlie, grinning, as he hugged Ginny good-bye./n/n"Why?" said Fred keenly./n/n"You'll see," said Charlie. "Just don't tell Percy I/nmentioned it ... it's 'classified information, until such/ntime as the Ministry sees fit to release it,' after all."/n/n"Yeah, I sort of wish I were back at Hogwarts this/nyear," said Bill, hands in his pockets, looking almost/nwistfully at the train./n/n"Why?" said George impatiently./n/n"You're going to have an interesting year," said Bill,/nhis eyes twinkling. "I might even get time off to come/nand watch a bit of it. ..."/n/n"A bit of what?" said Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut at that moment, the whistle blew, and Mrs./nWeasley chivvied them toward the train doors./n/n"Thanks for having us to stay, Mrs. Weasley," said/nHermione as they climbed on board, closed the door,/nand leaned out of the window to talk to her./n/n"Yeah, thanks for everything, Mrs. Weasley," said/nHarry./n/n"Oh it was my pleasure, dears," said Mrs. Weasley./n"Td invite you for Christmas, but ... well, I expect/nyou're all going to want to stay at Hogwarts, what/nwith ... one thing and another."/n/n"Mum!" said Ron irritably. "What d'you three know/nthat we don't?"/n/n"You'll find out this evening, I expect," said Mrs./nWeasley, smiling. "It's going to be very exciting —/nmind you, I'm very glad they've changed the rules — "/n/n"What rules?" said Harry, Ron, Fred, and George/ntogether./n/n"I'm sure Professor Dumbledore will tell you. ... Now,/nbehave, won't you? Won't you, Fred? And you,/nGeorge?"/n/nThe pistons hissed loudly and the train began to/nmove./n/n"Tell us what's happening at Hogwarts!" Fred/nbellowed out of the window as Mrs. Weasley, Bill, and/nCharlie sped away from them. "What rules are they/nchanging?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Mrs. Weasley only smiled and waved. Before the/ntrain had rounded the corner, she, Bill, and Charlie/nhad Disapparated./n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione went back to their/ncompartment. The thick rain splattering the windows/nmade it very difficult to see out of them. Ron undid/nhis trunk, pulled out his maroon dress robes, and/nflung them over Pigwidgeon's cage to muffle his/nhooting./n/n"Bagman wanted to tell us what's happening at/nHogwarts," he said grumpily, sitting down next to/nHarry. "At the World Cup, remember? But my own/nmother won't say. Wonder what — "/n/n"Shh!" Hermione whispered suddenly, pressing her/nfinger to her lips and pointing toward the/ncompartment next to theirs. Harry and Ron listened,/nand heard a familiar drawling voice drifting in/nthrough the open door./n/n"... Father actually considered sending me to/nDurmstrang rather than Hogwarts, you know. He/nknows the headmaster, you see. Well, you know his/nopinion of Dumbledore — the man's such a/nMudblood-lover — and Durmstrang doesn't admit/nthat sort of riffraff. But Mother didn't like the idea of/nme going to school so far away. Father says/nDurmstrang takes a far more sensible line than/nHogwarts about the Dark Arts. Durmstrang students/nactually learn them, not just the defense rubbish we/ndo. ..."/n/nHermione got up, tiptoed to the compartment door,/nand slid it shut, blocking out Malfoy's voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So he thinks Durmstrang would have suited him,/ndoes he?" she said angrily. "I wish he had gone, then/nwe wouldn't have to put up with him."/n/n"Durmstrang's another wizarding school?" said Harry./n/n"Yes," said Hermione sniffily, "and it's got a horrible/nreputation. According to An Appraisal of Magical/nEducation in Europe, it puts a lot of emphasis on the/nDark Arts."/n/n"I think I've heard of it," said Ron vaguely. "Where is/nit? What country?"/n/n"Well, nobody knows, do they?" said Hermione,/nraising her eyebrows./n/n"Er — why not?" said Harry./n/n"There's traditionally been a lot of rivalry between all/nthe magic schools. Durmstrang and Beauxbatons like/nto conceal their whereabouts so nobody can steal/ntheir secrets," said Hermione matter-of-factly./n/n"Come off it," said Ron, starting to laugh./n"Durmstrang's got to be about the same size as/nHogwarts — how are you going to hide a great big/ncastle?"/n/n"But Hogwarts is hidden," said Hermione, in surprise./n"Everyone knows that ... well, everyone who's read/nHogwarts, A History, anyway."/n/n"Just you, then," said Ron. "So go on — how d'you/nhide a place like Hogwarts?"/n/n"It's bewitched," said Hermione. "If a Muggle looks at/nit, all they see is a moldering old ruin with a sign over/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe entrance saying DANGER, DO NOT ENTER,/nUNSAFE."/n/n"So Durmstrangll just look like a min to an outsider/ntoo?"/n/n"Maybe," said Hermione, shrugging, "or it might have/nMuggle-repelling charms on it, like the World Cup/nstadium. And to keep foreign wizards from finding it,/nthey'll have made it Unplottable — "/n/n"Come again?"/n/n"Well, you can enchant a building so it's impossible to/nplot on a map, can't you?"/n/n"Er ... if you say so," said Harry./n/n"But I think Durmstrang must be somewhere in the/nfar north," said Hermione thoughtfully. "Somewhere/nvery cold, because they've got fur capes as part of/ntheir uniforms."/n/n"Ah, think of the possibilities," said Ron dreamily. "It/nwould've been so easy to push Malfoy off a glacier and/nmake it look like an accident. ... Shame his mother/nlikes him. ..."/n/nThe rain became heavier and heavier as the train/nmoved farther north. The sky was so dark and the/nwindows so steamy that the lanterns were lit by/nmidday. The lunch trolley came rattling along the/ncorridor, and Harry bought a large stack of Cauldron/nCakes for them to share./n/nSeveral of their friends looked in on them as the/nafternoon progressed, including Seamus Finnigan,/nDean Thomas, and Neville Longbottom, a round-/nfaced, extremely forgetful boy who had been brought/n/n/n/n/n/nup by his formidable witch of a grandmother. Seamus/nwas still wearing his Ireland rosette. Some of its/nmagic seemed to be wearing off now; it was still/nsqueaking " Troy — Mullet — Moran\" but in a very/nfeeble and exhausted sort of way. After half an hour/nor so, Hermione, growing tired of the endless/nQuidditch talk, buried herself once more in The/nStandard Book of Spells, Grade 4, and started trying/nto learn a Summoning Charm./n/nNeville listened jealously to the others' conversation/nas they relived the Cup match./n/n"Gran didn't want to go," he said miserably. "Wouldn't/nbuy tickets. It sounded amazing though."/n/n"It was," said Ron. "Look at this, Neville. ..."/n/nHe rummaged in his trunk up in the luggage rack and/npulled out the miniature figure of Viktor Krum./n/n"Oh wow," said Neville enviously as Ron tipped Krum/nonto his pudgy hand./n/n"We saw him right up close, as well," said Ron. "We/nwere in the Top Box — "/n/n"For the first and last time in your life, Weasley."/n/nDraco Malfoy had appeared in the doorway. Behind/nhim stood Crabbe and Goyle, his enormous, thuggish/ncronies, both of whom appeared to have grown at/nleast a foot during the summer. Evidently they had/noverheard the conversation through the compartment/ndoor, which Dean and Seamus had left ajar./n/n"Don't remember asking you to join us, Malfoy," said/nHarry coolly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Weasley ... what is that?" said Malfoy, pointing at/nPigwidgeon's cage. A sleeve of Ron's dress robes was/ndangling from it, swaying with the motion of the train,/nthe moldy lace cuff very obvious./n/nRon made to stuff the robes out of sight, but Malfoy/nwas too quick for him; he seized the sleeve and/npulled./n/n"Look at this!" said Malfoy in ecstasy, holding up/nRon's robes and showing Crabbe and Goyle, "Weasley,/nyou weren't thinking of wearing these, were you? I/nmean — they were very fashionable in about eighteen/nninety. ..."/n/n"Eat dung, Malfoy!" said Ron, the same color as the/ndress robes as he snatched them back out of Malfoy's/ngrip. Malfoy howled with derisive laughter; Crabbe/nand Goyle guffawed stupidly./n/n"So ... going to enter, Weasley? Going to try and bring/na bit of glory to the family name? There's money/ninvolved as well, you know ... you'd be able to afford/nsome decent robes if you won. ..."/n/n"What are you talking about?" snapped Ron./n/n" Are you going to enter?" Malfoy repeated. "I suppose/nyou will, Potter? You never miss a chance to show off,/ndo you?"/n/n"Either explain what you're on about or go away,/nMalfoy," said Hermione testily, over the top of The/nStandard Book of Spells, Grade 4./n/nA gleeful smile spread across Malfoy's pale face./n/n"Don't tell me you don't know?" he said delightedly./n"You've got a father and brother at the Ministry and/n/n/n/n/n/nyou don't even know ? My God, my father told me/nabout it ages ago ... heard it from Cornelius Fudge./nBut then, Father's always associated with the top/npeople at the Ministry. . . . Maybe your father's too/njunior to know about it, Weasley ... yes ... they/nprobably don't talk about important stuff in front of/nhim. ..."/n/nLaughing once more, Malfoy beckoned to Crabbe and/nGoyle, and the three of them disappeared./n/nRon got to his feet and slammed the sliding/ncompartment door so hard behind them that the glass/nshattered./n/n"Ronl" said Hermione reproachfully, and she pulled/nout her wand, muttered " ReparoV ' and the glass/nshards flew back into a single pane and back into the/ndoor./n/n"Well ... making it look like he knows everything and/nwe don't. ..." Ron snarled. " 'Father's always/nassociated with the top people at the Ministry.'... Dad/ncould've got a promotion any time ... he just likes it/nwhere he is. ..."/n/n"Of course he does," said Hermione quietly. "Don't let/nMalfoy get to you, Ron — "/n/n"Him! Get to me!? As if!" said Ron, picking up one of/nthe remaining Cauldron Cakes and squashing it into/na pulp./n/nRon's bad mood continued for the rest of the journey./nHe didn't talk much as they changed into their school/nrobes, and was still glowering when the Hogwarts/nExpress slowed down at last and finally stopped in/nthe pitch-darkness of Hogsmeade station./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAs the train doors opened, there was a rumble of/nthunder overhead. Hermione bundled up/nCrookshanks in her cloak and Ron left his dress/nrobes over Pigwidgeon as they left the train, heads/nbent and eyes narrowed against the downpour. The/nrain was now coming down so thick and fast that it/nwas as though buckets of ice-cold water were being/nemptied repeatedly over their heads./n/n"Hi, Hagrid!" Harry yelled, seeing a gigantic silhouette/nat the far end of the platform./n/n"All righ', Harry?" Hagrid bellowed back, waving. "See/nyeh at the feast if we don' drown!"/n/nFirst years traditionally reached Hogwarts Castle by/nsailing across the lake with Hagrid./n/n"Oooh, I wouldn't fancy crossing the lake in this/nweather," said Hermione fervently, shivering as they/ninched slowly along the dark platform with the rest of/nthe crowd. A hundred horseless carriages stood/nwaiting for them outside the station. Harry, Ron,/nHermione, and Neville climbed gratefully into one of/nthem, the door shut with a snap, and a few moments/nlater, with a great lurch, the long procession of/ncarriages was rumbling and splashing its way up the/ntrack toward Hogwarts Castle./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Triwizard Tournament
text: /nThrough the gates, flanked with statues of winged/nboars, and up the sweeping drive the carriages/ntrundled, swaying dangerously in what was fast/nbecoming a gale. Leaning against the window, Harry/ncould see Hogwarts coming nearer, its many lighted/nwindows blurred and shimmering behind the thick/ncurtain of rain. Lightning flashed across the sky as/ntheir carriage came to a halt before the great oak front/ndoors, which stood at the top of a flight of stone steps./nPeople who had occupied the carriages in front were/nalready hurrying up the stone steps into the castle./nHarry, Ron, Hermione, and Neville jumped down from/ntheir carriage and dashed up the steps too, looking up/nonly when they were safely inside the cavernous,/ntorch-lit entrance hall, with its magnificent marble/nstaircase./n/n"Blimey," said Ron, shaking his head and sending/nwater everywhere, "if that keeps up the lake's going to/noverflow. I'm soak — ARRGH!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA large, red, water-filled balloon had dropped from/nout of the ceiling onto Ron's head and exploded./nDrenched and sputtering, Ron staggered sideways/ninto Harry, just as a second water bomb dropped —/nnarrowly missing Hermione, it burst at Harry's feet,/nsending a wave of cold water over his sneakers into/nhis socks. People all around them shrieked and/nstarted pushing one another in their efforts to get out/nof the line of fire. Harry looked up and saw, floating/ntwenty feet above them, Peeves the Poltergeist, a little/nman in a bell-covered hat and orange bow tie, his/nwide, malicious face contorted with concentration as/nhe took aim again./n/n"PEEVES!" yelled an angry voice. "Peeves, come down/nhere at ONCE!"/n/nProfessor McGonagall, Deputy Headmistress and/nhead of Gryffindor House, had come dashing out of/nthe Great Hall; she skidded on the wet floor and/ngrabbed Hermione around the neck to stop herself/nfrom falling./n/n"Ouch — sorry, Miss Granger — "/n/n"That's all right, Professor!" Hermione gasped,/nmassaging her throat./n/n"Peeves, get down here NOW!" barked Professor/nMcGonagall, straightening her pointed hat and/nglaring upward through her square-rimmed/nspectacles./n/n"Not doing nothing!" cackled Peeves, lobbing a water/nbomb at several fifth-year girls, who screamed and/ndived into the Great Hall. "Already wet, aren't they?/nLittle squirts! Wheeeeeeeeee!" And he aimed another/nbomb at a group of second years who had just/narrived./n/n/n/n/n/n"I shall call the headmaster!" shouted Professor/nMcGonagall. "I'm warning you, Peeves — "/n/nPeeves stuck out his tongue, threw the last of his/nwater bombs into the air, and zoomed off up the/nmarble staircase, cackling insanely./n/n"Well, move along, then!" said Professor McGonagall/nsharply to the bedraggled crowd. "Into the Great Hall,/ncome on!"/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione slipped and slid across the/nentrance hall and through the double doors on the/nright, Ron muttering furiously under his breath as he/npushed his sopping hair off his face./n/nThe Great Hall looked its usual splendid self,/ndecorated for the start-of-term feast. Golden plates/nand goblets gleamed by the light of hundreds and/nhundreds of candles, floating over the tables in/nmidair. The four long House tables were packed with/nchattering students; at the top of the Hall, the staff/nsat along one side of a fifth table, facing their pupils./n/nIt was much warmer in here. Harry, Ron, and/nHermione walked past the Slytherins, the/nRavenclaws, and the Hufflepuffs, and sat down with/nthe rest of the Gryffindors at the far side of the Hall,/nnext to Nearly Headless Nick, the Gryffindor ghost./nPearly white and semitransparent, Nick was dressed/ntonight in his usual doublet, but with a particularly/nlarge ruff, which served the dual purpose of looking/nextra-festive, and insuring that his head didn't wobble/ntoo much on his partially severed neck./n/n"Good evening," he said, beaming at them./n/n"Says who?" said Harry, taking off his sneakers and/nemptying them of water. "Hope they hurry up with the/nSorting. I'm starving."/n/n/n/n/n/nThe Sorting of the new students into Houses took/nplace at the start of every school year, but by an/nunlucky combination of circumstances, Harry hadn't/nbeen present at one since his own. He was quite/nlooking forward to it. Just then, a highly excited,/nbreathless voice called down the table./n/n"Hiya, Harry!"/n/nIt was Colin Creevey, a third year to whom Harry was/nsomething of a hero./n/n"Hi, Colin," said Harry warily./n/n"Harry, guess what? Guess what, Harry? My brother's/nstarting! My brother Dennis!"/n/n"Er — good," said Harry./n/n"He's really excited!" said Colin, practically bouncing/nup and down in his seat. "I just hope he's in/nGryffindor! Keep your fingers crossed, eh, Harry?"/n/n"Er — yeah, all right," said Harry. He turned back to/nHermione, Ron, and Nearly Headless Nick. "Brothers/nand sisters usually go in the same Houses, don't/nthey?" he said. He was judging by the Weasleys, all/nseven of whom had been put into Gryffindor./n/n"Oh no, not necessarily," said Hermione. "Parvati/nPatil's twin's in Ravenclaw, and they're identical./nYou'd think they'd be together, wouldn't you?"/n/nHarry looked up at the staff table. There seemed to be/nrather more empty seats there than usual. Hagrid, of/ncourse, was still fighting his way across the lake with/nthe first years; Professor McGonagall was presumably/nsupervising the drying of the entrance hall floor, but/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthere was another empty chair too, and Harry/ncouldn't think who else was missing./n/n"Where's the new Defense Against the Dark Arts/nteacher?" said Hermione, who was also looking up at/nthe teachers./n/nThey had never yet had a Defense Against the Dark/nArts teacher who had lasted more than three terms./nHarry's favorite by far had been Professor Lupin, who/nhad resigned last year. He looked up and down the/nstaff table. There was definitely no new face there./n/n"Maybe they couldn't get anyone!" said Hermione,/nlooking anxious./n/nHarry scanned the table more carefully. Tiny little/nProfessor Flitwick, the Charms teacher, was sitting on/na large pile of cushions beside Professor Sprout, the/nHerbology teacher, whose hat was askew over her/nflyaway gray hair. She was talking to Professor/nSinistra of the Astronomy department. On Professor/nSinistra 's other side was the sallow-faced, hook-/nnosed, greasy-haired Potions master, Snape —/n/nHarry's least favorite person at Hogwarts. Harry's/nloathing of Snape was matched only by Snape 's/nhatred of him, a hatred which had, if possible,/nintensified last year, when Harry had helped Sirius/nescape right under Snape 's overlarge nose — Snape/nand Sirius had been enemies since their own school/ndays./n/nOn Snape 's other side was an empty seat, which/nHarry guessed was Professor McGonagall's. Next to it,/nand in the very center of the table, sat Professor/nDumbledore, the headmaster, his sweeping silver hair/nand beard shining in the candlelight, his magnificent/ndeep green robes embroidered with many stars and/nmoons. The tips of Dumbledore 's long, thin fingers/n/n/n/n/nwere together and he was resting his chin upon them,/nstaring up at the ceiling through his half-moon/nspectacles as though lost in thought. Harry glanced/nup at the ceiling too. It was enchanted to look like the/nsky outside, and he had never seen it look this/nstormy. Black and purple clouds were swirling across/nit, and as another thunderclap sounded outside, a/nfork of lightning flashed across it./n/n"Oh hurry up," Ron moaned, beside Harry, "I could/neat a hippogriff."/n/nThe words were no sooner out of his mouth than the/ndoors of the Great Hall opened and silence fell./nProfessor McGonagall was leading a long line of first/nyears up to the top of the Hall. If Harry, Ron, and/nHermione were wet, it was nothing to how these first/nyears looked. They appeared to have swum across the/nlake rather than sailed. All of them were shivering/nwith a combination of cold and nerves as they filed/nalong the staff table and came to a halt in a line/nfacing the rest of the school — all of them except the/nsmallest of the lot, a boy with mousy hair, who was/nwrapped in what Harry recognized as Hagrid's/nmoleskin overcoat. The coat was so big for him that it/nlooked as though he were draped in a furry black/ncircus tent. His small face protruded from over the/ncollar, looking almost painfully excited. When he had/nlined up with his terrified-looking peers, he caught/nColin Creevey's eye, gave a double thumbs-up, and/nmouthed, I fell in the lake\ He looked positively/ndelighted about it./n/nProfessor McGonagall now placed a three-legged stool/non the ground before the first years and, on top of it,/nan extremely old, dirty, patched wizard's hat. The first/nyears stared at it. So did everyone else. For a/nmoment, there was silence. Then a long tear near the/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbrim opened wide like a mouth, and the hat broke/ninto song:/n/nA thousand years or more ago,/n/nWhen I was newly sewn,/n/nThere lived four wizards of renown,/n/nWhose names are still well known:/n/nBold Gryffindor, from wild moor,/n/nFair Ravenclaw, from glen,/n/nSweet Hufflepuff, from valley broad,/n/nShrewd Slytherin, from fen./n/nThey shared a wish, a hope, a dream,/n/nThey hatched a daring plan/nTo educate young sorcerers/nThus Hogwarts School began./n/nNow each of these four founders/nFormed their own house, for each/nDid value different virtues/nIn the ones they had to teach./n/nBy Gryffindor, the bravest were/nPrized far beyond the rest;/n/nFor Ravenclaw, the cleverest/nWould always be the best;/n/nFor Hufflepuff, hard workers were/nMost worthy of admission;/n/nAnd power-hungry Slytherin/nLoved those of great ambition./n/nWhile still alive they did divide/nTheir favorites from the throng,/n/nYet how to pick the worthy ones/nWhen they were dead and gone?/n/nTwas Gryffindor who found the way,/n/nHe whipped me off his head/n/nThe founders put some brains in me/n/nSo I could choose instead!/n/nNow slip me snug about your ears,/n/nI've never yet been wrong,/n/n111 have a look inside your mind/nAnd tell where you belong!/n/n/n/n/n/nThe Great Hall rang with applause as the Sorting Hat/nfinished./n/n/n/n"That's not the song it sang when it Sorted us," said/nHarry, clapping along with everyone else./n/n"Sings a different one every year," said Ron. "It's got/nto be a pretty boring life, hasn't it, being a hat? I/nsuppose it spends all year making up the next one."/n/nProfessor McGonagall was now unrolling a large scroll/nof parchment./n/n"When I call out your name, you will put on the hat/nand sit on the stool," she told the first years. "When/nthe hat announces your House, you will go and sit at/nthe appropriate table./n/n"Ackerley, Stewart!"/n/nA boy walked forward, visibly trembling from head to/nfoot, picked up the Sorting Hat, put it on, and sat/ndown on the stool./n/n"RAVENCLAW!" shouted the hat./n/nStewart Ackerley took off the hat and hurried into a/nseat at the Ravenclaw table, where everyone was/napplauding him. Harry caught a glimpse of Cho, the/nRavenclaw Seeker, cheering Stewart Ackerley as he/nsat down. For a fleeting second, Harry had a strange/ndesire to join the Ravenclaw table too./n/n"Baddock, Malcolm!"/n/n"SLYTHERIN!"/n/nThe table on the other side of the hall erupted with/ncheers; Harry could see Malfoy clapping as Baddock/n/n/n/n/n/njoined the Slytherins. Harry wondered whether/nBaddock knew that Slytherin House had turned out/nmore Dark witches and wizards than any other. Fred/nand George hissed Malcolm Baddock as he sat down./n/n"Branstone, Eleanor!"/n/n"HUFFLEPUFF!"/n/n"Cauldwell, Owen!"/n/n"HUFFLEPUFF!"/n/n"Creevey, Dennis!"/n/nTiny Dennis Creevey staggered forward, tripping over/nHagrid 's moleskin, just as Hagrid himself sidled into/nthe Hall through a door behind the teachers' table./nAbout twice as tall as a normal man, and at least/nthree times as broad, Hagrid, with his long, wild,/ntangled black hair and beard, looked slightly alarming/n— a misleading impression, for Harry, Ron, and/nHermione knew Hagrid to possess a very kind nature./nHe winked at them as he sat down at the end of the/nstaff table and watched Dennis Creevey putting on/nthe Sorting Hat. The rip at the brim opened wide —/n/n"GRYFFINDOR!" the hat shouted./n/nHagrid clapped along with the Gryffindors as Dennis/nCreevey, beaming widely, took off the hat, placed it/nback on the stool, and hurried over to join his/nbrother./n/n"Colin, I fell in!" he said shrilly, throwing himself into/nan empty seat. "It was brilliant! And something in the/nwater grabbed me and pushed me back in the boat!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Cool!" said Colin, just as excitedly. "It was probably/nthe giant squid, Dennis!"/n/n"Wow\" said Dennis, as though nobody in their/nwildest dreams could hope for more than being/nthrown into a storm-tossed, fathoms-deep lake, and/npushed out of it again by a giant sea monster./n/n"Dennis! Dennis! See that boy down there? The one/nwith the black hair and glasses? See him? Know who/nhe is, Dennis ?"/n/nHarry looked away, staring very hard at the Sorting/nHat, now Sorting Emma Dobbs./n/nThe Sorting continued; boys and girls with varying/ndegrees of fright on their faces moving one by one to/nthe three-legged stool, the line dwindling slowly as/nProfessor McGonagall passed the L's./n/n"Oh hurry up," Ron moaned, massaging his stomach./n/n"Now, Ron, the Sorting's much more important than/nfood," said Nearly Headless Nick as "Madley, Laura!"/nbecame a Hufflepuff./n/n" 'Course it is, if you're dead," snapped Ron./n/n"I do hope this year's batch of Gryffindors are up to/nscratch," said Nearly Headless Nick, applauding as/n"McDonald, Natalie!" joined the Gryffindor table. "We/ndon't want to break our winning streak, do we?"/n/nGryffindor had won the Inter-House Championship/nfor the last three years in a row./n/n"Pritchard, Graham!"/n/n"SLYTHERIN!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Quirke, Orla!"/n/n/n/n"RAVENCLAW!"/n/nAnd finally, with "Whitby, Kevin!" ("HUFFLEPUFF!"),/nthe Sorting ended. Professor McGonagall picked up/nthe hat and the stool and carried them away./n/n"About time," said Ron, seizing his knife and fork and/nlooking expectantly at his golden plate./n/nProfessor Dumbledore had gotten to his feet. He was/nsmiling around at the students, his arms opened wide/nin welcome./n/n"I have only two words to say to you," he told them,/nhis deep voice echoing around the Hall. " Tuck in."/n/n"Hear, hear!" said Harry and Ron loudly as the empty/ndishes filled magically before their eyes./n/nNearly Headless Nick watched mournfully as Harry,/nRon, and Hermione loaded their own plates./n/n"Aaah, 'at's be'er," said Ron, with his mouth full of/nmashed potato./n/n"You're lucky there's a feast at all tonight, you know,"/nsaid Nearly Headless Nick. "There was trouble in the/nkitchens earlier."/n/n"Why? Wha' 'appened?" said Harry, through a sizable/nchunk of steak./n/n"Peeves, of course," said Nearly Headless Nick,/nshaking his head, which wobbled dangerously. He/npulled his ruff a little higher up on his neck. "The/nusual argument, you know. He wanted to attend the/nfeast — well, it's quite out of the question, you know/n/n/n/n/nwhat he's like, utterly uncivilized, can't see a plate of/nfood without throwing it. We held a ghost's council —/nthe Fat Friar was all for giving him the chance — but/nmost wisely, in my opinion, the Bloody Baron put his/nfoot down."/n/nThe Bloody Baron was the Slytherin ghost, a gaunt/nand silent specter covered in silver bloodstains. He/nwas the only person at Hogwarts who could really/ncontrol Peeves./n/n"Yeah, we thought Peeves seemed hacked off about/nsomething," said Ron darkly. "So what did he do in/nthe kitchens?"/n/n"Oh the usual," said Nearly Headless Nick, shrugging./n"Wreaked havoc and mayhem. Pots and pans/neverywhere. Place swimming in soup. Terrified the/nhouse-elves out of their wits — "/n/nClang./n/nHermione had knocked over her golden goblet./nPumpkin juice spread steadily over the tablecloth,/nstaining several feet of white linen orange, but/nHermione paid no attention./n/n"There are house-elves here?" she said, staring,/nhorror-struck, at Nearly Headless Nick. "Here at/nHogwarts ?"/n/n"Certainly," said Nearly Headless Nick, looking/nsurprised at her reaction. "The largest number in any/ndwelling in Britain, I believe. Over a hundred."/n/n"I've never seen one!" said Hermione./n/n"Well, they hardly ever leave the kitchen by day, do/nthey?" said Nearly Headless Nick. "They come out at/n/n/n/n/n/nnight to do a bit of cleaning . . . see to the fires and so/non. ... I mean, you're not supposed to see them, are/nyou? That's the mark of a good house-elf, isn't it, that/nyou don't know it's there?"/n/nHermione stared at him./n/n"But they get paid?" she said. "They get holidays,/ndon't they? And — and sick leave, and pensions, and/neverything?"/n/nNearly Headless Nick chortled so much that his ruff/nslipped and his head flopped off, dangling on the inch/nor so of ghostly skin and muscle that still attached it/nto his neck./n/n"Sick leave and pensions?" he said, pushing his head/nback onto his shoulders and securing it once more/nwith his ruff. "House-elves don't want sick leave and/npensions!"/n/nHermione looked down at her hardly touched plate of/nfood, then put her knife and fork down upon it and/npushed it away from her./n/n"Oh c'mon, 'Er-my-knee," said Ron, accidentally/nspraying Harry with bits of Yorkshire pudding. "Oops/n— sorry, 'Arry — " He swallowed. "You won't get them/nsick leave by starving yourself!"/n/n"Slave labor," said Hermione, breathing hard through/nher nose. "That's what made this dinner. Slave labor."/n/nAnd she refused to eat another bite./n/nThe rain was still drumming heavily against the high,/ndark glass. Another clap of thunder shook the/nwindows, and the stormy ceiling flashed, illuminating/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe golden plates as the remains of the first course/nvanished and were replaced, instantly, with puddings./n/n"Treacle tart, Hermione!" said Ron, deliberately/nwafting its smell toward her. "Spotted dick, look!/nChocolate gateau!"/n/nBut Hermione gave him a look so reminiscent of/nProfessor McGonagall that he gave up./n/nWhen the puddings too had been demolished, and the/nlast crumbs had faded off the plates, leaving them/nsparkling clean, Albus Dumbledore got to his feet/nagain. The buzz of chatter filling the Hall ceased/nalmost at once, so that only the howling wind and/npounding rain could be heard./n/n"So!" said Dumbledore, smiling around at them all./n"Now that we are all fed and watered," ("Hmph!" said/nHermione) "I must once more ask for your attention,/nwhile I give out a few notices./n/n"Mr. Filch, the caretaker, has asked me to tell you/nthat the list of objects forbidden inside the castle has/nthis year been extended to include Screaming Yo-yos,/nFanged Frisbees, and Ever-Bashing Boomerangs. The/nfull list comprises some four hundred and thirty-/nseven items, I believe, and can be viewed in Mr./n/nFilch 's office, if anybody would like to check it."/n/nThe corners of Dumbledore 's mouth twitched. He/ncontinued, "As ever, I would like to remind you all/nthat the forest on the grounds is out-of-bounds to/nstudents, as is the village of Hogsmeade to all below/nthird year./n/n"It is also my painful duty to inform you that the/nInter-House Quidditch Cup will not take place this/nyear."/n/n/n/n/n/n"What?" Harry gasped. He looked around at Fred and/nGeorge, his fellow members of the Quidditch team./nThey were mouthing soundlessly at Dumbledore,/napparently too appalled to speak. Dumbledore went/non, "This is due to an event that will be starting in/nOctober, and continuing throughout the school year,/ntaking up much of the teachers' time and energy —/nbut I am sure you will all enjoy it immensely. I have/ngreat pleasure in announcing that this year at/nHogwarts — "/n/nBut at that moment, there was a deafening rumble of/nthunder and the doors of the Great Hall banged open./n/nA man stood in the doorway, leaning upon a long/nstaff, shrouded in a black traveling cloak. Every head/nin the Great Hall swiveled toward the stranger,/nsuddenly brightly illuminated by a fork of lightning/nthat flashed across the ceiling. He lowered his hood,/nshook out a long mane of grizzled, dark gray hair,/nthen began to walk up toward the teachers' table./n/nA dull clunk echoed through the Hall on his every/nother step. He reached the end of the top table,/nturned right, and limped heavily toward Dumbledore./nAnother flash of lightning crossed the ceiling./nHermione gasped./n/nThe lightning had thrown the man's face into sharp/nrelief, and it was a face unlike any Harry had ever/nseen. It looked as though it had been carved out of/nweathered wood by someone who had only the/nvaguest idea of what human faces are supposed to/nlook like, and was none too skilled with a chisel./nEvery inch of skin seemed to be scarred. The mouth/nlooked like a diagonal gash, and a large chunk of the/nnose was missing. But it was the man's eyes that/nmade him frightening./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nOne of them was small, dark, and beady. The other/nwas large, round as a coin, and a vivid, electric blue./nThe blue eye was moving ceaselessly, without/nblinking, and was rolling up, down, and from side to/nside, quite independently of the normal eye — and/nthen it rolled right over, pointing into the back of the/nman's head, so that all they could see was whiteness./n/nThe stranger reached Dumbledore. He stretched out a/nhand that was as badly scarred as his face, and/nDumbledore shook it, muttering words Harry couldn't/nhear. He seemed to be making some inquiry of the/nstranger, who shook his head unsmilingly and replied/nin an undertone. Dumbledore nodded and gestured/nthe man to the empty seat on his right-hand side./n/nThe stranger sat down, shook his mane of dark gray/nhair out of his face, pulled a plate of sausages toward/nhim, raised it to what was left of his nose, and sniffed/nit. He then took a small knife out of his pocket,/nspeared a sausage on the end of it, and began to eat./nHis normal eye was fixed upon the sausages, but the/nblue eye was still darting restlessly around in its/nsocket, taking in the Hall and the students./n/n"May I introduce our new Defense Against the Dark/nArts teacher?" said Dumbledore brightly into the/nsilence. "Professor Moody."/n/nIt was usual for new staff members to be greeted with/napplause, but none of the staff or students clapped/nexcept Dumbledore and Hagrid, who both put their/nhands together and applauded, but the sound echoed/ndismally into the silence, and they stopped fairly/nquickly. Everyone else seemed too transfixed by/nMoody's bizarre appearance to do more than stare at/nhim./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Moody?" Harry muttered to Ron. "MacL-Eye Moody?/nThe one your dad went to help this morning?"/n/n"Must be," said Ron in a low, awed voice./n/n"What happened to him?" Hermione whispered. "What/nhappened to his face?"/n/n"Dunno," Ron whispered back, watching Moody with/nfascination./n/nMoody seemed totally indifferent to his less-than-/nwarm welcome. Ignoring the jug of pumpkin juice in/nfront of him, he reached again into his traveling cloak,/npulled out a hip flask, and took a long draught from/nit. As he lifted his arm to drink, his cloak was pulled a/nfew inches from the ground, and Harry saw, below the/ntable, several inches of carved wooden leg, ending in a/nclawed foot./n/nDumbledore cleared his throat./n/n"As I was saying," he said, smiling at the sea of/nstudents before him, all of whom were still gazing/ntransfixed at Mad-Eye Moody, "we are to have the/nhonor of hosting a very exciting event over the coming/nmonths, an event that has not been held for over a/ncentury. It is my very great pleasure to inform you/nthat the Triwizard Tournament will be taking place at/nHogwarts this year."/n/n"You're JOKING!" said Fred Weasley loudly./n/nThe tension that had filled the Hall ever since Moody's/narrival suddenly broke. Nearly everyone laughed, and/nDumbledore chuckled appreciatively./n/n"I am not joking, Mr. Weasley," he said, "though now/nthat you mention it, I did hear an excellent one over/n/n/n/n/n/nthe summer about a troll, a hag, and a leprechaun/nwho all go into a bar ..."/n/nProfessor McGonagall cleared her throat loudly./n/n"Er — but maybe this is not the time ... no ..." said/nDumbledore, "where was I? Ah yes, the Triwizard/nTournament ... well, some of you will not know what/nthis tournament involves, so I hope those who do/nknow will forgive me for giving a short explanation,/nand allow their attention to wander freely./n/n"The Triwizard Tournament was first established/nsome seven hundred years ago as a friendly/ncompetition between the three largest European/nschools of wizardry: Hogwarts, Beauxbatons, and/nDurmstrang. A champion was selected to represent/neach school, and the three champions competed in/nthree magical tasks. The schools took it in turns to/nhost the tournament once every five years, and it was/ngenerally agreed to be a most excellent way of/nestablishing ties between young witches and wizards/nof different nationalities — until, that is, the death toll/nmounted so high that the tournament was/ndiscontinued."/n/n" Death toll?" Hermione whispered, looking alarmed./nBut her anxiety did not seem to be shared by the/nmajority of students in the Hall; many of them were/nwhispering excitedly to one another, and Harry/nhimself was far more interested in hearing about the/ntournament than in worrying about deaths that had/nhappened hundreds of years ago./n/n"There have been several attempts over the centuries/nto reinstate the tournament," Dumbledore continued,/n"none of which has been very successful. However,/nour own departments of International Magical/nCooperation and Magical Games and Sports have/n/n/n/n/ndecided the time is ripe for another attempt. We have/nworked hard over the summer to ensure that this/ntime, no champion will find himself or herself in/nmortal danger./n/n"The heads of Beauxbatons and Durmstrang will be/narriving with their short-listed contenders in October,/nand the selection of the three champions will take/nplace at Halloween. An impartial judge will decide/nwhich students are most worthy to compete for the/nTriwizard Cup, the glory of their school, and a/nthousand Galleons personal prize money."/n/n"I'm going for it!" Fred Weasley hissed down the table,/nhis face lit with enthusiasm at the prospect of such/nglory and riches. He was not the only person who/nseemed to be visualizing himself as the Hogwarts/nchampion. At every House table, Harry could see/npeople either gazing raptly at Dumbledore, or else/nwhispering fervently to their neighbors. But then/nDumbledore spoke again, and the Hall quieted once/nmore./n/n"Eager though I know all of you will be to bring the/nTriwizard Cup to Hogwarts," he said, "the heads of the/nparticipating schools, along with the Ministry of/nMagic, have agreed to impose an age restriction on/ncontenders this year. Only students who are of age —/nthat is to say, seventeen years or older — will be/nallowed to put forward their names for consideration./nThis" — Dumbledore raised his voice slightly, for/nseveral people had made noises of outrage at these/nwords, and the Weasley twins were suddenly looking/nfurious — "is a measure we feel is necessary, given/nthat the tournament tasks will still be difficult and/ndangerous, whatever precautions we take, and it is/nhighly unlikely that students below sixth and seventh/nyear will be able to cope with them. I will personally/nbe ensuring that no underage student hoodwinks our/n/n/n/n/nimpartial judge into making them Hogwarts/nchampion." His light blue eyes twinkled as they/nflickered over Fred's and George's mutinous faces. "I/ntherefore beg you not to waste your time submitting/nyourself if you are under seventeen./n/n"The delegations from Beauxbatons and Durmstrang/nwill be arriving in October and remaining with us for/nthe greater part of this year. I know that you will all/nextend every courtesy to our foreign guests while they/nare with us, and will give your whole-hearted support/nto the Hogwarts champion when he or she is selected./nAnd now, it is late, and I know how important it is to/nyou all to be alert and rested as you enter your/nlessons tomorrow morning. Bedtime! Chop chop!"/n/nDumbledore sat down again and turned to talk to/nMad-Eye Moody. There was a great scraping and/nbanging as all the students got to their feet and/nswarmed toward the double doors into the entrance/nhall./n/n"They can't do that!" said George Weasley, who had/nnot joined the crowd moving toward the door, but was/nstanding up and glaring at Dumbledore. "We're/nseventeen in April, why can't we have a shot?"/n/n"They're not stopping me entering," said Fred/nstubbornly, also scowling at the top table. "The/nchampions'll get to do all sorts of stuff you'd never be/nallowed to do normally. And a thousand Galleons/nprize money!"/n/n"Yeah," said Ron, a faraway look on his face. "Yeah, a/nthousand Galleons ..."/n/n"Come on," said Hermione, "we'll be the only ones left/nhere if you don't move."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry, Ron, Hermione, Fred, and George set off for/nthe entrance hall, Fred and George debating the ways/nin which Dumbledore might stop those who were/nunder seventeen from entering the tournament./n/n"Who's this impartial judge who's going to decide who/nthe champions are?" said Harry./n/n"Dunno," said Fred, "but it's them we'll have to fool. I/nreckon a couple of drops of Aging Potion might do it,/nGeorge. ..."/n/n"Dumbledore knows you're not of age, though," said/nRon./n/n"Yeah, but he's not the one who decides who the/nchampion is, is he?" said Fred shrewdly. "Sounds to/nme like once this judge knows who wants to enter,/nhe'll choose the best from each school and never mind/nhow old they are. Dumbledore 's trying to stop us/ngiving our names."/n/n"People have died, though!" said Hermione in a/nworried voice as they walked through a door/nconcealed behind a tapestry and started up another,/nnarrower staircase./n/n"Yeah," said Fred airily, "but that was years ago,/nwasn't it? Anyway, where's the fun without a bit of/nrisk? Hey, Ron, what if we find out how to get 'round/nDumbledore? Fancy entering?"/n/n"What d'you reckon?" Ron asked Harry. "Be cool to/nenter, wouldn't it? But I s'pose they might want/nsomeone older. ... Dunno if we've learned enough. ..."/n/n"I definitely haven't," came Neville's gloomy voice from/nbehind Fred and George./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I expect my gran'd want me to try, though. She's/nalways going on about how I should be upholding the/nfamily honor. I'll just have to — oops. ..."/n/nNeville's foot had sunk right through a step halfway/nup the staircase. There were many of these trick/nstairs at Hogwarts; it was second nature to most of/nthe older students to jump this particular step, but/nNeville's memory was notoriously poor. Harry and/nRon seized him under the armpits and pulled him/nout, while a suit of armor at the top of the stairs/ncreaked and clanked, laughing wheezily./n/n"Shut it, you," said Ron, banging down its visor as/nthey passed./n/nThey made their way up to the entrance to Gryffindor/nTower, which was concealed behind a large portrait of/na fat lady in a pink silk dress./n/n"Password?" she said as they approached./n/n"Balderdash," said George, "a prefect downstairs told/nme."/n/nThe portrait swung forward to reveal a hole in the wall/nthrough which they all climbed. A crackling fire/nwarmed the circular common room, which was full of/nsquashy armchairs and tables. Hermione cast the/nmerrily dancing flames a dark look, and Harry/ndistinctly heard her mutter " Slave labor," before/nbidding them good night and disappearing through/nthe doorway to the girls' dormitory./n/nHarry, Ron, and Neville climbed up the last, spiral/nstaircase until they reached their own dormitory,/nwhich was situated at the top of the tower. Five four-/nposter beds with deep crimson hangings stood against/nthe walls, each with its owner's trunk at the foot./n/n/n/n/n/nDean and Seamus were already getting into bed;/nSeamus had pinned his Ireland rosette to his/nheadboard, and Dean had tacked up a poster of/nViktor Krum over his bedside table. His old poster of/nthe West Ham football team was pinned right next to/nit./n/n"Mental," Ron sighed, shaking his head at the/ncompletely stationary soccer players./n/nHarry, Ron, and Neville got into their pajamas and/ninto bed. Someone — a house-elf, no doubt — had/nplaced warming pans between the sheets. It was/nextremely comfortable, lying there in bed and/nlistening to the storm raging outside./n/n"I might go in for it, you know," Ron said sleepily/nthrough the darkness, "if Fred and George find out/nhow to ... the tournament ... you never know, do/nyou?"/n/n"S'pose not. ..."/n/nHarry rolled over in bed, a series of dazzling new/npictures forming in his mind's eye. ... He had/nhoodwinked the impartial judge into believing he was/nseventeen ... he had become Hogwarts champion .../nhe was standing on the grounds, his arms raised in/ntriumph in front of the whole school, all of whom were/napplauding and screaming ... he had just won the/nTriwizard Tournament. ... Cho's face stood out/nparticularly clearly in the blurred crowd, her face/nglowing with admiration. .../n/nHarry grinned into his pillow, exceptionally glad that/nRon couldn't see what he could./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Mad-Eye Moody
text: /nThe storm had blown itself out by the following/nmorning, though the ceiling in the Great Hall was still/ngloomy; heavy clouds of pewter gray swirled overhead/nas Harry, Ron, and Hermione examined their new/ncourse schedules at breakfast. A few seats along,/n/nFred, George, and Lee Jordan were discussing/nmagical methods of aging themselves and bluffing/ntheir way into the Triwizard Tournament./n/n"Today's not bad ... outside all morning," said Ron,/nwho was running his finger down the Monday column/nof his schedule. "Herbology with the Hufflepuffs and/nCare of Magical Creatures ... damn it, we're still with/nthe Slytherins. ..."/n/n"Double Divination this afternoon," Harry groaned,/nlooking down. Divination was his least favorite/nsubject, apart from Potions. Professor Trelawney kept/npredicting Harry's death, which he found extremely/nannoying./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You should have given it up like me, shouldn't you?"/nsaid Hermione briskly, buttering herself some toast./n"Then you'd be doing something sensible like/nArithmancy."/n/n"You're eating again, I notice," said Ron, watching/nHermione adding liberal amounts of jam to her toast/ntoo./n/n"I've decided there are better ways of making a stand/nabout elf rights," said Hermione haughtily./n/n"Yeah ... and you were hungry," said Ron, grinning./n/nThere was a sudden rustling noise above them, and a/nhundred owls came soaring through the open/nwindows carrying the morning mail. Instinctively,/nHarry looked up, but there was no sign of white/namong the mass of brown and gray. The owls circled/nthe tables, looking for the people to whom their letters/nand packages were addressed. A large tawny owl/nsoared down to Neville Longbottom and deposited a/nparcel into his lap — Neville almost always forgot to/npack something. On the other side of the Hall Draco/nMalfoy's eagle owl had landed on his shoulder,/ncarrying what looked like his usual supply of sweets/nand cakes from home. Trying to ignore the sinking/nfeeling of disappointment in his stomach, Harry/nreturned to his porridge. Was it possible that/nsomething had happened to Hedwig, and that Sirius/nhadn't even got his letter?/n/nHis preoccupation lasted all the way across the/nsodden vegetable patch until they arrived in/ngreenhouse three, but here he was distracted by/nProfessor Sprout showing the class the ugliest plants/nHarry had ever seen. Indeed, they looked less like/nplants than thick, black, giant slugs, protruding/nvertically out of the soil. Each was squirming slightly/n/n/n/n/nand had a number of large, shiny swellings upon it,/nwhich appeared to be full of liquid./n/n"Bubotubers," Professor Sprout told them briskly./n"They need squeezing. You will collect the pus — "/n/n"The what?" said Seamus Finnigan, sounding/nrevolted./n/n"Pus, Finnigan, pus," said Professor Sprout, "and it's/nextremely valuable, so don't waste it. You will collect/nthe pus, I say, in these bottles. Wear your dragon-/nhide gloves; it can do funny things to the skin when/nundiluted, bubotuber pus."/n/nSqueezing the bubotubers was disgusting, but oddly/nsatisfying. As each swelling was popped, a large/namount of thick yellowish-green liquid burst forth,/nwhich smelled strongly of petrol. They caught it in the/nbottles as Professor Sprout had indicated, and by the/nend of the lesson had collected several pints./n/n"This'll keep Madam Pomfrey happy," said Professor/nSprout, stoppering the last bottle with a cork. "An/nexcellent remedy for the more stubborn forms of acne,/nbubotuber pus. Should stop students resorting to/ndesperate measures to rid themselves of pimples."/n/n"Like poor Eloise Midgen," said Hannah Abbott, a/nHufflepuff, in a hushed voice. "She tried to curse hers/noff."/n/n"Silly girl," said Professor Sprout, shaking her head./n"But Madam Pomfrey fixed her nose back on in the/nend."/n/nA booming bell echoed from the castle across the wet/ngrounds, signaling the end of the lesson, and the/nclass separated; the Hufflepuffs climbing the stone/n/n/n/n/n/nsteps for Transfiguration, and the Gryffindors heading/nin the other direction, down the sloping lawn toward/nHagrid 's small wooden cabin, which stood on the edge/nof the Forbidden Forest./n/nHagrid was standing outside his hut, one hand on the/ncollar of his enormous black boarhound, Fang. There/nwere several open wooden crates on the ground at his/nfeet, and Fang was whimpering and straining at his/ncollar, apparently keen to investigate the contents/nmore closely. As they drew nearer, an odd rattling/nnoise reached their ears, punctuated by what/nsounded like minor explosions./n/n"Mornin'!" Hagrid said, grinning at Harry, Ron, and/nHermione. "Be'er wait fer the Slytherins, they won'/nwant ter miss this — Blast-Ended Skrewts!"/n/n"Come again?" said Ron./n/nHagrid pointed down into the crates./n/n"Eurgh!" squealed Lavender Brown, jumping/nbackward./n/n"Eurgh" just about summed up the Blast-Ended/nSkrewts in Harry's opinion. They looked like/ndeformed, shell-less lobsters, horribly pale and slimy -/nlooking, with legs sticking out in very odd places and/nno visible heads. There were about a hundred of them/nin each crate, each about six inches long, crawling/nover one another, bumping blindly into the sides of/nthe boxes. They were giving off a very powerful smell/nof rotting fish. Every now and then, sparks would fly/nout of the end of a skrewt, and with a small phut, it/nwould be propelled forward several inches./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"On'y jus' hatched," said Hagrid proudly, "so yeh'll be/nable ter raise 'em yerselves! Thought we'd make a bit/nof a project of it!"/n/n"And why would we want to raise them?" said a cold/nvoice./n/nThe Slytherins had arrived. The speaker was Draco/nMalfoy. Crabbe and Goyle were chuckling/nappreciatively at his words./n/nHagrid looked stumped at the question./n/n"I mean, what do they do?" asked Malfoy. "What is the/npoint of them?"/n/nHagrid opened his mouth, apparently thinking hard;/nthere was a few seconds' pause, then he said roughly,/n"Tha's next lesson, Malfoy. Yer jus' feedin' 'em today./nNow, yeh'll wan' ter try 'em on a few diff'rent things —/nI've never had 'em before, not sure what they'll go fer/n/n— I got ant eggs an' frog livers an' a bit o' grass snake/n/n— just try 'em out with a bit of each."/n/n"First pus and now this," muttered Seamus./n/nNothing but deep affection for Hagrid could have/nmade Harry, Ron, and Hermione pick up squelchy/nhandfuls of frog liver and lower them into the crates/nto tempt the Blast-Ended Skrewts. Harry couldn't/nsuppress the suspicion that the whole thing was/nentirely pointless, because the skrewts didn't seem to/nhave mouths./n/n"Ouch\" yelled Dean Thomas after about ten minutes./n"It got me!"/n/nHagrid hurried over to him, looking anxious./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Its end exploded!" said Dean angrily, showing Hagrid/na burn on his hand./n/n"Ah, yeah, that can happen when they blast off," said/nHagrid, nodding./n/n"Eurgh!" said Lavender Brown again. "Eurgh, Hagrid,/nwhat's that pointy thing on it?"/n/n"Ah, some of 'em have got stings," said Hagrid/nenthusiastically (Lavender quickly withdrew her hand/nfrom the box). "I reckon they're the males. ... The/nfemales Ve got sorta sucker things on their bellies. ... I/nthink they might be ter suck blood."/n/n"Well, I can certainly see why we're trying to keep/nthem alive," said Malfoy sarcastically. "Who wouldn't/nwant pets that can burn, sting, and bite all at once?"/n/n"Just because they're not very pretty, it doesn't mean/nthey're not useful," Hermione snapped. "Dragon/nblood's amazingly magical, but you wouldn't want a/ndragon for a pet, would you?"/n/nHarry and Ron grinned at Hagrid, who gave them a/nfurtive smile from behind his bushy beard. Hagrid/nwould have liked nothing better than a pet dragon, as/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione knew only too well — he/nhad owned one for a brief period during their first/nyear, a vicious Norwegian Ridgeback by the name of/nNorbert. Hagrid simply loved monstrous creatures,/nthe more lethal, the better./n/n"Well, at least the skrewts are small," said Ron as/nthey made their way back up to the castle for lunch/nan hour later./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They are now," said Hermione in an exasperated/nvoice, "but once Hagrid's found out what they eat, I/nexpect they'll be six feet long."/n/n"Well, that won't matter if they turn out to cure/nseasickness or something, will it?" said Ron, grinning/nslyly at her./n/n"You know perfectly well I only said that to shut/nMalfoy up," said Hermione. "As a matter of fact I/nthink he's right. The best thing to do would be to/nstamp on the lot of them before they start attacking/nus all."/n/nThey sat down at the Gryffindor table and helped/nthemselves to lamb chops and potatoes. Hermione/nbegan to eat so fast that Harry and Ron stared at her./n/n"Er — is this the new stand on elf rights?" said Ron./n"You're going to make yourself puke instead?"/n/n"No," said Hermione, with as much dignity as she/ncould muster with her mouth bulging with sprouts. "I/njust want to get to the library."/n/n"What?" said Ron in disbelief. "Hermione — it's the/nfirst day back! We haven't even got homework yet!"/n/nHermione shrugged and continued to shovel down her/nfood as though she had not eaten for days. Then she/nleapt to her feet, said, "See you at dinner!" and/ndeparted at high speed./n/nWhen the bell rang to signal the start of afternoon/nlessons, Harry and Ron set off for North Tower where,/nat the top of a tightly spiraling staircase, a silver/nstepladder led to a circular trapdoor in the ceiling,/nand the room where Professor Trelawney lived./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe familiar sweet perfume spreading from the fire/nmet their nostrils as they emerged at the top of the/nstepladder. As ever, the curtains were all closed; the/ncircular room was bathed in a dim reddish light cast/nby the many lamps, which were all draped with/nscarves and shawls. Harry and Ron walked through/nthe mass of occupied chintz chairs and poufs that/ncluttered the room, and sat down at the same small/ncircular table./n/n"Good day," said the misty voice of Professor/nTrelawney right behind Harry, making him jump./n/nA very thin woman with enormous glasses that made/nher eyes appear far too large for her face, Professor/nTrelawney was peering down at Harry with the tragic/nexpression she always wore whenever she saw him./nThe usual large amount of beads, chains, and bangles/nglittered upon her person in the firelight./n/n"You are preoccupied, my dear," she said mournfully/nto Harry. "My inner eye sees past your brave face to/nthe troubled soul within. And I regret to say that your/nworries are not baseless. I see difficult times ahead/nfor you, alas ... most difficult ... I fear the thing you/ndread will indeed come to pass ... and perhaps sooner/nthan you think. ..."/n/nHer voice dropped almost to a whisper. Ron rolled his/neyes at Harry, who looked stonily back. Professor/nTrelawney swept past them and seated herself in a/nlarge winged armchair before the fire, facing the class./nLavender Brown and Parvati Patil, who deeply/nadmired Professor Trelawney, were sitting on poufs/nvery close to her./n/n"My dears, it is time for us to consider the stars," she/nsaid. "The movements of the planets and the/nmysterious portents they reveal only to those who/n/n/n/n/n/nunderstand the steps of the celestial dance. Human/ndestiny may be deciphered by the planetary rays,/nwhich intermingle ..."/n/nBut Harry's thoughts had drifted. The perfumed fire/nalways made him feel sleepy and dull-witted, and/nProfessor Trelawney's rambling talks on fortune-/ntelling never held him exactly spellbound — though/nhe couldn't help thinking about what she had just/nsaid to him. " 'I fear the thing you dread will indeed/ncome to pass . . . ' "/n/nBut Hermione was right, Harry thought irritably,/nProfessor Trelawney really was an old fraud. He/nwasn't dreading anything at the moment at all ... well,/nunless you counted his fears that Sirius had been/ncaught ... but what did Professor Trelawney know? He/nhad long since come to the conclusion that her brand/nof fortune-telling was really no more than lucky/nguesswork and a spooky manner./n/nExcept, of course, for that time at the end of last/nterm, when she had made the prediction about/nVoldemort rising again . . . and Dumbledore himself/nhad said that he thought that trance had been/ngenuine, when Harry had described it to him. .../n/n"Harry\" Ron muttered./n/n"What?"/n/nHarry looked around; the whole class was staring at/nhim. He sat up straight; he had been almost dozing/noff, lost in the heat and his thoughts./n/n"I was saying, my dear, that you were clearly born/nunder the baleful influence of Saturn," said Professor/nTrelawney, a faint note of resentment in her voice at/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe fact that he had obviously not been hanging on/nher words./n/n"Born under — what, sorry?" said Harry./n/n"Saturn, dear, the planet Saturn!" said Professor/nTrelawney, sounding definitely irritated that he wasn't/nriveted by this news. "I was saying that Saturn was/nsurely in a position of power in the heavens at the/nmoment of your birth. ... Your dark hair ... your mean/nstature ... tragic losses so young in life ... I think I am/nright in saying, my dear, that you were born in/nmidwinter?"/n/n"No," said Harry, "I was born in July."/n/nRon hastily turned his laugh into a hacking cough./n/nHalf an hour later, each of them had been given a/ncomplicated circular chart, and was attempting to fill/nin the position of the planets at their moment of birth./nIt was dull work, requiring much consultation of/ntimetables and calculation of angles./n/n"I've got two Neptunes here," said Harry after a while,/nfrowning down at his piece of parchment, "that can't/nbe right, can it?"/n/n"Aaaaah," said Ron, imitating Professor Trelawney's/nmystical whisper, "when two Neptunes appear in the/nsky, it is a sure sign that a midget in glasses is being/nborn, Harry ..."/n/nSeamus and Dean, who were working nearby,/nsniggered loudly, though not loudly enough to mask/nthe excited squeals from Lavender Brown — "Oh/nProfessor, look! I think I've got an unaspected planet!/nOooh, which one's that, Professor?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It is Uranus, my dear," said Professor Trelawney,/npeering down at the chart./n/n"Can I have a look at Uranus too, Lavender?" said/nRon./n/nMost unfortunately, Professor Trelawney heard him,/nand it was this, perhaps, that made her give them so/nmuch homework at the end of the class./n/n"A detailed analysis of the way the planetary/nmovements in the coming month will affect you, with/nreference to your personal chart," she snapped,/nsounding much more like Professor McGonagall than/nher usual airy-fairy self. "I want it ready to hand in/nnext Monday, and no excuses!"/n/n"Miserable old bat," said Ron bitterly as they joined/nthe crowds descending the staircases back to the/nGreat Hall and dinner. "Thatll take all weekend, that/nwill. ..."/n/n"Lots of homework?" said Hermione brightly, catching/nup with them. "Professor Vector didn't give us any at/nall!"/n/n"Well, bully for Professor Vector," said Ron moodily./n/nThey reached the entrance hall, which was packed/nwith people queuing for dinner. They had just joined/nthe end of the line, when a loud voice rang out behind/nthem./n/n"Weasley! Hey, Weasley!"/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione turned. Malfoy, Crabbe,/nand Goyle were standing there, each looking/nthoroughly pleased about something./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What?" said Ron shortly./n/n/n/n"Your dad's in the paper, Weasley!" said Malfoy,/nbrandishing a copy of the Daily Prophet and speaking/nvery loudly, so that everyone in the packed entrance/nhall could hear. "Listen to this!/n/nFURTHER MISTAKES AT THE MINISTRY OF MAGIC/n/nIt seems as though the Ministry of Magic's troubles are/nnot yet at an end, writes Rita Skeeter, Special/nCorrespondent. Recently under fire for its poor crowd/ncontrol at the Quidditch World Cup, and still unable to/naccount for the disappearance of one of its witches, the/nMinistry was plunged into fresh embarrassment/nyesterday by the antics of Arnold Weasley, of the/nMisuse of Muggle Artifacts Office. "/n/nMalfoy looked up./n/n"Imagine them not even getting his name right,/nWeasley. It's almost as though he's a complete/nnonentity, isn't it?" he crowed./n/nEveryone in the entrance hall was listening now./nMalfoy straightened the paper with a flourish and/nread on:/n/nArnold Weasley, who was charged with possession of/na flying car two years ago, was yesterday involved in/na tussle with several Muggle law-keepers ("policemen")/nover a number of highly aggressive dustbins. Mr./nWeasley appears to have rushed to the aid of "Mad-/nEye" Moody, the aged ex-Auror who retired from the/nMinistry when no longer able to tell the difference/nbetween a handshake and attempted murder./nUnsurprisingly, Mr. Weasley found, upon arrival at Mr./nMoody 's heavily guarded house, that Mr. Moody had/nonce again raised a false alarm. Mr. Weasley was/n/n/n/n/nforced to modify several memories before he could/nescape from the policemen, but refused to answer/nDaily Prophet questions about why he had involved/nthe Ministry in such an undignified and potentially/nembarrassing scene./n/n"And there's a picture, Weasley!" said Malfoy, flipping/nthe paper over and holding it up. "A picture of your/nparents outside their house — if you can call it a/nhouse! Your mother could do with losing a bit of/nweight, couldn't she?"/n/nRon was shaking with fury. Everyone was staring at/nhim./n/n"Get stuffed, Malfoy," said Harry. "C'mon, Ron. ..."/n/n"Oh yeah, you were staying with them this summer,/nweren't you, Potter?" sneered Malfoy. "So tell me, is/nhis mother really that porky, or is it just the picture?"/n/n"You know your mother, Malfoy?" said Harry — both/nhe and Hermione had grabbed the back of Ron's/nrobes to stop him from launching himself at Malfoy —/n"that expression she's got, like she's got dung under/nher nose? Has she always looked like that, or was it/njust because you were with her?"/n/nMalfoy's pale face went slightly pink./n/n"Don't you dare insult my mother, Potter."/n/n"Keep your fat mouth shut, then," said Harry, turning/naway./n/nBANG!/n/nSeveral people screamed — Harry felt something/nwhite-hot graze the side of his face — he plunged his/n/n/n/n/n/nhand into his robes for his wand, but before he'd even/ntouched it, he heard a second loud BANG, and a roar/nthat echoed through the entrance hall./n/n"OH NO YOU DONT, LADDIE!"/n/nHarry spun around. Professor Moody was limping/ndown the marble staircase. His wand was out and it/nwas pointing right at a pure white ferret, which was/nshivering on the stone-flagged floor, exactly where/nMalfoy had been standing./n/nThere was a terrified silence in the entrance hall./nNobody but Moody was moving a muscle. Moody/nturned to look at Harry — at least, his normal eye was/nlooking at Harry; the other one was pointing into the/nback of his head./n/n"Did he get you?" Moody growled. His voice was low/nand gravelly./n/n"No," said Harry, "missed."/n/n"LEAVE IT!" Moody shouted./n/n"Leave — what?" Harry said, bewildered./n/n"Not you — him!" Moody growled, jerking his thumb/nover his shoulder at Crabbe, who had just frozen,/nabout to pick up the white ferret. It seemed that/nMoody's rolling eye was magical and could see out of/nthe back of his head./n/nMoody started to limp toward Crabbe, Goyle, and the/nferret, which gave a terrified squeak and took off,/nstreaking toward the dungeons./n/n"I don't think so!" roared Moody, pointing his wand at/nthe ferret again — it flew ten feet into the air, fell with/n/n/n/n/n/na smack to the floor, and then bounced upward once/nmore./n/n"I don't like people who attack when their opponent's/nback's turned," growled Moody as the ferret bounced/nhigher and higher, squealing in pain. "Stinking,/ncowardly, scummy thing to do. ..."/n/nThe ferret flew through the air, its legs and tail flailing/nhelplessly./n/n"Never — do — that — again — " said Moody, speaking/neach word as the ferret hit the stone floor and/nbounced upward again./n/n"Professor Moody!" said a shocked voice./n/nProfessor McGonagall was coming down the marble/nstaircase with her arms full of books./n/n"Hello, Professor McGonagall," said Moody calmly,/nbouncing the ferret still higher./n/n"What — what are you doing?" said Professor/nMcGonagall, her eyes following the bouncing ferret's/nprogress through the air./n/n"Teaching," said Moody./n/n"Teach — Moody, is that a student?" shrieked/nProfessor McGonagall, the books spilling out of her/narms./n/n"Yep," said Moody./n/n"No!" cried Professor McGonagall, running down the/nstairs and pulling out her wand; a moment later, with/na loud snapping noise, Draco Malfoy had reappeared,/nlying in a heap on the floor with his sleek blond hair/n/n/n/n/n/nall over his now brilliantly pink face. He got to his/nfeet, wincing./n/n"Moody, we never use Transfiguration as a/npunishment!" said Professor McGonagall weakly./n"Surely Professor Dumbledore told you that?"/n/n"He might've mentioned it, yeah," said Moody,/nscratching his chin unconcernedly, "but I thought a/ngood sharp shock — "/n/n"We give detentions, Moody! Or speak to the offender's/nHead of House!"/n/n"I'll do that, then," said Moody, staring at Malfoy with/ngreat dislike./n/nMalfoy, whose pale eyes were still watering with pain/nand humiliation, looked malevolently up at Moody/nand muttered something in which the words "my/nfather" were distinguishable./n/n"Oh yeah?" said Moody quietly, limping forward a few/nsteps, the dull clunk of his wooden leg echoing around/nthe hall. "Well, I know your father of old, boy. ... You/ntell him Moody's keeping a close eye on his son . . . you/ntell him that from me. ... Now, your Head of House'll/nbe Snape, will it?"/n/n"Yes," said Malfoy resentfully./n/n"Another old friend," growled Moody. "I've been/nlooking forward to a chat with old Snape. ... Come on,/nyou. ..."/n/nAnd he seized Malfoy's upper arm and marched him/noff toward the dungeons./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor McGonagall stared anxiously after them for/na few moments, then waved her wand at her fallen/nbooks, causing them to soar up into the air and back/ninto her arms./n/n"Don't talk to me," Ron said quietly to Harry and/nHermione as they sat down at the Gryffindor table a/nfew minutes later, surrounded by excited talk on all/nsides about what had just happened./n/n"Why not?" said Hermione in surprise./n/n"Because I want to fix that in my memory forever,"/nsaid Ron, his eyes closed and an uplifted expression/non his face. "Draco Malfoy, the amazing bouncing/nferret ..."/n/nHarry and Hermione both laughed, and Hermione/nbegan doling beef casserole onto each of their plates./n/n"He could have really hurt Malfoy, though," she said./n"It was good, really, that Professor McGonagall/nstopped it — "/n/n"Hermione!" said Ron furiously, his eyes snapping/nopen again, "you're ruining the best moment of my/nlife!"/n/nHermione made an impatient noise and began to eat/nat top speed again./n/n"Don't tell me you're going back to the library this/nevening?" said Harry, watching her./n/n"Got to," said Hermione thickly. "Loads to do."/n/n"But you told us Professor Vector — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's not schoolwork," she said. Within five minutes,/nshe had cleared her plate and departed. No sooner/nhad she gone than her seat was taken by Fred/nWeasley./n/n"Moody!" he said. "How cool is he?"/n/n"Beyond cool," said George, sitting down opposite/nFred./n/n"Supercool," said the twins' best friend, Lee Jordan,/nsliding into the seat beside George.
