"We had him this/nafternoon," he told Harry and Ron./n/n"What was it like?" said Harry eagerly./n/nFred, George, and Lee exchanged looks full of/nmeaning./n/n"Never had a lesson like it," said Fred./n/n"He knows, man," said Lee./n/n"Knows what?" said Ron, leaning forward./n/n"Knows what it's like to be out there doing it," said/nGeorge impressively./n/n"Doing what?" said Harry./n/n"Fighting the Dark Arts," said Fred./n/n"He's seen it all," said George./n/n" 'Mazing," said Lee./n/nRon dived into his bag for his schedule./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We haven't got him till Thursday!" he said in a/ndisappointed voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Unforgivable Curses
text: /nThe next two days passed without great incident,/nunless you counted Neville melting his sixth cauldron/nin Potions. Professor Snape, who seemed to have/nattained new levels of vindictiveness over the/nsummer, gave Neville detention, and Neville returned/nfrom it in a state of nervous collapse, having been/nmade to disembowel a barrel full of horned toads./n/n"You know why Snape 's in such a foul mood, don't/nyou?" said Ron to Harry as they watched Hermione/nteaching Neville a Scouring Charm to remove the frog/nguts from under his fingernails./n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "Moody."/n/nIt was common knowledge that Snape really wanted/nthe Dark Arts job, and he had now failed to get it for/nthe fourth year running. Snape had disliked all of/ntheir previous Dark Arts teachers, and shown it —/nbut he seemed strangely wary of displaying overt/nanimosity to Mad-Eye Moody. Indeed, whenever Harry/nsaw the two of them together — at mealtimes, or/n/n/n/n/nwhen they passed in the corridors — he had the/ndistinct impression that Snape was avoiding Moody's/neye, whether magical or normal./n/n"I reckon Snape's a bit scared of him, you know,"/nHarry said thoughtfully./n/n"Imagine if Moody turned Snape into a horned toad,"/nsaid Ron, his eyes misting over, "and bounced him all/naround his dungeon. ..."/n/nThe Gryffindor fourth years were looking forward to/nMoody's first lesson so much that they arrived early/non Thursday lunchtime and queued up outside his/nclassroom before the bell had even rung. The only/nperson missing was Hermione, who turned up just in/ntime for the lesson./n/n"Been in the — "/n/n"Library." Harry finished her sentence for her./n/n"C'mon, quick, or we won't get decent seats."/n/nThey hurried into three chairs right in front of the/nteacher's desk, took out their copies of The Dark/nForces: A Guide to Self-Protection, and waited,/nunusually quiet. Soon they heard Moody's distinctive/nclunking footsteps coming down the corridor, and he/nentered the room, looking as strange and frightening/nas ever. They could just see his clawed, wooden foot/nprotruding from underneath his robes./n/n"You can put those away," he growled, stumping over/nto his desk and sitting down, "those books. You won't/nneed them."/n/nThey returned the books to their bags, Ron looking/nexcited./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMoody took out a register, shook his long mane of/ngrizzled gray hair out of his twisted and scarred face,/nand began to call out names, his normal eye moving/nsteadily down the list while his magical eye swiveled/naround, fixing upon each student as he or she/nanswered./n/n"Right then," he said, when the last person had/ndeclared themselves present, "I've had a letter from/nProfessor Lupin about this class. Seems you've had a/npretty thorough grounding in tackling Dark creatures/n— you've covered boggarts, Red Caps, hinkypunks,/ngrindylows, Kappas, and werewolves, is that right?"/n/nThere was a general murmur of assent./n/n"But you're behind — very behind — on dealing with/ncurses," said Moody. "So I'm here to bring you up to/nscratch on what wizards can do to each other. I've got/none year to teach you how to deal with Dark — "/n/n"What, aren't you staying?" Ron blurted out./n/nMoody's magical eye spun around to stare at Ron;/n/nRon looked extremely apprehensive, but after a/nmoment Moody smiled — the first time Harry had/nseen him do so. The effect was to make his heavily/nscarred face look more twisted and contorted than/never, but it was nevertheless good to know that he/never did anything as friendly as smile. Ron looked/ndeeply relieved./n/n"You'll be Arthur Weasley's son, eh?" Moody said./n"Your father got me out of a very tight corner a few/ndays ago. ... Yeah, I'm staying just the one year./nSpecial favor to Dumbledore. ... One year, and then/nback to my quiet retirement."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe gave a harsh laugh, and then clapped his gnarled/nhands together./n/n"So — straight into it. Curses. They come in many/nstrengths and forms. Now, according to the Ministry/nof Magic, I'm supposed to teach you countercurses/nand leave it at that. I'm not supposed to show you/nwhat illegal Dark curses look like until you're in the/nsixth year. You're not supposed to be old enough to/ndeal with it till then. But Professor Dumbledore's got/na higher opinion of your nerves, he reckons you can/ncope, and I say, the sooner you know what you're up/nagainst, the better. How are you supposed to defend/nyourself against something you've never seen? A/nwizard who's about to put an illegal curse on you isn't/ngoing to tell you what he's about to do. He's not going/nto do it nice and polite to your face. You need to be/nprepared. You need to be alert and watchful. You/nneed to put that away, Miss Brown, when I'm/ntalking."/n/nLavender jumped and blushed. She had been showing/nParvati her completed horoscope under the desk./nApparently Moody's magical eye could see through/nsolid wood, as well as out of the back of his head./n/n"So ... do any of you know which curses are most/nheavily punished by wizarding law?"/n/nSeveral hands rose tentatively into the air, including/nRon's and Hermione's. Moody pointed at Ron, though/nhis magical eye was still fixed on Lavender./n/n"Er," said Ron tentatively, "my dad told me about one./n... Is it called the Imperius Curse, or something?"/n/n"Ah, yes," said Moody appreciatively. "Your father/nwould know that one. Gave the Ministry a lot of/ntrouble at one time, the Imperius Curse."/n/n/n/n/n/nMoody got heavily to his mismatched feet, opened his/ndesk drawer, and took out a glass jar. Three large/nblack spiders were scuttling around inside it. Harry/nfelt Ron recoil slightly next to him — Ron hated/nspiders./n/nMoody reached into the jar, caught one of the spiders,/nand held it in the palm of his hand so that they could/nall see it. He then pointed his wand at it and/nmuttered, "Imperio\"/n/nThe spider leapt from Moody's hand on a fine thread/nof silk and began to swing backward and forward as/nthough on a trapeze. It stretched out its legs rigidly,/nthen did a back flip, breaking the thread and landing/non the desk, where it began to cartwheel in circles./nMoody jerked his wand, and the spider rose onto two/nof its hind legs and went into what was unmistakably/na tap dance./n/nEveryone was laughing — everyone except Moody./n/n"Think it's funny, do you?" he growled. "You'd like it,/nwould you, if I did it to you?"/n/nThe laughter died away almost instantly./n/n"Total control," said Moody quietly as the spider/nballed itself up and began to roll over and over. "I/ncould make it jump out of the window, drown itself,/nthrow itself down one of your throats ..."/n/nRon gave an involuntary shudder./n/n"Years back, there were a lot of witches and wizards/nbeing controlled by the Imperius Curse," said Moody,/nand Harry knew he was talking about the days in/nwhich Voldemort had been all-powerful. "Some job for/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe Ministry, trying to sort out who was being forced/nto act, and who was acting of their own free will./n/n"The Imperius Curse can be fought, and I'll be/nteaching you how, but it takes real strength of/ncharacter, and not everyone's got it. Better avoid/nbeing hit with it if you can. CONSTANT VIGILANCE!"/nhe barked, and everyone jumped./n/nMoody picked up the somersaulting spider and threw/nit back into the jar./n/n"Anyone else know one? Another illegal curse?"/n/nHermione's hand flew into the air again and so, to/nHarry's slight surprise, did Neville's. The only class in/nwhich Neville usually volunteered information was/nHerbology, which was easily his best subject. Neville/nlooked surprised at his own daring./n/n"Yes?" said Moody, his magical eye rolling right over/nto fix on Neville./n/n"There's one — the Cruciatus Curse," said Neville in a/nsmall but distinct voice./n/nMoody was looking very intently at Neville, this time/nwith both eyes./n/n"Your name's Longbottom?" he said, his magical eye/nswooping down to check the register again./n/nNeville nodded nervously, but Moody made no further/ninquiries. Turning back to the class at large, he/nreached into the jar for the next spider and placed it/nupon the desktop, where it remained motionless,/napparently too scared to move./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The Cruciatus Curse," said Moody. "Needs to be a bit/nbigger for you to get the idea," he said, pointing his/nwand at the spider. "Engorgio\"/n/nThe spider swelled. It was now larger than a/ntarantula. Abandoning all pretense, Ron pushed his/nchair backward, as far away from Moody's desk as/npossible./n/nMoody raised his wand again, pointed it at the spider,/nand muttered, "CrucioV'/n/nAt once, the spider's legs bent in upon its body; it/nrolled over and began to twitch horribly, rocking from/nside to side. No sound came from it, but Harry was/nsure that if it could have given voice, it would have/nbeen screaming. Moody did not remove his wand, and/nthe spider started to shudder and jerk more violently/n/n/n/n"Stop it!" Hermione said shrilly./n/nHarry looked around at her. She was looking, not at/nthe spider, but at Neville, and Harry, following her/ngaze, saw that Neville's hands were clenched upon the/ndesk in front of him, his knuckles white, his eyes/nwide and horrified./n/nMoody raised his wand. The spider's legs relaxed, but/nit continued to twitch./n/n"Reducio," Moody muttered, and the spider shrank/nback to its proper size. He put it back into the jar./n/n"Pain," said Moody softly. "You don't need/nthumbscrews or knives to torture someone if you can/nperform the Cruciatus Curse. ... That one was very/npopular once too./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Right . . . anyone know any others?"/n/n/n/nHarry looked around. From the looks on everyone's/nfaces, he guessed they were all wondering what was/ngoing to happen to the last spider. Hermione's hand/nshook slightly as, for the third time, she raised it into/nthe air./n/n"Yes?" said Moody, looking at her./n/n"Avada Kedavra," Hermione whispered./n/nSeveral people looked uneasily around at her,/nincluding Ron./n/n"Ah," said Moody, another slight smile twisting his/nlopsided mouth. "Yes, the last and worst. Avada/nKedavra ... the Killing Curse."/n/nHe put his hand into the glass jar, and almost as/nthough it knew what was coming, the third spider/nscuttled frantically around the bottom of the jar,/ntrying to evade Moody's fingers, but he trapped it, and/nplaced it upon the desktop. It started to scuttle/nfrantically across the wooden surface./n/nMoody raised his wand, and Harry felt a sudden thrill/nof foreboding./n/n"Avada Kedavral" Moody roared./n/nThere was a flash of blinding green light and a/nrushing sound, as though a vast, invisible something/nwas soaring through the air — instantaneously the/nspider rolled over onto its back, unmarked, but/nunmistakably dead. Several of the students stifled/ncries; Ron had thrown himself backward and almost/ntoppled off his seat as the spider skidded toward him./n/n/n/n/n/nMoody swept the dead spider off the desk onto the/nfloor./n/n"Not nice," he said calmly. "Not pleasant. And there's/nno countercurse. There's no blocking it. Only one/nknown person has ever survived it, and he's sitting/nright in front of me."/n/nHarry felt his face redden as Moody's eyes (both of/nthem) looked into his own. He could feel everyone else/nlooking around at him too. Harry stared at the blank/nblackboard as though fascinated by it, but not really/nseeing it at all. .../n/nSo that was how his parents had died . . . exactly like/nthat spider. Had they been unblemished and/nunmarked too? Had they simply seen the flash of/ngreen light and heard the rush of speeding death,/nbefore life was wiped from their bodies?/n/nHarry had been picturing his parents' deaths over/nand over again for three years now, ever since he'd/nfound out they had been murdered, ever since he'd/nfound out what had happened that night: Wormtail/nhad betrayed his parents' whereabouts to Voldemort,/nwho had come to find them at their cottage. How/nVoldemort had killed Harry's father first. How James/nPotter had tried to hold him off, while he shouted at/nhis wife to take Harry and run ... Voldemort had/nadvanced on Lily Potter, told her to move aside so/nthat he could kill Harry . . . how she had begged him to/nkill her instead, refused to stop shielding her son . . ./nand so Voldemort had murdered her too, before/nturning his wand on Harry. . . ./n/nHarry knew these details because he had heard his/nparents' voices when he had fought the dementors/nlast year — for that was the terrible power of the/ndementors: to force their victims to relive the worst/n/n/n/n/n/nmemories of their lives, and drown, powerless, in their/nown despair. . . ./n/nMoody was speaking again, from a great distance, it/nseemed to Harry. With a massive effort, he pulled/nhimself back to the present and listened to what/nMoody was saying./n/n"Avada Kedavra's a curse that needs a powerful bit of/nmagic behind it — you could all get your wands out/nnow and point them at me and say the words, and I/ndoubt I'd get so much as a nosebleed. But that/ndoesn't matter. I'm not here to teach you how to do it./n/n"Now, if there's no countercurse, why am I showing/nyou? Because you've got to know. You've got to/nappreciate what the worst is. You don't want to find/nyourself in a situation where you're facing it./nCONSTANT VIGILANCE!" he roared, and the whole/nclass jumped again./n/n"Now ... those three curses — Avada Kedavra,/nImperius, and Cruciatus — are known as the/nUnforgivable Curses. The use of any one of them on a/nfellow human being is enough to earn a life sentence/nin Azkaban. That's what you're up against. That's/nwhat I've got to teach you to fight. You need/npreparing. You need arming. But most of all, you/nneed to practice constant, never-ceasing vigilance. Get/nout your quills ... copy this down. ..."/n/nThey spent the rest of the lesson taking notes on each/nof the Unforgivable Curses. No one spoke until the/nbell rang — but when Moody had dismissed them and/nthey had left the classroom, a torrent of talk burst/nforth. Most people were discussing the curses in awed/nvoices — "Did you see it twitch?" " — and when he/nkilled it — just like that!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey were talking about the lesson, Harry thought, as/nthough it had been some sort of spectacular show,/nbut he hadn't found it very entertaining — and nor, it/nseemed, had Hermione./n/n"Hurry up," she said tensely to Harry and Ron./n/n"Not the ruddy library again?" said Ron./n/n"No," said Hermione curtly, pointing up a side/npassage. "Neville."/n/nNeville was standing alone, halfway up the passage,/nstaring at the stone wall opposite him with the same/nhorrified, wide-eyed look he had worn when Moody/nhad demonstrated the Cruciatus Curse./n/n"Neville?" Hermione said gently./n/nNeville looked around./n/n"Oh hello," he said, his voice much higher than usual./n"Interesting lesson, wasn't it? I wonder what's for/ndinner, I'm — I'm starving, aren't you?"/n/n"Neville, are you all right?" said Hermione./n/n"Oh yes, I'm fine," Neville gabbled in the same/nunnaturally high voice. "Very interesting dinner — I/nmean lesson — what's for eating?"/n/nRon gave Harry a startled look./n/n"Neville, what — ?"/n/nBut an odd clunking noise sounded behind them, and/nthey turned to see Professor Moody limping toward/nthem. All four of them fell silent, watching him/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/napprehensively, but when he spoke, it was in a much/nlower and gentler growl than they had yet heard./n/n"It's all right, sonny," he said to Neville. "Why don't/nyou come up to my office? Come on . . . we can have a/ncup of tea. ..."/n/nNeville looked even more frightened at the prospect of/ntea with Moody. He neither moved nor spoke. Moody/nturned his magical eye upon Harry./n/n"You all right, are you, Potter?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry, almost defiantly./n/nMoody's blue eye quivered slightly in its socket as it/nsurveyed Harry. Then he said, "You've got to know. It/nseems harsh, maybe, but you've got to know. No point/npretending ... well ... come on, Longbottom, I've got/nsome books that might interest you."/n/nNeville looked pleadingly at Harry, Ron, and/nHermione, but they didn't say anything, so Neville/nhad no choice but to allow himself to be steered away,/none of Moody's gnarled hands on his shoulder./n/n"What was that about?" said Ron, watching Neville/nand Moody turn the corner./n/n"I don't know," said Hermione, looking pensive./n/n"Some lesson, though, eh?" said Ron to Harry as they/nset off for the Great Hall. "Fred and George were right,/nweren't they? He really knows his stuff, Moody,/ndoesn't he? When he did Avada Kedavra, the way that/nspider just died, just snuffed it right — "/n/nBut Ron fell suddenly silent at the look on Harry's/nface and didn't speak again until they reached the/n/n/n/n/n/nGreat Hall, when he said he supposed they had better/nmake a start on Professor Trelawney's predictions/ntonight, since they would take hours./n/nHermione did not join in with Harry and Ron's/nconversation during dinner, but ate furiously fast,/nand then left for the library again. Harry and Ron/nwalked back to Gryffindor Tower, and Harry, who had/nbeen thinking of nothing else all through dinner, now/nraised the subject of the Unforgivable Curses himself./n/n"Wouldn't Moody and Dumbledore be in trouble with/nthe Ministry if they knew we'd seen the curses?"/n/nHarry asked as they approached the Fat Lady./n/n"Yeah, probably," said Ron. "But Dumbledore's always/ndone things his way, hasn't he, and Moody's been/ngetting in trouble for years, I reckon. Attacks first and/nasks questions later — look at his dustbins./nBalderdash."/n/nThe Fat Lady swung forward to reveal the entrance/nhole, and they climbed into the Gryffindor common/nroom, which was crowded and noisy./n/n"Shall we get our Divination stuff, then?" said Harry./n/n"I s'pose," Ron groaned./n/nThey went up to the dormitory to fetch their books/nand charts, to find Neville there alone, sitting on his/nbed, reading. He looked a good deal calmer than at/nthe end of Moody's lesson, though still not entirely/nnormal. His eyes were rather red./n/n"You all right, Neville?" Harry asked him./n/n"Oh yes," said Neville, "I'm fine, thanks. Just reading/nthis book Professor Moody lent me. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe held up the book: Magical Water Plants of the/nMediterranean./n/n"Apparently, Professor Sprout told Professor Moody/nI'm really good at Herbology," Neville said. There was/na faint note of pride in his voice that Harry had rarely/nheard there before. "He thought I'd like this."/n/nTelling Neville what Professor Sprout had said, Harry/nthought, had been a very tactful way of cheering/nNeville up, for Neville very rarely heard that he was/ngood at anything. It was the sort of thing Professor/nLupin would have done./n/nHarry and Ron took their copies of Unfogging the/nFuture back down to the common room, found a/ntable, and set to work on their predictions for the/ncoming month. An hour later, they had made very/nlittle progress, though their table was littered with/nbits of parchment bearing sums and symbols, and/nHarry's brain was as fogged as though it had been/nfilled with the fumes from Professor Trelawney's fire./n/n"I haven't got a clue what this lot's supposed to/nmean," he said, staring down at a long list of/ncalculations./n/n"You know," said Ron, whose hair was on end/nbecause of all the times he had run his fingers/nthrough it in frustration, "I think it's back to the old/nDivination standby."/n/n"What — make it up?"/n/n"Yeah," said Ron, sweeping the jumble of scrawled/nnotes off the table, dipping his pen into some ink, and/nstarting to write./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Next Monday," he said as he scribbled, "I am likely to/ndevelop a cough, owing to the unlucky conjunction of/nMars and Jupiter." He looked up at Harry. "You know/nher — just put in loads of misery, shell lap it up."/n/n"Right," said Harry, crumpling up his first attempt/nand lobbing it over the heads of a group of chattering/nfirst years into the fire. "Okay ... on Monday, / will be/nin danger of — er — burns."/n/n"Yeah, you will be," said Ron darkly, "we're seeing the/nskrewts again on Monday. Okay, Tuesday, I'll ... erm/n/n/n/n"Lose a treasured possession," said Harry, who was/nflicking through Unfogging the Future for ideas./n/n"Good one," said Ron, copying it down. "Because of/n... erm ... Mercury. Why don't you get stabbed in the/nback by someone you thought was a friend?"/n/n"Yeah ... cool ..." said Harry, scribbling it down,/n"because ... Venus is in the twelfth house."/n/n"And on Wednesday, I think I'll come off worst in a/nfight."/n/n"Aaah, I was going to have a fight. Okay, I'll lose a/nbet."/n/n"Yeah, you'll be betting I'll win my fight. ..."/n/nThey continued to make up predictions (which grew/nsteadily more tragic) for another hour, while the/ncommon room around them slowly emptied as people/nwent up to bed. Crookshanks wandered over to them,/nleapt lightly into an empty chair, and stared/ninscrutably at Harry, rather as Hermione might look if/nshe knew they weren't doing their homework properly./n/n/n/n/nStaring around the room, trying to think of a kind of/nmisfortune he hadn't yet used, Harry saw Fred and/nGeorge sitting together against the opposite wall,/nheads together, quills out, poring over a single piece/nof parchment. It was most unusual to see Fred and/nGeorge hidden away in a corner and working silently;/nthey usually liked to be in the thick of things and the/nnoisy center of attention. There was something/nsecretive about the way they were working on the/npiece of parchment, and Harry was reminded of how/nthey had sat together writing something back at the/nBurrow. He had thought then that it was another/norder form for Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, but it didn't/nlook like that this time; if it had been, they would/nsurely have let Lee Jordan in on the joke. He/nwondered whether it had anything to do with entering/nthe Triwizard Tournament./n/nAs Harry watched, George shook his head at Fred,/nscratched out something with his quill, and said, in a/nvery quiet voice that nevertheless carried across the/nalmost deserted room, "No — that sounds like we're/naccusing him. Got to be careful ..."/n/nThen George looked over and saw Harry watching/nhim. Harry grinned and quickly returned to his/npredictions — he didn't want George to think he was/neavesdropping. Shortly after that, the twins rolled up/ntheir parchment, said good night, and went off to bed./n/nFred and George had been gone ten minutes or so/nwhen the portrait hole opened and Hermione climbed/ninto the common room carrying a sheaf of parchment/nin one hand and a box whose contents rattled as she/nwalked in the other. Crookshanks arched his back,/npurring./n/n"Hello," she said, "I've just finished!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So have I!" said Ron triumphantly, throwing down/nhis quill./n/nHermione sat down, laid the things she was carrying/nin an empty armchair, and pulled Ron's predictions/ntoward her./n/n"Not going to have a very good month, are you?" she/nsaid sardonically as Crookshanks curled up in her/nlap./n/n"Ah well, at least I'm forewarned," Ron yawned./n/n"You seem to be drowning twice," said Hermione./n/n"Oh am I?" said Ron, peering down at his predictions./n"I'd better change one of them to getting trampled by/na rampaging hippogriff."/n/n"Don't you think it's a bit obvious you've made these/nup?" said Hermione./n/n"How dare you!" said Ron, in mock outrage. "We've/nbeen working like house-elves here!"/n/nHermione raised her eyebrows./n/n"It's just an expression," said Ron hastily./n/nHarry laid down his quill too, having just finished/npredicting his own death by decapitation./n/n"What's in the box?" he asked, pointing at it./n/n"Funny you should ask," said Hermione, with a nasty/nlook at Ron. She took off the lid and showed them the/ncontents./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nInside were about fifty badges, all of different colors,/nbut all bearing the same letters: S.P.E.W./n/n" 'Spew?" said Harry, picking up a badge and looking/nat it. "What's this about?"/n/n"Not spew," said Hermione impatiently. "It's S-P-E-W./nStands for the Society for the Promotion of Elfish/nWelfare."/n/n"Never heard of it," said Ron./n/n"Well, of course you haven't," said Hermione briskly,/n"I've only just started it."/n/n"Yeah?" said Ron in mild surprise. "How many/nmembers have you got?"/n/n"Well — if you two join — three," said Hermione./n/n"And you think we want to walk around wearing/nbadges saying 'spew,' do you?" said Ron./n/n"S-P-E-W!" said Hermione hotly. "I was going to put/nStop the Outrageous Abuse of Our Fellow Magical/nCreatures and Campaign for a Change in Their Legal/nStatus — but it wouldn't fit. So that's the heading of/nour manifesto."/n/nShe brandished the sheaf of parchment at them./n/n"I've been researching it thoroughly in the library. Elf/nenslavement goes back centuries. I can't believe no/none's done anything about it before now."/n/n"Hermione — open your ears," said Ron loudly. "They./nLike. It. They like being enslaved!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Our short-term aims," said Hermione, speaking even/nmore loudly than Ron, and acting as though she/nhadn't heard a word, "are to secure house-elves fair/nwages and working conditions. Our long-term aims/ninclude changing the law about non-wand use, and/ntrying to get an elf into the Department for the/nRegulation and Control of Magical Creatures, because/nthey're shockingly underrepresented."/n/n"And how do we do all this?" Harry asked./n/n"We start by recruiting members," said Hermione/nhappily. "I thought two Sickles to join — that buys a/nbadge — and the proceeds can fund our leaflet/ncampaign. You're treasurer, Ron — I've got you a/ncollecting tin upstairs — and Harry, you're secretary,/nso you might want to write down everything I'm/nsaying now, as a record of our first meeting."/n/nThere was a pause in which Hermione beamed at the/npair of them, and Harry sat, torn between/nexasperation at Hermione and amusement at the look/non Ron's face. The silence was broken, not by Ron,/nwho in any case looked as though he was temporarily/ndumbstruck, but by a soft tap, tap on the window./nHarry looked across the now empty common room/nand saw, illuminated by the moonlight, a snowy owl/nperched on the windowsill./n/n"Hedwig!" he shouted, and he launched himself out of/nhis chair and across the room to pull open the/nwindow./n/nHedwig flew inside, soared across the room, and/nlanded on the table on top of Harry's predictions./n/n"About time!" said Harry, hurrying after her./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"She's got an answer!" said Ron excitedly, pointing at/nthe grubby piece of parchment tied to Hedwig's leg./n/nHarry hastily untied it and sat down to read,/nwhereupon Hedwig fluttered onto his knee, hooting/nsoftly./n/n"What does it say?" Hermione asked breathlessly./n/nThe letter was very short, and looked as though it had/nbeen scrawled in a great hurry. Harry read it aloud:/n/nHarry —/n/nI'm flying north immediately. This news about your/nscar is the latest in a series of strange rumors that/nhave reached me here. If it hurts again , go straight to/nDumbledore — they're saying he's got Mad-Eye out of/nretirement, which means he's reading the signs, even if/nno one else is./n/nI'll be in touch soon. My best to Ron and Hermione./n/nKeep your eyes open, Harry./n/nSirius/n/nHarry looked up at Ron and Hermione, who stared/nback at him./n/n"He's flying north?" Hermione whispered. "He's/ncoming back?"/n/n"Dumbledore's reading what signs?" said Ron, looking/nperplexed. "Harry — what's up?"/n/nFor Harry had just hit himself in the forehead with/nhis fist, jolting Hedwig out of his lap./n/n"I shouldn't've told him!" Harry said furiously./n/n/n/n/n/n"What are you on about?" said Ron in surprise./n/n/n/n"It's made him think he's got to come back!" said/nHarry, now slamming his fist on the table so that/nHedwig landed on the back of Ron's chair, hooting/nindignantly. "Coming back, because he thinks I'm in/ntrouble! And there's nothing wrong with me! And I/nhaven't got anything for you," Harry snapped at/nHedwig, who was clicking her beak expectantly,/n/n"you'll have to go up to the Owlery if you want food."/n/nHedwig gave him an extremely offended look and took/noff for the open window, cuffing him around the head/nwith her outstretched wing as she went./n/n"Harry," Hermione began, in a pacifying sort of voice./n/n"I'm going to bed," said Harry shortly. "See you in the/nmorning."/n/nUpstairs in the dormitory he pulled on his pajamas/nand got into his four-poster, but he didn't feel/nremotely tired./n/nIf Sirius came back and got caught, it would be his,/nHarry's, fault. Why hadn't he kept his mouth shut? A/nfew seconds' pain and he'd had to blab. ... If he'd just/nhad the sense to keep it to himself. . . ./n/nHe heard Ron come up into the dormitory a short/nwhile later, but did not speak to him. For a long time,/nHarry lay staring up at the dark canopy of his bed./nThe dormitory was completely silent, and, had he/nbeen less preoccupied, Harry would have realized that/nthe absence of Neville's usual snores meant that he/nwas not the only one lying awake./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Beauxbatons And Durmstrang
text: /nEarly next morning, Harry woke with a plan fully/nformed in his mind, as though his sleeping brain had/nbeen working on it all night. He got up, dressed in the/npale dawn light, left the dormitory without waking/nRon, and went back down to the deserted common/nroom. Here he took a piece of parchment from the/ntable upon which his Divination homework still lay/nand wrote the following letter:/n/nDear Sirius,/n/nI reckon I just imagined my scar hurting, I was half/nasleep when I wrote to you last time. There's no point/ncoming back, everything's fine here. Don't worry about/nme, my head feels completely normal./n/nHarry/n/nHe then climbed out of the portrait hole, up through/nthe silent castle (held up only briefly by Peeves, who/ntried to overturn a large vase on him halfway along/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe fourth-floor corridor), finally arriving at the/nOwlery, which was situated at the top of West Tower./n/nThe Owlery was a circular stone room, rather cold/nand drafty, because none of the windows had glass in/nthem. The floor was entirely covered in straw, owl/ndroppings, and the regurgitated skeletons of mice and/nvoles. Hundreds upon hundreds of owls of every/nbreed imaginable were nestled here on perches that/nrose right up to the top of the tower, nearly all of/nthem asleep, though here and there a round amber/neye glared at Harry. He spotted Hedwig nestled/nbetween a barn owl and a tawny, and hurried over to/nher, sliding a little on the dropping-strewn floor./n/nIt took him a while to persuade her to wake up and/nthen to look at him, as she kept shuffling around on/nher perch, showing him her tail. She was evidently/nstill furious about his lack of gratitude the previous/nnight. In the end, it was Harry suggesting she might/nbe too tired, and that perhaps he would ask Ron to/nborrow Pigwidgeon, that made her stick out her leg/nand allow him to tie the letter to it./n/n"Just find him, all right?" Harry said, stroking her/nback as he carried her on his arm to one of the holes/nin the wall. "Before the dementors do."/n/nShe nipped his finger, perhaps rather harder than she/nwould ordinarily have done, but hooted softly in a/nreassuring sort of way all the same. Then she spread/nher wings and took off into the sunrise. Harry/nwatched her fly out of sight with the familiar feeling of/nunease back in his stomach. He had been so sure/nthat Sirius's reply would alleviate his worries rather/nthan increasing them./n/n"That was a lie, Harry," said Hermione sharply over/nbreakfast, when he told her and Ron what he had/n/n/n/n/n/ndone. "You didn't imagine your scar hurting and you/nknow it."/n/n"So what?" said Harry. "He's not going back to/nAzkaban because of me."/n/n"Drop it," said Ron sharply to Hermione as she/nopened her mouth to argue some more, and for once,/nHermione heeded him, and fell silent./n/nHarry did his best not to worry about Sirius over the/nnext couple of weeks. True, he could not stop himself/nfrom looking anxiously around every morning when/nthe post owls arrived, nor, late at night before he went/nto sleep, prevent himself from seeing horrible visions/nof Sirius, cornered by dementors down some dark/nLondon street, but betweentimes he tried to keep his/nmind off his godfather. He wished he still had/nQuidditch to distract him; nothing worked so well on/na troubled mind as a good, hard training session. On/nthe other hand, their lessons were becoming more/ndifficult and demanding than ever before, particularly/nMoody's Defense Against the Dark Arts./n/nTo their surprise, Professor Moody had announced/nthat he would be putting the Imperius Curse on each/nof them in turn, to demonstrate its power and to see/nwhether they could resist its effects./n/n"But — but you said it's illegal, Professor," said/nHermione uncertainly as Moody cleared away the/ndesks with a sweep of his wand, leaving a large clear/nspace in the middle of the room. "You said — to use it/nagainst another human was — "/n/n"Dumbledore wants you taught what it feels like,"/nsaid Moody, his magical eye swiveling onto Hermione/nand fixing her with an eerie, unblinking stare. "If/nyou'd rather learn the hard way — when someone's/n/n/n/n/n/nputting it on you so they can control you completely/n— fine by me. You're excused. Off you go."/n/nHe pointed one gnarled finger toward the door./nHermione went very pink and muttered something/nabout not meaning that she wanted to leave. Harry/nand Ron grinned at each other. They knew Hermione/nwould rather eat bubotuber pus than miss such an/nimportant lesson./n/nMoody began to beckon students forward in turn and/nput the Imperius Curse upon them. Harry watched/nas, one by one, his classmates did the most/nextraordinary things under its influence. Dean/nThomas hopped three times around the room, singing/nthe national anthem. Lavender Brown imitated a/nsquirrel. Neville performed a series of quite/nastonishing gymnastics he would certainly not have/nbeen capable of in his normal state. Not one of them/nseemed to be able to fight off the curse, and each of/nthem recovered only when Moody had removed it./n/n"Potter," Moody growled, "you next."/n/nHarry moved forward into the middle of the/nclassroom, into the space that Moody had cleared of/ndesks. Moody raised his wand, pointed it at Harry,/nand said, "Imperio\"/n/nIt was the most wonderful feeling. Harry felt a floating/nsensation as every thought and worry in his head was/nwiped gently away, leaving nothing but a vague,/nuntraceable happiness. He stood there feeling/nimmensely relaxed, only dimly aware of everyone/nwatching him./n/nAnd then he heard Mad-Eye Moody's voice, echoing in/nsome distant chamber of his empty brain: Jump onto/nthe desk . . . jump onto the desk. . . ./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry bent his knees obediently, preparing to spring./nJump onto the desk. .../n/nWhy, though? Another voice had awoken in the back/nof his brain./n/nStupid thing to do, really, said the voice./n/nJump onto the desk. .../n/nNo, I don't think I will, thanks, said the other voice, a/nlittle more firmly ... no, I don't really want to. .../n/nJump\ NOW/n/nThe next thing Harry felt was considerable pain. He/nhad both jumped and tried to prevent himself from/njumping — the result was that he'd smashed/nheadlong into the desk, knocking it over, and, by the/nfeeling in his legs, fractured both his kneecaps./n/n"Now, that's more like it!" growled Moody's voice, and/nsuddenly, Harry felt the empty, echoing feeling in his/nhead disappear. He remembered exactly what was/nhappening, and the pain in his knees seemed to/ndouble./n/n"Look at that, you lot ... Potter fought! He fought it,/nand he damn near beat it! We'll try that again, Potter,/nand the rest of you, pay attention — watch his eyes,/nthat's where you see it — very good, Potter, very good/nindeed! They'll have trouble controlling you!"/n/n/n/n"The way he talks," Harry muttered as he hobbled out/nof the Defense Against the Dark Arts class an hour/nlater (Moody had insisted on putting Harry through/n/n/n/n/n/nhis paces four times in a row, until Harry could throw/noff the curse entirely), "you'd think we were all going/nto be attacked any second."/n/n"Yeah, I know," said Ron, who was skipping on every/nalternate step. He had had much more difficulty with/nthe curse than Harry, though Moody assured him the/neffects would wear off by lunch-time. "Talk about/nparanoid ..." Ron glanced nervously over his shoulder/nto check that Moody was definitely out of earshot and/nwent on. "No wonder they were glad to get shot of him/nat the Ministry. Did you hear him telling Seamus/nwhat he did to that witch who shouted 'Boo' behind/nhim on April Fools' Day? And when are we supposed/nto read up on resisting the Imperius Curse with/neverything else we've got to do?"/n/nAll the fourth years had noticed a definite increase in/nthe amount of work they were required to do this/nterm. Professor McGonagall explained why, when the/nclass gave a particularly loud groan at the amount of/nTransfiguration homework she had assigned./n/n"You are now entering a most important phase of your/nmagical education!" she told them, her eyes glinting/ndangerously behind her square spectacles. "Your/nOrdinary Wizarding Levels are drawing closer — "/n/n"We don't take O.W.L.s till fifth year!" said Dean/nThomas indignantly./n/n"Maybe not, Thomas, but believe me, you need all the/npreparation you can get! Miss Granger remains the/nonly person in this class who has managed to turn a/nhedgehog into a satisfactory pincushion. I might/nremind you that your pincushion, Thomas, still curls/nup in fright if anyone approaches it with a pin!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione, who had turned rather pink again, seemed/nto be trying not to look too pleased with herself./n/nHarry and Ron were deeply amused when Professor/nTrelawney told them that they had received top marks/nfor their homework in their next Divination class. She/nread out large portions of their predictions,/ncommending them for their unflinching acceptance of/nthe horrors in store for them — but they were less/namused when she asked them to do the same thing/nfor the month after next; both of them were running/nout of ideas for catastrophes./n/nMeanwhile Professor Binns, the ghost who taught/nHistory of Magic, had them writing weekly essays on/nthe goblin rebellions of the eighteenth century./nProfessor Snape was forcing them to research/nantidotes. They took this one seriously, as he had/nhinted that he might be poisoning one of them before/nChristmas to see if their antidote worked. Professor/nFlitwick had asked them to read three extra books in/npreparation for their lesson on Summoning Charms./n/nEven Hagrid was adding to their workload. The Blast-/nEnded Skrewts were growing at a remarkable pace/ngiven that nobody had yet discovered what they ate./nHagrid was delighted, and as part of their "project,"/nsuggested that they come down to his hut on/nalternate evenings to observe the skrewts and make/nnotes on their extraordinary behavior./n/n"I will not," said Draco Malfoy flatly when Hagrid had/nproposed this with the air of Father Christmas pulling/nan extra- large toy out of his sack. "I see enough of/nthese foul things during lessons, thanks."/n/nHagrid 's smile faded off his face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeh'll do wha'yer told," he growled, "or I'll be takin' a/nleaf outta Professor Moody's book. ... I hear yeh made/na good ferret, Malfoy."/n/nThe Gryffindors roared with laughter. Malfoy flushed/nwith anger, but apparently the memory of Moody's/npunishment was still sufficiently painful to stop him/nfrom retorting. Harry, Ron, and Hermione returned to/nthe castle at the end of the lesson in high spirits;/nseeing Hagrid put down Malfoy was particularly/nsatisfying, especially because Malfoy had done his/nvery best to get Hagrid sacked the previous year./n/nWhen they arrived in the entrance hall, they found/nthemselves unable to proceed owing to the large/ncrowd of students congregated there, all milling/naround a large sign that had been erected at the foot/nof the marble staircase. Ron, the tallest of the three,/nstood on tiptoe to see over the heads in front of them/nand read the sign aloud to the other two:/n/nTRIWIZARD TOURNAMENT/n/nThe delegations from Beauxbatons and Durmstrang/nwill be arriving at 6 o'clock on Friday the 30th of/nOctober. Lessons will end half an hour early —/n/n"Brilliant!" said Harry. "It's Potions last thing on/nFriday! Snape won't have time to poison us all!"/n/nStudents will return their bags and books to their/ndormitories and assemble in front of the castle to/ngreet our guests before the Welcoming Feast./n/n/n/n"Only a week away!" said Ernie Macmillan of/nHufflepuff, emerging from the crowd, his eyes/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ngleaming. "I wonder if Cedric knows? Think 111 go and/ntell him. ..."/n/n/n/n"Cedric?" said Ron blankly as Ernie hurried off./n/n"Diggory," said Harry. "He must be entering the/ntournament."/n/n"That idiot, Hogwarts champion?" said Ron as they/npushed their way through the chattering crowd/ntoward the staircase./n/n"He's not an idiot. You just don't like him because he/nbeat Gryffindor at Quidditch," said Hermione. "I've/nheard he's a really good student — and he's a/nprefect."/n/nShe spoke as though this settled the matter./n/n"You only like him because he's handsome," said Ron/nscathingly./n/n"Excuse me, I don't like people just because they're/nhandsome!" said Hermione indignantly./n/nRon gave a loud false cough, which sounded oddly/nlike "Lockhart\"/n/nThe appearance of the sign in the entrance hall had a/nmarked effect upon the inhabitants of the castle./nDuring the following week, there seemed to be only/none topic of conversation, no matter where Harry/nwent: the Triwizard Tournament. Rumors were flying/nfrom student to student like highly contagious germs:/nwho was going to try for Hogwarts champion, what/nthe tournament would involve, how the students from/nBeauxbatons and Durmstrang differed from/nthemselves./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry noticed too that the castle seemed to be/nundergoing an extra-thorough cleaning. Several grimy/nportraits had been scrubbed, much to the displeasure/nof their subjects, who sat huddled in their frames/nmuttering darkly and wincing as they felt their raw/npink faces. The suits of armor were suddenly/ngleaming and moving without squeaking, and Argus/nFilch, the caretaker, was behaving so ferociously to/nany students who forgot to wipe their shoes that he/nterrified a pair of first-year girls into hysterics./n/nOther members of the staff seemed oddly tense too./n/n"Longbottom, kindly do not reveal that you can't even/nperform a simple Switching Spell in front of anyone/nfrom Durmstrang!" Professor McGonagall barked at/nthe end of one particularly difficult lesson, during/nwhich Neville had accidentally transplanted his own/nears onto a cactus./n/nWhen they went down to breakfast on the morning of/nthe thirtieth of October, they found that the Great/nHall had been decorated overnight. Enormous silk/nbanners hung from the walls, each of them/nrepresenting a Hogwarts House: red with a gold lion/nfor Gryffindor, blue with a bronze eagle for/nRavenclaw, yellow with a black badger for Hufflepuff,/nand green with a silver serpent for Slytherin. Behind/nthe teachers' table, the largest banner of all bore the/nHogwarts coat of arms: lion, eagle, badger, and snake/nunited around a large letter H./n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione sat down beside Fred and/nGeorge at the Gryffindor table. Once again, and most/nunusually, they were sitting apart from everyone else/nand conversing in low voices. Ron led the way over to/nthem./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's a bummer, all right," George was saying gloomily/nto Fred. "But if he won't talk to us in person, we'll/nhave to send him the letter after all. Or we'll stuff it/ninto his hand. He can't avoid us forever."/n/n"Who's avoiding you?" said Ron, sitting down next to/nthem./n/n"Wish you would," said Fred, looking irritated at the/ninterruption./n/n"What's a bummer?" Ron asked George./n/n"Having a nosy git like you for a brother," said George./n/n"You two got any ideas on the Triwizard Tournament/nyet?" Harry asked. "Thought any more about trying to/nenter?"/n/n"I asked McGonagall how the champions are chosen/nbut she wasn't telling," said George bitterly. "She just/ntold me to shut up and get on with transfiguring my/nraccoon."/n/n"Wonder what the tasks are going to be?" said Ron/nthoughtfully. "You know, I bet we could do them,/nHarry. We've done dangerous stuff before. ..."/n/n"Not in front of a panel of judges, you haven't," said/nFred. "McGonagall says the champions get awarded/npoints according to how well they've done the tasks."/n/n"Who are the judges?" Harry asked./n/n"Well, the Heads of the participating schools are/nalways on the panel," said Hermione, and everyone/nlooked around at her, rather surprised, "because all/nthree of them were injured during the Tournament of/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n1792, when a cockatrice the champions were/nsupposed to be catching went on the rampage."/n/nShe noticed them all looking at her and said, with her/nusual air of impatience that nobody else had read all/nthe books she had, "It's all in Hogwarts, A History./nThough, of course, that book's not entirely reliable. A/nRevised History of Hogwarts would be a more/naccurate title. Or A Highly Biased and Selective/nHistory of Hogwarts, Which Glosses Over the Nastier/nAspects of the School."/n/n"What are you on about?" said Ron, though Harry/nthought he knew what was coming./n/n" House-elves\" said Hermione, her eyes flashing. "Not/nonce, in over a thousand pages, does Hogwarts, A/nHistory mention that we are all colluding in the/noppression of a hundred slaves!"/n/nHarry shook his head and applied himself to his/nscrambled eggs. His and Ron's lack of enthusiasm/nhad done nothing whatsoever to curb Hermione 's/ndetermination to pursue justice for house-elves. True,/nboth of them had paid two Sickles for a S.P.E.W./nbadge, but they had only done it to keep her quiet./nTheir Sickles had been wasted, however; if anything,/nthey seemed to have made Hermione more vociferous./nShe had been badgering Harry and Ron ever since,/nfirst to wear the badges, then to persuade others to do/nthe same, and she had also taken to rattling around/nthe Gryffindor common room every evening, cornering/npeople and shaking the collecting tin under their/nnoses./n/n"You do realize that your sheets are changed, your/nfires lit, your classrooms cleaned, and your food/ncooked by a group of magical creatures who are/nunpaid and enslaved?" she kept saying fiercely./n/n/n/n/n/nSome people, like Neville, had paid up just to stop/nHermione from glowering at them. A few seemed/nmildly interested in what she had to say, but were/nreluctant to take a more active role in campaigning./nMany regarded the whole thing as a joke./n/nRon now rolled his eyes at the ceiling, which was/nflooding them all in autumn sunlight, and Fred/nbecame extremely interested in his bacon (both twins/nhad refused to buy a S.P.E.W. badge). George,/nhowever, leaned in toward Hermione./n/n"Listen, have you ever been down in the kitchens,/nHermione?"/n/n"No, of course not," said Hermione curtly, "I hardly/nthink students are supposed to — "/n/n"Well, we have," said George, indicating Fred, "loads/nof times, to nick food. And we've met them, and/nthey're happy. They think they've got the best job in/nthe world — "/n/n"That's because they're uneducated and/nbrainwashed!" Hermione began hotly, but her next/nfew words were drowned out by the sudden/nwhooshing noise from overhead, which announced/nthe arrival of the post owls. Harry looked up at once,/nand saw Hedwig soaring toward him. Hermione/nstopped talking abruptly; she and Ron watched/nHedwig anxiously as she fluttered down onto Harry's/nshoulder, folded her wings, and held out her leg/nwearily./n/nHarry pulled off Sirius's reply and offered Hedwig his/nbacon rinds, which she ate gratefully. Then, checking/nthat Fred and George were safely immersed in further/ndiscussions about the Tri-wizard Tournament, Harry/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nread out Sirius's letter in a whisper to Ron and/nHermione./n/n/n/nNice try, Harry./n/nI'm back in the country and well hidden. I want you to/nkeep me posted on everything that's going on at/nHog warts. Don't use Hedwig, keep changing owls, and/ndon't worry about me, just watch out for yourself. Don't/nforget what I said about your scar./n/nSirius/n/n"Why d'you have to keep changing owls?" Ron asked/nin a low voice./n/n"Hedwig'll attract too much attention," said Hermione/nat once. "She stands out. A snowy owl that keeps/nreturning to wherever he's hiding ... I mean, they're/nnot native birds, are they?"/n/nHarry rolled up the letter and slipped it inside his/nrobes, wondering whether he felt more or less worried/nthan before. He supposed that Sirius managing to get/nback without being caught was something. He/ncouldn't deny either that the idea that Sirius was/nmuch nearer was reassuring; at least he wouldn't/nhave to wait so long for a response every time he/nwrote./n/n"Thanks, Hedwig," he said, stroking her. She hooted/nsleepily, dipped her beak briefly into his goblet of/norange juice, then took off again, clearly desperate for/na good long sleep in the Owlery./n/nThere was a pleasant feeling of anticipation in the air/nthat day. Nobody was very attentive in lessons, being/nmuch more interested in the arrival that evening of/nthe people from Beauxbatons and Durmstrang; even/n/n/n/n/n/nPotions was more bearable than usual, as it was half/nan hour shorter. When the bell rang early, Harry,/n/nRon, and Hermione hurried up to Gryffindor Tower,/ndeposited their bags and books as they had been/ninstructed, pulled on their cloaks, and rushed back/ndownstairs into the entrance hall./n/nThe Heads of Houses were ordering their students/ninto lines./n/n"Weasley, straighten your hat," Professor McGonagall/nsnapped at Ron. "Miss Patil, take that ridiculous/nthing out of your hair."/n/nParvati scowled and removed a large ornamental/nbutterfly from the end of her plait./n/n"Follow me, please," said Professor McGonagall. "First/nyears in front ... no pushing. ..."/n/nThey filed down the steps and lined up in front of the/ncastle. It was a cold, clear evening; dusk was falling/nand a pale, transparent-looking moon was already/nshining over the Forbidden Forest. Harry, standing/nbetween Ron and Hermione in the fourth row from/nthe front, saw Dennis Creevey positively shivering/nwith anticipation among the other first years./n/n"Nearly six," said Ron, checking his watch and then/nstaring down the drive that led to the front gates./n"How d'you reckon they're coming? The train?"/n/n"I doubt it," said Hermione./n/n"How, then? Broomsticks?" Harry suggested, looking/nup at the starry sky./n/n"I don't think so ... not from that far away. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"A Portkey?" Ron suggested. "Or they could Apparate/n— maybe you're allowed to do it under seventeen/nwherever they come from?"/n/n"You can't Apparate inside the Hogwarts grounds,/nhow often do I have to tell you?" said Hermione/nimpatiently./n/nThey scanned the darkening grounds excitedly, but/nnothing was moving; everything was still, silent, and/nquite as usual. Harry was starting to feel cold. He/nwished they'd hurry up. ... Maybe the foreign/nstudents were preparing a dramatic entrance. ... He/nremembered what Mr. Weasley had said back at the/ncampsite before the Quidditch World Cup: "always the/nsame — we can't resist showing off when we get/ntogether. ..."/n/nAnd then Dumbledore called out from the back row/nwhere he stood with the other teachers —/n/n"Aha! Unless I am very much mistaken, the delegation/nfrom Beauxbatons approaches!"/n/n"Where?" said many students eagerly, all looking in/ndifferent directions./n/n"There!" yelled a sixth year, pointing over the forest./n/nSomething large, much larger than a broomstick —/nor, indeed, a hundred broomsticks — was hurtling/nacross the deep blue sky toward the castle, growing/nlarger all the time./n/n"It's a dragon!" shrieked one of the first years, losing/nher head completely./n/n"Don't be stupid ... it's a flying house!" said Dennis/nCreevey./n/n/n/n/n/nDennis's guess was closer. ... As the gigantic black/nshape skimmed over the treetops of the Forbidden/nForest and the lights shining from the castle windows/nhit it, they saw a gigantic, powder-blue, horse-drawn/ncarriage, the size of a large house, soaring toward/nthem, pulled through the air by a dozen winged/nhorses, all palominos, and each the size of an/nelephant./n/nThe front three rows of students drew backward as/nthe carriage hurtled ever lower, coming in to land at a/ntremendous speed — then, with an almighty crash/nthat made Neville jump backward onto a Slytherin/nfifth year's foot, the horses' hooves, larger than dinner/nplates, hit the ground. A second later, the carriage/nlanded too, bouncing upon its vast wheels, while the/ngolden horses tossed their enormous heads and rolled/nlarge, fiery red eyes./n/nHarry just had time to see that the door of the/ncarriage bore a coat of arms (two crossed, golden/nwands, each emitting three stars) before it opened./n/nA boy in pale blue robes jumped down from the/ncarriage, bent forward, fumbled for a moment with/nsomething on the carriage floor, and unfolded a set of/ngolden steps. He sprang back respectfully. Then/nHarry saw a shining, high-heeled black shoe emerging/nfrom the inside of the carriage — a shoe the size of a/nchild's sled — followed, almost immediately, by the/nlargest woman he had ever seen in his life. The size of/nthe carriage, and of the horses, was immediately/nexplained. A few people gasped./n/nHarry had only ever seen one person as large as this/nwoman in his life, and that was Hagrid; he doubted/nwhether there was an inch difference in their heights./nYet somehow — maybe simply because he was used/nto Hagrid — this woman (now at the foot of the steps,/n/n/n/n/nand looking around at the waiting, wide-eyed crowd)/nseemed even more unnaturally large. As she stepped/ninto the light flooding from the entrance hall, she was/nrevealed to have a handsome, olive-skinned face;/nlarge, black, liquid-looking eyes; and a rather beaky/nnose. Her hair was drawn back in a shining knob at/nthe base of her neck. She was dressed from head to/nfoot in black satin, and many magnificent opals/ngleamed at her throat and on her thick fingers./n/nDumbledore started to clap; the students, following/nhis lead, broke into applause too, many of them/nstanding on tiptoe, the better to look at this woman./n/nHer face relaxed into a gracious smile and she walked/nforward toward Dumbledore, extending a glittering/nhand. Dumbledore, though tall himself, had barely to/nbend to kiss it./n/n"My dear Madame Maxime," he said. "Welcome to/nHogwarts."/n/n"Dumbly-dorr," said Madame Maxime in a deep voice./n"I 'ope I find you well?"/n/n"In excellent form, I thank you," said Dumbledore./n/n"My pupils," said Madame Maxime, waving one of her/nenormous hands carelessly behind her./n/nHarry, whose attention had been focused completely/nupon Madame Maxime, now noticed that about a/ndozen boys and girls, all, by the look of them, in their/nlate teens, had emerged from the carriage and were/nnow standing behind Madame Maxime. They were/nshivering, which was unsurprising, given that their/nrobes seemed to be made of fine silk, and none of/nthem were wearing cloaks. A few had wrapped scarves/nand shawls around their heads. From what Harry/n/n/n/n/ncould see of them (they were standing in Madame/nMaxime 's enormous shadow), they were staring up at/nHogwarts with apprehensive looks on their faces./n/n" 'As Karkaroff arrived yet?" Madame Maxime asked./n/n"He should be here any moment," said Dumbledore./n"Would you like to wait here and greet him or would/nyou prefer to step inside and warm up a trifle?"/n/n"Warm up, I think," said Madame Maxime. "But ze/n'orses — "/n/n"Our Care of Magical Creatures teacher will be/ndelighted to take care of them," said Dumbledore, "the/nmoment he has returned from dealing with a slight/nsituation that has arisen with some of his other — er/n— charges."/n/n"Skrewts," Ron muttered to Harry, grinning./n/n"My steeds require — er — forceful 'andling," said/nMadame Maxime, looking as though she doubted/nwhether any Care of Magical Creatures teacher at/nHogwarts could be up to the job. "Zey are very strong./n/n/n/n"I assure you that Hagrid will be well up to the job,"/nsaid Dumbledore, smiling./n/n"Very well," said Madame Maxime, bowing slightly./n"Will you please inform zis 'Agrid zat ze 'orses drink/nonly single-malt whiskey?"/n/n"It will be attended to," said Dumbledore, also bowing./n/n"Come," said Madame Maxime imperiously to her/nstudents, and the Hogwarts crowd parted to allow her/nand her students to pass up the stone steps./n/n/n/n/n/n"How big d'you reckon Durmstrang's horses are going/nto be?" Seamus Finnigan said, leaning around/nLavender and Parvati to address Harry and Ron./n/n"Well, if they're any bigger than this lot, even Hagrid/nwon't be able to handle them," said Harry. "That's if/nhe hasn't been attacked by his skrewts. Wonder/nwhat's up with them?"/n/n"Maybe they've escaped," said Ron hopefully./n/n"Oh don't say that," said Hermione with a shudder./n"Imagine that lot loose on the grounds. ..."/n/nThey stood, shivering slightly now, waiting for the/nDurmstrang party to arrive. Most people were gazing/nhopefully up at the sky. For a few minutes, the/nsilence was broken only by Madame Maxime's huge/nhorses snorting and stamping. But then —/n/n"Can you hear something?" said Ron suddenly./n/nHarry listened; a loud and oddly eerie noise was/ndrifting toward them from out of the darkness: a/nmuffled rumbling and sucking sound, as though an/nimmense vacuum cleaner were moving along a/nriverbed. .../n/n"The lake!" yelled Lee Jordan, pointing down at it./n"Look at the lake!"/n/nFrom their position at the top of the lawns/noverlooking the grounds, they had a clear view of the/nsmooth black surface of the water — except that the/nsurface was suddenly not smooth at all. Some/ndisturbance was taking place deep in the center; great/nbubbles were forming on the surface, waves were now/nwashing over the muddy banks — and then, out in/nthe very middle of the lake, a whirlpool appeared, as if/n/n/n/n/na giant plug had just been pulled out of the lake's/nfloor. .../n/nWhat seemed to be a long, black pole began to rise/nslowly out of the heart of the whirlpool . . . and then/nHarry saw the rigging. . . ./n/n"It's a mast!" he said to Ron and Hermione./n/nSlowly, magnificently, the ship rose out of the water,/ngleaming in the moonlight. It had a strangely skeletal/nlook about it, as though it were a resurrected wreck,/nand the dim, misty lights shimmering at its portholes/nlooked like ghostly eyes. Finally, with a great sloshing/nnoise, the ship emerged entirely, bobbing on the/nturbulent water, and began to glide toward the bank./nA few moments later, they heard the splash of an/nanchor being thrown down in the shallows, and the/nthud of a plank being lowered onto the bank./n/nPeople were disembarking; they could see their/nsilhouettes passing the lights in the ship's portholes./nAll of them, Harry noticed, seemed to be built along/nthe lines of Crabbe and Goyle . . . but then, as they/ndrew nearer, walking up the lawns into the light/nstreaming from the entrance hall, he saw that their/nbulk was really due to the fact that they were wearing/ncloaks of some kind of shaggy, matted fur. But the/nman who was leading them up to the castle was/nwearing furs of a different sort: sleek and silver, like/nhis hair./n/n"Dumbledore!" he called heartily as he walked up the/nslope. "How are you, my dear fellow, how are you?"/n/n"Blooming, thank you, Professor Karkaroff,"/nDumbledore replied./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nKarkaroff had a fruity, unctuous voice; when he/nstepped into the light pouring from the front doors of/nthe castle they saw that he was tall and thin like/nDumbledore, but his white hair was short, and his/ngoatee (finishing in a small curl) did not entirely hide/nhis rather weak chin. When he reached Dumbledore,/nhe shook hands with both of his own./n/n"Dear old Hogwarts," he said, looking up at the castle/nand smiling; his teeth were rather yellow, and Harry/nnoticed that his smile did not extend to his eyes,/nwhich remained cold and shrewd. "How good it is to/nbe here, how good. ... Viktor, come along, into the/nwarmth ... you don't mind, Dumbledore? Viktor has a/nslight head cold. ..."/n/nKarkaroff beckoned forward one of his students. As/nthe boy passed, Harry caught a glimpse of a/nprominent curved nose and thick black eyebrows. He/ndidn't need the punch on the arm Ron gave him, or/nthe hiss in his ear, to recognize that profile./n/n"Harry — it's Krum\"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nt'fyfflapier- l6/n/n/n/n

title: The Goblet Of Fire
text: /n"I don't believe it!" Ron said, in a stunned voice, as/nthe Hogwarts students filed back up the steps behind/nthe party from Durmstrang. "Krum, Harry! Viktor/nKruml"/n/n"For heaven's sake, Ron, he's only a Quidditch/nplayer," said Hermione./n/n"Only a Quidditch player?" Ron said, looking at her as/nthough he couldn't believe his ears. "Hermione — he's/none of the best Seekers in the world! I had no idea he/nwas still at school!"/n/nAs they recrossed the entrance hall with the rest of/nthe Hogwarts students heading for the Great Hall,/nHarry saw Lee Jordan jumping up and down on the/nsoles of his feet to get a better look at the back of/nKrum's head. Several sixth-year girls were frantically/nsearching their pockets as they walked —/n/n"Oh I don't believe it, I haven't got a single quill on me/n/n??/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"D'you think he'd sign my hat in lipstick?"/n/n/n/n"Really," Hermione said loftily as they passed the/ngirls, now squabbling over the lipstick./n/n"I'm getting his autograph if I can," said Ron. "You/nhaven't got a quill, have you, Harry?"/n/n"Nope, they're upstairs in my bag," said Harry./n/nThey walked over to the Gryffindor table and sat/ndown. Ron took care to sit on the side facing the/ndoorway, because Krum and his fellow Durmstrang/nstudents were still gathered around it, apparently/nunsure about where they should sit. The students/nfrom Beauxbatons had chosen seats at the Ravenclaw/ntable. They were looking around the Great Hall with/nglum expressions on their faces. Three of them were/nstill clutching scarves and shawls around their heads./n/n"It's not that cold," said Hermione defensively. "Why/ndidn't they bring cloaks?"/n/n"Over here! Come and sit over here!" Ron hissed./n/n"Over here! Hermione, budge up, make a space — "/n/n"What?"/n/n"Too late," said Ron bitterly./n/nViktor Krum and his fellow Durmstrang students had/nsettled themselves at the Slytherin table. Harry could/nsee Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle looking very smug/nabout this. As he watched, Malfoy bent forward to/nspeak to Krum./n/n"Yeah, that's right, smarm up to him, Malfoy," said/nRon scathingly. "I bet Krum can see right through/nhim, though ... bet he gets people fawning over him/n/n/n/n/n/nall the time. ... Where d'you reckon they're going to/nsleep? We could offer him a space in our dormitory,/nHarry ... I wouldn't mind giving him my bed, I could/nkip on a camp bed."/n/nHermione snorted./n/n"They look a lot happier than the Beauxbatons lot,"/nsaid Harry./n/nThe Durmstrang students were pulling off their heavy/nfurs and looking up at the starry black ceiling with/nexpressions of interest; a couple of them were picking/nup the golden plates and goblets and examining/nthem, apparently impressed./n/nUp at the staff table, Filch, the caretaker, was adding/nchairs. He was wearing his moldy old tailcoat in/nhonor of the occasion. Harry was surprised to see/nthat he added four chairs, two on either side of/nDumbledore's./n/n"But there are only two extra people," Harry said./n"Why's Filch putting out four chairs, who else is/ncoming?"/n/n"Eh?" said Ron vaguely. He was still staring avidly at/nKrum./n/nWhen all the students had entered the Hall and/nsettled down at their House tables, the staff entered,/nfiling up to the top table and taking their seats. Last/nin line were Professor Dumbledore, Professor/nKarkaroff, and Madame Maxime. When their/nheadmistress appeared, the pupils from Beauxbatons/nleapt to their feet. A few of the Hogwarts students/nlaughed. The Beauxbatons party appeared quite/nunembarrassed, however, and did not resume their/nseats until Madame Maxime had sat down on/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore 's left-hand side. Dumbledore remained/nstanding, and a silence fell over the Great Hall./n/n"Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, ghosts and —/nmost particularly — guests," said Dumbledore,/nbeaming around at the foreign students. "I have great/npleasure in welcoming you all to Hogwarts.
