Viktor Krum was walking side by/nside with Karkaroff, and the other Durmstrang/nstudents were straggling along behind them. Ron/nwatched Krum excitedly, but Krum did not look/naround as he reached the front doors a little ahead of/nHermione, Ron, and Harry and proceeded through/nthem./n/n/n/n/n/nWhen they entered the candlelit Great Hall it was/nalmost full. The Goblet of Fire had been moved; it was/nnow standing in front of Dumbledore 's empty chair at/nthe teachers' table. Fred and George — clean-shaven/nagain — seemed to have taken their disappointment/nfairly well./n/n"Hope it's Angelina," said Fred as Harry, Ron, and/nHermione sat down./n/n"So do I!" said Hermione breathlessly. "Well, we'll/nsoon know!"/n/nThe Halloween feast seemed to take much longer than/nusual. Perhaps because it was their second feast in/ntwo days, Harry didn't seem to fancy the/nextravagantly prepared food as much as he would/nhave normally. Like everyone else in the Hall, judging/nby the constantly craning necks, the impatient/nexpressions on every face, the fidgeting, and the/nstanding up to see whether Dumbledore had finished/neating yet, Harry simply wanted the plates to clear,/nand to hear who had been selected as champions./n/nAt long last, the golden plates returned to their/noriginal spotless state; there was a sharp upswing in/nthe level of noise within the Hall, which died away/nalmost instantly as Dumbledore got to his feet. On/neither side of him, Professor Karkaroff and Madame/nMaxime looked as tense and expectant as anyone./nLudo Bagman was beaming and winking at various/nstudents. Mr. Crouch, however, looked quite/nuninterested, almost bored./n/n"Well, the goblet is almost ready to make its decision,"/nsaid Dumbledore. "I estimate that it requires one/nmore minute. Now, when the champions' names are/ncalled, I would ask them please to come up to the top/nof the Hall, walk along the staff table, and go through/n/n/n/n/ninto the next chamber" — he indicated the door/nbehind the staff table — "where they will be receiving/ntheir first instructions."/n/nHe took out his wand and gave a great sweeping wave/nwith it; at once, all the candles except those inside the/ncarved pumpkins were extinguished, plunging them/ninto a state of semidarkness. The Goblet of Fire now/nshone more brightly than anything in the whole Hall,/nthe sparkling bright, bluey-whiteness of the flames/nalmost painful on the eyes. Everyone watched,/nwaiting. ... A few people kept checking their watches./n/n/n/n"Any second," Lee Jordan whispered, two seats away/nfrom Harry./n/nThe flames inside the goblet turned suddenly red/nagain. Sparks began to fly from it. Next moment, a/ntongue of flame shot into the air, a charred piece of/nparchment fluttered out of it — the whole room/ngasped./n/nDumbledore caught the piece of parchment and held/nit at arm's length, so that he could read it by the light/nof the flames, which had turned back to blue-white./n/n"The champion for Durmstrang," he read, in a strong,/nclear voice, "will be Viktor Krum."/n/n"No surprises there!" yelled Ron as a storm of/napplause and cheering swept the Hall. Harry saw/nViktor Krum rise from the Slytherin table and slouch/nup toward Dumbledore; he turned right, walked along/nthe staff table, and disappeared through the door into/nthe next chamber./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Bravo, Viktor!" boomed Karkaroff, so loudly that/neveryone could hear him, even over all the applause./n"Knew you had it in you!"/n/nThe clapping and chatting died down. Now everyone's/nattention was focused again on the goblet, which,/nseconds later, turned red once more. A second piece/nof parchment shot out of it, propelled by the flames./n/n"The champion for Beauxbatons," said Dumbledore,/n/n"is Fleur Delacour!"/n/n"It's her, Ron!" Harry shouted as the girl who so/nresembled a veela got gracefully to her feet, shook/nback her sheet of silvery blonde hair, and swept up/nbetween the Ravenclaw and Hufflepuff tables./n/n"Oh look, they're all disappointed," Hermione said/nover the noise, nodding toward the remainder of the/nBeauxbatons party. "Disappointed" was a bit of an/nunderstatement, Harry thought. Two of the girls who/nhad not been selected had dissolved into tears and/nwere sobbing with their heads on their arms./n/nWhen Fleur Delacour too had vanished into the side/nchamber, silence fell again, but this time it was a/nsilence so stiff with excitement you could almost taste/nit. The Hogwarts champion next .../n/nAnd the Goblet of Fire turned red once more; sparks/nshowered out of it; the tongue of flame shot high into/nthe air, and from its tip Dumbledore pulled the third/npiece of parchment./n/n"The Hogwarts champion," he called, "is Cedric/nDiggory!"/n/n"No!" said Ron loudly, but nobody heard him except/nHarry; the uproar from the next table was too great./n/n/n/n/n/nEvery single Hufflepuff had jumped to his or her feet,/nscreaming and stamping, as Cedric made his way/npast them, grinning broadly, and headed off toward/nthe chamber behind the teachers' table. Indeed, the/napplause for Cedric went on so long that it was some/ntime before Dumbledore could make himself heard/nagain./n/n"Excellent!" Dumbledore called happily as at last the/ntumult died down. "Well, we now have our three/nchampions. I am sure I can count upon all of you,/nincluding the remaining students from Beauxbatons/nand Durmstrang, to give your champions every ounce/nof support you can muster. By cheering your/nchampion on, you will contribute in a very real — "/n/nBut Dumbledore suddenly stopped speaking, and it/nwas apparent to everybody what had distracted him./n/nThe fire in the goblet had just turned red again./nSparks were flying out of it. A long flame shot/nsuddenly into the air, and borne upon it was another/npiece of parchment./n/nAutomatically, it seemed, Dumbledore reached out a/nlong hand and seized the parchment. He held it out/nand stared at the name written upon it. There was a/nlong pause, during which Dumbledore stared at the/nslip in his hands, and everyone in the room stared at/nDumbledore. And then Dumbledore cleared his throat/nand read out —/n/n" Harry Potter."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Four Champions
text: /nHarry sat there, aware that every head in the Great/nHall had turned to look at him. He was stunned. He/nfelt numb. He was surely dreaming. He had not heard/ncorrectly./n/nThere was no applause. A buzzing, as though of angry/nbees, was starting to fill the Hall; some students were/nstanding up to get a better look at Harry as he sat,/nfrozen, in his seat./n/nUp at the top table, Professor McGonagall had got to/nher feet and swept past Ludo Bagman and Professor/nKarkaroff to whisper urgently to Professor/nDumbledore, who bent his ear toward her, frowning/nslightly./n/nHarry turned to Ron and Hermione; beyond them, he/nsaw the long Gryffindor table all watching him,/nopenmouthed./n/n"I didn't put my name in," Harry said blankly. "You/nknow I didn't."/n/n/n/n/nBoth of them stared just as blankly back./n/nAt the top table, Professor Dumbledore had/nstraightened up, nodding to Professor McGonagall./n/n"Harry Potter!" he called again. "Harry! Up here, if you/nplease!"/n/n"Go on," Hermione whispered, giving Harry a slight/npush./n/nHarry got to his feet, trod on the hem of his robes,/nand stumbled slightly. He set off up the gap between/nthe Gryffindor and Hufflepuff tables. It felt like an/nimmensely long walk; the top table didn't seem to be/ngetting any nearer at all, and he could feel hundreds/nand hundreds of eyes upon him, as though each were/na searchlight. The buzzing grew louder and louder./nAfter what seemed like an hour, he was right in front/nof Dumbledore, feeling the stares of all the teachers/nupon him./n/n"Well ... through the door, Harry," said Dumbledore./nHe wasn't smiling./n/nHarry moved off along the teachers' table. Hagrid was/nseated right at the end. He did not wink at Harry, or/nwave, or give any of his usual signs of greeting. He/nlooked completely astonished and stared at Harry as/nhe passed like everyone else. Harry went through the/ndoor out of the Great Hall and found himself in a/nsmaller room, lined with paintings of witches and/nwizards. A handsome fire was roaring in the fireplace/nopposite him./n/nThe faces in the portraits turned to look at him as he/nentered. He saw a wizened witch flit out of the frame/nof her picture and into the one next to it, which/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncontained a wizard with a walrus mustache. The/nwizened witch started whispering in his ear./n/nViktor Krum, Cedric Diggory, and Fleur Delacour/nwere grouped around the fire. They looked strangely/nimpressive, silhouetted against the flames. Krum,/nhunched-up and brooding, was leaning against the/nmantelpiece, slightly apart from the other two. Cedric/nwas standing with his hands behind his back, staring/ninto the fire. Fleur Delacour looked around when/nHarry walked in and threw back her sheet of long,/nsilvery hair./n/n"What is it?" she said. "Do zey want us back in ze/nHall?"/n/nShe thought he had come to deliver a message. Harry/ndidn't know how to explain what had just happened./nHe just stood there, looking at the three champions. It/nstruck him how very tall all of them were./n/nThere was a sound of scurrying feet behind him, and/nLudo Bagman entered the room. He took Harry by the/narm and led him forward./n/n"Extraordinary!" he muttered, squeezing Harry's arm./n"Absolutely extraordinary! Gentlemen ... lady," he/nadded, approaching the fireside and addressing the/nother three. "May I introduce — incredible though it/nmay seem — the fourth Triwizard champion?"/n/nViktor Krum straightened up. His surly face darkened/nas he surveyed Harry. Cedric looked nonplussed. He/nlooked from Bagman to Harry and back again as/nthough sure he must have misheard what Bagman/nhad said. Fleur Delacour, however, tossed her hair,/nsmiling, and said, "Oh, vairy funny joke, Meester/nBagman."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Joke?" Bagman repeated, bewildered. "No, no, not at/nall! Harry's name just came out of the Goblet of Fire!"/n/nKrum's thick eyebrows contracted slightly. Cedric was/nstill looking politely bewildered. Fleur frowned./n/n"But evidently zair 'as been a mistake," she said/ncontemptuously to Bagman. " 'E cannot compete. 'E is/ntoo young."/n/n"Well ... it is amazing," said Bagman, rubbing his/nsmooth chin and smiling down at Harry. "But, as you/nknow, the age restriction was only imposed this year/nas an extra safety measure. And as his name's come/nout of the goblet ... I mean, I don't think there can be/nany ducking out at this stage. ... It's down in the/nrules, you're obliged ... Harry will just have to do the/nbest he — "/n/nThe door behind them opened again, and a large/ngroup of people came in: Professor Dumbledore,/nfollowed closely by Mr. Crouch, Professor Karkaroff,/nMadame Maxime, Professor McGonagall, and/nProfessor Snape. Harry heard the buzzing of the/nhundreds of students on the other side of the wall,/nbefore Professor McGonagall closed the door./n/n"Madame Maxime!" said Fleur at once, striding over to/nher headmistress. "Zey are saying zat zis little boy is/nto compete also!"/n/nSomewhere under Harry's numb disbelief he felt a/nripple of anger. Little boy ?/n/nMadame Maxime had drawn herself up to her full,/nand considerable, height. The top of her handsome/nhead brushed the candle-filled chandelier, and her/ngigantic black-satin bosom swelled./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What is ze meaning of zis, Dumbly-dorr?" she said/nimperiously./n/n"I'd rather like to know that myself, Dumbledore,"/nsaid Professor Karkaroff. He was wearing a steely/nsmile, and his blue eyes were like chips of ice. "Two/nHogwarts champions? I don't remember anyone/ntelling me the host school is allowed two champions/n— or have I not read the rules carefully enough?"/n/nHe gave a short and nasty laugh./n/n"C'est impossible," said Madame Maxime, whose/nenormous hand with its many superb opals was/nresting upon Fleur's shoulder. " 'Ogwarts cannot 'ave/ntwo champions. It is most injust."/n/n"We were under the impression that your Age Line/nwould keep out younger contestants, Dumbledore,"/nsaid Karkaroff, his steely smile still in place, though/nhis eyes were colder than ever. "Otherwise, we would,/nof course, have brought along a wider selection of/ncandidates from our own schools."/n/n"It's no one's fault but Potter's, Karkaroff," said Snape/nsoftly. His black eyes were alight with malice. "Don't/ngo blaming Dumbledore for Potter's determination to/nbreak rules. He has been crossing lines ever since he/narrived here — "/n/n"Thank you, Severus," said Dumbledore firmly, and/nSnape went quiet, though his eyes still glinted/nmalevolently through his curtain of greasy black hair./n/nProfessor Dumbledore was now looking down at/nHarry, who looked right back at him, trying to discern/nthe expression of the eyes behind the half-moon/nspectacles./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Did you put your name into the Goblet of Fire,/nHarry?" he asked calmly./n/n"No," said Harry. He was very aware of everybody/nwatching him closely. Snape made a soft noise of/nimpatient disbelief in the shadows./n/n"Did you ask an older student to put it into the Goblet/nof Fire for you?" said Professor Dumbledore, ignoring/nSnape./n/n"No," said Harry vehemently./n/n"Ah, but of course 'e is lying!" cried Madame Maxime./nSnape was now shaking his head, his lip curling./n/n"He could not have crossed the Age Line," said/nProfessor McGonagall sharply. "I am sure we are all/nagreed on that — "/n/n"Dumbly-dorr must 'ave made a mistake wiz ze line,"/nsaid Madame Maxime, shrugging./n/n"It is possible, of course," said Dumbledore politely/n/n"Dumbledore, you know perfectly well you did not/nmake a mistake!" said Professor McGonagall angrily./n"Really, what nonsense! Harry could not have crossed/nthe line himself, and as Professor Dumbledore/nbelieves that he did not persuade an older student to/ndo it for him, I'm sure that should be good enough for/neverybody else!"/n/nShe shot a very angry look at Professor Snape./n/n"Mr. Crouch ... Mr. Bagman," said Karkaroff, his voice/nunctuous once more, "you are our — er — objective/njudges. Surely you will agree that this is most/nirregular?"/n/n/n/n/n/nBagman wiped his round, boyish face with his/nhandkerchief and looked at Mr. Crouch, who was/nstanding outside the circle of the firelight, his face/nhalf hidden in shadow. He looked slightly eerie, the/nhalf darkness making him look much older, giving/nhim an almost skull-like appearance. When he spoke,/nhowever, it was in his usual curt voice./n/n"We must follow the rules, and the rules state clearly/nthat those people whose names come out of the/nGoblet of Fire are bound to compete in the/ntournament."/n/n"Well, Barty knows the rule book back to front," said/nBagman, beaming and turning back to Karkaroff and/nMadame Maxime, as though the matter was now/nclosed./n/n"I insist upon resubmitting the names of the rest of/nmy students," said Karkaroff. He had dropped his/nunctuous tone and his smile now. His face wore a/nvery ugly look indeed. "You will set up the Goblet of/nFire once more, and we will continue adding names/nuntil each school has two champions. It's only fair,/nDumbledore."/n/n"But Karkaroff, it doesn't work like that," said/nBagman. "The Goblet of Fire's just gone out — it won't/nreignite until the start of the next tournament — "/n/n" — in which Durmstrang will most certainly not be/ncompeting!" exploded Karkaroff. "After all our/nmeetings and negotiations and compromises, I little/nexpected something of this nature to occur! I have/nhalf a mind to leave now!"/n/n"Empty threat, Karkaroff," growled a voice from near/nthe door. "You can't leave your champion now. He's/ngot to compete. They've all got to compete. Binding/n/n/n/n/n/nmagical contract, like Dumbledore said. Convenient,/neh?"/n/n/n/nMoody had just entered the room. He limped toward/nthe fire, and with every right step he took, there was a/nloud clunk./n/n"Convenient?" said Karkaroff. "I'm afraid I don't/nunderstand you, Moody."/n/nHarry could tell he was trying to sound disdainful, as/nthough what Moody was saying was barely worth his/nnotice, but his hands gave him away; they had balled/nthemselves into fists./n/n"Don't you?" said Moody quietly. "It's very simple,/nKarkaroff. Someone put Potter's name in that goblet/nknowing he'd have to compete if it came out."/n/n"Evidently, someone 'oo wished to give 'Ogwarts two/nbites at ze apple!" said Madame Maxime./n/n"I quite agree, Madame Maxime," said Karkaroff,/nbowing to her. "I shall be lodging complaints with the/nMinistry of Magic and the International Confederation/nof Wizards — "/n/n"If anyone's got reason to complain, it's Potter,"/ngrowled Moody, "but ... funny thing ... I don't hear/nhim saying a word. ..."/n/n"Why should 'e complain?" burst out Fleur Delacour,/nstamping her foot. " 'E 'as ze chance to compete, 'asn't/n'e? We 'ave all been 'oping to be chosen for weeks and/nweeks! Ze honor for our schools! A thousand Galleons/nin prize money — zis is a chance many would die for!"/n/n"Maybe someone's hoping Potter is going to die for it,"/nsaid Moody, with the merest trace of a growl./n/n/n/n/n/nAn extremely tense silence followed these words. Ludo/nBagman, who was looking very anxious indeed,/nbounced nervously up and down on his feet and said,/n"Moody, old man ... what a thing to say!"/n/n"We all know Professor Moody considers the morning/nwasted if he hasn't discovered six plots to murder him/nbefore lunchtime," said Karkaroff loudly. "Apparently/nhe is now teaching his students to fear assassination/ntoo. An odd quality in a Defense Against the Dark/nArts teacher, Dumbledore, but no doubt you had your/nreasons."/n/n"Imagining things, am I?" growled Moody. "Seeing/nthings, eh? It was a skilled witch or wizard who put/nthe boy's name in that goblet. ..."/n/n"Ah, what evidence is zere of zat?" said Madame/nMaxime, throwing up her huge hands./n/n"Because they hoodwinked a very powerful magical/nobject!" said Moody. "It would have needed an/nexceptionally strong Confundus Charm to bamboozle/nthat goblet into forgetting that only three schools/ncompete in the tournament. ... I'm guessing they/nsubmitted Potter's name under a fourth school, to/nmake sure he was the only one in his category. ..."/n/n"You seem to have given this a great deal of thought,/nMoody," said Karkaroff coldly, "and a very ingenious/ntheory it is — though of course, I heard you recently/ngot it into your head that one of your birthday/npresents contained a cunningly disguised basilisk/negg, and smashed it to pieces before realizing it was a/ncarriage clock. So you'll understand if we don't take/nyou entirely seriously. ..."/n/n"There are those who'll turn innocent occasions to/ntheir advantage," Moody retorted in a menacing voice./n/n/n/n/n/n"It's my job to think the way Dark wizards do,/nKarkaroff — as you ought to remember. ..."/n/n"Alas tor!" said Dumbledore warningly. Harry/nwondered for a moment whom he was speaking to,/nbut then realized "Mad-Eye" could hardly be Moody's/nreal first name. Moody fell silent, though still/nsurveying Karkaroff with satisfaction — Karkaroff's/nface was burning./n/n"How this situation arose, we do not know," said/nDumbledore, speaking to everyone gathered in the/nroom. "It seems to me, however, that we have no/nchoice but to accept it. Both Cedric and Harry have/nbeen chosen to compete in the Tournament. This,/ntherefore, they will do. ..."/n/n"Ah, but Dumbly-dorr — "/n/n"My dear Madame Maxime, if you have an alternative,/n/nI would be delighted to hear it."/n/nDumbledore waited, but Madame Maxime did not/nspeak, she merely glared. She wasn't the only one/neither. Snape looked furious; Karkaroff livid; Bagman,/nhowever, looked rather excited./n/n"Well, shall we crack on, then?" he said, rubbing his/nhands together and smiling around the room. "Got to/ngive our champions their instructions, haven't we?/nBarty, want to do the honors?"/n/nMr. Crouch seemed to come out of a deep reverie./n/n"Yes," he said, "instructions. Yes ... the first task ..."/n/nHe moved forward into the firelight. Close up, Harry/nthought he looked ill. There were dark shadows/nbeneath his eyes and a thin, papery look about his/n/n/n/n/n/nwrinkled skin that had not been there at the/nQuidditch World Cup./n/n"The first task is designed to test your daring," he told/nHarry, Cedric, Fleur, and Viktor, "so we are not going/nto be telling you what it is. Courage in the face of the/nunknown is an important quality in a wizard . . . very/nimportant. .../n/n"The first task will take place on November the/ntwenty-fourth, in front of the other students and the/npanel of judges./n/n"The champions are not permitted to ask for or accept/nhelp of any kind from their teachers to complete the/ntasks in the tournament. The champions will face the/nfirst challenge armed only with their wands. They will/nreceive information about the second task when the/nfirst is over. Owing to the demanding and time-/nconsuming nature of the tournament, the champions/nare exempted from end-of-year tests."/n/nMr. Crouch turned to look at Dumbledore./n/n"I think that's all, is it, Albus?"/n/n"I think so," said Dumbledore, who was looking at Mr./nCrouch with mild concern. "Are you sure you/nwouldn't like to stay at Hogwarts tonight, Barty?"/n/n"No, Dumbledore, I must get back to the Ministry,"/nsaid Mr. Crouch. "It is a very busy, very difficult time/nat the moment. ... I've left young Weatherby in/ncharge. ... Very enthusiastic ... a little/noverenthusiastic, if truth be told. ..."/n/n"You'll come and have a drink before you go, at/nleast?" said Dumbledore./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Come on, Barty, I'm staying!" said Bagman brightly./n"It's all happening at Hogwarts now, you know, much/nmore exciting here than at the office!"/n/n"I think not, Ludo," said Crouch with a touch of his/nold impatience./n/n"Professor Karkaroff — Madame Maxime — a/nnightcap?" said Dumbledore./n/nBut Madame Maxime had already put her arm/naround Fleur's shoulders and was leading her swiftly/nout of the room. Harry could hear them both talking/nvery fast in French as they went off into the Great/nHall. Karkaroff beckoned to Krum, and they, too,/nexited, though in silence./n/n"Harry, Cedric, I suggest you go up to bed," said/nDumbledore, smiling at both of them. "I am sure/nGryffindor and Hufflepuff are waiting to celebrate with/nyou, and it would be a shame to deprive them of this/nexcellent excuse to make a great deal of mess and/nnoise."/n/nHarry glanced at Cedric, who nodded, and they left/ntogether./n/nThe Great Hall was deserted now; the candles had/nburned low, giving the jagged smiles of the pumpkins/nan eerie, flickering quality./n/n"So," said Cedric, with a slight smile. "We're playing/nagainst each other again!"/n/n"I s'pose," said Harry. He really couldn't think of/nanything to say. The inside of his head seemed to be/nin complete disarray, as though his brain had been/nransacked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So ... tell me ..." said Cedric as they reached the/nentrance hall, which was now lit only by torches in/nthe absence of the Goblet of Fire. "How did you get/nyour name in?"/n/n"I didn't," said Harry, staring up at him. "I didn't put/nit in. I was telling the truth."/n/n"Ah ... okay," said Cedric. Harry could tell Cedric/ndidn't believe him. "Well ... see you, then."/n/nInstead of going up the marble staircase, Cedric/nheaded for a door to its right. Harry stood listening to/nhim going down the stone steps beyond it, then,/nslowly, he started to climb the marble ones./n/nWas anyone except Ron and Hermione going to/nbelieve him, or would they all think he'd put himself/nin for the tournament? Yet how could anyone think/nthat, when he was facing competitors who'd had three/nyears' more magical education than he had — when/nhe was now facing tasks that not only sounded very/ndangerous, but which were to be performed in front of/nhundreds of people? Yes, he'd thought about it ... he'd/nfantasized about it ... but it had been a joke, really,/nan idle sort of dream ... he'd never really, seriously/nconsidered entering. .../n/nBut someone else had considered it ... someone else/nhad wanted him in the tournament, and had made/nsure he was entered. Why? To give him a treat? He/ndidn't think so, somehow. .../n/nTo see him make a fool of himself? Well, they were/nlikely to get their wish. .../n/nBut to get him killed?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWas Moody just being his usual paranoid self?/nCouldn't someone have put Harry's name in the/ngoblet as a trick, a practical joke? Did anyone really/nwant him dead?/n/nHarry was able to answer that at once. Yes, someone/nwanted him dead, someone had wanted him dead/never since he had been a year old ... Lord Voldemort./nBut how could Voldemort have ensured that Harry's/nname got into the Goblet of Fire? Voldemort was/nsupposed to be far away, in some distant country, in/nhiding, alone ... feeble and powerless. .../n/nYet in that dream he had had, just before he had/nawoken with his scar hurting, Voldemort had not/nbeen alone ... he had been talking to Wormtail .../nplotting Harry's murder. . . ./n/nHarry got a shock to find himself facing the Fat Lady/nalready. He had barely noticed where his feet were/ncarrying him. It was also a surprise to see that she/nwas not alone in her frame. The wizened witch who/nhad flitted into her neighbor's painting when he had/njoined the champions downstairs was now sitting/nsmugly beside the Fat Lady. She must have dashed/nthrough every picture lining seven staircases to reach/nhere before him. Both she and the Fat Lady were/nlooking down at him with the keenest interest./n/n"Well, well, well," said the Fat Lady, "Violet's just told/nme everything. Who's just been chosen as school/nchampion, then?"/n/n"Balderdash," said Harry dully./n/n"It most certainly isn't!" said the pale witch/nindignantly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No, no, Vi, it's the password," said the Fat Lady/nsoothingly, and she swung forward on her hinges to/nlet Harry into the common room./n/nThe blast of noise that met Harry's ears when the/nportrait opened almost knocked him backward. Next/nthing he knew, he was being wrenched inside the/ncommon room by about a dozen pairs of hands, and/nwas facing the whole of Gryffindor House, all of whom/nwere screaming, applauding, and whistling./n/n"You should've told us you'd entered!" bellowed Fred;/nhe looked half annoyed, half deeply impressed./n/n"How did you do it without getting a beard? Brilliant!"/nroared George./n/n"I didn't," Harry said. "I don't know how — "/n/nBut Angelina had now swooped down upon him; "Oh/nif it couldn't be me, at least it's a Gryffindor — "/n/n"You'll be able to pay back Diggory for that last/nQuidditch match, Harry!" shrieked Katie Bell, another/nof the Gryffindor Chasers./n/n"We've got food, Harry, come and have some — "/n/n"I'm not hungry, I had enough at the feast — "/n/nBut nobody wanted to hear that he wasn't hungry;/nnobody wanted to hear that he hadn't put his name in/nthe goblet; not one single person seemed to have/nnoticed that he wasn't at all in the mood to celebrate./n... Lee Jordan had unearthed a Gryffindor banner/nfrom somewhere, and he insisted on draping it/naround Harry like a cloak. Harry couldn't get away;/nwhenever he tried to sidle over to the staircase up to/nthe dormitories, the crowd around him closed ranks,/n/n/n/n/nforcing another butterbeer on him, stuffing crisps and/npeanuts into his hands. ... Everyone wanted to know/nhow he had done it, how he had tricked Dumbledore's/nAge Line and managed to get his name into the/ngoblet. .../n/n"I didn't," he said, over and over again, "I don't know/nhow it happened."/n/nBut for all the notice anyone took, he might just as/nwell not have answered at all./n/n"I'm tired!" he bellowed finally, after nearly half an/nhour. "No, seriously, George — I'm going to bed — "/n/nHe wanted more than anything to find Ron and/nHermione, to find a bit of sanity, but neither of them/nseemed to be in the common room. Insisting that he/nneeded to sleep, and almost flattening the little/nCreevey brothers as they attempted to waylay him at/nthe foot of the stairs, Harry managed to shake/neveryone off and climb up to the dormitory as fast as/nhe could./n/nTo his great relief, he found Ron was lying on his bed/nin the otherwise empty dormitory, still fully dressed./nHe looked up when Harry slammed the door behind/nhim./n/n"Where 've you been?" Harry said./n/n"Oh hello," said Ron./n/nHe was grinning, but it was a very odd, strained sort/nof grin. Harry suddenly became aware that he was/nstill wearing the scarlet Gryffindor banner that Lee/nhad tied around him. He hastened to take it off, but it/nwas knotted very tightly. Ron lay on the bed without/nmoving, watching Harry struggle to remove it./n/n/n/n/n/n"So," he said, when Harry had finally removed the/nbanner and thrown it into a corner./n/n"Congratulations . "/n/n"What d'you mean, congratulations?" said Harry,/nstaring at Ron. There was definitely something wrong/nwith the way Ron was smiling: It was more like a/ngrimace./n/n"Well ... no one else got across the Age Line," said/nRon. "Not even Fred and George. What did you use —/nthe Invisibility Cloak?"/n/n"The Invisibility Cloak wouldn't have got me over that/nline," said Harry slowly./n/n"Oh right," said Ron. "I thought you might've told me/nif it was the cloak ... because it would've covered both/nof us, wouldn't it? But you found another way, did/nyou?"/n/n"Listen," said Harry, "I didn't put my name in that/ngoblet. Someone else must've done it."/n/nRon raised his eyebrows./n/n"What would they do that for?"/n/n"I dunno," said Harry. He felt it would sound very/nmelodramatic to say, "To kill me."/n/nRon's eyebrows rose so high that they were in danger/nof disappearing into his hair./n/n"It's okay, you know, you can tell me the truth," he/nsaid. "If you don't want everyone else to know, fine,/nbut I don't know why you're bothering to lie, you/ndidn't get into trouble for it, did you? That friend of/nthe Fat Lady's, that Violet, she's already told us all/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore's letting you enter. A thousand Galleons/nprize money, eh? And you don't have to do end-of-/nyear tests either. ..."/n/n"I didn't put my name in that goblet!" said Harry,/nstarting to feel angry./n/n"Yeah, okay," said Ron, in exactly the same sceptical/ntone as Cedric. "Only you said this morning you'd/nhave done it last night, and no one would've seen you./n... I'm not stupid, you know."/n/n"You're doing a really good impression of it," Harry/nsnapped./n/n"Yeah?" said Ron, and there was no trace of a grin,/nforced or otherwise, on his face now. "You want to get/nto bed, Harry. I expect you'll need to be up early/ntomorrow for a photo-call or something."/n/nHe wrenched the hangings shut around his four-/nposter, leaving Harry standing there by the door,/nstaring at the dark red velvet curtains, now hiding/none of the few people he had been sure would believe/nhim./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Weighing Of The Wands
text: /nWhen Harry woke up on Sunday morning, it took him/na moment to remember why he felt so miserable and/nworried. Then the memory of the previous night rolled/nover him. He sat up and ripped back the curtains of/nhis own four-poster, intending to talk to Ron, to force/nRon to believe him — only to find that Ron's bed was/nempty; he had obviously gone down to breakfast./n/nHarry dressed and went down the spiral staircase into/nthe common room. The moment he appeared, the/npeople who had already finished breakfast broke into/napplause again. The prospect of going down into the/nGreat Hall and facing the rest of the Gryffindors, all/ntreating him like some sort of hero, was not inviting;/nit was that, however, or stay here and allow himself to/nbe cornered by the Creevey brothers, who were both/nbeckoning frantically to him to join them. He walked/nresolutely over to the portrait hole, pushed it open,/nclimbed out of it, and found himself face-to-face with/nHermione./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Hello," she said, holding up a stack of toast, which/nshe was carrying in a napkin. "I brought you this. .../nWant to go for a walk?"/n/n"Good idea," said Harry gratefully./n/nThey went downstairs, crossed the entrance hall/nquickly without looking in at the Great Hall, and were/nsoon striding across the lawn toward the lake, where/nthe Durmstrang ship was moored, reflected blackly in/nthe water. It was a chilly morning, and they kept/nmoving, munching their toast, as Harry told/nHermione exactly what had happened after he had left/nthe Gryffindor table the night before. To his immense/nrelief, Hermione accepted his story without question./n/n"Well, of course I knew you hadn't entered yourself,"/nshe said when he'd finished telling her about the/nscene in the chamber off the Hall. "The look on your/nface when Dumbledore read out your name! But the/nquestion is, who did put it in? Because Moody's right,/nHarry ... I don't think any student could have done it/n... they'd never be able to fool the Goblet, or get over/nDumbledore 's — "/n/n"Have you seen Ron?" Harry interrupted./n/nHermione hesitated./n/n"Erm ... yes ... he was at breakfast," she said./n/n"Does he still think I entered myself?"/n/n"Well ... no, I don't think so ... not really," said/nHermione awkwardly./n/n"What's that supposed to mean, 'not really'?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh Harry, isn't it obvious?" Hermione said/ndespairingly. "He's jealous!"/n/n/n/n"Jealous?" Harry said incredulously. "Jealous of/nwhat? He wants to make a prat of himself in front of/nthe whole school, does he?"/n/n"Look," said Hermione patiently, "it's always you who/ngets all the attention, you know it is. I know it's not/nyour fault," she added quickly, seeing Harry open his/nmouth furiously. "I know you don't ask for it ... but —/nwell — you know, Ron's got all those brothers to/ncompete against at home, and you're his best friend,/nand you're really famous — he's always shunted to/none side whenever people see you, and he puts up/nwith it, and he never mentions it, but I suppose this/nis just one time too many. ..."/n/n"Great," said Harry bitterly. "Really great. Tell him/nfrom me I'll swap any time he wants. Tell him from/nme he's welcome to it. ... People gawping at my/nforehead everywhere I go. ..."/n/n"I'm not telling him anything," Hermione said shortly./n"Tell him yourself. It's the only way to sort this out."/n/n"I'm not running around after him trying to make him/ngrow up!" Harry said, so loudly that several owls in a/nnearby tree took flight in alarm. "Maybe he'll believe/nI'm not enjoying myself once I've got my neck broken/nor — "/n/n/n/n"That's not funny," said Hermione quietly. "That's not/nfunny at all." She looked extremely anxious. "Harry,/nI've been thinking — you know what we've got to do,/ndon't you? Straight away, the moment we get back to/nthe castle?"/n/n"Yeah, give Ron a good kick up the — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Write to Sirius. You've got to tell him what's/nhappened. He asked you to keep him posted on/neverything that's going on at Hogwarts. ... It's almost/nas if he expected something like this to happen. I/nbrought some parchment and a quill out with me — "/n/n"Come off it," said Harry, looking around to check/nthat they couldn't be overheard, but the grounds were/nquite deserted. "He came back to the country just/nbecause my scar twinged. He'll probably come/nbursting right into the castle if I tell him someone's/nentered me in the Triwizard Tournament — "/n/n"He'd want you to tell him," said Hermione sternly./n"He's going to find out anyway — "/n/n"How?"/n/n"Harry, this isn't going to be kept quiet," said/nHermione, very seriously. "This tournament's famous,/nand you're famous. Ill be really surprised if there isn't/nanything in the Daily Prophet about you competing. . . ./nYou're already in half the books about You-Know-/nWho, you know ... and Sirius would rather hear it/nfrom you, I know he would."/n/n"Okay, okay, I'll write to him," said Harry, throwing/nhis last piece of toast into the lake. They both stood/nand watched it floating there for a moment, before a/nlarge tentacle rose out of the water and scooped it/nbeneath the surface. Then they returned to the castle./n/n"Whose owl am I going to use?" Harry said as they/nclimbed the stairs. "He told me not to use Hedwig/nagain."/n/n"Ask Ron if you can borrow — "/n/n"I'm not asking Ron for anything," Harry said flatly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, borrow one of the school owls, then, anyone/ncan use them," said Hermione./n/nThey went up to the Owlery Hermione gave Harry a/npiece of parchment, a quill, and a bottle of ink, then/nstrolled around the long lines of perches, looking at/nall the different owls, while Harry sat down against a/nwall and wrote his letter./n/nDear Sirius,/n/nYou told me to keep you posted on what's happening/nat Hogwarts, so here goes — I don't know if you've/nheard, but the Tri-wizard Tournament's happening this/nyear and on Saturday night I got picked as a fourth/nchampion. I don't know who put my name in the Goblet/nof Fire, because I didn't The other Hogwarts champion/nis Cedric Diggory, from Hufflepuff/n/nHe paused at this point, thinking. He had an urge to/nsay something about the large weight of anxiety that/nseemed to have settled inside his chest since last/nnight, but he couldn't think how to translate this into/nwords, so he simply dipped his quill back into the ink/nbottle and wrote,/n/nHope you're okay, and Buckbeak — Harry/n/n/n/n"Finished," he told Hermione, getting to his feet and/nbrushing straw off his robes. At this, Hedwig came/nfluttering down onto his shoulder and held out her/nleg./n/n"I can't use you," Harry told her, looking around for/nthe school owls. "I've got to use one of these. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHedwig gave a very loud hoot and took off so suddenly/nthat her talons cut into his shoulder. She kept her/nback to Harry all the time he was tying his letter to/nthe leg of a large barn owl. When the barn owl had/nflown off, Harry reached out to stroke Hedwig, but she/nclicked her beak furiously and soared up into the/nrafters out of reach./n/n"First Ron, then you," said Harry angrily. " This isn't/nmy fault."/n/nIf Harry had thought that matters would improve/nonce everyone got used to the idea of him being/nchampion, the following day showed him how/nmistaken he was. He could no longer avoid the rest of/nthe school once he was back at lessons — and it was/nclear that the rest of the school, just like the/nGryffindors, thought Harry had entered himself for/nthe tournament. Unlike the Gryffindors, however,/nthey did not seem impressed./n/nThe Hufflepuffs, who were usually on excellent terms/nwith the Gryffindors, had turned remarkably cold/ntoward the whole lot of them. One Herbology lesson/nwas enough to demonstrate this. It was plain that the/nHufflepuffs felt that Harry had stolen their/nchampion's glory; a feeling exacerbated, perhaps, by/nthe fact that Hufflepuff House very rarely got any/nglory, and that Cedric was one of the few who had/never given them any, having beaten Gryffindor once at/nQuidditch. Ernie Macmillan and Justin Finch-/nFletchley, with whom Harry normally got on very well,/ndid not talk to him even though they were repotting/nBouncing Bulbs at the same tray — though they did/nlaugh rather unpleasantly when one of the Bouncing/nBulbs wriggled free from Harry's grip and smacked/nhim hard in the face. Ron wasn't talking to Harry/neither. Hermione sat between them, making very/nforced conversation, but though both answered her/n/n/n/n/nnormally, they avoided making eye contact with each/nother. Harry thought even Professor Sprout seemed/ndistant with him — but then, she was Head of/nHufflepuff House./n/nHe would have been looking forward to seeing Hagrid/nunder normal circumstances, but Care of Magical/nCreatures meant seeing the Slytherins too — the first/ntime he would come face-to-face with them since/nbecoming champion./n/nPredictably, Malfoy arrived at Hagrid 's cabin with his/nfamiliar sneer firmly in place./n/n"Ah, look, boys, it's the champion," he said to Crabbe/nand Goyle the moment he got within earshot of Harry./n"Got your autograph books? Better get a signature/nnow, because I doubt he's going to be around much/nlonger. ... Half the Triwizard champions have died .../nhow long d'you reckon you're going to last, Potter?/n/nTen minutes into the first task's my bet."/n/nCrabbe and Goyle guffawed sycophantically, but/nMalfoy had to stop there, because Hagrid emerged/nfrom the back of his cabin balancing a teetering tower/nof crates, each containing a very large Blast-Ended/nSkrewt. To the class's horror, Hagrid proceeded to/nexplain that the reason the skrewts had been killing/none another was an excess of pent-up energy, and/nthat the solution would be for each student to fix a/nleash on a skrewt and take it for a short walk. The/nonly good thing about this plan was that it distracted/nMalfoy completely./n/n"Take this thing for a walk?" he repeated in disgust,/nstaring into one of the boxes. "And where exactly are/nwe supposed to fix the leash? Around the sting, the/nblasting end, or the sucker?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Roun' the middle," said Hagrid, demonstrating. "Er/n— yeh might want ter put on yer dragon-hide gloves,/njus' as an extra precaution, like. Harry — you come/nhere an' help me with this big one. ..."/n/nHagrid's real intention, however, was to talk to Harry/naway from the rest of the class. He waited until/neveryone else had set off with their skrewts, then/nturned to Harry and said, very seriously, "So — yer/ncompetin', Harry. In the tournament. School/nchampion."/n/n"One of the champions," Harry corrected him./n/nHagrid's beetle-black eyes looked very anxious under/nhis wild eyebrows./n/n"No idea who put yeh in fer it, Harry?"/n/n"You believe I didn't do it, then?" said Harry,/nconcealing with difficulty the rush of gratitude he felt/nat Hagrid's words./n/n" 'Course I do," Hagrid grunted. "Yeh say it wasn' you,/nan' I believe yeh — an' Dumbledore believes yer, an'/nall."/n/n"Wish I knew who did do it," said Harry bitterly./n/nThe pair of them looked out over the lawn; the class/nwas widely scattered now, and all in great difficulty./nThe skrewts were now over three feet long, and/nextremely powerful. No longer shell-less and colorless,/nthey had developed a kind of thick, grayish, shiny/narmor. They looked like a cross between giant/nscorpions and elongated crabs — but still without/nrecognizable heads or eyes. They had become/nimmensely strong and very hard to control./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Look like they're havin' fun, don' they?" Hagrid said/nhappily. Harry assumed he was talking about the/nskrewts, because his classmates certainly weren't;/nevery now and then, with an alarming bang, one of/nthe skrewts' ends would explode, causing it to shoot/nforward several yards, and more than one person was/nbeing dragged along on their stomach, trying/ndesperately to get back on their feet./n/n"Ah, I don' know, Harry," Hagrid sighed suddenly,/nlooking back down at him with a worried expression/non his face. "School champion ... everythin' seems ter/nhappen ter you, doesn' it?"/n/nHarry didn't answer. Yes, everything did seem to/nhappen to him ... that was more or less what/nHermione had said as they had walked around the/nlake, and that was the reason, according to her, that/nRon was no longer talking to him./n/nThe next few days were some of Harry's worst at/nHogwarts. The closest he had ever come to feeling like/nthis had been during those months, in his second/nyear, when a large part of the school had suspected/nhim of attacking his fellow students. But Ron had/nbeen on his side then. He thought he could have/ncoped with the rest of the school's behavior if he could/njust have had Ron back as a friend, but he wasn't/ngoing to try and persuade Ron to talk to him if Ron/ndidn't want to. Nevertheless, it was lonely with dislike/npouring in on him from all sides./n/nHe could understand the Hufflepuffs' attitude, even if/nhe didn't like it; they had their own champion to/nsupport. He expected nothing less than vicious/ninsults from the Slytherins — he was highly/nunpopular there and always had been, because he/nhad helped Gryffindor beat them so often, both at/nQuidditch and in the Inter-House Championship. But/n/n/n/n/nhe had hoped the Ravenclaws might have found it in/ntheir hearts to support him as much as Cedric. He/nwas wrong, however. Most Ravenclaws seemed to/nthink that he had been desperate to earn himself a bit/nmore fame by tricking the goblet into accepting his/nname./n/nThen there was the fact that Cedric looked the part of/na champion so much more than he did. Exceptionally/nhandsome, with his straight nose, dark hair, and gray/neyes, it was hard to say who was receiving more/nadmiration these days, Cedric or Viktor Krum. Harry/nactually saw the same sixth-year girls who had been/nso keen to get Krum's autograph begging Cedric to/nsign their school bags one lunchtime./n/nMeanwhile there was no reply from Sirius, Hedwig/nwas refusing to come anywhere near him, Professor/nTrelawney was predicting his death with even more/ncertainty than usual, and he did so badly at/nSummoning Charms in Professor Flitwick's class that/nhe was given extra homework — the only person to/nget any, apart from Neville./n/n"It's really not that difficult, Harry," Hermione tried to/nreassure him as they left Flitwick's class — she had/nbeen making objects zoom across the room to her all/nlesson, as though she were some sort of weird magnet/nfor board dusters, wastepaper baskets, and/nlunascopes. "You just weren't concentrating properly/n/n/n/n"Wonder why that was," said Harry darkly as Cedric/nDiggory walked past, surrounded by a large group of/nsimpering girls, all of whom looked at Harry as/nthough he were a particularly large Blast-Ended/nSkrewt. "Still — never mind, eh? Double Potions to/nlook forward to this afternoon. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDouble Potions was always a horrible experience, but/nthese days it was nothing short of torture. Being shut/nin a dungeon for an hour and a half with Snape and/nthe Slytherins, all of whom seemed determined to/npunish Harry as much as possible for daring to/nbecome school champion, was about the most/nunpleasant thing Harry could imagine. He had/nalready struggled through one Friday's worth, with/nHermione sitting next to him intoning "ignore them,/nignore them, ignore them" under her breath, and he/ncouldn't see why today should be any better./n/nWhen he and Hermione arrived at Snape 's dungeon/nafter lunch, they found the Slytherins waiting outside,/neach and every one of them wearing a large badge on/nthe front of his or her robes. For one wild moment/nHarry thought they were S.P.E.W. badges — then he/nsaw that they all bore the same message, in luminous/nred letters that burnt brightly in the dimly lit/nunderground passage:/n/nSupport CEDRIC DIGGORY —/n/nThe REAL Hogwarts Champion/n/n"Like them, Potter?" said Malfoy loudly as Harry/napproached. "And this isn't all they do — look!"/n/nHe pressed his badge into his chest, and the message/nupon it vanished, to be replaced by another one,/nwhich glowed green:/n/nPOTTER STINKS/n/nThe Slytherins howled with laughter. Each of them/npressed their badges too, until the message POTTER/nSTINKS was shining brightly all around Harry. He felt/nthe heat rise in his face and neck./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh very funny," Hermione said sarcastically to Pansy/nParkinson and her gang of Slytherin girls, who were/nlaughing harder than anyone, "really witty."/n/nRon was standing against the wall with Dean and/nSeamus. He wasn't laughing, but he wasn't sticking/nup for Harry either./n/n"Want one, Granger?" said Malfoy, holding out a/nbadge to Hermione. "I've got loads. But don't touch/nmy hand, now. I've just washed it, you see; don't want/na Mudblood sliming it up."/n/nSome of the anger Harry had been feeling for days/nand days seemed to burst through a dam in his chest./nHe had reached for his wand before he'd thought/nwhat he was doing. People all around them scrambled/nout of the way, backing down the corridor./n/n"Harry!" Hermione said warningly./n/n"Go on, then, Potter," Malfoy said quietly, drawing out/nhis own wand. "Moody's not here to look after you/nnow — do it, if you've got the guts — "/n/nFor a split second, they looked into each other's eyes,/nthen, at exactly the same time, both acted./n/n" FurnunculusV' Harry yelled./n/n" DensaugeoV' screamed Malfoy./n/nJets of light shot from both wands, hit each other in/nmidair, and ricocheted off at angles — Harry's hit/nGoyle in the face, and Malfoy's hit Hermione. Goyle/nbellowed and put his hands to his nose, where great/nugly boils were springing up — Hermione, whimpering/nin panic, was clutching her mouth./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Hermione!"/n/n/n/nRon had hurried forward to see what was wrong with/nher; Harry turned and saw Ron dragging Hermione 's/nhand away from her face. It wasn't a pretty sight./nHermione 's front teeth — already larger than average/n— were now growing at an alarming rate; she was/nlooking more and more like a beaver as her teeth/nelongated, past her bottom lip, toward her chin —/npanic-stricken, she felt them and let out a terrified/ncry./n/n"And what is all this noise about?" said a soft, deadly/nvoice./n/nSnape had arrived. The Slytherins clamored to give/ntheir explanations; Snape pointed a long yellow finger/nat Malfoy and said, "Explain."/n/n"Potter attacked me, sir — "/n/n"We attacked each other at the same time!" Harry/nshouted./n/n" — and he hit Goyle — look — "/n/nSnape examined Goyle, whose face now resembled/nsomething that would have been at home in a book/non poisonous fungi./n/n"Hospital wing, Goyle," Snape said calmly./n/n"Malfoy got Hermione!" Ron said. "Loo/d"/n/nHe forced Hermione to show Snape her teeth — she/nwas doing her best to hide them with her hands,/nthough this was difficult as they had now grown down/npast her collar. Pansy Parkinson and the other/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSlytherin girls were doubled up with silent giggles,/npointing at Hermione from behind Snape 's back./n/nSnape looked coldly at Hermione, then said, "I see no/ndifference."/n/nHermione let out a whimper; her eyes filled with tears,/nshe turned on her heel and ran, ran all the way up/nthe corridor and out of sight./n/nIt was lucky, perhaps, that both Harry and Ron/nstarted shouting at Snape at the same time; lucky/ntheir voices echoed so much in the stone corridor, for/nin the confused din, it was impossible for him to hear/nexactly what they were calling him. He got the gist,/nhowever./n/n"Let's see," he said, in his silkiest voice. "Fifty points/nfrom Gryffindor and a detention each for Potter and/nWeasley. Now get inside, or it'll be a week's worth of/ndetentions."/n/nHarry's ears were ringing. The injustice of it made/nhim want to curse Snape into a thousand slimy/npieces. He passed Snape, walked with Ron to the/nback of the dungeon, and slammed his bag down onto/nthe table. Ron was shaking with anger too — for a/nmoment, it felt as though everything was back to/nnormal between them, but then Ron turned and sat/ndown with Dean and Seamus instead, leaving Harry/nalone at his table. On the other side of the dungeon,/nMalfoy turned his back on Snape and pressed his/nbadge, smirking. POTTER STINKS flashed once more/nacross the room./n/nHarry sat there staring at Snape as the lesson began,/npicturing horrific things happening to him. ... If only/nhe knew how to do the Cruciatus Curse ... he'd have/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSnape flat on his back like that spider, jerking and/ntwitching. .../n/n"Antidotes!" said Snape, looking around at them all,/nhis cold black eyes glittering unpleasantly. "You/nshould all have prepared your recipes now. I want you/nto brew them carefully, and then, we will be selecting/nsomeone on whom to test one. ..."/n/nSnape's eyes met Harry's, and Harry knew what was/ncoming. Snape was going to poison him. Harry/nimagined picking up his cauldron, and sprinting to/nthe front of the class, and bringing it down on Snape's/ngreasy head —/n/nAnd then a knock on the dungeon door burst in on/nHarry's thoughts./n/nIt was Colin Creevey; he edged into the room,/nbeaming at Harry, and walked up to Snape's desk at/nthe front of the room./n/n"Yes?" said Snape curtly./n/n"Please, sir, I'm supposed to take Harry Potter/nupstairs."/n/nSnape stared down his hooked nose at Colin, whose/nsmile faded from his eager face./n/n"Potter has another hour of Potions to complete," said/nSnape coldly. "He will come upstairs when this class/nis finished."/n/nColin went pink./n/n"Sir — sir, Mr. Bagman wants him," he said/nnervously. "All the champions have got to go, I think/nthey want to take photographs. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry would have given anything he owned to have/nstopped Colin saying those last few words. He/nchanced half a glance at Ron, but Ron was staring/ndeterminedly at the ceiling./n/n"Very well, very well," Snape snapped. "Potter, leave/nyour things here, I want you back down here later to/ntest your antidote."/n/n"Please, sir — he's got to take his things with him,"/nsqueaked Colin. "All the champions — "/n/n"Very well\" said Snape. "Potter — take your bag and/nget out of my sight!"/n/nHarry swung his bag over his shoulder, got up, and/nheaded for the door. As he walked through the/nSlytherin desks, POTTER STINKS flashed at him from/nevery direction./n/n"It's amazing, isn't it, Harry?" said Colin, starting to/nspeak the moment Harry had closed the dungeon/ndoor behind him. "Isn't it, though? You being/nchampion?"/n/n"Yeah, really amazing," said Harry heavily as they set/noff toward the steps into the entrance hall. "What do/nthey want photos for, Colin?"/n/n"The Daily Prophet, I think!"/n/n"Great," said Harry dully. "Exactly what I need. More/npublicity."/n/n"Good luck!" said Colin when they had reached the/nright room. Harry knocked on the door and entered./n/nHe was in a fairly small classroom; most of the desks/nhad been pushed away to the back of the room,/n/n/n/n/n/nleaving a large space in the middle; three of them,/nhowever, had been placed end-to-end in front of the/nblackboard and covered with a long length of velvet./nFive chairs had been set behind the velvet-covered/ndesks, and Ludo Bagman was sitting in one of them,/ntalking to a witch Harry had never seen before, who/nwas wearing magenta robes./n/nViktor Krum was standing moodily in a corner as/nusual and not talking to anybody. Cedric and Fleur/nwere in conversation. Fleur looked a good deal/nhappier than Harry had seen her so far; she kept/nthrowing back her head so that her long silvery hair/ncaught the light. A paunchy man, holding a large/nblack camera that was smoking slightly, was/nwatching Fleur out of the corner of his eye./n/nBagman suddenly spotted Harry, got up quickly, and/nbounded forward./n/n"Ah, here he is! Champion number four! In you come,/nHarry, in you come ... nothing to worry about, it's just/nthe wand weighing ceremony, the rest of the judges/nwill be here in a moment — "/n/n"Wand weighing?" Harry repeated nervously./n/n"We have to check that your wands are fully/nfunctional, no problems, you know, as they're your/nmost important tools in the tasks ahead," said/nBagman. "The expert's upstairs now with/nDumbledore. And then there's going to be a little/nphoto shoot. This is Rita Skeeter," he added,/ngesturing toward the witch in magenta robes. "She's/ndoing a small piece on the tournament for the Daily/nProphet ..."/n/n"Maybe not that small, Ludo," said Rita Skeeter, her/neyes on Harry./n/n/n/n/n/nHer hair was set in elaborate and curiously rigid curls/nthat contrasted oddly with her heavy-jawed face. She/nwore jeweled spectacles. The thick fingers clutching/nher crocodile-skin handbag ended in two-inch nails,/npainted crimson./n/n"I wonder if I could have a little word with Harry/nbefore we start?" she said to Bagman, but still gazing/nfixedly at Harry. "The youngest champion, you know/n... to add a bit of color?"/n/n"Certainly!" cried Bagman. "That is — if Harry has no/nobjection?"/n/n"Er — " said Harry./n/n"Lovely," said Rita Skeeter, and in a second, her/nscarlet-taloned fingers had Harry's upper arm in a/nsurprisingly strong grip, and she was steering him/nout of the room again and opening a nearby door./n/n"We don't want to be in there with all that noise," she/nsaid. "Let's see ... ah, yes, this is nice and cozy."/n/nIt was a broom cupboard. Harry stared at her./n/n"Come along, dear — that's right — lovely," said Rita/nSkeeter again, perching herself precariously upon an/nupturned bucket, pushing Harry down onto a/ncardboard box, and closing the door, throwing them/ninto darkness. "Let's see now ..."/n/nShe unsnapped her crocodile-skin handbag and/npulled out a handful of candles, which she lit with a/nwave of her wand and magicked into midair, so that/nthey could see what they were doing./n/n"You won't mind, Harry, if I use a Quick-Quotes/nQuill? It leaves me free to talk to you normally. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"A what?" said Harry./n/n/n/nRita Skeeter's smile widened. Harry counted three/ngold teeth. She reached again into her crocodile bag/nand drew out a long acid-green quill and a roll of/nparchment, which she stretched out between them on/na crate of Mrs. Skower's All-Purpose Magical Mess/nRemover. She put the tip of the green quill into her/nmouth, sucked it for a moment with apparent relish,/nthen placed it upright on the parchment, where it/nstood balanced on its point, quivering slightly./n/n"Testing ... my name is Rita Skeeter, Daily Prophet/nreporter."/n/nHarry looked down quickly at the quill. The moment/nRita Skeeter had spoken, the green quill had started/nto scribble, skidding across the parchment:/n/nAttractive blonde Rita Skeeter, forty-three, whose/nsavage quill has punctured many inflated reputations/n/n/n/n"Lovely," said Rita Skeeter, yet again, and she ripped/nthe top piece of parchment off, crumpled it up, and/nstuffed it into her handbag. Now she leaned toward/nHarry and said, "So, Harry ... what made you decide/nto enter the Triwizard Tournament?"/n/n"Er — " said Harry again, but he was distracted by the/nquill. Even though he wasn't speaking, it was dashing/nacross the parchment, and in its wake he could make/nout a fresh sentence:/n/nAn ugly scar, souvenir of a tragic past, disfigures the/notherwise charming face of Harry Potter, whose eyes/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ignore the quill, Harry," said Rita Skeeter firmly./nReluctantly, Harry looked up at her instead. "Now —/nwhy did you decide to enter the tournament, Harry?"/n/n"I didn't," said Harry. "I don't know how my name got/ninto the Goblet of Fire. I didn't put it in there."/n/nRita Skeeter raised one heavily penciled eyebrow./n/n"Come now, Harry, there's no need to be scared of/ngetting into trouble. We all know you shouldn't really/nhave entered at all. But don't worry about that. Our/nreaders love a rebel."/n/n"But I didn't enter," Harry repeated. "I don't know/nwho — "/n/n"How do you feel about the tasks ahead?" said Rita/nSkeeter. "Excited? Nervous?"/n/n"I haven't really thought ... yeah, nervous, I suppose,"/nsaid Harry. His insides squirmed uncomfortably as he/nspoke./n/n"Champions have died in the past, haven't they?" said/nRita Skeeter briskly. "Have you thought about that at/nall?"/n/n"Well ... they say it's going to be a lot safer this year,"/nsaid Harry./n/nThe quill whizzed across the parchment between/nthem, back and forward as though it were skating./n/n"Of course, you've looked death in the face before,/nhaven't you?" said Rita Skeeter, watching him closely./n"How would you say that's affected you?"/n/n"Er," said Harry, yet again./n/n/n/n/n/n"Do you think that the trauma in your past might/nhave made you keen to prove yourself? To live up to/nyour name? Do you think that perhaps you were/ntempted to enter the Triwizard Tournament because/n/n/n/n"I didn't enter," said Harry, starting to feel irritated./n/n"Can you remember your parents at all?" said Rita/nSkeeter, talking over him./n/n"No," said Harry./n/n"How do you think they'd feel if they knew you were/ncompeting in the Triwizard Tournament? Proud?/nWorried? Angry?"/n/nHarry was feeling really annoyed now. How on earth/nwas he to know how his parents would feel if they/nwere alive? He could feel Rita Skeeter watching him/nvery intently. Frowning, he avoided her gaze and/nlooked down at words the quill had just written:/n/nTears fill those startling green eyes as our/nconversation turns to the parents he can barely/nremember./n/n"I have NOT got tears in my eyes!" said Harry loudly./n/nBefore Rita Skeeter could say a word, the door of the/nbroom cupboard was pulled open. Harry looked/naround, blinking in the bright light. Albus/nDumbledore stood there, looking down at both of/nthem, squashed into the cupboard./n/n" Dumbledorel" cried Rita Skeeter, with every/nappearance of delight — but Harry noticed that her/nquill and the parchment had suddenly vanished from/nthe box of Magical Mess Remover, and Rita's clawed/n/n/n/n/n/nfingers were hastily snapping shut the clasp of her/ncrocodile-skin bag. "How are you?" she said, standing/nup and holding out one of her large, mannish hands/nto Dumbledore. "I hope you saw my piece over the/nsummer about the International Confederation of/nWizards' Conference?"/n/n"Enchantingly nasty," said Dumbledore, his eyes/ntwinkling. "I particularly enjoyed your description of/nme as an obsolete dingbat."/n/nRita Skeeter didn't look remotely abashed./n/n"I was just making the point that some of your ideas/nare a little old-fashioned, Dumbledore, and that many/nwizards in the street — "/n/n"I will be delighted to hear the reasoning behind the/nrudeness, Rita," said Dumbledore, with a courteous/nbow and a smile, "but I'm afraid we will have to/ndiscuss the matter later. The Weighing of the Wands/nis about to start, and it cannot take place if one of our/nchampions is hidden in a broom cupboard."/n/nVery glad to get away from Rita Skeeter, Harry/nhurried back into the room. The other champions/nwere now sitting in chairs near the door, and he sat/ndown quickly next to Cedric, looking up at the velvet-/ncovered table, where four of the five judges were now/nsitting — Professor Karkaroff, Madame Maxime, Mr./nCrouch, and Ludo Bagman. Rita Skeeter settled/nherself down in a corner; Harry saw her slip the/nparchment out of her bag again, spread it on her/nknee, suck the end of the Quick-Quotes Quill, and/nplace it once more on the parchment./n/n"May I introduce Mr. Ollivander?" said Dumbledore,/ntaking his place at the judges' table and talking to the/nchampions. "He will be checking your wands to/n/n/n/n/n/nensure that they are in good condition before the/ntournament."/n/nHarry looked around, and with a jolt of surprise saw/nan old wizard with large, pale eyes standing quietly by/nthe window. Harry had met Mr. Ollivander before —/nhe was the wand-maker from whom Harry had/nbought his own wand over three years ago in Diagon/nAlley./n/n"Mademoiselle Delacour, could we have you first,/nplease?" said Mr. Ollivander, stepping into the empty/nspace in the middle of the room./n/nFleur Delacour swept over to Mr. Ollivander and/nhanded him her wand./n/n"Hmmm ..." he said./n/nHe twirled the wand between his long fingers like a/nbaton and it emitted a number of pink and gold/nsparks. Then he held it close to his eyes and/nexamined it carefully./n/n"Yes," he said quietly, "nine and a half inches .../ninflexible . . . rosewood . . . and containing . . . dear me/n/n/n/n"An 'air from ze 'ead of a veela," said Fleur. "One of/nmy grandmuzzer's."/n/nSo Fleur was part veela, thought Harry, making a/nmental note to tell Ron . . . then he remembered that/nRon wasn't speaking to him./n/n"Yes," said Mr. Ollivander, "yes, I've never used veela/nhair myself, of course. I find it makes for rather/ntemperamental wands . . . however, to each his own,/nand if this suits you ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nMr. Ollivander ran his fingers along the wand,/napparently checking for scratches or bumps; then he/nmuttered, " OrchideousV' and a bunch of flowers burst/nfrom the wand tip./n/n"Very well, very well, it's in fine working order," said/nMr. Ollivander, scooping up the flowers and handing/nthem to Fleur with her wand. "Mr. Diggory, you next."/n/nFleur glided back to her seat, smiling at Cedric as he/npassed her./n/n"Ah, now, this is one of mine, isn't it?" said Mr./nOllivander, with much more enthusiasm, as Cedric/nhanded over his wand. "Yes, I remember it well./nContaining a single hair from the tail of a particularly/nfine male unicorn . . . must have been seventeen/nhands; nearly gored me with his horn after I plucked/nhis tail. Twelve and a quarter inches ... ash .../npleasantly springy. It's in fine condition. ... You treat/nit regularly?"/n/n"Polished it last night," said Cedric, grinning./n/nHarry looked down at his own wand. He could see/nfinger marks all over it. He gathered a fistful of robe/nfrom his knee and tried to rub it clean surreptitiously./nSeveral gold sparks shot out of the end of it. Fleur/nDelacour gave him a very patronizing look, and he/ndesisted./n/nMr. Ollivander sent a stream of silver smoke rings/nacross the room from the tip of Cedric's wand,/npronounced himself satisfied, and then said, "Mr./nKrum, if you please."/n/nViktor Krum got up and slouched, round-shouldered/nand duck-footed, toward Mr. Ollivander. He thrust/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nout his wand and stood scowling, with his hands in/nthe pockets of his robes./n/n/n/n"Hmm," said Mr. Ollivander, "this is a Gregorovitch/ncreation, unless I'm much mistaken? A fine wand-/nmaker, though the styling is never quite what I . . ./nhowever ..."/n/nHe lifted the wand and examined it minutely, turning/nit over and over before his eyes./n/n"Yes . . . hornbeam and dragon heartstring?" he shot at/nKrum, who nodded. "Rather thicker than one usually/nsees . . . quite rigid . . . ten and a quarter inches . . ./n/nAvis'."/n/nThe hornbeam wand let off a blast like a gun, and a/nnumber of small, twittering birds flew out of the end/nand through the open window into the watery/nsunlight./n/n"Good," said Mr. Ollivander, handing Krum back his/nwand. "Which leaves ... Mr. Potter."/n/nHarry got to his feet and walked past Krum to Mr./nOllivander. He handed over his wand./n/n"Aaaah, yes," said Mr. Ollivander, his pale eyes/nsuddenly gleaming. "Yes, yes, yes. How well I/nremember."/n/nHarry could remember too. He could remember it as/nthough it had happened yesterday. . ./n/nFour summers ago, on his eleventh birthday, he had/nentered Mr. Ollivander's shop with Hagrid to buy a/nwand. Mr. Ollivander had taken his measurements/nand then started handing him wands to try. Harry/nhad waved what felt like every wand in the shop, until/n/n/n/n/nat last he had found the one that suited him — this/none, which was made of holly, eleven inches long, and/ncontained a single feather from the tail of a phoenix./nMr. Ollivander had been very surprised that Harry/nhad been so compatible with this wand. "Curious," he/nhad said, "curious," and not until Harry asked what/nwas curious had Mr. Ollivander explained that the/nphoenix feather in Harry's wand had come from the/nsame bird that had supplied the core of Lord/nVoldemort's./n/nHarry had never shared this piece of information with/nanybody. He was very fond of his wand, and as far as/nhe was concerned its relation to Voldemort's wand/nwas something it couldn't help — rather as he/ncouldn't help being related to Aunt Petunia. However,/nhe really hoped that Mr. Ollivander wasn't about to/ntell the room about it. He had a funny feeling Rita/nSkeeter's Quick-Quotes Quill might just explode with/nexcitement if he did./n/nMr. Ollivander spent much longer examining Harry's/nwand than anyone else's. Eventually, however, he/nmade a fountain of wine shoot out of it, and handed it/nback to Harry, announcing that it was still in perfect/ncondition./n/n"Thank you all," said Dumbledore, standing up at the/njudges' table. "You may go back to your lessons now/n— or perhaps it would be quicker just to go down to/ndinner, as they are about to end — "/n/nFeeling that at last something had gone right today,/nHarry got up to leave, but the man with the black/ncamera jumped up and cleared his throat./n/n"Photos, Dumbledore, photos!" cried Bagman/nexcitedly. "All the judges and champions, what do you/nthink, Rita?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Er — yes, let's do those first," said Rita Skeeter,/nwhose eyes were upon Harry again. "And then/nperhaps some individual shots."/n/nThe photographs took a long time. Madame Maxime/ncast everyone else into shadow wherever she stood,/nand the photographer couldn't stand far enough back/nto get her into the frame; eventually she had to sit/nwhile everyone else stood around her. Karkaroff kept/ntwirling his goatee around his finger to give it an extra/ncurl; Krum, whom Harry would have thought would/nhave been used to this sort of thing, skulked, half-/nhidden, at the back of the group. The photographer/nseemed keenest to get Fleur at the front, but Rita/nSkeeter kept hurrying forward and dragging Harry/ninto greater prominence. Then she insisted on/nseparate shots of all the champions. At last, they were/nfree to go./n/nHarry went down to dinner. Hermione wasn't there —/nhe supposed she was still in the hospital wing having/nher teeth fixed. He ate alone at the end of the table,/nthen returned to Gryffindor Tower, thinking of all the/nextra work on Summoning Charms that he had to do./nUp in the dormitory, he came across Ron./n/n"You've had an owl," said Ron brusquely the moment/nhe walked in. He was pointing at Harry's pillow. The/nschool barn owl was waiting for him there./n/n"Oh — right," said Harry./n/n"And we've got to do our detentions tomorrow night,/nSnape's dungeon," said Ron./n/nHe then walked straight out of the room, not looking/nat Harry. For a moment, Harry considered going after/nhim — he wasn't sure whether he wanted to talk to/nhim or hit him, both seemed quite appealing — but/n/n/n/n/n/nthe lure of Sirius's answer was too strong. Harry/nstrode over to the barn owl, took the letter off its leg,/nand unrolled it./n/nHarry —/n/nI can't say everything I would like to in a letter, it's too/nrisky in case the owl is intercepted — we need to talk/nface-to-face. Can you ensure that you are alone by the/nfire in Gryffindor Tower at one o'clock in the morning/non the 22nd of November?/n/nI know better than anyone that you can look after/nyourself and while you're around Dumbledore and/nMoody I don't think anyone will be able to hurt you./nHowever, someone seems to be having a good try./nEntering you in that tournament would have been very/nrisky, especially right under Dumbledore' s nose./n/nBe on the watch, Harry. I still want to hear about/nanything unusual. Let me know about the 22nd of/nNovember as quickly as you can./n/nSirius/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Hungarian Horntail
text: /nThe prospect of talking face-to-face with Sirius was all/nthat sustained Harry over the next fortnight, the only/nbright spot on a horizon that had never looked/ndarker. The shock of finding himself school champion/nhad worn off slightly now, and the fear of what was/nfacing him had started to sink in. The first task was/ndrawing steadily nearer; he felt as though it were/ncrouching ahead of him like some horrific monster,/nbarring his path. He had never suffered nerves like/nthese; they were way beyond anything he had/nexperienced before a Quidditch match, not even his/nlast one against Slytherin, which had decided who/nwould win the Quidditch Cup. Harry was finding it/nhard to think about the future at all; he felt as though/nhis whole life had been leading up to, and would/nfinish with, the first task. .../n/nAdmittedly, he didn't see how Sirius was going to/nmake him feel any better about having to perform an/nunknown piece of difficult and dangerous magic in/nfront of hundreds of people, but the mere sight of a/nfriendly face would be something at the moment./n/n/n/n/nHarry wrote back to Sirius saying that he would be/nbeside the common room fire at the time Sirius had/nsuggested, and he and Hermione spent a long time/ngoing over plans for forcing any stragglers out of the/ncommon room on the night in question. If the worst/ncame to the worst, they were going to drop a bag of/nDungbombs, but they hoped they wouldn't have to/nresort to that — Filch would skin them alive./n/nIn the meantime, life became even worse for Harry/nwithin the confines of the castle, for Rita Skeeter had/npublished her piece about the Triwizard Tournament,/nand it had turned out to be not so much a report on/nthe tournament as a highly colored life story of Harry./nMuch of the front page had been given over to a/npicture of Harry; the article (continuing on pages two,/nsix, and seven) had been all about Harry, the names/nof the Beauxbatons and Durmstrang champions/n(misspelled) had been squashed into the last line of/nthe article, and Cedric hadn't been mentioned at all./n/nThe article had appeared ten days ago, and Harry still/ngot a sick, burning feeling of shame in his stomach/nevery time he thought about it. Rita Skeeter had/nreported him saying an awful lot of things that he/ncouldn't remember ever saying in his life, let alone in/nthat broom cupboard./n/nI suppose I get my strength from my parents. I know/nthey'd be very proud of me if they could see me now./n/n... Yes, sometimes at night I still cry about them, I'm/nnot ashamed to admit it. ... I know nothing will hurt/nme during the tournament, because they're watching/nover me. .../n/nBut Rita Skeeter had gone even further than/ntransforming his "er's" into long, sickly sentences:/n/nShe had interviewed other people about him too./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry has at last found love at Hogwarts. His close/nfriend, Colin Creevey, says that Harry is rarely seen/nout of the company of one Hermione Granger, a/nstunningly pretty Muggle-born girl who, like Harry, is/none of the top students in the school./n/nFrom the moment the article had appeared, Harry/nhad had to endure people — Slytherins, mainly —/nquoting it at him as he passed and making sneering/ncomments./n/n"Want a hanky, Potter, in case you start crying in/nTransfiguration?"/n/n"Since when have you been one of the top students in/nthe school, Potter? Or is this a school you and/nLongbottom have set up together?"/n/n"Hey — Harry!"/n/n"Yeah, that's right!" Harry found himself shouting as/nhe wheeled around in the corridor, having had just/nabout enough. "I've just been crying my eyes out over/nmy dead mum, and I'm just off to do a bit more. ..."/n/n"No — it was just — you dropped your quill."/n/nIt was Cho. Harry felt the color rising in his face./n/n"Oh — right — sorry," he muttered, taking the quill/nback./n/n"Er ... good luck on Tuesday," she said. "I really hope/nyou do well."/n/nWhich left Harry feeling extremely stupid./n/nHermione had come in for her fair share of/nunpleasantness too, but she hadn't yet started yelling/n/n/n/n/n/nat innocent bystanders; in fact, Harry was full of/nadmiration for the way she was handling the/nsituation./n/n" Stunningly pretty? Her?" Pansy Parkinson had/nshrieked the first time she had come face-to-face with/nHermione after Rita's article had appeared. "What was/nshe judging against — a chipmunk?"/n/n"Ignore it," Hermione said in a dignified voice, holding/nher head in the air and stalking past the sniggering/nSlytherin girls as though she couldn't hear them./n/n"Just ignore it, Harry."/n/nBut Harry couldn't ignore it. Ron hadn't spoken to/nhim at all since he had told him about Snape's/ndetentions. Harry had half hoped they would make/nthings up during the two hours they were forced to/npickle rats' brains in Snape's dungeon, but that had/nbeen the day Rita's article had appeared, which/nseemed to have confirmed Ron's belief that Harry was/nreally enjoying all the attention./n/nHermione was furious with the pair of them; she went/nfrom one to the other, trying to force them to talk to/neach other, but Harry was adamant: He would talk to/nRon again only if Ron admitted that Harry hadn't put/nhis name in the Goblet of Fire and apologized for/ncalling him a liar./n/n"I didn't start this," Harry said stubbornly. "It's his/nproblem."/n/n"You miss him!" Hermione said impatiently. "And I/nknow he misses you — "/n/n"Miss him?" said Harry. "I don't miss him. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut this was a downright lie. Harry liked Hermione/nvery much, but she just wasn't the same as Ron./n/nThere was much less laughter and a lot more hanging/naround in the library when Hermione was your best/nfriend. Harry still hadn't mastered Summoning/nCharms, he seemed to have developed something of a/nblock about them, and Hermione insisted that/nlearning the theory would help. They consequently/nspent a lot of time poring over books during their/nlunchtimes./n/nViktor Krum was in the library an awful lot too, and/nHarry wondered what he was up to. Was he studying,/nor was he looking for things to help him through the/nfirst task? Hermione often complained about Krum/nbeing there — not that he ever bothered them — but/nbecause groups of giggling girls often turned up to spy/non him from behind bookshelves, and Hermione/nfound the noise distracting./n/n"He's not even good-looking!" she muttered angrily,/nglaring at Krum's sharp profile. "They only like him/nbecause he's famous! They wouldn't look twice at him/nif he couldn't do that Wonky- Faint thing — "/n/n"Wronski Feint," said Harry, through gritted teeth./nQuite apart from liking to get Quidditch terms/ncorrect, it caused him another pang to imagine Ron's/nexpression if he could have heard Hermione talking/nabout Wonky- Faints./n/nIt is a strange thing, but when you are dreading/nsomething, and would give anything to slow down/ntime, it has a disobliging habit of speeding up. The/ndays until the first task seemed to slip by as though/nsomeone had fixed the clocks to work at double/nspeed. Harry's feeling of barely controlled panic was/nwith him wherever he went, as everpresent as the/nsnide comments about the Daily Prophet article./n/n/n/n/n/nOn the Saturday before the first task, all students in/nthe third year and above were permitted to visit the/nvillage of Hogsmeade. Hermione told Harry that it/nwould do him good to get away from the castle for a/nbit, and Harry didn't need much persuasion./n/n"What about Ron, though?" he said. Karkaroff doesn't strike me as the type who'd go/nback to Voldemort unless he knew Voldemort was/npowerful enough to protect him. But whoever put/nyour name in that goblet did it for a reason, and I/ncan't help thinking the tournament would be a very/ngood way to attack you and make it look like an/naccident."/n/n"Looks like a really good plan from where I'm/nstanding," said Harry grinning bleakly. "They'll just/nhave to stand back and let the dragons do their stuff."/n/n"Right — these dragons," said Sirius, speaking very/nquickly now. "There's a way, Harry. Don't be tempted/n/n/n/n/n/nto try a Stunning Spell — dragons are strong and too/npowerfully magical to be knocked out by a single/nStunner, you need about half a dozen wizards at a/ntime to overcome a dragon — "/n/n"Yeah, I know, I just saw," said Harry./n/n"But you can do it alone," said Sirius. "There is a way,/nand a simple spell's all you need. Just — "/n/nBut Harry held up a hand to silence him, his heart/nsuddenly pounding as though it would burst. He/ncould hear footsteps coming down the spiral staircase/nbehind him./n/n"Go!" he hissed at Sirius. "Go!
