There's someone/ncoming!"/n/nHarry scrambled to his feet, hiding the fire — if/nsomeone saw Sirius's face within the walls of/nHogwarts, they would raise an almighty uproar — the/nMinistry would get dragged in — he, Harry, would be/nquestioned about Sirius's whereabouts —/n/nHarry heard a tiny pop\ in the fire behind him and/nknew Sirius had gone. He watched the bottom of the/nspiral staircase. Who had decided to go for a stroll at/none o'clock in the morning, and stopped Sirius from/ntelling him how to get past a dragon?/n/nIt was Ron. Dressed in his maroon paisley pajamas,/nRon stopped dead facing Harry across the room, and/nlooked around./n/n"Who were you talking to?" he said./n/n"What's that got to do with you?" Harry snarled./n/n"What are you doing down here at this time of night?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I just wondered where you — " Ron broke off,/nshrugging. "Nothing. I'm going back to bed."/n/n"Just thought you'd come nosing around, did you?"/nHarry shouted. He knew that Ron had no idea what/nhe'd walked in on, knew he hadn't done it on purpose,/nbut he didn't care — at this moment he hated/neverything about Ron, right down to the several/ninches of bare ankle showing beneath his pajama/ntrousers./n/n"Sorry about that," said Ron, his face reddening with/nanger. "Should've realized you didn't want to be/ndisturbed. I'll let you get on with practicing for your/nnext interview in peace."/n/nHarry seized one of the POTTER REALLY STINKS/nbadges off the table and chucked it, as hard as he/ncould, across the room. It hit Ron on the forehead/nand bounced off./n/n"There you go," Harry said. "Something for you to/nwear on Tuesday. You might even have a scar now, if/nyou're lucky. ... That's what you want, isn't it?"/n/nHe strode across the room toward the stairs; he half/nexpected Ron to stop him, he would even have liked/nRon to throw a punch at him, but Ron just stood/nthere in his too-small pajamas, and Harry, having/nstormed upstairs, lay awake in bed fuming for a long/ntime afterward and didn't hear him come up to bed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The First Task
text: /nHarry got up on Sunday morning and dressed so/ninattentively that it was a while before he realized he/nwas trying to pull his hat onto his foot instead of his/nsock. When he'd finally got all his clothes on the right/nparts of his body, he hurried off to find Hermione,/nlocating her at the Gryffindor table in the Great Hall,/nwhere she was eating breakfast with Ginny. Feeling/ntoo queasy to eat, Harry waited until Hermione had/nswallowed her last spoonful of porridge, then dragged/nher out onto the grounds. There, he told her all about/nthe dragons, and about everything Sirius had said,/nwhile they took another long walk around the lake./n/nAlarmed as she was by Sirius's warnings about/nKarkaroff, Hermione still thought that the dragons/nwere the more pressing problem./n/n"Let's just try and keep you alive until Tuesday/nevening," she said desperately, "and then we can/nworry about Karkaroff."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey walked three times around the lake, trying all/nthe way to think of a simple spell that would subdue/na dragon. Nothing whatsoever occurred to them, so/nthey retired to the library instead. Here, Harry pulled/ndown every book he could find on dragons, and both/nof them set to work searching through the large pile./n/n" 'Talon-clipping by charms ... treating scale-rot ...'/n/nThis is no good, this is for nutters like Hagrid who/nwant to keep them healthy. ..."/n/n" 'Dragons are extremely difficult to slay, owing to the/nancient magic that imbues their thick hides, which/nnone but the most powerful spells can penetrate ...'/n/nBut Sirius said a simple one would do it. ..."/n/n"Let's try some simple spellbooks, then," said Harry,/nthrowing aside Men Who Love Dragons Too Much./n/nHe returned to the table with a pile of spellbooks, set/nthem down, and began to flick through each in turn,/nHermione whispering nonstop at his elbow./n/n"Well, there are Switching Spells ... but what's the/npoint of Switching it? Unless you swapped its fangs/nfor wine-gums or something that would make it less/ndangerous. ... The trouble is, like that book said, not/nmuch is going to get through a dragon's hide. ... I'd/nsay Transfigure it, but something that big, you really/nhaven't got a hope, I doubt even Professor McGonagall/n... unless you're supposed to put the spell on/nyourself? Maybe to give yourself extra powers? But/nthey're not simple spells, I mean, we haven't done any/nof those in class, I only know about them because I've/nbeen doing O.W.L. practice papers. ..."/n/n"Hermione," Harry said, through gritted teeth, "will/nyou shut up for a bit, please? I'm trying to/nconcentrate."/n/n/n/n/n/nBut all that happened, when Hermione fell silent, was/nthat Harry's brain filled with a sort of blank buzzing,/nwhich didn't seem to allow room for concentration. He/nstared hopelessly down the index of Basic Hexes for/nthe Busy and Vexed. Instant scalping . . . but dragons/nhad no hair . . . pepper breath . . . that would probably/nincrease a dragon's firepower ... horn tongue ... just/nwhat he needed, to give it an extra weapon . . ./n/n"Oh no, he's back again, why can't he read on his/nstupid ship?" said Hermione irritably as Viktor Krum/nslouched in, cast a surly look over at the pair of them,/nand settled himself in a distant corner with a pile of/nbooks. "Come on, Harry, we'll go back to the common/nroom ... his fan club'll be here in a moment, twittering/naway. ..."/n/nAnd sure enough, as they left the library, a gang of/ngirls tiptoed past them, one of them wearing a/nBulgaria scarf tied around her waist./n/nHarry barely slept that night. When he awoke on/nMonday morning, he seriously considered for the first/ntime ever just running away from Hogwarts. But as/nhe looked around the Great Hall at breakfast time,/nand thought about what leaving the castle would/nmean, he knew he couldn't do it. It was the only place/nhe had ever been happy . . . well, he supposed he must/nhave been happy with his parents too, but he couldn't/nremember that./n/nSomehow, the knowledge that he would rather be/nhere and facing a dragon than back on Privet Drive/nwith Dudley was good to know; it made him feel/nslightly calmer. He finished his bacon with difficulty/n(his throat wasn't working too well), and as he and/nHermione got up, he saw Cedric Diggory leaving the/nHufflepuff table./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nCedric still didn't know about the dragons ... the only/nchampion who didn't, if Harry was right in thinking/nthat Maxime and Karkaroff would have told Fleur and/nKrum. .../n/n"Hermione, I'll see you in the greenhouses," Harry/nsaid, coming to his decision as he watched Cedric/nleaving the Hall. "Go on, I'll catch you up."/n/n"Harry, you'll be late, the bell's about to ring — "/n/n"I'll catch you up, okay?"/n/nBy the time Harry reached the bottom of the marble/nstaircase, Cedric was at the top. He was with a load of/nsixth-year friends. Harry didn't want to talk to Cedric/nin front of them; they were among those who had/nbeen quoting Rita Skeeter's article at him every time/nhe went near them. He followed Cedric at a distance/nand saw that he was heading toward the Charms/ncorridor. This gave Harry an idea. Pausing at a/ndistance from them, he pulled out his wand, and took/ncareful aim./n/n"Diffindol"/n/nCedric's bag split. Parchment, quills, and books/nspilled out of it onto the floor. Several bottles of ink/nsmashed./n/n"Don't bother," said Cedric in an exasperated voice as/nhis friends bent down to help him. "Tell Flitwick I'm/ncoming, go on. ..."/n/nThis was exactly what Harry had been hoping for. He/nslipped his wand back into his robes, waited until/nCedric's friends had disappeared into their classroom,/nand hurried up the corridor, which was now empty of/neveryone but himself and Cedric./n/n/n/n/n/n"Hi," said Cedric, picking up a copy of A Guide to/nAdvanced Transfiguration that was now splattered/nwith ink. "My bag just split ... brand-new and all ..."/n/n"Cedric," said Harry, "the first task is dragons."/n/n"What?" said Cedric, looking up./n/n"Dragons," said Harry, speaking quickly, in case/nProfessor Flitwick came out to see where Cedric had/ngot to. "They've got four, one for each of us, and we've/ngot to get past them."/n/nCedric stared at him. Harry saw some of the panic/nhe'd been feeling since Saturday night flickering in/nCedric's gray eyes./n/n"Are you sure?" Cedric said in a hushed voice./n/n"Dead sure," said Harry. "I've seen them."/n/n"But how did you find out? We're not supposed to/nknow. ..."/n/n"Never mind," said Harry quickly — he knew Hagrid/nwould be in trouble if he told the truth. "But I'm not/nthe only one who knows. Fleur and Krum will know/nby now — Maxime and Karkaroff both saw the/ndragons too."/n/nCedric straightened up, his arms full of inky quills,/nparchment, and books, his ripped bag dangling off/none shoulder. He stared at Harry, and there was a/npuzzled, almost suspicious look in his eyes./n/n"Why are you telling me?" he asked./n/nHarry looked at him in disbelief. He was sure Cedric/nwouldn't have asked that if he had seen the dragons/n/n/n/n/n/nhimself. Harry wouldn't have let his worst enemy face/nthose monsters unprepared — well, perhaps Malfoy or/nSnape .../n/n"It's just ... fair, isn't it?" he said to Cedric. "We all/nknow now ... we're on an even footing, aren't we?"/n/nCedric was still looking at him in a slightly suspicious/nway when Harry heard a familiar clunking noise/nbehind him. He turned around and saw Mad-Eye/nMoody emerging from a nearby classroom./n/n"Come with me, Potter," he growled. "Diggory, off you/ngo."/n/nHarry stared apprehensively at Moody. Had he/noverheard them?/n/n"Er — Professor, I'm supposed to be in Herbology — "/n/n"Never mind that, Potter. In my office, please. ..."/n/nHarry followed him, wondering what was going to/nhappen to him now. What if Moody wanted to know/nhow he'd found out about the dragons? Would Moody/ngo to Dumbledore and tell on Hagrid, or just turn/nHarry into a ferret? Well, it might be easier to get past/na dragon if he were a ferret, Harry thought dully, he'd/nbe smaller, much less easy to see from a height of fifty/nfeet .../n/nHe followed Moody into his office. Moody closed the/ndoor behind them and turned to look at Harry, his/nmagical eye fixed upon him as well as the normal one./n/n"That was a very decent thing you just did, Potter,"/nMoody said quietly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry didn't know what to say; this wasn't the/nreaction he had expected at all./n/n/n/n"Sit down," said Moody, and Harry sat, looking/naround./n/nHe had visited this office under two of its previous/noccupants. In Professor Lockhart's day, the walls had/nbeen plastered with beaming, winking pictures of/nProfessor Lockhart himself. When Lupin had lived/nhere, you were more likely to come across a specimen/nof some fascinating new Dark creature he had/nprocured for them to study in class. Now, however,/nthe office was full of a number of exceptionally odd/nobjects that Harry supposed Moody had used in the/ndays when he had been an Auror./n/nOn his desk stood what looked like a large, cracked,/nglass spinning top; Harry recognized it at once as a/nSneakoscope, because he owned one himself, though/nit was much smaller than Moody's. In the corner on a/nsmall table stood an object that looked something like/nan extra- squiggly, golden television aerial. It was/nhumming slightly. What appeared to be a mirror hung/nopposite Harry on the wall, but it was not reflecting/nthe room. Shadowy figures were moving around/ninside it, none of them clearly in focus./n/n"Like my Dark Detectors, do you?" said Moody, who/nwas watching Harry closely./n/n"What's that?" Harry asked, pointing at the squiggly/ngolden aerial./n/n"Secrecy Sensor. Vibrates when it detects/nconcealment and lies ... no use here, of course, too/nmuch interference — students in every direction lying/nabout why they haven't done their homework. Been/nhumming ever since I got here. I had to disable my/n/n/n/n/nSneakoscope because it wouldn't stop whistling. It's/nextra-sensitive, picks up stuff about a mile around. Of/ncourse, it could be picking up more than kid stuff," he/nadded in a growl./n/n"And what's the mirror for?"/n/n"Oh that's my Foe-Glass. See them out there,/nskulking around? I'm not really in trouble until I see/nthe whites of their eyes. That's when I open my/ntrunk."/n/nHe let out a short, harsh laugh, and pointed to the/nlarge trunk under the window. It had seven keyholes/nin a row. Harry wondered what was in there, until/nMoody's next question brought him sharply back to/nearth./n/n"So ... found out about the dragons, have you?"/n/nHarry hesitated. He'd been afraid of this — but he/nhadn't told Cedric, and he certainly wasn't going to/ntell Moody, that Hagrid had broken the rules./n/n"It's all right," said Moody, sitting down and/nstretching out his wooden leg with a groan./n/n"Cheating's a traditional part of the Tri-wizard/nTournament and always has been."/n/n"I didn't cheat," said Harry sharply. "It was — a sort/nof accident that I found out."/n/nMoody grinned. "I wasn't accusing you, laddie. I've/nbeen telling Dumbledore from the start, he can be as/nhigh-minded as he likes, but you can bet old/nKarkaroff and Maxime won't be. They'll have told their/nchampions everything they can. They want to win./nThey want to beat Dumbledore. They'd like to prove/nhe's only human."/n/n/n/n/n/nMoody gave another harsh laugh, and his magical eye/nswiveled around so fast it made Harry feel queasy to/nwatch it./n/n"So ... got any ideas how you're going to get past your/ndragon yet?" said Moody./n/n"No," said Harry./n/n"Well, I'm not going to tell you," said Moody gruffly. "I/ndon't show favoritism, me. I'm just going to give you/nsome good, general advice. And the first bit is — play/nto your strengths."/n/n"I haven't got any," said Harry, before he could stop/nhimself./n/n"Excuse me," growled Moody, "you've got strengths if I/nsay you've got them. Think now. What are you best/nat?"/n/nHarry tried to concentrate. What was he best at?/n/nWell, that was easy, really —/n/n"Quidditch," he said dully, "and a fat lot of help — "/n/n"That's right," said Moody, staring at him very hard,/nhis magical eye barely moving at all. "You're a damn/ngood flier from what I've heard."/n/n"Yeah, but ..." Harry stared at him. "I'm not allowed a/nbroom, I've only got my wand — "/n/n"My second piece of general advice," said Moody/nloudly, interrupting him, "is to use a nice, simple/nspell that will enable you to get what you need."/n/nHarry looked at him blankly. What did he need?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Come on, boy ..." whispered Moody. "Put them/ntogether ... it's not that difficult. ..."/n/nAnd it clicked. He was best at flying. He needed to/npass the dragon in the air. For that, he needed his/nFirebolt. And for his Firebolt, he needed —/n/n"Hermione," Harry whispered, when he had sped into/ngreenhouse three minutes later, uttering a hurried/napology to Professor Sprout as he passed her./n"Hermione — I need you to help me."/n/n"What d'you think I've been trying to do, Harry?" she/nwhispered back, her eyes round with anxiety over the/ntop of the quivering Flutterby Bush she was pruning./n/n"Hermione, I need to learn how to do a Summoning/nCharm properly by tomorrow afternoon."/n/nAnd so they practiced. They didn't have lunch, but/nheaded for a free classroom, where Harry tried with/nall his might to make various objects fly across the/nroom toward him. He was still having problems. The/nbooks and quills kept losing heart halfway across the/nroom and dropping like stones to the floor./n/n"Concentrate, Harry, concentrate. ..."/n/n"What d'you think I'm trying to do?" said Harry/nangrily. "A great big dragon keeps popping up in my/nhead for some reason. ... Okay, try again. ..."/n/nHe wanted to skip Divination to keep practicing, but/nHermione refused point-blank to skive off/nArithmancy, and there was no point in staying/nwithout her. He therefore had to endure over an hour/nof Professor Trelawney, who spent half the lesson/ntelling everyone that the position of Mars with relation/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nto Saturn at that moment meant that people born in/nJuly were in great danger of sudden, violent deaths./n/n"Well, that's good," said Harry loudly, his temper/ngetting the better of him, "just as long as it's not/ndrawn-out. I don't want to suffer."/n/nRon looked for a moment as though he was going to/nlaugh; he certainly caught Harry's eye for the first/ntime in days, but Harry was still feeling too resentful/ntoward Ron to care. He spent the rest of the lesson/ntrying to attract small objects toward him under the/ntable with his wand. He managed to make a fly zoom/nstraight into his hand, though he wasn't entirely sure/nthat was his prowess at Summoning Charms —/nperhaps the fly was just stupid./n/nHe forced down some dinner after Divination, then/nreturned to the empty classroom with Hermione,/nusing the Invisibility Cloak to avoid the teachers./n/nThey kept practicing until past midnight. They would/nhave stayed longer, but Peeves turned up and,/npretending to think that Harry wanted things thrown/nat him, started chucking chairs across the room./nHarry and Hermione left in a hurry before the noise/nattracted Filch, and went back to the Gryffindor/ncommon room, which was now mercifully empty./n/nAt two o'clock in the morning, Harry stood near the/nfireplace, surrounded by heaps of objects: books,/nquills, several upturned chairs, an old set of/nGobstones, and Neville's toad, Trevor. Only in the last/nhour had Harry really got the hang of the Summoning/nCharm./n/n"That's better, Harry, that's loads better," Hermione/nsaid, looking exhausted but very pleased./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, now we know what to do next time I can't/nmanage a spell," Harry said, throwing a rune/ndictionary back to Hermione, so he could try again,/n"threaten me with a dragon. Right ..." He raised his/nwand once more. "Accio Dictionary !"/n/nThe heavy book soared out of Hermione 's hand, flew/nacross the room, and Harry caught it./n/n"Harry, I really think you've got it!" said Hermione/ndelightedly./n/n"Just as long as it works tomorrow," Harry said. "The/nFirebolt's going to be much farther away than the/nstuff in here, it's going to be in the castle, and I'm/ngoing to be out there on the grounds. ..."/n/n"That doesn't matter," said Hermione firmly "Just as/nlong as you're concentrating really, really hard on it,/nit'll come. Harry, we'd better get some sleep ... you're/ngoing to need it."/n/nHarry had been focusing so hard on learning the/nSummoning Charm that evening that some of his/nblind panic had left him. It returned in full measure,/nhowever, on the following morning. The atmosphere/nin the school was one of great tension and excitement./nLessons were to stop at midday, giving all the/nstudents time to get down to the dragons' enclosure/n— though of course, they didn't yet know what they/nwould find there./n/nHarry felt oddly separate from everyone around him,/nwhether they were wishing him good luck or hissing/n" We'll have a box of tissues ready, Potted as he/npassed. It was a state of nervousness so advanced/nthat he wondered whether he mightn't just lose his/nhead when they tried to lead him out to his dragon,/nand start trying to curse everyone in sight. Time was/n/n/n/n/nbehaving in a more peculiar fashion than ever,/nrushing past in great dollops, so that one moment he/nseemed to be sitting down in his first lesson, History/nof Magic, and the next, walking into lunch . . . and/nthen (where had the morning gone? the last of the/ndragon-free hours?), Professor McGonagall was/nhurrying over to him in the Great Hall. Lots of people/nwere watching./n/n"Potter, the champions have to come down onto the/ngrounds now. ... You have to get ready for your first/ntask."/n/n"Okay," said Harry, standing up, his fork falling onto/nhis plate with a clatter./n/n"Good luck, Harry," Hermione whispered. "You'll be/nfine!"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry in a voice that was most unlike his/nown./n/nHe left the Great Hall with Professor McGonagall. She/ndidn't seem herself either; in fact, she looked nearly/nas anxious as Hermione. As she walked him down the/nstone steps and out into the cold November afternoon,/nshe put her hand on his shoulder./n/n"Now, don't panic," she said, "just keep a cool head./n/n... We've got wizards standing by to control the/nsituation if it gets out of hand. ... The main thing is/njust to do your best, and nobody will think any the/nworse of you. ... Are you all right?"/n/n"Yes," Harry heard himself say. "Yes, I'm fine."/n/nShe was leading him toward the place where the/ndragons were, around the edge of the forest, but when/nthey approached the clump of trees behind which the/n/n/n/n/n/nenclosure would be clearly visible, Harry saw that a/ntent had been erected, its entrance facing them,/nscreening the dragons from view./n/n"You're to go in here with the other champions," said/nProfessor McGonagall, in a rather shaky sort of voice,/n"and wait for your turn, Potter. Mr. Bagman is in/nthere ... he'll be telling you the — the procedure. .../nGood luck."/n/n"Thanks," said Harry, in a flat, distant voice. She left/nhim at the entrance of the tent. Harry went inside./n/nFleur Delacour was sitting in a corner on a low/nwooden stool. She didn't look nearly as composed as/nusual, but rather pale and clammy. Viktor Krum/nlooked even surlier than usual, which Harry/nsupposed was his way of showing nerves. Cedric was/npacing up and down. When Harry entered, Cedric/ngave him a small smile, which Harry returned, feeling/nthe muscles in his face working rather hard, as/nthough they had forgotten how to do it./n/n"Harry! Good-o!" said Bagman happily, looking/naround at him. "Come in, come in, make yourself at/nhome!"/n/nBagman looked somehow like a slightly overblown/ncartoon figure, standing amid all the pale-faced/nchampions. He was wearing his old Wasp robes again./n/n"Well, now we're all here — time to fill you in!" said/nBagman brightly. "When the audience has assembled,/nI'm going to be offering each of you this bag" — he/nheld up a small sack of purple silk and shook it at/nthem — "from which you will each select a small/nmodel of the thing you are about to face! There are/ndifferent — er — varieties, you see. And I have to tell/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nyou something else too . . . ah, yes . . . your task is to/ncollect the golden egg\"/n/nHarry glanced around. Cedric had nodded once, to/nshow that he understood Bagman's words, and then/nstarted pacing around the tent again; he looked/nslightly green. Fleur Delacour and Krum hadn't/nreacted at all. Perhaps they thought they might be/nsick if they opened their mouths; that was certainly/nhow Harry felt. But they, at least, had volunteered for/nthis. .../n/nAnd in no time at all, hundreds upon hundreds of/npairs of feet could be heard passing the tent, their/nowners talking excitedly, laughing, joking. ... Harry/nfelt as separate from the crowd as though they were a/ndifferent species. And then — it seemed like about a/nsecond later to Harry — Bagman was opening the/nneck of the purple silk sack./n/n"Ladies first," he said, offering it to Fleur Delacour./n/nShe put a shaking hand inside the bag and drew out/na tiny, perfect model of a dragon — a Welsh Green. It/nhad the number two around its neck. And Harry/nknew, by the fact that Fleur showed no sign of/nsurprise, but rather a determined resignation, that he/nhad been right: Madame Maxime had told her what/nwas coming./n/nThe same held true for Krum. He pulled out the/nscarlet Chinese Fireball. It had a number three/naround its neck. He didn't even blink, just sat back/ndown and stared at the ground./n/nCedric put his hand into the bag, and out came the/nblueish-gray Swedish Short-Snout, the number one/ntied around its neck. Knowing what was left, Harry/nput his hand into the silk bag and pulled out the/n/n/n/n/n/nHungarian Horntail, and the number four. It/nstretched its wings as he looked down at it, and bared/nits minuscule fangs./n/n"Well, there you are!" said Bagman. "You have each/npulled out the dragon you will face, and the numbers/nrefer to the order in which you are to take on the/ndragons, do you see? Now, I'm going to have to leave/nyou in a moment, because I'm commentating. Mr./nDiggory, you're first, just go out into the enclosure/nwhen you hear a whistle, all right? Now ... Harry .../ncould I have a quick word? Outside?"/n/n"Er ... yes," said Harry blankly, and he got up and/nwent out of the tent with Bagman, who walked him a/nshort distance away, into the trees, and then turned/nto him with a fatherly expression on his face./n/n"Feeling all right, Harry? Anything I can get you?"/n/n"What?" said Harry. "I — no, nothing."/n/n"Got a plan?" said Bagman, lowering his voice/nconspiratorially. "Because I don't mind sharing a few/npointers, if you'd like them, you know. I mean,"/nBagman continued, lowering his voice still further,/n"you're the underdog here, Harry. ... Anything I can/ndo to help ..."/n/n"No," said Harry so quickly he knew he had sounded/nrude, "no — I — I know what I'm going to do, thanks."/n/n"Nobody would know, Harry," said Bagman, winking/nat him./n/n"No, I'm fine," said Harry, wondering why he kept/ntelling people this, and wondering whether he had/never been less fine. "I've got a plan worked out, I — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA whistle had blown somewhere./n/n/n/n"Good lord, I've got to run!" said Bagman in alarm,/nand he hurried off./n/nHarry walked back to the tent and saw Cedric/nemerging from it, greener than ever. Harry tried to/nwish him luck as he walked past, but all that came/nout of his mouth was a sort of hoarse grunt./n/nHarry went back inside to Fleur and Krum. Seconds/nlater, they heard the roar of the crowd, which meant/nCedric had entered the enclosure and was now face-/nto-face with the living counterpart of his model. .../n/nIt was worse than Harry could ever have imagined,/nsitting there and listening. The crowd screamed . . ./nyelled . . . gasped like a single many-headed entity, as/nCedric did whatever he was doing to get past the/nSwedish Short-Snout. Krum was still staring at the/nground. Fleur had now taken to retracing Cedric's/nsteps, around and around the tent. And Bagman's/ncommentary made everything much, much worse. .../nHorrible pictures formed in Harry's mind as he heard:/n"Oooh, narrow miss there, very narrow" ... "He's/ntaking risks, this one!" ... "Clever move — pity it/ndidn't work!"/n/nAnd then, after about fifteen minutes, Harry heard/nthe deafening roar that could mean only one thing:/nCedric had gotten past his dragon and captured the/ngolden egg./n/n"Very good indeed!" Bagman was shouting. "And now/nthe marks from the judges!"/n/nBut he didn't shout out the marks; Harry supposed/nthe judges were holding them up and showing them/nto the crowd./n/n/n/n/n/n"One down, three to go!" Bagman yelled as the whistle/nblew again. "Miss Delacour, if you please!"/n/n/n/nFleur was trembling from head to foot; Harry felt more/nwarmly toward her than he had done so far as she left/nthe tent with her head held high and her hand/nclutching her wand. He and Krum were left alone, at/nopposite sides of the tent, avoiding each other's gaze./n/nThe same process started again. ... "Oh I'm not sure/nthat was wise!" they could hear Bagman shouting/ngleefully. "Oh . . . nearly! Careful now . . . good lord, I/nthought she'd had it then!"/n/nTen minutes later, Harry heard the crowd erupt into/napplause once more. ... Fleur must have been/nsuccessful too. A pause, while Fleur's marks were/nbeing shown . . . more clapping . . . then, for the third/ntime, the whistle./n/n"And here comes Mr. Krum!" cried Bagman, and/nKrum slouched out, leaving Harry quite alone./n/nHe felt much more aware of his body than usual; very/naware of the way his heart was pumping fast, and his/nfingers tingling with fear ... yet at the same time, he/nseemed to be outside himself, seeing the walls of the/ntent, and hearing the crowd, as though from far away./n/n/n/n"Very daring!" Bagman was yelling, and Harry heard/nthe Chinese Fireball emit a horrible, roaring shriek,/nwhile the crowd drew its collective breath. "That's/nsome nerve he's showing — and — yes, he's got the/negg!"/n/nApplause shattered the wintery air like breaking/nglass; Krum had finished — it would be Harry's turn/nany moment./n/n/n/n/n/nHe stood up, noticing dimly that his legs seemed to be/nmade of marshmallow. He waited. And then he heard/nthe whistle blow. He walked out through the entrance/nof the tent, the panic rising into a crescendo inside/nhim. And now he was walking past the trees, through/na gap in the enclosure fence./n/nHe saw everything in front of him as though it was a/nvery highly colored dream. There were hundreds and/nhundreds of faces staring down at him from stands/nthat had been magicked there since he'd last stood on/nthis spot. And there was the Horntail, at the other/nend of the enclosure, crouched low over her clutch of/neggs, her wings half-furled, her evil, yellow eyes upon/nhim, a monstrous, scaly, black lizard, thrashing her/nspiked tail, leaving yard-long gouge marks in the hard/nground. The crowd was making a great deal of noise,/nbut whether friendly or not, Harry didn't know or/ncare. It was time to do what he had to do ... to focus/nhis mind, entirely and absolutely, upon the thing that/nwas his only chance. .../n/nHe raised his wand./n/n"Accio Firebolti" he shouted./n/nHarry waited, every fiber of him hoping, praying. ... If/nit hadn't worked ... if it wasn't coming ... He seemed/nto be looking at everything around him through some/nsort of shimmering, transparent barrier, like a heat/nhaze, which made the enclosure and the hundreds of/nfaces around him swim strangely. .../n/nAnd then he heard it, speeding through the air behind/nhim; he turned and saw his Firebolt hurtling toward/nhim around the edge of the woods, soaring into the/nenclosure, and stopping dead in midair beside him,/nwaiting for him to mount. The crowd was making/neven more noise. ... Bagman was shouting something/n/n/n/n/n... but Harry's ears were not working properly/nanymore ... listening wasn't important. .../n/nHe swung his leg over the broom and kicked off from/nthe ground. And a second later, something/nmiraculous happened. .../n/nAs he soared upward, as the wind rushed through his/nhair, as the crowd's faces became mere flesh-colored/npinpricks below, and the Horntail shrank to the size/nof a dog, he realized that he had left not only the/nground behind, but also his fear. . . . He was back/nwhere he belonged. .../n/nThis was just another Quidditch match, that was all/n... just another Quidditch match, and that Horntail/nwas just another ugly opposing team. .../n/nHe looked down at the clutch of eggs and spotted the/ngold one, gleaming against its cement-colored fellows,/nresiding safely between the dragon's front legs./n"Okay," Harry told himself, "diversionary tactics .../nlet's go. ..."/n/nHe dived. The Horntail's head followed him; he knew/nwhat it was going to do and pulled out of the dive just/nin time; a jet of fire had been released exactly where/nhe would have been had he not swerved away . . . but/nHarry didn't care ... that was no more than dodging a/nBludger. .../n/n"Great Scott, he can fly!" yelled Bagman as the crowd/nshrieked and gasped. "Are you watching this, Mr./nKrum?"/n/nHarry soared higher in a circle; the Horntail was still/nfollowing his progress; its head revolving on its long/nneck — if he kept this up, it would be nicely dizzy —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbut better not push it too long, or it would be/nbreathing fire again —/n/nHarry plummeted just as the Horntail opened its/nmouth, but this time he was less lucky — he missed/nthe flames, but the tail came whipping up to meet/nhim instead, and as he swerved to the left, one of the/nlong spikes grazed his shoulder, ripping his robes —/n/nHe could feel it stinging, he could hear screaming and/ngroans from the crowd, but the cut didn't seem to be/ndeep. ... Now he zoomed around the back of the/nHorntail, and a possibility occurred to him. .../n/nThe Horntail didn't seem to want to take off, she was/ntoo protective of her eggs. Though she writhed and/ntwisted, furling and unfurling her wings and keeping/nthose fearsome yellow eyes on Harry, she was afraid/nto move too far from them . . . but he had to persuade/nher to do it, or he'd never get near them. ... The trick/nwas to do it carefully, gradually. . . ./n/nHe began to fly, first this way, then the other, not/nnear enough to make her breathe fire to stave him off,/nbut still posing a sufficient threat to ensure she kept/nher eyes on him. Her head swayed this way and that,/nwatching him out of those vertical pupils, her fangs/nbared. .../n/nHe flew higher. The Horntail's head rose with him, her/nneck now stretched to its fullest extent, still swaying,/nlike a snake before its charmer. . . ./n/nHarry rose a few more feet, and she let out a roar of/nexasperation. He was like a fly to her, a fly she was/nlonging to swat; her tail thrashed again, but he was/ntoo high to reach now. ... She shot fire into the air,/nwhich he dodged. ... Her jaws opened wide. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Come on," Harry hissed, swerving tantalizingly above/nher, "come on, come and get me ... up you get now ..."/n/nAnd then she reared, spreading her great, black,/nleathery wings at last, as wide as those of a small/nairplane — and Harry dived. Before the dragon knew/nwhat he had done, or where he had disappeared to,/nhe was speeding toward the ground as fast as he/ncould go, toward the eggs now unprotected by her/nclawed front legs — he had taken his hands off his/nFirebolt — he had seized the golden egg —/n/nAnd with a huge spurt of speed, he was off, he was/nsoaring out over the stands, the heavy egg safely/nunder his uninjured arm, and it was as though/nsomebody had just turned the volume back up — for/nthe first time, he became properly aware of the noise/nof the crowd, which was screaming and applauding as/nloudly as the Irish supporters at the World Cup —/n/n"Look at that!" Bagman was yelling. "Will you look at/nthat! Our youngest champion is quickest to get his/negg! Well, this is going to shorten the odds on Mr./nPotter!"/n/nHarry saw the dragon keepers rushing forward to/nsubdue the Horntail, and, over at the entrance to the/nenclosure, Professor McGonagall, Professor Moody,/nand Hagrid hurrying to meet him, all of them waving/nhim toward them, their smiles evident even from this/ndistance. He flew back over the stands, the noise of/nthe crowd pounding his eardrums, and came in/nsmoothly to land, his heart lighter than it had been in/nweeks. ... He had got through the first task, he had/nsurvived. .../n/n"That was excellent, Potter!" cried Professor/nMcGonagall as he got off the Firebolt — which from/nher was extravagant praise. He noticed that her hand/n/n/n/n/n/nshook as she pointed at his shoulder. "You'll need to/nsee Madam Pomfrey before the judges give out your/nscore. ... Over there, she's had to mop up Diggory/nalready. ..."/n/n"Yeh did it, Harry!" said Hagrid hoarsely. "Yeh did it!/nAn' agains' the Horntail an' all, an' yeh know Charlie/nsaid that was the wors' — "/n/n"Thanks, Hagrid," said Harry loudly, so that Hagrid/nwouldn't blunder on and reveal that he had shown/nHarry the dragons beforehand./n/nProfessor Moody looked very pleased too; his magical/neye was dancing in its socket./n/n"Nice and easy does the trick, Potter," he growled./n/n"Right then, Potter, the first aid tent, please ..." said/nProfessor McGonagall./n/nHarry walked out of the enclosure, still panting, and/nsaw Madam Pomfrey standing at the mouth of a/nsecond tent, looking worried./n/n"Dragons!" she said, in a disgusted tone, pulling/nHarry inside. The tent was divided into cubicles; he/ncould make out Cedric's shadow through the canvas,/nbut Cedric didn't seem to be badly injured; he was/nsitting up, at least. Madam Pomfrey examined Harry's/nshoulder, talking furiously all the while. "Last year/ndementors, this year dragons, what are they going to/nbring into this school next? You're very lucky ... this/nis quite shallow ... it'll need cleaning before I heal it/nup, though. ..."/n/nShe cleaned the cut with a dab of some purple liquid/nthat smoked and stung, but then poked his shoulder/nwith her wand, and he felt it heal instantly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Now, just sit quietly for a minute — sit! And then you/ncan go and get your score."/n/nShe bustled out of the tent and he heard her go next/ndoor and say, "How does it feel now, Diggory?"/n/nHarry didn't want to sit still: He was too full of/nadrenaline. He got to his feet, wanting to see what/nwas going on outside, but before he'd reached the/nmouth of the tent, two people had come darting inside/n— Hermione, followed closely by Ron./n/n"Harry, you were brilliant!" Hermione said squeakily./nThere were fingernail marks on her face where she/nhad been clutching it in fear. "You were amazing! You/nreally were!"/n/nBut Harry was looking at Ron, who was very white/nand staring at Harry as though he were a ghost./n/n"Harry," he said, very seriously, "whoever put your/nname in that goblet — I — I reckon they're trying to/ndo you in!"/n/nIt was as though the last few weeks had never/nhappened — as though Harry were meeting Ron for/nthe first time, right after he'd been made champion./n/n"Caught on, have you?" said Harry coldly. "Took you/nlong enough."/n/nHermione stood nervously between them, looking/nfrom one to the other. Ron opened his mouth/nuncertainly. Harry knew Ron was about to apologize/nand suddenly he found he didn't need to hear it./n/n"It's okay," he said, before Ron could get the words/nout. "Forget it."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Ron, "I shouldn't've — "/n/n/n/n" Forget it," Harry said./n/nRon grinned nervously at him, and Harry grinned/nback./n/nHermione burst into tears./n/n"There's nothing to cry about!" Harry told her,/nbewildered./n/n"You two are so stupid)." she shouted, stamping her/nfoot on the ground, tears splashing down her front./nThen, before either of them could stop her, she had/ngiven both of them a hug and dashed away, now/npositively howling./n/n"Barking mad," said Ron, shaking his head. "Harry,/nc'mon, they'll be putting up your scores. ..."/n/nPicking up the golden egg and his Firebolt, feeling/nmore elated than he would have believed possible an/nhour ago, Harry ducked out of the tent, Ron by his/nside, talking fast./n/n"You were the best, you know, no competition. Cedric/ndid this weird thing where he Transfigured a rock on/nthe ground . . . turned it into a dog ... he was trying to/nmake the dragon go for the dog instead of him. Well,/nit was a pretty cool bit of Transfiguration, and it sort/nof worked, because he did get the egg, but he got/nburned as well — the dragon changed its mind/nhalfway through and decided it would rather have/nhim than the Labrador; he only just got away. And/nthat Fleur girl tried this sort of charm, I think she/nwas trying to put it into a trance — well, that kind of/nworked too, it went all sleepy, but then it snored, and/nthis great jet of flame shot out, and her skirt caught/n/n/n/n/nfire — she put it out with a bit of water out of her/nwand. And Krum — you won't believe this, but he/ndidn't even think of flying! He was probably the best/nafter you, though. Hit it with some sort of spell right/nin the eye. Only thing is, it went trampling around in/nagony and squashed half the real eggs — they took/nmarks off for that, he wasn't supposed to do any/ndamage to them."/n/nRon drew breath as he and Harry reached the edge of/nthe enclosure. Now that the Horntail had been taken/naway, Harry could see where the five judges were/nsitting — right at the other end, in raised seats/ndraped in gold./n/n"It's marks out of ten from each one," Ron said, and/nHarry, squinting up the field, saw the first judge —/nMadame Maxime — raise her wand in the air. What/nlooked like a long silver ribbon shot out of it, which/ntwisted itself into a large figure eight./n/n"Not bad!" said Ron as the crowd applauded. "I/nsuppose she took marks off for your shoulder. ..."/n/nMr. Crouch came next. He shot a number nine into/nthe air./n/n"Looking good!" Ron yelled, thumping Harry on the/nback./n/nNext, Dumbledore. He too put up a nine. The crowd/nwas cheering harder than ever./n/nLudo Bagman — ten./n/n"Ten?" said Harry in disbelief. "But ... I got hurt. .../nWhat's he playing at?"/n/n"Harry, don't complain!" Ron yelled excitedly./n/n/n/n/n/nAnd now Karkaroff raised his wand. He paused for a/nmoment, and then a number shot out of his wand too/n— four./n/n/n/n"What?" Ron bellowed furiously. "Four? You lousy,/nbiased scumbag, you gave Krum ten!"/n/nBut Harry didn't care, he wouldn't have cared if/nKarkaroff had given him zero; Ron's indignation on/nhis behalf was worth about a hundred points to him./nHe didn't tell Ron this, of course, but his heart felt/nlighter than air as he turned to leave the enclosure./nAnd it wasn't just Ron ... those weren't only/nGryffindors cheering in the crowd. When it had come/nto it, when they had seen what he was facing, most of/nthe school had been on his side as well as Cedric's. .../nHe didn't care about the Slytherins, he could stand/nwhatever they threw at him now./n/n"You're tied in first place, Harry! You and Krum!" said/nCharlie Weasley, hurrying to meet them as they set off/nback toward the school. "Listen, I've got to run, I've/ngot to go and send Mum an owl, I swore I'd tell her/nwhat happened — but that was unbelievable! Oh yeah/n— and they told me to tell you you've got to hang/naround for a few more minutes. ... Bagman wants a/nword, back in the champions' tent."/n/nRon said he would wait, so Harry reentered the tent,/nwhich somehow looked quite different now: friendly/nand welcoming. He thought back to how he'd felt/nwhile dodging the Horntail, and compared it to the/nlong wait before he'd walked out to face it. ... There/nwas no comparison; the wait had been immeasurably/nworse./n/nFleur, Cedric, and Krum all came in together. One/nside of Cedric's face was covered in a thick orange/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/npaste, which was presumably mending his burn. He/ngrinned at Harry when he saw him./n/n"Good one, Harry."/n/n"And you," said Harry, grinning back./n/n"Well done, all of you!" said Ludo Bagman, bouncing/ninto the tent and looking as pleased as though he/npersonally had just got past a dragon. "Now, just a/nquick few words. You've got a nice long break before/nthe second task, which will take place at half past/nnine on the morning of February the twenty-fourth —/nbut we're giving you something to think about in the/nmeantime! If you look down at those golden eggs/nyou're all holding, you will see that they open ... see/nthe hinges there? You need to solve the clue inside/nthe egg — because it will tell you what the second/ntask is, and enable you to prepare for it! All clear?/nSure? Well, off you go, then!"/n/nHarry left the tent, rejoined Ron, and they started to/nwalk back around the edge of the forest, talking hard;/nHarry wanted to hear what the other champions had/ndone in more detail. Then, as they rounded the clump/nof trees behind which Harry had first heard the/ndragons roar, a witch leapt out from behind them./n/nIt was Rita Skeeter. She was wearing acid-green robes/ntoday; the Quick-Quotes Quill in her hand blended/nperfectly against them./n/n"Congratulations, Harry!" she said, beaming at him. "I/nwonder if you could give me a quick word? How you/nfelt facing that dragon? How you feel now, about the/nfairness of the scoring?"/n/n"Yeah, you can have a word," said Harry savagely./n"Good-bye."/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd he set off back to the castle with Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The House-Elf Liberation Front
text: /nHarry, Ron, and Hermione went up to the Owlery that/nevening to find Pigwidgeon, so that Harry could send/nSirius a letter telling him that he had managed to get/npast his dragon unscathed. On the way, Harry filled/nRon in on everything Sirius had told him about/nKarkaroff. Though shocked at first to hear that/nKarkaroff had been a Death Eater, by the time they/nentered the Owlery Ron was saying that they ought to/nhave suspected it all along./n/n"Fits, doesn't it?" he said. "Remember what Malfoy/nsaid on the train, about his dad being friends with/nKarkaroff? Now we know where they knew each other./nThey were probably running around in masks/ntogether at the World Cup. ... I'll tell you one thing,/nthough, Harry, if it was Karkaroff who put your name/nin the goblet, he's going to be feeling really stupid/nnow, isn't he? Didn't work, did it? You only got a/nscratch! Come here — I'll do it — "/n/nPigwidgeon was so overexcited at the idea of a delivery/nhe was flying around and around Harry's head,/n/n/n/n/nhooting incessantly. Ron snatched Pigwidgeon out of/nthe air and held him still while Harry attached the/nletter to his leg./n/n"There's no way any of the other tasks are going to be/nthat dangerous, how could they be?" Ron went on as/nhe carried Pigwidgeon to the window. "You know/nwhat? I reckon you could win this tournament, Harry,/nI'm serious."/n/nHarry knew that Ron was only saying this to make up/nfor his behavior of the last few weeks, but he/nappreciated it all the same. Hermione, however,/nleaned against the Owlery wall, folded her arms, and/nfrowned at Ron./n/n"Harry's got a long way to go before he finishes this/ntournament," she said seriously. "If that was the first/ntask, I hate to think what's coming next."/n/n"Right little ray of sunshine, aren't you?" said Ron./n"You and Professor Trelawney should get together/nsometime."/n/nHe threw Pigwidgeon out of the window. Pigwidgeon/nplummeted twelve feet before managing to pull/nhimself back up again; the letter attached to his leg/nwas much longer and heavier than usual — Harry/nhadn't been able to resist giving Sirius a blow-by-blow/naccount of exactly how he had swerved, circled, and/ndodged the Horntail. They watched Pigwidgeon/ndisappear into the darkness, and then Ron said,/n/n"Well, we'd better get downstairs for your surprise/nparty, Harry — Fred and George should have nicked/nenough food from the kitchens by now."/n/nSure enough, when they entered the Gryffindor/ncommon room it exploded with cheers and yells again./nThere were mountains of cakes and flagons of/n/n/n/n/n/npumpkin juice and butterbeer on every surface; Lee/nJordan had let off some Filibuster's Fireworks, so that/nthe air was thick with stars and sparks; and Dean/nThomas, who was very good at drawing, had put up/nsome impressive new banners, most of which depicted/nHarry zooming around the Horntail's head on his/nFirebolt, though a couple showed Cedric with his/nhead on fire./n/nHarry helped himself to food; he had almost forgotten/nwhat it was like to feel properly hungry, and sat down/nwith Ron and Hermione. He couldn't believe how/nhappy he felt; he had Ron back on his side, he'd/ngotten through the first task, and he wouldn't have to/nface the second one for three months./n/n"Blimey, this is heavy," said Lee Jordan, picking up/nthe golden egg, which Harry had left on a table, and/nweighing it in his hands. "Open it, Harry, go on! Let's/njust see what's inside it!"/n/n"He's supposed to work out the clue on his own,"/nHermione said swiftly. "It's in the tournament rules./n/n/n/n"I was supposed to work out how to get past the/ndragon on my own too," Harry muttered, so only/nHermione could hear him, and she grinned rather/nguiltily./n/n"Yeah, go on, Harry, open it!" several people echoed./n/nLee passed Harry the egg, and Harry dug his/nfingernails into the groove that ran all the way around/nit and prised it open./n/nIt was hollow and completely empty — but the/nmoment Harry opened it, the most horrible noise, a/nloud and screechy wailing, filled the room. The/n/n/n/n/n/nnearest thing to it Harry had ever heard was the ghost/norchestra at Nearly Headless Nick's deathday party,/nwho had all been playing the musical saw./n/n"Shut it!" Fred bellowed, his hands over his ears./n/n"What was that?" said Seamus Finnigan, staring at/nthe egg as Harry slammed it shut again. "Sounded/nlike a banshee. ... Maybe you've got to get past one of/nthose next, Harry!"/n/n"It was someone being tortured!" said Neville, who/nhad gone very white and spilled sausage rolls all over/nthe floor. "You're going to have to fight the Cruciatus/nCurse!"/n/n"Don't be a prat, Neville, that's illegal," said George./n"They wouldn't use the Cruciatus Curse on the/nchampions. I thought it sounded a bit like Percy/nsinging ... maybe you've got to attack him while he's/nin the shower, Harry."/n/n"Want a jam tart, Hermione?" said Fred./n/nHermione looked doubtfully at the plate he was/noffering her. Fred grinned./n/n"It's all right," he said. "I haven't done anything to/nthem. It's the custard creams you've got to watch — "/n/nNeville, who had just bitten into a custard cream,/nchoked and spat it out. Fred laughed./n/n"Just my little joke, Neville. ..."/n/nHermione took a jam tart. Then she said, "Did you get/nall this from the kitchens, Fred?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yep," said Fred, grinning at her. He put on a high-/npitched squeak and imitated a house-elf. " 'Anything/nwe can get you, sir, anything at all!' They're dead/nhelpful ... get me a roast ox if I said I was peckish."/n/n"How do you get in there?" Hermione said in an/ninnocently casual sort of voice./n/n"Easy," said Fred, "concealed door behind a painting/nof a bowl of fruit. Just tickle the pear, and it giggles/nand — " He stopped and looked suspiciously at her./n"Why?"/n/n"Nothing," said Hermione quickly./n/n"Going to try and lead the house-elves out on strike/nnow, are you?" said George. "Going to give up all the/nleaflet stuff and try and stir them up into rebellion?"/n/nSeveral people chortled. Hermione didn't answer./n/n"Don't you go upsetting them and telling them they've/ngot to take clothes and salaries!" said Fred warningly./n"You'll put them off their cooking!"/n/nJust then, Neville caused a slight diversion by turning/ninto a large canary./n/n"Oh — sorry, Neville!" Fred shouted over all the/nlaughter. "I forgot — it was the custard creams we/nhexed — "/n/nWithin a minute, however, Neville had molted, and/nonce his feathers had fallen off, he reappeared looking/nentirely normal. He even joined in laughing./n/n"Canary Creams!" Fred shouted to the excitable/ncrowd. "George and I invented them — seven Sickles/neach, a bargain!"/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was nearly one in the morning when Harry finally/nwent up to the dormitory with Ron, Neville, Seamus,/nand Dean. Before he pulled the curtains of his four-/nposter shut, Harry set his tiny model of the/nHungarian Horntail on the table next to his bed,/nwhere it yawned, curled up, and closed its eyes./n/nReally, Harry thought, as he pulled the hangings on/nhis four-poster closed, Hagrid had a point . . . they/nwere all right, really, dragons. .../n/nThe start of December brought wind and sleet to/nHogwarts. Drafty though the castle always was in/nwinter, Harry was glad of its fires and thick walls/nevery time he passed the Durmstrang ship on the/nlake, which was pitching in the high winds, its black/nsails billowing against the dark skies. He thought the/nBeauxbatons caravan was likely to be pretty chilly/ntoo. Hagrid, he noticed, was keeping Madame/nMaxime's horses well provided with their preferred/ndrink of single-malt whiskey; the fumes wafting from/nthe trough in the corner of their paddock was enough/nto make the entire Care of Magical Creatures class/nlight-headed. This was unhelpful, as they were still/ntending the horrible skrewts and needed their wits/nabout them./n/n"I'm not sure whether they hibernate or not," Hagrid/ntold the shivering class in the windy pumpkin patch/nnext lesson. "Thought we'd jus' try an' see if they/nfancied a kip ... we'll jus' settle 'em down in these/nboxes. ..."/n/nThere were now only ten skrewts left; apparently their/ndesire to kill one another had not been exercised out/nof them. Each of them was now approaching six feet/nin length. Their thick gray armor; their powerful,/nscuttling legs; their fire-blasting ends; their stings/nand their suckers, combined to make the skrewts the/nmost repulsive things Harry had ever seen. The class/n/n/n/n/nlooked dispiritedly at the enormous boxes Hagrid had/nbrought out, all lined with pillows and fluffy blankets./n/n"Well jus' lead 'em in here," Hagrid said, "an' put the/nlids on, and we'll see what happens."/n/nBut the skrewts, it transpired, did not hibernate, and/ndid not appreciate being forced into pillow-lined boxes/nand nailed in. Hagrid was soon yelling, "Don' panic,/nnow, don' panic!" while the skrewts rampaged around/nthe pumpkin patch, now strewn with the smoldering/nwreckage of the boxes. Most of the class — Malfoy,/nCrabbe, and Goyle in the lead — had fled into/nHagrid 's cabin through the back door and barricaded/nthemselves in; Harry, Ron, and Hermione, however,/nwere among those who remained outside trying to/nhelp Hagrid. Together they managed to restrain and/ntie up nine of the skrewts, though at the cost of/nnumerous burns and cuts; finally, only one skrewt/nwas left./n/n"Don' frighten him, now!" Hagrid shouted as Ron and/nHarry used their wands to shoot jets of fiery sparks at/nthe skrewt, which was advancing menacingly on/nthem, its sting arched, quivering, over its back. "Jus'/ntry an' slip the rope 'round his sting, so he won' hurt/nany o' the others!"/n/n"Yeah, we wouldn't want that!" Ron shouted angrily/nas he and Harry backed into the wall of Hagrid 's/ncabin, still holding the skrewt off with their sparks./n/n"Well, well, well ... this does look like fun."/n/nRita Skeeter was leaning on Hagrid 's garden fence,/nlooking in at the mayhem. She was wearing a thick/nmagenta cloak with a furry purple collar today, and/nher crocodile-skin handbag was over her arm./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid launched himself forward on top of the skrewt/nthat was cornering Harry and Ron and flattened it; a/nblast of fire shot out of its end, withering the/npumpkin plants nearby./n/n"Who 're you?" Hagrid asked Rita Skeeter as he/nslipped a loop of rope around the skrewt's sting and/ntightened it./n/n"Rita Skeeter, Daily Prophet reporter," Rita replied,/nbeaming at him. Her gold teeth glinted./n/n"Thought Dumbledore said you weren' allowed inside/nthe school anymore," said Hagrid, frowning slightly as/nhe got off the slightly squashed skrewt and started/ntugging it over to its fellows./n/nRita acted as though she hadn't heard what Hagrid/nhad said./n/n"What are these fascinating creatures called?" she/nasked, beaming still more widely./n/n"Blast-Ended Skrewts," grunted Hagrid./n/n"Really?" said Rita, apparently full of lively interest./n"I've never heard of them before ... where do they/ncome from?"/n/nHarry noticed a dull red flush rising up out of/nHagrid's wild black beard, and his heart sank. Where/nhad Hagrid got the skrewts from? Hermione, who/nseemed to be thinking along these lines, said quickly,/n"They're very interesting, aren't they? Aren't they,/nHarry?"/n/n"What? Oh yeah ... ouch ... interesting," said Harry as/nshe stepped on his foot./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah, you're here, Harry!" said Rita Skeeter as she/nlooked around. "So you like Care of Magical/nCreatures, do you? One of your favorite lessons?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry stoutly. Hagrid beamed at him./n/n"Lovely," said Rita. "Really lovely. Been teaching/nlong?" she added to Hagrid./n/nHarry noticed her eyes travel over Dean (who had a/nnasty cut across one cheek), Lavender (whose robes/nwere badly singed), Seamus (who was nursing several/nburnt fingers), and then to the cabin windows, where/nmost of the class stood, their noses pressed against/nthe glass waiting to see if the coast was clear./n/n"This is o'ny me second year," said Hagrid./n/n"Lovely... I don't suppose you'd like to give an/ninterview, would you? Share some of your experience/nof magical creatures? The Prophet does a zoological/ncolumn every Wednesday, as I'm sure you know. We/ncould feature these — er — Bang-Ended Scoots."/n/n"Blast-Ended Skrewts," Hagrid said eagerly. "Er —/nyeah, why not?"/n/nHarry had a very bad feeling about this, but there was/nno way of communicating it to Hagrid without Rita/nSkeeter seeing, so he had to stand and watch in/nsilence as Hagrid and Rita Skeeter made/narrangements to meet in the Three Broomsticks for a/ngood long interview later that week. Then the bell/nrang up at the castle, signaling the end of the lesson./n/n"Well, good-bye, Harry!" Rita Skeeter called merrily to/nhim as he set off with Ron and Hermione. "Until/nFriday night, then, Hagrid!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Shell twist everything he says," Harry said under his/nbreath./n/n"Just as long as he didn't import those skrewts/nillegally or anything," said Hermione desperately./n/nThey looked at one another — it was exactly the sort/nof thing Hagrid might do./n/n"Hagrid's been in loads of trouble before, and/nDumbledore's never sacked him," said Ron/nconsolingly. "Worst that can happen is Hagrid'll have/nto get rid of the skrewts. Sorry ... did I say worst? I/nmeant best."/n/nHarry and Hermione laughed, and, feeling slightly/nmore cheerful, went off to lunch./n/nHarry thoroughly enjoyed double Divination that/nafternoon; they were still doing star charts and/npredictions, but now that he and Ron were friends/nonce more, the whole thing seemed very funny again./nProfessor Trelawney, who had been so pleased with/nthe pair of them when they had been predicting their/nown horrific deaths, quickly became irritated as they/nsniggered through her explanation of the various/nways in which Pluto could disrupt everyday life./n/n"I would think," she said, in a mystical whisper that/ndid not conceal her obvious annoyance, "that some of/nus" — she stared very meaningfully at Harry —/n/n"might be a little less frivolous had they seen what I/nhave seen during my crystal gazing last night. As I sat/nhere, absorbed in my needlework, the urge to consult/nthe orb overpowered me. I arose, I settled myself/nbefore it, and I gazed into its crystalline depths . . . and/nwhat do you think I saw gazing back at me?"/n/n"An ugly old bat in outsize specs?" Ron muttered/nunder his breath./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry fought hard to keep his face straight./n/n"Death, my dears."/n/nParvati and Lavender both put their hands over their/nmouths, looking horrified./n/n"Yes," said Professor Trelawney, nodding impressively,/n"it comes, ever closer, it circles overhead like a/nvulture, ever lower ... ever lower over the castle. ..."/n/nShe stared pointedly at Harry, who yawned very/nwidely and obviously./n/n"It'd be a bit more impressive if she hadn't done it/nabout eighty times before," Harry said as they finally/nregained the fresh air of the staircase beneath/nProfessor Trelawney's room. "But if I'd dropped dead/nevery time she's told me I'm going to, I'd be a medical/nmiracle."/n/n"You'd be a sort of extra-concentrated ghost," said/nRon, chortling, as they passed the Bloody Baron going/nin the opposite direction, his wide eyes staring/nsinisterly. "At least we didn't get homework. I hope/nHermione got loads off Professor Vector, I love not/nworking when she is. ..."/n/nBut Hermione wasn't at dinner, nor was she in the/nlibrary when they went to look for her afterward. The/nonly person in there was Viktor Krum. Ron hovered/nbehind the bookshelves for a while, watching Krum,/ndebating in whispers with Harry whether he should/nask for an autograph — but then Ron realized that six/nor seven girls were lurking in the next row of books,/ndebating exactly the same thing, and he lost his/nenthusiasm for the idea./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wonder where she's got to?" Ron said as he and/nHarry went back to Gryffindor Tower./n/n/n/n"Dunno ... balderdash."/n/nBut the Fat Lady had barely begun to swing forward/nwhen the sound of racing feet behind them/nannounced Hermione's arrival./n/n"Harry!" she panted, skidding to a halt beside him/n(the Fat Lady stared down at her, eyebrows raised)./n"Harry, you've got to come — you've got to come, the/nmost amazing thing's happened — please — "/n/nShe seized Harry's arm and started to try to drag him/nback along the corridor./n/n"What's the matter?" Harry said./n/n"I'll show you when we get there — oh come on, quick/n/n/n/nHarry looked around at Ron; he looked back at Harry,/nintrigued./n/n"Okay," Harry said, starting off back down the/ncorridor with Hermione, Ron hurrying to keep up./n/n"Oh don't mind me!" the Fat Lady called irritably after/nthem. "Don't apologize for bothering me! I'll just hang/nhere, wide open, until you get back, shall I?"/n/n"Yeah, thanks!" Ron shouted over his shoulder./n/n"Hermione, where are we going?" Harry asked, after/nshe had led them down through six floors, and/nstarted down the marble staircase into the entrance/nhall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You'll see, you'll see in a minute!" said Hermione/nexcitedly./n/nShe turned left at the bottom of the staircase and/nhurried toward the door through which Cedric/nDiggory had gone the night after the Goblet of Fire/nhad regurgitated his and Harry's names. Harry had/nnever been through here before. He and Ron followed/nHermione down a flight of stone steps, but instead of/nending up in a gloomy underground passage like the/none that led to Snape's dungeon, they found/nthemselves in a broad stone corridor, brightly lit with/ntorches, and decorated with cheerful paintings that/nwere mainly of food./n/n"Oh hang on ..." said Harry slowly, halfway down the/ncorridor. "Wait a minute, Hermione. ..."/n/n"What?" She turned around to look at him,/nanticipation all over her face./n/n"I know what this is about," said Harry./n/nHe nudged Ron and pointed to the painting just/nbehind Hermione. It showed a gigantic silver fruit/nbowl./n/n"Hermione!" said Ron, cottoning on. "You're trying to/nrope us into that spew stuff again!"/n/n"No, no, I'm not!" she said hastily. "And it's not spew,/nRon — "/n/n"Changed the name, have you?" said Ron, frowning at/nher. "What are we now, then, the House-Elf Liberation/nFront? I'm not barging into that kitchen and trying to/nmake them stop work, I'm not doing it — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm not asking you to!" Hermione said impatiently. "I/ncame down here just now, to talk to them all, and I/nfound — oh come on, Harry, I want to show you!"/n/nShe seized his arm again, pulled him in front of the/npicture of the giant fruit bowl, stretched out her/nforefinger, and tickled the huge green pear. It began/nto squirm, chuckling, and suddenly turned into a/nlarge green door handle. Hermione seized it, pulled/nthe door open, and pushed Harry hard in the back,/nforcing him inside./n/nHe had one brief glimpse of an enormous, high-/nceilinged room, large as the Great Hall above it, with/nmounds of glittering brass pots and pans heaped/naround the stone walls, and a great brick fireplace at/nthe other end, when something small hurtled toward/nhim from the middle of the room, squealing, "Harry/nPotter, sir! Harry Potteri"/n/nNext second all the wind had been knocked out of/nhim as the squealing elf hit him hard in the midriff,/nhugging him so tightly he thought his ribs would/nbreak./n/n"D-Dobby?" Harry gasped./n/n"It is Dobby, sir, it is!" squealed the voice from/nsomewhere around his navel. "Dobby has been/nhoping and hoping to see Harry Potter, sir, and Harry/nPotter has come to see him, sir!"/n/nDobby let go and stepped back a few paces, beaming/nup at Harry, his enormous, green, tennis-ball-shaped/neyes brimming with tears of happiness. He looked/nalmost exactly as Harry remembered him; the pencil-/nshaped nose, the batlike ears, the long fingers and/nfeet — all except the clothes, which were very/ndifferent./n/n/n/n/n/nWhen Dobby had worked for the Malfoys, he had/nalways worn the same filthy old pillowcase. Now,/nhowever, he was wearing the strangest assortment of/ngarments Harry had ever seen; he had done an even/nworse job of dressing himself than the wizards at the/nWorld Cup. He was wearing a tea cozy for a hat, on/nwhich he had pinned a number of bright badges; a tie/npatterned with horseshoes over a bare chest, a pair of/nwhat looked like children's soccer shorts, and odd/nsocks. One of these, Harry saw, was the black one/nHarry had removed from his own foot and tricked Mr./nMalfoy into giving Dobby, thereby setting Dobby free./nThe other was covered in pink and orange stripes./n/n"Dobby, what're you doing here?" Harry said in/namazement./n/n"Dobby has come to work at Hogwarts, sir!" Dobby/nsquealed excitedly. "Professor Dumbledore gave/nDobby and Winky jobs, sir!"/n/n"Winky?" said Harry. "She's here too?"/n/n"Yes, sir, yes!" said Dobby, and he seized Harry's/nhand and pulled him off into the kitchen between the/nfour long wooden tables that stood there. Each of/nthese tables, Harry noticed as he passed them, was/npositioned exactly beneath the four House tables/nabove, in the Great Hall. At the moment, they were/nclear of food, dinner having finished, but he supposed/nthat an hour ago they had been laden with dishes/nthat were then sent up through the ceiling to their/ncounterparts above./n/nAt least a hundred little elves were standing around/nthe kitchen, beaming, bowing, and curtsying as/nDobby led Harry past them. They were all wearing the/nsame uniform: a tea towel stamped with the Hogwarts/ncrest, and tied, as Winky's had been, like a toga./n/n/n/n/n/nDobby stopped in front of the brick fireplace and/npointed./n/n"Winky, sir!" he said./n/nWinky was sitting on a stool by the fire. Unlike/nDobby, she had obviously not foraged for clothes. She/nwas wearing a neat little skirt and blouse with a/nmatching blue hat, which had holes in it for her large/nears. However, while every one of Dobby 's strange/ncollection of garments was so clean and well cared for/nthat it looked brand-new, Winky was plainly not/ntaking care of her clothes at all. There were soup/nstains all down her blouse and a burn in her skirt./n/n"Hello, Winky," said Harry./n/nWinky's lip quivered. Then she burst into tears, which/nspilled out of her great brown eyes and splashed/ndown her front, just as they had done at the/nQuidditch World Cup./n/n"Oh dear," said Hermione. She and Ron had followed/nHarry and Dobby to the end of the kitchen. "Winky,/ndon't cry, please don't ..."/n/nBut Winky cried harder than ever. Dobby, on the/nother hand, beamed up at Harry./n/n"Would Harry Potter like a cup of tea?" he squeaked/nloudly, over Winky's sobs./n/n"Er — yeah, okay," said Harry./n/nInstantly, about six house-elves came trotting up/nbehind him, bearing a large silver tray laden with a/nteapot, cups for Harry, Ron, and Hermione, a milk/njug, and a large plate of biscuits./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Good service!" Ron said, in an impressed voice./nHermione frowned at him, but the elves all looked/ndelighted; they bowed very low and retreated./n/n"How long have you been here, Dobby?" Harry asked/nas Dobby handed around the tea./n/n"Only a week, Harry Potter, sir!" said Dobby happily./n"Dobby came to see Professor Dumbledore, sir. You/nsee, sir, it is very difficult for a house-elf who has/nbeen dismissed to get a new position, sir, very difficult/nindeed — "/n/nAt this, Winky howled even harder, her squashed-/ntomato of a nose dribbling all down her front, though/nshe made no effort to stem the flow./n/n"Dobby has traveled the country for two whole years,/nsir, trying to find work!" Dobby squeaked. "But Dobby/nhasn't found work, sir, because Dobby wants paying/nnow!"/n/nThe house-elves all around the kitchen, who had been/nlistening and watching with interest, all looked away/nat these words, as though Dobby had said something/nrude and embarrassing. Hermione, however, said,/n"Good for you, Dobby!"/n/n"Thank you, miss!" said Dobby, grinning toothily at/nher. "But most wizards doesn't want a house-elf who/nwants paying, miss. That's not the point of a house-/nelf,' they says, and they slammed the door in Dobby 's/nface! Dobby likes work, but he wants to wear clothes/nand he wants to be paid, Harry Potter. . . . Dobby likes/nbeing free!"/n/nThe Hogwarts house-elves had now started edging/naway from Dobby, as though he were carrying/nsomething contagious. Winky, however, remained/n/n/n/n/n/nwhere she was, though there was a definite increase/nin the volume of her crying./n/n"And then, Harry Potter, Dobby goes to visit Winky,/nand finds out Winky has been freed too, sir!" said/nDobby delightedly./n/nAt this, Winky flung herself forward off her stool and/nlay facedown on the flagged stone floor, beating her/ntiny fists upon it and positively screaming with/nmisery. Hermione hastily dropped down to her knees/nbeside her and tried to comfort her, but nothing she/nsaid made the slightest difference. Dobby continued/nwith his story, shouting shrilly over Winky's/nscreeches./n/n"And then Dobby had the idea, Harry Potter, sir! Why/ndoesn't Dobby and Winky find work together?' Dobby/nsays. Where is there enough work for two house-/nelves?' says Winky. And Dobby thinks, and it comes/nto him, sir! Hogwarts\ So Dobby and Winky came to/nsee Professor Dumbledore, sir, and Professor/nDumbledore took us on!"/n/nDobby beamed very brightly, and happy tears welled/nin his eyes again./n/n"And Professor Dumbledore says he will pay Dobby,/nsir, if Dobby wants paying! And so Dobby is a free elf,/nsir, and Dobby gets a Galleon a week and one day off/na month!"/n/n"That's not very much!" Hermione shouted/nindignantly from the floor, over Winky's continued/nscreaming and fist-beating./n/n"Professor Dumbledore offered Dobby ten Galleons a/nweek, and weekends off," said Dobby, suddenly giving/na little shiver, as though the prospect of so much/n/n/n/n/n/nleisure and riches were frightening, "but Dobby beat/nhim down, miss. ... Dobby likes freedom, miss, but he/nisn't wanting too much, miss, he likes work better."/n/n"And how much is Professor Dumbledore paying you,/nWinky?" Hermione asked kindly./n/nIf she had thought this would cheer up Winky, she/nwas wildly mistaken. Winky did stop crying, but when/nshe sat up she was glaring at Hermione through her/nmassive brown eyes, her whole face sopping wet and/nsuddenly furious./n/n"Winky is a disgraced elf, but Winky is not yet getting/npaid!" she squeaked. "Winky is not sunk so low as/nthat! Winky is properly ashamed of being freed!"/n/n"Ashamed?" said Hermione blankly. "But — Winky,/ncome on! It's Mr. Crouch who should be ashamed, not/nyou! You didn't do anything wrong, he was really/nhorrible to you — "/n/nBut at these words, Winky clapped her hands over/nthe holes in her hat, flattening her ears so that she/ncouldn't hear a word, and screeched, "You is not/ninsulting my master, miss! You is not insulting Mr./nCrouch! Mr. Crouch is a good wizard, miss! Mr./nCrouch is right to sack bad Winky!"/n/n"Winky is having trouble adjusting, Harry Potter,"/nsqueaked Dobby confidentially. "Winky forgets she is/nnot bound to Mr. Crouch anymore; she is allowed to/nspeak her mind now, but she won't do it."/n/n"Can't house-elves speak their minds about their/nmasters, then?" Harry asked./n/n"Oh no, sir, no," said Dobby, looking suddenly/nserious. " Tis part of the house-elf's enslavement, sir./n/n/n/n/n/nWe keeps their secrets and our silence, sir. We/nupholds the family's honor, and we never speaks ill of/nthem — though Professor Dumbledore told Dobby he/ndoes not insist upon this. Professor Dumbledore said/nwe is free to — to — "/n/nDobby looked suddenly nervous and beckoned Harry/ncloser. Harry bent forward. Dobby whispered, "He/nsaid we is free to call him a — a barmy old codger if/nwe likes, sir!"/n/nDobby gave a frightened sort of giggle./n/n"But Dobby is not wanting to, Harry Potter," he said,/ntalking normally again, and shaking his head so that/nhis ears flapped. "Dobby likes Professor Dumbledore/nvery much, sir, and is proud to keep his secrets and/nour silence for him."/n/n"But you can say what you like about the Malfoys/nnow?" Harry asked him, grinning./n/nA slightly fearful look came into Dobby's immense/neyes./n/n"Dobby — Dobby could," he said doubtfully. He/nsquared his small shoulders. "Dobby could tell Harry/nPotter that his old masters were — were — bad Dark/nwizards'."/n/nDobby stood for a moment, quivering all over, horror-/nstruck by his own daring — then he rushed over to/nthe nearest table and began banging his head on it/nvery hard, squealing, " Bad Dobby ! Bad Dobby\"/n/nHarry seized Dobby by the back of his tie and pulled/nhim away from the table./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Thank you, Harry Potter, thank you," said Dobby/nbreathlessly, rubbing his head./n/n"You just need a bit of practice," Harry said./n/n"Practice!" squealed Winky furiously. "You is ought to/nbe ashamed of yourself, Dobby, talking that way/nabout your masters!"/n/n"They isn't my masters anymore, Winky!" said Dobby/ndefiantly. "Dobby doesn't care what they think/nanymore!"/n/n"Oh you is a bad elf, Dobby!" moaned Winky, tears/nleaking down her face once more. "My poor Mr./nCrouch, what is he doing without Winky? He is/nneeding me, he is needing my help! I is looking after/nthe Crouches all my life, and my mother is doing it/nbefore me, and my grandmother is doing it before her/n...oh what is they saying if they knew Winky was/nfreed? Oh the shame, the shame!" She buried her face/nin her skirt again and bawled./n/n"Winky," said Hermione firmly, "I'm quite sure Mr./nCrouch is getting along perfectly well without you./nWe've seen him, you know — "/n/n"You is seeing my master?" said Winky breathlessly,/nraising her tearstained face out of her skirt once more/nand goggling at Hermione. "You is seeing him here at/nHogwarts?"/n/n"Yes," said Hermione, "he and Mr. Bagman are judges/nin the Tri-wizard Tournament."/n/n"Mr. Bagman comes too?" squeaked Winky, and to/nHarry's great surprise (and Ron's and Hermione's too,/nby the looks on their faces), she looked angry again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mr. Bagman is a bad wizard! A very bad wizard! My/nmaster isn't liking him, oh no, not at all!"/n/n"Bagman — bad?" said Harry./n/n"Oh yes," Winky said, nodding her head furiously./n/n"My master is telling Winky some things! But Winky/nis not saying ... Winky — Winky keeps her master's/nsecrets. ..."/n/nShe dissolved yet again in tears; they could hear her/nsobbing into her skirt, "Poor master, poor master, no/nWinky to help him no more!"/n/nThey couldn't get another sensible word out of Winky./nThey left her to her crying and finished their tea,/nwhile Dobby chatted happily about his life as a free elf/nand his plans for his wages./n/n"Dobby is going to buy a sweater next, Harry Potter!"/nhe said happily, pointing at his bare chest./n/n"Tell you what, Dobby," said Ron, who seemed to have/ntaken a great liking to the elf, "I'll give you the one my/nmum knits me this Christmas, I always get one from/nher. You don't mind maroon, do you?"/n/nDobby was delighted./n/n"We might have to shrink it a bit to fit you," Ron told/nhim, "but it'll go well with your tea cozy."/n/nAs they prepared to take their leave, many of the/nsurrounding elves pressed in upon them, offering/nsnacks to take back upstairs. Hermione refused, with/na pained look at the way the elves kept bowing and/ncurtsying, but Harry and Ron loaded their pockets/nwith cream cakes and pies./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Thanks a lot!" Harry said to the elves, who had all/nclustered around the door to say good night. "See/nyou, Dobby!"/n/n"Harry Potter . . . can Dobby come and see you/nsometimes, sir?" Dobby asked tentatively./n/n" 'Course you can," said Harry, and Dobby beamed./n/n"You know what?" said Ron, once he, Hermione, and/nHarry had left the kitchens behind and were climbing/nthe steps into the entrance hall again. "All these years/nI've been really impressed with Fred and George,/nnicking food from the kitchens — well, it's not exactly/ndifficult, is it? They can't wait to give it away!"/n/n"I think this is the best thing that could have/nhappened to those elves, you know," said Hermione,/nleading the way back up the marble staircase. "Dobby/ncoming to work here, I mean. The other elves will see/nhow happy he is, being free, and slowly it'll dawn on/nthem that they want that too!"/n/n"Let's hope they don't look too closely at Winky," said/nHarry./n/n"Oh shell cheer up," said Hermione, though she/nsounded a bit doubtful. "Once the shock's worn off,/nand she's got used to Hogwarts, she'll see how much/nbetter off she is without that Crouch man."/n/n"She seems to love him," said Ron thickly (he had just/nstarted on a cream cake) ./n/n"Doesn't think much of Bagman, though, does she?"/nsaid Harry. "Wonder what Crouch says at home about/nhim?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Probably says he's not a very good Head of/nDepartment," said Hermione, "and let's face it ... he's/ngot a point, hasn't he?"/n/n"I'd still rather work for him than old Crouch," said/nRon. "At least Bagman's got a sense of humor."/n/n"Don't let Percy hear you saying that," Hermione said,/nsmiling slightly./n/n"Yeah, well, Percy wouldn't want to work for anyone/nwith a sense of humor, would he?" said Ron, now/nstarting on a chocolate eclair. "Percy wouldn't/nrecognize a joke if it danced naked in front of him/nwearing Dobby's tea cozy."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Unexpected Task
text: /n"Potter! Weasley! Will you pay attention?"/n/nProfessor McGonagall's irritated voice cracked like a/nwhip through the Transfiguration class on Thursday,/nand Harry and Ron both jumped and looked up./n/nIt was the end of the lesson; they had finished their/nwork; the guinea fowl they had been changing into/nguinea pigs had been shut away in a large cage on/nProfessor McGonagall's desk (Neville's still had/nfeathers); they had copied down their homework from/nthe blackboard ("Describe, with examples, the ways in/nwhich Transforming Spells must be adapted when/nperforming Cross-Species Switches"). The bell was due/nto ring at any moment, and Harry and Ron, who had/nbeen having a sword fight with a couple of Fred and/nGeorge's fake wands at the back of the class, looked/nup, Ron holding a tin parrot and Harry, a rubber/nhaddock./n/n"Now that Potter and Weasley have been kind enough/nto act their age," said Professor McGonagall, with an/n/n/n/n/nangry look at the pair of them as the head of Harry's/nhaddock drooped and fell silently to the floor — Ron's/nparrot's beak had severed it moments before — "I/nhave something to say to you all./n/n"The Yule Ball is approaching — a traditional part of/nthe Tri-wizard Tournament and an opportunity for us/nto socialize with our foreign guests. Now, the ball will/nbe open only to fourth years and above — although/nyou may invite a younger student if you wish — "/n/nLavender Brown let out a shrill giggle. Parvati Patil/nnudged her hard in the ribs, her face working/nfuriously as she too fought not to giggle. They both/nlooked around at Harry. Professor McGonagall/nignored them, which Harry thought was distinctly/nunfair, as she had just told off him and Ron./n/n"Dress robes will be worn," Professor McGonagall/ncontinued, "and the ball will start at eight o'clock on/nChristmas Day, finishing at midnight in the Great/nHall.
