Now then — "/n/nProfessor McGonagall stared deliberately around the/nclass./n/n"The Yule Ball is of course a chance for us all to — er/n— let our hair down," she said, in a disapproving/nvoice./n/nLavender giggled harder than ever, with her hand/npressed hard against her mouth to stifle the sound./nHarry could see what was funny this time: Professor/nMcGonagall, with her hair in a tight bun, looked as/nthough she had never let her hair down in any sense./n/n"But that does NOT mean," Professor McGonagall/nwent on, "that we will be relaxing the standards of/nbehavior we expect from Hogwarts students. I will be/n/n/n/n/n/nmost seriously displeased if a Gryffindor student/nembarrasses the school in any way."/n/nThe bell rang, and there was the usual scuffle of/nactivity as everyone packed their bags and swung/nthem onto their shoulders./n/nProfessor McGonagall called above the noise, "Potter/n— a word, if you please."/n/nAssuming this had something to do with his headless/nrubber haddock, Harry proceeded gloomily to the/nteacher's desk. Professor McGonagall waited until the/nrest of the class had gone, and then said, "Potter, the/nchampions and their partners — "/n/n"What partners?" said Harry./n/nProfessor McGonagall looked suspiciously at him, as/nthough she thought he was trying to be funny./n/n"Your partners for the Yule Ball, Potter," she said/ncoldly. "Your dance partners."/n/nHarry's insides seemed to curl up and shrivel./n/n"Dance partners?" He felt himself going red. "I don't/ndance," he said quickly./n/n"Oh yes, you do," said Professor McGonagall irritably./n"That's what I'm telling you. Traditionally, the/nchampions and their partners open the ball."/n/nHarry had a sudden mental image of himself in a top/nhat and tails, accompanied by a girl in the sort of/nfrilly dress Aunt Petunia always wore to Uncle/nVernon's work parties./n/n"I'm not dancing," he said./n/n/n/n/n/n"It is traditional," said Professor McGonagall firmly./n"You are a Hogwarts champion, and you will do what/nis expected of you as a representative of the school./n/nSo make sure you get yourself a partner, Potter."/n/n"But — I don't — "/n/n"You heard me, Potter," said Professor McGonagall in/na very final sort of way./n/nA week ago, Harry would have said finding a partner/nfor a dance would be a cinch compared to taking on a/nHungarian Horntail. But now that he had done the/nlatter, and was facing the prospect of asking a girl to/nthe ball, he thought he'd rather have another round/nwith the dragon./n/nHarry had never known so many people to put their/nnames down to stay at Hogwarts for Christmas; he/nalways did, of course, because the alternative was/nusually going back to Privet Drive, but he had always/nbeen very much in the minority before now. This year,/nhowever, everyone in the fourth year and above/nseemed to be staying, and they all seemed to Harry to/nbe obsessed with the coming ball — or at least all the/ngirls were, and it was amazing how many girls/nHogwarts suddenly seemed to hold; he had never/nquite noticed that before. Girls giggling and/nwhispering in the corridors, girls shrieking with/nlaughter as boys passed them, girls excitedly/ncomparing notes on what they were going to wear on/nChristmas night. .../n/n"Why do they have to move in packs?" Harry asked/nRon as a dozen or so girls walked past them,/nsniggering and staring at Harry. "How're you/nsupposed to get one on their own to ask them?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Lasso one?" Ron suggested. "Got any idea who you're/ngoing to try?"/n/nHarry didn't answer. He knew perfectly well whom/nhe'd like to ask, but working up the nerve was/nsomething else. ... Cho was a year older than he was;/nshe was very pretty; she was a very good Quidditch/nplayer, and she was also very popular./n/nRon seemed to know what was going on inside/nHarry's head./n/n"Listen, you're not going to have any trouble. You're a/nchampion. You've just beaten a Hungarian Horntail. I/nbet they 11 be queuing up to go with you."/n/nIn tribute to their recently repaired friendship, Ron/nhad kept the bitterness in his voice to a bare/nminimum. Moreover, to Harry's amazement, he/nturned out to be quite right./n/nA curly-haired third-year Hufflepuff girl to whom/nHarry had never spoken in his life asked him to go to/nthe ball with her the very next day. Harry was so/ntaken aback he said no before he'd even stopped to/nconsider the matter. The girl walked off looking rather/nhurt, and Harry had to endure Dean's, Seamus's, and/nRon's taunts about her all through History of Magic./nThe following day, two more girls asked him, a second/nyear and (to his horror) a fifth year who looked as/nthough she might knock him out if he refused./n/n"She was quite good-looking," said Ron fairly, after/nhe'd stopped laughing./n/n"She was a foot taller than me," said Harry, still/nunnerved. "Imagine what I'd look like trying to dance/nwith her."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione's words about Krum kept coming back to/nhim. "They only like him because he's famous!" Harry/ndoubted very much if any of the girls who had asked/nto be his partner so far would have wanted to go to/nthe ball with him if he hadn't been a school/nchampion. Then he wondered if this would bother/nhim if Cho asked him./n/nOn the whole, Harry had to admit that even with the/nembarrassing prospect of opening the ball before him,/nlife had definitely improved since he had got through/nthe first task. He wasn't attracting nearly as much/nunpleasantness in the corridors anymore, which he/nsuspected had a lot to do with Cedric — he had an/nidea Cedric might have told the Hufflepuffs to leave/nHarry alone, in gratitude for Harry's tip-off about the/ndragons. There seemed to be fewer Support Cedric/nDiggoryl badges around too. Draco Malfoy, of course,/nwas still quoting Rita Skeeter's article to him at every/npossible opportunity, but he was getting fewer and/nfewer laughs out of it — and just to heighten Harry's/nfeeling of well-being, no story about Hagrid had/nappeared in the Daily Prophet/n/n"She didn' seem very int'rested in magical creatures,/nter tell yeh the truth," Hagrid said, when Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione asked him how his interview with Rita/nSkeeter had gone during the last Care of Magical/nCreatures lesson of the term. To their very great relief,/nHagrid had given up on direct contact with the/nskrewts now, and they were merely sheltering behind/nhis cabin today, sitting at a trestle table and/npreparing a fresh selection of food with which to/ntempt the skrewts./n/n"She jus' wanted me ter talk about you, Harry,"/n/nHagrid continued in a low voice. "Well, I told her we'd/nbeen friends since I went ter fetch yeh from the/nDursleys. 'Never had to tell him off in four years?' she/n/n/n/n/n/nsaid. 'Never played you up in lessons, has he?' I told/nher no, an' she didn' seem happy at all. Yeh'd think/nshe wanted me to say yeh were horrible, Harry."/n/n" 'Course she did," said Harry, throwing lumps of/ndragon liver into a large metal bowl and picking up/nhis knife to cut some more. "She can't keep writing/nabout what a tragic little hero I am, it'll get boring."/n/n"She wants a new angle, Hagrid," said Ron wisely as/nhe shelled salamander eggs. "You were supposed to/nsay Harry's a mad delinquent!"/n/n"But he's not!" said Hagrid, looking genuinely/nshocked./n/n"She should've interviewed Snape," said Harry grimly./n"He'd give her the goods on me any day. 'Potter has/nbeen crossing lines ever since he first arrived at this/nschool. . . . ' "/n/n"Said that, did he?" said Hagrid, while Ron and/nHermione laughed. "Well, yeh might've bent a few/nrules, Harry, bu' yeh're all righ' really, aren' you?"/n/n"Cheers, Hagrid," said Harry, grinning./n/n"You coming to this ball thing on Christmas Day,/nHagrid?" said Ron./n/n"Though' I might look in on it, yeah," said Hagrid/ngruffly. "Should be a good do, I reckon. You'll be/nopenin' the dancin', won' yeh, Harry? Who 're you/ntakin'?"/n/n"No one, yet," said Harry, feeling himself going red/nagain. Hagrid didn't pursue the subject./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe last week of term became increasingly boisterous/nas it progressed. Rumors about the Yule Ball were/nflying everywhere, though Harry didn't believe half of/nthem — for instance, that Dumbledore had bought/neight hundred barrels of mulled mead from Madam/nRosmerta. It seemed to be fact, however, that he had/nbooked the Weird Sisters. Exactly who or what the/nWeird Sisters were Harry didn't know, never having/nhad access to a wizard's wireless, but he deduced/nfrom the wild excitement of those who had grown up/nlistening to the WWN (Wizarding Wireless Network)/nthat they were a very famous musical group./n/nSome of the teachers, like little Professor Flitwick,/ngave up trying to teach them much when their minds/nwere so clearly elsewhere; he allowed them to play/ngames in his lesson on Wednesday, and spent most of/nit talking to Harry about the perfect Summoning/nCharm Harry had used during the first task of the/nTriwizard Tournament. Other teachers were not so/ngenerous. Nothing would ever deflect Professor Binns,/nfor example, from plowing on through his notes on/ngoblin rebellions — as Binns hadn't let his own death/nstand in the way of continuing to teach, they/nsupposed a small thing like Christmas wasn't going to/nput him off. It was amazing how he could make even/nbloody and vicious goblin riots sound as boring as/nPercy's cauldron-bottom report. Professors/nMcGonagall and Moody kept them working until the/nvery last second of their classes too, and Snape, of/ncourse, would no sooner let them play games in class/nthan adopt Harry. Staring nastily around at them all,/nhe informed them that he would be testing them on/npoison antidotes during the last lesson of the term./n/n"Evil, he is," Ron said bitterly that night in the/nGryffindor common room. "Springing a test on us on/nthe last day. Ruining the last bit of term with a whole/nload of studying."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mmm ... you're not exactly straining yourself,/nthough, are you?" said Hermione, looking at him over/nthe top of her Potions notes. Ron was busy building a/ncard castle out of his Exploding Snap pack — a much/nmore interesting pastime than with Muggle cards,/nbecause of the chance that the whole thing would/nblow up at any second./n/n"It's Christmas, Hermione," said Harry lazily; he was/nrereading Flying with the Cannons for the tenth time/nin an armchair near the fire./n/nHermione looked severely over at him too. "I'd have/nthought you'd be doing something constructive,/n/nHarry, even if you don't want to learn your antidotes!"/n/n"Like what?" Harry said as he watched Joey Jenkins/nof the Cannons belt a Bludger toward a Ballycastle/nBats Chaser./n/n"That egg!" Hermione hissed./n/n"Come on, Hermione, I've got till February the twenty-/nfourth," Harry said./n/nHe had put the golden egg upstairs in his trunk and/nhadn't opened it since the celebration party after the/nfirst task. There were still two and a half months to go/nuntil he needed to know what all the screechy wailing/nmeant, after all./n/n"But it might take weeks to work it out!" said/nHermione. "You're going to look a real idiot if everyone/nelse knows what the next task is and you don't!"/n/n"Leave him alone, Hermione, he's earned a bit of a/nbreak," said Ron, and he placed the last two cards on/ntop of the castle and the whole lot blew up, singeing/nhis eyebrows./n/n/n/n/n/n"Nice look, Ron ... go well with your dress robes, that/nwill."/n/n/n/nIt was Fred and George. They sat down at the table/nwith Harry, Ron, and Hermione as Ron felt how much/ndamage had been done./n/n"Ron, can we borrow Pigwidgeon?" George asked./n/n"No, he's off delivering a letter," said Ron. "Why?"/n/n"Because George wants to invite him to the ball," said/nFred sarcastically./n/n"Because we want to send a letter, you stupid great/nprat," said George./n/n"Who d'you two keep writing to, eh?" said Ron./n/n"Nose out, Ron, or I'll burn that for you too," said/nFred, waving his wand threateningly. "So ... you lot/ngot dates for the ball yet?"/n/n"Nope," said Ron./n/n"Well, you'd better hurry up, mate, or all the good/nones will be gone," said Fred./n/n"Who're you going with, then?" said Ron./n/n"Angelina," said Fred promptly, without a trace of/nembarrassment./n/n"What?" said Ron, taken aback. "You've already asked/nher?"/n/n"Good point," said Fred. He turned his head and/ncalled across the common room, "Oi! Angelina!"/n/n/n/n/n/nAngelina, who had been chatting with Alicia Spinnet/nnear the fire, looked over at him./n/n/n/n"What?" she called back./n/n"Want to come to the ball with me?"/n/nAngelina gave Fred an appraising sort of look./n/n"All right, then," she said, and she turned back to/nAlicia and carried on chatting with a bit of a grin on/nher face./n/n"There you go," said Fred to Harry and Ron, "piece of/ncake."/n/nHe got to his feet, yawning, and said, "We'd better use/na school owl then, George, come on. ..."/n/nThey left. Ron stopped feeling his eyebrows and/nlooked across the smoldering wreck of his card castle/nat Harry./n/n"We should get a move on, you know ... ask someone./nHe's right. We don't want to end up with a pair of/ntrolls."/n/nHermione let out a sputter of indignation./n/n"A pair of . . . what, excuse me?"/n/n"Well — you know," said Ron, shrugging. "I'd rather/ngo alone than with — with Eloise Midgen, say."/n/n"Her acne's loads better lately — and she's really/nnice!"/n/n"Her nose is off-center," said Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh I see," Hermione said, bristling. "So basically,/nyou're going to take the best-looking girl who'll have/nyou, even if she's completely horrible?"/n/n"Er — yeah, that sounds about right," said Ron./n/n"I'm going to bed," Hermione snapped, and she swept/noff toward the girls' staircase without another word./n/nThe Hogwarts staff, demonstrating a continued desire/nto impress the visitors from Beauxbatons and/nDurmstrang, seemed determined to show the castle at/nits best this Christmas. When the decorations went/nup, Harry noticed that they were the most stunning/nhe had yet seen inside the school. Everlasting icicles/nhad been attached to the banisters of the marble/nstaircase; the usual twelve Christmas trees in the/nGreat Hall were bedecked with everything from/nluminous holly berries to real, hooting, golden owls,/nand the suits of armor had all been bewitched to sing/ncarols whenever anyone passed them. It was quite/nsomething to hear "O Come, All Ye Faithful" sung by/nan empty helmet that only knew half the words./nSeveral times, Filch the caretaker had to extract/nPeeves from inside the armor, where he had taken to/nhiding, filling in the gaps in the songs with lyrics of/nhis own invention, all of which were very rude./n/nAnd still, Harry hadn't asked Cho to the ball. He and/nRon were getting very nervous now, though as Harry/npointed out, Ron would look much less stupid than/nhe would without a partner; Harry was supposed to/nbe starting the dancing with the other champions./n/n"I suppose there's always Moaning Myrtle," he said/ngloomily, referring to the ghost who haunted the girls'/ntoilets on the second floor./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry — we've just got to grit our teeth and do it,"/nsaid Ron on Friday morning, in a tone that suggested/nthey were planning the storming of an impregnable/nfortress. "When we get back to the common room/ntonight, we'll both have partners — agreed?"/n/n"Er ... okay," said Harry./n/nBut every time he glimpsed Cho that day — during/nbreak, and then lunchtime, and once on the way to/nHistory of Magic — she was surrounded by friends./nDidn't she ever go anywhere alone? Could he perhaps/nambush her as she was going into a bathroom? But/nno — she even seemed to go there with an escort of/nfour or five girls. Yet if he didn't do it soon, she was/nbound to have been asked by somebody else./n/nHe found it hard to concentrate on Snape's Potions/ntest, and consequently forgot to add the key/ningredient — a bezoar — meaning that he received/nbottom marks. He didn't care, though; he was too/nbusy screwing up his courage for what he was about/nto do. When the bell rang, he grabbed his bag, and/nhurried to the dungeon door./n/n"I'll meet you at dinner," he said to Ron and/nHermione, and he dashed off upstairs./n/nHe'd just have to ask Cho for a private word, that was/nall. ... He hurried off through the packed corridors/nlooking for her, and (rather sooner than he had/nexpected) he found her, emerging from a Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts lesson./n/n"Er — Cho? Could I have a word with you?"/n/nGiggling should be made illegal, Harry thought/nfuriously, as all the girls around Cho started doing it./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe didn't, though. She said, "Okay," and followed/nhim out of earshot of her classmates./n/nHarry turned to look at her and his stomach gave a/nweird lurch as though he had missed a step going/ndownstairs./n/n"Er," he said./n/nHe couldn't ask her. He couldn't. But he had to. Cho/nstood there looking puzzled, watching him./n/nThe words came out before Harry had quite got his/ntongue around them./n/n"Wangoballwime?"/n/n"Sorry?" said Cho./n/n"D'you — d'you want to go to the ball with me?" said/nHarry. Why did he have to go red now? Why ?/n/n"Oh!" said Cho, and she went red too. "Oh Harry, I'm/nreally sorry," and she truly looked it. "I've already said/nI'll go with someone else."/n/n"Oh," said Harry./n/nIt was odd; a moment before his insides had been/nwrithing like snakes, but suddenly he didn't seem to/nhave any insides at all./n/n"Oh okay," he said, "no problem."/n/n"I'm really sorry," she said again./n/n"That's okay," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey stood there looking at each other, and then Cho/nsaid, "Well — "/n/n"Yeah," said Harry./n/n"Well, 'bye," said Cho, still very red. She walked away./nHarry called after her, before he could stop himself./n"Who 're you going with?"/n/n"Oh — Cedric," she said. "Cedric Diggory."/n/n"Oh right," said Harry./n/nHis insides had come back again. It felt as though/nthey had been filled with lead in their absence./n/nCompletely forgetting about dinner, he walked slowly/nback up to Gryffindor Tower, Cho's voice echoing in/nhis ears with every step he took. " Cedric — Cedric/nDiggory." He had been starting to quite like Cedric —/nprepared to overlook the fact that he had once beaten/nhim at Quidditch, and was handsome, and popular,/nand nearly everyone's favorite champion. Now he/nsuddenly realized that Cedric was in fact a useless/npretty boy who didn't have enough brains to fill an/neggcup./n/n"Fairy lights," he said dully to the Fat Lady — the/npassword had been changed the previous day./n/n"Yes, indeed, dear!" she trilled, straightening her new/ntinsel hair band as she swung forward to admit him./n/nEntering the common room, Harry looked around,/nand to his surprise he saw Ron sitting ashen-faced in/na distant corner. Ginny was sitting with him, talking/nto him in what seemed to be a low, soothing voice./n/n/n/n/n/n"What's up, Ron?" said Harry, joining them./n/n/n/nRon looked up at Harry, a sort of blind horror in his/nface./n/n"Why did I do it?" he said wildly. "I don't know what/nmade me do it!"/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"He — er — just asked Fleur Delacour to go to the/nball with him," said Ginny. She looked as though she/nwas fighting back a smile, but she kept patting Ron's/narm sympathetically./n/n"You what?" said Harry./n/n"I don't know what made me do it!" Ron gasped again./n"What was I playing at? There were people — all/naround — I've gone mad — everyone watching! I was/njust walking past her in the entrance hall — she was/nstanding there talking to Diggory — and it sort of/ncame over me — and I asked her!"/n/nRon moaned and put his face in his hands. He kept/ntalking, though the words were barely/ndistinguishable./n/n"She looked at me like I was a sea slug or something./nDidn't even answer. And then — I dunno — I just sort/nof came to my senses and ran for it."/n/n"She's part veela," said Harry. "You were right — her/ngrandmother was one. It wasn't your fault, I bet you/njust walked past when she was turning on the old/ncharm for Diggory and got a blast of it — but she was/nwasting her time. He's going with Cho Chang."/n/nRon looked up./n/n/n/n/n/n"I asked her to go with me just now," Harry said dully,/n"and she told me."/n/nGinny had suddenly stopped smiling./n/n"This is mad," said Ron. "We're the only ones left who/nhaven't got anyone — well, except Neville. Hey —/nguess who he asked? Hermionel"/n/n" What?" said Harry, completely distracted by this/nstartling news./n/n"Yeah, I know!" said Ron, some of the color coming/nback into his face as he started to laugh. "He told me/nafter Potions! Said she's always been really nice,/nhelping him out with work and stuff — but she told/nhim she was already going with someone. Ha! As if!/nShe just didn't want to go with Neville ... I mean, who/nwould?"/n/n"Don't!" said Ginny, annoyed. "Don't laugh — "/n/nJust then Hermione climbed in through the portrait/nhole./n/n"Why weren't you two at dinner?" she said, coming/nover to join them./n/n"Because — oh shut up laughing, you two — because/nthey've both just been turned down by girls they/nasked to the ball!" said Ginny./n/nThat shut Harry and Ron up./n/n"Thanks a bunch, Ginny," said Ron sourly./n/n"All the good-looking ones taken, Ron?" said/nHermione loftily. "Eloise Midgen starting to look quite/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/npretty now, is she? Well, I'm sure you'll find someone/nsomewhere who'll have you."/n/nBut Ron was staring at Hermione as though suddenly/nseeing her in a whole new light./n/n"Hermione, Neville's right — you are a girl. ..."/n/n"Oh well spotted," she said acidly./n/n"Well — you can come with one of us!"/n/n"No, I can't," snapped Hermione./n/n"Oh come on," he said impatiently, "we need partners,/nwe're going to look really stupid if we haven't got any,/neveryone else has ..."/n/n"I can't come with you," said Hermione, now blushing,/n"because I'm already going with someone."/n/n"No, you're not!" said Ron. "You just said that to get/nrid of Neville!"/n/n"Oh did I?" said Hermione, and her eyes flashed/ndangerously. "Just because it's taken you three years/nto notice, Ron, doesn't mean no one else has spotted/nI'm a girl!"/n/nRon stared at her. Then he grinned again./n/n"Okay, okay, we know you're a girl," he said. "That/ndo? Will you come now?"/n/n"I've already told you!" Hermione said very angrily./n/n"I'm going with someone else!"/n/nAnd she stormed off toward the girls' dormitories/nagain./n/n/n/n/n/n"She's lying," said Ron flatly, watching her go./n/n"She's not," said Ginny quietly./n/n"Who is it then?" said Ron sharply./n/n"I'm not telling you, it's her business," said Ginny./n/n"Right," said Ron, who looked extremely put out, "this/nis getting stupid. Ginny, you can go with Harry, and/nI'll just—"/n/n"I can't," said Ginny, and she went scarlet too. "I'm/ngoing with — with Neville. He asked me when/nHermione said no, and I thought ... well ... I'm not/ngoing to be able to go otherwise, I'm not in fourth/nyear." She looked extremely miserable. "I think I'll go/nand have dinner," she said, and she got up and/nwalked off to the portrait hole, her head bowed./n/nRon goggled at Harry./n/n"What's got into them?" he demanded./n/nBut Harry had just seen Parvati and Lavender come/nin through the portrait hole. The time had come for/ndrastic action./n/n"Wait here," he said to Ron, and he stood up, walked/nstraight up to Parvati, and said, "Parvati? Will you go/nto the ball with me?"/n/nParvati went into a fit of giggles. Harry waited for/nthem to subside, his fingers crossed in the pocket of/nhis robes./n/n"Yes, all right then," she said finally, blushing/nfuriously./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Thanks," said Harry, in relief. "Lavender — will you/ngo with Ron?"/n/n"She's going with Seamus," said Parvati, and the pair/nof them giggled harder than ever./n/nHarry sighed./n/n"Can't you think of anyone who'd go with Ron?" he/nsaid, lowering his voice so that Ron wouldn't hear./n/n"What about Hermione Granger?" said Parvati./n/n"She's going with someone else."/n/nParvati looked astonished./n/n"Ooooh — who?" she said keenly./n/nHarry shrugged. "No idea," he said. "So what about/nRon?"/n/n"Well ..." said Parvati slowly, "I suppose my sister/nmight ... Padma, you know ... in Ravenclaw. I'll ask/nher if you like."/n/n"Yeah, that would be great," said Harry. "Let me/nknow, will you?"/n/nAnd he went back over to Ron, feeling that this ball/nwas a lot more trouble than it was worth, and hoping/nvery much that Padma Patil's nose was dead center./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Yule Ball
text: /nDespite the very heavy load of homework that the/nfourth years had been given for the holidays, Harry/nwas in no mood to work when term ended, and spent/nthe week leading up to Christmas enjoying himself as/nfully as possible along with everyone else. Gryffindor/nTower was hardly less crowded now than during/nterm-time; it seemed to have shrunk slightly too, as/nits inhabitants were being so much rowdier than/nusual. Fred and George had had a great success with/ntheir Canary Creams, and for the first couple of days/nof the holidays, people kept bursting into feather all/nover the place. Before long, however, all the/nGryffindors had learned to treat food anybody else/noffered them with extreme caution, in case it had a/nCanary Cream concealed in the center, and George/nconfided to Harry that he and Fred were now working/non developing something else. Harry made a mental/nnote never to accept so much as a crisp from Fred/nand George in future. He still hadn't forgotten Dudley/nand the Ton-Tongue Toffee./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSnow was falling thickly upon the castle and its/ngrounds now. The pale blue Beauxbatons carriage/nlooked like a large, chilly, frosted pumpkin next to the/niced gingerbread house that was Hagrid's cabin, while/nthe Durmstrang ship's portholes were glazed with ice,/nthe rigging white with frost. The house-elves down in/nthe kitchen were outdoing themselves with a series of/nrich, warming stews and savory puddings, and only/nFleur Delacour seemed to be able to find anything to/ncomplain about./n/n"It is too 'eavy, all zis 'Ogwarts food," they heard her/nsaying grumpily as they left the Great Hall behind her/none evening (Ron skulking behind Harry, keen not to/nbe spotted by Fleur). "I will not fit into my dress/nrobes!"/n/n"Oooh there's a tragedy," Hermione snapped as Fleur/nwent out into the entrance hall. "She really thinks a/nlot of herself, that one, doesn't she?"/n/n"Hermione — who are you going to the ball with?"/nsaid Ron./n/nHe kept springing this question on her, hoping to/nstartle her into a response by asking it when she least/nexpected it. However, Hermione merely frowned and/nsaid, "I'm not telling you, you'll just make fun of me."/n/n"You're joking, Weasley!" said Malfoy, behind them./n"You're not telling me someone's asked that to the/nball? Not the long-molared Mudblood?"/n/nHarry and Ron both whipped around, but Hermione/nsaid loudly, waving to somebody over Malfoy's/nshoulder, "Hello, Professor Moody!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMalfoy went pale and jumped backward, looking/nwildly around for Moody, but he was still up at the/nstaff table, finishing his stew./n/n"Twitchy little ferret, aren't you, Malfoy?" said/nHermione scathingly, and she, Harry, and Ron went/nup the marble staircase laughing heartily./n/n"Hermione," said Ron, looking sideways at her,/nsuddenly frowning, "your teeth ..."/n/n"What about them?" she said./n/n"Well, they're different ... I've just noticed. ..."/n/n"Of course they are — did you expect me to keep/nthose fangs Malfoy gave me?"/n/n"No, I mean, they're different to how they were before/nhe put that hex on you. ... They're all ... straight and/n— and normal-sized."/n/nHermione suddenly smiled very mischievously, and/nHarry noticed it too: It was a very different smile from/nthe one he remembered./n/n"Well ... when I went up to Madam Pomfrey to get/nthem shrunk, she held up a mirror and told me to/nstop her when they were back to how they normally/nwere," she said. "And I just ... let her carry on a bit."/nShe smiled even more widely. "Mum and Dad won't be/ntoo pleased. I've been trying to persuade them to let/nme shrink them for ages, but they wanted me to carry/non with my braces. You know, they're dentists, they/njust don't think teeth and magic should — look!/nPigwidgeon's back!"/n/nRon's tiny owl was twittering madly on the top of the/nicicle-laden banisters, a scroll of parchment tied to/n/n/n/n/n/nhis leg. People passing him were pointing and/nlaughing, and a group of third-year girls paused and/nsaid, "Oh look at the weeny owl! Isn't he cute?"/n/n"Stupid little feathery git!" Ron hissed, hurrying up/nthe stairs and snatching up Pigwidgeon. "You bring/nletters to the addressee! You don't hang around/nshowing off!"/n/nPigwidgeon hooted happily, his head protruding over/nRon's fist. The third-year girls all looked very/nshocked./n/n"Clear off!" Ron snapped at them, waving the fist/nholding Pigwidgeon, who hooted more happily than/never as he soared through the air. "Here — take it,/nHarry," Ron added in an undertone as the third-year/ngirls scuttled away looking scandalized. He pulled/nSirius's reply off Pigwidgeon's leg, Harry pocketed it,/nand they hurried back to Gryffindor Tower to read it./n/nEveryone in the common room was much too busy in/nletting off more holiday steam to observe what anyone/nelse was up to. Ron, Harry, and Hermione sat apart/nfrom everyone else by a dark window that was/ngradually filling up with snow, and Harry read out:/n/nDear Harry,/n/nCongratulations on getting past the Horntail. Whoever/nput your name in that goblet shouldn't be feeling too/nhappy right now! I was going to suggest a/nConjunctivitis Curse, as a dragon's eyes are its/nweakest point — "That's what Krum did!" Hermione/nwhispered — but your way was better, I'm impressed./n/nDon't get complacent, though, Harry. You've only done/none task; whoever put you in for the tournament's got/nplenty more opportunity if they're trying to hurt you./n/n/n/n/n/nKeep your eyes open — particularly when the person/nwe discussed is around — and concentrate on keeping/nyourself out of trouble./n/nKeep in touch, I still want to hear about anything/nunusual./n/nSirius/n/n"He sounds exactly like Moody," said Harry quietly,/ntucking the letter away again inside his robes. "/n'Constant vigilance!' You'd think I walk around with/nmy eyes shut, banging off the walls. ..."/n/n"But he's right, Harry," said Hermione, "you have still/ngot two tasks to do. You really ought to have a look at/nthat egg, you know, and start working out what it/nmeans. ..."/n/n"Hermione, he's got ages!" snapped Ron. "Want a/ngame of chess, Harry?"/n/n"Yeah, okay," said Harry. Then, spotting the look on/nHermione 's face, he said, "Come on, how'm I/nsupposed to concentrate with all this noise going on?/n/nI won't even be able to hear the egg over this lot."/n/n"Oh I suppose not," she sighed, and she sat down to/nwatch their chess match, which culminated in an/nexciting checkmate of Ron's, involving a couple of/nrecklessly brave pawns and a very violent bishop./n/nHarry awoke very suddenly on Christmas Day./nWondering what had caused his abrupt return to/nconsciousness, he opened his eyes, and saw/nsomething with very large, round, green eyes staring/nback at him in the darkness, so close they were/nalmost nose to nose./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Dobbyl" Harry yelled, scrambling away from the elf/nso fast he almost fell out of bed. "Don't do that!"/n/n"Dobby is sorry, sir!" squeaked Dobby anxiously,/njumping backward with his long fingers over his/nmouth. "Dobby is only wanting to wish Harry Potter/n'Merry Christmas' and bring him a present, sir! Harry/nPotter did say Dobby could come and see him/nsometimes, sir!"/n/n"It's okay," said Harry, still breathing rather faster/nthan usual, while his heart rate returned to normal./n"Just — just prod me or something in future, all right,/ndon't bend over me like that. ..."/n/nHarry pulled back the curtains around his four-/nposter, took his glasses from his bedside table, and/nput them on. His yell had awoken Ron, Seamus,/n/nDean, and Neville. All of them were peering through/nthe gaps in their own hangings, heavy-eyed and/ntousle-haired./n/n"Someone attacking you, Harry?" Seamus asked/nsleepily./n/n"No, it's just Dobby," Harry muttered. "Go back to/nsleep."/n/n"Nah ... presents!" said Seamus, spotting the large/npile at the foot of his bed. Ron, Dean, and Neville/ndecided that now they were awake they might as well/nget down to some present-opening too. Harry turned/nback to Dobby, who was now standing nervously next/nto Harry's bed, still looking worried that he had upset/nHarry. There was a Christmas bauble tied to the loop/non top of his tea cozy./n/n"Can Dobby give Harry Potter his present?" he/nsqueaked tentatively./n/n/n/n/n/n" 'Course you can," said Harry. "Er ... I've got/nsomething for you too."/n/nIt was a lie; he hadn't bought anything for Dobby at/nall, but he quickly opened his trunk and pulled out a/nparticularly knobbly rolled-up pair of socks. They/nwere his oldest and foulest, mustard yellow, and had/nonce belonged to Uncle Vernon. The reason they were/nextra-knobbly was that Harry had been using them to/ncushion his Sneakoscope for over a year now. He/npulled out the Sneakoscope and handed the socks to/nDobby, saying, "Sorry, I forgot to wrap them. ..."/n/nBut Dobby was utterly delighted./n/n"Socks are Dobby's favorite, favorite clothes, sir!" he/nsaid, ripping off his odd ones and pulling on Uncle/nVernon's. "I has seven now, sir. ... But sir ..." he said,/nhis eyes widening, having pulled both socks up to/ntheir highest extent, so that they reached to the/nbottom of his shorts, "they has made a mistake in the/nshop, Harry Potter, they is giving you two the same!"/n/n"Ah, no, Harry, how come you didn't spot that?" said/nRon, grinning over from his own bed, which was now/nstrewn with wrapping paper. "Tell you what, Dobby —/nhere you go — take these two, and you can mix them/nup properly. And here's your sweater."/n/nHe threw Dobby a pair of violet socks he had just/nunwrapped, and the hand-knitted sweater Mrs./nWeasley had sent. Dobby looked quite overwhelmed./n/n"Sir is very kind!" he squeaked, his eyes brimming/nwith tears again, bowing deeply to Ron. "Dobby knew/nsir must be a great wizard, for he is Harry Potter's/ngreatest friend, but Dobby did not know that he was/nalso as generous of spirit, as noble, as selfless — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They're only socks," said Ron, who had gone slightly/npink around the ears, though he looked rather/npleased all the same. "Wow, Harry — " He had just/nopened Harry's present, a Chudley Cannon hat./n/n"Cool!" He jammed it onto his head, where it clashed/nhorribly with his hair./n/nDobby now handed Harry a small package, which/nturned out to be — socks./n/n"Dobby is making them himself, sir!" the elf said/nhappily. "He is buying the wool out of his wages, sir!"/n/nThe left sock was bright red and had a pattern of/nbroomsticks upon it; the right sock was green with a/npattern of Snitches./n/n"They're ... they're really ... well, thanks, Dobby," said/nHarry, and he pulled them on, causing Dobby's eyes/nto leak with happiness again./n/n"Dobby must go now, sir, we is already making/nChristmas dinner in the kitchens!" said Dobby, and/nhe hurried out of the dormitory, waving good-bye to/nRon and the others as he passed./n/nHarry's other presents were much more satisfactory/nthan Dobby's odd socks — with the obvious exception/nof the Dursleys', which consisted of a single tissue, an/nall-time low — Harry supposed they too were/nremembering the Ton-Tongue Toffee. Hermione had/ngiven Harry a book called Quidditch Teams of Britain/nand Ireland ; Ron, a bulging bag of Dungbombs;/n/nSirius, a handy penknife with attachments to unlock/nany lock and undo any knot; and Hagrid, a vast box/nof sweets including all Harry's favorites: Bertie Bott's/nEvery Flavor Beans, Chocolate Frogs, Drooble's Best/nBlowing Gum, and Fizzing Whizbees. There was also,/nof course, Mrs. Weasley's usual package, including a/n/n/n/n/nnew sweater (green, with a picture of a dragon on it —/nHarry supposed Charlie had told her all about the/nHorntail), and a large quantity of homemade mince/npies./n/nHarry and Ron met up with Hermione in the common/nroom, and they went down to breakfast together. They/nspent most of the morning in Gryffindor Tower, where/neveryone was enjoying their presents, then returned/nto the Great Hall for a magnificent lunch, which/nincluded at least a hundred turkeys and Christmas/npuddings, and large piles of Cribbage's Wizarding/nCrackers./n/nThey went out onto the grounds in the afternoon; the/nsnow was untouched except for the deep channels/nmade by the Durmstrang and Beauxbatons students/non their way up to the castle. Hermione chose to/nwatch Harry and the Weasleys' snowball fight rather/nthan join in, and at five o'clock said she was going/nback upstairs to get ready for the ball./n/n"What, you need three hours?" said Ron, looking at/nher incredulously and paying for his lapse in/nconcentration when a large snowball, thrown by/nGeorge, hit him hard on the side of the head. "Who 're/nyou going with?" he yelled after Hermione, but she/njust waved and disappeared up the stone steps into/nthe castle./n/nThere was no Christmas tea today, as the ball/nincluded a feast, so at seven o'clock, when it had/nbecome hard to aim properly, the others abandoned/ntheir snowball fight and trooped back to the common/nroom. The Fat Lady was sitting in her frame with her/nfriend Violet from downstairs, both of them extremely/ntipsy, empty boxes of chocolate liqueurs littering the/nbottom of her picture./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Lairy fights, that's the one!" she giggled when they/ngave the password, and she swung forward to let/nthem inside./n/nHarry, Ron, Seamus, Dean, and Neville changed into/ntheir dress robes up in their dormitory, all of them/nlooking very self-conscious, but none as much as/nRon, who surveyed himself in the long mirror in the/ncorner with an appalled look on his face. There was/njust no getting around the fact that his robes looked/nmore like a dress than anything else. In a desperate/nattempt to make them look more manly, he used a/nSevering Charm on the ruff and cuffs. It worked fairly/nwell; at least he was now lace-free, although he hadn't/ndone a very neat job, and the edges still looked/ndepressingly frayed as the boys set off downstairs./n/n"I still can't work out how you two got the best-/nlooking girls in the year," muttered Dean./n/n"Animal magnetism," said Ron gloomily, pulling stray/nthreads out of his cuffs./n/nThe common room looked strange, full of people/nwearing different colors instead of the usual mass of/nblack. Parvati was waiting for Harry at the foot of the/nstairs. She looked very pretty indeed, in robes of/nshocking pink, with her long dark plait braided with/ngold, and gold bracelets glimmering at her wrists./nHarry was relieved to see that she wasn't giggling./n/n"You — er — look nice," he said awkwardly./n/n"Thanks," she said. "Padma's going to meet you in the/nentrance hall," she added to Ron./n/n"Right," said Ron, looking around. "Where's/nHermione?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nParvati shrugged. "Shall we go down then, Harry?"/n/n/n/n"Okay," said Harry, wishing he could just stay in the/ncommon room. Fred winked at Harry as he passed/nhim on the way out of the portrait hole./n/nThe entrance hall was packed with students too, all/nmilling around waiting for eight o'clock, when the/ndoors to the Great Hall would be thrown open. Those/npeople who were meeting partners from different/nHouses were edging through the crowd trying to find/none another. Parvati found her sister, Padma, and led/nher over to Harry and Ron./n/n"Hi," said Padma, who was looking just as pretty as/nParvati in robes of bright turquoise. She didn't look/ntoo enthusiastic about having Ron as a partner,/nthough; her dark eyes lingered on the frayed neck and/nsleeves of his dress robes as she looked him up and/ndown./n/n"Hi," said Ron, not looking at her, but staring around/nat the crowd. "Oh no ..."/n/nHe bent his knees slightly to hide behind Harry,/nbecause Fleur Delacour was passing, looking/nstunning in robes of silver-gray satin, and/naccompanied by the Ravenclaw Quidditch captain,/nRoger Davies. When they had disappeared, Ron stood/nstraight again and stared over the heads of the crowd./n/n"Where is Hermione?" he said again./n/nA group of Slytherins came up the steps from their/ndungeon common room. Malfoy was in front; he was/nwearing dress robes of black velvet with a high collar,/nwhich in Harry's opinion made him look like a vicar./nPansy Parkinson in very frilly robes of pale pink was/nclutching Malfoy's arm. Crabbe and Goyle were both/n/n/n/n/nwearing green; they resembled moss-colored boulders,/nand neither of them, Harry was pleased to see, had/nmanaged to find a partner./n/nThe oak front doors opened, and everyone turned to/nlook as the Durmstrang students entered with/nProfessor Karkaroff. Krum was at the front of the/nparty, accompanied by a pretty girl in blue robes/nHarry didn't know. Over their heads he saw that an/narea of lawn right in front of the castle had been/ntransformed into a sort of grotto full of fairy lights —/nmeaning hundreds of actual living fairies were sitting/nin the rosebushes that had been conjured there, and/nfluttering over the statues of what seemed to be/nFather Christmas and his reindeer./n/nThen Professor McGonagall's voice called,/n/n"Champions over here, please!"/n/nParvati readjusted her bangles, beaming; she and/nHarry said "See you in a minute" to Ron and Padma/nand walked forward, the chattering crowd parting to/nlet them through. Professor McGonagall, who was/nwearing dress robes of red tartan and had arranged a/nrather ugly wreath of thistles around the brim of her/nhat, told them to wait on one side of the doors while/neveryone else went inside; they were to enter the/nGreat Hall in procession when the rest of the students/nhad sat down. Fleur Delacour and Roger Davies/nstationed themselves nearest the doors; Davies looked/nso stunned by his good fortune in having Fleur for a/npartner that he could hardly take his eyes off her./nCedric and Cho were close to Harry too; he looked/naway from them so he wouldn't have to talk to them./nHis eyes fell instead on the girl next to Krum. His jaw/ndropped./n/nIt was Hermione./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut she didn't look like Hermione at all. She had done/nsomething with her hair; it was no longer bushy but/nsleek and shiny, and twisted up into an elegant knot/nat the back of her head. She was wearing robes made/nof a floaty, periwinkle-blue material, and she was/nholding herself differently, somehow — or maybe it/nwas merely the absence of the twenty or so books she/nusually had slung over her back. She was also/nsmiling — rather nervously, it was true — but the/nreduction in the size of her front teeth was more/nnoticeable than ever; Harry couldn't understand how/nhe hadn't spotted it before./n/n"Hi, Harry!" she said. "Hi, Parvati!"/n/nParvati was gazing at Hermione in unflattering/ndisbelief. She wasn't the only one either; when the/ndoors to the Great Hall opened, Krum's fan club from/nthe library stalked past, throwing Hermione looks of/ndeepest loathing. Pansy Parkinson gaped at her as/nshe walked by with Malfoy, and even he didn't seem/nto be able to find an insult to throw at her. Ron,/nhowever, walked right past Hermione without looking/nat her./n/nOnce everyone else was settled in the Hall, Professor/nMcGonagall told the champions and their partners to/nget in line in pairs and to follow her. They did so, and/neveryone in the Great Hall applauded as they entered/nand started walking up toward a large round table at/nthe top of the Hall, where the judges were sitting./n/nThe walls of the Hall had all been covered in sparkling/nsilver frost, with hundreds of garlands of mistletoe/nand ivy crossing the starry black ceiling. The House/ntables had vanished; instead, there were about a/nhundred smaller, lantern-lit ones, each seating about/na dozen people./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry concentrated on not tripping over his feet./nParvati seemed to be enjoying herself; she was/nbeaming around at everybody, steering Harry so/nforcefully that he felt as though he were a show dog/nshe was putting through its paces. He caught sight of/nRon and Padma as he neared the top table. Ron was/nwatching Hermione pass with narrowed eyes. Padma/nwas looking sulky./n/nDumbledore smiled happily as the champions/napproached the top table, but Karkaroff wore an/nexpression remarkably like Ron's as he watched/nKrum and Hermione draw nearer. Ludo Bagman,/ntonight in robes of bright purple with large yellow/nstars, was clapping as enthusiastically as any of the/nstudents; and Madame Maxime, who had changed/nher usual uniform of black satin for a flowing gown of/nlavender silk, was applauding them politely. But Mr./nCrouch, Harry suddenly realized, was not there. The/nfifth seat at the table was occupied by Percy Weasley./n/nWhen the champions and their partners reached the/ntable, Percy drew out the empty chair beside him,/nstaring pointedly at Harry. Harry took the hint and/nsat down next to Percy, who was wearing brand-new,/nnavy-blue dress robes and an expression of such/nsmugness that Harry thought it ought to be fined./n/n"I've been promoted," Percy said before Harry could/neven ask, and from his tone, he might have been/nannouncing his election as supreme ruler of the/nuniverse. "I'm now Mr. Crouch's personal assistant,/nand I'm here representing him."/n/n"Why didn't he come?" Harry asked. He wasn't looking/nforward to being lectured on cauldron bottoms all/nthrough dinner./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm afraid to say Mr. Crouch isn't well, not well at all./nHasn't been right since the World Cup. Hardly/nsurprising — overwork. He's not as young as he was/n— though still quite brilliant, of course, the mind/nremains as great as it ever was. But the World Cup/nwas a fiasco for the whole Ministry, and then, Mr./nCrouch suffered a huge personal shock with the/nmisbehavior of that house-elf of his, Blinky, or/nwhatever she was called. Naturally, he dismissed her/nimmediately afterward, but — well, as I say, he's/ngetting on, he needs looking after, and I think he's/nfound a definite drop in his home comforts since she/nleft. And then we had the tournament to arrange, and/nthe aftermath of the Cup to deal with — that revolting/nSkeeter woman buzzing around — no, poor man, he's/nhaving a well earned, quiet Christmas. I'm just glad/nhe knew he had someone he could rely upon to take/nhis place."/n/nHarry wanted very much to ask whether Mr. Crouch/nhad stopped calling Percy "Weatherby" yet, but/nresisted the temptation./n/nThere was no food as yet on the glittering golden/nplates, but small menus were lying in front of each of/nthem. Harry picked his up uncertainly and looked/naround — there were no waiters. Dumbledore,/nhowever, looked carefully down at his own menu,/nthen said very clearly to his plate, "Pork chops!"/n/nAnd pork chops appeared. Getting the idea, the rest of/nthe table placed their orders with their plates too./nHarry glanced up at Hermione to see how she felt/nabout this new and more complicated method of/ndining — surely it meant plenty of extra work for the/nhouse-elves? — but for once, Hermione didn't seem to/nbe thinking about S.P.E.W. She was deep in talk with/nViktor Krum and hardly seemed to notice what she/nwas eating./n/n/n/n/n/nIt now occurred to Harry that he had never actually/nheard Krum speak before, but he was certainly/ntalking now, and very enthusiastically at that./n/n"Veil, ve have a castle also, not as big as this, nor as/ncomfortable, I am thinking," he was telling Hermione./n"Ve have just four floors, and the fires are lit only for/nmagical purposes. But ve have grounds larger even/nthan these — though in vinter, ve have very little/ndaylight, so ve are not enjoying them. But in summer/nve are flying every day, over the lakes and the/nmountains — "/n/n"Now, now, Viktor!" said Karkaroff with a laugh that/ndidn't reach his cold eyes, "don't go giving away/nanything else, now, or your charming friend will know/nexactly where to find us!"/n/nDumbledore smiled, his eyes twinkling. "Igor, all this/nsecrecy ... one would almost think you didn't want/nvisitors."/n/n"Well, Dumbledore," said Karkaroff, displaying his/nyellowing teeth to their fullest extent, "we are all/nprotective of our private domains, are we not? Do we/nnot jealously guard the halls of learning that have/nbeen entrusted to us? Are we not right to be proud/nthat we alone know our school's secrets, and right to/nprotect them?"/n/n"Oh I would never dream of assuming I know all/nHogwarts' secrets, Igor," said Dumbledore amicably./n"Only this morning, for instance, I took a wrong/nturning on the way to the bathroom and found myself/nin a beautifully proportioned room I have never seen/nbefore, containing a really rather magnificent/ncollection of chamber pots. When I went back to/ninvestigate more closely, I discovered that the room/nhad vanished. But I must keep an eye out for it./n/n/n/n/n/nPossibly it is only accessible at five-thirty in the/nmorning. Or it may only appear at the quarter moon/n— or when the seeker has an exceptionally full/nbladder."/n/nHarry snorted into his plate of goulash. Percy/nfrowned, but Harry could have sworn Dumbledore/nhad given him a very small wink./n/nMeanwhile Fleur Delacour was criticizing the/nHogwarts decorations to Roger Davies./n/n"Zis is nothing," she said dismissively, looking around/nat the sparkling walls of the Great Hall. "At ze Palace/nof Beauxbatons, we 'ave ice sculptures all around ze/ndining chamber at Chreestmas. Zey do not melt, of/ncourse . . . zey are like 'uge statues of diamond,/nglittering around ze place. And ze food is seemply/nsuperb. And we 'ave choirs of wood nymphs, 'oo/nserenade us as we eat. We 'ave none of zis ugly armor/nin ze 'alls, and eef a poltergeist ever entaired into/nBeauxbatons, 'e would be expelled like zat." She/nslapped her hand onto the table impatiently./n/nRoger Davies was watching her talk with a very dazed/nlook on his face, and he kept missing his mouth with/nhis fork. Harry had the impression that Davies was/ntoo busy staring at Fleur to take in a word she was/nsaying./n/n"Absolutely right," he said quickly, slapping his own/nhand down on the table in imitation of Fleur. "Like/nthat. Yeah."/n/nHarry looked around the Hall. Hagrid was sitting at/none of the other staff tables; he was back in his/nhorrible hairy brown suit and gazing up at the top/ntable. Harry saw him give a small wave, and looking/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/naround, saw Madame Maxime return it, her opals/nglittering in the candlelight./n/nHermione was now teaching Krum to say her name/nproperly; he kept calling her "Hermy-own."/n/n"Her-my-oh-nee," she said slowly and clearly./n/n"Herm-own-ninny."/n/n"Close enough," she said, catching Harry's eye and/ngrinning./n/nWhen all the food had been consumed, Dumbledore/nstood up and asked the students to do the same./n/nThen, with a wave of his wand, all the tables zoomed/nback along the walls leaving the floor clear, and then/nhe conjured a raised platform into existence along the/nright wall. A set of drums, several guitars, a lute, a/ncello, and some bagpipes were set upon it./n/nThe Weird Sisters now trooped up onto the stage to/nwildly enthusiastic applause; they were all extremely/nhairy and dressed in black robes that had been/nartfully ripped and torn. They picked up their/ninstruments, and Harry, who had been so interested/nin watching them that he had almost forgotten what/nwas coming, suddenly realized that the lanterns on all/nthe other tables had gone out, and that the other/nchampions and their partners were standing up./n/n"Come on!" Parvati hissed. "We're supposed to dance!"/n/nHarry tripped over his dress robes as he stood up./n/nThe Weird Sisters struck up a slow, mournful tune;/nHarry walked onto the brightly lit dance floor,/ncarefully avoiding catching anyone's eye (he could see/nSeamus and Dean waving at him and sniggering), and/nnext moment, Parvati had seized his hands, placed/n/n/n/n/none around her waist, and was holding the other/ntightly in hers./n/nIt wasn't as bad as it could have been, Harry thought,/nrevolving slowly on the spot (Parvati was steering) . He/nkept his eyes fixed over the heads of the watching/npeople, and very soon many of them too had come/nonto the dance floor, so that the champions were no/nlonger the center of attention. Neville and Ginny were/ndancing nearby — he could see Ginny wincing/nfrequently as Neville trod on her feet — and/nDumbledore was waltzing with Madame Maxime. He/nwas so dwarfed by her that the top of his pointed hat/nbarely tickled her chin; however, she moved very/ngracefully for a woman so large. Mad-Eye Moody was/ndoing an extremely ungainly two-step with Professor/nSinistra, who was nervously avoiding his wooden leg./n/n"Nice socks, Potter," Moody growled as he passed, his/nmagical eye staring through Harry's robes./n/n"Oh — yeah, Dobby the house-elf knitted them for/nme," said Harry, grinning./n/n"He is so creepy\" Parvati whispered as Moody/nclunked away. "I don't think that eye should be/nallowed]"/n/nHarry heard the final, quavering note from the/nbagpipe with relief. The Weird Sisters stopped playing,/napplause filled the hall once more, and Harry let go of/nParvati at once./n/n"Let's sit down, shall we?"/n/n"Oh — but — this is a really good one!" Parvati said/nas the Weird Sisters struck up a new song, which was/nmuch faster./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No, I don't like it," Harry lied, and he led her away/nfrom the dance floor, past Fred and Angelina, who/nwere dancing so exhuberantly that people around/nthem were backing away in fear of injury, and over to/nthe table where Ron and Padma were sitting./n/n"How's it going?" Harry asked Ron, sitting down and/nopening a bottle of butterbeer./n/nRon didn't answer. He was glaring at Hermione and/nKrum, who were dancing nearby. Padma was sitting/nwith her arms and legs crossed, one foot jiggling in/ntime to the music. Every now and then she threw a/ndisgruntled look at Ron, who was completely ignoring/nher. Parvati sat down on Harry's other side, crossed/nher arms and legs too, and within minutes was asked/nto dance by a boy from Beauxbatons./n/n"You don't mind, do you, Harry?" Parvati said./n/n"What?" said Harry, who was now watching Cho and/nCedric./n/n"Oh never mind," snapped Parvati, and she went off/nwith the boy from Beauxbatons. When the song/nended, she did not return./n/nHermione came over and sat down in Parvati's empty/nchair. She was a bit pink in the face from dancing./n/n"Hi," said Harry. Ron didn't say anything./n/n"It's hot, isn't it?" said Hermione, fanning herself with/nher hand. "Viktor's just gone to get some drinks."/n/nRon gave her a withering look. "Viktor?" he said./n"Hasn't he asked you to call him Vicky yet?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione looked at him in surprise. "What's up with/nyou?" she said./n/n"If you don't know," said Ron scathingly, "I'm not/ngoing to tell you."/n/nHermione stared at him, then at Harry, who/nshrugged./n/n"Ron, what — ?"/n/n"He's from Durmstrang!" spat Ron. "He's competing/nagainst Harry! Against Hogwarts! You — you're — "/nRon was obviously casting around for words strong/nenough to describe Hermione 's crime, " fraternizing/nwith the enemy, that's what you're doing!"/n/nHermione's mouth fell open./n/n"Don't be so stupid!" she said after a moment. "The/nenemy\ Honestly — who was the one who was all/nexcited when they saw him arrive? Who was the one/nwho wanted his autograph? Who's got a model of him/nup in their dormitory?"/n/nRon chose to ignore this. "I s'pose he asked you to/ncome with him while you were both in the library?"/n/n"Yes, he did," said Hermione, the pink patches on her/ncheeks glowing more brightly. "So what?"/n/n"What happened — trying to get him to join spew,/nwere you?"/n/n"No, I wasn't! If you really want to know, he — he said/nhe'd been coming up to the library every day to try/nand talk to me, but he hadn't been able to pluck up/nthe courage!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione said this very quickly, and blushed so/ndeeply that she was the same color as Parvati's robes./n/n"Yeah, well — that's his story," said Ron nastily./n/n"And what's that supposed to mean?"/n/n"Obvious, isn't it? He's Karkaroff's student, isn't he?/nHe knows who you hang around with. ... He's just/ntrying to get closer to Harry — get inside information/non him — or get near enough to jinx him — "/n/nHermione looked as though Ron had slapped her./nWhen she spoke, her voice quivered./n/n"For your information, he hasn't asked me one single/nthing about Harry, not one — "/n/nRon changed tack at the speed of light./n/n"Then he's hoping you'll help him find out what his/negg means! I suppose you've been putting your heads/ntogether during those cozy little library sessions — "/n/n"I'd never help him work out that egg!" said Hermione,/nlooking outraged. "Never. How could you say/nsomething like that — I want Harry to win the/ntournament, Harry knows that, don't you, Harry?"/n/n"You've got a funny way of showing it," sneered Ron./n/n"This whole tournament's supposed to be about/ngetting to know foreign wizards and making friends/nwith them!" said Hermione hotly./n/n"No it isn't!" shouted Ron. "It's about winning!"/n/nPeople were starting to stare at them./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ron," said Harry quietly, "I haven't got a problem/nwith Hermione coming with Krum — "/n/nBut Ron ignored Harry too./n/n"Why don't you go and find Vicky, he'll be wondering/nwhere you are," said Ron./n/n"Don't call him Vickyl"/n/nHermione jumped to her feet and stormed off across/nthe dance floor, disappearing into the crowd. Ron/nwatched her go with a mixture of anger and/nsatisfaction on his face./n/n"Are you going to ask me to dance at all?" Padma/nasked him./n/n"No," said Ron, still glaring after Hermione./n/n"Fine," snapped Padma, and she got up and went to/njoin Parvati and the Beauxbatons boy, who conjured/nup one of his friends to join them so fast that Harry/ncould have sworn he had zoomed him there by a/nSummoning Charm./n/n"Vare is Herm-own-ninny?" said a voice./n/nKrum had just arrived at their table clutching two/nbutterbeers./n/n"No idea," said Ron mulishly, looking up at him. "Lost/nher, have you?"/n/nKrum was looking surly again./n/n"Veil, if you see her, tell her I haff drinks," he said,/nand he slouched off./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Made friends with Viktor Krum, have you, Ron?"/n/n/n/nPercy had bustled over, rubbing his hands together/nand looking extremely pompous. "Excellent! That's/nthe whole point, you know — international magical/ncooperation!"/n/nTo Harry's displeasure, Percy now took Padma's/nvacated seat. The top table was now empty; Professor/nDumbledore was dancing with Professor Sprout, Ludo/nBagman with Professor McGonagall; Madame Maxime/nand Hagrid were cutting a wide path around the/ndance floor as they waltzed through the students, and/nKarkaroff was nowhere to be seen. When the next/nsong ended, everybody applauded once more, and/nHarry saw Ludo Bagman kiss Professor McGonagall's/nhand and make his way back through the crowds, at/nwhich point Fred and George accosted him./n/n"What do they think they're doing, annoying senior/nMinistry members?" Percy hissed, watching Fred and/nGeorge suspiciously. "No respect ..."/n/nLudo Bagman shook off Fred and George fairly/nquickly, however, and, spotting Harry, waved and/ncame over to their table./n/n"I hope my brothers weren't bothering you, Mr./nBagman?" said Percy at once./n/n"What? Oh not at all, not at all!" said Bagman. "No,/nthey were just telling me a bit more about those fake/nwands of theirs. Wondering if I could advise them on/nthe marketing. I've promised to put them in touch/nwith a couple of contacts of mine at Zonko's Joke/nShop. ..."/n/nPercy didn't look happy about this at all, and Harry/nwas prepared to bet he would be rushing to tell Mrs./n/n/n/n/n/nWeasley about this the moment he got home./nApparently Fred and George's plans had grown even/nmore ambitious lately, if they were hoping to sell to/nthe public. Bagman opened his mouth to ask Harry/nsomething, but Percy diverted him./n/n"How do you feel the tournament's going, Mr./n/nBagman? Our department's quite satisfied — the/nhitch with the Goblet of Fire" — he glanced at Harry/n— "was a little unfortunate, of course, but it seems to/nhave gone very smoothly since, don't you think?"/n/n"Oh yes," Bagman said cheerfully, "it's all been/nenormous fun. How's old Barty doing? Shame he/ncouldn't come."/n/n"Oh I'm sure Mr. Crouch will be up and about in no/ntime," said Percy importantly, "but in the meantime,/nI'm more than willing to take up the slack. Of course,/nit's not all attending balls" — he laughed airily — "oh/nno, I've had to deal with all sorts of things that have/ncropped up in his absence — you heard Ali Bashir/nwas caught smuggling a consignment of flying carpets/ninto the country? And then we've been trying to/npersuade the Transylvanians to sign the International/nBan on Dueling. I've got a meeting with their Head of/nMagical Cooperation in the new year — "/n/n"Let's go for a walk," Ron muttered to Harry, "get/naway from Percy. ..."/n/nPretending they wanted more drinks, Harry and Ron/nleft the table, edged around the dance floor, and/nslipped out into the entrance hall. The front doors/nstood open, and the fluttering fairy lights in the rose/ngarden winked and twinkled as they went down the/nfront steps, where they found themselves surrounded/nby bushes; winding, ornamental paths; and large/nstone statues. Harry could hear splashing water,/n/n/n/n/n/nwhich sounded like a fountain. Here and there, people/nwere sitting on carved benches. He and Ron set off/nalong one of the winding paths through the/nrosebushes, but they had gone only a short way when/nthey heard an unpleasantly familiar voice./n/n"... don't see what there is to fuss about, Igor."/n/n"Severus, you cannot pretend this isn't happening!"/nKarkaroff's voice sounded anxious and hushed, as/nthough keen not to be overheard. "It's been getting/nclearer and clearer for months. I am becoming/nseriously concerned, I can't deny it — "/n/n"Then flee," said Snape's voice curtly. "Flee — I will/nmake your excuses. I, however, am remaining at/nHogwarts."/n/nSnape and Karkaroff came around the corner. Snape/nhad his wand out and was blasting rosebushes apart,/nhis expression most ill-natured. Squeals issued from/nmany of the bushes, and dark shapes emerged from/nthem./n/n"Ten points from Ravenclaw, Fawcett!" Snape snarled/nas a girl ran past him. "And ten points from Hufflepuff/ntoo, Stebbins!" as a boy went rushing after her. "And/nwhat are you two doing?" he added, catching sight of/nHarry and Ron on the path ahead. Karkaroff, Harry/nsaw, looked slightly discomposed to see them/nstanding there. His hand went nervously to his/ngoatee, and he began winding it around his finger./n/n"We're walking," Ron told Snape shortly. "Not against/nthe law, is it?"/n/n"Keep walking, then!" Snape snarled, and he brushed/npast them, his long black cloak billowing out behind/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhim. Karkaroff hurried away after Snape. Harry and/nRon continued down the path./n/n"What's got Karkaroff all worried?" Ron muttered./n/n"And since when have he and Snape been on first-/nname terms?" said Harry slowly./n/nThey had reached a large stone reindeer now, over/nwhich they could see the sparkling jets of a tall/nfountain. The shadowy outlines of two enormous/npeople were visible on a stone bench, watching the/nwater in the moonlight. And then Harry heard Hagrid/nspeak./n/n"Momen' I saw yeh, I knew," he was saying, in an/noddly husky voice./n/nHarry and Ron froze. This didn't sound like the sort of/nscene they ought to walk in on, somehow. . . . Harry/nlooked around, back up the path, and saw Fleur/nDelacour and Roger Davies standing half-concealed in/na rosebush nearby. He tapped Ron on the shoulder/nand jerked his head toward them, meaning that they/ncould easily sneak off that way without being noticed/n(Fleur and Davies looked very busy to Harry), but/nRon, eyes widening in horror at the sight of Fleur,/nshook his head vigorously, and pulled Harry deeper/ninto the shadows behind the reindeer./n/n"What did you know, 'Agrid?" said Madame Maxime, a/npurr in her low voice./n/nHarry definitely didn't want to listen to this; he knew/nHagrid would hate to be overheard in a situation like/nthis (he certainly would have) — if it had been/npossible he would have put his fingers in his ears and/nhummed loudly, but that wasn't really an option./nInstead he tried to interest himself in a beetle/n/n/n/n/ncrawling along the stone reindeer's back, but the/nbeetle just wasn't interesting enough to block out/nHagrid's next words./n/n"I jus' knew ... knew you were like me. ... Was it yer/nmother or yer father?"/n/n"I — I don't know what you mean, 'Agrid. ..."/n/n"It was my mother," said Hagrid quietly. "She was one/no' the las' ones in Britain. 'Course, I can' remember/nher too well ... she left, see. When I was abou' three./nShe wasn' really the maternal sort. Well ... it's not in/ntheir natures, is it? Dunno what happened to her .../nmight be dead fer all I know. ..."/n/nMadame Maxime didn't say anything. And Harry, in/nspite of himself, took his eyes off the beetle and/nlooked over the top of the reindeer's antlers, listening./n/n. . . He had never heard Hagrid talk about his/nchildhood before./n/n"Me dad was broken-hearted when she wen'. Tiny/nlittle bloke, my dad was. By the time I was six I could/nlift him up an' put him on top o' the dresser if he/nannoyed me. Used ter make him laugh. ..." Hagrid's/ndeep voice broke. Madame Maxime was listening,/nmotionless, apparently staring at the silvery fountain./n"Dad raised me ... but he died, o' course, jus' after I/nstarted school. Sorta had ter make me own way after/nthat. Dumbledore was a real help, mind. Very kind ter/nme, he was. ..."/n/nHagrid pulled out a large spotted silk handkerchief/nand blew his nose heavily./n/n"So ... anyway ... enough abou' me. What about you?/nWhich side you got it on?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Madame Maxime had suddenly got to her feet./n/n"It is chilly," she said — but whatever the weather/nwas doing, it was nowhere near as cold as her voice./n/n"I think I will go in now."/n/n"Eh?" said Hagrid blankly. "No, don' go! I've — I've/nnever met another one before!"/n/n"Anuzzer what, precisely?" said Madame Maxime, her/ntone icy./n/nHarry could have told Hagrid it was best not to/nanswer; he stood there in the shadows gritting his/nteeth, hoping against hope he wouldn't — but it was/nno good./n/n"Another half-giant, o' course!" said Hagrid./n/n" 'Ow dare you!" shrieked Madame Maxime. Her voice/nexploded through the peaceful night air like a/nfoghorn; behind him, Harry heard Fleur and Roger fall/nout of their rosebush. "I 'ave nevair been more/ninsulted in my life! 'Alf-giant? Moi? I 'ave — I 'ave big/nbones!"/n/nShe stormed away; great multicolored swarms of/nfairies rose into the air as she passed, angrily pushing/naside bushes. Hagrid was still sitting on the bench,/nstaring after her. It was much too dark to make out/nhis expression. Then, after about a minute, he stood/nup and strode away, not back to the castle, but off/nout into the dark grounds in the direction of his/ncabin./n/n"C'mon," Harry said, very quietly to Ron. "Let's go. ..."/nBut Ron didn't move./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's up?" said Harry, looking at him./n/nRon looked around at Harry, his expression very/nserious indeed./n/n"Did you know?" he whispered. "About Hagrid being/nhalf-giant?"/n/n"No," Harry said, shrugging. "So what?"/n/nHe knew immediately, from the look Ron was giving/nhim, that he was once again revealing his ignorance/nof the wizarding world. Brought up by the Dursleys,/nthere were many things that wizards took for granted/nthat were revelations to Harry, but these surprises/nhad become fewer with each successive year. Now,/nhowever, he could tell that most wizards would not/nhave said "So what?" upon finding out that one of/ntheir friends had a giantess for a mother./n/n"I'll explain inside," said Ron quietly, "c'mon. ..."/n/nFleur and Roger Davies had disappeared, probably/ninto a more private clump of bushes. Harry and Ron/nreturned to the Great Hall. Parvati and Padma were/nnow sitting at a distant table with a whole crowd of/nBeauxbatons boys, and Hermione was once more/ndancing with Krum. Harry and Ron sat down at a/ntable far removed from the dance floor./n/n"So?" Harry prompted Ron. "What's the problem with/ngiants?"/n/n"Well, they're ... they're ..." Ron struggled for words./n"... not very nice," he finished lamely./n/n"Who cares?" Harry said. "There's nothing wrong with/nHagrid!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I know there isn't, but ... blimey, no wonder he keeps/nit quiet," Ron said, shaking his head. "I always/nthought he'd got in the way of a bad Engorgement/nCharm when he was a kid or something. Didn't like to/nmention it. ..."/n/n"But what's it matter if his mother was a giantess?"/nsaid Harry./n/n"Well ... no one who knows him will care, 'cos they'll/nknow he's not dangerous," said Ron slowly. "But .../nHarry, they're just vicious, giants. It's like Hagrid/nsaid, it's in their natures, they're like trolls ... they/njust like killing, everyone knows that. There aren't/nany left in Britain now, though."/n/n"What happened to them?"/n/n"Well, they were dying out anyway, and then loads got/nthemselves killed by Aurors. There 're supposed to be/ngiants abroad, though. ... They hide out in mountains/nmostly. ..."/n/n"I don't know who Maxime thinks she's kidding,"/n/nHarry said, watching Madame Maxime sitting alone at/nthe judges' table, looking very somber. "If Hagrid 's/nhalf-giant, she definitely is. Big bones ... the only/nthing that's got bigger bones than her is a dinosaur."/n/nHarry and Ron spent the rest of the ball discussing/ngiants in their corner, neither of them having any/ninclination to dance. Harry tried not to watch Cho/nand Cedric too much; it gave him a strong desire to/nkick something./n/nWhen the Weird Sisters finished playing at midnight,/neveryone gave them a last, loud round of applause/nand started to wend their way into the entrance hall./nMany people were expressing the wish that the ball/n/n/n/n/n/ncould have gone on longer, but Harry was perfectly/nhappy to be going to bed; as far as he was concerned,/nthe evening hadn't been much fun./n/nOut in the entrance hall, Harry and Ron saw/nHermione saying good night to Krum before he went/nback to the Durmstrang ship. She gave Ron a very/ncold look and swept past him up the marble staircase/nwithout speaking. Harry and Ron followed her, but/nhalfway up the staircase Harry heard someone calling/nhim./n/n"Hey — Harry!"/n/nIt was Cedric Diggory. Harry could see Cho waiting for/nhim in the entrance hall below./n/n"Yeah?" said Harry coldly as Cedric ran up the stairs/ntoward him./n/nCedric looked as though he didn't want to say/nwhatever it was in front of Ron, who shrugged,/nlooking bad-tempered, and continued to climb the/nstairs./n/n"Listen ..." Cedric lowered his voice as Ron/ndisappeared. "I owe you one for telling me about the/ndragons. You know that golden egg? Does yours wail/nwhen you open it?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry./n/n"Well ... take a bath, okay?"/n/n"What?"/n/n"Take a bath, and — er — take the egg with you, and/n— er — just mull things over in the hot water. It'll/nhelp you think. ... Trust me."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry stared at him./n/n"Tell you what," Cedric said, "use the prefects'/nbathroom. Fourth door to the left of that statue of/nBoris the Bewildered on the fifth floor. Password's/n'pine fresh. ' Gotta go . . . want to say good night — "/n/nHe grinned at Harry again and hurried back down the/nstairs to Cho./n/nHarry walked back to Gryffindor Tower alone. That/nhad been extremely strange advice. Why would a bath/nhelp him to work out what the wailing egg meant?/nWas Cedric pulling his leg? Was he trying to make/nHarry look like a fool, so Cho would like him even/nmore by comparison?/n/nThe Fat Lady and her friend Vi were snoozing in the/npicture over the portrait hole. Harry had to yell "Fairy/nlights!" before he woke them up, and when he did,/nthey were extremely irritated. He climbed into the/ncommon room and found Ron and Hermione having a/nblazing row. Standing ten feet apart, they were/nbellowing at each other, each scarlet in the face./n/n"Well, if you don't like it, you know what the solution/nis, don't you?" yelled Hermione; her hair was coming/ndown out of its elegant bun now, and her face was/nscrewed up in anger./n/n"Oh yeah?" Ron yelled back. "What's that?"/n/n"Next time there's a ball, ask me before someone else/ndoes, and not as a last resort!"/n/nRon mouthed soundlessly like a goldfish out of water/nas Hermione turned on her heel and stormed up the/ngirls' staircase to bed. Ron turned to look at Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well," he sputtered, looking thunderstruck, "well —/nthat just proves — completely missed the point — "/n/nHarry didn't say anything. He liked being back on/nspeaking terms with Ron too much to speak his mind/nright now — but he somehow thought that Hermione/nhad gotten the point much better than Ron had./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Rita Skeeter's Scoop
text: /nEverybody got up late on Boxing Day. The Gryffindor/ncommon room was much quieter than it had been/nlately, many yawns punctuating the lazy/nconversations. Hermione's hair was bushy again; she/nconfessed to Harry that she had used liberal amounts/nof Sleekeazy's Hair Potion on it for the ball, "but it's/nway too much bother to do every day," she said/nmatter-of-factly, scratching a purring Crookshanks/nbehind the ears./n/nRon and Hermione seemed to have reached an/nunspoken agreement not to discuss their argument./nThey were being quite friendly to each other, though/noddly formal. Ron and Harry wasted no time in telling/nHermione about the conversation they had overheard/nbetween Madame Maxime and Hagrid, but Hermione/ndidn't seem to find the news that Hagrid was a half-/ngiant nearly as shocking as Ron did./n/n"Well, I thought he must be," she said, shrugging. "I/nknew he couldn't be pure giant because they're about/ntwenty feet tall. But honestly, all this hysteria about/n/n/n/n/n/ngiants. They can't all be horrible. ... It's the same sort/nof prejudice that people have toward werewolves. .../n/nIt's just bigotry, isn't it?"/n/nRon looked as though he would have liked to reply/nscathingly, but perhaps he didn't want another row,/nbecause he contented himself with shaking his head/ndisbelievingly while Hermione wasn't looking./n/nIt was time now to think of the homework they had/nneglected during the first week of the holidays./nEverybody seemed to be feeling rather flat now that/nChristmas was over — everybody except Harry, that/nis, who was starting (once again) to feel slightly/nnervous./n/nThe trouble was that February the twenty-fourth/nlooked a lot closer from this side of Christmas, and he/nstill hadn't done anything about working out the clue/ninside the golden egg. He therefore started taking the/negg out of his trunk every time he went up to the/ndormitory, opening it, and listening intently, hoping/nthat this time it would make some sense. He strained/nto think what the sound reminded him of, apart from/nthirty musical saws, but he had never heard anything/nelse like it. He closed the egg, shook it vigorously, and/nopened it again to see if the sound had changed, but/nit hadn't. He tried asking the egg questions, shouting/nover all the wailing, but nothing happened. He even/nthrew the egg across the room — though he hadn't/nreally expected that to help./n/nHarry had not forgotten the hint that Cedric had/ngiven him, but his less-than-friendly feelings toward/nCedric just now meant that he was keen not to take/nhis help if he could avoid it. In any case, it seemed to/nhim that if Cedric had really wanted to give Harry a/nhand, he would have been a lot more explicit.
