"I'm serious, Hermione, she'll dig up/nsomething on you — "/n/n"My parents don't read the Daily Prophet She can't/nscare me into hiding!" said Hermione, now striding/nalong so fast that it was all Harry and Ron could do to/nkeep up with her. The last time Harry had seen/nHermione in a rage like this, she had hit Draco Malfoy/naround the face. "And Hagrid isn't hiding anymore!/n/nHe should never have let that excuse for a human/nbeing upset him! Come on!"/n/nBreaking into a run, she led them all the way back up/nthe road, through the gates flanked by winged boars,/nand up through the grounds to Hagrid 's cabin./n/nThe curtains were still drawn, and they could hear/nFang barking as they approached./n/n"Hagrid!" Hermione shouted, pounding on his front/ndoor. "Hagrid, that's enough! We know you're in there!/n/n/n/n/n/nNobody cares if your mum was a giantess, Hagrid!/n/nYou can't let that foul Skeeter woman do this to you!/nHagrid, get out here, you're just being — "/n/nThe door opened. Hermione said, "About t — !" and/nthen stopped, very suddenly, because she had found/nherself face-to-face, not with Hagrid, but with Albus/nDumbledore./n/n"Good afternoon," he said pleasantly, smiling down at/nthem./n/n"We — er — we wanted to see Hagrid," said Hermione/nin a rather small voice./n/n"Yes, I surmised as much," said Dumbledore, his eyes/ntwinkling. "Why don't you come in?"/n/n"Oh ... um ... okay," said Hermione./n/nShe, Ron, and Harry went into the cabin; Fang/nlaunched himself upon Harry the moment he entered,/nbarking madly and trying to lick his ears. Harry/nfended off Fang and looked around./n/nHagrid was sitting at his table, where there were two/nlarge mugs of tea. He looked a real mess. His face was/nblotchy, his eyes swollen, and he had gone to the/nother extreme where his hair was concerned; far from/ntrying to make it behave, it now looked like a wig of/ntangled wire./n/n"Hi, Hagrid," said Harry./n/nHagrid looked up./n/n" 'Lo," he said in a very hoarse voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"More tea, I think," said Dumbledore, closing the door/nbehind Harry, Ron, and Hermione, drawing out his/nwand, and twiddling it; a revolving tea tray appeared/nin midair along with a plate of cakes. Dumbledore/nmagicked the tray onto the table, and everybody sat/ndown. There was a slight pause, and then/nDumbledore said, "Did you by any chance hear what/nMiss Granger was shouting, Hagrid?"/n/nHermione went slightly pink, but Dumbledore smiled/nat her and continued, "Hermione, Harry, and Ron still/nseem to want to know you, judging by the way they/nwere attempting to break down the door."/n/n"Of course we still want to know you!" Harry said,/nstaring at Hagrid. "You don't think anything that/nSkeeter cow — sorry, Professor," he added quickly,/nlooking at Dumbledore./n/n"I have gone temporarily deaf and haven't any idea/nwhat you said, Harry," said Dumbledore, twiddling/nhis thumbs and staring at the ceiling./n/n"Er — right," said Harry sheepishly. "I just meant —/nHagrid, how could you think we'd care what that —/nwoman — wrote about you?"/n/nTwo fat tears leaked out of Hagrid 's beetle-black eyes/nand fell slowly into his tangled beard./n/n"Living proof of what I've been telling you, Hagrid,"/nsaid Dumbledore, still looking carefully up at the/nceiling. "I have shown you the letters from the/ncountless parents who remember you from their own/ndays here, telling me in no uncertain terms that if I/nsacked you, they would have something to say about/nit — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Not all of 'em," said Hagrid hoarsely. "Not all of 'em/nwan' me ter stay."/n/n"Really, Hagrid, if you are holding out for universal/npopularity, I'm afraid you will be in this cabin for a/nvery long time," said Dumbledore, now peering sternly/nover his half-moon spectacles. "Not a week has/npassed since I became headmaster of this school/nwhen I haven't had at least one owl complaining/nabout the way I run it. But what should I do?/nBarricade myself in my study and refuse to talk to/nanybody?"/n/n"Yeh — yeh're not half-giant!" said Hagrid croakily./n/n"Hagrid, look what I've got for relatives!" Harry said/nfuriously. "Look at the Dursleys!"/n/n"An excellent point," said Professor Dumbledore. "My/nown brother, Aberforth, was prosecuted for practicing/ninappropriate charms on a goat. It was all over the/npapers, but did Aberforth hide? No, he did not! He/nheld his head high and went about his business as/nusual! Of course, I'm not entirely sure he can read, so/nthat may not have been bravery. ..."/n/n"Come back and teach, Hagrid," said Hermione/nquietly, "please come back, we really miss you."/n/nHagrid gulped. More tears leaked out down his cheeks/nand into his tangled beard./n/nDumbledore stood up. "I refuse to accept your/nresignation, Hagrid, and I expect you back at work on/nMonday," he said. "You will join me for breakfast at/neight-thirty in the Great Hall. No excuses. Good/nafternoon to you all."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore left the cabin, pausing only to scratch/nFang's ears. When the door had shut behind him,/nHagrid began to sob into his dustbin-lid-sized hands./nHermione kept patting his arm, and at last, Hagrid/nlooked up, his eyes very red indeed, and said, "Great/nman, Dumbledore ... great man ..."/n/n"Yeah, he is," said Ron. "Can I have one of these/ncakes, Hagrid?"/n/n"Help yerself," said Hagrid, wiping his eyes on the/nback of his hand. "Ar, he's righ', o' course — yeh're all/nrigh' ... I bin stupid ... my ol' dad woulda bin/nashamed o' the way I've bin behavin'. ..." More tears/nleaked out, but he wiped them away more forcefully,/nand said, "Never shown you a picture of my old dad,/nhave I? Here ..."/n/nHagrid got up, went over to his dresser, opened a/ndrawer, and pulled out a picture of a short wizard/nwith Hagrid's crinkled black eyes, beaming as he sat/non top of Hagrid's shoulder. Hagrid was a good seven/nor eight feet tall, judging by the apple tree beside him,/nbut his face was beardless, young, round, and smooth/n— he looked hardly older than eleven./n/n"Tha' was taken jus' after I got inter Hogwarts,"/n/nHagrid croaked. "Dad was dead chuffed ... thought I/nmigh' not be a wizard, see, 'cos me mum ... well,/nanyway. 'Course, I never was great shakes at magic,/nreally ... but at least he never saw me expelled. Died,/nsee, in me second year. .../n/n"Dumbledore was the one who stuck up for me after/nDad went. Got me the gamekeeper job ... trusts/npeople, he does. Gives 'em second chances ... tha's/nwhat sets him apar' from other heads, see. He'll/naccept anyone at Hogwarts, s'long as they've got the/ntalent. Knows people can turn out okay even if their/n/n/n/n/nfamilies weren' ... well ... all tha' respectable. But/nsome don' understand that. There's some who'd/nalways hold it against yeh ... there's some who'd even/npretend they just had big bones rather than stand up/nan' say — I am what I am, an' I'm not ashamed./n/n'Never be ashamed,' my ol' dad used ter say, 'there's/nsome wholl hold it against you, but they're not worth/nbotherin' with.' An' he was right. I've bin an idiot. I'm/nnot botherin' with her no more, I promise yeh that./n/nBig bones ... I'll give her big bones."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione looked at one another/nnervously; Harry would rather have taken fifty Blast-/nEnded Skrewts for a walk than admit to Hagrid that/nhe had overheard him talking to Madame Maxime,/nbut Hagrid was still talking, apparently unaware that/nhe had said anything odd./n/n"Yeh know wha', Harry?" he said, looking up from the/nphotograph of his father, his eyes very bright, "when I/nfirs' met you, you reminded me o' me a bit. Mum an'/nDad gone, an' you was feelin' like yeh wouldn' fit in at/nHogwarts, remember? Not sure yeh were really up to/nit ... an' now look at yeh, Harry! School champion!"/n/nHe looked at Harry for a moment and then said, very/nseriously, "Yeh know what I'd love, Harry? I'd love yeh/nter win, I really would. It'd show 'em all ... yeh don'/nhave ter be pureblood ter do it. Yeh don' have ter be/nashamed of what yeh are. It'd show 'em Dumbledore's/nthe one who's got it righ', lettin' anyone in as long as/nthey can do magic. How you doin' with that egg,/nHarry?"/n/n"Great," said Harry. "Really great."/n/nHagrid 's miserable face broke into a wide, watery/nsmile./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Tha's my boy ... you show 'em, Harry, you show 'em./nBeat 'em all."/n/nLying to Hagrid wasn't quite like lying to anyone else./nHarry went back to the castle later that afternoon/nwith Ron and Hermione, unable to banish the image/nof the happy expression on Hagrid's whiskery face as/nhe had imagined Harry winning the tournament. The/nincomprehensible egg weighed more heavily than ever/non Harry's conscience that evening, and by the time/nhe had got into bed, he had made up his mind — it/nwas time to shelve his pride and see if Cedric's hint/nwas worth anything./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Egg And The Eye
text: /nAs Harry had no idea how long a bath he would need/nto work out the secret of the golden egg, he decided to/ndo it at night, when he would be able to take as much/ntime as he wanted. Reluctant though he was to accept/nmore favours from Cedric, he also decided to use the/nprefects' bathroom; far fewer people were allowed in/nthere, so it was much less likely that he would be/ndisturbed./n/nHarry planned his excursion carefully, because he/nhad been caught out of bed and out-of-bounds by/nFilch the caretaker in the middle of the night once/nbefore, and had no desire to repeat the experience./n/nThe Invisibility Cloak would, of course, be essential,/nand as an added precaution, Harry thought he would/ntake the Marauder's Map, which, next to the cloak,/nwas the most useful aid to rule-breaking Harry/nowned. The map showed the whole of Hogwarts,/nincluding its many shortcuts and secret passageways/nand, most important of all, it revealed the people/ninside the castle as minuscule, labeled dots, moving/naround the corridors, so that Harry would be/n/n/n/nforewarned if somebody was approaching the/nbathroom./n/n/n/nOn Thursday night, Harry sneaked up to bed, put on/nthe cloak, crept back downstairs, and, just as he had/ndone on the night when Hagrid had shown him the/ndragons, waited for the portrait hole to open. This/ntime it was Ron who waited outside to give the Fat/nLady the password ("banana fritters"). "Good luck,"/nRon muttered, climbing into the room as Harry crept/nout past him./n/nIt was awkward moving under the cloak tonight,/nbecause Harry had the heavy egg under one arm and/nthe map held in front of his nose with the other./nHowever, the moonlit corridors were empty and silent,/nand by checking the map at strategic intervals, Harry/nwas able to ensure that he wouldn't run into anyone/nhe wanted to avoid. When he reached the statue of/nBoris the Bewildered, a lost-looking wizard with his/ngloves on the wrong hands, he located the right door,/nleaned close to it, and muttered the password, "Pine/nfresh," just as Cedric had told him./n/nThe door creaked open. Harry slipped inside, bolted/nthe door behind him, and pulled off the Invisibility/nCloak, looking around./n/nHis immediate reaction was that it would be worth/nbecoming a prefect just to be able to use this/nbathroom. It was softly lit by a splendid candle-filled/nchandelier, and everything was made of white marble,/nincluding what looked like an empty, rectangular/nswimming pool sunk into the middle of the floor./n/nAbout a hundred golden taps stood all around the/npool's edges, each with a differently colored jewel set/ninto its handle. There was also a diving board. Long/nwhite linen curtains hung at the windows; a large pile/nof fluffy white towels sat in a corner, and there was a/n/n/n/n/nsingle golden-framed painting on the wall. It featured/na blonde mermaid who was fast asleep on a rock, her/nlong hair over her face. It fluttered every time she/nsnored./n/nHarry moved forward, looking around, his footsteps/nechoing off the walls. Magnificent though the/nbathroom was — and quite keen though he was to try/nout a few of those taps — now he was here he/ncouldn't quite suppress the feeling that Cedric might/nhave been having him on. How on earth was this/nsupposed to help solve the mystery of the egg?/nNevertheless, he put one of the fluffy towels, the/ncloak, the map, and the egg at the side of the/nswimming-pool-sized bath, then knelt down and/nturned on a few of the taps./n/nHe could tell at once that they carried different sorts/nof bubble bath mixed with the water, though it wasn't/nbubble bath as Harry had ever experienced it. One/ntap gushed pink and blue bubbles the size of/nfootballs; another poured ice-white foam so thick that/nHarry thought it would have supported his weight if/nhe'd cared to test it; a third sent heavily perfumed/npurple clouds hovering over the surface of the water./nHarry amused himself for a while turning the taps on/nand off, particularly enjoying the effect of one whose/njet bounced off the surface of the water in large arcs./nThen, when the deep pool was full of hot water, foam,/nand bubbles, which took a very short time/nconsidering its size, Harry turned off all the taps,/npulled off his pajamas, slippers, and dressing gown,/nand slid into the water./n/nIt was so deep that his feet barely touched the/nbottom, and he actually did a couple of lengths before/nswimming back to the side and treading water,/nstaring at the egg. Highly enjoyable though it was to/nswim in hot and foamy water with clouds of different-/n/n/n/n/ncolored steam wafting all around him, no stroke of/nbrilliance came to him, no sudden burst of/nunderstanding./n/nHarry stretched out his arms, lifted the egg in his wet/nhands, and opened it. The wailing, screeching sound/nfilled the bathroom, echoing and reverberating off the/nmarble walls, but it sounded just as/nincomprehensible as ever, if not more so with all the/nechoes. He snapped it shut again, worried that the/nsound would attract Filch, wondering whether that/nhadn't been Cedric's plan — and then, making him/njump so badly that he dropped the egg, which/nclattered away across the bathroom floor, someone/nspoke./n/n"I'd try putting it in the water, if I were you."/n/nHarry had swallowed a considerable amount of/nbubbles in shock. He stood up, sputtering, and saw/nthe ghost of a very glum-looking girl sitting cross-/nlegged on top of one of the taps. It was Moaning/nMyrtle, who was usually to be heard sobbing in the S-/nbend of a toilet three floors below./n/n"Myrtle!" Harry said in outrage, "I'm — I'm not/nwearing anything!"/n/nThe foam was so dense that this hardly mattered, but/nhe had a nasty feeling that Myrtle had been spying on/nhim from out of one of the taps ever since he had/narrived./n/n"I closed my eyes when you got in," she said, blinking/nat him through her thick spectacles. "You haven't/nbeen to see me for ages."/n/n"Yeah ... well ..." said Harry, bending his knees/nslightly, just to make absolutely sure Myrtle couldn't/n/n/n/n/n/nsee anything but his head, "I'm not supposed to come/ninto your bathroom, am I? It's a girls' one."/n/n/n/n"You didn't used to care," said Myrtle miserably. "You/nused to be in there all the time."/n/nThis was true, though only because Harry, Ron, and/nHermione had found Myrtle's out-of-order toilets a/nconvenient place to brew Polyjuice Potion in secret —/na forbidden potion that had turned him and Ron into/nliving replicas of Crabbe and Goyle for an hour, so/nthat they could sneak into the Slytherin common/nroom./n/n"I got told off for going in there," said Harry, which/nwas half-true; Percy had once caught him coming out/nof Myrtle's bathroom. "I thought I'd better not come/nback after that."/n/n"Oh ... I see ..." said Myrtle, picking at a spot on her/nchin in a morose sort of way. "Well... anyway ... I'd try/nthe egg in the water. That's what Cedric Diggory did."/n/n"Have you been spying on him too?" said Harry/nindignantly. "What d'you do, sneak up here in the/nevenings to watch the prefects take baths?"/n/n"Sometimes," said Myrtle, rather slyly, "but I've never/ncome out to speak to anyone before."/n/n"I'm honored," said Harry darkly. "You keep your eyes/nshut!"/n/nHe made sure Myrtle had her glasses well covered/nbefore hoisting himself out of the bath, wrapping the/ntowel firmly around his waist, and going to retrieve/nthe egg. Once he was back in the water, Myrtle peered/nthrough her fingers and said, "Go on, then . . . open it/nunder the water!"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry lowered the egg beneath the foamy surface and/nopened it ... and this time, it did not wail. A gurgling/nsong was coming out of it, a song whose words he/ncouldn't distinguish through the water./n/n"You need to put your head under too," said Myrtle,/nwho seemed to be thoroughly enjoying bossing him/naround. "Go on!"/n/nHarry took a great breath and slid under the surface/n— and now, sitting on the marble bottom of the/nbubble-filled bath, he heard a chorus of eerie voices/nsinging to him from the open egg in his hands:/n/n"Come seek us where our voices sound,/n/nWe cannot sing above the ground,/n/nAnd while you're searching ponder this:/n/nWe've taken what you'll sorely miss,/n/nAn hour long you'll have to look,/n/nAnd to recover what we took,/n/nBut past an hour — the prospect's black,/n/nToo late, it's gone, it won't come back."/n/nHarry let himself float back upward and broke the/nbubbly surface, shaking his hair out of his eyes./n/n"Hear it?" said Myrtle./n/n"Yeah ... 'Come seek us where our voices sound ...'/nand if I need persuading . . . hang on, I need to listen/nagain. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe sank back beneath the water. It took three more/nunderwater renditions of the egg's song before Harry/nhad it memorized; then he trod water for a while,/nthinking hard, while Myrtle sat and watched him./n/n"I've got to go and look for people who can't use their/nvoices above the ground. ..." he said slowly. "Er .../nwho could that be?"/n/n"Slow, aren't you?"/n/nHe had never seen Moaning Myrtle so cheerful, apart/nfrom the day when a dose of Polyjuice Potion had/ngiven Hermione the hairy face and tail of a cat. Harry/nstared around the bathroom, thinking ... if the voices/ncould only be heard underwater, then it made sense/nfor them to belong to underwater creatures. He ran/nthis theory past Myrtle, who smirked at him./n/n"Well, that's what Diggory thought," she said. "He lay/nthere talking to himself for ages about it. Ages and/nages ... nearly all the bubbles had gone. ..."/n/n"Underwater ..." Harry said slowly. "Myrtle ... what/nlives in the lake, apart from the giant squid?"/n/n"Oh all sorts," she said. "I sometimes go down there/n... sometimes don't have any choice, if someone/nflushes my toilet when I'm not expecting it. ..."/n/nTrying not to think about Moaning Myrtle zooming/ndown a pipe to the lake with the contents of a toilet,/nHarry said, "Well, does anything in there have a/nhuman voice? Hang on — "/n/nHarry's eyes had fallen on the picture of the snoozing/nmermaid on the wall./n/n"Myrtle, there aren't merpeople in there, are there?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oooh, very good," she said, her thick glasses/ntwinkling, "it took Diggory much longer than that!/n/nAnd that was with her awake too" — Myrtle jerked her/nhead toward the mermaid with an expression of great/ndislike on her glum face — "giggling and showing off/nand flashing her fins. ..."/n/n"That's it, isn't it?" said Harry excitedly. "The second/ntask's to go and find the merpeople in the lake and . . ./nand ..."/n/nBut he suddenly realized what he was saying, and he/nfelt the excitement drain out of him as though/nsomeone had just pulled a plug in his stomach. He/nwasn't a very good swimmer; he'd never had much/npractice. Dudley had had lessons in his youth, but/nAunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon, no doubt hoping/nthat Harry would drown one day, hadn't bothered to/ngive him any. A couple of lengths of this bath were all/nvery well, but that lake was very large, and very deep/n. . . and merpeople would surely live right at the/nbottom. .../n/n"Myrtle," Harry said slowly, "how am I supposed to/nbreathe ?"/n/nAt this, Myrtle's eyes filled with sudden tears again./n/n"Tactless!" she muttered, groping in her robes for a/nhandkerchief./n/n"What's tactless?" said Harry, bewildered./n/n"Talking about breathing in front of me!" she said/nshrilly, and her voice echoed loudly around the/nbathroom. "When I can't ... when I haven't ... not for/nages ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe buried her face in her handkerchief and sniffed/nloudly. Harry remembered how touchy Myrtle had/nalways been about being dead, but none of the other/nghosts he knew made such a fuss about it./n/n"Sorry," he said impatiently. "I didn't mean — I just/nforgot ..."/n/n"Oh yes, very easy to forget Myrtle's dead," said/nMyrtle, gulping, looking at him out of swollen eyes./n"Nobody missed me even when I was alive. Took them/nhours and hours to find my body — I know, I was/nsitting there waiting for them. Olive Hornby came into/nthe bathroom — 'Are you in here again, sulking,/nMyrtle?' she said, 'because Professor Dippet asked me/nto look for you — ' And then she saw my body . . ./nooooh, she didn't forget it until her dying day, I made/nsure of that . . . followed her around and reminded her,/nI did. I remember at her brother's wedding — "/n/nBut Harry wasn't listening; he was thinking about the/nmerpeople's song again. "We've taken what you'll/nsorely miss." That sounded as though they were going/nto steal something of his, something he had to get/nback. What were they going to take?/n/n" — and then, of course, she went to the Ministry of/nMagic to stop me stalking her, so I had to come back/nhere and live in my toilet."/n/n"Good," said Harry vaguely. "Well, I'm a lot further on/nthan I was. ... Shut your eyes again, will you? I'm/ngetting out."/n/nHe retrieved the egg from the bottom of the bath,/nclimbed out, dried himself, and pulled on his pajamas/nand dressing gown again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Will you come and visit me in my bathroom again/nsometime?" Moaning Myrtle asked mournfully as/nHarry picked up the Invisibility Cloak./n/n"Er ... I'll try," Harry said, though privately thinking/nthe only way he'd be visiting Myrtle's bathroom again/nwas if every other toilet in the castle got blocked. "See/nyou, Myrtle ... thanks for your help."/n/n" 'Bye, 'bye," she said gloomily, and as Harry put on/nthe Invisibility Cloak he saw her zoom back up the/ntap./n/nOut in the dark corridor, Harry examined the/nMarauder's Map to check that the coast was still/nclear. Yes, the dots belonging to Filch and his cat,/n/nMrs. Norris, were safely in their office ... nothing else/nseemed to be moving apart from Peeves, though he/nwas bouncing around the trophy room on the floor/nabove. ... Harry had taken his first step back toward/nGryffindor Tower when something else on the map/ncaught his eye ... something distinctly odd./n/nPeeves was not the only thing that was moving. A/nsingle dot was flitting around a room in the bottom/nleft-hand corner — Snape's office. But the dot wasn't/nlabeled "Severus Snape" ... it was Bartemius Crouch./n/nHarry stared at the dot. Mr. Crouch was supposed to/nbe too ill to go to work or to come to the Yule Ball —/nso what was he doing, sneaking into Hogwarts at one/no'clock in the morning? Harry watched closely as the/ndot moved around and around the room, pausing/nhere and there. .../n/nHarry hesitated, thinking . . . and then his curiosity got/nthe better of him. He turned and set off in the/nopposite direction toward the nearest staircase. He/nwas going to see what Crouch was up to./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry walked down the stairs as quietly as possible,/nthough the faces in some of the portraits still turned/ncuriously at the squeak of a floorboard, the rustle of/nhis pajamas. He crept along the corridor below,/npushed aside a tapestry about halfway along, and/nproceeded down a narrower staircase, a shortcut that/nwould take him down two floors. He kept glancing/ndown at the map, wondering ... It just didn't seem in/ncharacter, somehow, for correct, law-abiding Mr./nCrouch to be sneaking around somebody else's office/nthis late at night. .../n/nAnd then, halfway down the staircase, not thinking/nabout what he was doing, not concentrating on/nanything but the peculiar behavior of Mr. Crouch,/nHarry's leg suddenly sank right through the trick step/nNeville always forgot to jump. He gave an ungainly/nwobble, and the golden egg, still damp from the bath,/nslipped from under his arm. He lurched forward to try/nand catch it, but too late; the egg fell down the long/nstaircase with a bang as loud as a bass drum on/nevery step — the Invisibility Cloak slipped — Harry/nsnatched at it, and the Marauder's Map fluttered out/nof his hand and slid down six stairs, where, sunk in/nthe step to above his knee, he couldn't reach it./n/nThe golden egg fell through the tapestry at the bottom/nof the staircase, burst open, and began wailing loudly/nin the corridor below. Harry pulled out his wand and/nstruggled to touch the Marauder's Map, to wipe it/nblank, but it was too far away to reach —/n/nPulling the cloak back over himself Harry/nstraightened up, listening hard with his eyes screwed/nup with fear ... and, almost immediately —/n/n"PEEVES!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was the unmistakable hunting cry of Filch the/ncaretaker. Harry could hear his rapid, shuffling/nfootsteps coming nearer and nearer, his wheezy voice/nraised in fury./n/n"What's this racket? Wake up the whole castle, will/nyou? I'll have you, Peeves, I'll have you, you'll ... and/nwhat is this?"/n/nFilch 's footsteps halted; there was a clink of metal on/nmetal and the wailing stopped — Filch had picked up/nthe egg and closed it. Harry stood very still, one leg/nstill jammed tightly in the magical step, listening. Any/nmoment now, Filch was going to pull aside the/ntapestry, expecting to see Peeves . . . and there would/nbe no Peeves ... but if he came up the stairs, he would/nspot the Marauder's Map ... and Invisibility Cloak or/nnot, the map would show "Harry Potter" standing/nexactly where he was./n/n"Egg?" Filch said quietly at the foot of the stairs. "My/nsweet!" — Mrs. Norris was obviously with him — "This/nis a Triwizard clue! This belongs to a school/nchampion!"/n/nHarry felt sick; his heart was hammering very fast —/n/n"PEEVES!" Filch roared gleefully. "You've been/nstealing!"/n/nHe ripped back the tapestry below, and Harry saw his/nhorrible, pouchy face and bulging, pale eyes staring/nup the dark and (to Filch) deserted staircase./n/n"Hiding, are you?" he said softly. "I'm coming to get/nyou, Peeves. ... You've gone and stolen a Tri wizard/nclue, Peeves. ... Dumbledore'll have you out of here/nfor this, you filthy, pilfering poltergeist. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nFilch started to climb the stairs, his scrawny, dust-/ncolored cat at his heels. Mrs. Norris's lamp-like eyes,/nso very like her master's, were fixed directly upon/nHarry. He had had occasion before now to wonder/nwhether the Invisibility Cloak worked on cats. ... Sick/nwith apprehension, he watched Filch drawing nearer/nand nearer in his old flannel dressing gown — he/ntried desperately to pull his trapped leg free, but it/nmerely sank a few more inches — any second now,/nFilch was going to spot the map or walk right into him/n/n/n/n"Filch? What's going on?"/n/nFilch stopped a few steps below Harry and turned. At/nthe foot of the stairs stood the only person who could/nmake Harry's situation worse: Snape. He was wearing/na long gray nightshirt and he looked livid./n/n"It's Peeves, Professor," Filch whispered malevolently./n"He threw this egg down the stairs."/n/nSnape climbed up the stairs quickly and stopped/nbeside Filch. Harry gritted his teeth, convinced his/nloudly thumping heart would give him away at any/nsecond. .../n/n"Peeves?" said Snape softly, staring at the egg in/nFilch's hands. "But Peeves couldn't get into my office./n/n/n/n"This egg was in your office, Professor?"/n/n"Of course not," Snape snapped. "I heard banging and/nwailing — "/n/n"Yes, Professor, that was the egg — "/n/n" — I was coming to investigate — "/n/n/n/n/n/n" — Peeves threw it, Professor — "/n/n" — and when I passed my office, I saw that the/ntorches were lit and a cupboard door was ajar!/nSomebody has been searching it!"/n/n"But Peeves couldn't — "/n/n"I know he couldn't, Filch!" Snape snapped again. "I/nseal my office with a spell none but a wizard could/nbreak!" Snape looked up the stairs, straight through/nHarry, and then down into the corridor below. "I want/nyou to come and help me search for the intruder,/nFilch."/n/n"I — yes, Professor — but — "/n/nFilch looked yearningly up the stairs, right through/nHarry, who could see that he was very reluctant to/nforgo the chance of cornering Peeves. Go, Harry/npleaded with him silently, go with Snape ... go ... Mrs./nNorris was peering around Filch 's legs. ... Harry had/nthe distinct impression that she could smell him. .../nWhy had he filled that bath with so much perfumed/nfoam?/n/n"The thing is, Professor," said Filch plaintively, "the/nheadmaster will have to listen to me this time. Peeves/nhas been stealing from a student, it might be my/nchance to get him thrown out of the castle once and/nfor all — "/n/n"Filch, I don't give a damn about that wretched/npoltergeist; it's my office that's — "/n/nClunk. Clunk. Clunk./n/nSnape stopped talking very abruptly. He and Filch/nboth looked down at the foot of the stairs. Harry saw/n/n/n/n/n/nMad-Eye Moody limp into sight through the narrow/ngap between their heads. Moody was wearing his old/ntraveling cloak over his nightshirt and leaning on his/nstaff as usual./n/n"Pajama party, is it?" he growled up the stairs./n/n"Professor Snape and I heard noises, Professor," said/nFilch at once. "Peeves the Poltergeist, throwing things/naround as usual — and then Professor Snape/ndiscovered that someone had broken into his off — "/n/n"Shut up!" Snape hissed to Filch./n/nMoody took a step closer to the foot of the stairs./n/nHarry saw Moody's magical eye travel over Snape, and/nthen, unmistakably, onto himself./n/nHarry's heart gave a horrible jolt. Moody could see/nthrough Invisibility Cloaks ... he alone could see the/nfull strangeness of the scene: Snape in his nightshirt,/nFilch clutching the egg, and he, Harry, trapped in the/nstairs behind them. Moody's lopsided gash of a mouth/nopened in surprise. For a few seconds, he and Harry/nstared straight into each other's eyes. Then Moody/nclosed his mouth and turned his blue eye upon Snape/nagain./n/n"Did I hear that correctly, Snape?" he asked slowly./n"Someone broke into your office?"/n/n"It is unimportant," said Snape coldly./n/n"On the contrary," growled Moody, "it is very/nimportant. Who'd want to break into your office?"/n/n"A student, I daresay," said Snape. Harry could see a/nvein flickering horribly on Snape 's greasy temple. "It/nhas happened before. Potion ingredients have gone/n/n/n/n/n/nmissing from my private store cupboard ... students/nattempting illicit mixtures, no doubt. ..."/n/n"Reckon they were after potion ingredients, eh?" said/nMoody. "Not hiding anything else in your office, are/nyou?"/n/nHarry saw the edge of Snape 's sallow face turn a/nnasty brick color, the vein in his temple pulsing more/nrapidly./n/n"You know I'm hiding nothing, Moody," he said in a/nsoft and dangerous voice, "as you've searched my/noffice pretty thoroughly yourself."/n/nMoody's face twisted into a smile. "Auror's privilege,/nSnape. Dumbledore told me to keep an eye — "/n/n"Dumbledore happens to trust me," said Snape/nthrough clenched teeth. "I refuse to believe that he/ngave you orders to search my office!"/n/n" 'Course Dumbledore trusts you," growled Moody./n"He's a trusting man, isn't he? Believes in second/nchances. But me — I say there are spots that don't/ncome off, Snape. Spots that never come off, d'you/nknow what I mean?"/n/nSnape suddenly did something very strange. He/nseized his left forearm convulsively with his right/nhand, as though something on it had hurt him./n/nMoody laughed. "Get back to bed, Snape."/n/n"You don't have the authority to send me anywhere!"/nSnape hissed, letting go of his arm as though angry/nwith himself. "I have as much right to prowl this/nschool after dark as you do!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Prowl away," said Moody, but his voice was full of/nmenace. "I look forward to meeting you in a dark/ncorridor some time. ... You've dropped something, by/nthe way. ..."/n/nWith a stab of horror, Harry saw Moody point at the/nMarauder's Map, still lying on the staircase six steps/nbelow him. As Snape and Filch both turned to look at/nit, Harry threw caution to the winds; he raised his/narms under the cloak and waved furiously at Moody/nto attract his attention, mouthing "It's mine! Mine!"/n/nSnape had reached out for it, a horrible expression of/ndawning comprehension on his face —/n/n"Accio Parchments/n/nThe map flew up into the air, slipped through Snape 's/noutstretched fingers, and soared down the stairs into/nMoody's hand./n/n"My mistake," Moody said calmly. "It's mine —/nmust've dropped it earlier — "/n/nBut Snape 's black eyes were darting from the egg in/nFilch's arms to the map in Moody's hand, and Harry/ncould tell he was putting two and two together, as/nonly Snape could. .../n/n"Potter," he said quietly./n/n"What's that?" said Moody calmly, folding up the map/nand pocketing it./n/n"Potter!" Snape snarled, and he actually turned his/nhead and stared right at the place where Harry was,/nas though he could suddenly see him. "That egg is/nPotter's egg. That piece of parchment belongs to/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nPotter. I have seen it before, I recognize it! Potter is/nhere! Potter, in his Invisibility Cloak!"/n/nSnape stretched out his hands like a blind man and/nbegan to move up the stairs; Harry could have sworn/nhis over-large nostrils were dilating, trying to sniff/nHarry out — trapped, Harry leaned backward, trying/nto avoid Snape's fingertips, but any moment now —/n/n"There's nothing there, Snape!" barked Moody, "but/nI'll be happy to tell the headmaster how quickly your/nmind jumped to Harry Potter!"/n/n"Meaning what?" Snape turned again to look at/nMoody, his hands still outstretched, inches from/nHarry's chest./n/n"Meaning that Dumbledore's very interested to know/nwho's got it in for that boy!" said Moody, limping/nnearer still to the foot of the stairs. "And so am I,/nSnape ... very interested. ..." The torchlight flickered/nacross his mangled face, so that the scars, and the/nchunk missing from his nose, looked deeper and/ndarker than ever./n/nSnape was looking down at Moody, and Harry/ncouldn't see the expression on his face. For a/nmoment, nobody moved or said anything. Then Snape/nslowly lowered his hands./n/n"I merely thought," said Snape, in a voice of forced/ncalm, "that if Potter was wandering around after/nhours again ... it's an unfortunate habit of his ... he/nshould be stopped. For — for his own safety."/n/n"Ah, I see," said Moody softly. "Got Potter's best/ninterests at heart, have you?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was a pause. Snape and Moody were still/nstaring at each other. Mrs. Norris gave a loud meow,/nstill peering around Filch's legs, looking for the source/nof Harry's bubble-bath smell./n/n"I think I will go back to bed," Snape said curtly./n/n"Best idea you've had all night," said Moody. "Now,/nFilch, if you'll just give me that egg — "/n/n"No!" said Filch, clutching the egg as though it were/nhis firstborn son. "Professor Moody, this is evidence of/nPeeves' treachery!"/n/n"It's the property of the champion he stole it from,"/nsaid Moody. "Hand it over, now."/n/nSnape swept downstairs and passed Moody without/nanother word. Filch made a chirruping noise to Mrs./nNorris, who stared blankly at Harry for a few more/nseconds before turning and following her master. Still/nbreathing very fast, Harry heard Snape walking away/ndown the corridor; Filch handed Moody the egg and/ndisappeared from view too, muttering to Mrs. Norris./n"Never mind, my sweet ... we'll see Dumbledore in the/nmorning ... tell him what Peeves was up to. ..."/n/nA door slammed. Harry was left staring down at/nMoody, who placed his staff on the bottommost stair/nand started to climb laboriously toward him, a dull/nclunk on every other step./n/n"Close shave, Potter," he muttered./n/n"Yeah ... I — er ... thanks," said Harry weakly./n/n"What is this thing?" said Moody, drawing the/nMarauders Map out of his pocket and unfolding it./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Map of Hogwarts," said Harry, hoping Moody was/ngoing to pull him out of the staircase soon; his leg/nwas really hurting him./n/n"Merlin's beard," Moody whispered, staring at the/nmap, his magical eye going haywire. "This ... this is/nsome map, Potter!"/n/n"Yeah, it's ... quite useful," Harry said. His eyes were/nstarting to water from the pain. "Er — Professor/nMoody, d'you think you could help me — ?"/n/n"What? Oh! Yes ... yes, of course ..."/n/nMoody took hold of Harry's arms and pulled; Harry's/nleg came free of the trick step, and he climbed onto/nthe one above it. Moody was still gazing at the map./n/n"Potter ..." he said slowly, "you didn't happen, by any/nchance, to see who broke into Snape's office, did you?/nOn this map, I mean?"/n/n"Er ... yeah, I did ..." Harry admitted. "It was Mr./nCrouch."/n/nMoody's magical eye whizzed over the entire surface of/nthe map. He looked suddenly alarmed./n/n"Crouch?" he said. "You're — you're sure, Potter?"/n/n"Positive," said Harry./n/n"Well, he's not here anymore," said Moody, his eye/nstill whizzing over the map. "Crouch ... that's very —/nvery interesting. ..."/n/nHe said nothing for almost a minute, still staring at/nthe map. Harry could tell that this news meant/nsomething to Moody and very much wanted to know/n/n/n/n/n/nwhat it was. He wondered whether he dared ask./nMoody scared him slightly ... yet Moody had just/nhelped him avoid an awful lot of trouble. .../n/n"Er ... Professor Moody ... why d'you reckon Mr./nCrouch wanted to look around S nape's office?"/n/nMoody's magical eye left the map and fixed, quivering,/nupon Harry. It was a penetrating glare, and Harry had/nthe impression that Moody was sizing him up,/nwondering whether to answer or not, or how much to/ntell him./n/n"Put it this way, Potter," Moody muttered finally, "they/nsay old Mad-Eye's obsessed with catching Dark/nwizards ... but I'm nothing — nothing — compared to/nBarty Crouch."/n/nHe continued to stare at the map. Harry was burning/nto know more./n/n"Professor Moody?" he said again. "D'you think .../ncould this have anything to do with . . . maybe Mr./nCrouch thinks there's something going on. ..."/n/n"Like what?" said Moody sharply./n/nHarry wondered how much he dare say. He didn't/nwant Moody to guess that he had a source of/ninformation outside Hogwarts; that might lead to/ntricky questions about Sirius./n/n"I don't know," Harry muttered, "odd stuff's been/nhappening lately, hasn't it? It's been in the Daily/nProphet ... the Dark Mark at the World Cup, and the/nDeath Eaters and everything. ..."/n/nBoth of Moody's mismatched eyes widened./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're a sharp boy, Potter," he said. His magical eye/nroved back to the Marauder's Map. "Crouch could be/nthinking along those lines," he said slowly. "Very/npossible ... there have been some funny rumors flying/naround lately — helped along by Rita Skeeter, of/ncourse. It's making a lot of people nervous, I reckon."/n/nA grim smile twisted his lopsided mouth. "Oh if/nthere's one thing I hate," he muttered, more to himself/nthan to Harry, and his magical eye was fixed on the/nleft-hand corner of the map, "it's a Death Eater who/nwalked free. ..."/n/nHarry stared at him. Could Moody possibly mean/nwhat Harry thought he meant?/n/n"And now I want to ask you a question, Potter," said/nMoody in a more businesslike tone./n/nHarry's heart sank; he had thought this was coming./nMoody was going to ask where he had got this map,/nwhich was a very dubious magical object — and the/nstory of how it had fallen into his hands incriminated/nnot only him, but his own father, Fred and George/nWeasley, and Professor Lupin, their last Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts teacher. Moody waved the map/nin front of Harry, who braced himself —/n/n"Can I borrow this?"/n/n"Oh!" said Harry./n/nHe was very fond of his map, but on the other hand,/nhe was extremely relieved that Moody wasn't asking/nwhere he'd got it, and there was no doubt that he/nowed Moody a favor./n/n"Yeah, okay."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Good boy," growled Moody. "I can make good use of/nthis ... this might be exactly what I've been looking/nfor. ... Right, bed, Potter, come on, now. ..."/n/nThey climbed to the top of the stairs together, Moody/nstill examining the map as though it was a treasure/nthe like of which he had never seen before. They/nwalked in silence to the door of Moody's office, where/nhe stopped and looked up at Harry./n/n"You ever thought of a career as an Auror, Potter?"/n/n"No," said Harry, taken aback./n/n"You want to consider it," said Moody, nodding and/nlooking at Harry thoughtfully. "Yes, indeed ... and/nincidentally ... I'm guessing you weren't just taking/nthat egg for a walk tonight?"/n/n"Er — no," said Harry, grinning. "I've been working/nout the clue."/n/nMoody winked at him, his magical eye going haywire/nagain./n/n"Nothing like a nighttime stroll to give you ideas,/nPotter. ... See you in the morning. ..."/n/nHe went back into his office, staring down at the/nMarauder's Map again, and closed the door behind/nhim./n/nHarry walked slowly back to Gryffindor Tower, lost in/nthought about Snape, and Crouch, and what it all/nmeant. ... Why was Crouch pretending to be ill, if he/ncould manage to get to Hogwarts when he wanted to?/nWhat did he think Snape was concealing in his office?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd Moody thought he, Harry, ought to be an Auror!/nInteresting idea . . . but somehow, Harry thought, as/nhe got quietly into his four-poster ten minutes later,/nthe egg and the cloak now safely back in his trunk, he/nthought he'd like to check how scarred the rest of/nthem were before he chose it as a career./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Second Task
text: /n"You said you'd already worked out that egg clue!"/nsaid Hermione indignantly./n/n"Keep your voice down!" said Harry crossly. "I just/nneed to — sort of fine-tune it, all right?"/n/nHe, Ron, and Hermione were sitting at the very back/nof the Charms class with a table to themselves. They/nwere supposed to be practicing the opposite of the/nSummoning Charm today — the Banishing Charm./nOwing to the potential for nasty accidents when/nobjects kept flying across the room, Professor Flitwick/nhad given each student a stack of cushions on which/nto practice, the theory being that these wouldn't hurt/nanyone if they went off target. It was a good theory,/nbut it wasn't working very well. Neville's aim was so/npoor that he kept accidentally sending much heavier/nthings flying across the room — Professor Flitwick, for/ninstance./n/n"Just forget the egg for a minute, all right?" Harry/nhissed as Professor Flitwick went whizzing resignedly/n/n/n/n/npast them, landing on top of a large cabinet. "I'm/ntrying to tell you about Snape and Moody. ..."/n/nThis class was an ideal cover for a private/nconversation, as everyone was having far too much/nfun to pay them any attention. Harry had been/nrecounting his adventures of the previous night in/nwhispered installments for the last half hour./n/n"Snape said Moody's searched his office as well?" Ron/nwhispered, his eyes alight with interest as he/nBanished a cushion with a sweep of his wand (it/nsoared into the air and knocked Parvati's hat off)./n"What ... d'you reckon Moody's here to keep an eye on/nSnape as well as Karkaroff?"/n/n"Well, I dunno if that's what Dumbledore asked him/nto do, but he's definitely doing it," said Harry, waving/nhis wand without paying much attention, so that his/ncushion did an odd sort of belly flop off the desk./n"Moody said Dumbledore only lets Snape stay here/nbecause he's giving him a second chance or/nsomething. ..."/n/n"What?" said Ron, his eyes widening, his next cushion/nspinning high into the air, ricocheting off the/nchandelier, and dropping heavily onto Flitwick's desk./n"Harry . . . maybe Moody thinks Snape put your name/nin the Goblet of Fire!"/n/n"Oh Ron," said Hermione, shaking her head/nsceptically, "we thought Snape was trying to kill/nHarry before, and it turned out he was saving Harry's/nlife, remember?"/n/nShe Banished a cushion and it flew across the room/nand landed in the box they were all supposed to be/naiming at. Harry looked at Hermione, thinking ... it/nwas true that Snape had saved his life once, but the/n/n/n/n/n/nodd thing was, Snape definitely loathed him, just as/nhe'd loathed Harry's father when they had been at/nschool together. Snape loved taking points from/nHarry, and had certainly never missed an opportunity/nto give him punishments, or even to suggest that he/nshould be suspended from the school./n/n"I don't care what Moody says," Hermione went on./n"Dumbledore's not stupid. He was right to trust/nHagrid and Professor Lupin, even though loads of/npeople wouldn't have given them jobs, so why/nshouldn't he be right about Snape, even if Snape is a/nbit — "/n/n/n/n" — evil," said Ron promptly. "Come on, Hermione,/nwhy are all these Dark wizard catchers searching his/noffice, then?"/n/n"Why has Mr. Crouch been pretending to be ill?" said/nHermione, ignoring Ron. "It's a bit funny, isn't it, that/nhe can't manage to come to the Yule Ball, but he can/nget up here in the middle of the night when he wants/nto?"/n/n"You just don't like Crouch because of that elf,/nWinky," said Ron, sending a cushion soaring into the/nwindow./n/n"You just want to think Snape's up to something,"/nsaid Hermione, sending her cushion zooming neatly/ninto the box./n/n"I just want to know what Snape did with his first/nchance, if he's on his second one," said Harry grimly,/nand his cushion, to his very great surprise, flew/nstraight across the room and landed neatly on top of/nHermione 's./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nObedient to Sirius's wish of hearing about anything/nodd at Hogwarts, Harry sent him a letter by brown/nowl that night, explaining all about Mr. Crouch/nbreaking into Snape's office, and Moody and Snape's/nconversation. Then Harry turned his attention in/nearnest to the most urgent problem facing him: how/nto survive underwater for an hour on the twenty-/nfourth of February./n/nRon quite liked the idea of using the Summoning/nCharm again — Harry had explained about Aqua-/nLungs, and Ron couldn't see why Harry shouldn't/nSummon one from the nearest Muggle town./n/nHermione squashed this plan by pointing out that, in/nthe unlikely event that Harry managed to learn how/nto operate an Aqua-Lung within the set limit of an/nhour, he was sure to be disqualified for breaking the/nInternational Code of Wizarding Secrecy — it was too/nmuch to hope that no Muggles would spot an Aqua-/nLung zooming across the countryside to Hogwarts./n/n"Of course, the ideal solution would be for you to/nTransfigure yourself into a submarine or something,"/nHermione said. "If only we'd done human/nTransfiguration already! But I don't think we start/nthat until sixth year, and it can go badly wrong if you/ndon't know what you're doing. ..."/n/n"Yeah, I don't fancy walking around with a periscope/nsticking out of my head," said Harry. "I s'pose I could/nalways attack someone in front of Moody; he might do/nit for me. ..."/n/n"I don't think he'd let you choose what you wanted to/nbe turned into, though," said Hermione seriously./n/n"No, I think your best chance is some sort of charm."/n/nSo Harry, thinking that he would soon have had/nenough of the library to last him a lifetime, buried/n/n/n/n/n/nhimself once more among the dusty volumes, looking/nfor any spell that might enable a human to survive/nwithout oxygen. However, though he, Ron, and/nHermione searched through their lunchtimes,/nevenings, and whole weekends — though Harry asked/nProfessor McGonagall for a note of permission to use/nthe Restricted Section, and even asked the irritable,/nvulture-like librarian, Madam Pince, for help — they/nfound nothing whatsoever that would enable Harry to/nspend an hour underwater and live to tell the tale./n/nFamiliar flutterings of panic were starting to disturb/nHarry now, and he was finding it difficult to/nconcentrate in class again. The lake, which Harry had/nalways taken for granted as just another feature of/nthe grounds, drew his eyes whenever he was near a/nclassroom window, a great, iron-gray mass of chilly/nwater, whose dark and icy depths were starting to/nseem as distant as the moon./n/nJust as it had before he faced the Horntail, time was/nslipping away as though somebody had bewitched the/nclocks to go extra-fast. There was a week to go before/nFebruary the twenty-fourth (there was still time) .../nthere were five days to go (he was bound to find/nsomething soon) ... three days to go (please let me find/nsomething . . . please) . . ./n/nWith two days left, Harry started to go off food again./nThe only good thing about breakfast on Monday was/nthe return of the brown owl he had sent to Sirius. He/npulled off the parchment, unrolled it, and saw the/nshortest letter Sirius had ever written to him./n/nSend date of next Hogsmeade weekend by return owl./n/nHarry turned the parchment over and looked at the/nback, hoping to see something else, but it was blank./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Weekend after next," whispered Hermione, who had/nread the note over Harry's shoulder. "Here — take my/nquill and send this owl back straight away."/n/nHarry scribbled the dates down on the back of/nSirius's letter, tied it onto the brown owl's leg, and/nwatched it take flight again. What had he expected?/nAdvice on how to survive underwater? He had been so/nintent on telling Sirius all about Snape and Moody he/nhad completely forgotten to mention the egg's clue./n/n"What's he want to know about the next Hogsmeade/nweekend for?" said Ron./n/n"Dunno," said Harry dully. The momentary happiness/nthat had flared inside him at the sight of the owl had/ndied. "Come on ... Care of Magical Creatures."/n/nWhether Hagrid was trying to make up for the Blast-/nEnded Skrewts, or because there were now only two/nskrewts left, or because he was trying to prove he/ncould do anything that Professor Grubbly-Plank/ncould, Harry didn't know, but Hagrid had been/ncontinuing her lessons on unicorns ever since he'd/nreturned to work. It turned out that Hagrid knew/nquite as much about unicorns as he did about/nmonsters, though it was clear that he found their lack/nof poisonous fangs disappointing./n/nToday he had managed to capture two unicorn foals./nUnlike full-grown unicorns, they were pure gold./nParvati and Lavender went into transports of delight/nat the sight of them, and even Pansy Parkinson had/nto work hard to conceal how much she liked them./n/n"Easier ter spot than the adults," Hagrid told the/nclass. "They turn silver when they're abou' two years/nold, an' they grow horns at aroun' four. Don' go pure/nwhite till they're full grown, 'round about seven./n/n/n/n/n/nThey're a bit more trustin' when they're babies ... don'/nmind boys so much. ... C'mon, move in a bit, yeh can/npat 'em if yeh want ... give 'em a few o' these sugar/nlumps. .../n/n"You okay, Harry?" But still no sign./n/nThere was nothing to be done except . . ./n/nHe snatched up the stone, which Krum had dropped,/nbut the mermen now closed in around Ron and the/nlittle girl, shaking their heads at him. Harry pulled/nout his wand./n/n"Get out of the way!"/n/nOnly bubbles flew out of his mouth, but he had the/ndistinct impression that the mermen had understood/nhim, because they suddenly stopped laughing. Their/nyellowish eyes were fixed upon Harry's wand, and/nthey looked scared. There might be a lot more of them/nthan there were of him, but Harry could tell, by the/nlooks on their faces, that they knew no more magic/nthan the giant squid did./n/n"You've got until three!" Harry shouted; a great/nstream of bubbles burst from him, but he held up/nthree fingers to make sure they got the message. "One/n..." (he put down a finger) "two ..." (he put down a/nsecond one) —/n/nThey scattered. Harry darted forward and began to/nhack at the ropes binding the small girl to the statue,/nand at last she was free. He seized the little girl/naround the waist, grabbed the neck of Ron's robes,/nand kicked off from the bottom./n/nIt was very slow work. He could no longer use his/nwebbed hands to propel himself forward; he worked/nhis flippers furiously, but Ron and Fleur's sister were/nlike potato-filled sacks dragging him back down. .../n/nHe fixed his eyes skyward, though he knew he must/nstill be very deep, the water above him was so dark./n/n/n/n/n/nMerpeople were rising with him. He could see them/nswirling around him with ease, watching him struggle/nthrough the water. ... Would they pull him back down/nto the depths when the time was up? Did they/nperhaps eat humans? Harry's legs were seizing up/nwith the effort to keep swimming; his shoulders were/naching horribly with the effort of dragging Ron and/nthe girl. .../n/nHe was drawing breath with extreme difficulty. He/ncould feel pain on the sides of his neck again ... he/nwas becoming very aware of how wet the water was in/nhis mouth . . . yet the darkness was definitely thinning/nnow ... he could see daylight above him. .../n/nHe kicked hard with his flippers and discovered that/nthey were nothing more than feet . . . water was/nflooding through his mouth into his lungs ... he was/nstarting to feel dizzy, but he knew light and air were/nonly ten feet above him ... he had to get there ... he/nhad to . . ./n/nHarry kicked his legs so hard and fast it felt as/nthough his muscles were screaming in protest; his/nvery brain felt waterlogged, he couldn't breathe, he/nneeded oxygen, he had to keep going, he could not/nstop —/n/nAnd then he felt his head break the surface of the/nlake; wonderful, cold, clear air was making his wet/nface sting; he gulped it down, feeling as though he/nhad never breathed properly before, and, panting,/npulled Ron and the little girl up with him. All around/nhim, wild, green-haired heads were emerging out of/nthe water with him, but they were smiling at him./n/nThe crowd in the stands was making a great deal of/nnoise; shouting and screaming, they all seemed to be/non their feet; Harry had the impression they thought/n/n/n/n/n/nthat Ron and the little girl might be dead, but they/nwere wrong ... both of them had opened their eyes;/nthe girl looked scared and confused, but Ron merely/nexpelled a great spout of water, blinked in the bright/nlight, turned to Harry, and said, "Wet, this, isn't it?"/nThen he spotted Fleur's sister. "What did you bring/nher for?"/n/n"Fleur didn't turn up, I couldn't leave her," Harry/npanted./n/n"Harry, you prat," said Ron, "you didn't take that song/nthing seriously, did you? Dumbledore wouldn't have/nlet any of us drown!"/n/n"The song said — "/n/n"It was only to make sure you got back inside the time/nlimit!" said Ron. "I hope you didn't waste time down/nthere acting the hero!"/n/nHarry felt both stupid and annoyed. It was all very/nwell for Ron; he'd been asleep, he hadn't felt how/neerie it was down in the lake, surrounded by spear-/ncarrying merpeople who'd looked more than capable/nof murder./n/n"C'mon," Harry said shortly, "help me with her, I don't/nthink she can swim very well."/n/nThey pulled Fleur's sister through the water, back/ntoward the bank where the judges stood watching,/ntwenty merpeople accompanying them like a guard of/nhonor, singing their horrible screechy songs./n/nHarry could see Madam Pomfrey fussing over/nHermione, Krum, Cedric, and Cho, all of whom were/nwrapped in thick blankets. Dumbledore and Ludo/nBagman stood beaming at Harry and Ron from the/n/n/n/n/n/nbank as they swam nearer, but Percy, who looked/nvery white and somehow much younger than usual,/ncame splashing out to meet them. Meanwhile/nMadame Maxime was trying to restrain Fleur/nDelacour, who was quite hysterical, fighting tooth and/nnail to return to the water./n/n"Gabrielle! Gabrielle\ Is she alive ? Is she 'urt?"/n/n"She's fine!" Harry tried to tell her, but he was so/nexhausted he could hardly talk, let alone shout./n/nPercy seized Ron and was dragging him back to the/nbank ("Gerroff, Percy, I'm all right!"); Dumbledore and/nBagman were pulling Harry upright; Fleur had broken/nfree of Madame Maxime and was hugging her sister./n/n"It was ze grindylows . . . zey attacked me ... oh/nGabrielle, I thought ... I thought ..."/n/n"Come here, you," said Madam Pomfrey. She seized/nHarry and pulled him over to Hermione and the/nothers, wrapped him so tightly in a blanket that he/nfelt as though he were in a straitjacket, and forced a/nmeasure of very hot potion down his throat. Steam/ngushed out of his ears./n/n"Harry, well done!" Hermione cried. "You did it, you/nfound out how all by yourself!"/n/n"Well — " said Harry. He would have told her about/nDobby, but he had just noticed Karkaroff watching/nhim. He was the only judge who had not left the table;/nthe only judge not showing signs of pleasure and/nrelief that Harry, Ron, and Fleur's sister had got back/nsafely. "Yeah, that's right," said Harry, raising his/nvoice slightly so that Karkaroff could hear him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You haff a water beetle in your hair, Herm-own-/nninny," said Krum. Harry had the impression that/nKrum was drawing her attention back onto himself;/nperhaps to remind her that he had just rescued her/nfrom the lake, but Hermione brushed away the beetle/nimpatiently and said, "You're well outside the time/nlimit, though, Harry. . . . Did it take you ages to find/nus?"/n/n"No ... I found you okay. ..."/n/nHarry's feeling of stupidity was growing. Now he was/nout of the water, it seemed perfectly clear that/nDumbledore's safety precautions wouldn't have/npermitted the death of a hostage just because their/nchampion hadn't turned up. Why hadn't he just/ngrabbed Ron and gone? He would have been first/nback. ... Cedric and Krum hadn't wasted time/nworrying about anyone else; they hadn't taken the/nmersong seriously. .../n/nDumbledore was crouching at the water's edge, deep/nin conversation with what seemed to be the chief/nmerperson, a particularly wild and ferocious-looking/nfemale. He was making the same sort of screechy/nnoises that the merpeople made when they were/nabove water; clearly, Dumbledore could speak/nMermish. Finally he straightened up, turned to his/nfellow judges, and said, "A conference before we give/nthe marks, I think."/n/nThe judges went into a huddle. Madam Pomfrey had/ngone to rescue Ron from Percy's clutches; she led him/nover to Harry and the others, gave him a blanket and/nsome Pepperup Potion, then went to fetch Fleur and/nher sister. Fleur had many cuts on her face and arms/nand her robes were torn, but she didn't seem to care,/nnor would she allow Madam Pomfrey to clean them./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Look after Gabrielle," she told her, and then she/nturned to Harry. "You saved 'er," she said/nbreathlessly. "Even though she was not your 'ostage."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, who was now heartily wishing/nhe'd left all three girls tied to the statue./n/nFleur bent down, kissed Harry twice on each cheek/n(he felt his face burn and wouldn't have been/nsurprised if steam was coming out of his ears again),/nthen said to Ron, "And you too — you 'elped — "/n/n"Yeah," said Ron, looking extremely hopeful, "yeah, a/nbit — "/n/n/n/nFleur swooped down on him too and kissed him./nHermione looked simply furious, but just then, Ludo/nBagman's magically magnified voice boomed out/nbeside them, making them all jump, and causing the/ncrowd in the stands to go very quiet./n/n"Ladies and gentlemen, we have reached our decision./nMerchieftainess Murcus has told us exactly what/nhappened at the bottom of the lake, and we have/ntherefore decided to award marks out of fifty for each/nof the champions, as follows. .../n/n"Fleur Delacour, though she demonstrated excellent/nuse of the Bubble-Head Charm, was attacked by/ngrindylows as she approached her goal, and failed to/nretrieve her hostage. We award her twenty-five/npoints."/n/nApplause from the stands./n/n"I deserved zero," said Fleur throatily, shaking her/nmagnificent head./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Cedric Diggory, who also used the Bubble-Head/nCharm, was first to return with his hostage, though/nhe returned one minute outside the time limit of an/nhour." Enormous cheers from the Hufflepuffs in the/ncrowd; Harry saw Cho give Cedric a glowing look. "We/ntherefore award him forty-seven points."/n/nHarry's heart sank. If Cedric had been outside the/ntime limit, he most certainly had been./n/n"Viktor Krum used an incomplete form of/nTransfiguration, which was nevertheless effective, and/nwas second to return with his hostage. We award him/nforty points."/n/nKarkaroff clapped particularly hard, looking very/nsuperior./n/n"Harry Potter used gillyweed to great effect," Bagman/ncontinued. "He returned last, and well outside the/ntime limit of an hour. However, the Merchieftainess/ninforms us that Mr. Potter was first to reach the/nhostages, and that the delay in his return was due to/nhis determination to return all hostages to safety, not/nmerely his own."/n/nRon and Hermione both gave Harry half-exasperated,/nhalf-commiserating looks./n/n"Most of the judges," and here, Bagman gave/nKarkaroff a very nasty look, "feel that this shows/nmoral fiber and merits full marks. However ... Mr./nPotter's score is forty-five points."/n/nHarry's stomach leapt — he was now tying for first/nplace with Cedric. Ron and Hermione, caught by/nsurprise, stared at Harry, then laughed and started/napplauding hard with the rest of the crowd./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"There you go, Harry!" Ron shouted over the noise./n"You weren't being thick after all — you were showing/nmoral fiber!"/n/nFleur was clapping very hard too, but Krum didn't/nlook happy at all. He attempted to engage Hermione/nin conversation again, but she was too busy cheering/nHarry to listen./n/n"The third and final task will take place at dusk on/nthe twenty-fourth of June," continued Bagman. "The/nchampions will be notified of what is coming precisely/none month beforehand. Thank you all for your/nsupport of the champions."/n/nIt was over, Harry thought dazedly, as Madam/nPomfrey began herding the champions and hostages/nback to the castle to get into dry clothes ... it was/nover, he had got through ... he didn't have to worry/nabout anything now until June the twenty-fourth. .../n/nNext time he was in Hogsmeade, Harry decided as he/nwalked back up the stone steps into the castle, he/nwas going to buy Dobby a pair of socks for every day/nof the year./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Padfoot Returns
text: /nOne of the best things about the aftermath of the/nsecond task was that everybody was very keen to hear/ndetails of what had happened down in the lake, which/nmeant that Ron was getting to share Harry's limelight/nfor once. Harry noticed that Ron's version of events/nchanged subtly with every retelling. At first, he gave/nwhat seemed to be the truth; it tallied with/nHermione's story, anyway — Dumbledore had put all/nthe hostages into a bewitched sleep in Professor/nMcGonagall's office, first assuring them that they/nwould be quite safe, and would awake when they were/nback above the water. One week later, however, Ron/nwas telling a thrilling tale of kidnap in which he/nstruggled single-handedly against fifty heavily armed/nmerpeople who had to beat him into submission/nbefore tying him up./n/n"But I had my wand hidden up my sleeve," he assured/nPadma Patil, who seemed to be a lot keener on Ron/nnow that he was getting so much attention and was/nmaking a point of talking to him every time they/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/npassed in the corridors. "I could've taken those mer-/nidiots any time I wanted."/n/n"What were you going to do, snore at them?" said/nHermione waspishly. People had been teasing her so/nmuch about being the thing that Viktor Krum would/nmost miss that she was in a rather tetchy mood./n/nRon's ears went red, and thereafter, he reverted to the/nbewitched sleep version of events./n/nAs they entered March the weather became drier, but/ncruel winds skinned their hands and faces every time/nthey went out onto the grounds. There were delays in/nthe post because the owls kept being blown off/ncourse. The brown owl that Harry had sent to Sirius/nwith the dates of the Hogsmeade weekend turned up/nat breakfast on Friday morning with half its feathers/nsticking up the wrong way; Harry had no sooner torn/noff Sirius's reply than it took flight, clearly afraid it/nwas going to be sent outside again./n/nSirius's letter was almost as short as the previous/none./n/nBe at stile at end of road out of Hogsmeade (past/nDervish and Banges) at two o'clock on Saturday/nafternoon. Bring as much food as you can./n/n"He hasn't come back to Hogsmeade?" said Ron/nincredulously./n/n"It looks like it, doesn't it?" said Hermione./n/n"I can't believe him," said Harry tensely, "if he's/ncaught ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Made it so far, though, hasn't he?" said Ron. "And/nit's not like the place is swarming with dementors/nanymore."/n/nHarry folded up the letter, thinking. If he was honest/nwith himself, he really wanted to see Sirius again. He/ntherefore approached the final lesson of the afternoon/n— double Potions — feeling considerably more/ncheerful than he usually did when descending the/nsteps to the dungeons./n/nMalfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle were standing in a huddle/noutside the classroom door with Pansy Parkinson's/ngang of Slytherin girls. All of them were looking at/nsomething Harry couldn't see and sniggering heartily./nPansy's pug-like face peered excitedly around Goyle 's/nbroad back as Harry, Ron, and Hermione approached./n/n"There they are, there they are!" she giggled, and the/nknot of Slytherins broke apart. Harry saw that Pansy/nhad a magazine in her hands — Witch Weekly. The/nmoving picture on the front showed a curly-haired/nwitch who was smiling toothily and pointing at a large/nsponge cake with her wand./n/n"You might find something to interest you in there,/nGranger!" Pansy said loudly, and she threw the/nmagazine at Hermione, who caught it, looking/nstartled. At that moment, the dungeon door opened,/nand Snape beckoned them all inside./n/nHermione, Harry, and Ron headed for a table at the/nback of the dungeon as usual. Once Snape had/nturned his back on them to write up the ingredients/nof today's potion on the blackboard, Hermione hastily/nrifled through the magazine under the desk. At last,/nin the center pages, Hermione found what they were/nlooking for. Harry and Ron leaned in closer. A color/nphotograph of Harry headed a short piece entitled:/n/n/n/n/nHarry Potter's Secret Heartache/n/n/n/nA boy like no other, perhaps — yet a boy suffering all/nthe usual pangs of adolescence, writes Rita Skeeter./nDeprived of love since the tragic demise of his parents,/nfourteen-year-old Harry Potter thought he had found/nsolace in his steady girlfriend at Hogwarts, Muggle-/nborn Hermione Granger. Little did he know that he/nwould shortly be suffering yet another emotional blow/nin a life already littered with personal loss./n/nMiss Granger, a plain but ambitious girl, seems to/nhave a taste for famous wizards that Harry alone/ncannot satisfy. Since the arrival at Hogwarts of Viktor/nKrum, Bulgarian Seeker and hero of the last World/nQuidditch Cup, Miss Granger has been toying with/nboth boys' affections. Krum, who is openly smitten/nwith the devious Miss Granger, has already invited/nher to visit him in Bulgaria over the summer holidays,/nand insists that he has "never felt this way about any/nother girl."/n/nHowever, it might not be Miss Granger's doubtful/nnatural charms that have captured these unfortunate/nboys' interest./n/n"She's really ugly," says Pansy Parkinson, a pretty/nand vivacious fourth-year student, "but she'd be well/nup to making a Love Potion, she's quite brainy. I/nthink that's how she's doing it."/n/nLove Potions are, of course, banned at Hogwarts, and/nno doubt Albus Dumbledore will want to investigate/nthese claims. In the meantime, Harry Potter's well-/nwishers must hope that, next time, he bestows his/nheart on a worthier candidate./n/n"I told you!" Ron hissed at Hermione as she stared/ndown at the article. "I told you not to annoy Rita/n/n/n/n/n/nSkeeter! She's made you out to be some sort of — of/nscarlet woman!"/n/nHermione stopped looking astonished and snorted/nwith laughter. " Scarlet woman?" she repeated,/nshaking with suppressed giggles as she looked/naround at Ron./n/n"It's what my mum calls them," Ron muttered, his/nears going red./n/n"If that's the best Rita can do, she's losing her touch,"/nsaid Hermione, still giggling, as she threw Witch/nWeekly onto the empty chair beside her. "What a pile/nof old rubbish."/n/nShe looked over at the Slytherins, who were all/nwatching her and Harry closely across the room to see/nif they had been upset by the article. Hermione gave/nthem a sarcastic smile and a wave, and she, Harry,/nand Ron started unpacking the ingredients they/nwould need for their Wit-Sharpening Potion./n/n"There's something funny, though," said Hermione/nten minutes later, holding her pestle suspended over/na bowl of scarab beetles. "How could Rita Skeeter/nhave known ... ?"/n/n"Known what?" said Ron quickly. "You haven't been/nmixing up Love Potions, have you?"/n/n"Don't be stupid," Hermione snapped, starting to/npound up her beetles again. "No, it's just ... how did/nshe know Viktor asked me to visit him over the/nsummer?"/n/nHermione blushed scarlet as she said this and/ndeterminedly avoided Ron's eyes./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What?" said Ron, dropping his pestle with a loud/nclunk./n/n/n/n"He asked me right after he'd pulled me out of the/nlake," Hermione muttered. "After he'd got rid of his/nshark's head. Madam Pomfrey gave us both blankets/nand then he sort of pulled me away from the judges/nso they wouldn't hear, and he said, if I wasn't doing/nanything over the summer, would I like to — "/n/n"And what did you say?" said Ron, who had picked up/nhis pestle and was grinding it on the desk, a good six/ninches from his bowl, because he was looking at/nHermione./n/n"And he did say he'd never felt the same way about/nanyone else," Hermione went on, going so red now/nthat Harry could almost feel the heat coming from/nher, "but how could Rita Skeeter have heard him?/n/nShe wasn't there ... or was she? Maybe she has got an/nInvisibility Cloak; maybe she sneaked onto the/ngrounds to watch the second task. ..."/n/n"And what did you say?" Ron repeated, pounding his/npestle down so hard that it dented the desk./n/n"Well, I was too busy seeing whether you and Harry/nwere okay to — "/n/n"Fascinating though your social life undoubtedly is,/nMiss Granger," said an icy voice right behind them,/nand all three of them jumped, "I must ask you not to/ndiscuss it in my class. Ten points from Gryffindor."/n/nSnape had glided over to their desk while they were/ntalking. The whole class was now looking around at/nthem; Malfoy took the opportunity to flash POTTER/nSTINKS across the dungeon at Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah . . . reading magazines under the table as well?"/nSnape added, snatching up the copy of Witch Weekly./n"A further ten points from Gryffindor ... oh but of/ncourse ..." Snape's black eyes glittered as they fell on/nRita Skeeter's article. "Potter has to keep up with his/npress cuttings. ..."/n/nThe dungeon rang with the Slytherins' laughter, and/nan unpleasant smile curled Snape's thin mouth. To/nHarry's fury, he began to read the article aloud./n/n" 'Harry Potter's Secret Heartache . . . dear, dear,/n/nPotter, what's ailing you now? 'A boy like no other,/nperhaps ...' "/n/nHarry could feel his face burning. Snape was pausing/nat the end of every sentence to allow the Slytherins a/nhearty laugh. The article sounded ten times worse/nwhen read by Snape. Even Hermione was blushing/nscarlet now./n/n" '. . . Harry Potter's well-wishers must hope that, next/ntime, he bestows his heart upon a worthier candidate.'/nHow very touching," sneered Snape, rolling up the/nmagazine to continued gales of laughter from the/nSlytherins. "Well, I think I had better separate the/nthree of you, so you can keep your minds on your/npotions rather than on your tangled love lives./nWeasley, you stay here. Miss Granger, over there,/nbeside Miss Parkinson. Potter — that table in front of/nmy desk. Move. Now."/n/nFurious, Harry threw his ingredients and his bag into/nhis cauldron and dragged it up to the front of the/ndungeon to the empty table. Snape followed, sat down/nat his desk and watched Harry unload his cauldron./nDetermined not to look at Snape, Harry resumed the/nmashing of his scarab beetles, imagining each one to/nhave Snape's face./n/n/n/n/n/n"All this press attention seems to have inflated your/nalready over-large head, Potter," said Snape quietly,/nonce the rest of the class had settled down again./n/nHarry didn't answer. He knew Snape was trying to/nprovoke him; he had done this before. No doubt he/nwas hoping for an excuse to take a round fifty points/nfrom Gryffindor before the end of the class./n/n"You might be laboring under the delusion that the/nentire wizarding world is impressed with you," Snape/nwent on, so quietly that no one else could hear him/n(Harry continued to pound his scarab beetles, even/nthough he had already reduced them to a very fine/npowder), "but I don't care how many times your/npicture appears in the papers. To me, Potter, you are/nnothing but a nasty little boy who considers rules to/nbe beneath him."/n/nHarry tipped the powdered beetles into his cauldron/nand started cutting up his ginger roots. His hands/nwere shaking slightly out of anger, but he kept his/neyes down, as though he couldn't hear what Snape/nwas saying to him./n/n"So I give you fair warning, Potter," Snape continued/nin a softer and more dangerous voice, "pint-sized/ncelebrity or not — if I catch you breaking into my/noffice one more time — "/n/n"I haven't been anywhere near your office!" said Harry/nangrily, forgetting his feigned deafness./n/n"Don't lie to me," Snape hissed, his fathomless black/neyes boring into Harry's. "Boomslang skin. Gillyweed./nBoth come from my private stores, and I know who/nstole them."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry stared back at Snape, determined not to blink/nor to look guilty. In truth, he hadn't stolen either of/nthese things from Snape. Hermione had taken the/nboomslang skin back in their second year — they had/nneeded it for the Polyjuice Potion — and while Snape/nhad suspected Harry at the time, he had never been/nable to prove it. Dobby, of course, had stolen the/ngillyweed./n/n"I don't know what you're talking about," Harry lied/ncoldly./n/n"You were out of bed on the night my office was/nbroken into!" Snape hissed. "I know it, Potter! Now,/nMad-Eye Moody might have joined your fan club, but/nI will not tolerate your behavior! One more nighttime/nstroll into my office, Potter, and you will pay!"/n/n"Right," said Harry coolly, turning back to his ginger/nroots. "I'll bear that in mind if I ever get the urge to go/nin there."/n/nSnape's eyes flashed. He plunged a hand into the/ninside of his black robes. For one wild moment, Harry/nthought Snape was about to pull out his wand and/ncurse him — then he saw that Snape had drawn out a/nsmall crystal bottle of a completely clear potion. Harry/nstared at it./n/n"Do you know what this is, Potter?" Snape said, his/neyes glittering dangerously again./n/n"No," said Harry, with complete honesty this time./n/n"It is Veritaserum — a Truth Potion so powerful that/nthree drops would have you spilling your innermost/nsecrets for this entire class to hear," said Snape/nviciously. "Now, the use of this potion is controlled by/nvery strict Ministry guidelines. But unless you watch/n/n/n/n/nyour step, you might just find that my hand slips" —/nhe shook the crystal bottle slightly — "right over your/nevening pumpkin juice. And then, Potter ... then we'll/nfind out whether you've been in my office or not."/n/nHarry said nothing. He turned back to his ginger/nroots once more, picked up his knife, and started/nslicing them again. He didn't like the sound of that/nTruth Potion at all, nor would he put it past Snape to/nslip him some. He repressed a shudder at the thought/nof what might come spilling out of his mouth if Snape/ndid it . . . quite apart from landing a whole lot of people/nin trouble — Hermione and Dobby for a start — there/nwere all the other things he was concealing . . . like the/nfact that he was in contact with Sirius . . . and — his/ninsides squirmed at the thought — how he felt about/nCho. ... He tipped his ginger roots into the cauldron/ntoo, and wondered whether he ought to take a leaf out/nof Moody's book and start drinking only from a/nprivate hip flask./n/nThere was a knock on the dungeon door./n/n"Enter," said Snape in his usual voice./n/nThe class looked around as the door opened./n/nProfessor Karkaroff came in. Everyone watched him/nas he walked up toward Snape 's desk. He was/ntwisting his finger around his goatee and looking/nagitated./n/n"We need to talk," said Karkaroff abruptly when he/nhad reached Snape. He seemed so determined that/nnobody should hear what he was saying that he was/nbarely opening his lips; it was as though he were a/nrather poor ventriloquist.
