Here he allowed each of/nthem to pat him on the head, before turning and/nsetting off at a run around the outskirts of the village./nHarry, Ron, and Hermione made their way back into/nHogsmeade and up toward Hogwarts./n/n"Wonder if Percy knows all that stuff about Crouch?"/nRon said as they walked up the drive to the castle./n"But maybe he doesn't care ... it'd probably just make/nhim admire Crouch even more. Yeah, Percy loves/nrules. He'd just say Crouch was refusing to break/nthem for his own son."/n/n"Percy would never throw any of his family to the/ndementors," said Hermione severely./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't know," said Ron. "If he thought we were/nstanding in the way of his career . . . Percy's really/nambitious, you know. ..."/n/nThey walked up the stone steps into the entrance/nhall, where the delicious smells of dinner wafted/ntoward them from the Great Hall./n/n"Poor old Snuffles," said Ron, breathing deeply. "He/nmust really like you, Harry. ... Imagine having to live/noff rats."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Madness Of Mr. Crouch
text: /nHarry, Ron, and Hermione went up to the Owlery/nafter breakfast on Sunday to send a letter to Percy,/nasking, as Sirius had suggested, whether he had seen/nMr. Crouch lately. They used Hedwig, because it had/nbeen so long since she'd had a job. When they had/nwatched her fly out of sight through the Owlery/nwindow, they proceeded down to the kitchen to give/nDobby his new socks./n/nThe house-elves gave them a very cheery welcome,/nbowing and curtsying and bustling around making/ntea again. Dobby was ecstatic about his present./n/n"Harry Potter is too good to Dobby!" he squeaked,/nwiping large tears out of his enormous eyes./n/n"You saved my life with that gillyweed, Dobby, you/nreally did," said Harry./n/n"No chance of more of those eclairs, is there?" said/nRon, who was looking around at the beaming and/nbowing house-elves./n/n/n/n/n"You've just had breakfast!" said Hermione irritably,/nbut a great silver platter of eclairs was already/nzooming toward them, supported by four elves./n/n"We should get some stuff to send up to Snuffles,"/nHarry muttered./n/n"Good idea," said Ron. "Give Pig something to do. You/ncouldn't give us a bit of extra food, could you?" he/nsaid to the surrounding elves, and they bowed/ndelightedly and hurried off to get some more./n/n"Dobby, where's Winky?" said Hermione, who was/nlooking around./n/n"Winky is over there by the fire, miss," said Dobby/nquietly, his ears drooping slightly./n/n"Oh dear," said Hermione as she spotted Winky./n/nHarry looked over at the fireplace too. Winky was/nsitting on the same stool as last time, but she had/nallowed herself to become so filthy that she was not/nimmediately distinguishable from the smoke-/nblackened brick behind her. Her clothes were ragged/nand unwashed. She was clutching a bottle of/nbutterbeer and swaying slightly on her stool, staring/ninto the fire. As they watched her, she gave an/nenormous hiccup./n/n"Winky is getting through six bottles a day now,"/nDobby whispered to Harry./n/n"Well, it's not strong, that stuff," Harry said./n/nBut Dobby shook his head. " Tis strong for a house-/nelf, sir," he said./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWinky hiccuped again. The elves who had brought the/neclairs gave her disapproving looks as they returned/nto work./n/n"Winky is pining, Harry Potter," Dobby whispered/nsadly. "Winky wants to go home. Winky still thinks/nMr. Crouch is her master, sir, and nothing Dobby/nsays will persuade her that Professor Dumbledore is/nher master now."/n/n"Hey, Winky," said Harry, struck by a sudden/ninspiration, walking over to her, and bending down,/n"you don't know what Mr. Crouch might be up to, do/nyou? Because he's stopped turning up to judge the/nTriwizard Tournament."/n/nWinky's eyes flickered. Her enormous pupils focused/non Harry. She swayed slightly again and then said, "M/n— Master is stopped — hie — coming?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "we haven't seen him since the/nfirst task. The Daily Prophet's saying he's ill."/n/nWinky swayed some more, staring blurrily at Harry./n/n"Master — hie — ill?"/n/nHer bottom lip began to tremble./n/n"But we're not sure if that's true," said Hermione/nquickly./n/n"Master is needing his — hie — Winky!" whimpered/nthe elf. "Master cannot — hie — manage — hie — all/nby himself. ..."/n/n"Other people manage to do their own housework,/nyou know, Winky," Hermione said severely./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Winky — hie — is not only — hie — doing housework/nfor Mr. Crouch!" Winky squeaked indignantly,/nswaying worse than ever and slopping butterbeer/ndown her already heavily stained blouse. "Master is —/nhie — trusting Winky with — hie — the most/nimportant — hie — the most secret — "/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/nBut Winky shook her head very hard, spilling more/nbutterbeer down herself./n/n"Winky keeps — hie — her master's secrets," she said/nmutinously, swaying very heavily now, frowning up at/nHarry with her eyes crossed. "You is — hie — nosing,/nyou is."/n/n"Winky must not talk like that to Harry Potter!" said/nDobby angrily. "Harry Potter is brave and noble and/nHarry Potter is not nosy!"/n/n"He is nosing — hie — into my master's — hie —/nprivate and secret — hie — Winky is a good house-elf/n— hie — Winky keeps her silence — hie — people/ntrying to — hie — pry and poke — hie — "/n/nWinky's eyelids drooped and suddenly, without/nwarning, she slid off her stool into the hearth, snoring/nloudly. The empty bottle of butterbeer rolled away/nacross the stone-flagged floor. Half a dozen house-/nelves came hurrying forward, looking disgusted. One/nof them picked up the bottle; the others covered/nWinky with a large checked tablecloth and tucked the/nends in neatly, hiding her from view./n/n"We is sorry you had to see that, sirs and miss!"/nsqueaked a nearby elf, shaking his head and looking/nvery ashamed. "We is hoping you will not judge us all/nby Winky, sirs and miss!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"She's unhappy!" said Hermione, exasperated. "Why/ndon't you try and cheer her up instead of covering her/nup?"/n/n"Begging your pardon, miss," said the house-elf,/nbowing deeply again, "but house-elves has no right to/nbe unhappy when there is work to be done and/nmasters to be served."/n/n"Oh for heaven's sake!" Hermione cried. "Listen to me,/nall of you! You've got just as much right as wizards to/nbe unhappy! You've got the right to wages and/nholidays and proper clothes, you don't have to do/neverything you're told — look at Dobby!"/n/n"Miss will please keep Dobby out of this," Dobby/nmumbled, looking scared. The cheery smiles had/nvanished from the faces of the house-elves around the/nkitchen. They were suddenly looking at Hermione as/nthough she were mad and dangerous./n/n"We has your extra food!" squeaked an elf at Harry's/nelbow, and he shoved a large ham, a dozen cakes, and/nsome fruit into Harry's arms. "Good-bye!"/n/nThe house-elves crowded around Harry, Ron, and/nHermione and began shunting them out of the/nkitchen, many little hands pushing in the smalls of/ntheir backs./n/n"Thank you for the socks, Harry Potter!" Dobby called/nmiserably from the hearth, where he was standing/nnext to the lumpy tablecloth that was Winky./n/n"You couldn't keep your mouth shut, could you,/nHermione?" said Ron angrily as the kitchen door/nslammed shut behind them. "They won't want us/nvisiting them now! We could've tried to get more stuff/nout of Winky about Crouch!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh as if you care about that!" scoffed Hermione. "You/nonly like coming down here for the food!"/n/nIt was an irritable sort of day after that. Harry got so/ntired of Ron and Hermione sniping at each other over/ntheir homework in the common room that he took/nSirius's food up to the Owlery that evening on his/nown./n/nPigwidgeon was much too small to carry an entire/nham up to the mountain by himself, so Harry enlisted/nthe help of two school screech owls as well. When/nthey had set off into the dusk, looking extremely odd/ncarrying the large package between them, Harry/nleaned on the windowsill, looking out at the grounds,/nat the dark, rustling treetops of the Forbidden Forest,/nand the rippling sails of the Durmstrang ship. An/neagle owl flew through the coil of smoke rising from/nHagrid's chimney; it soared toward the castle, around/nthe Owlery, and out of sight. Looking down, Harry/nsaw Hagrid digging energetically in front of his cabin./nHarry wondered what he was doing; it looked as/nthough he were making a new vegetable patch. As he/nwatched, Madame Maxime emerged from the/nBeauxbatons carriage and walked over to Hagrid. She/nappeared to be trying to engage him in conversation./nHagrid leaned upon his spade, but did not seem keen/nto prolong their talk, because Madame Maxime/nreturned to the carriage shortly afterward./n/nUnwilling to go back to Gryffindor Tower and listen to/nRon and Hermione snarling at each other, Harry/nwatched Hagrid digging until the darkness swallowed/nhim and the owls around Harry began to awake,/nswooshing past him into the night./n/nBy breakfast the next day Ron's and Hermione's bad/nmoods had burnt out, and to Harry's relief, Ron's/ndark predictions that the house-elves would send/n/n/n/n/n/nsubstandard food up to the Gryffindor table because/nHermione had insulted them proved false; the bacon,/neggs, and kippers were quite as good as usual./n/nWhen the post owls arrived, Hermione looked up/neagerly; she seemed to be expecting something./n/n"Percy won't've had time to answer yet," said Ron. "We/nonly sent Hedwig yesterday."/n/n"No, it's not that," said Hermione. "I've taken out a/nsubscription to the Daily Prophet I'm getting sick of/nfinding everything out from the Slytherins."/n/n"Good thinking!" said Harry, also looking up at the/nowls. "Hey, Hermione, I think you're in luck — "/n/nA gray owl was soaring down toward Hermione./n/n"It hasn't got a newspaper, though," she said, looking/ndisappointed. "It's — "/n/nBut to her bewilderment, the gray owl landed in front/nof her plate, closely followed by four barn owls, a/nbrown owl, and a tawny./n/n"How many subscriptions did you take out?" said/nHarry, seizing Hermione 's goblet before it was/nknocked over by the cluster of owls, all of whom were/njostling close to her, trying to deliver their own letter/nfirst./n/n"What on earth — ?" Hermione said, taking the letter/nfrom the gray owl, opening it, and starting to read./n/n"Oh really!" she sputtered, going rather red./n/n"What's up?" said Ron./n/n"It's — oh how ridiculous — "/n/n/n/n/n/nShe thrust the letter at Harry, who saw that it was/nnot handwritten, but composed from pasted letters/nthat seemed to have been cut out of the Daily Prophet./n/nYou are a WickEd giRL. HarRy PotTER desErves/n/nBeTteR. GO back wherE you cAMe from mUGgle./n/n"They're all like it!" said Hermione desperately,/nopening one letter after another. " 'Harry Potter can do/nmuch better than the likes of you. ...' 'You deserve to/nbe boiled in frog spawn. ...' Ouch!"/n/nShe had opened the last envelope, and yellowish-/ngreen liquid smelling strongly of petrol gushed over/nher hands, which began to erupt in large yellow boils./n/n"Undiluted bubotuber pus!" said Ron, picking up the/nenvelope gingerly and sniffing it./n/n"Ow!" said Hermione, tears starting in her eyes as she/ntried to rub the pus off her hands with a napkin, but/nher fingers were now so thickly covered in painful/nsores that it looked as though she were wearing a pair/nof thick, knobbly gloves./n/n"You'd better get up to the hospital wing," said Harry/nas the owls around Hermione took flight. "We'll tell/nProfessor Sprout where you've gone. ..."/n/n"I warned her!" said Ron as Hermione hurried out of/nthe Great Hall, cradling her hands. "I warned her not/nto annoy Rita Skeeter! Look at this one ..." He read/nout one of the letters Hermione had left behind: " 'I/nread in Witch Weekly about how you are playing/nHarry Potter false and that boy has had enough/nhardship and I will be sending you a curse by next/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/npost as soon as I can find a big enough envelope.'/nBlimey, she'd better watch out for herself."/n/nHermione didn't turn up for Herbology. As Harry and/nRon left the greenhouse for their Care of Magical/nCreatures class, they saw Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle/ndescending the stone steps of the castle. Pansy/nParkinson was whispering and giggling behind them/nwith her gang of Slytherin girls. Catching sight of/nHarry, Pansy called, "Potter, have you split up with/nyour girlfriend? Why was she so upset at breakfast?"/n/nHarry ignored her; he didn't want to give her the/nsatisfaction of knowing how much trouble the Witch/nWeekly article had caused./n/nHagrid, who had told them last lesson that they had/nfinished with unicorns, was waiting for them outside/nhis cabin with a fresh supply of open crates at his/nfeet. Harry's heart sank at the sight of the crates —/nsurely not another skrewt hatching? — but when he/ngot near enough to see inside, he found himself/nlooking at a number of fluffy black creatures with/nlong snouts. Their front paws were curiously flat, like/nspades, and they were blinking up at the class,/nlooking politely puzzled at all the attention./n/n"These're nifflers," said Hagrid, when the class had/ngathered around. "Yeh find 'em down mines mostly./nThey like sparkly stuff. ... There yeh go, look."/n/nOne of the nifflers had suddenly leapt up and/nattempted to bite Pansy Parkinson's watch off her/nwrist. She shrieked and jumped backward./n/n"Useful little treasure detectors," said Hagrid happily./n"Thought we'd have some fun with 'em today. See over/nthere?" He pointed at the large patch of freshly turned/nearth Harry had watched him digging from the Owlery/n/n/n/n/n/nwindow. "I've buried some gold coins. I've got a prize/nfer whoever picks the niffler that digs up most. Jus'/ntake off all yer valuables, an' choose a niffler, an' get/nready ter set 'em loose."/n/nHarry took off his watch, which he was only wearing/nout of habit, as it didn't work anymore, and stuffed it/ninto his pocket. Then he picked up a niffler. It put its/nlong snout in Harry's ear and sniffed enthusiastically./nIt was really quite cuddly./n/n"Hang on," said Hagrid, looking down into the crate,/n"there's a spare niffler here ... who's missin'? Where's/nHermione?"/n/n"She had to go to the hospital wing," said Ron./n/n"Well explain later," Harry muttered; Pansy/nParkinson was listening./n/nIt was easily the most fun they had ever had in Care/nof Magical Creatures. The nifflers dived in and out of/nthe patch of earth as though it were water, each/nscurrying back to the student who had released it and/nspitting gold into their hands. Ron's was particularly/nefficient; it had soon filled his lap with coins./n/n"Can you buy these as pets, Hagrid?" he asked/nexcitedly as his niffler dived back into the soil,/nsplattering his robes./n/n"Yer mum wouldn' be happy, Ron," said Hagrid,/ngrinning. "They wreck houses, nifflers. I reckon/nthey've nearly got the lot, now," he added, pacing/naround the patch of earth while the nifflers continued/nto dive. "I on'y buried a hundred coins. Oh there/ny'are, Hermione!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione was walking toward them across the lawn./nHer hands were very heavily bandaged and she looked/nmiserable. Pansy Parkinson was watching her/nbeadily./n/n"Well, let's check how yeh've done!" said Hagrid./n"Count yer coins! An' there's no point tryin' ter steal/nany, Goyle," he added, his beetle-black eyes/nnarrowed. "It's leprechaun gold. Vanishes after a few/nhours."/n/nGoyle emptied his pockets, looking extremely sulky. It/nturned out that Ron's niffler had been most/nsuccessful, so Hagrid gave him an enormous slab of/nHoneydukes chocolate for a prize. The bell rang/nacross the grounds for lunch; the rest of the class set/noff back to the castle, but Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nstayed behind to help Hagrid put the nifflers back in/ntheir boxes. Harry noticed Madame Maxime watching/nthem out of her carriage window./n/n"What yeh done ter your hands, Hermione?" said/nHagrid, looking concerned./n/nHermione told him about the hate mail she had/nreceived that morning, and the envelope full of/nbubotuber pus./n/n"Aaah, don' worry," said Hagrid gently, looking down/nat her. "I got some o' those letters an' all, after Rita/nSkeeter wrote abou' me mum. 'Yeh're a monster an'/nyeh should be put down.' 'Yer mother killed innocent/npeople an' if you had any decency you'd jump in a/nlake. ' "/n/n"No!" said Hermione, looking shocked./n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid, heaving the niffler crates over by/nhis cabin wall. "They're jus' nutters, Hermione. Don'/n/n/n/n/n/nopen 'em if yeh get any more. Chuck 'em straigh' in/nthe fire."/n/n/n/n"You missed a really good lesson," Harry told/nHermione as they headed back toward the castle./n"They're good, nifflers, aren't they, Ron?"/n/nRon, however, was frowning at the chocolate Hagrid/nhad given him. He looked thoroughly put out about/nsomething./n/n"What's the matter?" said Harry. "Wrong flavor?"/n/n"No," said Ron shortly. "Why didn't you tell me about/nthe gold?"/n/n"What gold?" said Harry./n/n"The gold I gave you at the Quidditch World Cup,"/nsaid Ron. "The leprechaun gold I gave you for my/nOmnioculars. In the Top Box. Why didn't you tell me/nit disappeared?"/n/nHarry had to think for a moment before he realized/nwhat Ron was talking about./n/n"Oh ..." he said, the memory coming back to him at/nlast. "I dunno ... I never noticed it had gone. I was/nmore worried about my wand, wasn't I?"/n/nThey climbed the steps into the entrance hall and/nwent into the Great Hall for lunch./n/n"Must be nice," Ron said abruptly, when they had sat/ndown and started serving themselves roast beef and/nYorkshire puddings. "To have so much money you/ndon't notice if a pocketful of Galleons goes missing."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Listen, I had other stuff on my mind that night!" said/nHarry impatiently. "We all did, remember?"/n/n/n/n"I didn't know leprechaun gold vanishes," Ron/nmuttered. "I thought I was paying you back. You/nshouldn't 've given me that Chudley Cannon hat for/nChristmas."/n/n"Forget it, all right?" said Harry./n/nRon speared a roast potato on the end of his fork,/nglaring at it. Then he said, "I hate being poor."/n/nHarry and Hermione looked at each other. Neither of/nthem really knew what to say./n/n"It's rubbish," said Ron, still glaring down at his/npotato. "I don't blame Fred and George for trying to/nmake some extra money. Wish I could. Wish I had a/nniffler."/n/n"Well, we know what to get you next Christmas," said/nHermione brightly. Then, when Ron continued to look/ngloomy, she said, "Come on, Ron, it could be worse./n/nAt least your fingers aren't full of pus." Hermione was/nhaving a lot of difficulty managing her knife and fork,/nher fingers were so stiff and swollen. "I hate that/nSkeeter woman!" she burst out savagely. "I'll get her/nback for this if it's the last thing I do!"/n/n/n/nHate mail continued to arrive for Hermione over the/nfollowing week, and although she followed Hagrid's/nadvice and stopped opening it, several of her ill-/nwishers sent Howlers, which exploded at the/nGryffindor table and shrieked insults at her for the/nwhole Hall to hear. Even those people who didn't read/nWitch Weekly knew all about the supposed Harry-/n/n/n/n/nKrum-Hermione triangle now. Harry was getting sick/nof telling people that Hermione wasn't his girlfriend./n/n"It'll die down, though," he told Hermione, "if we just/nignore it. ... People got bored with that stuff she wrote/nabout me last time — "/n/n"I want to know how she's listening into private/nconversations when she's supposed to be banned/nfrom the grounds!" said Hermione angrily./n/nHermione hung back in their next Defense Against/nthe Dark Arts lesson to ask Professor Moody/nsomething. The rest of the class was very eager to/nleave; Moody had given them such a rigorous test of/nhex-deflection that many of them were nursing small/ninjuries. Harry had such a bad case of Twitchy Ears,/nhe had to hold his hands clamped over them as he/nwalked away from the class./n/n"Well, Rita's definitely not using an Invisibility Cloak!"/nHermione panted five minutes later, catching up with/nHarry and Ron in the entrance hall and pulling/nHarry's hand away from one of his wiggling ears so/nthat he could hear her. "Moody says he didn't see her/nanywhere near the judges' table at the second task, or/nanywhere near the lake!"/n/n"Hermione, is there any point in telling you to drop/nthis?" said Ron./n/n"No!" said Hermione stubbornly. "I want to know how/nshe heard me talking to Viktor! And how she found/nout about Hagrid's mum!"/n/n"Maybe she had you bugged," said Harry./n/n"Bugged?" said Ron blankly. "What ... put fleas on her/nor something?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry started explaining about hidden microphones/nand recording equipment. Ron was fascinated, but/nHermione interrupted them./n/n"Aren't you two ever going to read Hogwarts, A/nHistory?"/n/n"What's the point?" said Ron. "You know it by heart,/nwe can just ask you."/n/n"All those substitutes for magic Muggles use —/nelectricity, computers, and radar, and all those things/n— they all go haywire around Hogwarts, there's too/nmuch magic in the air. No, Rita's using magic to/neavesdrop, she must be. ... If I could just find out/nwhat it is ... ooh, if it's illegal, I'll have her ..."/n/n"Haven't we got enough to worry about?" Ron asked/nher. "Do we have to start a vendetta against Rita/nSkeeter as well?"/n/n"I'm not asking you to help!" Hermione snapped. "I'll/ndo it on my own!"/n/nShe marched back up the marble staircase without a/nbackward glance. Harry was quite sure she was going/nto the library./n/n"What's the betting she comes back with a box of //nHate Rita Skeeter badges?" said Ron./n/nHermione, however, did not ask Harry and Ron to/nhelp her pursue vengeance against Rita Skeeter, for/nwhich they were both grateful, because their workload/nwas mounting ever higher in the days before the/nEaster holidays. Harry frankly marveled at the fact/nthat Hermione could research magical methods of/neavesdropping as well as everything else they had to/ndo. He was working flat-out just to get through all/n/n/n/n/ntheir homework, though he made a point of sending/nregular food packages up to the cave in the mountain/nfor Sirius; after last summer, Harry had not forgotten/nwhat it felt like to be continually hungry. He enclosed/nnotes to Sirius, telling him that nothing out of the/nordinary had happened, and that they were still/nwaiting for an answer from Percy./n/nHedwig didn't return until the end of the Easter/nholidays. Percy's letter was enclosed in a package of/nEaster eggs that Mrs. Weasley had sent. Both Harry's/nand Ron's were the size of dragon eggs and full of/nhomemade toffee. Hermione's, however, was smaller/nthan a chicken egg. Her face fell when she saw it./n/n"Your mum doesn't read Witch Weekly, by any/nchance, does she, Ron?" she asked quietly./n/n"Yeah," said Ron, whose mouth was full of toffee./n/n"Gets it for the recipes."/n/nHermione looked sadly at her tiny egg./n/n"Don't you want to see what Percy's written?" Harry/nasked her hastily./n/nPercy's letter was short and irritated./n/nAs I am constantly telling the Daily Prophet, Mr./n/nCrouch is taking a well-deserved break. He is sending/nin regular owls with instructions. No, I haven't actually/nseen him, but I think I can be trusted to know my own/nsuperior's handwriting. I have quite enough to do at/nthe moment without trying to quash these ridiculous/nrumors. Please don't bother me again unless it's/nsomething important. Happy Easter./n/nThe start of the summer term would normally have/nmeant that Harry was training hard for the last/n/n/n/n/n/nQuidditch match of the season. This year, however, it/nwas the third and final task in the Triwizard/nTournament for which he needed to prepare, but he/nstill didn't know what he would have to do. Finally, in/nthe last week of May, Professor McGonagall held him/nback in Transfiguration./n/n"You are to go down to the Quidditch field tonight at/nnine o'clock, Potter," she told him. "Mr. Bagman will/nbe there to tell the champions about the third task."/n/nSo at half past eight that night, Harry left Ron and/nHermione in Gryffindor Tower and went downstairs./nAs he crossed the entrance hall, Cedric came up from/nthe Hufflepuff common room./n/n"What d'you reckon it's going to be?" he asked Harry/nas they went together down the stone steps, out into/nthe cloudy night. "Fleur keeps going on about/nunderground tunnels; she reckons we've got to find/ntreasure."/n/n"That wouldn't be too bad," said Harry, thinking that/nhe would simply ask Hagrid for a niffler to do the job/nfor him./n/nThey walked down the dark lawn to the Quidditch/nstadium, turned through a gap in the stands, and/nwalked out onto the field./n/n"What've they done to it?" Cedric said indignantly,/nstopping dead./n/nThe Quidditch field was no longer smooth and flat. It/nlooked as though somebody had been building long,/nlow walls all over it that twisted and crisscrossed in/nevery direction./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They're hedges!" said Harry, bending to examine the/nnearest one./n/n/n/n"Hello there!" called a cheery voice./n/nLudo Bagman was standing in the middle of the field/nwith Krum and Fleur. Harry and Cedric made their/nway toward them, climbing over the hedges. Fleur/nbeamed at Harry as he came nearer. Her attitude/ntoward him had changed completely since he had/nsaved her sister from the lake./n/n"Well, what d'you think?" said Bagman happily as/nHarry and Cedric climbed over the last hedge./n"Growing nicely, aren't they? Give them a month and/nHagrid'll have them twenty feet high. Don't worry," he/nadded, grinning, spotting the less-than-happy/nexpressions on Harry's and Cedric's faces, "you'll have/nyour Quidditch field back to normal once the task is/nover! Now, I imagine you can guess what we're/nmaking here?"/n/nNo one spoke for a moment. Then —/n/n"Maze," grunted Krum./n/n"That's right!" said Bagman. "A maze. The third task's/nreally very straightforward. The Triwizard Cup will be/nplaced in the center of the maze. The first champion/nto touch it will receive full marks."/n/n"We seemply 'ave to get through the maze?" said/nFleur./n/n"There will be obstacles," said Bagman happily,/nbouncing on the balls of his feet. "Hagrid is providing/na number of creatures . . . then there will be spells that/nmust be broken ... all that sort of thing, you know./nNow, the champions who are leading on points will/n/n/n/n/nget a head start into the maze." Bagman grinned at/nHarry and Cedric. "Then Mr. Krum will enter ... then/nMiss Delacour. But you 11 all be in with a fighting/nchance, depending how well you get past the/nobstacles. Should be fun, eh?"/n/nHarry, who knew only too well the kind of creatures/nthat Hagrid was likely to provide for an event like this,/nthought it was unlikely to be any fun at all. However,/nhe nodded politely like the other champions./n/n"Very well ... if you haven't got any questions, we'll go/nback up to the castle, shall we, it's a bit chilly. ..."/n/nBagman hurried alongside Harry as they began to/nwend their way out of the growing maze. Harry had/nthe feeling that Bagman was going to start offering to/nhelp him again, but just then, Krum tapped Harry on/nthe shoulder./n/n"Could I haff a vord?"/n/n"Yeah, all right," said Harry, slightly surprised./n/n"Vill you valk vith me?"/n/n"Okay," said Harry curiously./n/nBagman looked slightly perturbed./n/n"I'll wait for you, Harry, shall I?"/n/n"No, it's okay, Mr. Bagman," said Harry, suppressing/na smile, "I think I can find the castle on my own,/nthanks."/n/nHarry and Krum left the stadium together, but Krum/ndid not set a course for the Durmstrang ship. Instead,/nhe walked toward the forest./n/n/n/n/n/n"What 're we going this way for?" said Harry as they/npassed Hagrid's cabin and the illuminated/nBeauxbatons carriage./n/n"Don't vant to be overheard," said Krum shortly./n/nWhen at last they had reached a quiet stretch of/nground a short way from the Beauxbatons horses'/npaddock, Krum stopped in the shade of the trees and/nturned to face Harry./n/n"I vant to know," he said, glowering, "vot there is/nbetween you and Hermy-own-ninny."/n/nHarry, who from Krum's secretive manner had/nexpected something much more serious than this,/nstared up at Krum in amazement./n/n"Nothing," he said. But Krum glowered at him, and/nHarry, somehow struck anew by how tall Krum was,/nelaborated. "We're friends. She's not my girlfriend and/nshe never has been. It's just that Skeeter woman/nmaking things up."/n/n"Hermy-own-ninny talks about you very often," said/nKrum, looking suspiciously at Harry./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "because we're friends."/n/nHe couldn't quite believe he was having this/nconversation with Viktor Krum, the famous/nInternational Quidditch player. It was as though the/neighteen-year-old Krum thought he, Harry, was an/nequal — a real rival —/n/n"You haff never ... you haff not ..."/n/n"No," said Harry very firmly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nKrum looked slightly happier. He stared at Harry for a/nfew seconds, then said, "You fly very veil. I vos/nvotching at the first task."/n/n"Thanks," said Harry, grinning broadly and suddenly/nfeeling much taller himself. "I saw you at the/nQuidditch World Cup. The Wronski Feint, you really/n/n/n/nBut something moved behind Krum in the trees, and/nHarry, who had some experience of the sort of thing/nthat lurked in the forest, instinctively grabbed Krum's/narm and pulled him around./n/n"Vot is it?"/n/nHarry shook his head, staring at the place where he'd/nseen movement. He slipped his hand inside his robes,/nreaching for his wand./n/nSuddenly a man staggered out from behind a tall oak./nFor a moment, Harry didn't recognize him ... then he/nrealized it was Mr. Crouch./n/nHe looked as though he had been traveling for days./nThe knees of his robes were ripped and bloody, his/nface scratched; he was unshaven and gray with/nexhaustion. His neat hair and mustache were both in/nneed of a wash and a trim. His strange appearance,/nhowever, was nothing to the way he was behaving./nMuttering and gesticulating, Mr. Crouch appeared to/nbe talking to someone that he alone could see. He/nreminded Harry vividly of an old tramp he had seen/nonce when out shopping with the Dursleys. That man/ntoo had been conversing wildly with thin air; Aunt/nPetunia had seized Dudley's hand and pulled him/nacross the road to avoid him; Uncle Vernon had then/ntreated the family to a long rant about what he would/nlike to do with beggars and vagrants./n/n/n/n/n/n"Vosn't he a judge?" said Krum, staring at Mr./n/nCrouch. "Isn't he vith your Ministry?"/n/nHarry nodded, hesitated for a moment, then walked/nslowly toward Mr. Crouch, who did not look at him,/nbut continued to talk to a nearby tree./n/n"... and when you've done that, Weatherby, send an/nowl to Dumbledore confirming the number of/nDurmstrang students who will be attending the/ntournament, Karkaroff has just sent word there will/nbe twelve. ..."/n/n"Mr. Crouch?" said Harry cautiously./n/n"... and then send another owl to Madame Maxime,/nbecause she might want to up the number of/nstudents she's bringing, now Karkaroff's made it a/nround dozen ... do that, Weatherby, will you? Will/nyou? Will..."/n/nMr. Crouch's eyes were bulging. He stood staring at/nthe tree, muttering soundlessly at it. Then he/nstaggered sideways and fell to his knees./n/n"Mr. Crouch?" Harry said loudly. "Are you all right?"/n/nCrouch's eyes were rolling in his head. Harry looked/naround at Krum, who had followed him into the trees,/nand was looking down at Crouch in alarm./n/n"Vot is wrong with him?"/n/n"No idea," Harry muttered. "Listen, you'd better go/nand get someone — "/n/n"Dumbledore!" gasped Mr. Crouch. He reached out/nand seized a handful of Harry's robes, dragging him/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncloser, though his eyes were staring over Harry's/nhead. "I need ... see ... Dumbledore. ..."/n/n"Okay," said Harry, "if you get up, Mr. Crouch, we can/ngo up to the — "/n/n"I've done ... stupid ... thing ..." Mr. Crouch breathed./nHe looked utterly mad. His eyes were rolling and/nbulging, and a trickle of spittle was sliding down his/nchin. Every word he spoke seemed to cost him a/nterrible effort. "Must ... tell ... Dumbledore ..."/n/n"Get up, Mr. Crouch," said Harry loudly and clearly./n"Get up, I'll take you to Dumbledore!"/n/nMr. Crouch's eyes rolled forward onto Harry./n/n"Who ... you?" he whispered./n/n"I'm a student at the school," said Harry, looking/naround at Krum for some help, but Krum was/nhanging back, looking extremely nervous./n/n"You're not ... his?" whispered Crouch, his mouth/nsagging./n/n"No," said Harry, without the faintest idea what/nCrouch was talking about./n/n"Dumbledore 's?"/n/n"That's right," said Harry./n/nCrouch was pulling him closer; Harry tried to loosen/nCrouch's grip on his robes, but it was too powerful./n/n"Warn ... Dumbledore ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'll get Dumbledore if you let go of me," said Harry./n"Just let go, Mr. Crouch, and I'll get him. ..."/n/n"Thank you, Weatherby, and when you have done/nthat, I would like a cup of tea. My wife and son will be/narriving shortly, we are attending a concert tonight/nwith Mr. and Mrs. Fudge."/n/nCrouch was now talking fluently to a tree again, and/nseemed completely unaware that Harry was there,/nwhich surprised Harry so much he didn't notice that/nCrouch had released him./n/n"Yes, my son has recently gained twelve O.W.L.s,/nmost satisfactory, yes, thank you, yes, very proud/nindeed. Now, if you could bring me that memo from/nthe Andorran Minister of Magic, I think I will have/ntime to draft a response. ..."/n/n"You stay here with him!" Harry said to Krum. "I'll get/nDumbledore, I'll be quicker, I know where his office is/n/n/n/n"He is mad," said Krum doubtfully, staring down at/nCrouch, who was still gabbling to the tree, apparently/nconvinced it was Percy./n/n"Just stay with him," said Harry, starting to get up,/nbut his movement seemed to trigger another abrupt/nchange in Mr. Crouch, who seized him hard around/nthe knees and pulled Harry back to the ground./n/n"Don't ... leave ... me!" he whispered, his eyes bulging/nagain. "I ... escaped . . . must warn . . . must tell . . . see/nDumbledore . . . my fault ... all my fault . . . Bertha . . ./ndead ... all my fault . . . my son . . . my fault . . . tell/nDumbledore . . . Harry Potter . . . the Dark Lord . . ./nstronger ... Harry Potter ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'll get Dumbledore if you let me go, Mr. Crouch!"/nsaid Harry. He looked furiously around at Krum./n/n"Help me, will you?"/n/nLooking extremely apprehensive, Krum moved/nforward and squatted down next to Mr. Crouch./n/n"Just keep him here," said Harry, pulling himself free/nof Mr. Crouch. "I'll be back with Dumbledore."/n/n"Hurry, von't you?" Krum called after him as Harry/nsprinted away from the forest and up through the/ndark grounds. They were deserted; Bagman, Cedric,/nand Fleur had disappeared. Harry tore up the stone/nsteps, through the oak front doors, and off up the/nmarble staircase, toward the second floor./n/nFive minutes later he was hurtling toward a stone/ngargoyle standing halfway along an empty corridor./n/n"Sher — sherbet lemon!" he panted at it./n/nThis was the password to the hidden staircase to/nDumbledore 's office — or at least, it had been two/nyears ago. The password had evidently changed,/nhowever, for the stone gargoyle did not spring to life/nand jump aside, but stood frozen, glaring at Harry/nmalevolently./n/n"Move!" Harry shouted at it. "C'mon!"/n/nBut nothing at Hogwarts had ever moved just because/nhe shouted at it; he knew it was no good. He looked/nup and down the dark corridor. Perhaps Dumbledore/nwas in the staffroom? He started running as fast as/nhe could toward the staircase —/n/n"POTTER!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry skidded to a halt and looked around. Snape/nhad just emerged from the hidden staircase behind/nthe stone gargoyle. The wall was sliding shut behind/nhim even as he beckoned Harry back toward him./n/n"What are you doing here, Potter?"/n/n"I need to see Professor Dumbledore!" said Harry,/nrunning back up the corridor and skidding to a/nstandstill in front of Snape instead. "It's Mr. Crouch/n... he's just turned up ... he's in the forest ... he's/nasking — "/n/n"What is this rubbish?" said Snape, his black eyes/nglittering. "What are you talking about?"/n/n"Mr. Crouch!" Harry shouted. "From the Ministry!/n/nHe's ill or something — he's in the forest, he wants to/nsee Dumbledore! Just give me the password up to — "/n/n"The headmaster is busy, Potter," said Snape, his thin/nmouth curling into an unpleasant smile./n/n"I've got to tell Dumbledore!" Harry yelled./n/n"Didn't you hear me, Potter?"/n/nHarry could tell Snape was thoroughly enjoying/nhimself, denying Harry the thing he wanted when he/nwas so panicky./n/n"Look," said Harry angrily, "Crouch isn't right — he's/n— he's out of his mind — he says he wants to warn —/n/n/n/nThe stone wall behind Snape slid open. Dumbledore/nwas standing there, wearing long green robes and a/nmildly curious expression. "Is there a problem?" he/nsaid, looking between Harry and Snape./n/n/n/n/n/n"Professor!" Harry said, sidestepping Snape before/nSnape could speak, "Mr. Crouch is here — he's down/nin the forest, he wants to speak to you!"/n/nHarry expected Dumbledore to ask questions, but to/nhis relief, Dumbledore did nothing of the sort./n/n"Lead the way," he said promptly, and he swept off/nalong the corridor behind Harry, leaving Snape/nstanding next to the gargoyle and looking twice as/nugly./n/n"What did Mr. Crouch say, Harry?" said Dumbledore/nas they walked swiftly down the marble staircase./n/n"Said he wants to warn you ... said he's done/nsomething terrible ... he mentioned his son . . . and/nBertha Jorkins ... and — and Voldemort ... something/nabout Voldemort getting stronger. ..."/n/n"Indeed," said Dumbledore, and he quickened his/npace as they hurried out into the pitch-darkness./n/n"He's not acting normally," Harry said, hurrying along/nbeside Dumbledore. "He doesn't seem to know where/nhe is. He keeps talking like he thinks Percy Weasley's/nthere, and then he changes, and says he needs to see/nyou. ... I left him with Viktor Krum."/n/n"You did?" said Dumbledore sharply, and he began to/ntake longer strides still, so that Harry was running to/nkeep up. "Do you know if anybody else saw Mr./nCrouch?"/n/n"No," said Harry. "Krum and I were talking, Mr./nBagman had just finished telling us about the third/ntask, we stayed behind, and then we saw Mr. Crouch/ncoming out of the forest — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Where are they?" said Dumbledore as the/nBeauxbatons carriage emerged from the darkness./n/n"Over here," said Harry, moving in front of/nDumbledore, leading the way through the trees. He/ncouldn't hear Crouch's voice anymore, but he knew/nwhere he was going; it hadn't been much past the/nBeauxbatons carriage ... somewhere around here. .../n/n"Viktor?" Harry shouted./n/nNo one answered./n/n"They were here," Harry said to Dumbledore. "They/nwere definitely somewhere around here. ..."/n/n"Lumos," Dumbledore said, lighting his wand and/nholding it up./n/nIts narrow beam traveled from black trunk to black/ntrunk, illuminating the ground. And then it fell upon/na pair of feet./n/nHarry and Dumbledore hurried forward. Krum was/nsprawled on the forest floor. He seemed to be/nunconscious. There was no sign at all of Mr. Crouch./nDumbledore bent over Krum and gently lifted one of/nhis eyelids./n/n"Stunned," he said softly. His half-moon glasses/nglittered in the wandlight as he peered around at the/nsurrounding trees./n/n"Should I go and get someone?" said Harry. "Madam/nPomfrey?"/n/n"No," said Dumbledore swiftly. "Stay here."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe raised his wand into the air and pointed it in the/ndirection of Hagrid 's cabin. Harry saw something/nsilvery dart out of it and streak away through the/ntrees like a ghostly bird. Then Dumbledore bent over/nKrum again, pointed his wand at him, and muttered,/n"Renneruate."/n/nKrum opened his eyes. He looked dazed. When he saw/nDumbledore, he tried to sit up, but Dumbledore put a/nhand on his shoulder and made him lie still./n/n"He attacked me!" Krum muttered, putting a hand up/nto his head. "The old madman attacked me! I vos/nlooking around to see vare Potter had gone and he/nattacked from behind!"/n/n"Lie still for a moment," Dumbledore said./n/nThe sound of thunderous footfalls reached them, and/nHagrid came panting into sight with Fang at his/nheels. He was carrying his crossbow./n/n"Professor Dumbledore!" he said, his eyes widening./n"Harry — what the — ?"/n/n"Hagrid, I need you to fetch Professor Karkaroff," said/nDumbledore. "His student has been attacked. When/nyou've done that, kindly alert Professor Moody — "/n/n"No need, Dumbledore," said a wheezy growl. "I'm/nhere."/n/nMoody was limping toward them, leaning on his staff,/nhis wand lit./n/n"Damn leg," he said furiously. "Would've been here/nquicker ... what's happened? Snape said something/nabout Crouch — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Crouch?" said Hagrid blankly./n/n"Karkaroff, please, Hagrid!" said Dumbledore sharply./n/n"Oh yeah ... right y'are, Professor ..." said Hagrid, and/nhe turned and disappeared into the dark trees, Fang/ntrotting after him./n/n"I don't know where Barty Crouch is," Dumbledore/ntold Moody, "but it is essential that we find him."/n/n"I'm onto it," growled Moody, and he pulled out his/nwand and limped off into the forest./n/nNeither Dumbledore nor Harry spoke again until they/nheard the unmistakable sounds of Hagrid and Fang/nreturning. Karkaroff was hurrying along behind them./nHe was wearing his sleek silver furs, and he looked/npale and agitated./n/n"What is this?" he cried when he saw Krum on the/nground and Dumbledore and Harry beside him./n"What's going on?"/n/n"I vos attacked!" said Krum, sitting up now and/nrubbing his head. "Mr. Crouch or votever his name —/n/n/n/n"Crouch attacked you? Crouch attacked you? The/nTriwizard judge?"/n/n"Igor," Dumbledore began, but Karkaroff had drawn/nhimself up, clutching his furs around him, looking/nlivid./n/n"Treachery!" he bellowed, pointing at Dumbledore. "It/nis a plot! You and your Ministry of Magic have lured/nme here under false pretenses, Dumbledore! This is/nnot an equal competition! First you sneak Potter into/n/n/n/n/n/nthe tournament, though he is underage! Now one of/nyour Ministry friends attempts to put my champion/nout of action! I smell double-dealing and corruption in/nthis whole affair, and you, Dumbledore, you, with/nyour talk of closer international wizarding links, of/nrebuilding old ties, of forgetting old differences —/nhere's what I think of you!"/n/nKarkaroff spat onto the ground at Dumbledore's feet./nIn one swift movement, Hagrid seized the front of/nKarkaroff's furs, lifted him into the air, and slammed/nhim against a nearby tree./n/n"Apologize!" Hagrid snarled as Karkaroff gasped for/nbreath, Hagrid's massive fist at his throat, his feet/ndangling in midair./n/n"Hagrid, no\" Dumbledore shouted, his eyes flashing./n/nHagrid removed the hand pinning Karkaroff to the/ntree, and Karkaroff slid all the way down the trunk/nand slumped in a huddle at its roots; a few twigs and/nleaves showered down upon his head./n/n"Kindly escort Harry back up to the castle, Hagrid,"/nsaid Dumbledore sharply./n/nBreathing heavily, Hagrid gave Karkaroff a glowering/nlook./n/n"Maybe I'd better stay here, Headmaster. ..."/n/n"You will take Harry back to school, Hagrid,"/nDumbledore repeated firmly. "Take him right up to/nGryffindor Tower. And Harry — I want you to stay/nthere. Anything you might want to do — any owls you/nmight want to send — they can wait until morning, do/nyou understand me?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Er — yes," said Harry, staring at him. How had/nDumbledore known that, at that very moment, he had/nbeen thinking about sending Pigwidgeon straight to/nSirius, to tell him what had happened?/n/n"Ill leave Fang with yeh, Headmaster," Hagrid said,/nstaring menacingly at Karkaroff, who was still/nsprawled at the foot of the tree, tangled in furs and/ntree roots. "Stay, Fang. C'mon, Harry."/n/nThey marched in silence past the Beauxbatons/ncarriage and up toward the castle./n/n"How dare he," Hagrid growled as they strode past the/nlake. "How dare he accuse Dumbledore. Like/nDumbledore 'd do anythin' like that. Like Dumbledore/nwanted you in the tournament in the firs' place./nWorried! I dunno when I seen Dumbledore more/nworried than he's bin lately. An' you!" Hagrid/nsuddenly said angrily to Harry, who looked up at him,/ntaken aback. "What were yeh doin', wanderin' off with/nruddy Krum? He's from Durmstrang, Harry! Coulda/njinxed yeh right there, couldn' he? Hasn' Moody/ntaught yeh nothin'? 'Magine lettin' him lure yeh off on/nyer own — "/n/n"Krum's all right!" said Harry as they climbed the/nsteps into the entrance hall. "He wasn't trying to jinx/nme, he just wanted to talk about Hermione — "/n/n"I'll be havin' a few words with her, an' all," said/nHagrid grimly, stomping up the stairs. "The less you/nlot 'ave ter do with these foreigners, the happier yeh'll/nbe. Yeh can' trust any of 'em."/n/n"You were getting on all right with Madame Maxime,"/nHarry said, annoyed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Don' you talk ter me abou' her!" said Hagrid, and he/nlooked quite frightening for a moment. "I've got her/nnumber now! Tryin' ter get back in me good books,/ntryin' ter get me ter tell her what's cornin' in the third/ntask. Ha! You can' trust any of 'em!"/n/nHagrid was in such a bad mood, Harry was quite glad/nto say good-bye to him in front of the Fat Lady. He/nclambered through the portrait hole into the common/nroom and hurried straight for the corner where Ron/nand Hermione were sitting, to tell them what had/nhappened./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nz?/n/n/n/n

title: The Dream
text: /n"It comes down to this," said Hermione, rubbing her/nforehead. "Either Mr. Crouch attacked Viktor, or/nsomebody else attacked both of them when Viktor/nwasn't looking."/n/n"It must've been Crouch," said Ron at once. "That's/nwhy he was gone when Harry and Dumbledore got/nthere. He'd done a runner."/n/n"I don't think so," said Harry, shaking his head. "He/nseemed really weak — I don't reckon he was up to/nDisapparating or anything."/n/n"You can't Disapparate on the Hogwarts grounds,/nhaven't I told you enough times?" said Hermione./n/n"Okay ... how's this for a theory," said Ron excitedly./n"Krum attacked Crouch — no, wait for it — and then/nStunned himself!"/n/n"And Mr. Crouch evaporated, did he?" said Hermione/ncoldly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh yeah ..."/n/n/n/nIt was daybreak. Harry, Ron, and Hermione had crept/nout of their dormitories very early and hurried up to/nthe Owlery together to send a note to Sirius. Now they/nwere standing looking out at the misty grounds. All/nthree of them were puffy-eyed and pale because they/nhad been talking late into the night about Mr./n/nCrouch./n/n"Just go through it again, Harry," said Hermione./n"What did Mr. Crouch actually say?"/n/n"I've told you, he wasn't making much sense," said/nHarry. "He said he wanted to warn Dumbledore about/nsomething. He definitely mentioned Bertha Jorkins,/nand he seemed to think she was dead. He kept saying/nstuff was his fault. ... He mentioned his son."/n/n"Well, that was his fault," said Hermione testily./n/n"He was out of his mind," said Harry. "Half the time/nhe seemed to think his wife and son were still alive,/nand he kept talking to Percy about work and giving/nhim instructions."/n/n"And ... remind me what he said about You-Know-/nWho?" said Ron tentatively./n/n"I've told you," Harry repeated dully. "He said he's/ngetting stronger."/n/nThere was a pause. Then Ron said in a falsely/nconfident voice, "But he was out of his mind, like you/nsaid, so half of it was probably just raving. ..."/n/n"He was sanest when he was trying to talk about/nVoldemort," said Harry, and Ron winced at the sound/nof the name. "He was having real trouble stringing/n/n/n/n/n/ntwo words together, but that was when he seemed to/nknow where he was, and know what he wanted to do./nHe just kept saying he had to see Dumbledore."/n/nHarry turned away from the window and stared up/ninto the rafters. The many perches were half-empty;/nevery now and then, another owl would swoop in/nthrough one of the windows, returning from its night's/nhunting with a mouse in its beak./n/n"If Snape hadn't held me up," Harry said bitterly, "we/nmight've got there in time. The headmaster is busy,/nPotter ... what's this rubbish, Potter?' Why couldn't he/nhave just got out of the way?"/n/n"Maybe he didn't want you to get there!" said Ron/nquickly. "Maybe — hang on — how fast d'you reckon/nhe could've gotten down to the forest? D'you reckon/nhe could've beaten you and Dumbledore there?"/n/n"Not unless he can turn himself into a bat or/nsomething," said Harry./n/n"Wouldn't put it past him," Ron muttered./n/n"We need to see Professor Moody," said Hermione./n/n"We need to find out whether he found Mr. Crouch."/n/n"If he had the Marauder's Map on him, it would've/nbeen easy," said Harry./n/n"Unless Crouch was already outside the grounds,"/nsaid Ron, "because it only shows up to the/nboundaries, doesn't — "/n/n"Shh!" said Hermione suddenly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSomebody was climbing the steps up to the Owlery./nHarry could hear two voices arguing, coming closer/nand closer./n/n" — that's blackmail, that is, we could get into a lot of/ntrouble for that — "/n/n" — we've tried being polite; it's time to play dirty, like/nhim. He wouldn't like the Ministry of Magic knowing/nwhat he did — "/n/n"I'm telling you, if you put that in writing, it's/nblackmail!"/n/n"Yeah, and you won't be complaining if we get a nice/nfat payoff, will you?"/n/nThe Owlery door banged open. Fred and George came/nover the threshold, then froze at the sight of Harry,/nRon, and Hermione./n/n"What're you doing here?" Ron and Fred said at the/nsame time./n/n"Sending a letter," said Harry and George in unison./n"What, at this time?" said Hermione and Fred./n/nFred grinned./n/n"Fine — we won't ask you what you're doing, if you/ndon't ask us," he said./n/nHe was holding a sealed envelope in his hands. Harry/nglanced at it, but Fred, whether accidentally or on/npurpose, shifted his hand so that the name on it was/ncovered./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, don't let us hold you up," Fred said, making a/nmock bow and pointing at the door./n/nRon didn't move. "Who're you blackmailing?" he said./n/nThe grin vanished from Fred's face. Harry saw George/nhalf glance at Fred, before smiling at Ron./n/n"Don't be stupid, I was only joking," he said easily./n/n"Didn't sound like that," said Ron./n/nFred and George looked at each other. Then Fred said/nabruptly, "I've told you before, Ron, keep your nose/nout if you like it the shape it is. text: /nThe door of the office opened./n/n"Hello, Potter," said Moody. "Come in, then."/n/nHarry walked inside. "How are/nyou?"/n/n"Fine," Harry lied./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We were just talking about the night when Mr./nCrouch turned up on the grounds," said Fudge. "It/nwas you who found him, was it not?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry. Then, feeling it was pointless to/npretend that he hadn't overheard what they had been/nsaying, he added, "I didn't see Madame Maxime/nanywhere, though, and she'd have a job hiding,/nwouldn't she?"/n/nDumbledore smiled at Harry behind Fudge's back, his/neyes twinkling./n/n"Yes, well," said Fudge, looking embarrassed, "we're/nabout to go for a short walk on the grounds, Harry, if/nyou'll excuse us ... perhaps if you just go back to your/nclass — "/n/n"I wanted to talk to you, Professor," Harry said/nquickly, looking at Dumbledore, who gave him a swift,/nsearching look./n/n"Wait here for me, Harry," he said. "Our examination/nof the grounds will not take long."/n/nThey trooped out in silence past him and closed the/ndoor. After a minute or so, Harry heard the clunks of/nMoody's wooden leg growing fainter in the corridor/nbelow. He looked around./n/n"Hello, Fawkes," he said./n/nFawkes, Professor Dumbledore's phoenix, was/nstanding on his golden perch beside the door. The/nsize of a swan, with magnificent scarlet-and-gold/nplumage, he swished his long tail and blinked/nbenignly at Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry sat down in a chair in front of Dumbledore's/ndesk. For several minutes, he sat and watched the old/nheadmasters and headmistresses snoozing in their/nframes, thinking about what he had just heard, and/nrunning his fingers over his scar. It had stopped/nhurting now./n/nHe felt much calmer, somehow, now that he was in/nDumbledore's office, knowing he would shortly be/ntelling him about the dream. Harry looked up at the/nwalls behind the desk. The patched and ragged/nSorting Hat was standing on a shelf. A glass case next/nto it held a magnificent silver sword with large rubies/nset into the hilt, which Harry recognized as the one he/nhimself had pulled out of the Sorting Hat in his/nsecond year. The sword had once belonged to Godric/nGryffindor, founder of Harry's House. He was gazing/nat it, remembering how it had come to his aid when/nhe had thought all hope was lost, when he noticed a/npatch of silvery light, dancing and shimmering on the/nglass case. He looked around for the source of the/nlight and saw a sliver of silver-white shining brightly/nfrom within a black cabinet behind him, whose door/nhad not been closed properly. Harry hesitated,/nglanced at Fawkes, then got up, walked across the/noffice, and pulled open the cabinet door./n/nA shallow stone basin lay there, with odd carvings/naround the edge: runes and symbols that Harry did/nnot recognize. The silvery light was coming from the/nbasin's contents, which were like nothing Harry had/never seen before. He could not tell whether the/nsubstance was liquid or gas. It was a bright, whitish/nsilver, and it was moving ceaselessly; the surface of it/nbecame ruffled like water beneath wind, and then,/nlike clouds, separated and swirled smoothly. It looked/nlike light made liquid — or like wind made solid —/nHarry couldn't make up his mind./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe wanted to touch it, to find out what it felt like, but/nnearly four years' experience of the magical world told/nhim that sticking his hand into a bowl full of some/nunknown substance was a very stupid thing to do. He/ntherefore pulled his wand out of the inside of his/nrobes, cast a nervous look around the office, looked/nback at the contents of the basin, and prodded them./n/nThe surface of the silvery stuff inside the basin began/nto swirl very fast./n/nHarry bent closer, his head right inside the cabinet./nThe silvery substance had become transparent; it/nlooked like glass. He looked down into it, expecting to/nsee the stone bottom of the basin — and saw instead/nan enormous room below the surface of the/nmysterious substance, a room into which he seemed/nto be looking through a circular window in the ceiling./n/nThe room was dimly lit; he thought it might even be/nunderground, for there were no windows, merely/ntorches in brackets such as the ones that illuminated/nthe walls of Hogwarts. Lowering his face so that his/nnose was a mere inch away from the glassy/nsubstance, Harry saw that rows and rows of witches/nand wizards were seated around every wall on what/nseemed to be benches rising in levels. An empty chair/nstood in the very center of the room. There was/nsomething about the chair that gave Harry an/nominous feeling.
