The/nthoughts inside began to swirl so fast that Harry/ncouldn't make out anything clearly: It was merely a/nblur of color./n/n"Professor?" he said quietly, after a couple of minutes./n/nDumbledore stopped pacing and looked at Harry./n/n"My apologies," he said quietly. He sat back down at/nhis desk./n/n"D'you — d'you know why my scar's hurting me?"/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore looked very intently at Harry for a/nmoment, and then said, "I have a theory, no more/nthan that. ... It is my belief that your scar hurts both/nwhen Lord Voldemort is near you, and when he is/nfeeling a particularly strong surge of hatred."/n/n"But ... why?"/n/n"Because you and he are connected by the curse that/nfailed," said Dumbledore. "That is no ordinary scar."/n/n"So you think . . . that dream . . . did it really happen?"/n/n"It is possible," said Dumbledore. "I would say —/nprobable. Harry — did you see Voldemort?"/n/n"No," said Harry. "Just the back of his chair. But —/nthere wouldn't have been anything to see, would/nthere? I mean, he hasn't got a body, has he? But .../nbut then how could he have held the wand?" Harry/nsaid slowly./n/n"How indeed?" muttered Dumbledore. "How indeed/n/n/n/nNeither Dumbledore nor Harry spoke for a while./nDumbledore was gazing across the room, and, every/nnow and then, placing his wand tip to his temple and/nadding another shining silver thought to the seething/nmass within the Pensieve./n/n"Professor," Harry said at last, "do you think he's/ngetting stronger?"/n/n"Voldemort?" said Dumbledore, looking at Harry over/nthe Pensieve. It was the characteristic, piercing look/nDumbledore had given him on other occasions, and/nalways made Harry feel as though Dumbledore were/nseeing right through him in a way that even Moody's/n/n/n/n/nmagical eye could not. "Once again, Harry, I can only/ngive you my suspicions."/n/nDumbledore sighed again, and he looked older, and/nwearier, than ever./n/n"The years of Voldemort's ascent to power," he said,/n"were marked with disappearances. Bertha Jorkins/nhas vanished without a trace in the place where/nVoldemort was certainly known to be last. Mr. Crouch/ntoo has disappeared ... within these very grounds./n/nAnd there was a third disappearance, one which the/nMinistry, I regret to say, do not consider of any/nimportance, for it concerns a Muggle. His name was/nFrank Bryce, he lived in the village where Voldemort's/nfather grew up, and he has not been seen since last/nAugust. You see, I read the Muggle newspapers,/nunlike most of my Ministry friends."/n/nDumbledore looked very seriously at Harry./n/n"These disappearances seem to me to be linked. The/nMinistry disagrees — as you may have heard, while/nwaiting outside my office."/n/nHarry nodded. Silence fell between them again,/nDumbledore extracting thoughts every now and then./nHarry felt as though he ought to go, but his curiosity/nheld him in his chair./n/n"Professor?" he said again./n/n"Yes, Harry?" said Dumbledore./n/n"Er . . . could I ask you about . . . that court thing I was/nin ... in the Pensieve?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You could," said Dumbledore heavily. "I attended it/nmany times, but some trials come back to me more/nclearly than others ... particularly now. ..."/n/n"You know — you know the trial you found me in?/n/nThe one with Crouch's son? Well ... were they talking/nabout Neville's parents?"/n/nDumbledore gave Harry a very sharp look. "Has/nNeville never told you why he has been brought up by/nhis grandmother?" he said./n/nHarry shook his head, wondering, as he did so, how/nhe could have failed to ask Neville this, in almost four/nyears of knowing him./n/n"Yes, they were talking about Neville's parents," said/nDumbledore. "His father, Frank, was an Auror just/nlike Professor Moody. He and his wife were tortured/nfor information about Voldemort's whereabouts after/nhe lost his powers, as you heard."/n/n"So they're dead?" said Harry quietly./n/n"No," said Dumbledore, his voice full of a bitterness/nHarry had never heard there before. "They are insane./nThey are both in St. Mungo's Hospital for Magical/nMaladies and Injuries. I believe Neville visits them,/nwith his grandmother, during the holidays. They do/nnot recognize him."/n/nHarry sat there, horror-struck. He had never known/n... never, in four years, bothered to find out .../n/n"The Longbottoms were very popular," said/nDumbledore. "The attacks on them came after/nVoldemort's fall from power, just when everyone/nthought they were safe. Those attacks caused a wave/nof fury such as I have never known. The Ministry was/n/n/n/n/nunder great pressure to catch those who had done it./nUnfortunately, the Longbottoms' evidence was —/ngiven their condition — none too reliable."/n/n"Then Mr. Crouch's son might not have been/ninvolved?" said Harry slowly./n/nDumbledore shook his head./n/n"As to that, I have no idea."/n/nHarry sat in silence once more, watching the contents/nof the Pensieve swirl. There were two more questions/nhe was burning to ask . . . but they concerned the guilt/nof living people. .../n/n"Er," he said, "Mr. Bagman ..."/n/n"... has never been accused of any Dark activity/nsince," said Dumbledore calmly./n/n"Right," said Harry hastily, staring at the contents of/nthe Pensieve again, which were swirling more slowly/nnow that Dumbledore had stopped adding thoughts./n"And ... er ..."/n/nBut the Pensieve seemed to be asking his question for/nhim. Snape's face was swimming on the surface/nagain. Dumbledore glanced down into it, and then up/nat Harry./n/n"No more has Professor Snape," he said./n/nHarry looked into Dumbledore 's light blue eyes, and/nthe thing he really wanted to know spilled out of his/nmouth before he could stop it./n/n"What made you think he'd really stopped supporting/nVoldemort, Professor?"/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore held Harry's gaze for a few seconds, and/nthen said, "That, Harry, is a matter between Professor/nSnape and myself."/n/nHarry knew that the interview was over; Dumbledore/ndid not look angry, yet there was a finality in his tone/nthat told Harry it was time to go. He stood up, and so/ndid Dumbledore./n/n"Harry," he said as Harry reached the door. "Please do/nnot speak about Neville's parents to anybody else. He/nhas the right to let people know, when he is ready."/n/n"Yes, Professor," said Harry, turning to go./n/n"And — "/n/nHarry looked back. Dumbledore was standing over/nthe Pensieve, his face lit from beneath by its silvery/nspots of light, looking older than ever. He stared at/nHarry for a moment, and then said, "Good luck with/nthe third task."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Third Task
text: /n"Dumbledore reckons You- Know- Who's getting/nstronger again as well?" Ron whispered./n/nEverything Harry had seen in the Pensieve, nearly/neverything Dumbledore had told and shown him/nafterward, he had now shared with Ron and/nHermione — and, of course, with Sirius, to whom/nHarry had sent an owl the moment he had left/nDumbledore's office. Harry, Ron, and Hermione sat/nup late in the common room once again that night,/ntalking it all over until Harry's mind was reeling, until/nhe understood what Dumbledore had meant about a/nhead becoming so full of thoughts that it would have/nbeen a relief to siphon them off./n/nRon stared into the common room fire. Harry thought/nhe saw Ron shiver slightly, even though the evening/nwas warm./n/n"And he trusts Snape?" Ron said. "He really trusts/nSnape, even though he knows he was a Death Eater?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n/n/nHermione had not spoken for ten minutes. She was/nsitting with her forehead in her hands, staring at her/nknees. Harry thought she too looked as though she/ncould have done with a Pensieve./n/n"Rita Skeeter," she muttered finally./n/n"How can you be worrying about her now?" said Ron,/nin utter disbelief./n/n"I'm not worrying about her," Hermione said to her/nknees. "I'm just thinking ... remember what she said/nto me in the Three Broomsticks? 'I know things about/nLudo Bagman that would make your hair curl.' This/nis what she meant, isn't it? She reported his trial, she/nknew he'd passed information to the Death Eaters./nAnd Winky too, remember ... 'Ludo Bagman's a bad/nwizard.' Mr. Crouch would have been furious he got/noff, he would have talked about it at home."/n/n"Yeah, but Bagman didn't pass information on/npurpose, did he?"/n/nHermione shrugged./n/n"And Fudge reckons Madame Maxime attacked/nCrouch?" Ron said, turning back to Harry./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "but he's only saying that because/nCrouch disappeared near the Beauxbatons carriage."/n/n"We never thought of her, did we?" said Ron slowly./n"Mind you, she's definitely got giant blood, and she/ndoesn't want to admit it — "/n/n"Of course she doesn't," said Hermione sharply,/nlooking up. "Look what happened to Hagrid when Rita/n/n/n/n/n/nfound out about his mother. Look at Fudge, jumping/nto conclusions about her, just because she's part/ngiant. Who needs that sort of prejudice? I'd probably/nsay I had big bones if I knew that's what I'd get for/ntelling the truth."/n/nHermione looked at her watch. "We haven't done any/npracticing!" she said, looking shocked. "We were going/nto do the Impediment Curse! We'll have to really get/ndown to it tomorrow! Come on, Harry, you need to get/nsome sleep."/n/nHarry and Ron went slowly upstairs to their/ndormitory. As Harry pulled on his pajamas, he looked/nover at Neville's bed. True to his word to Dumbledore,/nhe had not told Ron and Hermione about Neville's/nparents. As Harry took off his glasses and climbed/ninto his four-poster, he imagined how it must feel to/nhave parents still living but unable to recognize you./nHe often got sympathy from strangers for being an/norphan, but as he listened to Neville's snores, he/nthought that Neville deserved it more than he did./nLying in the darkness, Harry felt a rush of anger and/nhate toward the people who had tortured Mr. and/nMrs. Longbottom. ... He remembered the jeers of the/ncrowd as Crouch's son and his companions had been/ndragged from the court by the dementors. ... He/nunderstood how they had felt. ... Then he/nremembered the milk-white face of the screaming boy/nand realized with a jolt that he had died a year later./n/n/n/nIt was Voldemort, Harry thought, staring up at the/ncanopy of his bed in the darkness, it all came back to/nVoldemort. ... He was the one who had torn these/nfamilies apart, who had ruined all these lives. .../n/nRon and Hermione were supposed to be studying for/ntheir exams, which would finish on the day of the/n/n/n/n/n/nthird task, but they were putting most of their efforts/ninto helping Harry prepare./n/n"Don't worry about it," Hermione said shortly when/nHarry pointed this out to them and said he didn't/nmind practicing on his own for a while, "at least we'll/nget top marks in Defense Against the Dark Arts. We'd/nnever have found out about all these hexes in class."/n/n"Good training for when we're all Aurors," said Ron/nexcitedly, attempting the Impediment Curse on a/nwasp that had buzzed into the room and making it/nstop dead in midair./n/nThe mood in the castle as they entered June became/nexcited and tense again. Everyone was looking/nforward to the third task, which would take place a/nweek before the end of term. Harry was practicing/nhexes at every available moment. He felt more/nconfident about this task than either of the others./nDifficult and dangerous though it would undoubtedly/nbe, Moody was right: Harry had managed to find his/nway past monstrous creatures and enchanted/nbarriers before now, and this time he had some/nnotice, some chance to prepare himself for what lay/nahead./n/nTired of walking in on Harry, Hermione, and Ron all/nover the school, Professor McGonagall had given them/npermission to use the empty Transfiguration/nclassroom at lunchtimes. Harry had soon mastered/nthe Impediment Curse, a spell to slow down and/nobstruct attackers; the Reductor Curse, which would/nenable him to blast solid objects out of his way; and/nthe Four-Point Spell, a useful discovery of Hermione's/nthat would make his wand point due north, therefore/nenabling him to check whether he was going in the/nright direction within the maze. He was still having/ntrouble with the Shield Charm, though. This was/n/n/n/n/nsupposed to cast a temporary, invisible wall around/nhimself that deflected minor curses; Hermione/nmanaged to shatter it with a well-placed Jelly-Legs/nJinx, and Harry wobbled around the room for ten/nminutes afterward before she had looked up the/ncounter-jinx./n/n"You're still doing really well, though," Hermione said/nencouragingly, looking down her list and crossing off/nthose spells they had already learned. "Some of these/nare bound to come in handy."/n/n"Come and look at this," said Ron, who was standing/nby the window. He was staring down onto the/ngrounds. "What's Malfoy doing?"/n/nHarry and Hermione went to see. Malfoy, Crabbe, and/nGoyle were standing in the shadow of a tree below./nCrabbe and Goyle seemed to be keeping a lookout;/nboth were smirking. Malfoy was holding his hand up/nto his mouth and speaking into it./n/n"He looks like he's using a walkie-talkie," said Harry/ncuriously./n/n"He can't be," said Hermione, "I've told you, those/nsorts of things don't work around Hogwarts. Come on,/nHarry," she added briskly, turning away from the/nwindow and moving back into the middle of the room,/n"let's try that Shield Charm again."/n/n/n/nSirius was sending daily owls now. Like Hermione, he/nseemed to want to concentrate on getting Harry/nthrough the last task before they concerned/nthemselves with anything else. He reminded Harry in/nevery letter that whatever might be going on outside/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe walls of Hogwarts was not Harry's responsibility,/nnor was it within his power to influence it./n/n/n/nIf Voldemort is really getting stronger again, he wrote,/nmy priority is to ensure your safety. He cannot hope to/nlay hands on you while you are under Dumbledore's/nprotection, but all the same, take no risks : Concentrate/non getting through that maze safely, and then we can/nturn our attention to other matters./n/nHarry's nerves mounted as June the twenty-fourth/ndrew closer, but they were not as bad as those he had/nfelt before the first and second tasks. For one thing,/nhe was confident that, this time, he had done/neverything in his power to prepare for the task. For/nanother, this was the final hurdle, and however well/nor badly he did, the tournament would at last be over,/nwhich would be an enormous relief./n/nBreakfast was a very noisy affair at the Gryffindor/ntable on the morning of the third task. The post owls/nappeared, bringing Harry a good-luck card from/nSirius. It was only a piece of parchment, folded over/nand bearing a muddy paw print on its front, but/nHarry appreciated it all the same. A screech owl/narrived for Hermione, carrying her morning copy of/nthe Daily Prophet as usual. She unfolded the paper,/nglanced at the front page, and spat out a mouthful of/npumpkin juice all over it./n/n"What?" said Harry and Ron together, staring at her./n/n"Nothing," said Hermione quickly, trying to shove the/npaper out of sight, but Ron grabbed it. He stared at/nthe headline and said, "No way. Not today. That old/ncow."/n/n"What?" said Harry. "Rita Skeeter again?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Ron, and just like Hermione, he attempted/nto push the paper out of sight./n/n/n/n"It's about me, isn't it?" said Harry./n/n"No," said Ron, in an entirely unconvincing tone./n/nBut before Harry could demand to see the paper,/nDraco Malfoy shouted across the Great Hall from the/nSlytherin table./n/n"Hey, Potter! Potteri How's your head? You feeling all/nright? Sure you're not going to go berserk on us?"/n/nMalfoy was holding a copy of the Daily Prophet too./nSlytherins up and down the table were sniggering,/ntwisting in their seats to see Harry's reaction./n/n"Let me see it," Harry said to Ron. "Give it here."/n/nVery reluctantly, Ron handed over the newspaper./nHarry turned it over and found himself staring at his/nown picture, beneath the banner headline:/n/nHARRY POTTER/n/n"DISTURBED AND DANGEROUS"/n/nThe boy who defeated He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named is/nunstable and possibly dangerous, writes Rita Skeeter,/nSpecial Correspondent. Alarming evidence has/nrecently come to light about Harry Potter's strange/nbehavior, which casts doubts upon his suitability to/ncompete in a demanding competition like the Triwizard/nTournament, or even to attend Hogwarts School./n/nPotter, the Daily Prophet can exclusively reveal,/nregularly collapses at school, and is often heard to/ncomplain of pain in the scar on his forehead (relic of the/n/n/n/n/n/ncurse with which You-Know-Who attempted to kill him)./nOn Monday last, midway through a Divination lesson,/nyour Daily Prophet reporter witnessed Potter storming/nfrom the class, claiming that his scar was hurting too/nbadly to continue studying./n/nIt is possible, say top experts at St. Mungo's Hospital/nfor Magical Maladies and Injuries, that Potter's brain/nwas affected by the attack inflicted upon him by You-/nKnow-Who, and that his insistence that the scar is/nstill hurting is an expression of his deep-seated/nconfusion./n/n"He might even be pretending," said one specialist./n"This could be a plea for attention."/n/nThe Daily Prophet, however, has unearthed worrying/nfacts about Harry Potter thatAlbus Dumbledore,/nHeadmaster of Hogwarts, has carefully concealed from/nthe wizarding public./n/n"Potter can speak Parseltongue, " reveals Draco Malfoy,/na Hogwarts fourth year. "There were a lot of attacks/non students a couple of years ago, and most people/nthought Potter was behind them after they saw him/nlose his temper at a dueling club and set a snake on/nanother boy. It was all hushed up, though. But he's/nmade friends with werewolves and giants too. We/nthink he'd do anything for a bit of power."/n/nParseltongue, the ability to converse with snakes, has/nlong been considered a Dark Art. Indeed, the most/nfamous Parselmouth of our times is none other than/nYou-Know-Who himself. A member of the Dark Force/nDefense League, who wished to remain unnamed,/nstated that he would regard any wizard who could/nspeak Parseltongue "as worthy of investigation./nPersonally, I would be highly suspicious of anybody/nwho could converse with snakes, as serpents are/n/n/n/n/noften used in the worst kinds of Dark Magic, and are/nhistorically associated with evildoers." Similarly,/n"anyone who seeks out the company of such vicious/ncreatures as werewolves and giants would appear to/nhave a fondness for violence."/n/nAlbus Dumbledore should surely consider whether a/nboy such as this should be allowed to compete in the/nTriwizard Tournament. Some fear that Potter might/nresort to the Dark Arts in his desperation to win the/ntournament, the third task of which takes place this/nevening./n/n"Gone off me a bit, hasn't she?" said Harry lightly,/nfolding up the paper./n/nOver at the Slytherin table, Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle/nwere laughing at him, tapping their heads with their/nfingers, pulling grotesquely mad faces, and waggling/ntheir tongues like snakes./n/n"How did she know your scar hurt in Divination?"/n/nRon said. "There's no way she was there, there's no/nway she could've heard — "/n/n"The window was open," said Harry. "I opened it to/nbreathe."/n/n"You were at the top of North Tower!" Hermione said./n"Your voice couldn't have carried all the way down to/nthe grounds!"/n/n"Well, you're the one who's supposed to be/nresearching magical methods of bugging!" said Harry./n"You tell me how she did it!"/n/n"I've been trying!" said Hermione. "But I ... but ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAn odd, dreamy expression suddenly came over/nHermione 's face. She slowly raised a hand and ran/nher fingers through her hair./n/n"Are you all right?" said Ron, frowning at her./n/n"Yes," said Hermione breathlessly. She ran her fingers/nthrough her hair again, and then held her hand up to/nher mouth, as though speaking into an invisible/nwalkie-talkie. Harry and Ron stared at each other./n/n"I've had an idea," Hermione said, gazing into space./n/n"I think I know . . . because then no one would be able/nto see ... even Moody ... and she'd have been able to/nget onto the window ledge ... but she's not allowed .../nshe's definitely not allowed ... I think we've got her!/nJust give me two seconds in the library — just to/nmake sure!"/n/nWith that, Hermione seized her school bag and/ndashed out of the Great Hall./n/n"Oi!" Ron called after her. "We've got our History of/nMagic exam in ten minutes! Blimey," he said, turning/nback to Harry, "she must really hate that Skeeter/nwoman to risk missing the start of an exam. What're/nyou going to do in Binns's class — read again?"/n/nExempt from the end-of-term tests as a Triwizard/nchampion, Harry had been sitting in the back of every/nexam class so far, looking up fresh hexes for the third/ntask./n/n"S'pose so," Harry said to Ron; but just then,/n/nProfessor McGonagall came walking alongside the/nGryffindor table toward him./n/n"Potter, the champions are congregating in the/nchamber off the Hall after breakfast," she said./n/n/n/n/n/n"But the task's not till tonight!" said Harry,/naccidentally spilling scrambled eggs down his front,/nafraid he had mistaken the time./n/n"I'm aware of that, Potter," she said. "The champions'/nfamilies are invited to watch the final task, you know./nThis is simply a chance for you to greet them."/n/nShe moved away. Harry gaped after her./n/n"She doesn't expect the Dursleys to turn up, does/nshe?" he asked Ron blankly./n/n"Dunno," said Ron. "Harry, I'd better hurry, I'm going/nto be late for Binns. See you later."/n/nHarry finished his breakfast in the emptying Great/nHall. He saw Fleur Delacour get up from the/nRavenclaw table and join Cedric as he crossed to the/nside chamber and entered. Krum slouched off to join/nthem shortly afterward. Harry stayed where he was./n/nHe really didn't want to go into the chamber. He had/nno family — no family who would turn up to see him/nrisk his life, anyway. But just as he was getting up,/nthinking that he might as well go up to the library/nand do a spot more hex research, the door of the side/nchamber opened, and Cedric stuck his head out./n/n"Harry, come on, they're waiting for you!"/n/nUtterly perplexed, Harry got up. The Dursleys/ncouldn't possibly be here, could they? He walked/nacross the Hall and opened the door into the/nchamber./n/nCedric and his parents were just inside the door./nViktor Krum was over in a corner, conversing with his/ndark-haired mother and father in rapid Bulgarian. He/nhad inherited his father's hooked nose. On the other/n/n/n/n/n/nside of the room, Fleur was jabbering away in French/nto her mother. Fleur's little sister, Gabrielle, was/nholding her mother's hand. She waved at Harry, who/nwaved back, grinning. Then he saw Mrs. Weasley and/nBill standing in front of the fireplace, beaming at him./n/n"Surprise!" Mrs. Weasley said excitedly as he smiled/nbroadly and walked over to them. "Thought we'd come/nand watch you, Harry!" She bent down and kissed/nhim on the cheek./n/n"You all right?" said Bill, grinning at Harry and/nshaking his hand. "Charlie wanted to come, but he/ncouldn't get time off. He said you were incredible/nagainst the Horntail."/n/nFleur Delacour, Harry noticed, was eyeing Bill with/ngreat interest over her mother's shoulder. Harry could/ntell she had no objection whatsoever to long hair or/nearrings with fangs on them./n/n"This is really nice of you," Harry muttered to Mrs./nWeasley. "I thought for a moment — the Dursleys — "/n/n"Hmm," said Mrs. Weasley, pursing her lips. She had/nalways refrained from criticizing the Dursleys in front/nof Harry, but her eyes flashed every time they were/nmentioned./n/n"It's great being back here," said Bill, looking around/nthe chamber (Violet, the Fat Lady's friend, winked at/nhim from her frame). "Haven't seen this place for five/nyears. Is that picture of the mad knight still around?/nSir Cadogan?"/n/n"Oh yeah," said Harry, who had met Sir Cadogan the/nprevious year./n/n"And the Fat Lady?" said Bill./n/n/n/n/n/n"She was here in my time," said Mrs. Weasley. "She/ngave me such a telling off one night when I got back/nto the dormitory at four in the morning — "/n/n"What were you doing out of your dormitory at four in/nthe morning?" said Bill, surveying his mother with/namazement./n/nMrs. Weasley grinned, her eyes twinkling./n/n"Your father and I had been for a nighttime stroll,"/nshe said. "He got caught by Apollyon Pringle — he/nwas the caretaker in those days — your father's still/ngot the marks."/n/n"Fancy giving us a tour, Harry?" said Bill./n/n"Yeah, okay," said Harry, and they made their way/nback toward the door into the Great Hall. As they/npassed Amos Diggory, he looked around./n/n"There you are, are you?" he said, looking Harry up/nand down. "Bet you're not feeling quite as full of/nyourself now Cedric's caught you up on points, are/nyou?"/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"Ignore him," said Cedric in a low voice to Harry,/nfrowning after his father. "He's been angry ever since/nRita Skeeter's article about the Triwizard Tournament/n— you know, when she made out you were the only/nHogwarts champion."/n/n"Didn't bother to correct her, though, did he?" said/nAmos Diggory, loudly enough for Harry to hear as he/nstarted to walk out of the door with Mrs. Weasley and/nBill. "Still ... you'll show him, Ced. Beaten him once/nbefore, haven't you?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Rita Skeeter goes out of her way to cause trouble,/nAmos!" Mrs. Weasley said angrily. "I would have/nthought you'd know that, working at the Ministry!"/n/nMr. Diggory looked as though he was going to say/nsomething angry, but his wife laid a hand on his arm,/nand he merely shrugged and turned away./n/nHarry had a very enjoyable morning walking over the/nsunny grounds with Bill and Mrs. Weasley, showing/nthem the Beauxbatons carriage and the Durmstrang/nship. Mrs. Weasley was intrigued by the Whomping/nWillow, which had been planted after she had left/nschool, and reminisced at length about the/ngamekeeper before Hagrid, a man called Ogg./n/n"How's Percy?" Harry asked as they walked around/nthe greenhouses./n/n"Not good," said Bill./n/n"He's very upset," said Mrs. Weasley, lowering her/nvoice and glancing around. "The Ministry wants to/nkeep Mr. Crouch's disappearance quiet, but Percy's/nbeen hauled in for questioning about the instructions/nMr. Crouch has been sending in. When they had reached it, they both held a/nhand out over one of the cup's gleaming handles./n/n"On three, right?" said Harry. "One — two — three — "/n/nHe and Cedric both grasped a handle./n/nInstantly, Harry felt a jerk somewhere behind his/nnavel. His feet had left the ground. He could not/nunclench the hand holding the Triwizard Cup; it was/npulling him onward in a howl of wind and swirling/ncolor, Cedric at his side./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Flesh, Blood, And Bone
text: /nHarry felt his feet slam into the ground; his injured/nleg gave way, and he fell forward; his hand let go of/nthe Triwizard Cup at last. He raised his head./n/n"Where are we?" he said./n/nCedric shook his head. He got up, pulled Harry to his/nfeet, and they looked around./n/nThey had left the Hogwarts grounds completely; they/nhad obviously traveled miles — perhaps hundreds of/nmiles — for even the mountains surrounding the/ncastle were gone. They were standing instead in a/ndark and overgrown graveyard; the black outline of a/nsmall church was visible beyond a large yew tree to/ntheir right. A hill rose above them to their left. Harry/ncould just make out the outline of a fine old house on/nthe hillside./n/nCedric looked down at the Triwizard Cup and then up/nat Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Did anyone tell you the cup was a Portkey?" he/nasked./n/n"Nope," said Harry. He was looking around the/ngraveyard. It was completely silent and slightly eerie./n"Is this supposed to be part of the task?"/n/n"I dunno," said Cedric. He sounded slightly nervous./n"Wands out, d'you reckon?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, glad that Cedric had made the/nsuggestion rather than him./n/nThey pulled out their wands. Harry kept looking/naround him. He had, yet again, the strange feeling/nthat they were being watched./n/n"Someone's coming," he said suddenly./n/nSquinting tensely through the darkness, they watched/nthe figure drawing nearer, walking steadily toward/nthem between the graves. Harry couldn't make out a/nface, but from the way it was walking and holding its/narms, he could tell that it was carrying something./nWhoever it was, he was short, and wearing a hooded/ncloak pulled up over his head to obscure his face. And/n— several paces nearer, the gap between them closing/nall the time — Harry saw that the thing in the/nperson's arms looked like a baby ... or was it merely a/nbundle of robes?/n/nHarry lowered his wand slightly and glanced sideways/nat Cedric. Cedric shot him a quizzical look. They both/nturned back to watch the approaching figure./n/nIt stopped beside a towering marble headstone, only/nsix feet from them. For a second, Harry and Cedric/nand the short figure simply looked at one another./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd then, without warning, Harry's scar exploded/nwith pain. It was agony such as he had never felt in/nall his life; his wand slipped from his fingers as he put/nhis hands over his face; his knees buckled; he was on/nthe ground and he could see nothing at all; his head/nwas about to split open./n/nFrom far away, above his head, he heard a high, cold/nvoice say, "Kill the spare."/n/nA swishing noise and a second voice, which screeched/nthe words to the night: "Avada KedavraV'/n/nA blast of green light blazed through Harry's eyelids,/nand he heard something heavy fall to the ground/nbeside him; the pain in his scar reached such a pitch/nthat he retched, and then it diminished; terrified of/nwhat he was about to see, he opened his stinging/neyes./n/nCedric was lying spread-eagled on the ground beside/nhim. He was dead./n/nFor a second that contained an eternity, Harry stared/ninto Cedric's face, at his open gray eyes, blank and/nexpressionless as the windows of a deserted house, at/nhis half-open mouth, which looked slightly surprised./nAnd then, before Harry's mind had accepted what he/nwas seeing, before he could feel anything but numb/ndisbelief, he felt himself being pulled to his feet./n/nThe short man in the cloak had put down his bundle,/nlit his wand, and was dragging Harry toward the/nmarble headstone. Harry saw the name upon it/nflickering in the wandlight before he was forced/naround and slammed against it./n/nTOM RIDDLE/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe cloaked man was now conjuring tight cords/naround Harry, tying him from neck to ankles to the/nheadstone. Harry could hear shallow, fast breathing/nfrom the depths of the hood; he struggled, and the/nman hit him — hit him with a hand that had a finger/nmissing. And Harry realized who was under the hood./nIt was Wormtail./n/n"You!" he gasped./n/nBut Wormtail, who had finished conjuring the ropes,/ndid not reply; he was busy checking the tightness of/nthe cords, his fingers trembling uncontrollably,/nfumbling over the knots. Once sure that Harry was/nbound so tightly to the headstone that he couldn't/nmove an inch, Wormtail drew a length of some black/nmaterial from the inside of his cloak and stuffed it/nroughly into Harry's mouth; then, without a word, he/nturned from Harry and hurried away. Harry couldn't/nmake a sound, nor could he see where Wormtail had/ngone; he couldn't turn his head to see beyond the/nheadstone; he could see only what was right in front/nof him./n/nCedric's body was lying some twenty feet away. Some/nway beyond him, glinting in the starlight, lay the/nTriwizard Cup. Harry's wand was on the ground at/nCedric's feet. The bundle of robes that Harry had/nthought was a baby was close by, at the foot of the/ngrave. It seemed to be stirring fretfully. Harry watched/nit, and his scar seared with pain again . . . and he/nsuddenly knew that he didn't want to see what was in/nthose robes ... he didn't want that bundle opened. .../n/nHe could hear noises at his feet. He looked down and/nsaw a gigantic snake slithering through the grass,/ncircling the headstone where he was tied. Wormtail's/nfast, wheezy breathing was growing louder again. It/nsounded as though he was forcing something heavy/n/n/n/n/nacross the ground. Then he came back within Harry's/nrange of vision, and Harry saw him pushing a stone/ncauldron to the foot of the grave. It was full of what/nseemed to be water — Harry could hear it slopping/naround — and it was larger than any cauldron Harry/nhad ever used; a great stone belly large enough for a/nfull-grown man to sit in./n/nThe thing inside the bundle of robes on the ground/nwas stirring more persistently, as though it was trying/nto free itself. Now Wormtail was busying himself at/nthe bottom of the cauldron with a wand. Suddenly/nthere were crackling flames beneath it. The large/nsnake slithered away into the darkness./n/nThe liquid in the cauldron seemed to heat very fast./nThe surface began not only to bubble, but to send out/nfiery sparks, as though it were on fire. Steam was/nthickening, blurring the outline of Wormtail tending/nthe fire. The movements beneath the robes became/nmore agitated. And Harry heard the high, cold voice/nagain./n/n"Hurry\"/n/nThe whole surface of the water was alight with sparks/nnow. It might have been encrusted with diamonds./n/n"It is ready, Master."/n/n"Now ..." said the cold voice./n/nWormtail pulled open the robes on the ground,/nrevealing what was inside them, and Harry let out a/nyell that was strangled in the wad of material blocking/nhis mouth./n/nIt was as though Wormtail had flipped over a stone/nand revealed something ugly, slimy, and blind — but/n/n/n/n/n/nworse, a hundred times worse. The thing Wormtail/nhad been carrying had the shape of a crouched/nhuman child, except that Harry had never seen/nanything less like a child. It was hairless and scaly -/nlooking, a dark, raw, reddish black. Its arms and legs/nwere thin and feeble, and its face — no child alive/never had a face like that — flat and snakelike, with/ngleaming red eyes./n/nThe thing seemed almost helpless; it raised its thin/narms, put them around Wormtail's neck, and/nWormtail lifted it. As he did so, his hood fell back,/nand Harry saw the look of revulsion on Wormtail's/nweak, pale face in the firelight as he carried the/ncreature to the rim of the cauldron. For one moment,/nHarry saw the evil, flat face illuminated in the sparks/ndancing on the surface of the potion. And then/nWormtail lowered the creature into the cauldron;/nthere was a hiss, and it vanished below the surface;/nHarry heard its frail body hit the bottom with a soft/nthud./n/nLet it drown, Harry thought, his scar burning almost/npast endurance, please ... let it drown. .../n/nWormtail was speaking. His voice shook; he seemed/nfrightened beyond his wits. He raised his wand,/nclosed his eyes, and spoke to the night./n/n"Bone of the father, unknowingly given, you will renew/nyour son!"/n/nThe surface of the grave at Harry's feet cracked./nHorrified, Harry watched as a fine trickle of dust rose/ninto the air at Wormtail's command and fell softly into/nthe cauldron. The diamond surface of the water broke/nand hissed; it sent sparks in all directions and turned/na vivid, poisonous-looking blue./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd now Wormtail was whimpering. He pulled a long,/nthin, shining silver dagger from inside his cloak. His/nvoice broke into petrified sobs./n/n" Flesh — of the servant — w-willingly given — you will/n— revive — your master."/n/nHe stretched his right hand out in front of him — the/nhand with the missing finger. He gripped the dagger/nvery tightly in his left hand and swung it upward./n/nHarry realized what Wormtail was about to do a/nsecond before it happened — he closed his eyes as/ntightly as he could, but he could not block the scream/nthat pierced the night, that went through Harry as/nthough he had been stabbed with the dagger too. He/nheard something fall to the ground, heard Wormtail's/nanguished panting, then a sickening splash, as/nsomething was dropped into the cauldron. Harry/ncouldn't stand to look ... but the potion had turned a/nburning red; the light of it shone through Harry's/nclosed eyelids.../n/nWormtail was gasping and moaning with agony. Not/nuntil Harry felt Wormtail's anguished breath on his/nface did he realize that Wormtail was right in front of/nhim./n/n"B-blood of the enemy ... forcibly taken ... you will .../nresurrect your foe."/n/nHarry could do nothing to prevent it, he was tied too/ntightly. ... Squinting down, struggling hopelessly at/nthe ropes binding him, he saw the shining silver/ndagger shaking in Wormtail's remaining hand. He felt/nits point penetrate the crook of his right arm and/nblood seeping down the sleeve of his torn robes./nWormtail, still panting with pain, fumbled in his/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/npocket for a glass vial and held it to Harry's cut, so/nthat a dribble of blood fell into it./n/nHe staggered back to the cauldron with Harry's blood./nHe poured it inside. The liquid within turned,/ninstantly, a blinding white. Wormtail, his job done,/ndropped to his knees beside the cauldron, then/nslumped sideways and lay on the ground, cradling the/nbleeding stump of his arm, gasping and sobbing./n/nThe cauldron was simmering, sending its diamond/nsparks in all directions, so blindingly bright that it/nturned all else to velvety blackness. Nothing/nhappened. .../n/nLet it have drowned, Harry thought, let it have gone/nwrong. .../n/nAnd then, suddenly, the sparks emanating from the/ncauldron were extinguished. A surge of white steam/nbillowed thickly from the cauldron instead,/nobliterating everything in front of Harry, so that he/ncouldn't see Wormtail or Cedric or anything but vapor/nhanging in the air. . . It's gone wrong, he thought . . . it's/ndrowned . . . please . . . please let it be dead. . ./n/nBut then, through the mist in front of him, he saw,/nwith an icy surge of terror, the dark outline of a man,/ntall and skeletally thin, rising slowly from inside the/ncauldron./n/n"Robe me," said the high, cold voice from behind the/nsteam, and Wormtail, sobbing and moaning, still/ncradling his mutilated arm, scrambled to pick up the/nblack robes from the ground, got to his feet, reached/nup, and pulled them one-handed over his master's/nhead./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe thin man stepped out of the cauldron, staring at/nHarry . . . and Harry stared back into the face that had/nhaunted his nightmares for three years. Whiter than a/nskull, with wide, livid scarlet eyes and a nose that/nwas flat as a snake's with slits for nostrils .../n/nLord Voldemort had risen again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Death Eaters
text: /nVoldemort looked away from Harry and began/nexamining his own body. His hands were like large,/npale spiders; his long white fingers caressed his own/nchest, his arms, his face; the red eyes, whose pupils/nwere slits, like a cat's, gleamed still more brightly/nthrough the darkness. He held up his hands and/nflexed the fingers, his expression rapt and exultant./n/nHe took not the slightest notice of Wormtail, who lay/ntwitching and bleeding on the ground, nor of the great/nsnake, which had slithered back into sight and was/ncircling Harry again, hissing. Voldemort slipped one of/nthose unnaturally long-fingered hands into a deep/npocket and drew out a wand. He caressed it gently/ntoo; and then he raised it, and pointed it at Wormtail,/nwho was lifted off the ground and thrown against the/nheadstone where Harry was tied; he fell to the foot of/nit and lay there, crumpled up and crying. Voldemort/nturned his scarlet eyes upon Harry, laughing a high,/ncold, mirthless laugh./n/nWormtail's robes were shining with blood now; he had/nwrapped the stump of his arm in them./n/n/n/n/n"My Lord ..." he choked, "my Lord ... you promised .../nyou did promise ..."/n/n"Hold out your arm," said Voldemort lazily./n/n"Oh Master ... thank you, Master ..."/n/nHe extended the bleeding stump, but Voldemort/nlaughed again./n/n"The other arm, Wormtail."/n/n"Master, please ... please ..."/n/nVoldemort bent down and pulled out Wormtail's left/narm; he forced the sleeve of Wormtail's robes up past/nhis elbow, and Harry saw something upon the skin/nthere, something like a vivid red tattoo — a skull with/na snake protruding from its mouth — the image that/nhad appeared in the sky at the Quidditch World Cup:/nthe Dark Mark. Voldemort examined it carefully,/nignoring Wormtail's uncontrollable weeping./n/n"It is back," he said softly, "they will all have noticed it/n... and now, we shall see ... now we shall know ..."/n/nHe pressed his long white forefinger to the brand on/nWormtail's arm./n/nThe scar on Harry's forehead seared with a sharp/npain again, and Wormtail let out a fresh howl;/nVoldemort removed his fingers from Wormtail's mark,/nand Harry saw that it had turned jet black./n/nA look of cruel satisfaction on his face, Voldemort/nstraightened up, threw back his head, and stared/naround at the dark graveyard./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"How many will be brave enough to return when they/nfeel it?" he whispered, his gleaming red eyes fixed/nupon the stars. "And how many will be foolish enough/nto stay away?"/n/nHe began to pace up and down before Harry and/nWormtail, eyes sweeping the graveyard all the while./nAfter a minute or so, he looked down at Harry again,/na cruel smile twisting his snakelike face./n/n"You stand, Harry Potter, upon the remains of my late/nfather," he hissed softly. "A Muggle and a fool ... very/nlike your dear mother. But they both had their uses,/ndid they not? Your mother died to defend you as a/nchild . . . and I killed my father, and see how useful he/nhas proved himself, in death. ..."/n/nVoldemort laughed again. Up and down he paced,/nlooking all around him as he walked, and the snake/ncontinued to circle in the grass./n/n"You see that house upon the hillside, Potter? My/nfather lived there. My mother, a witch who lived here/nin this village, fell in love with him. But he abandoned/nher when she told him what she was. ... He didn't like/nmagic, my father . . ./n/n"He left her and returned to his Muggle parents before/nI was even born, Potter, and she died giving birth to/nme, leaving me to be raised in a Muggle orphanage .../nbut I vowed to find him ... I revenged myself upon/nhim, that fool who gave me his name . . . Tom Riddle./n/n/n/nStill he paced, his red eyes darting from grave to/ngrave./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Listen to me, reliving family history ..." he said/nquietly, "why, I am growing quite sentimental. ... But/nlook, Harry! My true family returns. ..."/n/nThe air was suddenly full of the swishing of cloaks./nBetween graves, behind the yew tree, in every/nshadowy space, wizards were Apparating. All of them/nwere hooded and masked. And one by one they moved/nforward . . . slowly, cautiously, as though they could/nhardly believe their eyes. Voldemort stood in silence,/nwaiting for them. Then one of the Death Eaters fell to/nhis knees, crawled toward Voldemort, and kissed the/nhem of his black robes./n/n"Master ... Master ..." he murmured./n/nThe Death Eaters behind him did the same; each of/nthem approaching Voldemort on his knees and/nkissing his robes, before backing away and standing/nup, forming a silent circle, which enclosed Tom/nRiddle's grave, Harry, Voldemort, and the sobbing and/ntwitching heap that was Wormtail. Yet they left gaps/nin the circle, as though waiting for more people./nVoldemort, however, did not seem to expect more. He/nlooked around at the hooded faces, and though there/nwas no wind, a rustling seemed to run around the/ncircle, as though it had shivered./n/n"Welcome, Death Eaters," said Voldemort quietly./n"Thirteen years ... thirteen years since last we met./n/nYet you answer my call as though it were yesterday./n/n... We are still united under the Dark Mark, then! Or/nare we?"/n/nHe put back his terrible face and sniffed, his slit-like/nnostrils widening./n/n"I smell guilt," he said. "There is a stench of guilt/nupon the air."/n/n/n/n/n/nA second shiver ran around the circle, as though each/nmember of it longed, but did not dare, to step back/nfrom him./n/n"I see you all, whole and healthy, with your powers/nintact — such prompt appearances! — and I ask/nmyself . . . why did this band of wizards never come to/nthe aid of their master, to whom they swore eternal/nloyalty?"/n/nNo one spoke. No one moved except Wormtail, who/nwas upon the ground, still sobbing over his bleeding/narm./n/n"And I answer myself," whispered Voldemort, "they/nmust have believed me broken, they thought I was/ngone. They slipped back among my enemies, and they/npleaded innocence, and ignorance, and bewitchment./n/n/n/n"And then I ask myself, but how could they have/nbelieved I would not rise again? They, who knew the/nsteps I took, long ago, to guard myself against mortal/ndeath? They, who had seen proofs of the immensity of/nmy power in the times when I was mightier than any/nwizard living?/n/n"And I answer myself, perhaps they believed a still/ngreater power could exist, one that could vanquish/neven Lord Voldemort ... perhaps they now pay/nallegiance to another . . . perhaps that champion of/ncommoners, of Mudbloods and Muggles, Albus/nDumbledore?"/n/nAt the mention of Dumbledore's name, the members/nof the circle stirred, and some muttered and shook/ntheir heads. Voldemort ignored them./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It is a disappointment to me ... I confess myself/ndisappointed. ..."/n/nOne of the men suddenly flung himself forward,/nbreaking the circle. Trembling from head to foot, he/ncollapsed at Voldemort's feet./n/n"Master!" he shrieked, "Master, forgive me! Forgive us/nall!"/n/nVoldemort began to laugh. He raised his wand./n/n" Cruciol "/n/nThe Death Eater on the ground writhed and shrieked;/nHarry was sure the sound must carry to the houses/naround. ... Let the police come, he thought desperately/n... anyone ... anything .../n/n/n/nVoldemort raised his wand. The tortured Death Eater/nlay flat upon the ground, gasping./n/n"Get up, Avery," said Voldemort softly. "Stand up. You/nask for forgiveness? I do not forgive. I do not forget./nThirteen long years ... I want thirteen years'/nrepayment before I forgive you. Wormtail here has/npaid some of his debt already, have you not,/nWormtail?"/n/nHe looked down at Wormtail, who continued to sob./n/n"You returned to me, not out of loyalty, but out of fear/nof your old friends. You deserve this pain, Wormtail./nYou know that, don't you?"/n/n"Yes, Master," moaned Wormtail, "please, Master .../nplease ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yet you helped return me to my body," said/nVoldemort coolly, watching Wormtail sob on the/nground. "Worthless and traitorous as you are, you/nhelped me . . . and Lord Voldemort rewards his/nhelpers. ..."/n/nVoldemort raised his wand again and whirled it/nthrough the air. A streak of what looked like molten/nsilver hung shining in the wand's wake. Momentarily/nshapeless, it writhed and then formed itself into a/ngleaming replica of a human hand, bright as/nmoonlight, which soared downward and fixed itself/nupon Wormtail's bleeding wrist./n/nWormtail's sobbing stopped abruptly. His breathing/nharsh and ragged, he raised his head and stared in/ndisbelief at the silver hand, now attached seamlessly/nto his arm, as though he were wearing a dazzling/nglove. He flexed the shining fingers, then, trembling,/npicked up a small twig on the ground and crushed it/ninto powder./n/n"My Lord," he whispered. "Master ... it is beautiful .../nthank you ... thank you. ..."/n/nHe scrambled forward on his knees and kissed the/nhem of Voldemort's robes./n/n"May your loyalty never waver again, Wormtail," said/nVoldemort./n/n"No, my Lord ... never, my Lord ..."/n/nWormtail stood up and took his place in the circle,/nstaring at his powerful new hand, his face still/nshining with tears. Voldemort now approached the/nman on Wormtail's right./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Lucius, my slippery friend," he whispered, halting/nbefore him. "I am told that you have not renounced/nthe old ways, though to the world you present a/nrespectable face. You are still ready to take the lead in/na spot of Muggle-torture, I believe? Yet you never tried/nto find me, Lucius. ... Your exploits at the Quidditch/nWorld Cup were fun, I daresay ... but might not your/nenergies have been better directed toward finding and/naiding your master?"/n/n"My Lord, I was constantly on the alert," came Lucius/nMalfoy's voice swiftly from beneath the hood. "Had/nthere been any sign from you, any whisper of your/nwhereabouts, I would have been at your side/nimmediately, nothing could have prevented me — "/n/n"And yet you ran from my Mark, when a faithful/nDeath Eater sent it into the sky last summer?" said/nVoldemort lazily, and Mr. Malfoy stopped talking/nabruptly. "Yes, I know all about that, Lucius. ... You/nhave disappointed me. ... I expect more faithful/nservice in the future."/n/n"Of course, my Lord, of course. ... You are merciful,/nthank you. ..."/n/nVoldemort moved on, and stopped, staring at the/nspace — large enough for two people — that/nseparated Malfoy and the next man./n/n"The Lestranges should stand here," said Voldemort/nquietly. "But they are entombed in Azkaban. They/nwere faithful. They went to Azkaban rather than/nrenounce me. ... When Azkaban is broken open, the/nLestranges will be honored beyond their dreams. The/ndementors will join us ... they are our natural allies .../nwe will recall the banished giants ... I shall have all/nmy devoted servants returned to me, and an army of/ncreatures whom all fear. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe walked on. Some of the Death Eaters he passed in/nsilence, but he paused before others and spoke to/nthem./n/n"Macnair . . . destroying dangerous beasts for the/nMinistry of Magic now, Wormtail tells me? You shall/nhave better victims than that soon, Macnair. Lord/nVoldemort will provide. ..."/n/n"Thank you, Master ... thank you," murmured/nMacnair./n/n"And here" — Voldemort moved on to the two largest/nhooded figures — "we have Crabbe . . . you will do/nbetter this time, will you not, Crabbe? And you,/nGoyle?"/n/nThey bowed clumsily, muttering dully./n/n"Yes, Master ..."/n/n"We will, Master. ..."/n/n"The same goes for you, Nott," said Voldemort quietly/nas he walked past a stooped figure in Mr. Goyle 's/nshadow./n/n"My Lord, I prostrate myself before you, I am your/nmost faithful — "/n/n"That will do," said Voldemort./n/nHe had reached the largest gap of all, and he stood/nsurveying it with his blank, red eyes, as though he/ncould see people standing there./n/n"And here we have six missing Death Eaters . . . three/ndead in my service. One, too cowardly to return ... he/nwill pay. One, who I believe has left me forever ... he/n/n/n/n/n/nwill be killed, of course ... and one, who remains my/nmost faithful servant, and who has already reentered/nmy service."/n/nThe Death Eaters stirred, and Harry saw their eyes/ndart sideways at one another through their masks./n/n"He is at Hogwarts, that faithful servant, and it was/nthrough his efforts that our young friend arrived here/ntonight. .../n/n"Yes," said Voldemort, a grin curling his lipless mouth/nas the eyes of the circle flashed in Harry's direction./n"Harry Potter has kindly joined us for my rebirthing/nparty. One might go so far as to call him my guest of/nhonor."/n/nThere was a silence. Then the Death Eater to the right/nof Wormtail stepped forward, and Lucius Malfoy's/nvoice spoke from under the mask./n/n"Master, we crave to know . . . we beg you to tell us . . ./nhow you have achieved this . . . this miracle . . . how/nyou managed to return to us. ..."/n/n"Ah, what a story it is, Lucius," said Voldemort. "And/nit begins — and ends — with my young friend here."/n/nHe walked lazily over to stand next to Harry, so that/nthe eyes of the whole circle were upon the two of/nthem. The snake continued to circle./n/n"You know, of course, that they have called this boy/nmy downfall?" Voldemort said softly, his red eyes/nupon Harry, whose scar began to burn so fiercely that/nhe almost screamed in agony. "You all know that on/nthe night I lost my powers and my body, I tried to kill/nhim. His mother died in the attempt to save him —/nand unwittingly provided him with a protection I/n/n/n/n/nadmit I had not foreseen. ... I could not touch the/nboy."/n/nVoldemort raised one of his long white fingers and put/nit very close to Harry's cheek./n/n"His mother left upon him the traces of her sacrifice./n/n. . . This is old magic, I should have remembered it, I/nwas foolish to overlook it . . . but no matter. I can/ntouch him now."/n/nHarry felt the cold tip of the long white finger touch/nhim, and thought his head would burst with the pain./nVoldemort laughed softly in his ear, then took the/nfinger away and continued addressing the Death/nEaters./n/n"I miscalculated, my friends, I admit it. My curse was/ndeflected by the woman's foolish sacrifice, and it/nrebounded upon myself. Aaah . . . pain beyond pain,/nmy friends; nothing could have prepared me for it. I/nwas ripped from my body, I was less than spirit, less/nthan the meanest ghost ... but still, I was alive. What/nI was, even I do not know ... I, who have gone further/nthan anybody along the path that leads to/nimmortality. You know my goal — to conquer death./nAnd now, I was tested, and it appeared that one or/nmore of my experiments had worked . . . for I had not/nbeen killed, though the curse should have done it./nNevertheless, I was as powerless as the weakest/ncreature alive, and without the means to help myself/n. . . for I had no body, and every spell that might have/nhelped me required the use of a wand. .../n/n"I remember only forcing myself, sleeplessly,/nendlessly, second by second, to exist. ... I settled in a/nfaraway place, in a forest, and I waited. ... Surely, one/nof my faithful Death Eaters would try and find me . . ./none of them would come and perform the magic I/n/n/n/n/ncould not, to restore me to a body . . . but I waited in/nvain. ..."/n/nThe shiver ran once more around the circle of/nlistening Death Eaters. Voldemort let the silence/nspiral horribly before continuing./n/n"Only one power remained to me. I could possess the/nbodies of others. But I dared not go where other/nhumans were plentiful, for I knew that the Aurors/nwere still abroad and searching for me. I sometimes/ninhabited animals — snakes, of course, being my/npreference — but I was little better off inside them/nthan as pure spirit, for their bodies were ill adapted to/nperform magic ... and my possession of them/nshortened their lives; none of them lasted long. .../n/n"Then . . . four years ago . . . the means for my return/nseemed assured. A wizard — young, foolish, and/ngullible — wandered across my path in the forest I/nhad made my home. Oh, he seemed the very chance I/nhad been dreaming of . . . for he was a teacher at/nDumbledore's school ... he was easy to bend to my/nwill ... he brought me back to this country, and after/na while, I took possession of his body, to supervise/nhim closely as he carried out my orders. But my plan/nfailed. I did not manage to steal the Sorcerer's Stone. I/nwas not to be assured immortal life. I was thwarted .../nthwarted, once again, by Harry Potter. ..."/n/nSilence once more; nothing was stirring, not even the/nleaves on the yew tree. The Death Eaters were quite/nmotionless, the glittering eyes in their masks fixed/nupon Voldemort, and upon Harry./n/n"The servant died when I left his body, and I was left/nas weak as ever I had been," Voldemort continued. "I/nreturned to my hiding place far away, and I will not/npretend to you that I didn't then fear that I might/n/n/n/n/n/nnever regain my powers. ... Yes, that was perhaps my/ndarkest hour ... I could not hope that I would be sent/nanother wizard to possess ... and I had given up hope,/nnow, that any of my Death Eaters cared what had/nbecome of me. ..."/n/nOne or two of the masked wizards in the circle moved/nuncomfortably, but Voldemort took no notice./n/n"And then, not even a year ago, when I had almost/nabandoned hope, it happened at last ... a servant/nreturned to me. Wormtail here, who had faked his/nown death to escape justice, was driven out of hiding/nby those he had once counted friends, and decided to/nreturn to his master. He sought me in the country/nwhere it had long been rumored I was hiding . . ./nhelped, of course, by the rats he met along the way./nWormtail has a curious affinity with rats, do you not,/nWormtail? His filthy little friends told him there was a/nplace, deep in an Albanian forest, that they avoided,/nwhere small animals like themselves had met their/ndeaths by a dark shadow that possessed them. .../n/n"But his journey back to me was not smooth, was it,/nWormtail? For, hungry one night, on the edge of the/nvery forest where he had hoped to find me, he/nfoolishly stopped at an inn for some food . . . and who/nshould he meet there, but one Bertha Jorkins, a/nwitch from the Ministry of Magic./n/n"Now see the way that fate favors Lord Voldemort./n/nThis might have been the end of Wormtail, and of my/nlast hope for regeneration. But Wormtail — displaying/na presence of mind I would never have expected from/nhim — convinced Bertha Jorkins to accompany him/non a nighttime stroll. He overpowered her ... he/nbrought her to me. And Bertha Jorkins, who might/nhave ruined all, proved instead to be a gift beyond my/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwildest dreams . . . for — with a little persuasion — she/nbecame a veritable mine of information./n/n"She told me that the Triwizard Tournament would be/nplayed at Hogwarts this year. She told me that she/nknew of a faithful Death Eater who would be only too/nwilling to help me, if I could only contact him. She/ntold me many things . . . but the means I used to break/nthe Memory Charm upon her were powerful, and/nwhen I had extracted all useful information from her,/nher mind and body were both damaged beyond repair./nShe had now served her purpose. I could not possess/nher. I disposed of her."/n/nVoldemort smiled his terrible smile, his red eyes/nblank and pitiless./n/n"Wormtail's body, of course, was ill adapted for/npossession, as all assumed him dead, and would/nattract far too much attention if noticed. However, he/nwas the able-bodied servant I needed, and, poor/nwizard though he is, Wormtail was able to follow the/ninstructions I gave him, which would return me to a/nrudimentary, weak body of my own, a body I would be/nable to inhabit while awaiting the essential/ningredients for true rebirth ... a spell or two of my/nown invention ... a little help from my dear Nagini,"/nVoldemort's red eyes fell upon the continually circling/nsnake, "a potion concocted from unicorn blood, and/nthe snake venom Nagini provided ... I was soon/nreturned to an almost human form, and strong/nenough to travel./n/n"There was no hope of stealing the Sorcerer's Stone/nanymore, for I knew that Dumbledore would have/nseen to it that it was destroyed. But I was willing to/nembrace mortal life again, before chasing immortality./nI set my sights lower ... I would settle for my old body/nback again, and my old strength./n/n/n/n/n/n"I knew that to achieve this — it is an old piece of/nDark Magic, the potion that revived me tonight — I/nwould need three powerful ingredients. Well, one of/nthem was already at hand, was it not, Wormtail?/n/nFlesh given by a servant. .../n/n"My father's bone, naturally, meant that we would/nhave to come here, where he was buried. But the/nblood of a foe ... Wormtail would have had me use any/nwizard, would you not, Wormtail? Any wizard who/nhad hated me ... as so many of them still do. But I/nknew the one I must use, if I was to rise again, more/npowerful than I had been when I had fallen. I wanted/nHarry Potter's blood. I wanted the blood of the one/nwho had stripped me of power thirteen years ago . . ./nfor the lingering protection his mother once gave him/nwould then reside in my veins too. .../n/n"But how to get at Harry Potter? For he has been/nbetter protected than I think even he knows,/nprotected in ways devised by Dumbledore long ago,/nwhen it fell to him to arrange the boy's future./nDumbledore invoked an ancient magic, to ensure the/nboy's protection as long as he is in his relations' care./nNot even I can touch him there. ... Then, of course,/nthere was the Quidditch World Cup. ... I thought his/nprotection might be weaker there, away from his/nrelations and Dumbledore, but I was not yet strong/nenough to attempt kidnap in the midst of a horde of/nMinistry wizards. And then, the boy would return to/nHogwarts, where he is under the crooked nose of that/nMuggle-loving fool from morning until night. So how/ncould I take him?/n/n"Why ... by using Bertha Jorkins's information, of/ncourse. Use my one faithful Death Eater, stationed at/nHogwarts, to ensure that the boy's name was entered/ninto the Goblet of Fire. Use my Death Eater to ensure/nthat the boy won the tournament — that he touched/n/n/n/n/nthe Triwizard Cup first — the cup which my Death/nEater had turned into a Portkey, which would bring/nhim here, beyond the reach of Dumbledore's help and/nprotection, and into my waiting arms. And here he is/n... the boy you all believed had been my downfall..."/n/nVoldemort moved slowly forward and turned to face/nHarry. He raised his wand./n/n"Crucio\"/n/nIt was pain beyond anything Harry had ever/nexperienced; his very bones were on fire; his head was/nsurely splitting along his scar; his eyes were rolling/nmadly in his head; he wanted it to end ... to black out/n...to die .../n/nAnd then it was gone. He was hanging limply in the/nropes binding him to the headstone of Voldemort's/nfather, looking up into those bright red eyes through/na kind of mist. The night was ringing with the sound/nof the Death Eaters' laughter./n/n"You see, I think, how foolish it was to suppose that/nthis boy could ever have been stronger than me," said/nVoldemort. "But I want there to be no mistake in/nanybody's mind. Harry Potter escaped me by a lucky/nchance. And I am now going to prove my power by/nkilling him, here and now, in front of you all, when/nthere is no Dumbledore to help him, and no mother to/ndie for him. I will give him his chance. He will be/nallowed to fight, and you will be left in no doubt/nwhich of us is the stronger. Just a little longer,/nNagini," he whispered, and the snake glided away/nthrough the grass to where the Death Eaters stood/nwatching./n/n"Now untie him, Wormtail, and give him back his/nwand."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Priori Incantatem
text: /nWormtail approached Harry, who scrambled to find/nhis feet, to support his own weight before the ropes/nwere untied. Wormtail raised his new silver hand,/npulled out the wad of material gagging Harry, and/nthen, with one swipe, cut through the bonds tying/nHarry to the gravestone./n/nThere was a split second, perhaps, when Harry might/nhave considered running for it, but his injured leg/nshook under him as he stood on the overgrown grave,/nas the Death Eaters closed ranks, forming a tighter/ncircle around him and Voldemort, so that the gaps/nwhere the missing Death Eaters should have stood/nwere filled. Wormtail walked out of the circle to the/nplace where Cedric's body lay and returned with/nHarry's wand, which he thrust roughly into Harry's/nhand without looking at him. Then Wormtail resumed/nhis place in the circle of watching Death Eaters./n/n"You have been taught how to duel, Harry Potter?"/nsaid Voldemort softly, his red eyes glinting through/nthe darkness./n/n/n/n/nAt these words Harry remembered, as though from a/nformer life, the dueling club at Hogwarts he had/nattended briefly two years ago. ... All he had learned/nthere was the Disarming Spell, " Expelliarmus" ... and/nwhat use would it be to deprive Voldemort of his/nwand, even if he could, when he was surrounded by/nDeath Eaters, outnumbered by at least thirty to one?/nHe had never learned anything that could possibly fit/nhim for this. He knew he was facing the thing against/nwhich Moody had always warned . . . the un-blockable/nAvada Kedavra curse — and Voldemort was right —/nhis mother was not here to die for him this time. .../n/nHe was quite unprotected. .../n/n"We bow to each other, Harry," said Voldemort,/nbending a little, but keeping his snakelike face/nupturned to Harry. "Come, the niceties must be/nobserved. ... Dumbledore would like you to show/nmanners. ... Bow to death, Harry. ..."/n/nThe Death Eaters were laughing again. Voldemort's/nlipless mouth was smiling. Harry did not bow. He was/nnot going to let Voldemort play with him before killing/nhim ... he was not going to give him that satisfaction./n/n/n/n"I said, bow," Voldemort said, raising his wand — and/nHarry felt his spine curve as though a huge, invisible/nhand were bending him ruthlessly forward, and the/nDeath Eaters laughed harder than ever./n/n"Very good," said Voldemort softly, and as he raised/nhis wand the pressure bearing down upon Harry lifted/ntoo. "And now you face me, like a man ... straight-/nbacked and proud, the way your father died. .../n/n"And now — we duel."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nVoldemort raised his wand, and before Harry could do/nanything to defend himself, before he could even/nmove, he had been hit again by the Cruciatus Curse./nThe pain was so intense, so all-consuming, that he no/nlonger knew where he was. ... White-hot knives were/npiercing every inch of his skin, his head was surely/ngoing to burst with pain, he was screaming more/nloudly than he'd ever screamed in his life —/n/nAnd then it stopped. Harry rolled over and scrambled/nto his feet; he was shaking as uncontrollably as/nWormtail had done when his hand had been cut off;/nhe staggered sideways into the wall of watching Death/nEaters, and they pushed him away, back toward/nVoldemort./n/n"A little break," said Voldemort, the slit-like nostrils/ndilating with excitement, "a little pause . . . That hurt,/ndidn't it, Harry? You don't want me to do that again,/ndo you?"/n/nHarry didn't answer. He was going to die like Cedric,/nthose pitiless red eyes were telling him so ... he was/ngoing to die, and there was nothing he could do about/nit... but he wasn't going to play along. He wasn't going/nto obey Voldemort ... he wasn't going to beg. .../n/n"I asked you whether you want me to do that again,"/nsaid Voldemort softly. "Answer me! ImperioV'/n/nAnd Harry felt, for the third time in his life, the/nsensation that his mind had been wiped of all/nthought. ... Ah, it was bliss, not to think, it was as/nthough he were floating, dreaming ... just answer no/n. . . say no ... just answer no. . . ./n/nI will not, said a stronger voice, in the back of his/nhead, I won't answer. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nJust answer no. .../n/n/n/nI won't do it, I won't say it. .../n/nJust answer no. .../n/n"I WONT!"/n/nAnd these words burst from Harry's mouth; they/nechoed through the graveyard, and the dream state/nwas lifted as suddenly as though cold water had been/nthrown over him — back rushed the aches that the/nCruciatus Curse had left all over his body — back/nrushed the realization of where he was, and what he/nwas facing. .../n/n"You won't?" said Voldemort quietly, and the Death/nEaters were not laughing now. "You won't say no?/nHarry, obedience is a virtue I need to teach you before/nyou die. ... Perhaps another little dose of pain?"/n/nVoldemort raised his wand, but this time Harry was/nready; with the reflexes born of his Quidditch/ntraining, he flung himself sideways onto the ground;/nhe rolled behind the marble headstone of Voldemort's/nfather, and he heard it crack as the curse missed/nhim./n/n"We are not playing hide-and-seek, Harry," said/nVoldemort's soft, cold voice, drawing nearer, as the/nDeath Eaters laughed. "You cannot hide from me./n/nDoes this mean you are tired of our duel? Does this/nmean that you would prefer me to finish it now,/n/nHarry? Come out, Harry . . . come out and play, then/n...it will be quick ... it might even be painless ... I/nwould not know ... I have never died. ..."/n/nHarry crouched behind the headstone and knew the/nend had come. There was no hope ... no help to be/n/n/n/n/n/nhad. And as he heard Voldemort draw nearer still, he/nknew one thing only, and it was beyond fear or/nreason: He was not going to die crouching here like a/nchild playing hide-and-seek; he was not going to die/nkneeling at Voldemort's feet ... he was going to die/nupright like his father, and he was going to die trying/nto defend himself, even if no defense was possible. .../n/nBefore Voldemort could stick his snakelike face/naround the headstone, Harry stood up ... he gripped/nhis wand tightly in his hand, thrust it out in front of/nhim, and threw himself around the headstone, facing/nVoldemort./n/nVoldemort was ready. As Harry shouted,/n/n" ExpelliarmusV' Voldemort cried, "Avada KedavraV'/n/nA jet of green light issued from Voldemort's wand just/nas a jet of red light blasted from Harry's — they met/nin midair — and suddenly Harry's wand was vibrating/nas though an electric charge were surging through it;/nhis hand seized up around it; he couldn't have/nreleased it if he'd wanted to — and a narrow beam of/nlight connected the two wands, neither red nor green,/nbut bright, deep gold. Harry, following the beam with/nhis astonished gaze, saw that Voldemort's long white/nfingers too were gripping a wand that was shaking/nand vibrating./n/nAnd then — nothing could have prepared Harry for/nthis — he felt his feet lift from the ground. He and/nVoldemort were both being raised into the air, their/nwands still connected by that thread of shimmering/ngolden light. They glided away from the tombstone of/nVoldemort's father and then came to rest on a patch/nof ground that was clear and free of graves. ... The/nDeath Eaters were shouting; they were asking/nVoldemort for instructions; they were closing in,/nreforming the circle around Harry and Voldemort, the/n/n/n/n/nsnake slithering at their heels, some of them drawing/ntheir wands —/n/n/n/nThe golden thread connecting Harry and Voldemort/nsplintered; though the wands remained connected, a/nthousand more beams arced high over Harry and/nVoldemort, crisscrossing all around them, until they/nwere enclosed in a golden, dome-shaped web, a cage/nof light, beyond which the Death Eaters circled like/njackals, their cries strangely muffled now. .../n/n"Do nothing!" Voldemort shrieked to the Death/nEaters, and Harry saw his red eyes wide with/nastonishment at what was happening, saw him/nfighting to break the thread of light still connecting/nhis wand with Harry's; Harry held onto his wand/nmore tightly, with both hands, and the golden thread/nremained unbroken. "Do nothing unless I command/nyou!" Voldemort shouted to the Death Eaters./n/nAnd then an unearthly and beautiful sound filled the/nair. ... It was coming from every thread of the light-/nspun web vibrating around Harry and Voldemort. It/nwas a sound Harry recognized, though he had heard/nit only once before in his life: phoenix song./n/nIt was the sound of hope to Harry . . . the most/nbeautiful and welcome thing he had ever heard in his/nlife. ... He felt as though the song were inside him/ninstead of just around him. ... It was the sound he/nconnected with Dumbledore, and it was almost as/nthough a friend were speaking in his ear. . . ./n/nDon't break the connection./n/nI know, Harry told the music, I know I mustn't ... but/nno sooner had he thought it, than the thing became/nmuch harder to do. His wand began to vibrate more/npowerfully than ever . . . and now the beam between/n/n/n/n/n/nhim and Voldemort changed too ... it was as though/nlarge beads of light were sliding up and down the/nthread connecting the wands — Harry felt his wand/ngive a shudder under his hand as the light beads/nbegan to slide slowly and steadily his way. . . . The/ndirection of the beam's movement was now toward/nhim, from Voldemort, and he felt his wand shudder/nangrily. .../n/nAs the closest bead of light moved nearer to Harry's/nwand tip, the wood beneath his fingers grew so hot he/nfeared it would burst into flame. The closer that bead/nmoved, the harder Harry's wand vibrated; he was sure/nhis wand would not survive contact with it; it felt as/nthough it was about to shatter under his fingers —/n/nHe concentrated every last particle of his mind upon/nforcing the bead back toward Voldemort, his ears full/nof phoenix song, his eyes furious, fixed ... and slowly,/nvery slowly, the beads quivered to a halt, and then,/njust as slowly, they began to move the other way .../nand it was Voldemort 's wand that was vibrating extra-/nhard now ... Voldemort who looked astonished, and/nalmost fearful. .../n/nOne of the beads of light was quivering, inches from/nthe tip of Voldemort's wand. Harry didn't understand/nwhy he was doing it, didn't know what it might/nachieve . . . but he now concentrated as he had never/ndone in his life on forcing that bead of light right back/ninto Voldemort's wand ... and slowly ... very slowly .../nit moved along the golden thread ... it trembled for a/nmoment... and then it connected. .../n/nAt once, Voldemort's wand began to emit echoing/nscreams of pain ... then — Voldemort's red eyes/nwidened with shock — a dense, smoky hand flew out/nof the tip of it and vanished . . . the ghost of the hand/nhe had made Wormtail ... more shouts of pain ... and/n/n/n/n/nthen something much larger began to blossom from/nVoldemort's wand tip, a great, grayish something,/nthat looked as though it were made of the solidest,/ndensest smoke. ... It was a head ... now a chest and/narms . . . the torso of Cedric Diggory./n/nIf ever Harry might have released his wand from/nshock, it would have been then, but instinct kept him/nclutching his wand tightly, so that the thread of/ngolden light remained unbroken, even though the/nthick gray ghost of Cedric Diggory (was it a ghost? it/nlooked so solid) emerged in its entirety from the end of/nVoldemort's wand, as though it were squeezing itself/nout of a very narrow tunnel . . . and this shade of/nCedric stood up, and looked up and down the golden/nthread of light, and spoke./n/n"Hold on, Harry," it said./n/nIts voice was distant and echoing. Harry looked at/nVoldemort . . . his wide red eyes were still shocked . . ./nhe had no more expected this than Harry had . . . and,/nvery dimly, Harry heard the frightened yells of the/nDeath Eaters, prowling around the edges of the/ngolden dome. .../n/nMore screams of pain from the wand . . . and then/nsomething else emerged from its tip . . . the dense/nshadow of a second head, quickly followed by arms/nand torso ... an old man Harry had seen only in a/ndream was now pushing himself out of the end of the/nwand just as Cedric had done ... and his ghost, or his/nshadow, or whatever it was, fell next to Cedric's, and/nsurveyed Harry and Voldemort, and the golden web,/nand the connected wands, with mild surprise, leaning/non his walking stick. . . ./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He was a real wizard, then?" the old man said, his/neyes on Voldemort. "Killed me, that one did. ... You/nfight him, boy. ..."/n/nBut already, yet another head was emerging . . . and/nthis head, gray as a smoky statue, was a woman's. .../nHarry, both arms shaking now as he fought to keep/nhis wand still, saw her drop to the ground and/nstraighten up like the others, staring. .../n/nThe shadow of Bertha Jorkins surveyed the battle/nbefore her with wide eyes./n/n"Don't let go, now!" she cried, and her voice echoed/nlike Cedric's as though from very far away. "Don't let/nhim get you, Harry — don't let go!"/n/nShe and the other two shadowy figures began to pace/naround the inner walls of the golden web, while the/nDeath Eaters flitted around the outside of it ... and/nVoldemort's dead victims whispered as they circled/nthe duelers, whispered words of encouragement to/nHarry, and hissed words Harry couldn't hear to/nVoldemort./n/nAnd now another head was emerging from the tip of/nVoldemort's wand ... and Harry knew when he saw it/nwho it would be ... he knew, as though he had/nexpected it from the moment when Cedric had/nappeared from the wand . . . knew, because the woman/nwas the one he'd thought of more than any other/ntonight. .../n/nThe smoky shadow of a young woman with long hair/nfell to the ground as Bertha had done, straightened/nup, and looked at him ... and Harry, his arms shaking/nmadly now, looked back into the ghostly face of his/nmother./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Your father's coming ..." she said quietly. "Hold on/nfor your father ... it will be all right ... hold on. ..."/n/nAnd he came . . . first his head, then his body . . . tall/nand untidy-haired like Harry, the smoky, shadowy/nform of James Potter blossomed from the end of/nVoldemort's wand, fell to the ground, and/nstraightened like his wife. He walked close to Harry,/nlooking down at him, and he spoke in the same/ndistant, echoing voice as the others, but quietly, so/nthat Voldemort, his face now livid with fear as his/nvictims prowled around him, could not hear. . . ./n/n"When the connection is broken, we will linger for/nonly moments . . . but we will give you time . . . you/nmust get to the Portkey, it will return you to Hogwarts/n... do you understand, Harry?"/n/n"Yes," Harry gasped, fighting now to keep a hold on/nhis wand, which was slipping and sliding beneath his/nfingers./n/n"Harry ..." whispered the figure of Cedric, "take my/nbody back, will you? Take my body back to my/nparents. ..."/n/n"I will," said Harry, his face screwed up with the effort/nof holding the wand./n/n"Do it now," whispered his father's voice, "be ready to/nrun ... do it now. ..."/n/n"NOW!" Harry yelled; he didn't think he could have/nheld on for another moment anyway — he pulled his/nwand upward with an almighty wrench, and the/ngolden thread broke; the cage of light vanished, the/nphoenix song died — but the shadowy figures of/nVoldemort's victims did not disappear — they were/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nclosing in upon Voldemort, shielding Harry from his/ngaze —/n/nAnd Harry ran as he had never run in his life,/nknocking two stunned Death Eaters aside as he/npassed; he zigzagged behind headstones, feeling their/ncurses following him, hearing them hit the/nheadstones — he was dodging curses and graves,/npelting toward Cedric's body, no longer aware of the/npain in his leg, his whole being concentrated on what/nhe had to do —/n/n"Stun him\" he heard Voldemort scream./n/nTen feet from Cedric, Harry dived behind a marble/nangel to avoid the jets of red light and saw the tip of/nits wing shatter as the spells hit it. Gripping his wand/nmore tightly, he dashed out from behind the angel —/n/n"Impedimental" he bellowed, pointing his wand wildly/nover his shoulder at the Death Eaters running at him./n/nFrom a muffled yell, he thought he had stopped at/nleast one of them, but there was no time to stop and/nlook; he jumped over the cup and dived as he heard/nmore wand blasts behind him; more jets of light flew/nover his head as he fell, stretching out his hand to/ngrab Cedric's arm —/n/n"Stand aside! I will kill him! He is mine!" shrieked/nVoldemort./n/nHarry's hand had closed on Cedric's wrist; one/ntombstone stood between him and Voldemort, but/nCedric was too heavy to carry, and the cup was out of/nreach —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nVoldemort's red eyes flamed in the darkness. Harry/nsaw his mouth curl into a smile, saw him raise his/nwand./n/n"Acciol" Harry yelled, pointing his wand at the/nTriwizard Cup./n/nIt flew into the air and soared toward him.
