Harry/ncaught it by the handle —/n/nHe heard Voldemort's scream of fury at the same/nmoment that he felt the jerk behind his navel that/nmeant the Portkey had worked — it was speeding him/naway in a whirl of wind and color, and Cedric along/nwith him. ... They were going back./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Veritaserum
text: /nHarry felt himself slam flat into the ground; his face/nwas pressed into grass; the smell of it filled his/nnostrils. He had closed his eyes while the Portkey/ntransported him, and he kept them closed now. He/ndid not move. All the breath seemed to have been/nknocked out of him; his head was swimming so badly/nhe felt as though the ground beneath him were/nswaying like the deck of a ship. To hold himself/nsteady, he tightened his hold on the two things he/nwas still clutching: the smooth, cold handle of the Tri-/nwizard Cup and Cedric's body. He felt as though he/nwould slide away into the blackness gathering at the/nedges of his brain if he let go of either of them. Shock/nand exhaustion kept him on the ground, breathing in/nthe smell of the grass, waiting ... waiting for someone/nto do something . . . something to happen . . . and all/nthe while, his scar burned dully on his forehead. .../n/nA torrent of sound deafened and confused him; there/nwere voices everywhere, footsteps, screams. ... He/nremained where he was, his face screwed up against/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe noise, as though it were a nightmare that would/npass. .../n/nThen a pair of hands seized him roughly and turned/nhim over./n/n"Harry! HarryV'/n/nHe opened his eyes./n/nHe was looking up at the starry sky, and Albus/nDumbledore was crouched over him. The dark/nshadows of a crowd of people pressed in around/nthem, pushing nearer; Harry felt the ground beneath/nhis head reverberating with their footsteps./n/nHe had come back to the edge of the maze. He could/nsee the stands rising above him, the shapes of people/nmoving in them, the stars above./n/nHarry let go of the cup, but he clutched Cedric to him/neven more tightly. He raised his free hand and seized/nDumbledore 's wrist, while Dumbledore 's face swam in/nand out of focus./n/n"He's back," Harry whispered. "He's back. Voldemort."/n/n"What's going on? What's happened?"/n/nThe face of Cornelius Fudge appeared upside down/nover Harry; it looked white, appalled./n/n"My God — Diggory!" it whispered. "Dumbledore —/nhe's dead!"/n/nThe words were repeated, the shadowy figures/npressing in on them gasped it to those around them/n. . . and then others shouted it — screeched it — into/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe night — "He's dead!" "He's dead!" "Cedric Diggory!/nDead)."/n/n/n/n"Harry, let go of him," he heard Fudge's voice say, and/nhe felt fingers trying to pry him from Cedric's limp/nbody, but Harry wouldn't let him go. Then/nDumbledore's face, which was still blurred and/nmisted, came closer./n/n"Harry, you can't help him now. It's over. Let go."/n/n"He wanted me to bring him back," Harry muttered —/nit seemed important to explain this. "He wanted me to/nbring him back to his parents. ..."/n/n"That's right, Harry ... just let go now. ..."/n/nDumbledore bent down, and with extraordinary/nstrength for a man so old and thin, raised Harry from/nthe ground and set him on his feet. Harry swayed. His/nhead was pounding. His injured leg would no longer/nsupport his weight. The crowd around them jostled,/nfighting to get closer, pressing darkly in on him —/n"What's happened?" "What's wrong with him?"/n/n"Dig gory's dead\"/n/n"He'll need to go to the hospital wing!" Fudge was/nsaying loudly. "He's ill, he's injured — Dumbledore,/nDiggory's parents, they're here, they're in the stands./n/n/n/n"I'll take Harry, Dumbledore, I'll take him — "/n/n"No, I would prefer — "/n/n"Dumbledore, Amos Diggory's running ... he's coming/nover. ... Don't you think you should tell him — before/nhe sees — ?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, stay here — "/n/n/n/nGirls were screaming, sobbing hysterically. . . . The/nscene flickered oddly before Harry's eyes. .../n/n"It's all right, son, I've got you ... come on ... hospital/nwing ..."/n/n"Dumbledore said stay," said Harry thickly, the/npounding in his scar making him feel as though he/nwas about to throw up; his vision was blurring worse/nthan ever./n/n"You need to lie down. ... Come on now. ..."/n/nSomeone larger and stronger than he was was half/npulling, half carrying him through the frightened/ncrowd. Harry heard people gasping, screaming, and/nshouting as the man supporting him pushed a path/nthrough them, taking him back to the castle. Across/nthe lawn, past the lake and the Durmstrang ship,/nHarry heard nothing but the heavy breathing of the/nman helping him walk./n/n"What happened, Harry?" the man asked at last as he/nlifted Harry up the stone steps. Clunk. Clunk. Clunk./n/nIt was Mad-Eye Moody./n/n"Cup was a Portkey," said Harry as they crossed the/nentrance hall. "Took me and Cedric to a graveyard .../nand Voldemort was there ... Lord Voldemort ..."/n/nClunk. Clunk. Clunk. Up the marble stairs .../n/n"The Dark Lord was there? What happened then?"/n/n"Killed Cedric ... they killed Cedric. ..."/n/n"And then?"/n/n/n/n/n/nClunk. Clunk. Clunk. Along the corridor . . ./n/n"Made a potion ... got his body back. ..."/n/n"The Dark Lord got his body back? He's returned?"/n"And the Death Eaters came ... and then we dueled./n/n/n/n"You dueled with the Dark Lord?"/n/n"Got away . . . my wand . . . did something funny. ... I/nsaw my mum and dad ... they came out of his wand./n/n/n/n"In here, Harry ... in here, and sit down. ... You'll be/nall right now ... drink this. ..."/n/nHarry heard a key scrape in a lock and felt a cup/nbeing pushed into his hands./n/n"Drink it ... you'll feel better ... come on, now, Harry, I/nneed to know exactly what happened. ..."/n/nMoody helped tip the stuff down Harry's throat; he/ncoughed, a peppery taste burning his throat. Moody's/noffice came into sharper focus, and so did Moody/nhimself. ... He looked as white as Fudge had looked,/nand both eyes were fixed unblinkingly upon Harry's/nface./n/n"Voldemort's back, Harry? You're sure he's back? How/ndid he do it?"/n/n"He took stuff from his father's grave, and from/nWormtail, and me," said Harry. His head felt clearer;/nhis scar wasn't hurting so badly; he could now see/nMoody's face distinctly, even though the office was/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndark. He could still hear screaming and shouting/nfrom the distant Quidditch field./n/n/n/n"What did the Dark Lord take from you?" said Moody./n/n"Blood," said Harry, raising his arm. His sleeve was/nripped where Wormtail's dagger had torn it./n/nMoody let out his breath in a long, low hiss./n/n"And the Death Eaters? They returned?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry. "Loads of them ..."/n/n"How did he treat them?" Moody asked quietly. "Did/nhe forgive them?"/n/nBut Harry had suddenly remembered. He should have/ntold Dumbledore, he should have said it straightaway/n/n/n/n"There's a Death Eater at Hogwarts! There's a Death/nEater here — they put my name in the Goblet of Fire,/nthey made sure I got through to the end — "/n/nHarry tried to get up, but Moody pushed him back/ndown./n/n"I know who the Death Eater is," he said quietly./n/n"Karkaroff?" said Harry wildly. "Where is he? Have/nyou got him? Is he locked up?"/n/n"Karkaroff?" said Moody with an odd laugh./n/n"Karkaroff fled tonight, when he felt the Dark Mark/nburn upon his arm. He betrayed too many faithful/nsupporters of the Dark Lord to wish to meet them . . ./nbut I doubt he will get far. The Dark Lord has ways of/ntracking his enemies."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Karkaroff's gone? He ran away? But then — he didn't/nput my name in the goblet?"/n/n/n/n"No," said Moody slowly. "No, he didn't. It was I who/ndid that."/n/nHarry heard, but didn't believe./n/n"No, you didn't," he said. "You didn't do that ... you/ncan't have done ..."/n/n"I assure you I did," said Moody, and his magical eye/nswung around and fixed upon the door, and Harry/nknew he was making sure that there was no one/noutside it. At the same time, Moody drew out his/nwand and pointed it at Harry./n/n"He forgave them, then?" he said. "The Death Eaters/nwho went free? The ones who escaped Azkaban?"/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/nHe was looking at the wand Moody was pointing at/nhim. This was a bad joke, it had to be./n/n"I asked you," said Moody quietly, "whether he forgave/nthe scum who never even went to look for him. Those/ntreacherous cowards who wouldn't even brave/nAzkaban for him. The faithless, worthless bits of filth/nwho were brave enough to cavort in masks at the/nQuidditch World Cup, but fled at the sight of the Dark/nMark when I fired it into the sky."/n/n" You fired . . . What are you talking about ... ?"/n/n"I told you, Harry ... I told you. If there's one thing I/nhate more than any other, it's a Death Eater who/nwalked free. They turned their backs on my master/nwhen he needed them most. I expected him to punish/n/n/n/n/n/nthem. I expected him to torture them. Tell me he hurt/nthem, Harry. ..." Moody's face was suddenly lit with/nan insane smile. "Tell me he told them that I, I alone/nremained faithful . . . prepared to risk everything to/ndeliver to him the one thing he wanted above all .../nyou."/n/n"You didn't ... it — it can't be you. ..."/n/n"Who put your name in the Goblet of Fire, under the/nname of a different school? I did. Who frightened off/nevery person I thought might try to hurt you or/nprevent you from winning the tournament? I did. Who/nnudged Hagrid into showing you the dragons? I did./nWho helped you see the only way you could beat the/ndragon? I did."/n/nMoody's magical eye had now left the door. It was/nfixed upon Harry. His lopsided mouth leered more/nwidely than ever./n/n"It hasn't been easy, Harry, guiding you through these/ntasks without arousing suspicion. I have had to use/nevery ounce of cunning I possess, so that my hand/nwould not be detectable in your success. Dumbledore/nwould have been very suspicious if you had managed/neverything too easily. As long as you got into that/nmaze, preferably with a decent head start — then, I/nknew, I would have a chance of getting rid of the/nother champions and leaving your way clear. But I/nalso had to contend with your stupidity. The second/ntask . . . that was when I was most afraid we would/nfail. I was keeping watch on you, Potter. I knew you/nhadn't worked out the egg's clue, so I had to give you/nanother hint — "/n/n"You didn't," Harry said hoarsely. "Cedric gave me the/nclue — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Who told Cedric to open it underwater? I did. I/ntrusted that he would pass the information on to you./nDecent people are so easy to manipulate, Potter. I was/nsure Cedric would want to repay you for telling him/nabout the dragons, and so he did. But even then,/nPotter, even then you seemed likely to fail. I was/nwatching all the time ... all those hours in the library./nDidn't you realize that the book you needed was in/nyour dormitory all along? I planted it there early on, I/ngave it to the Longbottom boy, don't you remember?/nMagical Water Plants of the Mediterranean. It would/nhave told you all you needed to know about gillyweed./n/nI expected you to ask everyone and anyone you could/nfor help. Longbottom would have told you in an/ninstant. But you did not ... you did not. ... You have a/nstreak of pride and independence that might have/nruined all./n/n"So what could I do? Feed you information from/nanother innocent source. You told me at the Yule Ball/na house-elf called Dobby had given you a Christmas/npresent. I called the elf to the staffroom to collect/nsome robes for cleaning. I staged a loud conversation/nwith Professor McGonagall about the hostages who/nhad been taken, and whether Potter would think to/nuse gillyweed. And your little elf friend ran straight to/nSnape's office and then hurried to find you. ..."/n/nMoody's wand was still pointing directly at Harry's/nheart. Over his shoulder, foggy shapes were moving in/nthe Foe-Glass on the wall./n/n"You were so long in that lake, Potter, I thought you/nhad drowned. But luckily, Dumbledore took your/nidiocy for nobility, and marked you high for it. I/nbreathed again./n/n"You had an easier time of it than you should have in/nthat maze tonight, of course," said Moody. "I was/n/n/n/n/n/npatrolling around it, able to see through the outer/nhedges, able to curse many obstacles out of your way./nI Stunned Fleur Delacour as she passed. I put the/nImperius Curse on Krum, so that he would finish/nDiggory and leave your path to the cup clear."/n/nHarry stared at Moody. He just didn't see how this/ncould be. ... Dumbledore's friend, the famous Auror/n. . . the one who had caught so many Death Eaters . . ./n/nIt made no sense ... no sense at all. .../n/nThe foggy shapes in the Foe-Glass were sharpening,/nhad become more distinct. Harry could see the/noutlines of three people over Moody's shoulder,/nmoving closer and closer. But Moody wasn't watching/nthem. His magical eye was upon Harry./n/n"The Dark Lord didn't manage to kill you, Potter, and/nhe so wanted to," whispered Moody. "Imagine how he/nwill reward me when he finds I have done it for him. I/ngave you to him — the thing he needed above all to/nregenerate — and then I killed you for him. I will be/nhonored beyond all other Death Eaters. I will be his/ndearest, his closest supporter ... closer than a son. ..."/n/nMoody's normal eye was bulging, the magical eye/nfixed upon Harry. The door was barred, and Harry/nknew he would never reach his own wand in time. .../n/n"The Dark Lord and I," said Moody, and he looked/ncompletely insane now, towering over Harry, leering/ndown at him, "have much in common. Both of us, for/ninstance, had very disappointing fathers ... very/ndisappointing indeed. Both of us suffered the/nindignity, Harry, of being named after those fathers./nAnd both of us had the pleasure . . . the very great/npleasure ... of killing our fathers to ensure the/ncontinued rise of the Dark Order!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're mad," Harry said — he couldn't stop himself/n— "you're mad!"/n/n/n/n"Mad, am I?" said Moody, his voice rising/nuncontrollably. "We'll see! We'll see who's mad, now/nthat the Dark Lord has returned, with me at his side!/nHe is back, Harry Potter, you did not conquer him —/nand now — I conquer you!"/n/nMoody raised his wand, he opened his mouth; Harry/nplunged his own hand into his robes —/n/n"Stupefy\" There was a blinding flash of red light, and/nwith a great splintering and crashing, the door of/nMoody's office was blasted apart —/n/nMoody was thrown backward onto the office floor./nHarry, still staring at the place where Moody's face/nhad been, saw Albus Dumbledore, Professor Snape,/nand Professor McGonagall looking back at him out of/nthe Foe-Glass. He looked around and saw the three of/nthem standing in the doorway, Dumbledore in front,/nhis wand outstretched./n/nAt that moment, Harry fully understood for the first/ntime why people said Dumbledore was the only wizard/nVoldemort had ever feared. The look upon/nDumbledore 's face as he stared down at the/nunconscious form of Mad-Eye Moody was more/nterrible than Harry could have ever imagined. There/nwas no benign smile upon Dumbledore 's face, no/ntwinkle in the eyes behind the spectacles. There was/ncold fury in every line of the ancient face; a sense of/npower radiated from Dumbledore as though he were/ngiving off burning heat./n/nHe stepped into the office, placed a foot underneath/nMoody's unconscious body, and kicked him over onto/nhis back, so that his face was visible. Snape followed/n/n/n/n/n/nhim, looking into the Foe-Glass, where his own face/nwas still visible, glaring into the room. Professor/nMcGonagall went straight to Harry./n/n"Come along, Potter," she whispered. The thin line of/nher mouth was twitching as though she was about to/ncry. "Come along ... hospital wing ..."/n/n"No," said Dumbledore sharply./n/n"Dumbledore, he ought to — look at him — he's been/nthrough enough tonight — "/n/n"He will stay, Minerva, because he needs to/nunderstand," said Dumbledore curtly. "Understanding/nis the first step to acceptance, and only with/nacceptance can there be recovery. He needs to know/nwho has put him through the ordeal he has suffered/ntonight, and why."/n/n"Moody," Harry said. He was still in a state of/ncomplete disbelief. "How can it have been Moody?"/n/n"This is not Alastor Moody," said Dumbledore quietly./n"You have never known Alastor Moody. The real/nMoody would not have removed you from my sight/nafter what happened tonight. The moment he took/nyou, I knew — and I followed."/n/nDumbledore bent down over Moody's limp form and/nput a hand inside his robes. He pulled out Moody's/nhip flask and a set of keys on a ring. Then he turned/nto Professors McGonagall and Snape./n/n"Severus, please fetch me the strongest Truth Potion/nyou possess, and then go down to the kitchens and/nbring up the house-elf called Winky. Minerva, kindly/ngo down to Hagrid's house, where you will find a large/nblack dog sitting in the pumpkin patch. Take the dog/n/n/n/n/nup to my office, tell him I will be with him shortly,/nthen come back here."/n/nIf either Snape or McGonagall found these/ninstructions peculiar, they hid their confusion. Both/nturned at once and left the office. Dumbledore walked/nover to the trunk with seven locks, fitted the first key/nin the lock, and opened it. It contained a mass of/nspell-books. Dumbledore closed the trunk, placed a/nsecond key in the second lock, and opened the trunk/nagain. The spellbooks had vanished; this time it/ncontained an assortment of broken Sneako-scopes,/nsome parchment and quills, and what looked like a/nsilvery Invisibility Cloak. Harry watched, astounded,/nas Dumbledore placed the third, fourth, fifth, and/nsixth keys in their respective locks, reopening the/ntrunk, and each time revealing different contents./nThen he placed the seventh key in the lock, threw/nopen the lid, and Harry let out a cry of amazement./n/nHe was looking down into a kind of pit, an/nunderground room, and lying on the floor some ten/nfeet below, apparently fast asleep, thin and starved in/nappearance, was the real Mad-Eye Moody. His/nwooden leg was gone, the socket that should have/nheld the magical eye looked empty beneath its lid,/nand chunks of his grizzled hair were missing. Harry/nstared, thunderstruck, between the sleeping Moody in/nthe trunk and the unconscious Moody lying on the/nfloor of the office./n/nDumbledore climbed into the trunk, lowered himself,/nand fell lightly onto the floor beside the sleeping/nMoody. He bent over him./n/n"Stunned — controlled by the Imperius Curse — very/nweak," he said. "Of course, they would have needed to/nkeep him alive. Harry, throw down the imposter's/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncloak — he's freezing. Madam Pomfrey will need to see/nhim, but he seems in no immediate danger."/n/nHarry did as he was told; Dumbledore covered Moody/nin the cloak, tucked it around him, and clambered/nout of the trunk again. Then he picked up the hip/nflask that stood upon the desk, unscrewed it, and/nturned it over. A thick glutinous liquid splattered onto/nthe office floor./n/n"Polyjuice Potion, Harry," said Dumbledore. "You see/nthe simplicity of it, and the brilliance. For Moody/nnever does drink except from his hip flask, he's well/nknown for it. The imposter needed, of course, to keep/nthe real Moody close by, so that he could continue/nmaking the potion. You see his hair ..." Dumbledore/nlooked down on the Moody in the trunk. "The/nimposter has been cutting it off all year, see where it/nis uneven? But I think, in the excitement of tonight,/nour fake Moody might have forgotten to take it as/nfrequently as he should have done ... on the hour . . ./nevery hour. ... We shall see."/n/nDumbledore pulled out the chair at the desk and sat/ndown upon it, his eyes fixed upon the unconscious/nMoody on the floor. Harry stared at him too. Minutes/npassed in silence. .../n/nThen, before Harry's very eyes, the face of the man on/nthe floor began to change. The scars were/ndisappearing, the skin was becoming smooth; the/nmangled nose became whole and started to shrink./nThe long mane of grizzled gray hair was withdrawing/ninto the scalp and turning the color of straw./nSuddenly, with a loud clunk, the wooden leg fell away/nas a normal leg regrew in its place; next moment, the/nmagical eyeball had popped out of the man's face as a/nreal eye replaced it; it rolled away across the floor and/ncontinued to swivel in every direction./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry saw a man lying before him, pale-skinned,/nslightly freckled, with a mop of fair hair. He knew who/nhe was. He had seen him in Dumbledore's Pensieve,/nhad watched him being led away from court by the/ndementors, trying to convince Mr. Crouch that he was/ninnocent . . . but he was lined around the eyes now/nand looked much older. . . ./n/nThere were hurried footsteps outside in the corridor./nSnape had returned with Winky at his heels./n/nProfessor McGonagall was right behind them./n/n"Crouch!" Snape said, stopping dead in the doorway./n"Barty Crouch!"/n/n"Good heavens," said Professor McGonagall, stopping/ndead and staring down at the man on the floor./n/nFilthy, disheveled, Winky peered around Snape's legs./nHer mouth opened wide and she let out a piercing/nshriek./n/n"Master Barty, Master Barty, what is you doing here?"/n/nShe flung herself forward onto the young man's chest./n/n"You is killed him! You is killed him! You is killed/nMaster's son!"/n/n"He is simply Stunned, Winky," said Dumbledore./n"Step aside, please. Severus, you have the potion?"/n/nSnape handed Dumbledore a small glass bottle of/ncompletely clear liquid: the Veritaserum with which/nhe had threatened Harry in class. Dumbledore got up,/nbent over the man on the floor, and pulled him into a/nsitting position against the wall beneath the Foe-/nGlass, in which the reflections of Dumbledore, Snape,/nand McGonagall were still glaring down upon them/n/n/n/n/nall. Winky remained on her knees, trembling, her/nhands over her face. Dumbledore forced the man's/nmouth open and poured three drops inside it. Then/nhe pointed his wand at the man's chest and said,/n"Rennervate."/n/nCrouch's son opened his eyes. His face was slack, his/ngaze unfocused. Dumbledore knelt before him, so that/ntheir faces were level./n/n"Can you hear me?" Dumbledore asked quietly./n/nThe man's eyelids flickered./n/n"Yes," he muttered./n/n"I would like you to tell us," said Dumbledore softly,/n"how you came to be here. How did you escape from/nAzkaban?"/n/nCrouch took a deep, shuddering breath, then began/nto speak in a flat, expressionless voice./n/n"My mother saved me. She knew she was dying. She/npersuaded my father to rescue me as a last favor to/nher. He loved her as he had never loved me. He/nagreed. They came to visit me. They gave me a draft of/nPolyjuice Potion containing one of my mother's hairs./nShe took a draft of Polyjuice Potion containing one of/nmy hairs. We took on each other's appearance."/n/nWinky was shaking her head, trembling./n/n"Say no more, Master Barty, say no more, you is/ngetting your father into trouble!"/n/nBut Crouch took another deep breath and continued/nin the same flat voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The dementors are blind. They sensed one healthy,/none dying person entering Azkaban. They sensed one/nhealthy, one dying person leaving it. My father/nsmuggled me out, disguised as my mother, in case/nany prisoners were watching through their doors./n/n"My mother died a short while afterward in Azkaban./nShe was careful to drink Polyjuice Potion until the/nend. She was buried under my name and bearing my/nappearance. Everyone believed her to be me."/n/nThe man's eyelids flickered./n/n"And what did your father do with you, when he had/ngot you home?" said Dumbledore quietly./n/n"Staged my mother's death. A quiet, private funeral./nThat grave is empty. The house-elf nursed me back to/nhealth. Then I had to be concealed. I had to be/ncontrolled. My father had to use a number of spells to/nsubdue me. When I had recovered my strength, I/nthought only of finding my master ... of returning to/nhis service."/n/n"How did your father subdue you?" said Dumbledore./n/n"The Imperius Curse," Crouch said. "I was under my/nfather's control. I was forced to wear an Invisibility/nCloak day and night. I was always with the house-elf./nShe was my keeper and caretaker. She pitied me. She/npersuaded my father to give me occasional treats./nRewards for my good behavior."/n/n"Master Barty, Master Barty," sobbed Winky through/nher hands. "You isn't ought to tell them, we is getting/nin trouble. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Did anybody ever discover that you were still alive?"/nsaid Dumbledore softly. "Did anyone know except/nyour father and the house-elf?"/n/n"Yes," said Crouch, his eyelids flickering again. "A/nwitch in my father's office. Bertha Jorkins. She came/nto the house with papers for my father's signature. He/nwas not at home. Winky showed her inside and/nreturned to the kitchen, to me. But Bertha Jorkins/nheard Winky talking to me. She came to investigate./nShe heard enough to guess who was hiding under the/nInvisibility Cloak. My father arrived home. She/nconfronted him. He put a very powerful Memory/nCharm on her to make her forget what she'd found/nout. Too powerful. He said it damaged her memory/npermanently."/n/n"Why is she coming to nose into my master's private/nbusiness?" sobbed Winky. "Why isn't she leaving us/nbe?"/n/n"Tell me about the Quidditch World Cup," said/nDumbledore./n/n"Winky talked my father into it," said Crouch, still in/nthe same monotonous voice. "She spent months/npersuading him. I had not left the house for years. I/nhad loved Quidditch. Let him go, she said. He will be/nin his Invisibility Cloak. He can watch. Let him smell/nfresh air for once. She said my mother would have/nwanted it. She told my father that my mother had/ndied to give me freedom. She had not saved me for a/nlife of imprisonment. He agreed in the end./n/n"It was carefully planned. My father led me and Winky/nup to the Top Box early in the day. Winky was to say/nthat she was saving a seat for my father. I was to sit/nthere, invisible. When everyone had left the box, we/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwould emerge. Winky would appear to be alone./nNobody would ever know./n/n"But Winky didn't know that I was growing stronger. I/nwas starting to fight my father's Imperius Curse./n/nThere were times when I was almost myself again./nThere were brief periods when I seemed outside his/ncontrol. It happened, there, in the Top Box. It was like/nwaking from a deep sleep. I found myself out in/npublic, in the middle of the match, and I saw, in front/nof me, a wand sticking out of a boy's pocket. I had not/nbeen allowed a wand since before Azkaban. I stole it./nWinky didn't know. Winky is frightened of heights./n/nShe had her face hidden."/n/n"Master Barty, you bad boy!" whispered Winky, tears/ntrickling between her fingers./n/n"So you took the wand," said Dumbledore, "and what/ndid you do with it?"/n/n"We went back to the tent," said Crouch. "Then we/nheard them. We heard the Death Eaters. The ones/nwho had never been to Azkaban. The ones who had/nnever suffered for my master. They had turned their/nbacks on him. They were not enslaved, as I was. They/nwere free to seek him, but they did not. They were/nmerely making sport of Muggles. The sound of their/nvoices awoke me. My mind was clearer than it had/nbeen in years. I was angry. I had the wand. I wanted/nto attack them for their disloyalty to my master. My/nfather had left the tent; he had gone to free the/nMuggles. Winky was afraid to see me so angry. She/nused her own brand of magic to bind me to her. She/npulled me from the tent, pulled me into the forest,/naway from the Death Eaters. I tried to hold her back. I/nwanted to return to the campsite. I wanted to show/nthose Death Eaters what loyalty to the Dark Lord/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmeant, and to punish them for their lack of it. I used/nthe stolen wand to cast the Dark Mark into the sky./n/n"Ministry wizards arrived. They shot Stunning Spells/neverywhere. One of the spells came through the trees/nwhere Winky and I stood. The bond connecting us/nwas broken. We were both Stunned./n/n"When Winky was discovered, my father knew I must/nbe nearby. He searched the bushes where she had/nbeen found and felt me lying there. He waited until/nthe other Ministry members had left the forest. He put/nme back under the Imperius Curse and took me/nhome. He dismissed Winky. She had failed him. She/nhad let me acquire a wand. She had almost let me/nescape."/n/nWinky let out a wail of despair./n/n"Now it was just Father and I, alone in the house. And/nthen ... and then ..." Crouch's head rolled on his/nneck, and an insane grin spread across his face. "My/nmaster came for me./n/n"He arrived at our house late one night in the arms of/nhis servant Wormtail. My master had found out that I/nwas still alive. He had captured Bertha Jorkins in/nAlbania. He had tortured her. She told him a great/ndeal. She told him about the Triwizard Tournament./nShe told him the old Auror, Moody, was going to teach/nat Hogwarts. He tortured her until he broke through/nthe Memory Charm my father had placed upon her./nShe told him I had escaped from Azkaban. She told/nhim my father kept me imprisoned to prevent me from/nseeking my master. And so my master knew that I/nwas still his faithful servant — perhaps the most/nfaithful of all. My master conceived a plan, based/nupon the information Bertha had given him. He/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nneeded me. He arrived at our house near midnight./n/nMy father answered the door."/n/nThe smile spread wider over Crouch's face, as though/nrecalling the sweetest memory of his life. Winky's/npetrified brown eyes were visible through her fingers./nShe seemed too appalled to speak./n/n"It was very quick. My father was placed under the/nImperius Curse by my master. Now my father was the/none imprisoned, controlled. My master forced him to/ngo about his business as usual, to act as though/nnothing was wrong. And I was released. I awoke. I/nwas myself again, alive as I hadn't been in years."/n/n"And what did Lord Voldemort ask you to do?" said/nDumbledore./n/n"He asked me whether I was ready to risk everything/nfor him. I was ready. It was my dream, my greatest/nambition, to serve him, to prove myself to him. He/ntold me he needed to place a faithful servant at/nHogwarts. A servant who would guide Harry Potter/nthrough the Triwizard Tournament without appearing/nto do so. A servant who would watch over Harry/nPotter. Ensure he reached the Triwizard Cup. Turn/nthe cup into a Portkey, which would take the first/nperson to touch it to my master. But first — "/n/n"You needed Alastor Moody," said Dumbledore. His/nblue eyes were blazing, though his voice remained/ncalm./n/n"Wormtail and I did it. We had prepared the Polyjuice/nPotion beforehand. We journeyed to his house. Moody/nput up a struggle. There was a commotion. We/nmanaged to subdue him just in time. Forced him into/na compartment of his own magical trunk. Took some/nof his hair and added it to the potion. I drank it; I/n/n/n/n/nbecame Moody's double. I took his leg and his eye. I/nwas ready to face Arthur Weasley when he arrived to/nsort out the Muggles who had heard a disturbance. I/nmade the dustbins move around the yard. I told/nArthur Weasley I had heard intruders in my yard,/nwho had set off the dustbins. Then I packed up/nMoody's clothes and Dark detectors, put them in the/ntrunk with Moody, and set off for Hogwarts. I kept/nhim alive, under the Imperius Curse. I wanted to be/nable to question him. To find out about his past, learn/nhis habits, so that I could fool even Dumbledore. I/nalso needed his hair to make the Polyjuice Potion. The/nother ingredients were easy. I stole boom-slang skin/nfrom the dungeons. When the Potions master found/nme in his office, I said I was under orders to search/nit."/n/n"And what became of Wormtail after you attacked/nMoody?" said Dumbledore./n/n"Wormtail returned to care for my master, in my/nfather's house, and to keep watch over my father."/n/n"But your father escaped," said Dumbledore./n/n"Yes. After a while he began to fight the Imperius/nCurse just as I had done. There were periods when he/nknew what was happening. My master decided it was/nno longer safe for my father to leave the house. He/nforced him to send letters to the Ministry instead. He/nmade him write and say he was ill. But Wormtail/nneglected his duty. He was not watchful enough. My/nfather escaped. My master guessed that he was/nheading for Hogwarts. My father was going to tell/nDumbledore everything, to confess. He was going to/nadmit that he had smuggled me from Azkaban./n/n"My master sent me word of my father's escape. He/ntold me to stop him at all costs. So I waited and/n/n/n/n/n/nwatched. I used the map I had taken from Harry/nPotter. The map that had almost mined everything."/n/n"Map?" said Dumbledore quickly. "What map is this?"/n/n"Potter's map of Hogwarts. Potter saw me on it. Potter/nsaw me stealing more ingredients for the Polyjuice/nPotion from Snape's office one night. He thought I was/nmy father. We have the same first name. I took the/nmap from Potter that night. I told him my father/nhated Dark wizards. Potter believed my father was/nafter Snape./n/n"For a week I waited for my father to arrive at/nHogwarts. At last, one evening, the map showed my/nfather entering the grounds. I pulled on my Invisibility/nCloak and went down to meet him. He was walking/naround the edge of the forest. Then Potter came, and/nKrum. I waited. I could not hurt Potter; my master/nneeded him. Potter ran to get Dumbledore. I Stunned/nKrum. I killed my father."/n/n"iVoooo!" wailed Winky. "Master Barty, Master Barty,/nwhat is you saying?"/n/n"You killed your father," Dumbledore said, in the/nsame soft voice. "What did you do with the body?"/n/n"Carried it into the forest. Covered it with the/nInvisibility Cloak. I had the map with me. I watched/nPotter run into the castle. He met Snape. Dumbledore/njoined them. I watched Potter bringing Dumbledore/nout of the castle. I walked back out of the forest,/ndoubled around behind them, went to meet them. I/ntold Dumbledore Snape had told me where to come./n/n"Dumbledore told me to go and look for my father. I/nwent back to my father's body. Watched the map./nWhen everyone was gone, I Transfigured my father's/n/n/n/n/n/nbody. He became a bone ... I buried it, while wearing/nthe Invisibility Cloak, in the freshly dug earth in front/nof Hagrid's cabin."/n/nThere was complete silence now, except for Winky's/ncontinued sobs. Then Dumbledore said, "And tonight/n/n/n/n"I offered to carry the Triwizard Cup into the maze/nbefore dinner," whispered Barty Crouch. "Turned it/ninto a Portkey. My master's plan worked. He is/nreturned to power and I will be honored by him/nbeyond the dreams of wizards."/n/nThe insane smile lit his features once more, and his/nhead drooped onto his shoulder as Winky wailed and/nsobbed at his side./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Parting Of The Ways
text: /nDumbledore stood up. He stared down at Barty/nCrouch for a moment with disgust on his face. Then/nhe raised his wand once more and ropes flew out of it,/nropes that twisted themselves around Barty Crouch,/nbinding him tightly. He turned to Professor/nMcGonagall./n/n"Minerva, could I ask you to stand guard here while I/ntake Harry upstairs?"/n/n"Of course," said Professor McGonagall. She looked/nslightly nauseous, as though she had just watched/nsomeone being sick. However, when she drew out her/nwand and pointed it at Barty Crouch, her hand was/nquite steady./n/n"Severus" — Dumbledore turned to Snape — "please/ntell Madam Pomfrey to come down here; we need to/nget Alastor Moody into the hospital wing. Then go/ndown into the grounds, find Cornelius Fudge, and/nbring him up to this office. He will undoubtedly want/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nto question Crouch himself. Tell him I will be in the/nhospital wing in half an hour's time if he needs me."/n/nSnape nodded silently and swept out of the room./n/n"Harry?" Dumbledore said gently./n/nHarry got up and swayed again; the pain in his leg,/nwhich he had not noticed all the time he had been/nlistening to Crouch, now returned in full measure. He/nalso realized that he was shaking. Dumbledore/ngripped his arm and helped him out into the dark/ncorridor./n/n"I want you to come up to my office first, Harry," he/nsaid quietly as they headed up the passageway./n/n"Sirius is waiting for us there."/n/nHarry nodded. A kind of numbness and a sense of/ncomplete unreality were upon him, but he did not/ncare; he was even glad of it. He didn't want to have to/nthink about anything that had happened since he had/nfirst touched the Triwizard Cup. He didn't want to/nhave to examine the memories, fresh and sharp as/nphotographs, which kept flashing across his mind./nMad-Eye Moody, inside the trunk. Wormtail, slumped/non the ground, cradling his stump of an arm./nVoldemort, rising from the steaming cauldron. Cedric/n. . . dead . . . Cedric, asking to be returned to his/nparents. .../n/n"Professor," Harry mumbled, "where are Mr. and Mrs./nDiggory?"/n/n"They are with Professor Sprout," said Dumbledore./nHis voice, which had been so calm throughout the/ninterrogation of Barty Crouch, shook very slightly for/nthe first time. "She was Head of Cedric's house, and/nknew him best."/n/n/n/n/n/nThey had reached the stone gargoyle. Dumbledore/ngave the password, it sprang aside, and he and Harry/nwent up the moving spiral staircase to the oak door./nDumbledore pushed it open. Sirius was standing/nthere. His face was white and gaunt as it had been/nwhen he had escaped Azkaban. In one swift moment,/nhe had crossed the room./n/n"Harry, are you all right? I knew it — I knew/nsomething like this — what happened?"/n/nHis hands shook as he helped Harry into a chair in/nfront of the desk./n/n"What happened?" he asked more urgently./n/nDumbledore began to tell Sirius everything Barty/nCrouch had said. Harry was only half listening. So/ntired every bone in his body was aching, he wanted/nnothing more than to sit here, undisturbed, for hours/nand hours, until he fell asleep and didn't have to/nthink or feel anymore./n/nThere was a soft rush of wings. Fawkes the phoenix/nhad left his perch, flown across the office, and landed/non Harry's knee./n/n" 'Lo, Fawkes," said Harry quietly. He stroked the/nphoenix's beautiful scarlet-and-gold plumage. Fawkes/nblinked peacefully up at him. There was something/ncomforting about his warm weight./n/nDumbledore stopped talking. He sat down opposite/nHarry, behind his desk. He was looking at Harry, who/navoided his eyes. Dumbledore was going to question/nhim. He was going to make Harry relive everything./n/n"I need to know what happened after you touched the/nPortkey in the maze, Harry," said Dumbledore./n/n/n/n/n/n"We can leave that till morning, can't we,/nDumbledore?" said Sirius harshly. He had put a hand/non Harry's shoulder. "Let him have a sleep. Let him/nrest."/n/nHarry felt a rush of gratitude toward Sirius, but/nDumbledore took no notice of Sirius's words. He/nleaned forward toward Harry. Very unwillingly, Harry/nraised his head and looked into those blue eyes./n/n"If I thought I could help you," Dumbledore said/ngently, "by putting you into an enchanted sleep and/nallowing you to postpone the moment when you/nwould have to think about what has happened/ntonight, I would do it. But I know better. Numbing the/npain for a while will make it worse when you finally/nfeel it. You have shown bravery beyond anything I/ncould have expected of you. I ask you to demonstrate/nyour courage one more time. I ask you to tell us what/nhappened."/n/nThe phoenix let out one soft, quavering note. It/nshivered in the air, and Harry felt as though a drop of/nhot liquid had slipped down his throat into his/nstomach, warming him, and strengthening him./n/nHe took a deep breath and began to tell them. As he/nspoke, visions of everything that had passed that/nnight seemed to rise before his eyes; he saw the/nsparkling surface of the potion that had revived/nVoldemort; he saw the Death Eaters Apparating/nbetween the graves around them; he saw Cedric's/nbody, lying on the ground beside the cup./n/nOnce or twice, Sirius made a noise as though about to/nsay something, his hand still tight on Harry's/nshoulder, but Dumbledore raised his hand to stop/nhim, and Harry was glad of this, because it was easier/nto keep going now he had started. It was even a relief;/n/n/n/n/nhe felt almost as though something poisonous were/nbeing extracted from him. It was costing him every bit/nof determination he had to keep talking, yet he sensed/nthat once he had finished, he would feel better./n/nWhen Harry told of Wormtail piercing his arm with/nthe dagger, however, Sirius let out a vehement/nexclamation and Dumbledore stood up so quickly that/nHarry started. Dumbledore walked around the desk/nand told Harry to stretch out his arm. Harry showed/nthem both the place where his robes were torn and/nthe cut beneath them./n/n"He said my blood would make him stronger than if/nhe'd used someone else's," Harry told Dumbledore./n/n"He said the protection my — my mother left in me —/nhe'd have it too. And he was right — he could touch/nme without hurting himself, he touched my face."/n/nFor a fleeting instant, Harry thought he saw a gleam/nof something like triumph in Dumbledore 's eyes. But/nnext second, Harry was sure he had imagined it, for/nwhen Dumbledore had returned to his seat behind/nthe desk, he looked as old and weary as Harry had/never seen him./n/n"Very well," he said, sitting down again. "Voldemort/nhas overcome that particular barrier. Harry, continue,/nplease."/n/nHarry went on; he explained how Voldemort had/nemerged from the cauldron, and told them all he/ncould remember of Voldemort's speech to the Death/nEaters. Then he told how Voldemort had untied him,/nreturned his wand to him, and prepared to duel./n/nBut when he reached the part where the golden beam/nof light had connected his and Voldemort's wands, he/nfound his throat obstructed. He tried to keep talking,/n/n/n/n/n/nbut the memories of what had come out of/nVoldemort's wand were flooding into his mind. He/ncould see Cedric emerging, see the old man, Bertha/nJorkins ... his father ... his mother .../n/nHe was glad when Sirius broke the silence./n/n"The wands connected?" he said, looking from Harry/nto Dumbledore. "Why?"/n/nHarry looked up at Dumbledore again, on whose face/nthere was an arrested look./n/n"Priori Incantatem," he muttered./n/nHis eyes gazed into Harry's and it was almost as/nthough an invisible beam of understanding shot/nbetween them./n/n"The Reverse Spell effect?" said Sirius sharply./n/n"Exactly," said Dumbledore. "Harry's wand and/nVoldemort's wand share cores. Each of them contains/na feather from the tail of the same phoenix. This/nphoenix, in fact," he added, and he pointed at the/nscarlet-and-gold bird, perching peacefully on Harry's/nknee./n/n"My wand's feather came from Fawkes?" Harry said,/namazed./n/n"Yes," said Dumbledore. "Mr. Ollivander wrote to tell/nme you had bought the second wand, the moment/nyou left his shop four years ago."/n/n"So what happens when a wand meets its brother?"/nsaid Sirius./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They will not work properly against each other," said/nDumbledore. "If, however, the owners of the wands/nforce the wands to do battle ... a very rare effect will/ntake place. One of the wands will force the other to/nregurgitate spells it has performed — in reverse. The/nmost recent first ... and then those which preceded it./n/n/n/nHe looked interrogatively at Harry, and Harry nodded./n/n"Which means," said Dumbledore slowly, his eyes/nupon Harry's face, "that some form of Cedric must/nhave reappeared."/n/nHarry nodded again./n/n"Diggory came back to life?" said Sirius sharply./n/n"No spell can reawaken the dead," said Dumbledore/nheavily. "All that would have happened is a kind of/nreverse echo. A shadow of the living Cedric would/nhave emerged from the wand . . . am I correct, Harry?"/n/n"He spoke to me," Harry said. He was suddenly/nshaking again. "The ... the ghost Cedric, or whatever/nhe was, spoke."/n/n"An echo," said Dumbledore, "which retained Cedric's/nappearance and character. I am guessing other such/nforms appeared ... less recent victims of Voldemort's/nwand. ..."/n/n"An old man," Harry said, his throat still constricted./n"Bertha Jorkins. And ..."/n/n"Your parents?" said Dumbledore quietly./n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSirius's grip on Harry's shoulder was now so tight it/nwas painful./n/n"The last murders the wand performed," said/nDumbledore, nodding. "In reverse order. More would/nhave appeared, of course, had you maintained the/nconnection. Very well, Harry, these echoes, these/nshadows . . . what did they do?"/n/nHarry described how the figures that had emerged/nfrom the wand had prowled the edges of the golden/nweb, how Voldemort had seemed to fear them, how/nthe shadow of Harry's father had told him what to do,/nhow Cedric's had made its final request./n/nAt this point, Harry found he could not continue. He/nlooked around at Sirius and saw that he had his face/nin his hands./n/nHarry suddenly became aware that Fawkes had left/nhis knee. The phoenix had fluttered to the floor. It/nwas resting its beautiful head against Harry's injured/nleg, and thick, pearly tears were falling from its eyes/nonto the wound left by the spider. The pain vanished./nThe skin mended. His leg was repaired./n/n"I will say it again," said Dumbledore as the phoenix/nrose into the air and resettled itself upon the perch/nbeside the door. "You have shown bravery beyond/nanything I could have expected of you tonight, Harry./nYou have shown bravery equal to those who died/nfighting Voldemort at the height of his powers. You/nhave shouldered a grown wizard's burden and found/nyourself equal to it — and you have now given us all/nthat we have a right to expect. You will come with me/nto the hospital wing. I do not want you returning to/nthe dormitory tonight. A Sleeping Potion, and some/npeace ... Sirius, would you like to stay with him?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSirius nodded and stood up. He transformed back/ninto the great black dog and walked with Harry and/nDumbledore out of the office, accompanying them/ndown a flight of stairs to the hospital wing./n/nWhen Dumbledore pushed open the door, Harry saw/nMrs. Weasley, Bill, Ron, and Hermione grouped/naround a harassed-looking Madam Pomfrey. They/nappeared to be demanding to know where Harry was/nand what had happened to him. All of them whipped/naround as Harry, Dumbledore, and the black dog/nentered, and Mrs. Weasley let out a kind of muffled/nscream./n/n"Harry! Oh Harry!"/n/nShe started to hurry toward him, but Dumbledore/nmoved between them./n/n"Molly," he said, holding up a hand, "please listen to/nme for a moment. Harry has been through a terrible/nordeal tonight. He has just had to relive it for me./nWhat he needs now is sleep, and peace, and quiet. If/nhe would like you all to stay with him," he added,/nlooking around at Ron, Hermione, and Bill too, "you/nmay do so. But I do not want you questioning him/nuntil he is ready to answer, and certainly not this/nevening."/n/nMrs. Weasley nodded. She was very white. She/nrounded on Ron, Hermione, and Bill as though they/nwere being noisy, and hissed, "Did you hear? He/nneeds quiet!"/n/n"Headmaster," said Madam Pomfrey, staring at the/ngreat black dog that was Sirius, "may I ask what — ?"/n/n"This dog will be remaining with Harry for a while,"/nsaid Dumbledore simply. "I assure you, he is/n/n/n/n/n/nextremely well trained. Harry — I will wait while you/nget into bed."/n/nHarry felt an inexpressible sense of gratitude to/nDumbledore for asking the others not to question/nhim. It wasn't as though he didn't want them there;/nbut the thought of explaining it all over again, the/nidea of reliving it one more time, was more than he/ncould stand./n/n"I will be back to see you as soon as I have met with/nFudge, Harry," said Dumbledore. "I would like you to/nremain here tomorrow until I have spoken to the/nschool." He left./n/nAs Madam Pomfrey led Harry to a nearby bed, he/ncaught sight of the real Moody lying motionless in a/nbed at the far end of the room. His wooden leg and/nmagical eye were lying on the bedside table./n/n"Is he okay?" Harry asked./n/n"He'll be fine," said Madam Pomfrey, giving Harry/nsome pajamas and pulling screens around him. He/ntook off his robes, pulled on the pajamas, and got into/nbed. Ron, Hermione, Bill, Mrs. Weasley, and the black/ndog came around the screen and settled themselves/nin chairs on either side of him. Ron and Hermione/nwere looking at him almost cautiously, as though/nscared of him./n/n"I'm all right," he told them. "Just tired."/n/nMrs. Weasley's eyes filled with tears as she smoothed/nhis bedcovers unnecessarily./n/nMadam Pomfrey, who had bustled off to her office,/nreturned holding a small bottle of some purple potion/nand a goblet./n/n/n/n/n/n"You'll need to drink all of this, Harry," she said. "It's/na potion for dreamless sleep."/n/nHarry took the goblet and drank a few mouthfuls. He/nfelt himself becoming drowsy at once. Everything/naround him became hazy; the lamps around the/nhospital wing seemed to be winking at him in a/nfriendly way through the screen around his bed; his/nbody felt as though it was sinking deeper into the/nwarmth of the feather matress. Before he could finish/nthe potion, before he could say another word, his/nexhaustion had carried him off to sleep./n/nHarry woke up, so warm, so very sleepy, that he/ndidn't open his eyes, wanting to drop off again. The/nroom was still dimly lit; he was sure it was still/nnighttime and had a feeling that he couldn't have/nbeen asleep very long./n/nThen he heard whispering around him./n/n"They'll wake him if they don't shut up!"/n/n"What are they shouting about? Nothing else can/nhave happened, can it?"/n/nHarry opened his eyes blearily Someone had removed/nhis glasses. He could see the fuzzy outlines of Mrs./nWeasley and Bill close by. Mrs. Weasley was on her/nfeet./n/n"That's Fudge's voice," she whispered. "And that's/nMinerva McGonagall's, isn't it? But what are they/narguing about?"/n/nNow Harry could hear them too: people shouting and/nrunning toward the hospital wing./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Regrettable, but all the same, Minerva — " Cornelius/nFudge was saying loudly./n/n"You should never have brought it inside the castle!"/nyelled Professor McGonagall. "When Dumbledore/nfinds out — "/n/nHarry heard the hospital doors burst open. Unnoticed/nby any of the people around his bed, all of whom were/nstaring at the door as Bill pulled back the screens,/nHarry sat up and put his glasses back on./n/nFudge came striding up the ward. Professors/nMcGonagall and Snape were at his heels./n/n"Where's Dumbledore?" Fudge demanded of Mrs./nWeasley./n/n"He's not here," said Mrs. Weasley angrily. "This is a/nhospital wing, Minister, don't you think you'd do/nbetter to — "/n/nBut the door opened, and Dumbledore came sweeping/nup the ward./n/n"What has happened?" said Dumbledore sharply,/nlooking from Fudge to Professor McGonagall. "Why/nare you disturbing these people? Minerva, I'm/nsurprised at you — I asked you to stand guard over/nBarty Crouch — "/n/n"There is no need to stand guard over him anymore,/nDumbledore!" she shrieked. "The Minister has seen to/nthat!"/n/nHarry had never seen Professor McGonagall lose/ncontrol like this. There were angry blotches of color in/nher cheeks, and her hands were balled into fists; she/nwas trembling with fury./n/n/n/n/n/n"When we told Mr. Fudge that we had caught the/nDeath Eater responsible for tonight's events," said/nSnape, in a low voice, "he seemed to feel his personal/nsafety was in question. He insisted on summoning a/ndementor to accompany him into the castle. He/nbrought it up to the office where Barty Crouch — "/n/n"I told him you would not agree, Dumbledore!"/nProfessor McGonagall fumed. "I told him you would/nnever allow dementors to set foot inside the castle,/nbut — "/n/n"My dear woman!" roared Fudge, who likewise looked/nangrier than Harry had ever seen him, "as Minister of/nMagic, it is my decision whether I wish to bring/nprotection with me when interviewing a possibly/ndangerous — "/n/nBut Professor McGonagall's voice drowned Fudge's./n/n"The moment that — that thing entered the room,"/nshe screamed, pointing at Fudge, trembling all over,/n"it swooped down on Crouch and — and — "/n/nHarry felt a chill in his stomach as Professor/nMcGonagall struggled to find words to describe what/nhad happened. He did not need her to finish her/nsentence. He knew what the dementor must have/ndone. It had administered its fatal kiss to Barty/nCrouch. It had sucked his soul out through his/nmouth. He was worse than dead./n/n"By all accounts, he is no loss!" blustered Fudge. "It/nseems he has been responsible for several deaths!"/n/n"But he cannot now give testimony, Cornelius," said/nDumbledore. He was staring hard at Fudge, as/nthough seeing him plainly for the first time. "He/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncannot give evidence about why he killed those/npeople."/n/n/n/n"Why he killed them? Well, that's no mystery, is it?"/nblustered Fudge. "He was a raving lunatic! From what/nMinerva and Severus have told me, he seems to have/nthought he was doing it all on You-Know- Who's/ninstructions!"/n/n"Lord Voldemort was giving him instructions,/nCornelius," Dumbledore said. "Those people's deaths/nwere mere by-products of a plan to restore Voldemort/nto full strength again. The plan succeeded. Voldemort/nhas been restored to his body."/n/nFudge looked as though someone had just swung a/nheavy weight into his face. Dazed and blinking, he/nstared back at Dumbledore as if he couldn't quite/nbelieve what he had just heard. He began to sputter,/nstill goggling at Dumbledore./n/n"You-Know- Who ... returned? Preposterous. Come/nnow, Dumbledore ..."/n/n"As Minerva and Severus have doubtless told you,"/nsaid Dumbledore, "we heard Barry Crouch confess./nUnder the influence of Veritaserum, he told us how/nhe was smuggled out of Azkaban, and how Voldemort/n— learning of his continued existence from Bertha/nJorkins — went to free him from his father and used/nhim to capture Harry. The plan worked, I tell you./nCrouch has helped Voldemort to return."/n/n"See here, Dumbledore," said Fudge, and Harry was/nastonished to see a slight smile dawning on his face,/n"you — you can't seriously believe that. You-Know-/nWho — back? Come now, come now . . . certainly,/nCrouch may have believed himself to be acting upon/n/n/n/n/n/nYou-Know- Who's orders — but to take the word of a/nlunatic like that, Dumbledore ..."/n/n"When Harry touched the Triwizard Cup tonight, he/nwas transported straight to Voldemort," said/nDumbledore steadily. "He witnessed Lord Voldemort's/nrebirth. I will explain it all to you if you will step up to/nmy office."/n/nDumbledore glanced around at Harry and saw that he/nwas awake, but shook his head and said, "I am afraid/nI cannot permit you to question Harry tonight."/n/nFudge's curious smile lingered. He too glanced at/nHarry, then looked back at Dumbledore, and said,/n"You are — er — prepared to take Harry's word on/nthis, are you, Dumbledore?"/n/nThere was a moment's silence, which was broken by/nSirius growling. His hackles were raised, and he was/nbaring his teeth at Fudge./n/n"Certainly, I believe Harry," said Dumbledore. His/neyes were blazing now. "I heard Crouch's confession,/nand I heard Harry's account of what happened after/nhe touched the Triwizard Cup; the two stories make/nsense, they explain everything that has happened/nsince Bertha Jorkins disappeared last summer."/n/nFudge still had that strange smile on his face. Once/nagain, he glanced at Harry before answering./n/n"You are prepared to believe that Lord Voldemort has/nreturned, on the word of a lunatic murderer, and a/nboy who ... well ..."/n/nFudge shot Harry another look, and Harry suddenly/nunderstood./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You've been reading Rita Skeeter, Mr. Fudge," he/nsaid quietly./n/nRon, Hermione, Mrs. Weasley, and Bill all jumped./nNone of them had realized that Harry was awake./n/nFudge reddened slightly, but a defiant and obstinate/nlook came over his face./n/n"And if I have?" he said, looking at Dumbledore. "If I/nhave discovered that you've been keeping certain facts/nabout the boy very quiet? A Parselmouth, eh? And/nhaving funny turns all over the place — "/n/n"I assume that you are referring to the pains Harry/nhas been experiencing in his scar?" said Dumbledore/ncoolly./n/n"You admit that he has been having these pains,/nthen?" said Fudge quickly. "Headaches? Nightmares?/nPossibly — hallucinations?"/n/n"Listen to me, Cornelius," said Dumbledore, taking a/nstep toward Fudge, and once again, he seemed to/nradiate that indefinable sense of power that Harry/nhad felt after Dumbledore had Stunned young/nCrouch. "Harry is as sane as you or I. That scar upon/nhis forehead has not addled his brains. I believe it/nhurts him when Lord Voldemort is close by, or feeling/nparticularly murderous."/n/nFudge had taken half a step back from Dumbledore,/nbut he looked no less stubborn./n/n"You'll forgive me, Dumbledore, but I've never heard/nof a curse scar acting as an alarm bell before. ..."/n/n"Look, I saw Voldemort come back!" Harry shouted./n/nHe tried to get out of bed again, but Mrs. Weasley/n/n/n/n/n/nforced him back. "I saw the Death Eaters! I can give/nyou their names! Lucius Malfoy — "/n/nSnape made a sudden movement, but as Harry/nlooked at him, Snape's eyes flew back to Fudge./n/n"Malfoy was cleared!" said Fudge, visibly affronted. "A/nvery old family — donations to excellent causes — "/n/n"Macnair!" Harry continued./n/n"Also cleared! Now working for the Ministry!"/n/n"Avery — Nott — Crabbe — Goyle — "/n/n"You are merely repeating the names of those who/nwere acquitted of being Death Eaters thirteen years/nago!" said Fudge angrily. "You could have found those/nnames in old reports of the trials! For heaven's sake,/nDumbledore — the boy was full of some crackpot/nstory at the end of last year too — his tales are getting/ntaller, and you're still swallowing them — the boy can/ntalk to snakes, Dumbledore, and you still think he's/ntrustworthy?"/n/n"You fool!" Professor McGonagall cried. "Cedric/nDiggory! Mr. Crouch! These deaths were not the/nrandom work of a lunatic!"/n/n"I see no evidence to the contrary!" shouted Fudge,/nnow matching her anger, his face purpling. "It seems/nto me that you are all determined to start a panic that/nwill destabilize everything we have worked for these/nlast thirteen years!"/n/nHarry couldn't believe what he was hearing. He had/nalways thought of Fudge as a kindly figure, a little/nblustering, a little pompous, but essentially good-/nnatured. But now a short, angry wizard stood before/n/n/n/n/n/nhim, refusing, point-blank, to accept the prospect of/ndisruption in his comfortable and ordered world — to/nbelieve that Voldemort could have risen./n/n"Voldemort has returned," Dumbledore repeated. "If/nyou accept that fact straightaway, Fudge, and take/nthe necessary measures, we may still be able to save/nthe situation. The first and most essential step is to/nremove Azkaban from the control of the dementors — "/n/n"Preposterous!" shouted Fudge again. "Remove the/ndementors? I'd be kicked out of office for suggesting/nit! Half of us only feel safe in our beds at night/nbecause we know the dementors are standing guard/nat Azkaban!"/n/n"The rest of us sleep less soundly in our beds,/nCornelius, knowing that you have put Lord/nVoldemort 's most dangerous supporters in the care of/ncreatures who will join him the instant he asks them!"/nsaid Dumbledore. "They will not remain loyal to you,/nFudge! Voldemort can offer them much more scope/nfor their powers and their pleasures than you can!/nWith the dementors behind him, and his old/nsupporters returned to him, you will be hard-pressed/nto stop him regaining the sort of power he had/nthirteen years ago!"/n/nFudge was opening and closing his mouth as though/nno words could express his outrage./n/n"The second step you must take — and at once,"/nDumbledore pressed on, "is to send envoys to the/ngiants."/n/n"Envoys to the giants?" Fudge shrieked, finding his/ntongue again. "What madness is this?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Extend them the hand of friendship, now, before it is/ntoo late," said Dumbledore, "or Voldemort will/npersuade them, as he did before, that he alone among/nwizards will give them their rights and their freedom!"/n/n"You — you cannot be serious!" Fudge gasped,/nshaking his head and retreating further from/nDumbledore. "If the magical community got wind that/nI had approached the giants — people hate them,/nDumbledore — end of my career — "/n/n"You are blinded," said Dumbledore, his voice rising/nnow, the aura of power around him palpable, his eyes/nblazing once more, "by the love of the office you hold,/nCornelius! You place too much importance, and you/nalways have done, on the so-called purity of blood!/n/nYou fail to recognize that it matters not what someone/nis born, but what they grow to be! Your dementor has/njust destroyed the last remaining member of a pure-/nblood family as old as any — and see what that man/nchose to make of his life! I tell you now — take the/nsteps I have suggested, and you will be remembered,/nin office or out, as one of the bravest and greatest/nMinisters of Magic we have ever known. Fail to act —/nand history will remember you as the man who/nstepped aside and allowed Voldemort a second chance/nto destroy the world we have tried to rebuild!"/n/n"Insane," whispered Fudge, still backing away. "Mad/n/n/n/nAnd then there was silence. Madam Pomfrey was/nstanding frozen at the foot of Harry's bed, her hands/nover her mouth. Mrs. Weasley was still standing over/nHarry, her hand on his shoulder to prevent him from/nrising. Bill, Ron, and Hermione were staring at Fudge./n/n"If your determination to shut your eyes will carry you/nas far as this, Cornelius," said Dumbledore, "we have/n/n/n/n/n/nreached a parting of the ways. You must act as you/nsee fit. And I — I shall act as I see fit."/n/nDumbledore 's voice carried no hint of a threat; it/nsounded like a mere statement, but Fudge bristled as/nthough Dumbledore were advancing upon him with a/nwand./n/n"Now, see here, Dumbledore," he said, waving a/nthreatening finger. "I've given you free rein, always./n/nI've had a lot of respect for you. I might not have/nagreed with some of your decisions, but I've kept/nquiet. There aren't many who'd have let you hire/nwerewolves, or keep Hagrid, or decide what to teach/nyour students without reference to the Ministry. But if/nyou're going to work against me — "/n/n"The only one against whom I intend to work," said/nDumbledore, "is Lord Voldemort. If you are against/nhim, then we remain, Cornelius, on the same side."/n/nIt seemed Fudge could think of no answer to this. He/nrocked backward and forward on his small feet for a/nmoment and spun his bowler hat in his hands./n/nFinally, he said, with a hint of a plea in his voice, "He/ncan't be back, Dumbledore, he just can't be ..."/n/nSnape strode forward, past Dumbledore, pulling up/nthe left sleeve of his robes as he went. He stuck out/nhis forearm and showed it to Fudge, who recoiled./n/n"There," said Snape harshly. "There. The Dark Mark./n/nIt is not as clear as it was an hour or so ago, when it/nburned black, but you can still see it. Every Death/nEater had the sign burned into him by the Dark Lord./nIt was a means of distinguishing one another, and his/nmeans of summoning us to him. When he touched/nthe Mark of any Death Eater, we were to Disapparate,/nand Apparate, instantly, at his side. This Mark has/n/n/n/n/nbeen growing clearer all year. Karkaroff's too. Why do/nyou think Karkaroff fled tonight? We both felt the/nMark burn. We both knew he had returned. Karkaroff/nfears the Dark Lord's vengeance. He betrayed too/nmany of his fellow Death Eaters to be sure of a/nwelcome back into the fold."/n/nFudge stepped back from Snape too. He was shaking/nhis head. He did not seem to have taken in a word/nSnape had said. He stared, apparently repelled by the/nugly mark on Snape 's arm, then looked up at/nDumbledore and whispered, "I don't know what you/nand your staff are playing at, Dumbledore, but I have/nheard enough. I have no more to add. I will be in/ntouch with you tomorrow, Dumbledore, to discuss the/nrunning of this school. I must return to the Ministry."/n/nHe had almost reached the door when he paused. He/nturned around, strode back down the dormitory, and/nstopped at Harry's bed./n/n"Your winnings," he said shortly, taking a large bag of/ngold out of his pocket and dropping it onto Harry's/nbedside table. "One thousand Galleons. There should/nhave been a presentation ceremony, but under the/ncircumstances ..."/n/nHe crammed his bowler hat onto his head and walked/nout of the room, slamming the door behind him. The/nmoment he had disappeared, Dumbledore turned to/nlook at the group around Harry's bed./n/n"There is work to be done," he said. "Molly ... am I/nright in thinking that I can count on you and/nArthur?"/n/n"Of course you can," said Mrs. Weasley. She was/nwhite to the lips, but she looked resolute. "We know/nwhat Fudge is. It's Arthur's fondness for Muggles that/n/n/n/n/n/nhas held him back at the Ministry all these years./nFudge thinks he lacks proper wizarding pride."/n/n"Then I need to send a message to Arthur," said/nDumbledore. "All those that we can persuade of the/ntruth must be notified immediately, and he is well/nplaced to contact those at the Ministry who are not as/nshortsighted as Cornelius."/n/n"Ill go to Dad," said Bill, standing up. "Ill go now."/n/n"Excellent," said Dumbledore. "Tell him what has/nhappened. Tell him I will be in direct contact with him/nshortly. He will need to be discreet, however. If Fudge/nthinks I am interfering at the Ministry — "/n/n"Leave it to me," said Bill./n/nHe clapped a hand on Harry's shoulder, kissed his/nmother on the cheek, pulled on his cloak, and strode/nquickly from the room./n/n"Minerva," said Dumbledore, turning to Professor/nMcGonagall, "I want to see Hagrid in my office as/nsoon as possible. Also — if she will consent to come —/nMadame Maxime."/n/nProfessor McGonagall nodded and left without a word./n/n"Poppy," Dumbledore said to Madam Pomfrey, "would/nyou be very kind and go down to Professor Moody's/noffice, where I think you will find a house-elf called/nWinky in considerable distress? Do what you can for/nher, and take her back to the kitchens. I think Dobby/nwill look after her for us."/n/n"Very — very well," said Madam Pomfrey, looking/nstartled, and she too left./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore made sure that the door was closed, and/nthat Madam Pomfrey's footsteps had died away,/nbefore he spoke again./n/n"And now," he said, "it is time for two of our number/nto recognize each other for what they are. Sirius ... if/nyou could resume your usual form."/n/nThe great black dog looked up at Dumbledore, then,/nin an instant, turned back into a man./n/nMrs. Weasley screamed and leapt back from the bed./n/n"Sirius Black!" she shrieked, pointing at him./n/n"Mum, shut up!" Ron yelled. "It's okay!"/n/nSnape had not yelled or jumped backward, but the/nlook on his face was one of mingled fury and horror./n/n"Him!" he snarled, staring at Sirius, whose face/nshowed equal dislike. "What is he doing here?"/n/n"He is here at my invitation," said Dumbledore,/nlooking between them, "as are you, Severus. I trust/nyou both. It is time for you to lay aside your old/ndifferences and trust each other."/n/nHarry thought Dumbledore was asking for a near/nmiracle. Sirius and Snape were eyeing each other/nwith the utmost loathing./n/n"I will settle, in the short term," said Dumbledore,/nwith a bite of impatience in his voice, "for a lack of/nopen hostility. You will shake hands. You are on the/nsame side now. Time is short, and unless the few of/nus who know the truth do not stand united, there is/nno hope for any of us."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nVery slowly — but still glaring at each other as/nthough each wished the other nothing but ill — Sirius/nand Snape moved toward each other and shook/nhands. They let go extremely quickly./n/n"That will do to be going on with," said Dumbledore,/nstepping between them once more. "Now I have work/nfor each of you. Fudge's attitude, though not/nunexpected, changes everything. Sirius, I need you to/nset off at once. You are to alert Remus Lupin, Arabella/nFigg, Mundungus Fletcher — the old crowd. Lie low at/nLupins for a while; I will contact you there."/n/n"But — " said Harry./n/nHe wanted Sirius to stay. He did not want to have to/nsay goodbye again so quickly./n/n"You'll see me very soon, Harry," said Sirius, turning/nto him. "I promise you. But I must do what I can, you/nunderstand, don't you?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "Yeah ... of course I do."/n/nSirius grasped his hand briefly, nodded to/nDumbledore, transformed again into the black dog,/nand ran the length of the room to the door, whose/nhandle he turned with a paw. Then he was gone./n/n"Severus," said Dumbledore, turning to Snape, "you/nknow what I must ask you to do. If you are ready ... if/nyou are prepared ..."/n/n"I am," said Snape./n/nHe looked slightly paler than usual, and his cold,/nblack eyes glittered strangely./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Then good luck," said Dumbledore, and he watched,/nwith a trace of apprehension on his face, as Snape/nswept wordlessly after Sirius./n/nIt was several minutes before Dumbledore spoke/nagain./n/n"I must go downstairs," he said finally. "I must see the/nDiggorys. Harry — take the rest of your potion. I will/nsee all of you later."/n/nHarry slumped back against his pillows as/nDumbledore disappeared. Hermione, Ron, and Mrs./nWeasley were all looking at him. None of them spoke/nfor a very long time./n/n"You've got to take the rest of your potion, Harry,"/n/nMrs. Weasley said at last. Her hand nudged the sack/nof gold on his bedside cabinet as she reached for the/nbottle and the goblet. "You have a good long sleep. Try/nand think about something else for a while . . . think/nabout what you're going to buy with your winnings!"/n/n"I don't want that gold," said Harry in an/nexpressionless voice. "You have it. Anyone can have/nit. I shouldn't have won it. It should've been Cedric's."/n/nThe thing against which he had been fighting on and/noff ever since he had come out of the maze was/nthreatening to overpower him. He could feel a/nburning, prickling feeling in the inner corners of his/neyes. He blinked and stared up at the ceiling./n/n"It wasn't your fault, Harry," Mrs. Weasley whispered./n/n"I told him to take the cup with me," said Harry./n/nNow the burning feeling was in his throat too. He/nwished Ron would look away./n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley set the potion down on the bedside/ncabinet, bent down, and put her arms around Harry./nHe had no memory of ever being hugged like this, as/nthough by a mother. The full weight of everything he/nhad seen that night seemed to fall in upon him as/nMrs. Weasley held him to her. His mother's face, his/nfather's voice, the sight of Cedric, dead on the ground/nall started spinning in his head until he could hardly/nbear it, until he was screwing up his face against the/nhowl of misery fighting to get out of him./n/nThere was a loud slamming noise, and Mrs. Weasley/nand Harry broke apart. Hermione was standing by the/nwindow. She was holding something tight in her/nhand./n/n"Sorry," she whispered./n/n"Your potion, Harry," said Mrs. Weasley quickly,/nwiping her eyes on the back of her hand./n/nHarry drank it in one gulp. The effect was/ninstantaneous. Heavy, irresistible waves of dreamless/nsleep broke over him; he fell back onto his pillows and/nthought no more./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Beginning
text: /nWhen he looked back, even a month later, Harry/nfound he had only scattered memories of the next few/ndays. It was as though he had been through too much/nto take in any more. The recollections he did have/nwere very painful. The worst, perhaps, was the/nmeeting with the Diggorys that took place the/nfollowing morning./n/nThey did not blame him for what had happened; on/nthe contrary, both thanked him for returning Cedric's/nbody to them. Mr. Diggory sobbed through most of/nthe interview. Mrs. Diggory 's grief seemed to be/nbeyond tears./n/n"He suffered very little then," she said, when Harry/nhad told her how Cedric had died. "And after all,/n/nAmos ... he died just when he'd won the tournament./nHe must have been happy."/n/nWhen they got to their feet, she looked down at Harry/nand said, "You look after yourself, now."/n/n/n/n/nHarry seized the sack of gold on the bedside table./n/n"You take this," he muttered to her. "It should've been/nCedric's, he got there first, you take it — "/n/nBut she backed away from him./n/n"Oh no, it's yours, dear, I couldn't ... you keep it."/n/nHarry returned to Gryffindor Tower the following/nevening. From what Hermione and Ron told him,/nDumbledore had spoken to the school that morning/nat breakfast. He had merely requested that they leave/nHarry alone, that nobody ask him questions or badger/nhim to tell the story of what had happened in the/nmaze. Most people, he noticed, were skirting him in/nthe corridors, avoiding his eyes. Some whispered/nbehind their hands as he passed. He guessed that/nmany of them had believed Rita Skeeter's article/nabout how disturbed and possibly dangerous he was./nPerhaps they were formulating their own theories/nabout how Cedric had died. He found he didn't care/nvery much. He liked it best when he was with Ron/nand Hermione and they were talking about other/nthings, or else letting him sit in silence while they/nplayed chess. He felt as though all three of them had/nreached an understanding they didn't need to put/ninto words; that each was waiting for some sign, some/nword, of what was going on outside Hogwarts — and/nthat it was useless to speculate about what might be/ncoming until they knew anything for certain. The only/ntime they touched upon the subject was when Ron/ntold Harry about a meeting Mrs. Weasley had had/nwith Dumbledore before going home./n/n"She went to ask him if you could come straight to us/nthis summer," he said. "But he wants you to go back/nto the Dursleys, at least at first."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Why?" said Harry./n/n"She said Dumbledore's got his reasons," said Ron,/nshaking his head darkly. "I suppose we've got to trust/nhim, haven't we?"/n/nThe only person apart from Ron and Hermione that/nHarry felt able to talk to was Hagrid. As there was no/nlonger a Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher, they/nhad those lessons free. They used the one on/nThursday afternoon to go down and visit Hagrid in his/ncabin. It was a bright and sunny day; Fang bounded/nout of the open door as they approached, barking and/nwagging his tail madly./n/n"Who's that?" called Hagrid, coming to the door./n/n" Harry\"/n/nHe strode out to meet them, pulled Harry into a one-/narmed hug, ruffled his hair, and said, "Good ter see/nyeh, mate. Good ter see yeh."/n/nThey saw two bucket-size cups and saucers on the/nwooden table in front of the fireplace when they/nentered Hagrid 's cabin./n/n"Bin havin' a cuppa with Olympe," Hagrid said. "She's/njus' left."/n/n"Who?" said Ron curiously./n/n"Madame Maxime, o' course!" said Hagrid./n/n"You two made up, have you?" said Ron./n/n"Dunno what yeh're talkin' about," said Hagrid airily,/nfetching more cups from the dresser. When he had/nmade tea and offered around a plate of doughy/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncookies, he leaned back in his chair and surveyed/nHarry closely through his beetle-black eyes./n/n"You all righ'?" he said gruffly./n/n"Yeah," said Harry./n/n"No, yeh're not," said Hagrid. " 'Course yeh're not. But/nyeh will be."/n/nHarry said nothing./n/n"Knew he was goin' ter come back," said Hagrid, and/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione looked up at him, shocked./n"Known it fer years, Harry. Knew he was out there,/nbidin' his time. It had ter happen. Well, now it has,/nan' we'll jus' have ter get on with it. We'll fight. Migh'/nbe able ter stop him before he gets a good hold. That's/nDumbledore's plan, anyway. Great man, Dumbledore./n'S long as we've got him, I'm not too worried."/n/nHagrid raised his bushy eyebrows at the disbelieving/nexpressions on their faces./n/n"No good sittin' worryin' abou' it," he said. "What's/ncornin' will come, an' we'll meet it when it does./nDumbledore told me wha' you did, Harry."/n/nHagrid's chest swelled as he looked at Harry./n/n"Yeh did as much as yer father would've done, an' I/ncan' give yeh no higher praise than that."/n/nHarry smiled back at him. It was the first time he'd/nsmiled in days. "What's Dumbledore asked you to do,/nHagrid?" he asked. "He sent Professor McGonagall to/nask you and Madame Maxime to meet him — that/nnight."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Got a little job fer me over the summer," said Hagrid./n"Secret, though. I'm not s'pposed ter talk abou' it, no,/nnot even ter you lot. Olympe — Madame Maxime ter/nyou — might be cornin' with me. I think she will./nThink I got her persuaded."/n/n"Is it to do with Voldemort?"/n/nHagrid flinched at the sound of the name./n/n"Migh' be," he said evasively. "Now ... who'd like ter/ncome an' visit the las' skrewt with me? I was jokin' —/njokin'!" he added hastily, seeing the looks on their/nfaces./n/n/n/nk k k/n/n/n/nIt was with a heavy heart that Harry packed his trunk/nup in the dormitory on the night before his return to/nPrivet Drive. He was dreading the Leaving Feast,/nwhich was usually a cause for celebration, when the/nwinner of the Inter-House Championship would be/nannounced. He had avoided being in the Great Hall/nwhen it was full ever since he had left the hospital/nwing, preferring to eat when it was nearly empty to/navoid the stares of his fellow students./n/nWhen he, Ron, and Hermione entered the Hall, they/nsaw at once that the usual decorations were missing./nThe Great Hall was normally decorated with the/nwinning House's colors for the Leaving Feast. Tonight,/nhowever, there were black drapes on the wall behind/nthe teachers' table. Harry knew instantly that they/nwere there as a mark of respect to Cedric./n/nThe real Mad-Eye Moody was at the staff table now,/nhis wooden leg and his magical eye back in place. He/nwas extremely twitchy, jumping every time someone/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nspoke to him. Harry couldn't blame him; Moody's fear/nof attack was bound to have been increased by his/nten-month imprisonment in his own trunk. Professor/nKarkaroff's chair was empty. Harry wondered, as he/nsat down with the other Gryffindors, where Karkaroff/nwas now, and whether Voldemort had caught up with/nhim./n/nMadame Maxime was still there. She was sitting next/nto Hagrid. They were talking quietly together. Further/nalong the table, sitting next to Professor McGonagall,/nwas Snape. His eyes lingered on Harry for a moment/nas Harry looked at him. His expression was difficult to/nread. He looked as sour and unpleasant as ever./n/nHarry continued to watch him, long after Snape had/nlooked away./n/nWhat was it that Snape had done on Dumbledore's/norders, the night that Voldemort had returned? And/nwhy ... why ... was Dumbledore so convinced that/nSnape was truly on their side? He had been their spy,/nDumbledore had said so in the Pensieve. Snape had/nturned spy against Voldemort, "at great personal/nrisk." Was that the job he had taken up again?
