Had/nhe made contact with the Death Eaters, perhaps?/nPretended that he had never really gone over to/nDumbledore, that he had been, like Voldemort/nhimself, biding his time?/n/nHarry's musings were ended by Professor/nDumbledore, who stood up at the staff table. The/nGreat Hall, which in any case had been less noisy/nthan it usually was at the Leaving Feast, became very/nquiet./n/n"The end," said Dumbledore, looking around at them/nall, "of another year."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe paused, and his eyes fell upon the Hufflepuff/ntable. Theirs had been the most subdued table before/nhe had gotten to his feet, and theirs were still the/nsaddest and palest faces in the Hall./n/n"There is much that I would like to say to you all/ntonight," said Dumbledore, "but I must first/nacknowledge the loss of a very fine person, who/nshould be sitting here," he gestured toward the/nHufflepuffs, "enjoying our feast with us. I would like/nyou all, please, to stand, and raise your glasses, to/nCedric Diggory."/n/nThey did it, all of them; the benches scraped as/neveryone in the Hall stood, and raised their goblets,/nand echoed, in one loud, low, rumbling voice, "Cedric/nDiggory."/n/nHarry caught a glimpse of Cho through the crowd./nThere were tears pouring silently down her face. He/nlooked down at the table as they all sat down again./n/n"Cedric was a person who exemplified many of the/nqualities that distinguish Hufflepuff house,"/nDumbledore continued. "He was a good and loyal/nfriend, a hard worker, he valued fair play. His death/nhas affected you all, whether you knew him well or/nnot. I think that you have the right, therefore, to/nknow exactly how it came about."/n/nHarry raised his head and stared at Dumbledore./n/n"Cedric Diggory was murdered by Lord Voldemort."/n/nA panicked whisper swept the Great Hall. People were/nstaring at Dumbledore in disbelief, in horror. He/nlooked perfectly calm as he watched them mutter/nthemselves into silence./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The Ministry of Magic," Dumbledore continued, "does/nnot wish me to tell you this. It is possible that some of/nyour parents will be horrified that I have done so —/neither because they will not believe that Lord/nVoldemort has returned, or because they think I/nshould not tell you so, young as you are. It is my/nbelief, however, that the truth is generally preferable/nto lies, and that any attempt to pretend that Cedric/ndied as the result of an accident, or some sort of/nblunder of his own, is an insult to his memory."/n/nStunned and frightened, every face in the Hall was/nturned toward Dumbledore now ... or almost every/nface. Over at the Slytherin table, Harry saw Draco/nMalfoy muttering something to Crabbe and Goyle./nHarry felt a hot, sick swoop of anger in his stomach./nHe forced himself to look back at Dumbledore./n/n"There is somebody else who must be mentioned in/nconnection with Cedric's death," Dumbledore went/non. "I am talking, of course, about Harry Potter."/n/nA kind of ripple crossed the Great Hall as a few heads/nturned in Harry's direction before flicking back to face/nDumbledore./n/n"Harry Potter managed to escape Lord Voldemort,"/nsaid Dumbledore. "He risked his own life to return/nCedric's body to Hogwarts. He showed, in every/nrespect, the sort of bravery that few wizards have ever/nshown in facing Lord Voldemort, and for this, I honor/nhim."/n/nDumbledore turned gravely to Harry and raised his/ngoblet once more. Nearly everyone in the Great Hall/nfollowed suit. They murmured his name, as they had/nmurmured Cedric's, and drank to him. But through a/ngap in the standing figures, Harry saw that Malfoy,/nCrabbe, Goyle, and many of the other Slytherins had/n/n/n/n/nremained defiantly in their seats, their goblets/nuntouched. Dumbledore, who after all possessed no/nmagical eye, did not see them./n/nWhen everyone had once again resumed their seats,/nDumbledore continued, "The Triwizard Tournament's/naim was to further and promote magical/nunderstanding. In the light of what has happened —/nof Lord Voldemort's return — such ties are more/nimportant than ever before."/n/nDumbledore looked from Madame Maxime and/nHagrid, to Fleur Delacour and her fellow Beauxbatons/nstudents, to Viktor Krum and the Durmstrangs at the/nSlytherin table. Krum, Harry saw, looked wary,/nalmost frightened, as though he expected Dumbledore/nto say something harsh./n/n"Every guest in this Hall," said Dumbledore, and his/neyes lingered upon the Durmstrang students, "will be/nwelcomed back here at any time, should they wish to/ncome. I say to you all, once again — in the light of/nLord Voldemort's return, we are only as strong as we/nare united, as weak as we are divided. Lord/nVoldemort's gift for spreading discord and enmity is/nvery great. We can fight it only by showing an equally/nstrong bond of friendship and trust. Differences of/nhabit and language are nothing at all if our aims are/nidentical and our hearts are open./n/n"It is my belief — and never have I so hoped that I am/nmistaken — that we are all facing dark and difficult/ntimes. Some of you in this Hall have already suffered/ndirectly at the hands of Lord Voldemort. Many of your/nfamilies have been torn asunder. A week ago, a/nstudent was taken from our midst./n/n"Remember Cedric. Remember, if the time should/ncome when you have to make a choice between what/n/n/n/n/n/nis right and what is easy, remember what happened/nto a boy who was good, and kind, and brave, because/nhe strayed across the path of Lord Voldemort./nRemember Cedric Diggory."/n/nHarry's trunk was packed; Hedwig was back in her/ncage on top of it. He, Ron, and Hermione were waiting/nin the crowded entrance hall with the rest of the/nfourth years for the carriages that would take them/nback to Hogsmeade station. It was another beautiful/nsummer's day. He supposed that Privet Drive would/nbe hot and leafy, its flower beds a riot of color, when/nhe arrived there that evening. The thought gave him/nno pleasure at all./n/n" 'Arry!"/n/nHe looked around. Fleur Delacour was hurrying up/nthe stone steps into the castle. Beyond her, far across/nthe grounds, Harry could see Hagrid helping Madame/nMaxime to back two of the giant horses into their/nharness. The Beauxbatons carriage was about to take/noff./n/n"We will see each uzzer again, I 'ope," said Fleur as/nshe reached him, holding out her hand. "I am 'oping/nto get a job 'ere, to improve my Eenglish."/n/n"It's very good already," said Ron in a strangled sort of/nvoice. Fleur smiled at him; Hermione scowled./n/n"Good-bye, 'Arry," said Fleur, turning to go. "It 'az/nbeen a pleasure meeting you!"/n/nHarry's spirits couldn't help but lift slightly as he/nwatched Fleur hurry back across the lawns to/nMadame Maxime, her silvery hair rippling in the/nsunlight./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wonder how the Durmstrang students are getting/nback," said Ron. "D'you reckon they can steer that/nship without Karkaroff?"/n/n"Karkaroff did not steer," said a gruff voice. "He/nstayed in his cabin and let us do the vork."/n/nKrum had come to say good-bye to Hermione./n/n"Could I have a vord?" he asked her./n/n"Oh ... yes ... all right," said Hermione, looking/nslightly flustered, and following Krum through the/ncrowd and out of sight./n/n"You'd better hurry up!" Ron called loudly after her./n"The carriages'll be here in a minute!"/n/nHe let Harry keep a watch for the carriages, however,/nand spent the next few minutes craning his neck over/nthe crowd to try and see what Krum and Hermione/nmight be up to. They returned quite soon. Ron stared/nat Hermione, but her face was quite impassive./n/n"I liked Diggory," said Krum abruptly to Harry. "He/nvos alvays polite to me. Alvays. Even though I vos/nfrom Durmstrang — with Karkaroff," he added,/nscowling./n/n"Have you got a new headmaster yet?" said Harry./n/nKrum shrugged. He held out his hand as Fleur had/ndone, shook Harry's hand, and then Ron's. Ron/nlooked as though he was suffering some sort of/npainful internal struggle. Krum had already started/nwalking away when Ron burst out, "Can I have your/nautograph?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione turned away, smiling at the horseless/ncarriages that were now trundling toward them up the/ndrive, as Krum, looking surprised but gratified, signed/na fragment of parchment for Ron./n/n/n/nThe weather could not have been more different on/nthe journey back to King's Cross than it had been on/ntheir way to Hogwarts the previous September. There/nwasn't a single cloud in the sky. Harry, Ron, and/nHermione had managed to get a compartment to/nthemselves. Pigwidgeon was once again hidden under/nRon's dress robes to stop him from hooting/ncontinually; Hedwig was dozing, her head under her/nwing, and Crookshanks was curled up in a spare seat/nlike a large, furry ginger cushion. Harry, Ron, and/nHermione talked more fully and freely than they had/nall week as the train sped them southward. Harry felt/nas though Dumbledore's speech at the Leaving Feast/nhad unblocked him, somehow. It was less painful to/ndiscuss what had happened now. They broke off their/nconversation about what action Dumbledore might be/ntaking, even now, to stop Voldemort only when the/nlunch trolley arrived./n/nWhen Hermione returned from the trolley and put her/nmoney back into her schoolbag, she dislodged a copy/nof the Daily Prophet that she had been carrying in/nthere. Harry looked at it, unsure whether he really/nwanted to know what it might say, but Hermione,/nseeing him looking at it, said calmly, "There's nothing/nin there. You can look for yourself, but there's/nnothing at all. I've been checking every day. Just a/nsmall piece the day after the third task saying you/nwon the tournament. They didn't even mention/nCedric. Nothing about any of it. If you ask me, Fudge/nis forcing them to keep quiet."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He'll never keep Rita quiet," said Harry. "Not on a/nstory like this."/n/n"Oh, Rita hasn't written anything at all since the third/ntask," said Hermione in an oddly constrained voice./n"As a matter of fact," she added, her voice now/ntrembling slightly, "Rita Skeeter isn't going to be/nwriting anything at all for a while. Not unless she/nwants me to spill the beans on her."/n/n"What are you talking about?" said Ron./n/n"I found out how she was listening in on private/nconversations when she wasn't supposed to be/ncoming onto the grounds," said Hermione in a rush./n/nHarry had the impression that Hermione had been/ndying to tell them this for days, but that she had/nrestrained herself in light of everything else that had/nhappened./n/n"How was she doing it?" said Harry at once./n/n"How did you find out?" said Ron, staring at her./n/n"Well, it was you, really, who gave me the idea,/n/nHarry," she said./n/n"Did I?" said Harry, perplexed. "How?"/n/n"Bugging," said Hermione happily./n/n"But you said they didn't work — "/n/n"Oh not electronic bugs," said Hermione. "No, you see/n... Rita Skeeter" — Hermione 's voice trembled with/nquiet triumph — "is an unregistered Animagus. She/ncan turn — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione pulled a small sealed glass jar out of her/nbag./n/n" — into a beetle."/n/n"You're kidding," said Ron. "You haven't ... she's not/n/n/n/n"Oh yes she is," said Hermione happily, brandishing/nthe jar at them./n/nInside were a few twigs and leaves and one large, fat/nbeetle./n/n"That's never — you're kidding — " Ron whispered,/nlifting the jar to his eyes./n/n"No, I'm not," said Hermione, beaming. "I caught her/non the windowsill in the hospital wing. Look very/nclosely, and you 11 notice the markings around her/nantennae are exactly like those foul glasses she/nwears."/n/nHarry looked and saw that she was quite right. He/nalso remembered something./n/n"There was a beetle on the statue the night we heard/nHagrid telling Madame Maxime about his mum!"/n/n"Exactly," said Hermione. "And Viktor pulled a beetle/nout of my hair after we'd had our conversation by the/nlake. And unless I'm very much mistaken, Rita was/nperched on the windowsill of the Divination class the/nday your scar hurt. She's been buzzing around for/nstories all year."/n/n"When we saw Malfoy under that tree ..." said Ron/nslowly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He was talking to her, in his hand," said Hermione./n"He knew, of course. That's how she's been getting all/nthose nice little interviews with the Slytherins. They/nwouldn't care that she was doing something illegal, as/nlong as they were giving her horrible stuff about us/nand Hagrid."/n/nHermione took the glass jar back from Ron and/nsmiled at the beetle, which buzzed angrily against the/nglass./n/n"I've told her I'll let her out when we get back to/nLondon," said Hermione. "I've put an Unbreakable/nCharm on the jar, you see, so she can't transform./n/nAnd I've told her she's to keep her quill to herself for a/nwhole year. See if she can't break the habit of writing/nhorrible lies about people."/n/nSmiling serenely, Hermione placed the beetle back/ninside her schoolbag./n/nThe door of the compartment slid open./n/n"Very clever, Granger," said Draco Malfoy./n/nCrabbe and Goyle were standing behind him. All/nthree of them looked more pleased with themselves,/nmore arrogant and more menacing, than Harry had/never seen them./n/n"So," said Malfoy slowly, advancing slightly into the/ncompartment and looking slowly around at them, a/nsmirk quivering on his lips. "You caught some/npathetic reporter, and Potter's Dumbledore's favorite/nboy again. Big deal."/n/nHis smirk widened. Crabbe and Goyle leered./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Trying not to think about it, are we?" said Malfoy/nsoftly, looking around at all three of them. "Trying to/npretend it hasn't happened?"/n/n"Get out," said Harry./n/nHe had not been this close to Malfoy since he had/nwatched him muttering to Crabbe and Goyle during/nDumbledore's speech about Cedric. He could feel a/nkind of ringing in his ears. His hand gripped his wand/nunder his robes./n/n"You've picked the losing side, Potter! I warned you! I/ntold you you ought to choose your company more/ncarefully, remember? When we met on the train, first/nday at Hogwarts? I told you not to hang around with/nriffraff like this!" He jerked his head at Ron and/nHermione. "Too late now, Potter! They'll be the first to/ngo, now the Dark Lord's back! Mudbloods and/nMuggle-lovers first! Well — second — Diggory was the/nf— "/n/nIt was as though someone had exploded a box of/nfireworks within the compartment. Blinded by the/nblaze of the spells that had blasted from every/ndirection, deafened by a series of bangs, Harry/nblinked and looked down at the floor./n/nMalfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle were all lying unconscious/nin the doorway. He, Ron, and Hermione were on their/nfeet, all three of them having used a different hex. Nor/nwere they the only ones to have done so./n/n"Thought we'd see what those three were up to," said/nFred matter-of-factly, stepping onto Goyle and into/nthe compartment. He had his wand out, and so did/nGeorge, who was careful to tread on Malfoy as he/nfollowed Fred inside./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Interesting effect," said George, looking down at/nCrabbe. "Who used the Furnunculus Curse?"/n/n"Me," said Harry./n/n"Odd," said George lightly. "I used Jelly-Legs. Looks/nas though those two shouldn't be mixed. He seems to/nhave sprouted little tentacles all over his face. Well,/nlet's not leave them here, they don't add much to the/ndecor."/n/nRon, Harry, and George kicked, rolled, and pushed/nthe unconscious Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle — each of/nwhom looked distinctly the worse for the jumble of/njinxes with which they had been hit — out into the/ncorridor, then came back into the compartment and/nrolled the door shut./n/n"Exploding Snap, anyone?" said Fred, pulling out a/npack of cards./n/nThey were halfway through their fifth game when/nHarry decided to ask them./n/n"You going to tell us, then?" he said to George. "Who/nyou were blackmailing?"/n/n"Oh," said George darkly. " That/n/n"It doesn't matter," said Fred, shaking his head/nimpatiently. "It wasn't anything important. Not now,/nanyway."/n/n"We've given up," said George, shrugging./n/nBut Harry, Ron, and Hermione kept on asking, and/nfinally, Fred said, "All right, all right, if you really/nwant to know ... it was Ludo Bagman."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Bagman?" said Harry sharply. "Are you saying he/nwas involved in — "/n/n"Nah," said George gloomily. "Nothing like that./n/nStupid git. He wouldn't have the brains."/n/n"Well, what, then?" said Ron./n/nFred hesitated, then said, "You remember that bet we/nhad with him at the Quidditch World Cup? About how/nIreland would win, but Krum would get the Snitch?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry and Ron slowly./n/n"Well, the git paid us in leprechaun gold he'd caught/nfrom the Irish mascots."/n/n"So?"/n/n"So," said Fred impatiently, "it vanished, didn't it? By/nnext morning, it had gone!"/n/n"But — it must've been an accident, mustn't it?" said/nHermione./n/nGeorge laughed very bitterly./n/n"Yeah, that's what we thought, at first. We thought if/nwe just wrote to him, and told him he'd made a/nmistake, he'd cough up. But nothing doing. Ignored/nour letter. We kept trying to talk to him about it at/nHogwarts, but he was always making some excuse to/nget away from us."/n/n"In the end, he turned pretty nasty," said Fred. "Told/nus we were too young to gamble, and he wasn't giving/nus anything."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So we asked for our money back," said George/nglowering./n/n"He didn't refuse!" gasped Hermione./n/n"Right in one," said Fred./n/n"But that was all your savings!" said Ron./n/n"Tell me about it," said George. " 'Course, we found/nout what was going on in the end. Lee Jordan's dad/nhad had a bit of trouble getting money off Bagman as/nwell. Turns out he's in big trouble with the goblins./nBorrowed loads of gold off them. A gang of them/ncornered him in the woods after the World Cup and/ntook all the gold he had, and it still wasn't enough to/ncover all his debts. They followed him all the way to/nHogwarts to keep an eye on him. He's lost everything/ngambling. Hasn't got two Galleons to rub together./nAnd you know how the idiot tried to pay the goblins/nback?"/n/n"How?" said Harry./n/n"He put a bet on you, mate," said Fred. "Put a big bet/non you to win the tournament. Bet against the/ngoblins."/n/n"So that's why he kept trying to help me win!" said/nHarry. "Well — I did win, didn't I? So he can pay you/nyour gold!"/n/n"Nope," said George, shaking his head. "The goblins/nplay as dirty as him. They say you drew with Diggory,/nand Bagman was betting you'd win outright. So/nBagman had to run for it. He did run for it right after/nthe third task."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGeorge sighed deeply and started dealing out the/ncards again./n/nThe rest of the journey passed pleasantly enough;/nHarry wished it could have gone on all summer, in/nfact, and that he would never arrive at King's Cross . . ./nbut as he had learned the hard way that year, time/nwill not slow down when something unpleasant lies/nahead, and all too soon, the Hogwarts Express was/npulling in at platform nine and three-quarters. The/nusual confusion and noise filled the corridors as the/nstudents began to disembark. Ron and Hermione/nstruggled out past Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle,/ncarrying their trunks. Harry, however, stayed put./n/n"Fred — George — wait a moment."/n/nThe twins turned. Harry pulled open his trunk and/ndrew out his Triwizard winnings./n/n"Take it," he said, and he thrust the sack into/nGeorge's hands./n/n"What?" said Fred, looking flabbergasted./n/n"Take it," Harry repeated firmly. "I don't want it."/n/n"You're mental," said George, trying to push it back at/nHarry./n/n"No, I'm not," said Harry. "You take it, and get/ninventing. It's for the joke shop."/n/n"He is mental," Fred said in an almost awed voice./n/n"Listen," said Harry firmly. "If you don't take it, I'm/nthrowing it down the drain. I don't want it and I don't/nneed it. But I could do with a few laughs. We could all/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndo with a few laughs. I've got a feeling we're going to/nneed them more than usual before long."/n/n"Harry," said George weakly, weighing the money bag/nin his hands, "there's got to be a thousand Galleons/nin here."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, grinning. "Think how many/nCanary Creams that is."/n/nThe twins stared at him./n/n"Just don't tell your mum where you got it .../nalthough she might not be so keen for you to join the/nMinistry anymore, come to think of it. ..."/n/n"Harry," Fred began, but Harry pulled out his wand./n/n"Look," he said flatly, "take it, or I'll hex you. I know/nsome good ones now. Just do me one favor, okay?/n/nBuy Ron some different dress robes and say they're/nfrom you."/n/nHe left the compartment before they could say/nanother word, stepping over Malfoy, Crabbe, and/nGoyle, who were still lying on the floor, covered in hex/nmarks./n/nUncle Vernon was waiting beyond the barrier. Mrs./nWeasley was close by him. She hugged Harry very/ntightly when she saw him and whispered in his ear, "I/nthink Dumbledore will let you come to us later in the/nsummer. Keep in touch, Harry."/n/n"See you, Harry," said Ron, clapping him on the back./n/n" 'Bye, Harry!" said Hermione, and she did something/nshe had never done before, and kissed him on the/ncheek./n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry — thanks," George muttered, while Fred/nnodded fervently at his side./n/nHarry winked at them, turned to Uncle Vernon, and/nfollowed him silently from the station. There was no/npoint worrying yet, he told himself, as he got into the/nback of the Dursleys' car./n/nAs Hagrid had said, what would come, would come.../nand he would have to meet it when it did./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Dudley Demented
text: /nThe hottest day of the summer so far was drawing to/na close and a drowsy silence lay over the large, square/nhouses of Privet Drive. Cars that were usually/ngleaming stood dusty in their drives and lawns that/nwere once emerald green lay parched and yellowing;/nthe use of hosepipes had been banned due to/ndrought. Deprived of their usual car-washing and/nlawn-mowing pursuits, the inhabitants of Privet Drive/nhad retreated into the shade of their cool houses,/nwindows thrown wide in the hope of tempting in a/nnonexistent breeze. The only person left outdoors was/na teenage boy who was lying flat on his back in a/nflower bed outside number four./n/nHe was a skinny, black-haired, bespectacled boy who/nhad the pinched, slightly unhealthy look of someone/nwho has grown a lot in a short space of time. His/njeans were torn and dirty, his T-shirt baggy and/nfaded, and the soles of his trainers were peeling away/nfrom the uppers. Harry Potter's appearance did not/nendear him to the neighbors, who were the sort of/npeople who thought scruffiness ought to be/n/n/n/npunishable by law, but as he had hidden himself/nbehind a large hydrangea bush this evening he was/nquite invisible to passersby. In fact, the only way he/nwould be spotted was if his Uncle Vernon or Aunt/nPetunia stuck their heads out of the living room/nwindow and looked straight down into the flower bed/nbelow./n/nOn the whole, Harry thought he was to be/ncongratulated on his idea of hiding here. He was not,/nperhaps, very comfortable lying on the hot, hard/nearth, but on the other hand, nobody was glaring at/nhim, grinding their teeth so loudly that he could not/nhear the news, or shooting nasty questions at him, as/nhad happened every time he had tried sitting down in/nthe living room and watching television with his aunt/nand uncle./n/nAlmost as though this thought had fluttered through/nthe open window, Vernon Dursley, Harry's uncle,/nsuddenly spoke. "Glad to see the boy's stopped trying/nto butt in. Where is he anyway?"/n/n"I don't know," said Aunt Petunia unconcernedly. "Not/nin the house."/n/nUncle Vernon grunted./n/n"Watching the news ..." he said scathingly. "I'd like to/nknow what he's really up to. As if a normal boy cares/nwhat's on the news — Dudley hasn't got a clue what's/ngoing on, doubt he knows who the Prime Minister is!/nAnyway, it's not as if there 'd be anything about his lot/non our news — "/n/n"Vernon, shh\" said Aunt Petunia. "The window's/nopen!"/n/n"Oh — yes — sorry, dear ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nThe Dursleys fell silent. Harry listened to a jingle/nabout Fruit 'N Bran breakfast cereal while he watched/nMrs. Figg, a batty, cat-loving old lady from nearby/nWisteria Walk, amble slowly past. She was frowning/nand muttering to herself. Harry was very pleased that/nhe was concealed behind the bush; Mrs. Figg had/nrecently taken to asking him around for tea whenever/nshe met him in the street.
