"Where's — wand — come on — Lumosl"/n/nHe said the spell automatically, desperate for light to/nhelp him in his search — and to his disbelieving/nrelief, light flared inches from his right hand — the/nwand tip had ignited. Harry snatched it up,/nscrambled to his feet, and turned around./n/nHis stomach turned over./n/nA towering, hooded figure was gliding smoothly/ntoward him, hovering over the ground, no feet or face/nvisible beneath its robes, sucking on the night as it/ncame./n/nStumbling backward, Harry raised his wand./n/n"Expecto Patronurrd"/n/nA silvery wisp of vapor shot from the tip of the wand/nand the dementor slowed, but the spell hadn't worked/nproperly; tripping over his feet, Harry retreated/nfarther as the dementor bore down upon him, panic/nfogging his brain — concentrate —/n/nA pair of gray, slimy, scabbed hands slid from inside/nthe dementor's robes, reaching for him. A rushing/nnoise filled Harry's ears./n/n"Expecto PatronumV'/n/nHis voice sounded dim and distant... Another wisp of/nsilver smoke, feebler than the last, drifted from the/nwand — he couldn't do it anymore, he couldn't work/nthe spell —/n/nThere was laughter inside his own head, shrill, high-/npitched laughter... He could smell the dementor's/n/n/n/n/n/nputrid, death-cold breath, filling his own lungs,/ndrowning him — Think ... something happy.../n/nBut there was no happiness in him... The dementor's/nicy fingers were closing on his throat — the high-/npitched laughter was growing louder and louder, and/na voice spoke inside his head — "Bow to death,/n/nHarry. . . It might even be painless. . . I would not/nknow... I have never died..."/n/nHe was never going to see Ron and Hermione again —/n/nAnd their faces burst clearly into his mind as he/nfought for breath —/n/n"EXPECTO PATRONUM"/n/nAn enormous silver stag erupted from the tip of/nHarry's wand; its antlers caught the dementor in the/nplace where the heart should have been; it was/nthrown backward, weightless as darkness, and as the/nstag charged, the dementor swooped away, batlike/nand defeated./n/n"THIS WAY!" Harry shouted at the stag. Wheeling/naround, he sprinted down the alleyway, holding the lit/nwand aloft. "DUDLEY? DUDLEY!"/n/nHe had run barely a dozen steps when he reached/nthem: Dudley was curled on the ground, his arms/nclamped over his face; a second dementor was/ncrouching low over him, gripping his wrists in its/nslimy hands, prizing them slowly, almost lovingly/napart, lowering its hooded head toward Dudley's face/nas though about to kiss him.../n/n"GET IT!" Harry bellowed, and with a rushing, roaring/nsound, the silver stag he had conjured came galloping/nback past him. The dementor's eyeless face was/n/n/n/n/n/nbarely an inch from Dudley's when the silver antlers/ncaught it; the thing was thrown up into the air and,/nlike its fellow, it soared away and was absorbed into/nthe darkness. The stag cantered to the end of the/nalleyway and dissolved into silver mist./n/nMoon, stars, and streetlamps burst back into life. A/nwarm breeze swept the alleyway. Trees rustled in/nneighboring gardens and the mundane rumble of cars/nin Magnolia Crescent filled the air again. Harry stood/nquite still, all his senses vibrating, taking in the/nabrupt return to normality. After a moment he/nbecame aware that his T-shirt was sticking to him; he/nwas drenched in sweat./n/nHe could not believe what had just happened./nDementors here, in Little Whinging . . ./n/nDudley lay curled up on the ground, whimpering and/nshaking. Harry bent down to see whether he was in a/nfit state to stand up, but then heard loud, running/nfootsteps behind him; instinctively raising his wand/nagain, he spun on his heel to face the newcomer./n/nMrs. Figg, their batty old neighbor, came panting into/nsight. Her grizzled gray hair was escaping from its/nhairnet, a clanking string shopping bag was swinging/nfrom her wrist, and her feet were halfway out of her/ntartan carpet slippers. Harry made to stow his wand/nhurriedly out of sight, but —/n/n"Don't put it away, idiot boy!" she shrieked. "What if/nthere are more of them around? Oh, I'm going to kill/nMundungus Fletcher!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: A Peck Of Owls
text: /n"What?" said Harry blankly./n/n"He left!" said Mrs. Figg, wringing her hands. "Left to/nsee someone about a batch of cauldrons that fell off/nthe back of a broom! I told him I'd flay him alive if he/nwent, and now look! Dementors! It's just lucky I put/nMr. Tibbies on the case! But we haven't got time to/nstand around! Hurry, now, we've got to get you back!/nOh, the trouble this is going to cause! I will kill him!"/n/n"But — "/n/nThe revelation that his batty old cat-obsessed/nneighbor knew what dementors were was almost as/nbig a shock to Harry as meeting two of them down the/nalleyway. "You're — you're a witch?"/n/n"I'm a Squib, as Mundungus knows full well, so how/non earth was I supposed to help you fight off/ndementors? He left you completely without cover/nwhen I warned him — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"This bloke Mundungus has been following me? Hang/non — it was him). He Disapparated from the front of/nmy house!"/n/n"Yes, yes, yes, but luckily I'd stationed Mr. Tibbies/nunder a car just in case, and Mr. Tibbies came and/nwarned me, but by the time I got to your house you'd/ngone — and now — oh, what's Dumbledore going to/nsay? You!" she shrieked at Dudley, still supine on the/nalley floor. "Get your fat bottom off the ground,/nquick!"/n/n"You know Dumbledore?" said Harry, staring at her./n/n"Of course I know Dumbledore, who doesn't know/nDumbledore? But come on — I'll be no help if they/ncome back, I've never so much as Transfigured a/nteabag — "/n/nShe stooped down, seized one of Dudley's massive/narms in her wizened hands, and tugged./n/n"Get up, you useless lump, get up!"/n/nBut Dudley either could not or would not move. He/nwas still on the ground, trembling and ashen-faced,/nhis mouth shut very tight./n/n"I'll do it." Harry took hold of Dudley's arm and/nheaved: With an enormous effort he managed to hoist/nDudley to his feet. Dudley seemed to be on the point/nof fainting: His small eyes were rolling in their sockets/nand sweat was beading his face; the moment Harry let/ngo of him he swayed dangerously./n/n"Hurry up!" said Mrs. Figg hysterically./n/nHarry pulled one of Dudley's massive arms around/nhis own shoulders and dragged him toward the road,/n/n/n/n/n/nsagging slightly under his weight. Mrs. Figg tottered/nalong in front of them, peering anxiously around the/ncorner./n/n"Keep your wand out," she told Harry, as they entered/nWisteria Walk. "Never mind the Statute of Secrecy/nnow, there's going to be hell to pay anyway, we might/nas well be hanged for a dragon as an egg. Talk about/nthe Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery .../nThis was exactly what Dumbledore was afraid of —/nwhat's that at the end of the street? Oh, it's just Mr./nPrentice... Don't put your wand away, boy, don't I/nkeep telling you I'm no use?"/n/nIt was not easy to hold a wand steady and carry/nDudley along at the same time. Harry gave his cousin/nan impatient dig in the ribs, but Dudley seemed to/nhave lost all desire for independent movement. He/nwas slumped on Harry's shoulder, his large feet/ndragging along the ground./n/n"Why didn't you tell me you're a Squib?" Harry asked/nMrs. Figg, panting with the effort to keep walking. "All/nthose times I came round your house — why didn't/nyou say anything?"/n/n"Dumbledore 's orders. I was to keep an eye on you/nbut not say anything, you were too young. I'm sorry I/ngave you such a miserable time, but the Dursleys/nwould never have let you come if they'd thought you/nenjoyed it. It wasn't easy, you know... But oh my/nword," she said tragically, wringing her hands once/nmore, "when Dumbledore hears about this — how/ncould Mundungus have left, he was supposed to be/non duty until midnight — where is he? How am I/ngoing to tell Dumbledore what's happened, I can't/nApparate — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I've got an owl, you can borrow her," Harry groaned,/nwondering whether his spine was going to snap under/nDudley's weight./n/n"Harry, you don't understand! Dumbledore will need/nto act as quickly as possible, the Ministry have their/nown ways of detecting underage magic, they'll know/nalready, you mark my words — "/n/n"But I was getting rid of dementors, I had to use/nmagic — they're going to be more worried what/ndementors were doing floating around Wisteria Walk,/nsurely?"/n/n"Oh my dear, I wish it were so but I'm afraid —/nMUNDUNGUS FLETCHER, I AM GOING TO KILL/nYOU!"/n/nThere was a loud crack and a strong smell of mingled/ndrink and stale tobacco filled the air as a squat,/nunshaven man in a tattered overcoat materialized/nright in front of them. He had short bandy legs, long/nstraggly ginger hair, and bloodshot baggy eyes that/ngave him the doleful look of a basset hound; he was/nalso clutching a silvery bundle that Harry recognized/nat once as an Invisibility Cloak./n/n" 'S' up, Figgy?" he said, staring from Mrs. Figg to/nHarry and Dudley. "What 'appened to staying/nundercover?"/n/n"I'll give you undercover!" cried Mrs. Figg. "Dementors,/nyou useless, skiving sneak thief!"/n/n"Dementors?" repeated Mundungus, aghast./n"Dementors here?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, here, you worthless pile of bat droppings, here!"/nshrieked Mrs. Figg. "Dementors attacking the boy on/nyour watch!"/n/n"Blimey," said Mundungus weakly, looking from Mrs./nFigg to Harry and back again. "Blimey, I ..."/n/n"And you off buying stolen cauldrons! Didn't I tell you/nnot to go? Didn't i?"/n/n"I — well, I — " Mundungus looked deeply/nuncomfortable. "It ... it was a very good business/nopportunity, see ..."/n/nMrs. Figg raised the arm from which her string bag/ndangled and whacked Mundungus around the face/nand neck with it; judging by the clanking noise it/nmade it was full of cat food./n/n"Ouch — gerroff — gerroff, you mad old bat!/n/nSomeone's gotta tell Dumbledore!"/n/n"Yes — they — have!" yelled Mrs. Figg, still swinging/nthe bag of cat food at every bit of Mundungus she/ncould reach. "And — it — had — better — be — you —/nand — you — can — tell — him — why — you —/nweren't — there — to — help!"/n/n"Keep your 'airnet on!" said Mundungus, his arms/nover his head, cowering. "I'm going, I'm going!"/n/nAnd with another loud crack, he vanished./n/n"I hope Dumbledore murders him!" said Mrs. Figg/nfuriously. "Now come on, Harry, what are you waiting/nfor?"/n/nHarry decided not to waste his remaining breath on/npointing out that he could barely walk under Dudley's/n/n/n/n/n/nbulk. He gave the semiconscious Dudley a heave and/nstaggered onward./n/n"I'll take you to the door," said Mrs. Figg, as they/nturned into Privet Drive. "Just in case there are more/nof them around... Oh my word, what a catastrophe .../nand you had to fight them off yourself . . . and/nDumbledore said we were to keep you from doing/nmagic at all costs... Well, it's no good crying over/nspilled potion, I suppose ... but the cat's among the/npixies now ..."/n/n"So," Harry panted, "Dumbledore 's ... been having .../nme followed?"/n/n"Of course he has," said Mrs. Figg impatiently. "Did/nyou expect him to let you wander around on your own/nafter what happened in June? Good Lord, boy, they/ntold me you were intelligent... Right ... get inside and/nstay there," she said as they reached number four. "I/nexpect someone will be in touch with you soon/nenough."/n/n"What are you going to do?" asked Harry quickly./n/n"I'm going straight home," said Mrs. Figg, staring/naround the dark street and shuddering. "I'll need to/nwait for more instructions. Just stay in the house./nGood night."/n/n"Hang on, don't go yet! I want to know — "/n/nBut Mrs. Figg had already set off at a trot, carpet/nslippers flopping, string bag clanking./n/n"Wait!" Harry shouted after her; he had a million/nquestions to ask anyone who was in contact with/nDumbledore; but within seconds Mrs. Figg was/nswallowed by the darkness. Scowling, Harry/n/n/n/n/n/nreadjusted Dudley on his shoulder and made his/nslow, painful way up number four's garden path./n/nThe hall light was on. Harry stuck his wand back/ninside the waistband of his jeans, rang the bell, and/nwatched Aunt Petunia's outline grow larger and/nlarger, oddly distorted by the rippling glass in the/nfront door./n/n"Diddy! About time too, I was getting quite — quite —/nDiddy, what's the matter?"/n/nHarry looked sideways at Dudley and ducked out/nfrom under his arm just in time. Dudley swayed for a/nmoment on the spot, his face pale green, then he/nopened his mouth at last and vomited all over the/ndoormat./n/n"DIDDY! Diddy, what's the matter with you? Vernon?/nVERNON!"/n/nHarry's uncle came galumphing out of the living/nroom, walrus mustache blowing hither and thither as/nit always did when he was agitated. He hurried/nforward to help Aunt Petunia negotiate a weak-kneed/nDudley over the threshold while avoiding stepping in/nthe pool of sick./n/n"He's ill, Vernon!"/n/n"What is it, son? What's happened? Did Mrs. Polkiss/ngive you something foreign for tea?"/n/n"Why are you all covered in dirt, darling? Have you/nbeen lying on the ground?"/n/n"Hang on — you haven't been mugged, have you,/nson?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAunt Petunia screamed./n/n/n/n"Phone the police, Vernon! Phone the police! Diddy,/ndarling, speak to Mummy! What did they do to you?"/n/nIn all the kerfuffle, nobody seemed to have noticed/nHarry, which suited him perfectly. He managed to slip/ninside just before Uncle Vernon slammed the door/nand while the Dursleys made their noisy progress/ndown the hall toward the kitchen, Harry moved/ncarefully and quietly toward the stairs./n/n"Who did it, son? Give us names. Well get them, don't/nworry."/n/n"Shh! He's trying to say something, Vernon! What is/nit, Diddy? Tell Mummy!"/n/nHarry's foot was on the bottommost stair when/nDudley found his voice./n/n"Him"/n/nHarry froze, foot on the stair, face screwed up, braced/nfor the explosion./n/n"BOY! COME HERE!"/n/nWith a feeling of mingled dread and anger, Harry/nremoved his foot slowly from the stair and turned to/nfollow the Dursleys./n/nThe scrupulously clean kitchen had an oddly unreal/nglitter after the darkness outside. Aunt Petunia was/nushering Dudley into a chair; he was still very green/nand clammy looking. Uncle Vernon was standing in/nfront of the draining board, glaring at Harry through/ntiny, narrowed eyes./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What have you done to my son?" he said in a/nmenacing growl./n/n/n/n"Nothing," said Harry, knowing perfectly well that/nUncle Vernon wouldn't believe him./n/n"What did he do to you, Diddy?" Aunt Petunia said in/na quavering voice, now sponging sick from the front of/nDudley's leather jacket. "Was it — was it you-know-/nwhat, darling? Did he use — his thing?"/n/nSlowly, tremulously, Dudley nodded./n/n"I didn't!" Harry said sharply, as Aunt Petunia let out/na wail and Uncle Vernon raised his fists. "I didn't do/nanything to him, it wasn't me, it was — "/n/nBut at that precise moment a screech owl swooped in/nthrough the kitchen window. Narrowly missing the/ntop of Uncle Vernon's head, it soared across the/nkitchen, dropped the large parchment envelope it was/ncarrying in its beak at Harry's feet, and turned/ngracefully, the tips of its wings just brushing the top/nof the fridge, then zoomed outside again and off/nacross the garden./n/n"OWLS!" bellowed Uncle Vernon, the well-worn vein in/nhis temple pulsing angrily as he slammed the kitchen/nwindow shut. "OWLS AGAIN! I WILL NOT HAVE ANY/nMORE OWLS IN MY HOUSE!"/n/nBut Harry was already ripping open the envelope and/npulling out the letter inside, his heart pounding/nsomewhere in the region of his Adam's apple./n/nDear Mr. Potter,/n/nWe have received intelligence that you performed the/nPatronus Charm at twenty-three minutes past nine this/n/n/n/n/n/nevening in a Muggle-inhabited area and in the/npresence of a Muggle./n/nThe severity of this breach of the Decree for the/nReasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery has/nresulted in your expulsion from Hog warts School of/nWitchcraft and Wizardry. Ministry representatives will/nbe calling at your place of residence shortly to destroy/nyour wand./n/nAs you have already received an official warning for a/nprevious offense under section 13 of the International/nConfederation of Wizards' Statute of Secrecy, we regret/nto inform you that your presence is required at a/ndisciplinary hearing at the Ministry of Magic at 9 a. m./non August 12th./n/nHoping you are well,/n/nYours sincerely,/n/nMafalda Hopkirk/n/nIMPROPER USE OF MAGIC OFFICE/nMinistry of Magic/n/nHarry read the letter through twice. He was only/nvaguely aware of Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia/ntalking in the vicinity. Inside his head, all was icy and/nnumb. One fact had penetrated his consciousness/nlike a paralyzing dart. He was expelled from/nHogwarts. It was all over. He was never going back./n/nHe looked up at the Dursleys. Uncle Vernon was/npurple-faced, shouting, his fists still raised; Aunt/nPetunia had her arms around Dudley, who was/nretching again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's temporarily stupefied brain seemed to/nreawaken. Ministry representatives will be calling at/nyour place of residence shortly to destroy your wand./nThere was only one thing for it. He would have to run/n— now. Where he was going to go, Harry didn't know,/nbut he was certain of one thing: At Hogwarts or/noutside it, he needed his wand. In an almost/ndreamlike state, he pulled his wand out and turned to/nleave the kitchen./n/n"Where d'you think you're going?" yelled Uncle/nVernon. When Harry didn't reply, he pounded across/nthe kitchen to block the doorway into the hall. "I/nhaven't finished with you, boy!"/n/n"Get out of the way," said Harry quietly./n/n"You're going to stay here and explain how my son — "/n/n"If you don't get out of the way I'm going to jinx you,"/nsaid Harry, raising the wand./n/n"You can't pull that one on me!" snarled Uncle/nVernon. "I know you're not allowed to use it outside/nthat madhouse you call a school!"/n/n"The madhouse has chucked me out," said Harry. "So/nI can do whatever I like. You've got three seconds./n/nOne — two — "/n/nA resounding CRACK filled the kitchen; Aunt Petunia/nscreamed, Uncle Vernon yelled and ducked, but for/nthe third time that night Harry was staring for the/nsource of a disturbance he had not made. He spotted/nit at once: A dazed and ruffled-looking barn owl was/nsitting outside on the kitchen sill, having just collided/nwith the closed window./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIgnoring Uncle Vernon's anguished yell of "OWLS!"/nHarry crossed the room at a run and wrenched the/nwindow open again. The owl stuck out its leg, to/nwhich a small roll of parchment was tied, shook its/nfeathers, and took off the moment Harry had pulled/noff the letter. Hands shaking, Harry unfurled the/nsecond message, which was written very hastily and/nblotchily in black ink./n/nHarry —/n/nDumbledore's just arrived at the Ministry, and he's/ntrying to sort it all out. DO NOT LEAVE YOUR AUNT/nAND UNCLE'S HOUSE. DO NOT DO ANYMORE/nMAGIC. DO NOT SURRENDER YOUR WAND./n/nArthur Weasley/n/nDumbledore was trying to sort it all out... What did/nthat mean? How much power did Dumbledore have to/noverride the Ministry of Magic? Was there a chance/nthat he might be allowed back to Hogwarts, then? A/nsmall shoot of hope burgeoned in Harry's chest,/nalmost immediately strangled by panic — how was he/nsupposed to refuse to surrender his wand without/ndoing magic? He'd have to duel with the Ministry/nrepresentatives, and if he did that, he'd be lucky to/nescape Azkaban, let alone expulsion./n/nHis mind was racing. . . He could run for it and risk/nbeing captured by the Ministry, or stay put and wait/nfor them to find him here. He was much more/ntempted by the former course, but he knew that Mr./nWeasley had his best interests at heart ... and, after/nall, Dumbledore had sorted out much worse than this/nbefore.../n/n"Right," Harry said, "I've changed my mind, I'm/nstaying."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe flung himself down at the kitchen table and faced/nDudley and Aunt Petunia. The Dursleys appeared/ntaken aback at his abrupt change of mind. Aunt/nPetunia glanced despairingly at Uncle Vernon. The/nvein in Uncle Vernon's purple temple was throbbing/nworse than ever./n/n"Who are all these ruddy owls from?" he growled./n/n"The first one was from the Ministry of Magic,/nexpelling me," said Harry calmly; he was straining his/nears to catch noises outside in case the Ministry/nrepresentatives were approaching, and it was easier/nand quieter to answer Uncle Vernon's questions than/nto have him start raging and bellowing. "The second/none was from my friend Ron's dad, he works at the/nMinistry."/n/n"Ministry of Magic?" bellowed Uncle Vernon. "People/nlike you in government? Oh this explains everything,/neverything, no wonder the country's going to the/ndogs..."/n/nWhen Harry did not respond, Uncle Vernon glared at/nhim, then spat, "And why have you been expelled?"/n/n"Because I did magic."/n/n"AHA!" roared Uncle Vernon, slamming his fist down/non the top of the fridge, which sprang open; several of/nDudley's low-fat snacks toppled out and burst on the/nfloor. "So you admit it! What did you do to Dudley?"/n/n"Nothing," said Harry, slightly less calmly. "That/nwasn't me — "/n/n"Was," muttered Dudley unexpectedly, and Uncle/nVernon and Aunt Petunia instantly made flapping/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ngestures at Harry to quiet him while they both bent/nlow over Dudley./n/n"Go on, son," said Uncle Vernon, "what did he do?"/n/n"Tell us, darling," whispered Aunt Petunia./n/n"Pointed his wand at me," Dudley mumbled./n/n"Yeah, I did, but I didn't use — " Harry began angrily,/nbut .../n/n"SHUT UP!" roared Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia in/nunison. "Go on, son," repeated Uncle Vernon,/nmustache blowing about furiously./n/n"All dark," Dudley said hoarsely, shuddering./n"Everything dark. And then I h-heard . . . things. Inside/nm-my head ..."/n/nUncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia exchanged looks of/nutter horror. If their least favorite thing in the world/nwas magic, closely followed by neighbors who cheated/nmore than they did on the hosepipe ban, people who/nheard voices were definitely in the bottom ten. They/nobviously thought Dudley was losing his mind./n/n"What sort of things did you hear, popkin?" breathed/nAunt Petunia, very white-faced and with tears in her/neyes./n/nBut Dudley seemed incapable of saying. He/nshuddered again and shook his large blond head, and/ndespite the sense of numb dread that had settled on/nHarry since the arrival of the first owl, he felt a/ncertain curiosity. Dementors caused a person to relive/nthe worst moments of their life... What would spoiled,/npampered, bullying Dudley have been forced to hear?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"How come you fell over, son?" said Uncle Vernon in/nan unnaturally quiet voice, the kind of voice he would/nadopt at the bedside of a very ill person./n/n"T-tripped," said Dudley shakily. "And then — "/n/nHe gestured at his massive chest. Harry understood:/nDudley was remembering the clammy cold that filled/nthe lungs as hope and happiness were sucked out of/nyou./n/n"Horrible," croaked Dudley. "Cold. Really cold."/n/n"Okay," said Uncle Vernon in a voice of forced calm,/nwhile Aunt Petunia laid an anxious hand on Dudley's/nforehead to feel his temperature. "What happened/nthen, Dudders?"/n/n"Felt ... felt ... felt ... as if... as if ..."/n/n"As if you'd never be happy again," Harry supplied/ntonelessly./n/n"Yes," Dudley whispered, still trembling./n/n"So," said Uncle Vernon, voice restored to full and/nconsiderable volume as he straightened up. "So you/nput some crackpot spell on my son so he'd hear/nvoices and believe he was — was doomed to misery,/nor something, did you?"/n/n"How many times do I have to tell you?" said Harry,/ntemper and voice rising together. "It wasn't me\ It was/na couple of dementors!"/n/n"A couple of — what's this codswallop?"/n/n"De — men — tors," said Harry slowly and clearly./n"Two of them."/n/n/n/n/n/n"And what the ruddy hell are dementors?"/n/n/n/n"They guard the wizard prison, Azkaban," said Aunt/nPetunia./n/nTwo seconds' ringing silence followed these words and/nthen Aunt Petunia clapped her hand over her mouth/nas though she had let slip a disgusting swear word./nUncle Vernon was goggling at her. Harry's brain/nreeled. Mrs. Figg was one thing — but Aunt Petunia?/n/n"How d'you know that?" he asked her, astonished./n/nAunt Petunia looked quite appalled with herself. She/nglanced at Uncle Vernon in fearful apology, then/nlowered her hand slightly to reveal her horsey teeth./n/n"I heard — that awful boy — telling her about them —/nyears ago," she said jerkily./n/n"If you mean my mum and dad, why don't you use/ntheir names?" said Harry loudly, but Aunt Petunia/nignored him. She seemed horribly flustered./n/nHarry was stunned. Except for one outburst years/nago, in the course of which Aunt Petunia had/nscreamed that Harry's mother had been a freak, he/nhad never heard her mention her sister. He was/nastounded that she had remembered this scrap of/ninformation about the magical world for so long, when/nshe usually put all her energies into pretending it/ndidn't exist./n/nUncle Vernon opened his mouth, closed it again,/nopened it once more, shut it, then, apparently/nstruggling to remember how to talk, opened it for a/nthird time and croaked, "So — so — they — er — they/n— er — they actually exist, do they — er — dementy-/nwhatsits?"/n/n/n/n/n/nAunt Petunia nodded./n/n/n/nUncle Vernon looked from Aunt Petunia to Dudley to/nHarry as if hoping somebody was going to shout/n"April Fool!" When nobody did, he opened his mouth/nyet again, but was spared the struggle to find more/nwords by the arrival of the third owl of the evening,/nwhich zoomed through the still-open window like a/nfeathery cannonball and landed with a clatter on the/nkitchen table, causing all three of the Dursleys to/njump with fright. Harry tore a second official-looking/nenvelope from the owl's beak and ripped it open as/nthe owl swooped back out into the night./n/n"Enough — effing — owls ..." muttered Uncle Vernon/ndistractedly, stomping over to the window and/nslamming it shut again./n/nDear Mr. Potter,/n/nFurther to our letter of approximately twenty-two/nminutes ago, the Ministry of Magic has revised its/ndecision to destroy your wand forthwith. You may/nretain your wand until your disciplinary hearing on/n12th August, at which time an official decision will be/ntaken./n/nFollowing discussions with the Headmaster of/nHogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, the/nMinistry has agreed that the question of your expulsion/nwill also be decided at that time. You should therefore/nconsider yourself suspended from school pending/nfurther inquiries./n/nWith best wishes,/n/nYours sincerely,/n/nMafalda Hopkirk/n/n/n/n/n/nIMPROPER USE OF MAGIC OFFICE/n/n/n/nMinistry of Magic/n/nHarry read this letter through three times in quick/nsuccession. The miserable knot in his chest loosened/nslightly at the thought that he was not definitely/nexpelled, though his fears were by no means/nbanished. Everything seemed to hang on this hearing/non the twelfth of August./n/n"Well?" said Uncle Vernon, recalling Harry to his/nsurroundings. "What now? Have they sentenced you/nto anything? Do your lot have the death penalty?" he/nadded as a hopeful afterthought./n/n"I've got to go to a hearing," said Harry./n/n"And they'll sentence you there?"/n/n"I suppose so."/n/n"I won't give up hope, then," said Uncle Vernon/nnastily./n/n"Well, if that's all," said Harry, getting to his feet. He/nwas desperate to be alone, to think, perhaps to send a/nletter to Ron, Hermione, or Sirius./n/n"NO, IT RUDDY WELL IS NOT ALL!" bellowed Uncle/nVernon. "SIT BACK DOWN!"/n/n"What now?" said Harry impatiently./n/n"DUDLEY!" roared Uncle Vernon. "I want to know/nexactly what happened to my son!"/n/n"FINE!" yelled Harry, and in his temper, red and gold/nsparks shot out of the end of his wand, still clutched/n/n/n/n/n/nin his hand. All three Dursleys flinched, looking/nterrified./n/n"Dudley and I were in the alleyway between Magnolia/nCrescent and Wisteria Walk," said Harry, speaking/nfast, fighting to control his temper. "Dudley thought/nhe'd be smart with me, I pulled out my wand but/ndidn't use it. Then two dementors turned up — "/n/n"But what ARE dementoids?" asked Uncle Vernon/nfuriously. "What do they DO?"/n/n"I told you — they suck all the happiness out of you,"/nsaid Harry, "and if they get the chance, they kiss you/n/n/n/n"Kiss you?" said Uncle Vernon, his eyes popping/nslightly. "Kiss you?"/n/n"It's what they call it when they suck the soul out of/nyour mouth."/n/nAunt Petunia uttered a soft scream./n/n"His soul? They didn't take — he's still got his — "/n/nShe seized Dudley by the shoulders and shook him,/nas though testing to see whether she could hear his/nsoul rattling around inside him./n/n"Of course they didn't get his soul, you'd know if they/nhad," said Harry, exasperated./n/n"Fought 'em off, did you, son?" said Uncle Vernon/nloudly, with the appearance of a man struggling to/nbring the conversation back onto a plane he/nunderstood. "Gave 'em the old one-two, did you?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You can't give a dementor the old one-two," said/nHarry through clenched teeth./n/n"Why's he all right, then?" blustered Uncle Vernon./n"Why isn't he all empty, then?"/n/n"Because I used the Patronus — "/n/nWHOOSH. With a clattering, a whirring of wings, and/na soft fall of dust, a fourth owl came shooting out of/nthe kitchen fireplace./n/n"FOR GOD'S SAKE!" roared Uncle Vernon, pulling/ngreat clumps of hair out of his mustache, something/nhe hadn't been driven to in a long time. "I WILL NOT/nHAVE OWLS HERE, I WILL NOT TOLERATE THIS, I/nTELL YOU!"/n/nBut Harry was already pulling a roll of parchment/nfrom the owl's leg. He was so convinced that this/nletter had to be from Dumbledore, explaining/neverything — the dementors, Mrs. Figg, what the/nMinistry was up to, how he, Dumbledore, intended to/nsort everything out — that for the first time in his life/nhe was disappointed to see Sirius's handwriting./nIgnoring Uncle Vernon's ongoing rant about owls and/nnarrowing his eyes against a second cloud of dust as/nthe most recent owl took off back up the chimney,/nHarry read Sirius's message./n/nArthur's just told us what's happened./n/nDon't leave the house again, whatever you do./n/nHarry found this such an inadequate response to/neverything that had happened tonight that he turned/nthe piece of parchment over, looking for the rest of the/nletter, but there was nothing there./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd now his temper was rising again. Wasn't/nanybody going to say "well done" for fighting off two/ndementors single-handedly? Both Mr. Weasley and/nSirius were acting as though he'd misbehaved and/nthey were saving their tellings-off until they could/nascertain how much damage had been done./n/n" — a peck, I mean, pack of owls shooting in and out/nof my house and I won't have it, boy, I won't — "/n/n"I can't stop the owls coming," Harry snapped,/ncrushing Sirius's letter in his fist./n/n"I want the truth about what happened tonight!"/nbarked Uncle Vernon. "If it was demenders who hurt/nDudley, how come you've been expelled? You did you-/nknow-what, you've admitted it!"/n/nHarry took a deep, steadying breath. His head was/nbeginning to ache again. He wanted more than/nanything to get out of the kitchen, away from the/nDursleys./n/n"I did the Patronus Charm to get rid of the/ndementors," he said, forcing himself to remain calm./n"It's the only thing that works against them."/n/n"But what were dementoids doing in Little Whinging?"/nsaid Uncle Vernon in tones of outrage./n/n"Couldn't tell you," said Harry wearily. "No idea."/n/nHis head was pounding in the glare of the strip/nlighting now. His anger was ebbing away. He felt/ndrained, exhausted. The Dursleys were all staring at/nhim./n/n"It's you," said Uncle Vernon forcefully. "It's got/nsomething to do with you, boy, I know it. Why else/n/n/n/n/n/nwould they turn up here? Why else would they be/ndown that alleyway? You've got to be the only — the/nonly — " Evidently he couldn't bring himself to say the/nword "wizard." "The only you-know-what for miles."/n/n"I don't know why they were here..."/n/nBut at these words of Uncle Vernon's, Harry's/nexhausted brain ground back into action. Why had/nthe dementors come to Little Whinging? How could it/nbe coincidence that they had arrived in the alleyway/nwhere Harry was? Had they been sent? Had the/nMinistry of Magic lost control of the dementors, had/nthey deserted Azkaban and joined Voldemort, as/nDumbledore had predicted they would?/n/n"These demembers guard some weirdos' prison?" said/nUncle Vernon, lumbering in the wake of Harry's train/nof thought./n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/nIf only his head would stop hurting, if only he could/njust leave the kitchen and get to his dark bedroom/nand think.../n/n"Oho! They were coming to arrest you!" said Uncle/nVernon, with the triumphant air of a man reaching an/nunassailable conclusion. "That's it, isn't it, boy?/n/nYou're on the run from the law!"/n/n"Of course I'm not," said Harry, shaking his head as/nthough to scare off a fly, his mind racing now./n/n"Then why — ?"/n/n"He must have sent them," said Harry quietly, more to/nhimself than to Uncle Vernon./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's that? Who must have sent them?"/n/n"Lord Voldemort," said Harry./n/nHe registered dimly how strange it was that the/nDursleys, who flinched, winced, and squawked if they/nheard words like "wizard," "magic," or "wand," could/nhear the name of the most evil wizard of all time/nwithout the slightest tremor./n/n"Lord — hang on," said Uncle Vernon, his face/nscrewed up, a look of dawning comprehension in his/npiggy eyes. "I've heard that name ... that was the one/nwho ..."/n/n"Murdered my parents, yes," Harry said./n/n"But he's gone," said Uncle Vernon impatiently,/nwithout the slightest sign that the murder of Harry's/nparents might be a painful topic to anybody. "That/ngiant bloke said so. He's gone."/n/n"He's back," said Harry heavily./n/nIt felt very strange to be standing here in Aunt/nPetunia's surgically clean kitchen, beside the top-of-/nthe-range fridge and the wide-screen television, and/ntalking calmly of Lord Voldemort to Uncle Vernon./n/nThe arrival of the dementors in Little Whinging/nseemed to have caused a breach in the great, invisible/nwall that divided the relentlessly non-magical world of/nPrivet Drive and the world beyond. Harry's two lives/nhad somehow become fused and everything had been/nturned upside down: The Dursleys were asking for/ndetails about the magical world and Mrs. Figg knew/nAlbus Dumbledore; dementors were soaring around/nLittle Whinging and he might never go back to/nHogwarts. Harry's head throbbed more painfully./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Back?" whispered Aunt Petunia./n/nShe was looking at Harry as she had never looked at/nhim before. And all of a sudden, for the very first time/nin his life, Harry fully appreciated that Aunt Petunia/nwas his mother's sister. He could not have said why/nthis hit him so very powerfully at this moment. All he/nknew was that he was not the only person in the/nroom who had an inkling of what Lord Voldemort/nbeing back might mean. Aunt Petunia had never in/nher life looked at him like that before. Her large, pale/neyes (so unlike her sister's) were not narrowed in/ndislike or anger: They were wide and fearful. The/nfurious pretense that Aunt Petunia had maintained/nall Harry's life — that there was no magic and no/nworld other than the world she inhabited with Uncle/nVernon — seemed to have fallen away./n/n"Yes," Harry said, talking directly to Aunt Petunia/nnow. "He came back a month ago. I saw him."/n/nHer hands found Dudley's massive leather-clad/nshoulders and clutched them./n/n"Hang on," said Uncle Vernon, looking from his wife/nto Harry and back again, apparently dazed and/nconfused by the unprecedented understanding that/nseemed to have sprung up between them. "Hang on./nThis Lord Voldything's back, you say."/n/n"Yes."/n/n"The one who murdered your parents."/n/n"Yes."/n/n"And now he's sending dismembers after you?"/n/n"Looks like it," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n"I see," said Uncle Vernon, looking from his white-/nfaced wife to Harry and hitching up his trousers. He/nseemed to be swelling, his great purple face stretching/nbefore Harry's eyes. "Well, that settles it," he said, his/nshirt front straining as he inflated himself, "you can/nget out of this house, boy\"/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"You heard me — OUT!" Uncle Vernon bellowed, and/neven Aunt Petunia and Dudley jumped. "OUT! OUT! I/nshould've done it years ago! Owls treating the place/nlike a rest home, puddings exploding, half the lounge/ndestroyed, Dudley's tail, Marge bobbing around on/nthe ceiling, and that flying Ford Anglia — OUT! OUT!/nYou've had it! You're history! You're not staying here if/nsome loony's after you, you're not endangering my/nwife and son, you're not bringing trouble down on us,/nif you're going the same way as your useless parents,/nI've had it! OUT!"/n/nHarry stood rooted to the spot. The letters from the/nMinistry, Mr. Weasley, and Sirius were crushed in his/nleft hand. Don't leave the house again, whatever you/ndo. DO NOT LEA VE YOUR A UNT AND UNCLE'S/nHOUSE./n/n"You heard me!" said Uncle Vernon, bending forward/nnow, so that his massive purple face came closer to/nHarry's, so that Harry actually felt flecks of spit hit/nhis face. "Get going! You were all keen to leave half an/nhour ago! I'm right behind you! Get out and never/ndarken our doorstep again! Why we ever kept you in/nthe first place I don't know. Marge was right, it should/nhave been the orphanage, we were too damn soft for/nour own good, thought we could squash it out of you,/nthought we could turn you normal, but you've been/nrotten from the beginning, and I've had enough —/nOWLS!"/n/n/n/n/n/nThe fifth owl zoomed down the chimney so fast it/nactually hit the floor before zooming into the air again/nwith a loud screech. Harry raised his hand to seize/nthe letter, which was in a scarlet envelope, but it/nsoared straight over his head, flying directly at Aunt/nPetunia, who let out a scream and ducked, her arms/nover her face. The owl dropped the red envelope on/nher head, turned, and flew straight up the chimney/nagain./n/nHarry darted forward to pick up the letter, but Aunt/nPetunia beat him to it./n/n"You can open it if you like," said Harry, "but I'll hear/nwhat it says anyway. That's a Howler."/n/n"Let go of it, Petunia!" roared Uncle Vernon. "Don't/ntouch it, it could be dangerous!"/n/n"It's addressed to me," said Aunt Petunia in a shaking/nvoice. "It's addressed to me, Vernon, look! Mrs./n/nPetunia Dursley, The Kitchen, Number Four, Privet/nDrive — "/n/nShe caught her breath, horrified. The red envelope/nhad begun to smoke./n/n"Open it!" Harry urged her. "Get it over with! It'll/nhappen anyway — "/n/n"No — "/n/n/n/nAunt Petunia's hand was trembling. She looked wildly/naround the kitchen as though looking for an escape/nroute, but too late — the envelope burst into flames./nAunt Petunia screamed and dropped it./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAn awful voice filled the kitchen, echoing in the/nconfined space, issuing from the burning letter on the/ntable./n/n/n/n"REMEMBER MY LAST, PETUNIA."/n/nAunt Petunia looked as though she might faint. She/nsank into the chair beside Dudley, her face in her/nhands. The remains of the envelope smoldered into/nash in the silence./n/n"What is this?" Uncle Vernon said hoarsely. "What —/n/nI don't — Petunia?"/n/nAunt Petunia said nothing. Dudley was staring/nstupidly at his mother, his mouth hanging open. The/nsilence spiraled horribly. Harry was watching his/naunt, utterly bewildered, his head throbbing fit to/nburst./n/n"Petunia, dear?" said Uncle Vernon timidly. "P-/nPetunia?"/n/nShe raised her head. She was still trembling. She/nswallowed./n/n"The boy — the boy will have to stay, Vernon," she/nsaid weakly./n/n"W-what?"/n/n"He stays," she said. She was not looking at Harry./n/nShe got to her feet again./n/n"He ... but Petunia ..."/n/n"If we throw him out, the neighbors will talk," she/nsaid. She was regaining her usual brisk, snappish/nmanner rapidly, though she was still very pale./n/n/n/n/n/n"They'll ask awkward questions, they'll want to know/nwhere he's gone. We'll have to keep him."/n/nUncle Vernon was deflating like an old tire./n/n"But Petunia, dear — "/n/nAunt Petunia ignored him. She turned to Harry./n/n"You're to stay in your room," she said. "You're not to/nleave the house. Now get to bed."/n/nHarry didn't move./n/n"Who was that Howler from?"/n/n"Don't ask questions," Aunt Petunia snapped./n/n"Are you in touch with wizards?"/n/n"I told you to get to bed!"/n/n"What did it mean? Remember the last what?"/n/n"Go to bed!"/n/n"How come — ?"/n/n"YOU HEARD YOUR AUNT, NOW GET TO BED!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Advance Guard
text: /n"Fve just been attacked by dementors and I might be/nexpelled from Hogwarts. I want to know what's going/non and when I'm going to get out of here. "/n/nHarry copied these words onto three separate pieces/nof parchment the moment he reached the desk in his/ndark bedroom. He addressed the first to Sirius, the/nsecond to Ron, and the third to Hermione. His owl,/nHedwig, was off hunting; her cage stood empty on the/ndesk. Harry paced the bedroom waiting for her to/ncome back, his head pounding, his brain too busy for/nsleep even though his eyes stung and itched with/ntiredness. His back ached from carrying Dudley/nhome, and the two lumps on his head where the/nwindow and Dudley had hit him were throbbing/npainfully./n/nUp and down he paced, consumed with anger and/nfrustration, grinding his teeth and clenching his fists,/ncasting angry looks out at the empty, star-strewn sky/nevery time he passed the window. Dementors sent to/nget him, Mrs. Figg and Mundungus Fletcher tailing/n/n/n/nhim in secret, then suspension from Hogwarts and a/nhearing at the Ministry of Magic — and still no one/nwas telling him what was going on./n/nAnd what, what, had that Howler been about? Whose/nvoice had echoed so horribly, so menacingly, through/nthe kitchen?/n/nWhy was he still trapped here without information?/nWhy was everyone treating him like some naughty/nkid? Don't do any more magic, stay in the house.../n/nHe kicked his school trunk as he passed it, but far/nfrom relieving his anger he felt worse, as he now had/na sharp pain in his toe to deal with in addition to the/npain in the rest of his body./n/nJust as he limped past the window, Hedwig soared/nthrough it with a soft rustle of wings like a small/nghost./n/n"About time!" Harry snarled, as she landed lightly on/ntop of her cage. "You can put that down, IVe got work/nfor you!"/n/nHedwig's large round amber eyes gazed reproachfully/nat him over the dead frog clamped in her beak./n/n"Come here," said Harry, picking up the three small/nrolls of parchment and a leather thong and tying the/nscrolls to her scaly leg. "Take these straight to Sirius,/nRon, and Hermione and don't come back here without/ngood long replies. Keep pecking them till they've/nwritten decent-length answers if you've got to./nUnderstand?"/n/nHedwig gave a muffled hooting noise, beak still full of/nfrog./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Get going, then," said Harry./n/nShe took off immediately. The moment she'd gone,/nHarry threw himself down onto his bed without/nundressing and stared at the dark ceiling. In addition/nto every other miserable feeling, he now felt guilty/nthat he'd been irritable with Hedwig; she was the only/nfriend he had at number four, Privet Drive. But he'd/nmake it up to her when she came back with Sirius's,/nRon's, and Hermione's answers./n/nThey were bound to write back quickly; they couldn't/npossibly ignore a dementor attack. He'd probably/nwake up tomorrow to three fat letters full of sympathy/nand plans for his immediate removal to the Burrow./nAnd with that comforting idea, sleep rolled over him,/nstifling all further thought./n/n•k Jc k/n/n/n/nBut Hedwig didn't return next morning. Harry spent/nthe day in his bedroom, leaving it only to go to the/nbathroom. Three times that day Aunt Petunia shoved/nfood into his room through the cat flap Uncle Vernon/nhad installed three summers ago. Every time Harry/nheard her approaching he tried to question her about/nthe Howler, but he might as well have interrogated/nthe doorknob for all the answers he got. Otherwise/nthe Dursleys kept well clear of his bedroom. Harry/ncouldn't see the point of forcing his company on/nthem; another row would achieve nothing except/nperhaps making him so angry he'd perform more/nillegal magic./n/nSo it went on for three whole days. Harry was filled/nalternately with restless energy that made him unable/nto settle to anything, during which he paced his/nbedroom again, furious at the whole lot of them for/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nleaving him to stew in this mess, and with a lethargy/nso complete that he could lie on his bed for an hour/nat a time, staring dazedly into space, aching with/ndread at the thought of the Ministry hearing./n/nWhat if they ruled against him? What if he was/nexpelled and his wand was snapped in half? What/nwould he do, where would he go? He could not return/nto living full-time with the Dursleys, not now that he/nknew the other world, the one to which he really/nbelonged... Was it possible that he might be able to/nmove into Sirius's house, as Sirius had suggested a/nyear ago, before he had been forced to flee from the/nMinistry himself? Would he be allowed to live there/nalone, given that he was still underage? Or would the/nmatter of where he went next be decided for him; had/nhis breach of the International Statute of Secrecy/nbeen severe enough to land him in a cell in Azkaban?/nWhenever this thought occurred, Harry invariably slid/noff his bed and began pacing again./n/nOn the fourth night after Hedwig's departure Harry/nwas lying in one of his apathetic phases, staring at/nthe ceiling, his exhausted mind quite blank, when his/nuncle entered his bedroom. Harry looked slowly/naround at him. Uncle Vernon was wearing his best/nsuit and an expression of enormous smugness./n/n"We're going out," he said./n/n"Sorry?"/n/n"We — that is to say, your aunt, Dudley, and I — are/ngoing out."/n/n"Fine," said Harry dully, looking back at the ceiling./n/n"You are not to leave your bedroom while we are/naway."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Okay."/n/n/n/n"You are not to touch the television, the stereo, or any/nof our possessions."/n/n"Right."/n/n"You are not to steal food from the fridge."/n/n"Okay."/n/n"I am going to lock your door."/n/n"You do that."/n/nUncle Vernon glared at Harry, clearly suspicious of/nthis lack of argument, then stomped out of the room/nand closed the door behind him. Harry heard the key/nturn in the lock and Uncle Vernon's footsteps walking/nheavily down the stairs. A few minutes later he heard/nthe slamming of car doors, the rumble of an engine,/nand the unmistakable sound of the car sweeping out/nof the drive./n/nHarry had no particular feeling about the Dursleys/nleaving. It made no difference to him whether they/nwere in the house or not. He could not even summon/nthe energy to get up and turn on his bedroom light./nThe room grew steadily darker around him as he lay/nlistening to the night sounds through the window he/nkept open all the time, waiting for the blessed/nmoment when Hedwig returned./n/nThe empty house creaked around him. The pipes/ngurgled. Harry lay there in a kind of stupor, thinking/nof nothing, suspended in misery./n/nAnd then, quite distinctly, he heard a crash in the/nkitchen below./n/n/n/n/n/nHe sat bolt upright, listening intently. The Dursleys/ncouldn't be back, it was much too soon, and in any/ncase he hadn't heard their car./n/nThere was silence for a few seconds, and then he/nheard voices./n/nBurglars, he thought, sliding off the bed onto his feet/n— but a split second later it occurred to him that/nburglars would keep their voices down, and whoever/nwas moving around in the kitchen was certainly not/ntroubling to do so./n/nHe snatched up his wand from his bedside table and/nstood facing his bedroom door, listening with all his/nmight. Next moment he jumped as the lock gave a/nloud click and his door swung open./n/nHarry stood motionless, staring through the open/ndoor at the dark upstairs landing, straining his ears/nfor further sounds, but none came. He hesitated for a/nmoment and then moved swiftly and silently out of/nhis room to the head of the stairs./n/nHis heart shot upward into his throat. There were/npeople standing in the shadowy hall below,/nsilhouetted against the streetlight glowing through/nthe glass door; eight or nine of them, all, as far as he/ncould see, looking up at him./n/n"Lower your wand, boy, before you take someone's eye/nout," said a low, growling voice./n/nHarry's heart was thumping uncontrollably. He knew/nthat voice, but he did not lower his wand./n/n"Professor Moody?" he said uncertainly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't know so much about 'Professor,' " growled the/nvoice, "never got round to much teaching, did I? Get/ndown here, we want to see you properly."/n/nHarry lowered his wand slightly but did not relax his/ngrip on it, nor did he move. He had very good reason/nto be suspicious. He had recently spent nine months/nin what he had thought was Mad-Eye Moody's/ncompany only to find out that it wasn't Moody at all,/nbut an impostor; an impostor, moreover, who had/ntried to kill Harry before being unmasked. But before/nhe could make a decision about what to do next, a/nsecond, slightly hoarse voice floated upstairs./n/n"It's all right, Harry. We've come to take you away."/n/nHarry's heart leapt. He knew that voice too, though he/nhadn't heard it for more than a year./n/n"P-Professor Lupin?" he said disbelievingly. "Is that/nyou?"/n/n"Why are we all standing in the dark?" said a third/nvoice, this one completely unfamiliar, a woman's./n"Lumos."/n/nA wand tip flared, illuminating the hall with magical/nlight. Harry blinked. The people below were crowded/naround the foot of the stairs, gazing intently up at/nhim, some craning their heads for a better look./n/nRemus Lupin stood nearest to him. Though still quite/nyoung, Lupin looked tired and rather ill; he had more/ngray hair than when Harry had said good-bye to him,/nand his robes were more patched and shabbier than/never. Nevertheless, he was smiling broadly at Harry,/nwho tried to smile back through his shock./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oooh, he looks just like I thought he would," said the/nwitch who was holding her lit wand aloft. She looked/nthe youngest there; she had a pale heart-shaped face,/ndark twinkling eyes, and short spiky hair that was a/nviolent shade of violet. "Wotcher, Harry!"/n/n"Yeah, I see what you mean, Remus," said a bald/nblack wizard standing farthest back; he had a deep,/nslow voice and wore a single gold hoop in his ear. "He/nlooks exactly like James."/n/n"Except the eyes," said a wheezy-voiced, silver-haired/nwizard at the back. "Lily's eyes."/n/nMad-Eye Moody, who had long grizzled gray hair and/na large chunk missing from his nose, was squinting/nsuspiciously at Harry through his mismatched eyes./nOne of the eyes was small, dark, and beady, the other/nlarge, round, and electric blue — the magical eye that/ncould see through walls, doors, and the back of/nMoody's own head./n/n"Are you quite sure it's him, Lupin?" he growled. "It'd/nbe a nice lookout if we bring back some Death Eater/nimpersonating him. We ought to ask him something/nonly the real Potter would know. Unless anyone/nbrought any Veritaserum?"/n/n"Harry, what form does your Patronus take?" said/nLupin./n/n"A stag," said Harry nervously./n/n"That's him, Mad-Eye," said Lupin./n/nHarry descended the stairs, very conscious of/neverybody still staring at him, stowing his wand into/nthe back pocket of his jeans as he came./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't put your wand there, boy!" roared Moody./n"What if it ignited? Better wizards than you have lost/nbuttocks, you know!"/n/n"Who d'you know who's lost a buttock?" the violet-/nhaired woman asked Mad-Eye interestedly./n/n"Never you mind, you just keep your wand out of your/nback pocket!" growled Mad-Eye. "Elementary wand/nsafety, nobody bothers about it anymore..." He/nstumped off toward the kitchen. "And I saw that," he/nadded irritably, as the woman rolled her eyes at the/nceiling./n/nLupin held out his hand and shook Harry's./n/n"How are you?" he asked, looking at Harry closely./n"F-fine ..."/n/nHarry could hardly believe this was real. Four weeks/nwith nothing, not the tiniest hint of a plan to remove/nhim from Privet Drive, and suddenly a whole bunch of/nwizards was standing matter-of-factly in the house as/nthough this were a long-standing arrangement. He/nglanced at the people surrounding Lupin; they were/nstill gazing avidly at him. He felt very conscious of the/nfact that he had not combed his hair for four days./n/n"I'm — you're really lucky the Dursleys are out ..." he/nmumbled./n/n"Lucky, ha!" said the violet-haired woman. "It was me/nthat lured them out of the way. Sent a letter by/nMuggle post telling them they'd been short-listed for/nthe All-England Best-Kept Suburban Lawn/nCompetition. They're heading off to the prize-giving/nright now... Or they think they are."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry had a fleeting vision of Uncle Vernon's face/nwhen he realized there was no All-England Best-Kept/nSuburban Lawn Competition./n/n"We are leaving, aren't we?" he asked. "Soon?"/n/n"Almost at once," said Lupin, "we're just waiting for/nthe all-clear."/n/n"Where are we going? The Burrow?" Harry asked/nhopefully./n/n"Not the Burrow, no," said Lupin, motioning Harry/ntoward the kitchen; the little knot of wizards followed,/nall still eyeing Harry curiously. "Too risky. We've set/nup headquarters somewhere undetectable. It's taken/na while..."/n/nMad-Eye Moody was now sitting at the kitchen table/nswigging from a hip flask, his magical eye spinning in/nall directions, taking in the Dursleys' many labor-/nsaving appliances./n/n"This is Alastor Moody, Harry," Lupin continued,/npointing toward Moody./n/n"Yeah, I know," said Harry uncomfortably; it felt odd/nto be introduced to somebody he'd thought he'd/nknown for a year./n/n"And this is Nymphadora — "/n/n" Don't call me Nymphadora, Remus," said the young/nwitch with a shudder. "It's Tonks."/n/n" — Nymphadora Tonks, who prefers to be known by/nher surname only," finished Lupin./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So would you if your fool of a mother had called you/n'Nymphadora, ' " muttered Tonks./n/n"And this is Kingsley Shacklebolt" — he indicated the/ntall black wizard, who bowed — "Elphias Doge" — the/nwheezy-voiced wizard nodded — "Dedalus Diggle — "/n/n"We've met before," squeaked the excitable Diggle,/ndropping his top hat./n/n" — Emmeline Vance" — a stately looking witch in an/nemerald-green shawl inclined her head — "Sturgis/nPodmore" — a square-jawed wizard with thick, straw-/ncolored hair winked — "and Hestia Jones." A pink-/ncheeked, black-haired witch waved from next to the/ntoaster./n/nHarry inclined his head awkwardly at each of them as/nthey were introduced. He wished they would look at/nsomething other than him; it was as though he had/nsuddenly been ushered onstage. He also wondered/nwhy so many of them were there./n/n"A surprising number of people volunteered to come/nand get you," said Lupin, as though he had read/nHarry's mind; the corners of his mouth twitched/nslightly./n/n"Yeah, well, the more the better," said Moody darkly./n"We're your guard, Potter."/n/n"We're just waiting for the signal to tell us it's safe to/nset off," said Lupin, glancing out of the kitchen/nwindow. "We've got about fifteen minutes."/n/n"Very clean, aren't they, these Muggles?" said the/nwitch called Tonks, who was looking around the/nkitchen with great interest. "My dad's Muggle-born/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nand he's a right old slob. I suppose it varies, just like/nwith wizards?"/n/n"Er — yeah," said Harry. "Look" — he turned back to/nLupin — "what's going on, I haven't heard anything/nfrom anyone, what's Vol — ?"/n/nSeveral of the witches and wizards made odd hissing/nnoises; Dedalus Diggle dropped his hat again, and/nMoody growled, "Shut up\"/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"We're not discussing anything here, it's too risky,"/nsaid Moody, turning his normal eye on Harry; his/nmagical eye remained pointing up at the ceiling./n"Damn it," he added angrily, putting a hand up to the/nmagical eye, "it keeps sticking — ever since that scum/nwore it — "/n/nAnd with a nasty squelching sound much like a/nplunger being pulled from a sink, he popped out his/neye./n/n"Mad-Eye, you do know that's disgusting, don't you?"/nsaid Tonks conversationally./n/n"Get me a glass of water, would you, Harry?" asked/nMoody./n/nHarry crossed to the dishwasher, took out a clean/nglass, and filled it with water at the sink, still watched/neagerly by the band of wizards. Their relentless/nstaring was starting to annoy him./n/n"Cheers," said Moody, when Harry handed him the/nglass. He dropped the magical eyeball into the water/nand prodded it up and down; the eye whizzed around,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nstaring at them all in turn. "I want three-hundred-/nand-sixty degrees visibility on the return journey."/n/n"How're we getting — wherever we're going?" Harry/nasked./n/n"Brooms," said Lupin. "Only way. You're too young to/nApparate, they'll be watching the Floo Network, and/nit's more than our life's worth to set up an/nunauthorized Portkey."/n/n"Remus says you're a good flier," said Kingsley/nShacklebolt in his deep voice./n/n"He's excellent," said Lupin, who was checking his/nwatch. "Anyway, you'd better go and get packed,/nHarry, we want to be ready to go when the signal/ncomes."/n/n"I'll come and help you," said Tonks brightly./n/nShe followed Harry back into the hall and up the/nstairs, looking around with much curiosity and/ninterest./n/n"Funny place," she said, "it's a bit too clean, d'you/nknow what I mean? Bit unnatural. Oh, this is better,"/nshe added, as they entered Harry's bedroom and he/nturned on the light./n/nHis room was certainly much messier than the rest of/nthe house. Confined to it for four days in a very bad/nmood, Harry had not bothered tidying up after/nhimself. Most of the books he owned were strewn over/nthe floor where he'd tried to distract himself with each/nin turn and thrown it aside. Hedwig's cage needed/ncleaning out and was starting to smell, and his trunk/nlay open, revealing a jumbled mixture of Muggle/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nclothes and wizard's robes that had spilled onto the/nfloor around it./n/nHarry started picking up books and throwing them/nhastily into his trunk. Tonks paused at his open/nwardrobe to look critically at her reflection in the/nmirror on the inside of the door./n/n"You know, I don't think purple's really my color," she/nsaid pensively, tugging at a lock of spiky hair. "D'you/nthink it makes me look a bit peaky?"/n/n"Er — " said Harry, looking up at her over the top of/nQuidditch Teams of Britain and Ireland./n/n"Yeah, it does," said Tonks decisively. She screwed up/nher eyes in a strained expression as though she were/nstruggling to remember something. A second later,/nher hair had turned bubble-gum pink./n/n"How did you do that?" said Harry, gaping at her as/nshe opened her eyes again./n/n"I'm a Metamorphmagus," she said, looking back at/nher reflection and turning her head so that she could/nsee her hair from all directions. "It means I can/nchange my appearance at will," she added, spotting/nHarry's puzzled expression in the mirror behind her./n/n"I was born one. I got top marks in Concealment and/nDisguise during Auror training without any study at/nall, it was great."/n/n"You're an Auror?" said Harry, impressed. Being a/nDark wizard catcher was the only career he'd ever/nconsidered after Hogwarts./n/n"Yeah," said Tonks, looking proud. "Kingsley is as/nwell; he's a bit higher up than I am, though. I only/nqualified a year ago. Nearly failed on Stealth and/n/n/n/n/n/nTracking, I'm dead clumsy, did you hear me break/nthat plate when we arrived downstairs?"/n/n/n/n"Can you learn how to be a Metamorphmagus?" Harry/nasked her, straightening up, completely forgetting/nabout packing./n/nTonks chuckled./n/n"Bet you wouldn't mind hiding that scar sometimes,/neh?"/n/nHer eyes found the lightning-shaped scar on Harry's/nforehead./n/n"No, I wouldn't mind," Harry mumbled, turning away./nHe did not like people staring at his scar./n/n"Well, you 11 have to learn the hard way, I'm afraid,"/nsaid Tonks. "Metamorphmagi are really rare, they're/nborn, not made. Most wizards need to use a wand or/npotions to change their appearance... But we've got to/nget going, Harry, we're supposed to be packing," she/nadded guiltily, looking around at all the mess on the/nfloor./n/n"Oh — yeah," said Harry, grabbing up a few more/nbooks./n/n"Don't be stupid, it'll be much quicker if I — pack)."/ncried Tonks, waving her wand in a long, sweeping/nmovement over the floor./n/nBooks, clothes, telescope, and scales all soared into/nthe air and flew pell-mell into the trunk./n/n"It's not very neat," said Tonks, walking over to the/ntrunk and looking down at the jumble inside. "My/nmum's got this knack of getting stuff to fit itself in/n/n/n/n/n/nneatly — she even gets the socks to fold themselves —/nbut I've never mastered how she does it — it's a kind/nof flick — "/n/nShe flicked her wand hopefully; one of Harry's socks/ngave a feeble sort of wiggle and flopped back on top of/nthe mess within./n/n"Ah, well," said Tonks, slamming the trunk's lid shut,/n"at least it's all in. That could do with a bit of/ncleaning, too — Scourgify — " She pointed her wand at/nHedwig's cage; a few feathers and droppings/nvanished. "Well, that's a bit better — I've never quite/ngot the hang of these sort of householdy spells. Right/n— got everything? Cauldron? Broom? Wow! A/nFirebolt?"/n/nHer eyes widened as they fell on the broomstick in/nHarry's right hand. It was his pride and joy, a gift/nfrom Sirius, an international standard broomstick./n/n"And I'm still riding a Comet Two Sixty," said Tonks/nenviously. "Ah well ... wand still in your jeans? Both/nbuttocks still on? Okay, let's go. Locomotor Trunk."/n/nHarry's trunk rose a few inches into the air. Holding/nher wand like a conductor's baton, Tonks made it/nhover across the room and out of the door ahead of/nthem, Hedwig's cage in her left hand. Harry followed/nher down the stairs carrying his broomstick./n/nBack in the kitchen, Moody had replaced his eye,/nwhich was spinning so fast after its cleaning it made/nHarry feel sick. Kingsley Shacklebolt and Sturgis/nPodmore were examining the microwave and Hestia/nJones was laughing at a potato peeler she had come/nacross while rummaging in the drawers. Lupin was/nsealing a letter addressed to the Dursleys./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Excellent," said Lupin, looking up as Tonks and/nHarry entered. "We've got about a minute, I think. We/nshould probably get out into the garden so we're/nready. Harry, I've left a letter telling your aunt and/nuncle not to worry — "/n/n"They won't," said Harry./n/n"That you're safe — "/n/n"That'll just depress them."/n/n" — and you'll see them next summer."/n/n"Do I have to?"/n/nLupin smiled but made no answer./n/n"Come here, boy," said Moody gruffly, beckoning/nHarry toward him with his wand. "I need to/nDisillusion you."/n/n"You need to what?" said Harry nervously./n/n"Disillusionment Charm," said Moody, raising his/nwand. "Lupin says you've got an Invisibility Cloak,/nbut it won't stay on while we're flying; this'll disguise/nyou better. Here you go — "/n/nHe rapped Harry hard on the top of the head and/nHarry felt a curious sensation as though Moody had/njust smashed an egg there; cold trickles seemed to be/nrunning down his body from the point the wand had/nstruck./n/n"Nice one, Mad-Eye," said Tonks appreciatively,/nstaring at Harry's midriff./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry looked down at his body, or rather, what had/nbeen his body, for it didn't look anything like his/nanymore. It was not invisible; it had simply taken on/nthe exact color and texture of the kitchen unit behind/nhim. He seemed to have become a human chameleon./n/n"Come on," said Moody, unlocking the back door with/nhis wand./n/nThey all stepped outside onto Uncle Vernon's/nbeautifully kept lawn./n/n"Clear night," grunted Moody, his magical eye/nscanning the heavens. "Could've done with a bit more/ncloud cover. Right, you," he barked at Harry, "we're/ngoing to be flying in close formation. Tonks'll be right/nin front of you, keep close on her tail. Lupin'll be/ncovering you from below. I'm going to be behind you./nThe rest'll be circling us. We don't break ranks for/nanything, got me? If one of us is killed — "/n/n"Is that likely?" Harry asked apprehensively, but/nMoody ignored him./n/n" — the others keep flying, don't stop, don't break/nranks. If they take out all of us and you survive,/n/nHarry, the rear guard are standing by to take over;/nkeep flying east and they'll join you."/n/n"Stop being so cheerful, Mad-Eye, he'll think we're not/ntaking this seriously," said Tonks, as she strapped/nHarry's trunk and Hedwig's cage into a harness/nhanging from her broom./n/n"I'm just telling the boy the plan," growled Moody./n"Our job's to deliver him safely to headquarters and if/nwe die in the attempt — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No one's going to die," said Kingsley Shacklebolt in/nhis deep, calming voice./n/n"Mount your brooms, that's the first signal!" said/nLupin sharply, pointing into the sky./n/nFar, far above them, a shower of bright red sparks/nhad flared among the stars. Harry recognized them at/nonce as wand sparks. He swung his right leg over his/nFirebolt, gripped its handle tightly, and felt it/nvibrating very slightly, as though it was as keen as he/nwas to be up in the air once more./n/n"Second signal, let's go!" said Lupin loudly, as more/nsparks, green this time, exploded high above them./n/nHarry kicked off hard from the ground. The cool night/nair rushed through his hair as the neat square/ngardens of Privet Drive fell away, shrinking rapidly/ninto a patchwork of dark greens and blacks, and/nevery thought of the Ministry hearing was swept from/nhis mind as though the rush of air had blown it out of/nhis head. He felt as though his heart was going to/nexplode with pleasure; he was flying again, flying/naway from Privet Drive as he'd been fantasizing about/nall summer, he was going home... For a few glorious/nmoments, all his problems seemed to recede into/nnothing, insignificant in the vast, starry sky./n/n"Hard left, hard left, there's a Muggle looking up!"/nshouted Moody from behind him. Tonks swerved and/nHarry followed her, watching his trunk swinging/nwildly beneath her broom. "We need more height.../nGive it another quarter of a mile!"/n/nHarry's eyes watered in the chill as they soared/nupward; he could see nothing below now but tiny/npinpricks of light that were car headlights and/nstreetlamps. Two of those tiny lights might belong to/n/n/n/n/n/nUncle Vernon's car... The Dursleys would be heading/nback to their empty house right now, full of rage/nabout the nonexistent lawn competition . . . and Harry/nlaughed aloud at the thought, though his voice was/ndrowned by the flapping of the others' robes, the/ncreaking of the harness holding his trunk and the/ncage, the whoosh of the wind in their ears as they/nsped through the air. He had not felt this alive in a/nmonth, or this happy.../n/n"Bearing south!" shouted Mad-Eye. "Town ahead!"/n/nThey soared right, so that they did not pass directly/nover the glittering spiderweb of lights below./n/n"Bear southeast and keep climbing, there's some low/ncloud ahead we can lose ourselves in!" called Moody./n/n"We're not going through clouds!" shouted Tonks/nangrily. "We'll get soaked, Mad-Eye!"/n/nHarry was relieved to hear her say this; his hands/nwere growing numb on the Firebolt's handle. He/nwished he had thought to put on a coat; he was/nstarting to shiver./n/nThey altered their course every now and then/naccording to Mad-Eye 's instructions. Harry's eyes/nwere screwed up against the rush of icy wind that/nwas starting to make his ears ache. He could/nremember being this cold on a broom only once/nbefore, during the Quidditch match against Hufflepuff/nin his third year, which had taken place in a storm./nThe guard around him was circling continuously like/ngiant birds of prey. Harry lost track of time. He/nwondered how long they had been flying; it felt like an/nhour at least./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Turning southwest!" yelled Moody. "We want to avoid/nthe motorway!"/n/nHarry was now so chilled that he thought longingly/nfor a moment of the snug, dry interiors of the cars/nstreaming along below, then, even more longingly, of/ntraveling by Floo powder; it might be uncomfortable to/nspin around in fireplaces but it was at least warm in/nthe flames... Kingsley Shacklebolt swooped around/nhim, bald pate and earring gleaming slightly in the/nmoonlight... Now Emmeline Vance was on his right,/nher wand out, her head turning left and right . . . then/nshe too swooped over him, to be replaced by Sturgis/nPodmore.../n/n"We ought to double back for a bit, just to make sure/nwe're not being followed!" Moody shouted./n/n"ARE YOU MAD, MAD-EYE?" Tonks screamed from/nthe front. "We're all frozen to our brooms! If we keep/ngoing off course we're not going to get there until next/nweek! We're nearly there now!"/n/n"Time to start the descent!" came Lupin's voice./n"Follow Tonks, Harry!"/n/nHarry followed Tonks into a dive. They were heading/nfor the largest collection of lights he had yet seen, a/nhuge, sprawling, crisscrossing mass, glittering in lines/nand grids, interspersed with patches of deepest black./nLower and lower they flew, until Harry could see/nindividual headlights and streetlamps, chimneys, and/ntelevision aerials. He wanted to reach the ground very/nmuch, though he felt sure that someone would have/nto unfreeze him from his broom./n/n"Here we go!" called Tonks, and a few seconds later/nshe had landed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry touched down right behind her and/ndismounted on a patch of unkempt grass in the/nmiddle of a small square. Tonks was already/nunbuckling Harry's trunk. Shivering, Harry looked/naround. The grimy fronts of the surrounding houses/nwere not welcoming; some of them had broken/nwindows, glimmering dully in the light from the/nstreet-lamps, paint was peeling from many of the/ndoors, and heaps of rubbish lay outside several sets/nof front steps./n/n"Where are we?" Harry asked, but Lupin said quietly,/n"In a minute."/n/nMoody was rummaging in his cloak, his gnarled/nhands clumsy with cold./n/n"Got it," he muttered, raising what looked like a silver/ncigarette lighter into the air and clicking it./n/nThe nearest streetlamp went out with a pop. He/nclicked the un-lighter again; the next lamp went out./nHe kept clicking until every lamp in the square was/nextinguished and the only light in the square came/nfrom curtained windows and the sickle moon/noverhead./n/n"Borrowed it from Dumbledore," growled Moody,/npocketing the Put-Outer. "That'll take care of any/nMuggles looking out of the window, see? Now, come/non, quick."/n/nHe took Harry by the arm and led him from the patch/nof grass, across the road, and onto the pavement./nLupin and Tonks followed, carrying Harry's trunk/nbetween them, the rest of the guard, all with their/nwands out, flanking them./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe muffled pounding of a stereo was coming from an/nupper window in the nearest house. A pungent smell/nof rotting rubbish came from the pile of bulging bin-/nbags just inside the broken gate./n/n"Here," Moody muttered, thrusting a piece of/nparchment toward Harry's Disillusioned hand and/nholding his lit wand close to it, so as to illuminate the/nwriting. "Read quickly and memorize."/n/nHarry looked down at the piece of paper. The narrow/nhandwriting was vaguely familiar. It said:/n/nThe headquarters of the Order of the Phoenix may he/nfound at number twelve, Grimmauld Place, London./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Number Twelve, Grimmauld Place
text: /n"What's the Order of the — ?" Harry began./n/n"Not here, boy!" snarled Moody. "Wait till we're/ninside!"/n/nHe pulled the piece of parchment out of Harry's hand/nand set fire to it with his wand tip. As the message/ncurled into flames and floated to the ground, Harry/nlooked around at the houses again. They were/nstanding outside number eleven; he looked to the left/nand saw number ten; to the right, however, was/nnumber thirteen./n/n"But where's — ?"/n/n"Think about what you've just memorized," said Lupin/nquietly./n/nHarry thought, and no sooner had he reached the/npart about number twelve, Grimmauld Place, than a/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbattered door emerged out of nowhere between/nnumbers eleven and thirteen, followed swiftly by dirty/nwalls and grimy windows. It was as though an extra/nhouse had inflated, pushing those on either side out/nof its way. Harry gaped at it. The stereo in number/neleven thudded on. Apparently the Muggles inside/nhadn't even felt anything./n/n"Come on, hurry," growled Moody, prodding Harry in/nthe back./n/nHarry walked up the worn stone steps, staring at the/nnewly materialized door. Its black paint was shabby/nand scratched. The silver door knocker was in the/nform of a twisted serpent. There was no keyhole or/nletterbox./n/nLupin pulled out his wand and tapped the door once./nHarry heard many loud, metallic clicks and what/nsounded like the clatter of a chain. The door creaked/nopen./n/n"Get in quick, Harry," Lupin whispered. "But don't go/nfar inside and don't touch anything."/n/nHarry stepped over the threshold into the almost total/ndarkness of the hall. He could smell damp, dust, and/na sweetish, rotting smell; the place had the feeling of/na derelict building. He looked over his shoulder and/nsaw the others filing in behind him, Lupin and Tonks/ncarrying his trunk and Hedwig's cage. Moody was/nstanding on the top step and releasing the balls of/nlight the Put-Outer had stolen from the street-lamps;/nthey flew back to their bulbs and the square beyond/nglowed momentarily with orange light before Moody/nlimped inside and closed the front door, so that the/ndarkness in the hall became complete./n/n"Here — "/n/n/n/n/n/nHe rapped Harry hard over the head with his wand;/nHarry felt as though something hot was trickling/ndown his back this time and knew that the/nDisillusionment Charm must have lifted./n/n"Now stay still, everyone, while I give us a bit of light/nin here," Moody whispered./n/nThe others' hushed voices were giving Harry an odd/nfeeling of foreboding; it was as though they had just/nentered the house of a dying person. He heard a soft/nhissing noise and then old-fashioned gas lamps/nsputtered into life all along the walls, casting a/nflickering insubstantial light over the peeling/nwallpaper and threadbare carpet of a long, gloomy/nhallway, where a cobwebby chandelier glimmered/noverhead and age-blackened portraits hung crooked/non the walls. Harry heard something scuttling behind/nthe baseboard. Both the chandelier and the/ncandelabra on a rickety table nearby were shaped like/nserpents./n/nThere were hurried footsteps and Ron's mother, Mrs./nWeasley, emerged from a door at the far end of the/nhall. She was beaming in welcome as she hurried/ntoward them, though Harry noticed that she was/nrather thinner and paler than she had been last time/nhe had seen her./n/n"Oh, Harry, it's lovely to see you!" she whispered,/npulling him into a rib-cracking hug before holding/nhim at arm's length and examining him critically./n"You're looking peaky; you need feeding up, but you'll/nhave to wait a bit for dinner, I'm afraid..."/n/nShe turned to the gang of wizards behind him and/nwhispered urgently, "He's just arrived, the meeting's/nstarted..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe wizards behind Harry all made noises of interest/nand excitement and began filing past Harry toward/nthe door through which Mrs. Weasley had just come;/nHarry made to follow Lupin, but Mrs. Weasley held/nhim back./n/n"No, Harry, the meeting's only for members of the/nOrder. Ron and Hermione are upstairs, you can wait/nwith them until the meeting's over and then we'll have/ndinner. And keep your voice down in the hall," she/nadded in an urgent whisper./n/n"Why?"/n/n"I don't want to wake anything up."/n/n"What d'you — ?"/n/n"I'll explain later, I've got to hurry, I'm supposed to be/nat the meeting — I'll just show you where you're/nsleeping."/n/nPressing her finger to her lips, she led him on tiptoes/npast a pair of long, moth-eaten curtains, behind/nwhich Harry supposed there must be another door,/nand after skirting a large umbrella stand that looked/nas though it had been made from a severed troll's leg,/nthey started up the dark staircase, passing a row of/nshrunken heads mounted on plaques on the wall. A/ncloser look showed Harry that the heads belonged to/nhouse-elves. All of them had the same rather/nsnoutlike nose./n/nHarry's bewilderment deepened with every step he/ntook. C'mon."/n/n"And don't forget to keep your voice down in the hall,/nHarry," Hermione whispered./n/nAs they passed the row of house-elf heads on the wall/nthey saw Lupin, Mrs. Weasley, and Tonks at the front/ndoor, magically sealing its many locks and bolts/nbehind those who had just left./n/n"We're eating down in the kitchen," Mrs. Weasley/nwhispered, meeting them at the bottom of the stairs./n"Harry, dear, if youll just tiptoe across the hall, it's/nthrough this door here — "/n/nCRASH./n/n"Tonksl" cried Mrs. Weasley exasperatedly, turning to/nlook behind her./n/n"I'm sorry!" wailed Tonks, who was lying flat on the/nfloor. "It's that stupid umbrella stand, that's the/nsecond time I've tripped over — "/n/nBut the rest of her words were drowned by a horrible,/nearsplitting, bloodcurdling screech./n/nThe moth-eaten velvet curtains Harry had passed/nearlier had flown apart, but there was no door behind/nthem. For a split second, Harry thought he was/nlooking through a window, a window behind which an/nold woman in a black cap was screaming and/nscreaming as though she was being tortured — then/n/n/n/n/nhe realized it was simply a life-size portrait, but the/nmost realistic, and the most unpleasant, he had ever/nseen in his life./n/nThe old woman was drooling, her eyes were rolling,/nthe yellowing skin of her face stretched taut as she/nscreamed, and all along the hall behind them, the/nother portraits awoke and began to yell too, so that/nHarry actually screwed up his eyes at the noise and/nclapped his hands over his ears./n/nLupin and Mrs. Weasley darted forward and tried to/ntug the curtains shut over the old woman, but they/nwould not close and she screeched louder than ever,/nbrandishing clawed hands as though trying to tear at/ntheir faces./n/n"Filth! Scum! By-products of dirt and vileness! Half-/nbreeds, mutants, freaks, begone from this place! How/ndare you befoul the house of my fathers — "/n/nTonks apologized over and over again, at the same/ntime dragging the huge, heavy troll's leg back off the/nfloor. Mrs. Weasley abandoned the attempt to close/nthe curtains and hurried up and down the hall,/nStunning all the other portraits with her wand. Then/na man with long black hair came charging out of a/ndoor facing Harry./n/n"Shut up, you horrible old hag, shut UP!" he roared,/nseizing the curtain Mrs. Weasley had abandoned./n/nThe old woman's face blanched./n/n"Yooooul" she howled, her eyes popping at the sight of/nthe man.
