"Blood traitor, abomination, shame of my/nfleshl"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I said — shut — UP!" roared the man, and with a/nstupendous effort he and Lupin managed to force the/ncurtains closed again./n/nThe old woman's screeches died and an echoing/nsilence fell./n/nPanting slightly and sweeping his long dark hair out/nof his eyes, Harry's godfather, Sirius, turned to face/nhim./n/n"Hello, Harry," he said grimly, "I see you've met my/nmother."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n5/n/n/n/n

title: The Order Of The Phoenix
text: /n"Your — ?"/n/n"My dear old mum, yeah," said Sirius. "We've been/ntrying to get her down for a month but we think she/nput a Permanent Sticking Charm on the back of the/ncanvas. Let's get downstairs, quick, before they all/nwake up again."/n/n"But what's a portrait of your mother doing here?"/nHarry asked, bewildered, as they went through the/ndoor from the hall and led the way down a flight of/nnarrow stone steps, the others just behind them./n/n"Hasn't anyone told you? This was my parents'/nhouse," said Sirius. "But I'm the last Black left, so it's/nmine now. I offered it to Dumbledore for headquarters/n— about the only useful thing I've been able to do."/n/nHarry, who had expected a better welcome, noted how/nhard and bitter Sirius's voice sounded. He followed/nhis godfather to the bottom of the stairs and through/na door leading into the basement kitchen./n/n/n/n/nIt was scarcely less gloomy than the hall above, a/ncavernous room with rough stone walls. Most of the/nlight was coming from a large fire at the far end of the/nroom. A haze of pipe smoke hung in the air like battle/nfumes, through which loomed the menacing shapes of/nheavy iron pots and pans hanging from the dark/nceiling. Many chairs had been crammed into the room/nfor the meeting and a long wooden table stood in the/nmiddle of the room, littered with rolls of parchment,/ngoblets, empty wine bottles, and a heap of what/nappeared to be rags. Mr. Weasley and his eldest son,/nBill, were talking quietly with their heads together at/nthe end of the table./n/nMrs. Weasley cleared her throat. Her husband, a thin,/nbalding, red-haired man, who wore horn-rimmed/nglasses, looked around and jumped to his feet./n/n"Harry!" Mr. Weasley said, hurrying forward to greet/nhim and shaking his hand vigorously. "Good to see/nyou!"/n/nOver his shoulder Harry saw Bill, who still wore his/nlong hair in a ponytail, hastily rolling up the lengths/nof parchment left on the table./n/n"Journey all right, Harry?" Bill called, trying to gather/nup twelve scrolls at once. "Mad-Eye didn't make you/ncome via Greenland, then?"/n/n"He tried," said Tonks, striding over to help Bill and/nimmediately sending a candle toppling onto the last/npiece of parchment. "Oh no — sorry — "/n/n"Here, dear," said Mrs. Weasley, sounding/nexasperated, and she repaired the parchment with a/nwave of her wand: In the flash of light caused by Mrs./nWeasley's charm, Harry caught a glimpse of what/nlooked like the plan of a building./n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley had seen him looking. She snatched the/nplan off the table and stuffed it into Bill's heavily/nladen arms./n/n"This sort of thing ought to be cleared away promptly/nat the end of meetings," she snapped before sweeping/noff toward an ancient dresser from which she started/nunloading dinner plates./n/nBill took out his wand, muttered "Evanescol" and the/nscrolls vanished./n/n"Sit down, Harry," said Sirius. "You've met/nMundungus, haven't you?"/n/nThe thing Harry had taken to be a pile of rags gave a/nprolonged, grunting snore and then jerked awake./n/n"Some'n say m' name?" Mundungus mumbled/nsleepily. "I 'gree with Sirius..."/n/nHe raised a very grubby hand in the air as though/nvoting, his droopy, bloodshot eyes unfocused. Ginny/ngiggled./n/n"The meeting's over, Dung," said Sirius, as they all sat/ndown around him at the table. "Harry's arrived."/n/n"Eh?" said Mundungus, peering balefully at Harry/nthrough his matted ginger hair. "Blimey, so 'e 'as./n/nYeah ... you all right, 'arry?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry./n/nMundungus fumbled nervously in his pockets, still/nstaring at Harry, and pulled out a grimy black pipe./n/nHe stuck it in his mouth, ignited the end of it with his/nwand, and took a deep pull on it. Great billowing/nclouds of greenish smoke obscured him in seconds./n/n/n/n/n"Owe you a 'pology," grunted a voice from the middle/nof the smelly cloud./n/n"For the last time, Mundungus," called Mrs. Weasley,/n"will you please not smoke that thing in the kitchen,/nespecially not when we're about to eat!"/n/n"Ah," said Mundungus. "Right. Sorry, Molly."/n/nThe cloud of smoke vanished as Mundungus stowed/nhis pipe back in his pocket, but an acrid smell of/nburning socks lingered./n/n"And if you want dinner before midnight I'll need a/nhand," Mrs. Weasley said to the room at large. "No,/nyou can stay where you are, Harry dear, you've had a/nlong journey — "/n/n"What can I do, Molly?" said Tonks enthusiastically,/nbounding forward./n/nMrs. Weasley hesitated, looking apprehensive./n/n"Er — no, it's all right, Tonks, you have a rest too,/nyou've done enough today — "/n/n"No, no, I want to help!" said Tonks brightly, knocking/nover a chair as she hurried toward the dresser from/nwhich Ginny was collecting cutlery./n/nSoon a series of heavy knives were chopping meat/nand vegetables of their own accord, supervised by Mr./nWeasley, while Mrs. Weasley stirred a cauldron/ndangling over the fire and the others took out plates,/nmore goblets, and food from the pantry. Harry was/nleft at the table with Sirius and Mundungus, who was/nstill blinking mournfully at him./n/n"Seen old Figgy since?" he asked./n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Harry, "I haven't seen anyone."/n/n/n/n"See, I wouldn't 'ave left," said Mundungus, leaning/nforward, a pleading note in his voice, "but I 'ad a/nbusiness opportunity — "/n/nHarry felt something brush against his knees and/nstarted, but it was only Crookshanks, Hermione's/nbandy-legged ginger cat, who wound himself once/naround Harry's legs, purring, then jumped onto/nSirius's lap and curled up. Sirius scratched him/nabsentmindedly behind the ears as he turned, still/ngrim-faced, to Harry./n/n"Had a good summer so far?"/n/n"No, it's been lousy," said Harry./n/nFor the first time, something like a grin flitted across/nSirius's face./n/n"Don't know what you're complaining about, myself."/n/n" What?" said Harry incredulously./n/n"Personally, I'd have welcomed a dementor attack. A/ndeadly struggle for my soul would have broken the/nmonotony nicely. You think you've had it bad, at least/nyou've been able to get out and about, stretch your/nlegs, get into a few fights... I've been stuck inside for a/nmonth."/n/n"How come?" asked Harry, frowning./n/n"Because the Ministry of Magic's still after me, and/nVoldemort will know all about me being an Animagus/nby now, Wormtail will have told him, so my big/ndisguise is useless. There's not much I can do for the/nOrder of the Phoenix ... or so Dumbledore feels."/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was something about the slightly flattened tone/nof voice in which Sirius uttered Dumbledore's name/nthat told Harry that Sirius was not very happy with/nthe headmaster either. Harry felt a sudden upsurge of/naffection for his godfather./n/n"At least you've known what's been going on," he said/nbracingly./n/n"Oh yeah," said Sirius sarcastically. "Listening to/nSnape's reports, having to take all his snide hints that/nhe's out there risking his life while I'm sat on my/nbackside here having a nice comfortable time . . ./nasking me how the cleaning's going — "/n/n"What cleaning?" asked Harry./n/n"Trying to make this place fit for human habitation,"/nsaid Sirius, waving a hand around the dismal/nkitchen. "No one's lived here for ten years, not since/nmy dear mother died, unless you count her old/nhouse-elf, and he's gone round the twist, hasn't/ncleaned anything in ages — "/n/n"Sirius?" said Mundungus, who did not appear to/nhave paid any attention to this conversation, but had/nbeen minutely examining an empty goblet. "This solid/nsilver, mate?"/n/n"Yes," said Sirius, surveying it with distaste. "Finest/nfifteenth-century goblin-wrought silver, embossed/nwith the Black family crest."/n/n"That'd come off, though," muttered Mundungus,/npolishing it with his cuff./n/n"Fred — George — NO, JUST CARRY THEM!" Mrs./nWeasley shrieked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry, Sirius, and Mundungus looked around and, a/nsplit second later, dived away from the table. Fred/nand George had bewitched a large cauldron of stew,/nan iron flagon of butterbeer, and a heavy wooden/nbreadboard, complete with knife, to hurtle through/nthe air toward them. The stew skidded the length of/nthe table and came to a halt just before the end,/nleaving a long black burn on the wooden surface, the/nflagon of butterbeer fell with a crash, spilling its/ncontents everywhere, and the bread knife slipped off/nthe board and landed, point down and quivering/nominously, exactly where Sirius's right hand had/nbeen seconds before./n/n"FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE!" screamed Mrs. Weasley./n"THERE WAS NO NEED — IVE HAD ENOUGH OF/nTHIS — JUST BECAUSE YOU'RE ALLOWED TO USE/nMAGIC NOW YOU DONT HAVE TO WHIP YOUR/nWANDS OUT FOR EVERY TINY LITTLE THING!"/n/n"We were just trying to save a bit of time!" said Fred,/nhurrying forward and wrenching the bread knife out/nof the table. "Sorry Sirius, mate — didn't mean to — "/n/nHarry and Sirius were both laughing. Mundungus,/nwho had toppled backward off his chair, was swearing/nas he got to his feet. Crookshanks had given an angry/nhiss and shot off under the dresser, from whence his/nlarge yellow eyes glowed in the darkness./n/n"Boys," Mr. Weasley said, lifting the stew back into/nthe middle of the table, "your mother's right, you're/nsupposed to show a sense of responsibility now you've/ncome of age — "/n/n" — none of your brothers caused this sort of trouble!"/nMrs. Weasley raged at the twins, slamming a fresh/nflagon of butterbeer onto the table and spilling almost/nas much again. "Bill didn't feel the need to Apparate/n/n/n/n/n/nevery few feet! Charlie didn't Charm everything he/nmet! Percy — "/n/nShe stopped dead, catching her breath with a/nfrightened look at her husband, whose expression/nwas suddenly wooden./n/n"Let's eat," said Bill quickly./n/n"It looks wonderful, Molly," said Lupin, ladling stew/nonto a plate for her and handing it across the table./n/nFor a few minutes there was silence but for the chink/nof plates and cutlery and the scraping of chairs as/neveryone settled down to their food. Then Mrs./n/nWeasley turned to Sirius and said, "I've been meaning/nto tell you, there's something trapped in that writing/ndesk in the drawing room, it keeps rattling and/nshaking. Of course, it could just be a boggart, but I/nthought we ought to ask Alastor to have a look at it/nbefore we let it out."/n/n"Whatever you like," said Sirius indifferently./n/n"The curtains in there are full of doxies too," Mrs./nWeasley went on. "I thought we might try and tackle/nthem tomorrow."/n/n"I look forward to it," said Sirius. Harry heard the/nsarcasm in his voice, but he was not sure that anyone/nelse did./n/nOpposite Harry, Tonks was entertaining Hermione/nand Ginny by transforming her nose between/nmouthfuls. Screwing up her eyes each time with the/nsame pained expression she had worn back in Harry's/nbedroom, her nose swelled to a beaklike protuberance/nlike Snape's, shrank to something resembling a/nbutton mushroom, and then sprouted a great deal of/n/n/n/n/nhair from each nostril. Apparently this was a regular/nmealtime entertainment, because after a while/nHermione and Ginny started requesting their favorite/nnoses./n/n"Do that one like a pig snout, Tonks ..."/n/nTonks obliged, and Harry, looking up, had the fleeting/nimpression that a female Dudley was grinning at him/nfrom across the table./n/nMr. Weasley, Bill, and Lupin were having an intense/ndiscussion about goblins./n/n"They're not giving anything away yet," said Bill. "I/nstill can't work out whether they believe he's back or/nnot. 'Course, they might prefer not to take sides at all./nKeep out of it."/n/n"I'm sure they'd never go over to You-Know-Who,"/nsaid Mr. Weasley, shaking his head. "They've suffered/nlosses too. Remember that goblin family he murdered/nlast time, somewhere near Nottingham?"/n/n"I think it depends what they're offered," said Lupin./n"And I'm not talking about gold; if they're offered/nfreedoms we've been denying them for centuries/nthey're going to be tempted. Have you still not had/nany luck with Ragnok, Bill?"/n/n"He's feeling pretty anti-wizard at the moment," said/nBill. "He hasn't stopped raging about the Bagman/nbusiness, he reckons the Ministry did a cover-up,/nthose goblins never got their gold from him, you know/n/n/n/nA gale of laughter from the middle of the table/ndrowned the rest of Bill's words. Fred, George, Ron,/nand Mundungus were rolling around in their seats./n/n/n/n/n/n"... and then," choked Mundungus, tears running/ndown his face, "and then, if you'll believe it, 'e says to/nme, 'e says, ''ere, Dung, where didja get all them toads/nfrom? 'Cos some son of a Bludger's gone and nicked/nall mine!' And I says, 'Nicked all your toads, Will,/nwhat next? So you'll be wanting some more, then?'/nAnd if you'll believe me, lads, the gormless gargoyle/nbuys all 'is own toads back orf me for twice what 'e/npaid in the first place — ■"/n/n"I don't think we need to hear any more of your/nbusiness dealings, thank you very much,/nMundungus," said Mrs. Weasley sharply, as Ron/nslumped forward onto the table, howling with/nlaughter./n/n"Beg pardon, Molly," said Mundungus at once, wiping/nhis eyes and winking at Harry. "But, you know, Will/nnicked 'em orf Warty Harris in the first place so I/nwasn't really doing nothing wrong — "/n/n"I don't know where you learned about right and/nwrong, Mundungus, but you seem to have missed a/nfew crucial lessons," said Mrs. Weasley coldly./n/nFred and George buried their faces in their goblets of/nbutterbeer; George was hiccuping. For some reason,/nMrs. Weasley threw a very nasty look at Sirius before/ngetting to her feet and going to fetch a large rhubarb/ncrumble for pudding. Harry looked round at his/ngodfather./n/n"Molly doesn't approve of Mundungus," said Sirius in/nan undertone./n/n"How come he's in the Order?" Harry said very/nquietly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He's useful," Sirius muttered. "Knows all the crooks/n— well, he would, seeing as he's one himself. But he's/nalso very loyal to Dumbledore, who helped him out of/na tight spot once. It pays to have someone like Dung/naround, he hears things we don't. But Molly thinks/ninviting him to stay for dinner is going too far. She/nhasn't forgiven him for slipping off duty when he was/nsupposed to be tailing you."/n/nThree helpings of rhubarb crumble and custard later/nand the waistband on Harry's jeans was feeling/nuncomfortably tight (which was saying something, as/nthe jeans had once been Dudley's). He lay down his/nspoon in a lull in the general conversation. Mr./nWeasley was leaning back in his chair, looking replete/nand relaxed, Tonks was yawning widely, her nose now/nback to normal, and Ginny, who had lured/nCrookshanks out from under the dresser, was sitting/ncross-legged on the floor, rolling butterbeer corks for/nhim to chase./n/n"Nearly time for bed, I think," said Mrs. Weasley on a/nyawn./n/n"Not just yet, Molly," said Sirius, pushing away his/nempty plate and turning to look at Harry. "You know,/nI'm surprised at you. I thought the first thing you'd do/nwhen you got here would be to start asking questions/nabout Voldemort."/n/nThe atmosphere in the room changed with the/nrapidity Harry associated with the arrival of/ndementors. Where seconds before it had been sleepily/nrelaxed, it was now alert, even tense. A frisson had/ngone around the table at the mention of Voldemort's/nname. Lupin, who had been about to take a sip of/nwine, lowered his goblet slowly, looking wary./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I did!" said Harry indignantly. "I asked Ron and/nHermione but they said we're not allowed in the/nOrder, so — "/n/n"And they're quite right," said Mrs. Weasley. "You're/ntoo young."/n/nShe was sitting bolt upright in her chair, her fists/nclenched upon its arms, every trace of drowsiness/ngone./n/n"Since when did someone have to be in the Order of/nthe Phoenix to ask questions?" asked Sirius. "Harry's/nbeen trapped in that Muggle house for a month. He's/ngot the right to know what's been happen — "/n/n"Hang on!" interrupted George loudly./n/n"How come Harry gets his questions answered?" said/nFred angrily./n/n" We've been trying to get stuff out of you for a month/nand you haven't told us a single stinking thing!" said/nGeorge./n/n" 'You're too young, you're not in the Order,' " said/nFred, in a high-pitched voice that sounded uncannily/nlike his mother's. "Harry's not even of age!"/n/n"It's not my fault you haven't been told what the/nOrder's doing," said Sirius calmly. "That's your/nparents' decision. Harry, on the other hand — "/n/n"It's not down to you to decide what's good for Harry!"/nsaid Mrs. Weasley sharply. Her normally kindly face/nlooked dangerous. "You haven't forgotten what/nDumbledore said, I suppose?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Which bit?" Sirius asked politely, but with an air as/nthough readying himself for a fight./n/n"The bit about not telling Harry more than he needs/nto know," said Mrs. Weasley, placing a heavy/nemphasis on the last three words./n/nRon, Hermione, Fred, and George's heads turned from/nSirius to Mrs. Weasley as though following a tennis/nrally. Ginny was kneeling amid a pile of abandoned/nbutterbeer corks, watching the conversation with her/nmouth slightly open. Lupin's eyes were fixed on/nSirius./n/n"I don't intend to tell him more than he needs to/nknow, Molly," said Sirius. "But as he was the one who/nsaw Voldemort come back" (again, there was a/ncollective shudder around the table at the name), "he/nhas more right than most to — "/n/n"He's not a member of the Order of the Phoenix!" said/nMrs. Weasley. "He's only fifteen and — "/n/n" — and he's dealt with as much as most in the/nOrder," said Sirius, "and more than some — "/n/n"No one's denying what he's done!" said Mrs. Weasley,/nher voice rising, her fists trembling on the arms of her/nchair. "But he's still — "/n/n"He's not a child!" said Sirius impatiently./n/n"He's not an adult either!" said Mrs. Weasley, the/ncolor rising in her cheeks. "He's not James, Sirius!"/n/n"I'm perfectly clear who he is, thanks, Molly," said/nSirius coldly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm not sure you are!" said Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Sometimes, the way you talk about him, it's as/nthough you think you've got your best friend back!"/n/n"What's wrong with that?" said Harry./n/n"What's wrong, Harry, is that you are not your father,/nhowever much you might look like him!" said Mrs./nWeasley, her eyes still boring into Sirius. "You are still/nat school and adults responsible for you should not/nforget it!"/n/n"Meaning I'm an irresponsible godfather?" demanded/nSirius, his voice rising./n/n"Meaning you've been known to act rashly, Sirius,/nwhich is why Dumbledore keeps reminding you to/nstay at home and — "/n/n"We'll leave my instructions from Dumbledore out of/nthis, if you please!" said Sirius loudly./n/n"Arthur!" said Mrs. Weasley, rounding on her/nhusband. "Arthur, back me up!"/n/nMr. Weasley did not speak at once. He took off his/nglasses and cleaned them slowly on his robes, not/nlooking at his wife. Only when he had replaced them/ncarefully on his nose did he say, "Dumbledore knows/nthe position has changed, Molly. He accepts that/nHarry will have to be filled in to a certain extent now/nthat he is staying at headquarters — "/n/n"Yes, but there's a difference between that and/ninviting him to ask whatever he likes!"/n/n"Personally," said Lupin quietly, looking away from/nSirius at last, as Mrs. Weasley turned quickly to him,/nhopeful that finally she was about to get an ally, "I/n/n/n/n/n/nthink it better that Harry gets the facts — not all the/nfacts, Molly, but the general picture — from us, rather/nthan a garbled version from ... others."/n/nHis expression was mild, but Harry felt sure that/nLupin, at least, knew that some Extendable Ears had/nsurvived Mrs. Weasley's purge./n/n"Well," said Mrs. Weasley, breathing deeply and/nlooking around the table for support that did not/ncome, "well ... I can see I'm going to be overruled. I'll/njust say this: Dumbledore must have had his reasons/nfor not wanting Harry to know too much, and/nspeaking as someone who has got Harry's best/ninterests at heart — "/n/n"He's not your son," said Sirius quietly./n/n"He's as good as," said Mrs. Weasley fiercely. "Who/nelse has he got?"/n/n"He's got me!"/n/n"Yes," said Mrs. Weasley, her lip curling. "The thing/nis, it's been rather difficult for you to look after him/nwhile you've been locked up in Azkaban, hasn't it?"/n/nSirius started to rise from his chair./n/n"Molly, you're not the only person at this table who/ncares about Harry," said Lupin sharply. "Sirius, sit/ndown."/n/nMrs. Weasley's lower lip was trembling. Sirius sank/nslowly back into his chair, his face white./n/n"I think Harry ought to be allowed a say in this,"/n/nLupin continued. "He's old enough to decide for/nhimself."/n/n/n/n/n/n"I want to know what's been going on," Harry said at/nonce./n/nHe did not look at Mrs. Weasley. He had been touched/nby what she had said about his being as good as a/nson, but he was also impatient at her mollycoddling. . ./nSirius was right, he was not a child./n/n"Very well," said Mrs. Weasley, her voice cracking./n"Ginny — Ron — Hermione — Fred — George — I/nwant you out of this kitchen, now."/n/nThere was instant uproar./n/n"We're of age!" Fred and George bellowed together./n/n"If Harry's allowed, why can't I?" shouted Ron./n/n"Mum, I want to!" wailed Ginny./n/n"NO!" shouted Mrs. Weasley, standing up, her eyes/noverbright. "I absolutely forbid — "/n/n"Molly, you can't stop Fred and George," said Mr./nWeasley wearily. "They are of age — "/n/n"They're still at school — "/n/n"But they're legally adults now," said Mr. Weasley in/nthe same tired voice./n/nMrs. Weasley was now scarlet in the face./n/n"I — oh, all right then, Fred and George can stay, but/nRon — "/n/n"Harry'll tell me and Hermione everything you say/nanyway!" said Ron hotly. "Won't — won't you?" he/nadded uncertainly, meeting Harry's eyes./n/n/n/n/n/nFor a split second, Harry considered telling Ron that/nhe wouldn't tell him a single word, that he could try a/ntaste of being kept in the dark and see how he liked/nit. But the nasty impulse vanished as they looked at/neach other./n/n" 'Course I will," Harry said. Ron and Hermione/nbeamed./n/n"Fine!" shouted Mrs. Weasley. "Fine! Ginny — BED!"/n/nGinny did not go quietly. They could hear her raging/nand storming at her mother all the way up the stairs,/nand when she reached the hall Mrs. Black's/nearsplitting shrieks were added to the din. Lupin/nhurried off to the portrait to restore calm. It was only/nafter he had returned, closing the kitchen door/nbehind him and taking his seat at the table again,/nthat Sirius spoke./n/n"Okay, Harry ... what do you want to know?"/n/nHarry took a deep breath and asked the question that/nhad been obsessing him for a month./n/n"Where's Voldemort? What's he doing? I've been trying/nto watch the Muggle news," he said, ignoring the/nrenewed shudders and winces at the name, "and/nthere hasn't been anything that looks like him yet, no/nfunny deaths or anything — "/n/n"That's because there haven't been any suspicious/ndeaths yet," said Sirius, "not as far as we know,/nanyway... And we know quite a lot."/n/n"More than he thinks we do anyway," said Lupin./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"How come he's stopped killing people?" Harry asked./nHe knew that Voldemort had murdered more than/nonce in the last year alone./n/n"Because he doesn't want to draw attention to himself/nat the moment," said Sirius. "It would be dangerous/nfor him. His comeback didn't come off quite the way/nhe wanted it to, you see. He messed it up."/n/n"Or rather, you messed it up for him," said Lupin with/na satisfied smile./n/n"How?" Harry asked perplexedly./n/n"You weren't supposed to survive!" said Sirius./n"Nobody apart from his Death Eaters was supposed to/nknow he'd come back. But you survived to bear/nwitness."/n/n"And the very last person he wanted alerted to his/nreturn the moment he got back was Dumbledore,"/nsaid Lupin. "And you made sure Dumbledore knew at/nonce."/n/n"How has that helped?" Harry asked./n/n"Are you kidding?" said Bill incredulously./n"Dumbledore was the only one You-Know-Who was/never scared of!"/n/n"Thanks to you, Dumbledore was able to recall the/nOrder of the Phoenix about an hour after Voldemort/nreturned," said Sirius./n/n"So what's the Order been doing?" said Harry, looking/naround at them all./n/n"Working as hard as we can to make sure Voldemort/ncan't carry out his plans," said Sirius./n/n/n/n/n/n"How d'you know what his plans are?" Harry asked/nquickly./n/n/n/n"Dumbledore's got a shrewd idea," said Lupin, "and/nDumbledore's shrewd ideas normally turn out to be/naccurate."/n/n"So what does Dumbledore reckon he's planning?"/n/n"Well, firstly, he wants to build up his army again,"/nsaid Sirius. "In the old days he had huge numbers at/nhis command; witches and wizards he'd bullied or/nbewitched into following him, his faithful Death/nEaters, a great variety of Dark creatures. You heard/nhim planning to recruit the giants; well, they'll be just/none group he's after. He's certainly not going to try/nand take on the Ministry of Magic with only a dozen/nDeath Eaters."/n/n"So you're trying to stop him getting more followers?"/n"We're doing our best," said Lupin./n/n"How?"/n/n"Well, the main thing is to try and convince as many/npeople as possible that You-Know-Who really has/nreturned, to put them on their guard," said Bill. "It's/nproving tricky, though."/n/n"Why?"/n/n"Because of the Ministry's attitude," said Tonks. "You/nsaw Cornelius Fudge after You-Know-Who came back,/nHarry. Well, he hasn't shifted his position at all. He's/nabsolutely refusing to believe it's happened."/n/n"But why?" said Harry desperately. "Why's he being/nso stupid? If Dumbledore — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ah, well, you've put your finger on the problem," said/nMr. Weasley with a wry smile. "Dumbledore."/n/n"Fudge is frightened of him, you see," said Tonks/nsadly./n/n"Frightened of Dumbledore?" said Harry/nincredulously./n/n"Frightened of what he's up to," said Mr. Weasley./n"You see, Fudge thinks Dumbledore's plotting to/noverthrow him. He thinks Dumbledore wants to be/nMinister of Magic."/n/n"But Dumbledore doesn't want — "/n/n"Of course he doesn't," said Mr. Weasley. "He's never/nwanted the Minister's job, even though a lot of people/nwanted him to take it when Millicent Bagnold retired./nFudge came to power instead, but he's never quite/nforgotten how much popular support Dumbledore/nhad, even though Dumbledore never applied for the/njob."/n/n"Deep down, Fudge knows Dumbledore's much/ncleverer than he is, a much more powerful wizard,/nand in the early days of his Ministry he was forever/nasking Dumbledore for help and advice," said Lupin./n"But it seems that he's become fond of power now,/nand much more confident. He loves being Minister of/nMagic, and he's managed to convince himself that/nhe's the clever one and Dumbledore's simply stirring/nup trouble for the sake of it."/n/n"How can he think that?" said Harry angrily. "How/ncan he think Dumbledore would just make it all up —/nthat I'd make it all up?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Because accepting that Voldemort's back would/nmean trouble like the Ministry hasn't had to cope/nwith for nearly fourteen years," said Sirius bitterly./n"Fudge just can't bring himself to face it. It's so much/nmore comfortable to convince himself Dumbledore's/nlying to destabilize him."/n/n"You see the problem," said Lupin. "While the/nMinistry insists there is nothing to fear from/nVoldemort, it's hard to convince people he's back,/nespecially as they really don't want to believe it in the/nfirst place. What's more, the Ministry's leaning heavily/non the Daily Prophet not to report any of what they're/ncalling Dumbledore's rumormongering, so most of the/nWizarding community are completely unaware/nanything's happened, and that makes them easy/ntargets for the Death Eaters if they're using the/nImperius Curse."/n/n"But you're telling people, aren't you?" said Harry,/nlooking around at Mr. Weasley, Sirius, Bill,/nMundungus, Lupin, and Tonks. "You're letting people/nknow he's back?"/n/nThey all smiled humorlessly./n/n"Well, as everyone thinks I'm a mad mass murderer/nand the Ministry's put a ten-thousand-Galleon price/non my head, I can hardly stroll up the street and start/nhanding out leaflets, can I?" said Sirius restlessly./n/n"And I'm not a very popular dinner guest with most of/nthe community," said Lupin. "It's an occupational/nhazard of being a werewolf."/n/n"Tonks and Arthur would lose their jobs at the/nMinistry if they started shooting their mouths off,"/nsaid Sirius, "and it's very important for us to have/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nspies inside the Ministry, because you can bet/nVoldemort will have them."/n/n"We've managed to convince a couple of people,/nthough," said Mr. Weasley. "Tonks here, for one —/nshe's too young to have been in the Order of the/nPhoenix last time, and having Aurors on our side is a/nhuge advantage — Kingsley Shacklebolt's been a real/nasset too. He's in charge of the hunt for Sirius, so he's/nbeen feeding the Ministry information that Sirius is in/nTibet."/n/n"But if none of you's putting the news out that/nVoldemort 's back — " Harry began./n/n"Who said none of us was putting the news out?" said/nSirius. "Why d'you think Dumbledore's in such/ntrouble?"/n/n"What d'you mean?" Harry asked./n/n"They're trying to discredit him," said Lupin. "Didn't/nyou see the Daily Prophet last week? They reported/nthat he'd been voted out of the Chairmanship of the/nInternational Confederation of Wizards because he's/ngetting old and losing his grip, but it's not true, he/nwas voted out by Ministry wizards after he made a/nspeech announcing Voldemort's return. They've/ndemoted him from Chief Warlock on the Wizengamot/n— that's the Wizard High Court — and they're talking/nabout taking away his Order of Merlin, First Class,/ntoo."/n/n"But Dumbledore says he doesn't care what they do/nas long as they don't take him off the Chocolate Frog/ncards," said Bill, grinning./n/n"It's no laughing matter," said Mr. Weasley shortly. "If/nhe carries on defying the Ministry like this, he could/n/n/n/n/n/nend up in Azkaban and the last thing we want is/nDumbledore locked up. While You-Know-Who knows/nDumbledore's out there and wise to what he's up to,/nhe's going to go cautiously for a while. If/nDumbledore's out of the way — well, You-Know-Who/nwill have a clear field."/n/n"But if Voldemort's trying to recruit more Death/nEaters, it's bound to get out that he's come back, isn't/nit?" asked Harry desperately./n/n"Voldemort doesn't march up to people's houses and/nbang on their front doors, Harry," said Sirius. "He/ntricks, jinxes, and blackmails them. He's well-/npracticed at operating in secrecy. In any case,/ngathering followers is only one thing he's interested/nin, he's got other plans too, plans he can put into/noperation very quietly indeed, and he's concentrating/non them at the moment."/n/n"What's he after apart from followers?" Harry asked/nswiftly./n/nHe thought he saw Sirius and Lupin exchange the/nmost fleeting of looks before Sirius said, "Stuff he can/nonly get by stealth."/n/nWhen Harry continued to look puzzled, Sirius said,/n"Like a weapon. Something he didn't have last time."/n/n"When he was powerful before?"/n/n"Yes."/n/n"Like what kind of weapon?" said Harry. "Something/nworse than the Avada Kedavra — ?"/n/n"That's enough."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley spoke from the shadows beside the/ndoor. Harry had not noticed her return from taking/nGinny upstairs. Her arms were crossed and she/nlooked furious./n/n"I want you in bed, now. All of you," she added,/nlooking around at Fred, George, Ron, and Hermione./n/n"You can't boss us — " Fred began./n/n"Watch me," snarled Mrs. Weasley. She was trembling/nslightly as she looked at Sirius. "You've given Harry/nplenty of information. Any more and you might just/nas well induct him into the Order straightaway."/n/n"Why not?" said Harry quickly. "I'll join, I want to join,/nI want to fight — "/n/n"No."/n/nIt was not Mrs. Weasley who spoke this time, but/nLupin./n/n"The Order is comprised only of overage wizards," he/nsaid. "Wizards who have left school," he added, as/nFred and George opened their mouths. "There are/ndangers involved of which you can have no idea, any/nof you ... I think Molly's right, Sirius. We've said/nenough."/n/nSirius half-shrugged but did not argue. Mrs. Weasley/nbeckoned imperiously to her sons and Hermione. One/nby one they stood up and Harry, recognizing defeat,/nfollowed suit./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Noble And Most Ancient House Of Black
text: /nMrs. Weasley followed them upstairs looking grim./n/n"I want you all to go straight to bed, no talking," she/nsaid as they reached the first landing. "We've got a/nbusy day tomorrow. I expect Ginny's asleep," she/nadded to Hermione, "so try not to wake her up."/n/n"Asleep, yeah, right," said Fred in an undertone, after/nHermione bade them good night and they were/nclimbing to the next floor. "If Ginny's not lying awake/nwaiting for Hermione to tell her everything they said/ndownstairs, then I'm a flobberworm..."/n/n"All right, Ron, Harry," said Mrs. Weasley on the/nsecond landing, pointing them into their bedroom./n/n"Off to bed with you."/n/n" 'Night," Harry and Ron said to the twins./n/n"Sleep tight," said Fred, winking./n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley closed the door behind Harry with a/nsharp snap. The bedroom looked, if anything, even/ndanker and gloomier than it had on first sight. The/nblank picture on the wall was now breathing very/nslowly and deeply, as though its invisible occupant/nwas asleep. Harry put on his pajamas, took off his/nglasses, and climbed into his chilly bed while Ron/nthrew Owl Treats up on top of the wardrobe to pacify/nHedwig and Pigwidgeon, who were clattering around/nand rustling their wings restlessly./n/n"We can't let them out to hunt every night," Ron/nexplained as he pulled on his maroon pajamas./n"Dumbledore doesn't want too many owls swooping/naround the square, thinks it'll look suspicious. Oh/nyeah ... I forgot..."/n/nHe crossed to the door and bolted it./n/n"What 're you doing that for?"/n/n"Kreacher," said Ron as he turned off the light. "First/nnight I was here he came wandering in at three in the/nmorning. Trust me, you don't want to wake up and/nfind him prowling around your room. Anyway ..." He/ngot into his bed, settled down under the covers, then/nturned to look at Harry in the darkness. Harry could/nsee his outline by the moonlight filtering in through/nthe grimy window. "What d'you reckon?"/n/nHarry didn't need to ask what Ron meant./n/n"Well, they didn't tell us much we couldn't have/nguessed, did they?" he said, thinking of all that had/nbeen said downstairs. "I mean, all they've really said/nis that the Order's trying to stop people joining Vol — "/n/nThere was a sharp intake of breath from Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" — demort" said Harry firmly. "When are you going to/nstart using his name? Sirius and Lupin do."/n/n/n/nRon ignored this last comment. "Yeah, you're right,"/nhe said. "We already knew nearly everything they told/nus, from using the Extendable Ears. The only new bit/nwas — "/n/nCrack./n/n"OUCH!"/n/n"Keep your voice down, Ron, or Mum'll be back up/nhere."/n/n"You two just Apparated on my knees!"/n/n"Yeah, well, it's harder in the dark — "/n/nHarry saw the blurred outlines of Fred and George/nleaping down from Ron's bed. There was a groan of/nbedsprings and Harry's mattress descended a few/ninches as George sat down near his feet./n/n"So, got there yet?" said George eagerly./n/n"The weapon Sirius mentioned?" said Harry./n/n"Let slip, more like," said Fred with relish, now sitting/nnext to Ron. "We didn't hear about that on the old/nExtendables, did we?"/n/n"What d'you reckon it is?" said Harry./n/n"Could be anything," said Fred./n/n"But there can't be anything worse than the Avada/nKedavra curse, can there?" said Ron. "What's worse/nthan death?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Maybe it's something that can kill loads of people at/nonce," suggested George./n/n"Maybe it's some particularly painful way of killing/npeople," said Ron fearfully./n/n"He's got the Cruciatus Curse for causing pain," said/nHarry. "He doesn't need anything more efficient than/nthat."/n/nThere was a pause and Harry knew that the others,/nlike him, were wondering what horrors this weapon/ncould perpetrate./n/n"So who d'you thinks got it now?" asked George./n/n"I hope it's our side," said Ron, sounding slightly/nnervous./n/n"If it is, Dumbledore's probably keeping it," said Fred./n/n"Where?" said Ron quickly. "Hogwarts?"/n/n"Bet it is!" said George. "That's where he hid the/nSorcerer's Stone!"/n/n"A weapon's going to be a lot bigger than the Stone,/nthough!" said Ron./n/n"Not necessarily," said Fred./n/n"Yeah, size is no guarantee of power," said George./n"Look at Ginny."/n/n"What d'you mean?" said Harry./n/n"You've never been on the receiving end of one of her/nBat-Bogey Hexes, have you?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Shhh!" said Fred, half-rising from the bed. "Listen!"/n/n/n/nThey fell silent. Footsteps were coming up the stairs/nagain./n/n"Mum," said George, and without further ado there/nwas a loud crack and Harry felt the weight vanish/nfrom the end of his bed. A few seconds later and they/nheard the floorboard creak outside their door; Mrs./nWeasley was plainly listening to see whether they/nwere talking or not./n/nHedwig and Pigwidgeon hooted dolefully. The/nfloorboard creaked again and they heard her heading/nupstairs to check on Fred and George./n/n"She doesn't trust us at all, you know," said Ron/nregretfully./n/nHarry was sure he would not be able to fall asleep;/nthe evening had been so packed with things to think/nabout that he fully expected to lie awake for hours/nmulling it all over. He wanted to continue talking to/nRon, but Mrs. Weasley was now creaking back/ndownstairs again, and once she had gone he distinctly/nheard others making their way upstairs... In fact,/nmany-legged creatures were cantering softly up and/ndown outside the bedroom door, and Hagrid, the Care/nof Magical Creatures teacher, was saying, "Beauties,/naren' they, eh, Harry? We'll be study in' weapons this/nterm..." And Harry saw that the creatures had/ncannons for heads and were wheeling to face him.../n/nHe ducked.../n/nThe next thing he knew, he was curled in a warm ball/nunder his bedclothes, and George's loud voice was/nfilling the room./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mum says get up, your breakfast is in the kitchen/nand then she needs you in the drawing room, there/nare loads more doxies than she thought and she's/nfound a nest of dead puffskeins under the sofa."/n/nHalf an hour later, Harry and Ron, who had dressed/nand breakfasted quickly, entered the drawing room, a/nlong, high-ceilinged room on the first floor with olive-/ngreen walls covered in dirty tapestries. The carpet/nexhaled little clouds of dust every time someone put/ntheir foot on it and the long, moss-green velvet/ncurtains were buzzing as though swarming with/ninvisible bees. It was around these that Mrs. Weasley,/nHermione, Ginny, Fred, and George were grouped, all/nlooking rather peculiar, as they had tied cloths over/ntheir noses and mouths. Each of them was also/nholding a large bottle of black liquid with a nozzle at/nthe end./n/n"Cover your faces and take a spray," Mrs. Weasley/nsaid to Harry and Ron the moment she saw them,/npointing to two more bottles of black liquid standing/non a spindle-legged table. "It's Doxycide. I've never/nseen an infestation this bad — what that house-elf's/nbeen doing for the last ten years — "/n/nHermione 's face was half concealed by a tea towel but/nHarry distinctly saw her throw a reproachful look at/nMrs. Weasley at these words./n/n"Kreacher's really old, he probably couldn't manage —/n/n/n/n"You'd be surprised what Kreacher can manage when/nhe wants to, Hermione," said Sirius, who had just/nentered the room carrying a bloodstained bag of what/nappeared to be dead rats. "I've just been feeding/nBuckbeak," he added, in reply to Harry's inquiring/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nlook. "I keep him upstairs in my mother's bedroom./nAnyway ... this writing desk ..."/n/nHe dropped the bag of rats onto an armchair, then/nbent over to examine the locked cabinet which, Harry/nnow noticed for the first time, was shaking slightly./n/n"Well, Molly, I'm pretty sure this is a boggart," said/nSirius, peering through the keyhole, "but perhaps we/nought to let Mad-Eye have a shifty at it before we let it/nout — knowing my mother it could be something/nmuch worse."/n/n"Right you are, Sirius," said Mrs. Weasley./n/nThey were both speaking in carefully light, polite/nvoices that told Harry quite plainly that neither had/nforgotten their disagreement of the night before./n/nA loud, clanging bell sounded from downstairs,/nfollowed at once by the cacophony of screams and/nwails that had been triggered the previous night by/nTonks knocking over the umbrella stand./n/n"I keep telling them not to ring the doorbell!" said/nSirius exasperatedly, hurrying back out of the room./nThey heard him thundering down the stairs as Mrs./nBlack's screeches echoed up through the house once/nmore: "Stains of dishonor, filthy half-breeds, blood/ntraitors, children of filth ..."/n/n"Close the door, please, Harry," said Mrs. Weasley./n/nHarry took as much time as he dared to close the/ndrawing room door; he wanted to listen to what was/ngoing on downstairs. Sirius had obviously managed to/nshut the curtains over his mother's portrait because/nshe had stopped screaming. He heard Sirius walking/ndown the hall, then the clattering of the chain on the/n/n/n/n/nfront door, and then a deep voice he recognized as/nKingsley Shacklebolt's saying, "Hestia's just relieved/nme, so she's got Moody's cloak now, thought I'd leave/na report for Dumbledore..."/n/nFeeling Mrs. Weasley's eyes on the back of his head,/nHarry regretfully closed the drawing room door and/nrejoined the doxy party./n/nMrs. Weasley was bending over to check the page on/ndoxies in Gilderoy Lockhart's Guide to Household/nPests, which was lying open on the sofa./n/n"Right, you lot, you need to be careful, because doxies/nbite and their teeth are poisonous. I've got a bottle of/nantidote here, but I'd rather nobody needed it."/n/nShe straightened up, positioned herself squarely in/nfront of the curtains, and beckoned them all forward./n/n"When I say the word, start spraying immediately,"/nshe said. "They'll come flying out at us, I expect, but it/nsays on the sprays one good squirt will paralyze them./nWhen they're immobilized, just throw them in this/nbucket."/n/nShe stepped carefully out of their line of fire and/nraised her own spray. "All right — squirti"/n/nHarry had been spraying only a few seconds when a/nfully grown doxy came soaring out of a fold in the/nmaterial, shiny beetlelike wings whirring, tiny needle-/nsharp teeth bared, its fairylike body covered with/nthick black hair and its four tiny fists clenched with/nfury. Harry caught it full in the face with a blast of/nDoxycide; it froze in midair and fell, with a/nsurprisingly loud thunk, onto the worn carpet below./nHarry picked it up and threw it in the bucket./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Fred, what are you doing?" said Mrs. Weasley/nsharply. "Spray that at once and throw it away!"/n/nHarry looked around. Fred was holding a struggling/ndoxy between his forefinger and thumb./n/n"Right-o," Fred said brightly, spraying the doxy/nquickly in the face so that it fainted, but the moment/nMrs. Weasley's back was turned he pocketed it with a/nwink./n/n"We want to experiment with doxy venom for our/nSkiving Snack-boxes," George told Harry under his/nbreath./n/nDeftly spraying two doxies at once as they soared/nstraight for his nose, Harry moved closer to George/nand muttered out of the corner of his mouth, "What/nare Skiving Snackboxes?"/n/n"Range of sweets to make you ill," George whispered,/nkeeping a wary eye on Mrs. Weasley's back. "Not/nseriously ill, mind, just ill enough to get you out of a/nclass when you feel like it. Fred and I have been/ndeveloping them this summer. They're double-ended,/ncolor-coded chews. If you eat the orange half of the/nPuking Pastilles, you throw up. Moment you've been/nrushed out of the lesson for the hospital wing, you/nswallow the purple half — "/n/n" ' — which restores you to full fitness, enabling you to/npursue the leisure activity of your own choice during/nan hour that would otherwise have been devoted to/nunprofitable boredom.' That's what we're putting in/nthe adverts, anyway," whispered Fred, who had edged/nover out of Mrs. Weasley's line of vision and was now/nsweeping a few stray doxies from the floor and adding/nthem to his pocket. "But they still need a bit of work./nAt the moment our testers are having a bit of trouble/n/n/n/n/nstopping puking long enough to swallow the purple/nend."/n/n/n/n"Testers?"/n/n"Us," said Fred. "We take it in turns. George did the/nFainting Fancies — we both tried the Nosebleed/nNougat — "/n/n"Mum thought we'd been dueling," said George./n/n"Joke shop still on, then?" Harry muttered,/npretending to be adjusting the nozzle on his spray./n/n"Well, we haven't had a chance to get premises yet,"/nsaid Fred, dropping his voice even lower as Mrs./nWeasley mopped her brow with her scarf before/nreturning to the attack, "so we're running it as a mail-/norder service at the moment. We put advertisements/nin the Daily Prophet last week."/n/n"All thanks to you, mate," said George. "But don't/nworry ... Mum hasn't got a clue. She won't read the/nDaily Prophet anymore, 'cause of it telling lies about/nyou and Dumbledore."/n/nHarry grinned. He had forced the Weasley twins to/ntake the thousand-Galleon prize money he had won/nin the Triwizard Tournament to help them realize/ntheir ambition to open a joke shop, but he was still/nglad to know that his part in furthering their plans/nwas unknown to Mrs. Weasley, who did not think that/nrunning a joke shop was a suitable career for two of/nher sons./n/nThe de-doxying of the curtains took most of the/nmorning. It was past midday when Mrs. Weasley/nfinally removed her protective scarf, sank into a/nsagging armchair, and sprang up again with a cry of/n/n/n/n/n/ndisgust, having sat on the bag of dead rats. The/ncurtains were no longer buzzing; they hung limp and/ndamp from the intensive spraying; unconscious/ndoxies lay crammed in the bucket at the foot of them/nbeside a bowl of their black eggs, at which/nCrookshanks was now sniffing and Fred and George/nwere shooting covetous looks./n/n"I think well tackle those after lunch."/n/nMrs. Weasley pointed at the dusty glass-fronted/ncabinets standing on either side of the mantelpiece./nThey were crammed with an odd assortment of/nobjects: a selection of rusty daggers, claws, a coiled/nsnakeskin, a number of tarnished silver boxes/ninscribed with languages Harry could not understand/nand, least pleasant of all, an ornate crystal bottle with/na large opal set into the stopper, full of what Harry/nwas quite sure was blood./n/nThe clanging doorbell rang again. Everyone looked at/nMrs. Weasley./n/n"Stay here," she said firmly, snatching up the bag of/nrats as Mrs. Blacks screeches started up again from/ndown below. "I'll bring up some sandwiches."/n/nShe left the room, closing the door carefully behind/nher. At once, everyone dashed over to the window to/nlook down onto the doorstep. They could see the top/nof an unkempt gingery head and a stack of/nprecariously balanced cauldrons./n/n"Mundungus!" said Hermione. "What's he brought all/nthose cauldrons for?"/n/n"Probably looking for a safe place to keep them," said/nHarry. "Isn't that what he was doing the night he was/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nsupposed to be tailing me? Picking up dodgy/ncauldrons?"/n/n/n/n"Yeah, you're right!" said Fred, as the front door/nopened; Mundungus heaved his cauldrons through it/nand disappeared from view. "Blimey, Mum won't like/nthat..."/n/nHe and George crossed to the door and stood beside/nit, listening intently. Mrs. Black's screaming had/nstopped again./n/n"Mundungus is talking to Sirius and Kingsley," Fred/nmuttered, frowning with concentration. "Can't hear/nproperly ... d'you reckon we can risk the Extendable/nEars?"/n/n"Might be worth it," said George. "I could sneak/nupstairs and get a pair — "/n/nBut at that precise moment there was an explosion of/nsound from downstairs that rendered Extendable/nEars quite unnecessary. All of them could hear/nexactly what Mrs. Weasley was shouting at the top of/nher voice./n/n"WE ARE NOT RUNNING A HIDEOUT FOR STOLEN/nGOODS!"/n/n"I love hearing Mum shouting at someone else," said/nFred, with a satisfied smile on his face as he opened/nthe door an inch or so to allow Mrs. Weasley 's voice to/npermeate the room better. "It makes such a nice/nchange."/n/nCOMPLETELY IRRESPONSIBLE, AS IF WE/nHAVENT GOT ENOUGH TO WORRY ABOUT/nWITHOUT YOU DRAGGING STOLEN CAULDRONS/nINTO THE HOUSE — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"The idiots are letting her get into her stride," said/nGeorge, shaking his head. "You've got to head her off/nearly, otherwise she builds up a head of steam and/ngoes on for hours. And she's been dying to have a go/nat Mundungus ever since he sneaked off when he was/nsupposed to be following you, Harry — and there goes/nSirius's mum again — "/n/nMrs. Weasley's voice was lost amid fresh shrieks and/nscreams from the portraits in the hall. George made/nto shut the door to drown the noise, but before he/ncould do so, a house-elf edged into the room./n/nExcept for the filthy rag tied like a loincloth around/nits middle, it was completely naked. It looked very old./nIts skin seemed to be several times too big for it and/nthough it was bald like all house-elves, there was a/nquantity of white hair growing out of its large, batlike/nears. Its eyes were a bloodshot and watery gray, and/nits fleshy nose was large and rather snoutlike./n/nThe elf took absolutely no notice of Harry and the/nrest. Acting as though it could not see them, it/nshuffled hunchbacked, slowly and doggedly, toward/nthe far end of the room, muttering under its breath all/nthe while in a hoarse, deep voice like a bullfrog's, ".../nSmells like a drain and a criminal to boot, but she's/nno better, nasty old blood traitor with her brats/nmessing up my Mistress's house, oh my poor/nMistress, if she knew, if she knew the scum they've let/nin her house, what would she say to old Kreacher, oh/nthe shame of it, Mudbloods and werewolves and/ntraitors and thieves, poor old Kreacher, what can he/ndo..."/n/n"Hello, Kreacher," said Fred very loudly, closing the/ndoor with a snap./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe house-elf froze in his tracks, stopped muttering,/nand then gave a very pronounced and very/nunconvincing start of surprise./n/n"Kreacher did not see Young Master," he said, turning/naround and bowing to Fred. Still facing the carpet, he/nadded, perfectly audibly, "Nasty little brat of a blood/ntraitor it is."/n/n"Sorry?" said George. "Didn't catch that last bit."/n/n"Kreacher said nothing," said the elf, with a second/nbow to George, adding in a clear undertone, "and/nthere's its twin, unnatural little beasts they are."/n/nHarry didn't know whether to laugh or not. The elf/nstraightened up, eyeing them all very malevolently,/nand apparently convinced that they could not hear/nhim as he continued to mutter./n/n"... and there's the Mudblood, standing there bold as/nbrass, oh if my Mistress knew, oh how she'd cry, and/nthere's a new boy, Kreacher doesn't know his name,/nwhat is he doing here, Kreacher doesn't know ..."/n/n"This is Harry, Kreacher," said Hermione tentatively./n"Harry Potter."/n/nKreacher's pale eyes widened and he muttered faster/nand more furiously than ever./n/n"The Mudblood is talking to Kreacher as though she/nis my friend, if Kreacher's Mistress saw him in such/ncompany, oh what would she say — "/n/n"Don't call her a Mudblood!" said Ron and Ginny/ntogether, very angrily./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It doesn't matter," Hermione whispered, "he's not in/nhis right mind, he doesn't know what he's — "/n/n"Don't kid yourself, Hermione, he knows exactly what/nhe's saying," said Fred, eyeing Kreacher with great/ndislike./n/nKreacher was still muttering, his eyes on Harry./n/n"Is it true? Is it Harry Potter? Kreacher can see the/nscar, it must be true, that's that boy who stopped the/nDark Lord, Kreacher wonders how he did it — "/n/n"Don't we all, Kreacher?" said Fred./n/n"What do you want anyway?" George asked./n/nKreacher 's huge eyes darted onto George./n/n"Kreacher is cleaning," he said evasively./n/n"A likely story," said a voice behind Harry./n/nSirius had come back; he was glowering at the elf/nfrom the doorway. The noise in the hall had abated;/nperhaps Mrs. Weasley and Mundungus had moved/ntheir argument down into the kitchen. At the sight of/nSirius, Kreacher flung himself into a ridiculously low/nbow that flattened his snoutlike nose on the floor./n/n"Stand up straight," said Sirius impatiently. "Now,/nwhat are you up to?"/n/n"Kreacher is cleaning," the elf repeated. "Kreacher/nlives to serve the noble house of Black — "/n/n" — and it's getting blacker every day, it's filthy," said/nSirius./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Master always liked his little joke," said Kreacher,/nbowing again, and continuing in an undertone,/n"Master was a nasty ungrateful swine who broke his/nmother's heart — "/n/n"My mother didn't have a heart, Kreacher," Sirius/nsnapped. "She kept herself alive out of pure spite."/n/nKreacher bowed again and said, "Whatever Master/nsays," then muttered furiously, "Master is not fit to/nwipe slime from his mother's boots, oh my poor/nMistress, what would she say if she saw Kreacher/nserving him, how she hated him, what a/ndisappointment he was — "/n/n"I asked you what you were up to," said Sirius coldly./n"Every time you show up pretending to be cleaning,/nyou sneak something off to your room so we can't/nthrow it out."/n/n"Kreacher would never move anything from its proper/nplace in Master's house," said the elf, then muttered/nvery fast, "Mistress would never forgive Kreacher if/nthe tapestry was thrown out, seven centuries it's been/nin the family, Kreacher must save it, Kreacher will not/nlet Master and the blood traitors and the brats/ndestroy it — "/n/n"I thought it might be that," said Sirius, casting a/ndisdainful look at the opposite wall. "She'll have put/nanother Permanent Sticking Charm on the back of it,/n/nI don't doubt, but if I can get rid of it I certainly will./nNow go away, Kreacher."/n/nIt seemed that Kreacher did not dare disobey a direct/norder; nevertheless, the look he gave Sirius as he/nshuffled out past him was redolent of deepest loathing/nand he muttered all the way out of the room./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" — comes back from Azkaban ordering Kreacher/naround, oh my poor Mistress, what would she say if/nshe saw the house now, scum living in it, her/ntreasures thrown out, she swore he was no son of/nhers and he's back, they say he's a murderer too — "/n/n"Keep muttering and I will be a murderer!" said Sirius/nirritably, and he slammed the door shut on the elf./n/n"Sirius, he's not right in the head," said Hermione/npleadingly, "I don't think he realizes we can hear/nhim."/n/n"He's been alone too long," said Sirius, "taking mad/norders from my mother's portrait and talking to/nhimself, but he was always a foul little — "/n/n"If you just set him free," said Hermione hopefully,/n"maybe — "/n/n"We can't set him free, he knows too much about the/nOrder," said Sirius curtly. "And anyway, the shock/nwould kill him. You suggest to him that he leaves this/nhouse, see how he takes it."/n/nSirius walked across the room, where the tapestry/nKreacher had been trying to protect hung the length/nof the wall. Harry and the others followed./n/nThe tapestry looked immensely old; it was faded and/nlooked as though doxies had gnawed it in places;/nnevertheless, the golden thread with which it was/nembroidered still glinted brightly enough to show/nthem a sprawling family tree dating back (as far as/nHarry could tell) to the Middle Ages. Large words at/nthe very top of the tapestry read:/n/nTHE NOBLE AND MOST ANCIENT HOUSE OF BLACK/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"TOUJOURS PUR"/n/n/n/n"You're not on here!" said Harry, after scanning the/nbottom of the tree./n/n"I used to be there," said Sirius, pointing at a small,/nround, charred hole in the tapestry, rather like a/ncigarette burn. "My sweet old mother blasted me off/nafter I ran away from home — Kreacher's quite fond of/nmuttering the story under his breath."/n/n"You ran away from home?"/n/n"When I was about sixteen," said Sirius. "I'd had/nenough."/n/n"Where did you go?" asked Harry, staring at him./n/n"Your dad's place," said Sirius. "Your grandparents/nwere really good about it; they sort of adopted me as a/nsecond son. Yeah, I camped out at your dad's during/nthe school holidays, and then when I was seventeen I/ngot a place of my own, my Uncle Alphard had left me/na decent bit of gold — he's been wiped off here too,/nthat's probably why — anyway, after that I looked/nafter myself. I was always welcome at Mr. and Mrs./nPotter's for Sunday lunch, though."/n/n"But . . . why did you ... ?"/n/n"Leave?" Sirius smiled bitterly and ran a hand/nthrough his long, unkempt hair. "Because I hated the/nwhole lot of them: my parents, with their pure-blood/nmania, convinced that to be a Black made you/npractically royal . . . my idiot brother, soft enough to/nbelieve them ... that's him."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSirius jabbed a finger at the very bottom of the tree,/nat the name REGULUS BLACK. A date of death (some/nfifteen years previously) followed the date of birth./n/n"He was younger than me," said Sirius, "and a much/nbetter son, as I was constantly reminded."/n/n"But he died," said Harry./n/n"Yeah," said Sirius. "Stupid idiot ... he joined the/nDeath Eaters."/n/n"You're kidding!"/n/n"Come on, Harry, haven't you seen enough of this/nhouse to tell what kind of wizards my family were?"/nsaid Sirius testily./n/n"Were — were your parents Death Eaters as well?"/n/n"No, no, but believe me, they thought Voldemort had/nthe right idea, they were all for the purification of the/nWizarding race, getting rid of Muggle-borns and/nhaving purebloods in charge. They weren't alone/neither, there were quite a few people, before/nVoldemort showed his true colors, who thought he/nhad the right idea about things... They got cold feet/nwhen they saw what he was prepared to do to get/npower, though. But I bet my parents thought Regulus/nwas a right little hero for joining up at first."/n/n"Was he killed by an Auror?" Harry asked tentatively./n/n"Oh no," said Sirius. "No, he was murdered by/nVoldemort. Or on Voldemort's orders, more likely, I/ndoubt Regulus was ever important enough to be killed/nby Voldemort in person. From what I found out after/nhe died, he got in so far, then panicked about what he/nwas being asked to do and tried to back out. Well, you/n/n/n/n/ndon't just hand in your resignation to Voldemort. It's/na lifetime of service or death."/n/n"Lunch," said Mrs. Weasley's voice./n/nShe was holding her wand high in front of her,/nbalancing a huge tray loaded with sandwiches and/ncake on its tip. She was very red in the face and still/nlooked angry. The others moved over to her, eager for/nsome food, but Harry remained with Sirius, who had/nbent closer to the tapestry./n/n"I haven't looked at this for years. There's Phineas/nNigellus ... my great-great-grandfather, see? Least/npopular headmaster Hogwarts ever had . . . and/nAraminta Meliflua . . . cousin of my mother's . . . tried to/nforce through a Ministry Bill to make Muggle-hunting/nlegal . . . and dear Aunt Elladora . . . she started the/nfamily tradition of beheading house-elves when they/ngot too old to carry tea trays ... of course, anytime the/nfamily produced someone halfway decent they were/ndisowned. I see Tonks isn't on here. Maybe that's why/nKreacher won't take orders from her — he's supposed/nto do whatever anyone in the family asks him..."/n/n"You and Tonks are related?" Harry asked, surprised./n/n"Oh yeah, her mother, Andromeda, was my favorite/ncousin," said Sirius, examining the tapestry carefully./n"No, Andromeda's not on here either, look — "/n/nHe pointed to another small round burn mark/nbetween two names, Bellatrix and Narcissa./n/n"Andromeda's sisters are still here because they made/nlovely, respectable pure-blood marriages, but/nAndromeda married a Muggle-born, Ted Tonks, so — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSirius mimed blasting the tapestry with a wand and/nlaughed sourly. Harry, however, did not laugh; he was/ntoo busy staring at the names to the right of/nAndromeda's burn mark. A double line of gold/nembroidery linked Narcissa Black with Lucius Malfoy,/nand a single vertical gold line from their names led to/nthe name Draco./n/n"You're related to the Malfoys!"/n/n"The pure-blood families are all interrelated," said/nSirius. "If you're only going to let your sons and/ndaughters marry purebloods your choice is very/nlimited, there are hardly any of us left. Molly and I are/ncousins by marriage and Arthur's something like my/nsecond cousin once removed. But there's no point/nlooking for them on here — if ever a family was a/nbunch of blood traitors it's the Weasleys."/n/nBut Harry was now looking at the name to the left of/nAndromeda's burn: Bellatrix Black, which was/nconnected by a double line to Rodolphus Lestrange./n/n"Lestrange ..." Harry said aloud. The name had/nstirred something in his memory; he knew it from/nsomewhere, but for a moment he couldn't think/nwhere, though it gave him an odd, creeping sensation/nin the pit of his stomach./n/n"They're in Azkaban," said Sirius shortly./n/nHarry looked at him curiously./n/n"Bellatrix and her husband Rodolphus came in with/nBarty Crouch, Junior," said Sirius in the same/nbrusque voice. "Rodolphus 's brother, Rabastan, was/nwith them too."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd Harry remembered: He had seen Bellatrix/nLestrange inside Dumbledore's Pensieve, the strange/ndevice in which thoughts and memories could be/nstored: a tall dark woman with heavy-lidded eyes,/nwho had stood at her trial and proclaimed her/ncontinuing allegiance to Lord Voldemort, her pride/nthat she had tried to find him after his downfall and/nher conviction that she would one day be rewarded/nfor her loyalty./n/n"You never said she was your — "/n/n"Does it matter if she's my cousin?" snapped Sirius./n"As far as I'm concerned, they're not my family. She's/ncertainly not my family. I haven't seen her since I was/nyour age, unless you count a glimpse of her coming in/nto Azkaban. D'you think I'm proud of having relatives/nlike her?"/n/n"Sorry," said Harry quickly, "I didn't mean — I was/njust surprised, that's all — "/n/n"It doesn't matter, don't apologize," Sirius mumbled at/nonce. He turned away from the tapestry, his hands/ndeep in his pockets. "I don't like being back here," he/nsaid, staring across the drawing room. "I never/nthought I'd be stuck in this house again."/n/nHarry understood completely. He knew how he would/nfeel if forced, when he was grown up and thought he/nwas free of the place forever, to return and live at/nnumber four, Privet Drive./n/n"It's ideal for headquarters, of course," Sirius said./n/n"My father put every security measure known to/nWizard-kind on it when he lived here. It's Unplottable,/nso Muggles could never come and call — as if they'd/nhave wanted to — and now Dumbledore's added his/nprotection, you'd be hard put to find a safer house/n/n/n/n/nanywhere. Dumbledore's Secret-Keeper for the Order,/nyou know — nobody can find headquarters unless he/ntells them personally where it is — that note Moody/nshowed you last night, that was from Dumbledore..."/nSirius gave a short, barklike laugh. "If my parents/ncould see the use it was being put to now ... well, my/nmother's portrait should give you some idea..."/n/nHe scowled for a moment, then sighed./n/n"I wouldn't mind if I could just get out occasionally/nand do something useful. I've asked Dumbledore/nwhether I can escort you to your hearing — as/nSnuffles, obviously — so I can give you a bit of moral/nsupport, what d'you think?"/n/nHarry felt as though his stomach had sunk through/nthe dusty carpet. He had not thought about the/nhearing once since dinner the previous evening; in the/nexcitement of being back with the people he liked/nbest, of hearing everything that was going on, it had/ncompletely flown his mind. At Sirius's words,/nhowever, the crushing sense of dread returned to/nhim. He stared at Hermione and the Weasleys, all/ntucking into their sandwiches, and thought how he/nwould feel if they went back to Hogwarts without him./n/n"Don't worry," Sirius said. Harry looked up and/nrealized that Sirius had been watching him. "I'm sure/nthey're going to clear you, there's definitely something/nin the International Statute of Secrecy about being/nallowed to use magic to save your own life."/n/n"But if they do expel me," said Harry, quietly, "can I/ncome back here and live with you?"/n/nSirius smiled sadly./n/n"We'll see."/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'd feel a lot better about the hearing if I knew I didn't/nhave to go back to the Dursleys," Harry pressed him./n/n/n/n"They must be bad if you prefer this place," said/nSirius gloomily./n/n"Hurry up, you two, or there won't be any food left,"/nMrs. Weasley called./n/nSirius heaved another great sigh, cast a dark look at/nthe tapestry, and he and Harry went to join the/nothers./n/nHarry tried his best not to think about the hearing/nwhile they emptied the glass cabinets that afternoon./nFortunately for him, it was a job that required a lot of/nconcentration, as many of the objects in there seemed/nvery reluctant to leave their dusty shelves. Sirius/nsustained a bad bite from a silver snuffbox; within/nseconds, his bitten hand had developed an/nunpleasant crusty covering like a tough brown glove./n/n"It's okay," he said, examining the hand with interest/nbefore tapping it lightly with his wand and restoring/nits skin to normal, "must be Wartcap powder in/nthere."/n/nHe threw the box aside into the sack where they were/ndepositing the debris from the cabinets; Harry saw/nGeorge wrap his own hand carefully in a cloth/nmoments later and sneak the box into his already/ndoxy-filled pocket./n/nThey found an unpleasant-looking silver instrument,/nsomething like a many-legged pair of tweezers, which/nscuttled up Harry's arm like a spider when he picked/nit up, and attempted to puncture his skin; Sirius/nseized it and smashed it with a heavy book entitled/nNature's Nobility: A Wizarding Genealogy. There was a/n/n/n/n/nmusical box that emitted a faintly sinister, tinkling/ntune when wound, and they all found themselves/nbecoming curiously weak and sleepy until Ginny had/nthe sense to slam the lid shut; also a heavy locket/nthat none of them could open, a number of ancient/nseals and, in a dusty box, an Order of Merlin, First/nClass, that had been awarded to Sirius's grandfather/nfor "Services to the Ministry."/n/n"It means he gave them a load of gold," said Sirius/ncontemptuously, throwing the medal into the rubbish/nsack./n/nSeveral times, Kreacher sidled into the room and/nattempted to smuggle things away under his/nloincloth, muttering horrible curses every time they/ncaught him at it. When Sirius wrested a large golden/nring bearing the Black crest from his grip Kreacher/nactually burst into furious tears and left the room/nsobbing under his breath and calling Sirius names/nHarry had never heard before./n/n"It was my father's," said Sirius, throwing the ring/ninto the sack. "Kreacher wasn't quite as devoted to/nhim as to my mother, but I still caught him snogging/na pair of my father's old trousers last week."/n/nMrs. Weasley kept them all working very hard over/nthe next few days. The drawing room took three days/nto decontaminate; finally the only undesirable things/nleft in it were the tapestry of the Black family tree,/nwhich resisted all their attempts to remove it from the/nwall, and the rattling writing desk; Moody had not/ndropped by headquarters yet, so they could not be/nsure what was inside it./n/nThey moved from the drawing room to a dining room/non the ground floor where they found spiders large as/nsaucers lurking in the dresser (Ron left the room/n/n/n/n/n/nhurriedly to make a cup of tea and did not return for/nan hour and a half) . The china, which bore the Black/ncrest and motto, was all thrown unceremoniously into/na sack by Sirius, and the same fate met a set of old/nphotographs in tarnished silver frames, all of whose/noccupants squealed shrilly as the glass covering them/nsmashed./n/nSnape might refer to their work as "cleaning," but in/nHarry's opinion they were really waging war on the/nhouse, which was putting up a very good fight, aided/nand abetted by Kreacher. The house-elf kept/nappearing wherever they were congregated, his/nmuttering becoming more and more offensive as he/nattempted to remove anything he could from the/nrubbish sacks. Sirius went as far as to threaten him/nwith clothes, but Kreacher fixed him with a watery/nstare and said, "Master must do as Master wishes,"/nbefore turning away and muttering very loudly, "but/nMaster will not turn Kreacher away, no, because/nKreacher knows what they are up to, oh yes, he is/nplotting against the Dark Lord, yes, with these/nMudbloods and traitors and scum..."/n/nAt which Sirius, ignoring Hermione's protests, seized/nKreacher by the back of his loincloth and threw him/nbodily from the room./n/nThe doorbell rang several times a day, which was the/ncue for Sirius's mother to start shrieking again, and/nfor Harry and the others to attempt to eavesdrop on/nthe visitor, though they gleaned very little from the/nbrief glimpses and snatches of conversation they were/nable to sneak before Mrs. Weasley recalled them to/ntheir tasks. Snape flitted in and out of the house/nseveral times more, though to Harry's relief they never/ncame face-to-face; he also caught sight of his/nTransfiguration teacher, Professor McGonagall,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nlooking very odd in a Muggle dress and coat, though/nshe also seemed too busy to linger./n/nSometimes, however, the visitors stayed to help;/n/nTonks joined them for a memorable afternoon in/nwhich they found a murderous old ghoul lurking in/nan upstairs toilet, and Lupin, who was staying in the/nhouse with Sirius but who left it for long periods to do/nmysterious work for the Order, helped them repair a/ngrandfather clock that had developed the unpleasant/nhabit of shooting heavy bolts at passersby./nMundungus redeemed himself slightly in Mrs./nWeasley's eyes by rescuing Ron from an ancient set of/npurple robes that had tried to strangle him when he/nremoved them from their wardrobe./n/nDespite the fact that he was still sleeping badly, still/nhaving dreams about corridors and locked doors that/nmade his scar prickle, Harry was managing to have/nfun for the first time all summer. As long as he was/nbusy he was happy; when the action abated, however,/nwhenever he dropped his guard, or lay exhausted in/nbed watching blurred shadows move across the/nceiling, the thought of the looming Ministry hearing/nreturned to him. Fear jabbed at his insides like/nneedles as he wondered what was going to happen to/nhim if he was expelled. The idea was so terrible that/nhe did not dare voice it aloud, not even to Ron and/nHermione, who, though he often saw them whispering/ntogether and casting anxious looks in his direction,/nfollowed his lead in not mentioning it. Sometimes he/ncould not prevent his imagination showing him a/nfaceless Ministry official who was snapping his wand/nin two and ordering him back to the Dursleys' ... but/nhe would not go. He was determined on that. He/nwould come back here to Grimmauld Place and live/nwith Sirius./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe felt as though a brick had dropped into his/nstomach when Mrs. Weasley turned to him during/ndinner on Wednesday evening and said quietly, "I've/nironed your best clothes for tomorrow morning,/n/nHarry, and I want you to wash your hair tonight too./n/nA good first impression can work wonders."/n/nRon, Hermione, Fred, George, and Ginny all stopped/ntalking and looked over at him. Harry nodded and/ntried to keep eating his chops, but his mouth had/nbecome so dry he could not chew./n/n"How am I getting there?" he asked Mrs. Weasley,/ntrying to sound unconcerned./n/n"Arthur's taking you to work with him," said Mrs./nWeasley gently./n/nMr. Weasley smiled encouragingly at Harry across the/ntable./n/n"You can wait in my office until it's time for the/nhearing," he said./n/nHarry looked over at Sirius, but before he could ask/nthe question, Mrs. Weasley had answered it./n/n"Professor Dumbledore doesn't think it's a good idea/nfor Sirius to go with you, and I must say I — "/n/n" — think he's quite right," said Sirius through/nclenched teeth./n/nMrs. Weasley pursed her lips./n/n"When did Dumbledore tell you that?" Harry said,/nstaring at Sirius./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He came last night, when you were in bed," said Mr./nWeasley./n/nSirius stabbed moodily at a potato with his fork./nHarry dropped his own eyes to his plate. The thought/nthat Dumbledore had been in the house on the eve of/nhis hearing and not asked to see him made him feel,/nif that were possible, even worse./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n7/n/n/n/n

title: The Ministry Of Magic
text: /nHarry awoke at half-past five the next morning as/nabruptly and completely as if somebody had yelled in/nhis ear. For a few moments he lay immobile as the/nprospect of the hearing filled every tiny particle of his/nbrain, then, unable to bear it, he leapt out of bed and/nput on his glasses. Mrs. Weasley had laid out his/nfreshly laundered jeans and T-shirt at the foot of his/nbed. Harry scrambled into them. The blank picture on/nthe wall sniggered again./n/nRon was lying sprawled on his back with his mouth/nwide open, fast asleep. He did not stir as Harry/ncrossed the room, stepped out onto the landing, and/nclosed the door softly behind him. Trying not to think/nof the next time he would see Ron, when they might/nno longer be fellow students at Hogwarts, Harry/nwalked quietly down the stairs, past the heads of/nKreacher's ancestors, and into the kitchen./n/nHe had expected it to be empty, but it was not. When/nhe reached the door he heard the soft rumble of/nvoices on the other side and when he pushed it open/n/n/n/n/nhe saw Mr. and Mrs. Weasley, Sirius, Lupin, and/nTonks sitting there almost as though they were/nwaiting for him. All were fully dressed except Mrs./nWeasley, who was wearing a quilted, purple dressing/ngown. She leapt to her feet the moment he entered./n/n"Breakfast," she said as she pulled out her wand and/nhurried over to the fire./n/n"M-m-morning, Harry," yawned Tonks. Her hair was/nblonde and curly this morning. "Sleep all right?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry./n/n"I've b-b-been up all night," she said, with another/nshuddering yawn. "Come and sit down..."/n/nShe drew out a chair, knocking over the one beside it/nin the process./n/n"What do you want, Harry?" Mrs. Weasley called./n"Porridge? Muffins? Kippers? Bacon and eggs?/n/nToast?"/n/n"Just — just toast, thanks," said Harry./n/nLupin glanced at Harry, then said to Tonks, "What/nwere you saying about Scrimgeour?"/n/n"Oh ... yeah ... well, we need to be a bit more careful,/nhe's been asking Kingsley and me funny questions..."/n/nHarry felt vaguely grateful that he was not required to/njoin in the conversation. His insides were squirming./nMrs. Weasley placed a couple of pieces of toast and/nmarmalade in front of him; he tried to eat, but it was/nlike chewing carpet. Mrs. Weasley sat down on his/nother side and started fussing with his T-shirt,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ntucking in the label and smoothing out creases across/nthe shoulders. He wished she wouldn't./n/n"... and I'll have to tell Dumbledore I can't do night/nduty tomorrow, I'm just t-t-too tired," Tonks finished,/nyawning hugely again./n/n"I'll cover for you," said Mr. Weasley. "I'm okay, I've/ngot a report to finish anyway..."/n/nMr. Weasley was not wearing wizard's robes but a/npair of pinstriped trousers and an old bomber jacket./nHe turned from Tonks to Harry./n/n"How are you feeling?"/n/nHarry shrugged./n/n"It'll all be over soon," Mr. Weasley said bracingly. "In/na few hours' time you'll be cleared."/n/nHarry said nothing./n/n"The hearing's on my floor, in Amelia Bones 's office./nShe's Head of the Department of Magical Law/nEnforcement and she's the one who'll be questioning/nyou."/n/n"Amelia Bones is okay, Harry," said Tonks earnestly./n"She's fair, she'll hear you out."/n/nHarry nodded, still unable to think of anything to say./n/n"Don't lose your temper," said Sirius abruptly. "Be/npolite and stick to the facts."/n/nHarry nodded again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The law's on your side," said Lupin quietly. "Even/nunderage wizards are allowed to use magic in life-/nthreatening situations."/n/nSomething very cold trickled down the back of Harry's/nneck; for a moment he thought someone was putting/na Disillusionment Charm on him again, then he/nrealized that Mrs. Weasley was attacking his hair with/na wet comb. She pressed hard on the top of his head./n/n"Doesn't it ever lie flat?" she said desperately./n/nHarry shook his head./n/nMr. Weasley checked his watch and looked up at/nHarry./n/n"I think we'll go now," he said. "We're a bit early, but I/nthink you'll be better off there than hanging around/nhere."/n/n"Okay," said Harry automatically, dropping his toast/nand getting to his feet./n/n"You'll be all right, Harry," said Tonks, patting him on/nthe arm./n/n"Good luck," said Lupin. "I'm sure it will be fine."/n/n"And if it's not," said Sirius grimly, "I'll see to Amelia/nBones for you..."/n/nHarry smiled weakly. Mrs. Weasley hugged him./n/n"We've all got our fingers crossed," she said./n/n"Right," said Harry. "Well ... see you later then."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe followed Mr. Weasley upstairs and along the hall./nHe could hear Sirius's mother grunting in her sleep/nbehind her curtains. Mr. Weasley unbolted the door/nand they stepped out into the cold, gray dawn./n/n"You don't normally walk to work, do you?" Harry/nasked him, as they set off briskly around the square./n/n"No, I usually Apparate," said Mr. Weasley, "but/nobviously you can't, and I think it's best we arrive in a/nthoroughly non-magical fashion . . . makes a better/nimpression, given what you're being disciplined for..."/n/nMr. Weasley kept his hand inside his jacket as they/nwalked. Harry knew it was clenched around his wand./nThe run-down streets were almost deserted, but when/nthey arrived at the miserable little Underground/nstation they found it already full of early morning/ncommuters. As ever when he found himself in close/nproximity to Muggles going about their daily business,/nMr. Weasley was hard put to contain his enthusiasm./n/n"Simply fabulous," he whispered, indicating the/nautomatic ticket machines.
