"Wonderfully ingenious."/n/n"They're out of order," said Harry, pointing at the/nsign./n/n"Yes, but even so ..." said Mr. Weasley, beaming/nfondly at them./n/nThey bought their tickets instead from a sleepy-/nlooking guard (Harry handled the transaction, as Mr./nWeasley was not very good with Muggle money) and/nfive minutes later they were boarding an Underground/ntrain that rattled them off toward the center of/nLondon. Mr. Weasley kept anxiously checking and/nrechecking the Underground map above the windows./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Four stops, Harry ... three stops left now ... two/nstops to go, Harry ..."/n/nThey got off at a station in the very heart of London,/nswept from the train in a tide of besuited men and/nwomen carrying briefcases. Up the escalator they/nwent, through the ticket barrier (Mr. Weasley/ndelighted with the way the stile swallowed his ticket),/nand emerged onto a broad street lined with imposing-/nlooking buildings, already full of traffic./n/n"Where are we?" said Mr. Weasley blankly, and for/none heart-stopping moment Harry thought they had/ngotten off at the wrong station despite Mr. Weasley's/ncontinual references to the map; but a second later he/nsaid, "Ah yes ... this way, Harry," and led him down a/nside road./n/n"Sorry," he said, "but I never come by train and it all/nlooks rather different from a Muggle perspective. As a/nmatter of fact I've never even used the visitor's/nentrance before."/n/nThe farther they walked, the smaller and less/nimposing the buildings became, until finally they/nreached a street that contained several rather/nshabby-looking offices, a pub, and an overflowing/ndumpster. Harry had expected a rather more/nimpressive location for the Ministry of Magic./n/n"Here we are," said Mr. Weasley brightly, pointing at/nan old red telephone box, which was missing several/npanes of glass and stood before a heavily graffittied/nwall. "After you, Harry."/n/nHe opened the telephone box door./n/nHarry stepped inside, wondering what on earth this/nwas about. Mr. Weasley folded himself in beside Harry/n/n/n/n/n/nand closed the door. It was a tight fit; Harry was/njammed against the telephone apparatus, which was/nhanging crookedly from the wall as though a vandal/nhad tried to rip it off. Mr. Weasley reached past Harry/nfor the receiver./n/n"Mr. Weasley, I think this might be out of order too,"/nHarry said./n/n"No, no, I'm sure it's fine," said Mr. Weasley, holding/nthe receiver above his head and peering at the dial./n"Let's see ... six ..." he dialed the number, "two ... four/n... and another four ... and another two ..."/n/nAs the dial whirred smoothly back into place, a cool/nfemale voice sounded inside the telephone box, not/nfrom the receiver in Mr. Weasley's hand, but as loudly/nand plainly as though an invisible woman were/nstanding right beside them./n/n"Welcome to the Ministry of Magic. Please state your/nname and business."/n/n"Er ..." said Mr. Weasley, clearly uncertain whether he/nshould talk into the receiver or not; he compromised/nby holding the mouthpiece to his ear, "Arthur/nWeasley, Misuse of Muggle Artifacts Office, here to/nescort Harry Potter, who has been asked to attend a/ndisciplinary hearing..."/n/n"Thank you," said the cool female voice. "Visitor,/nplease take the badge and attach it to the front of/nyour robes."/n/nThere was a click and a rattle, and Harry saw/nsomething slide out of the metal chute where/nreturned coins usually appeared. He picked it up: It/nwas a square silver badge with Harry Potter,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDisciplinary Hearing on it. He pinned it to the front of/nhis T-shirt as the female voice spoke again./n/n"Visitor to the Ministry, you are required to submit to/na search and present your wand for registration at the/nsecurity desk, which is located at the far end of the/nAtrium."/n/nThe floor of the telephone box shuddered. They were/nsinking slowly into the ground. Harry watched/napprehensively as the pavement rose up past the/nglass windows of the telephone box until darkness/nclosed over their heads. Then he could see nothing at/nall; he could only hear a dull grinding noise as the/ntelephone box made its way down through the earth./nAfter about a minute, though it felt much longer to/nHarry, a chink of golden light illuminated his feet/nand, widening, rose up his body, until it hit him in/nthe face and he had to blink to stop his eyes from/nwatering./n/n"The Ministry of Magic wishes you a pleasant day,"/nsaid the woman's voice./n/nThe door of the telephone box sprang open and Mr./nWeasley stepped out of it, followed by Harry, whose/nmouth had fallen open./n/nThey were standing at one end of a very long and/nsplendid hall with a highly polished, dark wood floor./nThe peacock-blue ceiling was inlaid with gleaming/ngolden symbols that were continually moving and/nchanging like some enormous heavenly notice board./nThe walls on each side were paneled in shiny dark/nwood and had many gilded fireplaces set into them./nEvery few seconds a witch or wizard would emerge/nfrom one of the left-hand fireplaces with a soft/nwhoosh ; on the right-hand side, short queues of/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwizards were forming before each fireplace, waiting to/ndepart./n/nHalfway down the hall was a fountain. A group of/ngolden statues, larger than life-size, stood in the/nmiddle of a circular pool. Tallest of them all was a/nnoble-looking wizard with his wand pointing straight/nup in the air. Grouped around him were a beautiful/nwitch, a centaur, a goblin, and a house-elf. The last/nthree were all looking adoringly up at the witch and/nwizard. Glittering jets of water were flying from the/nends of the two wands, the point of the centaur's/narrow, the tip of the goblin's hat, and each of the/nhouse-elf's ears, so that the tinkling hiss of falling/nwater was added to the pops and cracks of/nApparators and the clatter of footsteps as hundreds of/nwitches and wizards, most of whom were wearing/nglum, early-morning looks, strode toward a set of/ngolden gates at the far end of the hall./n/n"This way," said Mr. Weasley./n/nThey joined the throng, wending their way between/nthe Ministry workers, some of whom were carrying/ntottering piles of parchment, others battered/nbriefcases, still others reading the Daily Prophet as/nthey walked. As they passed the fountain Harry saw/nsilver Sickles and bronze Knuts glinting up at him/nfrom the bottom of the pool. A small, smudged sign/nbeside it read:/n/nAll proceeds from the Fountain of Magical Brethren will/nbe given to/n/nSt. Mungo's Hospital for Magical Maladies and Injuries/n/nIf I'm not expelled from Hogwarts, I'll put in ten/nGalleons, Harry found himself thinking desperately./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Over here, Harry," said Mr. Weasley, and they/nstepped out of the stream of Ministry employees/nheading for the golden gates, toward a desk on the/nleft, over which hung a sign saying SECURITY. A/nbadly shaven wizard in peacock-blue robes looked up/nas they approached and put down his Daily Prophet./n/n"I'm escorting a visitor," said Mr. Weasley, gesturing/ntoward Harry./n/n"Step over here," said the wizard in a bored voice./n/nHarry walked closer to him and the wizard held up a/nlong golden rod, thin and flexible as a car aerial, and/npassed it up and down Harry's front and back./n/n"Wand," grunted the security wizard at Harry, putting/ndown the golden instrument and holding out his/nhand./n/nHarry produced his wand. The wizard dropped it onto/na strange brass instrument, which looked something/nlike a set of scales with only one dish. It began to/nvibrate. A narrow strip of parchment came speeding/nout of a slit in the base. The wizard tore this off and/nread the writing upon it./n/n"Eleven inches, phoenix-feather core, been in use four/nyears. That correct?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry nervously./n/n"I keep this," said the wizard, impaling the slip of/nparchment on a small brass spike. "You get this/nback," he added, thrusting the wand at Harry./n/n"Thank you."/n/n"Hang on..." said the wizard slowly./n/n/n/n/n/nHis eyes had darted from the silver visitor's badge on/nHarry's chest to his forehead./n/n"Thank you, Eric," said Mr. Weasley firmly, and/ngrasping Harry by the shoulder, he steered him away/nfrom the desk and back into the stream of wizards/nand witches walking through the golden gates./n/nJostled slightly by the crowd, Harry followed Mr./nWeasley through the gates into the smaller hall/nbeyond, where at least twenty lifts stood behind/nwrought golden grilles. Harry and Mr. Weasley joined/nthe crowd around one of them. A big, bearded wizard/nholding a large cardboard box stood nearby. The box/nwas emitting rasping noises./n/n"All right, Arthur?" said the wizard, nodding at Mr./nWeasley./n/n"What've you got there, Bob?" asked Mr. Weasley,/nlooking at the box./n/n"We're not sure," said the wizard seriously. "We/nthought it was a bog-standard chicken until it started/nbreathing fire. Looks like a serious breach of the Ban/non Experimental Breeding to me."/n/nWith a great jangling and clattering a lift descended in/nfront of them; the golden grille slid back and Harry/nand Mr. Weasley moved inside it with the rest of the/ncrowd. Harry found himself jammed against the back/nwall of the lift. Several witches and wizards were/nlooking at him curiously; he stared at his feet to avoid/ncatching anyone's eye, flattening his fringe as he did/nso. The grilles slid shut with a crash and the lift/nascended slowly, chains rattling all the while, while/nthe same cool female voice Harry had heard in the/ntelephone box rang out again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Level seven, Department of Magical Games and/nSports, incorporating the British and Irish Quidditch/nLeague Headquarters, Official Gobstones Club, and/nLudicrous Patents Office."/n/nThe lift doors opened; Harry glimpsed an untidy-/nlooking corridor, with various posters of Quidditch/nteams tacked lopsidedly on the walls; one of the/nwizards in the lift, who was carrying an armful of/nbroomsticks, extricated himself with difficulty and/ndisappeared down the corridor. The doors closed, the/nlift juddered upward again, and the woman's voice/nsaid, "Level six, Department of Magical Transport,/nincorporating the Floo Network Authority, Broom/nRegulatory Control, Portkey Office, and Apparation/nTest Center."/n/nOnce again the lift doors opened and four or five/nwitches and wizards got out; at the same time, several/npaper airplanes swooped into the lift. Harry stared up/nat them as they flapped idly around above his head;/nthey were a pale violet color and he could see/nMINISTRY OF MAGIC stamped along the edges of/ntheir wings./n/n"Just Interdepartmental memos," Mr. Weasley/nmuttered to him. "We used to use owls, but the mess/nwas unbelievable ... droppings all over the desks ..."/n/nAs they clattered upward again, the memos flapped/naround the swaying lamp in the lift's ceiling./n/n"Level five, Department of International Magical/nCooperation, incorporating the International Magical/nTrading Standards Body, the International Magical/nOffice of Law, and the International Confederation of/nWizards, British Seats."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWhen the doors opened, two of the memos zoomed/nout with a few more witches and wizards, but several/nmore memos zoomed in, so that the light from the/nlamp in the ceiling flickered and flashed as they/ndarted around it./n/n"Level four, Department for the Regulation and/nControl of Magical Creatures, incorporating Beast,/nBeing, and Spirit Divisions, Goblin Liaison Office, and/nPest Advisory Bureau."/n/n" 'S'cuse," said the wizard carrying the fire-breathing/nchicken and he left the lift pursued by a little flock of/nmemos. The doors clanged shut yet again./n/n"Level three, Department of Magical Accidents and/nCatastrophes, including the Accidental Magic/nReversal Squad, Obliviator Headquarters, and/nMuggle-Worthy Excuse Committee."/n/nEverybody left the lift on this floor except Mr./n/nWeasley, Harry, and a witch who was reading an/nextremely long piece of parchment that was trailing/non the ground. The remaining memos continued to/nsoar around the lamp as the lift juddered upward/nagain, and then the doors opened and the voice said,/n"Level two, Department of Magical Law Enforcement,/nincluding the Improper Use of Magic Office, Auror/nHeadquarters, and Wizengamot Administration/nServices."/n/n"This is us, Harry," said Mr. Weasley, and they/nfollowed the witch out of the lift into a corridor lined/nwith doors. "My office is on the other side of the floor."/n/n"Mr. Weasley," said Harry, as they passed a window/nthrough which sunlight was streaming, "aren't we/nunderground?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, we are," said Mr. Weasley, "those are enchanted/nwindows; Magical Maintenance decide what weather/nwe're getting every day. We had two months of/nhurricanes last time they were angling for a pay/nraise... Just round here, Harry."/n/nThey turned a corner, walked through a pair of heavy/noak doors, and emerged in a cluttered, open area/ndivided into cubicles, which were buzzing with talk/nand laughter. Memos were zooming in and out of/ncubicles like miniature rockets. A lopsided sign on the/nnearest cubicle read AUROR HEADQUARTERS./n/nHarry looked surreptitiously through the doorways as/nthey passed. The Aurors had covered their cubicle/nwalls with everything from pictures of wanted wizards/nand photographs of their families, to posters of their/nfavorite Quidditch teams and articles from the Daily/nProphet A scarlet-robed man with a ponytail longer/nthan Bill's was sitting with his boots up on his desk,/ndictating a report to his quill. A little farther along, a/nwitch with a patch over her eye was talking over the/ntop of her cubicle wall to Kingsley Shacklebolt./n/n"Morning, Weasley," said Kingsley carelessly, as they/ndrew nearer. "I've been wanting a word with you, have/nyou got a second?"/n/n"Yes, if it really is a second," said Mr. Weasley, "I'm in/nrather a hurry."/n/nThey were talking to each other as though they hardly/nknew each other, and when Harry opened his mouth/nto say hello to Kingsley, Mr. Weasley stood on his/nfoot. They followed Kingsley along the row and into/nthe very last cubicle./n/nHarry received a slight shock; Sirius's face was/nblinking down at him from every direction. Newspaper/n/n/n/n/n/ncuttings and old photographs — even the one of/nSirius being best man at the Potters' wedding —/npapered the walls. The only Sirius-free space was a/nmap of the world in which little red pins were glowing/nlike jewels./n/n"Here," said Kingsley brusquely to Mr. Weasley,/nshoving a sheaf of parchment into his hand, "I need/nas much information as possible on flying Muggle/nvehicles sighted in the last twelve months. We've/nreceived information that Black might still be using/nhis old motorcycle."/n/nKingsley tipped Harry an enormous wink and added,/nin a whisper, "Give him the magazine, he might find it/ninteresting." Then he said in normal tones, "And don't/ntake too long, Weasley, the delay on that firelegs/nreport held our investigation up for a month."/n/n"If you had read my report you would know that the/nterm is 'firearms,' " said Mr. Weasley coolly. "And I'm/nafraid you'll have to wait for information on/nmotorcycles, we're extremely busy at the moment." He/ndropped his voice and said, "If you can get away/nbefore seven, Molly's making meatballs."/n/nHe beckoned to Harry and led him out of Kingsley's/ncubicle, through a second set of oak doors, into/nanother passage, turned left, marched along another/ncorridor, turned right into a dimly lit and distinctly/nshabby corridor, and finally reached a dead end,/nwhere a door on the left stood ajar, revealing a broom/ncupboard, and a door on the right bore a tarnished/nbrass plaque reading MISUSE OF MUGGLE/nARTIFACTS./n/nMr. Weasley's dingy office seemed to be slightly/nsmaller than the broom cupboard. Two desks had/nbeen crammed inside it and there was barely room to/n/n/n/n/n/nmove around them because of all the overflowing/nfiling cabinets lining the walls, on top of which were/ntottering piles of files. The little wall space available/nbore witness to Mr. Weasley's obsessions; there were/nseveral posters of cars, including one of a dismantled/nengine, two illustrations of postboxes he seemed to/nhave cut out of Muggle children's books, and a/ndiagram showing how to wire a plug./n/nSitting on top of Mr. Weasley's overflowing in-tray was/nan old toaster that was hiccuping in a disconsolate/nway and a pair of empty leather gloves that were/ntwiddling their thumbs. A photograph of the Weasley/nfamily stood beside the in-tray. Harry noticed that/nPercy appeared to have walked out of it./n/n"We haven't got a window," said Mr. Weasley/napologetically, taking off his bomber jacket and/nplacing it on the back of his chair. "We've asked, but/nthey don't seem to think we need one. Have a seat,/nHarry, doesn't look as if Perkins is in yet."/n/nHarry squeezed himself into the chair behind/nPerkins's desk while Mr. Weasley rifled through the/nsheaf of parchment Kingsley Shacklebolt had given/nhim./n/n"Ah," he said, grinning, as he extracted a copy of a/nmagazine entitled The Quibbler from its midst, "yes/n..." He flicked through it. "Yes, he's right, I'm sure/nSirius will find that very amusing — oh dear, what's/nthis now?"/n/nA memo had just zoomed in through the open door/nand fluttered to rest on top of the hiccuping toaster./nMr. Weasley unfolded it and read aloud, " Third/nregurgitating public toilet reported in Bethnal Green,/nkindly investigate immediately. ' This is getting/nridiculous..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"A regurgitating toilet?"/n/n/n/n"Anti-Muggle pranksters," said Mr. Weasley, frowning./n"We had two last week, one in Wimbledon, one in/nElephant and Castle. Muggles are pulling the flush/nand instead of everything disappearing — well, you/ncan imagine. The poor things keep calling in those —/nthose pumbles, I think they're called — you know, the/nones who mend pipes and things — "/n/n"Plumbers?"/n/n" — exactly, yes, but of course they're flummoxed. I/nonly hope we can catch whoever's doing it."/n/n"Will it be Aurors who catch them?"/n/n"Oh no, this is too trivial for Aurors, it'll be the/nordinary Magical Law Enforcement Patrol — ah,/n/nHarry, this is Perkins."/n/nA stooped, timid-looking old wizard with fluffy white/nhair had just entered the room, panting./n/n"Oh Arthur!" he said desperately, without looking at/nHarry. "Thank goodness, I didn't know what to do for/nthe best, whether to wait here for you or not, I've just/nsent an owl to your home but you've obviously missed/nit — an urgent message came ten minutes ago — "/n/n"I know about the regurgitating toilet," said Mr./nWeasley./n/n"No, no, it's not the toilet, it's the Potter boy's hearing/n— they've changed the time and venue — it starts at/neight o'clock now and it's down in old Courtroom Ten/n/n/n/n"Down in old — but they told me — Merlin's beard — "/n/n/n/n/n/nMr. Weasley looked at his watch, let out a yelp, and/nleapt from his chair./n/n"Quick, Harry, we should have been there five/nminutes ago!"/n/nPerkins flattened himself against the filing cabinets as/nMr. Weasley left the office at a run, Harry on his/nheels./n/n"Why have they changed the time?" Harry said/nbreathlessly as they hurtled past the Auror cubicles;/npeople poked out their heads and stared as they/nstreaked past. Harry felt as though he had left all his/ninsides back at Perkins's desk./n/n"I've no idea, but thank goodness we got here so early,/nif you'd missed it it would have been catastrophic!"/n/nMr. Weasley skidded to a halt beside the lifts and/njabbed impatiently at the down button./n/n"Come ON!"/n/nThe lift clattered into view and they hurried inside./nEvery time it stopped Mr. Weasley cursed furiously/nand pummelled the number nine button./n/n"Those courtrooms haven't been used in years," said/nMr. Weasley angrily. "I can't think why they're doing it/ndown there — unless — but no ..."/n/nA plump witch carrying a smoking goblet entered the/nlift at that moment, and Mr. Weasley did not/nelaborate./n/n"The Atrium," said the cool female voice and the/ngolden grilles slid open, showing Harry a distant/nglimpse of the golden statues in the fountain. The/n/n/n/n/n/nplump witch got out and a sallow-skinned wizard with/na very mournful face got in./n/n/n/n"Morning, Arthur," he said in a sepulchral voice as/nthe lift began to descend. "Don't often see you down/nhere..."/n/n"Urgent business, Bode," said Mr. Weasley, who was/nbouncing on the balls of his feet and throwing/nanxious looks over at Harry./n/n"Ah, yes," said Bode, surveying Harry unblinkingly./n/n"Of course."/n/nHarry barely had emotion to spare for Bode, but his/nunfaltering gaze did not make him feel any more/ncomfortable./n/n"Department of Mysteries," said the cool female voice,/nand left it at that./n/n"Quick, Harry," said Mr. Weasley as the lift doors/nrattled open, and they sped up a corridor that was/nquite different from those above. The walls were bare;/nthere were no windows and no doors apart from a/nplain black one set at the very end of the corridor./nHarry expected them to go through it, but instead Mr./nWeasley seized him by the arm and dragged him to/nthe left, where there was an opening leading to a flight/nof steps./n/n"Down here, down here," panted Mr. Weasley, taking/ntwo steps at a time. "The lift doesn't even come down/nthis far ... why they're doing it there ..."/n/nThey reached the bottom of the steps and ran along/nyet another corridor, which bore a great resemblance/nto that which led to Snape's dungeon at Hogwarts,/nwith rough stone walls and torches in brackets. The/n/n/n/n/n/ndoors they passed here were heavy wooden ones with/niron bolts and keyholes./n/n"Courtroom ... ten ... I think ... we're nearly ... yes."/n/nMr. Weasley stumbled to a halt outside a grimy dark/ndoor with an immense iron lock and slumped against/nthe wall, clutching at a stitch in his chest./n/n"Go on," he panted, pointing his thumb at the door./n"Get in there."/n/n"Aren't — aren't you coming with — ?"/n/n"No, no, I'm not allowed. Good luck!"/n/nHarry's heart was beating a violent tattoo against his/nAdam's apple. He swallowed hard, turned the heavy/niron door handle, and stepped inside the courtroom./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n8/n/n/n/n

title: The Hearing
text: /nHarry gasped; he could not help himself. The large/ndungeon he had entered was horribly familiar. He had/nnot only seen it before, he had been here before: This/nwas the place he had visited inside Dumbledore's/nPensieve, the place where he had watched the/nLestranges sentenced to life imprisonment in/nAzkaban./n/nThe walls were made of dark stone, dimly lit by/ntorches. Empty benches rose on either side of him,/nbut ahead, in the highest benches of all, were many/nshadowy figures. They had been talking in low voices,/nbut as the heavy door swung closed behind Harry an/nominous silence fell./n/nA cold male voice rang across the courtroom./n/n"You're late."/n/n"Sorry," said Harry nervously. "I-I didn't know the/ntime had changed."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"That is not the Wizengamot's fault," said the voice./n"An owl was sent to you this morning. Take your/nseat."/n/nHarry dropped his gaze to the chair in the center of/nthe room, the arms of which were covered in chains./nHe had seen those chains spring to life and bind/nwhoever sat between them. His footsteps echoed/nloudly as he walked across the stone floor. When he/nsat gingerly on the edge of the chair the chains/nclinked rather threateningly but did not bind him./nFeeling rather sick he looked up at the people seated/nat the bench above./n/nThere were about fifty of them, all, as far as he could/nsee, wearing plum-colored robes with an elaborately/nworked silver W on the left-hand side of the chest and/nall staring down their noses at him, some with very/naustere expressions, others looks of frank curiosity./n/nIn the very middle of the front row sat Cornelius/nFudge, the Minister of Magic. Fudge was a portly man/nwho often sported a lime-green bowler hat, though/ntoday he had dispensed with it; he had dispensed too/nwith the indulgent smile he had once worn when he/nspoke to Harry. A broad, square-jawed witch with/nvery short gray hair sat on Fudge's left; she wore a/nmonocle and looked forbidding. On Fudge's right was/nanother witch, but she was sitting so far back on the/nbench that her face was in shadow./n/n"Very well," said Fudge. "The accused being present/n— finally — let us begin. Are you ready?" he called/ndown the row./n/n"Yes, sir," said an eager voice Harry knew. Ron's/nbrother Percy was sitting at the very end of the front/nbench. Harry looked at Percy, expecting some sign of/nrecognition from him, but none came. Percy's eyes,/n/n/n/n/n/nbehind his horn-rimmed glasses, were fixed on his/nparchment, a quill poised in his hand./n/n/n/n"Disciplinary hearing of the twelfth of August," said/nFudge in a ringing voice, and Percy began taking/nnotes at once, "into offenses committed under the/nDecree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage/nSorcery and the International Statute of Secrecy by/nHarry James Potter, resident at number four, Privet/nDrive, Little Whinging, Surrey./n/n"Interrogators: Cornelius Oswald Fudge, Minister of/nMagic; Amelia Susan Bones, Head of the Department/nof Magical Law Enforcement; Dolores Jane Umbridge,/nSenior Undersecretary to the Minister. Court Scribe,/nPercy Ignatius Weasley — "/n/n" — Witness for the defense, Albus Percival Wulfric/nBrian Dumbledore," said a quiet voice from behind/nHarry, who turned his head so fast he cricked his/nneck./n/nDumbledore was striding serenely across the room/nwearing long midnight-blue robes and a perfectly/ncalm expression. His long silver beard and hair/ngleamed in the torchlight as he drew level with Harry/nand looked up at Fudge through the half-moon/nspectacles that rested halfway down his very crooked/nnose./n/nThe members of the Wizengamot were muttering. All/neyes were now on Dumbledore. Some looked annoyed,/nothers slightly frightened; two elderly witches in the/nback row, however, raised their hands and waved in/nwelcome./n/nA powerful emotion had risen in Harry's chest at the/nsight of Dumbledore, a fortified, hopeful feeling rather/nlike that which phoenix song gave him. He wanted to/n/n/n/n/n/ncatch Dumbledore's eye, but Dumbledore was not/nlooking his way; he was continuing to look up at the/nobviously flustered Fudge./n/n"Ah," said Fudge, who looked thoroughly/ndisconcerted. "Dumbledore. Yes. You — er — got our/n/n— er — message that the time and — er — place of/nthe hearing had been changed, then?"/n/n"I must have missed it," said Dumbledore cheerfully./n"However, due to a lucky mistake I arrived at the/nMinistry three hours early, so no harm done."/n/n"Yes — well — I suppose well need another chair — I/n/n— Weasley, could you — ?"/n/n"Not to worry, not to worry," said Dumbledore/npleasantly; he took out his wand, gave it a little flick,/nand a squashy chintz armchair appeared out of/nnowhere next to Harry. Dumbledore sat down, put the/ntips of his long fingers together, and looked at Fudge/nover them with an expression of polite interest. The/nWizengamot was still muttering and fidgeting/nrestlessly; only when Fudge spoke again did they/nsettle down./n/n"Yes," said Fudge again, shuffling his notes. "Well,/nthen. So. The charges. Yes."/n/nHe extricated a piece of parchment from the pile/nbefore him, took a deep breath, and read, "The/ncharges against the accused are as follows: That he/ndid knowingly, deliberately, and in full awareness of/nthe illegality of his actions, having received a previous/nwritten warning from the Ministry of Magic on a/nsimilar charge, produce a Patronus Charm in a/nMuggle-inhabited area, in the presence of a Muggle,/non August the second at twenty-three minutes past/nnine, which constitutes an offense under paragraph C/n/n/n/n/nof the Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of/nUnderage Sorcery, 1875, and also under section/nthirteen of the International Confederation of Wizards'/nStatute of Secrecy./n/n"You are Harry James Potter, of number four, Privet/nDrive, Little Whinging, Surrey?" Fudge said, glaring at/nHarry over the top of his parchment./n/n"Yes," Harry said./n/n"You received an official warning from the Ministry for/nusing illegal magic three years ago, did you not?"/n/n"Yes, but — "/n/n"And yet you conjured a Patronus on the night of the/nsecond of August?" said Fudge./n/n"Yes," said Harry, "but — "/n/n"Knowing that you are not permitted to use magic/noutside school while you are under the age of/nseventeen?"/n/n"Yes, but — "/n/n"Knowing that you were in an area full of Muggles?"/n"Yes, but — "/n/n"Fully aware that you were in close proximity to a/nMuggle at the time?/n/n"Yes," said Harry angrily, "but I only used it because/nwe were — "/n/nThe witch with the monocle on Fudge's left cut across/nhim in a booming voice./n/n/n/n/n/n"You produced a fully fledged Patronus?"/n/n/n/n"Yes," said Harry, "because — "/n/n"A corporeal Patronus?"/n/n"A — what?" said Harry./n/n"Your Patronus had a clearly defined form? I mean to/nsay, it was more than vapor or smoke?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry, feeling both impatient and slightly/ndesperate, "it's a stag, it's always a stag."/n/n"Always?" boomed Madam Bones. "You have/nproduced a Patronus before now?"/n/n"Yes" said Harry, "I've been doing it for over a year —/n/n/n/n"And you are fifteen years old?"/n/n"Yes, and — "/n/n"You learned this at school?"/n/n"Yes, Professor Lupin taught me in my third year,/nbecause of the — "/n/n"Impressive," said Madam Bones, staring down at/nhim, "a true Patronus at that age ... very impressive/nindeed."/n/nSome of the wizards and witches around her were/nmuttering again; a few nodded, but others were/nfrowning and shaking their heads./n/n"It's not a question of how impressive the magic was,"/nsaid Fudge in a testy voice. "In fact, the more/n/n/n/n/n/nimpressive the worse it is, I would have thought, given/nthat the boy did it in plain view of a Muggle!"/n/n/n/nThose who had been frowning now murmured in/nagreement, but it was the sight of Percy's/nsanctimonious little nod that goaded Harry into/nspeech./n/n"I did it because of the dementors!" he said loudly,/nbefore anyone could interrupt him again./n/nHe had expected more muttering, but the silence that/nfell seemed to be somehow denser than before./n/n"Dementors?" said Madam Bones after a moment,/nraising her thick eyebrows so that her monocle looked/nin danger of falling out. "What do you mean, boy?"/n/n"I mean there were two dementors down that alleyway/nand they went for me and my cousin!"/n/n"Ah," said Fudge again, smirking unpleasantly as he/nlooked around at the Wizengamot, as though inviting/nthem to share the joke. "Yes. Yes, I thought we'd be/nhearing something like this."/n/n"Dementors in Little Whinging?" Madam Bones said/nin tones of great surprise. "I don't understand — "/n/n"Don't you, Amelia?" said Fudge, still smirking. "Let/nme explain. He's been thinking it through and decided/ndementors would make a very nice little cover story,/nvery nice indeed. Muggles can't see dementors, can/nthey, boy? Highly convenient, highly convenient ... so/nit's just your word and no witnesses..."/n/n"I'm not lying!" said Harry loudly, over another/noutbreak of muttering from the court. "There were two/nof them, coming from opposite ends of the alley,/n/n/n/n/n/neverything went dark and cold and my cousin felt/nthem and ran for it — "/n/n"Enough, enough!" said Fudge with a very/nsupercilious look on his face. "I'm sorry to interrupt/nwhat I'm sure would have been a very well-rehearsed/nstory — "/n/nDumbledore cleared his throat. The Wizengamot fell/nsilent again./n/n"We do, in fact, have a witness to the presence of/ndementors in that alleyway," he said, "other than/nDudley Dursley, I mean."/n/nFudge's plump face seemed to slacken, as though/nsomebody had let air out of it. He stared down at/nDumbledore for a moment or two, then, with the/nappearance of a man pulling himself back together,/nsaid, "We haven't got time to listen to more/ntaradiddles, I'm afraid, Dumbledore. I want this dealt/nwith quickly — "/n/n"I may be wrong," said Dumbledore pleasantly, "but I/nam sure that under the Wizengamot Charter of/nRights, the accused has the right to present witnesses/nfor his or her case? Isn't that the policy of the/nDepartment of Magical Law Enforcement, Madam/nBones?" he continued, addressing the witch in the/nmonocle./n/n"True," said Madam Bones. "Perfectly true."/n/n"Oh, very well, very well," snapped Fudge. "Where is/nthis person?"/n/n"I brought her with me," said Dumbledore. "She's just/noutside the door. Should I — ?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No — Weasley, you go," Fudge barked at Percy, who/ngot up at once, hurried down the stone steps from the/njudge's balcony, and hastened past Dumbledore and/nHarry without glancing at them./n/nA moment later, Percy returned, followed by Mrs./n/nFigg. She looked scared and more batty than ever./nHarry wished she had thought to change out of her/ncarpet slippers./n/nDumbledore stood up and gave Mrs. Figg his chair,/nconjuring a second one for himself./n/n"Full name?" said Fudge loudly, when Mrs. Figg had/nperched herself nervously on the very edge of her/nseat./n/n"Arabella Doreen Figg," said Mrs. Figg in her quavery/nvoice./n/n"And who exactly are you?" said Fudge, in a bored/nand lofty voice./n/n"I'm a resident of Little Whinging, close to where/nHarry Potter lives," said Mrs. Figg./n/n"We have no record of any witch or wizard living in/nLittle Whinging other than Harry Potter," said Madam/nBones at once. "That situation has always been/nclosely monitored, given ... given past events."/n/n"I'm a Squib," said Mrs. Figg. "So you wouldn't have/nme registered, would you?"/n/n"A Squib, eh?" said Fudge, eyeing her suspiciously./n"We'll be checking that. You'll leave details of your/nparentage with my assistant, Weasley. Incidentally,/ncan Squibs see dementors?" he added, looking left/nand right along the bench where he sat./n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, we can!" said Mrs. Figg indignantly./n/n/n/nFudge looked back down at her, his eyebrows raised./n"Very well," he said coolly. "What is your story?"/n/n"I had gone out to buy cat food from the corner shop/nat the end of Wisteria Walk, shortly after nine on the/nevening of the second of August," gabbled Mrs. Figg at/nonce, as though she had learned what she was saying/nby heart, "when I heard a disturbance down the/nalleyway between Magnolia Crescent and Wisteria/nWalk. On approaching the mouth of the alleyway I/nsaw dementors running — "/n/n"Running?" said Madam Bones sharply. "Dementors/ndon't run, they glide."/n/n"That's what I meant to say," said Mrs. Figg quickly,/npatches of pink appearing in her withered cheeks./n"Gliding along the alley toward what looked like two/nboys."/n/n"What did they look like?" said Madam Bones,/nnarrowing her eyes so that the monocle's edges/ndisappeared into her flesh./n/n"Well, one was very large and the other one rather/nskinny — "/n/n"No, no," said Madam Bones impatiently, "the/ndementors ... describe them."/n/n"Oh," said Mrs. Figg, the pink flush creeping up her/nneck now. "They were big. Big and wearing cloaks."/n/nHarry felt a horrible sinking in the pit of his stomach./nWhatever Mrs. Figg said to the contrary, it sounded to/nhim as though the most she had ever seen was a/npicture of a dementor, and a picture could never/n/n/n/n/n/nconvey the truth of what these beings were like: the/neerie way they moved, hovering inches over the/nground, or the rotting smell of them, or that terrible,/nrattling noise they made as they sucked on the/nsurrounding air ... A dumpy wizard with a large black/nmustache in the second row leaned close to his/nneighbor, a frizzy-haired witch, and whispered/nsomething in her ear. She smirked and nodded./n/n"Big and wearing cloaks," repeated Madam Bones/ncoolly, while Fudge snorted derisively. "I see. Anything/nelse?"/n/n"Yes," said Mrs. Figg. "I felt them. Everything went/ncold, and this was a very warm summer's night, mark/nyou. And I felt ... as though all happiness had gone/nfrom the world . . . and I remembered . . . dreadful/nthings..."/n/nHer voice shook and died./n/nMadam Bones' eyes widened slightly. Harry could see/nred marks under her eyebrow where the monocle had/ndug into it./n/n"What did the dementors do?" she asked, and Harry/nfelt a rush of hope./n/n"They went for the boys," said Mrs. Figg, her voice/nstronger and more confident now, the pink flush/nebbing away from her face. "One of them had fallen./nThe other was backing away, trying to repel the/ndementor. That was Harry. He tried twice and/nproduced silver vapor. On the third attempt, he/nproduced a Patronus, which charged down the first/ndementor and then, with his encouragement, chased/naway the second from his cousin. And that ... that/nwas what happened," Mrs. Figg finished, somewhat/nlamely./n/n/n/n/n/nMadam Bones looked down at Mrs. Figg in silence;/nFudge was not looking at her at all, but fidgeting with/nhis papers. Finally he raised his eyes and said, rather/naggressively "That's what you saw, is it?"/n/n"That was what happened," Mrs. Figg repeated./n/n"Very well," said Fudge. "You may go."/n/nMrs. Figg cast a frightened look from Fudge to/nDumbledore, then got up and shuffled off toward the/ndoor again. Harry heard it thud shut behind her./n/n"Not a very convincing witness," said Fudge loftily./n/n"Oh, I don't know," said Madam Bones in her/nbooming voice. "She certainly described the effects of/na dementor attack very accurately. And I can't/nimagine why she would say they were there if they/nweren't — "/n/n"But dementors wandering into a Muggle suburb and/njust happening to come across a wizard?" snorted/nFudge. "The odds on that must be very, very long,/neven Bagman wouldn't have bet — "/n/n"Oh, I don't think any of us believe the dementors/nwere there by coincidence," said Dumbledore lightly./n/nThe witch sitting to the right of Fudge with her face in/nshadow moved slightly, but everyone else was quite/nstill and silent./n/n"And what is that supposed to mean?" asked Fudge/nicily./n/n"It means that I think they were ordered there," said/nDumbledore./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I think we might have a record of it if someone had/nordered a pair of dementors to go strolling through/nLittle Whinging!" barked Fudge./n/n"Not if the dementors are taking orders from someone/nother than the Ministry of Magic these days," said/nDumbledore calmly. "I have already given you my/nviews on this matter, Cornelius."/n/n"Yes, you have," said Fudge forcefully, "and I have no/nreason to believe that your views are anything other/nthan bilge, Dumbledore. The dementors remain in/nplace in Azkaban and are doing everything we ask/nthem to."/n/n"Then," said Dumbledore, quietly but clearly, "we/nmust ask ourselves why somebody within the/nMinistry ordered a pair of dementors into that/nalleyway on the second of August."/n/nIn the complete silence that greeted these words, the/nwitch to the right of Fudge leaned forward so that/nHarry saw her for the first time./n/nHe thought she looked just like a large, pale toad. She/nwas rather squat with a broad, flabby face, as little/nneck as Uncle Vernon, and a very wide, slack mouth./nHer eyes were large, round, and slightly bulging. Even/nthe little black velvet bow perched on top of her short/ncurly hair put him in mind of a large fly she was/nabout to catch on a long sticky tongue./n/n"The Chair recognizes Dolores Jane Umbridge, Senior/nUndersecretary to the Minister," said Fudge./n/nThe witch spoke in a fluttery, girlish, high-pitched/nvoice that took Harry aback; he had been expecting a/ncroak./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'm sure I must have misunderstood you, Professor/nDumbledore," she said with a simper that left her big,/nround eyes as cold as ever. "So silly of me. But it/nsounded for a teensy moment as though you were/nsuggesting that the Ministry of Magic had ordered an/nattack on this boy!"/n/nShe gave a silvery laugh that made the hairs on the/nback of Harry's neck stand up. A few other members/nof the Wizengamot laughed with her. It could not have/nbeen plainer that not one of them was really amused./n/n"If it is true that the dementors are taking orders only/nfrom the Ministry of Magic, and it is also true that two/ndementors attacked Harry and his cousin a week ago,/nthen it follows logically that somebody at the Ministry/nmight have ordered the attacks," said Dumbledore/npolitely. "Of course, these particular dementors may/nhave been outside Ministry control — "/n/n"There are no dementors outside Ministry control!"/nsnapped Fudge, who had turned brick red./n/nDumbledore inclined his head in a little bow./n/n"Then undoubtedly the Ministry will be making a full/ninquiry into why two dementors were so very far from/nAzkaban and why they attacked without/nauthorization."/n/n"It is not for you to decide what the Ministry of Magic/ndoes or does not do, Dumbledore!" snapped Fudge,/nnow a shade of magenta of which Uncle Vernon would/nhave been proud./n/n"Of course it isn't," said Dumbledore mildly. "I was/nmerely expressing my confidence that this matter will/nnot go uninvestigated."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe glanced at Madam Bones, who readjusted her/nmonocle and stared back at him, frowning slightly./n/n"I would remind everybody that the behavior of these/ndementors, if indeed they are not figments of this/nboy's imagination, is not the subject of this hearing!"/nsaid Fudge. "We are here to examine Harry Potter's/noffenses under the Decree for the Reasonable/nRestriction of Underage Sorcery!"/n/n"Of course we are," said Dumbledore, "but the/npresence of dementors in that alleyway is highly/nrelevant. Clause seven of the Decree states that magic/nmay be used before Muggles in exceptional/ncircumstances, and as those exceptional/ncircumstances include situations that threaten the/nlife of the wizard or witch himself, or witches, wizards,/nor Muggles present at the time of the — "/n/n"We are familiar with clause seven, thank you very/nmuch!" snarled Fudge./n/n"Of course you are," said Dumbledore courteously./n"Then we are in agreement that Harry's use of the/nPatronus Charm in these circumstances falls/nprecisely into the category of exceptional/ncircumstances it describes?"/n/n"If there were dementors, which I doubt — "/n/n"You have heard from an eyewitness," Dumbledore/ninterrupted. "If you still doubt her truthfulness, call/nher back, question her again. I am sure she would not/nobject."/n/n"I — that — not — " blustered Fudge, fiddling with the/npapers before him. "It's — I want this over with today,/nDumbledore!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But naturally, you would not care how many times/nyou heard from a witness, if the alternative was a/nserious miscarriage of justice," said Dumbledore./n/n"Serious miscarriage, my hat!" said Fudge at the top/nof his voice. "Have you ever bothered to tot up the/nnumber of cock-and-bull stories this boy has come/nout with, Dumbledore, while trying to cover up his/nflagrant misuse of magic out of school? I suppose/nyou've forgotten the Hover Charm he used three years/nago -"/n/n"That wasn't me, it was a house-elf!" said Harry./n/n"YOU SEE?" roared Fudge, gesturing flamboyantly in/nHarry's direction. "A house-elf! In a Muggle house! I/nask you — "/n/n"The house-elf in question is currently in the employ/nof Hogwarts School," said Dumbledore. "I can/nsummon him here in an instant to give evidence if/nyou wish."/n/n"I — not — I haven't got time to listen to house-elves!/nAnyway, that's not the only — he blew up his aunt,/nfor God's sake!" Fudge shouted, banging his fist on/nthe judge's bench and upsetting a bottle of ink./n/n"And you very kindly did not press charges on that/noccasion, accepting, I presume, that even the best/nwizards cannot always control their emotions," said/nDumbledore calmly, as Fudge attempted to scrub the/nink off his notes./n/n"And I haven't even started on what he gets up to at/nschool — "/n/n" — but as the Ministry has no authority to punish/nHogwarts students for misdemeanors at school,/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's behavior there is not relevant to this inquiry,"/nsaid Dumbledore, politely as ever, but now with a/nsuggestion of coolness behind his words./n/n"Oho!" said Fudge. "Not our business what he does at/nschool, eh? You think so?"/n/n"The Ministry does not have the power to expel/nHogwarts students, Cornelius, as I reminded you on/nthe night of the second of August," said Dumbledore./n"Nor does it have the right to confiscate wands until/ncharges have been successfully proven, again, as I/nreminded you on the night of the second of August. In/nyour admirable haste to ensure that the law is/nupheld, you appear, inadvertently I am sure, to have/noverlooked a few laws yourself."/n/n"Laws can be changed," said Fudge savagely./n/n"Of course they can," said Dumbledore, inclining his/nhead. "And you certainly seem to be making many/nchanges, Cornelius. Why, in the few short weeks/nsince I was asked to leave the Wizengamot, it has/nalready become the practice to hold a full criminal/ntrial to deal with a simple matter of underage magic!"/n/nA few of the wizards above them shifted/nuncomfortably in their seats. Fudge turned a slightly/ndeeper shade of puce. The toadlike witch on his right,/nhowever, merely gazed at Dumbledore, her face quite/nexpressionless./n/n"As far as I am aware, however," Dumbledore/ncontinued, "there is no law yet in place that says this/ncourt's job is to punish Harry for every bit of magic he/nhas ever performed. He has been charged with a/nspecific offense and he has presented his defense. All/nhe and I can do now is to await your verdict."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore put his fingertips together again and said/nno more. Fudge glared at him, evidently incensed./nHarry glanced sideways at Dumbledore, seeking/nreassurance; he was not at all sure that Dumbledore/nwas right in telling the Wizengamot, in effect, that it/nwas about time they made a decision. Again, however,/nDumbledore seemed oblivious to Harry's attempt to/ncatch his eye. He continued to look up at the benches/nwhere the entire Wizengamot had fallen into urgent,/nwhispered conversations./n/nHarry looked at his feet. His heart, which seemed to/nhave swollen to an unnatural size, was thumping/nloudly under his ribs. He had expected the hearing to/nlast longer than this. He was not at all sure that he/nhad made a good impression. He had not really said/nvery much. He ought to have explained more fully/nabout the dementors, about how he had fallen over,/nabout how both he and Dudley had nearly been/nkissed.../n/nTwice he looked up at Fudge and opened his mouth to/nspeak, but his swollen heart was now constricting his/nair passages and both times he merely took a deep/nbreath and looked back at his shoes./n/nThen the whispering stopped. Harry wanted to look/nup at the judges, but found that it was really much,/nmuch easier to keep examining his laces./n/n"Those in favor of clearing the accused of all/ncharges?" said Madam Bones 's booming voice./n/nHarry's head jerked upward. There were hands in the/nair, many of them . . . more than half! Breathing very/nfast, he tried to count, but before he could finish/nMadam Bones had said, "And those in favor of/nconviction?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nFudge raised his hand; so did half a dozen others,/nincluding the witch on his right and the heavily/nmustached wizard and the frizzy-haired witch in the/nsecond row./n/nFudge glanced around at them all, looking as though/nthere was something large stuck in his throat, then/nlowered his own hand. He took two deep breaths and/nthen said, in a voice distorted by suppressed rage,/n"Very well, very well ... cleared of all charges."/n/n"Excellent," said Dumbledore briskly, springing to his/nfeet, pulling out his wand, and causing the two chintz/narmchairs to vanish. "Well, I must be getting along./nGood day to you all."/n/nAnd without looking once at Harry, he swept from the/ndungeon./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Woes Of Mrs. Weasley
text: /nDumbledore's abrupt departure took Harry/ncompletely by surprise. He remained sitting where he/nwas in the chained chair, struggling with his feelings/nof shock and relief. The Wizengamot were all getting/nto their feet, talking, and gathering up their papers/nand packing them away. Harry stood up. Nobody/nseemed to be paying him the slightest bit of attention/nexcept the toadlike witch on Fudge's right, who was/nnow gazing down at him instead of at Dumbledore./nIgnoring her, he tried to catch Fudge's eye, or Madam/nBones's, wanting to ask whether he was free to go,/nbut Fudge seemed quite determined not to notice/nHarry, and Madam Bones was busy with her/nbriefcase, so he took a few tentative steps toward the/nexit and when nobody called him back, broke into a/nvery fast walk./n/nHe took the last few steps at a run, wrenched open/nthe door, and almost collided with Mr. Weasley, who/nwas standing right outside, looking pale and/napprehensive./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Dumbledore didn't say — "/n/n/n/n"Cleared," Harry said, pulling the door closed behind/nhim, "of all charges!"/n/nBeaming, Mr. Weasley seized Harry by the shoulders./n/n"Harry, that's wonderful! Well, of course, they couldn't/nhave found you guilty, not on the evidence, but even/nso, I can't pretend I wasn't — "/n/nBut Mr. Weasley broke off, because the courtroom/ndoor had just opened again. The Wizengamot were/nfiling out./n/n"Merlin's beard," said Mr. Weasley wonderingly,/npulling Harry aside to let them all pass, "you were/ntried by the full court?"/n/n"I think so," said Harry quietly./n/nOne or two of the passing wizards nodded to Harry as/nthey passed and a few, including Madam Bones, said,/n"Morning, Arthur," to Mr. Weasley, but most averted/ntheir eyes. "She says she'll/nget the Cleansweep if she can."/n/n"Cool," Harry said, and he was relieved to hear that/nhis voice had stopped sounding hearty. "Listen — Ron/n— well done, mate."/n/n/n/n/n/nThe smile faded off Ron's face./n/n/n/n"I never thought it would be me!" he said, shaking his/nhead, "I thought it would be you!"/n/n"Nah, I've caused too much trouble," Harry said,/nechoing Fred./n/n"Yeah," said Ron, "yeah, I suppose... Well, we'd better/nget our trunks packed, hadn't we?"/n/nIt was odd how widely their possessions seemed to/nhave scattered themselves since they had arrived. It/ntook them most of the afternoon to retrieve their/nbooks and belongings from all over the house and/nstow them back inside their school trunks. Harry/nnoticed that Ron kept moving his prefect's badge/naround, first placing it on his bedside table, then/nputting it into his jeans pocket, then taking it out and/nlaying it on his folded robes, as though to see the/neffect of the red on the black. Only when Fred and/nGeorge dropped in and offered to attach it to his/nforehead with a Permanent Sticking Charm did he/nwrap it tenderly in his maroon socks and lock it in his/ntrunk./n/nMrs. Weasley returned from Diagon Alley around six/no'clock, laden with books and carrying a long package/nwrapped in thick brown paper that Ron took from her/nwith a moan of longing./n/n"Never mind unwrapping it now, people are arriving/nfor dinner, I want you all downstairs," she said, but/nthe moment she was out of sight Ron ripped off the/npaper in a frenzy and examined every inch of his new/nbroom, an ecstatic expression on his face./n/nDown in the basement Mrs. Weasley had hung a/nscarlet banner over the heavily laden dinner table,/n/n/n/n/n/nwhich read CONGRATULATIONS RON AND/nHERMIONE — NEW PREFECTS. She looked in a/nbetter mood than Harry had seen her all holiday./n/n"I thought we'd have a little party, not a sit-down/ndinner," she told Harry, Ron, Hermione, Fred, George,/nand Ginny as they entered the room. "Your father and/nBill are on their way, Ron, I've sent them both owls/nand they're thrilled," she added, beaming./n/nFred rolled his eyes./n/nSirius, Lupin, Tonks, and Kingsley Shacklebolt were/nalready there and Mad-Eye Moody stumped in shortly/nafter Harry had got himself a butterbeer./n/n"Oh, Alastor, I am glad you're here," said Mrs./n/nWeasley brightly, as Mad-Eye shrugged off his/ntraveling cloak. "We've been wanting to ask you for/nages — could you have a look in the writing desk in/nthe drawing room and tell us what's inside it? We/nhaven't wanted to open it just in case it's something/nreally nasty."/n/n"No problem, Molly ..."/n/nMoody's electric-blue eye swiveled upward and stared/nfixedly through the ceiling of the kitchen./n/n"Drawing room ..." he growled, as the pupil/ncontracted. "Desk in the corner? Yeah, I see it... Yeah,/nit's a boggart... Want me to go up and get rid of it,/nMolly?"/n/n"No, no, I'll do it myself later," beamed Mrs. Weasley./n"You have your drink. We're having a little bit of a/ncelebration, actually..." She gestured at the scarlet/nbanner. "Fourth prefect in the family!" she said/nfondly, ruffling Ron's hair./n/n/n/n/n/n"Prefect, eh?" growled Moody, his normal eye on Ron/nand his magical eye swiveling around to gaze into the/nside of his head. Harry had the very uncomfortable/nfeeling it was looking at him and moved away toward/nSirius and Lupin./n/n"Well, congratulations," said Moody, still glaring at/nRon with his normal eye, "authority figures always/nattract trouble, but I suppose Dumbledore thinks you/ncan withstand most major jinxes or he wouldn't have/nappointed you..."/n/nRon looked rather startled at this view of the matter/nbut was saved the trouble of responding by the arrival/nof his father and eldest brother. Mrs. Weasley was in/nsuch a good mood she did not even complain that/nthey had brought Mundungus with them too; he was/nwearing a long overcoat that seemed oddly lumpy in/nunlikely places and declined the offer to remove it and/nput it with Moody's traveling cloak./n/n"Well, I think a toast is in order," said Mr. Weasley,/nwhen everyone had a drink. He raised his goblet. "To/nRon and Hermione, the new Gryffindor prefects!"/n/nRon and Hermione beamed as everyone drank to/nthem and then applauded./n/n"I was never a prefect myself," said Tonks brightly/nfrom behind Harry as everybody moved toward the/ntable to help themselves to food. Her hair was tomato-/nred and waist length today; she looked like Ginny's/nolder sister. "My Head of House said I lacked certain/nnecessary qualities."/n/n"Like what?" said Ginny, who was choosing a baked/npotato./n/n"Like the ability to behave myself," said Tonks./n/n/n/n/n/nGinny laughed; Hermione looked as though she did/nnot know whether to smile or not and compromised/nby taking an extra large gulp of butterbeer and/nchoking on it./n/n"What about you, Sirius?" Ginny asked, thumping/nHermione on the back./n/nSirius, who was right beside Harry, let out his usual/nbarklike laugh./n/n"No one would have made me a prefect, I spent too/nmuch time in detention with James. Lupin was the/ngood boy, he got the badge."/n/n"I think Dumbledore might have hoped that I would/nbe able to exercise some control over my best friends,"/nsaid Lupin. "I need scarcely say that I failed dismally."/n/nHarry's mood suddenly lifted. His father had not been/na prefect either. All at once the party seemed much/nmore enjoyable; he loaded up his plate, feeling/nunusually fond of everyone in the room./n/nRon was rhapsodizing about his new broom to/nanybody who would listen./n/n"... naught to seventy in ten seconds, not bad, is it?/nWhen you think the Comet Two Ninety's only naught/nto sixty and that's with a decent tailwind according to/nWhich Broomstick?"/n/nHermione was talking very earnestly to Lupin about/nher view of elf rights./n/n"I mean, it's the same kind of nonsense as werewolf/nsegregation, isn't it? It all stems from this horrible/nthing wizards have of thinking they're superior to/nother creatures..."/n/n/n/n/n/nMrs. Weasley and Bill were having their usual/nargument about Bill's hair./n/n"... getting really out of hand, and you're so good-/nlooking, it would look much better shorter, wouldn't/nit, Harry?"/n/n"Oh — I dunno — " said Harry, slightly alarmed at/nbeing asked his opinion; he slid away from them in/nthe direction of Fred and George, who were huddled/nin a corner with Mundungus./n/nMundungus stopped talking when he saw Harry, but/nFred winked and beckoned Harry closer./n/n"It's okay," he told Mundungus, "we can trust Harry,/nhe's our financial backer."/n/n"Look what Dung's gotten us," said George, holding/nout his hand to Harry. It was full of what looked like/nshriveled black pods. A faint rattling noise was/ncoming from them, even though they were completely/nstationary./n/n"Venomous Tentacula seeds," said George. "We need/nthem for the Skiving Snackboxes but they're a Class/nC Non-Tradeable Substance so we've been having a/nbit of trouble getting hold of them."/n/n"Ten Galleons the lot, then, Dung?" said Fred./n/n"Wiv all the trouble I went to to get 'em?" said/nMundungus, his saggy, bloodshot eyes stretching/neven wider. "I'm sorry, lads, but I'm not taking a Knut/nunder twenty."/n/n"Dung likes his little joke," Fred said to Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, his best one so far has been six Sickles for a/nbag of knarl quills," said George./n/n"Be careful," Harry warned them quietly./n/n"What?" said Fred. "Mum's busy cooing over Prefect/nRon, we're okay."/n/n"But Moody could have his eye on you," Harry pointed/nout./n/nMundungus looked nervously over his shoulder./n/n"Good point, that," he grunted. "All right, lads, ten it/nis, if you'll take 'em quick."/n/n"Cheers, Harry!" said Fred delightedly, when/nMundungus had emptied his pockets into the twins'/noutstretched hands and scuttled off toward the food./n"We'd better get these upstairs..."/n/nHarry watched them go, feeling slightly uneasy. It had/njust occurred to him that Mr. and Mrs. Weasley would/nwant to know how Fred and George were financing/ntheir joke shop business when, as was inevitable,/nthey finally found out about it. Giving the twins his/nTri-wizard winnings had seemed a simple thing to do/nat the time, but what if it led to another family row/nand a Percy-like estrangement? Would Mrs. Weasley/nstill feel that Harry was as good as her son if she/nfound out he had made it possible for Fred and/nGeorge to start a career she thought quite/nunsuitable?/n/nStanding where the twins had left him with nothing/nbut a guilty weight in the pit of his stomach for/ncompany, Harry caught the sound of his own name./nKingsley Shacklebolt's deep voice was audible even/nover the surrounding chatter./n/n/n/n/n/n"... why Dumbledore didn't make Potter a prefect?"/nsaid Kingsley./n/n"He'll have had his reasons," replied Lupin./n/n"But it would've shown confidence in him. It's what/nI'd've done," persisted Kingsley, " 'specially with the/nDaily Prophet having a go at him every few days..."/n/nHarry did not look around; he did not want Lupin or/nKingsley to know he had heard. He followed/nMundungus back toward the table, though not/nremotely hungry. His pleasure in the party had/nevaporated as quickly as it had come; he wished he/nwere upstairs in bed./n/nMad-Eye Moody was sniffing at a chicken leg with/nwhat remained of his nose; evidently he could not/ndetect any trace of poison, because he then tore a/nstrip off it with his teeth./n/n"... the handle's made of Spanish oak with anti-jinx/nvarnish and in-built vibration control — " Ron was/nsaying to Tonks./n/nMrs. Weasley yawned widely./n/n"Well, I think I'll sort out that boggart before I turn/nin... Arthur, I don't want this lot up too late, all right?/n'Night, Harry, dear."/n/nShe left the kitchen. Harry set down his plate and/nwondered whether he could follow her without/nattracting attention./n/n"You all right, Potter?" grunted Moody./n/n"Yeah, fine," lied Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMoody took a swig from his hip flask, his electric blue/neye staring sideways at Harry./n/n"Come here, I've got something that might interest/nyou," he said./n/nFrom an inner pocket of his robes Moody pulled a/nvery tattered old Wizarding photograph./n/n"Original Order of the Phoenix," growled Moody./n"Found it last night when I was looking for my spare/nInvisibility Cloak, seeing as Podmore hasn't had the/nmanners to return my best one... Thought people/nmight like to see it."/n/nHarry took the photograph. A small crowd of people,/nsome waving at him, others lifting their glasses,/nlooked back up at him./n/n"There's me," said Moody unnecessarily, pointing at/nhimself. The Moody in the picture was unmistakable,/nthough his hair was slightly less gray and his nose/nwas intact. "And there's Dumbledore beside me,/nDedalus Diggle on the other side ... That's Marlene/nMcKinnon, she was killed two weeks after this was/ntaken, they got her whole family. That's Frank and/nAlice Longbottom — "/n/nHarry's stomach, already uncomfortable, clenched as/nhe looked at Alice Longbottom; he knew her round,/nfriendly face very well, even though he had never met/nher, because she was the image of her son, Neville./n/n"Poor devils," growled Moody. "Better dead than what/nhappened to them ... and that's Emmeline Vance,/nyou've met her, and that there's Lupin, obviously .../nBenjy Fenwick, he copped it too, we only ever found/nbits of him ... shift aside there," he added, poking the/npicture, and the little photographic people edged/n/n/n/n/nsideways, so that those who were partially obscured/ncould move to the front./n/n/n/n"That's Edgar Bones ... brother of Amelia Bones, they/ngot him and his family too, he was a great wizard .../nSturgis Podmore, blimey, he looks young ... Caradoc/nDearborn, vanished six months after this, we never/nfound his body ... Hagrid, of course, looks exactly the/nsame as ever ... Elphias Doge, you've met him, I'd/nforgotten he used to wear that stupid hat . . . Gideon/nPrewett, it took five Death Eaters to kill him and his/nbrother Fabian, they fought like heroes ... budge/nalong, budge along ..."/n/nThe little people in the photograph jostled among/nthemselves, and those hidden right at the back/nappeared at the forefront of the picture./n/n"That's Dumbledore's brother, Aberforth, only time I/never met him, strange bloke ... That's Dorcas/nMeadowes, Voldemort killed her personally ... Sirius,/nwhen he still had short hair ... and ... there you go,/nthought that would interest you!"/n/nHarry's heart turned over. His mother and father were/nbeaming up at him, sitting on either side of a small,/nwatery-eyed man Harry recognized at once as/nWormtail: He was the one who had betrayed their/nwhereabouts to Voldemort and so helped bring about/ntheir deaths./n/n"Eh?" said Moody./n/nHarry looked up into Moody's heavily scarred and/npitted face. Evidently Moody was under the/nimpression he had just given Harry a bit of a treat./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, attempting to grin again. "Er .../nlisten, I've just remembered, I haven't packed my ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe was spared the trouble of inventing an object he/nhad not packed; Sirius had just said, "What's that/nyou've got there, Mad-Eye?" and Moody had turned/ntoward him. Harry crossed the kitchen, slipped/nthrough the door and up the stairs before anyone/ncould call him back./n/nHe did not know why he had received such a shock;/nhe had seen his parents' pictures before, after all, and/nhe had met Wormtail ... but to have them sprung on/nhim like that, when he was least expecting it ... No/none would like that, he thought angrily. . ./n/nAnd then, to see them surrounded by all those other/nhappy faces ... Benjy Fenwick, who had been found in/nbits, and Gideon Prewett, who had died like a hero,/nand the Longbottoms, who had been tortured into/nmadness ... all waving happily out of the photograph/nforevermore, not knowing that they were doomed.../nWell, Moody might find that interesting ... he, Harry,/nfound it disturbing.../n/nHarry tiptoed up the stairs in the hall past the stuffed/nelf heads, glad to be on his own again, but as he/napproached the first landing he heard noises./nSomeone was sobbing in the drawing room./n/n"Hello?" Harry said./n/nThere was no answer but the sobbing continued. He/nclimbed the remaining stairs two at a time, walked/nacross the landing, and opened the drawing-room/ndoor./n/nSomeone was cowering against the dark wall, her/nwand in her hand, her whole body shaking with sobs./nSprawled on the dusty old carpet in a patch of/nmoonlight, clearly dead, was Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAll the air seemed to vanish from Harry's lungs; he/nfelt as though he were falling through the floor; his/nbrain turned icy cold — Ron dead, no, it couldn't be/n/n/n/nBut wait a moment, it couldn't be — Ron was/ndownstairs —/n/n"Mrs. Weasley?" Harry croaked./n/n" R-r-riddikulus\" Mrs. Weasley sobbed, pointing her/nshaking wand at Ron's body./n/nCrack./n/nRon's body turned into Bill's, spread-eagled on his/nback, his eyes wide open and empty. Mrs. Weasley/nsobbed harder than ever./n/n" R-riddikulus\" she sobbed again./n/nCrack./n/nMr. Weasley's body replaced Bill's, his glasses askew,/na trickle of blood running down his face./n/n"No!" Mrs. Weasley moaned. "No ... riddikulus\/nRiddikulusl RIDDIKULUSl"/n/nCrack. Dead twins. Crack. Dead Percy. Crack. Dead/nHarry .../n/n"Mrs. Weasley, just get out of here!" shouted Harry,/nstaring down at his own dead body on the floor. "Let/nsomeone else — "/n/n"What's going on?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nLupin had come running into the room, closely/nfollowed by Sirius, with Moody stumping along behind/nthem. Lupin looked from Mrs. Weasley to the dead/nHarry on the floor and seemed to understand in an/ninstant. Pulling out his own wand he said, very firmly/nand clearly, " RiddikulusV'/n/nHarry's body vanished. A silvery orb hung in the air/nover the spot where it had lain. Lupin waved his wand/nonce more and the orb vanished in a puff of smoke./n/n"Oh — oh — oh!" gulped Mrs. Weasley, and she broke/ninto a storm of crying, her face in her hands./n/n"Molly," said Lupin bleakly, walking over to her,/n/n"Molly, don't ..."/n/nNext second she was sobbing her heart out on Lupin's/nshoulder./n/n"Molly, it was just a boggart," he said soothingly,/npatting her on the head. "Just a stupid boggart ..."/n/n"I see them d-d-dead all the time!" Mrs. Weasley/nmoaned into his shoulder. "All the t-t-time! I d-d-/ndream about it ..."/n/nSirius was staring at the patch of carpet where the/nboggart, pretending to be Harry's body, had lain./nMoody was looking at Harry, who avoided his gaze. He/nhad a funny feeling Moody's magical eye had followed/nhim all the way out of the kitchen./n/n"D-d-don't tell Arthur," Mrs. Weasley was gulping/nnow, mopping her eyes frantically with her cuffs. "I d-/nd-don't want him to know... Being silly ..."/n/nLupin handed her a handkerchief and she blew her/nnose./n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, I'm so sorry, what must you think of me?" she/nsaid shakily. "Not even able to get rid of a boggart ..."/n/n"Don't be stupid," said Harry, trying to smile./n/n"I'm just s-s-so worried," she said, tears spilling out of/nher eyes again. "Half the f-f-family's in the Order, it'll/nb-b-be a miracle if we all come through this... and P-/nP-Percy's not talking to us... What if something d-d-/ndreadful happens and we had never m-m-made up?/nAnd what's going to happen if Arthur and I get killed,/nwho's g-g-going to look after Ron and Ginny?"/n/n"Molly, that's enough," said Lupin firmly. "This isn't/nlike last time. The Order is better prepared, we've got/na head start, we know what Voldemort's up to — "/n/nMrs. Weasley gave a little squeak of fright at the/nsound of the name./n/n"Oh, Molly, come on, it's about time you got used to/nhearing it — look, I can't promise no one's going to get/nhurt, nobody can promise that, but we're much better/noff than we were last time, you weren't in the Order/nthen, you don't understand, last time we were/noutnumbered twenty to one by the Death Eaters and/nthey were picking us off one by one..."/n/nHarry thought of the photograph again, of his parents'/nbeaming faces. He knew Moody was still watching/nhim./n/n"Don't worry about Percy," said Sirius abruptly. "He'll/ncome round. It's a matter of time before Voldemort/nmoves into the open; once he does, the whole/nMinistry's going to be begging us to forgive them. And/nI'm not sure I'll be accepting their apology," he added/nbitterly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And as for who's going to look after Ron and Ginny if/nyou and Arthur died," said Lupin, smiling slightly,/n"what do you think we'd do, let them starve?"/n/nMrs. Weasley smiled tremulously./n/n"Being silly," she muttered again, mopping her eyes./n/nBut Harry, closing his bedroom door behind him/nsome ten minutes later, could not think Mrs. Weasley/nsilly. He could still see his parents beaming up at him/nfrom the tattered old photograph, unaware that their/nlives, like so many of those around them, were/ndrawing to a close. The image of the boggart posing as/nthe corpse of each member of Mrs. Weasley's family in/nturn kept flashing before his eyes./n/nWithout warning, the scar on his forehead seared/nwith pain again and his stomach churned horribly./n/n"Cut it out," he said firmly, rubbing the scar as the/npain receded again./n/n"First sign of madness, talking to your own head,"/nsaid a sly voice from the empty picture on the wall./n/nHarry ignored it. He felt older than he had ever felt in/nhis life, and it seemed extraordinary to him that/nbarely an hour ago he had been worried about a joke/nshop and who had gotten a prefect's badge./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n10/n/n/n/n

title: Luna Lovegood
text: /nHarry had a troubled night's sleep. His parents wove/nin and out of his dreams, never speaking; Mrs./nWeasley sobbed over Kreacher's dead body watched/nby Ron and Hermione, who were wearing crowns, and/nyet again Harry found himself walking down a/ncorridor ending in a locked door. He awoke abruptly/nwith his scar prickling to find Ron already dressed/nand talking to him./n/n"... better hurry up, Mum's going ballistic, she says/nwe're going to miss the train..."/n/nThere was a lot of commotion in the house. From/nwhat he heard as he dressed at top speed, Harry/ngathered that Fred and George had bewitched their/ntrunks to fly downstairs to save the bother of carrying/nthem, with the result that they had hurtled straight/ninto Ginny and knocked her down two flights of stairs/ninto the hall; Mrs. Black and Mrs. Weasley were both/nscreaming at the top of their voices./n/n/n/n/n/n/nCOULD HAVE DONE HER A SERIOUS INJURY,/nYOU IDIOTS — "/n/nFILTHY HALF-BREEDS, BESMIRCHING THE/nHOUSE OF MY FATHERS — "/n/nHermione came hurrying into the room looking/nflustered just as Harry was putting on his trainers;/nHedwig was swaying on her shoulder, and she was/ncarrying a squirming Crookshanks in her arms./n/n"Mum and Dad just sent Hedwig back" — the owl/nfluttered obligingly over and perched on top of her/ncage — "are you ready yet?"/n/n"Nearly — Ginny all right?" Harry asked, shoving on/nhis glasses./n/n"Mrs. Weasley's patched her up," said Hermione. "But/nnow Mad-Eye's complaining that we can't leave unless/nSturgis Podmore's here, otherwise the guard will be/none short."/n/n"Guard?" said Harry. "We have to go to King's Cross/nwith a guard?"/n/n" You have to go to King's Cross with a guard,"/nHermione corrected him./n/n"Why?" said Harry irritably. "I thought Voldemort was/nsupposed to be lying low, or are you telling me he's/ngoing to jump out from behind a dustbin to try and do/nme in?"/n/n"I don't know, it's just what Mad-Eye says," said/nHermione distractedly, looking at her watch. "But if/nwe don't leave soon we're definitely going to miss the/ntrain..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"WILL YOU LOT GET DOWN HERE NOW, PLEASE!"/nMrs. Weasley bellowed and Hermione jumped as/nthough scalded and hurried out of the room. Harry/nseized Hedwig, stuffed her unceremoniously into her/ncage, and set off downstairs after Hermione, dragging/nhis trunk./n/nMrs. Black's portrait was howling with rage but/nnobody was bothering to close the curtains over her;/nall the noise in the hall was bound to rouse her again/nanyway./n/n"Harry, you're to come with me and Tonks," shouted/nMrs. Weasley over the repeated screeches of/n"MUDBLOODSl SCUM CREATURES OF DIRV." "Leave/nyour trunk and your owl, Alastor's going to deal with/nthe luggage... Oh, for heaven's sake, Sirius,/nDumbledore said no!"/n/nA bearlike black dog had appeared at Harry's side as/nHarry clambered over the various trunks cluttering/nthe hall to get to Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Oh honestly ..." said Mrs. Weasley despairingly,/n"well, on your own head be it!"/n/nShe wrenched open the front door and stepped out/ninto the weak September sunlight. Harry and the dog/nfollowed her. The door slammed behind them and/nMrs. Black's screeches were cut off instantly./n/n"Where's Tonks?" Harry said, looking around as they/nwent down the stone steps of number twelve, which/nvanished the moment they reached the pavement./n/n"She's waiting for us just up here," said Mrs. Weasley/nstiffly, averting her eyes from the lolloping black dog/nbeside Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAn old woman greeted them on the corner. She had/ntightly curled gray hair and wore a purple hat shaped/nlike a porkpie./n/n"Wotcher, Harry," she said, winking. "Better hurry up,/nhadn't we, Molly?" she added, checking her watch./n/n"I know, I know," moaned Mrs. Weasley, lengthening/nher stride, "but Mad-Eye wanted to wait for Sturgis.../nIf only Arthur could have got us cars from the/nMinistry again ... but Fudge wouldn't let him borrow/nso much as an empty ink bottle these days... How/nMuggles can stand traveling without magic ..."/n/nBut the great black dog gave a joyful bark and/ngamboled around them, snapping at pigeons, and/nchasing its own tail. Harry couldn't help laughing./nSirius had been trapped inside for a very long time./nMrs. Weasley pursed her lips in an almost Aunt/nPetunia-ish way./n/nIt took them twenty minutes to reach King's Cross by/nfoot and nothing more eventful happened during that/ntime than Sirius scaring a couple of cats for Harry's/nentertainment. Once inside the station they lingered/ncasually beside the barrier between platforms nine/nand ten until the coast was clear, then each of them/nleaned against it in turn and fell easily through onto/nplatform nine and three quarters, where the Hogwarts/nExpress stood belching sooty steam over a platform/npacked with departing students and their families./nHarry inhaled the familiar smell and felt his spirits/nsoar. . . He was really going back. . ./n/n"I hope the others make it in time," said Mrs. Weasley/nanxiously, staring behind her at the wrought-iron/narch spanning the platform, through which new/narrivals would come./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Nice dog, Harry!" called a tall boy with dreadlocks./n/n"Thanks, Lee," said Harry, grinning, as Sirius wagged/nhis tail frantically./n/n"Oh good," said Mrs. Weasley, sounding relieved,/n"here's Alas tor with the luggage, look ..."/n/nA porter's cap pulled low over his mismatched eyes,/nMoody came limping through the archway pushing a/ncart full of their trunks./n/n"All okay," he muttered to Mrs. Weasley and Tonks./n"Don't think we were followed..."/n/nSeconds later, Mr. Weasley emerged onto the platform/nwith Ron and Hermione. They had almost unloaded/nMoody's luggage cart when Fred, George, and Ginny/nturned up with Lupin./n/n"No trouble?" growled Moody./n/n"Nothing," said Lupin./n/n"I'll still be reporting Sturgis to Dumbledore," said/nMoody. "That's the second time he's not turned up in/na week. Getting as unreliable as Mundungus."/n/n"Well, look after yourselves," said Lupin, shaking/nhands all round. He reached Harry last and gave him/na clap on the shoulder. "You too, Harry. Be careful."/n/n"Yeah, keep your head down and your eyes peeled,"/nsaid Moody, shaking Harry's hand too.
