Harry/nsaid, as he, Ron, and Luna made for the carriage in/nwhich Hermione and Ginny were already sitting./n/n/n/n/n/n"What horse things?"/n/n/n/n"The horse things pulling the carriages!" said Harry/nimpatiently; they were, after all, about three feet from/nthe nearest one; it was watching them with empty/nwhite eyes. Ron, however, gave Harry a perplexed/nlook./n/n"What are you talking about?"/n/n"I'm talking about — look!"/n/nHarry grabbed Ron's arm and wheeled him about so/nthat he was face-to-face with the winged horse. Ron/nstared straight at it for a second, then looked back at/nHarry./n/n"What am I supposed to be looking at?"/n/n"At the — there, between the shafts! Harnessed to the/ncoach! It's right there in front — "/n/nBut as Ron continued to look bemused, a strange/nthought occurred to Harry./n/n"Can't ... can't you see them?"/n/n"See what?"/n/n"Can't you see what's pulling the carriages?"/n/nRon looked seriously alarmed now./n/n"Are you feeling all right, Harry?"/n/n"I ... yeah ..."/n/nHarry felt utterly bewildered. The horse was there in/nfront of him, gleaming solidly in the dim light issuing/n/n/n/n/n/nfrom the station windows behind them, vapor rising/nfrom its nostrils in the chilly night air. Yet unless Ron/nwas faking — and it was a very feeble joke if he was —/nRon could not see it at all./n/n"Shall we get in, then?" said Ron uncertainly, looking/nat Harry as though worried about him./n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "Yeah, go on ..."/n/n"It's all right," said a dreamy voice from beside Harry/nas Ron vanished into the coach's dark interior./n/n"You're not going mad or anything. I can see them/ntoo."/n/n"Can you?" said Harry desperately, turning to Luna./nHe could see the bat-winged horses reflected in her/nwide, silvery eyes./n/n"Oh yes," said Luna, "I've been able to see them ever/nsince my first day here. They've always pulled the/ncarriages. Don't worry. You're just as sane as I am."/n/nSmiling faintly, she climbed into the musty interior of/nthe carriage after Ron. Not altogether reassured,/n/nHarry followed her./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nXX/n/n/n/n

title: The Sorting Hat's New Song
text: /nHarry did not want to tell the others that he and Luna/nwere having the same hallucination, if that was what/nit was, so he said nothing about the horses as he sat/ndown inside the carriage and slammed the door/nbehind him. Nevertheless, he could not help watching/nthe silhouettes of the horses moving beyond the/nwindow./n/n"Did everyone see that Grubbly-Plank woman?" asked/nGinny. "What's she doing back here? Hagrid can't/nhave left, can he?"/n/n"I'll be quite glad if he has," said Luna. "He isn't a/nvery good teacher, is he?"/n/n"Yes, he is!" said Harry, Ron, and Ginny angrily./n/nHarry glared at Hermione; she cleared her throat and/nquickly said, "Erm ... yes ... he's very good."/n/n"Well, we think he's a bit of a joke in Ravenclaw," said/nLuna, unfazed./n/n/n/n/n/n"You've got a rubbish sense of humor then," Ron/nsnapped, as the wheels below them creaked into/nmotion./n/nLuna did not seem perturbed by Ron's rudeness; on/nthe contrary, she simply watched him for a while as/nthough he were a mildly interesting television/nprogram./n/nRattling and swaying, the carriages moved in convoy/nup the road. When they passed between the tall stone/npillars topped with winged boars on either side of the/ngates to the school grounds, Harry leaned forward to/ntry and see whether there were any lights on in/nHagrid's cabin by the Forbidden Forest, but the/ngrounds were in complete darkness. Hogwarts Castle,/nhowever, loomed ever closer: a towering mass of/nturrets, jet-black against the dark sky, here and there/na window blazing fiery bright above them./n/nThe carriages jingled to a halt near the stone steps/nleading up to the oak front doors and Harry got out of/nthe carriage first. He turned again to look for lit/nwindows down by the forest, but there was definitely/nno sign of life within Hagrid's cabin. Unwillingly,/nbecause he had half hoped they would have vanished,/nhe turned his eyes instead upon the strange, skeletal/ncreatures standing quietly in the chill night air, their/nblank white eyes gleaming./n/nHarry had once before had the experience of seeing/nsomething that Ron could not, but that had been a/nreflection in a mirror, something much more/ninsubstantial than a hundred very solid-looking/nbeasts strong enough to pull a fleet of carriages. If/nLuna was to be believed, the beasts had always been/nthere but invisible; why, then, could Harry suddenly/nsee them, and why could Ron not?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Are you coming or what?" said Ron beside him./n/n/n/n"Oh ... yeah," said Harry quickly, and they joined the/ncrowd hurrying up the stone steps into the castle./n/nThe entrance hall was ablaze with torches and/nechoing with footsteps as the students crossed the/nflagged stone floor for the double doors to the right,/nleading to the Great Hall and the start-of-term feast./n/nThe four long House tables in the Great Hall were/nfilling up under the starless black ceiling, which was/njust like the sky they could glimpse through the high/nwindows. Candles floated in midair all along the/ntables, illuminating the silvery ghosts who were/ndotted about the Hall and the faces of the students/ntalking eagerly to one another, exchanging summer/nnews, shouting greetings at friends from other/nHouses, eyeing one another's new haircuts and robes./nAgain Harry noticed people putting their heads/ntogether to whisper as he passed; he gritted his teeth/nand tried to act as though he neither noticed nor/ncared./n/nLuna drifted away from them at the Ravenclaw table./nThe moment they reached Gryffindor's, Ginny was/nhailed by some fellow fourth years and left to sit with/nthem; Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Neville found seats/ntogether about halfway down the table between Nearly/nHeadless Nick, the Gryffindor House ghost, and/nParvati Patil and Lavender Brown, the last two of/nwhom gave Harry airy, overly friendly greetings that/nmade him quite sure they had stopped talking about/nhim a split second before. He had more important/nthings to worry about, however: He was looking over/nthe students' heads to the staff table that ran along/nthe top wall of the Hall./n/n"He's not there."/n/n/n/n/n/nRon and Hermione scanned the staff table too, though/nthere was no real need; Hagrid's size made him/ninstantly obvious in any lineup./n/n"He can't have left," said Ron, sounding slightly/nanxious./n/n"Of course he hasn't," said Harry firmly./n/n"You don't think he's ... hurt, or anything, do you?"/nsaid Hermione uneasily./n/n"No," said Harry at once./n/n"But where is he, then?"/n/nThere was a pause, then Harry said very quietly, so/nthat Neville, Parvati, and Lavender could not hear,/n"Maybe he's not back yet. You know — from his/nmission — the thing he was doing over the summer/nfor Dumbledore."/n/n"Yeah ... yeah, that'll be it," said Ron, sounding/nreassured, but Hermione bit her lip, looking up and/ndown the staff table as though hoping for some/nconclusive explanation of Hagrid's absence./n/n"Who's that?" she said sharply, pointing toward the/nmiddle of the staff table./n/nHarry's eyes followed hers. They lit first upon/nProfessor Dumbledore, sitting in his high-backed/ngolden chair at the center of the long staff table,/nwearing deep-purple robes scattered with silvery stars/nand a matching hat. Dumbledore's head was inclined/ntoward the woman sitting next to him, who was/ntalking into his ear. She looked, Harry thought, like/nsomebody's maiden aunt: squat, with short, curly,/nmouse-brown hair in which she had placed a horrible/n/n/n/n/npink Alice band that matched the fluffy pink cardigan/nshe wore over her robes. Then she turned her face/nslightly to take a sip from her goblet and he saw, with/na shock of recognition, a pallid, toadlike face and a/npair of prominent, pouchy eyes./n/n"It's that Umbridge woman!"/n/n"Who?" said Hermione./n/n"She was at my hearing, she works for Fudge!"/n/n"Nice cardigan," said Ron, smirking./n/n"She works for Fudge?" Hermione repeated, frowning./n"What on earth's she doing here, then?"/n/n"Dunno ..."/n/nHermione scanned the staff table, her eyes narrowed./n/n"No," she muttered, "no, surely not ..."/n/nHarry did not understand what she was talking about/nbut did not ask; his attention had just been caught by/nProfessor Grubbly-Plank who had just appeared/nbehind the staff table; she worked her way along to/nthe very end and took the seat that ought to have/nbeen Hagrid's. That meant that the first years must/nhave crossed the lake and reached the castle, and/nsure enough, a few seconds later, the doors from the/nentrance hall opened. A long line of scared-looking/nfirst years entered, led by Professor McGonagall, who/nwas carrying a stool on which sat an ancient wizard's/nhat, heavily patched and darned with a wide rip near/nthe frayed brim./n/nThe buzz of talk in the Great Hall faded away. The/nfirst years lined up in front of the staff table facing the/n/n/n/n/n/nrest of the students, and Professor McGonagall placed/nthe stool carefully in front of them, then stood back./n/nThe first years' faces glowed palely in the candlelight./nA small boy right in the middle of the row looked as/nthough he was trembling. Harry recalled, fleetingly,/nhow terrified he had felt when he had stood there,/nwaiting for the unknown test that would determine to/nwhich House he belonged./n/nThe whole school waited with bated breath. Then the/nrip near the hat's brim opened wide like a mouth and/nthe Sorting Hat burst into song:/n/nIn times of old when I was new/nAnd Hogwarts barely started/nThe founders of our noble school/nThought never to be parted:/n/nUnited by a common goal,/n/nThey had the selfsame yearning,/n/nTo make the world's best magic school/nAnd pass along their learning./n/n"Together we will build and teach!"/n/nThe four good friends decided/nAnd never did they dream that they/nMight someday be divided,/n/nFor were there such friends anywhere/nAs Slytherin and Gryffndor?/n/nUnless it was the second pair/nOf Huffepuff and Ravenclaw?/n/nSo how could it have gone so wrong?/n/nHow could such friendships fail?/n/nWhy, I was there and so can tell/nThe whole sad, sorry tale./n/nSaid Slytherin, "We'll teach just those/nWhose ancestry is purest."/n/nSaid Ravenclaw, "We'll teach those whose/nIntelligence is surest."/n/nSaid Gryffindor, "We'll teach all those/n/n/n/n/n/nWith brave deeds to their name,"/n/nSaid Hufflepuff, "111 teach the lot,/n/nAnd treat them just the same."/n/nThese differences caused little strife/nWhen first they came to light,/n/nFor each of the four founders had/nA House in which they might/nTake only those they wanted, so,/n/nFor instance, Slytherin/nTook only pure-blood wizards/nOf great cunning, just like him,/n/nAnd only those of sharpest mind/nWere taught by Ravenclaw/nWhile the bravest and the boldest/nWent to daring Gryffindor./n/nGood Hufflepuff she took the rest,/n/nAnd taught them all she knew,/n/nThus the Houses and their founders/nRetained friendships firm and true./n/nSo Hogwarts worked in harmony/nFor several happy years,/n/nBut then discord crept among us/nFeeding on our faults and fears./n/nThe Houses that, like pillars four,/n/nHad once held up our school,/n/nNow turned upon each other and,/n/nDivided, sought to rule./n/nAnd for a while it seemed the school/nMust meet an early end,/n/nWhat with dueling and with fighting/nAnd the clash of friend on friend/nAnd at last there came a morning/nWhen old Slytherin departed/nAnd though the fighting then died out/nHe left us quite downhearted./n/nAnd never since the founders four/nWere whittled down to three/nHave the Houses been united/nAs they once were meant to be./n/n/n/n/n/nAnd now the Sorting Hat is here/nAnd you all know the score:/n/nI sort you into Houses/nBecause that is what I'm for,/n/nBut this year I'll go further,/n/nListen closely to my song:/n/nThough condemned I am to split you/nStill I worry that it's wrong,/n/nThough I must fulfill my duty/nAnd must quarter every year/nStill I wonder whether sorting/nMay not bring the end I fear./n/nOh, know the perils, read the signs,/n/nThe warning history shows,/n/nFor our Hogwarts is in danger/nFrom external, deadly foes/nAnd we must unite inside her/nOr we'll crumble from within./n/nI have told you, I have warned you.../n/nLet the Sorting now begin./n/nThe hat became motionless once more; applause/nbroke out, though it was punctured, for the first time/nin Harry's memory, with muttering and whispers. All/nacross the Great Hall students were exchanging/nremarks with their neighbors and Harry, clapping/nalong with everyone else, knew exactly what they were/ntalking about./n/n"Branched out a bit this year, hasn't it?" said Ron, his/neyebrows raised./n/n"Too right it has," said Harry./n/nThe Sorting Hat usually confined itself to describing/nthe different qualities looked for by each of the four/nHogwarts Houses and its own role in sorting them;/nHarry could not remember it ever trying to give the/nschool advice before./n/n/n/n/n/n"I wonder if it's ever given warnings before?" said/nHermione, sounding slightly anxious./n/n/n/n"Yes, indeed," said Nearly Headless Nick/nknowledgeably, leaning across Neville toward her/n(Neville winced, it was very uncomfortable to have a/nghost lean through you). "The hat feels itself honor-/nbound to give the school due warning whenever it/nfeels — "/n/nBut Professor McGonagall, who was waiting to read/nout the list of first years' names, was giving the/nwhispering students the sort of look that scorches./nNearly Headless Nick placed a see-through finger to/nhis lips and sat primly upright again as the muttering/ncame to an abrupt end. With a last frowning look that/nswept the four House tables, Professor McGonagall/nlowered her eyes to her long piece of parchment and/ncalled out,/n/n"Abercrombie, Euan."/n/nThe terrified-looking boy Harry had noticed earlier/nstumbled forward and put the hat on his head; it was/nonly prevented from falling right down to his/nshoulders by his very prominent ears. The hat/nconsidered for a moment, then the rip near the brim/nopened again and shouted, " GR YFFIND OR ! "/n/nHarry clapped loudly with the rest of Gryffindor/nHouse as Euan Abercrombie staggered to their table/nand sat down, looking as though he would like very/nmuch to sink through the floor and never be looked at/nagain./n/nSlowly the long line of first years thinned; in the/npauses between the names and the Sorting Hat's/ndecisions, Harry could hear Ron's stomach rumbling/nloudly. Finally, "Zeller, Rose" was sorted into/n/n/n/n/n/nHufflepuff, and Professor McGonagall picked up the/nhat and stool and marched them away as Professor/nDumbledore rose to his feet./n/nHarry was somehow soothed to see Dumbledore/nstanding before them all, whatever his recent bitter/nfeelings toward his headmaster. Between the absence/nof Hagrid and the presence of those dragonish horses,/nhe had felt that his return to Hogwarts, so long/nanticipated, was full of unexpected surprises like/njarring notes in a familiar song. But this, at least, was/nhow it was supposed to be: their headmaster rising to/ngreet them all before the start-of-term feast./n/n"To our newcomers," said Dumbledore in a ringing/nvoice, his arms stretched wide and a beaming smile/non his lips, "welcome! To our old hands — welcome/nback! There is a time for speech making, but this is/nnot it. Tuck in!"/n/nThere was an appreciative laugh and an outbreak of/napplause as Dumbledore sat down neatly and threw/nhis long beard over his shoulder so as to keep it out of/nthe way of his plate — for food had appeared out of/nnowhere, so that the five long tables were groaning/nunder joints and pies and dishes of vegetables, bread,/nsauces, and flagons of pumpkin juice./n/n"Excellent," said Ron, with a kind of groan of longing,/nand he seized the nearest plate of chops and began/npiling them onto his plate, watched wistfully by/nNearly Headless Nick./n/n"What were you saying before the Sorting?" Hermione/nasked the ghost. "About the hat giving warnings?"/n/n"Oh yes," said Nick, who seemed glad of a reason to/nturn away from Ron, who was now eating roast/npotatoes with almost indecent enthusiasm. "Yes, I/n/n/n/n/n/nhave heard the hat give several warnings before,/nalways at times when it detects periods of great/ndanger for the school. And always, of course, its/nadvice is the same: Stand together, be strong from/nwithin."/n/n"Ow kunnit nofe skusin danger ifzat?" said Ron./n/nHis mouth was so full Harry thought it was quite an/nachievement for him to make any noise at all./n/n"I beg your pardon?" said Nearly Headless Nick/npolitely, while Hermione looked revolted. Ron gave an/nenormous swallow and said, "How can it know if the/nschool's in danger if it's a hat?"/n/n"I have no idea," said Nearly Headless Nick. "Of/ncourse, it lives in Dumbledore's office, so I daresay it/npicks things up there."/n/n"And it wants all the Houses to be friends?" said/nHarry, looking over at the Slytherin table, where/nDraco Malfoy was holding court. "Fat chance."/n/n"Well, now, you shouldn't take that attitude," said/nNick reprovingly. "Peaceful cooperation, that's the/nkey. We ghosts, though we belong to separate Houses,/nmaintain links of friendship. In spite of the/ncompetitiveness between Gryffindor and Slytherin, I/nwould never dream of seeking an argument with the/nBloody Baron."/n/n"Only because you're terrified of him," said Ron./n/nNearly Headless Nick looked highly affronted./n/n"Terrified? I hope I, Sir Nicholas de Mimsy-/nPorpington, have never been guilty of cowardice in my/nlife! The noble blood that runs in my veins — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"What blood?" asked Ron. "Surely you haven't still got/n— ?"/n/n"It's a figure of speech!" said Nearly Headless Nick,/nnow so annoyed his head was trembling ominously on/nhis partially severed neck. "I assume I am still allowed/nto enjoy the use of whichever words I like, even if the/npleasures of eating and drinking are denied me! But I/nam quite used to students poking fun at my death, I/nassure you!"/n/n"Nick, he wasn't really laughing at you!" said/nHermione, throwing a furious look at Ron./n/nUnfortunately, Ron's mouth was packed to exploding/npoint again and all he could manage was "node/niddum eentup sechew," which Nick did not seem to/nthink constituted an adequate apology. Rising into/nthe air, he straightened his feathered hat and swept/naway from them to the other end of the table, coming/nto rest between the Creevey brothers, Colin and/nDennis./n/n"Well done, Ron," snapped Hermione./n/n"What?" said Ron indignantly, having managed,/nfinally, to swallow his food. "I'm not allowed to ask a/nsimple question?"/n/n"Oh forget it," said Hermione irritably, and the pair of/nthem spent the rest of the meal in huffy silence./n/nHarry was too used to their bickering to bother trying/nto reconcile them; he felt it was a better use of his/ntime to eat his way steadily through his steak-and-/nkidney pie, then a large plateful of his favorite treacle/ntart./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWhen all the students had finished eating and the/nnoise level in the hall was starting to creep upward/nagain, Dumbledore got to his feet once more. Talking/nceased immediately as all turned to face the/nheadmaster. Harry was feeling pleasantly drowsy/nnow. His four-poster bed was waiting somewhere/nabove, wonderfully warm and soft.../n/n"Well, now that we are all digesting another/nmagnificent feast, I beg a few moments of your/nattention for the usual start-of-term notices," said/nDumbledore. "First years ought to know that the/nforest in the grounds is out of bounds to students —/nand a few of our older students ought to know by now/ntoo." (Harry, Ron, and Hermione exchanged smirks.)/n/n"Mr. Filch, the caretaker, has asked me, for what he/ntells me is the four hundred and sixty-second time, to/nremind you all that magic is not permitted in/ncorridors between classes, nor are a number of other/nthings, all of which can be checked on the extensive/nlist now fastened to Mr. Filch's office door./n/n"We have had two changes in staffing this year. We/nare very pleased to welcome back Professor Grubbly-/nPlank, who will be taking Care of Magical Creatures/nlessons; we are also delighted to introduce Professor/nUmbridge, our new Defense Against the Dark Arts/nteacher."/n/nThere was a round of polite but fairly unenthusiastic/napplause during which Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nexchanged slightly panicked looks; Dumbledore had/nnot said for how long Grubbly-Plank would be/nteaching./n/nDumbledore continued, "Tryouts for the House/nQuidditch teams will take place on the — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe broke off, looking inquiringly at Professor/nUmbridge. As she was not much taller standing than/nsitting, there was a moment when nobody understood/nwhy Dumbledore had stopped talking, but then/nProfessor Umbridge said, "Hem, hem," and it became/nclear that she had got to her feet and was intending to/nmake a speech./n/nDumbledore only looked taken aback for a moment,/nthen he sat back down smartly and looked alertly at/nProfessor Umbridge as though he desired nothing/nbetter than to listen to her talk. Other members of/nstaff were not as adept at hiding their surprise./nProfessor Sprout's eyebrows had disappeared into her/nflyaway hair, and Professor McGonagall's mouth was/nas thin as Harry had ever seen it. No new teacher had/never interrupted Dumbledore before. Many of the/nstudents were smirking; this woman obviously did not/nknow how things were done at Hogwarts./n/n"Thank you, Headmaster," Professor Umbridge/nsimpered, "for those kind words of welcome."/n/nHer voice was high-pitched, breathy, and little-girlish/nand again, Harry felt a powerful rush of dislike that/nhe could not explain to himself; all he knew was that/nhe loathed everything about her, from her stupid/nvoice to her fluffy pink cardigan. She gave another/nlittle throat-clearing cough ("Hem, hem") and/ncontinued: "Well, it is lovely to be back at Hogwarts, I/nmust say!" She smiled, revealing very pointed teeth./n"And to see such happy little faces looking back at/nme!"/n/nHarry glanced around. None of the faces he could see/nlooked happy; on the contrary, they all looked rather/ntaken aback at being addressed as though they were/nfive years old./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I am very much looking forward to getting to know/nyou all, and I'm sure well be very good friends!"/n/nStudents exchanged looks at this; some of them were/nbarely concealing grins./n/n"I'll be her friend as long as I don't have to borrow/nthat cardigan," Parvati whispered to Lavender, and/nboth of them lapsed into silent giggles./n/nProfessor Umbridge cleared her throat again ("Hem,/nhem"), but when she continued, some of the/nbreathiness had vanished from her voice. She/nsounded much more businesslike and now her words/nhad a dull learned-by-heart sound to them./n/n"The Ministry of Magic has always considered the/neducation of young witches and wizards to be of vital/nimportance. The rare gifts with which you were born/nmay come to nothing if not nurtured and honed by/ncareful instruction. The ancient skills unique to the/nWizarding community must be passed down through/nthe generations lest we lose them forever. The/ntreasure trove of magical knowledge amassed by our/nancestors must be guarded, replenished, and polished/nby those who have been called to the noble profession/nof teaching."/n/nProfessor Umbridge paused here and made a little/nbow to her fellow staff members, none of whom bowed/nback. Professor McGonagall's dark eyebrows had/ncontracted so that she looked positively hawklike, and/nHarry distinctly saw her exchange a significant glance/nwith Professor Sprout as Umbridge gave another little/n"Hem, hem" and went on with her speech./n/n"Every headmaster and headmistress of Hogwarts has/nbrought something new to the weighty task of/ngoverning this historic school, and that is as it should/n/n/n/n/n/nbe, for without progress there will be stagnation and/ndecay. There again, progress for progress's sake must/nbe discouraged, for our tried and tested traditions/noften require no tinkering. A balance, then, between/nold and new, between permanence and change,/nbetween tradition and innovation ..."/n/nHarry found his attentiveness ebbing, as though his/nbrain was slipping in and out of tune. The quiet that/nalways filled the Hall when Dumbledore was speaking/nwas breaking up as students put their heads/ntogether, whispering and giggling. Over at the/nRavenclaw table, Cho Chang was chatting animatedly/nwith her friends. A few seats along from Cho, Luna/nLovegood had got out The Quibbler again. Meanwhile/nat the Hufflepuff table, Ernie Macmillan was one of/nthe few still staring at Professor Umbridge, but he was/nglassy-eyed and Harry was sure he was only/npretending to listen in an attempt to live up to the/nnew prefect's badge gleaming on his chest./n/nProfessor Umbridge did not seem to notice the/nrestlessness of her audience. Harry had the/nimpression that a full-scale riot could have broken/nout under her nose and she would have plowed on/nwith her speech. The teachers, however, were still/nlistening very attentively, and Hermione seemed to be/ndrinking in every word Umbridge spoke, though/njudging by her expression, they were not at all to her/ntaste./n/n"... because some changes will be for the better, while/nothers will come, in the fullness of time, to be/nrecognized as errors of judgment. Meanwhile, some/nold habits will be retained, and rightly so, whereas/nothers, outmoded and outworn, must be abandoned./nLet us move forward, then, into a new era of/nopenness, effectiveness, and accountability, intent on/npreserving what ought to be preserved, perfecting/n/n/n/n/nwhat needs to be perfected, and pruning wherever we/nfind practices that ought to be prohibited."/n/nShe sat down. Dumbledore clapped. The staff followed/nhis lead, though Harry noticed that several of them/nbrought their hands together only once or twice/nbefore stopping. A few students joined in, but most/nhad been taken unawares by the end of the speech,/nnot having listened to more than a few words of it,/nand before they could start applauding properly,/nDumbledore had stood up again./n/n"Thank you very much, Professor Umbridge, that was/nmost illuminating," he said, bowing to her. "Now — as/nI was saying, Quidditch tryouts will be held ..."/n/n"Yes, it certainly was illuminating," said Hermione in/na low voice./n/n"You're not telling me you enjoyed it?" Ron said/nquietly, turning a glazed face upon Hermione. "That/nwas about the dullest speech I've ever heard, and I/ngrew up with Percy."/n/n"I said illuminating, not enjoyable," said Hermione. "It/nexplained a lot."/n/n"Did it?" said Harry in surprise. "Sounded like a load/nof waffle to me."/n/n"There was some important stuff hidden in the/nwaffle," said Hermione grimly./n/n"Was there?" said Ron blankly./n/n"How about 'progress for progress's sake must be/ndiscouraged'? How about 'pruning wherever we find/npractices that ought to be prohibited'?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, what does that mean?" said Ron impatiently./n/n/n/n"Ill tell you what it means," said Hermione ominously./n"It means the Ministry's interfering at Hogwarts."/n/nThere was a great clattering and banging all around/nthem; Dumbledore had obviously just dismissed the/nschool, because everyone was standing up ready to/nleave the Hall. Hermione jumped up, looking/nflustered./n/n"Ron, we're supposed to show the first years where to/ngo!"/n/n"Oh yeah," said Ron, who had obviously forgotten./n"Hey — hey you lot! Midgets!"/n/n"Ron\"/n/n"Well, they are, they're titchy..."/n/n"I know, but you can't call them midgets... First/nyears!" Hermione called commandingly along the/ntable. "This way, please!"/n/nA group of new students walked shyly up the gap/nbetween the Gryffindor and Hufflepuff tables, all of/nthem trying hard not to lead the group. They did/nindeed seem very small; Harry was sure he had not/nappeared that young when he had arrived here. He/ngrinned at them. A blond boy next to Euan/nAbercrombie looked petrified, nudged Euan, and/nwhispered something in his ear. Euan Abercrombie/nlooked equally frightened and stole a horrified look at/nHarry, who felt the grin slide off his face like/nStinksap./n/n"See you later," he said to Ron and Hermione and he/nmade his way out of the Great Hall alone, doing/n/n/n/n/n/neverything he could to ignore more whispering,/nstaring, and pointing as he passed. He kept his eyes/nfixed ahead as he wove his way through the crowd in/nthe entrance hall, then he hurried up the marble/nstaircase, took a couple of concealed shortcuts, and/nhad soon left most of the crowds behind./n/nHe had been stupid not to expect this, he thought/nangrily, as he walked through much emptier upstairs/ncorridors. Of course everyone was staring at him: He/nhad emerged from the Triwizard maze two months ago/nclutching the dead body of a fellow student and/nclaiming to have seen Lord Voldemort return to/npower. There had not been time last term to explain/nhimself before everyone went home, even if he had felt/nup to giving the whole school a detailed account of the/nterrible events in that graveyard./n/nHe had reached the end of the corridor to the/nGryffindor common room and had come to a halt in/nfront of the portrait of the Fat Lady before he realized/nthat he did not know the new password./n/n"Er ..." he said glumly, staring up at the Fat Lady,/nwho smoothed the folds of her pink satin dress and/nlooked sternly back at him./n/n"No password, no entrance," she said loftily./n/n"Harry, I know it!" someone panted from behind him,/nand he turned to see Neville jogging toward him./n"Guess what it is? I'm actually going to be able to/nremember it for once — " He waved the stunted little/ncactus he had shown them on the train. "Mimbulus/nmimbletonio 1"/n/n"Correct," said the Fat Lady, and her portrait swung/nopen toward them like a door, revealing a circular/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhole in the wall behind, through which Harry and/nNeville now climbed./n/nThe Gryffindor common room looked as welcoming as/never, a cozy circular tower room full of dilapidated/nsquashy armchairs and rickety old tables. A fire was/ncrackling merrily in the grate and a few people were/nwarming their hands before going up to their/ndormitories; on the other side of the room Fred and/nGeorge Weasley were pinning something up on the/nnotice board. Harry waved good night to them and/nheaded straight for the door to the boys' dormitories;/nhe was not in much of a mood for talking at the/nmoment. Neville followed him./n/nDean Thomas and Seamus Finnigan had reached the/ndormitory first and were in the process of covering the/nwalls beside their beds with posters and photographs./nThey had been talking as Harry pushed open the door/nbut stopped abruptly the moment they saw him./n/nHarry wondered whether they had been talking about/nhim, then whether he was being paranoid./n/n"Hi," he said, moving across to his own trunk and/nopening it./n/n"Hey, Harry," said Dean, who was putting on a pair of/npajamas in the West Ham colors. "Good holiday?"/n/n"Not bad," muttered Harry, as a true account of his/nholiday would have taken most of the night to relate/nand he could not face it. "You?"/n/n"Yeah, it was okay," chuckled Dean. "Better than/nSeamus's anyway, he was just telling me."/n/n"Why, what happened, Seamus?" Neville asked as he/nplaced his Mimbulus mimbletonia tenderly on his/nbedside cabinet./n/n/n/n/n/nSeamus did not answer immediately; he was making/nrather a meal of ensuring that his poster of the/nKenmare Kestrels Quidditch team was quite straight./nThen he said, with his back still turned to Harry, "Me/nmam didn't want me to come back."/n/n"What?" said Harry, pausing in the act of pulling off/nhis robes./n/n"She didn't want me to come back to Hogwarts."/n/nSeamus turned away from his poster and pulled his/nown pajamas out of his trunk, still not looking at/nHarry./n/n"But — why?" said Harry, astonished. He knew that/nSeamus's mother was a witch and could not/nunderstand, therefore, why she should have come/nover so Dursley-ish./n/nSeamus did not answer until he had finished/nbuttoning his pajamas./n/n"Well," he said in a measured voice, "I suppose .../nbecause of you."/n/n"What d'you mean?" said Harry quickly. His heart was/nbeating rather fast. He felt vaguely as though/nsomething was closing in on him./n/n"Well," said Seamus again, still avoiding Harry's eyes,/n"she ... er ... well, it's not just you, it's Dumbledore/ntoo ..."/n/n"She believes the Daily Prophet?" said Harry. "She/nthinks I'm a liar and Dumbledore 's an old fool?"/n/nSeamus looked up at him. "Yeah, something like/nthat."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry said nothing. He threw his wand down onto his/nbedside table, pulled off his robes, stuffed them/nangrily into his trunk, and pulled on his pajamas. He/nwas sick of it; sick of being the person who was stared/nat and talked about all the time. If any of them knew,/nif any of them had the faintest idea what it felt like to/nbe the one all these things had happened to ... Mrs./nFinnigan had no idea, the stupid woman, he thought/nsavagely./n/nHe got into bed and made to pull the hangings closed/naround him, but before he could do so, Seamus said,/n"Look . . . what did happen that night when . . . you/nknow, when . . . with Cedric Diggory and all?"/n/nSeamus sounded nervous and eager at the same time./nDean, who had been bending over his trunk, trying to/nretrieve a slipper, went oddly still and Harry knew he/nwas listening hard./n/n"What are you asking me for?" Harry retorted. "Just/nread the Daily Prophet like your mother, why don't/nyou? That'll tell you all you need to know."/n/n"Don't you have a go at my mother," snapped/nSeamus./n/n"I'll have a go at anyone who calls me a liar," said/nHarry./n/n"Don't talk to me like that!"/n/n"I'll talk to you how I want," said Harry, his temper/nrising so fast he snatched his wand back from his/nbedside table. "If you've got a problem sharing a/ndormitory with me, go and ask McGonagall if you can/nbe moved, stop your mummy worrying — "/n/n"Leave my mother out of this, Potter!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's going on?"/n/nRon had appeared in the doorway. His wide eyes/ntraveled from Harry, who was kneeling on his bed/nwith his wand pointing at Seamus, to Seamus, who/nwas standing there with his fists raised./n/n"He's having a go at my mother!" Seamus yelled./n/n"What?" said Ron. "Harry wouldn't do that — we met/nyour mother, we liked her..."/n/n"That's before she started believing every word the/nstinking Daily Prophet writes about me!" said Harry at/nthe top of his voice./n/n"Oh," said Ron, comprehension dawning across his/nfreckled face. "Oh ... right."/n/n"You know what?" said Seamus heatedly, casting/nHarry a venomous look. "He's right, I don't want to/nshare a dormitory with him anymore, he's a/nmadman."/n/n"That's out of order, Seamus," said Ron, whose ears/nwere starting to glow red, always a danger sign./n/n"Out of order, am I?" shouted Seamus, who in/ncontrast with Ron was turning paler. "You believe all/nthe rubbish he's come out with about You-Know-Who,/ndo you, you reckon he's telling the truth?"/n/n"Yeah, I do!" said Ron angrily./n/n"Then you're mad too," said Seamus in disgust./n/n"Yeah? Well unfortunately for you, pal, I'm also a/nprefect!" said Ron, jabbing himself in the chest with a/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nfinger. "So unless you want detention, watch your/nmouth!"/n/nSeamus looked for a few seconds as though detention/nwould be a reasonable price to pay to say what was/ngoing through his mind; but with a noise of contempt/nhe turned on his heel, vaulted into bed, and pulled/nthe hangings shut with such violence that they were/nripped from the bed and fell in a dusty pile to the/nfloor. Ron glared at Seamus, then looked at Dean and/nNeville./n/n"Anyone else's parents got a problem with Harry?" he/nsaid aggressively./n/n"My parents are Muggles, mate," said Dean,/nshrugging. "They don't know nothing about no deaths/nat Hogwarts, because I'm not stupid enough to tell/nthem."/n/n"You don't know my mother, she'll weasel anything/nout of anyone!" Seamus snapped at him. "Anyway,/nyour parents don't get the Daily Prophet, they don't/nknow our headmaster's been sacked from the/nWizengamot and the International Confederation of/nWizards because he's losing his marbles — "/n/n"My gran says that's rubbish," piped up Neville. "She/nsays it's the Daily Prophet that's going downhill, not/nDumbledore. She's canceled our subscription. We/nbelieve Harry," he said simply. He climbed into bed/nand pulled the covers up to his chin, looking owlishly/nover them at Seamus. "My gran's always said You-/nKnow-Who would come back one day. She says if/nDumbledore says he's back, he's back."/n/nHarry felt a rush of gratitude toward Neville. Nobody/nelse said anything. Seamus got out his wand, repaired/nthe bed hangings, and vanished behind them. Dean/n/n/n/n/n/ngot into bed, rolled over, and fell silent. Neville, who/nappeared to have nothing more to say either, was/ngazing fondly at his moonlit cactus./n/nHarry lay back on his pillows while Ron bustled/naround the next bed, putting his things away. He felt/nshaken by the argument with Seamus, whom he had/nalways liked very much. How many more people were/ngoing to suggest that he was lying or unhinged?/n/nHad Dumbledore suffered like this all summer, as/nfirst the Wizengamot, then the International/nConfederation of Wizards had thrown him from their/nranks? Was it anger at Harry, perhaps, that had/nstopped Dumbledore getting in touch with him for/nmonths? The two of them were in this together, after/nall; Dumbledore had believed Harry, announced his/nversion of events to the whole school and then to the/nwider Wizarding community. Anyone who thought/nHarry was a liar had to think that Dumbledore was/ntoo or else that Dumbledore had been hoodwinked.../n/nThey'll know we're right in the end, thought Harry/nmiserably, as Ron got into bed and extinguished the/nlast candle in the dormitory. But he wondered how/nmany attacks like Seamus's he would have to endure/nbefore that time came./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Professor Umbridge
text: /nSeamus dressed at top speed next morning and left/nthe dormitory before Harry had even put on his socks./n/n"Does he think hell turn into a nutter if he stays in a/nroom with me too long?" asked Harry loudly, as the/nhem of Seamus's robes whipped out of sight./n/n"Don't worry about it, Harry," Dean muttered,/nhoisting his school-bag onto his shoulder. "He's just/n..." But apparently he was unable to say exactly what/nSeamus was, and after a slightly awkward pause/nfollowed him out of the room./n/nNeville and Ron both gave Harry it's-his-problem-not-/nyours looks, but Harry was not much consoled. How/nmuch more of this was he going to have to take?/n/n"What's the matter?" asked Hermione five minutes/nlater, catching up with Harry and Ron halfway across/nthe common room as they all headed toward/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbreakfast. "You look absolutely — oh for heaven's/nsake."/n/n/n/nShe was staring at the common room notice board,/nwhere a large new sign had been put up./n/nGALLONS OF GALLEONS!/n/nPocket money failing to keep pace with your/noutgoings?/n/nLike to earn a little extra gold?/n/n/n/nContact Fred and George Weasley,/n/nGryffindor common room,/n/nfor simple, part-time, virtually painless jobs/n/n(WE REGRET THAT ALL WORK IS UNDERTAKEN AT/nAPPLICANT'S OWN RISK)/n/n"They are the limit," said Hermione grimly, taking/ndown the sign, which Fred and George had pinned up/nover a poster giving the date of the first Hogsmeade/nweekend in October. "We'll have to talk to them, Ron."/n/nRon looked positively alarmed./n/n"Why?"/n/n"Because we're prefects!" said Hermione, as they/nclimbed out through the portrait hole. "It's up to us to/nstop this kind of thing!"/n/nRon said nothing; Harry could tell from his glum/nexpression that the prospect of stopping Fred and/n/n/n/n/n/nGeorge doing exactly what they liked was not one that/nhe found inviting./n/n"Anyway, what's up, Harry?" Hermione continued, as/nthey walked down a flight of stairs lined with portraits/nof old witches and wizards, all of whom ignored them,/nbeing engrossed in their own conversation. "You look/nreally angry about something."/n/n"Seamus reckons Harry's lying about You-Know-/nWho," said Ron succinctly, when Harry did not/nrespond./n/nHermione, whom Harry had expected to react angrily/non his behalf, sighed./n/n"Yes, Lavender thinks so too," she said gloomily./n/n"Been having a nice little chat with her about whether/nor not I'm a lying, attention-seeking prat, have you?"/nHarry said loudly./n/n"No," said Hermione calmly, "I told her to keep her big/nfat mouth shut about you, actually. And it would be/nquite nice if you stopped jumping down Ron's and my/nthroats, Harry, because if you haven't noticed, we're/non your side."/n/nThere was a short pause./n/n"Sorry," said Harry in a low voice./n/n"That's quite all right," said Hermione with dignity./nThen she shook her head. "Don't you remember what/nDumbledore said at the end-of-term feast last year?"/n/nHarry and Ron both looked at her blankly, and/nHermione sighed again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"About You-Know-Who. He said, 'His gift for spreading/ndiscord and enmity is very great. We can fight it only/nby showing an equally strong bond of friendship and/ntrust — ' "/n/n"How do you remember stuff like that?" asked Ron,/nlooking at her in admiration./n/n"I listen, Ron," said Hermione with a touch of/nasperity./n/n"So do I, but I still couldn't tell you exactly what — "/n/n"The point," Hermione pressed on loudly, "is that this/nsort of thing is exactly what Dumbledore was talking/nabout. You-Know- Who's only been back two months,/nand we've started fighting among ourselves. And the/nSorting Hat's warning was the same — stand/ntogether, be united — "/n/n"And Harry said it last night," retorted Ron, "if that/nmeans we're supposed to get matey with the/nSlytherins, fat chance."/n/n"Well, I think it's a pity we're not trying for a bit of/ninter-House unity," said Hermione crossly./n/nThey had reached the foot of the marble staircase. A/nline of fourth-year Ravenclaws was crossing the/nentrance hall; they caught sight of Harry and hurried/nto form a tighter group, as though frightened he/nmight attack stragglers./n/n"Yeah, we really ought to be trying to make friends/nwith people like that," said Harry sarcastically./n/nThey followed the Ravenclaws into the Great Hall,/nlooking instinctively at the staff table as they entered./nProfessor Grubbly-Plank was chatting to Professor/n/n/n/n/n/nSinistra, the Astronomy teacher, and Hagrid was once/nagain conspicuous only by his absence. The/nenchanted ceiling above them echoed Harry's mood; it/nwas a miserable rain-cloud gray./n/n"Dumbledore didn't even mention how long that/nGrubbly-Plank woman's staying," he said, as they/nmade their way across to the Gryffindor table./n/n"Maybe ..." said Hermione thoughtfully./n/n"What?" said both Harry and Ron together./n/n"Well ... maybe he didn't want to draw attention to/nHagrid not being here."/n/n"What d'you mean, draw attention to it?" said Ron,/nhalf laughing. "How could we not notice?"/n/nBefore Hermione could answer, a tall black girl with/nlong, braided hair had marched up to Harry./n/n"Hi, Angelina."/n/n"Hi," she said briskly, "good summer?" And without/nwaiting for an answer, "Listen, I've been made/nGryffindor Quidditch Captain."/n/n"Nice one," said Harry, grinning at her; he suspected/nAngelina's pep talks might not be as long-winded as/nOliver Wood's had been, which could only be an/nimprovement./n/n"Yeah, well, we need a new Keeper now Oliver's left./nTryouts are on Friday at five o'clock and I want the/nwhole team there, all right? Then we can see how the/nnew person'll fit in."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Okay," said Harry, and she smiled at him and/ndeparted./n/n"I'd forgotten Wood had left," said Hermione vaguely,/nsitting down beside Ron and pulling a plate of toast/ntoward her. "I suppose that will make quite a/ndifference to the team?"/n/n"I s'pose," said Harry, taking the bench opposite. "He/nwas a good Keeper..."/n/n"Still, it won't hurt to have some new blood, will it?"/nsaid Ron./n/nWith a whoosh and a clatter, hundreds of owls came/nsoaring in through the upper windows. They/ndescended all over the Hall, bringing letters and/npackages to their owners and showering the/nbreakfasters with droplets of water; it was clearly/nraining hard outside. Hedwig was nowhere to be seen,/nbut Harry was hardly surprised; his only/ncorrespondent was Sirius, and he doubted Sirius/nwould have anything new to tell him after only/ntwenty-four hours apart. Hermione, however, had to/nmove her orange juice aside quickly to make way for a/nlarge damp barn owl bearing a sodden Daily Prophet/nin its beak./n/n"What are you still getting that for?" said Harry/nirritably, thinking of Seamus, as Hermione placed a/nKnut in the leather pouch on the owl's leg and it took/noff again. "I'm not bothering ... load of rubbish."/n/n"It's best to know what the enemy are saying," said/nHermione darkly, and she unfurled the newspaper/nand disappeared behind it, not emerging until Harry/nand Ron had finished eating./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Nothing," she said simply, rolling up the newspaper/nand laying it down by her plate. "Nothing about you/nor Dumbledore or anything."/n/nProfessor McGonagall was now moving along the table/nhanding out schedules./n/n"Look at today!" groaned Ron. "History of Magic,/ndouble Potions, Divination, and double Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts ... Binns, Snape, Trelawney,/nand that Umbridge woman all in one day! I wish Fred/nand George 'd hurry up and get those Skiving/nSnackboxes sorted..."/n/n"Do mine ears deceive me?" said Fred, arriving with/nGeorge and squeezing onto the bench beside Harry./n"Hogwarts prefects surely don't wish to skive off/nlessons?"/n/n"Look what we've got today," said Ron grumpily,/nshoving his schedule under Fred's nose. "That's the/nworst Monday I've ever seen."/n/n"Fair point, little bro," said Fred, scanning the/ncolumn. "You can have a bit of Nosebleed Nougat/ncheap if you like."/n/n"Why's it cheap?" said Ron suspiciously./n/n"Because you'll keep bleeding till you shrivel up, we/nhaven't got an antidote yet," said George, helping/nhimself to a kipper./n/n"Cheers," said Ron moodily, pocketing his schedule,/n"but I think I'll take the lessons."/n/n"And speaking of your Skiving Snackboxes," said/nHermione, eyeing Fred and George beadily, "you can't/nadvertise for testers on the Gryffindor notice board."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Says who?" said George, looking astonished./n/n"Says me," said Hermione. "And Ron."/n/n"Leave me out of it," said Ron hastily./n/nHermione glared at him. Fred and George sniggered./n/n"You'll be singing a different tune soon enough,/nHermione," said Fred, thickly buttering a crumpet./n"You're starting your fifth year, you'll be begging us/nfor a Snackbox before long."/n/n"And why would starting fifth year mean I want a/nSkiving Snackbox?" asked Hermione./n/n"Fifth year's O.W.L. year," said George./n/n"So?"/n/n"So you've got your exams coming up, haven't you?/nThey'll be keeping your noses so hard to that/ngrindstone they'll be rubbed raw," said Fred with/nsatisfaction./n/n"Half our year had minor breakdowns coming up to/nO.W.L.s," said George happily. "Tears and tantrums/n... Patricia Stimpson kept coming over faint..."/n/n"Kenneth Towler came out in boils, d'you remember?"/nsaid Fred reminiscently./n/n"That's 'cause you put Bulbadox Powder in his/npajamas," said George./n/n"Oh yeah," said Fred, grinning. "I'd forgotten... Hard/nto keep track sometimes, isn't it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Anyway, it's a nightmare of a year, the fifth," said/nGeorge. "If you care about exam results anyway. Fred/nand I managed to keep our spirits up somehow."/n/n"Yeah ... you got, what was it, three O.W.L.s each?"/nsaid Ron./n/n"Yep," said Fred unconcernedly. "But we feel our/nfutures lie outside the world of academic/nachievement."/n/n"We seriously debated whether we were going to/nbother coming back for our seventh year," said/nGeorge brightly, "now that we've got — "/n/nHe broke off at a warning look from Harry, who knew/nGeorge had been about to mention the Triwizard/nwinnings he had given them./n/n" — now that we've got our O.W.L.s," George said/nhastily. "I mean, do we really need N.E.W.T.s? But we/ndidn't think Mum could take us leaving school early,/nnot on top of Percy turning out to be the world's/nbiggest prat."/n/n"We're not going to waste our last year here, though,"/nsaid Fred, looking affectionately around at the Great/nHall. "We're going to use it to do a bit of market/nresearch, find out exactly what the average Hogwarts/nstudent requires from his joke shop, carefully/nevaluate the results of our research, and then/nproduce the products to fit the demand."/n/n"But where are you going to get the gold to start a/njoke shop?" asked Hermione skeptically. "You're going/nto need all the ingredients and materials — and/npremises too, I suppose..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry did not look at the twins. His face felt hot; he/ndeliberately dropped his fork and dived down to/nretrieve it. He heard Fred say overhead, "Ask us no/nquestions and well tell you no lies, Hermione. C'mon,/nGeorge, if we get there early we might be able to sell a/nfew Extendable Ears before Herbology."/n/nHarry emerged from under the table to see Fred and/nGeorge walking away, each carrying a stack of toast./n/n"What did that mean?" said Hermione, looking from/nHarry to Ron. " 'Ask us no questions ...' Does that/nmean they've already got some gold to start a joke/nshop?"/n/n"You know, I've been wondering about that," said/nRon, his brow furrowed. "They bought me a new set of/ndress robes this summer, and I couldn't understand/nwhere they got the Galleons..."/n/nHarry decided it was time to steer the conversation/nout of these dangerous waters./n/n"D'you reckon it's true this year's going to be really/ntough? Because of the exams?"/n/n"Oh yeah," said Ron. "Bound to be, isn't it? O.W.L.s/nare really important, affect the jobs you can apply for/nand everything. We get career advice too, later this/nyear, Bill told me. So you can choose what N.E.W.T.s/nyou want to do next year."/n/n"D'you know what you want to do after Hogwarts?"/nHarry asked the other two, as they left the Great Hall/nshortly afterward and set off toward their History of/nMagic classroom./n/n"Not really," said Ron slowly. "Except ... well ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe looked slightly sheepish./n/n/n/n"What?" Harry urged him./n/n"Well, it'd be cool to be an Auror," said Ron in an/noffhand voice./n/n"Yeah, it would," said Harry fervently./n/n"But they're, like, the elite," said Ron. "You've got to/nbe really good. What about you, Hermione?"/n/n"I don't know," said Hermione. "I think I'd really like/nto do something worthwhile."/n/n"An Auror's worthwhile!" said Harry./n/n"Yes, it is, but it's not the only worthwhile thing," said/nHermione thoughtfully. "I mean, if I could take/nS.P.E.W. further ..."/n/nHarry and Ron carefully avoided looking at each/nother./n/nHistory of Magic was by common consent the most/nboring subject ever devised by Wizard-kind. Professor/nBinns, their ghost teacher, had a wheezy, droning/nvoice that was almost guaranteed to cause severe/ndrowsiness within ten minutes, five in warm weather./nHe never varied the form of their lessons, but lectured/nthem without pausing while they took notes, or/nrather, gazed sleepily into space. Harry and Ron had/nso far managed to scrape passes in this subject only/nby copying Hermione's notes before exams; she alone/nseemed able to resist the soporific power of Binns 's/nvoice./n/nToday they suffered through three quarters of an/nhour's droning on the subject of giant wars. Harry/n/n/n/n/n/nheard just enough within the first ten minutes to/nappreciate dimly that in another teacher's hands this/nsubject might have been mildly interesting, but then/nhis brain disengaged, and he spent the remaining/nthirty-five minutes playing hangman on a corner of/nhis parchment with Ron, while Hermione shot them/nfilthy looks out of the corner of her eye./n/n"How would it be," she asked them coldly as they left/nthe classroom for break (Binns drifting away through/nthe blackboard), "if I refused to lend you my notes/nthis year?"/n/n"We'd fail our O.W.L.s," said Ron. "If you want that on/nyour conscience, Hermione ..."/n/n"Well, you'd deserve it," she snapped. "You don't even/ntry to listen to him, do you?"/n/n"We do try," said Ron. "We just haven't got your/nbrains or your memory or your concentration —/nyou're just cleverer than we are — is it nice to rub it/nin?"/n/n/n/n"Oh, don't give me that rubbish," said Hermione, but/nshe looked slightly mollified as she led the way out/ninto the damp courtyard./n/nA fine misty drizzle was falling, so that the people/nstanding in huddles around the yard looked blurred/nat the edges. Everyone was/nstaring at either Umbridge or Harry./n/n"Now, let me make a few things quite plain."/n/nProfessor Umbridge stood up and leaned toward/nthem, her stubby-fingered hands splayed on her desk./n/n"You have been told that a certain Dark wizard has/nreturned from the dead — "/n/n"He wasn't dead," said Harry angrily, "but yeah, he's/nreturned!"/n/n"Mr.-Potter-you-have-already-lost-your-House-ten-/npoints-do-not-make-matters-worse-for-yourself," said/nProfessor Umbridge in one breath without looking at/nhim. "As I was saying, you have been informed that a/ncertain Dark wizard is at large once again. This is a/nlie."/n/n"It is NOT a lie!" said Harry. "I saw him, I fought him!"/n/n"Detention, Mr. Potter!" said Professor Umbridge/ntriumphantly. "Tomorrow evening. Five o'clock. My/noffice. I repeat, this is a lie. The Ministry of Magic/nguarantees that you are not in danger from any Dark/nwizard. If you are still worried, by all means come and/nsee me outside class hours. If someone is alarming/nyou with fibs about reborn Dark wizards, I would like/nto hear about it. I am here to help. I am your friend./nAnd now, you will kindly continue your reading. Page/nfive, 'Basics for Beginners.' "/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor Umbridge sat down behind her desk again./nHarry, however, stood up. Everyone was staring at/nhim; Seamus looked half-scared, half-fascinated./n/n"Harry, no!" Hermione whispered in a warning voice,/ntugging at his sleeve, but Harry jerked his arm out of/nher reach./n/n"So, according to you, Cedric Diggory dropped dead of/nhis own accord, did he?" Harry asked, his voice/nshaking./n/nThere was a collective intake of breath from the class,/nfor none of them, apart from Ron and Hermione, had/never heard Harry talk about what had happened on/nthe night that Cedric had died. They stared avidly/nfrom Harry to Professor Umbridge, who had raised/nher eyes and was staring at him without a trace of a/nfake smile on her face./n/n"Cedric Diggory's death was a tragic accident," she/nsaid coldly./n/n"It was murder," said Harry. He could feel himself/nshaking. He had hardly talked to anyone about this,/nleast of all thirty eagerly listening classmates./n"Voldemort killed him, and you know it."/n/nProfessor Umbridge's face was quite blank. For a/nmoment he thought she was going to scream at him./nThen she said, in her softest, most sweetly girlish/nvoice, "Come here, Mr. Potter, dear."/n/nHe kicked his chair aside, strode around Ron and/nHermione and up to the teacher's desk. He could feel/nthe rest of the class holding its breath. He felt so/nangry he did not care what happened next./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor Umbridge pulled a small roll of pink/nparchment out of her handbag, stretched it out on the/ndesk, dipped her quill into a bottle of ink, and started/nscribbling, hunched over so that Harry could not see/nwhat she was writing. Nobody spoke. After a minute/nor so she rolled up the parchment and tapped it with/nher wand; it sealed itself seamlessly so that he could/nnot open it./n/n"Take this to Professor McGonagall, dear," said/nProfessor Umbridge, holding out the note to him./n/nHe took it from her without saying a word and left the/nroom, not even looking back at Ron and Hermione,/nand slamming the classroom door shut behind him./nHe walked very fast along the corridor, the note to/nMcGonagall clutched tight in his hand, and turning a/ncorner walked slap into Peeves the Poltergeist, a wide-/nfaced little man floating on his back in midair,/njuggling several inkwells./n/n"Why, it's Potty Wee Potter!" cackled Peeves, allowing/ntwo of the inkwells to fall to the ground where they/nsmashed and spattered the walls with ink; Harry/njumped backward out of the way with a snarl./n/n"Get out of it, Peeves."/n/n"Oooh, Crackpot's feeling cranky," said Peeves,/npursuing Harry along the corridor, leering as he/nzoomed along above him. "What is it this time, my/nfine Potty friend? Hearing voices? Seeing visions?/nSpeaking in" — Peeves blew a gigantic raspberry —/n"tongues?"/n/n"I said, leave me ALONE!" Harry shouted, running/ndown the nearest flight of stairs, but Peeves merely/nslid down the banister on his back beside him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh, most think he's barking, the Potty wee lad,/n/nBut some are more kindly and think he's just sad,/n/nBut Peevesy knows better and says that he's mad — "/n"SHUT UP!"/n/nA door to his left flew open and Professor McGonagall/nemerged from her office looking grim and slightly/nharassed./n/n"What on earth are you shouting about, Potter?" she/nsnapped, as Peeves cackled gleefully and zoomed out/nof sight. "Why aren't you in class?"/n/n"I've been sent to see you," said Harry stiffly./n/n"Sent? What do you mean, sent?"/n/nHe held out the note from Professor Umbridge./nProfessor McGonagall took it from him, frowning, slit/nit open with a tap of her wand, stretched it out, and/nbegan to read. Her eyes zoomed from side to side/nbehind their square spectacles as she read what/nUmbridge had written, and with each line they/nbecame narrower./n/n"Come in here, Potter."/n/nHe followed her inside her study. The door closed/nautomatically behind him./n/n"Well?" said Professor McGonagall, rounding on him./n"Is this true?"/n/n"Is what true?" Harry asked, rather more aggressively/nthan he had intended. "Professor?" he added in an/nattempt to sound more polite./n/n/n/n/n/n"Is it true that you shouted at Professor Umbridge?"/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n"You called her a liar?"/n/n"Yes."/n/n"You told her He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named is back?"/n"Yes."/n/nProfessor McGonagall sat down behind her desk,/nfrowning at Harry. Then she said, "Have a biscuit,/nPotter."/n/n"Have — what?"/n/n"Have a biscuit," she repeated impatiently, indicating/na tartan tin of cookies lying on top of one of the piles/nof papers on her desk. "And sit down."/n/nThere had been a previous occasion when Harry,/nexpecting to be caned by Professor McGonagall, had/ninstead been appointed by her to the Gryffindor/nQuidditch team. He sank into a chair opposite her/nand helped himself to a Ginger Newt, feeling just as/nconfused and wrong-footed as he had done on that/noccasion./n/nProfessor McGonagall set down Professor Umbridge's/nnote and looked very seriously at Harry./n/n"Potter, you need to be careful."/n/nHarry swallowed his mouthful of Ginger Newt and/nstared at her. Her tone of voice was not at all what he/nwas used to; it was not brisk, crisp, and stern; it was/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nlow and anxious and somehow much more human/nthan usual./n/n"Misbehavior in Dolores Umbridge's class could cost/nyou much more than House points and a detention."/n/n"What do you — ?"/n/n"Potter, use your common sense," snapped Professor/nMcGonagall, with an abrupt return to her usual/nmanner. "You know where she comes from, you must/nknow to whom she is reporting."/n/nThe bell rang for the end of the lesson. Overhead and/nall around came the elephantine sounds of hundreds/nof students on the move./n/n"It says here she's given you detention every evening/nthis week, starting tomorrow," Professor McGonagall/nsaid, looking down at Umbridge's note again./n/n"Every evening this week!" Harry repeated, horrified./n"But, Professor, couldn't you — ?"/n/n"No, I couldn't," said Professor McGonagall flatly./n/n"But — "/n/n"She is your teacher and has every right to give you/ndetention. You will go to her room at five o'clock/ntomorrow for the first one. Just remember: Tread/ncarefully around Dolores Umbridge."/n/n"But I was telling the truth!" said Harry, outraged./n"Voldemort's back, you know he is, Professor/nDumbledore knows he is — "/n/n"For heaven's sake, Potter!" said Professor/nMcGonagall, straightening her glasses angrily (she/n/n/n/n/n/nhad winced horribly when he had used Voldemort's/nname). "Do you really think this is about truth or/nlies? It's about keeping your head down and your/ntemper under control!"/n/nShe stood up, nostrils wide and mouth very thin, and/nhe stood too./n/n"Have another biscuit," she said irritably, thrusting/nthe tin at him./n/n"No, thanks," said Harry coldly./n/n"Don't be ridiculous," she snapped./n/nHe took one./n/n"Thanks," he said grudgingly./n/n"Didn't you listen to Dolores Umbridge's speech at the/nstart-of-term feast, Potter?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "Yeah ... she said ... progress will/nbe prohibited or ... well, it meant that ... that the/nMinistry of Magic is trying to interfere at Hogwarts."/n/nProfessor McGonagall eyed him for a moment, then/nsniffed, walked around her desk, and held open the/ndoor for him./n/n"Well, I'm glad you listen to Hermione Granger at any/nrate," she said, pointing him out of her office./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Detention With Dolores
text: /nDinner in the Great Hall that night was not a pleasant/nexperience for Harry. The news about his shouting/nmatch with Umbridge seemed to have traveled/nexceptionally fast even by Hogwarts standards. He/nheard whispers all around him as he sat eating/nbetween Ron and Hermione. The funny thing was that/nnone of the whisperers seemed to mind him/noverhearing what they were saying about him — on/nthe contrary, it was as though they were hoping he/nwould get angry and start shouting again, so that/nthey could hear his story firsthand./n/n"He says he saw Cedric Diggory murdered..."/n/n"He reckons he dueled with You-Know-Who..."/n/n"Come off it..."/n/n"Who does he think he's kidding?"/n/n"Pur - lease ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What I don't get," said Harry in a shaking voice,/nlaying down his knife and fork (his hands were/ntrembling too much to hold them steady), "is why they/nall believed the story two months ago when/nDumbledore told them..."/n/n"The thing is, Harry, I'm not sure they did," said/nHermione grimly. "Oh, let's get out of here."/n/nShe slammed down her own knife and fork; Ron/nlooked sadly at his half-finished apple pie but/nfollowed suit. People stared at them all the way out of/nthe Hall./n/n"What d'you mean, you're not sure they believed/nDumbledore?" Harry asked Hermione when they/nreached the first-floor landing./n/n"Look, you don't understand what it was like after it/nhappened," said Hermione quietly. "You arrived back/nin the middle of the lawn clutching Cedric's dead/nbody... None of us saw what happened in the maze.../nWe just had Dumbledore's word for it that You-Know-/nWho had come back and killed Cedric and fought/nyou."/n/n"Which is the truth!" said Harry loudly./n/n"I know it is, Harry, so will you please stop biting my/nhead off?" said Hermione wearily. "It's just that before/nthe truth could sink in, everyone went home for the/nsummer, where they spent two months reading about/nhow you're a nutcase and Dumbledore's going senile!"/n/nRain pounded on the windowpanes as they strode/nalong the empty corridors back to Gryffindor Tower./nHarry felt as though his first day had lasted a week,/nbut he still had a mountain of homework to do before/nbed. A dull pounding pain was developing over his/n/n/n/n/nright eye. He glanced out of a rain-washed window at/nthe dark grounds as they turned into the Fat Lady's/ncorridor. There was still no light in Hagrid's cabin./n/n"Mimbulus mimbletonia," said Hermione, before the/nFat Lady could ask. The portrait swung open to reveal/nthe hole behind and the three of them scrambled/nback through it./n/nThe common room was almost empty; nearly everyone/nwas still down at dinner. Crookshanks uncoiled/nhimself from an armchair and trotted to meet them,/npurring loudly, and when Harry, Ron, and Hermione/ntook their three favorite chairs at the fireside he leapt/nlightly into Hermione 's lap and curled up there like a/nfurry ginger cushion. Harry gazed into the flames,/nfeeling drained and exhausted./n/n"How can Dumbledore have let this happen?"/nHermione cried suddenly, making Harry and Ron/njump; Crookshanks leapt off her, looking affronted./nShe pounded the arms of her chair in fury, so that/nbits of stuffing leaked out of the holes. "How can he/nlet that terrible woman teach us? And in our O.W.L./nyear too!"/n/n"Well, we've never had great Defense Against the Dark/nArts teachers, have we?" said Harry. "You know what/nit's like, Hagrid told us, nobody wants the job, they/nsay it's jinxed."/n/n"Yes, but to employ someone who's actually refusing/nto let us do magic! What's Dumbledore playing at?"/n/n"And she's trying to get people to spy for her," said/nRon darkly. "Remember when she said she wanted us/nto come and tell her if we hear anyone saying You-/nKnow- Who's back?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Of course she's here to spy on us all, that's obvious,/nwhy else would Fudge have wanted her to come?"/nsnapped Hermione./n/n"Don't start arguing again," said Harry wearily, as/nRon opened his mouth to retaliate. "Can't we just .../nLet's just do that homework, get it out of the way..."/n/nThey collected their schoolbags from a corner and/nreturned to the chairs by the fire. People were coming/nback from dinner now. Harry kept his face averted/nfrom the portrait hole, but could still sense the stares/nhe was attracting./n/n"Shall we do Snape's stuff first?" said Ron, dipping/nhis quill into his ink. " 'The properties ...of moonstone/n... and its uses ...in potion-making ...' " he muttered,/nwriting the words across the top of his parchment as/nhe spoke them. "There." He underlined the title, then/nlooked up expectantly at Hermione./n/n"So what are the properties of moonstone and its uses/nin potion-making?"/n/nBut Hermione was not listening; she was squinting/nover into the far corner of the room, where Fred,/nGeorge, and Lee Jordan were now sitting at the center/nof a knot of innocent-looking first years, all of whom/nwere chewing something that seemed to have come/nout of a large paper bag that Fred was holding./n/n"No, I'm sorry, they've gone too far," she said,/nstanding up and looking positively furious. "Come on,/nRon."/n/n"I — what?" said Ron, plainly playing for time. "No —/ncome on, Hermione — we can't tell them off for giving/nout sweets..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You know perfectly well that those are bits of/nNosebleed Nougat or — or Puking Pastilles or — "/n/n"Fainting Fancies?" Harry suggested quietly./n/nOne by one, as though hit over the heads with/ninvisible mallets, the first years were slumping/nunconscious in their seats; some slid right onto the/nfloor, others merely hung over the arms of their/nchairs, their tongues lolling out. Most of the people/nwatching were laughing; Hermione, however, squared/nher shoulders and marched directly over to where/nFred and George now stood with clipboards, closely/nobserving the unconscious first years. Ron rose/nhalfway out of his chair, hovered uncertainly for a/nmoment or two, then muttered to Harry, "She's got it/nunder control," before sinking as low in his chair as/nhis lanky frame permitted./n/n"That's enough!" Hermione said forcefully to Fred and/nGeorge, both of whom looked up in mild surprise./n/n"Yeah, you're right," said George, nodding, "this/ndosage looks strong enough, doesn't it?"/n/n"I told you this morning, you can't test your rubbish/non students!"/n/n"We're paying them!" said Fred indignantly./n/n"I don't care, it could be dangerous!"/n/n"Rubbish," said Fred./n/n"Calm down, Hermione, they're fine!" said Lee/nreassuringly as he walked from first year to first year,/ninserting purple sweets into their open mouths./n/n"Yeah, look, they're coming round now," said George./n/n/n/n/n/nA few of the first years were indeed stirring. Several/nlooked so shocked to find themselves lying on the/nfloor, or dangling off their chairs, that Harry was sure/nFred and George had not warned them what the/nsweets were going to do./n/n"Feel all right?" said George kindly to a small dark-/nhaired girl lying at his feet./n/n"I-I think so," she said shakily./n/n"Excellent," said Fred happily, but the next second/nHermione had snatched both his clipboard and the/npaper bag of Fainting Fancies from his hands./n/n"It is NOT excellent!"/n/n" 'Course it is, they're alive, aren't they?" said Fred/nangrily./n/n"You can't do this, what if you made one of them/nreally ill?"/n/n"We're not going to make them ill, we've already tested/nthem all on ourselves, this is just to see if everyone/nreacts the same — "/n/n"If you don't stop doing it, I'm going to — "/n/n"Put us in detention?" said Fred in an I'd-like-to-see-/nyou-try-it voice./n/n"Make us write lines?" said George, smirking./n/nOnlookers all over the room were laughing. Hermione/ndrew herself up to her full height; her eyes were/nnarrowed and her bushy hair seemed to crackle with/nelectricity./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," she said, her voice quivering with anger, "but I/nwill write to your mother."/n/n/n/n"You wouldn't," said George, horrified, taking a step/nback from her./n/n"Oh, yes, I would," said Hermione grimly. "I can't stop/nyou eating the stupid things yourselves, but you're/nnot giving them to first years."/n/nFred and George looked thunderstruck. It was clear/nthat as far as they were concerned, Hermione 's threat/nwas way below the belt. With a last threatening look/nat them, she thrust Fred's clipboard and the bag of/nFancies back into his arms and stalked back to her/nchair by the fire./n/nRon was now so low in his seat that his nose was/nroughly level with his knees./n/n"Thank you for your support, Ron," Hermione said/nacidly./n/n"You handled it fine by yourself," Ron mumbled./n/nHermione stared down at her blank piece of/nparchment for a few seconds, then said edgily, "Oh,/nit's no good, I can't concentrate now. I'm going to/nbed."/n/nShe wrenched her bag open; Harry thought she was/nabout to put her books away, but instead she pulled/nout two misshapen woolly objects, placed them/ncarefully on a table by the fireplace, covered them/nwith a few screwed-up bits of parchment and a/nbroken quill, and stood back to admire the effect./n/n"What in the name of Merlin are you doing?" said/nRon, watching her as though fearful for her sanity./n/n/n/n/n/n"They're hats for house-elves," she said briskly, now/nstuffing her books back into her bag. "I did them over/nthe summer. I'm a really slow knitter without magic,/nbut now I'm back at school I should be able to make/nlots more."/n/n"You're leaving out hats for the house-elves?" said/nRon slowly. "And you're covering them up with/nrubbish first?"/n/n"Yes," said Hermione defiantly, swinging her bag onto/nher back./n/n"That's not on," said Ron angrily. "You're trying to/ntrick them into picking up the hats. You're setting/nthem free when they might not want to be free."/n/n"Of course they want to be free!" said Hermione at/nonce, though her face was turning pink. "Don't you/ndare touch those hats, Ron!"/n/nShe left. Ron waited until she had disappeared/nthrough the door to the girls' dormitories, then/ncleared the rubbish off the woolly hats./n/n"They should at least see what they're picking up," he/nsaid firmly. "Anyway ..." He rolled up the parchment/non which he had written the title of Snape's essay./n"There's no point trying to finish this now, I can't do it/nwithout Hermione, I haven't got a clue what you're/nsupposed to do with moonstones, have you?"/n/nHarry shook his head, noticing as he did so that the/nache in his right temple was getting worse. He/nthought of the long essay on giant wars and the pain/nstabbed at him sharply. Knowing perfectly well that/nhe would regret not finishing his homework tonight/nwhen the morning came, he piled his books back into/nhis bag./n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm going to bed too."/n/nHe passed Seamus on the way to the door leading to/nthe dormitories, but did not look at him. Harry had a/nfleeting impression that Seamus had opened his/nmouth to speak, but sped up, and reached the/nsoothing peace of the stone spiral staircase without/nhaving to endure any more provocation./n/nThe following day dawned just as leaden and rainy as/nthe previous one. Hagrid was still absent from the/nstaff table at breakfast./n/n"But on the plus side, no Snape today," said Ron/nbracingly./n/nHermione yawned widely and poured herself some/ncoffee. She looked mildly pleased about something,/nand when Ron asked her what she had to be so happy/nabout, she simply said, "The hats have gone. Seems/nthe house-elves do want freedom after all."/n/n"I wouldn't bet on it," Ron told her cuttingly. "They/nmight not count as clothes. They didn't look anything/nlike hats to me, more like woolly bladders."/n/nHermione did not speak to him all morning./n/nDouble Charms was succeeded by double/nTransfiguration. Professor Flitwick and Professor/nMcGonagall both spent the first fifteen minutes of/ntheir lessons lecturing the class on the importance of/nO.W.L.s./n/n"What you must remember," said little Professor/nFlitwick squeakily, perched as ever on a pile of books/nso that he could see over the top of his desk, "is that/nthese examinations may influence your futures for/nmany years to come! If you have not already given/n/n/n/n/nserious thought to your careers, now is the time to do/nso. And in the meantime, I'm afraid, we shall be/nworking harder than ever to ensure that you all do/nyourselves justice!"/n/nThey then spent more than an hour reviewing/nSummoning Charms, which according to Professor/nFlitwick were bound to come up in their O.W.L., and/nhe rounded off the lesson by setting them their largest/namount of Charms homework ever./n/nIt was the same, if not worse, in Transfiguration./n/n"You cannot pass an O.W.L.," said Professor/nMcGonagall grimly, "without serious application,/npractice, and study. I see no reason why everybody in/nthis class should not achieve an O.W.L. in/nTransfiguration as long as they put in the work."/nNeville made a sad little disbelieving noise. "Yes, you/ntoo, Longbottom," said Professor McGonagall. "There's/nnothing wrong with your work except lack of/nconfidence. So ... today we are starting Vanishing/nSpells. These are easier than Conjuring Spells, which/nyou would not usually attempt until N.E.W.T. level,/nbut they are still among the most difficult magic you/nwill be tested on in your O.W.L."/n/nShe was quite right; Harry found the Vanishing Spells/nhorribly difficult. By the end of a double period,/nneither he nor Ron had managed to vanish the snails/non which they were practicing, though Ron said/nhopefully that he thought his looked a bit paler./nHermione, on the other hand, successfully vanished/nher snail on the third attempt, earning her a ten-point/nbonus for Gryffindor from Professor McGonagall. She/nwas the only person not given homework; everybody/nelse was told to practice the spell overnight, ready for/na fresh attempt on their snails the following/nafternoon./n/n/n/n/n/nNow panicking slightly about the amount of/nhomework they had to do, Harry and Ron spent their/nlunch hour in the library looking up the uses of/nmoonstones in potion-making. Still angry about Ron's/nslur on her woolly hats, Hermione did not join them./nBy the time they reached Care of Magical Creatures in/nthe afternoon, Harry's head was aching again./n/nThe day had become cool and breezy, and, as they/nwalked down the sloping lawn toward Hagrid's cabin/non the edge of the Forbidden Forest, they felt the/noccasional drop of rain on their faces. Professor/nGrubbly-Plank stood waiting for the class some ten/nyards from Hagrid's front door, a long trestle table in/nfront of her laden with many twigs. As Harry and Ron/nreached her, a loud shout of laughter sounded behind/nthem; turning, they saw Draco Malfoy striding toward/nthem, surrounded by his usual gang of Slytherin/ncronies. He had clearly just said something highly/namusing, because Crabbe, Goyle, Pansy Parkinson,/nand the rest continued to snigger heartily as they/ngathered around the trestle table. Judging by the fact/nthat all of them kept looking over at Harry, he was/nable to guess the subject of the joke without too much/ndifficulty./n/n"Everyone here?" barked Professor Grubbly-Plank,/nonce all the Slytherins and Gryffindors had arrived./n"Let's crack on then — who can tell me what these/nthings are called?"/n/nShe indicated the heap of twigs in front of her./nHermione 's hand shot into the air. Behind her back,/nMalfoy did a buck-toothed imitation of her jumping/nup and down in eagerness to answer a question./n/nPansy Parkinson gave a shriek of laughter that turned/nalmost at once into a scream, as the twigs on the/ntable leapt into the air and revealed themselves to be/nwhat looked like tiny pixieish creatures made of wood,/n/n/n/n/neach with knobbly brown arms and legs, two twiglike/nfingers at the end of each hand, and a funny, flat,/nbarklike face in which a pair of beetle-brown eyes/nglittered./n/n"Oooooh!" said Parvati and Lavender, thoroughly/nirritating Harry: Anyone would have thought that/nHagrid never showed them impressive creatures;/nadmittedly the flobberworms had been a bit dull, but/nthe salamanders and hippogriffs had been interesting/nenough, and the Blast-Ended Skrewts perhaps too/nmuch so./n/n"Kindly keep your voices down, girls!" said Professor/nGrubbly-Plank sharply, scattering a handful of what/nlooked like brown rice among the stick-creatures, who/nimmediately fell upon the food. "So — anyone know/nthe names of these creatures? Miss Granger?"/n/n"Bowtruckles," said Hermione. "They're tree-/nguardians, usually live in wand-trees."/n/n"Five points for Gryffindor," said Professor Grubbly-/nPlank. "Yes, these are bowtruckles and, as Miss/nGranger rightly says, they generally live in trees/nwhose wood is of wand quality. Anybody know what/nthey eat?"/n/n"Wood lice," said Hermione promptly, which explained/nwhy what Harry had taken for grains of brown rice/nwere moving. "But fairy eggs if they can get them."/n/n"Good girl, take another five points. So whenever you/nneed leaves or wood from a tree in which a/nbowtruckle lodges, it is wise to have a gift of wood lice/nready to distract or placate it.
