It was impossible to tell which one/nwas Ron at this distance./n/nI must not tell lies, Harry wrote. The cut in the back of/nhis right hand opened and began to bleed afresh./n/nI must not tell lies. The cut dug deeper, stinging and/nsmarting./n/nI must not tell lies. Blood trickled down his wrist./n/nHe chanced another glance out of the window./nWhoever was defending the goalposts now was doing/na very poor job indeed. Katie Bell scored twice in the/nfew seconds Harry dared watch. Hoping very much/nthat the Keeper wasn't Ron, he dropped his eyes back/nto the parchment dotted with blood./n/nI must not tell lies./n/nI must not tell lies./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe looked up whenever he thought he could risk it,/nwhen he could hear the scratching of Umbridge's quill/nor the opening of a desk drawer. The third person to/ntry out was pretty good, the fourth was terrible, the/nfifth dodged a Bludger exceptionally well but then/nfumbled an easy save. The sky was darkening so that/nHarry doubted he would be able to watch the sixth/nand seventh people at all./n/nI must not tell lies./n/nI must not tell lies./n/nThe parchment was now shining with drops of blood/nfrom the back of his hand, which was searing with/npain. When he next looked up, night had fallen and/nthe Quidditch pitch was no longer visible./n/n"Let's see if you've gotten the message yet, shall we?"/nsaid Umbridge's soft voice half an hour later./n/nShe moved toward him, stretching out her short be-/nringed fingers for his arm. And then, as she took hold/nof him to examine the words now cut into his skin,/npain seared, not across the back of his hand, but/nacross the scar on his forehead. At the same time, he/nhad a most peculiar sensation somewhere around his/nmidriff./n/nHe wrenched his arm out of her grip and leapt to his/nfeet, staring at her. She looked back at him, a smile/nstretching her wide, slack mouth./n/n"Yes, it hurts, doesn't it?" she said softly./n/nHe did not answer. His heart was thumping very hard/nand fast. Was she talking about his hand or did she/nknow what he had just felt in his forehead?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, I think I've made my point, Mr. Potter. You may/ngo."/n/nHe caught up his schoolbag and left the room as/nquickly as he could./n/nStay calm, he told himself as he sprinted up the/nstairs. Stay calm, it doesn't necessarily mean what/nyou think it means.../n/n" Mimbulus mimbletoniaV ' he gasped at the Fat Lady,/nwho swung forward once more./n/nA roar of sound greeted him. Ron came running/ntoward him, beaming all over his face and slopping/nbutterbeer down his front from the goblet he was/nclutching./n/n"Harry, I did it, I'm in, I'm Keeper!"/n/n"What? Oh — brilliant!" said Harry, trying to smile/nnaturally, while his heart continued to race and his/nhand throbbed and bled./n/n"Have a butterbeer." Ron pressed a bottle onto him. "I/ncan't believe it — where's Hermione gone?"/n/n"She's there," said Fred, who was also swigging/nbutterbeer, and pointed to an armchair by the fire./nHermione was dozing in it, her drink tipping/nprecariously in her hand./n/n"Well, she said she was pleased when I told her," said/nRon, looking slightly put out./n/n"Let her sleep," said George hastily. It was a few/nmoments before Harry noticed that several of the first/nyears gathered around them bore unmistakable signs/nof recent nosebleeds./n/n/n/n/n/n"Come here, Ron, and see if Oliver's old robes fit you,"/ncalled Katie Bell. "We can take off his name and put/nyours on instead..."/n/nAs Ron moved away, Angelina came striding up to/nHarry./n/n"Sorry I was a bit short with you earlier, Potter," she/nsaid abruptly. "It's stressful, this managing lark, you/nknow, I'm starting to think I was a bit hard on Wood/nsometimes." She was watching Ron over the rim of/nher goblet with a slight frown on her face./n/n"Look, I know he's your best mate, but he's not/nfabulous," she said bluntly. "I think with a bit of/ntraining he'll be all right, though. He comes from a/nfamily of good Quidditch players. I'm banking on him/nturning out to have a bit more talent than he showed/ntoday, to be honest. Vicky Frobisher and Geoffrey/nHooper both flew better this evening, but Hooper's a/nreal whiner, he's always moaning about something or/nother, and Vicky's involved in all sorts of societies,/nshe admitted herself that if training clashed with her/nCharm Club she'd put Charms first. Anyway, we're/nhaving a practice session at two o'clock tomorrow, so/njust make sure you're there this time. And do me a/nfavor and help Ron as much as you can, okay?"/n/nHe nodded and Angelina strolled back to Alicia/nSpinnet. Harry moved over to sit next to Hermione,/nwho awoke with a jerk as he put down his bag./n/n"Oh, Harry, it's you... Good about Ron, isn't it?" she/nsaid blearily. "I'm just so — so — so tired," she/nyawned. "I was up until one o'clock making more/nhats. They're disappearing like mad!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd sure enough, now that he looked, Harry saw that/nthere were woolly hats concealed all around the room/nwhere unwary elves might accidentally pick them up./n/n"Great," said Harry distractedly; if he did not tell/nsomebody soon, he would burst. "Listen, Hermione, I/nwas just up in Umbridge's office and she touched my/narm ..."/n/nHermione listened closely. When Harry had finished/nshe said slowly, "You're worried that You-Know- Who's/ncontrolling her like he controlled Quirrell?"/n/n"Well," said Harry, dropping his voice, "it's a/npossibility, isn't it?"/n/n"I suppose so," said Hermione, though she sounded/nunconvinced. "But I don't think he can be possessing/nher the way he possessed Quirrell, I mean, he's/nproperly alive again now, isn't he, he's got his own/nbody, he wouldn't need to share someone else's. He/ncould have her under the Imperius Curse, I/nsuppose..."/n/nHarry watched Fred, George, and Lee Jordan juggling/nempty butterbeer bottles for a moment. Then/nHermione said, "But last year your scar hurt when/nnobody was touching you, and didn't Dumbledore say/nit had to do with what You- Know- Who was feeling at/nthe time? I mean, maybe this hasn't got anything to/ndo with Umbridge at all, maybe it's just coincidence it/nhappened while you were with her?"/n/n"She's evil," said Harry flatly. "Twisted."/n/n"She's horrible, yes, but ... Harry, I think you ought to/ntell Dumbledore your scar hurt."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was the second time in two days he had been/nadvised to go to Dumbledore and his answer to/nHermione was just the same as his answer to Ron./n/n"I'm not bothering him with this. Like you just said,/nit's not a big deal. It's been hurting on and off all/nsummer — it was just a bit worse tonight, that's all —/n/n/n/n"Harry, I'm sure Dumbledore would want to be/nbothered by this — "/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, before he could stop himself,/n"that's the only bit of me Dumbledore cares about,/nisn't it, my scar?"/n/n"Don't say that, it's not true!"/n/n"I think I'll write and tell Sirius about it, see what he/nthinks — "/n/n"Harry, you can't put something like that in a letter!"/nsaid Hermione, looking alarmed. "Don't you/nremember, Moody told us to be careful what we put in/nwriting! We just can't guarantee owls aren't being/nintercepted anymore!"/n/n"All right, all right, I won't tell him, then!" said Harry/nirritably. He got to his feet. "I'm going to bed. Tell Ron/nfor me, will you?"/n/n"Oh no," said Hermione, looking relieved, "if you're/ngoing that means I can go without being rude too, I'm/nabsolutely exhausted and I want to make some more/nhats tomorrow. Listen, you can help me if you like,/nit's quite fun, I'm getting better, I can do patterns and/nbobbles and all sorts of things now."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry looked into her face, which was shining with/nglee, and tried to look as though he was vaguely/ntempted by this offer./n/n"Er ... no, I don't think I will, thanks," he said. "Er —/nnot tomorrow. I've got loads of homework to do..."/n/nAnd he traipsed off to the boys' stairs, leaving her/nlooking slightly disappointed behind him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Percy And Padfoot
text: /nHarry was the first to awake in his dormitory next/nmorning. He lay for a moment watching dust swirl in/nthe chink of sunlight falling through the gap in his/nfour-poster's hangings and savored the thought that/nit was Saturday. The first week of term seemed to/nhave dragged on forever, like one gigantic History of/nMagic lesson./n/nJudging by the sleepy silence and the freshly minted/nlook of that beam of sunlight, it was just after/ndaybreak. He pulled open the curtains around his/nbed, got up, and started to dress. The only sound/napart from the distant twittering of birds was the/nslow, deep breathing of his fellow Gryffindors. He/nopened his schoolbag carefully, pulled out parchment/nand quill, and headed out of the dormitory for the/ncommon room./n/nMaking straight for his favorite squashy old armchair/nbeside the now extinct fire, Harry settled himself/ndown comfortably and unrolled his parchment while/nlooking around the room. The detritus of crumpled-up/n/n/n/n/nbits of parchment, old Gobstones, empty ingredient/njars, and candy wrappers that usually covered the/ncommon room at the end of each day was gone, as/nwere all Hermione's elf hats. Wondering vaguely how/nmany elves had now been set free whether they/nwanted to be or not, Harry uncorked his ink bottle,/ndipped his quill into it, and then held it suspended an/ninch above the smooth yellowish surface of his/nparchment, thinking hard... But after a minute or so/nhe found himself staring into the empty grate, at a/ncomplete loss for what to say./n/nHe could now appreciate how hard it had been for/nRon and Hermione to write him letters over the/nsummer. How was he supposed to tell Sirius/neverything that had happened over the past week and/npose all the questions he was burning to ask without/ngiving potential letter-thieves a lot of information he/ndid not want them to have?/n/nHe sat quite motionless for a while, gazing into the/nfireplace, then, finally coming to a decision, he dipped/nhis quill into the ink bottle once more and set it/nresolutely upon the parchment./n/nDear Snuffles,/n/nHope you're okay, the first week back here's been/nterrible, I'm really glad it's the weekend./n/nWe've got a new Defense Against the Dark Arts/nteacher, Professor Umbridge. She's nearly as nice as/nyour mum. I'm writing because that thing I wrote to/nyou about last summer happened again last night/nwhen I was doing a detention with Umbridge./n/nWe're all missing our biggest friend, we hope he'll be/nback soon./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nPlease write back quickly./n/nBest,/n/nHarry/n/nHarry reread this letter several times, trying to see it/nfrom the point of view of an outsider. He could not see/nhow they would know what he was talking about — or/nwho he was talking to — just from reading this letter./nHe did hope Sirius would pick up the hint about/nHagrid and tell them when he might be back: Harry/ndid not want to ask directly in case it drew too much/nattention to what Hagrid might be up to while he was/nnot at Hogwarts./n/nConsidering it was a very short letter it had taken a/nlong time to write; sunlight had crept halfway across/nthe room while he had been working on it, and he/ncould now hear distant sounds of movement from the/ndormitories above. Sealing the parchment carefully he/nclimbed through the portrait hole and headed off for/nthe Owlery./n/n"I would not go that way if I were you," said Nearly/nHeadless Nick, drifting disconcertingly through a wall/njust ahead of him as he walked down the passage./n"Peeves is planning an amusing joke on the next/nperson to pass the bust of Paracelsus halfway down/nthe corridor."/n/n"Does it involve Paracelsus falling on top of the/nperson's head?" asked Harry./n/n"Funnily enough, it does," said Nearly Headless Nick/nin a bored voice. "Subtlety has never been Peeves 's/nstrong point. I'm off to try and find the Bloody/nBaron... He might be able to put a stop to it... See/nyou, Harry..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, 'bye," said Harry and instead of turning right,/nhe turned left, taking a longer but safer route up to/nthe Owlery. His spirits rose as he walked past window/nafter window showing brilliantly blue sky; he had/ntraining later, he would be back on the Quidditch/npitch at last —/n/nSomething brushed his ankles. He looked down and/nsaw the caretaker's skeletal gray cat, Mrs. Norris,/nslinking past him. She turned lamplike yellow eyes/nupon him for a moment before disappearing behind a/nstatue of Wilfred the Wistful./n/n"I'm not doing anything wrong," Harry called after/nher. She had the unmistakable air of a cat that was/noff to report to her boss, yet Harry could not see why;/nhe was perfectly entitled to walk up to the Owlery on/na Saturday morning./n/nThe sun was high in the sky now and when Harry/nentered the Owlery the glassless windows dazzled his/neyes; thick silvery beams of sunlight crisscrossed the/ncircular room in which hundreds of owls nestled on/nrafters, a little restless in the early morning light,/nsome clearly just returned from hunting. The straw-/ncovered floor crunched a little as he stepped across/ntiny animal bones, craning his neck for a sight of/nHedwig./n/n"There you are," he said, spotting her somewhere near/nthe very top of the vaulted ceiling. "Get down here,/n/nI've got a letter for you."/n/nWith a low hoot she stretched her great white wings/nand soared down onto his shoulder./n/n"Right, I know this says 'Snuffles' on the outside," he/ntold her, giving her the letter to clasp in her beak and,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwithout knowing exactly why, whispering, "but it's for/nSirius, okay?"/n/nShe blinked her amber eyes once and he took that to/nmean that she understood./n/n"Safe flight, then," said Harry and he carried her to/none of the windows; with a moment's pressure on his/narm Hedwig took off into the blindingly bright sky. He/nwatched her until she became a tiny black speck and/nvanished, then switched his gaze to Hagrid's hut,/nclearly visible from this window, and just as clearly/nuninhabited, the chimney smokeless, the curtains/ndrawn./n/nThe treetops of the Forbidden Forest swayed in a light/nbreeze. Harry watched them, savoring the fresh air on/nhis face, thinking about Quidditch later ... and then/nhe saw it. A great, reptilian winged horse, just like the/nones pulling the Hogwarts carriages, with leathery/nblack wings spread wide like a pterodactyl's, rose up/nout of the trees like a grotesque, giant bird. It soared/nin a great circle and then plunged once more into the/ntrees. The whole thing had happened so quickly Harry/ncould hardly believe what he had seen, except that/nhis heart was hammering madly./n/nThe Owlery door opened behind him. He leapt in/nshock, and turning quickly, saw Cho Chang holding a/nletter and a parcel in her hands./n/n"Hi," said Harry automatically./n/n"Oh ... hi," she said breathlessly. "I didn't think/nanyone would be up here this early. . . I only/nremembered five minutes ago, it's my mum's/nbirthday."/n/n/n/nShe held up the parcel./n/n/n/n/n/n"Right," said Harry. His brain seemed to have/njammed. He wanted to say something funny and/ninteresting, but the memory of that terrible winged/nhorse was fresh in his mind./n/n"Nice day," he said, gesturing to the windows. His/ninsides seemed to shrivel with embarrassment. The/nweather. He was talking about the weather.../n/n"Yeah," said Cho, looking around for a suitable owl./n"Good Quidditch conditions. I haven't been out all/nweek, have you?"/n/n"No," said Harry./n/nCho had selected one of the school barn owls. She/ncoaxed it down onto her arm where it held out an/nobliging leg so that she could attach the parcel./n/n"Hey, has Gryffindor got a new Keeper yet?" she/nasked./n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "It's my friend Ron Weasley, d'you/nknow him?"/n/n"The Tornado-hater?" said Cho rather coolly. "Is he/nany good?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "I think so. I didn't see his tryout,/nthough, I was in detention."/n/nCho looked up, the parcel only half-attached to the/nowl's legs./n/n"That Umbridge woman's foul," she said in a low/nvoice. "Putting you in detention just because you told/nthe truth about how — how — how he died. Everyone/nheard about it, it was all over the school. You were/nreally brave standing up to her like that."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's insides reinflated so rapidly he felt as though/nhe might actually float a few inches off the dropping-/nstrewn floor. Who cared about a stupid flying horse,/nCho thought he had been really brave... For a/nmoment he considered accidentally-on-purpose/nshowing her his cut hand as he helped her tie her/nparcel onto her owl... But the very instant that this/nthrilling thought occurred, the Owlery door opened/nagain./n/nFilch, the caretaker, came wheezing into the room./nThere were purple patches on his sunken, veined/ncheeks, his jowls were aquiver and his thin gray hair/ndisheveled; he had obviously run here. Mrs. Norris/ncame trotting at his heels, gazing up at the owls/noverhead and mewing hungrily. There was a restless/nshifting of wings from above, and a large brown owl/nsnapped his beak in a menacing fashion./n/n"Aha!" said Filch, taking a flat-footed step toward/nHarry, his pouchy cheeks trembling with anger. "I've/nhad a tip-off that you are intending to place a massive/norder for Dungbombs!"/n/nHarry folded his arms and stared at the caretaker./n/n"Who told you I was ordering Dungbombs?"/n/nCho was looking from Harry to Filch, also frowning;/nthe barn owl on her arm, tired of standing on one leg,/ngave an admonitory hoot but she ignored it./n/n"I have my sources," said Filch in a self-satisfied hiss./n"Now hand over whatever it is you're sending."/n/nFeeling immensely thankful that he had not dawdled/nin posting off the letter, Harry said, "I can't, it's gone."/n/n"Gone?" said Filch, his face contorting with rage./n/n/n/n/n/n"Gone," said Harry calmly./n/n/n/nFilch opened his mouth furiously, mouthed for a few/nseconds, then raked Harry's robes with his eyes. "How/ndo I know you haven't got it in your pocket?"/n/n"Because — "/n/n"I saw him send it," said Cho angrily./n/nFilch rounded on her./n/n"You saw him — ?"/n/n"That's right, I saw him," she said fiercely./n/nThere was a moment's pause in which Filch glared at/nCho and Cho glared right back, then the caretaker/nturned and shuffled back toward the door. He/nstopped with his hand on the handle and looked back/nat Harry./n/n"If I get so much as a whiff of a Dungbomb ..."/n/nHe stumped off down the stairs. Mrs. Norris cast a/nlast longing look at the owls and followed him./n/nHarry and Cho looked at each other./n/n"Thanks," Harry said./n/n"No problem," said Cho, finally fixing the parcel to the/nbarn owl's other leg, her face slightly pink. "You/nweren't ordering Dungbombs, were you?"/n/n"No," said Harry./n/n"I wonder why he thought you were, then?" she said,/nas she carried the owl to the window./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry shrugged; he was quite as mystified by that as/nshe was, though, oddly, it was not bothering him very/nmuch at the moment./n/nThey left the Owlery together. At the entrance of a/ncorridor that led toward the west wing of the castle,/nCho said, "I'm going this way. Well, I'll ... I'll see you/naround, Harry."/n/n"Yeah ... see you."/n/nShe smiled at him and departed. He walked on,/nfeeling quietly elated. He had managed to have an/nentire conversation with her and not embarrassed/nhimself once... You were really brave standing up to/nher like that... She had called him brave... She did not/nhate him for being alive.../n/nOf course, she had preferred Cedric, he knew that.../nThough if he'd only asked her to the ball before Cedric/nhad, things might have turned out differently... She/nhad seemed sincerely sorry that she had to refuse/nwhen Harry had asked her. . ./n/n"Morning," Harry said brightly to Ron and Hermione,/njoining them at the Gryffindor table in the Great Hall./n/n"What are you looking so pleased about?" said Ron,/neyeing Harry in surprise./n/n"Erm ... Quidditch later," said Harry happily, pulling/na large platter of bacon and eggs toward him./n/n"Oh ... yeah ..." said Ron. He put down the bit of toast/nhe was eating and took a large swig of pumpkin juice./nThen he said, "Listen ... you don't fancy going out a/nbit earlier with me, do you? Just to — er — give me/nsome practice before training? So I can, you know, get/nmy eye in a bit ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, okay," said Harry./n/n/n/n"Look, I don't think you should," said Hermione/nseriously, "you're both really behind on homework as/n/n/n/nit — "/n/n/n/nBut she broke off; the morning post was arriving and,/nas usual, the Daily Prophet was soaring toward her in/nthe beak of a screech owl, which landed perilously/nclose to the sugar bowl and held out a leg; Hermione/npushed a Knut into its leather pouch, took the/nnewspaper, and scanned the front page critically as/nthe owl took off again./n/n"Anything interesting?" said Ron; Harry smiled — he/nknew Ron was keen to get her off the subject of/nhomework./n/n"No," she sighed, "just some guff about the bass/nplayer in the Weird Sisters getting married..."/n/nShe opened the paper and disappeared behind it./nHarry devoted himself to another helping of eggs and/nbacon; Ron was staring up at the high windows,/nlooking slightly preoccupied./n/n"Wait a moment," said Hermione suddenly. "Oh no .../nSirius!"/n/n"What's happened?" said Harry, and he snatched at/nthe paper so violently that it ripped down the middle/nso that he and Hermione were holding half each./n/n" 'The Ministry of Magic has received a tip-off from a/nreliable source that Sirius Black, notorious mass/nmurderer . . . blah blah blah ...is currently hiding in/nLondon\ ' " Hermione read from her half in an/nanguished whisper./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Lucius Malfoy, I'll bet anything," said Harry in a low,/nfurious voice. "He did recognize Sirius on the/nplatform..."/n/n"What?" said Ron, looking alarmed. "You didn't say —/n/n/n/n"Shh!" said the other two./n/n"... 'Ministry warns Wizarding community that Black is/nvery dangerous . . . killed thirteen people . . . broke out of/nAzkaban ...' the usual rubbish," Hermione concluded,/nlaying down her half of the paper and looking fearfully/nat Harry and Ron. "Well, he just won't be able to leave/nthe house again, that's all," she whispered./n"Dumbledore did warn him not to."/n/nHarry looked down glumly at the bit of the Prophet he/nhad torn off. Most of the page was devoted to an/nadvertisement for Madame Malkin's Robes for All/nOccasions, which was apparently having a sale./n/n"Hey!" he said, flattening it down so Hermione and/nRon could both see it. "Look at this!"/n/n"I've got all the robes I want," said Ron./n/n"No," said Harry, "look ... this little piece here ..."/n/nRon and Hermione bent closer to read it; the item was/nbarely an inch long and placed right at the bottom of/na column. It was headlined:/n/nTRESPASS AT MINISTRY/n/nSturgis Podmore, 38, of number two, Laburnum/nGardens, Clapham, has appeared in front of the/nWizengamot charged with trespass and attempted/nrobbery at the Ministry of Magic on 31st August./n/n/n/n/n/nPodmore was arrested by Ministry of Magic watch-/nwizard Eric Munch, who found him attempting to/nforce his way through a top-security door at one/no'clock in the morning. Podmore, who refused to/nspeak in his own defense, was convicted on both/ncharges and sentenced to six months in Azkaban./n/n"Sturgis Podmore?" said Ron slowly, "but he's that/nbloke who looks like his head's been thatched, isn't/nhe? He's one of the Ord — "/n/n"Ron, shh\" said Hermione, casting a terrified look/naround them./n/n"Six months in Azkaban!" whispered Harry, shocked./n"Just for trying to get through a door!"/n/n"Don't be silly, it wasn't just for trying to get through/na door — what on earth was he doing at the Ministry/nof Magic at one o'clock in the morning?" breathed/nHermione./n/n"D'you reckon he was doing something for the Order?"/nRon muttered./n/n"Wait a moment..." said Harry slowly. "Sturgis was/nsupposed to come and see us off, remember?"/n/nThe other two looked at him./n/n"Yeah, he was supposed to be part of our guard going/nto King's Cross, remember? And Moody was all/nannoyed because he didn't turn up, so that doesn't/nseem like he was supposed to be on a iob for them,/ndoes it?"/n/n"Well, maybe they didn't expect him to get caught,"/nsaid Hermione./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It could be a frame-up!" Ron exclaimed excitedly. "No/n— listen!" he went on, dropping his voice dramatically/nat the threatening look on Hermione's face. "The/nMinistry suspects he's one of Dumbledore's lot so — I/ndunno — they lured him to the Ministry, and he/nwasn't trying to get through a door at all! Maybe/nthey've just made something up to get him!"/n/nThere was a pause while Harry and Hermione/nconsidered this. Harry thought it seemed far-fetched;/nHermione, on the other hand, looked rather/nimpressed and said, "Do you know, I wouldn't be at/nall surprised if that were true."/n/nShe folded up her half of the newspaper thoughtfully./nWhen Harry laid down his knife and fork she seemed/nto come out of a reverie./n/n"Right, well, I think we should tackle that essay for/nSprout on Self-Fertilizing Shrubs first, and if we're/nlucky we'll be able to start McGonagall's Inanimatus/nConjurus before lunch..."/n/nHarry felt a small twinge of guilt at the thought of the/npile of homework awaiting him upstairs, but the sky/nwas a clear, exhilarating blue, and he had not been/non his Firebolt for a week.../n/n"I mean, we can do it tonight," said Ron, as he and/nHarry walked down the sloping lawns toward the/nQuidditch pitch, their broomsticks over their/nshoulders, Hermione's dire warnings that they would/nfail all their O.W.L.s still ringing in their ears. "And/nwe've got tomorrow. She gets too worked up about/nwork, that's her trouble..." There was a pause and he/nadded, in a slightly more anxious tone, "D'you think/nshe meant it when she said we weren't copying from/nher?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, I do," said Harry. It's just/nbeen Kreacher and me here..."/n/nThere was a definite note of bitterness in Sirius's/nvoice./n/n"So you haven't had any news about Hagrid, either?"/n/n"Ah ..." said Sirius, "well, he was supposed to be back/nby now, no one's sure what's happened to him." Then,/nseeing their stricken faces, he added quickly, "But/nDumbledore's not worried, so don't you three get/nyourselves in a state; I'm sure Hagrid's fine."/n/n"But if he was supposed to be back by now ..." said/nHermione in a small, worried voice./n/n"Madame Maxime was with him, we've been in touch/nwith her and she says they got separated on the/njourney home — but there's nothing to suggest he's/nhurt or — well, nothing to suggest he's not perfectly/nokay."/n/nUnconvinced, Harry, Ron, and Hermione exchanged/nworried looks./n/n"Listen, don't go asking too many questions about/nHagrid," said Sirius hastily, "it'll just draw even more/nattention to the fact that he's not back, and I know/nDumbledore doesn't want that. Hagrid's tough, he'll/nbe okay." And when they did not appear cheered by/nthis, Sirius added, "When's your next Hogsmeade/nweekend anyway? I was thinking, we got away with/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe dog disguise at the station, didn't we? I thought I/ncould — "/n/n/n/n"NO!" said Harry and Hermione together, very loudly./n/n"Sirius, didn't you see the Daily Prophet?" said/nHermione anxiously./n/n"Oh that," said Sirius, grinning, "they're always/nguessing where I am, they haven't really got a clue — "/n/n"Yeah, but we think this time they have," said Harry./n"Something Malfoy said on the train made us think he/nknew it was you, and his father was on the platform,/nSirius — you know, Lucius Malfoy — so don't come/nup here, whatever you do, if Malfoy recognizes you/nagain — "/n/n"All right, all right, I've got the point," said Sirius. He/nlooked most displeased. "Just an idea, thought you/nmight like to get together — "/n/n"I would, I just don't want you chucked back in/nAzkaban!" said Harry./n/nThere was a pause in which Sirius looked out of the/nfire at Harry, a crease between his sunken eyes./n/n"You're less like your father than I thought," he said/nfinally, a definite coolness in his voice. "The risk/nwould've been what made it fun for James."/n/n"Look — "/n/n"Well, I'd better get going, I can hear Kreacher coming/ndown the stairs," said Sirius, but Harry was sure he/nwas lying. "I'll write to tell you a time I can make it/nback into the fire, then, shall I? If you can stand to/nrisk it?"/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was a tiny pop, and the place where Sirius's/nhead had been was flickering flame once more./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Hogwarts High Inquisitor
text: /nThey had expected to have to comb Hermione's Daily/nProphet carefully next morning to find the article/nPercy had mentioned in his letter. However, the/ndeparting delivery owl had barely cleared the top of/nthe milk jug when Hermione let out a huge gasp and/nflattened the newspaper to reveal a large photograph/nof Dolores Umbridge, smiling widely and blinking/nslowly at them from beneath the headline:/n/nMINISTRY SEEKS EDUCATIONAL REFORM/n/nDOLORES UMBRIDGE APPOINTED FIRST-EVER/n"HIGH INQUISITOR"/n/n" "High Inquisitor'?" said Harry darkly, his half-eaten/nbit of toast slipping from his fingers. "What does that/nmean?"/n/nHermione read aloud:/n/n"In a surprise move last night the Ministry of Magic/npassed new legislation giving itself an unprecedented/n/n/n/n/nlevel of control at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and/nWizardry./n/n" 'The Minister has been growing uneasy about goings-/non at Hogwarts for some time,' said Junior Assistant to/nthe Minister, Percy Weasley. 'He is now responding to/nconcerns voiced by anxious parents, who feel the/nschool may be moving in a direction they do not/napprove.'/n/n"This is not the first time in recent weeks Fudge has/nused new laws to effect improvements at the/nWizarding school. As recently as August 30th/nEducational Decree Twenty -two was passed, to ensure/nthat, in the event of the current headmaster being/nunable to provide a candidate for a teaching post, the/nMinistry should select an appropriate person./n/n" 'That's how Dolores Umbridge came to be appointed/nto the teaching staff at Hogwarts,' said Weasley last/nnight. 'Dumbledore couldn't find anyone, so the/nMinister put in Umbridge and of course, she's been an/nimmediate success — ' "/n/n"She's been a WHAT?" said Harry loudly./n/n"Wait, there's more," said Hermione grimly./n/n" ' — an immediate success, totally revolutionizing the/nteaching of Defense Against the Dark Arts and/nproviding the Minister with on-the-ground feedback/nabout what's really happening at Hogwarts.'/n/n"It is this last function that the Ministry has now/nformalized with the passing of Educational Decree/nTwenty-three, which creates the new position of/n'Hogwarts High Inquisitor.'/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" 'This is an exciting new phase in the Minister's plan/nto get to grips with what some are calling the "falling/nstandards" at Hog warts,' said Weasley. 'The Inquisitor/nwill have powers to inspect her fellow educators and/nmake sure that they are coming up to scratch./n/nProfessor Umbridge has been offered this position in/naddition to her own teaching post, and we are/ndelighted to say that she has accepted.'/n/n"The Ministry's new moves have received enthusiastic/nsupport from parents of students at Hogwarts./n/n" 'I feel much easier in my mind now that I know that/nDumbledore is being subjected to fair and objective/nevaluation,' said Mr. Lucius Malfoy, 41, speaking from/nhis Wiltshire mansion last night. 'Many of us with our/nchildren's best interests at heart have been concerned/nabout some of Dumbledore's eccentric decisions in the/nlast few years and will be glad to know that the/nMinistry is keeping an eye on the situation.'/n/n"Among those 'eccentric decisions' are undoubtedly the/ncontroversial staff appointments previously described/nin this newspaper, which have included the hiring of/nwerewolf Remus Lupin, half giant Rubeus Hagrid, and/ndelusional ex-Auror 'Mad-Eye' Moody./n/n"Rumors abound, of course, that Albus Dumbledore,/nonce Supreme Mugwump of the International/nConfederation of Wizards and Chief Warlock of the/nWizengamot, is no longer up to the task of managing/nthe prestigious school of Hogwarts./n/n" 'I think the appointment of the Inquisitor is a first step/ntoward ensuring that Hogwarts has a headmaster in/nwhom we can all repose confidence,' said a Ministry/ninsider last night./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wizengamot elders Gris elda M archbanks and Tiberius/nOgden have resigned in protest at the introduction of/nthe post of Inquisitor to Hogwarts./n/n" 'Hogwarts is a school, not an outpost of Cornelius/nFudge's office,' said Madam Marchbanks. 'This is a/nfurther disgusting attempt to discredit Albus/nDumbledore.' (For a full account of Madam/nMarchbanks' alleged links to subversive goblin groups,/nturn to page 17]."/n/nHermione finished reading and looked across the/ntable at the other two./n/n"So now we know how we ended up with Umbridge!/nFudge passed this 'Educational Decree' and forced/nher on us! And now he's given her the power to/ninspect other teachers!" Hermione was breathing fast/nand her eyes were very bright. "I can't believe this. It's/noutrageous..."/n/n"I know it is," said Harry. He looked down at his right/nhand, clenched upon the tabletop, and saw the faint/nwhite outline of the words Umbridge had forced him/nto cut into his skin./n/nBut a grin was unfurling on Ron's face./n/n"What?" said Harry and Hermione together, staring at/nhim./n/n"Oh, I can't wait to see McGonagall inspected," said/nRon happily. "Umbridge won't know what's hit her."/n/n"Well, come on," said Hermione, jumping up, "we'd/nbetter get going, if she's inspecting Binns's class we/ndon't want to be late..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Professor Umbridge was not inspecting their/nHistory of Magic lesson, which was just as dull as the/nprevious Monday, nor was she in Snape's dungeon/nwhen they arrived for double Potions, where Harry's/nmoonstone essay was handed back to him with a/nlarge, spiky black D scrawled in an upper corner./n/n"I have awarded you the grades you would have/nreceived if you presented this work in your O.W.L,"/nsaid Snape with a smirk, as he swept among them,/npassing back their homework. "This should give you a/nrealistic idea of what to expect in your examination."/n/nSnape reached the front of the class and turned to/nface them./n/n"The general standard of this homework was abysmal./nMost of you would have failed had this been your/nexamination. I expect to see a great deal more effort/nfor this week's essay on the various varieties of venom/nantidotes, or I shall have to start handing out/ndetentions to those dunces who get D's."/n/nHe smirked as Malfoy sniggered and said in a/ncarrying whisper, "Some people got D's? Ha!"/n/nHarry realized that Hermione was looking sideways to/nsee what grade he had received; he slid his/nmoonstone essay back into his bag as quickly as/npossible, feeling that he would rather keep that/ninformation private./n/nDetermined not to give Snape an excuse to fail him/nthis lesson, Harry read and reread every line of the/ninstructions on the blackboard at least three times/nbefore acting on them. His Strengthening Solution/nwas not precisely the clear turquoise shade of/nHermione 's but it was at least blue rather than pink,/nlike Neville's, and he delivered a flask of it to Snape's/n/n/n/n/ndesk at the end of the lesson with a feeling of mingled/ndefiance and relief./n/n"Well, that wasn't as bad as last week, was it?" said/nHermione, as they climbed the steps out of the/ndungeon and made their way across the entrance hall/ntoward lunch. "And the homework didn't go too badly/neither, did it?"/n/nWhen neither Ron nor Harry answered, she pressed/non, "I mean, all right, I didn't expect the top grade,/nnot if he's marking to O.W.L. standard, but a pass is/nquite encouraging at this stage, wouldn't you say?"/n/nHarry made a noncommittal noise in his throat./n/n"Of course, a lot can happen between now and the/nexam, we've got plenty of time to improve, but the/ngrades we're getting now are a sort of baseline, aren't/nthey? Something we can build on ..."/n/nThey sat down together at the Gryffindor table./n/n"Obviously, I'd have been thrilled if I'd gotten an O — "/n/n"Hermione," said Ron sharply, "if you want to know/nwhat grades we got, ask."/n/n"I don't — I didn't mean — well, if you want to tell me/n/n/n/n"I got a P," said Ron, ladling soup into his bowl./n"Happy?"/n/n"Well, that's nothing to be ashamed of," said Fred,/nwho had just arrived at the table with George and Lee/nJordan and was sitting down on Harry's right./n"Nothing wrong with a good healthy P."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But," said Hermione, "doesn't P stand for ..."/n/n" Boor,' yeah," said Lee Jordan. "Still, better than D,/nisn't it? 'Dreadful'?"/n/nHarry felt his face grow warm and faked a small/ncoughing fit over his roll. When he emerged from this/nhe was sorry to find that Hermione was still in full/nflow about O.W.L. grades./n/n"So top grade's O for 'Outstanding,' " she was saying,/n"and then there's A — "/n/n"No, E," George corrected her, "E for 'Exceeds/nExpectations.' And I've always thought Fred and I/nshould've got E in everything, because we exceeded/nexpectations just by turning up for the exams."/n/nThey all laughed except Hermione, who plowed on,/n/n"So after E, it's A for 'Acceptable,' and that's the last/npass grade, isn't it?"/n/n"Yep," said Fred, dunking an entire roll in his soup,/ntransferring it to his mouth, and swallowing it whole./n/n"Then you get P for 'Poor' " — Ron raised both his/narms in mock celebration — "and D for 'Dreadful.' "/n/n"And then T," George reminded him./n/n"T?" asked Hermione, looking appalled. "Even lower/nthan a D? What on earth does that stand for?"/n/n" Troll,' " said George promptly./n/nHarry laughed again, though he was not sure whether/nor not George was joking. He imagined trying to/nconceal from Hermione that he had received T's in all/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhis O.W.L.s and immediately resolved to work harder/nfrom now on./n/n"You lot had an inspected lesson yet?" Fred asked/nthem./n/n"No," said Hermione at once, "have you?"/n/n"Just now, before lunch," said George. "Charms."/n/n"What was it like?" Harry and Hermione asked/ntogether./n/nFred shrugged./n/n"Not that bad. Umbridge just lurked in the corner/nmaking notes on a clipboard. You know what/nFlitwick's like, he treated her like a guest, didn't seem/nto bother him at all. She didn't say much. Asked/nAlicia a couple of questions about what the classes/nare normally like, Alicia told her they were really/ngood, that was it."/n/n"I can't see old Flitwick getting marked down," said/nGeorge, "he usually gets everyone through their/nexams all right."/n/n"Who've you got this afternoon?" Fred asked Harry./n"Trelawney — "/n/n"A T if ever I saw one — "/n/n" — and Umbridge herself."/n/n"Well, be a good boy and keep your temper with/nUmbridge today," said George. "Angelina'll do her nut/nif you miss any more Quidditch practices."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Harry did not have to wait for Defense Against/nthe Dark Arts to meet Professor Umbridge. He was/npulling out his dream diary in a seat at the very back/nof the shadowy Divination room when Ron elbowed/nhim in the ribs and, looking round, he saw Professor/nUmbridge emerging through the trapdoor in the floor./nThe class, which had been talking cheerily, fell silent/nat once. The abrupt fall in the noise level made/nProfessor Trelawney, who had been wafting about/nhanding out Dream Oracles, look round./n/n"Good afternoon, Professor Trelawney," said Professor/nUmbridge with her wide smile. "You received my note,/n/nI trust? Giving the time and date of your inspection?"/n/nProfessor Trelawney nodded curtly and, looking very/ndisgruntled, turned her back on Professor Umbridge/nand continued to give out books. Still smiling,/nProfessor Umbridge grasped the back of the nearest/narmchair and pulled it to the front of the class so that/nit was a few inches behind Professor Trelawney's seat./nShe then sat down, took her clipboard from her/nflowery bag, and looked up expectantly, waiting for/nthe class to begin./n/nProfessor Trelawney pulled her shawls tight about her/nwith slightly trembling hands and surveyed the class/nthrough her hugely magnifying lenses. "We shall be/ncontinuing our study of prophetic dreams today," she/nsaid in a brave attempt at her usual mystic tones,/nthough her voice shook slightly. "Divide into pairs,/nplease, and interpret each other's latest nighttime/nvisions with the aid of the Oracle."/n/nShe made as though to sweep back to her seat, saw/nProfessor Umbridge sitting right beside it, and/nimmediately veered left toward Parvati and Lavender,/nwho were already deep in discussion about Parvati's/nmost recent dream./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry opened his copy of The Dream Oracle, watching/nUmbridge covertly. She was making notes on her/nclipboard now. After a few minutes she got to her feet/nand began to pace the room in Trelawney's wake,/nlistening to her conversations with students and/nposing questions here and there. Harry bent his head/nhurriedly over his book./n/n"Think of a dream, quick," he told Ron, "in case the/nold toad comes our way."/n/n"I did it last time," Ron protested, "it's your turn, you/ntell me one."/n/n"Oh, I dunno ..." said Harry desperately, who could/nnot remember dreaming anything at all over the last/nfew days. "Let's say I dreamed I was ... drowning/nSnape in my cauldron. Yeah, that'll do..."/n/nRon chortled as he opened his Dream Oracle./n/n"Okay, we've got to add your age to the date you had/nthe dream, the number of letters in the subject .../nwould that be 'drowning' or 'cauldron' or 'Snape'?"/n/n"It doesn't matter, pick any of them," said Harry,/nchancing a glance behind him. Professor Umbridge/nwas now standing at Professor Trelawney's shoulder/nmaking notes while the Divination teacher questioned/nNeville about his dream diary./n/n"What night did you dream this again?" Ron said,/nimmersed in calculations./n/n"I dunno, last night, whenever you like," Harry told/nhim, trying to listen to what Umbridge was saying to/nProfessor Trelawney. They were only a table away/nfrom him and Ron now. Professor Umbridge was/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmaking another note on her clipboard and Professor/nTrelawney was looking extremely put out./n/n"Now," said Umbridge, looking up at Trelawney,/n"you've been in this post how long, exactly?"/n/nProfessor Trelawney scowled at her, arms crossed and/nshoulders hunched as though wishing to protect/nherself as much as possible from the indignity of the/ninspection. After a slight pause in which she seemed/nto decide that the question was not so offensive that/nshe could reasonably ignore it, she said in a deeply/nresentful tone, "Nearly sixteen years."/n/n"Quite a period," said Professor Umbridge, making a/nnote on her clipboard. "So it was Professor/nDumbledore who appointed you?"/n/n"That's right," said Professor Trelawney shortly./n/nProfessor Umbridge made another note./n/n"And you are a great-great-granddaughter of the/ncelebrated Seer Cassandra Trelawney?"/n/n"Yes," said Professor Trelawney, holding her head a/nlittle higher./n/nAnother note on the clipboard./n/n"But I think — correct me if I am mistaken — that/nyou are the first in your family since Cassandra to be/npossessed of second sight?"/n/n"These things often skip — er — three generations,"/nsaid Professor Trelawney./n/nProfessor Umbridge's toadlike smile widened./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Of course," she said sweetly, making yet another/nnote. "Well, if you could just predict something for/nme, then?"/n/nShe looked up inquiringly, still smiling. Professor/nTrelawney had stiffened as though unable to believe/nher ears./n/n"I don't understand you," said Professor Trelawney,/nclutching convulsively at the shawl around her/nscrawny neck./n/n"I'd like you to make a prediction for me," said/nProfessor Umbridge very clearly./n/nHarry and Ron were not the only people watching and/nlistening sneakily from behind their books now; most/nof the class were staring transfixed at Professor/nTrelawney as she drew herself up to her full height,/nher beads and bangles clinking./n/n"The Inner Eye does not See upon command!" she/nsaid in scandalized tones./n/n"I see," said Professor Umbridge softly, making yet/nanother note on her clipboard./n/n"I — but — but ... wait\" said Professor Trelawney/nsuddenly, in an attempt at her usual ethereal voice,/nthough the mystical effect was ruined somewhat by/nthe way it was shaking with anger. "I ... I think I do/nsee something ... something that concerns you... Why,/nI sense something . . . something dark . . . some grave/nperil ..."/n/nProfessor Trelawney pointed a shaking finger at/nProfessor Umbridge who continued to smile blandly at/nher, eyebrows raised./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I am afraid ... I am afraid that you are in grave/ndanger!" Professor Trelawney finished dramatically./n/n/n/nThere was a pause. Professor Umbridge's eyebrows/nwere still raised./n/n"Right," she said softly, scribbling on her clipboard/nonce more. "Well, if that's really the best you can do/n/n/n/nShe turned away, leaving Professor Trelawney/nstanding rooted to the spot, her chest heaving. Harry/ncaught Ron's eye and knew that Ron was thinking/nexactly the same as he was: They both knew that/nProfessor Trelawney was an old fraud, but on the/nother hand, they loathed Umbridge so much that they/nfelt very much on Trelawney's side — until she/nswooped down on them a few seconds later, that was./n/n"Well?" she said, snapping her long fingers under/nHarry's nose, uncharacteristically brisk. "Let me see/nthe start you've made on your dream diary, please."/n/nAnd by the time she had interpreted Harry's dreams/nat the top of her voice (all of which, even the ones that/ninvolved eating porridge, apparently foretold a/ngruesome and early death), he was feeling much less/nsympathetic toward her. All the while, Professor/nUmbridge stood a few feet away, making notes on that/nclipboard, and when the bell rang she descended the/nsilver ladder first so that she was waiting for them all/nwhen they reached their Defense Against the Dark/nArts lesson ten minutes later./n/nShe was humming and smiling to herself when they/nentered the room. Harry and Ron told Hermione, who/nhad been in Arithmancy, exactly what had happened/nin Divination while they all took out their copies of/nDefensive Magical Theory, but before Hermione could/n/n/n/n/nask any questions Professor Umbridge had called/nthem all to order and silence fell./n/n"Wands away," she instructed them all smilingly, and/nthose people who had been hopeful enough to take/nthem out sadly returned them to their bags. "As we/nfinished chapter one last lesson, I would like you all/nto turn to page nineteen today and commence chapter/ntwo, 'Common Defensive Theories and Their/nDerivation. ' There will be no need to talk."/n/nStill smiling her wide, self-satisfied smile, she sat/ndown at her desk. The class gave an audible sigh as it/nturned, as one, to page nineteen. Harry wondered/ndully whether there were enough chapters in the book/nto keep them reading through all this year's lessons/nand was on the point of checking the contents when/nhe noticed that Hermione had her hand in the air/nagain./n/nProfessor Umbridge had noticed too, and what was/nmore, she seemed to have worked out a strategy for/njust such an eventuality. Instead of trying to pretend/nshe had not noticed Hermione, she got to her feet and/nwalked around the front row of desks until they were/nface-to-face, then she bent down and whispered, so/nthat the rest of the class could not hear, "What is it/nthis time, Miss Granger?"/n/n"I've already read chapter two," said Hermione./n/n"Well then, proceed to chapter three."/n/n"I've read that too. I've read the whole book."/n/nProfessor Umbridge blinked but recovered her poise/nalmost instantly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, then, you should be able to tell me what/nSlinkhard says about counterjinxes in chapter/nfifteen."/n/n/n/n"He says that counterjinxes are improperly named,"/nsaid Hermione promptly. "He says 'counterjinx' is just/na name people give their jinxes when they want to/nmake them sound more acceptable."/n/nProfessor Umbridge raised her eyebrows, and Harry/nknew she was impressed against her will./n/n"But I disagree," Hermione continued./n/nProfessor Umbridge's eyebrows rose a little higher and/nher gaze became distinctly colder./n/n"You disagree?"/n/n"Yes, I do," said Hermione, who, unlike Umbridge,/nwas not whispering, but speaking in a clear, carrying/nvoice that had by now attracted the rest of the class's/nattention. "Mr. Slinkhard doesn't like jinxes, does he?/nBut I think they can be very useful when they're used/ndefensively."/n/n"Oh, you do, do you?" said Professor Umbridge,/nforgetting to whisper and straightening up. "Well, I'm/nafraid it is Mr. Slinkhard 's opinion, and not yours,/nthat matters within this classroom, Miss Granger."/n/n"But — " Hermione began./n/n"That is enough," said Professor Umbridge. She/nwalked back to the front of the class and stood before/nthem, all the jauntiness she had shown at the/nbeginning of the lesson gone. "Miss Granger, I am/ngoing to take five points from Gryffindor House."/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was an outbreak of muttering at this./n/n"What for?" said Harry angrily./n/n"Don't you get involved!" Hermione whispered/nurgently to him./n/n"For disrupting my class with pointless/ninterruptions," said Professor Umbridge smoothly. "I/nam here to teach you using a Ministry-approved/nmethod that does not include inviting students to give/ntheir opinions on matters about which they/nunderstand very little. Your previous teachers in this/nsubject may have allowed you more license, but as/nnone of them — with the possible exception of/nProfessor Quirrell, who did at least appear to have/nrestricted himself to age-appropriate subjects —/nwould have passed a Ministry inspection — "/n/n"Yeah, Quirrell was a great teacher," said Harry/nloudly, "there was just that minor drawback of him/nhaving Lord Voldemort sticking out of the back of his/nhead."/n/nThis pronouncement was followed by one of the/nloudest silences Harry had ever heard. Then —/n/n"I think another week's detentions would do you some/ngood, Mr. Potter," said Umbridge sleekly./n/nk k k/n/n/n/nThe cut on the back of Harry's hand had barely/nhealed and by the following morning, it was bleeding/nagain. He did not complain during the evening's/ndetention; he was determined not to give Umbridge/nthe satisfaction; over and over again he wrote I must/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nnot tell lies and not a sound escaped his lips, though/nthe cut deepened with every letter./n/nThe very worst part of this second week's worth of/ndetentions was, just as George had predicted,/nAngelina's reaction. She cornered him just as he/narrived at the Gryffindor table for breakfast on/nTuesday and shouted so loudly that Professor/nMcGonagall came sweeping down upon the pair of/nthem from the staff table./n/n"Miss Johnson, how dare you make such a racket in/nthe Great Hall! Five points from Gryffindor!"/n/n"But Professor — he's gone and landed himself in/ndetention again — "/n/n"What's this, Potter?" said Professor McGonagall/nsharply, rounding on Harry. "Detention? From/nwhom?"/n/n"From Professor Umbridge," muttered Harry, not/nmeeting Professor McGonagall's beady, square-framed/neyes./n/n"Are you telling me," she said, lowering her voice so/nthat the group of curious Ravenclaws behind them/ncould not hear, "that after the warning I gave you last/nMonday you lost your temper in Professor Umbridge's/nclass again?"/n/n"Yes," Harry muttered, speaking to the floor./n/n"Potter, you must get a grip on yourself! You are/nheading for serious trouble! Another five points from/nGryffindor!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But — what? Professor, no!" Harry said, furious at/nthis injustice. "I'm already being punished by her,/nwhy do you have to take points as well?"/n/n"Because detentions do not appear to have any effect/non you whatsoever!" said Professor McGonagall tartly./n"No, not another word of complaint, Potter! And as for/nyou, Miss Johnson, you will confine your shouting/nmatches to the Quidditch pitch in future or risk/nlosing the team Captaincy!"/n/nShe strode back toward the staff table. Angelina gave/nHarry a look of deepest disgust and stalked away,/nupon which Harry flung himself onto the bench/nbeside Ron, fuming./n/n"She's taken points off Gryffindor because I'm having/nmy hand sliced open every night! How is that fair,/nhow?"/n/n"I know, mate," said Ron sympathetically, tipping/nbacon onto Harry's plate, "she's bang out of order."/n/nHermione, however, merely rustled the pages of her/nDaily Prophet and said nothing./n/n"You think McGonagall was right, do you?" said Harry/nangrily to the picture of Cornelius Fudge obscuring/nHermione 's face./n/n"I wish she hadn't taken points from you, but I think/nshe's right to warn you not to lose your temper with/nUmbridge," said Hermione's voice, while Fudge/ngesticulated forcefully from the front page, clearly/ngiving some kind of speech./n/nHarry did not speak to Hermione all through Charms,/nbut when they entered Transfiguration he forgot his/nanger; Professor Umbridge and her clipboard were/n/n/n/n/n/nsitting in a corner and the sight of her drove the/nmemory of breakfast right out of his head./n/n"Excellent," whispered Ron, as they sat down in their/nusual seats. "Let's see Umbridge get what she/ndeserves."/n/nProfessor McGonagall marched into the room without/ngiving the slightest indication that she knew Professor/nUmbridge was there./n/n"That will do," she said and silence fell immediately./n"Mr. Finnigan, kindly come here and hand back the/nhomework — Miss Brown, please take this box of/nmice — don't be silly, girl, they won't hurt you — and/nhand one to each student — "/n/n"Hem, hem," said Professor Umbridge, employing the/nsame silly little cough she had used to interrupt/nDumbledore on the first night of term. Professor/nMcGonagall ignored her. Seamus handed back/nHarry's essay; Harry took it without looking at him/nand saw, to his relief, that he had managed an A./n/n"Right then, everyone, listen closely — Dean Thomas,/nif you do that to the mouse again I shall put you in/ndetention — most of you have now successfully/nvanished your snails and even those who were left/nwith a certain amount of shell have the gist of the/nspell. Today we shall be — "/n/n"Hem, hem," said Professor Umbridge./n/n"Yes?" said Professor McGonagall, turning round, her/neyebrows so close together they seemed to form one/nlong, severe line./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I was just wondering, Professor, whether you/nreceived my note telling you of the date and time of/nyour inspec — "/n/n"Obviously I received it, or I would have asked you/nwhat you are doing in my classroom," said Professor/nMcGonagall, turning her back firmly on Professor/nUmbridge. Many of the students exchanged looks of/nglee. "As I was saying, today we shall be practicing/nthe altogether more difficult vanishment of mice. Now,/nthe Vanishing Spell — "/n/n"Hem, hem."/n/n"I wonder," said Professor McGonagall in cold fury,/nturning on Professor Umbridge, "how you expect to/ngain an idea of my usual teaching methods if you/ncontinue to interrupt me? You see, I do not generally/npermit people to talk when I am talking."/n/nProfessor Umbridge looked as though she had just/nbeen slapped in the face. She did not speak, but/nstraightened the parchment on her clipboard and/nbegan scribbling furiously. Looking supremely/nunconcerned, Professor McGonagall addressed the/nclass once more./n/n"As I was saying, the Vanishing Spell becomes more/ndifficult with the complexity of the animal to be/nvanished. The snail, as an invertebrate, does not/npresent much of a challenge; the mouse, as a/nmammal, offers a much greater one. This is not,/ntherefore, magic you can accomplish with your mind/non your dinner. So — you know the incantation, let/nme see what you can do..."/n/n"How she can lecture me about not losing my temper/nwith Umbridge!" Harry said to Ron under his voice,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbut he was grinning; his anger with Professor/nMcGonagall had quite evaporated./n/nProfessor Umbridge did not follow Professor/nMcGonagall around the class as she had followed/nProfessor Trelawney; perhaps she thought that/nProfessor McGonagall would not permit it. She did,/nhowever, take many more notes while she sat in her/ncorner, and when Professor McGonagall finally told/nthem all to pack away, rose with a grim expression on/nher face./n/n"Well, it's a start," said Ron, holding up a long,/nwriggling mouse tail and dropping it back into the box/nLavender was passing around./n/nAs they filed out of the classroom, Harry saw/nProfessor Umbridge approach the teacher's desk; he/nnudged Ron, who nudged Hermione in turn, and the/nthree of them deliberately fell back to eavesdrop./n/n"How long have you been teaching at Hogwarts?"/nProfessor Umbridge asked./n/n"Thirty-nine years this December," said Professor/nMcGonagall brusquely, snapping her bag shut./n/nProfessor Umbridge made a note./n/n"Very well," she said, "you will receive the results of/nyour inspection in ten days' time."/n/n"I can hardly wait," said Professor McGonagall in a/ncoldly indifferent voice, and she strode off toward the/ndoor. "Hurry up, you three," she added, sweeping/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione before her. Harry could not/nhelp giving her a faint smile and could have sworn he/nreceived one in return./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe had thought that the next time he would see/nUmbridge would be in his detention that evening, but/nhe was wrong. When they walked down the lawns/ntoward the forest for Care of Magical Creatures, they/nfound her and her clipboard waiting for them beside/nProfessor Grubbly-Plank./n/n"You do not usually take this class, is that correct?"/nHarry heard her ask as they arrived at the trestle/ntable where the group of captive bowtruckles were/nscrabbling around for wood lice like so many living/ntwigs./n/n"Quite correct," said Professor Grubbly-Plank, hands/nbehind her back and bouncing on the balls of her/nfeet. "I am a substitute teacher standing in for/nProfessor Hagrid."/n/nHarry exchanged uneasy looks with Ron and/nHermione. Malfoy was whispering with Crabbe and/nGoyle; he would surely love this opportunity to tell/ntales on Hagrid to a member of the Ministry./n/n"Hmm," said Professor Umbridge, dropping her voice,/nthough Harry could still hear her quite clearly, "I/nwonder — the headmaster seems strangely reluctant/nto give me any information on the matter — can you/ntell me what is causing Professor Hagrid's very/nextended leave of absence?"/n/nHarry saw Malfoy look up eagerly./n/n" 'Fraid I can't," said Professor Grubbly-Plank/nbreezily. "Don't know anything more about it than/nyou do. Got an owl from Dumbledore, would I like a/ncouple of weeks teaching work, accepted — that's as/nmuch as I know. Well ... shall I get started then?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, please do," said Professor Umbridge, scribbling/nupon her clipboard./n/nUmbridge took a different tack in this class and/nwandered among the students, questioning them on/nmagical creatures. Most people were able to answer/nwell and Harry's spirits lifted somewhat; at least the/nclass was not letting Hagrid down./n/n"Overall," said Professor Umbridge, returning to/nProfessor Grubbly-Plank's side after a lengthy/ninterrogation of Dean Thomas, "how do you, as a/ntemporary member of staff — an objective outsider, I/nsuppose you might say — how do you find Hogwarts?/nDo you feel you receive enough support from the/nschool management?"/n/n"Oh, yes, Dumbledore's excellent," said Professor/nGrubbly-Plank heartily. "No, I'm very happy with the/nway things are run, very happy indeed."/n/nLooking politely incredulous, Umbridge made a tiny/nnote on her clipboard and went on, "And what are you/nplanning to cover with this class this year —/nassuming, of course, that Professor Hagrid does not/nreturn?"/n/n"Oh, I'll take them through the creatures that most/noften come up in O.W.L.," said Professor Grubbly-/nPlank. "Not much left to do — they've studied/nunicorns and nifflers, I thought we'd cover porlocks/nand kneazles, make sure they can recognize crups/nand knarls, you know..."/n/n"Well, you seem to know what you're doing, at any/nrate," said Professor Umbridge, making a very obvious/ntick on her clipboard. Harry did not like the emphasis/nshe put on "you" and liked it even less when she put/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nher next question to Goyle: "Now, I hear there have/nbeen injuries in this class?"/n/nGoyle gave a stupid grin. Malfoy hastened to answer/nthe question./n/n"That was me," he said. "I was slashed by a/nhippogriff."/n/n"A hippogriff?" said Professor Umbridge, now/nscribbling frantically./n/n"Only because he was too stupid to listen to what/nHagrid told him to do," said Harry angrily./n/nBoth Ron and Hermione groaned. Professor Umbridge/nturned her head slowly in Harry's direction./n/n"Another night's detention, I think," she said softly./n"Well, thank you very much, Professor Grubbly-Plank,/nI think that's all I need here. You will be receiving the/nresults of your inspection within ten days."/n/n"Jolly good," said Professor Grubbly-Plank, and/nProfessor Umbridge set off back across the lawn to/nthe castle./n/n/n/nie ie ie/n/n/n/nIt was nearly midnight when Harry left Umbridge's/noffice that night, his hand now bleeding so severely/nthat it was staining the scarf he had wrapped around/nit. He expected the common room to be empty when/nhe returned, but Ron and Hermione had sat up/nwaiting for him. He was pleased to see them,/nespecially as Hermione was disposed to be/nsympathetic rather than critical./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Here," she said anxiously, pushing a small bowl of/nyellow liquid toward him, "soak your hand in that, it's/na solution of strained and pickled murtlap tentacles,/nit should help."/n/nHarry placed his bleeding, aching hand into the bowl/nand experienced a wonderful feeling of relief./nCrookshanks curled around his legs, purring loudly,/nand then leapt into his lap and settled down./n/n"Thanks," he said gratefully, scratching behind/nCrookshanks 's ears with his left hand./n/n"I still reckon you should complain about this," said/nRon in a low voice./n/n"No," said Harry flatly./n/n"McGonagall would go nuts if she knew — "/n/n"Yeah, she probably would," said Harry. "And how/nlong d'you reckon it'd take Umbridge to pass another/nDecree saying anyone who complains about the High/nInquisitor gets sacked immediately?"/n/nRon opened his mouth to retort but nothing came out/nand after a moment he closed it again in a defeated/nsort of way./n/n"She's an awful woman," said Hermione in a small/nvoice. "Awful. You know, I was just saying to Ron/nwhen you came in ... we've got to do something about/nher." "/n/n"I suggested poison," said Ron grimly./n/n"No ... I mean, something about what a dreadful/nteacher she is, and how we're not going to learn any/ndefense from her at all," said Hermione./n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, what can we do about that?" said Ron,/nyawning. " 'S too late, isn't it? She got the job, she's/nhere to stay, Fudge'll make sure of that."/n/n"Well," said Hermione tentatively. "You know, I was/nthinking today..." She shot a slightly nervous look at/nHarry and then plunged on, "I was thinking that —/nmaybe the time's come when we should just — just/ndo it ourselves."/n/n"Do what ourselves?" said Harry suspiciously, still/nfloating his hand in the essence of murtlap tentacles./n/n"Well — learn Defense Against the Dark Arts/nourselves," said Hermione./n/n"Come off it," groaned Ron. "You want us to do extra/nwork? D'you realize Harry and I are behind on/nhomework again and it's only the second week?"/n/n"But this is much more important than homework!"/nsaid Hermione./n/nHarry and Ron goggled at her./n/n"I didn't think there was anything in the universe/nmore important than homework," said Ron./n/n"Don't be silly, of course there is!" said Hermione, and/nHarry saw, with an ominous feeling, that her face was/nsuddenly alight with the kind of fervor that S.P.E.W./nusually inspired in her. "It's about preparing/nourselves, like Harry said in Umbridge's first lesson,/nfor what's waiting out there. It's about making sure/nwe really can defend ourselves. If we don't learn/nanything for a whole year — "/n/n"We can't do much by ourselves," said Ron in a/ndefeated voice. "I mean, all right, we can go and look/n/n/n/n/n/njinxes up in the library and try and practice them, I/nsuppose — "/n/n"No, I agree, we've gone past the stage where we can/njust learn things out of books," said Hermione. "We/nneed a teacher, a proper one, who can show us how/nto use the spells and correct us if we're going wrong."/n/n"If you're talking about Lupin ..." Harry began./n/n"No, no, I'm not talking about Lupin," said Hermione./n"He's too busy with the Order and anyway, the most/nwe could see him is during Hogsmeade weekends and/nthat's not nearly often enough."/n/n"Who, then?" said Harry, frowning at her./n/nHermione heaved a very deep sigh./n/n"Isn't it obvious?" she said. "I'm talking about you,/nHarry."/n/nThere was a moment's silence. A light night breeze/nrattled the windowpanes behind Ron and the fire/nguttered./n/n"About me what?" said Harry./n/n"I'm talking about you teaching us Defense Against/nthe Dark Arts."/n/nHarry stared at her. Then he turned to Ron, ready to/nexchange the exasperated looks they sometimes/nshared when Hermione elaborated on far-fetched/nschemes like S.P.E.W. To Harry's consternation,/nhowever, Ron did not look exasperated. He was/nfrowning slightly, apparently thinking. Then he said,/n"That's an idea."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's an idea?" said Harry./n/n"You," said Ron. "Teaching us to do it."/n/n"But ..."/n/nHarry was grinning now, sure the pair of them were/npulling his leg./n/n"But I'm not a teacher, I can't — "/n/n"Harry, you're the best in the year at Defense Against/nthe Dark Arts," said Hermione./n/n"Me?" said Harry, now grinning more broadly than/never. "No I'm not, you've beaten me in every test — "/n/n"Actually, I haven't," said Hermione coolly. "You beat/nme in our third year — the only year we both sat the/ntest and had a teacher who actually knew the subject/nBut I'm not talking about test results, Harry. Look/nwhat you've done\"/n/n"How d'you mean?"/n/n"You know what, I'm not sure I want someone this/nstupid teaching me," Ron said to Hermione, smirking/nslightly. He turned to Harry. "Let's think," he said,/npulling a face like Goyle concentrating. "Uh . . . first/nyear — you saved the Stone from You-Know-Who."/n/n"But that was luck," said Harry, "that wasn't skill — "/n/n"Second year," Ron interrupted, "you killed the/nbasilisk and destroyed Riddle."/n/n"Yeah, but if Fawkes hadn't turned up I — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Third year," said Ron, louder still, "you fought off/nabout a hundred dementors at once — "/n/n"You know that was a fluke, if the Time-Turner hadn't/n??/n/n/n/n"Last year," Ron said, almost shouting now, "you/nfought off You-Know-Who again — "/n/n"Listen to me!" said Harry, almost angrily, because/nRon and Hermione were both smirking now. "Just/nlisten to me, all right? It sounds great when you say it/nlike that, but all that stuff was luck — I didn't know/nwhat I was doing half the time, I didn't plan any of it,/n/nI just did whatever I could think of, and I nearly/nalways had help — "/n/nRon and Hermione were still smirking and Harry felt/nhis temper rise; he wasn't even sure why he was/nfeeling so angry./n/n"Don't sit there grinning like you know better than I/ndo, I was there, wasn't I?" he said heatedly. "I know/nwhat went on, all right? And I didn't get through any/nof that because I was brilliant at Defense Against the/nDark Arts, I got through it all because — because/nhelp came at the right time, or because I guessed/nright — but I just blundered through it all, I didn't/nhave a clue what I was doing — STOP LAUGHING!"/n/nThe bowl of murtlap essence fell to the floor and/nsmashed. He became aware that he was on his feet,/nthough he couldn't remember standing up./nCrookshanks streaked away under a sofa; Ron and/nHermione 's smiles had vanished./n/n" You don't know what it's likel You — neither of you/n— you've never had to face him, have you? You think/nit's just memorizing a bunch of spells and throwing/n/n/n/n/n/nthem at him, like you're in class or something? The/nwhole time you know there's nothing between you/nand dying except your own — your own brain or guts/nor whatever — like you can think straight when you/nknow you're about a second from being murdered, or/ntortured, or watching your friends die — they've never/ntaught us that in their classes, what it's like to deal/nwith things like that — and you two sit there acting/nlike I'm a clever little boy to be standing here, alive,/nlike Diggory was stupid, like he messed up — you just/ndon't get it, that could just as easily have been me, it/nwould have been if Voldemort hadn't needed me — "/n/n"We weren't saying anything like that, mate," said/nRon, looking aghast. "We weren't having a go at/nDiggory, we didn't — you've got the wrong end of the/n/n/n/nHe looked helplessly at Hermione, whose face was/nstricken./n/n"Harry," she said timidly, "don't you see? This ... this/nis exactly why we need you... We need to know what/nit's r-really like ... facing him ... facing V-Voldemort."/n/nIt was the first time she had ever said Voldemort's/nname, and it was this, more than anything else, that/ncalmed Harry. Still breathing hard, he sank back into/nhis chair, becoming aware as he did so that his hand/nwas throbbing horribly again. He wished he had not/nsmashed the bowl of murtlap essence./n/n"Well ... think about it," said Hermione quietly./n"Please?"/n/nHarry could not think of anything to say. He was/nfeeling ashamed of his outburst already. He nodded,/nhardly aware of what he was agreeing to./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione stood up./n/n"Well, I'm off to bed," she said in a voice that was/nclearly as natural as she could make it. "Erm .../n'night."/n/nRon had gotten to his feet too./n/n"Coming?" he said awkwardly to Harry./n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "In ... in a minute. I'll just clear/nthis up."/n/nHe indicated the smashed bowl on the floor. Ron/nnodded and left./n/n"Reparo," Harry muttered, pointing his wand at the/nbroken pieces of china. They flew back together, good/nas new, but there was no returning the murtlap/nessence to the bowl./n/nHe was suddenly so tired that he was tempted to sink/nback into his armchair and sleep there, but instead/nhe got to his feet and followed Ron upstairs. His/nrestless night was punctuated once more by dreams/nof long corridors and locked doors, and he awoke next/nday with his scar prickling again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: In The Hog's Head
text: /nHermione made no mention of Harry giving Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts lessons for two whole weeks/nafter her original suggestion. Harry's detentions with/nUmbridge were finally over (he doubted whether the/nwords now etched on the back of his hand would ever/nfade entirely); Ron had had four more Quidditch/npractices and not been shouted at during the last/ntwo; and all three of them had managed to vanish/ntheir mice in Transfiguration (Hermione had actually/nprogressed to vanishing kittens), before the subject/nwas broached again, on a wild, blustery evening at/nthe end of September, when the three of them were/nsitting in the library, looking up potion ingredients for/nSnape./n/n"I was wondering," Hermione said suddenly, "whether/nyou'd thought any more about Defense Against the/nDark Arts, Harry."/n/n" 'Course I have," said Harry grumpily. "Can't forget it,/ncan we, with that hag teaching us — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I meant the idea Ron and I had" — Ron cast her an/nalarmed, threatening kind of look; she frowned at him/n— "oh, all right, the idea / had, then — about you/nteaching us."/n/nHarry did not answer at once. He pretended to be/nperusing a page of Asiatic Anti-Venoms, because he/ndid not want to say what was in his mind./n/nThe fact was that he had given the matter a great deal/nof thought over the past fortnight. Sometimes it/nseemed an insane idea, just as it had on the night/nHermione had proposed it, but at others, he had/nfound himself thinking about the spells that had/nserved him best in his various encounters with Dark/ncreatures and Death Eaters — found himself, in fact,/nsubconsciously planning lessons.../n/n"Well," he said slowly, when he could not pretend to/nfind Asiatic anti-venoms interesting much longer,/n"yeah, I — I've thought about it a bit."/n/n"And?" said Hermione eagerly./n/n"I dunno," said Harry, playing for time. He looked up/nat Ron./n/n"I thought it was a good idea from the start," said/nRon, who seemed keener to join in this conversation/nnow that he was sure that Harry was not going to/nstart shouting again./n/nHarry shifted uncomfortably in his chair./n/n"You did listen to what I said about a load of it being/nluck, didn't you?"/n/n"Yes, Harry," said Hermione gently, "but all the same,/nthere's no point pretending that you're not good at/n/n/n/n/n/nDefense Against the Dark Arts, because you are. You/nwere the only person last year who could throw off the/nImperius Curse completely, you can produce a/nPatronus, you can do all sorts of stuff that full-grown/nwizards can't, Viktor always said — "/n/nRon looked around at her so fast he appeared to crick/nhis neck; rubbing it, he said, "Yeah? What did Vicky/nsay?"/n/n"Ho ho," said Hermione in a bored voice. "He said/nHarry knew how to do stuff even he didn't, and he/nwas in the final year at Durmstrang."/n/nRon was looking at Hermione suspiciously./n/n"You're not still in contact with him, are you?"/n/n"So what if I am?" said Hermione coolly, though her/nface was a little pink. "I can have a pen pal if I — "/n/n"He didn't only want to be your pen pal," said Ron/naccusingly./n/nHermione shook her head exasperatedly and, ignoring/nRon, who was continuing to watch her, said to Harry,/n"Well, what do you think? Will you teach us?"/n/n"Just you and Ron, yeah?"/n/n"Well," said Hermione, now looking a mite anxious/nagain. "Well ... now, don't fly off the handle again,/nHarry, please... But I really think you ought to teach/nanyone who wants to learn. I mean, we're talking/nabout defending ourselves against V-Voldemort — oh,/ndon't be pathetic, Ron — it doesn't seem fair if we/ndon't offer the chance to other people."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry considered this for a moment, then said, "Yeah,/nbut I doubt anyone except you two would want to be/ntaught by me. I'm a nutter, remember?"/n/n"Well, I think you might be surprised how many/npeople would be interested in hearing what you've got/nto say," said Hermione seriously. "Look," she leaned/ntoward him; Ron, who was still watching her with a/nfrown on his face, leaned forward to listen too, "you/nknow the first weekend in October's a Hogsmeade/nweekend? How would it be if we tell anyone who's/ninterested to meet us in the village and we can talk it/nover?"/n/n"Why do we have to do it outside school?" said Ron./n/n"Because," said Hermione, returning to the diagram of/nthe Chinese Chomping Cabbage she was copying, "I/ndon't think Umbridge would be very happy if she/nfound out what we were up to."/n/nHarry had been looking forward to the weekend trip/ninto Hogsmeade, but there was one thing worrying/nhim. Sirius had maintained a stony silence since he/nhad appeared in the fire at the beginning of/nSeptember; Harry knew they had made him angry by/nsaying that they did not want him to come — but he/nstill worried from time to time that Sirius might throw/ncaution to the winds and turn up anyway. What were/nthey going to do if the great black dog came bounding/nup the street toward them in Hogsmeade, perhaps/nunder the nose of Draco Malfoy?/n/n"Well, you can't blame him for wanting to get out and/nabout," said Ron, when Harry discussed his fears/nwith him and Hermione. "I mean, he's been on the/nrun for over two years, hasn't he, and I know that/ncan't have been a laugh, but at least he was free,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwasn't he? And now he's just shut up all the time/nwith that lunatic elf."/n/nHermione scowled at Ron, but otherwise ignored the/nslight on Kreacher./n/n"The trouble is," she said to Harry, "until V-Voldemort/n— oh for heaven's sake, Ron — comes out into the/nopen, Sirius is going to have to stay hidden, isn't he? I/nmean, the stupid Ministry isn't going to realize Sirius/nis innocent until they accept that Dumbledore's been/ntelling the truth about him all along. And once the/nfools start catching real Death Eaters again it'll be/nobvious Sirius isn't one ... I mean, he hasn't got the/nMark, for one thing."/n/n"I don't reckon he'd be stupid enough to turn up,"/nsaid Ron bracingly. "Dumbledore'd go mad if he did/nand Sirius listens to Dumbledore even if he doesn't/nlike what he hears."/n/nWhen Harry continued to look worried, Hermione/nsaid, "Listen, Ron and I have been sounding out/npeople who we thought might want to learn some/nproper Defense Against the Dark Arts, and there are a/ncouple who seem interested. We've told them to meet/nus in Hogsmeade."/n/n"Right," said Harry vaguely, his mind still on Sirius./n/n"Don't worry, Harry," Hermione said quietly. "You've/ngot enough on your plate without Sirius too."/n/nShe was quite right, of course; he was barely keeping/nup with his homework, though he was doing much/nbetter now that he was no longer spending every/nevening in detention with Umbridge. Ron was even/nfurther behind with his work than Harry, because/nwhile they both had Quidditch practices twice a week,/n/n/n/n/nRon also had prefect duties. However, Hermione, who/nwas taking more subjects than either of them, had/nnot only finished all her homework but was also/nfinding time to knit more elf clothes. Harry had to/nadmit that she was getting better; it was now almost/nalways possible to distinguish between the hats and/nthe socks./n/nThe morning of the Hogsmeade visit dawned bright/nbut windy. After breakfast they queued up in front of/nFilch, who matched their names to the long list of/nstudents who had permission from their parents or/nguardian to visit the village. With a slight pang, Harry/nremembered that if it hadn't been for Sirius, he would/nnot have been going at all./n/nWhen Harry reached Filch, the caretaker gave a great/nsniff as though trying to detect a whiff of something/nfrom Harry. Then he gave a curt nod that set his jowls/naquiver again and Harry walked on, out onto the/nstone steps and the cold, sunlit day./n/n"Er — why was Filch sniffing you?" asked Ron, as he,/nHarry, and Hermione set off at a brisk pace down the/nwide drive to the gates./n/n"I suppose he was checking for the smell of/nDungbombs," said Harry with a small laugh.
