Hermione rolled her eyes at/nHarry and then said in an undertone, while Ron was/nmuttering imprecations about Michael Corner, "And/ntalking about Michael and Ginny . . . what about Cho/nand you?"/n/n"What d'you mean?" said Harry quickly./n/nIt was as though boiling water was rising rapidly/ninside him; a burning sensation that was causing his/nface to smart in the cold — had he been that obvious?/n/n"Well," said Hermione, smiling slightly, "she just/ncouldn't keep her eyes off you, could she?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry had never before appreciated just how beautiful/nthe village of Hogsmeade was./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Educational Decree Number Twenty-Four
text: /nHarry felt happier for the rest of the weekend than he/nhad done all term. He and Ron spent much of Sunday/ncatching up with all their homework again, and/nalthough this could hardly be called fun, the last/nburst of autumn sunshine persisted, so rather than/nsitting hunched over tables in the common room, they/ntook their work outside and lounged in the shade of a/nlarge beech tree on the edge of the lake. Hermione,/nwho of course was up to date with all her work,/nbrought more wool outside with her and bewitched/nher knitting needles so that they flashed and clicked/nin midair beside her, producing more hats and/nscarves./n/nThe knowledge that they were doing something to/nresist Umbridge and the Ministry, and that he was a/nkey part of the rebellion, gave Harry a feeling of/nimmense satisfaction. He kept reliving Saturday's/nmeeting in his mind: all those people, coming to him/nto learn Defense Against the Dark Arts . . . and the/nlooks on their faces as they had heard some of the/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthings he had done . . . and Cho praising his/nperformance in the Triwizard Tournament... The/nknowledge that all those people did not think him a/nlying weirdo, but someone to be admired, buoyed him/nup so much that he was still cheerful on Monday/nmorning, despite the imminent prospect of all his/nleast favorite classes./n/nHe and Ron headed downstairs from their dormitory/ntogether, discussing Angelina's idea that they were to/nwork on a new move called the Sloth Grip Roll during/nthat night's Quidditch practice, and not until they/nwere halfway across the sunlit common room did they/nnotice the addition to the room that had already/nattracted the attention of a small group of people./n/nA large sign had been affixed to the Gryffindor notice/nboard, so large that it covered everything else on there/n— the lists of secondhand spellbooks for sale, the/nregular reminders of school rules from Argus Filch,/nthe Quidditch team training schedule, the offers to/nbarter certain Chocolate Frog cards for others, the/nWeasleys' new advertisement for testers, the dates of/nthe Hogsmeade weekends, and the lost-and-found/nnotices. The new sign was printed in large black/nletters and there was a highly official-looking seal at/nthe bottom beside a neat and curly signature./n/n/n/n— BY ORDER OF —/n/nTHE HIGH INQUISITOR OF HOGWARTS/n/nAll Student Organizations, Societies, Teams, Groups,/nand Clubs are henceforth disbanded./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAn Organization, Society, Team, Group, or Club is/nhereby defined as a regular meeting of three or more/nstudents./n/nPermission to re-form may be sought from the High/nInquisitor (Professor Umbridge)./n/nNo Student Organization, Society, Team, Group, or/nClub may exist without the knowledge and approval/nof the High Inquisitor./n/nAny student found to have formed, or to belong to, an/nOrganization, Society, Team, Group, or Club that has/nnot been approved by the High Inquisitor will be/nexpelled./n/nThe above is in accordance with/nEducational Decree Number Twenty-four./n/nSigned:/n/nDolores Jane Umbridge/nHIGH INQUISITOR/n/nHarry and Ron read the notice over the heads of some/nanxious-looking second years./n/n"Does this mean they're going to shut down the/nGobstones Club?" one of them asked his friend./n/n"I reckon you'll be okay with Gobstones," Ron said/ndarkly, making the second year jump. "I don't think/nwe're going to be as lucky, though, do you?" he asked/nHarry as the second years hurried away./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry was reading the notice through again. The/nhappiness that had filled him since Saturday was/ngone. His insides were pulsing with rage./n/n"This isn't a coincidence," he said, his hands forming/nfists. "She knows."/n/n"She can't," said Ron at once./n/n"There were people listening in that pub. And let's/nface it, we don't know how many of the people who/nturned up we can trust... Any of them could have run/noff and told Umbridge..."/n/nAnd he had thought they believed him, thought they/neven admired him . . ./n/n"Zacharias Smith!" said Ron at once, punching a fist/ninto his hand. "Or — I thought that Michael Corner/nhad a really shifty look too — "/n/n"I wonder if Hermione's seen this yet?" Harry said,/nlooking around at the door to the girls' dormitories./n/n"Let's go and tell her," said Ron. He bounded forward,/npulled open the door, and set off up the spiral/nstaircase./n/nHe was on the sixth stair when it happened. There/nwas a loud, wailing, klaxonlike sound and the steps/nmelted together to make a long, smooth stone slide./nThere was a brief moment when Ron tried to keep/nrunning, arms working madly like windmills, then he/ntoppled over backward and shot down the newly/ncreated slide, coming to rest on his back at Harry's/nfeet./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Er — I don't think we're allowed in the girls'/ndormitories," said Harry, pulling Ron to his feet and/ntrying not to laugh./n/nTwo fourth-year girls came zooming gleefully down/nthe stone slide./n/n"Oooh, who tried to get upstairs?" they giggled/nhappily, leaping to their feet and ogling Harry and/nRon./n/n"Me," said Ron, who was still rather disheveled. "I/ndidn't realize that would happen. It's not fair!" he/nadded to Harry, as the girls headed off for the portrait/nhole, still giggling madly. "Hermione's allowed in our/ndormitory, how come we're not allowed — ?"/n/n"Well, it's an old-fashioned rule," said Hermione, who/nhad just slid neatly onto a rug in front of them and/nwas now getting to her feet, "but it says in Hogwarts,/nA History that the founders thought boys were less/ntrustworthy than girls. Anyway, why were you trying/nto get in there?"/n/n"To see you — look at this!" said Ron, dragging her/nover to the notice board./n/nHermione's eyes slid rapidly down the notice. Her/nexpression became stony./n/n"Someone must have blabbed to her!" Ron said/nangrily./n/n"They can't have done," said Hermione in a low voice./n/n"You're so naive," said Ron, "you think just because/nyou're all honorable and trustworthy — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No, they can't have done because I put a jinx on that/npiece of parchment we all signed," said Hermione/ngrimly. "Believe me, if anyone's run off and told/nUmbridge, well know exactly who they are and they/nwill really regret it."/n/n"What'll happen to them?" said Ron eagerly./n/n"Well, put it this way," said Hermione, "it'll make/nEloise Midgen's acne look like a couple of cute/nfreckles. Come on, let's get down to breakfast and see/nwhat the others think. . . I wonder whether this has/nbeen put up in all the Houses?"/n/nIt was immediately apparent on entering the Great/nHall that Umbridge's sign had not only appeared in/nGryffindor Tower. There was a peculiar intensity/nabout the chatter and an extra measure of movement/nin the Hall as people scurried up and down their/ntables conferring on what they had read. Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione had barely taken their seats when/nNeville, Dean, Fred, George, and Ginny descended/nupon them./n/n"Did you see it?"/n/n"D'you reckon she knows?"/n/n"What are we going to do?"/n/nThey were all looking at Harry. He glanced around to/nmake sure there were no teachers near them./n/n"We're going to do it anyway, of course," he said/nquietly./n/n"Knew you'd say that," said George, beaming and/nthumping Harry on the arm./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The prefects as well?" said Fred, looking quizzically/nat Ron and Hermione./n/n"Of course," said Hermione coolly./n/n"Here comes Ernie and Hannah Abbott," said Ron,/nlooking over his shoulder. "And those Ravenclaw/nblokes and Smith ... and no one looks very spotty."/n/nHermione looked alarmed./n/n"Never mind spots, the idiots can't come over here/nnow, it'll look really suspicious — sit down!" she/nmouthed to Ernie and Hannah, gesturing frantically/nto them to rejoin the Hufflepuff table. "Later! We'll —/ntalk — to — you — lateri"/n/n"I'll tell Michael," said Ginny impatiently, swinging/nherself off her bench. "The fool, honestly ..."/n/nShe hurried off toward the Ravenclaw table; Harry/nwatched her go. Cho was sitting not far away, talking/nto the curly-haired friend she had brought along to/nthe Hog's Head. Would Umbridge's notice scare her off/nmeeting them again?/n/nBut the full repercussions of the sign were not felt/nuntil they were leaving the Great Hall for History of/nMagic./n/n"Harry! Ron\"/n/nIt was Angelina and she was hurrying toward them/nlooking perfectly desperate./n/n"It's okay," said Harry quietly, when she was near/nenough to hear him. "We're still going to — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You realize she's including Quidditch in this?"/nAngelina said over him. "We have to go and ask/npermission to re-form the Gryffindor team!"/n/n"What?" said Harry./n/n"No way," said Ron, appalled./n/n"You read the sign, it mentions teams too! So listen,/nHarry ... I am saying this for the last time... Please,/nplease don't lose your temper with Umbridge again or/nshe might not let us play anymore!"/n/n"Okay, okay," said Harry, for Angelina looked as/nthough she was on the verge of tears. "Don't worry, I'll/nbehave myself..."/n/n"Bet Umbridge is in History of Magic," said Ron/ngrimly, as they set off for Binns's lesson. "She hasn't/ninspected Binns yet... Bet you anything she's there..."/n/nBut he was wrong; the only teacher present when/nthey entered was Professor Binns, floating an inch or/nso above his chair as usual and preparing to continue/nhis monotonous drone on giant wars. Harry did not/neven attempt to follow what he was saying today; he/ndoodled idly on his parchment ignoring Hermione's/nfrequent glares and nudges, until a particularly/npainful poke in the ribs made him look up angrily./n/n"What?"/n/nShe pointed at the window. Harry looked around./nHedwig was perched on the narrow window ledge,/ngazing through the thick glass at him, a letter tied to/nher leg. Harry could not understand it; they had just/nhad breakfast, why on earth hadn't she delivered the/nletter then, as usual? Many of his classmates were/npointing out Hedwig to each other too./n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh, I've always loved that owl, she's so beautiful,"/nHarry heard Lavender sigh to Parvati./n/n/n/nHe glanced around at Professor Binns who continued/nto read his notes, serenely unaware that the class's/nattention was even less focused upon him than usual./nHarry slipped quietly off his chair, crouched down,/nand hurried along the row to the window, where he/nslid the catch and opened it very slowly./n/nHe had expected Hedwig to hold out her leg so that he/ncould remove the letter and then fly off to the Owlery,/nbut the moment the window was open wide enough/nshe hopped inside, hooting dolefully. He closed the/nwindow with an anxious glance at Professor Binns,/ncrouched low again, and sped back to his seat with/nHedwig on his shoulder. He regained his seat,/ntransferred Hedwig to his lap, and made to remove/nthe letter tied to her leg./n/nIt was only then that he realized that Hedwig's/nfeathers were oddly ruffled; some were bent the wrong/nway, and she was holding one of her wings at an odd/nangle./n/n"She's hurt!" Harry whispered, bending his head low/nover her. Hermione and Ron leaned in closer;/nHermione even put down her quill. "Look — there's/nsomething wrong with her wing — "/n/nHedwig was quivering; when Harry made to touch the/nwing she gave a little jump, all her feathers on end as/nthough she was inflating herself, and gazed at him/nreproachfully./n/n"Professor Binns," said Harry loudly, and everyone in/nthe class turned to look at him. "I'm not feeling well."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor Binns raised his eyes from his notes,/nlooking amazed, as always, to find the room in front/nof him full of people./n/n"Not feeling well?" he repeated hazily./n/n"Not at all well," said Harry firmly, getting to his feet/nwhile concealing Hedwig behind his back. "So I think/nI'll need to go to the hospital wing."/n/n"Yes," said Professor Binns, clearly very much wrong-/nfooted. "Yes ... yes, hospital wing ... well, off you go,/nthen, Perkins ..."/n/nOnce outside the room Harry returned Hedwig to his/nshoulder and hurried off up the corridor, pausing to/nthink only when he was out of sight of Binns's door./nHis first choice of somebody to cure Hedwig would/nhave been Hagrid, of course, but as he had no idea/nwhere Hagrid was, his only remaining option was to/nfind Professor Grubbly-Plank and hope she would/nhelp./n/nHe peered out of a window at the blustery, overcast/ngrounds. There was no sign of her anywhere near/nHagrid's cabin; if she was not teaching, she was/nprobably in the staffroom. He set off downstairs,/nHedwig hooting feebly as she swayed on his shoulder./n/nTwo stone gargoyles flanked the staffroom door. As/nHarry approached, one of them croaked, "You should/nbe in class, sunny Jim."/n/n"This is urgent," said Harry curtly./n/n"Ooooh, urgent, is it?" said the other gargoyle in a/nhigh-pitched voice. "Well, that's put us in our place,/nhasn't it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry knocked; he heard footsteps and then the door/nopened and he found himself face-to-face with/nProfessor McGonagall./n/n"You haven't been given another detention!" she said/nat once, her square spectacles flashing alarmingly./n/n"No, Professor!" said Harry hastily./n/n"Well then, why are you out of class?"/n/n"It's urgent, apparently," said the second gargoyle/nsnidely./n/n"I'm looking for Professor Grubbly-Plank," Harry/nexplained. "It's my owl, she's injured."/n/n"Injured owl, did you say?"/n/nProfessor Grubbly-Plank appeared at Professor/nMcGonagall's shoulder, smoking a pipe and holding a/ncopy of the Daily Prophet/n/n"Yes," said Harry, lifting Hedwig carefully off his/nshoulder, "she turned up after the other post owls/nand her wing's all funny, look — "/n/nProfessor Grubbly-Plank stuck her pipe firmly/nbetween her teeth and took Hedwig from Harry while/nProfessor McGonagall watched./n/n"Hmm," said Professor Grubbly-Plank, her pipe/nwaggling slightly as she talked. "Looks like/nsomething's attacked her. Can't think what would/nhave done it, though... Thestrals will sometimes go for/nbirds, of course, but Hagrid's got the Hogwarts/nthestrals well trained not to touch owls ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry neither knew nor cared what thestrals were, he/njust wanted to know that Hedwig was going to be all/nright. Professor McGonagall, however, looked sharply/nat Harry and said, "Do you know how far this owl's/ntraveled, Potter?"/n/n"Er," said Harry. "From London, I think."/n/nHe met her eyes briefly and knew that she understood/n"London" to mean "number twelve, Grimmauld Place"/nby the way her eyebrows had joined in the middle./n/nProfessor Grubbly-Plank pulled a monocle out of the/ninside of her robes and screwed it into her eye to/nexamine Hedwig's wing closely. "I should be able to/nsort this out if you leave her with me, Potter," she/nsaid. "She shouldn't be flying long distances for a few/ndays, in any case."/n/n"Er — right — thanks," said Harry, just as the bell/nrang for break./n/n"No problem," said Professor Grubbly-Plank gruffly,/nturning back into the staffroom./n/n"Just a moment, Wilhelmina!" said Professor/nMcGonagall. "Potter's letter!"/n/n"Oh yeah!" said Harry, who had momentarily/nforgotten the scroll tied to Hedwig's leg. Professor/nGrubbly-Plank handed it over and then disappeared/ninto the staffroom carrying Hedwig, who was staring/nat Harry as though unable to believe he would give/nher away like this. Feeling slightly guilty, he turned to/ngo, but Professor McGonagall called him back./n/n"Potter!"/n/n"Yes, Professor?"/n/n/n/n/n/nShe glanced up and down the corridor; there were/nstudents coming from both directions./n/n"Bear in mind," she said quickly and quietly, her eyes/non the scroll in his hand, "that channels of/ncommunication in and out of Hogwarts may be being/nwatched, won't you?"/n/n"I — " said Harry, but the flood of students rolling/nalong the corridor was almost upon him. Professor/nMcGonagall gave him a curt nod and retreated into/nthe staffroom, leaving Harry to be swept out into the/ncourtyard with the crowd. Here he spotted Ron and/nHermione already standing in a sheltered corner,/ntheir cloak collars turned up against the wind. Harry/nslit open the scroll as he hurried toward them and/nfound five words in Sirius's handwriting:/n/nToday, same time, same place./n/n"Is Hedwig okay?" asked Hermione anxiously, the/nmoment he was within earshot./n/n"Where did you take her?" asked Ron./n/n"To Grubbly-Plank," said Harry. "And I met/nMcGonagall... Listen..."/n/nAnd he told them what Professor McGonagall had/nsaid. To his surprise, neither of the others looked/nshocked; on the contrary, they exchanged significant/nlooks./n/n"What?" said Harry, looking from Ron to Hermione/nand back again./n/n"Well, I was just saying to Ron ... what if someone/nhad tried to intercept Hedwig? I mean, she's never/nbeen hurt on a flight before, has she?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Who's the letter from anyway?" asked Ron, taking/nthe note from Harry./n/n"Snuffles," said Harry quietly./n/n" 'Same time, same place'? Does he mean the fire in/nthe common room?"/n/n"Obviously," said Hermione, also reading the note./n/nShe looked uneasy. "I just hope nobody else has read/nthis..."/n/n"But it was still sealed and everything," said Harry,/ntrying to convince himself as much as her. "And/nnobody would understand what it meant if they didn't/nknow where we'd spoken to him before, would they?"/n/n"I don't know," said Hermione anxiously, hitching her/nbag back over her shoulder as the bell rang again. "It/nwouldn't be exactly difficult to reseal the scroll by/nmagic... And if anyone's watching the Floo Network .../nbut I don't really see how we can warn him not to/ncome without that being intercepted too!"/n/nThey trudged down the stone steps to the dungeons/nfor Potions, all three of them lost in thought, but as/nthey reached the bottom of the stairs they were/nrecalled to themselves by the voice of Draco Malfoy,/nwho was standing just outside Snape's classroom/ndoor, waving around an official-looking piece of/nparchment and talking much louder than was/nnecessary so that they could hear every word./n/n"Yeah, Umbridge gave the Slytherin Quidditch team/npermission to continue playing straightaway, I went/nto ask her first thing this morning. Well, it was pretty/nmuch automatic, I mean, she knows my father really/nwell, he's always popping in and out of the Ministry.../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt'll be interesting to see whether Gryffindor are/nallowed to keep playing, wont it?"/n/n"Don't rise," Hermione whispered imploringly to Harry/nand Ron, who were both watching Malfoy, faces set/nand fists clenched. "It's what he wants..."/n/n"I mean," said Malfoy, raising his voice a little more,/nhis gray eyes glittering malevolently in Harry and/nRon's direction, "if it's a question of influence with the/nMinistry, I don't think they've got much chance.../n/nFrom what my father says, they've been looking for an/nexcuse to sack Arthur Weasley for years... And as for/nPotter ... My father says it's a matter of time before/nthe Ministry has him carted off to St. Mungo's.../napparently they've got a special ward for people whose/nbrains have been addled by magic..."/n/nMalfoy made a grotesque face, his mouth sagging/nopen and his eyes rolling. Crabbe and Goyle gave/ntheir usual grunts of laughter, Pansy Parkinson/nshrieked with glee./n/nSomething collided hard with Harry's shoulder,/nknocking him sideways. A split second later he/nrealized that Neville had just charged past him,/nheading straight for Malfoy./n/n"Neville, no!"/n/nHarry leapt forward and seized the back of Neville's/nrobes; Neville struggled frantically, his fists flailing,/ntrying desperately to get at Malfoy who looked, for a/nmoment, extremely shocked./n/n"Help me!" Harry flung at Ron, managing to get an/narm around Neville's neck and dragging him/nbackward, away from the Slytherins. Crabbe and/nGoyle were now flexing their arms, closing in front of/n/n/n/n/n/nMalfoy, ready for the fight. Ron hurried forward and/nseized Neville's arms; together, he and Harry/nsucceeded in dragging Neville back into the Gryffindor/nline. Neville's face was scarlet; the pressure Harry was/nexerting on his throat rendered him quite/nincomprehensible, but odd words spluttered from his/nmouth./n/n"Not... funny ... don't ... Mungo's ... show ... him ..."/n/nThe dungeon door opened. Snape appeared there. His/nblack eyes swept up the Gryffindor line to the point/nwhere Harry and Ron were wrestling with Neville./n/n"Fighting, Potter, Weasley, Longbottom?" Snape said/nin his cold, sneering voice. "Ten points from/nGryffindor. Release Longbottom, Potter, or it will be/ndetention. Inside, all of you."/n/nHarry let go of Neville, who stood panting and glaring/nat him./n/n"I had to stop you," Harry gasped, picking up his bag./n"Crabbe and Goyle would've torn you apart."/n/nNeville said nothing, he merely snatched up his own/nbag and stalked off into the dungeon./n/n"What in the name of Merlin," said Ron slowly, as/nthey followed Neville, "was that about?"/n/nHarry did not answer. He knew exactly why the/nsubject of people who were in St. Mungo's because of/nmagical damage to their brains was highly distressing/nto Neville, but he had sworn to Dumbledore that he/nwould not tell anyone Neville's secret. Even Neville did/nnot know that Harry knew./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione took their usual seats at/nthe back of the class and pulled out parchment,/nquills, and their copies of One Thousand Magical/nHerbs and Fungi. The class around them was/nwhispering about what Neville had just done, but/nwhen Snape closed the dungeon door with an echoing/nbang everybody fell silent immediately./n/n"You will notice," said Snape in his low, sneering/nvoice, "that we have a guest with us today."/n/nHe gestured toward the dim corner of the dungeon,/nand Harry saw Professor Umbridge sitting there,/nclipboard on her knee. He glanced sideways at Ron/nand Hermione, his eyebrows raised. Snape and/nUmbridge, the two teachers he hated most ... it was/nhard to decide which he wanted to triumph over the/nother./n/n"We are continuing with our Strengthening Solutions/ntoday, you will find your mixtures as you left them/nlast lesson, if correctly made they should have/nmatured well over the weekend — instructions" — he/nwaved his wand again — "on the board. Carry on."/n/nProfessor Umbridge spent the first half hour of the/nlesson making notes in her corner. Harry was very/ninterested in hearing her question Snape, so/ninterested, that he was becoming careless with his/npotion again./n/n"Salamander blood, Harry!" Hermione moaned,/ngrabbing his wrist to prevent him adding the wrong/ningredient for the third time. "Not pomegranate juice!"/n/n"Right," said Harry vaguely, putting down the bottle/nand continuing to watch the corner. Umbridge had/njust gotten to her feet. "Ha," he said softly, as she/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nstrode between two lines of desks toward Snape, who/nwas bending over Dean Thomas's cauldron./n/n"Well, the class seems fairly advanced for their level,"/nshe said briskly to Snape 's back. "Though I would/nquestion whether it is advisable to teach them a/npotion like the Strengthening Solution. I think the/nMinistry would prefer it if that was removed from the/nsyllabus."/n/nSnape straightened up slowly and turned to look at/nher./n/n"Now ... how long have you been teaching at/nHogwarts?" she asked, her quill poised over her/nclipboard./n/n"Fourteen years," Snape replied. His expression was/nunfathomable. His eyes on Snape, Harry added a few/ndrops to his potion; it hissed menacingly and turned/nfrom turquoise to orange./n/n"You applied first for the Defense Against the Dark/nArts post, I believe?" Professor Umbridge asked/nSnape./n/n"Yes," said Snape quietly./n/n"But you were unsuccessful?"/n/nSnape 's lip curled./n/n"Obviously."/n/nProfessor Umbridge scribbled on her clipboard./n/n"And you have applied regularly for the Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts post since you first joined the/nschool, I believe?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes," said Snape quietly, barely moving his lips. He/nlooked very angry./n/n"Do you have any idea why Dumbledore has/nconsistently refused to appoint you?" asked/nUmbridge./n/n"I suggest you ask him," said Snape jerkily./n/n"Oh I shall," said Professor Umbridge with a sweet/nsmile./n/n"I suppose this is relevant?" Snape asked, his black/neyes narrowed./n/n"Oh yes," said Professor Umbridge. "Yes, the Ministry/nwants a thorough understanding of teachers' — er —/nbackgrounds..."/n/nShe turned away, walked over to Pansy Parkinson/nand began questioning her about the lessons. Snape/nlooked around at Harry and their eyes met for a/nsecond. Harry hastily dropped his gaze to his potion,/nwhich was now congealing foully and giving off a/nstrong smell of burned rubber./n/n"No marks again, then, Potter," said Snape/nmaliciously, emptying Harry's cauldron with a wave of/nhis wand. "You will write me an essay on the correct/ncomposition of this potion, indicating how and why/nyou went wrong, to be handed in next lesson, do you/nunderstand?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry furiously. Snape had already given/nthem homework, and he had Quidditch practice this/nevening; this would mean another couple of sleepless/nnights. It did not seem possible that he had awoken/nthat morning feeling very happy. All he felt now was a/nfervent desire for this day to end as soon as possible./n/n/n/n/n"Maybe I'll skive off Divination," he said glumly as/nthey stood again in the courtyard after lunch, the/nwind whipping at the hems of robes and brims of/nhats. "I'll pretend to be ill and do Snape's essay/ninstead, then I won't have to stay up half the night..."/n/n"You can't skive off Divination," said Hermione/nseverely./n/n"Hark who's talking, you walked out of Divination,/nyou hate Trelawney!" said Ron indignantly./n/n"I don't hate her," said Hermione loftily. "I just think/nshe's an absolutely appalling teacher and a real old/nfraud... But Harry's already missed History of Magic/nand I don't think he ought to miss anything else/ntoday!"/n/nThere was too much truth in this to ignore, so half an/nhour later Harry took his seat in the hot, over-/nperfumed atmosphere of the Divination classroom/nfeeling angry at everybody. Professor Trelawney was/nhanding out copies of The Dream Oracle yet again; he/nwould surely be much better employed doing Snape's/npunishment essay than sitting here trying to find/nmeaning in a lot of made-up dreams./n/nIt seemed, however, that he was not the only person/nin Divination who was in a temper. Professor/nTrelawney slammed a copy of the Oracle down on the/ntable between Harry and Ron and swept away, her/nlips pursed; she threw the next copy of the Oracle at/nSeamus and Dean, narrowly avoiding Seamus's head,/nand thrust the final one into Neville's chest with such/nforce that he slipped off his pouf./n/n"Well, carry on!" said Professor Trelawney loudly, her/nvoice high pitched and somewhat hysterical. "You/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nknow what to do! Or am I such a substandard teacher/nthat you have never learned how to open a book?"/n/nThe class stared perplexedly at her and then at each/nother. Harry, however, thought he knew what was the/nmatter. As Professor Trelawney flounced back to the/nhigh-backed teacher's chair, her magnified eyes full of/nangry tears, he leaned his head closer to Ron's and/nmuttered, "I think she's got the results of her/ninspection back."/n/n"Professor?" said Parvati Patil in a hushed voice (she/nand Lavender had always rather admired Professor/nTrelawney). "Professor, is there anything — er —/nwrong?"/n/n"Wrong!" cried Professor Trelawney in a voice/nthrobbing with emotion. "Certainly not! I have been/ninsulted, certainly... Insinuations have been made/nagainst me... Unfounded accusations levelled ... but/nno, there is nothing wrong, certainly not..."/n/nShe took a great shuddering breath and looked away/nfrom Parvati, angry tears spilling from under her/nglasses./n/n"I say nothing," she choked, "of sixteen years' devoted/nservice... It has passed, apparently, unnoticed... But I/nshall not be insulted, no, I shall not!"/n/n"But Professor, who's insulting you?" asked Parvati/ntimidly./n/n"The establishment!" said Professor Trelawney in a/ndeep, dramatic, wavering voice. "Yes, those with eyes/ntoo clouded by the Mundane to See as I See, to Know/nas I Know ... Of course, we Seers have always been/nfeared, always persecuted... It is — alas — our fate..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe gulped, dabbed at her wet cheeks with the end of/nher shawl, and then pulled a small, embroidered/nhandkerchief from her sleeve, into which she blew her/nnose very hard with a sound like Peeves blowing a/nraspberry. Ron sniggered. Lavender shot him a/ndisgusted look./n/n"Professor," said Parvati, "do you mean ... is it/nsomething Professor Umbridge ... ?"/n/n"Do not speak to me about that woman!" cried/nProfessor Trelawney, leaping to her feet, her beads/nrattling and her spectacles flashing. "Kindly continue/nwith your work!"/n/nAnd she spent the rest of the lesson striding among/nthem, tears still leaking from behind her glasses,/nmuttering what sounded like threats under her/nbreath./n/n"... may well choose to leave ... the indignity of it ... on/nprobation ... we shall see ... how she dares ..."/n/n"You and Umbridge have got something in common,"/nHarry told Hermione quietly when they met again in/nDefense Against the Dark Arts. "She obviously/nreckons Trelawney's an old fraud too... Looks like/nshe's put her on probation."/n/nUmbridge entered the room as he spoke, wearing her/nblack velvet bow and an expression of great/nsmugness./n/n"Good afternoon, class."/n/n"Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge," they chanted/ndrearily./n/n"Wands away, please ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nBut there was no answering flurry of movement this/ntime; nobody had bothered to take out their wands./n/n"Please turn to page thirty-four of Defensive Magical/nTheory and read the third chapter, entitled The Case/nfor Non-Offensive Responses to Magical Attack.' There/nwill be — "/n/n" — no need to talk," Harry, Ron, and Hermione said/ntogether under their breaths./n/n"No Quidditch practice," said Angelina in hollow tones/nwhen Harry, Ron, and Hermione entered the common/nroom that night after dinner./n/n"But I kept my temper!" said Harry, horrified. "I didn't/nsay anything to her, Angelina, I swear, I — "/n/n"I know, I know," said Angelina miserably. "She just/nsaid she needed a bit of time to consider."/n/n"Consider what?" said Ron angrily. "She's given the/nSlytherins permission, why not us?"/n/nBut Harry could imagine how much Umbridge was/nenjoying holding the threat of no Gryffindor Quidditch/nteam over their heads and could easily understand/nwhy she would not want to relinquish that weapon/nover them too soon./n/n"Well," said Hermione, "look on the bright side — at/nleast now you'll have time to do Snape's essay!"/n/n"That's a bright side, is it?" snapped Harry, while Ron/nstared incredulously at Hermione. "No Quidditch/npractice and extra Potions?"/n/nHarry slumped down into a chair, dragged his Potions/nessay reluctantly from his bag, and set to work./n/n/n/n/n/nIt was very hard to concentrate; even though he knew/nthat Sirius was not due in the fire until much later he/ncould not help glancing into the flames every few/nminutes just in case. There was also an incredible/namount of noise in the room: Fred and George/nappeared finally to have perfected one type of Skiving/nSnackbox, which they were taking turns to/ndemonstrate to a cheering and whooping crowd./n/nFirst, Fred would take a bite out of the orange end of/na chew, at which he would vomit spectacularly into a/nbucket they had placed in front of them. Then he/nwould force down the purple end of the chew, at/nwhich the vomiting would immediately cease. Lee/nJordan, who was assisting the demonstration, was/nlazily vanishing the vomit at regular intervals with the/nsame Vanishing Spell Snape kept using on Harry's/npotions./n/nWhat with the regular sounds of retching, cheering,/nand Fred and George taking advance orders from the/ncrowd, Harry was finding it exceptionally difficult to/nfocus on the correct method for Strengthening/nSolutions. Hermione was not helping matters; the/ncheers and sound of vomit hitting the bottom of Fred/nand George's bucket were punctuated by loud and/ndisapproving sniffs that Harry found, if anything,/nmore distracting./n/n"Just go and stop them, then!" he said irritably, after/ncrossing out the wrong weight of powdered griffin/nclaw for the fourth time./n/n"I can't, they're not technically doing anything wrong,"/nsaid Hermione through gritted teeth. "They're quite/nwithin their rights to eat the foul things themselves,/nand I can't find a rule that says the other idiots aren't/nentitled to buy them, not unless they're proven to be/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndangerous in some way, and it doesn't look as though/nthey are..."/n/nShe, Harry, and Ron watched George projectile-vomit/ninto the bucket, gulp down the rest of the chew, and/nstraighten up, beaming with his arms wide to/nprotracted applause./n/n"You know, I don't get why Fred and George only got/nthree O.W.L.s each," said Harry, watching as Fred,/nGeorge, and Lee collected gold from the eager crowd./n"They really know their stuff..."/n/n"Oh, they only know flashy stuff that's no real use to/nanyone," said Hermione disparagingly./n/n"No real use?" said Ron in a strained voice./n/n"Hermione, they've got about twenty-six Galleons/nalready..."/n/nIt was a long while before the crowd around the/nWeasleys dispersed, and then Fred, Lee, and George/nsat up counting their takings even longer, so that it/nwas well past midnight when Harry, Ron, and/nHermione finally had the common room to themselves/nagain. At long last, Fred closed the doorway to the/nboys' dormitories behind him, rattling his box of/nGalleons ostentatiously so that Hermione scowled./nHarry, who was making very little progress with his/nPotions essay, decided to give it up for the night. As/nhe put his books away, Ron, who was dozing lightly in/nan armchair, gave a muffled grunt, awoke, looked/nblearily into the fire and said, "Sirius!"/n/nHarry whipped around; Sirius's untidy dark head was/nsitting in the fire again./n/n"Hi," he said, grinning./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Hi," chorused Harry, Ron, and Hermione, all three/nkneeling down upon the hearthrug. Crookshanks/npurred loudly and approached the fire, trying, despite/nthe heat, to put his face close to Sirius's./n/n"How're things?" said Sirius./n/n"Not that good," said Harry, as Hermione pulled/nCrookshanks back to stop him singeing his whiskers./n"The Ministry's forced through another decree, which/nmeans we're not allowed to have Quidditch teams — "/n/n" — or secret Defense Against the Dark Arts groups?"/nsaid Sirius./n/nThere was a short pause./n/n"How did you know about that?" Harry demanded./n/n"You want to choose your meeting places more/ncarefully," said Sirius, grinning still more broadly./n"The Hog's Head, I ask you ..."/n/n"Well, it was better than the Three Broomsticks!" said/nHermione defensively. "That's always packed with/npeople — "/n/n" — which means you'd have been harder to overhear,"/nsaid Sirius. "You've got a lot to learn, Hermione."/n/n"Who overheard us?" Harry demanded./n/n"Mundungus, of course," said Sirius, and when they/nall looked puzzled he laughed. "He was the witch/nunder the veil."/n/n"That was Mundungus?" Harry said, stunned. "What/nwas he doing in the Hog's Head?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What do you think he was doing?" said Sirius/nimpatiently. "Keeping an eye on you, of course."/n/n"I'm still being followed?" asked Harry angrily./n/n"Yeah, you are," said Sirius, "and just as well, isn't it,/nif the first thing you're going to do on your weekend/noff is organize an illegal defense group."/n/nBut he looked neither angry nor worried; on the/ncontrary, he was looking at Harry with distinct pride./n/n"Why was Dung hiding from us?" asked Ron,/nsounding disappointed. "We'd've liked to've seen him."/n/n"He was banned from the Hog's Head twenty years/nago," said Sirius, "and that barman's got a long/nmemory. We lost Moody's spare Invisibility Cloak/nwhen Sturgis was arrested, so Dung's been dressing/nas a witch a lot lately... Anyway ... First of all, Ron —/nI've sworn to pass on a message from your mother."/n/n"Oh yeah?" said Ron, sounding apprehensive./n/n"She says on no account whatsoever are you to take/npart in an illegal secret Defense Against the Dark Arts/ngroup. She says you'll be expelled for sure and your/nfuture will be ruined. She says there will be plenty of/ntime to learn how to defend yourself later and that/nyou are too young to be worrying about that right/nnow. She also" — Sirius's eyes turned to the other two/n— "advises Harry and Hermione not to proceed with/nthe group, though she accepts that she has no/nauthority over either of them and simply begs them to/nremember that she has their best interests at heart./nShe would have written all this to you, but if the owl/nhad been intercepted you'd all have been in real/ntrouble, and she can't say it for herself because she's/non duty tonight."/n/n/n/n/n/n"On duty doing what?" said Ron quickly./n/n"Never you mind, just stuff for the Order," said Sirius./n"So it's fallen to me to be the messenger and make/nsure you tell her I passed it all on, because I don't/nthink she trusts me to."/n/nThere was another pause in which Crookshanks,/nmewing, attempted to paw Sirius's head, and Ron/nfiddled with a hole in the hearthrug./n/n"So you want me to say I'm not going to take part in/nthe defense group?" he muttered finally./n/n"Me? Certainly not!" said Sirius, looking surprised. "I/nthink it's an excellent idea!"/n/n"You do?" said Harry, his heart lifting./n/n"Of course I do!" said Sirius. "D'you think your father/nand I would've lain down and taken orders from an/nold hag like Umbridge?"/n/n"But — last term all you did was tell me to be careful/nand not take risks — "/n/n"Last year all the evidence was that someone inside/nHogwarts was trying to kill you, Harry!" said Sirius/nimpatiently. "This year we know that there's someone/noutside Hogwarts who'd like to kill us all, so I think/nlearning to defend yourselves properly is a very good/nidea!"/n/n"And if we do get expelled?" Hermione asked, a/nquizzical look on her face./n/n"Hermione, this whole thing was your idea!" said/nHarry, staring at her./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I know it was... I just wondered what Sirius/nthought," she said, shrugging./n/n"Well, better expelled and able to defend yourselves/nthan sitting safely in school without a clue," said/nSirius./n/n"Hear, hear," said Harry and Ron enthusiastically./n/n"So," said Sirius, "how are you organizing this group?/nWhere are you meeting?"/n/n"Well, that's a bit of a problem now," said Harry./n"Dunno where we're going to be able to go..."/n/n"How about the Shrieking Shack?" suggested Sirius./n/n"Hey, that's an idea!" said Ron excitedly, but/nHermione made a skeptical noise and all three of/nthem looked at her, Sirius's head turning in the/nflames./n/n"Well, Sirius, it's just that there were only four of you/nmeeting in the Shrieking Shack when you were at/nschool," said Hermione, "and all of you could/ntransform into animals and I suppose you could all/nhave squeezed under a single Invisibility Cloak if/nyou'd wanted to. But there are twenty-eight of us and/nnone of us is an Animagus, so we wouldn't need so/nmuch an Invisibility Cloak as an Invisibility Marquee/n/n/n/n"Fair point," said Sirius, looking slightly crestfallen./n"Well, I'm sure you'll come up with somewhere.../nThere used to be a pretty roomy secret passageway/nbehind that big mirror on the fourth floor, you might/nhave enough space to practice jinxes in there — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Fred and George told me it's blocked," said Harry,/nshaking his head. "Caved in or something."/n/n"Oh ..." said Sirius, frowning. "Well, 111 have a think/nand get back to — "/n/nHe broke off. His face was suddenly tense, alarmed./nHe turned sideways, apparently looking into the solid/nbrick wall of the fireplace./n/n"Sirius?" said Harry anxiously./n/nBut he had vanished. Harry gaped at the flames for a/nmoment, then turned to look at Ron and Hermione./n/n"Why did he — ?"/n/nHermione gave a horrified gasp and leapt to her feet,/nstill staring at the fire./n/nA hand had appeared amongst the flames, groping as/nthough to catch hold of something; a stubby, short-/nfingered hand covered in ugly old-fashioned rings.../n/nThe three of them ran for it; at the door of the boys'/ndormitory Harry looked back. Umbridge's hand was/nstill making snatching movements amongst the/nflames, as though she knew exactly where Sirius's/nhair had been moments before and was determined to/nseize it./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Dumbledore's Army
text: /n"Umbridge has been reading your mail, Harry. There's/nno other explanation."/n/n"You think Umbridge attacked Hedwig?" he said,/noutraged./n/n"I'm almost certain of it," said Hermione grimly./n/n"Watch your frog, it's escaping."/n/nHarry pointed his wand at the bullfrog that had been/nhopping hopefully toward the other side of the table/n— "Acciol " — and it zoomed gloomily back into his/nhand./n/nCharms was always one of the best lessons in which/nto enjoy a private chat: There was generally so much/nmovement and activity that the danger of being/noverheard was very slight. Today, with the room full of/ncroaking bullfrogs and cawing ravens, and with a/nheavy downpour of rain clattering and pounding/nagainst the classroom windows, Harry, Ron, and/nHermione 's whispered discussion about how/n/n/n/nUmbridge had nearly caught Sirius went quite/nunnoticed./n/n"I've been suspecting this ever since Filch accused/nyou of ordering Dungbombs, because it seemed such/na stupid lie," Hermione whispered. "I mean, once your/nletter had been read, it would have been quite clear/nyou weren't ordering them, so you wouldn't have been/nin trouble at all — it's a bit of a feeble joke, isn't it?/nBut then I thought, what if somebody just wanted an/nexcuse to read your mail? Well then, it would be a/nperfect way for Umbridge to manage it — tip off Filch,/nlet him do the dirty work and confiscate the letter,/nthen either find a way of stealing it from him or else/ndemand to see it — I don't think Filch would object,/nwhen's he ever stuck up for a student's rights? Harry,/nyou're squashing your frog."/n/nHarry looked down; he was indeed squeezing his/nbullfrog so tightly its eyes were popping; he replaced/nit hastily upon the desk./n/n"It was a very, very close call last night," said/nHermione. "I just wonder if Umbridge knows how/nclose it was. Silenciol"/n/nThe bullfrog on which she was practicing her/nSilencing Charm was struck dumb mid-croak and/nglared at her reproachfully./n/n"If she'd caught Snuffles ..."/n/nHarry finished the sentence for her./n/n"He'd probably be back in Azkaban this morning." He/nwaved his wand without really concentrating; his/nbullfrog swelled like a green balloon and emitted a/nhigh-pitched whistle./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Silenciol" said Hermione hastily, pointing her wand/nat Harry's frog, which deflated silently before them./n"Well, he mustn't do it again, that's all. I just don't/nknow how we're going to let him know. We can't send/nhim an owl."/n/n"I don't reckon he'll risk it again," said Ron. "He's not/nstupid, he knows she nearly got him. Silenciol"/n/nThe large and ugly raven in front of him let out a/nderisive caw./n/n" Silenciol SILENCIO"/n/nThe raven cawed more loudly./n/n"It's the way you're moving your wand," said/nHermione, watching Ron critically. "You don't want to/nwave it, it's more a sharp jab."/n/n"Ravens are harder than frogs," said Ron testily./n/n"Fine, let's swap," said Hermione, seizing Ron's raven/nand replacing it with her own fat bullfrog. "Silencio\"/nThe raven continued to open and close its sharp beak,/nbut no sound came out./n/n"Very good, Miss Granger!" said Professor Flitwick's/nsqueaky little voice and Harry, Ron, and Hermione all/njumped. "Now, let me see you try, Mr. Weasley!"/n/n"Wha — ? Oh — oh, right," said Ron, very flustered./n"Er — Silenciol"/n/nHe jabbed at the bullfrog so hard that he poked it in/nthe eye; the frog gave a deafening croak and leapt off/nthe desk./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt came as no surprise to any of them that Harry and/nRon were given additional practice of the Silencing/nCharm for homework./n/nThey were allowed to remain inside over break due to/nthe downpour outside. They found seats in a noisy/nand overcrowded classroom on the first floor in which/nPeeves was floating dreamily up near the chandelier,/noccasionally blowing an ink pellet at the top of/nsomebody's head. They had barely sat down when/nAngelina came struggling toward them through the/ngroups of gossiping students./n/n"I've got permission!" she said. "To re-form the/nQuidditch team!"/n/n"Excellent." said Ron and Harry together./n/n"Yeah," said Angelina, beaming. "I went to/nMcGonagall and I think she might have appealed to/nDumbledore — anyway, Umbridge had to give in. Ha!/nSo I want you down at the pitch at seven o'clock/ntonight, all right, because we've got to make up time,/nyou realize we're only three weeks away from our first/nmatch?"/n/nShe squeezed away from them, narrowly dodged an/nink pellet from Peeves, which hit a nearby first year/ninstead, and vanished from sight./n/nRon's smile slipped slightly as he looked out of the/nwindow, which was now opaque with hammering/nrain./n/n"Hope this clears up ... What's up with you,/nHermione?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe too was gazing at the window, but not as though/nshe really saw it. Her eyes were unfocused and there/nwas a frown on her face./n/n"Just thinking ..." she said, still frowning at the rain-/nwashed window./n/n"About Siri . . . Snuffles?" said Harry./n/n"No ... not exactly ..." said Hermione slowly. "More .../nwondering ... I suppose we're doing the right thing .../n/nI think ... aren't we?/n/nHarry and Ron looked at each other./n/n"Well, that clears that up," said Ron. "It would've been/nreally annoying if you hadn't explained yourself/nproperly."/n/nHermione looked at him as though she had only just/nrealized he was there./n/n"I was just wondering," she said, her voice stronger/nnow, "whether we're doing the right thing, starting/nthis Defense Against the Dark Arts group."/n/n"What!" said Harry and Ron together./n/n"Hermione, it was your idea in the first place!" said/nRon indignantly./n/n"I know," said Hermione, twisting her fingers together./n"But after talking to Snuffles ..."/n/n"But he's all for it!" said Harry./n/n"Yes," said Hermione, staring at the window again./n"Yes, that's what made me think maybe it wasn't a/ngood idea after all..."/n/n/n/n/n/nPeeves floated over them on his stomach, peashooter/nat the ready; automatically all three of them lifted/ntheir bags to cover their heads until he had passed./n/n"Let's get this straight," said Harry angrily, as they/nput their bags back on the floor, "Sirius agrees with/nus, so you don't think we should do it anymore?"/n/nHermione looked tense and rather miserable. Now/nstaring at her own hands she said, "Do you honestly/ntrust his judgment?"/n/n"Yes, I do!" said Harry at once. "He's always given us/ngreat advice!"/n/nAn ink pellet whizzed past them, striking Katie Bell/nsquarely in the ear. Hermione watched Katie leap to/nher feet and start throwing things at Peeves; it was a/nfew moments before Hermione spoke again and it/nsounded as though she was choosing her words very/ncarefully./n/n"You don't think he has become ... sort of ... reckless/n... since he's been cooped up in Grimmauld Place?/n/nYou don't think he's ... kind of ... living through us?"/n/n"What d'you mean, 'living through us'?" Harry/nretorted./n/n"I mean ... well, I think he'd love to be forming secret/ndefense societies right under the nose of someone/nfrom the Ministry... I think he's really frustrated at/nhow little he can do where he is ... so I think he's/nkeen to kind of ... egg us on."/n/nRon looked utterly perplexed./n/n"Sirius is right," he said, "you do sound just like my/nmother."/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione bit her lip and did not answer. The bell/nrang just as Peeves swooped down upon Katie and/nemptied an entire ink bottle over her head./n/nThe weather did not improve as the day wore on, so/nthat at seven o'clock that evening, when Harry and/nRon went down to the Quidditch pitch for practice,/nthey were soaked through within minutes, their feet/nslipping and sliding on the sodden grass. The sky was/na deep, thundery gray and it was a relief to gain the/nwarmth and light of the changing rooms, even if they/nknew the respite was only temporary. They found/nFred and George debating whether to use one of their/nown Skiving Snackboxes to get out of flying./n/n" — but I bet she'd know what we'd done," Fred said/nout of the corner of his mouth. "If only I hadn't offered/nto sell her some Puking Pastilles yesterday — "/n/n"We could try the Fever Fudge," George muttered, "no/none's seen that yet — "/n/n"Does it work?" inquired Ron hopefully, as the/nhammering of rain on the roof intensified and wind/nhowled around the building./n/n"Well, yeah," said Fred, "your temperature'll go right/nup — "/n/n/n/n" — but you get these massive pus-filled boils too,"/nsaid George, "and we haven't worked out how to get/nrid of them yet."/n/n"I can't see any boils," said Ron, staring at the twins./n/n"No, well, you wouldn't," said Fred darkly, "they're not/nin a place we generally display to the public — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" — but they make sitting on a broom a right pain in/nthe — "/n/n/n/n"All right, everyone, listen up," said Angelina loudly,/nemerging from the Captain's office. "I know it's not/nideal weather, but there's a good chance we'll be/nplaying Slytherin in conditions like this so it's a good/nidea to work out how we're going to cope with them./nHarry, didn't you do something to your glasses to stop/nthe rain fogging them up when we played Hufflepuff/nin that storm?"/n/n"Hermione did it," said Harry. He pulled out his wand,/ntapped his glasses and said, "Imperviusl"/n/n"I think we all ought to try that," said Angelina. "If we/ncould just keep the rain off our faces it would really/nhelp visibility — all together, come on — Imperviusl/nOkay. Let's go."/n/nThey all stowed their wands back in the inside/npockets of their robes, shouldered their brooms, and/nfollowed Angelina out of the changing rooms./n/nThey squelched through the deepening mud to the/nmiddle of the pitch; visibility was still very poor even/nwith the Impervius Charm; light was fading fast and/ncurtains of rain were sweeping the grounds./n/n"All right, on my whistle," shouted Angelina./n/nHarry kicked off from the ground, spraying mud in all/ndirections, and shot upward, the wind pulling him/nslightly off course. He had no idea how he was going/nto see the Snitch in this weather; he was having/nenough difficulty seeing the one Bludger with which/nthey were practicing; a minute into the practice it/nalmost unseated him and he had to use the Sloth/nGrip Roll to avoid it. Unfortunately Angelina did not/n/n/n/n/nsee this; in fact, she did not appear to be able to see/nanything; none of them had a clue what the others/nwere doing. The wind was picking up; even at a/ndistance Harry could hear the swishing, pounding/nsounds of the rain pummeling the surface of the lake./n/nAngelina kept them at it for nearly an hour before/nconceding defeat. She led her sodden and disgruntled/nteam back into the changing rooms, insisting that the/npractice had not been a waste of time, though without/nany real conviction in her voice. Fred and George were/nlooking particularly annoyed; both were bandy-legged/nand winced with every movement. Harry could hear/nthem complaining in low voices as he toweled his hair/ndry./n/n"I think a few of mine have ruptured," said Fred in a/nhollow voice./n/n"Mine haven't," said George, wincing. "They're/nthrobbing like mad ... feel bigger if anything ..."/n/n"OUCH!" said Harry./n/nHe pressed the towel to his face, his eyes screwed/ntight with pain. The scar on his forehead had seared/nagain, more painfully than in months./n/n"What's up?" said several voices./n/nHarry emerged from behind his towel; the changing/nroom was blurred because he was not wearing his/nglasses; but he could still tell that everyone's face was/nturned toward him./n/n"Nothing," he muttered, "I — poked myself in the eye,/nthat's all..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut he gave Ron a significant look and the two of/nthem hung back as the rest of the team filed back/noutside, muffled in their cloaks, their hats pulled low/nover their ears./n/n"What happened?" said Ron, the moment that Alicia/nhad disappeared through the door. "Was it your/nscar?"/n/nHarry nodded./n/n"But ..."
