"Blimey ... inspectin' people, is she?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, pulling the cloak off. "Trelawney's/non probation already..."/n/n"Um ... what sort of thing are you planning to do with/nus in class, Hagrid?" asked Hermione./n/n"Oh, don' you worry abou' that, I've got a great load o'/nlessons planned," said Hagrid enthusiastically,/nscooping up his dragon steak from the table and/nslapping it over his eye again. "I've bin keepin' a/ncouple o' creatures saved fer yer O.W.L. year, you/nwait, they're somethin' really special."/n/n"Erm . . . special in what way?" asked Hermione/ntentatively./n/n"I'm not sayin'," said Hagrid happily. "I don' want ter/nspoil the surprise."/n/n"Look, Hagrid," said Hermione urgently, dropping all/npretense, "Professor Umbridge won't be at all happy if/nyou bring anything to class that's too dangerous — "/n/n"Dangerous?" said Hagrid, looking genially bemused./n"Don' be silly, I wouldn' give yeh anythin' dangerous! I/nmean, all righ', they can look after themselves — "/n/n"Hagrid, you've got to pass Umbridge's inspection,/nand to do that it would really be better if she saw you/n/n/n/n/n/nteaching us how to look after porlocks, how to tell the/ndifference between knarls and hedgehogs, stuff like/nthat!" said Hermione earnestly./n/n"But tha's not very interestin', Hermione," said/nHagrid. "The stuff I've got's much more impressive,/n/nI've bin bringin' 'em on fer years, I reckon I've got the/non'y domestic herd in Britain — "/n/n"Hagrid ... please ..." said Hermione, a note of real/ndesperation in her voice. "Umbridge is looking for any/nexcuse to get rid of teachers she thinks are too close/nto Dumbledore. Please, Hagrid, teach us something/ndull that's bound to come up in our O.W.L..."/n/nBut Hagrid merely yawned widely and cast a one-eyed/nlook of longing toward the vast bed in the corner./n/n"Lis'en, it's bin a long day an' it's late," he said,/npatting Hermione gently on the shoulder, so that her/nknees gave way and hit the floor with a thud. "Oh —/nsorry — " He pulled her back up by the neck of her/nrobes. "Look, don' you go worryin' abou' me, I promise/nyeh I've got really good stuff planned fer yer lessons/nnow I'm back... Now you lot had better get back up to/nthe castle, an' don' forget ter wipe yer footprints out/nbehind yeh!"/n/n"I dunno if you got through to him," said Ron a short/nwhile later when, having checked that the coast was/nclear, they walked back up to the castle through the/nthickening snow, leaving no trace behind them due to/nthe Obliteration Charm Hermione was performing as/nthey went./n/n"Then I'll go back again tomorrow," said Hermione/ndeterminedly. "I'll plan his lessons for him if I have to./nI don't care if she throws out Trelawney but she's not/ntaking Hagrid!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Eye Of The Snake
text: /nHermione plowed her way back to Hagrid's cabin/nthrough two feet of snow on Sunday morning. Harry/nand Ron wanted to go with her, but their mountain of/nhomework had reached an alarming height again, so/nthey grudgingly remained in the common room, trying/nto ignore the gleeful shouts drifting up from the/ngrounds outside, where students were enjoying/nthemselves skating on the frozen lake, tobogganing,/nand worst of all, bewitching snowballs to zoom up to/nGryffindor Tower and rap hard on the windows./n/n"Oy!" bellowed Ron, finally losing patience and/nsticking his head out of the window, "I am a prefect/nand if one more snowball hits this window — OUCH!"/n/nHe withdrew his head sharply, his face covered in/nsnow./n/n"It's Fred and George," he said bitterly, slamming the/nwindow behind him. "Gits ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione returned from Hagrid's just before lunch,/nshivering slightly, her robes damp to the knees./n/n/n/n"So?" said Ron, looking up when she entered. "Got all/nhis lessons planned for him?"/n/n"Well, I tried," she said dully, sinking into a chair/nbeside Harry. She pulled out her wand and gave it a/ncomplicated little wave so that hot air streamed out of/nthe tip; she then pointed this at her robes, which/nbegan to steam as they dried out. "He wasn't even/nthere when I arrived, I was knocking for at least half/nan hour. And then he came stumping out of the forest/n/n/n/nHarry groaned. The Forbidden Forest was teeming/nwith the kind of creatures most likely to get Hagrid/nthe sack. "What's he keeping in there? Did he say?"/nasked Harry./n/n"No," said Hermione miserably. "He says he wants/nthem to be a surprise. I tried to explain about/nUmbridge, but he just doesn't get it. He kept saying/nnobody in their right mind would rather study knarls/nthan chimaeras — oh I don't think he's got a/nchimaera," she added at the appalled look on Harry/nand Ron's faces, "but that's not for lack of trying from/nwhat he said about how hard it is to get eggs... I don't/nknow how many times I told him he'd be better off/nfollowing Grubbly-Plank's plan, I honestly don't think/nhe listened to half of what I said. He's in a bit of a/nfunny mood, you know. He still won't say how he got/nall those injuries..."/n/nHagrid's reappearance at the staff table at breakfast/nnext day was not greeted by enthusiasm from all/nstudents. Some, like Fred, George, and Lee, roared/nwith delight and sprinted up the aisle between the/nGryffindor and Hufflepuff tables to wring Hagrid's/n/n/n/n/nenormous hand; others, like Parvati and Lavender,/nexchanged gloomy looks and shook their heads. Harry/nknew that many of them preferred Professor Grubbly-/nPlank's lessons, and the worst of it was that a very/nsmall, unbiased part of him knew that they had good/nreason: Grubbly-Plank's idea of an interesting class/nwas not one where there was a risk that somebody/nmight have their head ripped off./n/nIt was with a certain amount of apprehension that/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione headed down to Hagrid's/non Tuesday, heavily muffled against the cold. Harry/nwas worried, not only about what Hagrid might have/ndecided to teach them, but also about how the rest of/nthe class, particularly Malfoy and his cronies, would/nbehave if Umbridge was watching them./n/nHowever, the High Inquisitor was nowhere to be seen/nas they struggled through the snow toward Hagrid,/nwho stood waiting for them on the edge of the forest./nHe did not present a reassuring sight; the bruises/nthat had been purple on Saturday night were now/ntinged with green and yellow and some of his cuts still/nseemed to be bleeding. Harry could not understand/nthis: Had Hagrid perhaps been attacked by some/ncreature whose venom prevented the wounds it/ninflicted from healing? As though to complete the/nominous picture, Hagrid was carrying what looked/nlike half a dead cow over his shoulder./n/n"We're workin' in here today!" Hagrid called happily to/nthe approaching students, jerking his head back at/nthe dark trees behind him. "Bit more sheltered!/nAnyway, they prefer the dark..."/n/n"What prefers the dark?" Harry heard Malfoy say/nsharply to Crabbe and Goyle, a trace of panic in his/nvoice. "What did he say prefers the dark — did you/nhear?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry remembered the only occasion on which Malfoy/nhad entered the forest before now; he had not been/nvery brave then either. He smiled to himself; after the/nQuidditch match anything that caused Malfoy/ndiscomfort was all right with him./n/n"Ready?" said Hagrid happily, looking around at the/nclass. "Right, well, I've bin savin' a trip inter the forest/nfer yer fifth year. Thought we'd go an' see these/ncreatures in their natural habitat. Now, what we're/nstudyin' today is pretty rare, I reckon I'm probably the/non'y person in Britain who's managed ter train 'em — "/n/n"And you're sure they're trained, are you?" said/nMalfoy, the panic in his voice even more pronounced/nnow. "Only it wouldn't be the first time you'd brought/nwild stuff to class, would it?"/n/nThe Slytherins murmured agreement and a few/nGryffindors looked as though they thought Malfoy had/na fair point too./n/n" 'Course they're trained," said Hagrid, scowling and/nhoisting the dead cow a little higher on his shoulder./n/n"So what happened to your face, then?" demanded/nMalfoy./n/n"Mind yer own business!" said Hagrid, angrily. "Now if/nyeh've finished askin' stupid questions, follow me!"/n/nHe turned and strode straight into the forest. Nobody/nseemed much disposed to follow. Harry glanced at/nRon and Hermione, who sighed but nodded, and the/nthree of them set off after Hagrid, leading the rest of/nthe class./n/nThey walked for about ten minutes until they reached/na place where the trees stood so closely together that/n/n/n/n/n/nit was as dark as twilight and there was no snow on/nthe ground at all. Hagrid deposited his half a cow with/na grunt on the ground, stepped back, and turned to/nface his class again, most of whom were creeping/ntoward him from tree to tree, peering around/nnervously as though expecting to be set upon at any/nmoment./n/n"Gather roun', gather roun'," said Hagrid/nencouragingly. "Now, they'll be attracted by the smell/no' the meat but I'm goin' ter give 'em a call anyway,/n'cause they'll like ter know it's me..."/n/nHe turned, shook his shaggy head to get the hair out/nof his face, and gave an odd, shrieking cry that/nechoed through the dark trees like the call of some/nmonstrous bird. Nobody laughed; most of them/nlooked too scared to make a sound./n/nHagrid gave the shrieking cry again. A minute passed/nin which the class continued to peer nervously over/ntheir shoulders and around trees for a first glimpse of/nwhatever it was that was coming. And then, as Hagrid/nshook his hair back for a third time and expanded his/nenormous chest, Harry nudged Ron and pointed into/nthe black space between two gnarled yew trees./n/nA pair of blank, white, shining eyes were growing/nlarger through the gloom and a moment later the/ndragonish face, neck, and then skeletal body of a/ngreat, black, winged horse emerged from the/ndarkness. It looked around at the class for a few/nseconds, swishing its long black tail, then bowed its/nhead and began to tear flesh from the dead cow with/nits pointed fangs./n/nA great wave of relief broke over Harry. Here at last/nwas proof that he had not imagined these creatures,/nthat they were real: Hagrid knew about them too. He/n/n/n/n/n/nlooked eagerly at Ron, but Ron was still staring/naround into the trees and after a few seconds he/nwhispered, "Why doesn't Hagrid call again?"/n/nMost of the rest of the class were wearing expressions/nas confused and nervously expectant as Ron's and/nwere still gazing everywhere but at the horse standing/nfeet from them. There were only two other people who/nseemed to be able to see them: a stringy Slytherin boy/nstanding just behind Goyle was watching the horse/neating with an expression of great distaste on his face,/nand Neville, whose eyes were following the swishing/nprogress of the long black tail./n/n"Oh, an' here comes another one!" said Hagrid/nproudly, as a second black horse appeared out of the/ndark trees, folded its leathery wings closer to its body,/nand dipped its head to gorge on the meat. "Now ... put/nyer hands up, who can see 'em?"/n/nImmensely pleased to feel that he was at last going to/nunderstand the mystery of these horses, Harry raised/nhis hand. Hagrid nodded at him./n/n"Yeah ... yeah, I knew you'd be able ter, Harry," he/nsaid seriously. "An' you too, Neville, eh? An' — "/n/n"Excuse me," said Malfoy in a sneering voice, "but/nwhat exactly are we supposed to be seeing?"/n/nFor answer, Hagrid pointed at the cow carcass on the/nground. The whole class stared at it for a few seconds,/nthen several people gasped and Parvati squealed./nHarry understood why: Bits of flesh stripping/nthemselves away from the bones and vanishing into/nthin air had to look very odd indeed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's doing it?" Parvati demanded in a terrified/nvoice, retreating behind the nearest tree. "What's/neating it?"/n/n"Thestrals," said Hagrid proudly and Hermione gave a/nsoft "oh!" of comprehension at Harry's shoulder./n"Hogwarts has got a whole herd of 'em in here. Now,/nwho knows — ?"/n/n"But they're really, really unlucky!" interrupted/nParvati, looking alarmed. "They're supposed to bring/nall sorts of horrible misfortune on people who see/nthem. Professor Trelawney told me once — "/n/n"No, no, no," said Hagrid, chuckling, "tha's jus'/nsuperstition, that is, they aren' unlucky, they're dead/nclever an' useful! 'Course, this lot don' get a lot o'/nwork, it's mainly jus' pullin' the school carriages/nunless Dumbledore's takin' a long journey an' don'/nwant ter Apparate — an' here's another couple, look/n/n/n/nTwo more horses came quietly out of the trees, one of/nthem passing very close to Parvati, who shivered and/npressed herself closer to the tree, saying, "I think I felt/nsomething, I think it's near me!"/n/n"Don' worry, it won' hurt yeh," said Hagrid patiently./n"Righ', now, who can tell me why some o' you can see/nthem an' some can't?"/n/nHermione raised her hand./n/n"Go on then," said Hagrid, beaming at her./n/n"The only people who can see thestrals," she said,/n/n"are people who have seen death."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Tha's exactly right," said Hagrid solemnly, "ten/npoints ter Gryffindor. Now, thestrals — "/n/n"Hem, hem."/n/nProfessor Umbridge had arrived. She was standing a/nfew feet away from Harry, wearing her green hat and/ncloak again, her clipboard at the ready. Hagrid, who/nhad never heard Umbridge 's fake cough before, was/ngazing in some concern at the closest thestral,/nevidently under the impression that it had made the/nsound./n/n"Hem, hem."/n/n"Oh hello!" Hagrid said, smiling, having located the/nsource of the noise./n/n"You received the note I sent to your cabin this/nmorning?" said Umbridge, in the same loud, slow/nvoice she had used with him earlier, as though she/nwas addressing somebody both foreign and very slow./n"Telling you that I would be inspecting your lesson?"/n/n"Oh yeah," said Hagrid brightly. "Glad yeh found the/nplace all righ'! Well, as you can see — or, I dunno —/ncan you? We're doin' thestrals today — "/n/n"I'm sorry?" said Umbridge loudly, cupping her hand/naround her ear and frowning. "What did you say?"/n/nHagrid looked a little confused./n/n"Er — thestralsl" he said loudly. "Big — er — winged/nhorses, yeh know!"/n/nHe flapped his gigantic arms hopefully. Professor/nUmbridge raised her eyebrows at him and muttered/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nas she made a note on her clipboard, " 'has ... to .../nresort ... to ... crude . . . sign . . . language "/n/n"Well ... anyway ..." said Hagrid, turning back to the/nclass and looking slightly flustered. "Erm ... what was/nI sayin'?"/n/n" 'Appears ... to ... have . . . poor . . . short . . . term . . ./nmemory " muttered Umbridge, loudly enough for/neveryone to hear her. Draco Malfoy looked as though/nChristmas had come a month early; Hermione, on the/nother hand, had turned scarlet with suppressed rage./n/n"Oh yeah," said Hagrid, throwing an uneasy glance at/nUmbridge's clipboard, but plowing on valiantly. "Yeah,/nI was gonna tell yeh how come we got a herd. Yeah,/nso, we started off with a male an' five females. This/none," he patted the first horse to have appeared,/n/n"name o' Tenebrus, he's my special favorite, firs' one/nborn here in the forest — "/n/n"Are you aware," Umbridge said loudly, interrupting/nhim, "that the Ministry of Magic has classified/nthestrals as 'dangerous'?"/n/nHarry's heart sank like a stone, but Hagrid merely/nchuckled./n/n"Thestrals aren' dangerous! All righ, they might take a/nbite outta you if yeh really annoy them — "/n/n" 'Shows . . . signs ... of ... pleasure ... at ... idea ...of/n... violence ... ' " muttered Umbridge, scribbling on her/nclipboard again./n/n"No — come on!" said Hagrid, looking a little anxious/nnow. "I mean, a dog'll bite if yeh bait it, won' it — but/nthestrals have jus' got a bad reputation because o' the/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndeath thing — people used ter think they were bad/nomens, didn' they? Jus' didn' understand, did they?"/n/n/n/nUmbridge did not answer; she finished writing her/nlast note, then looked up at Hagrid and said, again/nvery loudly and slowly, "Please continue teaching as/nusual. I am going to walk" — she mimed walking —/nMalfoy and Pansy Parkinson were having silent fits of/nlaughter — "among the students" — she pointed/naround at individual members of the class — "and/nask them questions." She pointed at her mouth to/nindicate talking./n/nHagrid stared at her, clearly at a complete loss to/nunderstand why she was acting as though he did not/nunderstand normal English. Hermione had tears of/nfury in her eyes now./n/n"You hag, you evil hag!" she whispered, as Umbridge/nwalked toward Pansy Parkinson. "I know what you're/ndoing, you awful, twisted, vicious — "/n/n"Erm ... anyway," said Hagrid, clearly struggling to/nregain the flow of his lesson, "so — thestrals. Yeah./nWell, there's loads o' good stuff abou' them..."/n/n"Do you find," said Professor Umbridge in a ringing/nvoice to Pansy Parkinson, "that you are able to/nunderstand Professor Hagrid when he talks?"/n/nJust like Hermione, Pansy had tears in her eyes, but/nthese were tears of laughter; indeed, her answer was/nalmost incoherent because she was trying to suppress/nher giggles. "No ... because ... well ... it sounds ... like/ngrunting a lot of the time..."/n/nUmbridge scribbled on her clipboard. The few/nunbruised bits of Hagrid 's face flushed, but he tried/nto act as though he had not heard Pansy's answer./n/n/n/n/n/n"Er ... yeah ... good stuff abou' thestrals. Well, once/nthey're tamed, like this lot, yehll never be lost again./n'Mazin' senses o' direction, jus' tell 'em where yeh/nwant ter go — "/n/n"Assuming they can understand you, of course," said/nMalfoy loudly, and Pansy Parkinson collapsed in a fit/nof renewed giggles. Professor Umbridge smiled/nindulgently at them and then turned to Neville./n/n"You can see the thestrals, Longbottom, can you?"/nshe said./n/nNeville nodded./n/n"Whom did you see die?" she asked, her tone/nindifferent./n/n"My ... my grandad," said Neville./n/n"And what do you think of them?" she said, waving/nher stubby hand at the horses, who by now had/nstripped a great deal of the carcass down to bone./n/n"Erm," said Neville nervously, with a glance at Hagrid./n"Well, they're ... er ... okay..."/n/n" 'Students ... are ... too ... intimidated ... to ... admit/n... they ... are ... frightened...' " muttered Umbridge,/nmaking another note on her clipboard./n/n"No!" said Neville, looking upset, "no, I'm not scared of/nthem — !"/n/n"It's quite all right," said Umbridge, patting Neville on/nthe shoulder with what she evidently intended to be/nan understanding smile, though it looked more like a/nleer to Harry. "Well, Hagrid," she turned to look up at/nhim again, speaking once more in that loud, slow/n/n/n/n/nvoice, "I think I've got enough to be getting along/nwith... You will receive" — she mimed taking/nsomething from the air in front of her — "the results/nof your inspection" — she pointed at the clipboard —/n"in ten days' time." She held up ten stubby little/nfingers, then, her smile wider and more toadlike than/never before beneath her green hat, she bustled from/ntheir midst, leaving Malfoy and Pansy Parkinson in/nfits of laughter, Hermione actually shaking with fury,/nand Neville looking confused and upset./n/n"That foul, lying, twisting old gargoyle!" stormed/nHermione half an hour later, as they made their way/nback up to the castle through the channels they had/nmade earlier in the snow. "You see what she's up to?/nIt's her thing about half-breeds all over again — she's/ntrying to make out Hagrid's some kind of dim-witted/ntroll, just because he had a giantess for a mother —/nand oh, it's not fair, that really wasn't a bad lesson at/nall — I mean, all right, if it had been Blast-Ended/nSkrewts again, but thestrals are fine — in fact, for/nHagrid, they're really good!"/n/n"Umbridge said they're dangerous," said Ron./n/n"Well, it's like Hagrid said, they can look after/nthemselves," said Hermione impatiently, "and I/nsuppose a teacher like Grubbly-Plank wouldn't/nusually show them to us before N.E.W.T. level, but,/nwell, they are very interesting, aren't they? The way/nsome people can see them and some can't! I wish I/ncould."/n/n"Do you?" Harry asked her quietly./n/nShe looked horrorstruck./n/n"Oh Harry — I'm sorry — no, of course I don't — that/nwas a really stupid thing to say — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's okay," he said quickly, "don't worry..."/n/n/n/n"I'm surprised so many people could see them," said/nRon. "Three in a class — "/n/n"Yeah, Weasley, we were just wondering," said a/nmalicious voice nearby. Unheard by any of them in/nthe muffling snow, Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle were/nwalking along right behind them. "D'you reckon if you/nsaw someone snuff it you'd be able to see the Quaffle/nbetter?"/n/nHe, Crabbe, and Goyle roared with laughter as they/npushed past on their way to the castle and then broke/ninto a chorus of "Weasley Is Our King." Ron's ears/nturned scarlet./n/n"Ignore them, just ignore them," intoned Hermione,/npulling out her wand and performing the charm to/nproduce hot air again, so that she could melt them an/neasier path through the untouched snow between/nthem and the greenhouses./n/nDecember arrived, bringing with it more snow and a/npositive avalanche of homework for the fifth years./n/nRon and Hermione 's prefect duties also became more/nand more onerous as Christmas approached. They/nwere called upon to supervise the decoration of the/ncastle ("You try putting up tinsel when Peeves has got/nthe other end and is trying to strangle you with it,"/nsaid Ron), to watch over first and second years/nspending their break times inside because of the/nbitter cold ("And they're cheeky little snotrags, you/nknow, we definitely weren't that rude when we were in/nfirst year," said Ron), and to patrol the corridors in/nshifts with Argus Filch, who suspected that the/nholiday spirit might show itself in an outbreak of/nwizard duels ("He's got dung for brains, that one,"/nsaid Ron furiously). They were so busy that Hermione/n/n/n/n/nhad stopped knitting elf hats and was fretting that/nshe was down to her last three./n/n"All those poor elves I haven't set free yet, having to/nstay over during Christmas because there aren't/nenough hats!"/n/nHarry, who had not had the heart to tell her that/nDobby was taking everything she made, bent lower/nover his History of Magic essay. In any case, he did/nnot want to think about Christmas. For the first time/nin his school career, he very much wanted to spend/nthe holidays away from Hogwarts. Between his/nQuidditch ban and worry about whether or not/nHagrid was going to be put on probation, he felt/nhighly resentful toward the place at the moment. The/nonly thing he really looked forward to were the D.A./nmeetings, and they would have to stop over the/nholidays, as nearly everybody in the D.A. would be/nspending the time with their families. Hermione was/ngoing skiing with her parents, something that greatly/namused Ron, who had never before heard of Muggles/nstrapping narrow strips of wood to their feet to slide/ndown mountains. Ron, meanwhile, was going home to/nthe Burrow. Harry endured several days of jealousy/nbefore Ron said, in response to Harry asking how Ron/nwas going to get home for Christmas, "But you're/ncoming too! Didn't I say? Mum wrote and told me to/ninvite you weeks ago!"/n/nHermione rolled her eyes, but Harry's spirits soared:/nThe thought of Christmas at the Burrow was truly/nwonderful, only slightly marred by Harry's guilty/nfeeling that he would not be able to spend the holiday/nwith Sirius. He wondered whether he could possibly/npersuade Mrs. Weasley to invite his godfather for the/nfestivities too, but apart from the fact that he doubted/nwhether Dumbledore would permit Sirius to leave/nGrimmauld Place, he could not help but feel that Mrs./n/n/n/n/nWeasley might not want him; they were so often at/nloggerheads. Sirius had not contacted Harry at all/nsince his last appearance in the fire, and although/nHarry knew that with Umbridge on the constant/nwatch it would be unwise to attempt to contact him,/nhe did not like to think of Sirius alone in his mother's/nold house, perhaps pulling a lonely cracker with/nKreacher./n/nHarry arrived early in the Room of Requirement for/nthe last D.A. meeting before the holidays and was/nvery glad he had, because when the lamps burst into/nlight he saw that Dobby had taken it upon himself to/ndecorate the place for Christmas. He could tell the elf/nhad done it, because nobody else would have strung a/nhundred golden baubles from the ceiling, each/nshowing a picture of Harry's face and bearing the/nlegend HAVE A VERY HARRY CHRISTMAS!/n/nHarry had only just managed to get the last of them/ndown before the door creaked open and Luna/nLovegood entered, looking dreamy as always./n/n"Hello," she said vaguely, looking around at what/nremained of the decorations. "These are nice, did you/nput them up?"/n/n"No," said Harry, "it was Dobby the house-elf."/n/n"Mistletoe," said Luna dreamily, pointing at a large/nclump of white berries placed almost over Harry's/nhead. He jumped out from under it. "Good thinking,"/nsaid Luna very seriously. "It's often infested with/nnargles."/n/nHarry was saved the necessity of asking what nargles/nwere by the arrival of Angelina, Katie, and Alicia. All/nthree of them were breathless and looked very cold./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well," said Angelina dully, pulling off her cloak and/nthrowing it into a corner, "we've replaced you."/n/n/n/n"Replaced me?" said Harry blankly./n/n"You and Fred and George," she said impatiently./n"We've got another Seeker!"/n/n"Who?" said Harry quickly./n/n"Ginny Weasley," said Katie./n/nHarry gaped at her./n/n"Yeah, I know," said Angelina, pulling out her wand/nand flexing her arm. "But she's pretty good, actually./nNothing on you, of course," she said, throwing him a/nvery dirty look, "but as we can't have you ..."/n/nHarry bit back the retort he was longing to utter: Did/nshe imagine for a second that he did not regret his/nexpulsion from the team a hundred times more than/nshe did?/n/n"And what about the Beaters?" he asked, trying to/nkeep his voice even./n/n"Andrew Kirke," said Alicia without enthusiasm, "and/nJack Sloper. Neither of them are brilliant, but/ncompared with the rest of the idiots who turned up/n/n/n/nThe arrival of Ron, Hermione, and Neville brought this/ndepressing discussion to an end and within five/nminutes, the room was full enough to prevent him/nseeing Angelina's burning, reproachful looks./n/n"Okay," he said, calling them all to order. "I thought/nthis evening we should just go over the things we've/n/n/n/n/n/ndone so far, because it's the last meeting before the/nholidays and there's no point starting anything new/nright before a three-week break — "/n/n"We're not doing anything new?" said Zacharias/nSmith, in a disgruntled whisper loud enough to carry/nthrough the room. "If I'd known that, I wouldn't have/ncome..."/n/n"We're all really sorry Harry didn't tell you, then," said/nFred loudly./n/nSeveral people sniggered. Harry saw Cho laughing/nand felt the familiar swooping sensation in his/nstomach, as though he had missed a step going/ndownstairs./n/n"We can practice in pairs," said Harry. "Well start/nwith the Impediment Jinx, just for ten minutes, then/nwe can get out the cushions and try Stunning again."/n/nThey all divided up obediently; Harry partnered/nNeville as usual. The room was soon full of/nintermittent cries of " Impedimental " People froze for a/nminute or so, during which their partners would stare/naimlessly around the room watching other pairs at/nwork, then would unfreeze and take their turn at the/njinx./n/nNeville had improved beyond all recognition. After a/nwhile, when Harry had unfrozen three times in a row,/nhe had Neville join Ron and Hermione again so that/nhe could walk around the room and watch the others./nWhen he passed Cho she beamed at him; he resisted/nthe temptation to walk past her several more times./n/nAfter ten minutes on the Impediment Jinx, they laid/nout cushions all over the floor and started practicing/nStunning again. Space was really too confined to/n/n/n/n/n/nallow them all to work this spell at once; half the/ngroup observed the others for a while, then swapped/nover. Harry felt himself positively swelling with pride/nas he watched them all. True, Neville did Stun Padma/nPatil rather than Dean, at whom he had been aiming,/nbut it was a much closer miss than usual, and/neverybody else had made enormous progress./n/nAt the end of an hour, Harry called a halt./n/n"You're getting really good," he said, beaming around/nat them. "When we get back from the holidays we can/nstart doing some of the big stuff — maybe even/nPatronuses."/n/nThere was a murmur of excitement. The room began/nto clear in the usual twos and threes; most people/nwished Harry a Happy Christmas as they went./n/nFeeling cheerful, he collected up the cushions with/nRon and Hermione and stacked them neatly away./n/nRon and Hermione left before he did; he hung back a/nlittle, because Cho was still there and he was hoping/nto receive a Merry Christmas from her./n/n"No, you go on," he heard her say to her friend/nMarietta, and his heart gave a jolt that seemed to take/nit into the region of his Adam's apple./n/nHe pretended to be straightening the cushion pile. He/nwas quite sure they were alone now and waited for/nher to speak. Instead, he heard a hearty sniff./n/nHe turned and saw Cho standing in the middle of the/nroom, tears pouring down her face./n/n"Wha — ?"/n/n/n/nHe didn't know what to do. She was simply standing/nthere, crying silently./n/n/n/n/n/n"What's up?" he said feebly./n/n/n/nShe shook her head and wiped her eyes on her sleeve./n"I'm — sorry," she said thickly. "I suppose ... it's just/n... learning all this stuff... It just makes me ... wonder/nwhether ... if he'd known it all ... he'd still be alive..."/n/nHarry's heart sank right back past its usual spot and/nsettled somewhere around his navel. He ought to have/nknown. She wanted to talk about Cedric./n/n"He did know this stuff," Harry said heavily. "He was/nreally good at it, or he could never have got to the/nmiddle of that maze. But if Voldemort really wants to/nkill you, you don't stand a chance."/n/nShe hiccuped at the sound of Voldemort's name, but/nstared at Harry without flinching./n/n" You survived when you were just a baby," she said/nquietly./n/n"Yeah, well," said Harry wearily, moving toward the/ndoor, "I dunno why, nor does anyone else, so it's/nnothing to be proud of."/n/n"Oh don't go!" said Cho, sounding tearful again. "I'm/nreally sorry to get all upset like this... I didn't mean/nto..."/n/nShe hiccuped again. She was very pretty even when/nher eyes were red and puffy. Harry felt thoroughly/nmiserable. He'd have been so pleased just with a/nMerry Christmas.../n/n"I know it must be horrible for you," she said,/nmopping her eyes on her sleeve again. "Me/nmentioning Cedric, when you saw him die... I suppose/nyou just want to forget about it..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry did not say anything to this; it was quite true,/nbut he felt heartless saying it./n/n"You're a r-really good teacher, you know," said Cho,/nwith a watery smile. "I've never been able to Stun/nanything before."/n/n"Thanks," said Harry awkwardly./n/nThey looked at each other for a long moment. Harry/nfelt a burning desire to run from the room and, at the/nsame time, a complete inability to move his feet./n/n"Mistletoe," said Cho quietly, pointing at the ceiling/nover his head./n/n"Yeah," said Harry. His mouth was very dry. "It's/nprobably full of nargles, though."/n/n"What are nargles?"/n/n"No idea," said Harry. She had moved closer. His/nbrain seemed to have been Stunned. "You'd have to/nask Loony. Luna, I mean."/n/nCho made a funny noise halfway between a sob and a/nlaugh. She was even nearer him now. He could have/ncounted the freckles on her nose./n/n"I really like you, Harry."/n/nHe could not think. A tingling sensation was/nspreading throughout him, paralyzing his arms, legs,/nand brain./n/nShe was much too close. He could see every tear/nclinging to her eyelashes.../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe returned to the common room half an hour later to/nfind Hermione and Ron in the best seats by the fire;/nnearly everybody else had gone to bed. Hermione was/nwriting a very long letter; she had already filled half a/nroll of parchment, which was dangling from the edge/nof the table. Ron was lying on the hearthrug, trying to/nfinish his Transfiguration homework./n/n"What kept you?" he asked, as Harry sank into the/narmchair next to Hermione 's./n/nHarry did not answer. He was in a state of shock. Half/nof him wanted to tell Ron and Hermione what had/njust happened, but the other half wanted to take the/nsecret with him to the grave./n/n"Are you all right, Harry?" Hermione asked, peering at/nhim over the tip of her quill./n/nHarry gave a halfhearted shrug. In truth, he didn't/nknow whether he was all right or not. "What's up?"/nsaid Ron, hoisting himself up on his elbow to get a/nclearer view of Harry. "What's happened?"/n/nHarry didn't quite know how to set about telling them,/nand still wasn't sure whether he wanted to. Just as he/nhad decided not to say anything, Hermione took/nmatters out of his hands./n/n"Is it Cho?" she asked in a businesslike way. "Did she/ncorner you after the meeting?"/n/nNumbly surprised, Harry nodded. Ron sniggered,/nbreaking off when Hermione caught his eye./n/n"So — er — what did she want?" he asked in a mock/ncasual voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"She — " Harry began, rather hoarsely; he cleared his/nthroat and tried again. "She — er — "/n/n/n/n"Did you kiss?" asked Hermione briskly./n/nRon sat up so fast that he sent his ink bottle flying all/nover the rug. Disregarding this completely he stared/navidly at Harry./n/n"Well?" he demanded./n/nHarry looked from Ron's expression of mingled/ncuriosity and hilarity to Hermione's slight frown, and/nnodded./n/n"HA!"/n/nRon made a triumphant gesture with his fist and/nwent into a raucous peal of laughter that made/nseveral timid-looking second years over beside the/nwindow jump. A reluctant grin spread over Harry's/nface as he watched Ron rolling around on the/nhearthrug. Hermione gave Ron a look of deep disgust/nand returned to her letter./n/n"Well?" Ron said finally, looking up at Harry. "How/nwas it?"/n/nHarry considered for a moment./n/n"Wet," he said truthfully./n/nRon made a noise that might have indicated/njubilation or disgust, it was hard to tell./n/n"Because she was crying," Harry continued heavily./n/n"Oh," said Ron, his smile fading slightly. "Are you that/nbad at kissing?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Dunno," said Harry, who hadn't considered this, and/nimmediately felt rather worried. "Maybe I am."/n/n/n/n"Of course you're not," said Hermione absently, still/nscribbling away at her letter./n/n"How do you know?" said Ron in a sharp voice./n/n"Because Cho spends half her time crying these/ndays," said Hermione vaguely. "She does it at/nmealtimes, in the loos, all over the place."/n/n"You'd think a bit of kissing would cheer her up," said/nRon, grinning./n/n"Ron," said Hermione in a dignified voice, dipping the/npoint of her quill into her ink pot, "you are the most/ninsensitive wart I have ever had the misfortune to/nmeet."/n/n"What's that supposed to mean?" said Ron/nindignantly. "What sort of person cries while/nsomeone's kissing them?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, slightly desperately, "who does?"/n/nHermione looked at the pair of them with an almost/npitying expression on her face./n/n"Don't you understand how Cho's feeling at the/nmoment?" she asked./n/n"No," said Harry and Ron together./n/nHermione sighed and laid down her quill./n/n"Well, obviously, she's feeling very sad, because of/nCedric dying. Then I expect she's feeling confused/nbecause she liked Cedric and now she likes Harry,/n/n/n/n/n/nand she can't work out who she likes best. Then she'll/nbe feeling guilty, thinking it's an insult to Cedric's/nmemory to be kissing Harry at all, and she'll be/nworrying about what everyone else might say about/nher if she starts going out with Harry. And she/nprobably can't work out what her feelings toward/nHarry are anyway, because he was the one who was/nwith Cedric when Cedric died, so that's all very mixed/nup and painful. Oh, and she's afraid she's going to be/nthrown off the Ravenclaw Quidditch team because/nshe's been flying so badly."/n/nA slightly stunned silence greeted the end of this/nspeech, then Ron said, "One person can't feel all that/nat once, they'd explode."/n/n"Just because you've got the emotional range of a/nteaspoon doesn't mean we all have," said Hermione/nnastily, picking up her quill again./n/n"She was the one who started it," said Harry. "I/nwouldn't've — she just sort of came at me — and next/nthing she's crying all over me — I didn't know what to/ndo — "/n/n/n/n"Don't blame you, mate," said Ron, looking alarmed at/nthe very thought./n/n"You just had to be nice to her," said Hermione,/nlooking up anxiously. "You were, weren't you?"/n/n"Well," said Harry, an unpleasant heat creeping up/nhis face, "I sort of — patted her on the back a bit."/n/nHermione looked as though she was restraining/nherself from rolling her eyes with extreme difficulty./n/n"Well, I suppose it could have been worse," she said./n"Are you going to see her again?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'll have to, won't I?" said Harry. "We've got D.A./nmeetings, haven't we?"/n/n/n/n"You know what I mean," said Hermione impatiently./n/nHarry said nothing. Hermione 's words opened up a/nwhole new vista of frightening possibilities. He tried to/nimagine going somewhere with Cho — Hogsmeade,/nperhaps — and being alone with her for hours at a/ntime. Of course, she would have been expecting him/nto ask her out after what had just happened... The/nthought made his stomach clench painfully./n/n"Oh well," said Hermione distantly, buried in her/nletter once more, "you'll have plenty of opportunities/nto ask her..."/n/n"What if he doesn't want to ask her?" said Ron, who/nhad been watching Harry with an unusually shrewd/nexpression on his face./n/n"Don't be silly," said Hermione vaguely, "Harry's liked/nher for ages, haven't you, Harry?"/n/nHe did not answer. Yes, he had liked Cho for ages,/nbut whenever he had imagined a scene involving the/ntwo of them it had always featured a Cho who was/nenjoying herself, as opposed to a Cho who was/nsobbing uncontrollably into his shoulder./n/n"Who 're you writing the novel to anyway?" Ron asked/nHermione, trying to read the bit of parchment now/ntrailing on the floor. Hermione hitched it up out of/nsight./n/n"Viktor."/n/n"Krum?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"How many other Viktors do we know?"/n/n/n/nRon said nothing, but looked disgruntled. They sat in/nsilence for another twenty minutes, Ron finishing his/nTransfiguration essay with many snorts of impatience/nand crossings-out, Hermione writing steadily to the/nvery end of the parchment, rolling it up carefully and/nsealing it, and Harry staring into the fire, wishing/nmore than anything that Sirius's head would appear/nthere and give him some advice about girls. But the/nfire merely crackled lower and lower, until the red-hot/nembers crumbled into ash and, looking around, Harry/nsaw that they were, yet again, the last in the common/nroom./n/n"Well, 'night," said Hermione, yawning widely, and/nshe set off up the girls' staircase./n/n"What does she see in Krum?" Ron demanded as he/nand Harry climbed the boys' stairs./n/n"Well," said Harry, considering the matter, "I s'pose/nhe's older, isn't he ... and he's an international/nQuidditch player..."/n/n"Yeah, but apart from that," said Ron, sounding/naggravated. "I mean he's a grouchy git, isn't he?"/n/n"Bit grouchy, yeah," said Harry, whose thoughts were/nstill on Cho./n/nThey pulled off their robes and put on pajamas in/nsilence; Dean, Seamus, and Neville were already/nasleep. Harry put his glasses on his bedside table and/ngot into bed but did not pull the hangings closed/naround his four-poster; instead he stared at the patch/nof starry sky visible through the window next to/nNeville's bed. If he had known, this time last night,/n/n/n/n/n/nthat in twenty-four hours' time he would have kissed/nCho Chang .../n/n/n/n" 'Night," grunted Ron, from somewhere to his right./n/n" 'Night," said Harry./n/nMaybe next time ... if there was a next time ... she'd/nbe a bit happier. He ought to have asked her out; she/nhad probably been expecting it and was now really/nangry with him ... or was she lying in bed, still crying/nabout Cedric? He did not know what to think./nHermione's explanation had made it all seem more/ncomplicated rather than easier to understand./n/nThat's what they should teach us here, he thought,/nturning over onto his side, how girls' brains work .../nit'd be more useful than Divination anyway.../n/nNeville snuffled in his sleep. An owl hooted/nsomewhere out in the night./n/nHarry dreamed he was back in the D.A. room. Cho/nwas accusing him of luring her there under false/npretenses; she said that he had promised her a/nhundred and fifty Chocolate Frog cards if she showed/nup. Harry protested... Cho shouted, " Cedric gave me/nloads of Chocolate Frog cards, look\" And she pulled/nout fistfuls of cards from inside her robes and threw/nthem into the air, and then turned into Hermione,/nwho said, "You did promise her, you know, Harry... I/nthink you'd better give her something else instead.../nHow about your Firebolt?" And Harry was protesting/nthat he could not give Cho his Firebolt because/nUmbridge had it, and anyway the whole thing was/nridiculous, he'd only come to the D.A. room to put up/nsome Christmas baubles shaped like Dobby's head.../n/nThe dream changed.../n/n/n/n/n/nHis body felt smooth, powerful, and flexible. He was/ngliding between shining metal bars, across dark, cold/nstone... He was flat against the floor, sliding along on/nhis belly... It was dark, yet he could see objects/naround him shimmering in strange, vibrant colors.../nHe was turning his head... At first glance, the corridor/nwas empty . . . but no ... a man was sitting on the floor/nahead, his chin drooping onto his chest, his outline/ngleaming in the dark. . ./n/nHarry put out his tongue... He tasted the man's scent/non the air. . . He was alive but drowsing . . . sitting in/nfront of a door at the end of the corridor . . ./n/nHarry longed to bite the man . . . but he must master/nthe impulse... He had more important work to do.../n/nBut the man was stirring ... a silvery cloak fell from/nhis legs as he jumped to his feet; and Harry saw his/nvibrant, blurred outline towering above him, saw a/nwand withdrawn from a belt... He had no choice... He/nreared high from the floor and struck once, twice,/nthree times, plunging his fangs deeply into the man's/nflesh, feeling his ribs splinter beneath his jaws, feeling/nthe warm gush of blood.../n/nThe man was yelling in pain ... then he fell silent... He/nslumped backward against the wall... Blood was/nsplattering onto the floor.../n/nHis forehead hurt terribly. . . It was aching fit to/nburst.../n/n"Harry! HARRY!"/n/nHe opened his eyes. Every inch of his body was/ncovered in icy sweat; his bedcovers were twisted all/naround him like a straitjacket; he felt as though a/nwhite-hot poker was being applied to his forehead./n/n/n/n/n/n"Harryl"/n/n/n/nRon was standing over him looking extremely/nfrightened. There were more figures at the foot of/nHarry's bed. He clutched his head in his hands; the/npain was blinding him... He rolled right over and/nvomited over the edge of the mattress./n/n"He's really ill," said a scared voice. "Should we call/nsomeone?"/n/n"Harry! Harryl"/n/nHe had to tell Ron, it was very important that he tell/nhim... Taking great gulps of air, Harry pushed himself/nup in bed, willing himself not to throw up again, the/npain half-blinding him./n/n"Your dad," he panted, his chest heaving. "Your dad's/n... been attacked..."/n/n"What?" said Ron uncomprehendingly./n/n"Your dad! He's been bitten, it's serious, there was/nblood everywhere..."/n/n"I'm going for help," said the same scared voice, and/nHarry heard footsteps running out of the dormitory./n/n"Harry, mate," said Ron uncertainly, "you ... you were/njust dreaming..."/n/n"No!" said Harry furiously; it was crucial that Ron/nunderstand. "It wasn't a dream ... not an ordinary/ndream... I was there, I saw it... I did it..."/n/nHe could hear Seamus and Dean muttering but did/nnot care. The pain in his forehead was subsiding/nslightly, though he was still sweating and shivering/n/n/n/n/n/nfeverishly. He retched again and Ron leapt backward/nout of the way./n/n"Harry, you're not well," he said shakily. "Neville's/ngone for help..."/n/n"I'm fine!" Harry choked, wiping his mouth on his/npajamas and shaking uncontrollably. "There's nothing/nwrong with me, it's your dad you've got to worry/nabout — we need to find out where he is — he's/nbleeding like mad — I was — it was a huge snake..."/n/nHe tried to get out of bed but Ron pushed him back/ninto it; Dean and Seamus were still whispering/nsomewhere nearby. Whether one minute passed or/nten, Harry did not know; he simply sat there shaking,/nfeeling the pain recede very slowly from his scar. . ./nThen there were hurried footsteps coming up the/nstairs, and he heard Neville's voice again./n/n"Over here, Professor ..."/n/nProfessor McGonagall came hurrying into the/ndormitory in her tartan dressing gown, her glasses/nperched lopsidedly on the bridge of her bony nose./n/n"What is it, Potter? Where does it hurt?"/n/nHe had never been so pleased to see her; it was a/nmember of the Order of the Phoenix he needed now,/nnot someone fussing over him and prescribing useless/npotions./n/n"It's Ron's dad," he said, sitting up again. "He's been/nattacked by a snake and it's serious, I saw it happen."/n/n"What do you mean, you saw it happen?" said/nProfessor McGonagall, her dark eyebrows contracting./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't know... I was asleep and then I was there..."/n/n"You mean you dreamed this?"/n/n"No!" said Harry angrily. Would none of them/nunderstand? "I was having a dream at first about/nsomething completely different, something stupid . . ./nand then this interrupted it. It was real, I didn't/nimagine it, Mr. Weasley was asleep on the floor and/nhe was attacked by a gigantic snake, there was a load/nof blood, he collapsed, someone's got to find out/nwhere he is..."/n/nProfessor McGonagall was gazing at him through her/nlopsided spectacles as though horrified at what she/nwas seeing./n/n"I'm not lying, and I'm not mad!" Harry told her, his/nvoice rising to a shout. "I tell you, I saw it happen!"/n/n"I believe you, Potter," said Professor McGonagall/ncurtly. "Put on your dressing-gown — we're going to/nsee the headmaster."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n&/n/n/n

title: St. Mungo's Hospital For Magical Maladies And Injuries
text: /nHarry was so relieved that she was taking him/nseriously that he did not hesitate, but jumped out of/nbed at once, pulled on his dressing gown, and pushed/nhis glasses back onto his nose./n/n"Weasley, you ought to come too," said Professor/nMcGonagall./n/nThey followed Professor McGonagall past the silent/nfigures of Neville, Dean, and Seamus, out of the/ndormitory, down the spiral stairs into the common/nroom, through the portrait hole, and off along the Fat/nLady's moonlit corridor. Harry felt as though the/npanic inside him might spill over at any moment; he/nwanted to run, to yell for Dumbledore. Mr. Weasley/nwas bleeding as they walked along so sedately, and/nwhat if those fangs (Harry tried hard not to think "my/nfangs") had been poisonous? They passed Mrs. Norris,/nwho turned her lamplike eyes upon them and hissed/nfaintly, but Professor McGonagall said, "Shoo!" Mrs./n/n/n/n/n/n/nNorris slunk away into the shadows, and in a few/nminutes they had reached the stone gargoyle/nguarding the entrance to Dumbledore's office./n/n"Fizzing Whizbee," said Professor McGonagall./n/nThe gargoyle sprang to life and leapt aside; the wall/nbehind it split in two to reveal a stone staircase that/nwas moving continuously upward like a spiral/nescalator. The three of them stepped onto the moving/nstairs; the wall closed behind them with a thud, and/nthey were moving upward in tight circles until they/nreached the highly polished oak door with the brass/nknocker shaped like a griffin./n/nThough it was now well past midnight, there were/nvoices coming from inside the room, a positive babble/nof them. It sounded as though Dumbledore was/nentertaining at least a dozen people./n/nProfessor McGonagall rapped three times with the/ngriffin knocker, and the voices ceased abruptly as/nthough someone had switched them all off. The door/nopened of its own accord and Professor McGonagall/nled Harry and Ron inside./n/nThe room was in half darkness; the strange silver/ninstruments standing on tables were silent and still/nrather than whirring and emitting puffs of smoke as/nthey usually did. The portraits of old headmasters/nand headmistresses covering the walls were all/nsnoozing in their frames. Behind the door, a/nmagnificent red-and-gold bird the size of a swan/ndozed on its perch with its head under its wing./n/n"Oh, it's you, Professor McGonagall ... and ... ah."/n/nDumbledore was sitting in a high-backed chair/nbehind his desk; he leaned forward into the pool of/n/n/n/n/n/ncandlelight illuminating the papers laid out before/nhim. He was wearing a magnificently embroidered/npurple-and-gold dressing gown over a snowy-white/nnightshirt, but seemed wide awake, his penetrating/nlight-blue eyes fixed intently upon Professor/nMcGonagall./n/n"Professor Dumbledore, Potter has had a ... well, a/nnightmare," said Professor McGonagall. "He says ..."/n/n"It wasn't a nightmare," said Harry quickly./n/nProfessor McGonagall looked around at Harry,/nfrowning slightly./n/n"Very well, then, Potter, you tell the headmaster about/nit." ~/n/n"I ... well, I was asleep..." said Harry and even in his/nterror and his desperation to make Dumbledore/nunderstand he felt slightly irritated that the/nheadmaster was not looking at him, but examining/nhis own interlocked fingers. "But it wasn't an ordinary/ndream ... it was real... I saw it happen..." He took a/ndeep breath, "Ron's dad — Mr. Weasley — has been/nattacked by a giant snake."/n/nThe words seemed to reverberate in the air after he/nhad said them, slightly ridiculous, even comic. There/nwas a pause in which Dumbledore leaned back and/nstared meditatively at the ceiling. Ron looked from/nHarry to Dumbledore, white-faced and shocked./n/n"How did you see this?" Dumbledore asked quietly,/nstill not looking at Harry./n/n"Well ... I don't know," said Harry, rather angrily —/nwhat did it matter? "Inside my head, I suppose — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You misunderstand me," said Dumbledore, still in/nthe same calm tone. "I mean ... can you remember —/ner — where you were positioned as you watched this/nattack happen? Were you perhaps standing beside/nthe victim, or else looking down on the scene from/nabove?"/n/nThis was such a curious question that Harry gaped at/nDumbledore; it was almost as though he knew .../n/n"I was the snake," he said. Theory was sick wizards could/ncome and go and just blend in with the crowd..."/n/nHe seized Harry's shoulder to prevent them being/nseparated by a gaggle of shoppers plainly intent on/nnothing but making it into a nearby shop full of/nelectrical gadgets./n/n"Here we go," said Moody a moment later./n/nThey had arrived outside a large, old-fashioned, red/nbrick department store called Purge and Dowse Ltd./nThe place had a shabby, miserable air; the window/ndisplays consisted of a few chipped dummies with/ntheir wigs askew, standing at random and modeling/nfashions at least ten years out of date. Large signs on/nall the dusty doors read CLOSED FOR/nREFURBISHMENT. Harry distinctly heard a large/nwoman laden with plastic shopping bags say to her/nfriend as they passed, "It's never open, that place..."/n/n"Right," said Tonks, beckoning them forward to a/nwindow displaying nothing but a particularly ugly/n/n/n/n/n/nfemale dummy whose false eyelashes were hanging off/nand who was modeling a green nylon pinafore dress./n"Everybody ready?"/n/nThey nodded, clustering around her; Moody gave/nHarry another shove between the shoulder blades to/nurge him forward and Tonks leaned close to the glass,/nlooking up at the very ugly dummy and said, her/nbreath steaming up the glass, "Wotcher ... We're here/nto see Arthur Weasley."/n/nFor a split second, Harry thought how absurd it was/nfor Tonks to expect the dummy to hear her talking/nthat quietly through a sheet of glass, when there were/nbuses rumbling along behind her and all the racket of/na street full of shoppers. Then he reminded himself/nthat dummies could not hear anyway. Next second/nhis mouth opened in shock as the dummy gave a tiny/nnod, beckoned its jointed finger, and Tonks had/nseized Ginny and Mrs. Weasley by the elbows,/nstepped right through the glass and vanished./n/nFred, George, and Ron stepped after them; Harry/nglanced around at the jostling crowd; not one of them/nseemed to have a glance to spare for window displays/nas ugly as Purge and Dowse Ltd.'s, nor did any of/nthem seem to have noticed that six people had just/nmelted into thin air in front of them./n/n"C'mon," growled Moody, giving Harry yet another/npoke in the back and together they stepped forward/nthrough what felt like a sheet of cool water, emerging/nquite warm and dry on the other side./n/nThere was no sign of the ugly dummy or the space/nwhere she had stood. They had arrived in what/nseemed to be a crowded reception area where rows of/nwitches and wizards sat upon rickety wooden chairs,/nsome looking perfectly normal and perusing out-of-/n/n/n/n/ndate copies of Witch Weekly, others sporting gruesome/ndisfigurements such as elephant trunks or extra/nhands sticking out of their chests. The room was/nscarcely less quiet than the street outside, for many of/nthe patients were making very peculiar noises. A/nsweaty-faced witch in the center of the front row, who/nwas fanning herself vigorously with a copy of the/nDaily Prophet, kept letting off a high-pitched whistle/nas steam came pouring out of her mouth, and a/ngrubby-looking warlock in the corner clanged like a/nbell every time he moved, and with each clang his/nhead vibrated horribly, so that he had to seize himself/nby the ears and hold it steady./n/nWitches and wizards in lime-green robes were walking/nup and down the rows, asking questions and making/nnotes on clipboards like Umbridge's. Harry noticed/nthe emblem embroidered on their chests: a wand and/nbone, crossed./n/n"Are they doctors?" he asked Ron quietly./n/n"Doctors?" said Ron, looking startled. "Those Muggle/nnutters that cut people up? Nah, they're Healers."/n/n"Over here!" called Mrs. Weasley over the renewed/nclanging of the warlock in the corner, and they/nfollowed her to the queue in front of a plump blonde/nwitch seated at a desk marked inquiries. The wall/nbehind her was covered in notices and posters saying/nthings like A CLEAN CAULDRON KEEPS POTIONS/nFROM BECOMING POISONS and ANTIDOTES ARE/nANTI-DONTS UNLESS APPROVED BY A QUALIFIED/nHEALER./n/nThere was also a large portrait of a witch with long/nsilver ringlets that was labelled/n/nDILYS DERWENT/n/n/n/n/n

title: St. Mungo's Healer 1722-1741
text: /n/n/nHEADMISTRESS OF HOGWARTS SCHOOL OF/n/nWITCHCRAFT AND WIZARDRY, I74I-I768/n/nDilys was eyeing the Weasley party as though/ncounting them; when Harry caught her eye she gave a/ntiny wink, walked sideways out of her portrait, and/nvanished./n/nMeanwhile, at the front of the queue, a young wizard/nwas performing an odd on-the-spot jig and trying, in/nbetween yelps of pain, to explain his predicament to/nthe witch behind the desk./n/n"It's these — ouch — shoes my brother gave me — ow/n— they're eating my — OUCH — feet — look at them,/nthere must be some kind of — AARGH — jinx on them/nand I can't — AAAAARGH — get them off — "/n/nHe hopped from one foot to the other as though/ndancing on hot coals./n/n"The shoes don't prevent you reading, do they?" said/nthe blonde witch irritably, pointing at a large sign to/nthe left of her desk. "You want Spell Damage, fourth/nfloor. Just like it says on the floor guide. Next!"/n/nThe wizard hobbled and pranced sideways out of the/nway, the Weasley party moved forward a few steps/nand Harry read the floor guide:/n/nARTIFACT ACCIDENTS Ground Floor/n/n(Cauldron explosion, wand backfiring, broom crashes,/netc.)/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nCREATURE-INDUCED INJURIES/n/n/n/nFirst Floor/n/n/n/n(Bites, stings, burns, embedded spines, etc.)/n/nMAGICAL BUGS Second Floor/n/n(Contagious maladies, e.g., dragon pox, vanishing/nsickness, scrofungulus)/n/nPOTION AND PLANT POISONING .... Third Floor/n/n(Rashes, regurgitation, uncontrollable giggling, etc.)/n/nSPELL DAMAGE Fourth Floor/n/n(Unliftable jinxes, hexes, and incorrectly applied/ncharms, etc.)/n/nVISITORS' TEAROOM AND HOSPITAL SHOP... .Fifth/nFloor/n/nIf you are unsure where to go, incapable, of normal/nspeech, or unable to remember why you are here, our/nWelcome Witch will be pleased to help./n/nA very old, stooped wizard with a hearing trumpet/nhad shuffled to the front of the queue now./n/n"I'm here to see Broderick Bode!" he wheezed./n/n"Ward forty-nine, but I'm afraid you're wasting your/ntime," said the witch dismissively "He's completely/naddled, you know, still thinks he's a teapot... Next!"/n/nA harassed-looking wizard was holding his small/ndaughter tightly by the ankle while she flapped/naround his head using the immensely large, feathery/nwings that had sprouted right out the back of her/nromper suit./n/n/n/n/n/n"Fourth floor," said the witch in a bored voice, without/nasking, and the man disappeared through the double/ndoors beside the desk, holding his daughter like an/noddly shaped balloon. "Next!"/n/nMrs. Weasley moved forward to the desk./n/n"Hello," she said. "My husband, Arthur Weasley, was/nsupposed to be moved to a different ward this/nmorning, could you tell us — ?"/n/n"Arthur Weasley?" said the witch, running her finger/ndown a long list in front of her. "Yes, first floor,/nsecond door on the right, Dai Llewellyn ward."/n/n"Thank you," said Mrs. Weasley. "Come on, you lot."/n/nThey followed through the double doors and along the/nnarrow corridor beyond, which was lined with more/nportraits of famous Healers and lit by crystal bubbles/nfull of candles that floated up on the ceiling, looking/nlike giant soapsuds. More witches and wizards in/nlime-green robes walked in and out of the doors they/npassed; a foul-smelling yellow gas wafted into the/npassageway as they passed one door, and every now/nand then they heard distant wailing. They climbed a/nflight of stairs and entered the "Creature-Induced/nInjuries" corridor, where the second door on the right/nbore the words "DANGEROUS" DAI LLEWELLYN/nWARD: SERIOUS BITES. Underneath this was a card/nin a brass holder on which had been handwritten/nHealer-in-Charge: Hippocrates Smethwyck, Trainee/nHealer: Augustus Pye./n/n"Well wait outside, Molly," Tonks said. "Arthur won't/nwant too many visitors at once... It ought to be just/nthe family first."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMad-Eye growled his approval of this idea and set/nhimself with his back against the corridor wall, his/nmagical eye spinning in all directions. Harry drew/nback too, but Mrs. Weasley reached out a hand and/npushed him through the door, saying, "Don't be silly,/nHarry, Arthur wants to thank you..."/n/nThe ward was small and rather dingy as the only/nwindow was narrow and set high in the wall facing/nthe door. Most of the light came from more shining/ncrystal bubbles clustered in the middle of the ceiling./nThe walls were of panelled oak and there was a/nportrait of a rather vicious-looking wizard on the wall,/ncaptioned URQUHART RACKHARROW, 1612-1697,/nINVENTOR OF THE ENTRAIL- EXPELLING CURSE./n/nThere were only three patients. Mr. Weasley was/noccupying the bed at the far end of the ward beside/nthe tiny window. Harry was pleased and relieved to/nsee that he was propped up on several pillows and/nreading the Daily Prophet by the solitary ray of/nsunlight falling onto his bed. He looked around as/nthey walked toward him and, seeing whom it was,/nbeamed./n/n"Hello!" he called, throwing the Prophet aside. "Bill/njust left, Molly, had to get back to work, but he says/nhe'll drop in on you later..."/n/n"How are you, Arthur?" asked Mrs. Weasley, bending/ndown to kiss his cheek and looking anxiously into his/nface. "You're still looking a bit peaky..."/n/n"I feel absolutely fine," said Mr. Weasley brightly,/nholding out his good arm to give Ginny a hug. "If they/ncould only take the bandages off, I'd be fit to go/nhome."/n/n"Why can't they take them off, Dad?" asked Fred./n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, I start bleeding like mad every time they try,"/nsaid Mr. Weasley cheerfully, reaching across for his/nwand, which lay on his bedside cabinet, and waving it/nso that six extra chairs appeared at his bedside to/nseat them all. "It seems there was some rather/nunusual kind of poison in that snake's fangs that/nkeeps wounds open... They're sure they'll find an/nantidote, though, they say they've had much worse/ncases than mine, and in the meantime I just have to/nkeep taking a Blood-Replenishing Potion every hour./nBut that fellow over there," he said, dropping his voice/nand nodding toward the bed opposite in which a man/nlay looking green and sickly and staring at the ceiling./n"Bitten by a werewolf, poor chap. No cure at all."/n/n"A werewolf?" whispered Mrs. Weasley, looking/nalarmed. "Is he safe in a public ward? Shouldn't he be/nin a private room?"/n/n"It's two weeks till full moon," Mr. Weasley reminded/nher quietly. "They've been talking to him this/nmorning, the Healers, you know, trying to persuade/nhim he'll be able to lead an almost normal life. I said/nto him — didn't mention names, of course — but I/nsaid I knew a werewolf personally, very nice man, who/nfinds the condition quite easy to manage..."/n/n"What did he say?" asked George./n/n"Said he'd give me another bite if I didn't shut up,"/nsaid Mr. Weasley sadly. "And that woman over there,"/nhe indicated the only other occupied bed, which was/nright beside the door, "won't tell the Healers what bit/nher, which makes us all think it must have been/nsomething she was handling illegally. Whatever it was/ntook a real chunk out of her leg, very nasty smell/nwhen they take off the dressings."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So, you going to tell us what happened, Dad?" asked/nFred, pulling his chair closer to the bed./n/n"Well, you already know, don't you?" said Mr./n/nWeasley, with a significant smile at Harry. "It's very/nsimple — I'd had a very long day, dozed off, got/nsneaked up on, and bitten."/n/n"Is it in the Prophet, you being attacked?" asked Fred,/nindicating the newspaper Mr. Weasley had cast aside./n/n"No, of course not," said Mr. Weasley, with a slightly/nbitter smile, "the Ministry wouldn't want everyone to/nknow a dirty great serpent got — "/n/n"Arthur!" said Mrs. Weasley warningly./n/n" — got — er — me," Mr. Weasley said hastily, though/nHarry was quite sure that was not what he had meant/nto say./n/n"So where were you when it happened, Dad?" asked/nGeorge./n/n"That's my business," said Mr. Weasley, though with/na small smile. He snatched up the Daily Prophet,/nshook it open again and said, "I was just reading/nabout Willy Widdershins's arrest when you arrived./nYou know Willy turned out to be behind those/nregurgitating toilets last summer? One of his jinxes/nbackfired, the toilet exploded, and they found him/nlying unconscious in the wreckage covered from head/nto foot in — "/n/n"When you say you were 'on duty,' " Fred interrupted/nin a low voice, "what were you doing?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You heard your father," whispered Mrs. Weasley, "we/nare not discussing this here! Go on about Willy/nWiddershins, Arthur — "/n/n"Well, don't ask me how, but he actually got off on the/ntoilet charge," said Mr. Weasley grimly. "I can only/nsuppose gold changed hands — "/n/n"You were guarding it, weren't you?" said George/nquietly. "The weapon? The thing You-Know- Who's/nafter?"/n/n"George, be quiet!" snapped Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Anyway," said Mr. Weasley in a raised voice, "this/ntime Willy's been caught selling biting doorknobs to/nMuggles, and I don't think he'll be able to worm his/nway out of it because according to this article, two/nMuggles have lost fingers and are now in St. Mungo's/nfor emergency bone regrowth and memory/nmodification. Just think of it, Muggles in St. Mungo's!/nI wonder which ward they're in?"/n/nAnd he looked eagerly around as though hoping to/nsee a signpost./n/n"Didn't you say You-Know- Who's got a snake, Harry?"/nasked Fred, looking at his father for a reaction. "A/nmassive one? You saw it the night he returned, didn't/nyou?"/n/n"That's enough," said Mrs. Weasley crossly. "Mad-Eye/nand Tonks are outside, Arthur, they want to come/nand see you. And you lot can wait outside," she added/nto her children and Harry. "You can come and say/ngood-bye afterward. Go on..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey trooped back into the corridor. Mad-Eye and/nTonks went in and closed the door of the ward behind/nthem. Fred raised his eyebrows./n/n"Fine," he said coolly, rummaging in his pockets, "be/nlike that. Don't tell us anything."/n/n"Looking for these?" said George, holding out what/nlooked like a tangle of flesh-colored string./n/n"You read my mind," said Fred, grinning. "Let's see if/nSt. Mungo's puts Imperturbable Charms on its ward/ndoors, shall we?"/n/nHe and George disentangled the string and separated/nfive Extendable Ears from each other. Fred and/nGeorge handed them around. Harry hesitated to take/none./n/n"Go on, Harry, take it! You saved Dad's life, if/nanyone's got the right to eavesdrop on him it's you..."/n/nGrinning in spite of himself, Harry took the end of the/nstring and inserted it into his ear as the twins had/ndone./n/n"Okay, go!" Fred whispered./n/nThe flesh-colored strings wriggled like long skinny/nworms, then snaked under the door. For a few/nseconds Harry could hear nothing, then he heard/nTonks whispering as clearly as though she were/nstanding right beside him./n/n"... they searched the whole area but they couldn't/nfind the snake anywhere, it just seems to have/nvanished after it attacked you, Arthur... But You-/nKnow-Who can't have expected a snake to get in, can/nhe?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"I reckon he sent it as a lookout," growled Moody, "/n'cause he's not had any luck so far, has he? No, I/nreckon he's trying to get a clearer picture of what he's/nfacing and if Arthur hadn't been there the beast/nwould've had much more time to look around. So/nPotter says he saw it all happen?"/n/n"Yes," said Mrs. Weasley. She sounded rather uneasy./n"You know, Dumbledore seems almost to have been/nwaiting for Harry to see something like this..."/n/n"Yeah, well," said Moody, "there's something funny/nabout the Potter kid, we all know that."/n/n"Dumbledore seemed worried about Harry when I/nspoke to him this morning," whispered Mrs. Weasley./n/n" 'Course he's worried," growled Moody. "The boy's/nseeing things from inside You-Know- Who's snake.../nObviously, Potter doesn't realize what that means, but/nif You- Know- Who's possessing him — "/n/nHarry pulled the Extendable Ear out of his own, his/nheart hammering very fast and heat rushing up his/nface. He looked around at the others. They were all/nstaring at him, the strings still trailing from their/nears, looking suddenly fearful./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Christmas On The Closed Ward
text: /nWas this why Dumbledore would no longer meet/nHarry's eyes? Did he expect to see Voldemort staring/nout of them, afraid, perhaps, that their vivid green/nmight turn suddenly to scarlet, with catlike slits for/npupils? Harry remembered how the snakelike face of/nVoldemort had once forced itself out of the back of/nProfessor Quirrell's head, and he ran his hand over/nthe back of his own, wondering what it would feel like/nif Voldemort burst out of his skull.../n/nHe felt dirty, contaminated, as though he were/ncarrying some deadly germ, unworthy to sit on the/nunderground train back from the hospital with/ninnocent, clean people whose minds and bodies were/nfree of the taint of Voldemort... He had not merely/nseen the snake, he had been the snake, he knew it/nnow. . ./n/nAnd then a truly terrible thought occurred to him, a/nmemory bobbing to the surface of his mind, one that/nmade his insides writhe and squirm like serpents.../n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What's he after apart from followers?"/n/n"Stuff he can only get by stealth ... like a weapon./nSomething he didn't have last time."/n/nI'm the weapon, Harry thought, and it was as though/npoison were pumping through his veins, chilling him,/nbringing him out in a sweat as he swayed with the/ntrain through the dark tunnel. I'm the one Voldemort's/ntrying to use, that's why they've got guards around me/neverywhere I go, it's not for my protection, it's for other/npeople's, only it's not working, they can't have/nsomeone on me all the time at Hogwarts... I did attack/nMr. Weasley last night, it was me, Voldemort made me/ndo it and he could be inside me, listening to my/nthoughts right now.../n/n"Are you all right, Harry, dear?" whispered Mrs./nWeasley, leaning across Ginny to speak to him as the/ntrain rattled along through its dark tunnel. "You don't/nlook very well. Are you feeling sick?"/n/nThey were all watching him. He shook his head/nviolently and stared up at an advertisement for home/ninsurance./n/n"Harry, dear, are you sure you're all right?" said Mrs./nWeasley in a worried voice, as they walked around the/nunkempt patch of grass in the middle of Grimmauld/nPlace. "You look ever so pale... Are you sure you slept/nthis morning? You go upstairs to bed right now, and/nyou can have a couple of hours' sleep before dinner,/nall right?"/n/nHe nodded; here was a ready-made excuse not to talk/nto any of the others, which was precisely what he/nwanted, so when she opened the front door he/nproceeded straight past the troll's leg umbrella stand/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nand up the stairs and hurried into his and Ron's/nbedroom./n/nHere he began to pace up and down, past the two/nbeds and Phineas Nigellus's empty portrait, his brain/nteeming and seething with questions and ever more/ndreadful ideas.../n/nHow had he become a snake? Perhaps he was an/nAnimagus... No, he couldn't be, he would know.../nperhaps Voldemort was an Animagus... Yes, thought/nHarry, that would fit, he would turn into a snake of/ncourse ... and when he's possessing me, then we both/ntransform... That still doesn't explain how come I got to/nLondon and back to my bed in the space of about five/nminutes, though... But then Voldemort' s about the most/npowerful wizard in the world, apart from Dumbledore,/nit's probably no problem at all to him to transport/npeople like that.../n/nAnd then, with a terrible stab of panic he thought, but/nthis is insane — if Voldemort's possessing me, I'm/ngiving him a clear view into the headquarters of the/nOrder of the Phoenix right now! He'll know who's in the/nOrder and where Sirius is ... and I've heard loads of/nstuff I shouldn't have, everything Sirius told me the/nfirst night I was here.../n/nThere was only one thing for it: He would have to/nleave Grimmauld Place straightaway. He would spend/nChristmas at Hogwarts without the others, which/nwould keep them safe over the holidays at least... But/nno, that wouldn't do, there were still plenty of people/nat Hogwarts to maim and injure, what if it was/nSeamus, Dean, or Neville next time? He stopped his/npacing and stood staring at Phineas Nigellus's empty/nframe. A leaden sensation was settling in the pit of his/nstomach. He had no alternative: He was going to have/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nto return to Privet Drive, cut himself off from other/nwizards entirely.../n/n/n/nWell, if he had to do it, he thought, there was no point/nhanging around. Trying with all his might not to think/nhow the Dursleys were going to react when they found/nhim on their doorstep six months earlier than they/nhad expected, he strode over to his trunk, slammed/nthe lid shut and locked it, then glanced around/nautomatically for Hedwig before remembering that she/nwas still at Hogwarts — well, her cage would be one/nless thing to carry — he seized one end of his trunk/nand had dragged it halfway toward the door when a/nsneaky voice said, "Running away, are we?"/n/nHe looked around. Phineas Nigellus had appeared/nupon the canvas of his portrait and was leaning/nagainst the frame, watching Harry with an amused/nexpression on his face./n/n"Not running away, no," said Harry shortly, dragging/nhis trunk a few more feet across the room./n/n"I thought," said Phineas Nigellus, stroking his/npointed beard, "that to belong in Gryffindor House/nyou were supposed to be brave? It looks to me as/nthough you would have been better off in my own/nhouse. We Slytherins are brave, yes, but not stupid./nFor instance, given the choice, we will always choose/nto save our own necks."/n/n"It's not my own neck I'm saving," said Harry tersely,/ntugging the trunk over a patch of particularly uneven,/nmoth-eaten carpet right in front of the door./n/n"Oh I see," said Phineas Nigellus, still stroking his/nbeard. "This is no cowardly flight — you are being/nnoble."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry ignored him. His hand was on the doorknob/nwhen Phineas Nigellus said lazily, "I have a message/nfor you from Albus Dumbledore."/n/nHarry spun around./n/n"What is it?"/n/n"Stay where you are."/n/n"I haven't moved!" said Harry, his hand still upon the/ndoorknob. "So what's the message?"/n/n"I have just given it to you, dolt," said Phineas/nNigellus smoothly. "Dumbledore says, 'Stay where/nyou are. ' "/n/n"Why?" said Harry eagerly, dropping the end of his/ntrunk. "Why does he want me to stay? What else did/nhe say?"/n/n"Nothing whatsoever," said Phineas Nigellus, raising a/nthin black eyebrow as though he found Harry/nimpertinent./n/nHarry's temper rose to the surface like a snake/nrearing from long grass. He was exhausted, he was/nconfused beyond measure, he had experienced terror,/nrelief, and then terror again in the last twelve hours,/nand still Dumbledore did not want to talk to him!/n/n"So that's it, is it?" he said loudly. "Stay there? That's/nall anyone could tell me after I got attacked by those/ndementors too! Just stay put while the grown-ups/nsort it out, Harry! We won't bother telling you/nanything, though, because your tiny little brain might/nnot be able to cope with it!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You know," said Phineas Nigellus, even more loudly/nthan Harry, "this is precisely why I loathed being a/nteacher! Young people are so infernally convinced that/nthey are absolutely right about everything. Has it not/noccurred to you, my poor puffed-up popinjay, that/nthere might be an excellent reason why the/nheadmaster of Hogwarts is not confiding every tiny/ndetail of his plans to you? Have you never paused,/nwhile feeling hard-done-by, to note that following/nDumbledore 's orders has never yet led you into harm?/nNo. No, like all young people, you are quite sure that/nyou alone feel and think, you alone recognize danger,/nyou alone are the only one clever enough to realize/nwhat the Dark Lord may be planning..."/n/n"He is planning something to do with me, then?" said/nHarry swiftly./n/n"Did I say that?" said Phineas Nigellus, idly examining/nhis silk gloves. "Now, if you will excuse me, I have/nbetter things to do than to listen to adolescent/nagonizing... Good day to you..."/n/nAnd he strolled into his frame and out of sight./n/n"Fine, go then!" Harry bellowed at the empty frame./n"And tell Dumbledore thanks for nothing!"/n/nThe empty canvas remained silent. Fuming, Harry/ndragged his trunk back to the foot of his bed, then/nthrew himself facedown upon the moth-eaten covers,/nhis eyes shut, his body heavy and aching. . ./n/nHe felt he had journeyed miles and miles... It seemed/nimpossible that less than twenty-four hours ago Cho/nChang had been approaching him under the/nmistletoe... He was so tired... He was scared to sleep/n... yet he did not know how long he could fight it.../nDumbledore had told him to stay... That must mean/n/n/n/n/nhe was allowed to sleep... But he was scared... What if/nit happened again ... ?/n/nHe was sinking into shadows.../n/nIt was as though a film in his head had been waiting/nto start. He was walking down a deserted corridor/ntoward a plain black door, past rough stone walls,/ntorches, and an open doorway onto a flight of stone/nsteps leading downstairs on the left.../n/nHe reached the black door but could not open it... He/nstood gazing at it, desperate for entry. . . Something he/nwanted with all his heart lay beyond... A prize beyond/nhis dreams... If only his scar would stop prickling .../nthen he would be able to think more clearly. . ./n/n"Harry," said Ron's voice, from far, far away, "Mum/nsays dinner's ready, but she'll save you something if/nyou want to stay in bed..."/n/nHarry opened his eyes, but Ron had already left the/nroom./n/nHe doesn't want to be on his own with me, Harry/nthought.
