The moment/nhe had been deposited in his chair by the Healer,/nGilderoy pulled a fresh stack of photographs toward/nhim, seized a quill, and started signing them all/nfeverishly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You can put them in envelopes," he said to Ginny,/nthrowing the signed pictures into her lap one by one/nas he finished them. "I am not forgotten, you know,/nno, I still receive a very great deal of fan mail... Gladys/nGudgeon writes weekly... I just wish I knew why..."/n/nHe paused, looking faintly puzzled, then beamed/nagain and returned to his signing with renewed vigor./n"I suspect it is simply my good looks..."/n/nA sallow-skinned, mournful-looking wizard lay in the/nbed opposite, staring at the ceiling; he was mumbling/nto himself and seemed quite unaware of anything/naround him. Two beds along was a woman whose/nentire head was covered in fur; Harry remembered/nsomething similar happening to Hermione during/ntheir second year, although fortunately the damage,/nin her case, had not been permanent. At the far end/nof the ward flowery curtains had been drawn around/ntwo beds to give the occupants and their visitors some/nprivacy./n/n"Here you are, Agnes," said the Healer brightly to the/nfurry-faced woman, handing her a small pile of/nChristmas presents. "See, not forgotten, are you? And/nyour son's sent an owl to say he's visiting tonight, so/nthat's nice, isn't it?"/n/nAgnes gave several loud barks./n/n"And look, Broderick, you've been sent a potted plant/nand a lovely calendar with a different fancy hippogriff/nfor each month, they'll brighten things up, won't/nthey?" said the Healer, bustling along to the/nmumbling man, setting a rather ugly plant with long,/nswaying tentacles on the bedside cabinet and fixing/nthe calendar to the wall with her wand. "And — oh,/nMrs. Longbottom, are you leaving already?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's head spun round. The curtains had been/ndrawn back from the two beds at the end of the ward/nand two visitors were walking back down the aisle/nbetween the beds: a formidable-looking old witch/nwearing a long green dress, a moth-eaten fox fur, and/na pointed hat decorated with what was unmistakably/na stuffed vulture and, trailing behind her looking/nthoroughly depressed — Neville./n/nWith a sudden rush of understanding, Harry realized/nwho the people in the end beds must be. He cast/naround wildly for some means of distracting the/nothers so that Neville could leave the ward unnoticed/nand unquestioned, but Ron had looked up at the/nsound of the name "Longbottom" too, and before/nHarry could stop him had called, "Neville\"/n/nNeville jumped and cowered as though a bullet had/nnarrowly missed him./n/n"It's us, Neville!" said Ron brightly, getting to his feet./n"Have you seen? Lockhart's here! Who've you been/nvisiting?"/n/n"Friends of yours, Neville, dear?" said Neville's/ngrandmother graciously, bearing down upon them all./n/nNeville looked as though he would rather be anywhere/nin the world but here. A dull purple flush was/ncreeping up his plump face and he was not making/neye contact with any of them./n/n"Ah, yes," said his grandmother, looking closely at/nHarry and sticking out a shriveled, clawlike hand for/nhim to shake. "Yes, yes, I know who you are, of/ncourse. Neville speaks most highly of you."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Er — thanks," said Harry, shaking hands. Neville did/nnot look at him, but stared at his own feet, the color/ndeepening in his face all the while./n/n"And you two are clearly Weasleys," Mrs. Longbottom/ncontinued, proffering her hand regally to Ron and/nGinny in turn. "Yes, I know your parents — not well,/nof course — but fine people, fine people ... and you/nmust be Hermione Granger?"/n/nHermione looked rather startled that Mrs./n/nLongbottom knew her name, but shook hands all the/nsame./n/n"Yes, Neville's told me all about you. Helped him out/nof a few sticky spots, haven't you? He's a good boy,"/nshe said, casting a sternly appraising look down her/nrather bony nose at Neville, "but he hasn't got his/nfather's talent, I'm afraid to say..." And she jerked her/nhead in the direction of the two beds at the end of the/nward, so that the stuffed vulture on her hat trembled/nalarmingly./n/n"What?" said Ron, looking amazed (Harry wanted to/nstamp on Ron's foot, but that sort of thing was much/nharder to bring off unnoticed when you were wearing/njeans rather than robes). "Is that your dad down the/nend, Neville?"/n/n"What's this?" said Mrs. Longbottom sharply. "Haven't/nyou told your friends about your parents, Neville?"/n/nNeville took a deep breath, looked up at the ceiling,/nand shook his head. Harry could not remember ever/nfeeling sorrier for anyone, but he could not think of/nany way of helping Neville out of the situation./n/n"Well, it's nothing to be ashamed of!" said Mrs./nLongbottom angrily. "You should be proud, Neville,/n/n/n/n/n/nproud). They didn't give their health and their sanity/nso their only son would be ashamed of them, you/nknow!"/n/n"I'm not ashamed," said Neville very faintly, still/nlooking anywhere but at Harry and the others. Ron/nwas now standing on tiptoe to look over at the/ninhabitants of the two beds./n/n"Well, you've got a funny way of showing it!" said Mrs./nLongbottom. "My son and his wife," she said, turning/nhaughtily to Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Ginny, "were/ntortured into insanity by You-Know- Who's followers."/n/nHermione and Ginny both clapped their hands over/ntheir mouths. Ron stopped craning his neck to catch/na glimpse of Neville's parents and looked mortified./n/n"They were Aurors, you know, and very well respected/nwithin the Wizarding community," Mrs. Longbottom/nwent on. "Highly gifted, the pair of them. I — yes,/n/nAlice dear, what is it?"/n/nNeville's mother had come edging down the ward in/nher nightdress. She no longer had the plump, happy-/nlooking face Harry had seen in Moody's old/nphotograph of the original Order of the Phoenix. Her/nface was thin and worn now, her eyes seemed/noverlarge, and her hair, which had turned white, was/nwispy and dead-looking. She did not seem to want to/nspeak, or perhaps she was not able to, but she made/ntimid motions toward Neville, holding something in/nher outstretched hand./n/n"Again?" said Mrs. Longbottom, sounding slightly/nweary. "Very well, Alice dear, very well — Neville, take/nit, whatever it is..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Neville had already stretched out his hand, into/nwhich his mother dropped an empty Droobles/nBlowing Gum wrapper./n/n"Very nice, dear," said Neville's grandmother in a/nfalsely cheery voice, patting his mother on the/nshoulder. But Neville said quietly, "Thanks Mum."/n/nHis mother tottered away, back up the ward,/nhumming to herself. Neville looked around at the/nothers, his expression defiant, as though daring them/nto laugh, but Harry did not think he'd ever found/nanything less funny in his life./n/n"Well, we'd better get back," sighed Mrs. Longbottom,/ndrawing on long green gloves. "Very nice to have met/nyou all. Neville, put that wrapper in the bin, she must/nhave given you enough of them to paper your/nbedroom by now..."/n/nBut as they left, Harry was sure he saw Neville slip/nthe wrapper into his pocket./n/nThe door closed behind them./n/n"I never knew," said Hermione, who looked tearful./n"Nor did I," said Ron rather hoarsely./n/n"Nor me," whispered Ginny./n/nThey all looked at Harry./n/n"I did," he said glumly. "Dumbledore told me but I/npromised I wouldn't mention it ... that's what/nBellatrix Lestrange got sent to Azkaban for, using the/nCruciatus Curse on Neville's parents until they lost/ntheir minds."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Bellatrix Lestrange did that?" whispered Hermione,/nhorrified. "That woman Kreacher's got a photo of in/nhis den?"/n/n/n/nThere was a long silence, broken by Lockhart's angry/nvoice. "Look, I didn't learn joined-up writing for/nnothing, you know!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Occlumency
text: /nKreacher, it transpired, had been lurking in the attic./nSirius said he had found him up there, covered in/ndust, no doubt looking for more relics of the Black/nfamily to hide in his cupboard. Though Sirius seemed/nsatisfied with this story, it made Harry uneasy./nKreacher seemed to be in a better mood on his/nreappearance, his bitter muttering had subsided/nsomewhat, and he submitted to orders more docilely/nthan usual, though once or twice Harry caught the/nhouse-elf staring avidly at him, always looking quickly/naway when he saw that Harry had noticed./n/nHarry did not mention his vague suspicions to Sirius,/nwhose cheerfulness was evaporating fast now that/nChristmas was over. As the date of their departure/nback to Hogwarts drew nearer, he became more and/nmore prone to what Mrs. Weasley called "fits of the/nsullens," in which he would become taciturn and/ngrumpy, often withdrawing to Buckbeak's room for/nhours at a time. His gloom seeped through the house,/noozing under doorways like some noxious gas, so that/nall of them became infected by it./n/n/n/n/nHarry did not want to leave Sirius all alone again with/nonly Kreacher for company. In fact, for the first time/nin his life, he was not looking forward to returning to/nHogwarts. Going back to school would mean placing/nhimself once again under the tyranny of Dolores/nUmbridge, who had no doubt managed to force/nthrough another dozen decrees in their absence. Then/nthere was no Quidditch to look forward to now that he/nhad been banned; there was every likelihood that/ntheir burden of homework would increase as the/nexams drew even nearer; Dumbledore remained as/nremote as ever; in fact, if it had not been for the D.A.,/nHarry felt he might have gone to Sirius and begged/nhim to let him leave Hogwarts and remain in/nGrimmauld Place./n/nThen, on the very last day of the holidays, something/nhappened that made Harry positively dread his return/nto school./n/n"Harry dear," said Mrs. Weasley, poking her head into/nhis and Ron's bedroom, where the pair of them were/nplaying wizard chess watched by Hermione, Ginny,/nand Crookshanks, "could you come down to the/nkitchen? Professor Snape would like a word with/nyou."/n/nHarry did not immediately register what she had said;/none of his castles was engaged in a violent tussle with/na pawn of Ron's, and he was egging it on/nenthusiastically./n/n"Squash him — squash him, he's only a pawn, you/nidiot — sorry, Mrs. Weasley, what did you say?"/n/n"Professor Snape, dear. In the kitchen. He'd like a/nword."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's mouth fell open in horror. He looked around/nat Ron, Hermione, and Ginny, all of whom were/ngaping back at him. Crookshanks, whom Hermione/nhad been restraining with difficulty for the past/nquarter of an hour, leapt gleefully upon the board and/nset the pieces running for cover, squealing at the top/nof their voices./n/n"Snape?" said Harry blankly./n/n"Professor Snape, dear," said Mrs. Weasley/nreprovingly. "Now come on, quickly, he says he can't/nstay long."/n/n"What's he want with you?" said Ron, looking/nunnerved as Mrs. Weasley withdrew from the room./n/n"You haven't done anything, have you?"/n/n"No!" said Harry indignantly, racking his brains to/nthink what he could have done that would make/nSnape pursue him to Grimmauld Place. Had his last/npiece of homework perhaps earned a T?/n/nHe pushed open the kitchen door a minute or two/nlater to find Sirius and Snape both seated at the long/nkitchen table, glaring in opposite directions. The/nsilence between them was heavy with mutual dislike./n/nA letter lay open on the table in front of Sirius./n/n"Er," said Harry to announce his presence./n/nSnape looked around at him, his face framed between/ncurtains of greasy black hair./n/n"Sit down, Potter."/n/n"You know," said Sirius loudly, leaning back on his/nrear chair legs and speaking to the ceiling, "I think I'd/n/n/n/n/n/nprefer it if you didn't give orders here, Snape. It's my/nhouse, you see."/n/nAn ugly flush suffused Snape 's pallid face. Harry sat/ndown in a chair beside Sirius, facing Snape across the/ntable./n/n"I was supposed to see you alone, Potter," said Snape,/nthe familiar sneer curling his mouth, "but Black — "/n/n"I'm his godfather," said Sirius, louder than ever./n/n"I am here on Dumbledore's orders," said Snape,/nwhose voice, by contrast, was becoming more and/nmore quietly waspish, "but by all means stay, Black, I/nknow you like to feel ... involved."/n/n"What's that supposed to mean?" said Sirius, letting/nhis chair fall back onto all four legs with a loud bang./n/n"Merely that I am sure you must feel — ah —/nfrustrated by the fact that you can do nothing useful,"/nSnape laid a delicate stress on the word, "for the/nOrder."/n/nIt was Sirius's turn to flush. Snape 's lip curled in/ntriumph as he turned to Harry./n/n"The headmaster has sent me to tell you, Potter, that/nit is his wish for you to study Occlumency this term."/n/n"Study what?" said Harry blankly./n/nSnape's sneer became more pronounced./n/n"Occlumency, Potter. The magical defense of the mind/nagainst external penetration. An obscure branch of/nmagic, but a highly useful one."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's heart began to pump very fast indeed./n/nDefense against external penetration? But he was not/nbeing possessed, they had all agreed on that.../n/n"Why do I have to study Occlu — thing?" he blurted/nout./n/n"Because the headmaster thinks it a good idea," said/nSnape smoothly. "You will receive private lessons/nonce a week, but you will not tell anybody what you/nare doing, least of all Dolores Umbridge. You/nunderstand?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry. "Who's going to be teaching me?"/nSnape raised an eyebrow./n/n"I am," he said./n/nHarry had the horrible sensation that his insides were/nmelting. Extra lessons with Snape — what on earth/nhad he done to deserve this? He looked quickly/naround at Sirius for support./n/n"Why can't Dumbledore teach Harry?" asked Sirius/naggressively. "Why you?"/n/n"I suppose because it is a headmaster's privilege to/ndelegate less enjoyable tasks," said Snape silkily. "I/nassure you I did not beg for the job." He got to his/nfeet. "I will expect you at six o'clock on Monday/nevening, Potter. My office. If anybody asks, you are/ntaking Remedial Potions. Nobody who has seen you in/nmy classes could deny you need them."/n/nHe turned to leave, his black traveling cloak billowing/nbehind him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Wait a moment," said Sirius, sitting up straighter in/nhis chair./n/nSnape turned back to face them, sneering./n/n"I am in rather a hurry, Black ... unlike you, I do not/nhave unlimited leisure time..."/n/n"I'll get to the point, then," said Sirius, standing up./n/nHe was rather taller than Snape who, Harry noticed,/nhad balled his fist in the pocket of his cloak over what/nHarry was sure was the handle of his wand. "If I hear/nyou're using these Occlumency lessons to give Harry/na hard time, you'll have me to answer to."/n/n"How touching," Snape sneered. "But surely you have/nnoticed that Potter is very like his father?"/n/n"Yes, I have," said Sirius proudly./n/n"Well then, you'll know he's so arrogant that criticism/nsimply bounces off him," Snape said sleekly./n/nSirius pushed his chair roughly aside and strode/naround the table toward Snape, pulling out his wand/nas he went; Snape whipped out his own. They were/nsquaring up to each other, Sirius looking livid, Snape/ncalculating, his eyes darting from Sirius's wand tip to/nhis face./n/n"Sirius!" said Harry loudly, but Sirius appeared not to/nhear him./n/n"I've warned you, Snivellus," said Sirius, his face/nbarely a foot from Snape 's, "I don't care if Dumbledore/nthinks you've reformed, I know better — "/n/n"Oh, but why don't you tell him so?" whispered/nSnape. "Or are you afraid he might not take the/n/n/n/n/n/nadvice of a man who has been hiding inside his/nmother's house for six months very seriously?"/n/n"Tell me, how is Lucius Malfoy these days? I expect/nhe's delighted his lapdog's working at Hogwarts, isn't/nhe?"/n/n"Speaking of dogs," said Snape softly, "did you know/nthat Lucius Malfoy recognized you last time you/nrisked a little jaunt outside? Clever idea, Black,/ngetting yourself seen on a safe station platform . . ./ngave you a cast-iron excuse not to leave your hidey-/nhole in future, didn't it?"/n/nSirius raised his wand./n/n"NO!" Harry yelled, vaulting over the table and trying/nto get in between them, "Sirius, don't — "/n/n"Are you calling me a coward?" roared Sirius, trying to/npush Harry out of the way, but Harry would not/nbudge./n/n"Why, yes, I suppose I am," said Snape./n/n"Harry — get — out — of — it!" snarled Sirius,/npushing him out of the way with his free hand./n/nThe kitchen door opened and the entire Weasley/nfamily, plus Hermione, came inside, all looking very/nhappy, with Mr. Weasley walking proudly in their/nmidst dressed in a pair of striped pajamas covered by/na mackintosh./n/n"Cured!" he announced brightly to the kitchen at/nlarge. "Completely cured!"/n/nHe and all the other Weasleys froze on the threshold,/ngazing at the scene in front of them, which was also/n/n/n/n/n/nsuspended in mid-action, both Sirius and Snape/nlooking toward the door with their wands pointing/ninto each other's faces and Harry immobile between/nthem, a hand stretched out to each of them, trying to/nforce them apart./n/n"Merlin's beard," said Mr. Weasley, the smile sliding/noff his face, "what's going on here?"/n/nBoth Sirius and Snape lowered their wands. Harry/nlooked from one to the other. Each wore an/nexpression of utmost contempt, yet the unexpected/nentrance of so many witnesses seemed to have/nbrought them to their senses. Snape pocketed his/nwand and swept back across the kitchen, passing the/nWeasleys without comment. At the door he looked/nback./n/n"Six o'clock Monday evening, Potter."/n/nHe was gone. Sirius glared after him, his wand at his/nside./n/n"But what's been going on?" asked Mr. Weasley again./n/n"Nothing, Arthur," said Sirius, who was breathing/nheavily as though he had just run a long distance./n"Just a friendly little chat between two old school/nfriends..." With what looked like an enormous effort,/nhe smiled. "So ... you're cured? That's great news,/nreally great..."/n/n"Yes, isn't it?" said Mrs. Weasley, leading her/nhusband forward into a chair. "Healer Smethwyck/nworked his magic in the end, found an antidote to/nwhatever that snake's got in its fangs, and Arthur's/nlearned his lesson about dabbling in Muggle/nmedicine, haven't you, dear?" she added, rather/nmenacingly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, Molly dear," said Mr. Weasley meekly./n/nThat night's meal should have been a cheerful one/nwith Mr. Weasley back amongst them; Harry could/ntell Sirius was trying to make it so, yet when his/ngodfather was not forcing himself to laugh loudly at/nFred and George's jokes or offering everyone more/nfood, his face fell back into a moody, brooding/nexpression. Harry was separated from him by/nMundungus and Mad-Eye, who had dropped in to/noffer Mr. Weasley their congratulations; he wanted to/ntalk to Sirius, to tell him that he should not listen to a/nword Snape said, that Snape was goading him/ndeliberately and that the rest of them did not think/nSirius was a coward for doing as Dumbledore told/nhim and remaining in Grimmauld Place, but he had/nno opportunity to do so, and wondered occasionally,/neyeing the ugly look on Sirius's face, whether he/nwould have dared to even if he had the chance./n/nInstead he told Ron and Hermione under his voice/nabout having to take Occlumency lessons with Snape./n/n"Dumbledore wants to stop you having those dreams/nabout Voldemort," said Hermione at once. "Well, you/nwon't be sorry not to have them anymore, will you?"/n/n"Extra lessons with Snape?" said Ron, sounding/naghast. "I'd rather have the nightmares!"/n/nThey were to return to Hogwarts on the Knight Bus/nthe following day, escorted once again by Tonks and/nLupin, both of whom were eating breakfast in the/nkitchen when Harry, Ron, and Hermione arrived there/nnext morning. The adults seemed to have been/nmidway through a whispered conversation when the/ndoor opened; all of them looked around hastily and/nfell silent./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAfter a hurried breakfast they pulled on jackets and/nscarves against the chilly gray January morning./n/nHarry had an unpleasant constricted sensation in his/nchest; he did not want to say good-bye to Sirius. He/nhad a bad feeling about this parting; he did not know/nwhen they would next see each other and felt that it/nwas incumbent upon him to say something to Sirius/nto stop him doing anything stupid — Harry was/nworried that Snape's accusation of cowardice had/nstung Sirius so badly he might even now be planning/nsome foolhardy trip beyond Grimmauld Place. Before/nhe could think of what to say, however, Sirius had/nbeckoned him to his side./n/n"I want you to take this," he said quietly, thrusting a/nbadly wrapped package roughly the size of a/npaperback book into Harry's hands./n/n"What is it?" Harry asked./n/n"A way of letting me know if Snape's giving you a hard/ntime. No, don't open it in here!" said Sirius, with a/nwary look at Mrs. Weasley, who was trying to/npersuade the twins to wear hand-knitted mittens. "I/ndoubt Molly would approve — but I want you to use it/nif you need me, all right?"/n/n"Okay," said Harry, stowing the package away in the/ninside pocket of his jacket, but he knew he would/nnever use whatever it was. It would not be he, Harry,/nwho lured Sirius from his place of safety, no matter/nhow foully Snape treated him in their forthcoming/nOcclumency classes./n/n"Let's go, then," said Sirius, clapping Harry on the/nshoulder and smiling grimly, and before Harry could/nsay anything else, they were heading upstairs,/nstopping before the heavily chained and bolted front/ndoor, surrounded by Weasleys./n/n/n/n/n/n"Good-bye, Harry, take care," said Mrs. Weasley,/nhugging him./n/n"See you Harry, and keep an eye out for snakes for/nme!" said Mr. Weasley genially, shaking his hand./n/n"Right — yeah," said Harry distractedly. It was his/nlast chance to tell Sirius to be careful; he turned,/nlooked into his godfather's face and opened his mouth/nto speak, but before he could do so Sirius was giving/nhim a brief, one-armed hug. He said gruffly, "Look/nafter yourself, Harry," and next moment Harry found/nhimself being shunted out into the icy winter air, with/nTonks (today heavily disguised as a tall, tweedy/nwoman with iron-gray hair) chivvying him down the/nsteps./n/nThe door of number twelve slammed shut behind/nthem. They followed Lupin down the front steps. As/nhe reached the pavement, Harry looked around./nNumber twelve was shrinking rapidly as those on/neither side of it stretched sideways, squeezing it out of/nsight; one blink later, it had gone./n/n"Come on, the quicker we get on the bus the better,"/nsaid Tonks, and Harry thought there was/nnervousness in the glance she threw around the/nsquare. Lupin flung out his right arm./n/nBANG./n/nA violently purple, triple-decker bus had appeared out/nof thin air in front of them, narrowly avoiding the/nnearest lamppost, which jumped backward out of its/nway./n/nA thin, pimply, jug-eared youth in a purple uniform/nleapt down onto the pavement and said, "Welcome to/nthe — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, yes, we know, thank you," said Tonks swiftly./n"On, on, get on —/n/nAnd she shoved Harry forward toward the steps, past/nthe conductor, who goggled at Harry as he passed./n/n" 'Ere — it's 'Arry — !"/n/n/n/n"If you shout his name I will curse you into oblivion,"/nmuttered Tonks menacingly, now shunting Ginny and/nHermione forward./n/n"I've always wanted to go on this thing," said Ron/nhappily, joining Harry on board and looking around./n/nIt had been evening the last time Harry had traveled/nby Knight Bus and its three decks had been full of/nbrass bedsteads. Now, in the early morning, it was/ncrammed with an assortment of mismatched chairs/ngrouped haphazardly around windows. Some of these/nappeared to have fallen over when the bus stopped/nabruptly in Grimmauld Place; a few witches and/nwizards were still getting to their feet, grumbling, and/nsomebody's shopping bag had slid the length of the/nbus; an unpleasant mixture of frog spawn,/ncockroaches, and custard creams was scattered all/nover the floor./n/n"Looks like we'll have to split up," said Tonics briskly,/nlooking around for empty chairs. "Fred, George, and/nGinny, if you just take those seats at the back .../nRemus can stay with you..."/n/nShe, Harry, Ron, and Hermione proceeded up to the/nvery top deck, where there were two chairs at the very/nfront of the bus and two at the back. Stan Shunpike,/nthe conductor, followed Harry and Ron eagerly to the/nback. Heads turned as Harry passed and when he sat/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndown, he saw all the faces flick back to the front/nagain./n/nAs Harry and Ron handed Stan eleven Sickles each,/nthe bus set off again, swaying ominously. It rumbled/naround Grimmauld Square, weaving on and off the/npavement, then, with another tremendous BANG,/nthey were all flung backward; Ron's chair toppled/nright over and Pigwidgeon, who had been on his lap,/nburst out of his cage and flew twittering wildly up to/nthe front of the bus where he fluttered down upon/nHermione's shoulder instead. Harry, who had/nnarrowly avoided falling by seizing a candle bracket,/nlooked out of the window: they were now speeding/ndown what appeared to be a motorway./n/n"Just outside Birmingham," said Stan happily,/nanswering Harry's unasked question as Ron struggled/nup from the floor. "You keepin' well, then, 'Arry? I/nseen your name in the paper loads over the summer,/nbut it weren't never nuffink very nice... I said to Ern, I/nsaid, ''e didn't seem like a nutter when we met 'im,/njust goes to show, dunnit?' "/n/nHe handed over their tickets and continued to gaze,/nenthralled, at Harry; apparently Stan did not care/nhow nutty somebody was if they were famous enough/nto be in the paper. I'd imagine the/ncharm wouldn't have a very long life though..."/n/nHarry did not answer; he was still feeling ill./n/n"I'm going to have to do this tomorrow," he muttered,/npushing the books he had just taken out of his bag/nback inside it./n/n"Well, write it in your homework planner then!" said/nHermione encouragingly. "So you don't forget!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry and Ron exchanged looks as he reached into/nhis bag, withdrew the planner and opened it/ntentatively./n/n" Don't leave it till later, you big second-rateri" chided/nthe book as Harry scribbled down Umbridge's/nhomework. Hermione beamed at it./n/n"I think 111 go to bed," said Harry, stuffing the/nhomework planner back into his bag and making a/nmental note to drop it in the fire the first opportunity/nhe got./n/nHe walked across the common room, dodging George,/nwho tried to put a Headless Hat on him, and reached/nthe peace and cool of the stone staircase to the boys'/ndormitories. He was feeling sick again, just as he had/nthe night he had had the vision of the snake, but/nthought that if he could just lie down for a while he/nwould be all right./n/nHe opened the door of his dormitory and was one step/ninside it when he experienced pain so severe he/nthought that someone must have sliced into the top of/nhis head. He did not know where he was, whether he/nwas standing or lying down, he did not even know his/nown name.../n/nManiacal laughter was ringing in his ears... He was/nhappier than he had been in a very long time.../nJubilant, ecstatic, triumphant ... A wonderful,/nwonderful thing had happened.../n/n"Harry? HARRY!"/n/nSomeone had hit him around the face. The insane/nlaughter was punctuated with a cry of pain. The/nhappiness was draining out of him, but the laughter/ncontinued.../n/n/n/n/n/nHe opened his eyes and as he did so, he became/naware that the wild laughter was coming out of his/nown mouth. The moment he realized this, it died/naway; Harry lay panting on the floor, staring up at the/nceiling, the scar on his forehead throbbing horribly./nRon was bending over him, looking very worried./n/n"What happened?" he said./n/n"I ... dunno ..." Harry gasped, sitting up again. "He's/nreally happy ... really happy ..."/n/n"You-Know-Who is?"/n/n"Something good's happened," mumbled Harry. He/nwas shaking as badly as he had done after seeing the/nsnake attack Mr. Weasley and felt very sick./n"Something he's been hoping for."/n/nThe words came, just as they had back in the/nGryffindor changing room, as though a stranger was/nspeaking them through Harry's mouth, yet he knew/nthey were true. He took deep breaths, willing himself/nnot to vomit all over Ron. He was very glad that Dean/nand Seamus were not here to watch this time./n/n"Hermione told me to come and check on you," said/nRon in a low voice, helping Harry to his feet. "She/nsays your defenses will be low at the moment, after/nSnape's been fiddling around with your mind... Still, I/nsuppose it'll help in the long run, won't it?"/n/nHe looked doubtfully at Harry as he helped him/ntoward bed. Harry nodded without any conviction and/nslumped back on his pillows, aching all over from/nhaving fallen to the floor so often that evening, his/nscar still prickling painfully. He could not help feeling/nthat his first foray into Occlumency had weakened his/nmind's resistance rather than strengthening it, and/n/n/n/n/nhe wondered, with a feeling of great trepidation, what/nhad happened to make Lord Voldemort the happiest/nhe had been in fourteen years./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Beetle At Bay
text: /nHarry's question was answered the very next/nmorning. When Hermione's Daily Prophet arrived she/nsmoothed it out, gazed for a moment at the front/npage, and then gave a yelp that caused everyone in/nthe vicinity to stare at her./n/n"What?" said Harry and Ron together./n/nFor an answer she spread the newspaper on the table/nin front of them and pointed at ten black-and-white/nphotographs that filled the whole of the front page,/nnine showing wizards' faces and the tenth, a witch's./nSome of the people in the photographs were silently/njeering; others were tapping their fingers on the frame/nof their pictures, looking insolent. Each picture was/ncaptioned with a name and the crime for which the/nperson had been sent to Azkaban./n/nAntonin Dolohov, read the legend beneath a wizard/nwith a long, pale, twisted face who was sneering up at/nHarry, convicted of the brutal murders of Gideon and/nFabian Prewett./n/n/n/n/nAugustus Rookwood, said the caption beneath a/npockmarked man with greasy hair who was leaning/nagainst the edge of his picture, looking bored,/nconvicted of leaking Ministry of Magic Secrets to He-/nWho-Must-Not-Be-Named./n/nBut Harry's eyes were drawn to the picture of the/nwitch. Her face had leapt out at him the moment he/nhad seen the page. She had long, dark hair that/nlooked unkempt and straggly in the picture, though/nhe had seen it sleek, thick, and shining. She glared/nup at him through heavily lidded eyes, an arrogant,/ndisdainful smile playing around her thin mouth. Like/nSirius, she retained vestiges of great good looks, but/nsomething — perhaps Azkaban — had taken most of/nher beauty./n/nBellatrix Lestrange, convicted of the torture and/npermanent incapacitation of Frank and Alice/nLongbottom./n/nHermione nudged Harry and pointed at the headline/nover the pictures, which Harry, concentrating on/nBellatrix, had not yet read./n/nMASS BREAKOUT FROM AZKABAN/n/nMINISTRY FEARS BLACK IS "RALLYING POINT"/n/nFOR OLD DEATH EATERS/n/n"Black?" said Harry loudly. "Not — ?"/n/n" Shhh\ " whispered Hermione desperately. "Not so loud/n— just read it!"/n/nThe Ministry of Magic announced late last night that/nthere has been a mass breakout from Azkaban./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSpeaking to reporters in his private office, Cornelius/nFudge, Minister of Magic, confirmed that ten high-/nsecurity prisoners escaped in the early hours of/nyesterday evening, and that he has already informed/nthe Muggle Prime Minister of the dangerous nature of/nthese individuals./n/n"We find ourselves, most unfortunately, in the same/nposition we were two and a half years ago when the/nmurderer Sirius Black escaped, " said Fudge last night./n"Nor do we think the two breakouts are unrelated. An/nescape of this magnitude suggests outside help, and/nwe must remember that Black, as the first person ever/nto break out of Azkaban, would be ideally placed to/nhelp others follow in his footsteps. We think it likely/nthat these individuals, who include Black's cousin,/nBellatrix Lestrange, have rallied around Black as their/nleader. We are, however, doing all we can to round up/nthe criminals and beg the magical community to remain/nalert and cautious. On no account should any of these/nindividuals be approached. "/n/n"There you are, Harry," said Ron, looking awestruck./n"That's why he was happy last night..."/n/n"I don't believe this," snarled Harry, "Fudge is blaming/nthe breakout on Sirius?"/n/n"What other options does he have?" said Hermione/nbitterly. "He can hardly say, 'Sorry everyone,/nDumbledore warned me this might happen, the/nAzkaban guards have joined Lord Voldemort' — stop/nwhimpering, Ron — 'and now Voldemort's worst/nsupporters have broken out too.' I mean, he's spent a/ngood six months telling everyone you and Dumbledore/nare liars, hasn't he?"/n/nHermione ripped open the newspaper and began to/nread the report inside while Harry looked around the/n/n/n/n/n/nGreat Hall. He could not understand why his fellow/nstudents were not looking scared or at least/ndiscussing the terrible piece of news on the front/npage, but very few of them took the newspaper every/nday like Hermione. There they all were, talking about/nhomework and Quidditch and who knew what other/nrubbish, and outside these walls ten more Death/nEaters had swollen Voldemort's ranks.../n/nHe glanced up at the staff table. It was a different/nstory here: Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall/nwere deep in conversation, both looking extremely/ngrave. Professor Sprout had the Prophet propped/nagainst a bottle of ketchup and was reading the front/npage with such concentration that she was not/nnoticing the gentle drip of egg yolk falling into her lap/nfrom her stationary spoon. Meanwhile, at the far end/nof the table, Professor Umbridge was tucking into a/nbowl of porridge. For once her pouchy toad's eyes/nwere not sweeping the Great Hall looking for/nmisbehaving students. She scowled as she gulped/ndown her food and every now and then she shot a/nmalevolent glance up the table to where Dumbledore/nand McGonagall were talking so intently./n/n"Oh my — " said Hermione wonderingly, still staring at/nthe newspaper./n/n"What now?" said Harry quickly; he was feeling/njumpy./n/n"It's ... horrible," said Hermione, looking shaken. She/nfolded back page ten of the newspaper and handed it/nback to Harry and Ron./n/nTRAGIC DEMISE OF/n/nMINISTRY OF MAGIC WORKER/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSt. Mungo's Hospital promised a full inquiry last/nnight after Ministry of Magic worker Broderick Bode,/n49, was discovered dead in his bed, strangled by a/npotted-plant. Healers called to the scene were unable/nto revive Mr. Bode, who had been injured in a/nworkplace accident some weeks prior to his death./n/nHealer Miriam Strout, who was in charge of Mr./n/nBode's ward at the time of the incident, has been/nsuspended on full pay and was unavailable for/ncomment yesterday, but a spokeswizard for the/nhospital said in a statement, "St. Mungo's deeply/nregrets the death of Mr. Bode, whose health was/nimproving steadily prior to this tragic accident./n/n"We have strict guidelines on the decorations/npermitted on our wards but it appears that Healer/nStrout, busy over the Christmas period, overlooked/nthe dangers of the plant on Mr. Bode's bedside table./nAs his speech and mobility improved, Healer Strout/nencouraged Mr. Bode to look after the plant himself,/nunaware that it was not an innocent Flitterbloom, but/na cutting of Devil's Snare, which, when touched by/nthe convalescent Mr. Bode, throttled him instantly./n/n"St. Mungo's is as yet unable to account for the/npresence of the plant on the ward and asks any witch/nor wizard with information to come forward."/n/n"Bode ..." said Ron. "Bode. It rings a bell..."/n/n"We saw him," Hermione whispered. "In St. Mungo's,/nremember? He was in the bed opposite Lockhart's,/njust lying there, staring at the ceiling. And we saw the/nDevil's Snare arrive. She — the Healer — said it was a/nChristmas present..."/n/nHarry looked back at the story. A feeling of horror was/nrising like bile in his throat./n/n/n/n/n/n"How come we didn't recognize Devil's Snare ... ?/nWe've seen it before ... we could've stopped this from/nhappening ..."/n/n"Who expects Devil's Snare to turn up in a hospital/ndisguised as a potted plant?" said Ron sharply. "It's/nnot our fault, whoever sent it to the bloke is to blame!/nThey must be a real prat, why didn't they check what/nthey were buying?"/n/n"Oh come on, Ron!" said Hermione shakily, "I don't/nthink anyone could put Devil's Snare in a pot and not/nrealize it tries to kill whoever touches it? This — this/nwas murder... A clever murder, as well... If the plant/nwas sent anonymously, how's anyone ever going to/nfind out who did it?"/n/nHarry was not thinking about Devil's Snare. He was/nremembering taking the lift down to the ninth level of/nthe Ministry on the day of his hearing, and the/nsallow-faced man who had got in on the Atrium level./n/n"I met Bode," he said slowly. "I saw him at the/nMinistry with your dad ..."/n/nRon's mouth fell open./n/n"I've heard Dad talk about him at home! He was an/nUnspeakable — he worked in the Department of/nMysteries!"/n/nThey looked at one another for a moment, then/nHermione pulled the newspaper back toward her,/nclosed it, glared for a moment at the pictures of the/nten escaped Death Eaters on the front, then leapt to/nher feet./n/n"Where are you going?" said Ron, startled./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"To send a letter," said Hermione, swinging her bag/nonto her shoulder. "It ... well, I don't know whether .../nbut it's worth trying ... and I'm the only one who can/n/n/n/n"I hate it when she does that," grumbled Ron as he/nand Harry got up from the table and made their own,/nslower way out of the Great Hall. "Would it kill her to/ntell us what she's up to for once? It'd take her about/nten more seconds — hey, Hagrid!"/n/nHagrid was standing beside the doors into the/nentrance hall, waiting for a crowd of Ravenclaws to/npass. He was still as heavily bruised as he had been/non the day he had come back from his mission to the/ngiants and there was a new cut right across the/nbridge of his nose./n/n"All righ', you two?" he said, trying to muster a smile/nbut managing only a kind of pained grimace./n/n"Are you okay, Hagrid?" asked Harry, following him as/nhe lumbered after the Ravenclaws./n/n"Fine, fine," said Hagrid with a feeble assumption of/nairiness; he waved a hand and narrowly missed/nconcussing a frightened-looking Professor Vector, who/nwas passing. "Jus' busy, yeh know, usual stuff —/nlessons ter prepare — couple o' salamanders got scale/nrot — an' I'm on probation," he mumbled./n/n" You're on probation?" said Ron very loudly, so that/nmany students passing looked around curiously./n"Sorry — I mean — you're on probation?" he/nwhispered./n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid. " 'S'no more'n I expected, ter tell/nyeh the truth. Yeh migh' not've picked up on it, bu'/nthat inspection didn' go too well, yeh know .../n/n/n/n/n/nanyway," he sighed deeply. "Bes' go an mb a bit more/nchili powder on them salamanders or their tails'll be/nhangin' off 'em next. See yeh, Harry ... Ron ..."/n/nHe trudged away, out the front doors and down the/nstone steps into the damp grounds. Harry watched/nhim go, wondering how much more bad news he/ncould stand./n/nThe fact that Hagrid was now on probation became/ncommon knowledge within the school over the next/nfew days, but to Harry's indignation, hardly anybody/nappeared to be upset about it; indeed, some people,/nDraco Malfoy prominent among them, seemed/npositively gleeful. As for the freakish death of an/nobscure Department of Mysteries employee in St./nMungo's, Harry, Ron, and Hermione seemed to be the/nonly people who knew or cared. There was only one/ntopic of conversation in the corridors now: the ten/nescaped Death Eaters, whose story had finally filtered/nthrough the school from those few people who read/nthe newspapers. Rumors were flying that some of the/nconvicts had been spotted in Hogsmeade, that they/nwere supposed to be hiding out in the Shrieking/nShack and that they were going to break into/nHogwarts, just as Sirius Black had done./n/nThose who came from Wizarding families had grown/nup hearing the names of these Death Eaters spoken/nwith almost as much fear as Voldemort's; the crimes/nthey had committed during the days of Voldemort's/nreign of terror were legendary. There were relatives of/ntheir victims among the Hogwarts students, who now/nfound themselves the unwilling objects of a gruesome/nsort of reflected fame as they walked the corridors:/nSusan Bones, who had an uncle, aunt, and cousins/nwho had all died at the hands of one of the ten, said/nmiserably during Herbology that she now had a good/nidea what it felt like to be Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n"And I don't know how you stand it, it's horrible," she/nsaid bluntly, dumping far too much dragon manure/non her tray of Screechsnap seedlings, causing them to/nwriggle and squeak in discomfort./n/nIt was true that Harry was the subject of much/nrenewed muttering and pointing in the corridors these/ndays, yet he thought he detected a slight difference in/nthe tone of the whisperers' voices. They sounded/ncurious rather than hostile now, and once or twice he/nwas sure he overheard snatches of conversation that/nsuggested that the speakers were not satisfied with/nthe Prophet's version of how and why ten Death/nEaters had managed to break out of Azkaban fortress./nIn their confusion and fear, these doubters now/nseemed to be turning to the only other explanation/navailable to them, the one that Harry and/nDumbledore had been expounding since the previous/nyear./n/nIt was not only the students' mood that had changed./nIt was now quite common to come across two or three/nteachers conversing in low, urgent whispers in the/ncorridors, breaking off their conversations the/nmoment they saw students approaching./n/n"They obviously can't talk freely in the staffroom/nanymore," said Hermione in a low voice, as she,/n/nHarry, and Ron passed Professors McGonagall,/nFlitwick, and Sprout huddled together outside the/nCharms classroom one day. "Not with Umbridge/nthere."/n/n"Reckon they know anything new?" said Ron, gazing/nback over his shoulder at the three teachers./n/n"If they do, we're not going to hear about it, are we?"/nsaid Harry angrily. "Not after Decree ... What number/nare we on now?"/n/n/n/n/n/nFor new signs had appeared on the house notice/nboards the morning after news of the Azkaban/nbreakout:/n/n— BY ORDER OF —/n/nTHE HIGH INQUISITOR OF HOGWARTS/n/nTeachers are hereby banned from giving students any/ninformation that is not strictly related to the subjects/nthey are paid to teach./n/nThe above is in accordance with/n/nEducational Decree Number Twenty-six./n/nSigned:/n/nDolores Jane Umbridge/nHIGH INQUISITOR/n/nThis latest decree had been the subject of a great/nnumber of jokes among the students. Lee Jordan had/npointed out to Umbridge that by the terms of the new/nrule she was not allowed to tell Fred and George off/nfor playing Exploding Snap in the back of the class./n/n"Exploding Snap's got nothing to do with Defense/nAgainst the Dark Arts, Professor! That's not/ninformation relating to your subject!"/n/nWhen Harry next saw Lee, the back of his hand was/nbleeding rather badly. Harry recommended essence of/nmurtlap./n/nHarry had thought that the breakout from Azkaban/nmight have humbled Umbridge a little, that she might/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhave been abashed at the catastrophe that had/noccurred right under her beloved Fudge's nose. It/nseemed, however, to have only intensified her furious/ndesire to bring every aspect of life at Hogwarts under/nher personal control. She seemed determined at the/nvery least to achieve a sacking before long, and the/nonly question was whether it would be Professor/nTrelawney or Hagrid who went first./n/nEvery single Divination and Care of Magical Creatures/nlesson was now conducted in the presence of/nUmbridge and her clipboard. She lurked by the fire in/nthe heavily perfumed tower room, interrupting/nProfessor Trelawney's increasingly hysterical talks/nwith difficult questions about Ornithomancy and/nHeptomology, insisting that she predict students'/nanswers before they gave them and demanding that/nshe demonstrate her skill at the crystal ball, the tea/nleaves, and the rune stones in turn. Harry thought/nthat Professor Trelawney might soon crack under the/nstrain; several times he passed her in the corridors (in/nitself a very unusual occurrence as she generally/nremained in her tower room), muttering wildly to/nherself, wringing her hands, and shooting terrified/nglances over her shoulder, all the time giving off a/npowerful smell of cooking sherry. If he had not been/nso worried about Hagrid, he would have felt sorry for/nher — but if one of them was to be ousted out of a/njob, there could be only one choice for Harry as to/nwho should remain./n/nUnfortunately, Harry could not see that Hagrid was/nputting up a better show than Trelawney. Though he/nseemed to be following Hermione's advice and had/nshown them nothing more frightening than a crup, a/ncreature indistinguishable from a Jack Russell terrier/nexcept for its forked tail, since before Christmas, he/nalso seemed to have lost his nerve. He was oddly/ndistracted and jumpy in lessons, losing the thread of/n/n/n/n/nwhat he was saying while talking to the class,/nanswering questions wrongly and glancing anxiously/nat Umbridge all the time. He was also more distant/nwith Harry, Ron, and Hermione than he had ever/nbeen before, expressly forbidding them to visit him/nafter dark./n/n"If she catches yeh, it'll be all of our necks on the/nline," he told them flatly, and with no desire to do/nanything that jeopardized his job further, they/nabstained from walking down to his hut in the/nevenings. It seemed to Harry that Umbridge was/nsteadily depriving him of everything that made his life/nat Hogwarts worth living: visits to Hagrid's house,/nletters from Sirius, his Firebolt, and Quidditch. He/ntook his revenge the only way he had: redoubling his/nefforts for the D.A./n/nHarry was pleased to see that all of them, even/nZacharias Smith, had been spurred to work harder/nthan ever by the news that ten more Death Eaters/nwere now on the loose, but in nobody was this/nimprovement more pronounced than in Neville. The/nnews of his parents' attacker's escape had wrought a/nstrange and even slightly alarming change in him. He/nhad not once mentioned his meeting with Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione on the closed ward in St. Mungo's, and/ntaking their lead from him, they had kept quiet about/nit too. Nor had he said anything on the subject of/nBellatrix and her fellow torturers' escape; in fact, he/nbarely spoke during D.A. meetings anymore, but/nworked relentlessly on every new jinx and/ncountercurse Harry taught them, his plump face/nscrewed up in concentration, apparently indifferent to/ninjuries or accidents, working harder than anyone/nelse in the room. He was improving so fast it was/nquite unnerving and when Harry taught them the/nShield Charm, a means of deflecting minor jinxes so/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthat they rebounded upon the attacker, only/nHermione mastered the charm faster than Neville./n/nIn fact Harry would have given a great deal to be/nmaking as much progress at Occlumency as Neville/nwas making during D.A. meetings. Harry's sessions/nwith Snape, which had started badly enough, were/nnot improving; on the contrary, Harry felt he was/ngetting worse with every lesson./n/nBefore he had started studying Occlumency, his scar/nhad prickled occasionally, usually during the night, or/nelse following one of those strange flashes of/nVoldemort's thoughts or moods that he experienced/nevery now and then. Nowadays, however, his scar/nhardly ever stopped prickling, and he often felt/nlurches of annoyance or cheerfulness that were/nunrelated to what was happening to him at the time,/nwhich were always accompanied by a particularly/npainful twinge from his scar. He had the horrible/nimpression that he was slowly turning into a kind of/naerial that was tuned in to tiny fluctuations in/nVoldemort's mood, and he was sure he could date this/nincreased sensitivity firmly from his first Occlumency/nlesson with Snape. What was more, he was now/ndreaming about walking down the corridor toward the/nentrance to the Department of Mysteries almost every/nnight, dreams that always culminated in him/nstanding longingly in front of the plain black door./n/n"Maybe it's a bit like an illness," said Hermione,/nlooking concerned when Harry confided in her and/nRon. "A fever or something. It has to get worse before/nit gets better."/n/n"It's lessons with Snape that are making it worse,"/nsaid Harry flatly. "I'm getting sick of my scar hurting,/nand I'm getting bored walking down that corridor/nevery night." He rubbed his forehead angrily. "I just/n/n/n/n/n/nwish the door would open, I'm sick of standing staring/nat it — "/n/n"That's not funny," said Hermione sharply./n"Dumbledore doesn't want you to have dreams about/nthat corridor at all, or he wouldn't have asked Snape/nto teach you Occlumency. You're just going to have to/nwork a bit harder in your lessons."/n/n"I am working!" said Harry, nettled. "You try it/nsometime, Snape trying to get inside your head, it's/nnot a bundle of laughs, you know!"/n/n"Maybe ..." said Ron slowly./n/n"Maybe what?" said Hermione rather snappishly./n/n"Maybe it's not Harry's fault he can't close his mind,"/nsaid Ron darkly./n/n"What do you mean?" said Hermione./n/n"Well, maybe Snape isn't really trying to help Harry..."/n/nHarry and Hermione stared at him. Ron looked darkly/nand meaningfully from one to the other./n/n"Maybe," he said again in a lower voice, "he's actually/ntrying to open Harry's mind a bit wider . . . make it/neasier for You-Know — "/n/n"Shut up, Ron," said Hermione angrily. "How many/ntimes have you suspected Snape, and when have you/never been right? Dumbledore trusts him, he works for/nthe Order, that ought to be enough."/n/n"He used to be a Death Eater," said Ron stubbornly./n"And we've never seen proof that he really swapped/nsides..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Dumbledore trusts him," Hermione repeated. "And if/nwe can't trust Dumbledore, we can't trust anyone."/n/nWith so much to worry about and so much to do —/nstartling amounts of homework that frequently kept/nthe fifth years working until past midnight, secret/nD.A. meetings, and regular classes with Snape —/nJanuary seemed to be passing alarmingly fast. Before/nHarry knew it, February had arrived, bringing with it/nwetter and warmer weather and the prospect of the/nsecond Hogsmeade visit of the year. Harry had had/nvery little time to spare on conversations with Cho/nsince they had agreed to visit the village together, but/nsuddenly found himself facing a Valentine's Day/nspent entirely in her company./n/nOn the morning of the fourteenth he dressed/nparticularly carefully. He and Ron arrived at breakfast/njust in time for the arrival of the post owls. Hedwig/nwas not there — not that he had expected her — but/nHermione was tugging a letter from the beak of an/nunfamiliar brown owl as they sat down./n/n"And about time! If it hadn't come today ..." she said/neagerly, tearing open the envelope and pulling out a/nsmall piece of parchment. Her eyes sped from left to/nright as she read through the message and a grimly/npleased expression spread across her face./n/n"Listen, Harry," she said, looking up at him. "This is/nreally important... Do you think you could meet me in/nthe Three Broomsticks around midday?"/n/n"Well ... I dunno," said Harry dubiously. "Cho might/nbe expecting me to spend the whole day with her. We/nnever said what we were going to do."/n/n"Well, bring her along if you must," said Hermione/nurgently. "But will you come?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well ... all right, but why?"/n/n/n/n"I haven't got time to tell you now, I've got to answer/nthis quickly — "/n/nAnd she hurried out of the Great Hall, the letter/nclutched in one hand and a piece of uneaten toast in/nthe other./n/n"Are you coming?" Harry asked Ron, but he shook his/nhead, looking glum./n/n"I can't come into Hogsmeade at all, Angelina wants a/nfull day's training. Like it's going to help — we're the/nworst team I've ever seen. You should see Sloper and/nKirke, they're pathetic, even worse than I am." He/nheaved a great sigh. "I dunno why Angelina won't just/nlet me resign..."/n/n"It's because you're good when you're on form, that's/nwhy," said Harry irritably./n/nHe found it very hard to be sympathetic to Ron's/nplight when he himself would have given almost/nanything to be playing in the forthcoming match/nagainst Hufflepuff. Ron seemed to notice Harry's tone,/nbecause he did not mention Quidditch again during/nbreakfast, and there was a slight frostiness in the way/nthey said good-bye to each other shortly afterward./nRon departed for the Quidditch pitch and Harry, after/nattempting to flatten his hair while staring at his/nreflection in the back of a teaspoon, proceeded alone/nto the entrance hall to meet Cho, feeling very/napprehensive and wondering what on earth they were/ngoing to talk about./n/nShe was waiting for him a little to the side of the oak/nfront doors, looking very pretty with her hair tied/nback in a long ponytail. Harry's feet seemed to be too/n/n/n/n/n/nbig for his body as he walked toward her, and he was/nsuddenly horribly aware of his arms and how stupid/nthey looked swinging at his sides./n/n"Hi," said Cho slightly breathlessly./n/n"Hi," said Harry./n/nThey stared at each other for a moment, then Harry/nsaid, "Well — er — shall we go, then?"/n/n"Oh — yes ..."/n/nThey joined the queue of people being signed out by/nFilch, occasionally catching each other's eye and/ngrinning shiftily, but not talking to each other. Harry/nwas relieved when they reached the fresh air, finding/nit easier to walk along in silence than just stand there/nlooking awkward. It was a fresh, breezy sort of day/nand as they passed the Quidditch stadium, Harry/nglimpsed Ron and Ginny skimming over the stands/nand felt a horrible pang that he was not up there with/nthem.../n/n"You really miss it, don't you?" said Cho./n/nHe looked around and saw her watching him./n/n"Yeah," sighed Harry. "I do."/n/n"Remember the first time we played against each/nother, in the third year?" she asked him./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, grinning. "You kept blocking me."/n/n"And Wood told you not to be a gentleman and knock/nme off my broom if you had to," said Cho, smiling/nreminiscently. "I heard he got taken on by Pride of/nPortree, is that right?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Nah, it was Puddlemere United, I saw him at the/nWorld Cup last year."/n/n"Oh, I saw you there too, remember? We were on the/nsame campsite. It was really good, wasn't it?"/n/nThe subject of the Quidditch World Cup carried them/nall the way down the drive and out through the gates./nHarry could hardly believe how easy it was to talk to/nher, no more difficult, in fact, than talking to Ron and/nHermione, and he was just starting to feel confident/nand cheerful when a large gang of Slytherin girls/npassed them, including Pansy Parkinson./n/n"Potter and Chang!" screeched Pansy to a chorus of/nsnide giggles. "Urgh, Chang, I don't think much of/nyour taste... At least Diggory was good-looking!"/n/nThey sped up, talking and shrieking in a pointed/nfashion with many exaggerated glances back at Harry/nand Cho, leaving an embarrassed silence in their/nwake. Harry could think of nothing else to say about/nQuidditch, and Cho, slightly flushed, was watching/nher feet./n/n"So ... where d'you want to go?" Harry asked as they/nentered Hogsmeade. The High Street was full of/nstudents ambling up and down, peering into the shop/nwindows and messing about together on the/npavements./n/n"Oh ... I don't mind," said Cho, shrugging. "Um .../nshall we just have a look in the shops or something?"/n/nThey wandered toward Dervish and Banges. A large/nposter had been stuck up in the window and a few/nHogsmeaders were looking at it. They moved aside/nwhen Harry and Cho approached and Harry found/nhimself staring once more at the ten pictures of the/n/n/n/n/nescaped Death Eaters. The poster ("By Order of the/nMinistry of Magic") offered a thousand-Galleon reward/nto any witch or wizard with information relating to the/nrecapture of any of the convicts pictured./n/n"It's funny, isn't it," said Cho in a low voice, also/ngazing up at the pictures of the Death Eaters./n"Remember when that Sirius Black escaped, and/nthere were dementors all over Hogsmeade looking for/nhim? And now ten Death Eaters are on the loose and/nthere aren't dementors anywhere..."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, tearing his eyes away from/nBellatrix Lestrange's face to glance up and down the/nHigh Street. "Yeah, it is weird..."/n/nHe was not sorry that there were no dementors/nnearby, but now he came to think of it, their absence/nwas highly significant. They had not only let the/nDeath Eaters escape, they were not bothering to look/nfor them... It looked as though they really were/noutside Ministry control now./n/nThe ten escaped Death Eaters were staring out of/nevery shop window he and Cho passed. It started to/nrain as they passed Scrivenshaft's; cold, heavy drops/nof water kept hitting Harry's face and the back of his/nneck./n/n"Um ... d'you want to get a coffee?" said Cho/ntentatively, as the rain began to fall more heavily./n/n"Yeah, all right," said Harry, looking around. "Where/n— ?"/n/n"Oh, there's a really nice place just up here, haven't/nyou ever been to Madam Puddifoot's?" she said/nbrightly, and she led him up a side road and into a/nsmall tea shop that Harry had never noticed before. It/n/n/n/n/n/nwas a cramped, steamy little place where everything/nseemed to have been decorated with frills or bows./nHarry was reminded unpleasantly of Umbridge's/noffice./n/n"Cute, isn't it?" said Cho happily./n/n"Er ... yeah," said Harry untruthfully./n/n"Look, she's decorated it for Valentine's Day!" said/nCho, indicating a number of golden cherubs that were/nhovering over each of the small, circular tables,/noccasionally throwing pink confetti over the/noccupants./n/n"Aaah ..."/n/nThey sat down at the last remaining table, which was/nsituated in the steamy window. Roger Davies, the/nRavenclaw Quidditch Captain, was sitting about a/nfoot and a half away with a pretty blonde girl. They/nwere holding hands. The sight made Harry feel/nuncomfortable, particularly when, looking around the/ntea shop, he saw that it was full of nothing but/ncouples, all of them holding hands. Perhaps Cho/nwould expect him to hold her hand./n/n"What can I get you, m'dears?" said Madam/nPuddifoot, a very stout woman with a shiny black/nbun, squeezing between their table and Roger/nDavies's with great difficulty./n/n"Two coffees, please," said Cho./n/nIn the time it took for their coffees to arrive, Roger/nDavies and his girlfriend started kissing over their/nsugar bowl. Harry wished they wouldn't; he felt that/nDavies was setting a standard with which Cho would/nsoon expect him to compete. He felt his face growing/n/n/n/n/nhot and tried staring out of the window, but it was so/nsteamed up he could not see the street outside. To/npostpone the moment when he had to look at Cho he/nstared up at the ceiling as though examining the/npaintwork and received a handful of confetti in the/nface from their hovering cherub./n/nAfter a few more painful minutes Cho mentioned/nUmbridge; Harry seized on the subject with relief and/nthey passed a few happy moments abusing her, but/nthe subject had already been so thoroughly canvassed/nduring D.A. meetings it did not last very long. Silence/nfell again. Harry was very conscious of the slurping/nnoises coming from the table next door and cast/nwildly around for something else to say./n/n"Er ... listen, d'you want to come with me to the Three/nBroomsticks at lunchtime? I'm meeting Hermione/nGranger there."/n/nCho raised her eyebrows./n/n"You're meeting Hermione Granger? Today?"/n/n"Yeah. Well, she asked me to, so I thought I would./nD'you want to come with me? She said it wouldn't/nmatter if you did."/n/n"Oh ... well ... that was nice of her."/n/nBut Cho did not sound as though she thought it was/nnice at all; on the contrary, her tone was cold and all/nof a sudden she looked rather forbidding./n/nA few more minutes passed in total silence, Harry/ndrinking his coffee so fast that he would soon need a/nfresh cup. Next door, Roger Davies and his girlfriend/nseemed glued together by the lips./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nCho's hand was lying on the table beside her coffee,/nand Harry was feeling a mounting pressure to take/nhold of it. Just do it, he told himself, as a fount of/nmingled panic and excitement surged up inside his/nchest. Just reach out and grab it... Amazing how much/nmore difficult it was to extend his arm twelve inches/nand touch her hand than to snatch a speeding Snitch/nfrom midair .../n/nBut just as he moved his hand forward, Cho took/nhers off the table. She was now watching Roger/nDavies kissing his girlfriend with a mildly interested/nexpression./n/n"He asked me out, you know," she said in a quiet/nvoice. "A couple of weeks ago. Roger. I turned him/ndown, though."/n/nHarry, who had grabbed the sugar bowl to excuse his/nsudden lunging movement across the table, could not/nthink why she was telling him this. If she wished she/nwere sitting at the table next door being heartily/nkissed by Roger Davies, why had she agreed to come/nout with him?/n/nHe said nothing. Their cherub threw another handful/nof confetti over them; some of it landed in the last/ncold dregs of coffee Harry had been about to drink./n/n"I came in here with Cedric last year," said Cho./n/nIn the second or so it took for him to take in what she/nhad said, Harry's insides had become glacial. He/ncould not believe she wanted to talk about Cedric/nnow, while kissing couples surrounded them and a/ncherub floated over their heads./n/nCho's voice was rather higher when she spoke again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I've been meaning to ask you for ages... Did Cedric —/ndid he m-m-mention me at all before he died?"/n/nThis was the very last subject on earth Harry wanted/nto discuss, and least of all with Cho./n/n"Well — no — " he said quietly. "There — there wasn't/ntime for him to say anything. Erm ... so ... d'you .../nd'you get to see a lot of Quidditch in the holidays?/n/nYou support the Tornados, right?"/n/nHis voice sounded falsely bright and cheery. To his/nhorror, he saw that her eyes were swimming with/ntears again, just as they had been after the last D.A./nmeeting before Christmas./n/n"Look," he said desperately, leaning in so that nobody/nelse could overhear, "let's not talk about Cedric right/nnow... Let's talk about something else..."/n/nBut this, apparently, was quite the wrong thing to/nsay./n/n"I thought," she said, tears spattering down onto the/ntable. "I thought you'd u-u-understand! I need to talk/nabout it! Surely you n-need to talk about it t-too! I/nmean, you saw it happen, d-didn't you?"/n/nEverything was going nightmarishly wrong; Roger/nDavies' girlfriend had even unglued herself to look/naround at Cho crying./n/n"Well — I have talked about it," Harry said in a/nwhisper, "to Ron and Hermione, but — "/n/n"Oh, you'll talk to Hermione Granger!" she said/nshrilly, her face now shining with tears, and several/nmore kissing couples broke apart to stare. "But you/nwon't talk to me! P-perhaps it would be best if we just/n/n/n/n/n/n... just p-paid and you went and met up with/nHermione G-Granger, like you obviously want to!"/n/nHarry stared at her, utterly bewildered, as she seized/na frilly napkin and dabbed at her shining face with it./n/n"Cho?" he said weakly, wishing Roger would seize his/ngirlfriend and start kissing her again to stop her/ngoggling at him and Cho./n/n"Go on, leave!" she said, now crying into the napkin./n/n"I don't know why you asked me out in the first place/nif you're going to make arrangements to meet other/ngirls right after me... How many are you meeting after/nHermione?"/n/n"It's not like that!" said Harry, and he was so relieved/nat finally understanding what she was annoyed about/nthat he laughed, which he realized a split second too/nlate was a mistake./n/nCho sprang to her feet. The whole tearoom was quiet,/nand everybody was watching them now./n/n"I'll see you around, Harry," she said dramatically,/nand hiccuping slightly she dashed to the door,/nwrenched it open, and hurried off into the pouring/nrain./n/n"Cho!" Harry called after her, but the door had/nalready swung shut behind her with a tuneful tinkle./n/nThere was total silence within the tea shop. Every eye/nwas upon Harry. He threw a Galleon down onto the/ntable, shook pink confetti out of his eyes, and/nfollowed Cho out of the door./n/nIt was raining hard now, and she was nowhere to be/nseen. He simply did not understand what had/n/n/n/n/n/nhappened; half an hour ago they had been getting/nalong fine./n/n"Women!" he muttered angrily, sloshing down the/nrain-washed street with his hands in his pockets./n"What did she want to talk about Cedric for anyway?/nWhy does she always want to drag up a subject that/nmakes her act like a human hosepipe?"/n/nHe turned right and broke into a splashy run, and/nwithin minutes he was turning into the doorway of/nthe Three Broomsticks. He knew he was too early to/nmeet Hermione, but he thought it likely there would/nbe someone in here with whom he could spend the/nintervening time. He shook his wet hair out of his/neyes and looked around. Hagrid was sitting alone in a/ncorner, looking morose./n/n"Hi, Hagrid!" he said, when he had squeezed through/nthe crammed tables and pulled up a chair beside him./n/nHagrid jumped and looked down at Harry as though/nhe barely recognized him. Harry saw that he had two/nfresh cuts on his face and several new bruises./n/n"Oh, it's you, Harry," said Hagrid. "You all righ'?"/n/n"Yeah, I'm fine," lied Harry; in fact, next to this/nbattered and mournful-looking Hagrid, he felt he did/nnot have much to complain about. "Er — are you/nokay?"/n/n"Me?" said Hagrid. "Oh yeah, I'm grand, Harry,/ngrand..."/n/nHe gazed into the depths of his pewter tankard, which/nwas the size of a large bucket, and sighed. Harry did/nnot know what to say to him. They sat side by side in/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nsilence for a moment. Then Hagrid said abruptly, "In/nthe same boat, you an' me, aren' we, Harry?"/n/n"Er — " said Harry./n/n"Yeah ... I've said it before... Both outsiders, like,"/nsaid Hagrid, nodding wisely. "An' both orphans. Yeah/n... both orphans."/n/nHe took a great swig from his tankard./n/n"Makes a diff'rence, havin' a decent family," he said./n"Me dad was decent. An' your mum an' dad were/ndecent. If they'd lived, life woulda bin diff'rent, eh?"/n/n"Yeah ... I s'pose," said Harry cautiously. Hagrid/nseemed to be in a very strange mood./n/n"Family," said Hagrid gloomily. "Whatever yeh say,/nblood's important..."/n/nAnd he wiped a trickle of it out of his eye./n/n"Hagrid," said Harry, unable to stop himself, "where/nare you getting all these injuries?"/n/n"Eh?" said Hagrid, looking startled. "Wha' injuries?"/n/n"All those!" said Harry, pointing at Hagrid 's face./n/n"Oh ... tha's jus' normal bumps an' bruises, Harry,"/nsaid Hagrid dismissively. "I got a rough job."/n/nHe drained his tankard, set it back upon the table,/nand got to his feet./n/n"I'll be seein'yeh, Harry... Take care now..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd he lumbered out of the pub looking wretched and/nthen disappeared into the torrential rain. Harry/nwatched him go, feeling miserable. Hagrid was/nunhappy and he was hiding something, but he/nseemed determined not to accept help. What was/ngoing on? But before Harry could think about the/nmatter any further, he heard a voice calling his name./n/n"Harry! Harry, over here!"/n/nHermione was waving at him from the other side of/nthe room. He got up and made his way toward her/nthrough the crowded pub. He was still a few tables/naway when he realized that Hermione was not alone;/nshe was sitting at a table with the unlikeliest pair of/ndrinking mates he could ever have imagined: Luna/nLovegood and none other than Rita Skeeter, ex-/njournalist on the Daily Prophet and one of Hermione's/nleast favorite people in the world./n/n"You're early!" said Hermione, moving along to give/nhim room to sit down. "I thought you were with Cho, I/nwasn't expecting you for another hour at least!"/n/n"Cho?" said Rita at once, twisting around in her seat/nto stare avidly at Harry. "A girl?"/n/nShe snatched up her crocodile-skin handbag and/ngroped within it./n/n"It's none of your business if Harry's been with a/nhundred girls," Hermione told Rita coolly. "So you can/nput that away right now."/n/nRita had been on the point of withdrawing an acid-/ngreen quill from her bag. Looking as though she had/nbeen forced to swallow Stinksap, she snapped her bag/nshut again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What are you up to?" Harry asked, sitting down and/nstaring from Rita to Luna to Hermione./n/n/n/n"Little Miss Perfect was just about to tell me when you/narrived," said Rita, taking a large slurp of her drink. "I/nsuppose I'm allowed to talk to him, am I?" she shot at/nHermione./n/n"Yes, I suppose you are," said Hermione coldly./n/nUnemployment did not suit Rita. The hair that had/nonce been set in elaborate curls now hung lank and/nunkempt around her face. The scarlet paint on her/ntwo-inch talons was chipped and there were a couple/nof false jewels missing from her winged glasses. She/ntook another great gulp of her drink and said out of/nthe corner of her mouth, "Pretty girl, is she, Harry?"/n/n"One more word about Harry's love life and the deal's/noff and that's a promise," said Hermione irritably./n/n"What deal?" said Rita, wiping her mouth on the back/nof her hand. "You haven't mentioned a deal yet, Miss/nPrissy, you just told me to turn up. Oh, one of these/ndays ..." She took a deep shuddering breath./n/n"Yes, yes, one of these days you'll write more horrible/nstories about Harry and me," said Hermione/nindifferently. "Find someone who cares, why don't/nyou?"/n/n"They've run plenty of horrible stories about Harry/nthis year without my help," said Rita, shooting a/nsideways look at him over the top of her glass and/nadding in a rough whisper, "How has that made you/nfeel, Harry? Betrayed? Distraught? Misunderstood?"/n/n"He feels angry, of course," said Hermione in a hard,/nclear voice. "Because he's told the Minister of Magic/n/n/n/n/n/nthe truth and the Minister's too much of an idiot to/nbelieve him."/n/n"So you actually stick to it, do you, that He-Who-/nMust-Not-Be-Named is back?" said Rita, lowering her/nglass and subjecting Harry to a piercing stare while/nher finger strayed longingly to the clasp of the/ncrocodile bag. "You stand by all this garbage/nDumbledore's been telling everybody about You-/nKnow-Who returning and you being the sole witness/n— ?"/n/n"I wasn't the sole witness," snarled Harry. "There were/na dozen-odd Death Eaters there as well. Want their/nnames?"/n/n"I'd love them," breathed Rita, now fumbling in her/nbag once more and gazing at him as though he was/nthe most beautiful thing she had ever seen. "A great/nbold headline: 'Potter Accuses ...'A subheading:/n/n'Harry Potter Names Death Eaters Still Among Us.' And/nthen, beneath a nice big photograph of you:/n/n'Disturbed teenage survivor of You-Know-Who's attack,/nHarry Potter, 1 5, caused outrage yesterday by/naccusing respectable and prominent members of the/nWizarding community of being Death Eaters...' "/n/nThe Quick-Quotes Quill was actually in her hand and/nhalfway to her mouth when the rapturous expression/ndied out of her face./n/n"But of course," she said, lowering the quill and/nlooking daggers at Hermione, "Little Miss Perfect/nwouldn't want that story out there, would she?"/n/n"As a matter of fact," said Hermione sweetly, "that's/nexactly what Little Miss Perfect does want."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRita stared at her. So did Harry. Luna, on the other/nhand, sang, "Weasley Is Our King" dreamily under her/nbreath and stirred her drink with a cocktail onion on/na stick./n/n"You want me to report what he says about He-Who-/nMust-Not-Be-Named?" Rita asked Hermione in a/nhushed voice./n/n"Yes, I do," said Hermione. "The true story. All the/nfacts. Exactly as Harry reports them. Hell give you all/nthe details, hell tell you the names of the/nundiscovered Death Eaters he saw there, hell tell you/nwhat Voldemort looks like now — oh, get a grip on/nyourself," she added contemptuously, throwing a/nnapkin across the table, for at the sound of/nVoldemort's name, Rita had jumped so badly that she/nhad slopped half her glass of firewhisky down herself./n/nRita blotted the front of her grubby raincoat, still/nstaring at Hermione. Then she said baldly, "The/nProphet wouldn't print it. In case you haven't noticed,/nnobody believes his cock-and-bull story. Everyone/nthinks he's delusional. Now, if you let me write the/nstory from that angle — "/n/n"We don't need another story about how Harry's lost/nhis marbles!" said Hermione angrily. "We've had/nplenty of those already, thank you! I want him given/nthe opportunity to tell the truth!"/n/n"There's no market for a story like that," said Rita/ncoldly./n/n"You mean the Prophet won't print it because Fudge/nwon't let them," said Hermione irritably./n/nRita gave Hermione a long, hard look. Then, leaning/nforward across the table toward her, she said in a/n/n/n/n/n/nbusinesslike tone, "All right, Fudge is leaning on the/nProphet, but it comes to the same thing. They won't/nprint a story that shows Harry in a good light. Nobody/nwants to read it. It's against the public mood. This/nlast Azkaban breakout has got people quite worried/nenough. People just don't want to believe You-Know-/nWho's back."/n/n"So the Daily Prophet exists to tell people what they/nwant to hear, does it?" said Hermione scathingly./n/nRita sat up straight again, her eyebrows raised, and/ndrained her glass of firewhisky./n/n"The Prophet exists to sell itself, you silly girl," she/nsaid coldly./n/n"My dad thinks it's an awful paper," said Luna,/nchipping into the conversation unexpectedly. Sucking/non her cocktail onion, she gazed at Rita with her/nenormous, protuberant, slightly mad eyes. "He/npublishes important stories that he thinks the public/nneeds to know. He doesn't care about making money."/n/nRita looked disparagingly at Luna./n/n"I'm guessing your father runs some stupid little/nvillage newsletter?" she said. " Twenty-five Ways to/nMingle with Muggles' and the dates of the next Bring-/nand-Fly Sale?"/n/n"No," said Luna, dipping her onion back into her/ngillywater, "he's the editor of The Quibbler."/n/nRita snorted so loudly that people at a nearby table/nlooked around in alarm./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" 'Important stories he thinks the public needs to/nknow'?" she said witheringly. "I could manure my/ngarden with the contents of that rag."/n/n"Well, this is your chance to raise the tone of it a bit,/nisn't it?" said Hermione pleasantly. "Luna says her/nfather's quite happy to take Harry's interview. That's/nwho'll be publishing it."/n/nRita stared at them both for a moment and then let/nout a great whoop of laughter./n/n" The Quibbleii" she said, cackling. "You think people/nwill take him seriously if he's published in The/nQuibbler?"/n/n"Some people won't," said Hermione in a level voice./n"But the Daily Prophet's version of the Azkaban/nbreakout had some gaping holes in it. I think a lot of/npeople will be wondering whether there isn't a better/nexplanation of what happened, and if there's an/nalternative story available, even if it is published in a"/n— she glanced sideways at Luna, "in a — well, an/nunusual magazine — I think they might be rather/nkeen to read it."/n/nRita did not say anything for a while, but eyed/nHermione shrewdly, her head a little to one side./n/n"All right, let's say for a moment I'll do it," she said/nabruptly. "What kind of fee am I going to get?"/n/n"I don't think Daddy exactly pays people to write for/nthe magazine," said Luna dreamily. "They do it/nbecause it's an honor, and, of course, to see their/nnames in print."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRita Skeeter looked as though the taste of Stinksap/nwas strong in her mouth again as she rounded on/nHermione. "I'm supposed to do this for free?"/n/n"Well, yes," said Hermione calmly, taking a sip of her/ndrink. "Otherwise, as you very well know, I will inform/nthe authorities that you are an unregistered/nAnimagus. Of course, the Prophet might give you/nrather a lot for an insider's account of life in/nAzkaban..."/n/nRita looked as though she would have liked nothing/nbetter than to seize the paper umbrella sticking out of/nHermione 's drink and thrust it up her nose./n/n"I don't suppose I've got any choice, have I?" said Rita,/nher voice shaking slightly. She opened her crocodile/nbag once more, withdrew a piece of parchment, and/nraised her Quick-Quotes Quill./n/n"Daddy will be pleased," said Luna brightly. A muscle/ntwitched in Rita's jaw./n/n"Okay, Harry?" said Hermione, turning to him. "Ready/nto tell the public the truth?"/n/n"I suppose," said Harry, watching Rita balancing the/nQuick-Quotes Quill at the ready on the parchment/nbetween them./n/n"Fire away, then, Rita," said Hermione serenely,/nfishing a cherry out of the bottom of her glass./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Seen And Unforeseen
text: /nLuna said vaguely that she did not know how soon/nRita's interview with Harry would appear in The/nQuibbler, that her father was expecting a lovely long/narticle on recent sightings of Crumple-Horned/nSnorkacks. "And, of course, that'll be a very/nimportant story, so Harry's might have to wait for the/nfollowing issue," said Luna./n/nHarry had not found it an easy experience to talk/nabout the night when Voldemort had returned. Rita/nhad pressed him for every little detail, and he had/ngiven her everything he could remember, knowing/nthat this was his one big opportunity to tell the world/nthe truth. He wondered how people would react to the/nstory. He guessed that it would confirm a lot of people/nin the view that he was completely insane, not least/nbecause his story would be appearing alongside utter/nrubbish about Crumple-Horned Snorkacks. But the/nbreakout of Bellatrix Lestrange and her fellow Death/nEaters had given Harry a burning desire to do/nsomething, whether it worked or not.../n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Can't wait to see what Umbridge thinks of you going/npublic," said Dean, sounding awestruck at dinner on/nMonday night. Seamus was shoveling down large/namounts of chicken-and-ham pie on Dean's other/nside, but Harry knew he was listening./n/n"It's the right thing to do, Harry," said Neville, who/nwas sitting opposite him. He was rather pale, but/nwent on in a low voice, "It must have been ... tough .../ntalking about it...
