For a few seconds/nhe did not know where he was; he was convinced that/nhe was about to see the white, skull-like face looming/nat him out of the dark again, then Ron's voice spoke/nvery near to him./n/n"Will you stop acting like a maniac, and I can get you/nout of here!"/n/nRon wrenched the hangings apart, and Harry stared/nup at him in the moonlight, as he lay flat on his back,/nhis scar searing with pain. Ron looked as though he/nhad just been getting ready for bed; one arm was out/nof his robes./n/n"Has someone been attacked again?" asked Ron,/npulling Harry roughly to his feet. "Is it Dad? Is it that/nsnake?"/n/n"No — everyone's fine — " gasped Harry, whose/nforehead felt as though it was on fire again. "Well .../nAvery isn't... He's in trouble... He gave him the wrong/ninformation... He's really angry..."/n/nHarry groaned and sank, shaking, onto his bed,/nrubbing his scar./n/n"But Rookwood's going to help him now... He's on the/nright track again..."/n/n"What are you talking about?" said Ron, sounding/nscared. "D'you mean ... did you just see You-Know-/nWho?"/n/n"I was You-Know-Who," said Harry, and he stretched/nout his hands in the darkness and held them up to/n/n/n/n/n/nhis face to check that they were no longer deathly/nwhite and long-fingered. "He was with Rookwood, he's/none of the Death Eaters who escaped from Azkaban,/nremember? Rookwood's just told him Bode couldn't/nhave done it..."/n/n"Done what?"/n/n"Remove something. . . He said Bode would have/nknown he couldn't have done it... Bode was under the/nImperius Curse... I think he said Malfoy's dad put it/non him..."/n/n"Bode was bewitched to remove something?" Ron/nsaid. "But — Harry, that's got to be — "/n/n"The weapon," Harry finished the sentence for him. "I/nknow."/n/nThe dormitory door opened; Dean and Seamus came/nin. Harry swung his legs back into bed. He did not/nwant to look as though anything odd had just/nhappened, seeing as Seamus had only just stopped/nthinking Harry was a nutter./n/n"Did you say," murmured Ron, putting his head close/nto Harry's on the pretense of helping himself to water/nfrom the jug on his bedside table, "that you were You-/nKnow-Who?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry quietly./n/nRon took an unnecessarily large gulp of water. Harry/nsaw it spill over his chin onto his chest./n/n"Harry," he said, as Dean and Seamus clattered/naround noisily, pulling off their robes, and talking,/n"you've got to tell — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I haven't got to tell anyone," said Harry shortly. "I/nwouldn't have seen it at all if I could do Occlumency./nI'm supposed to have learned to shut this stuff out./nThat's what they want."/n/nBy "they" he meant Dumbledore. He got back into bed/nand rolled over onto his side with his back to Ron and/nafter a while he heard Ron's mattress creak as he lay/nback down too. His scar began to burn; he bit hard on/nhis pillow to stop himself making a noise. Somewhere,/nhe knew, Avery was being punished.../n/nHarry and Ron waited until break next morning to tell/nHermione exactly what had happened. They wanted/nto be absolutely sure they could not be overheard./nStanding in their usual corner of the cool and breezy/ncourtyard, Harry told her every detail of the dream he/ncould remember. When he had finished, she said/nnothing at all for a few moments, but stared with a/nkind of painful intensity at Fred and George, who/nwere both headless and selling their magical hats/nfrom under their cloaks on the other side of the yard./n/n"So that's why they killed him," she said quietly,/nwithdrawing her gaze from Fred and George at last./n"When Bode tried to steal this weapon, something/nfunny happened to him. I think there must be/ndefensive spells on it, or around it, to stop people/nfrom touching it. That's why he was in St. Mungo's,/nhis brain had gone all funny and he couldn't talk. But/nremember what the Healer told us? He was/nrecovering. And they couldn't risk him getting better,/ncould they? I mean, the shock of whatever happened/nwhen he touched that weapon probably made the/nImperius Curse lift. Once he'd got his voice back, he'd/nexplain what he'd been doing, wouldn't he? They/nwould have known he'd been sent to steal the/nweapon. Of course, it would have been easy for/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nLucius Malfoy to put the curse on him. Never out of/nthe Ministry, is he?"/n/n"He was even hanging around that day I had my/nhearing," said Harry. "In the — hang on ..." he said/nslowly. "He was in the Department of Mysteries/ncorridor that day! Your dad said he was probably/ntrying to sneak down and find out what happened in/nmy hearing, but what if — "/n/n"Sturgis," gasped Hermione, looking thunderstruck./n/n"Sorry?" said Ron, looking bewildered./n/n"Sturgis Podmore," said Hermione, breathlessly./n"Arrested for trying to get through a door. Lucius/nMalfoy got him too. I bet he did it the day you saw/nhim there, Harry. Sturgis had Moody's Invisibility/nCloak, right? So what if he was standing guard by the/ndoor, invisible, and Malfoy heard him move, or/nguessed he was there, or just did the Imperius Curse/non the off chance that a guard was there? So when/nSturgis next had an opportunity — probably when it/nwas his turn on guard duty again — he tried to get/ninto the department to steal the weapon for Voldemort/n— Ron, be quiet — but he got caught and sent to/nAzkaban..."/n/nShe gazed at Harry./n/n"And now Rookwood's told Voldemort how to get the/nweapon?"/n/n"I didn't hear all the conversation, but that's what it/nsounded like," said Harry. "Rookwood used to work/nthere... Maybe Voldemort'll send Rookwood to do it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione nodded, apparently still lost in thought./nThen, quite abruptly, she said, "But you shouldn't/nhave seen this at all, Harry."/n/n"What?" he said, taken aback./n/n"You're supposed to be learning how to close your/nmind to this sort of thing," said Hermione, suddenly/nstern./n/n"I know I am," said Harry. "But — "/n/n"Well, I think we should just try and forget what you/nsaw," said Hermione firmly. "And you ought to put in/na bit more effort on your Occlumency from now on."/n/nHarry was so angry with her that he did not talk to/nher for the rest of the day, which proved to be another/nbad one. When people were not discussing the/nescaped Death Eaters in the corridors today, they/nwere laughing at Gryffindor's abysmal performance in/ntheir match against Hufflepuff; the Slytherins were/nsinging "Weasley Is Our King" so loudly and/nfrequently that by sundown Filch had banned it from/nthe corridors out of sheer irritation./n/nThe week did not improve as it progressed: Harry/nreceived two more D's in Potions, was still on/ntenterhooks that Hagrid might get the sack, and/ncould not stop himself from dwelling on the dream in/nwhich he had seen Voldemort, though he did not/nbring it up with Ron and Hermione again because he/ndid not want another telling-off from Hermione. He/nwished very much that he could have talked to Sirius/nabout it, but that was out of the question, so he tried/nto push the matter to the back of his mind./n/nUnfortunately, the back of his mind was no longer the/nsecure place it had once been./n/n/n/n/n/n"Get up, Potter."/n/n/n/nA couple of weeks after his dream of Rookwood, Harry/nwas to be found, yet again, kneeling on the floor of/nSnape's office, trying to clear his head. He had just/nbeen forced, yet again, to relive a stream of very early/nmemories he had not even realized he still had, most/nof them concerning humiliations Dudley and his gang/nhad inflicted upon him in primary school./n/n"That last memory," said Snape. "What was it?"/n/n"I don't know," said Harry, getting wearily to his feet./nHe was finding it increasingly difficult to disentangle/nseparate memories from the rush of images and/nsound that Snape kept calling forth. "You mean the/none where my cousin tried to make me stand in the/ntoilet?"/n/n"No," said Snape softly. "I mean the one concerning a/nman kneeling in the middle of a darkened room..."/n/n"It's ... nothing," said Harry./n/nSnape's dark eyes bored into Harry's. Remembering/nwhat Snape had said about eye contact being crucial/nto Legilimency, Harry blinked and looked away./n/n"How do that man and that room come to be inside/nyour head, Potter?" said Snape./n/n"It — " said Harry, looking everywhere but at Snape,/n/n"it was — just a dream I had."/n/n"A dream," repeated Snape./n/nThere was a pause during which Harry stared fixedly/nat a large dead frog suspended in a purple liquid in/nits jar./n/n/n/n/n/n"You do know why we are here, don't you, Potter?"/nsaid Snape in a low, dangerous voice. "You do know/nwhy I am giving up my evenings to this tedious job?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry stiffly./n/n"Remind me why we are here, Potter."/n/n"So I can learn Occlumency," said Harry, now glaring/nat a dead eel./n/n"Correct, Potter. And dim though you may be" —/nHarry looked back at Snape, hating him — "I would/nhave thought that after two months' worth of lessons/nyou might have made some progress. How many other/ndreams about the Dark Lord have you had?"/n/n"Just that one," lied Harry./n/n"Perhaps," said Snape, his dark, cold eyes narrowing/nslightly, "perhaps you actually enjoy having these/nvisions and dreams, Potter. Maybe they make you feel/nspecial — important?"/n/n"No, they don't," said Harry, his jaw set and his/nfingers clenched tightly around the handle of his/nwand./n/n"That is just as well, Potter," said Snape coldly,/n"because you are neither special nor important, and it/nis not up to you to find out what the Dark Lord is/nsaying to his Death Eaters."/n/n"No — that's your job, isn't it?" Harry shot at him./n/nHe had not meant to say it; it had burst out of him in/ntemper. For a long moment they stared at each other,/nHarry convinced he had gone too far. But there was a/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncurious, almost satisfied expression on Snape's face/nwhen he answered./n/n/n/n"Yes, Potter," he said, his eyes glinting. "That is my/njob. Now, if you are ready, we will start again..."/n/nHe raised his wand. "One — two — three —/nLegilimensV'/n/nA hundred dementors were swooping toward Harry/nacross the lake in the grounds... He screwed up his/nface in concentration... They were coming closer... He/ncould see the dark holes beneath their hoods . . . yet/nhe could also see Snape standing in front of him, his/neyes fixed upon Harry's face, muttering under his/nbreath... And somehow, Snape was growing clearer,/nand the dementors were growing fainter . . ./n/nHarry raised his own wand./n/n"Protegol"/n/nSnape staggered; his wand flew upward, away from/nHarry — and suddenly Harry's mind was teeming/nwith memories that were not his — a hook-nosed man/nwas shouting at a cowering woman, while a small/ndark-haired boy cried in a corner. . . A greasy-haired/nteenager sat alone in a dark bedroom, pointing his/nwand at the ceiling, shooting down flies... A girl was/nlaughing as a scrawny boy tried to mount a bucking/nbroomstick —/n/n"ENOUGH!"/n/nHarry felt as though he had been pushed hard in the/nchest; he took several staggering steps backward, hit/nsome of the shelves covering Snape's walls and heard/nsomething crack. Snape was shaking slightly, very/nwhite in the face./n/n/n/n/n/nThe back of Harry's robes were damp. One of the jars/nbehind him had broken when he fell against it; the/npickled slimy thing within was swirling in its draining/npotion./n/n"Reparo\" hissed Snape, and the jar sealed itself once/nmore. "Well, Potter ... that was certainly an/nimprovement..." Panting slightly, Snape straightened/nthe Pensieve in which he had again stored some of his/nthoughts before starting the lesson, almost as though/nchecking that they were still there. "I don't remember/ntelling you to use a Shield Charm . . . but there is no/ndoubt that it was effective..."/n/nHarry did not speak; he felt that to say anything/nmight be dangerous. He was sure he had just broken/ninto Snape's memories, that he had just seen scenes/nfrom Snape's childhood, and it was unnerving to/nthink that the crying little boy who had watched his/nparents shouting was actually standing in front of/nhim with such loathing in his eyes.../n/n"Let's try again, shall we?" said Snape./n/nHarry felt a thrill of dread: He was about to pay for/nwhat had just happened, he was sure of it. They/nmoved back into position with the desk between/nthem, Harry feeling he was going to find it much/nharder to empty his mind this time.../n/n"On the count of three, then," said Snape, raising his/nwand once more. "One — two — "/n/nHarry did not have time to gather himself together/nand attempt to clear his mind, for Snape had already/ncried " Legilimens\"/n/nHe was hurtling along the corridor toward the/nDepartment of Mysteries, past the blank stone walls,/n/n/n/n/n/npast the torches — the plain black door was growing/never larger; he was moving so fast he was going to/ncollide with it, he was feet from it and he could see/nthat chink of faint blue light again —/n/nThe door had flown open! He was through it at last,/ninside a black-walled, black-floored circular room lit/nwith blue-flamed candles, and there were more doors/nall around him — he needed to go on — but which/ndoor ought he to take — ?/n/n"POTTER!"/n/nHarry opened his eyes. He was flat on his back again/nwith no memory of having gotten there; he was also/npanting as though he really had run the length of the/nDepartment of Mysteries corridor, really had sprinted/nthrough the black door and found the circular room.../n/n"Explain yourself!" said Snape, who was standing over/nhim, looking furious./n/n"I ... dunno what happened," said Harry truthfully,/nstanding up. There was a lump on the back of his/nhead from where he had hit the ground and he felt/nfeverish. "I've never seen that before. I mean, I told/nyou, I've dreamed about the door ... but it's never/nopened before..."/n/n"You are not working hard enough!"/n/nFor some reason, Snape seemed even angrier than he/nhad done two minutes before, when Harry had seen/ninto his own memories./n/n"You are lazy and sloppy, Potter, it is small wonder/nthat the Dark Lord — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Can you tell me something, sir?" said Harry, firing up/nagain. "Why do you call Voldemort the Dark Lord, I've/nonly ever heard Death Eaters call him that — "/n/nSnape opened his mouth in a snarl — and a woman/nscreamed from somewhere outside the room./n/nSnape's head jerked upward; he was gazing at the/nceiling./n/n"What the — ?" he muttered./n/nHarry could hear a muffled commotion coming from/nwhat he thought might be the entrance hall. Snape/nlooked around at him, frowning./n/n"Did you see anything unusual on your way down/nhere, Potter?"/n/nHarry shook his head. Somewhere above them, the/nwoman screamed again. Snape strode to his office/ndoor, his wand still held at the ready, and swept out/nof sight. Harry hesitated for a moment, then followed./n/nThe screams were indeed coming from the entrance/nhall; they grew louder as Harry ran toward the stone/nsteps leading up from the dungeons. When he/nreached the top he found the entrance hall packed./nStudents had come flooding out of the Great Hall,/nwhere dinner was still in progress, to see what was/ngoing on. Others had crammed themselves onto the/nmarble staircase. Harry pushed forward through a/nknot of tall Slytherins and saw that the onlookers had/nformed a great ring, some of them looking shocked,/nothers even frightened. Professor McGonagall was/ndirectly opposite Harry on the other side of the hall;/nshe looked as though what she was watching made/nher feel faintly sick./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor Trelawney was standing in the middle of the/nentrance hall with her wand in one hand and an/nempty sherry bottle in the other, looking utterly mad./nHer hair was sticking up on end, her glasses were/nlopsided so that one eye was magnified more than the/nother; her innumerable shawls and scarves were/ntrailing haphazardly from her shoulders, giving the/nimpression that she was falling apart at the seams./nTwo large trunks lay on the floor beside her, one of/nthem upside down; it looked very much as though it/nhad been thrown down the stairs after her. Professor/nTrelawney was staring, apparently terrified, at/nsomething Harry could not see but that seemed to be/nstanding at the foot of the stairs./n/n"No!" she shrieked. "NO! This cannot be happening.../n/nIt cannot ... I refuse to accept it!"/n/n"You didn't realize this was coming?" said a high/ngirlish voice, sounding callously amused, and Harry,/nmoving slightly to his right, saw that Trelawney's/nterrifying vision was nothing other than Professor/nUmbridge. "Incapable though you are of predicting/neven tomorrow's weather, you must surely have/nrealized that your pitiful performance during my/ninspections, and lack of any improvement, would/nmake it inevitable you would be sacked?"/n/n"You c-can't!" howled Professor Trelawney, tears/nstreaming down her face from behind her enormous/nlenses, "you c-can't sack me! I've b-been here sixteen/nyears! H-Hogwarts is m-my h-home!"/n/n"It was your home," said Professor Umbridge, and/nHarry was revolted to see the enjoyment stretching/nher toadlike face as she watched Professor Trelawney/nsink, sobbing uncontrollably, onto one of her trunks,/n"until an hour ago, when the Minister of Magic/ncountersigned the order for your dismissal. Now/n/n/n/n/nkindly remove yourself from this hall. You are/nembarrassing us."/n/nBut she stood and watched, with an expression of/ngloating enjoyment, as Professor Trelawney/nshuddered and moaned, rocking backward and/nforward on her trunk in paroxysms of grief. Harry/nheard a sob to his left and looked around. Lavender/nand Parvati were both crying silently, their arms/naround each other. Then he heard footsteps./n/nProfessor McGonagall had broken away from the/nspectators, marched straight up to Professor/nTrelawney and was patting her firmly on the back/nwhile withdrawing a large handkerchief from within/nher robes./n/n"There, there, Sibyll ... Calm down... Blow your nose/non this... It's not as bad as you think, now... You are/nnot going to have to leave Hogwarts..."/n/n"Oh really, Professor McGonagall?" said Umbridge in/na deadly voice, taking a few steps forward. "And your/nauthority for that statement is . . . ?"/n/n"That would be mine," said a deep voice./n/nThe oak front doors had swung open. Students beside/nthem scuttled out of the way as Dumbledore appeared/nin the entrance. What he had been doing out in the/ngrounds Harry could not imagine, but there was/nsomething impressive about the sight of him framed/nin the doorway against an oddly misty night. Leaving/nthe doors wide behind him, he strode forward through/nthe circle of onlookers toward the place where/nProfessor Trelawney sat, tearstained and trembling,/nupon her trunk, Professor McGonagall alongside her./n/n"Yours, Professor Dumbledore?" said Umbridge with a/nsingularly unpleasant little laugh. "I'm afraid you do/n/n/n/n/n/nnot understand the position. I have here" — she/npulled a parchment scroll from within her robes —/n/n"an Order of Dismissal signed by myself and the/nMinister of Magic. Under the terms of Educational/nDecree Number Twenty-three, the High Inquisitor of/nHogwarts has the power to inspect, place upon/nprobation, and sack any teacher she — that is to say,/n/nI — feel is not performing up to the standard required/nby the Ministry of Magic. I have decided that Professor/nTrelawney is not up to scratch. I have dismissed her."/n/nTo Harry's very great surprise, Dumbledore continued/nto smile. He looked down at Professor Trelawney, who/nwas still sobbing and choking on her trunk, and said,/n"You are quite right, of course, Professor Umbridge./n/nAs High Inquisitor you have every right to dismiss my/nteachers. You do not, however, have the authority to/nsend them away from the castle. I am afraid," he went/non, with a courteous little bow, "that the power to do/nthat still resides with the headmaster, and it is my/nwish that Professor Trelawney continue to live at/nHogwarts."/n/nAt this, Professor Trelawney gave a wild little laugh in/nwhich a hiccup was barely hidden./n/n"No — no, I'll g-go, Dumbledore! I sh-shall 1-leave/nHogwarts and s-seek my fortune elsewhere — "/n/n"No," said Dumbledore sharply. "It is my wish that/nyou remain, Sibyll."/n/nHe turned to Professor McGonagall./n/n"Might I ask you to escort Sibyll back upstairs,/nProfessor McGonagall?"/n/n"Of course," said McGonagall. "Up you get, Sibyll..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nProfessor Sprout came hurrying forward out of the/ncrowd and grabbed Professor Trelawney's other arm./nTogether they guided her past Umbridge and up the/nmarble stairs. Professor Flitwick went scurrying after/nthem, his wand held out before him; he squeaked,/n"Locomotor trunksl" and Professor Trelawney's luggage/nrose into the air and proceeded up the staircase after/nher, Professor Flitwick bringing up the rear./n/nProfessor Umbridge was standing stock-still, staring/nat Dumbledore, who continued to smile benignly./n/n"And what," she said in a whisper that nevertheless/ncarried all around the entrance hall, "are you going to/ndo with her once I appoint a new Divination teacher/nwho needs her lodgings?"/n/n"Oh, that won't be a problem," said Dumbledore/npleasantly. "You see, I have already found us a new/nDivination teacher, and he will prefer lodgings on the/nground floor."/n/n"You've found — ?" said Umbridge shrilly. "You've/nfound? Might I remind you, Dumbledore, that under/nEducational Decree Twenty-two — "/n/n" — the Ministry has the right to appoint a suitable/ncandidate if — and only if — the headmaster is/nunable to find one," said Dumbledore. "And I am/nhappy to say that on this occasion I have succeeded./nMay I introduce you?"/n/nHe turned to face the open front doors, through which/nnight mist was now drifting. Harry heard hooves./nThere was a shocked murmur around the hall and/nthose nearest the doors hastily moved even farther/nbackward, some of them tripping over in their haste/nto clear a path for the newcomer./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThrough the mist came a face Harry had seen once/nbefore on a dark, dangerous night in the Forbidden/nForest: white-blond hair and astonishingly blue eyes,/nthe head and torso of a man joined to the palomino/nbody of a horse./n/n"This is Firenze," said Dumbledore happily to a/nthunderstruck Umbridge. "I think you 11 find him/nsuitable."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Centaur And The Sneak
text: /n"I'll bet you wish you hadn't given up Divination now,/ndon't you, Hermione?" asked Parvati, smirking./n/nIt was breakfast time a few days after the sacking of/nProfessor Trelawney, and Parvati was curling her/neyelashes around her wand and examining the effect/nin the back of her spoon. They were to have their first/nlesson with Firenze that morning./n/n"Not really," said Hermione indifferently, who was/nreading the Daily Prophet "I've never really liked/nhorses."/n/nShe turned a page of the newspaper, scanning its/ncolumns./n/n"He's not a horse, he's a centaur!" said Lavender,/nsounding shocked./n/n"A gorgeous centaur ..." sighed Parvati./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Either way, he's still got four legs," said Hermione/ncoolly. "Anyway, I thought you two were all upset that/nTrelawney had gone?"/n/n"We are!" Lavender assured her. "We went up to her/noffice to see her, we took her some daffodils — not the/nhonking ones that Sprout's got, nice ones..."/n/n"How is she?" asked Harry./n/n"Not very good, poor thing," said Lavender/nsympathetically. "She was crying and saying she'd/nrather leave the castle forever than stay here if/nUmbridge is still here, and I don't blame her./n/nUmbridge was horrible to her, wasn't she?"/n/n"I've got a feeling Umbridge has only just started/nbeing horrible," said Hermione darkly./n/n"Impossible," said Ron, who was tucking into a large/nplate of eggs and bacon. "She can't get any worse/nthan she's been already."/n/n"You mark my words, she's going to want revenge on/nDumbledore for appointing a new teacher without/nconsulting her," said Hermione, closing the/nnewspaper. "Especially another part-human. You saw/nthe look on her face when she saw Firenze..."/n/nAfter breakfast Hermione departed for her Arithmancy/nclass and Harry and Ron followed Parvati and/nLavender into the entrance hall, heading for/nDivination./n/n"Aren't we going up to North Tower?" asked Ron,/nlooking puzzled, as Parvati bypassed the marble/nstaircase./n/nParvati looked scornfully over her shoulder at him./n/n/n/n/n/n"How d'you expect Firenze to climb that ladder? We're/nin classroom eleven now, it was on the notice board/nyesterday."/n/nClassroom eleven was situated in the ground-floor/ncorridor leading off the entrance hall on the opposite/nside to the Great Hall. Harry knew it to be one of/nthose classrooms that were never used regularly, and/nthat it therefore had the slightly neglected feeling of a/ncupboard or storeroom. When he entered it right/nbehind Ron, and found himself right in the middle of/na forest clearing, he was therefore momentarily/nstunned./n/n"What the — ?"/n/nThe classroom floor had become springily mossy and/ntrees were growing out of it; their leafy branches/nfanned across the ceiling and windows, so that the/nroom was full of slanting shafts of soft, dappled, green/nlight. The students who had already arrived were/nsitting on the earthy floor with their backs resting/nagainst tree trunks or boulders, arms wrapped/naround their knees or folded tightly across their/nchests, looking rather nervous. In the middle of the/nroom, where there were no trees, stood Firenze./n/n"Harry Potter," he said, holding out a hand when/nHarry entered./n/n"Er — hi," said Harry, shaking hands with the/ncentaur, who surveyed him unblinkingly through/nthose astonishingly blue eyes but did not smile. "Er —/ngood to see you ..."/n/n"And you," said the centaur, inclining his white-blond/nhead. "It was foretold that we would meet again."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry noticed that there was the shadow of a hoof-/nshaped bruise on Firenze's chest. He could have sworn too that he felt/nsomething brush against his side, a gentle something/nlike a draft or bird wings, but looking down he saw/nnothing there./n/n"Evidence?" repeated Umbridge with that horrible/nwide toadlike smile. "Have you not been listening,/nDumbledore? Why do you think Miss Edgecombe is/nhere?"/n/n"Oh, can she tell us about six months' worth of/nmeetings?" said Dumbledore, raising his eyebrows. "I/nwas under the impression that she was merely/nreporting a meeting tonight."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Miss Edgecombe," said Umbridge at once, "tell us/nhow long these meetings have been going on, dear./nYou can simply nod or shake your head, I'm sure that/nwon't make the spots worse. Have they been/nhappening regularly over the last six months?"/n/nHarry felt a horrible plummeting in his stomach. This/nwas it, they had hit a dead end of solid evidence that/nnot even Dumbledore would be able to shift aside.../n/n"Just nod or shake your head, dear," Umbridge said/ncoaxingly to Marietta. "Come on, now, that won't/nactivate the jinx further..."/n/nEveryone in the room was gazing at the top of/nMarietta's face. Only her eyes were visible between/nthe pulled up robes and her curly fringe. Perhaps it/nwas a trick of the firelight, but her eyes looked oddly/nblank. And then — to Harry's utter amazement —/nMarietta shook her head./n/nUmbridge looked quickly at Fudge and then back at/nMarietta./n/n"I don't think you understood the question, did you,/ndear? I'm asking whether you've been going to these/nmeetings for the past six months? You have, haven't/nyou?"/n/nAgain, Marietta shook her head./n/n"What do you mean by shaking your head, dear?"/nsaid Umbridge in a testy voice./n/n"I would have thought her meaning was quite clear,"/nsaid Professor McGonagall harshly. "There have been/nno secret meetings for the past six months. Is that/ncorrect, Miss Edgecombe?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMarietta nodded./n/n/n/n"But there was a meeting tonight!" said Umbridge/nfuriously. "There was a meeting, Miss Edgecombe,/nyou told me about it, in the Room of Requirement!/n/nAnd Potter was the leader, was he not, Potter/norganized it, Potter — why are you shaking your head,/ngirl?"/n/n"Well, usually when a person shakes their head," said/nMcGonagall coldly, "they mean 'no.' So unless Miss/nEdgecombe is using a form of sign language as yet/nunknown to humans — "/n/nProfessor Umbridge seized Marietta, pulled her/naround to face her, and began shaking her very hard./nA split second later Dumbledore was on his feet, his/nwand raised. Kingsley started forward and Umbridge/nleapt back from Marietta, waving her hands in the air/nas though they had been burned./n/n"I cannot allow you to manhandle my students,/nDolores," said Dumbledore, and for the first time, he/nlooked angry./n/n"You want to calm yourself, Madam Umbridge," said/nKingsley in his deep, slow voice. "You don't want to/nget yourself into trouble now."/n/n"No," said Umbridge breathlessly, glancing up at the/ntowering figure of Kingsley. "I mean, yes — you're/nright, Shacklebolt — I — I forgot myself."/n/nMarietta was standing exactly where Umbridge had/nreleased her. She seemed neither perturbed by/nUmbridge's sudden attack, nor relieved by her/nrelease. She was still clutching her robe up to her/noddly blank eyes, staring straight ahead of her. A/nsudden suspicion connected to Kingsley's whisper/n/n/n/n/nand the thing he had felt shoot past him sprang into/nHarry's mind./n/n/n/n"Dolores," said Fudge, with the air of trying to settle/nsomething once and for all, "the meeting tonight —/nthe one we know definitely happened — "/n/n"Yes," said Umbridge, pulling herself together, "yes .../nwell, Miss Edgecombe tipped me off and I proceeded/nat once to the seventh floor, accompanied by certain/ntrustworthy students, so as to catch those in the/nmeeting red-handed. It appears that they were/nforewarned of my arrival, however, because when we/nreached the seventh floor they were running in every/ndirection. It does not matter, however. I have all their/nnames here, Miss Parkinson ran into the Room of/nRequirement for me to see if they had left anything/nbehind... We needed evidence and the room provided/n/n/n/nAnd to Harry's horror, she withdrew from her pocket/nthe list of names that had been pinned upon the/nRoom of Requirement's wall and handed it to Fudge./n/n"The moment I saw Potter's name on the list, I knew/nwhat we were dealing with," she said softly./n/n"Excellent," said Fudge, a smile spreading across his/nface. "Excellent, Dolores. And ... by thunder ..."/n/nHe looked up at Dumbledore, who was still standing/nbeside Marietta, his wand held loosely in his hand./n/n"See what they've named themselves?" said Fudge/nquietly. "Dumbledore'sArmy."/n/nDumbledore reached out and took the piece of/nparchment from Fudge. He gazed at the heading/nscribbled by Hermione months before and for a/n/n/n/n/n/nmoment seemed unable to speak. Then he looked up,/nsmiling./n/n/n/n"Well, the game is up," he said simply. "Would you/nlike a written confession from me, Cornelius — or will/na statement before these witnesses suffice?"/n/nHarry saw McGonagall and Kingsley look at each/nother. There was fear in both faces. He did not/nunderstand what was going on, and neither,/napparently, did Fudge./n/n"Statement?" said Fudge slowly. "What — I don't — ?"/n/n"Dumbledore's Army, Cornelius," said Dumbledore,/nstill smiling as he waved the list of names before/nFudge's face. "Not Potter's Army. Dumbledore's Army."/n/n"But — but — "/n/nUnderstanding blazed suddenly in Fudge's face. He/ntook a horrified step backward, yelped, and jumped/nout of the fire again./n/n"You?" he whispered, stamping again on his/nsmoldering cloak./n/n"That's right," said Dumbledore pleasantly./n/n"You organized this?"/n/n"I did," said Dumbledore./n/n"You recruited these students for — for your army?"/n/n"Tonight was supposed to be the first meeting," said/nDumbledore, nodding. "Merely to see whether they/nwould be interested in joining me. I see now that it/nwas a mistake to invite Miss Edgecombe, of course."/n/n/n/n/n/nMarietta nodded. Fudge looked from her to/nDumbledore, his chest swelling./n/n/n/n"Then you have been plotting against me!" he yelled./n"That's right," said Dumbledore cheerfully./n/n"NO!" shouted Harry./n/nKingsley flashed a look of warning at him,/n/nMcGonagall widened her eyes threateningly, but it/nhad suddenly dawned upon Harry what Dumbledore/nwas about to do, and he could not let it happen./n/n"No — Professor Dumbledore!"/n/n"Be quiet, Harry, or I am afraid you will have to leave/nmy office," said Dumbledore calmly./n/n"Yes, shut up, Potter!" barked Fudge, who was still/nogling Dumbledore with a kind of horrified delight./n"Well, well, well — I came here tonight expecting to/nexpel Potter and instead — "/n/n"Instead you get to arrest me," said Dumbledore,/nsmiling. "It's like losing a Knut and finding a Galleon,/nisn't it?"/n/n"Weasley!" cried Fudge, now positively quivering with/ndelight, "Weasley, have you written it all down,/neverything he's said, his confession, have you got it?"/n/n"Yes, sir, I think so, sir!" said Percy eagerly, whose/nnose was splattered with ink from the speed of his/nnote-taking./n/n"The bit about how he's been trying to build up an/narmy against the Ministry, how he's been working to/ndestabilize me?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, sir, I've got it, yes!" said Percy, scanning his/nnotes joyfully./n/n"Very well, then," said Fudge, now radiant with glee./n"Duplicate your notes, Weasley, and send a copy to/nthe Daily Prophet at once. If we send a fast owl we/nshould make the morning edition!" Percy dashed from/nthe room, slamming the door behind him, and Fudge/nturned back to Dumbledore. "You will now be/nescorted back to the Ministry, where you will be/nformally charged and then sent to Azkaban to await/ntrial!"/n/n"Ah," said Dumbledore gently, "yes. Yes, I thought we/nmight hit that little snag."/n/n"Snag?" said Fudge, his voice still vibrating with joy./n/n"I see no snag, Dumbledore!"/n/n"Well," said Dumbledore apologetically, "I'm afraid I/ndo."/n/n"Oh really?"/n/n"Well — it's just that you seem to be laboring under/nthe delusion that I am going to — what is the phrase?/n'Come quietly. ' I am afraid I am not going to come/nquietly at all, Cornelius. I have absolutely no/nintention of being sent to Azkaban. I could break out,/nof course — but what a waste of time, and frankly, I/ncan think of a whole host of things I would rather be/ndoing."/n/nUmbridge's face was growing steadily redder, she/nlooked as though she was being filled with boiling/nwater. Fudge stared at Dumbledore with a very silly/nexpression on his face, as though he had just been/nstunned by a sudden blow and could not quite believe/nit had happened. He made a small choking noise and/n/n/n/n/nthen looked around at Kingsley and the man with/nshort gray hair, who alone of everyone in the room/nhad remained entirely silent so far. The latter gave/nFudge a reassuring nod and moved forward a little,/naway from the wall. Harry saw his hand drift, almost/ncasually, toward his pocket./n/n"Don't be silly, Dawlish," said Dumbledore kindly./n/n"I'm sure you are an excellent Auror, I seem to/nremember that you achieved 'Outstanding' in all your/nN.E.W.T.s, but if you attempt to — er — 'bring me in'/nby force, I will have to hurt you."/n/nThe man called Dawlish blinked, looking rather/nfoolish. He looked toward Fudge again, but this time/nseemed to be hoping for a clue as to what to do next./n/n"So," sneered Fudge, recovering himself, "you intend/nto take on Dawlish, Shacklebolt, Dolores, and myself/nsingle-handed, do you, Dumbledore?"/n/n"Merlin's beard, no," said Dumbledore, smiling. "Not/nunless you are foolish enough to force me to."/n/n"He will not be single-handed!" said Professor/nMcGonagall loudly, plunging her hand inside her/nrobes./n/n"Oh yes he will, Minerva!" said Dumbledore sharply./n"Hogwarts needs you!"/n/n"Enough of this rubbish!" said Fudge, pulling out his/nown wand. "Dawlish! Shacklebolt! Take him ). "/n/nA streak of silver light flashed around the room. There/nwas a bang like a gunshot, and the floor trembled. A/nhand grabbed the scruff of Harry's neck and forced/nhim down on the floor as a second silver flash went/noff — several of the portraits yelled, Fawkes/n/n/n/n/nscreeched, and a cloud of dust filled the air. Coughing/nin the dust, Harry saw a dark figure fall to the ground/nwith a crash in front of him. There was a shriek and a/nthud and somebody cried, "No!" Then the sound of/nbreaking glass, frantically scuffling footsteps, a groan/n/n— and silence./n/nHarry struggled around to see who was half-/nstrangling him and saw Professor McGonagall/ncrouched beside him. She had forced both him and/nMarietta out of harm's way. Dust was still floating/ngently down through the air onto them. Panting/nslightly, Harry saw a very tall figure moving toward/nthem./n/n"Are you all right?" said Dumbledore./n/n"Yes!" said Professor McGonagall, getting up and/ndragging Harry and Marietta with her./n/nThe dust was clearing. The wreckage of the office/nloomed into view: Dumbledore's desk had been/noverturned, all of the spindly tables had been/nknocked to the floor, their silver instruments in/npieces. Fudge, Umbridge, Kingsley, and Dawlish lay/nmotionless on the floor. Fawkes the phoenix soared in/nwide circles above them, singing softly./n/n"Unfortunately, I had to hex Kingsley too, or it would/nhave looked very suspicious," said Dumbledore in a/nlow voice. "He was remarkably quick on the uptake,/nmodifying Miss Edgecombe's memory like that while/neveryone was looking the other way — thank him for/nme, won't you, Minerva?/n/n"Now, they will all awake very soon and it will be best/nif they do not know that we had time to communicate/n/n— you must act as though no time has passed, as/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthough they were merely knocked to the ground, they/nwill not remember — "/n/n"Where will you go, Dumbledore?" whispered/nProfessor McGonagall. "Grimmauld Place?"/n/n"Oh no," said Dumbledore with a grim smile. "I am/nnot leaving to go into hiding. Fudge will soon wish/nhe'd never dislodged me from Hogwarts, I promise/nyou..."/n/n"Professor Dumbledore ..." Harry began./n/nHe did not know what to say first: how sorry he was/nthat he had started the D.A. in the first place and/ncaused all this trouble, or how terrible he felt that/nDumbledore was leaving to save him from expulsion?/nBut Dumbledore cut him off before he could say/nanother word./n/n"Listen to me, Harry," he said urgently, "you must/nstudy Occlumency as hard as you can, do you/nunderstand me? Do everything Professor Snape tells/nyou and practice it particularly every night before/nsleeping so that you can close your mind to bad/ndreams — you will understand why soon enough, but/nyou must promise me — "/n/nThe man called Dawlish was stirring. Dumbledore/nseized Harry's wrist./n/n"Remember — close your mind — "/n/nBut as Dumbledore 's fingers closed over Harry's skin,/na pain shot through the scar on his forehead, and he/nfelt again that terrible, snakelike longing to strike/nDumbledore, to bite him, to hurt him —/n/n" — you will understand," whispered Dumbledore./n/n/n/n/n/nFawkes circled the office and swooped low over him./nDumbledore released Harry, raised his hand, and/ngrasped the phoenix's long golden tail. There was a/nflash of fire and the pair of them had gone./n/n"Where is he?" yelled Fudge, pushing himself up from/nthe ground. "Where is he?"/n/n"I don't know!" shouted Kingsley, also leaping to his/nfeet./n/n"Well, he can't have Disapparated!" cried Umbridge./n"You can't inside this school — "/n/n"The stairs!" cried Dawlish, and he flung himself upon/nthe door, wrenched it open, and disappeared, followed/nclosely by Kingsley and Umbridge. Fudge hesitated,/nthen got to his feet slowly, brushing dust from his/nfront. There was a long and painful silence./n/n"Well, Minerva," said Fudge nastily, straightening his/ntorn shirtsleeve, "I'm afraid this is the end of your/nfriend Dumbledore."/n/n"You think so, do you?" said Professor McGonagall/nscornfully./n/nFudge seemed not to hear her. He was looking around/nat the wrecked office. A few of the portraits hissed at/nhim; one or two even made rude hand gestures./n/n"You'd better get those two off to bed," said Fudge,/nlooking back at Professor McGonagall with a/ndismissive nod toward Harry and Marietta./n/nShe said nothing, but marched Harry and Marietta to/nthe door. As it swung closed behind them, Harry/nheard Phineas Nigellus's voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You know, Minister, I disagree with Dumbledore on/nmany counts ... but you cannot deny he's got style..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Snape's Worst Memory
text: /n— BY ORDER OF —/n/nTHE MINISTRY OF MAGIC/n/nDolores Jane Umbridge (High Inquisitor) has replaced/nAlbus Dumbledore as Head of Hogwarts School of/nWitchcraft and Wizardry./n/nThe above is in accordance with/n/nEducational Decree Number Twenty-eight./n/nSigned:/n/nCornelius Oswald Fudge/nMINISTER OF MAGIC/n/nThe notices had gone up all over the school overnight,/nbut they did not explain how every single person/nwithin the castle seemed to know that Dumbledore/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhad overcome two Aurors, the High Inquisitor, the/nMinister of Magic, and his Junior Assistant to escape./nNo matter where Harry went within the castle next/nday, the sole topic of conversation was Dumbledore's/nflight, and though some of the details might have/ngone awry in the retelling (Harry overheard one/nsecond-year girl assuring another that Fudge was/nnow lying in St. Mungo's with a pumpkin for a head),/nit was surprising how accurate the rest of their/ninformation was. Everybody seemed aware, for/ninstance, that Harry and Marietta were the only/nstudents to have witnessed the scene in Dumbledore's/noffice, and as Marietta was now in the hospital wing,/nHarry found himself besieged with requests to give a/nfirsthand account wherever he went./n/n"Dumbledore will be back before long," said Ernie/nMacmillan confidently on the way back from/nHerbology after listening intently to Harry's story./n"They couldn't keep him away in our second year and/nthey won't be able to this time. The Fat Friar told me/n..." He dropped his voice conspiratorially, so that/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione had to lean closer to him/nto hear, "... that Umbridge tried to get back into his/noffice last night after they'd searched the castle and/ngrounds for him. Couldn't get past the gargoyle. The/nHead's office has sealed itself against her." Ernie/nsmirked. "Apparently she had a right little tantrum..."/n/n"Oh, I expect she really fancied herself sitting up/nthere in the Head's office," said Hermione viciously, as/nthey walked up the stone steps into the entrance hall./n"Lording it over all the other teachers, the stupid/npuffed-up, power-crazy old — "/n/n"Now, do you really want to finish that sentence,/nGranger?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDraco Malfoy had slid out from behind the door,/nfollowed by Crabbe and Goyle. His pale, pointed face/nwas alight with malice./n/n"Afraid I'm going to have to dock a few points from/nGryffindor and Hufflepuff," he drawled./n/n"It's only teachers that can dock points from Houses,/nMalfoy," said Ernie at once./n/n"Yeah, we're prefects too, remember?" snarled Ron./n/n"I know prefects can't dock points, Weasel King,"/nsneered Malfoy; Crabbe and Goyle sniggered. "But/nmembers of the Inquisitorial Squad — "/n/n"The what?" said Hermione sharply./n/n"The Inquisitorial Squad, Granger," said Malfoy,/npointing toward a tiny silver I upon his robes just/nbeneath his prefect's badge. "A select group of/nstudents who are supportive of the Ministry of Magic,/nhand-picked by Professor Umbridge. Anyway,/nmembers of the Inquisitorial Squad do have the power/nto dock points... So, Granger, I'll have five from you/nfor being rude about our new headmistress.../nMacmillan, five for contradicting me... Five because I/ndon't like you, Potter ... Weasley, your shirt's/nuntucked, so I'll have another five for that... Oh yeah,/n/nI forgot, you're a Mudblood, Granger, so ten for/nthat..."/n/nRon pulled out his wand, but Hermione pushed it/naway, whispering, "Don't!"/n/n"Wise move, Granger," breathed Malfoy. "New Head,/nnew times ... Be good now, Potty ... Weasel King ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe strode away, laughing heartily with Crabbe and/nGoyle./n/n"He was bluffing," said Ernie, looking appalled. "He/ncan't be allowed to dock points ... that would be/nridiculous... It would completely undermine the/nprefect system..."/n/nBut Harry, Ron, and Hermione had turned/nautomatically toward the giant hourglasses set in/nniches along the wall behind them, which recorded/nthe House points. Gryffindor and Ravenclaw had been/nneck and neck in the lead that morning. Even as they/nwatched, stones flew upward, reducing the amounts/nin the lower bulbs. In fact, the only glass that seemed/nunchanged was the emerald-filled one of Slytherin./n/n"Noticed, have you?" said Fred's voice./n/nHe and George had just come down the marble/nstaircase and joined Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Ernie/nin front of the hourglasses./n/n"Malfoy just docked us all about fifty points," said/nHarry furiously, as they watched several more stones/nfly upward from the Gryffindor hourglass./n/n"Yeah, Montague tried to do us during break," said/nGeorge./n/n"What do you mean, 'tried'?" said Ron quickly./n/n"He never managed to get all the words out," said/nFred, "due to the fact that we forced him headfirst/ninto that Vanishing Cabinet on the first floor."/n/nHermione looked very shocked./n/n"But you'll get into terrible trouble!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Not until Montague reappears, and that could take/nweeks, I dunno where we sent him," said Fred coolly./n"Anyway ... we've decided we don't care about getting/ninto trouble anymore."/n/n"Have you ever?" asked Hermione./n/n" 'Course we have," said George. "Never been expelled,/nhave we?"/n/n"We've always known where to draw the line," said/nFred./n/n"We might have put a toe across it occasionally," said/nGeorge./n/n"But we've always stopped short of causing real/nmayhem," said Fred./n/n"But now?" said Ron tentatively./n/n"Well, now — " said George./n/n" — what with Dumbledore gone — " said Fred./n/n" — we reckon a bit of mayhem — " said George./n/n" — is exactly what our dear new Head deserves," said/nFred./n/n"You mustn't!" whispered Hermione. "You really/nmustn't! She'd love a reason to expel you!"/n/n"You don't get it, Hermione, do you?" said Fred,/nsmiling at her. "We don't care about staying anymore./nWe'd walk out right now if we weren't determined to/ndo our bit for Dumbledore first. So anyway," he/nchecked his watch, "phase one is about to begin. I'd/nget in the Great Hall for lunch if I were you, that way/n/n/n/n/n/nthe teachers will see you can't have had anything to/ndo with it."/n/n"Anything to do with what?" said Hermione anxiously./n/n"You'll see," said George. "Run along, now."/n/nFred and George turned away and disappeared in the/nswelling crowd descending the stairs toward lunch./nLooking highly disconcerted, Ernie muttered/nsomething about unfinished Transfiguration/nhomework and scurried away./n/n"I think we should get out of here, you know," said/nHermione nervously. "Just in case ..."/n/n"Yeah, all right," said Ron, and the three of them/nmoved toward the doors to the Great Hall, but Harry/nhad barely glimpsed today's ceiling of scudding white/nclouds when somebody tapped him on the shoulder/nand, turning, he found himself almost nose to nose/nwith Filch, the caretaker. He took several hasty steps/nbackward; Filch was best viewed at a distance./n/n"The headmistress would like to see you, Potter," he/nleered./n/n"I didn't do it," said Harry stupidly, thinking of/nwhatever Fred and George were planning. Filch's/njowls wobbled with silent laughter./n/n"Guilty conscience, eh?" he wheezed. "Follow me..."/n/nHarry glanced back at Ron and Hermione, who were/nboth looking worried. He shrugged and followed Filch/nback into the entrance hall, against the tide of hungry/nstudents./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nFilch seemed to be in an extremely good mood; he/nhummed creakily under his breath as they climbed/nthe marble staircase. As they reached the first landing/nhe said, "Things are changing around here, Potter."/n/n"I've noticed," said Harry coldly./n/n"Yerse ... I've been telling Dumbledore for years and/nyears he's too soft with you all," said Filch, chuckling/nnastily. "You filthy little beasts would never have/ndropped Stinkpellets if you'd known I had it in my/npower to whip you raw, would you, now? Nobody/nwould have thought of throwing Fanged Frisbees/ndown the corridors if I could've strung you up by the/nankles in my office, would they? But when/nEducational Decree Twenty-nine comes in, Potter, I'll/nbe allowed to do them things... And she's asked the/nMinister to sign an order for the expulsion of Peeves.../nOh, things are going to be very different around here/nwith her in charge..."/n/nUmbridge had obviously gone to some lengths to get/nFilch on her side, Harry thought, and the worst of it/nwas that he would probably prove an important/nweapon; his knowledge of the school's secret/npassageways and hiding places was probably second/nonly to the Weasley twins./n/n"Here we are," he said, leering down at Harry as he/nrapped three times upon Professor Umbridge's door/nand pushed it open. "The Potter boy to see you,/nma'am."/n/nUmbridge's office, so very familiar to Harry from his/nmany detentions, was the same as usual except for/nthe large wooden block lying across the front of her/ndesk on which golden letters spelled the word/nHEADMISTRESS; also his Firebolt, and Fred's and/nGeorge's Clean-sweeps, which he saw with a pang/n/n/n/n/nwere now chained and padlocked to a stout iron peg/nin the wall behind the desk. Umbridge was sitting/nbehind the desk, busily scribbling upon some of her/npink parchment, but looked up and smiled widely at/ntheir entrance./n/n"Thank you, Argus," she said sweetly./n/n"Not at all, ma'am, not at all," said Filch, bowing as/nlow as his rheumatism would permit, and exiting/nbackward./n/n"Sit," said Umbridge curtly, pointing toward a chair,/nand Harry sat. She continued to scribble for a few/nmoments. He watched some of the foul kittens/ngamboling around the plates over her head,/nwondering what fresh horror she had in store for him./n/n"Well now," she said finally, setting down her quill/nand looking like a toad about to swallow a/nparticularly juicy fly. "What would you like to drink?"/n/n"What?" said Harry, quite sure he had misheard her./n/n"To drink, Mr. Potter," she said, smiling still more/nwidely. "Tea? Coffee? Pumpkin juice?"/n/nAs she named each drink, she gave her short wand a/nwave, and a cup or glass of it appeared upon her/ndesk./n/n"Nothing, thank you," said Harry./n/n"I wish you to have a drink with me," she said, her/nvoice becoming more dangerously sweet. "Choose/none."/n/n"Fine ... tea then," said Harry, shrugging./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe got up and made quite a performance of adding/nmilk with her back to him. She then bustled around/nthe desk with it, smiling in sinisterly sweet fashion./n/n"There," she said, handing it to him. "Drink it before it/ngets cold, won't you? Well, now, Mr. Potter ... I/nthought we ought to have a little chat, after the/ndistressing events of last night."/n/nHe said nothing. She settled herself back into her seat/nand waited. When several long moments had passed/nin silence, she said gaily, "You're not drinking up!"/n/nHe raised the cup to his lips and then, just as/nsuddenly, lowered it. One of the horrible painted/nkittens behind Umbridge had great round blue eyes/njust like Mad-Eye Moody's magical one, and it had/njust occurred to Harry what Mad-Eye would say if he/never heard that Harry had drunk anything offered by/na known enemy./n/n"What's the matter?" said Umbridge, who was still/nwatching him. "Do you want sugar?"/n/n"No," said Harry./n/nHe raised the cup to his lips again and pretended to/ntake a sip, though keeping his mouth tightly closed./nUmbridge's smile widened./n/n"Good," she whispered. "Wish it was full moon."/n/n"You might," said Lupin darkly from behind his book./n"We've still got Transfiguration, if you're bored you/ncould test me... Here." He held out his book./n/nSirius snorted. "I don't need to look at that rubbish, I/nknow it all."/n/n"This'll liven you up, Padfoot," said James quietly./n"Look who it is..."/n/nSirius's head turned. He had become very still, like a/ndog that has scented a rabbit./n/n"Excellent," he said softly. " Snivellus."/n/nHarry turned to see what Sirius was looking at./n/nSnape was on his feet again, and was stowing the/nO.W.L. paper in his bag. As he emerged from the/nshadows of the bushes and set off across the grass,/nSirius and James stood up. Lupin and Wormtail/nremained sitting: Lupin was still staring down at his/nbook, though his eyes were not moving and a faint/nfrown line had appeared between his eyebrows./nWormtail was looking from Sirius and James to/nSnape with a look of avid anticipation on his face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"All right, Snivellus?" said James loudly./n/n/n/nSnape reacted so fast it was as though he had been/nexpecting an attack: Dropping his bag, he plunged his/nhand inside his robes, and his wand was halfway into/nthe air when James shouted, " ExpelliarmusV'/n/nSnape 's wand flew twelve feet into the air and fell with/na little thud in the grass behind him. Sirius let out a/nbark of laughter./n/n" Impedimental " he said, pointing his wand at Snape,/nwho was knocked off his feet, halfway through a dive/ntoward his own fallen wand./n/nStudents all around had turned to watch. Some of/nthem had gotten to their feet and were edging nearer/nto watch. Some looked apprehensive, others/nentertained./n/nSnape lay panting on the ground. James and Sirius/nadvanced on him, wands up, James glancing over his/nshoulder at the girls at the water's edge as he went./nWormtail was on his feet now, watching hungrily,/nedging around Lupin to get a clearer view./n/n"How'd the exam go, Snivelly?" said James./n/n"I was watching him, his nose was touching the/nparchment," said Sirius viciously. "There'll be great/ngrease marks all over it, they won't be able to read a/nword."/n/nSeveral people watching laughed; Snape was clearly/nunpopular. Wormtail sniggered shrilly. Snape was/ntrying to get up, but the jinx was still operating on/nhim; he was struggling, as though bound by invisible/nropes./n/n/n/n/n/n"You — wait," he panted, staring up at James with an/nexpression of purest loathing. "You — wait..."/n/n"Wait for what?" said Sirius coolly. "What're you going/nto do, Snivelly, wipe your nose on us?"/n/nSnape let out a stream of mixed swearwords and/nhexes, but his wand being ten feet away nothing/nhappened./n/n"Wash out your mouth," said James coldly./n/n" Scourgifyl"/n/nPink soap bubbles streamed from Snape's mouth at/nonce; the froth was covering his lips, making him gag,/nchoking him —/n/n"Leave him ALONE!"/n/nJames and Sirius looked around. James's free hand/njumped to his hair again./n/nIt was one of the girls from the lake edge. She had/nthick, dark red hair that fell to her shoulders and/nstartlingly green almond-shaped eyes — Harry's eyes./n/nHarry's mother .../n/n"All right, Evans?" said James, and the tone of his/nvoice was suddenly pleasant, deeper, more mature./n/n"Leave him alone," Lily repeated. She was looking at/nJames with every sign of great dislike. "What's he/ndone to you?"/n/n"Well," said James, appearing to deliberate the point,/n"it's more the fact that he exists, if you know what I/nmean..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nMany of the surrounding watchers laughed, Sirius/nand Wormtail included, but Lupin, still apparently/nintent on his book, didn't, and neither did Lily./n/n"You think you're funny," she said coldly. "But you're/njust an arrogant, bullying toerag, Potter. Leave him/nalone."/n/n"I will if you go out with me, Evans," said James/nquickly. "Go on ... Go out with me, and I'll never lay a/nwand on old Snivelly again."/n/nBehind him, the Impediment Jinx was wearing off./nSnape was beginning to inch toward his fallen wand,/nspitting out soapsuds as he crawled./n/n"I wouldn't go out with you if it was a choice between/nyou and the giant squid," said Lily./n/n"Bad luck, Prongs," said Sirius briskly, turning back/nto Snape. "OY!"/n/nBut too late; Snape had directed his wand straight at/nJames; there was a flash of light and a gash appeared/non the side of James's face, spattering his robes with/nblood. James whirled about; a second flash of light/nlater, Snape was hanging upside down in the air, his/nrobes falling over his head to reveal skinny, pallid legs/nand a pair of graying underpants./n/nMany people in the small crowd watching cheered./nSirius, James, and Wormtail roared with laughter./n/nLily, whose furious expression had twitched for an/ninstant as though she was going to smile, said, "Let/nhim down!"/n/n"Certainly," said James and he jerked his wand/nupward. Snape fell into a crumpled heap on the/n/n/n/n/n/nground. Disentangling himself from his robes, he got/nquickly to his feet, wand up, but Sirius said,/n/n"Petrificus Totalusl" and Snape keeled over again at/nonce, rigid as a board./n/n"LEAVE HIM ALONE!" Lily shouted. She had her own/nwand out now. James and Sirius eyed it warily./n/n"Ah, Evans, don't make me hex you," said James/nearnestly./n/n"Take the curse off him, then!"/n/nJames sighed deeply, then turned to Snape and/nmuttered the countercurse./n/n"There you go," he said, as Snape struggled to his feet/nagain, "you're lucky Evans was here, Snivellus — "/n/n"I don't need help from filthy little Mudbloods like/nher!"/n/nLily blinked. "Fine," she said coolly. "I won't bother in/nfuture. And I'd wash your pants if I were you,/nSnivellus."/n/n"Apologize to Evans!" James roared at Snape, his/nwand pointed threateningly at him./n/n"I don't want you to make him apologize," Lily/nshouted, rounding on James. "You're as bad as he/nis..."/n/n"What?" yelped James. "I'd NEVER call you a — you-/nknow-what!"/n/n"Messing up your hair because you think it looks cool/nto look like you've just got off your broomstick,/nshowing off with that stupid Snitch, walking down/n/n/n/n/n/ncorridors and hexing anyone who annoys you just/nbecause you can — I'm surprised your broomstick/ncan get off the ground with that fat head on it. You/nmake me SICK."/n/nShe turned on her heel and hurried away./n/n"Evans!" James shouted after her, "Hey, EVANS!"/n/nBut she didn't look back./n/n"What is it with her?" said James, trying and failing to/nlook as though this was a throwaway question of no/nreal importance to him./n/n"Reading between the lines, I'd say she thinks you're/na bit conceited, mate," said Sirius./n/n"Right," said James, who looked furious now, "right —/n/n/n/nThere was another flash of light, and Snape was once/nagain hanging upside down in the air./n/n"Who wants to see me take off Snivelly's pants?"/n/nBut whether James really did take off Snape's pants,/nHarry never found out. A hand had closed tight over/nhis upper arm, closed with a pincerlike grip. Wincing,/nHarry looked around to see who had hold of him, and/nsaw, with a thrill of horror, a fully grown, adult-sized/nSnape standing right beside him, white with rage./n/n"Having fun?"/n/nHarry felt himself rising into the air. The summer's/nday evaporated around him, he was floating upward/nthrough icy blackness, Snape's hand still tight upon/nhis upper arm. Then, with a swooping feeling as/n/n/n/n/n/nthough he had turned head over heels in midair, his/nfeet hit the stone floor of Snape's dungeon, and he/nwas standing again beside the Pensieve on Snape's/ndesk in the shadowy, present-day Potions master's/nstudy./n/n"So," said Snape, gripping Harry's arm so tightly/nHarry's hand was starting to feel numb. "So ... been/nenjoying yourself, Potter?"/n/n"N-no ..." said Harry, trying to free his arm./n/nIt was scary: Snape's lips were shaking, his face was/nwhite, his teeth were bared./n/n"Amusing man, your father, wasn't he?" said Snape,/nshaking Harry so hard that his glasses slipped down/nhis nose./n/n"I — didn't — "/n/nSnape threw Harry from him with all his might. Harry/nfell hard onto the dungeon floor./n/n"You will not tell anybody what you saw!" Snape/nbellowed./n/n"No," said Harry, getting to his feet as far from Snape/nas he could. "No, of course I w — "/n/n"Get out, get out, I don't want to see you in this office/never again!"/n/nAnd as Harry hurtled toward the door, ajar of dead/ncockroaches exploded over his head. He wrenched the/ndoor open and flew away up the corridor, stopping/nonly when he had put three floors between himself/nand Snape. There he leaned against the wall, panting,/nand rubbing his bruised arm./n/n/n/n/n/nHe had no desire at all to return to Gryffindor Tower/nso early, nor to tell Ron and Hermione what he had/njust seen. What was making Harry feel so horrified/nand unhappy was not being shouted at or having jars/nthrown at him — it was that he knew how it felt to be/nhumiliated in the middle of a circle of onlookers, knew/nexactly how Snape had felt as his father had taunted/nhim, and that judging from what he had just seen, his/nfather had been every bit as arrogant as Snape had/nalways told him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Career Advice
text: /n"But why haven't you got Occlumency lessons/nanymore?" said Hermione, frowning./n/n"I've told you," Harry muttered. "Snape reckons I can/ncarry on by myself now I've got the basics..."/n/n"So you've stopped having funny dreams?" said/nHermione skeptically./n/n"Pretty much," said Harry, not looking at her./n/n"Well, I don't think Snape should stop until you're/nabsolutely sure you can control them!" said Hermione/nindignantly. "Harry, I think you should go back to/nhim and ask — "/n/n"No," said Harry forcefully. "Just drop it, Hermione,/nokay?"/n/nIt was the first day of the Easter holidays and/nHermione, as was her custom, had spent a large part/nof the day drawing up study schedules for the three of/n/n/n/n/nthem. Harry and Ron had let her do it — it was easier/nthan arguing with her and, in any case, they might/ncome in useful./n/nRon had been startled to discover that there were only/nsix weeks left until their exams./n/n"How can that come as a shock?" Hermione/ndemanded, as she tapped each little square on Ron's/nschedule with her wand so that it flashed a different/ncolor according to its subject./n/n"I dunno ..." said Ron, "there's been a lot going on..."/n/n"Well, there you are," she said, handing him his/nschedule, "if you follow that you should do fine."/n/nRon looked down it gloomily, but then brightened./n/n"You've given me an evening off every week!"/n/n"That's for Quidditch practice," said Hermione./n/nThe smile faded from Ron's face./n/n"What's the point?" he said. "We've got about as much/nchance of winning the Quidditch Cup this year as/nDad's got of becoming Minister of Magic..."/n/nHermione said nothing. She was looking at Harry,/nwho was staring blankly at the opposite wall of the/ncommon room while Crookshanks pawed at his hand,/ntrying to get his ears scratched./n/n"What's wrong, Harry?"/n/n"What?" he said quickly. "Nothing ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe seized his copy of Defensive Magical Theory and/npretended to be looking something up in the index./nCrookshanks gave him up as a bad job and slunk/naway under Hermione's chair./n/n"I saw Cho earlier," said Hermione tentatively, "and/nshe looked really miserable too... Have you two had a/nrow again?"/n/n"Wha — oh yeah, we have," said Harry, seizing/ngratefully on the excuse./n/n"What about?"/n/n"That sneak friend of hers, Marietta," said Harry./n/n"Yeah, well, I don't blame you!" said Ron angrily,/nsetting down his study schedule. "If it hadn't been for/nher ..."/n/nRon went into a rant about Marietta Edgecombe,/nwhich Harry found helpful. All he had to do was look/nangry, nod, and say "yeah" and "that's right"/nwhenever Ron drew breath, leaving his mind free to/ndwell, ever more miserably, on what he had seen in/nthe Pensieve./n/nHe felt as though the memory of it was eating him/nfrom inside. He had been so sure that his parents had/nbeen wonderful people that he never had the slightest/ndifficulty in disbelieving Snape's aspersions on his/nfather's character. Hadn't people like Hagrid and/nSirius told Harry how wonderful his father had been?/n/n( Yeah, well, look what Sirius was like himself, said a/nnagging voice inside Harry's head... He was as bad,/nwasn't he?) Yes, he had once overheard Professor/nMcGonagall saying that his father and Sirius had/nbeen troublemakers at school, but she had described/nthem as forerunners of the Weasley twins, and Harry/n/n/n/n/ncould not imagine Fred and George dangling someone/nupside down for the fun of it ... not unless they really/nloathed them . . . Perhaps Malfoy, or somebody who/nreally deserved it . . ./n/nHarry tried to make a case for Snape having deserved/nwhat he had suffered at James's hands — but hadn't/nLily asked, "What's he done to you?" And hadn't/nJames replied, "It's more the fact that he exists, if you/nknow what I mean?" Hadn't James started it all/nsimply because Sirius said he was bored? Harry/nremembered Lupin saying back in Grimmauld Place/nthat Dumbledore had made him prefect in the hope/nthat he would be able to exercise some control over/nJames and Sirius... But in the Pensieve, he had sat/nthere and let it all happen.../n/nHarry reminded himself that Lily had intervened; his/nmother had been decent, yet the memory of the look/non her face as she had shouted at James disturbed/nhim quite as much as anything else. She had clearly/nloathed James and Harry simply could not/nunderstand how they could have ended up married./nOnce or twice he even wondered whether James had/nforced her into it.../n/nFor nearly five years the thought of his father had/nbeen a source of comfort, of inspiration. Whenever/nsomeone had told him he was like James he had/nglowed with pride inside. And now ... now he felt cold/nand miserable at the thought of him./n/nThe weather grew breezier, brighter, and warmer as/nthe holidays passed, but Harry was stuck with the/nrest of the fifth and seventh years, who were all/ntrapped inside, traipsing back and forth to the library./nHarry pretended that his bad mood had no other/ncause but the approaching exams, and as his fellow/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGryffindors were sick of studying themselves, his/nexcuse went unchallenged./n/n"Harry, I'm talking to you, can you hear me?"/n/n"Huh?"/n/nHe looked around. Ginny Weasley, looking very/nwindswept, had joined him at the library table where/nhe had been sitting alone. It was late on Sunday/nevening; Hermione had gone back to Gryffindor Tower/nto review Ancient Runes; Ron had Quidditch practice./n/n"Oh hi," said Harry, pulling his books back toward/nhim. "How come you're not at practice?"/n/n"It's over," said Ginny. "Ron had to take Jack Sloper/nup to the hospital wing."/n/n"Why?"/n/n"Well, we're not sure, but we think he knocked himself/nout with his own bat." She sighed heavily. "Anyway .../na package just arrived, it's only just got through/nUmbridge's new screening process..."/n/nShe hoisted a box wrapped in brown paper onto the/ntable; it had clearly been unwrapped and carelessly/nrewrapped, and there was a scribbled note across it in/nred ink, reading INSPECTED AND PASSED BY THE/nHOGWARTS HIGH INQUISITOR./n/n"It's Easter eggs from Mum," said Ginny. "There's one/nfor you... There you go..."/n/nShe handed him a handsome chocolate egg decorated/nwith small, iced Snitches and, according to the/npackaging, containing a bag of Fizzing Whizbees./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry looked at it for a moment, then, to his horror,/nfelt a hard lump rise in his throat./n/n/n/n"Are you okay, Harry?" asked Ginny quietly./n/n"Yeah, I'm fine," said Harry gruffly. The lump in his/nthroat was painful. He did not understand why an/nEaster egg should have made him feel like this./n/n"You seem really down lately," Ginny persisted. "You/nknow, I'm sure if you just talked to Cho ..."/n/n"It's not Cho I want to talk to," said Harry brusquely./n/n"Who is it, then?" asked Ginny./n/n/n/nHe glanced around to make quite sure that nobody/nwas listening; Madam Pince was several shelves away,/nstamping out a pile of books for a frantic-looking/nHannah Abbott./n/n"I wish I could talk to Sirius," he muttered. "But I/nknow I can't."/n/nMore to give himself something to do than because he/nreally wanted any, Harry unwrapped his Easter egg,/nbroke off a large bit, and put it into his mouth./n/n"Well," said Ginny slowly, helping herself to a bit of/negg too, "if you really want to talk to Sirius, I expect/nwe could think of a way to do it..."/n/n"Come on," said Harry hopelessly. "With Umbridge/npolicing the fires and reading all our mail?"/n/n"The thing about growing up with Fred and George,"/nsaid Ginny thoughtfully, "is that you sort of start/n/n/n/n/n/nthinking anything's possible if you've got enough/nnerve."/n/nHarry looked at her. Perhaps it was the effect of the/nchocolate — Lupin had always advised eating some/nafter encounters with dementors — or simply because/nhe had finally spoken aloud the wish that had been/nburning inside him for a week, but he felt a bit more/nhopeful.../n/n"WHAT DO YOU THINK YOU ARE DOING?"/n/n"Oh damn," whispered Ginny, jumping to her feet. "I/nforgot—"/n/nMadam Pince was swooping down upon them, her/nshriveled face contorted with rage./n/n" Chocolate in the library\" she screamed. "Out — out/n— OUT!"/n/nAnd whipping out her wand, she caused Harry's/nbooks, bag, and ink bottle to chase him and Ginny/nfrom the library, whacking them repeatedly over the/nhead as they ran./n/nAs though to underline the importance of their/nupcoming examinations, a batch of pamphlets,/nleaflets, and notices concerning various Wizarding/ncareers appeared on the tables in Gryffindor Tower/nshortly before the end of the holidays, along with yet/nanother notice on the board, which read:/n/nCAREER ADVICE/n/nAll fifth years will be required to attend a short/nmeeting with their Head of House during the first/nweek of the Summer term, in which they will be given/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthe opportunity to discuss their future careers. Times/nof individual appointments are listed below./n/n/n/nHarry looked down the list and found that he was/nexpected in Professor McGonagall's office at half-past/ntwo on Monday, which would mean missing most of/nDivination. He and the other fifth years spent a/nconsiderable part of the final weekend of the Easter/nbreak reading all the career information that had/nbeen left there for their perusal./n/n"Well, I don't fancy Healing," said Ron on the last/nevening of the holidays. He was immersed in a leaflet/nthat carried the crossed bone-and-wand emblem of/nSt. Mungo's on its front. "It says here you need at/nleast an E at N.E.W.T. level in Potions, Herbology,/nTransfiguration, Charms, and Defense Against the/nDark Arts. I mean ... blimey... Don't want much, do/nthey?"/n/n"Well, it's a very responsible job, isn't it?" said/nHermione absently. She was poring over a bright/npink-and-orange leaflet that was headed SO YOU/nTHINK YOU'D LIKE TO WORK IN MUGGLE/nRELATIONS? "You don't seem to need many/nqualifications to liaise with Muggles... All they want is/nan O.W.L. in Muggle Studies... 'Much more important/nis your enthusiasm, patience, and a good sense offunV/n/n/n/n"You'd need more than a good sense of fun to liaise/nwith my uncle," said Harry darkly. "Good sense of/nwhen to duck, more like ..." He was halfway through/na pamphlet on Wizard banking. "Listen to this:/n/n" 'Are you seeking a challenging career involving travel,/nadventure, and substantial, danger-related treasure/nbonuses? Then consider a position with Gringotts/nWizarding Bank, who are currently recruiting Curse-/n/n/n/n/n/nBreakers for thrilling opportunities abroad...' They/nwant Arithmancy, though... You could do it,/nHermione!"/n/n"I don't much fancy banking," said Hermione vaguely,/nnow immersed in HAVE YOU GOT WHAT IT TAKES/nTO TRAIN SECURITY TROLLS?/n/n"Hey," said a voice in Harry's ear. He looked around;/nFred and George had come to join them. "Ginny's had/na word with us about you," said Fred, stretching out/nhis legs on the table in front of them and causing/nseveral booklets on careers with the Ministry of Magic/nto slide off onto the floor. "She says you need to talk/nto Sirius?"/n/n"What?" said Hermione sharply, freezing with her/nhand halfway toward picking up MAKE A BANG AT/nTHE DEPARTMENT OF MAGICAL ACCIDENTS AND/nCATASTROPHES./n/n"Yeah ..." said Harry, trying to sound casual, "yeah, I/nthought I'd like — "/n/n"Don't be so ridiculous," said Hermione, straightening/nup and looking at him as though she could not/nbelieve her eyes. "With Umbridge groping around in/nthe fires and frisking all the owls?"/n/n"Well, we think we can find a way around that," said/nGeorge, stretching and smiling. "It's a simple matter/nof causing a diversion. Now, you might have noticed/nthat we have been rather quiet on the mayhem front/nduring the Easter holidays?"/n/n"What was the point, we asked ourselves, of/ndisrupting leisure time?" continued Fred. "No point at/nall, we answered ourselves. And of course, we'd have/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmessed up people's studying too, which would be the/nvery last thing we'd want to do."/n/nHe gave Hermione a sanctimonious little nod. She/nlooked rather taken aback by this thoughtfulness./n/n"But it's business as usual from tomorrow," Fred/ncontinued briskly. "And if we're going to be causing a/nbit of uproar, why not do it so that Harry can have his/nchat with Sirius?"/n/n"Yes, but still," said Hermione with an air of/nexplaining something very simple to somebody very/nobtuse, "even if you do cause a diversion, how is/nHarry supposed to talk to him?"/n/n"Umbridge's office," said Harry quietly./n/nHe had been thinking about it for a fortnight and/ncould think of no alternative; Umbridge herself had/ntold him that the only fire that was not being watched/nwas her own./n/n"Are — you — insane?" said Hermione in a hushed/nvoice./n/nRon had lowered his leaflet on jobs in the cultivated/nfungus trade and was watching the conversation/nwarily./n/n"I don't think so," said Harry, shrugging./n/n"And how are you going to get in there in the first/nplace?"/n/nHarry was ready for this question./n/n"Sirius's knife," he said./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Excuse me?"/n/n/n/n"Christmas before last Sirius gave me a knife that'll/nopen any lock," said Harry. "So even if she's/nbewitched the door so Alohomora won't work, which I/nbet she has — "/n/n"What do you think about this?" Hermione demanded/nof Ron, and Harry was reminded irresistibly of Mrs./nWeasley appealing to her husband during Harry's first/ndinner in Grimmauld Place./n/n"I dunno," said Ron, looking alarmed at being asked/nto give an opinion. "If Harry wants to do it, it's up to/nhim, isn't it?"/n/n"Spoken like a true friend and Weasley," said Fred,/nclapping Ron hard on the back. "Right, then. We're/nthinking of doing it tomorrow, just after lessons,/nbecause it should cause maximum impact if/neverybody's in the corridors — Harry, we'll set it off in/nthe east wing somewhere, draw her right away from/nher own office — I reckon we should be able to/nguarantee you, what, twenty minutes?" he said,/nlooking at George./n/n"Easy," said George./n/n"What sort of diversion is it?" asked Ron./n/n"You'll see, little bro," said Fred, as he and George got/nup again. "At least, you will if you trot along to/nGregory the Smarmy's corridor round about five/no'clock tomorrow."/n/nHarry awoke very early the next day, feeling almost as/nanxious as he had done on the morning of his hearing/nat the Ministry of Magic. It was not only the prospect/nof breaking into Umbridge's office and using her fire/n/n/n/n/n/nto speak to Sirius that was making him feel nervous,/nthough that was certainly bad enough — today also/nhappened to be the first time he would be in close/nproximity with Snape since Snape had thrown him/nout of his office, as they had Potions that day./n/nAfter lying in bed for a while thinking about the day/nahead, Harry got up very quietly and moved across to/nthe window beside Neville's bed, staring out on a truly/nglorious morning. The sky was a clear, misty,/nopalescent blue. Directly ahead of him, Harry could/nsee the towering beech tree below which his father/nhad once tormented Snape. He was not sure what/nSirius could possibly say to him that would make up/nfor what he had seen in the Pensieve, but he was/ndesperate to hear Sirius's own account of what had/nhappened, to know of any mitigating factors there/nmight have been, any excuse at all for his father's/nbehavior. . ./n/nSomething caught Harry's attention: movement on/nthe edge of the Forbidden Forest. Harry squinted into/nthe sun and saw Hagrid emerging from between the/ntrees. He seemed to be limping. As Harry watched,/nHagrid staggered to the door of his cabin and/ndisappeared inside it.
