"I don't think we are."/n/nHe turned to his twin./n/n"George," said Fred, "I think we've outgrown full-time/neducation."/n/n"Yeah, I've been feeling that way myself," said George/nlightly./n/n"Time to test our talents in the real world, d'you/nreckon?" asked Fred./n/n"Definitely," said George./n/nAnd before Umbridge could say a word, they raised/ntheir wands and said together, "Accio BroomsV'/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry heard a loud crash somewhere in the distance./nLooking to his left he ducked just in time — Fred and/nGeorge's broomsticks, one still trailing the heavy/nchain and iron peg with which Umbridge had fastened/nthem to the wall, were hurtling along the corridor/ntoward their owners. They turned left, streaked down/nthe stairs, and stopped sharply in front of the twins,/nthe chain clattering loudly on the flagged stone floor./n/n"We won't be seeing you," Fred told Professor/nUmbridge, swinging his leg over his broomstick./n/n"Yeah, don't bother to keep in touch," said George,/nmounting his own./n/nFred looked around at the assembled students, and/nat the silent, watchful crowd./n/n"If anyone fancies buying a Portable Swamp, as/ndemonstrated upstairs, come to number ninety-three,/nDiagon Alley — Weasleys' Wizarding Wheezes," he/nsaid in a loud voice. "Our new premises!"/n/n"Special discounts to Hogwarts students who swear/nthey're going to use our products to get rid of this old/nbat," added George, pointing at Professor Umbridge./n/n"STOP THEM!" shrieked Umbridge, but it was too late./nAs the Inquisitorial Squad closed in, Fred and George/nkicked off from the floor, shooting fifteen feet into the/nair, the iron peg swinging dangerously below. Fred/nlooked across the hall at the poltergeist bobbing on/nhis level above the crowd./n/n"Give her hell from us, Peeves."/n/nAnd Peeves, whom Harry had never seen take an/norder from a student before, swept his belled hat from/nhis head and sprang to a salute as Fred and George/n/n/n/n/n/nwheeled about to tumultuous applause from the/nstudents below and sped out of the open front doors/ninto the glorious sunset./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Grawp
text: /nThe story of Fred and George's flight to freedom was/nretold so often over the next few days that Harry/ncould tell it would soon become the stuff of Hogwarts/nlegend. Within a week, even those who had been/neyewitnesses were half- convinced that they had seen/nthe twins dive-bomb Umbridge on their brooms,/npelting her with Dungbombs before zooming out of/nthe doors. In the immediate aftermath of their/ndeparture there was a great wave of talk about/ncopying them, so that Harry frequently heard/nstudents saying things like, "Honestly, some days I/njust feel like jumping on my broom and leaving this/nplace," or else, "One more lesson like that and I might/njust do a Weasley..."/n/nFred and George had made sure that nobody was/nlikely to forget them very soon. For one thing, they/nhad not left instructions on how to remove the swamp/nthat now filled the corridor on the fifth floor of the/neast wing. Umbridge and Filch had been observed/ntrying different means of removing it but without/nsuccess. Eventually the area was roped off and Filch,/n/n/n/ngnashing his teeth furiously, was given the task of/npunting students across it to their classrooms. Harry/nwas certain that teachers like McGonagall or Flitwick/ncould have removed the swamp in an instant, but just/nas in the case of Fred and George's Wildfire Whiz-/nBangs, they seemed to prefer to watch Umbridge/nstruggle./n/nThen there were the two large broom-shaped holes in/nUmbridge 's office door, through which Fred and/nGeorge's Cleansweeps had smashed to rejoin their/nmasters. Filch fitted a new door and removed Harry's/nFirebolt to the dungeons where, it was rumored,/nUmbridge had set an armed security troll to guard it./nHowever, her troubles were far from over./n/nInspired by Fred and George's example, a great/nnumber of students were now vying for the newly/nvacant positions of Troublemakers-in-Chief. In spite/nof the new door, somebody managed to slip a hairy-/nsnouted niffler into Umbridge 's office, which promptly/ntore the place apart in its search for shiny objects,/nleapt on Umbridge on her re-entrance, and tried to/ngnaw the rings off her stubby fingers. Dungbombs/nand Stinkpellets were dropped so frequently in the/ncorridors that it became the new fashion for students/nto perform Bubble-Head Charms on themselves/nbefore leaving lessons, which ensured them a supply/nof fresh clean air, even though it gave them all the/npeculiar appearance of wearing upside-down goldfish/nbowls on their heads./n/nFilch prowled the corridors with a horsewhip ready in/nhis hands, desperate to catch miscreants, but the/nproblem was that there were now so many of them/nthat he did not know which way to turn. The/nInquisitorial Squad were attempting to help him, but/nodd things kept happening to its members./n/nWarrington of the Slytherin Quidditch team reported/n/n/n/n/nto the hospital wing with a horrible skin complaint/nthat made him look as though he had been coated in/ncornflakes. Pansy Parkinson, to Hermione's delight,/nmissed all her lessons the following day, as she had/nsprouted antlers./n/nMeanwhile it became clear just how many Skiving/nSnackboxes Fred and George had managed to sell/nbefore leaving Hogwarts. Umbridge only had to enter/nher classroom for the students assembled there to/nfaint, vomit, develop dangerous fevers, or else spout/nblood from both nostrils. Shrieking with rage and/nfrustration she attempted to trace the mysterious/nsymptoms to their source, but the students told her/nstubbornly they were suffering "Umbridge-itis." After/nputting four successive classes in detention and/nfailing to discover their secret she was forced to give/nup and allow the bleeding, swooning, sweating, and/nvomiting students to leave her classes in droves./n/nBut not even the users of the Snackboxes could/ncompete with that master of chaos, Peeves, who/nseemed to have taken Fred's parting words deeply to/nheart. Cackling madly, he soared through the school,/nupending tables, bursting out of blackboards, and/ntoppling statues and vases. Twice he shut Mrs. Norris/ninside suits of armor, from which she was rescued,/nyowling loudly, by the furious caretaker. He smashed/nlanterns and snuffed out candles, juggled burning/ntorches over the heads of screaming students, caused/nneatly stacked piles of parchment to topple into fires/nor out of windows, flooded the second floor when he/npulled off all the taps in the bathrooms, dropped a/nbag of tarantulas in the middle of the Great Hall/nduring breakfast and, whenever he fancied a break,/nspent hours at a time floating along after Umbridge/nand blowing loud raspberries every time she spoke./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNone of the staff but Filch seemed to be stirring/nthemselves to help her. Indeed, a week after Fred and/nGeorge's departure Harry witnessed Professor/nMcGonagall walking right past Peeves, who was/ndeterminedly loosening a crystal chandelier, and/ncould have sworn he heard her tell the poltergeist out/nof the corner of her mouth, "It unscrews the other/nway."/n/nTo cap matters, Montague had still not recovered from/nhis sojourn in the toilet. He remained confused and/ndisorientated and his parents were to be observed one/nTuesday morning striding up the front drive, looking/nextremely angry./n/n"Should we say something?" said Hermione in a/nworried voice, pressing her cheek against the Charms/nwindow so that she could see Mr. and Mrs. Montague/nmarching inside. "About what happened to him? In/ncase it helps Madam Pomfrey cure him?"/n/n" 'Course not, he'll recover," said Ron indifferently./n/n"Anyway, more trouble for Umbridge, isn't it?" said/nHarry in a satisfied voice./n/nHe and Ron both tapped the teacups they were/nsupposed to be charming with their wands. Harry's/nspouted four very short legs that would not reach the/ndesk and wriggled pointlessly in midair. Ron's grew/nfour very thin spindly legs that hoisted the cup off the/ndesk with great difficulty, trembled for a few seconds,/nthen folded, causing the cup to crack into two./n/n"Reparo\" said Hermione quickly, mending Ron's cup/nwith a wave of her wand. "That's all very well, but/nwhat if Montague's permanently injured?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Who cares?" said Ron irritably, while his teacup/nstood drunkenly again, trembling violently at the/nknees. "Montague shouldn't have tried to take all/nthose points from Gryffindor, should he? If you want/nto worry about anyone, Hermione, worry about me!"/n/n"You?" she said, catching her teacup as it scampered/nhappily away across the desk on four sturdy little/nwillow-patterned legs and replacing it in front of her./n"Why should I be worried about you?"/n/n"When Mum's next letter finally gets through/nUmbridge's screening process," said Ron bitterly, now/nholding his cup up while its frail legs tried feebly to/nsupport its weight, "I'm going to be in deep trouble. I/nwouldn't be surprised if she's sent a Howler again."/n/n"But — "/n/n"It'll be my fault Fred and George left, you wait," said/nRon darkly. "She'll say I should've stopped them/nleaving, I should've grabbed the ends of their brooms/nand hung on or something... Yeah, it'll be all my/nfault..."/n/n"Well, if she does say that it'll be very unfair, you/ncouldn't have done anything! But I'm sure she won't, I/nmean, if it's really true they've got premises in Diagon/nAlley now, they must have been planning this for/nages..."/n/n"Yeah, but that's another thing, how did they get/npremises?" said Ron, hitting his teacup so hard with/nhis wand that its legs collapsed again and it lay/ntwitching before him. "It's a bit dodgy, isn't it? They'll/nneed loads of Galleons to afford the rent on a place in/nDiagon Alley, she'll want to know what they've been/nup to, to get their hands on that sort of gold..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, yes, that occurred to me too," said Hermione,/nallowing her teacup to jog in neat little circles around/nHarry's, whose stubby little legs were still unable to/ntouch the desktop. "I've been wondering whether/nMundungus has persuaded them to sell stolen goods/nor something awful..."/n/n"He hasn't," said Harry curtly./n/n"How do you know?" said Ron and Hermione together./n/n"Because — " Harry hesitated, but the moment to/nconfess finally seemed to have come. There was no/ngood to be gained in keeping silent if it meant anyone/nsuspected that Fred and George were criminals./n"Because they got the gold from me. I gave them my/nTriwizard winnings last June."/n/nThere was a shocked silence, then Hermione's teacup/njogged right over the edge of the desk and smashed on/nthe floor./n/n"Oh, Harry, you didn't" she said./n/n"Yes, I did," said Harry mutinously. "And I don't regret/nit either — I didn't need the gold, and they'll be great/nat a joke shop..."/n/n"But this is excellent!" said Ron, looking thrilled. "It's/nall your fault, Harry — Mum can't blame me at all!/n/nCan I tell her?"/n/n"Yeah, I suppose you'd better," said Harry dully. "/n'Specially if she thinks they're receiving stolen/ncauldrons or something..."/n/nHermione said nothing at all for the rest of the lesson,/nbut Harry had a shrewd suspicion that her self-/nrestraint was bound to crack before long. Sure/n/n/n/n/n/nenough, once they had left the castle for break and/nwere standing around in the weak May sunshine, she/nfixed Harry with a beady eye and opened her mouth/nwith a determined air./n/nHarry interrupted her before she had even started./n/n"It's no good nagging me, it's done," he said firmly./n"Fred and George have got the gold — spent a good/nbit of it too, by the sounds of it — and I can't get it/nback from them and I don't want to. So save your/nbreath, Hermione."/n/n"I wasn't going to say anything about Fred and/nGeorge!" she said in an injured voice./n/nRon snorted disbelievingly and Hermione threw him a/nvery dirty look./n/n"No, I wasn't!" she said angrily. "As a matter of fact, I/nwas going to ask Harry when he's going to go back to/nSnape and ask for Occlumency lessons again!"/n/nHarry's heart sank. Once they had exhausted the/nsubject of Fred and George's dramatic departure,/nwhich admittedly had taken many hours, Ron and/nHermione had wanted to hear news of Sirius. As/nHarry had not confided in them the reason he had/nwanted to talk to Sirius in the first place, it had been/nhard to think of things to tell them. He had ended up/nsaying to them truthfully that Sirius wanted Harry to/nresume Occlumency lessons. He had been regretting/nthis ever since; Hermione would not let the subject/ndrop and kept reverting to it when Harry least/nexpected it./n/n"You can't tell me you've stopped having funny/ndreams," Hermione said now, "because Ron told me/nlast night you were muttering in your sleep again..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry threw Ron a furious look. Ron had the grace to/nlook ashamed of himself./n/n"You were only muttering a bit," he mumbled/napologetically. "Something about 'just a bit farther.' "/n/n"I dreamed I was watching you lot play Quidditch,"/nHarry lied brutally. "I was trying to get you to stretch/nout a bit farther to grab the Quaffle."/n/nRon's ears went red. Harry felt a kind of vindictive/npleasure: He had not, of course, dreamed anything of/nthe sort./n/nLast night he had once again made the journey along/nthe Department of Mysteries corridor. He had passed/nthrough the circular room, then the room full of/nclicking and dancing light, until he found himself/nagain inside that cavernous room full of shelves on/nwhich were ranged dusty glass spheres.../n/nHe had hurried straight toward row number ninety-/nseven, turned left, and ran along it... It had probably/nbeen then that he had spoken aloud... Just a bit/nfarther . . . for he could feel his conscious self/nstruggling to wake . . . and before he had reached the/nend of the row, he had found himself lying in bed/nagain, gazing up at the canopy of his four-poster./n/n"You are trying to block your mind, aren't you?" said/nHermione, looking beadily at Harry. "You are keeping/ngoing with your Occlumency?"/n/n"Of course I am," said Harry, trying to sound as/nthough this question was insulting, but not quite/nmeeting her eye. The truth was that he was so/nintensely curious about what was hidden in that/nroom full of dusty orbs that he was quite keen for the/ndreams to continue./n/n/n/n/n/nThe problem was that with just under a month to go/nuntil the exams and every free moment devoted to/nstudying, his mind seemed saturated with/ninformation when he went to bed so that he found it/nvery difficult to get to sleep at all. When he did, his/noverwrought brain presented him most nights with/nstupid dreams about the exams. He also suspected/nthat part of his mind — the part that often spoke in/nHermione's voice — now felt guilty on the occasions it/nstrayed down that corridor ending in the black door,/nand sought to wake him before he could reach/njourney's end./n/n"You know," said Ron, whose ears were still flaming/nred, "if Montague doesn't recover before Slytherin play/nHufflepuff, we might be in with a chance of winning/nthe Cup."/n/n"Yeah, I s'pose so," said Harry, glad of a change of/nsubject./n/n"I mean, we've won one, lost one — if Slytherin lose to/nHufflepuff next Saturday — "/n/n"Yeah, that's right," said Harry, losing track of what/nhe was agreeing to: Cho Chang had just walked/nacross the courtyard, determinedly not looking at/nhim./n/nThe final match of the Quidditch season, Gryffindor/nversus Ravenclaw, was to take place on the last/nweekend of May. Although Slytherin had been/nnarrowly defeated by Hufflepuff in their last match,/nGryffindor was not daring to hope for victory, due/nmainly (though of course nobody said it to him) to/nRon's abysmal goalkeeping record. He, however,/nseemed to have found a new optimism./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I mean, I can't get any worse, can I?" he told Harry/nand Hermione grimly over breakfast on the morning/nof the match. "Nothing to lose now, is there?"/n/n"You know," said Hermione, as she and Harry walked/ndown to the pitch a little later in the midst of a very/nexcitable crowd, "I think Ron might do better without/nFred and George around. They never exactly gave him/na lot of confidence..."/n/nLuna Lovegood overtook them with what appeared to/nbe a live eagle perched on top of her head./n/n"Oh gosh, I forgot!" said Hermione, watching the eagle/nflapping its wings as Luna walked serenely past a/ngroup of cackling and pointing Slytherins. "Cho will/nbe playing, won't she?"/n/nHarry, who had not forgotten this, merely grunted./n/nThey found seats in the topmost row of the stands. It/nwas a fine, clear day. Ron could not wish for better,/nand Harry found himself hoping against hope that/nRon would not give the Slytherins cause for more/nrousing choruses of "Weasley Is Our King."/n/nLee Jordan, who had been very dispirited since Fred/nand George had left, was commentating as usual. As/nthe teams zoomed out onto the pitches he named the/nplayers with something less than his usual gusto./n/n"... Bradley ... Davies ... Chang," he said, and Harry/nfelt his stomach perform, less of a back flip, more a/nfeeble lurch as Cho walked out onto the pitch, her/nshiny black hair rippling in the slight breeze. He was/nnot sure what he wanted to happen anymore, except/nthat he could not stand any more rows. Even the/nsight of her chatting animatedly to Roger Davies as/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthey prepared to mount their brooms caused him only/na slight twinge of jealousy./n/n"And they're off!" said Lee. "And Davies takes the/nQuaffle immediately, Ravenclaw Captain Davies with/nthe Quaffle, he dodges Johnson, he dodges Bell, he/ndodges Spinnet as well... He's going straight for goal!/nHe's going to shoot — and — and — " Lee swore very/nloudly. "And he's scored."/n/nHarry and Hermione groaned with the rest of the/nGryffindors. Predictably, horribly, the Slytherins on/nthe other side of the stands began to sing:/n/nWeasley cannot save a thing,/n/nHe cannot block a single ring . . ./n/n"Harry," said a hoarse voice in Harry's ear. "Hermione/n/n/n/nHarry looked around and saw Hagrid's enormous/nbearded face sticking between the seats; apparently/nhe had squeezed his way all along the row behind, for/nthe first and second years he had just passed had a/nruffled, flattened look about them. For some reason,/nHagrid was bent double as though anxious not to be/nseen, though he was still at least four feet taller than/neverybody else./n/n"Listen," he whispered, "can yeh come with me? Now?/nWhile ev'ryone's watchin' the match?"/n/n"Er ... can't it wait, Hagrid?" asked Harry. "Till the/nmatch is over?/n/n"No," said Hagrid. "No, Harry, it's gotta be now .../nwhile ev'ryone's lookin' the other way... Please?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid's nose was gently dripping blood. His eyes/nwere both blackened. Harry had not seen him this/nclose up since his return to the school; he looked/nutterly woebegone./n/n" 'Course," said Harry at once, " 'course we'll come..."/n/nHe and Hermione edged back along their row of seats,/ncausing much grumbling among the students who/nhad to stand up for them. The people in Hagrid's row/nwere not complaining, merely attempting to make/nthemselves as small as possible./n/n"I 'ppreciate this, you two, I really do," said Hagrid as/nthey reached the stairs. He kept looking around/nnervously as they descended toward the lawn below./n/n"I jus' hope she doesn' notice us goin'..."/n/n"You mean Umbridge?" said Harry. "She won't, she's/ngot her whole Inquisitorial Squad sitting with her,/ndidn't you see? She must be expecting trouble at the/nmatch."/n/n"Yeah, well, a bit o' trouble wouldn' hurt," said/nHagrid, pausing to peer around the edge of the stands/nto make sure the stretch of lawn between there and/nhis cabin was deserted. "Give us more time ..."/n/n"What is it, Hagrid?" said Hermione, looking up at/nhim with a concerned expression on her face as they/nhurried across the lawn toward the edge of the forest./n/n"Yeh — yeh'll see in a mo'," said Hagrid, looking over/nhis shoulder as a great roar rose from the stands/nbehind them. "Hey — did someone jus' score?"/n/n"It'll be Ravenclaw," said Harry heavily./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Good ... good ..." said Hagrid distractedly. "Tha's/ngood..."/n/nThey had to jog to keep up with him as he strode/nacross the lawn, looking around with every other step./nWhen they reached his cabin, Hermione turned/nautomatically left toward the front door; Hagrid,/nhowever, walked straight past it into the shade of the/ntrees on the outermost edge of the forest, where he/npicked up a crossbow that was leaning against a tree./nWhen he realized they were no longer with him, he/nturned./n/n"We're goin' in here," he said, jerking his shaggy head/nbehind him./n/n"Into the forest?" said Hermione, perplexed./n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid. "C'mon now, quick, before we're/nspotted!"/n/nHarry and Hermione looked at each other, then/nducked into the cover of the trees behind Hagrid, who/nwas already striding away from them into the green/ngloom, his crossbow over his arm. Harry and/nHermione ran to catch up with him./n/n"Hagrid, why are you armed?" said Harry./n/n"Jus' a precaution," said Hagrid, shrugging his/nmassive shoulders./n/n"You didn't bring your crossbow the day you showed/nus the thestrals," said Hermione timidly./n/n"Nah, well, we weren' goin' in so far then," said/nHagrid. "An' anyway, tha' was before Firenze left the/nforest, wasn' it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Why does Firenze leaving make a difference?" asked/nHermione curiously./n/n/n/n" 'Cause the other centaurs are good an' riled at me,/ntha's why," said Hagrid quietly, glancing around./n"They used ter be — well, yeh couldn' call 'em friendly/n— but we got on all righ'. Kept 'emselves to 'emselves,/nbu' always turned up if I wanted a word. Not anymore/n/n/n/nHe sighed deeply./n/n"Firenze said that they're angry because he went to/nwork for Dumbledore?" Harry asked, tripping on a/nprotruding root because he was busy watching/nHagrid 's profile./n/n"Yeah," said Hagrid heavily. "Well, angry doesn' cover/nit. Ruddy livid. If I hadn' stepped in, I reckon they'd 've/nkicked Firenze ter death — "/n/n"They attacked him?" said Hermione, sounding/nshocked./n/n"Yep," said Hagrid gruffly, forcing his way through/nseveral low-hanging branches. "He had half the herd/nonto him — "/n/n"And you stopped it?" said Harry, amazed and/nimpressed. "By yourself?"/n/n" 'Course I did, couldn't stand by an' watch 'em kill/nhim, could I?" said Hagrid. "Lucky I was passin',/nreally ... an' I'd've thought Firenze mighta/nremembered tha' before he started sendin' me stupid/nwarnin's!" he added hotly and unexpectedly./n/nHarry and Hermione looked at each other, startled,/nbut Hagrid, scowling, did not elaborate./n/n/n/n/n/n"Anyway," he said, breathing a little more heavily/nthan usual, "since then the other centaurs Ve bin livid/nwith me an' the trouble is, they've got a lot of/ninfluence in the forest... Cleverest creatures in here/n/n/n/n"Is that why we're here, Hagrid?" asked Hermione./n"The centaurs?"/n/n"Ah no," said Hagrid, shaking his head dismissively,/n"no, it's not them... Well, o' course, they could/ncomplicate the problem, yeah... But yeh'll see what I/nmean in a bit..."/n/nOn this incomprehensible note he fell silent and/nforged a little ahead, taking one stride for every three/nof theirs, so that they had great trouble keeping up/nwith him./n/nThe path was becoming increasingly overgrown and/nthe trees grew so closely together as they walked/nfarther and farther into the forest that it was as dark/nas dusk. They were soon a long way past the clearing/nwhere Hagrid had shown them the thestrals, but/nHarry felt no sense of unease until Hagrid stepped/nunexpectedly off the path and began wending his way/nin and out of trees toward the dark heart of the forest./n/n"Hagrid?" said Harry, fighting his way through thickly/nknotted brambles over which Hagrid had stepped/neasily and remembering very vividly what had/nhappened to him on the other occasions he had/nstepped off the forest path. "Where are we going?"/n/n"Bit further," said Hagrid over his shoulder. "C'mon,/nHarry... We need ter keep together now..."/n/nIt was a great struggle to keep up with Hagrid, what/nwith branches and thickets of thorn through which/n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid marched as easily as though they were/ncobwebs, but which snagged Harry and Hermione's/nrobes, frequently entangling them so severely that/nthey had to stop for minutes at a time to free/nthemselves. Harry's arms and legs were soon covered/nin small cuts and scratches. They were so deep in the/nforest now that sometimes all Harry could see of/nHagrid in the gloom was a massive dark shape ahead/nof him. Any sound seemed threatening in the muffled/nsilence. The breaking of a twig echoed loudly and the/ntiniest rustle of movement, though it might have been/nmade by an innocent sparrow, caused Harry to peer/nthrough the gloom for a culprit. It occurred to him/nthat he had never managed to get this far into the/nforest without meeting some kind of creature — their/nabsence struck him as rather ominous./n/n"Hagrid, would it be all right if we lit our wands?" said/nHermione quietly./n/n"Er ... all righ'," Hagrid whispered back. "In fact ..."/n/nHe stopped suddenly and turned around; Hermione/nwalked right into him and was knocked over/nbackward. Harry caught her just before she hit the/nforest floor./n/n"Maybe we bes' jus' stop fer a momen', so I can ... fill/nyeh in," said Hagrid. "Before we ge' there, like."/n/n"Good!" said Hermione, as Harry set her back on her/nfeet. They both murmured "Lumos\" and their wand/ntips ignited. Hagrid 's face swam through the gloom by/nthe light of the two wavering beams and Harry saw/nthat he looked nervous and sad again./n/n"Righ," said Hagrid. "Well ... see ... the thing is ..."/n/nHe took a great breath./n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, there's a good chance I'm goin' ter be gettin' the/nsack any day now," he said./n/n/n/nHarry and Hermione looked at each other, then back/nat him./n/n"But you've lasted this long — " Hermione said/ntentatively. "What makes you think — "/n/n"Umbridge reckons it was me that put tha' niffler in/nher office."/n/n"And was it?" said Harry, before he could stop/nhimself./n/n"No, it ruddy well wasn'!" said Hagrid indignantly./n"On'y anythin' ter do with magical creatures an' she/nthinks it's got somethin' ter do with me. Yeh know/nshe's bin lookin' fer a chance ter get rid of me ever/nsince I got back. I don' wan' ter go, o' course, but if it/nwasn' fer ... well ... the special circumstances I'm/nabou' ter explain to yeh, I'd leave righ now, before/nshe's go' the chance ter do it in front o' the whole/nschool, like she did with Trelawney."/n/nHarry and Hermione both made noises of protest, but/nHagrid overrode them with a wave of one of his/nenormous hands./n/n"It's not the end o' the world, I'll be able ter help/nDumbledore once I'm outta here, I can be useful ter/nthe Order. An' you lot'll have Grubbly-Plank, yeh'll —/nyeh'll get through yer exams fine..." His voice/ntrembled and broke./n/n"Don' worry abou' me," he said hastily, as Hermione/nmade to pat his arm. He pulled his enormous spotted/nhandkerchief from the pocket of his waistcoat and/nmopped his eyes with it. "Look, I wouldn' be tellin' yer/n/n/n/n/n/nthis at all if I didn' have ter. See, if I go ... well, I can'/nleave withou' ... withou' fellin' someone ... because I'll/n— I'll need you two ter help me. An' Ron, if he's/nwillin'."/n/n"Of course well help you," said Harry at once. "What/ndo you want us to do?"/n/nHagrid gave a great sniff and patted Harry wordlessly/non the shoulder with such force that Harry was/nknocked sideways into a tree./n/n"I knew yeh'd say yes," said Hagrid into his/nhandkerchief, "but I won' ... never ... forget ... Well .../nc'mon ... jus' a little bit further through here ... Watch/nyerselves, now, there's nettles..."/n/nThey walked on in silence for another fifteen minutes./nHarry had opened his mouth to ask how much farther/nthey had to go when Hagrid threw out his right arm to/nsignal that they should stop./n/n"Really easy," he said softly. "Very quiet, now ..."/n/nThey crept forward and Harry saw that they were/nfacing a large, smooth mound of earth nearly as tall/nas Hagrid that he thought, with a jolt of dread, was/nsure to be the lair of some enormous animal. Trees/nhad been ripped up at the roots all around the/nmound, so that it stood on a bare patch of ground/nsurrounded by heaps of trunks and boughs that/nformed a kind of fence or barricade, behind which/nHarry, Hermione, and Hagrid now stood./n/n"Sleepin'," breathed Hagrid./n/nSure enough, Harry could hear a distant, rhythmic/nrumbling that sounded like a pair of enormous lungs/nat work. He glanced sideways at Hermione, who was/n/n/n/n/n/ngazing at the mound with her mouth slightly open./n/nShe looked utterly terrified./n/n"Hagrid," she said in a whisper barely audible over/nthe sound of the sleeping creature, "who is he?"/n/nHarry found this an odd question... "What is it?" was/nthe one he had been planning on asking./n/n"Hagrid, you told us," said Hermione, her wand now/nshaking in her hand, "you told us none of them/nwanted to come!"/n/nHarry looked from her to Hagrid and then, as/nrealization hit him, he looked back at the mound with/na small gasp of horror./n/nThe great mound of earth, on which he, Hermione,/nand Hagrid could easily have stood, was moving/nslowly up and down in time with the deep, grunting/nbreathing. It was not a mound at all. It was the/ncurved back of what was clearly . . ./n/n"Well — no — he didn' want ter come," said Hagrid,/nsounding desperate. "But I had ter bring him,/nHermione, I had ter!"/n/n"But why?" asked Hermione, who sounded as though/nshe wanted to cry. "Why — what — oh, Hagrid\"/n/n"I knew if I jus' got him back," said Hagrid, sounding/nclose to tears himself, "an' — an' taught him a few/nmanners — I'd be able ter take him outside an' show/nev'ryone he's harmless!"/n/n"Harmless!" said Hermione shrilly, and Hagrid made/nfrantic hushing noises with his hands as the/nenormous creature before them grunted loudly and/nshifted in its sleep. "He's been hurting you all this/n/n/n/n/n/ntime, hasn't he? That's why you've had all these/ninjuries!"/n/n"He don' know his own strength!" said Hagrid/nearnestly. "An' he's gettin' better, he's not fightin' so/nmuch anymore — "/n/n"So this is why it took you two months to get home!"/nsaid Hermione distractedly. "Oh Hagrid, why did you/nbring him back if he didn't want to come, wouldn't he/nhave been happier with his own people?"/n/n"They were all bullyin' him, Hermione, 'cause he's so/nsmall!" said Hagrid./n/n"Small?" said Hermione. "Small?"/n/n"Hermione, I couldn' leave him," said Hagrid, tears/nnow trickling down his bruised face into his beard./n"See — he's my brother!"/n/nHermione simply stared at him, her mouth open./n/n"Hagrid, when you say 'brother,' " said Harry slowly,/n"do you mean — ?"/n/n"Well — half-brother," amended Hagrid. "Turns out/nme mother took up with another giant when she left/nme dad, an' she went an' had Grawp here — "/n/n"Grawp?" said Harry./n/n"Yeah ... well, tha's what it sounds like when he says/nhis name," said Hagrid anxiously. "He don' speak a lot/nof English... I've bin tryin' ter teach him... Anyway,/nshe don' seem ter have liked him much more'n she/nliked me... See, with giantesses, what counts is/nproducin' good big kids, and he's always been a bit on/nthe runty side fer a giant — on'y sixteen foot — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh yes, tiny!" said Hermione, with a kind of/nhysterical sarcasm. "Absolutely minuscule!"/n/n"He was bein' kicked around by all o' them — I jus'/ncouldn' leave him — "/n/n"Did Madame Maxime want to bring him back?"/nasked Harry./n/n"She — well, she could see it was right importan' ter/nme," said Hagrid, twisting his enormous hands. "Bu'/n— bu' she got a bit tired of him after a while, I must/nadmit ... so we split up on the journey home... She/npromised not ter tell anyone though..."/n/n"How on earth did you get him back without anyone/nnoticing?" said Harry./n/n"Well, tha's why it took so long, see," said Hagrid./n"Could on'y travel by nigh an' through wild country/nan' stuff. 'Course, he covers the ground pretty well/nwhen he wants ter, but he kep' wantin' ter go back..."/n/n"Oh Hagrid, why on earth didn't you let him!" said/nHermione, flopping down onto a ripped-up tree and/nburying her face in her hands. "What do you think/nyou're going to do with a violent giant who doesn't/neven want to be here!"/n/n"Well, now — Violent' — tha's a bit harsh," said/nHagrid, still twisting his hands agitatedly. "I'll admit/nhe mighta taken a couple o' swings at me when he's/nbin in a bad mood, but he's gettin' better, loads/nbetter, settlin' down well..."/n/n"What are those ropes for, then?" Harry asked./n/nHe had just noticed ropes thick as saplings stretching/nfrom around the trunks of the largest nearby trees/n/n/n/n/n/ntoward the place where Grawp lay curled on the/nground with his back to them./n/n"You have to keep him tied up?" said Hermione/nfaintly./n/n"Well ... yeah ..." said Hagrid, looking anxious. "See —/nit's like I say — he doesn' really know his strength — "/n/nHarry understood now why there had been such a/nsuspicious lack of any other living creature in this/npart of the forest./n/n"So what is it you want Harry and Ron and me to do?"/nHermione asked apprehensively./n/n"Look after him," said Hagrid croakily. "After I'm/ngone."/n/nHarry and Hermione exchanged miserable looks,/n/nHarry uncomfortably aware that he had already/npromised Hagrid that he would do whatever he asked./n/n"What — what does that involve, exactly?" Hermione/ninquired./n/n"Not food or anythin'!" said Hagrid eagerly. "He can/nget his own food, no problem. Birds an' deer an' stuff/n... No, it's company he needs. If I jus' knew someone/nwas carryin' on tryin' ter help him a bit ... teachin'/nhim, yeh know ..."/n/nHarry said nothing, but turned to look back at the/ngigantic form lying asleep on the ground in front of/nthem. Grawp had his back to them. Unlike Hagrid,/nwho simply looked like a very oversize human, Grawp/nlooked strangely misshapen. What Harry had taken to/nbe a vast mossy boulder to the left of the great/nearthen mound he now recognized as Grawp 's head./n/n/n/n/nIt was much larger in proportion to the body than a/nhuman head, almost perfectly round and covered with/ntightly curling, close-growing hair the color of/nbracken. The rim of a single large, fleshy ear was/nvisible on top of the head, which seemed to sit, rather/nlike Uncle Vernon's, directly upon the shoulders with/nlittle or no neck in between. The back, under what/nlooked like a dirty brownish smock comprised of/nanimal skins sewn roughly together, was very broad,/nand as Grawp slept, it seemed to strain a little at the/nrough seams of the skins. The legs were curled up/nunder the body; Harry could see the soles of/nenormous, filthy, bare feet, large as sledges, resting/none on top of the other on the earthy forest floor./n/n"You want us to teach him," Harry said in a hollow/nvoice. He now understood what Firenze's warning had/nmeant. His attempt is not working. He would do better/nto abandon it. Of course, the other creatures who lived/nin the forest would have heard Hagrid's fruitless/nattempts to teach Grawp English.../n/n"Yeah — even if yeh jus' talk ter him a bit," said/nHagrid hopefully. " 'Cause I reckon, if he can talk ter/npeople, he'll understand more that we all like him/nreally, an' want him to stay..."/n/nHarry looked at Hermione, who peered back at him/nfrom between the fingers over her face./n/n"Kind of makes you wish we had Norbert back,/ndoesn't it?" he said and she gave a very shaky laugh./n/n"Yeh'll do it, then?" said Hagrid, who did not seem to/nhave caught what Harry had just said./n/n"We'll ..." said Harry, already bound by his promise./n"We'll try, Hagrid..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I knew I could count on yeh, Harry," Hagrid said,/nbeaming in a very watery way and dabbing at his face/nwith his handkerchief again. "An' I don' wan' yeh ter/nput yerself out too much, like... I know yeh've got/nexams... If yeh could jus' nip down here in yer/nInvisibility Cloak maybe once a week an' have a little/nchat with him ... I'll wake him up, then — introduce/nyou — "/n/n"Wha — no!" said Hermione, jumping up, "Hagrid, no,/ndon't wake him, really, we don't need — "/n/nBut Hagrid had already stepped over the great trunk/nin front of them and was proceeding toward Grawp./nWhen he was around ten feet away, he lifted a long,/nbroken bough from the ground, smiled reassuringly/nover his shoulder at Harry and Hermione, and then/npoked Grawp hard in the middle of the back with the/nend of the bough./n/nThe giant gave a roar that echoed around the silent/nforest. Birds in the treetops overhead rose twittering/nfrom their perches and soared away. In front of Harry/nand Hermione, meanwhile, the gigantic Grawp was/nrising from the ground, which shuddered as he placed/nan enormous hand upon it to push himself onto his/nknees and turned his head to see who and what had/ndisturbed him./n/n"All righ', Grawpy?" said Hagrid in a would-be cheery/nvoice, backing away with the long bough raised, ready/nto poke Grawp again. "Had a nice sleep, eh?"/n/nHarry and Hermione retreated as far as they could/nwhile still keeping the giant within their sights. Grawp/nknelt between two trees he had not yet uprooted./n/nThey looked up into his startlingly huge face, which/nresembled a gray full moon swimming in the gloom of/nthe clearing. It was as though the features had been/n/n/n/n/nhewn onto a great stone ball. The nose was stubby/nand shapeless, the mouth lopsided and full of/nmisshapen yellow teeth the size of half-bricks. The/nsmall eyes were a muddy greenish-brown and just/nnow were half gummed together with sleep. Grawp/nraised dirty knuckles as big as cricket balls to his/neyes, rubbed vigorously, then, without warning,/npushed himself to his feet with surprising speed and/nagility./n/n"Oh my ..." Harry heard Hermione squeal, terrified,/nbeside him./n/nThe trees to which the other ends of the ropes around/nGrawp's wrists and ankles were attached creaked/nominously. He was, as Hagrid had said, at least/nsixteen feet tall. Gazing blearily around, he reached/nout a hand the size of a beach umbrella, seized a/nbird's nest from the upper branches of a towering/npine and turned it upside down with a roar of/napparent displeasure that there was no bird in it —/neggs fell like grenades toward the ground and Hagrid/nthrew his arms over his head to protect himself./n/n"Anyway, Grawpy," shouted Hagrid, looking up/napprehensively in case of further falling eggs, "I've/nbrought some friends ter meet yeh. Remember, I told/nyeh I might? Remember, when I said I might have ter/ngo on a little trip an' leave them ter look after yeh fer/na bit? Remember that, Grawpy?"/n/nBut Grawp merely gave another low roar; it was hard/nto say whether he was listening to Hagrid or whether/nhe even recognized the sounds Hagrid was making as/nspeech. He had now seized the top of the pine tree/nand was pulling it toward him, evidently for the/nsimple pleasure of seeing how far it would spring/nback when he let go./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Now, Grawpy, don' do that!" shouted Hagrid. "Tha's/nhow you ended up pullin' up the others — "/n/nAnd sure enough, Harry could see the earth around/nthe tree's roots beginning to crack./n/n"I got company fer yeh!" Hagrid shouted. "Company,/nsee! Look down, yeh big buffoon, I brought yeh some/nfriends!"/n/n"Oh Hagrid, don't," moaned Hermione, but Hagrid/nhad already raised the bough again and gave Grawp's/nknee a sharp poke./n/nThe giant let go of the top of the pine tree, which/nswayed menacingly and deluged Hagrid with a rain of/nneedles, and looked down./n/n"This," said Hagrid, hastening over to where Harry/nand Hermione stood, "is Harry, Grawp! Harry Potter!/nHe migh' be cornin' ter visit yeh if I have ter go away,/nunderstand?"/n/nThe giant had only just realized that Harry and/nHermione were there. They watched, in great/ntrepidation, as he lowered his huge boulder of a head/nso that he could peer blearily at them./n/n"An' this is Hermione, see? Her — " Hagrid hesitated./nTurning to Hermione he said, "Would yeh mind if he/ncalled yeh Hermy, Hermione? On'y it's a difficult/nname fer him ter remember..."/n/n"No, not at all," squeaked Hermione./n/n"This is Hermy, Grawp! An' she's gonna be cornin' an'/nall! Is'n tha' nice? Eh? Two friends fer yeh ter —/nGRAWPY, NO!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGrawp's hand had shot out of nowhere toward/nHermione — Harry seized her and pulled her/nbackward behind the tree, so that Grawp's fist/nscraped the trunk but closed on thin air./n/n"BAD BOY, GRAWPY!" Harry heard Hagrid yelling, as/nHermione clung to Harry behind the tree, shaking/nand whimpering. "VERY BAD BOY! YEH DON' GRAB/n/n— OUCH!"/n/nHarry poked his head out from around the trunk and/nsaw Hagrid lying on his back, his hand over his nose./nGrawp, apparently losing interest, had straightened/nup again and was again engaged in pulling back the/npine as far as it would go./n/n"Righ'," said Hagrid thickly, getting up with one hand/npinching his bleeding nose and the other grasping his/ncrossbow. "Well ... there yeh are... Yeh've met him an'/n/n— an' now he'll know yeh when yeh come back. Yeah/n...well..."/n/nHe looked up at Grawp, who was now pulling back/nthe pine with an expression of detached pleasure on/nhis boulderish face; the roots were creaking as he/nripped them away from the ground.../n/n"Well, I reckon tha's enough fer one day," said Hagrid./n"We'll — er — we'll go back now, shall we?"/n/nHarry and Hermione nodded. Hagrid shouldered his/ncrossbow again and, still pinching his nose, led the/nway back into the trees./n/nNobody spoke for a while, not even when they heard/nthe distant crash that meant Grawp had pulled over/nthe pine tree at last. Hermione's face was pale and/nset. Harry could not think of a single thing to say./nWhat on earth was going to happen when somebody/n/n/n/n/nfound out that Hagrid had hidden Grawp in the/nforest? And he had promised that he, Ron, and/nHermione would continue Hagrid's totally pointless/nattempts to civilize the giant... How could Hagrid,/neven with his immense capacity to delude himself/nthat fanged monsters were lovably harmless, fool/nhimself that Grawp would ever be fit to mix with/nhumans?/n/n"Hold it," said Hagrid abruptly, just as Harry and/nHermione were struggling through a patch of thick/nknotgrass behind him. He pulled an arrow out of the/nquiver over his shoulder and fitted it into the/ncrossbow. Harry and Hermione raised their wands;/nnow that they had stopped walking, they too could/nhear movement close by./n/n"Oh blimey," said Hagrid quietly./n/n"I thought that we told you, Hagrid," said a deep male/nvoice, "that you are no longer welcome here?"/n/nA man's naked torso seemed for an instant to be/nfloating toward them through the dappled green half-/nlight. Then they saw that his waist joined smoothly/nwith a horse's chestnut body. This centaur had a/nproud, high-cheekboned face and long black hair./n/nLike Hagrid, he was armed: A quiverful of arrows and/na long bow were slung over his shoulders./n/n"How are yeh, Magorian?" said Hagrid warily./n/nThe trees behind the centaur rustled and four or five/nmore emerged behind him. Harry recognized the/nblack-bodied and bearded Bane, whom he had met/nnearly four years ago on the same night he had met/nFirenze. Bane gave no sign that he had ever seen/nHarry before./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So," he said, with a nasty inflection in his voice,/nbefore turning immediately to Magorian. "We agreed, I/nthink, what we would do if this human showed his/nface in the forest again?"/n/n" This human' now, am I?" said Hagrid testily. "Jus'/nfer stoppin' all of yeh committin' murder?"/n/n"You ought not to have meddled, Hagrid," said/nMagorian. "Our ways are not yours, nor are our laws./nFirenze has betrayed and dishonored us."/n/n"I dunno how yeh work that out," said Hagrid/nimpatiently. "He's done nothin' except help Albus/nDumbledore — "/n/n"Firenze has entered into servitude to humans," said/na gray centaur with a hard, deeply lined face./n/n" Servitude !" said Hagrid scathingly. "He's doin'/nDumbledore a favor is all — "/n/n"He is peddling our knowledge and secrets among/nhumans," said Magorian quietly. "There can be no/nreturn from such disgrace."/n/n"If yeh say so," said Hagrid, shrugging, "but/npersonally I think yeh 're makin' a big mistake — "/n/n"As are you, human," said Bane, "coming back into/nour forest when we warned you — "/n/n"Now, you listen ter me," said Hagrid angrily. "I'll have/nless of the 'our' forest, if it's all the same ter you. It's/nnot up ter you who comes an' goes in here — "/n/n"No more is it up to you, Hagrid," said Magorian/nsmoothly. "I shall let you pass today because you are/naccompanied by your young — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"They're not his!" interrupted Bane contemptuously./n"Students, Magorian, from up at the school! They/nhave probably already profited from the traitor/nF irenze 's teachings ..."/n/n"Nevertheless," said Magorian calmly, "the slaughter/nof foals is a terrible crime... We do not touch the/ninnocent. Today, Hagrid, you pass. Henceforth, stay/naway from this place. You forfeited the friendship of/nthe centaurs when you helped the traitor Firenze/nescape us."/n/n"I won' be kept outta the fores' by a bunch of mules/nlike you!" said Hagrid loudly./n/n"Hagrid," said Hermione in a high-pitched and/nterrified voice, as both Bane and the gray centaur/npawed at the ground, "let's go, please lets go!/n/nHagrid moved forward, but his crossbow was still/nraised and his eyes were still fixed threateningly upon/nMagorian./n/n"We know what you are keeping in the forest, Hagrid!"/nMagorian called after them, as the centaurs slipped/nout of sight. "And our tolerance is waning!"/n/nHagrid turned and gave every appearance of wanting/nto walk straight back to Magorian again./n/n"You'll tolerate him as long as he's here, it's as much/nhis forest as yours!" he yelled, while Harry and/nHermione both pushed with all their might against/nHagrid 's moleskin waistcoat in an effort to keep him/nmoving forward. Still scowling, he looked down; his/nexpression changed to mild surprise at the sight of/nthem both pushing him. He seemed not to have felt it./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Calm down, you two," he said, turning to walk on/nwhile they panted along behind him. "Ruddy old nags/nthough, eh?"/n/n"Hagrid," said Hermione breathlessly, skirting the/npatch of nettles they had passed on their way there,/n"if the centaurs don't want humans in the forest, it/ndoesn't really look as though Harry and I will be able/n/n/n/n"Ah, you heard what they said," said Hagrid/ndismissively "They wouldn't hurt foals — I mean,/nkids. Anyway, we can' let ourselves be pushed around/nby that lot..."/n/n"Nice try," Harry murmured to Hermione, who looked/ncrestfallen./n/nAt last they rejoined the path and after another ten/nminutes, the trees began to thin. They were able to/nsee patches of clear blue sky again and hear, in the/ndistance, the definite sounds of cheering and/nshouting./n/n"Was that another goal?" asked Hagrid, pausing in/nthe shelter of the trees as the Quidditch stadium/ncame into view. "Or d'you reckon the match is over?"/n/n"I don't know," said Hermione miserably. Harry saw/nthat she looked much the worse for wear; her hair/nwas full of bits of twig and leaves, her robes were/nripped in several places and there were numerous/nscratches on her face and arms. He knew he could/nlook little better./n/n"I reckon it's over, yeh know!" said Hagrid, still/nsquinting toward the stadium. "Look — there's people/ncornin' out already — if you two hurry yeh 'll be able/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nter blend in with the crowd an' no one'll know you/nweren't there!"/n/n/n/n"Good idea," said Harry. "Well ... see you later, then,/nHagrid..."/n/n"I don't believe him," said Hermione in a very/nunsteady voice, the moment they were out of earshot/nof Hagrid. "I don't believe him. I really don't believe/nhim..."/n/n"Calm down," said Harry./n/n"Calm down!" she said feverishly. "A giant! A giant in/nthe forest! And we're supposed to give him English/nlessons! Always assuming, of course, we can get past/nthe herd of murderous centaurs on the way in and/nout! I — don't — believe — him!"/n/n"We haven't got to do anything yet!" Harry tried to/nreassure her in a quiet voice, as they joined a stream/nof jabbering Hufflepuffs heading back toward the/ncastle. "He's not asking us to do anything unless he/ngets chucked out and that might not even happen — "/n/n"Oh come off it, Harry!" said Hermione angrily,/nstopping dead in her tracks so that the people behind/nher had to swerve to avoid her. "Of course he's going/nto be chucked out and to be perfectly honest, after/nwhat we've just seen, who can blame Umbridge?"/n/nThere was a pause in which Harry glared at her, and/nher eyes filled slowly with tears./n/n"You didn't mean that," said Harry quietly./n/n"No ... well ... all right ... I didn't," she said, wiping/nher eyes angrily. "But why does he have to make life/nso difficult for himself — for us?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"I dunno — "/n/n/n/nWeasley is our King,/n/nWeasley is our King,/n/nHe didn't let the Quaffle in,/n/nWeasley is our King . . ./n/n"And I wish they'd stop singing that stupid song," said/nHermione miserably, "haven't they gloated enough?"/n/nA great tide of students was moving up the sloping/nlawns from the pitch./n/n"Oh, let's get in before we have to meet the/nSlytherins," said Hermione./n/nWeasley can save anything,/n/nHe never leaves a single ring/nThat's why Gryffindors all sing:/n/nWeasley is our King./n/n"Hermione ..." said Harry slowly./n/nThe song was growing louder, but it was issuing not/nfrom a crowd of green-and-silver-clad Slytherins, but/nfrom a mass of red and gold moving slowly toward the/ncastle, which was bearing a solitary figure upon its/nmany shoulders.../n/nWeasley is our King,/n/nWeasley is our King,/n/nHe didn't let the Quaffle in,/n/nWeasley is our King . . ./n/n"No!" said Hermione in a hushed voice./n/n"YES!" said Harry loudly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"HARRY! HERMIONE!" yelled Ron, waving the silver/nQuidditch Cup in the air and looking quite beside/nhimself. "WE DID IT! WE WON!"/n/n/n/nThey beamed up at him as he passed; there was a/nscrum at the door of the castle and Ron's head got/nrather badly bumped on the lintel, but nobody/nseemed to want to put him down. Still singing, the/ncrowd squeezed itself into the entrance hall and out of/nsight. Harry and Hermione watched them go,/nbeaming, until the last echoing strains of "Weasley Is/nOur King" died away. Then they turned to each other,/ntheir smiles fading./n/n"We'll save our news till tomorrow, shall we?" said/nHarry./n/n"Yes, all right," said Hermione wearily. "I'm not in any/nhurry..."/n/nThey climbed the steps together. At the front doors/nboth instinctively looked back at the Forbidden/nForest. Harry was not sure whether it was his/nimagination or not, but he rather thought he saw a/nsmall cloud of birds erupting into the air over the/ntreetops in the distance, almost as though the tree in/nwhich they had been nesting had just been pulled up/nby the roots./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: O.W.L.S
text: /n/n/nRon's euphoria at helping Gryffindor scrape the/nQuidditch Cup was such that he could not settle to/nanything next day. He might as well have tried to/nsee moving pictures in the desktop as in the/nstubbornly blank crystal ball; he lost his head/ncompletely during tea-leaf reading, saying it looked to/nhim as though Professor Marchbanks would shortly/nbe meeting a round, dark, soggy stranger, and/nrounded off the whole fiasco by mixing up the life and/nhead lines on her palm and informing her that she/nought to have died the previous Tuesday./n/n"Well, we were always going to fail that one," said Ron/ngloomily as they ascended the marble staircase. He/nhad just made Harry feel rather better by telling him/nhow he told the examiner in detail about the ugly/nman with a wart on his nose in his crystal ball, only/nto look up and realize he had been describing his/nexaminer's reflection./n/n"We shouldn't have taken the stupid subject in the/nfirst place," said Harry./n/n"Still, at least we can give it up now."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "No more pretending we care what/nhappens when Jupiter and Uranus get too friendly ..."/n/n"And from now on, I don't care if my tea leaves spell/ndie, Ron, die — I'm just chucking them in the bin/nwhere they belong."/n/nHarry laughed just as Hermione came running up/nbehind them. He stopped laughing at once, in case it/nannoyed her./n/n"Well, I think I've done all right in Arithmancy," she/nsaid, and Harry and Ron both sighed with relief. "Just/ntime for a quick look over our star charts before/ndinner, then ..."/n/nWhen they reached the top of the Astronomy Tower at/neleven o'clock they found a perfect night for/nstargazing, cloudless and still. The grounds were/nbathed in silvery moonlight, and there was a slight/nchill in the air. Each of them set up his or her/ntelescope and, when Professor Marchbanks gave the/nword, proceeded to fill in the blank star chart he or/nshe had been given./n/nProfessors Marchbanks and Tofty strolled among/nthem, watching as they entered the precise positions/nof the stars and planets they were observing. All was/nquiet except for the rustle of parchment, the/noccasional creak of a telescope as it was adjusted on/nits stand, and the scribbling of many quills. Half an/nhour passed, then an hour; the little squares of/nreflected gold light flickering on the ground below/nstarted to vanish as lights in the castle windows were/nextinguished./n/nAs Harry completed the constellation Orion on his/nchart, however, the front doors of the castle opened/ndirectly below the parapet where he was standing, so/n/n/n/n/n/nthat light spilled down the stone steps a little way/nacross the lawn. Harry glanced down as he made a/nslight adjustment to the position of his telescope and/nsaw five or six elongated shadows moving over the/nbrightly lit grass before the doors swung shut and the/nlawn became a sea of darkness once more./n/nHarry put his eye back to his telescope and refocused/nit, now examining Venus. He looked down at his chart/nto enter the planet there, but something distracted/nhim. Pausing with his quill suspended over the/nparchment, he squinted down into the shadowy/ngrounds and saw half a dozen figures walking over/nthe lawn. If they had not been moving, and the/nmoonlight had not been gilding the tops of their/nheads, they would have been indistinguishable from/nthe dark ground on which they stood. Even at this/ndistance, Harry had a funny feeling that he/nrecognized the walk of the squattest among them,/nwho seemed to be leading the group./n/nHe could not think why Umbridge would be taking a/nstroll outside past midnight, much less accompanied/nby five others. Then somebody coughed behind him,/nand he remembered that he was halfway through an/nexam. He had quite forgotten Venus's position —/njamming his eye to his telescope, he found it again/nand was again on the point of entering it on his chart/nwhen, alert for any odd sound, he heard a distant/nknock that echoed through the deserted grounds,/nfollowed immediately by the muffled barking of a large/ndog./n/nHe looked up, his heart hammering. There were lights/non in Hagrid's windows and the people he had/nobserved crossing the lawn were now silhouetted/nagainst them. The door opened and he distinctly saw/nsix tiny but sharply defined figures walk over the/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nthreshold. The door closed again and there was/nsilence./n/nHarry felt very uneasy. He glanced around to see/nwhether Ron or Hermione had noticed what he had,/nbut Professor Marchbanks came walking behind him/nat that moment, and not wanting to appear as though/nhe was sneaking looks at anyone else's work, he/nhastily bent over his star chart and pretended to be/nadding notes to it while really peering over the top of/nthe parapet toward Hagrid's cabin. Figures were now/nmoving across the cabin windows, temporarily/nblocking the light./n/nHe could feel Professor Marchbanks's eyes on the/nback of his neck and pressed his eye again to his/ntelescope, staring up at the moon though he had/nmarked its position an hour ago, but as Professor/nMarchbanks moved on he heard a roar from the/ndistant cabin that echoed through the darkness right/nto the top of the Astronomy Tower. Several of the/npeople around Harry ducked out from behind their/ntelescopes and peered instead in the direction of/nHagrid's cabin./n/nProfessor Tofty gave another dry little cough./n/n"Try and concentrate, now, boys and girls," he said/nsoftly./n/nMost people returned to their telescopes. Harry looked/nto his left. Hermione was gazing transfixed at/nHagrid's./n/n"Ahem — twenty minutes to go," said Professor Tofty./n/nHermione jumped and returned at once to her star/nchart; Harry looked down at his own and noticed that/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhe had mislabelled Venus as Mars. He bent to correct/nit./n/nThere was a loud BANG from the grounds. Several/npeople said "Ouch!" as they poked themselves in the/nface with the ends of their telescopes, hastening to/nsee what was going on below./n/nHagrid's door had burst open and by the light flooding/nout of the cabin they saw him quite clearly, a massive/nfigure roaring and brandishing his fists, surrounded/nby six people, all of whom, judging by the tiny threads/nof red light they were casting in his direction, seemed/nto be attempting to Stun him./n/n"No!" cried Hermione./n/n"My dear!" said Professor Tofty in a scandalized voice./n"This is an examination!"/n/nBut nobody was paying the slightest attention to their/nstar charts anymore: Jets of red light were still flying/nbeside Hagrid's cabin, yet somehow they seemed to be/nbouncing off him. He was still upright and still, as far/nas Harry could see, fighting. Cries and yells echoed/nacross the grounds; a man yelled, "Be reasonable,/nHagrid!" and Hagrid roared, "Reasonable be damned,/nyeh won' take me like this, Dawlish!"/n/nHarry could see the tiny outline of Fang, attempting/nto defend Hagrid, leaping at the wizards surrounding/nhim until a Stunning Spell caught him and he fell to/nthe ground. Hagrid gave a howl of fury, lifted the/nculprit bodily from the ground, and threw him: The/nman flew what looked like ten feet and did not get up/nagain. Hermione gasped, both hands over her mouth;/nHarry looked around at Ron and saw that he too was/nlooking scared. None of them had ever seen Hagrid in/na real temper before.../n/n/n/n/n/n"Look!" squealed Parvati, who was leaning over the/nparapet and pointing to the foot of the castle where/nthe front doors seemed to have opened again; more/nlight had spilled out onto the dark lawn and a single/nlong black shadow was now rippling across the lawn./n/n"Now, really!" said Professor Tofty anxiously. "Only/nsixteen minutes left, you know!"/n/nBut nobody paid him the slightest attention: They/nwere watching the person now sprinting toward the/nbattle beside Hagrid's cabin./n/n"How dare you!" the figure shouted as she ran. "How/ndare you!"/n/n"It's McGonagall!" whispered Hermione./n/n"Leave him alone! Alone, I say!" said Professor/nMcGonagall's voice through the darkness. "On what/ngrounds are you attacking him? He has done nothing,/nnothing to warrant such — "/n/nHermione, Parvati, and Lavender all screamed. No/nfewer than four Stunners had shot from the figures/naround the cabin toward Professor McGonagall./nHalfway between cabin and castle the red beams/ncollided with her. For a moment she looked luminous,/nilluminated by an eerie red glow, then was lifted right/noff her feet, landed hard on her back, and moved no/nmore./n/n"Galloping gargoyles!" shouted Professor Tofty, who/nseemed to have forgotten the exam completely. "Not/nso much as a warning! Outrageous behavior!"/n/n"COWARDS!" bellowed Hagrid, his voice carrying/nclearly to the top of the tower, and several lights/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nflickered back on inside the castle. "RUDDY/nCOWARDS! HAVE SOME O' THAT — AN' THAT — "/n/n"Oh my — " gasped Hermione./n/nHagrid took two massive swipes at his closest/nattackers; judging by their immediate collapse, they/nhad been knocked cold. Harry saw him double over/nand thought for a moment that he had finally been/novercome by a spell, but on the contrary, next/nmoment Hagrid was standing again with what/nappeared to be a sack on his back — then Harry/nrealized that Fang's limp body was draped around his/nshoulders./n/n"Get him, get him!" screamed Umbridge, but her/nremaining helper seemed highly reluctant to go within/nreach of Hagrid 's fists. Indeed, he was backing away/nso fast he tripped over one of his unconscious/ncolleagues and fell over. Hagrid had turned and/nbegun to run with Fang still hung around his neck;/nUmbridge sent one last Stunning Spell after him but/nit missed, and Hagrid, running full-pelt toward the/ndistant gates, disappeared into the darkness./n/nThere was a long minute's quivering silence,/neverybody gazing openmouthed into the grounds./nThen Professor Tofty's voice said feebly, "Um ... five/nminutes to go, everybody ..."/n/nThough he had only filled in two-thirds of his chart,/nHarry was desperate for the end of the exam. When it/ncame at last he, Ron, and Hermione forced their/ntelescopes haphazardly back into their holders and/ndashed back down the spiral staircase. None of the/nstudents were going to bed — they were all talking/nloudly and excitedly at the foot of the stairs about/nwhat they had witnessed./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"That evil woman!" gasped Hermione, who seemed to/nbe having difficulty talking due to rage. "Trying to/nsneak up on Hagrid in the dead of night!"/n/n"She clearly wanted to avoid another scene like/nTrelawney's," said Ernie Macmillan sagely, squeezing/nover to join them./n/n"Hagrid did well, didn't he?" said Ron, who looked/nmore alarmed than impressed. "How come all the/nspells bounced off him?"/n/n"It'll be his giant blood," said Hermione shakily. "It's/nvery hard to Stun a giant, they're like trolls, really/ntough... But poor Professor McGonagall... Four/nStunners straight in the chest, and she's not exactly/nyoung, is she?"/n/n"Dreadful, dreadful," said Ernie, shaking his head/npompously. "Well, I'm off to bed... 'Night, all ..."/n/nPeople around them were drifting away, still talking/nexcitedly about what they had just seen./n/n"At least they didn't get to take Hagrid off to/nAzkaban," said Ron. "I 'spect he's gone to join/nDumbledore, hasn't he?"/n/n"I suppose so," said Hermione, who looked tearful./n"Oh, this is awful, I really thought Dumbledore would/nbe back before long, but now we've lost Hagrid too..."/n/nThey traipsed back to the Gryffindor common room to/nfind it full. The commotion out in the grounds had/nwoken several people, who had hastened to rouse/ntheir friends. Seamus and Dean, who had arrived/nahead of Harry, Ron, and Hermione, were now telling/neveryone what they had heard from the top of the/nAstronomy Tower./n/n/n/n/n/n"But why sack Hagrid now?" asked Angelina Johnson,/nshaking her head. "It's not like Trelawney, he's been/nteaching much better than usual this year!"/n/n"Umbridge hates part-humans," said Hermione/nbitterly, flopping down into an armchair. "She was/nalways going to try and get Hagrid out."/n/n"And she thought Hagrid was putting nifflers in her/noffice," piped up Katie Bell./n/n"Oh blimey," said Lee Jordan, covering his mouth./n/n"It's me's been putting the nifflers in her office, Fred/nand George left me a couple, I've been levitating them/nin through her window..."/n/n"She'd have sacked him anyway," said Dean. "He was/ntoo close to Dumbledore."/n/n"That's true," said Harry, sinking into an armchair/nbeside Hermione 's./n/n"I just hope Professor McGonagall's all right," said/nLavender tearfully./n/n"They carried her back up to the castle, we watched/nthrough the dormitory window," said Colin Creevey./n"She didn't look very well..."/n/n"Madam Pomfrey will sort her out," said Alicia/nSpinnet firmly. "She's never failed yet."/n/nIt was nearly four in the morning before the common/nroom cleared. Harry felt wide awake — the image of/nHagrid sprinting away into the dark was haunting/nhim. He was so angry with Umbridge he could not/nthink of a punishment bad enough for her, though/nRon's suggestion of having her fed to a box of starving/nBlast-Ended Skrewts had its merits. He fell asleep/n/n/n/n/ncontemplating hideous revenges and arose from bed/nthree hours later feeling distinctly unrested./n/n/n/nTheir final exam, History of Magic, was not to take/nplace until that afternoon. Harry would very much/nhave liked to go back to bed after breakfast, but he/nhad been counting on the morning for a spot of last-/nminute studying, so instead he sat with his head in/nhis hands by the common room window, trying hard/nnot to doze off as he read through some of the notes/nstacked three-and-a-half feet high that Hermione had/nlent him./n/nThe fifth years entered the Great Hall at two o'clock/nand took their places in front of their overturned/nexamination papers. Harry felt exhausted. He just/nwanted this to be over so that he could go and sleep./nThen tomorrow, he and Ron were going to go down to/nthe Quidditch pitch — he was going to have a fly on/nRon's broom and savor their freedom from studying.../n/n"Turn over your papers," said Professor Marchbanks/nfrom the front of the Hall, flicking over the giant/nhourglass. "You may begin..."/n/nHarry stared fixedly at the first question. It was/nseveral seconds before it occurred to him that he had/nnot taken in a word of it; there was a wasp buzzing/ndistractingly against one of the high windows. Slowly,/ntortuously, he began to write an answer./n/nHe was finding it very difficult to remember names/nand kept confusing dates. He simply skipped question/nfour: In your opinion, did wand legislation contribute/nto, or lead to better control of, goblin riots of the/neighteenth century? thinking that he would go back to/nit if he had time at the end. He had a stab at question/nfive: How was the Statute of Secrecy breached in 1 749/nand what measures were introduced to prevent a/n/n/n/n/nrecurrence? but had a nagging suspicion that he had/nmissed several important points. He had a feeling/nvampires had come into the story somewhere.../n/nHe looked ahead for a question he could definitely/nanswer and his eyes alighted upon number ten./n/nDescribe the circumstances that led to the Formation/nof the International Confederation of Wizards and/nexplain why the warlocks of Liechtenstein refused to/njoin./n/nI know this, Harry thought, though his brain felt/ntorpid and slack. He could visualize a heading, in/nHermione's handwriting: The Formation of the/nInternational Confederation of Wizards. . . He had read/nthese notes only this morning.../n/nHe began to write, looking up now and again to check/nthe large hourglass on the desk beside Professor/nMarchbanks. He was sitting right behind Parvati/nPatil, whose long dark hair fell below the back of her/nchair. Once or twice he found himself staring at the/ntiny golden lights that glistened in it when she moved/nher head very slightly and had to give his own head a/nlittle shake to clear it./n/n... the first Supreme Mugwump of the International/nConfederation of Wizards was Pierre Bonaccord, but/nhis appointment was contested by the Wizarding/ncommunity of Liechtenstein, because —/n/nAll around Harry quills were scratching on parchment/nlike scurrying, burrowing rats. The sun was very hot/non the back of his head. What was it that Bonaccord/nhad done to offend the wizards of Liechtenstein?/n/nHarry had a feeling it had something to do with/ntrolls... He gazed blankly at the back of Parvati 's head/nagain. If he could only perform Legilimency and open/n/n/n/n/na window in the back of her head and see what it was/nabout trolls that had caused the breach between/nPierre Bonaccord and Liechtenstein.../n/n/n/nHarry closed his eyes and buried his face in his/nhands, so that the glowing red of his eyelids grew/ndark and cool. Bonaccord had wanted to stop troll-/nhunting and give the trolls rights . . . but Liechtenstein/nwas having problems with a tribe of particularly/nvicious mountain trolls... That was it.../n/nHe opened his eyes; they stung and watered at the/nsight of the blazing- white parchment. Slowly he wrote/ntwo lines about the trolls then read through what he/nhad done so far. It did not seem very informative or/ndetailed, yet he was sure Hermione's notes on the/nconfederation had gone on for pages and pages.../n/nHe closed his eyes again, trying to see them, trying to/nremember. . . The confederation had met for the first/ntime in France, yes, he had written that already.../n/nGoblins had tried to attend and been ousted... He had/nwritten that too.../n/nAnd nobody from Liechtenstein had wanted to come/n/n/n/nThink, he told himself, his face in his hands, while all/naround him quills scratched out never-ending/nanswers and the sand trickled through the hourglass/nat the front.../n/nHe was walking along the cool, dark corridor to the/nDepartment of Mysteries again, walking with a firm/nand purposeful tread, breaking occasionally into a/nrun, determined to reach his destination at last... The/nblack door swung open for him as usual, and here he/nwas in the circular room with its many doors.../n/n/n/n/n/nStraight across the stone floor and through the/nsecond door . . . patches of dancing light on the walls/nand floor and that odd mechanical clicking, but no/ntime to explore, he must hurry.../n/nHe jogged the last few feet to the third door, which/nswung open just like the others.../n/nOnce again he was in the cathedral-sized room full of/nshelves and glass spheres... His heart was beating/nvery fast now... He was going to get there this time.../nWhen he reached number ninety-seven he turned left/nand hurried along the aisle between two rows.../n/nBut there was a shape on the floor at the very end, a/nblack shape moving upon the floor like a wounded/nanimal... Harry's stomach contracted with fear ... with/nexcitement.../n/nA voice issued from his own mouth, a high, cold voice/nempty of any human kindness, "Take it for me... Lift it/ndown, now... I cannot touch it ... but you can..."/n/nThe black shape upon the floor shifted a little. Harry/nsaw a long-fingered white hand clutching a wand rise/non the end of his own arm . . . heard the high, cold/nvoice say, " Cruciol "/n/nThe man on the floor let out a scream of pain,/nattempted to stand but fell back, writhing. Harry was/nlaughing. He raised his wand, the curse lifted, and/nthe figure groaned and became motionless./n/n"Lord Voldemort is waiting..."/n/nVery slowly, his arms trembling, the man on the/nground raised his shoulders a few inches and lifted/nhis head. His face was bloodstained and gaunt,/ntwisted in pain yet rigid with defiance.../n/n/n/n/n/n"You'll have to kill me," whispered Sirius./n/n"Undoubtedly I shall in the end," said the cold voice./n"But you will fetch it for me first, Black... You think/nyou have felt pain thus far? Think again... We have/nhours ahead of us and nobody to hear you scream..."/n/nBut somebody screamed as Voldemort lowered his/nwand again; somebody yelled and fell sideways off a/nhot desk onto the cold stone floor. Harry hit the/nground and awoke, still yelling, his scar on fire, as the/nGreat Hall erupted all around him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Out Of The Fire
text: /n"I'm not going... I don't need the hospital wing... I/ndon't want ..."/n/nHe was gibbering, trying to pull away from Professor/nTofty, who was looking at him with much concern,/nand who had just helped Harry out into the entrance/nhall while the students all around them stared./n/n"I'm — I'm fine, sir," Harry stammered, wiping the/nsweat from his face. "Really ... I just fell asleep... Had/na nightmare ..."/n/n"Pressure of examinations!" said the old wizard/nsympathetically, patting Harry shakily on the/nshoulder. "It happens, young man, it happens! Now, a/ncooling drink of water, and perhaps you will be ready/nto return to the Great Hall? The examination is nearly/nover, but you may be able to round off your last/nanswer nicely?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry wildly. "I mean ... no ... I've done —/ndone as much as I can, I think..."/n/n/n/n/n"Very well, very well," said the old wizard gently. "I/nshall go and collect your examination paper, and I/nsuggest that you go and have a nice lie down..."/n/n"I'll do that," said Harry, nodding vigorously. "Thanks/nvery much."/n/nHe waited for the second when the old man's heels/ndisappeared over the threshold into the Great Hall,/nthen ran up the marble staircase and then more/nstaircases toward the hospital wing, hurtling along/nthe corridors so fast that the portraits he passed/nmuttered reproaches, and burst through the double/ndoors like a hurricane, causing Madam Pomfrey, who/nhad been spooning some bright blue liquid into/nMontague's open mouth, to shriek in alarm./n/n"Potter, what do you think you're doing?"/n/n"I need to see Professor McGonagall," gasped Harry,/nthe breath tearing his lungs. "Now ... It's urgent..."/n/n"She's not here, Potter," said Madam Pomfrey sadly./n"She was transferred to St. Mungo's this morning./nFour Stunning Spells straight to the chest at her age?/nIt's a wonder they didn't kill her."/n/n"She's ... gone?" said Harry, stunned./n/nThe bell rang just outside the dormitory, and he/nheard the usual distant rumbling of students starting/nto flood out into the corridors above and below him./nHe remained quite still, looking at Madam Pomfrey./nTerror was rising inside him./n/nThere was nobody left to tell. Dumbledore had gone,/nHagrid had gone, but he had always expected/nProfessor McGonagall to be there, irascible and/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ninflexible, perhaps, but always dependably, solidly/npresent.../n/n"I don't wonder you're shocked, Potter," said Madam/nPomfrey with a kind of fierce approval in her face. "As/nif one of them could have Stunned Minerva/nMcGonagall face on by daylight! Cowardice, that's/nwhat it was... Despicable cowardice ... If I wasn't/nworried what would happen to you students without/nme, I'd resign in protest..."/n/n"Yes," said Harry blankly./n/nHe strode blindly from the hospital wing into the/nteeming corridor where he stood, buffeted by the/ncrowd, the panic expanding inside him like poison gas/nso that his head swam and he could not think what to/ndo.../n/nRon and Hermione, said a voice in his head./n/nHe was running again, pushing students out of the/nway, oblivious to their angry protests and shouts. He/nsprinted back down two floors and was at the top of/nthe marble staircase when he saw them hurrying/ntoward him./n/n"Harry!" said Hermione at once, looking very/nfrightened. "What happened? Are you all right? Are/nyou ill?"/n/n"Where have you been?" demanded Ron./n/n"Come with me," Harry said quickly. "Come on, I've/ngot to tell you something..."/n/nHe led them along the first-floor corridor, peering/nthrough doorways, and at last found an empty/nclassroom into which he dived, closing the door/n/n/n/n/n/nbehind Ron and Hermione the moment they were/ninside and leaning against it, facing them./n/n"Voldemort's got Sirius."/n/n"What?"/n/n"How d'you — ?"/n/n"Saw it. Just now. When I fell asleep in the exam."/n/n"But — but where? How?" said Hermione, whose face/nwas white./n/n"I dunno how," said Harry. "But I know exactly where./nThere's a room in the Department of Mysteries full of/nshelves covered in these little glass balls, and they're/nat the end of row ninety-seven ... He's trying to use/nSirius to get whatever it is he wants from in there.../nHe's torturing him... Says he'll end by killing him ..."/n/nHarry found his voice was shaking, as were his knees./nHe moved over to a desk and sat down on it, trying to/nmaster himself./n/n"How're we going to get there?" he asked them./n/nThere was a moment's silence. Then Ron said, "G-get/nthere?"/n/n"Get to the Department of Mysteries, so we can rescue/nSirius!" Harry said loudly./n/n"But — Harry ..." said Ron weakly./n/n"What? What?" said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe could not understand why they were both gaping/nat him as though he was asking them something/nunreasonable./n/n"Harry," said Hermione in a rather frightened voice,/n/n"er . . . how . . . how did Voldemort get into the Ministry/nof Magic without anybody realizing he was there?"/n/n"How do I know?" bellowed Harry. "The question is/nhow we're going to get in there!"/n/n"But ... Harry, think about this," said Hermione,/ntaking a step toward him, "it's five o'clock in the/nafternoon... The Ministry of Magic must be full of/nworkers... How would Voldemort and Sirius have got/nin without being seen? Harry . . . they're probably the/ntwo most wanted wizards in the world... You think/nthey could get into a building full of Aurors/nundetected?"/n/n"I dunno, Voldemort used an Invisibility Cloak or/nsomething!" Harry shouted. "Anyway, the Department/nof Mysteries has always been completely empty/nwhenever I've been — "/n/n"You've never been there, Harry," said Hermione/nquietly. "You've dreamed about the place, that's all."/n/n"They're not normal dreams!" Harry shouted in her/nface, standing up and taking a step closer to her in/nturn. He wanted to shake her. "How d'you explain/nRon's dad then, what was all that about, how come I/nknew what had happened to him?"/n/n"He's got a point," said Ron quietly, looking at/nHermione./n/n"But this is just — just so unlikely\" said Hermione/ndesperately. "Harry, how on earth could Voldemort/n/n/n/n/n/nhave got hold of Sirius when he's been in Grimmauld/nPlace all the time?"/n/n"Sirius might've cracked and just wanted some fresh/nair," said Ron, sounding worried. "He's been/ndesperate to get out of that house for ages — "/n/n"But why," Hermione persisted, "why on earth would/nVoldemort want to use Sirius to get the weapon, or/nwhatever the thing is?"/n/n"I dunno, there could be loads of reasons!" Harry/nyelled at her. "Maybe Sirius is just someone/nVoldemort doesn't care about seeing hurt — "/n/n"You know what, I've just thought of something," said/nRon in a hushed voice. Come on then, girl, come on!"/n/n"Er — my — nee — no!" shouted Ron through his gag./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGinny was staring at Hermione as though she had/nnever seen her before; Neville, still choking for breath,/nwas gazing at her too. But Harry had just noticed/nsomething. Though Hermione was sobbing/ndesperately into her hands, there was no trace of a/ntear.../n/n"I'm — I'm sorry everyone," said Hermione. "But — I/ncan't stand it — ■"/n/n"That's right, that's right, girl!" said Umbridge, seizing/nHermione by the shoulders, thrusting her into the/nabandoned chintz chair and leaning over her. "Now/nthen ... with whom was Potter communicating just/nnow?"/n/n"Well," gulped Hermione into her hands, "well, he was/ntrying to speak to Professor Dumbledore..."/n/nRon froze, his eyes wide; Ginny stopped trying to/nstamp on her Slytherin captor's toes; even Luna/nlooked mildly surprised. Fortunately, the attention of/nUmbridge and her minions was focused too/nexclusively upon Hermione to notice these suspicious/nsigns./n/n"Dumbledore?" said Umbridge eagerly. "You know/nwhere Dumbledore is, then?"/n/n"Well ... no!" sobbed Hermione.
