Ron/nlooked white and shocked. Tears were falling thick/nand fast into both Ginny 's and Hermione's laps./n/nThey could not see clearly what was happening at the/nfront. Hagrid seemed to have placed the body/ncarefully upon the table. Now he retreated down the/naisle, blowing his nose with loud trumpeting noises/nthat drew scandalized looks from some, including,/nHarry saw, Dolores Umbridge ... but Harry knew that/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore would not have cared. He tried to make a/nfriendly gesture to Hagrid as he passed, but Hagrid's/neyes were so swollen it was a wonder he could see/nwhere he was going. Harry glanced at the back row to/nwhich Hagrid was heading and realized what was/nguiding him, for there, dressed in a jacket and/ntrousers each the size of a small marquee, was the/ngiant Grawp, his great ugly boulderlike head bowed,/ndocile, almost human. Hagrid sat down next to his/nhalf-brother, and Grawp patted Hagrid hard on the/nhead, so that his chair legs sank into the ground./nHarry had a wonderful momentary urge to laugh. But/nthen the music stopped, and he turned to face the/nfront again./n/nA little tufty-haired man in plain black robes had got/nto his feet and stood now in front of Dumbledore 's/nbody. Harry could not hear what he was saying. Odd/nwords floated back to them over the hundreds of/nheads. "Nobility of spirit" ... "intellectual contribution"/n... "greatness of heart" ... It did not mean very much./n/nIt had little to do with Dumbledore as Harry had/nknown him. He suddenly remembered Dumbledore 's/nidea of a few words, "nitwit," "oddment," "blubber,"/nand "tweak," and again had to suppress a grin. .../nWhat was the matter with him?/n/nThere was a soft splashing noise to his left and he/nsaw that the merpeople had broken the surface to/nlisten too. He remembered Dumbledore crouching at/nthe water's edge two years ago, very close to where/nHarry now sat, and conversing in Mermish with the/nMerchieftainess. Harry wondered where Dumbledore/nhad learned Mermish. There was so much he had/nnever asked him, so much he should have said. .../n/nAnd then, without warning, it swept over him, the/ndreadful truth, more completely and undeniably than/nit had until now. Dumbledore was dead, gone. ... He/n/n/n/n/n/nclutched the cold locket in his hand so tightly that it/nhurt, but he could not prevent hot tears spilling from/nhis eyes: He looked away from Ginny and the others/nand stared out over the lake, toward the forest, as the/nlittle man in black droned on. ... There was movement/namong the trees. The centaurs had come to pay their/nrespects too. They did not move into the open but/nHarry saw them standing quite still, half hidden in/nshadow, watching the wizards, their bows hanging at/ntheir sides. And Harry remembered his first/nnightmarish trip into the forest, the first time he had/never encountered the thing that was then Voldemort,/nand how he had faced him, and how he and/nDumbledore had discussed fighting a losing battle not/nlong thereafter. It was important, Dumbledore said, to/nfight, and fight again, and keep fighting, for only then/ncould evil be kept at bay, though never quite/neradicated. .../n/nAnd Harry saw very clearly as he sat there under the/nhot sun how people who cared about him had stood/nin front of him one by one, his mother, his father, his/ngodfather, and finally Dumbledore, all determined to/nprotect him; but now that was over. He could not let/nanybody else stand between him and Voldemort; he/nmust abandon forever the illusion he ought to have/nlost at the age of one, that the shelter of a parent's/narms meant that nothing could hurt him. There was/nno waking from his nightmare, no comforting whisper/nin the dark that he was safe really, that it was all in/nhis imagination; the last and greatest of his protectors/nhad died, and he was more alone than he had ever/nbeen before./n/nThe little man in black had stopped speaking at last/nand resumed his seat. Harry waited for somebody else/nto get to their feet; he expected speeches, probably/nfrom the Minister, but nobody moved./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThen several people screamed. Bright, white flames/nhad erupted around Dumbledore's body and the table/nupon which it lay: Higher and higher they rose,/nobscuring the body. White smoke spiraled into the air/nand made strange shapes: Harry thought, for one/nheart- stopping moment, that he saw a phoenix fly/njoyfully into the blue, but next second the fire had/nvanished. In its place was a white marble tomb,/nencasing Dumbledore's body and the table on which/nhe had rested./n/nThere were a few more cries of shock as a shower of/narrows soared through the air, but they fell far short/nof the crowd. It was, Harry knew, the centaurs'/ntribute: He saw them turn tail and disappear back/ninto the cool trees. Likewise, the merpeople sank/nslowly back into the green water and were lost from/nview./n/nHarry looked at Ginny, Ron, and Hermione: Ron's/nface was screwed up as though the sunlight were/nblinding him. Hermione 's face was glazed with tears,/nbut Ginny was no longer crying. She met Harry's gaze/nwith the same hard, blazing look that he had seen/nwhen she had hugged him after winning the/nQuidditch Cup in his absence, and he knew that at/nthat moment they understood each other perfectly,/nand that when he told her what he was going to do/nnow, she would not say, "Be careful," or "Don't do it,"/nbut accept his decision, because she would not have/nexpected anything less of him. And so he steeled/nhimself to say what he had known he must say ever/nsince Dumbledore had died./n/n"Ginny, listen ..." he said very quietly, as the buzz of/nconversation grew louder around them and people/nbegan to get to their feet, "I can't be involved with you/nanymore. We've got to stop seeing each other. We/ncan't be together."/n/n/n/n/n/nShe said, with an oddly twisted smile, "It's for some/nstupid, noble reason, isn't it?"/n/n"It's been like ... like something out of someone else's/nlife, these last few weeks with you," said Harry. "But I/ncan't ... we can't ... I've got things to do alone now."/n/nShe did not cry, she simply looked at him./n/n"Voldemort uses people his enemies are close to. He's/nalready used you as bait once, and that was just/nbecause you're my best friend's sister. Think how/nmuch danger you'll be in if we keep this up. He'll/nknow, hell find out. He'll try and get to me through/nyou."/n/n"What if I don't care?" said Ginny fiercely./n/n"I care," said Harry. "How do you think I'd feel if this/nwas your funeral ... and it was my fault. ..."/n/nShe looked away from him, over the lake./n/n"I never really gave up on you," she said. "Not really. I/nalways hoped. ... Hermione told me to get on with life,/nmaybe go out with some other people, relax a bit/naround you, because I never used to be able to talk if/nyou were in the room, remember? And she thought/nyou might take a bit more notice if I was a bit more —/nmyself."/n/n"Smart girl, that Hermione," said Harry, trying to/nsmile. "I just wish I'd asked you sooner. We could've/nhad ages ... months ... years maybe. ..."/n/n"But you've been too busy saving the Wizarding/nworld," said Ginny, half laughing. "Well ... I can't say/nI'm surprised. I knew this would happen in the end. I/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nknew you wouldn't be happy unless you were hunting/nVoldemort. Maybe that's why I like you so much."/n/nHarry could not bear to hear these things, nor did he/nthink his resolution would hold if he remained sitting/nbeside her. Ron, he saw, was now holding Hermione/nand stroking her hair while she sobbed into his/nshoulder, tears dripping from the end of his own long/nnose. With a miserable gesture, Harry got up, turned/nhis back on Ginny and on Dumbledore's tomb, and/nwalked away around the lake. Moving felt much more/nbearable than sitting still, just as setting out as soon/nas possible to track down the Horcruxes and kill/nVoldemort would feel better than waiting to do it. .../n/n"Harry!"/n/nHe turned. Rufus Scrimgeour was limping rapidly/ntoward him around the bank, leaning on his walking/nstick./n/n"I've been hoping to have a word ... do you mind if I/nwalk a little way with you?"/n/n"No," said Harry indifferently, and set off again./n/n"Harry, this was a dreadful tragedy," said Scrimgeour/nquietly. "I cannot tell you how appalled I was to hear/nof it. Dumbledore was a very great wizard. We had our/ndisagreements, as you know, but no one knows better/nthan I — "/n/n"What do you want?" asked Harry flatly./n/nScrimgeour looked annoyed, but as before, hastily/nmodified his expression to one of sorrowful/nunderstanding./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You are, of course, devastated," he said. "I know that/nyou were very close to Dumbledore. I think you may/nhave been his favorite pupil ever. The bond between/nthe two of you — "/n/n"What do you want?" Harry repeated, coming to a/nhalt./n/nScrimgeour stopped too, leaned on his stick, and/nstared at Harry, his expression shrewd now./n/n"The word is that you were with him when he left the/nschool the night that he died."/n/n"Whose word?" said Harry./n/n"Somebody Stupefied a Death Eater on top of the/ntower after Dumbledore died. There were also two/nbroomsticks up there. The Ministry can add two and/ntwo, Harry."/n/n"Glad to hear it," said Harry. "Well, where I went with/nDumbledore and what we did is my business. He/ndidn't want people to know."/n/n"Such loyalty is admirable, of course," said/nScrimgeour, who seemed to be restraining his/nirritation with difficulty, "but Dumbledore is gone,/nHarry. He's gone."/n/n"He will only be gone from the school when none here/nare loyal to him," said Harry, smiling in spite of/nhimself./n/n"My dear boy . . . even Dumbledore cannot return from/nthe — "/n/n"I am not saying he can. You wouldn't understand./n/nBut I've got nothing to tell you."/n/n/n/n/n/nScrimgeour hesitated, then said, in what was/nevidently supposed to be a tone of delicacy, "The/nMinistry can offer you all sorts of protection, you/nknow, Harry. I would be delighted to place a couple of/nmy Aurors at your service — "/n/nHarry laughed. "Voldemort wants to kill me himself,/nand Aurors won't stop him. So thanks for the offer,/nbut no thanks."/n/n"So," said Scrimgeour, his voice cold now, "the/nrequest I made of you at Christmas — "/n/n"What request? Oh yeah . . . the one where I tell the/nworld what a great job you're doing in exchange for — "/n/n" — for raising everyone's morale!" snapped/nScrimgeour./n/nHarry considered him for a moment./n/n"Released Stan Shunpike yet?"/n/nScrimgeour turned a nasty purple color highly/nreminiscent of Uncle Vernon./n/n"I see you are — "/n/n"Dumbledore's man through and through," said/nHarry. "That's right."/n/nScrimgeour glared at him for another moment, then/nturned and limped away without another word. Harry/ncould see Percy and the rest of the Ministry delegation/nwaiting for him, casting nervous glances at the/nsobbing Hagrid and Grawp, who were still in their/nseats. Ron and Hermione were hurrying toward/nHarry, passing Scrimgeour going in the opposite/ndirection. Harry turned and walked slowly on, waiting/n/n/n/n/nfor them to catch up, which they finally did in the/nshade of a beech tree under which they had sat in/nhappier times./n/n"What did Scrimgeour want?" Hermione whispered./n/n"Same as he wanted at Christmas," shrugged Harry./n"Wanted me to give him inside information on/nDumbledore and be the Ministry's new poster boy."/n/nRon seemed to struggle with himself for a moment,/nthen he said loudly to Hermione, "Look, let me go/nback and hit Percy!"/n/n"No," she said firmly, grabbing his arm./n/n"It'll make me feel better!"/n/nHarry laughed. Even Hermione grinned a little,/nthough her smile faded as she looked up at the castle./n/n"I can't bear the idea that we might never come back,"/nshe said softly. "How can Hogwarts close?"/n/n"Maybe it won't," said Ron. "We're not in any more/ndanger here than we are at home, are we?/nEverywhere's the same now. I'd even say Hogwarts is/nsafer, there are more wizards inside to defend the/nplace. What d'you reckon, Harry?"/n/n"I'm not coming back even if it does reopen," said/nHarry./n/nRon gaped at him, but Hermione said sadly, "I knew/nyou were going to say that. But then what will you/ndo?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm going back to the Dursleys' once more, because/nDumbledore wanted me to," said Harry. "But it'll be a/nshort visit, and then I'll be gone for good."/n/n"But where will you go if you don't come back to/nschool?"/n/n"I thought I might go back to Godric's Hollow," Harry/nmuttered. He had had the idea in his head ever since/nthe night of Dumbledore's death. "For me, it started/nthere, all of it. I've just got a feeling I need to go there./nAnd I can visit my parents' graves, I'd like that."/n/n"And then what?" said Ron./n/n"Then I've got to track down the rest of the Horcruxes,/nhaven't I?" said Harry, his eyes upon Dumbledore's/nwhite tomb, reflected in the water on the other side of/nthe lake. "That's what he wanted me to do, that's why/nhe told me all about them. If Dumbledore was right —/nand I'm sure he was — there are still four of them out/nthere. I've got to find them and destroy them, and/nthen I've got to go after the seventh bit of Voldemort's/nsoul, the bit that's still in his body, and I'm the one/nwho's going to kill him. And if I meet Severus Snape/nalong the way," he added, "so much the better for me,/nso much the worse for him."/n/nThere was a long silence. The crowd had almost/ndispersed now, the stragglers giving the monumental/nfigure of Grawp a wide berth as he cuddled Hagrid,/nwhose howls of grief were still echoing across the/nwater./n/n"Well be there, Harry," said Ron./n/n"What?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"At your aunt and uncle's house," said Ron. "And/nthen well go with you wherever you're going."/n/n"No — " said Harry quickly; he had not counted on/nthis, he had meant them to understand that he was/nundertaking this most dangerous journey alone./n/n"You said to us once before," said Hermione quietly,/n"that there was time to turn back if we wanted to./nWe've had time, haven't we?/n/n"We're with you whatever happens," said Ron. "But/nmate, you're going to have to come round my mum/nand dad's house before we do anything else, even/nGodric's Hollow."/n/n"Why?"/n/n"Bill and Fleur's wedding, remember?"/n/nHarry looked at him, startled; the idea that anything/nas normal as a wedding could still exist seemed/nincredible and yet wonderful./n/n"Yeah, we shouldn't miss that," he said finally./n/nHis hand closed automatically around the fake/nHorcrux, but in spite of everything, in spite of the/ndark and twisting path he saw stretching ahead for/nhimself, in spite of the final meeting with Voldemort/nhe knew must come, whether in a month, in a year,/nor in ten, he felt his heart lift at the thought that/nthere was still one last golden day of peace left to/nenjoy with Ron and Hermione./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Dark Lord Ascending
text: /nThe two men appeared out of nowhere, a few yards/napart in the narrow, moonlit lane. For a second they/nstood quite still, wands directed at each other's/nchests; then, recognizing each other, they stowed/ntheir wands beneath their cloaks and started walking/nbriskly in the same direction./n/n"News?" asked the taller of the two./n/n"The best," replied Severus Snape./n/nThe lane was bordered on the left by wild, low-/ngrowing brambles, on the right by a high, neatly/nmanicured hedge. The men's long cloaks flapped/naround their ankles as they marched./n/n"Thought I might be late," said Yaxley, his blunt/nfeatures sliding in and out of sight as the branches of/noverhanging trees broke the moonlight. "It was a little/ntrickier than I expected. But I hope he will be/nsatisfied. You sound confident that your reception will/nbe good?"/n/n/n/n/n/nSnape nodded, but did not elaborate. They turned/nright, into a wide driveway that led off the lane. The/nhigh hedge curved with them, running off into the/ndistance beyond the pair of impressive wrought-iron/ngates barring the men's way. Neither of them broke/nstep: In silence both raised their left arms in a kind of/nsalute and passed straight through, as though the/ndark metal were smoke./n/nThe yew hedges muffled the sound of the men's/nfootsteps. There was a rustle somewhere to their/nright: Yaxley drew his wand again, pointing it over his/ncompanion's head, but the source of the noise proved/nto be nothing more than a pure-white peacock,/nstrutting majestically along the top of the hedge./n/n"He always did himself well, Lucius. Peacocks ..."/nYaxley thrust his wand back under his cloak with a/nsnort./n/nA handsome manor house grew out of the darkness at/nthe end of the straight drive, lights glinting in the/ndiamond-paned downstairs windows. Somewhere in/nthe dark garden beyond the hedge a fountain was/nplaying. Gravel crackled beneath their feet as Snape/nand Yaxley sped toward the front door, which swung/ninward at their approach, though nobody had visibly/nopened it./n/nThe hallway was large, dimly lit, and sumptuously/ndecorated, with a magnificent carpet covering most of/nthe stone floor. The eyes of the pale-faced portraits on/nthe walls followed Snape and Yaxley as they strode/npast. The two men halted at a heavy wooden door/nleading into the next room, hesitated for the space of/na heartbeat, then Snape turned the bronze handle./n/nThe drawing room was full of silent people, sitting at a/nlong and ornate table. The room's usual furniture had/n/n/n/n/n/nbeen pushed carelessly up against the walls./nIllumination came from a roaring fire beneath a/nhandsome marble mantelpiece surmounted by a/ngilded mirror. Snape and Yaxley lingered for a/nmoment on the threshold. As their eyes grew/naccustomed to the lack of light, they were drawn/nupward to the strangest feature of the scene: an/napparently unconscious human figure hanging upside/ndown over the table, revolving slowly as if suspended/nby an invisible rope, and reflected in the mirror and in/nthe bare, polished surface of the table below. None of/nthe people seated underneath this singular sight was/nlooking at it except for a pale young man sitting/nalmost directly below it. He seemed unable to prevent/nhimself from glancing upward every minute or so./n/n"Yaxley. Snape," said a high, clear voice from the head/nof the table. "You are very nearly late."/n/nThe speaker was seated directly in front of the/nfireplace, so that it was difficult, at first, for the new/narrivals to make out more than his silhouette. As they/ndrew nearer, however, his face shone through the/ngloom, hairless, snakelike, with slits for nostrils and/ngleaming red eyes whose pupils were vertical. He was/nso pale that he seemed to emit a pearly glow./n/n"Severus, here," said Voldemort, indicating the seat/non his immediate right. "Yaxley — beside Dolohov."/n/nThe two men took their allotted places. Most of the/neyes around the table followed Snape, and it was to/nhim that Voldemort spoke first./n/n"So?"/n/n"My Lord, the Order of the Phoenix intends to move/nHarry Potter from his current place of safety on/nSaturday next, at nightfall."/n/n/n/n/n/nThe interest around the table sharpened palpably:/nSome stiffened, others fidgeted, all gazing at Snape/nand Voldemort./n/n"Saturday ... at nightfall," repeated Voldemort. His/nred eyes fastened upon Snape 's black ones with such/nintensity that some of the watchers looked away,/napparently fearful that they themselves would be/nscorched by the ferocity of the gaze. Snape, however,/nlooked calmly back into Voldemort's face and, after a/nmoment or two, Voldemort's lipless mouth curved into/nsomething like a smile./n/n"Good. Very good. And this information comes — "/n/n" — from the source we discussed," said Snape./n/n"My Lord."/n/nYaxley had leaned forward to look down the long table/nat Voldemort and Snape. All faces turned to him./n/n"My Lord, I have heard differently."/n/nYaxley waited, but Voldemort did not speak, so he/nwent on, "Dawlish, the Auror, let slip that Potter will/nnot be moved until the thirtieth, the night before the/nboy turns seventeen."/n/nSnape was smiling./n/n"My source told me that there are plans to lay a false/ntrail; this must be it. No doubt a Confundus Charm/nhas been placed upon Dawlish. It would not be the/nfirst time; he is known to be susceptible."/n/n"I assure you, my Lord, Dawlish seemed quite/ncertain," said Yaxley./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"If he has been Confunded, naturally he is certain,"/nsaid Snape. "I assure you, Yaxley, the Auror Office/nwill play no further part in the protection of Harry/nPotter. The Order believes that we have infiltrated the/nMinistry."/n/n"The Order's got one thing right, then, eh?" said a/nsquat man sitting a short distance from Yaxley; he/ngave a wheezy giggle that was echoed here and there/nalong the table./n/nVoldemort did not laugh. His gaze had wandered/nupward to the body revolving slowly overhead, and he/nseemed to be lost in thought./n/n"My Lord," Yaxley went on, "Dawlish believes an/nentire party of Aurors will be used to transfer the boy/n/n/n/nVoldemort held up a large white hand, and Yaxley/nsubsided at once, watching resentfully as Voldemort/nturned back to Snape./n/n"Where are they going to hide the boy next?"/n/n"At the home of one of the Order," said Snape. "The/nplace, according to the source, has been given every/nprotection that the Order and Ministry together could/nprovide. I think that there is little chance of taking/nhim once he is there, my Lord, unless, of course, the/nMinistry has fallen before next Saturday, which might/ngive us the opportunity to discover and undo enough/nof the enchantments to break through the rest."/n/n"Well, Yaxley?" Voldemort called down the table, the/nfirelight glinting strangely in his red eyes. "Will the/nMinistry have fallen by next Saturday?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nOnce again, all heads turned. Yaxley squared his/nshoulders./n/n"My Lord, I have good news on that score. I have —/nwith difficulty, and after great effort — suceeded in/nplacing an Imperius Curse upon Pius Thicknesse."/n/nMany of those sitting around Yaxley looked/nimpressed; his neighbor, Dolohov, a man with a long,/ntwisted face, clapped him on the back./n/n"It is a start," said Voldemort. "But Thicknesse is only/none man. Scrimgeour must be surrounded by our/npeople before I act. One failed attempt on the/nMinister's life will set me back a long way."/n/n"Yes — my Lord, that is true — but you know, as/nHead of the Department of Magical Law Enforcement,/nThicknesse has regular contact not only with the/nMinister himself, but also with the Heads of all the/nother Ministry departments. It will, I think, be easy/nnow that we have such a high-ranking official under/nour control, to subjugate the others, and then they/ncan all work together to bring Scrimgeour down."/n/n"As long as our friend Thicknesse is not discovered/nbefore he has converted the rest," said Voldemort. "At/nany rate, it remains unlikely that the Ministry will be/nmine before next Saturday. If we cannot touch the/nboy at his destination, then it must be done while he/ntravels."/n/n"We are at an advantage there, my Lord," said Yaxley,/nwho seemed determined to receive some portion of/napproval. "We now have several people planted within/nthe Department of Magical Transport. If Potter/nApparates or uses the Floo Network, we shall know/nimmediately."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"He will not do either," said Snape. "The Order is/neschewing any form of transport that is controlled or/nregulated by the Ministry; they mistrust everything to/ndo with the place."/n/n"All the better," said Voldemort. "He will have to move/nin the open. Easier to take, by far."/n/nAgain, Voldemort looked up at the slowly revolving/nbody as he went on, "I shall attend to the boy in/nperson. There have been too many mistakes where/nHarry Potter is concerned. Some of them have been/nmy own. That Potter lives is due more to my errors/nthan to his triumphs."/n/nThe company around the table watched Voldemort/napprehensively, each of them, by his or her/nexpression, afraid that they might be blamed for/nHarry Potter's continued existence. Voldemort,/nhowever, seemed to be speaking more to himself than/nto any of them, still addressing the unconscious body/nabove him./n/n"I have been careless, and so have been thwarted by/nluck and chance, those wreckers of all but the best-/nlaid plans. But I know better now. I understand those/nthings that I did not understand before. I must be the/none to kill Harry Potter, and I shall be."/n/nAt these words, seemingly in response to them, a/nsudden wail sounded, a terrible, drawn-out cry of/nmisery and pain. Many of those at the table looked/ndownward, startled, for the sound had seemed to/nissue from below their feet./n/n"Wormtail," said Voldemort, with no change in his/nquiet, thoughtful tone, and without removing his eyes/nfrom the revolving body above, "have I not spoken to/nyou about keeping our prisoner quiet?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, m-my Lord," gasped a small man halfway down/nthe table, who had been sitting so low in his chair/nthat it had appeared, at first glance, to be/nunoccupied. Now he scrambled from his seat and/nscurried from the room, leaving nothing behind him/nbut a curious gleam of silver./n/n"As I was saying," continued Voldemort, looking again/nat the tense faces of his followers, "I understand/nbetter now. I shall need, for instance, to borrow a/nwand from one of you before I go to kill Potter."/n/nThe faces around him displayed nothing but shock;/nhe might have announced that he wanted to borrow/none of their arms./n/n"No volunteers?" said Voldemort. "Let's see ... Lucius,/nI see no reason for you to have a wand anymore."/n/nLucius Malfoy looked up. His skin appeared yellowish/nand waxy in the firelight, and his eyes were sunken/nand shadowed. When he spoke, his voice was hoarse./n/n"My Lord?"/n/n"Your wand, Lucius. I require your wand."/n/n/n/nMalfoy glanced sideways at his wife. She was staring/nstraight ahead, quite as pale as he was, her long/nblonde hair hanging down her back, but beneath the/ntable her slim fingers closed briefly on his wrist. At/nher touch, Malfoy put his hand into his robes,/nwithdrew a wand, and passed it along to Voldemort,/nwho held it up in front of his red eyes, examining it/nclosely./n/n"What is it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Elm, my Lord," whispered Malfoy./n/n/n/n"And the core?"/n/n"Dragon — dragon heartstring."/n/n"Good," said Voldemort. He drew out his own wand/nand compared the lengths. Lucius Malfoy made an/ninvoluntary movement; for a fraction of a second, it/nseemed he expected to receive Voldemort's wand in/nexchange for his own. The gesture was not missed by/nVoldemort, whose eyes widened maliciously./n/n"Give you my wand, Lucius? My wand?"/n/nSome of the throng sniggered./n/n"I have given you your liberty, Lucius, is that not/nenough for you? But I have noticed that you and your/nfamily seem less than happy of late. ... What is it/nabout my presence in your home that displeases you,/nLucius?"/n/n"Nothing — nothing, my Lord!"/n/n"Such lies, Lucius ..."/n/nThe soft voice seemed to hiss on even after the cruel/nmouth had stopped moving. One or two of the wizards/nbarely repressed a shudder as the hissing grew/nlouder; something heavy could be heard sliding/nacross the floor beneath the table./n/nThe huge snake emerged to climb slowly up/nVoldemort's chair. It rose, seemingly endlessly, and/ncame to rest across Voldemort's shoulders: its neck/nthe thickness of a man's thigh; its eyes, with their/nvertical slits for pupils, unblinking. Voldemort stroked/n/n/n/n/n/nthe creature absently with long thin fingers, still/nlooking at Lucius Malfoy./n/n"Why do the Malfoys look so unhappy with their lot?/n/nIs my return, my rise to power, not the very thing they/nprofessed to desire for so many years?"/n/n"Of course, my Lord," said Lucius Malfoy. His hand/nshook as he wiped sweat from his upper lip. "We did/ndesire it — we do."/n/nTo Malfoy's left, his wife made an odd, stiff nod, her/neyes averted from Voldemort and the snake. To his/nright, his son, Draco, who had been gazing up at the/ninert body overhead, glanced quickly at Voldemort/nand away again, terrified to make eye contact./n/n"My Lord," said a dark woman halfway down the/ntable, her voice constricted with emotion, "it is an/nhonor to have you here, in our family's house. There/ncan be no higher pleasure."/n/nShe sat beside her sister, as unlike her in looks, with/nher dark hair and heavily lidded eyes, as she was in/nbearing and demeanor; where Narcissa sat rigid and/nimpassive, Bellatrix leaned toward Voldemort, for/nmere words could not demonstrate her longing for/ncloseness./n/n"No higher pleasure," repeated Voldemort, his head/ntilted a little to one side as he considered Bellatrix./n"That means a great deal, Bellatrix, from you."/n/nHer face flooded with color; her eyes welled with tears/nof delight./n/n"My Lord knows I speak nothing but the truth!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No higher pleasure ... even compared with the happy/nevent that, I hear, has taken place in your family this/nweek?"/n/n/n/nShe stared at him, her lips parted, evidently confused./n/n"I don't know what you mean, my Lord."/n/n"I'm talking about your niece, Bellatrix. And yours,/nLucius and Narcissa. She has just married the/nwerewolf, Remus Lupin. You must be so proud."/n/nThere was an eruption of jeering laughter from/naround the table. Many leaned forward to exchange/ngleeful looks; a few thumped the table with their fists./nThe great snake, disliking the disturbance, opened its/nmouth wide and hissed angrily, but the Death Eaters/ndid not hear it, so jubilant were they at Bellatrix and/nthe Malfoys' humiliation. Bellatrix's face, so recently/nflushed with happiness, had turned an ugly, blotchy/nred./n/n"She is no niece of ours, my Lord," she cried over the/noutpouring of mirth. "We — Narcissa and I — have/nnever set eyes on our sister since she married the/nMudblood. This brat has nothing to do with either of/nus, nor any beast she marries."/n/n"What say you, Draco?" asked Voldemort, and though/nhis voice was quiet, it carried clearly through the/ncatcalls and jeers. "Will you babysit the cubs?"/n/nThe hilarity mounted; Draco Malfoy looked in terror at/nhis father, who was staring down into his own lap,/nthen caught his mother's eye. She shook her head/nalmost imperceptibly, then resumed her own deadpan/nstare at the opposite wall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Enough," said Voldemort, stroking the angry snake./n"Enough."/n/nAnd the laughter died at once./n/n"Many of our oldest family trees become a little/ndiseased over time," he said as Bellatrix gazed at him,/nbreathless and imploring. "You must prune yours,/nmust you not, to keep it healthy? Cut away those/nparts that threaten the health of the rest."/n/n"Yes, my Lord," whispered Bellatrix, and her eyes/nswam with tears of gratitude again. "At the first/nchance!"/n/n"You shall have it," said Voldemort. "And in your/nfamily, so in the world . . . we shall cut away the/ncanker that infects us until only those of the true/nblood remain. ..."/n/nVoldemort raised Lucius Malfoy's wand, pointed it/ndirectly at the slowly revolving figure suspended over/nthe table, and gave it a tiny flick. The figure came to/nlife with a groan and began to struggle against/ninvisible bonds./n/n"Do you recognize our guest, Severus?" asked/nVoldemort./n/nSnape raised his eyes to the upside-down face. All of/nthe Death Eaters were looking up at the captive now,/nas though they had been given permission to show/ncuriosity. As she revolved to face the firelight, the/nwoman said in a cracked and terrified voice, "Severus!/nHelp me!"/n/n"Ah, yes," said Snape as the prisoner turned slowly/naway again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And you, Draco?" asked Voldemort, stroking the/nsnake's snout with his wand-free hand. Draco shook/nhis head jerkily. Now that the woman had woken, he/nseemed unable to look at her anymore./n/n"But you would not have taken her classes," said/nVoldemort. "For those of you who do not know, we are/njoined here tonight by Charity Burbage who, until/nrecently, taught at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and/nWizardry."/n/nThere were small noises of comprehension around the/ntable. A broad, hunched woman with pointed teeth/ncackled./n/n"Yes . . . Professor Burbage taught the children of/nwitches and wizards all about Muggles . . . how they/nare not so different from us ..."/n/nOne of the Death Eaters spat on the floor. Charity/nBurbage revolved to face Snape again./n/n"Severus ... please ... please ..."/n/n"Silence," said Voldemort, with another twitch of/nMalfoy's wand, and Charity fell silent as if gagged./n/n"Not content with corrupting and polluting the minds/nof Wizarding children, last week Professor Burbage/nwrote an impassioned defense of Mudbloods in the/nDaily Prophet Wizards, she says, must accept these/nthieves of their knowledge and magic. The dwindling/nof the purebloods is, says Professor Burbage, a most/ndesirable circumstance. ... She would have us all/nmate with Muggles ... or, no doubt, werewolves. ..."/n/nNobody laughed this time: There was no mistaking/nthe anger and contempt in Voldemort's voice. For the/nthird time, Charity Burbage revolved to face Snape./nTears were pouring from her eyes into her hair. Snape/n/n/n/n/n/nlooked back at her, quite impassive, as she turned/nslowly away from him again./n/n"Avada Kedavra."/n/nThe flash of green light illuminated every corner of the/nroom. Charity fell, with a resounding crash, onto the/ntable below, which trembled and creaked. Several of/nthe Death Eaters leapt back in their chairs. Draco fell/nout of his onto the floor./n/n"Dinner, Nagini," said Voldemort softly, and the great/nsnake swayed and slithered from his shoulders onto/nthe polished wood./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: In Memoriam
text: /nHarry was bleeding. Clutching his right hand in his/nleft and swearing under his breath, he shouldered/nopen his bedroom door. There was a crunch of/nbreaking china: He had trodden on a cup of cold tea/nthat had been sitting on the floor outside his bedroom/ndoor./n/n"What the — ?"/n/nHe looked around; the landing of number four, Privet/nDrive, was deserted. Possibly the cup of tea was/nDudley's idea of a clever booby trap. Keeping his/nbleeding hand elevated, Harry scraped the fragments/nof cup together with the other hand and threw them/ninto the already crammed bin just visible inside his/nbedroom door. Then he tramped across to the/nbathroom to run his finger under the tap./n/nIt was stupid, pointless, irritating beyond belief that/nhe still had four days left of being unable to perform/nmagic . . . but he had to admit to himself that this/njagged cut in his finger would have defeated him. He/n/n/n/n/nhad never learned how to repair wounds, and now he/ncame to think of it — particularly in light of his/nimmediate plans — this seemed a serious flaw in his/nmagical education. Making a mental note to ask/nHermione how it was done, he used a large wad of/ntoilet paper to mop up as much of the tea as he could,/nbefore returning to his bedroom and slamming the/ndoor behind him./n/nHarry had spent the morning completely emptying his/nschool trunk for the first time since he had packed it/nsix years ago. At the start of the intervening school/nyears, he had merely skimmed off the topmost three/nquarters of the contents and replaced or updated/nthem, leaving a layer of general debris at the bottom/n— old quills, desiccated beetle eyes, single socks that/nno longer fit. Minutes previously, Harry had plunged/nhis hand into this mulch, experienced a stabbing pain/nin the fourth finger of his right hand, and withdrawn/nit to see a lot of blood./n/nHe now proceeded a little more cautiously. Kneeling/ndown beside the trunk again, he groped around in the/nbottom and, after retrieving an old badge that/nflickered feebly between Support CEDRIC DIGGORY/nand POTTER STINKS , a cracked and worn-out/nSneakoscope, and a gold locket inside which a note/nsigned R.A.B. had been hidden, he finally discovered/nthe sharp edge that had done the damage. He/nrecognized it at once. It was a two-inch-long fragment/nof the enchanted mirror that his dead godfather,/nSirius, had given him. Harry laid it aside and felt/ncautiously around the trunk for the rest, but nothing/nmore remained of his godfather's last gift except/npowdered glass, which clung to the deepest layer of/ndebris like glittering grit./n/nHarry sat up and examined the jagged piece on which/nhe had cut himself, seeing nothing but his own bright/n/n/n/n/n/ngreen eye reflected back at him. Then he placed the/nfragment on top of that morning's Daily Prophet,/nwhich lay unread on the bed, and attempted to stem/nthe sudden upsurge of bitter memories, the stabs of/nregret and of longing the discovery of the broken/nmirror had occasioned, by attacking the rest of the/nrubbish in the trunk./n/nIt took another hour to empty it completely, throw/naway the useless items, and sort the remainder in/npiles according to whether or not he would need them/nfrom now on. His school and Quidditch robes,/ncauldron, parchment, quills, and most of his/ntextbooks were piled in a corner, to be left behind. He/nwondered what his aunt and uncle would do with/nthem; burn them in the dead of night, probably, as if/nthey were the evidence of some dreadful crime. His/nMuggle clothing, Invisibility Cloak, potion-making kit,/ncertain books, the photograph album Hagrid had once/ngiven him, a stack of letters, and his wand had been/nrepacked into an old rucksack. In a front pocket were/nthe Marauder's Map and the locket with the note/nsigned R.A.B. inside it. The locket was accorded this/nplace of honor not because it was valuable — in all/nusual senses it was worthless — but because of what/nit had cost to attain it./n/nThis left a sizable stack of newspapers sitting on his/ndesk beside his snowy owl, Hedwig: one for each of/nthe days Harry had spent at Privet Drive this/nsummer./n/nHe got up off the floor, stretched, and moved across to/nhis desk. Hedwig made no movement as he began to/nflick through the newspapers, throwing them onto the/nrubbish pile one by one. The owl was asleep, or else/nfaking; she was angry with Harry about the limited/namount of time she was allowed out of her cage at the/nmoment./n/n/n/n/n/nAs he neared the bottom of the pile of newspapers,/nHarry slowed down, searching for one particular issue/nthat he knew had arrived shortly after he had/nreturned to Privet Drive for the summer; he/nremembered that there had been a small mention on/nthe front about the resignation of Charity Burbage,/nthe Muggle Studies teacher at Hogwarts. At last he/nfound it. Turning to page ten, he sank into his desk/nchair and reread the article he had been looking for./n/nALBUS DUMBLEDORE REMEMBERED/n/nby Elphias Doge/n/nI met Albus Dumbledore at the age of eleven, on our/nfirst day at Hogwarts. Our mutual attraction was/nundoubtedly due to the fact that we both felt/nourselves to be outsiders. I had contracted dragon/npox shortly before arriving at school, and while I was/nno longer contagious, my pockmarked visage and/ngreenish hue did not encourage many to approach/nme. For his part, Albus had arrived at Hogwarts/nunder the burden of unwanted notoriety. Scarcely a/nyear previously, his father, Percival, had been/nconvicted of a savage and well-publicized attack upon/nthree young Muggles./n/nAlbus never attempted to deny that his father (who/nwas to die in Azkaban) had committed this crime; on/nthe contrary, when I plucked up courage to ask him, he/nassured me that he knew his father to be guilty./nBeyond that, Dumbledore refused to speak of the sad/nbusiness, though many attempted to make him do so./nSome, indeed, were disposed to praise his father's/naction and assumed that Albus too was a Muggle-/nhater. They could not have been more mistaken: As/nanybody who knew Albus would attest, he never/nrevealed the remotest anti-Muggle tendency. Indeed,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhis determined support for Muggle rights gained him/nmany enemies in subsequent years./n/nIn a matter of months, however, Albus's own fame/nhad begun to eclipse that of his father. By the end of/nhis first year he would never again be known as the/nson of a Muggle-hater, but as nothing more or less/nthan the most brilliant student ever seen at the/nschool. Those of us who were privileged to be his/nfriends benefited from his example, not to mention his/nhelp and encouragement, with which he was always/ngenerous. He confessed to me in later life that he/nknew even then that his greatest pleasure lay in/nteaching./n/nHe not only won every prize of note that the school/noffered, he was soon in regular correspondence with/nthe most notable magical names of the day, including/nNicolas Flamel, the celebrated alchemist ; Bathilda/nBagshot, the noted historian; and Adalbert Waffling,/nthe magical theoretician. Several of his papers found/ntheir way into learned publications such as/nTransfiguration Today, Challenges in Charming, and/nThe Practical Potioneer. Dumbledore's future career/nseemed likely to be meteoric, and the only question/nthat remained was when he would become Minister of/nMagic. Though it was often predicted in later years that/nhe was on the point of taking the job, however, he/nnever had Ministerial ambitions./n/nThree years after we had started at Hogwarts, Albus's/nbrother, Aberforth, arrived at school. They were not/nalike; Aberforth was never bookish and, unlike Albus,/npreferred to settle arguments by dueling rather than/nthrough reasoned discussion. However, it is quite/nwrong to suggest, as some have, that the brothers/nwere not friends. They rubbed along as comfortably as/ntwo such different boys could do. In fairness to/nAberforth, it must be admitted that living in Albus's/n/n/n/n/nshadow cannot have been an altogether comfortable/nexperience. Being continually outshone was an/noccupational hazard of being his friend and cannot/nhave been any more pleasurable as a brother./n/nWhen Albus and I left Hogwarts we intended to take/nthe then- traditional tour of the world together, visiting/nand observing foreign wizards, before pursuing our/nseparate careers. However, tragedy intervened. On the/nvery eve of our trip, Albus's mother, Kendra, died,/nleaving Albus the head, and sole breadwinner, of the/nfamily. I postponed my departure long enough to pay/nmy respects at Kendra's funeral, then left for what/nwas now to be a solitary journey. With a younger/nbrother and sister to care for, and little gold left to/nthem, there could no longer be any question of Albus/naccompanying me./n/nThat was the period of our lives when we had least/ncontact. I wrote to Albus, describing, perhaps/ninsensitively, the wonders of my journey, from narrow/nescapes from chimaeras in Greece to the experiments/nof the Egyptian alchemists. His letters told me little of/nhis day-to-day life, which I guessed to be frustratingly/ndull for such a brilliant wizard. Immersed in my own/nexperiences, it was with horror that I heard, toward/nthe end of my year's travels, that yet another tragedy/nhad struck the Dumbledores: the death of his sister,/nAriana./n/nThough Ariana had been in poor health for a long/ntime, the blow, coming so soon after the loss of their/nmother, had a profound effect on both of her/nbrothers. All those closest to Albus — and I count/nmyself one of that lucky number — agree that/nAriana 's death, and Albus's feeling of personal/nresponsibility for it (though, of course, he was/nguiltless), left their mark upon him forevermore./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nI returned home to find a young man who had/nexperienced a much older person's suffering. Albus/nwas more reserved than before, and much less light-/nhearted. To add to his misery, the loss of Ariana had/nled, not to a renewed closeness between Albus and/nAberforth, but to an estrangement. (In time this would/nlift — in later years they reestablished, if not a close/nrelationship, then certainly a cordial one.) However,/nhe rarely spoke of his parents or of Ariana from then/non, and his friends learned not to mention them./n/nOther quills will describe the triumphs of the following/nyears. Dumbledore's innumerable contributions to the/nstore of Wizarding knowledge, including his discovery/nof the twelve uses of dragon's blood, will benefit/ngenerations to come, as will the wisdom he displayed/nin the many judgments he made while Chief Warlock of/nthe Wizengamot. They say, still, that no Wizarding duel/never matched that between Dumbledore and/nGrindelwald in 1 945. Those who witnessed it have/nwritten of the terror and the awe they felt as they/nwatched these two extraordinary wizards do battle./nDumbledore's triumph, and its consequences for the/nWizarding world, are considered a turning point in/nmagical history to match the introduction of the/nInternational Statute of Secrecy or the downfall of He-/nWho-Must-Not-Be-Named./n/nAlbus Dumbledore was never proud or vain; he could/nfind something to value in anyone, however/napparently insignificant or wretched, and I believe/nthat his early losses endowed him with great/nhumanity and sympathy. I shall miss his friendship/nmore than I can say, but my loss is as nothing/ncompared to the Wizarding world's. That he was the/nmost inspiring and the best loved of all Hogwarts/nheadmasters cannot be in question. He died as he/nlived: working always for the greater good and, to his/nlast hour, as willing to stretch out a hand to a small/n/n/n/n/nboy with dragon pox as he was on the day that I met/nhim./n/nHarry finished reading but continued to gaze at the/npicture accompanying the obituary. Dumbledore was/nwearing his familiar, kindly smile, but as he peered/nover the top of his half-moon spectacles, he gave the/nimpression, even in newsprint, of X-raying Harry,/nwhose sadness mingled with a sense of humiliation./n/nHe had thought he knew Dumbledore quite well, but/never since reading this obituary he had been forced to/nrecognize that he had barely known him at all. Never/nonce had he imagined Dumbledore 's childhood or/nyouth; it was as though he had sprung into being as/nHarry had known him, venerable and silver-haired/nand old. The idea of a teenage Dumbledore was/nsimply odd, like trying to imagine a stupid Hermione/nor a friendly Blast-Ended Skrewt./n/nHe had never thought to ask Dumbledore about his/npast. No doubt it would have felt strange, impertinent/neven, but after all, it had been common knowledge/nthat Dumbledore had taken part in that legendary/nduel with Grindelwald, and Harry had not thought to/nask Dumbledore what that had been like, nor about/nany of his other famous achievements. No, they had/nalways discussed Harry, Harry's past, Harry's future,/nHarry's plans ... and it seemed to Harry now, despite/nthe fact that his future was so dangerous and so/nuncertain, that he had missed irreplaceable/nopportunities when he had failed to ask Dumbledore/nmore about himself, even though the only personal/nquestion he had ever asked his headmaster was also/nthe only one he suspected that Dumbledore had not/nanswered honestly:/n/n" What do you see when you look in the mirror?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"/? I see myself holding a pair of thick, woolen socks."/n/nAfter several minutes' thought, Harry tore the/nobituary out of the Prophet, folded it carefully, and/ntucked it inside the first volume of Practical Defensive/nMagic and Its Use Against the Dark Arts. Then he/nthrew the rest of the newspaper onto the rubbish pile/nand turned to face the room. It was much tidier. The/nonly things left out of place were today's Daily/nProphet, still lying on the bed, and on top of it, the/npiece of broken mirror./n/nHarry moved across the room, slid the mirror/nfragment off today's Prophet, and unfolded the/nnewspaper. He had merely glanced at the headline/nwhen he had taken the rolled-up paper from the/ndelivery owl early that morning and thrown it aside,/nafter noting that it said nothing about Voldemort./nHarry was sure that the Ministry was leaning on the/nProphet to suppress news about Voldemort. It was/nonly now, therefore, that he saw what he had missed./n/nAcross the bottom half of the front page a smaller/nheadline was set over a picture of Dumbledore/nstriding along looking harried:/n/nDUMBLEDORE — THE TRUTH AT LAST?/n/nComing next week, the shocking story of the flawed/ngenius considered by many to be the greatest wizard/nof his generation. Stripping away the popular image of/nserene, silver-bearded wisdom, Rita Skeeter reveals/nthe disturbed childhood, the lawless youth, the/nlifelong feuds, and the guilty secrets that Dumbledore/ncarried to his grave. WHY was the man tipped to be/nMinister of Magic content to remain a mere/nheadmaster? WHAT was the real purpose of the secret/norganization known as the Order of the Phoenix?/n/nHOW did Dumbledore really meet his end?/n/n/n/n/n/nThe answers to these and many more questions are/nexplored in the explosive new biography, The Life and/nLies of Albus Dumbledore, by Rita Skeeter, exclusively/ninterviewed by Betty Braithwaite, page 13, inside./n/nHarry ripped open the paper and found page thirteen./nThe article was topped with a picture showing/nanother familiar face: a woman wearing jeweled/nglasses with elaborately curled blonde hair, her teeth/nbared in what was clearly supposed to be a winning/nsmile, wiggling her fingers up at him. Doing his best/nto ignore this nauseating image, Harry read on./n/nIn person, Rita Skeeter is much warmer and softer/nthan her famously ferocious quill-portraits might/nsuggest. Greeting me in the hallway of her cozy home,/nshe leads me straight into the kitchen for a cup of tea,/na slice of pound cake and, it goes without saying, a/nsteaming vat of freshest gossip./n/n"Well, of course, Dumbledore is a biographer's dream,"/nsays Skeeter. "Such a long, full life. I'm sure my book/nwill be the first of very, very many."/n/nSkeeter was certainly quick off the mark. Her nine-/nhundred-page book was completed a mere four weeks/nafter Dumbledore 's mysterious death in June. I ask/nher how she managed this superfast feat./n/n"Oh, when you've been a journalist as long as I have,/nworking to a deadline is second nature. I knew that/nthe Wizarding world was clamoring for the full story/nand I wanted to be the first to meet that need."/n/nI mention the recent, widely publicized remarks of/nElphias Doge, Special Advisor to the Wizengamot and/nlongstanding friend of Albus Dumbledore's, that/n"Skeeter's book contains less fact than a Chocolate/nFrog card. "/n/n/n/n/n/nSkeeter throws back her head and laughs./n/n/n/n"Darling Dodgy! I remember interviewing him a few/nyears back about merpeople rights, bless him./nCompletely gaga, seemed to think we were sitting at/nthe bottom of Lake Windermere, kept telling me to/nwatch out for trout."/n/nAnd yet Elphias Doge's accusations of inaccuracy/nhave been echoed in many places. Does Skeeter really/nfeel that four short weeks have been enough to gain a/nfull picture of Dumbledore's long and extraordinary/nlife?/n/n"Oh, my dear," beams Skeeter, rapping me/naffectionately across the knuckles, "you know as well/nas I do how much information can be generated by a/nfat bag of Galleons, a refusal to hear the word 'no,'/nand a nice sharp Quick-Quotes Quill! People were/nqueuing to dish the dirt on Dumbledore anyway. Not/neveryone thought he was so wonderful, you know —/nhe trod on an awful lot of important toes. But old/nDodgy Doge can get off his high hippogriff, because/nI've had access to a source most journalists would/nswap their wands for, one who has never spoken in/npublic before and who was close to Dumbledore/nduring the most turbulent and disturbing phase of/nhis youth."/n/nThe advance publicity for Skeeter' s biography has/ncertainly suggested that there will be shocks in store/nfor those who believe Dumbledore to have led a/nblameless life. What were the biggest surprises she/nuncovered, I ask?/n/n"Now, come off it, Betty, I'm not giving away all the/nhighlights before anybody's bought the book!" laughs/nSkeeter. "But I can promise that anybody who still/nthinks Dumbledore was white as his beard is in for a/n/n/n/n/n/nrude awakening! Let's just say that nobody hearing/nhim rage against You-Know-Who would have dreamed/nthat he dabbled in the Dark Arts himself in his youth!/nAnd for a wizard who spent his later years pleading/nfor tolerance, he wasn't exactly broad-minded when/nhe was younger! Yes, Albus Dumbledore had an/nextremely murky past, not to mention that very fishy/nfamily, which he worked so hard to keep hushed up."/n/nI ask whether Skeeter is referring to Dumbledore 's/nbrother, Aberforth, whose conviction by the/nWizengamot for misuse of magic caused a minor/nscandal fifteen years ago./n/n"Oh, Aberforth is just the tip of the dung heap, " laughs/nSkeeter. "No, no, I'm talking about much worse than a/nbrother with a fondness for fiddling about with goats,/nworse even than the Muggle-maiming father —/nDumbledore couldn't keep either of them quiet anyway,/nthey were both charged by the Wizengamot. No, it's the/nmother and the sister that intrigued me, and a little/ndigging uncovered a positive nest of nastiness — but,/nas I say, you'll have to wait for chapters nine to twelve/nfor full details. All I can say now is, it's no wonder/nDumbledore never talked about how his nose got/nbroken. "/n/nFamily skeletons notwithstanding, does Skeeter deny/nthe brilliance that led to Dumbledore 's many magical/ndiscoveries?/n/n"He had brains," she concedes, "although many now/nquestion whether he could really take full credit for all/nof his supposed achievements. As I reveal in chapter/nsixteen, Ivor Dillonsby claims he had already/ndiscovered eight uses of dragon's blood when/nDumbledore 'borrowed' his papers."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut the importance of some of Dumbledore's/nachievements cannot, I venture, be denied. What of/nhis famous defeat of Grindelwald?/n/n"Oh, now, I'm glad you mentioned Grindelwald," says/nSkeeter with a tantalizing smile. "I'm afraid those who/ngo dewy-eyed over Dumbledore's spectacular victory/nmust brace themselves for a bombshell — or perhaps/na Dungbomb. Very dirty business indeed. All I'll say/nis, don't be so sure that there really was the/nspectacular duel of legend. After they've read my/nbook, people may be forced to conclude that/nGrindelwald simply conjured a white handkerchief/nfrom the end of his wand and came quietly!"/n/nSkeeter refuses to give any more away on this/nintriguing subject, so we turn instead to the/nrelationship that will undoubtedly fascinate her/nreaders more than any other./n/n"Oh yes," says Skeeter, nodding briskly, "I devote an/nentire chapter to the whole Potter-Dumbledore/nrelationship. It's been called unhealthy, even sinister./nAgain, your readers will have to buy my book for the/nwhole story, but there is no question that/nDumbledore took an unnatural interest in Potter from/nthe word go. Whether that was really in the boy's best/ninterests — well, we'll see. It's certainly an open secret/nthat Potter has had a most troubled adolescence."/n/nI ask whether Skeeter is still in touch with Harry/nPotter, whom she so famously interviewed last year: a/nbreakthrough piece in which Potter spoke exclusively/nof his conviction that You-Know-Who had returned./n/n"Oh, yes, we've developed a close bond," says Skeeter./n"Poor Potter has few real friends, and we met at one of/nthe most testing moments of his life — the Triwizard/nTournament. I am probably one of the only people/n/n/n/n/n/nalive who can say that they know the real Harry/nPotter."/n/nWhich leads us neatly to the many rumors still/ncirculating about Dumbledore's final hours. Does/nSkeeter believe that Potter was there when/nDumbledore died?/n/n"Well, I don't want to say too much — it's all in the/nbook — but eyewitnesses inside Hogwarts castle saw/nPotter running away from the scene moments after/nDumbledore fell, jumped, or was pushed. Potter later/ngave evidence against Severus Snape, a man against/nwhom he has a notorious grudge. Is everything as it/nseems? That is for the Wizarding community to decide/n— once they've read my book."/n/nOn that intriguing note, I take my leave. There can be/nno doubt that Skeeter has quilled an instant/nbestseller. Dumbledore's legions of admirers,/nmeanwhile, may well be trembling at what is soon to/nemerge about their hero./n/nHarry reached the bottom of the article, but/ncontinued to stare blankly at the page. Revulsion and/nfury rose in him like vomit; he balled up the/nnewspaper and threw it, with all his force, at the wall,/nwhere it joined the rest of the rubbish heaped around/nhis overflowing bin./n/nHe began to stride blindly around the room, opening/nempty drawers and picking up books only to replace/nthem on the same piles, barely conscious of what he/nwas doing, as random phrases from Rita's article/nechoed in his head: An entire chapter to the whole/nPotter-Dumbledore relationship . . . It's been called/nunhealthy, even sinister. . . . He dabbled in the Dark/nArts himself in his youth . . . I've had access to a source/nmost journalists would swap their wands for .../n/n/n/n/n/n"Lies!" Harry bellowed, and through the window he/nsaw the next-door neighbor, who had paused to/nrestart his lawn mower, look up nervously./n/nHarry sat down hard on the bed. The broken bit of/nmirror danced away from him; he picked it up and/nturned it over in his fingers, thinking, thinking of/nDumbledore and the lies with which Rita Skeeter was/ndefaming him. .../n/nA flash of brightest blue. Harry froze, his cut finger/nslipping on the jagged edge of the mirror again. He/nhad imagined it, he must have done. He glanced over/nhis shoulder, but the wall was a sickly peach color of/nAunt Petunia's choosing: There was nothing blue/nthere for the mirror to reflect. He peered into the/nmirror fragment again, and saw nothing but his own/nbright green eye looking back at him./n/nHe had imagined it, there was no other explanation;/nimagined it, because he had been thinking of his dead/nheadmaster. If anything was certain, it was that the/nbright blue eyes of Albus Dumbledore would never/npierce him again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n3/n/n/n/n

title: The Dursleys Departing
text: /nThe sound of the front door slamming echoed up the/nstairs and a voice yelled, "Oi! You!"/n/nSixteen years of being addressed thus left Harry in no/ndoubt whom his uncle was calling; nevertheless, he/ndid not immediately respond. He was still gazing at/nthe mirror fragment in which, for a split second, he/nhad thought he saw Dumbledore's eye. It was not/nuntil his uncle bellowed, "BOY!" that Harry got slowly/nto his feet and headed for the bedroom door, pausing/nto add the piece of broken mirror to the rucksack/nfilled with things he would be taking with him./n/n"You took your time!" roared Vernon Dursley when/nHarry appeared at the top of the stairs. "Get down/nhere, I want a word!"/n/nHarry strolled downstairs, his hands deep in his jeans/npockets. When he reached the living room he found/nall three Dursleys. They were dressed for traveling:/nUncle Vernon in a fawn zip-up jacket, Aunt Petunia in/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/na neat salmon-colored coat, and Dudley, Harry's/nlarge, blond, muscular cousin, in his leather jacket./n/n/n/n"Yes?" asked Harry./n/n"Sit down!" said Uncle Vernon. Harry raised his/neyebrows. "Please!" added Uncle Vernon, wincing/nslightly as though the word was sharp in his throat./n/nHarry sat. He thought he knew what was coming. His/nuncle began to pace up and down, Aunt Petunia and/nDudley following his movements with anxious/nexpressions. Finally, his large purple face crumpled/nwith concentration, Uncle Vernon stopped in front of/nHarry and spoke./n/n"I've changed my mind," he said./n/n"What a surprise," said Harry./n/n"Don't you take that tone — " began Aunt Petunia in a/nshrill voice, but Vernon Dursley waved her down./n/n"It's all a lot of claptrap," said Uncle Vernon, glaring/nat Harry with piggy little eyes. "I've decided I don't/nbelieve a word of it. We're staying put, we're not going/nanywhere."/n/nHarry looked up at his uncle and felt a mixture of/nexasperation and amusement. Vernon Dursley had/nbeen changing his mind every twenty-four hours for/nthe past four weeks, packing and unpacking and/nrepacking the car with every change of heart. Harry's/nfavorite moment had been the one when Uncle/nVernon, unaware that Dudley had added his/ndumbbells to his case since the last time it had been/nunpacked, had attempted to hoist it back into the/nboot and collapsed with roars of pain and much/nswearing./n/n/n/n/n/n"According to you," Vernon Dursley said now,/nresuming his pacing up and down the living room,/n"we — Petunia, Dudley, and I — are in danger. From/n/n/n/n— from — "/n/n/n/n"Some of 'my lot,' right," said Harry./n/n"Well, I don't believe it," repeated Uncle Vernon,/ncoming to a halt in front of Harry again. "I was awake/nhalf the night thinking it all over, and I believe it's a/nplot to get the house."/n/n"The house?" repeated Harry. "What house?"/n/n" This house!" shrieked Uncle Vernon, the vein in his/nforehead starting to pulse. "Our house! House prices/nare skyrocketing around here! You want us out of the/nway and then you're going to do a bit of hocus-pocus/nand before we know it the deeds will be in your name/nand — "/n/n"Are you out of your mind?" demanded Harry. "A plot/nto get this house? Are you actually as stupid as you/nlook?"/n/n"Don't you dare — !" squealed Aunt Petunia, but/nagain, Vernon waved her down: Slights on his/npersonal appearance were, it seemed, as nothing to/nthe danger he had spotted./n/n"Just in case you've forgotten," said Harry, "I've/nalready got a house, my godfather left me one. So why/nwould I want this one? All the happy memories?"/n/nThere was silence. Harry thought he had rather/nimpressed his uncle with this argument./n/n"You claim," said Uncle Vernon, starting to pace yet/nagain, "that this Lord Thing — "/n/n/n/n/n/n" — Voldemort," said Harry impatiently, "and we've/nbeen through this about a hundred times already./n/nThis isn't a claim, it's fact, Dumbledore told you last/nyear, and Kingsley and Mr. Weasley — "/n/nVernon Dursley hunched his shoulders angrily, and/nHarry guessed that his uncle was attempting to ward/noff recollections of the unannounced visit, a few days/ninto Harry's summer holidays, of two fully grown/nwizards. The arrival on the doorstep of Kingsley/nShacklebolt and Arthur Weasley had come as a most/nunpleasant shock to the Dursleys. Harry had to/nadmit, however, that as Mr. Weasley had once/ndemolished half of the living room, his reappearance/ncould not have been expected to delight Uncle/nVernon./n/n" — Kingsley and Mr. Weasley explained it all as well,"/nHarry pressed on remorselessly. "Once I'm seventeen,/nthe protective charm that keeps me safe will break,/nand that exposes you as well as me. The Order is sure/nVoldemort will target you, whether to torture you to/ntry and find out where I am, or because he thinks by/nholding you hostage I'd come and try to rescue you."/n/nUncle Vernon's and Harry's eyes met. Harry was sure/nthat in that instant they were both wondering the/nsame thing. Then Uncle Vernon walked on and Harry/nresumed, "You've got to go into hiding and the Order/nwants to help. You're being offered serious protection,/nthe best there is."/n/nUncle Vernon said nothing, but continued to pace up/nand down. Outside the sun hung low over the privet/nhedges. The next-door neighbor's lawn mower stalled/nagain./n/n"I thought there was a Ministry of Magic?" asked/nVernon Dursley abruptly./n/n/n/n/n/n"There is," said Harry, surprised./n/n/n/n"Well, then, why can't they protect us? It seems to me/nthat, as innocent victims, guilty of nothing more than/nharboring a marked man, we ought to qualify for/ngovernment protection!"/n/nHarry laughed; he could not help himself. It was so/nvery typical of his uncle to put his hopes in the/nestablishment, even within this world that he/ndespised and mistrusted./n/n"You heard what Mr. Weasley and Kingsley said,"/nHarry replied. "We think the Ministry has been/ninfiltrated."/n/nUncle Vernon strode to the fireplace and back,/nbreathing so heavily that his great black mustache/nrippled, his face still purple with concentration./n/n"All right," he said, stopping in front of Harry yet/nagain. "All right, let's say, for the sake of argument,/nwe accept this protection. I still don't see why we can't/nhave that Kingsley bloke."/n/nHarry managed not to roll his eyes, but with difficulty./nThis question had also been addressed half a dozen/ntimes./n/n"As I've told you," he said through gritted teeth,/n"Kingsley is protecting the Mug — I mean, your Prime/nMinister."/n/n"Exactly — he's the best!" said Uncle Vernon, pointing/nat the blank television screen. The Dursleys had/nspotted Kingsley on the news, walking along/ndiscreetly behind the Muggle Prime Minister as he/nvisited a hospital. This, and the fact that Kingsley had/nmastered the knack of dressing like a Muggle, not to/n/n/n/n/nmention a certain reassuring something in his slow,/ndeep voice, had caused the Dursleys to take to/nKingsley in a way that they had certainly not done/nwith any other wizard, although it was true that they/nhad never seen him with his earring in./n/n"Well, he's taken," said Harry. "But Hestia Jones and/nDedalus Diggle are more than up to the job — "/n/n"If we'd even seen CVs ..." began Uncle Vernon, but/nHarry lost patience. Getting to his feet, he advanced/non his uncle, now pointing at the TV set himself./n/n"These accidents aren't accidents — the crashes and/nexplosions and derailments and whatever else has/nhappened since we last watched the news. People are/ndisappearing and dying and he's behind it —/nVoldemort. I've told you this over and over again, he/nkills Muggles for fun. Even the fogs — they're caused/nby dementors, and if you can't remember what they/nare, ask your son!"/n/nDudley's hands jerked upward to cover his mouth./nWith his parents' and Harry's eyes upon him, he/nslowly lowered them again and asked, "There are . . ./nmore of them?"/n/n"More?" laughed Harry. "More than the two that/nattacked us, you mean? Of course there are, there are/nhundreds, maybe thousands by this time, seeing as/nthey feed off fear and despair — "/n/n"All right, all right," blustered Vernon Dursley./n/n"You've made your point — "/n/n"I hope so," said Harry, "because once I'm seventeen,/nall of them — Death Eaters, dementors, maybe even/nInferi — which means dead bodies enchanted by a/nDark wizard — will be able to find you and will/n/n/n/n/n/ncertainly attack you. And if you remember the last/ntime you tried to outrun wizards, I think you 11 agree/nyou need help."/n/nThere was a brief silence in which the distant echo of/nHagrid smashing down a wooden front door seemed/nto reverberate through the intervening years. Aunt/nPetunia was looking at Uncle Vernon; Dudley was/nstaring at Harry. Finally Uncle Vernon blurted out,/n"But what about my work? What about Dudley's/nschool? I don't suppose those things matter to a/nbunch of layabout wizards — "/n/n"Don't you understand?" shouted Harry. "They will/ntorture and kill you like they did my parents !"/n/n"Dad," said Dudley in a loud voice, "Dad — I'm going/nwith these Order people."/n/n"Dudley," said Harry, "for the first time in your life,/nyou're talking sense."/n/nHe knew that the battle was won. If Dudley was/nfrightened enough to accept the Order's help, his/nparents would accompany him: There could be no/nquestion of being separated from their Diddykins./nHarry glanced at the carriage clock on the/nmantelpiece./n/n"They'll be here in about five minutes," he said, and/nwhen none of the Dursleys replied, he left the room./nThe prospect of parting — probably forever — from/nhis aunt, uncle, and cousin was one that he was able/nto contemplate quite cheerfully, but there was/nnevertheless a certain awkwardness in the air. What/ndid you say to one another at the end of sixteen years'/nsolid dislike?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBack in his bedroom, Harry fiddled aimlessly with his/nrucksack, then poked a couple of owl nuts through/nthe bars of Hedwig's cage. They fell with dull thuds to/nthe bottom, where she ignored them./n/n"We're leaving soon, really soon," Harry told her. "And/nthen you'll be able to fly again."/n/nThe doorbell rang. Harry hesitated, then headed back/nout of his room and downstairs. It was too much to/nexpect Hestia and Dedalus to cope with the Dursleys/non their own./n/n"Harry Potter!" squeaked an excited voice, the/nmoment Harry had opened the door; a small man in a/nmauve top hat was sweeping him a deep bow. "An/nhonor, as ever!"/n/n"Thanks, Dedalus," said Harry, bestowing a small and/nembarrassed smile upon the dark-haired Hestia. "It's/nreally good of you to do this. ... They're through here,/nmy aunt and uncle and cousin. ..."/n/n"Good day to you, Harry Potter's relatives!" said/nDedalus happily, striding into the living room. The/nDursleys did not look at all happy to be addressed/nthus; Harry half expected another change of mind./nDudley shrank nearer to his mother at the sight of/nthe witch and wizard./n/n"I see you are packed and ready. Excellent! The plan,/nas Harry has told you, is a simple one," said Dedalus,/npulling an immense pocket watch out of his waistcoat/nand examining it. "We shall be leaving before Harry/ndoes. Due to the danger of using magic in your house/n— Harry being still underage, it could provide the/nMinistry with an excuse to arrest him — we shall be/ndriving, say, ten miles or so, before Disapparating to/nthe safe location we have picked out for you. You/n/n/n/n/nknow how to drive, I take it?" he asked Uncle Vernon/npolitely./n/n"Know how to — ? Of course I ruddy well know how to/ndrive!" spluttered Uncle Vernon./n/n"Very clever of you, sir, very clever, I personally would/nbe utterly bamboozled by all those buttons and/nknobs," said Dedalus. He was clearly under the/nimpression that he was flattering Vernon Dursley,/nwho was visibly losing confidence in the plan with/nevery word Dedalus spoke./n/n"Can't even drive," he muttered under his breath, his/nmustache rippling indignantly, but fortunately neither/nDedalus nor Hestia seemed to hear him./n/n"You, Harry," Dedalus continued, "will wait here for/nyour guard. There has been a little change in the/narrangements — "/n/n"What d'you mean?" said Harry at once. "I thought/nMad-Eye was going to come and take me by Side-/nAlong- Apparition?"/n/n"Can't do it," said Hestia tersely. "Mad-Eye will/nexplain."/n/nThe Dursleys, who had listened to all of this with/nlooks of utter incomprehension on their faces, jumped/nas a loud voice screeched, "Hurry up\" Harry looked/nall around the room before realizing that the voice/nhad issued from Dedalus's pocket watch./n/n"Quite right, we're operating to a very tight schedule,"/nsaid Dedalus, nodding at his watch and tucking it/nback into his waistcoat. "We are attempting to time/nyour departure from the house with your family's/nDisapparition, Harry; thus, the charm breaks at the/n/n/n/n/nmoment you all head for safety." He turned to the/nDursleys. "Well, are we all packed and ready to go?"/n/nNone of them answered him. Uncle Vernon was still/nstaring, appalled, at the bulge in Dedalus's waistcoat/npocket./n/n"Perhaps we should wait outside in the hall,/n/nDedalus," murmured Hestia. She clearly felt that it/nwould be tactless for them to remain in the room/nwhile Harry and the Dursleys exchanged loving,/npossibly tearful farewells./n/n"There's no need," Harry muttered, but Uncle Vernon/nmade any further explanation unnecessary by saying/nloudly,/n/n"Well, this is good-bye, then, boy."/n/nHe swung his right arm upward to shake Harry's/nhand, but at the last moment seemed unable to face/nit, and merely closed his fist and began swinging it/nbackward and forward like a metronome./n/n"Ready, Diddy?" asked Aunt Petunia, fussily checking/nthe clasp of her handbag so as to avoid looking at/nHarry altogether./n/nDudley did not answer, but stood there with his/nmouth slightly ajar, reminding Harry a little of the/ngiant, Grawp./n/n"Come along, then," said Uncle Vernon./n/nHe had already reached the living room door when/nDudley mumbled, "I don't understand."/n/n"What don't you understand, popkin?" asked Aunt/nPetunia, looking up at her son./n/n/n/n/n/nDudley raised a large, hamlike hand to point at/nHarry./n/n"Why isn't he coming with us?"/n/nUncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia froze where they/nstood, staring at Dudley as though he had just/nexpressed a desire to become a ballerina./n/n"What?" said Uncle Vernon loudly./n/n"Why isn't he coming too?" asked Dudley./n/n"Well, he — he doesn't want to," said Uncle Vernon,/nturning to glare at Harry and adding, "You don't want/nto, do you?"/n/n"Not in the slightest," said Harry./n/n"There you are," Uncle Vernon told Dudley. "Now/ncome on, we're off."/n/nHe marched out of the room. They heard the front/ndoor open, but Dudley did not move and after a few/nfaltering steps Aunt Petunia stopped too./n/n"What now?" barked Uncle Vernon, reappearing in the/ndoorway./n/nIt seemed that Dudley was struggling with concepts/ntoo difficult to put into words. After several moments/nof apparently painful internal struggle he said, "But/nwhere's he going to go?"/n/nAunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon looked at each other./nIt was clear that Dudley was frightening them. Hestia/nJones broke the silence./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But . . . surely you know where your nephew is/ngoing?" she asked, looking bewildered./n/n"Certainly we know," said Vernon Dursley. "He's off/nwith some of your lot, isn't he? Right, Dudley, let's get/nin the car, you heard the man, we're in a hurry."/n/nAgain, Vernon Dursley marched as far as the front/ndoor, but Dudley did not follow./n/n"Off with some of our lot?"/n/nHestia looked outraged. Harry had met this attitude/nbefore: Witches and wizards seemed stunned that his/nclosest living relatives took so little interest in the/nfamous Harry Potter./n/n"It's fine," Harry assured her. "It doesn't matter,/nhonestly."/n/n"Doesn't matter?" repeated Hestia, her voice rising/nominously. "Don't these people realize what you've/nbeen through? What danger you are in? The unique/nposition you hold in the hearts of the anti-Voldemort/nmovement?"/n/n"Er — no, they don't," said Harry. "They think I'm a/nwaste of space, actually, but I'm used to — "/n/n"I don't think you're a waste of space."/n/nIf Harry had not seen Dudley's lips move, he might/nnot have believed it. As it was, he stared at Dudley for/nseveral seconds before accepting that it must have/nbeen his cousin who had spoken; for one thing,/n/nDudley had turned red. Harry was embarrassed and/nastonished himself./n/n"Well ... er ... thanks, Dudley."/n/n/n/n/n/nAgain, Dudley appeared to grapple with thoughts too/nunwieldy for expression before mumbling, "You saved/nmy life."/n/n"Not really," said Harry. "It was your soul the/ndementor would have taken. ..."/n/nHe looked curiously at his cousin. They had had/nvirtually no contact during this summer or last, as/nHarry had come back to Privet Drive so briefly and/nkept to his room so much. It now dawned on Harry,/nhowever, that the cup of cold tea on which he had/ntrodden that morning might not have been a booby/ntrap at all. Although rather touched, he was/nnevertheless quite relieved that Dudley appeared to/nhave exhausted his ability to express his feelings./nAfter opening his mouth once or twice more, Dudley/nsubsided into scarlet-faced silence./n/nAunt Petunia burst into tears. Hestia Jones gave her/nan approving look that changed to outrage as Aunt/nPetunia ran forward and embraced Dudley rather/nthan Harry./n/n"S-so sweet, Dudders ..." she sobbed into his massive/nchest. "S-such a lovely b-boy ... s-saying thank you/n/n/n/n"But he hasn't said thank you at all!" said Hestia/nindignantly. "He only said he didn't think Harry was a/nwaste of space!"/n/n"Yeah, but coming from Dudley that's like 'I love you,'/n" said Harry, torn between annoyance and a desire to/nlaugh as Aunt Petunia continued to clutch at Dudley/nas if he had just saved Harry from a burning building./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Are we going or not?" roared Uncle Vernon,/nreappearing yet again at the living room door. "I/nthought we were on a tight schedule!"/n/n"Yes — yes, we are," said Dedalus Diggle, who had/nbeen watching these exchanges with an air of/nbemusement and now seemed to pull himself/ntogether. "We really must be off. Harry — "/n/nHe tripped forward and wrung Harry's hand with both/nof his own./n/n" — good luck. I hope we meet again. The hopes of the/nWizarding world rest upon your shoulders."/n/n"Oh," said Harry, "right. Thanks."/n/n"Farewell, Harry," said Hestia, also clasping his hand./n"Our thoughts go with you."/n/n"I hope everything's okay," said Harry with a glance/ntoward Aunt Petunia and Dudley./n/n"Oh, I'm sure we shall end up the best of chums,"/nsaid Diggle brightly, waving his hat as he left the/nroom. Hestia followed him./n/nDudley gently released himself from his mother's/nclutches and walked toward Harry, who had to/nrepress an urge to threaten him with magic. Then/nDudley held out his large, pink hand./n/n"Blimey, Dudley," said Harry over Aunt Petunia's/nrenewed sobs, "did the dementors blow a different/npersonality into you?"/n/n"Dunno," muttered Dudley. "See you, Harry."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah ..." said Harry, taking Dudley's hand and/nshaking it. "Maybe. Take care, Big D."/n/nDudley nearly smiled, then lumbered from the room./nHarry heard his heavy footfalls on the graveled drive,/nand then a car door slammed./n/nAunt Petunia, whose face had been buried in her/nhandkerchief, looked around at the sound. She did/nnot seem to have expected to find herself alone with/nHarry. Hastily stowing her wet handkerchief into her/npocket, she said, "Well — good-bye," and marched/ntoward the door without looking at him./n/n"Good-bye," said Harry./n/nShe stopped and looked back. For a moment Harry/nhad the strangest feeling that she wanted to say/nsomething to him: She gave him an odd, tremulous/nlook and seemed to teeter on the edge of speech, but/nthen, with a little jerk of her head, she bustled out of/nthe room after her husband and son./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Seven Potters
text: /nHarry ran back upstairs to his bedroom, arriving at/nthe window just in time to see the Dursleys' car/nswinging out of the drive and off up the road./nDedalus's top hat was visible between Aunt Petunia/nand Dudley in the backseat. The car turned right at/nthe end of Privet Drive, its windows burned scarlet for/na moment in the now setting sun, and then it was/ngone./n/nHarry picked up Hedwig's cage, his Firebolt, and his/nrucksack, gave his unnaturally tidy bedroom one last/nsweeping look, and then made his ungainly way back/ndownstairs to the hall, where he deposited cage,/nbroomstick, and bag near the foot of the stairs. The/nlight was fading rapidly now, the hall full of shadows/nin the evening light. It felt most strange to stand here/nin the silence and know that he was about to leave/nthe house for the last time. Long ago, when he had/nbeen left alone while the Dursleys went out to enjoy/nthemselves, the hours of solitude had been a rare/ntreat: Pausing only to sneak something tasty from the/nfridge, he had rushed upstairs to play on Dudley's/n/n/n/n/ncomputer, or put on the television and flicked through/nthe channels to his heart's content.
