It gave him an/nodd, empty feeling to remember those times; it was/nlike remembering a younger brother whom he had/nlost./n/n"Don't you want to take a last look at the place?" he/nasked Hedwig, who was still sulking with her head/nunder her wing. "We'll never be here again. Don't you/nwant to remember all the good times? I mean, look at/nthis doormat. What memories ... Dudley puked on it/nafter I saved him from the dementors. ... Turns out he/nwas grateful after all, can you believe it? ... And last/nsummer, Dumbledore walked through that front door./n/n/n/nHarry lost the thread of his thoughts for a moment/nand Hedwig did nothing to help him retrieve it, but/ncontinued to sit with her head under her wing. Harry/nturned his back on the front door./n/n"And under here, Hedwig" — Harry pulled open a door/nunder the stairs — "is where I used to sleep! You/nnever knew me then — Blimey, it's small, I'd/nforgotten. ..."/n/nHarry looked around at the stacked shoes and/numbrellas, remembering how he used to wake every/nmorning looking up at the underside of the staircase,/nwhich was more often than not adorned with a spider/nor two. Those had been the days before he had known/nanything about his true identity; before he had found/nout how his parents had died or why such strange/nthings often happened around him. But Harry could/nstill remember the dreams that had dogged him, even/nin those days: confused dreams involving flashes of/ngreen light and once — Uncle Vernon had nearly/ncrashed the car when Harry had recounted it — a/nflying motorbike . . ./n/n/n/n/n/nThere was a sudden, deafening roar from somewhere/nnearby. Harry straightened up with a jerk and/nsmacked the top of his head on the low door frame./nPausing only to employ a few of Uncle Vernon's/nchoicest swear words, he staggered back into the/nkitchen, clutching his head and staring out of the/nwindow into the back garden./n/nThe darkness seemed to be rippling, the air itself/nquivering. Then, one by one, figures began to pop into/nsight as their Disillusionment Charms lifted./nDominating the scene was Hagrid, wearing a helmet/nand goggles and sitting astride an enormous/nmotorbike with a black sidecar attached. All around/nhim other people were dismounting from brooms and,/nin two cases, skeletal, black winged horses./n/nWrenching open the back door, Harry hurtled into/ntheir midst. There was a general cry of greeting as/nHermione flung her arms around him, Ron clapped/nhim on the back, and Hagrid said, "All righ', Harry?/nReady fer the off?"/n/n"Definitely," said Harry, beaming around at them all./n"But I wasn't expecting this many of you!"/n/n"Change of plan," growled Mad-Eye, who was holding/ntwo enormous, bulging sacks, and whose magical eye/nwas spinning from darkening sky to house to garden/nwith dizzying rapidity. "Let's get undercover before we/ntalk you through it."/n/nHarry led them all back into the kitchen where,/nlaughing and chattering, they settled on chairs, sat/nthemselves upon Aunt Petunia's gleaming work/nsurfaces, or leaned up against her spotless/nappliances: Ron, long and lanky; Hermione, her/nbushy hair tied back in a long plait; Fred and George,/ngrinning identically; Bill, badly scarred and long-/n/n/n/n/nhaired; Mr. Weasley, kind-faced, balding, his/nspectacles a little awry; Mad-Eye, battle-worn, one-/nlegged, his bright blue magical eye whizzing in its/nsocket; Tonks, whose short hair was her favorite/nshade of bright pink; Lupin, grayer, more lined; Fleur,/nslender and beautiful, with her long silvery blonde/nhair; Kingsley, bald, black, broad-shouldered; Hagrid,/nwith his wild hair and beard, standing hunchbacked/nto avoid hitting his head on the ceiling; and/nMundungus Fletcher, small, dirty, and hangdog, with/nhis droopy basset hound's eyes and matted hair./nHarry's heart seemed to expand and glow at the sight:/nHe felt incredibly fond of all of them, even/nMundungus, whom he had tried to strangle the last/ntime they had met./n/n"Kingsley, I thought you were looking after the Muggle/nPrime Minister?" he called across the room./n/n"He can get along without me for one night," said/nKingsley. "You're more important."/n/n"Harry, guess what?" said Tonks from her perch on/ntop of the washing machine, and she wiggled her left/nhand at him; a ring glittered there./n/n"You got married?" Harry yelped, looking from her to/nLupin./n/n"I'm sorry you couldn't be there, Harry, it was very/nquiet."/n/n"That's brilliant, congrat — "/n/n"All right, all right, we'll have time for a cozy catch-up/nlater!" roared Moody over the hubbub, and silence fell/nin the kitchen. Moody dropped his sacks at his feet/nand turned to Harry. "As Dedalus probably told you,/nwe had to abandon Plan A. Pius Thicknesse has gone/n/n/n/n/nover, which gives us a big problem. He's made it an/nimprisonable offense to connect this house to the Floo/nNetwork, place a Portkey here, or Apparate in or out./nAll done in the name of your protection, to prevent/nYou-Know-Who getting in at you. Absolutely/npointless, seeing as your mother's charm does that/nalready. What he's really done is to stop you getting/nout of here safely./n/n"Second problem: You're underage, which means/nyou've still got the Trace on you."/n/n"I don't — "/n/n"The Trace, the Trace!" said Mad-Eye impatiently./n/n"The charm that detects magical activity around/nunder-seventeens, the way the Ministry finds out/nabout underage magic! If you, or anyone around you,/ncasts a spell to get you out of here, Thicknesse is/ngoing to know about it, and so will the Death Eaters./n/n"We can't wait for the Trace to break, because the/nmoment you turn seventeen you'll lose all the/nprotection your mother gave you. In short: Pius/nThicknesse thinks he's got you cornered good and/nproper."/n/nHarry could not help but agree with the unknown/nThicknesse./n/n"So what are we going to do?"/n/n"We're going to use the only means of transport left to/nus, the only ones the Trace can't detect, because we/ndon't need to cast spells to use them: brooms,/nthestrals, and Hagrid's motorbike."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry could see flaws in this plan; however, he held/nhis tongue to give Mad-Eye the chance to address/nthem./n/n"Now, your mother's charm will only break under two/nconditions: when you come of age, or" — Moody/ngestured around the pristine kitchen — "you no/nlonger call this place home. You and your aunt and/nuncle are going your separate ways tonight, in the full/nunderstanding that you're never going to live together/nagain, correct?"/n/nHarry nodded./n/n"So this time, when you leave, there'll be no going/nback, and the charm will break the moment you get/noutside its range. We're choosing to break it early,/nbecause the alternative is waiting for You-Know-Who/nto come and seize you the moment you turn/nseventeen./n/n"The one thing we've got on our side is that You-/nKnow-Who doesn't know we're moving you tonight./nWe've leaked a fake trail to the Ministry: They think/nyou're not leaving until the thirtieth. However, this is/nYou-Know-Who we're dealing with, so we can't just/nrely on him getting the date wrong; he's bound to/nhave a couple of Death Eaters patrolling the skies in/nthis general area, just in case. So, we've given a dozen/ndifferent houses every protection we can throw at/nthem. They all look like they could be the place we're/ngoing to hide you, they've all got some connection/nwith the Order: my house, Kingsley's place, Molly's/nAuntie Muriel's — you get the idea."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, not entirely truthfully, because he/ncould still spot a gaping hole in the plan./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You'll be going to Tonks's parents. Once you're/nwithin the boundaries of the protective enchantments/nwe've put on their house, you'll be able to use a/nPortkey to the Burrow. Any questions?"/n/n"Er — yes," said Harry. "Maybe they won't know/nwhich of the twelve secure houses I'm heading for at/nfirst, but won't it be sort of obvious once" — he/nperformed a quick headcount — "fourteen of us fly off/ntoward Tonks's parents'?"/n/n"Ah," said Moody, "I forgot to mention the key point./nFourteen of us won't be flying to Tonks's parents'./nThere will be seven Harry Potters moving through the/nskies tonight, each of them with a companion, each/npair heading for a different safe house."/n/nFrom inside his cloak Moody now withdrew a flask of/nwhat looked like mud. There was no need for him to/nsay another word; Harry understood the rest of the/nplan immediately./n/n"No!" he said loudly, his voice ringing through the/nkitchen. "No way!"/n/n"I told them you'd take it like this," said Hermione/nwith a hint of complacency./n/n"If you think I'm going to let six people risk their lives/n/n— !"/n/n" — because it's the first time for all of us," said Ron./n/n"This is different, pretending to be me — "/n/n"Well, none of us really fancy it, Harry," said Fred/nearnestly. "Imagine if something went wrong and we/nwere stuck as specky, scrawny gits forever."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry did not smile./n/n/n/n"You can't do it if I don't cooperate, you need me to/ngive you some hair."/n/n"Well, that's that plan scuppered," said George./n"Obviously there's no chance at all of us getting a bit/nof your hair unless you cooperate."/n/n"Yeah, thirteen of us against one bloke who's not/nallowed to use magic; we've got no chance," said Fred./n/n"Funny," said Harry, "really amusing."/n/n"If it has to come to force, then it will," growled/nMoody, his magical eye now quivering a little in its/nsocket as he glared at Harry. "Everyone here's/noverage, Potter, and they're all prepared to take the/nrisk."/n/nMundungus shrugged and grimaced; the magical eye/nswerved sideways to glare at him out of the side of/nMoody's head./n/n"Let's have no more arguments. Time's wearing on. I/nwant a few of your hairs, boy, now."/n/n"But this is mad, there's no need — "/n/n"No need!" snarled Moody. "With You-Know-Who out/nthere and half the Ministry on his side? Potter, if/nwe're lucky hell have swallowed the fake bait and/nhe'll be planning to ambush you on the thirtieth, but/nhe'd be mad not to have a Death Eater or two keeping/nan eye out, it's what I'd do. They might not be able to/nget at you or this house while your mother's charm/nholds, but it's about to break and they know the/nrough position of the place. Our only chance is to use/n/n/n/n/n/ndecoys. Even You-Know-Who can't split himself into/nseven."/n/nHarry caught Hermione's eye and looked away at/nonce./n/n"So, Potter — some of your hair, if you please."/n/nHarry glanced at Ron, who grimaced at him in a just-/ndo-it sort of way./n/n"Now!" barked Moody./n/nWith all of their eyes upon him, Harry reached up to/nthe top of his head, grabbed a hank of hair, and/npulled./n/n"Good," said Moody, limping forward as he pulled the/nstopper out of the flask of potion. "Straight in here, if/nyou please."/n/nHarry dropped the hair into the mudlike liquid. The/nmoment it made contact with its surface, the potion/nbegan to froth and smoke, then, all at once, it turned/na clear, bright gold./n/n"Ooh, you look much tastier than Crabbe and Goyle,/nHarry," said Hermione, before catching sight of Ron's/nraised eyebrows, blushing slightly, and saying, "Oh,/nyou know what I mean — Goyle 's potion looked like/nbogies."/n/n"Right then, fake Potters line up over here, please,"/nsaid Moody./n/nRon, Hermione, Fred, George, and Fleur lined up in/nfront of Aunt Petunia's gleaming sink./n/n"We're one short," said Lupin./n/n/n/n/n/n"Here," said Hagrid gruffly, and he lifted Mundungus/nby the scruff of the neck and dropped him down/nbeside Fleur, who wrinkled her nose pointedly and/nmoved along to stand between Fred and George/ninstead./n/n"I've toldjer, I'd sooner be a protector," said/nMundungus./n/n"Shut it," growled Moody. "As I've already told you,/nyou spineless worm, any Death Eaters we run into/nwill be aiming to capture Potter, not kill him./nDumbledore always said You-Know-Who would want/nto finish Potter in person. It'll be the protectors who/nhave got the most to worry about, the Death Eaters'll/nwant to kill them."/n/nMundungus did not look particularly reassured, but/nMoody was already pulling half a dozen eggcup-sized/nglasses from inside his cloak, which he handed out,/nbefore pouring a little Polyjuice Potion into each one./n/n"Altogether, then ..."/n/nRon, Hermione, Fred, George, Fleur, and Mundungus/ndrank. All of them gasped and grimaced as the potion/nhit their throats: At once, their features began to/nbubble and distort like hot wax. Hermione and/nMundungus were shooting upward; Ron, Fred, and/nGeorge were shrinking; their hair was darkening,/nHermione's and Fleur's appearing to shoot backward/ninto their skulls./n/nMoody, quite unconcerned, was now loosening the/nties of the large sacks he had brought with him. When/nhe straightened up again, there were six Harry Potters/ngasping and panting in front of him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nFred and George turned to each other and said/ntogether, "Wow — we're identical!"/n/n"I dunno, though, I think I'm still better-looking," said/nFred, examining his reflection in the kettle./n/n"Bah," said Fleur, checking herself in the microwave/ndoor, "Bill, don't look at me — I'm 'ideous."/n/n"Those whose clothes are a bit roomy, I've got smaller/nhere," said Moody, indicating the first sack, "and vice/nversa. Don't forget the glasses, there's six pairs in the/nside pocket. And when you're dressed, there's luggage/nin the other sack."/n/nThe real Harry thought that this might just be the/nmost bizarre thing he had ever seen, and he had seen/nsome extremely odd things. He watched as his six/ndoppelgangers rummaged in the sacks, pulling out/nsets of clothes, putting on glasses, stuffing their own/nthings away. He felt like asking them to show a little/nmore respect for his privacy as they all began/nstripping off with impunity, clearly much more at ease/nwith displaying his body than they would have been/nwith their own./n/n"I knew Ginny was lying about that tattoo," said Ron,/nlooking down at his bare chest./n/n"Harry, your eyesight really is awful," said Hermione,/nas she put on glasses./n/nOnce dressed, the fake Harrys took rucksacks and/nowl cages, each containing a stuffed snowy owl, from/nthe second sack./n/n"Good," said Moody, as at last seven dressed,/nbespectacled, and luggage-laden Harrys faced him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The pairs will be as follows: Mundungus will be/ntraveling with me, by broom — "/n/n"Why'm I with you?" grunted the Harry nearest the/nback door./n/n"Because you're the one that needs watching,"/ngrowled Moody, and sure enough, his magical eye did/nnot waver from Mundungus as he continued, "Arthur/nand Fred — "/n/n"I'm George," said the twin at whom Moody was/npointing. "Can't you even tell us apart when we're/nHarry?"/n/n"Sorry, George — "/n/n"I'm only yanking your wand, I'm Fred really — "/n/n"Enough messing around!" snarled Moody. "The other/none — George or Fred or whoever you are — you're/nwith Remus. Miss Delacour — "/n/n"I'm taking Fleur on a thestral," said Bill. "She's not/nthat fond of brooms."/n/nFleur walked over to stand beside him, giving him a/nsoppy, slavish look that Harry hoped with all his/nheart would never appear on his face again./n/n"Miss Granger with Kingsley, again by thestral — "/n/nHermione looked reassured as she answered/nKingsley's smile; Harry knew that Hermione too/nlacked confidence on a broomstick./n/n"Which leaves you and me, Ron!" said Tonks brightly,/nknocking over a mug tree as she waved at him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRon did not look quite as pleased as Hermione./n/n/n/n"An' you're with me, Harry. That all righ'?" said/nHagrid, looking a little anxious. "We'll be on the bike,/nbrooms an' thestrals can't take me weight, see. Not a/nlot o' room on the seat with me on it, though, so you'll/nbe in the sidecar."/n/n"That's great," said Harry, not altogether truthfully./n/n"We think the Death Eaters will expect you to be on a/nbroom," said Moody, who seemed to guess how Harry/nwas feeling. "Snape's had plenty of time to tell them/neverything about you he's never mentioned before, so/nif we do run into any Death Eaters, we're betting/nthey'll choose one of the Potters who look at home on/na broomstick. All right then," he went on, tying up the/nsack with the fake Potters' clothes in it and leading/nthe way back to the door, "I make it three minutes/nuntil we're supposed to leave. No point locking the/nback door, it won't keep the Death Eaters out when/nthey come looking. ... Come on. ..."/n/nHarry hurried into the hall to fetch his rucksack,/nFirebolt, and Hedwig's cage before joining the others/nin the dark back garden. On every side broomsticks/nwere leaping into hands; Hermione had already been/nhelped up onto a great black thestral by Kingsley,/nFleur onto the other by Bill. Hagrid was standing/nready beside the motorbike, goggles on./n/n"Is this it? Is this Sirius's bike?"/n/n"The very same," said Hagrid, beaming down at Harry./n"An' the last time yeh was on it, Harry, I could fit yeh/nin one hand!"/n/nHarry could not help but feel a little humiliated as he/ngot into the sidecar. It placed him several feet below/n/n/n/n/n/neverybody else: Ron smirked at the sight of him/nsitting there like a child in a bumper car. Harry/nstuffed his rucksack and broomstick down by his feet/nand rammed Hedwig's cage between his knees. It was/nextremely uncomfortable./n/n"Arthur's done a bit o' tinkerin'," said Hagrid, quite/noblivious to Harry's discomfort. He settled himself/nastride the motorcycle, which creaked slightly and/nsank inches into the ground. "It's got a few tricks up/nits handlebars now. Tha' one was my idea."/n/nHe pointed a thick finger at a purple button near the/nspeedometer./n/n"Please be careful, Hagrid," said Mr. Weasley, who/nwas standing beside them, holding his broomstick./n"I'm still not sure that was advisable and it's certainly/nonly to be used in emergencies."/n/n"All right then," said Moody. "Everyone ready, please;/n/nI want us all to leave at exactly the same time or the/nwhole point of the diversion's lost."/n/nEverybody mounted their brooms./n/n"Hold tight now, Ron," said Tonks, and Harry saw/nRon throw a furtive, guilty look at Lupin before/nplacing his hands on either side of her waist. Hagrid/nkicked the motorbike into life: It roared like a dragon,/nand the sidecar began to vibrate./n/n"Good luck, everyone," shouted Moody. "See you all in/nabout an hour at the Burrow. On the count of three./nOne ... two ... THREE."/n/nThere was a great roar from the motorbike, and Harry/nfelt the sidecar give a nasty lurch: He was rising/nthrough the air fast, his eyes watering slightly, hair/n/n/n/n/n/nwhipped back off his face. Around him brooms were/nsoaring upward too; the long black tail of a thestral/nflicked past. His legs, jammed into the sidecar by/nHedwig's cage and his rucksack, were already sore/nand starting to go numb. So great was his discomfort/nthat he almost forgot to take a last glimpse of number/nfour, Privet Drive; by the time he looked over the edge/nof the sidecar he could no longer tell which one it/nwas. Higher and higher they climbed into the sky —/n/nAnd then, out of nowhere, out of nothing, they were/nsurrounded. At least thirty hooded figures, suspended/nin midair, formed a vast circle in the midst of which/nthe Order members had risen, oblivious —/n/nScreams, a blaze of green light on every side: Hagrid/ngave a yell and the motorbike rolled over. Harry lost/nany sense of where they were: Streetlights above him,/nyells around him, he was clinging to the sidecar for/ndear life. Hedwig's cage, the Firebolt, and his/nrucksack slipped from beneath his knees —/n/n"No — HEDWIG!"/n/nThe broomstick spun to earth, but he just managed/nto seize the strap of his rucksack and the top of the/ncage as the motorbike swung the right way up again./nA second's relief, and then another burst of green/nlight. The owl screeched and fell to the floor of the/ncage./n/n"No — NO!"/n/nThe motorbike zoomed forward; Harry glimpsed/nhooded Death Eaters scattering as Hagrid blasted/nthrough their circle./n/n"Hedwig — Hedwig — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut the owl lay motionless and pathetic as a toy on/nthe floor of her cage. He could not take it in, and his/nterror for the others was paramount. He glanced over/nhis shoulder and saw a mass of people moving, flares/nof green light, two pairs of people on brooms soaring/noff into the distance, but he could not tell who they/nwere —/n/n"Hagrid, we've got to go back, we've got to go back!" he/nyelled over the thunderous roar of the engine, pulling/nout his wand, ramming Hedwig's cage onto the floor,/nrefusing to believe that she was dead. "Hagrid, TURN/nAROUND!"/n/n"My job's ter get you there safe, Harry!" bellowed/nHagrid, and he opened the throttle./n/n"Stop — STOP!" Harry shouted, but as he looked back/nagain two jets of green light flew past his left ear: Four/nDeath Eaters had broken away from the circle and/nwere pursuing them, aiming for Hagrid 's broad back./nHagrid swerved, but the Death Eaters were keeping/nup with the bike; more curses shot after them, and/nHarry had to sink low into the sidecar to avoid them./nWriggling around he cried, "Stupefy\" and a red bolt of/nlight shot from his own wand, cleaving a gap between/nthe four pursuing Death Eaters as they scattered to/navoid it./n/n"Hold on, Harry, this'll do for 'em!" roared Hagrid, and/nHarry looked up just in time to see Hagrid slamming/na thick finger into a green button near the fuel gauge./n/nA wall, a solid brick wall, erupted out of the exhaust/npipe. Craning his neck, Harry saw it expand into/nbeing in midair. Three of the Death Eaters swerved/nand avoided it, but the fourth was not so lucky: He/nvanished from view and then dropped like a boulder/nfrom behind it, his broomstick broken into pieces./n/n/n/n/nOne of his fellows slowed up to save him, but they/nand the airborne wall were swallowed by darkness as/nHagrid leaned low over the handlebars and sped up./n/nMore Killing Curses flew past Harry's head from the/ntwo remaining Death Eaters' wands; they were aiming/nfor Hagrid. Harry responded with further Stunning/nSpells: Red and green collided in midair in a shower/nof multicolored sparks, and Harry thought wildly of/nfireworks, and the Muggles below who would have no/nidea what was happening —/n/n"Here we go again, Harry, hold on!" yelled Hagrid, and/nhe jabbed at a second button. This time a great net/nburst from the bike's exhaust, but the Death Eaters/nwere ready for it. Not only did they swerve to avoid it,/nbut the companion who had slowed to save their/nunconscious friend had caught up. He bloomed/nsuddenly out of the darkness and now three of them/nwere pursuing the motorbike, all shooting curses after/nit./n/n"This'll do it, Harry, hold on tight!" yelled Hagrid, and/nHarry saw him slam his whole hand onto the purple/nbutton beside the speedometer./n/nWith an unmistakable bellowing roar, dragon fire/nburst from the exhaust, white-hot and blue, and the/nmotorbike shot forward like a bullet with a sound of/nwrenching metal. Harry saw the Death Eaters swerve/nout of sight to avoid the deadly trail of flame, and at/nthe same time felt the sidecar sway ominously: Its/nmetal connections to the bike had splintered with the/nforce of acceleration./n/n"It's all righ', Harry!" bellowed Hagrid, now thrown flat/nonto his back by the surge of speed; nobody was/nsteering now, and the sidecar was starting to twist/nviolently in the bike's slipstream./n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm on it, Harry, don' worry!" Hagrid yelled, and from/ninside his jacket pocket he pulled his flowery pink/numbrella./n/n"Hagrid! No! Let me!"/n/n"REPAROl"/n/nThere was a deafening bang and the sidecar broke/naway from the bike completely: Harry sped forward,/npropelled by the impetus of the bike's flight, then the/nsidecar began to lose height —/n/nIn desperation Harry pointed his wand at the sidecar/nand shouted, "Wingardium Leviosal"/n/nThe sidecar rose like a cork, unsteerable but at least/nstill airborne: He had but a split second's relief,/nhowever, as more curses streaked past him: The three/nDeath Eaters were closing in./n/n"I'm cornin', Harry!" Hagrid yelled from out of the/ndarkness, but Harry could feel the sidecar beginning/nto sink again: Crouching as low as he could, he/npointed at the middle of the oncoming figures and/nyelled, "Impedimental"/n/nThe jinx hit the middle Death Eater in the chest: For/na moment the man was absurdly spread-eagled in/nmidair as though he had hit an invisible barrier: One/nof his fellows almost collided with him —/n/nThen the sidecar began to fall in earnest, and the/nremaining Death Eater shot a curse so close to Harry/nthat he had to duck below the rim of the car,/nknocking out a tooth on the edge of his seat —/n/n"I'm cornin', Harry, I'm cornin'!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA huge hand seized the back of Harry's robes and/nhoisted him out of the plummeting sidecar; Harry/npulled his rucksack with him as he dragged himself/nonto the motorbike's seat and found himself back-to-/nback with Hagrid. As they soared upward, away from/nthe two remaining Death Eaters, Harry spat blood out/nof his mouth, pointed his wand at the falling sidecar,/nand yelled, "Confringo\"/n/nHe knew a dreadful, gut-wrenching pang for Hedwig/nas it exploded; the Death Eater nearest it was blasted/noff his broom and fell from sight; his companion fell/nback and vanished./n/n"Harry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry," moaned Hagrid, "I/nshouldn'ta tried ter repair it meself — yeh've got no/nroom — "/n/n"It's not a problem, just keep flying!" Harry shouted/nback, as two more Death Eaters emerged out of the/ndarkness, drawing closer./n/nAs the curses came shooting across the intervening/nspace again, Hagrid swerved and zigzagged: Harry/nknew that Hagrid did not dare use the dragon-fire/nbutton again, with Harry seated so insecurely. Harry/nsent Stunning Spell after Stunning Spell back at their/npursuers, barely holding them off. He shot another/nblocking jinx at them: The closest Death Eater/nswerved to avoid it and his hood slipped, and by the/nred light of his next Stunning Spell, Harry saw the/nstrangely blank face of Stanley Shunpike — Stan —/n/n" ExpelliarmusV' Harry yelled./n/n"That's him, it's him, it's the real one!"/n/nThe hooded Death Eater's shout reached Harry even/nabove the thunder of the motorbike's engine: Next/n/n/n/n/n/nmoment, both pursuers had fallen back and/ndisappeared from view./n/n/n/n"Harry, what's happened?" bellowed Hagrid./n/n"Where Ve they gone?"/n/n"I don't know!"/n/nBut Harry was afraid: The hooded Death Eater had/nshouted "It's the real one!"; how had he known? He/ngazed around at the apparently empty darkness and/nfelt its menace. Where were they?/n/nHe clambered around on the seat to face forward and/nseized hold of the back of Hagrid 's jacket./n/n"Hagrid, do the dragon-fire thing again, let's get out of/nhere!"/n/n"Hold on tight, then, Harry!"/n/nThere was a deafening, screeching roar again and the/nwhite-blue fire shot from the exhaust: Harry felt/nhimself slipping backward off what little of the seat he/nhad, Hagrid flung backward upon him, barely/nmaintaining his grip on the handlebars —/n/n"I think we've lost 'em Harry, I think we've done it!"/nyelled Hagrid./n/nBut Harry was not convinced: Fear lapped at him as/nhe looked left and right for pursuers he was sure/nwould come. ... Why had they fallen back? One of/nthem had still had a wand. ... It's him ... it's the real/none. . . . They had said it right after he had tried to/nDisarm Stan. .../n/n"We're nearly there, Harry, we've nearly made it!"/nshouted Hagrid./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry felt the bike drop a little, though the lights/ndown on the ground still seemed remote as stars./n/nThen the scar on his forehead burned like fire; as a/nDeath Eater appeared on either side of the bike, two/nKilling Curses missed Harry by millimeters, cast from/nbehind —/n/nAnd then Harry saw him. Voldemort was flying like/nsmoke on the wind, without broomstick or thestral to/nhold him, his snakelike face gleaming out of the/nblackness, his white fingers raising his wand again —/n/nHagrid let out a bellow of fear and steered the/nmotorbike into a vertical dive. Clinging on for dear/nlife, Harry sent Stunning Spells flying at random into/nthe whirling night. He saw a body fly past him and/nknew he had hit one of them, but then he heard a/nbang and saw sparks from the engine; the motorbike/nspiraled through the air, completely out of control —/n/nGreen jets of light shot past them again. Harry had no/nidea which way was up, which down: His scar was/nstill burning; he expected to die at any second. A/nhooded figure on a broomstick was feet from him, he/nsaw it raise its arm —/n/n"NO!"/n/nWith a shout of fury Hagrid launched himself off the/nbike at the Death Eater; to his horror, Harry saw both/nHagrid and the Death Eater falling out of sight, their/ncombined weight too much for the broomstick —/n/nBarely gripping the plummeting bike with his knees,/nHarry heard Voldemort scream, "Mine\"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was over: He could not see or hear where Voldemort/nwas; he glimpsed another Death Eater swooping out/nof the way and heard, "Avada — "/n/nAs the pain from Harry's scar forced his eyes shut,/nhis wand acted of its own accord. He felt it drag his/nhand around like some great magnet, saw a spurt of/ngolden fire through his half-closed eyelids, heard a/ncrack and a scream of fury. The remaining Death/nEater yelled; Voldemort screamed, " No\ Somehow,/nHarry found his nose an inch from the dragon-fire/nbutton. He punched it with his wand-free hand and/nthe bike shot more flames into the air, hurtling/nstraight toward the ground./n/n"Hagrid!" Harry called, holding on to the bike for dear/nlife. "Hagrid — Accio Hagridl"/n/nThe motorbike sped up, sucked toward the earth./n/nFace level with the handlebars, Harry could see/nnothing but distant lights growing nearer and nearer:/nHe was going to crash and there was nothing he could/ndo about it. Behind him came another scream, "Your/nwand, Selwyn, give me your wand\"/n/nHe felt Voldemort before he saw him. Looking/nsideways, he stared into the red eyes and was sure/nthey would be the last thing he ever saw: Voldemort/npreparing to curse him once more —/n/nAnd then Voldemort vanished. Harry looked down/nand saw Hagrid spread-eagled on the ground below/nhim. He pulled hard at the handlebars to avoid hitting/nhim, groped for the brake, but with an earsplitting,/nground-trembling crash, he smashed into a muddy/npond./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n5/n/n/n/n

title: Fallen Warrior
text: /n/n/n"Hagrid?"/n/nHarry struggled to raise himself out of the debris of/nmetal and leather that surrounded him; his hands/nsank into inches of muddy water as he tried to stand./nHe could not understand where Voldemort had gone/nand expected him to swoop out of the darkness at any/nmoment. Something hot and wet was trickling down/nhis chin and from his forehead. He crawled out of the/npond and stumbled toward the great dark mass on/nthe ground that was Hagrid./n/n"Hagrid? Hagrid, talk to me — "/n/nBut the dark mass did not stir./n/n"Who's there? Is it Potter? Are you Harry Potter?"/n/nHarry did not recognize the man's voice. Then a/nwoman shouted, "They've crashed, Ted! Crashed in/nthe garden!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's head was swimming./n/n/n/n"Hagrid," he repeated stupidly, and his knees/nbuckled./n/nThe next thing he knew, he was lying on his back on/nwhat felt like cushions, with a burning sensation in/nhis ribs and right arm. His missing tooth had been/nregrown. The scar on his forehead was still throbbing./n/n"Hagrid?"/n/nHe opened his eyes and saw that he was lying on a/nsofa in an unfamiliar, lamplit sitting room. His/nrucksack lay on the floor a short distance away, wet/nand muddy. A fair-haired, big-bellied man was/nwatching Harry anxiously./n/n"Hagrid's fine, son," said the man, "the wife's seeing/nto him now. How are you feeling? Anything else/nbroken? I've fixed your ribs, your tooth, and your/narm. I'm Ted, by the way, Ted Tonks — Dora's father."/n/nHarry sat up too quickly: Lights popped in front of his/neyes and he felt sick and giddy./n/n"Voldemort — "/n/n"Easy, now," said Ted Tonks, placing a hand on/nHarry's shoulder and pushing him back against the/ncushions. "That was a nasty crash you just had. What/nhappened, anyway? Something go wrong with the/nbike? Arthur Weasley overstretch himself again, him/nand his Muggle contraptions?"/n/n"No," said Harry, as his scar pulsed like an open/nwound. "Death Eaters, loads of them — we were/nchased — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Death Eaters?" said Ted sharply. "What d'you mean,/nDeath Eaters? I thought they didn't know you were/nbeing moved tonight, I thought — "/n/n"They knew," said Harry./n/nTed Tonks looked up at the ceiling as though he could/nsee through it to the sky above./n/n"Well, we know our protective charms hold, then,/ndon't we? They shouldn't be able to get within a/nhundred yards of the place in any direction."/n/nNow Harry understood why Voldemort had vanished;/nit had been at the point when the motorbike crossed/nthe barrier of the Order's charms. He only hoped they/nwould continue to work: He imagined Voldemort, a/nhundred yards above them as they spoke, looking for/na way to penetrate what Harry visualized as a great/ntransparent bubble./n/nHe swung his legs off the sofa; he needed to see/nHagrid with his own eyes before he would believe that/nhe was alive. He had barely stood up, however, when/na door opened and Hagrid squeezed through it, his/nface covered in mud and blood, limping a little but/nmiraculously alive./n/n"Harry!"/n/nKnocking over two delicate tables and an aspidistra,/nhe covered the floor between them in two strides and/npulled Harry into a hug that nearly cracked his newly/nrepaired ribs. "Blimey, Harry, how did yeh get out o'/nthat? I thought we were both goners."/n/n"Yeah, me too. I can't believe — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry broke off. He had just noticed the woman who/nhad entered the room behind Hagrid./n/n"You!" he shouted, and he thrust his hand into his/npocket, but it was empty./n/n"Your wand's here, son," said Ted, tapping it on/nHarry's arm. "It fell right beside you, I picked it up./nAnd that's my wife you're shouting at."/n/n"Oh, I'm — I'm sorry."/n/nAs she moved forward into the room, Mrs. Tonks's/nresemblance to her sister Bellatrix became much less/npronounced: Her hair was a light, soft brown and her/neyes were wider and kinder. Nevertheless, she looked/na little haughty after Harry's exclamation./n/n"What happened to our daughter?" she asked. "Hagrid/nsaid you were ambushed; where is Nymphadora?"/n/n"I don't know," said Harry. "We don't know what/nhappened to anyone else."/n/nShe and Ted exchanged looks. A mixture of fear and/nguilt gripped Harry at the sight of their expressions; if/nany of the others had died, it was his fault, all his/nfault. He had consented to the plan, given them his/nhair. .../n/n"The Portkey," he said, remembering all of a sudden./n"We've got to get back to the Burrow and find out —/nthen well be able to send you word, or — or Tonks/nwill, once she's — "/n/n"Dora'll be okay, 'Dromeda," said Ted. "She knows her/nstuff, she's been in plenty of tight spots with the/nAurors. The Portkey 's through here," he added to/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry. "It's supposed to leave in three minutes, if you/nwant to take it."/n/n/n/n"Yeah, we do," said Harry. He seized his rucksack,/nswung it onto his shoulders. "I — "/n/nHe looked at Mrs. Tonks, wanting to apologize for the/nstate of fear in which he left her and for which he felt/nso terribly responsible, but no words occurred to him/nthat did not seem hollow and insincere./n/n"Ill tell Tonks — Dora — to send word, when she .../nThanks for patching us up, thanks for everything. I —/n/n/n/nHe was glad to leave the room and follow Ted Tonks/nalong a short hallway and into a bedroom. Hagrid/ncame after them, bending low to avoid hitting his/nhead on the door lintel./n/n"There you go, son. That's the Portkey."/n/nMr. Tonks was pointing to a small, silver-backed/nhairbrush lying on the dressing table./n/n"Thanks," said Harry, reaching out to place a finger/non it, ready to leave./n/n"Wait a moment," said Hagrid, looking around./n/n"Harry, where's Hedwig?"/n/n"She ... she got hit," said Harry./n/nThe realization crashed over him: He felt ashamed of/nhimself as the tears stung his eyes. The owl had been/nhis companion, his one great link with the magical/nworld whenever he had been forced to return to the/nDursleys./n/n/n/n/n/nHagrid reached out a great hand and patted him/npainfully on the shoulder./n/n"Never mind," he said gruffly. "Never mind. She had a/ngreat old life — "/n/n"Hagrid!" said Ted Tonks warningly, as the hairbrush/nglowed bright blue, and Hagrid only just got his/nforefinger to it in time./n/nWith a jerk behind the navel as though an invisible/nhook and line had dragged him forward, Harry was/npulled into nothingness, spinning uncontrollably, his/nfinger glued to the Portkey as he and Hagrid hurtled/naway from Mr. Tonks. Seconds later Harry's feet/nslammed onto hard ground and he fell onto his hands/nand knees in the yard of the Burrow. He heard/nscreams. Throwing aside the no longer glowing/nhairbrush, Harry stood up, swaying slightly, and saw/nMrs. Weasley and Ginny running down the steps by/nthe back door as Hagrid, who had also collapsed on/nlanding, clambered laboriously to his feet./n/n"Harry? You are the real Harry? What happened?/nWhere are the others?" cried Mrs. Weasley./n/n"What d'you mean? Isn't anyone else back?" Harry/npanted./n/nThe answer was clearly etched in Mrs. Weasley 's pale/nface./n/n"The Death Eaters were waiting for us," Harry told/nher. "We were surrounded the moment we took off —/nthey knew it was tonight — I don't know what/nhappened to anyone else, four of them chased us, it/nwas all we could do to get away, and then Voldemort/ncaught up with us — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe could hear the self-justifying note in his voice, the/nplea for her to understand why he did not know what/nhad happened to her sons, but —/n/n"Thank goodness you're all right," she said, pulling/nhim into a hug he did not feel he deserved./n/n"Haven't go' any brandy, have yeh, Molly?" asked/nHagrid a little shakily. "Fer medicinal purposes?"/n/nShe could have summoned it by magic, but as she/nhurried back toward the crooked house, Harry knew/nthat she wanted to hide her face. He turned to Ginny/nand she answered his unspoken plea for information/nat once./n/n"Ron and Tonks should have been back first, but they/nmissed their Portkey, it came back without them," she/nsaid, pointing at a rusty oil can lying on the ground/nnearby. "And that one," she pointed at an ancient/nsneaker, "should have been Dad and Fred's, they/nwere supposed to be second. You and Hagrid were/nthird and," she checked her watch, "if they made it,/nGeorge and Lupin ought to be back in about a/nminute."/n/nMrs. Weasley reappeared carrying a bottle of brandy,/nwhich she handed to Hagrid. He uncorked it and/ndrank it straight down in one./n/n"Mum!" shouted Ginny, pointing to a spot several feet/naway./n/nA blue light had appeared in the darkness: It grew/nlarger and brighter, and Lupin and George appeared,/nspinning and then falling. Harry knew immediately/nthat there was something wrong: Lupin was/nsupporting George, who was unconscious and whose/nface was covered in blood./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry ran forward and seized George's legs. Together,/nhe and Lupin carried George into the house and/nthrough the kitchen to the sitting room, where they/nlaid him on the sofa. As the lamplight fell across/nGeorge's head, Ginny gasped and Harry's stomach/nlurched: One of George's ears was missing. The side/nof his head and neck were drenched in wet,/nshockingly scarlet blood./n/nNo sooner had Mrs. Weasley bent over her son than/nLupin grabbed Harry by the upper arm and dragged/nhim, none too gently, back into the kitchen, where/nHagrid was still attempting to ease his bulk through/nthe back door./n/n"Oi!" said Hagrid indignantly. "Le' go of him! Le' go of/nHarry!"/n/nLupin ignored him./n/n"What creature sat in the corner the first time that/nHarry Potter visited my office at Hogwarts?" he said,/ngiving Harry a small shake. "Answer me!"/n/n"A — a grindylow in a tank, wasn't it?"/n/nLupin released Harry and fell back against a kitchen/ncupboard./n/n"Wha' was tha' about?" roared Hagrid./n/n"I'm sorry, Harry, but I had to check," said Lupin/ntersely. "We've been betrayed. Voldemort knew that/nyou were being moved tonight and the only people/nwho could have told him were directly involved in the/nplan. You might have been an impostor."/n/n"So why aren' you checkin' me?" panted Hagrid, still/nstruggling to fit through the door./n/n/n/n/n/n"You're half-giant," said Lupin, looking up at Hagrid./n"The Polyjuice Potion is designed for human use/nonly."/n/n"None of the Order would have told Voldemort we/nwere moving tonight," said Harry. The idea was/ndreadful to him, he could not believe it of any of them./n"Voldemort only caught up with me toward the end,/nhe didn't know which one I was in the beginning. If/nhe'd been in on the plan he'd have known from the/nstart I was the one with Hagrid."/n/n"Voldemort caught up with you?" said Lupin sharply./n"What happened? How did you escape?"/n/nHarry explained briefly how the Death Eaters/npursuing them had seemed to recognize him as the/ntrue Harry, how they had abandoned the chase, how/nthey must have summoned Voldemort, who had/nappeared just before he and Hagrid had reached the/nsanctuary of Tonks's parents./n/n"They recognized you? But how? What had you/ndone?"/n/n"I ..." Harry tried to remember; the whole journey/nseemed like a blur of panic and confusion. "I saw/nStan Shunpike. ... You know, the bloke who was the/nconductor on the Knight Bus? And I tried to Disarm/nhim instead of — well, he doesn't know what he's/ndoing, does he? He must be Imperiused!"/n/nLupin looked aghast./n/n"Harry, the time for Disarming is past! These people/nare trying to capture and kill you! At least Stun if you/naren't prepared to kill!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We were hundreds of feet up! Stan's not himself, and/nif I Stunned him and he'd fallen, he'd have died the/nsame as if I'd used Avada Kedavra! Expelliarmus/nsaved me from Voldemort two years ago," Harry added/ndefiantly. Lupin was reminding him of the sneering/nHufflepuff Zacharias Smith, who had jeered at Harry/nfor wanting to teach Dumbledore's Army how to/nDisarm./n/n"Yes, Harry," said Lupin with painful restraint, "and a/ngreat number of Death Eaters witnessed that/nhappening! Forgive me, but it was a very unusual/nmove then, under imminent threat of death./n/nRepeating it tonight in front of Death Eaters who/neither witnessed or heard about the first occasion was/nclose to suicidal!"/n/n"So you think I should have killed Stan Shunpike?"/nsaid Harry angrily./n/n"Of course not," said Lupin, "but the Death Eaters —/nfrankly, most people! — would have expected you to/nattack back! Expelliarmus is a useful spell, Harry, but/nthe Death Eaters seem to think it is your signature/nmove, and I urge you not to let it become so!"/n/nLupin was making Harry feel idiotic, and yet there/nwas still a grain of defiance inside him./n/n"I won't blast people out of my way just because/nthey're there," said Harry. "That's Voldemort's job."/n/nLupin's retort was lost: Finally succeeding in/nsqueezing through the door, Hagrid staggered to a/nchair and sat down; it collapsed beneath him./n/nIgnoring his mingled oaths and apologies, Harry/naddressed Lupin again./n/n"Will George be okay?"/n/n/n/n/n/nAll Lupin's frustration with Harry seemed to drain/naway at the question./n/n"I think so, although there's no chance of replacing/nhis ear, not when it's been cursed off — "/n/nThere was a scuffling from outside. Lupin dived for/nthe back door; Harry leapt over Hagrid's legs and/nsprinted into the yard./n/nTwo figures had appeared in the yard, and as Harry/nran toward them he realized they were Hermione, now/nreturning to her normal appearance, and Kingsley,/nboth clutching a bent coat hanger. Hermione flung/nherself into Harry's arms, but Kingsley showed no/npleasure at the sight of any of them. Over Hermione 's/nshoulder Harry saw him raise his wand and point it/nat Lupin's chest./n/n"The last words Albus Dumbledore spoke to the pair/nof us?"/n/n" 'Harry is the best hope we have. Trust him,' " said/nLupin calmly./n/nKingsley turned his wand on Harry, but Lupin said,/n"It's him, I've checked!"/n/n"All right, all right!" said Kingsley, stowing his wand/nback beneath his cloak. "But somebody betrayed us!/nThey knew, they knew it was tonight!"/n/n"So it seems," replied Lupin, "but apparently they did/nnot realize that there would be seven Harrys."/n/n"Small comfort!" snarled Kingsley. "Who else is back?"/n/n"Only Harry, Hagrid, George, and me."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHermione stifled a little moan behind her hand./n/n/n/n"What happened to you?" Lupin asked Kingsley./n/n"Followed by five, injured two, might've killed one,"/nKingsley reeled off, "and we saw You-Know-Who as/nwell, he joined the chase halfway through but/nvanished pretty quickly. Remus, he can — "/n/n"Fly," supplied Harry. "I saw him too, he came after/nHagrid and me."/n/n"So that's why he left, to follow you!" said Kingsley. "I/ncouldn't understand why he'd vanished. But what/nmade him change targets?"/n/n"Harry behaved a little too kindly to Stan Shunpike,"/nsaid Lupin./n/n"Stan?" repeated Hermione. "But I thought he was in/nAzkaban?"/n/nKingsley let out a mirthless laugh./n/n"Hermione, there's obviously been a mass breakout/nwhich the Ministry has hushed up. Travers's hood fell/noff when I cursed him, he's supposed to be inside too./nBut what happened to you, Remus? Where's George?"/n/n"He lost an ear," said Lupin./n/n"Lost an — ?" repeated Hermione in a high voice./n/n"Snape's work," said Lupin./n/n" Snape ?" shouted Harry. "You didn't say — "/n/n"He lost his hood during the chase. Sectumsempra/nwas always a specialty of Snape's. I wish I could say/n/n/n/n/n/nI'd paid him back in kind, but it was all I could do to/nkeep George on the broom after he was injured, he/nwas losing so much blood."/n/nSilence fell between the four of them as they looked/nup at the sky. There was no sign of movement; the/nstars stared back, unblinking, indifferent,/nunobscured by flying friends. Where was Ron? Where/nwere Fred and Mr. Weasley? Where were Bill, Fleur,/nTonks, Mad-Eye, and Mundungus?/n/n"Harry, give us a hand!" called Hagrid hoarsely from/nthe door, in which he was stuck again. Glad of/nsomething to do, Harry pulled him free, then headed/nthrough the empty kitchen and back into the sitting/nroom, where Mrs. Weasley and Ginny were still/ntending to George. Mrs. Weasley had staunched his/nbleeding now, and by the lamplight Harry saw a/nclean, gaping hole where George's ear had been./n/n"How is he?"/n/nMrs. Weasley looked around and said, "I can't make it/ngrow back, not when it's been removed by Dark/nMagic. But it could have been so much worse. ... He's/nalive."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "Thank God."/n/n"Did I hear someone else in the yard?" Ginny asked./n/n"Hermione and Kingsley," said Harry./n/n"Thank goodness," Ginny whispered. They looked at/neach other; Harry wanted to hug her, hold on to her;/nhe did not even care much that Mrs. Weasley was/nthere, but before he could act on the impulse there/nwas a great crash from the kitchen./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'll prove who I am, Kingsley, after I've seen my son,/nnow back off if you know what's good for you!"/n/nHarry had never heard Mr. Weasley shout like that/nbefore. He burst into the living room, his bald patch/ngleaming with sweat, his spectacles askew, Fred right/nbehind him, both pale but uninjured./n/n"Arthur!" sobbed Mrs. Weasley. "Oh thank goodness!"/n/n"How is he?"/n/nMr. Weasley dropped to his knees beside George. For/nthe first time since Harry had known him, Fred/nseemed to be lost for words. He gaped over the back/nof the sofa at his twin's wound as if he could not/nbelieve what he was seeing./n/nPerhaps roused by the sound of Fred and their/nfather's arrival, George stirred./n/n"How do you feel, Georgie?" whispered Mrs. Weasley./nGeorge's fingers groped for the side of his head./n"Saintlike," he murmured./n/n"What's wrong with him?" croaked Fred, looking/nterrified. "Is his mind affected?"/n/n"Saintlike," repeated George, opening his eyes and/nlooking up at his brother. "You see ... I'm holy. Hole v,/nFred, geddit?"/n/nMrs. Weasley sobbed harder than ever. Color flooded/nFred's pale face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Pathetic," he told George. "Pathetic! With the whole/nwide world of ear-related humor before you, you go for/nholey?"/n/n"Ah well," said George, grinning at his tear-soaked/nmother. "You'll be able to tell us apart now, anyway,/nMum."/n/nHe looked around./n/n"Hi, Harry — you are Harry, right?"/n/n"Yeah, I am," said Harry, moving closer to the sofa./n/n"Well, at least we got you back okay," said George./n"Why aren't Ron and Bill huddled round my sickbed?"/n/n"They're not back yet, George," said Mrs. Weasley./nGeorge's grin faded./n/nHarry glanced at Ginny and motioned to her to/naccompany him back outside. As they walked through/nthe kitchen she said in a low voice, "Ron and Tonks/nshould be back by now. They didn't have a long/njourney; Auntie Muriel's not that far from here."/n/nHarry said nothing. He had been trying to keep fear at/nbay ever since reaching the Burrow, but now it/nenveloped him, seeming to crawl over his skin,/nthrobbing in his chest, clogging his throat. As they/nwalked down the back steps into the dark yard, Ginny/ntook his hand./n/nKingsley was striding backward and forward, glancing/nup at the sky every time he turned. Harry was/nreminded of Uncle Vernon pacing the living room a/nmillion years ago. Hagrid, Hermione, and Lupin stood/nshoulder to shoulder, gazing upward in silence. None/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nof them looked around when Harry and Ginny joined/ntheir silent vigil./n/nThe minutes stretched into what might as well have/nbeen years. The slightest breath of wind made them/nall jump and turn toward the whispering bush or tree/nin the hope that one of the missing Order members/nmight leap unscathed from its leaves —/n/nAnd then a broom materialized directly above them/nand streaked toward the ground —/n/n"It's them!" screamed Hermione./n/nTonks landed in a long skid that sent earth and/npebbles everywhere./n/n"Remus!" Tonks cried as she staggered off the broom/ninto Lupin's arms. His face was set and white: He/nseemed unable to speak. Ron tripped dazedly toward/nHarry and Hermione./n/n"You're okay," he mumbled, before Hermione flew at/nhim and hugged him tightly./n/n"I thought — I thought — "/n/n" 'M all right," said Ron, patting her on the back. " 'M/nfine."/n/n"Ron was great," said Tonks warmly, relinquishing/nher hold on Lupin. "Wonderful. Stunned one of the/nDeath Eaters, straight to the head, and when you're/naiming at a moving target from a flying broom — "/n/n"You did?" said Hermione, gazing up at Ron with her/narms still around his neck./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Always the tone of surprise," he said a little/ngrumpily, breaking free. "Are we the last back?"/n/n"No," said Ginny, "we're still waiting for Bill and Fleur/nand Mad-Eye and Mundungus. I'm going to tell Mum/nand Dad you're okay, Ron — "/n/nShe ran back inside./n/n"So what kept you? What happened?" Lupin sounded/nalmost angry at Tonks./n/n"Bellatrix," said Tonks. "She wants me quite as much/nas she wants Harry, Remus, she tried very hard to kill/nme. I just wish I'd got her, I owe Bellatrix. But we/ndefinitely injured Rodolphus. ... Then we got to Ron's/nAuntie Muriel's and we'd missed our Portkey and she/nwas fussing over us — "/n/nA muscle was jumping in Lupin's jaw. He nodded, but/nseemed unable to say anything else./n/n"So what happened to you lot?" Tonks asked, turning/nto Harry, Hermione, and Kingsley./n/nThey recounted the stories of their own journeys, but/nall the time the continued absence of Bill, Fleur, Mad-/nEye, and Mundungus seemed to lie upon them like a/nfrost, its icy bite harder and harder to ignore./n/n"I'm going to have to get back to Downing Street, I/nshould have been there an hour ago," said Kingsley/nfinally, after a last sweeping gaze at the sky. "Let me/nknow when they're back."/n/nLupin nodded. With a wave to the others, Kingsley/nwalked away into the darkness toward the gate. Harry/nthought he heard the faintest pop as Kingsley/nDisapparated just beyond the Burrow's boundaries./n/n/n/n/n/nMr. and Mrs. Weasley came racing down the back/nsteps, Ginny behind them. Both parents hugged Ron/nbefore turning to Lupin and Tonks./n/n"Thank you," said Mrs. Weasley, "for our sons."/n/n"Don't be silly, Molly," said Tonks at once./n/n"How's George?" asked Lupin./n/n"What's wrong with him?" piped up Ron./n/n"He's lost — "/n/nBut the end of Mrs. Weasley 's sentence was drowned/nin a general outcry: A thestral had just soared into/nsight and landed a few feet from them. Bill and Fleur/nslid from its back, windswept but unhurt./n/n"Bill! Thank God, thank God — "/n/nMrs. Weasley ran forward, but the hug Bill bestowed/nupon her was perfunctory. Looking directly at his/nfather, he said, "Mad-Eye's dead."/n/nNobody spoke, nobody moved. Harry felt as though/nsomething inside him was falling, falling through the/nearth, leaving him forever./n/n"We saw it," said Bill; Fleur nodded, tear tracks/nglittering on her cheeks in the light from the kitchen/nwindow. "It happened just after we broke out of the/ncircle: Mad-Eye and Dung were close by us, they were/nheading north too. Voldemort — he can fly — went/nstraight for them. Dung panicked, I heard him cry/nout, Mad-Eye tried to stop him, but he Disapparated./nVoldemort's curse hit Mad-Eye full in the face, he fell/nbackward off his broom and — there was nothing we/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ncould do, nothing, we had half a dozen of them on our/nown tail — "/n/n/n/nBill's voice broke./n/n"Of course you couldn't have done anything," said/nLupin./n/nThey all stood looking at each other. Harry could not/nquite comprehend it. Mad-Eye dead; it could not be./n/n... Mad-Eye, so tough, so brave, the consummate/nsurvivor .../n/nAt last it seemed to dawn on everyone, though nobody/nsaid it, that there was no point waiting in the yard/nanymore, and in silence they followed Mr. and Mrs./nWeasley back into the Burrow, and into the living/nroom, where Fred and George were laughing together./n/n"What's wrong?" said Fred, scanning their faces as/nthey entered. "What's happened? Who's — ?"/n/n"Mad-Eye," said Mr. Weasley. "Dead."/n/nThe twins' grins turned to grimaces of shock. Nobody/nseemed to know what to do. Tonks was crying silently/ninto a handkerchief: She had been close to Mad-Eye,/nHarry knew, his favorite and his protegee at the/nMinistry of Magic. Hagrid, who had sat down on the/nfloor in the corner where he had most space, was/ndabbing at his eyes with his tablecloth-sized/nhandkerchief./n/nBill walked over to the sideboard and pulled out a/nbottle of fire-whisky and some glasses./n/n"Here," he said, and with a wave of his wand he sent/ntwelve full glasses soaring through the room to each/nof them, holding the thirteenth aloft. "Mad-Eye."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mad-Eye," they all said, and drank./n/n"Mad-Eye," echoed Hagrid, a little late, with a hiccup./n/nThe firewhisky seared Harry's throat. It seemed to/nburn feeling back into him, dispelling the numbness/nand sense of unreality, firing him with something that/nwas like courage./n/n"So Mundungus disappeared?" said Lupin, who had/ndrained his own glass in one./n/nThe atmosphere changed at once. Everybody looked/ntense, watching Lupin, both wanting him to go on, it/nseemed to Harry, and slightly afraid of what they/nmight hear./n/n"I know what you're thinking," said Bill, "and I/nwondered that too, on the way back here, because/nthey seemed to be expecting us, didn't they? But/nMundungus can't have betrayed us. They didn't know/nthere would be seven Harrys, that confused them the/nmoment we appeared, and in case you've forgotten, it/nwas Mundungus who suggested that little bit of/nskullduggery. Why wouldn't he have told them the/nessential point? I think Dung panicked, it's as simple/nas that. He didn't want to come in the first place, but/nMad-Eye made him, and You-Know-Who went/nstraight for them. It was enough to make anyone/npanic."/n/n"You-Know-Who acted exactly as Mad-Eye expected/nhim to," sniffed Tonks. "Mad-Eye said he'd expect the/nreal Harry to be with the toughest, most skilled/nAurors. He chased Mad-Eye first, and when/nMundungus gave them away he switched to Kingsley./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, and zat eez all very good," snapped Fleur, "but/nstill eet does not explain 'ow zey knew we were moving/n'Arry tonight, does eet? Somebody must 'ave been/ncareless. Somebody let slip ze date to an outsider. It is/nze only explanation for zem knowing ze date but not/nze 'ole plan."/n/nShe glared around at them all, tear tracks still etched/non her beautiful face, silently daring any of them to/ncontradict her. Nobody did. The only sound to break/nthe silence was that of Hagrid hiccuping from behind/nhis handkerchief. Harry glanced at Hagrid, who had/njust risked his own life to save Harry's — Hagrid,/nwhom he loved, whom he trusted, who had once been/ntricked into giving Voldemort crucial information in/nexchange for a dragon's egg. .../n/n"No," Harry said aloud, and they all looked at him,/nsurprised: The firewhisky seemed to have amplified/nhis voice. "I mean ... if somebody made a mistake,"/nHarry went on, "and let something slip, I know they/ndidn't mean to do it. It's not their fault," he repeated,/nagain a little louder than he would usually have/nspoken. "We've got to trust each other. I trust all of/nyou, I don't think anyone in this room would ever sell/nme to Voldemort."/n/nMore silence followed his words. They were all looking/nat him; Harry felt a little hot again, and drank some/nmore firewhisky for something to do. As he drank, he/nthought of Mad-Eye. Mad-Eye had always been/nscathing about Dumbledore's willingness to trust/npeople./n/n"Well said, Harry," said Fred unexpectedly./n/n"Yeah, 'ear, 'ear," said George, with half a glance at/nFred, the corner of whose mouth twitched./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nLupin was wearing an odd expression as he looked at/nHarry. It was close to pitying./n/n"You think I'm a fool?" demanded Harry./n/n"No, I think you're like James," said Lupin, "who/nwould have regarded it as the height of dishonor to/nmistrust his friends."/n/nHarry knew what Lupin was getting at: that his father/nhad been betrayed by his friend, Peter Pettigrew. He/nfelt irrationally angry. He wanted to argue, but Lupin/nhad turned away from him, set down his glass upon a/nside table, and addressed Bill, "There's work to do. I/ncan ask Kingsley whether — "/n/n"No," said Bill at once, "I'll do it, I'll come."/n/n"Where are you going?" said Tonks and Fleur/ntogether./n/n"Mad-Eye's body," said Lupin. "We need to recover it."/n/n"Can't it — ?" began Mrs. Weasley with an appealing/nlook at Bill./n/n"Wait?" said Bill. "Not unless you'd rather the Death/nEaters took it?"/n/nNobody spoke. Lupin and Bill said good-bye and left./n/nThe rest of them now dropped into chairs, all except/nfor Harry, who remained standing. The suddenness/nand completeness of death was with them like a/npresence./n/n"I've got to go too," said Harry./n/n/n/nTen pairs of startled eyes looked at him./n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't be silly, Harry," said Mrs. Weasley. "What are/nyou talking about?"/n/n"I can't stay here."/n/nHe rubbed his forehead; it was prickling again, it had/nnot hurt like this for more than a year./n/n"You're all in danger while I'm here. I don't want — "/n/n"But don't be so silly!" said Mrs. Weasley. "The whole/npoint of tonight was to get you here safely, and thank/ngoodness it worked. And Fleur's agreed to get married/nhere rather than in France, we've arranged everything/nso that we can all stay together and look after you — "/n/nShe did not understand; she was making him feel/nworse, not better./n/n"If Voldemort finds out I'm here — "/n/n"But why should he?" asked Mrs. Weasley./n/n"There are a dozen places you might be now, Harry,"/nsaid Mr. Weasley. "He's got no way of knowing which/nsafe house you're in."/n/n"It's not me I'm worried for!" said Harry./n/n"We know that," said Mr. Weasley quietly, "but it/nwould make our efforts tonight seem rather pointless/nif you left."/n/n"Yer not goin' anywhere," growled Hagrid. "Blimey,/nHarry, after all we wen' through ter get you here?"/n/n"Yeah, what about my bleeding ear?" said George,/nhoisting himself up on his cushions./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I know that — "/n/n/n/n"Mad-Eye wouldn't want — "/n/n"I KNOW!" Harry bellowed./n/nHe felt beleaguered and blackmailed: Did they think/nhe did not know what they had done for him, didn't/nthey understand that it was for precisely that reason/nthat he wanted to go now, before they had to suffer/nany more on his behalf? There was a long and/nawkward silence in which his scar continued to/nprickle and throb, and which was broken at last by/nMrs. Weasley./n/n"Where's Hedwig, Harry?" she said coaxingly. "We can/nput her up with Pigwidgeon and give her something to/neat."/n/nHis insides clenched like a fist. He could not tell her/nthe truth. He drank the last of his firewhisky to avoid/nanswering./n/n"Wait till it gets out yeh did it again, Harry," said/nHagrid. "Escaped him, fought him off when he was/nright on top of yeh!"/n/n"It wasn't me," said Harry flatly. "It was my wand. My/nwand acted of its own accord."/n/nAfter a few moments, Hermione said gently, "But/nthat's impossible, Harry. You mean that you did/nmagic without meaning to; you reacted instinctively."/n/n"No," said Harry. "The bike was falling, I couldn't have/ntold you where Voldemort was, but my wand spun in/nmy hand and found him and shot a spell at him, and/nit wasn't even a spell I recognized. I've never made/ngold flames appear before."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Often," said Mr. Weasley, "when you're in a/npressured situation you can produce magic you never/ndreamed of. Small children often find, before they're/ntrained — "/n/n"It wasn't like that," said Harry through gritted teeth./nHis scar was burning: He felt angry and frustrated; he/nhated the idea that they were all imagining him to/nhave power to match Voldemort's./n/nNo one said anything. He knew that they did not/nbelieve him. Now that he came to think of it, he had/nnever heard of a wand performing magic on its own/nbefore./n/nHis scar seared with pain; it was all he could do not/nto moan aloud. Muttering about fresh air, he set/ndown his glass and left the room./n/nAs he crossed the dark yard, the great skeletal/nthestral looked up, rustled its enormous batlike/nwings, then resumed its grazing. Harry stopped at the/ngate into the garden, staring out at its overgrown/nplants, rubbing his pounding forehead and thinking/nof Dumbledore./n/nDumbledore would have believed him, he knew it./nDumbledore would have known how and why Harry's/nwand had acted independently, because Dumbledore/nalways had the answers; he had known about wands,/nhad explained to Harry the strange connection that/nexisted between his wand and Voldemort's. ... But/nDumbledore, like Mad-Eye, like Sirius, like his/nparents, like his poor owl, all were gone where Harry/ncould never talk to them again. He felt a burning in/nhis throat that had nothing to do with firewhisky . . ./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd then, out of nowhere, the pain in his scar/npeaked. As he clutched his forehead and closed his/neyes, a voice screamed inside his head./n/n/n/n" You told me the problem would be solved by using/nanother's wand\"/n/nAnd into his mind burst the vision of an emaciated/nold man lying in rags upon a stone floor, screaming, a/nhorrible, drawn-out scream, a scream of unendurable/nagony. .../n/n"No! No! I beg you, I beg you. ..."/n/n"You lied to Lord Voldemort, Ollivander!"/n/n"I did not. ... I swear I did not. ..."/n/n"You sought to help Potter, to help him escape me!"/n/n"I swear I did not. ... I believed a different wand would/nwork. ..."/n/n"Explain, then, what happened. Lucius's wand is/ndestroyed!"/n/n"I cannot understand. ... The connection ... exists/nonly ... between your two wands. ..."/n/n"Lies!"/n/n"Please ... I beg you. ..."/n/nAnd Harry saw the white hand raise its wand and felt/nVoldemort 's surge of vicious anger, saw the frail old/nman on the floor writhe in agony —/n/n"Harry?"/n/n/n/n/n/nIt was over as quickly as it had come: Harry stood/nshaking in the darkness, clutching the gate into the/ngarden, his heart racing, his scar still tingling. It was/nseveral moments before he realized that Ron and/nHermione were at his side./n/n"Harry, come back in the house," Hermione/nwhispered. "You aren't still thinking of leaving?"/n/n"Yeah, you've got to stay, mate," said Ron, thumping/nHarry on the back./n/n"Are you all right?" Hermione asked, close enough/nnow to look into Harry's face. "You look awful!"/n/n"Well," said Harry shakily, "I probably look better/nthan Ollivander. ..."/n/nWhen he had finished telling them what he had seen,/nRon looked appalled, but Hermione downright/nterrified./n/n"But it was supposed to have stopped! Your scar — it/nwasn't supposed to do this anymore! You mustn't let/nthat connection open up again — Dumbledore wanted/nyou to close your mind!"/n/nWhen he did not reply, she gripped his arm./n/n"Harry, he's taking over the Ministry and the/nnewspapers and half the Wizarding world! Don't let/nhim inside your head too!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n6/n/n/n/n

title: The Ghoul In Pajamas
text: /nThe shock of losing Mad-Eye hung over the house in/nthe days that followed; Harry kept expecting to see/nhim stumping in through the back door like the other/nOrder members, who passed in and out to relay news./nHarry felt that nothing but action would assuage his/nfeelings of guilt and grief and that he ought to set out/non his mission to find and destroy Horcruxes as soon/nas possible./n/n"Well, you can't do anything about the" — Ron/nmouthed the word Horcruxes — "till you're seventeen./nYou've still got the Trace on you. And we can plan/nhere as well as anywhere, can't we? Or," he dropped/nhis voice to a whisper, "d'you reckon you already/nknow where the You-Know-Whats are?"/n/n"No," Harry admitted./n/n"I think Hermione's been doing a bit of research," said/nRon. "She said she was saving it for when you got/nhere."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThey were sitting at the breakfast table; Mr. Weasley/nand Bill had just left for work. Mrs. Weasley had gone/nupstairs to wake Hermione and Ginny, while Fleur/nhad drifted off to take a bath./n/n"The Trace'll break on the thirty- first," said Harry./n"That means I only need to stay here four days. Then/nI can — "/n/n"Five days," Ron corrected him firmly. "We've got to/nstay for the wedding. They'll kill us if we miss it."/n/nHarry understood "they" to mean Fleur and Mrs./nWeasley./n/n"It's one extra day," said Ron, when Harry looked/nmutinous./n/n"Don't they realize how important — ?"/n/n" 'Course they don't," said Ron. "They haven't got a/nclue. And now you mention it, I wanted to talk to you/nabout that."/n/nRon glanced toward the door into the hall to check/nthat Mrs. Weasley was not returning yet, then leaned/nin closer to Harry./n/n"Mum's been trying to get it out of Hermione and me./nWhat we're off to do. She'll try you next, so brace/nyourself. Dad and Lupin 've both asked as well, but/nwhen we said Dumbledore told you not to tell anyone/nexcept us, they dropped it. Not Mum, though. She's/ndetermined."/n/nRon's prediction came true within hours. Shortly/nbefore lunch, Mrs. Weasley detached Harry from the/nothers by asking him to help identify a lone man's/nsock that she thought might have come out of his/n/n/n/n/n/nrucksack. Once she had him cornered in the tiny/nscullery off the kitchen, she started./n/n"Ron and Hermione seem to think that the three of/nyou are dropping out of Hogwarts," she began in a/nlight, casual tone./n/n"Oh," said Harry. "Well, yeah. We are."/n/nThe mangle turned of its own accord in a corner,/nwringing out what looked like one of Mr. Weasley's/nvests./n/n"May I ask why you are abandoning your education?"/nsaid Mrs. Weasley./n/n"Well, Dumbledore left me ... stuff to do," mumbled/nHarry. "Ron and Hermione know about it, and they/nwant to come too."/n/n"What sort of 'stuff'?"/n/n"I'm sorry, I can't — "/n/n"Well, frankly, I think Arthur and I have a right to/nknow, and I'm sure Mr. and Mrs. Granger would/nagree!" said Mrs. Weasley. Harry had been afraid of/nthe "concerned parent" attack. He forced himself to/nlook directly into her eyes, noticing as he did so that/nthey were precisely the same shade of brown as/nGinny's. This did not help./n/n"Dumbledore didn't want anyone else to know, Mrs./nWeasley. I'm sorry. Ron and Hermione don't have to/ncome, it's their choice — "/n/n"I don't see that you have to go either!" she snapped,/ndropping all pretense now. "You're barely of age, any/nof you!
