It can't exist without it."/n/n"That diary sort of died when I stabbed it," said Harry,/nremembering ink pouring like blood from the/npunctured pages, and the screams of the piece of/nVoldemort's soul as it vanished./n/n"And once the diary was properly destroyed, the bit of/nsoul trapped in it could no longer exist. Ginny tried to/nget rid of the diary before you did, flushing it away,/nbut obviously it came back good as new."/n/n"Hang on," said Ron, frowning. "The bit of soul in that/ndiary was possessing Ginny, wasn't it? How does that/nwork, then?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"While the magical container is still intact, the bit of/nsoul inside it can flit in and out of someone if they get/ntoo close to the object. I don't mean holding it for too/nlong, it's nothing to do with touching it," she added/nbefore Ron could speak. "I mean close emotionally./nGinny poured her heart out into that diary, she made/nherself incredibly vulnerable. You're in trouble if you/nget too fond of or dependent on the Horcrux."/n/n"I wonder how Dumbledore destroyed the ring?" said/nHarry. "Why didn't I ask him? I never really ..."/n/nHis voice tailed away: He was thinking of all the/nthings he should have asked Dumbledore, and of/nhow, since the headmaster had died, it seemed to/nHarry that he had wasted so many opportunities/nwhen Dumbledore had been alive, to find out more .../nto find out everything. . . ./n/nThe silence was shattered as the bedroom door flew/nopen with a wall-shaking crash. Hermione shrieked/nand dropped Secrets of the Darkest Art; Crookshanks/nstreaked under the bed, hissing indignantly; Ron/njumped off the bed, skidded on a discarded Chocolate/nFrog wrapper, and smacked his head on the opposite/nwall; and Harry instinctively dived for his wand before/nrealizing that he was looking up at Mrs. Weasley,/nwhose hair was disheveled and whose face was/ncontorted with rage./n/n"I'm so sorry to break up this cozy little gathering,"/nshe said, her voice trembling. "I'm sure you all need/nyour rest . . . but there are wedding presents stacked/nin my room that need sorting out and I was under the/nimpression that you had agreed to help."/n/n"Oh yes," said Hermione, looking terrified as she leapt/nto her feet, sending books flying in every direction,/n/n"we will ... we're sorry ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nWith an anguished look at Harry and Ron, Hermione/nhurried out of the room after Mrs. Weasley./n/n"It's like being a house-elf," complained Ron in an/nundertone, still massaging his head as he and Harry/nfollowed. "Except without the job satisfaction. The/nsooner this wedding's over, the happier I'll be."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "then we'll have nothing to do/nexcept find Horcruxes. ... It'll be like a holiday, won't/nit?"/n/n/n/nRon started to laugh, but at the sight of the enormous/npile of wedding presents waiting for them in Mrs./nWeasley's room, stopped quite abruptly./n/nThe Delacours arrived the following morning at eleven/no'clock. Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Ginny were feeling/nquite resentful toward Fleur's family by this time, and/nit was with ill grace that Ron stumped back upstairs/nto put on matching socks, and Harry attempted to/nflatten his hair. Once they had all been deemed smart/nenough, they trooped out into the sunny backyard to/nawait the visitors./n/nHarry had never seen the place looking so tidy. The/nrusty cauldrons and old Wellington boots that usually/nlittered the steps by the back door were gone,/nreplaced by two new Flutterby bushes standing either/nside of the door in large pots; though there was no/nbreeze, the leaves waved lazily, giving an attractive/nrippling effect. The chickens had been shut away, the/nyard had been swept, and the nearby garden had/nbeen pruned, plucked, and generally spruced up,/nalthough Harry, who liked it in its overgrown state,/nthought that it looked rather forlorn without its usual/ncontingent of capering gnomes./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe had lost track of how many security enchantments/nhad been placed upon the Burrow by both the Order/nand the Ministry; all he knew was that it was no/nlonger possible for anybody to travel by magic directly/ninto the place. Mr. Weasley had therefore gone to/nmeet the Delacours on top of a nearby hill, where they/nwere to arrive by Portkey. The first sound of their/napproach was an unusually high-pitched laugh,/nwhich turned out to be coming from Mr. Weasley, who/nappeared at the gate moments later, laden with/nluggage and leading a beautiful blonde woman in/nlong, leaf-green robes, who could only be Fleur's/nmother./n/n"Maman!" cried Fleur, rushing forward to embrace/nher. "Papa!"/n/nMonsieur Delacour was nowhere near as attractive as/nhis wife; he was a head shorter and extremely plump,/nwith a little, pointed black beard. However, he looked/ngood-natured. Bouncing toward Mrs. Weasley on/nhigh-heeled boots, he kissed her twice on each cheek,/nleaving her flustered./n/n"You 'ave been to much trouble," he said in a deep/nvoice. "Fleur tells us you 'ave been working very 'ard."/n/n"Oh, it's been nothing, nothing!" trilled Mrs. Weasley./n"No trouble at all!"/n/nRon relieved his feelings by aiming a kick at a gnome/nwho was peering out from behind one of the new/nFlutterby bushes./n/n"Dear lady!" said Monsieur Delacour, still holding/nMrs. Weasley's hand between his own two plump/nones and beaming. "We are most honored at the/napproaching union of our two families! Let me present/nmy wife, Apolline."/n/n/n/n/n/nMadame Delacour glided forward and stooped to kiss/nMrs. Weasley too./n/n" Enchantee," she said. "Your 'usband 'as been telling/nus such amusing stories!"/n/nMr. Weasley gave a maniacal laugh; Mrs. Weasley/nthrew him a look, upon which he became immediately/nsilent and assumed an expression appropriate to the/nsickbed of a close friend./n/n"And, of course, you 'ave met my leetle daughter,/nGabrielle!" said Monsieur Delacour. Gabrielle was/nFleur in miniature; eleven years old, with waist-length/nhair of pure, silvery blonde, she gave Mrs. Weasley a/ndazzling smile and hugged her, then threw Harry a/nglowing look, batting her eyelashes. Ginny cleared her/nthroat loudly./n/n"Well, come in, do!" said Mrs. Weasley brightly, and/nshe ushered the Delacours into the house, with many/n"No, please!"s and "After you!"s and "Not at all!"s./n/nThe Delacours, it soon transpired, were helpful,/npleasant guests. They were pleased with everything/nand keen to assist with the preparations for the/nwedding. Monsieur Delacour pronounced everything/nfrom the seating plan to the bridesmaids' shoes/n"Charmanti" Madame Delacour was most/naccomplished at household spells and had the oven/nproperly cleaned in a trice; Gabrielle followed her/nelder sister around, trying to assist in any way she/ncould and jabbering away in rapid French./n/nOn the downside, the Burrow was not built to/naccommodate so many people. Mr. and Mrs. Weasley/nwere now sleeping in the sitting room, having shouted/ndown Monsieur and Madame Delacour's protests and/ninsisted they take their bedroom. Gabrielle was/n/n/n/n/nsleeping with Fleur in Percy's old room, and Bill/nwould be sharing with Charlie, his best man, once/nCharlie arrived from Romania. Opportunities to make/nplans together became virtually nonexistent, and it/nwas in desperation that Harry, Ron, and Hermione/ntook to volunteering to feed the chickens just to/nescape the overcrowded house./n/n"But she still won't leave us alone!" snarled Ron, as/ntheir second attempt at a meeting in the yard was/nfoiled by the appearance of Mrs. Weasley carrying a/nlarge basket of laundry in her arms./n/n"Oh, good, you've fed the chickens," she called as she/napproached them. "We'd better shut them away again/nbefore the men arrive tomorrow ... to put up the tent/nfor the wedding," she explained, pausing to lean/nagainst the henhouse. She looked exhausted./n"Millamant's Magic Marquees ... they're very good,/nBill's escorting them. ... You'd better stay inside while/nthey're here, Harry. I must say it does complicate/norganizing a wedding, having all these security spells/naround the place."/n/n"I'm sorry," said Harry humbly./n/n"Oh, don't be silly, dear!" said Mrs. Weasley at once. "I/ndidn't mean — well, your safety's much more/nimportant! Actually, I've been wanting to ask you how/nyou want to celebrate your birthday, Harry./n/nSeventeen, after all, it's an important day. ..."/n/n"I don't want a fuss," said Harry quickly, envisaging/nthe additional strain this would put on them all./n"Really, Mrs. Weasley, just a normal dinner would be/nfine. ... It's the day before the wedding. ..."/n/n"Oh, well, if you're sure, dear. I'll invite Remus and/nTonks, shall I? And how about Hagrid?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"That'd be great," said Harry. "But please don't go to/nloads of trouble."/n/n"Not at all, not at all ... It's no trouble. ..."/n/nShe looked at him, a long, searching look, then smiled/na little sadly, straightened up, and walked away./n/nHarry watched as she waved her wand near the/nwashing line, and the damp clothes rose into the air/nto hang themselves up, and suddenly he felt a great/nwave of remorse for the inconvenience and the pain/nhe was giving her./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n7/n/n/n/n

title: The Will Of Albus Dumbledore
text: /nHe was walking along a mountain road in the cool/nblue light of dawn. Far below, swathed in mist, was/nthe shadow of a small town. Was the man he sought/ndown there, the man he needed so badly he could/nthink of little else, the man who held the answer, the/nanswer to his problem . . . ?/n/n"Oi, wake up."/n/nHarry opened his eyes. He was lying again on the/ncamp bed in Ron's dingy attic room. The sun had not/nyet risen and the room was still shadowy. Pigwidgeon/nwas asleep with his head under his tiny wing. The/nscar on Harry's forehead was prickling./n/n"You were muttering in your sleep."/n/n"Was I?"/n/n"Yeah. 'Gregorovitch.' You kept saying 'Gregorovitch.'/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry was not wearing his glasses; Ron's face/nappeared slightly blurred./n/n/n/n"Who's Gregorovitch?"/n/n"I dunno, do I? You were the one saying it."/n/nHarry rubbed his forehead, thinking. He had a vague/nidea he had heard the name before, but he could not/nthink where./n/n"I think Voldemort's looking for him."/n/n"Poor bloke," said Ron fervently./n/nHarry sat up, still rubbing his scar, now wide awake./nHe tried to remember exactly what he had seen in the/ndream, but all that came back was a mountainous/nhorizon and the outline of the little village cradled in a/ndeep valley./n/n"I think he's abroad."/n/n"Who, Gregorovitch?"/n/n"Voldemort. I think he's somewhere abroad, looking/nfor Gregorovitch. It didn't look like anywhere in/nBritain."/n/n"You reckon you were seeing into his mind again?"/nRon sounded worried./n/n"Do me a favor and don't tell Hermione," said Harry./n"Although how she expects me to stop seeing stuff in/nmy sleep ..."/n/nHe gazed up at little Pigwidgeon's cage, thinking .../nWhy was the name "Gregorovitch" familiar?/n/n/n/n/n/n"I think," he said slowly, "he's got something to do/nwith Quidditch. There's some connection, but I can't/n— I can't think what it is."/n/n"Quidditch?" said Ron. "Sure you're not thinking of/nGorgovitch?"/n/n"Who?"/n/n"Dragomir Gorgovitch, Chaser, transferred to the/nChudley Cannons for a record fee two years ago./nRecord holder for most Quaffle drops in a season."/n/n"No," said Harry. "I'm definitely not thinking of/nGorgovitch."/n/n"I try not to either," said Ron. "Well, happy birthday/nanyway."/n/n"Wow — that's right, I forgot! I'm seventeen!"/n/nHarry seized the wand lying beside his camp bed,/npointed it at the cluttered desk where he had left his/nglasses, and said, "Accio Glasses!" Although they were/nonly around a foot away, there was something/nimmensely satisfying about seeing them zoom toward/nhim, at least until they poked him in the eye./n/n"Slick," snorted Ron./n/nReveling in the removal of his Trace, Harry sent Ron's/npossessions flying around the room, causing/nPigwidgeon to wake up and flutter excitedly around/nhis cage. Harry also tried tying the laces of his/ntrainers by magic (the resultant knot took several/nminutes to untie by hand) and, purely for the/npleasure of it, turned the orange robes on Ron's/nChudley Cannons posters bright blue./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'd do your fly by hand, though," Ron advised Harry,/nsniggering when Harry immediately checked it./n/n"Here's your present. Unwrap it up here, it's not for/nmy mother's eyes."/n/n"A book?" said Harry as he took the rectangular/nparcel. "Bit of a departure from tradition, isn't it?"/n/n"This isn't your average book," said Ron. "It's pure/ngold: Twelve Fail-Safe Ways to Charm Witches./nExplains everything you need to know about girls. If/nonly I'd had this last year I'd have known exactly how/nto get rid of Lavender and I would've known how to/nget going with ... Well, Fred and George gave me a/ncopy, and I've learned a lot. You'd be surprised, it's/nnot all about wandwork, either."/n/nWhen they arrived in the kitchen they found a pile of/npresents waiting on the table. Bill and Monsieur/nDelacour were finishing their breakfasts, while Mrs./nWeasley stood chatting to them over the frying pan./n/n"Arthur told me to wish you a happy seventeenth,/nHarry," said Mrs. Weasley, beaming at him. "He had/nto leave early for work, but hell be back for dinner./nThat's our present on top."/n/nHarry sat down, took the square parcel she had/nindicated, and unwrapped it. Inside was a watch very/nlike the one Mr. and Mrs. Weasley had given Ron for/nhis seventeenth; it was gold, with stars circling/naround the face instead of hands./n/n"It's traditional to give a wizard a watch when he/ncomes of age," said Mrs. Weasley, watching him/nanxiously from beside the cooker. "I'm afraid that one/nisn't new like Ron's, it was actually my brother/nFabian's and he wasn't terribly careful with his/npossessions, it's a bit dented on the back, but — "/n/n/n/n/nThe rest of her speech was lost; Harry had got up and/nhugged her. He tried to put a lot of unsaid things into/nthe hug and perhaps she understood them, because/nshe patted his cheek clumsily when he released her,/nthen waved her wand in a slightly random way,/ncausing half a pack of bacon to flop out of the frying/npan onto the floor./n/n"Happy birthday, Harry!" said Hermione, hurrying/ninto the kitchen and adding her own present to the/ntop of the pile. "It's not much, but I hope you like it./nWhat did you get him?" she added to Ron, who/nseemed not to hear her./n/n"Come on, then, open Hermione's!" said Ron./n/nShe had bought him a new Sneakoscope. The other/npackages contained an enchanted razor from Bill and/nFleur ("Ah yes, zis will give you ze smoothest shave/nyou will ever 'ave," Monsieur Delacour assured him,/n"but you must tell it clearly what you want . . ./nozzerwise you might find you 'ave a leetle less hair/nzan you would like. ..."), chocolates from the/nDelacours, and an enormous box of the latest/nWeasleys' Wizard Wheezes merchandise from Fred/nand George./n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione did not linger at the table,/nas the arrival of Madame Delacour, Fleur, and/nGabrielle made the kitchen uncomfortably crowded./n/n"I'll pack these for you," Hermione said brightly,/ntaking Harry's presents out of his arms as the three of/nthem headed back upstairs. "I'm nearly done, I'm just/nwaiting for the rest of your underpants to come out of/nthe wash, Ron — "/n/nRon's splutter was interrupted by the opening of a/ndoor on the first-floor landing./n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, will you come in here a moment?"/n/nIt was Ginny. Ron came to an abrupt halt, but/nHermione took him by the elbow and tugged him on/nup the stairs. Feeling nervous, Harry followed Ginny/ninto her room./n/nHe had never been inside it before. It was small, but/nbright. There was a large poster of the Wizarding/nband the Weird Sisters on one wall, and a picture of/nGwenog Jones, Captain of the all-witch Quidditch/nteam the Holyhead Harpies, on the other. A desk/nstood facing the open window, which looked out over/nthe orchard where he and Ginny had once played/ntwo-a-side Quidditch with Ron and Hermione, and/nwhich now housed a large, pearly white marquee. The/ngolden flag on top was level with Ginny's window./n/nGinny looked up into Harry's face, took a deep breath,/nand said, "Happy seventeenth."/n/n"Yeah ... thanks."/n/nShe was looking at him steadily; he, however, found it/ndifficult to look back at her; it was like gazing into a/nbrilliant light./n/n"Nice view," he said feebly, pointing toward the/nwindow./n/nShe ignored this. He could not blame her./n/n"I couldn't think what to get you," she said./n/n"You didn't have to get me anything."/n/nShe disregarded this too./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I didn't know what would be useful. Nothing too big,/nbecause you wouldn't be able to take it with you."/n/nHe chanced a glance at her. She was not tearful; that/nwas one of the many wonderful things about Ginny,/nshe was rarely weepy. He had sometimes thought that/nhaving six brothers must have toughened her up./n/nShe took a step closer to him./n/n"So then I thought, I'd like you to have something to/nremember me by, you know, if you meet some veela/nwhen you're off doing whatever you're doing."/n/n"I think dating opportunities are going to be pretty/nthin on the ground, to be honest."/n/n"There's the silver lining I've been looking for," she/nwhispered, and then she was kissing him as she had/nnever kissed him before, and Harry was kissing her/nback, and it was blissful oblivion, better than/nfirewhisky; she was the only real thing in the world,/nGinny, the feel of her, one hand at her back and one/nin her long, sweet-smelling hair —/n/nThe door banged open behind them and they jumped/napart./n/n"Oh," said Ron pointedly. "Sorry."/n/n"Ron!" Hermione was just behind him, slightly out of/nbreath. There was a strained silence, then Ginny said/nin a flat little voice,/n/n"Well, happy birthday anyway, Harry."/n/nRon's ears were scarlet; Hermione looked nervous./nHarry wanted to slam the door in their faces, but it/nfelt as though a cold draft had entered the room when/n/n/n/n/n/nthe door opened, and his shining moment had popped/nlike a soap bubble. All the reasons for ending his/nrelationship with Ginny, for staying well away from/nher, seemed to have slunk inside the room with Ron,/nand all happy forgetfulness was gone./n/nHe looked at Ginny, wanting to say something,/nthough he hardly knew what, but she had turned her/nback on him. He thought that she might have/nsuccumbed, for once, to tears. He could not do/nanything to comfort her in front of Ron./n/n"I'll see you later," he said, and followed the other two/nout of the bedroom./n/nRon marched downstairs, through the still-crowded/nkitchen and into the yard, and Harry kept pace with/nhim all the way, Hermione trotting along behind them/nlooking scared./n/nOnce he reached the seclusion of the freshly mown/nlawn, Ron rounded on Harry./n/n"You ditched her. What are you doing now, messing/nher around?"/n/n"I'm not messing her around," said Harry, as/nHermione caught up with them./n/n"Ron — "/n/nBut Ron held up a hand to silence her./n/n"She was really cut up when you ended it — "/n/n"So was I. You know why I stopped it, and it wasn't/nbecause I wanted to."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, but you go snogging her now and she's just/ngoing to get her hopes up again — "/n/n"She's not an idiot, she knows it can't happen, she's/nnot expecting us to — to end up married, or — "/n/nAs he said it, a vivid picture formed in Harry's mind of/nGinny in a white dress, marrying a tall, faceless, and/nunpleasant stranger. In one spiraling moment it/nseemed to hit him: Her future was free and/nunencumbered, whereas his ... he could see nothing/nbut Voldemort ahead./n/n"If you keep groping her every chance you get — "/n/n"It won't happen again," said Harry harshly. The day/nwas cloudless, but he felt as though the sun had gone/nin. "Okay?"/n/nRon looked half resentful, half sheepish; he rocked/nbackward and forward on his feet for a moment, then/nsaid, "Right then, well, that's ... yeah."/n/nGinny did not seek another one-to-one meeting with/nHarry for the rest of the day, nor by any look or/ngesture did she show that they had shared more than/npolite conversation in her room. Nevertheless,/n/nCharlie's arrival came as a relief to Harry. It provided/na distraction, watching Mrs. Weasley force Charlie/ninto a chair, raise her wand threateningly, and/nannounce that he was about to get a proper haircut./n/nAs Harry's birthday dinner would have stretched the/nBurrow's kitchen to breaking point even before the/narrival of Charlie, Lupin, Tonks, and Hagrid, several/ntables were placed end to end in the garden. Fred and/nGeorge bewitched a number of purple lanterns, all/nemblazoned with a large number 17, to hang in/nmidair over the guests. Thanks to Mrs. Weasley's/n/n/n/n/nministrations, George's wound was neat and clean,/nbut Harry was not yet used to the dark hole in the/nside of his head, despite the twins' many jokes about/nit./n/nHermione made purple and gold streamers erupt from/nthe end of her wand and drape themselves artistically/nover the trees and bushes./n/n"Nice," said Ron, as with one final flourish of her/nwand, Hermione turned the leaves on the crabapple/ntree to gold. "You've really got an eye for that sort of/nthing."/n/n"Thank you, Ron!" said Hermione, looking both/npleased and a little confused. Harry turned away,/nsmiling to himself. He had a funny notion that he/nwould find a chapter on compliments when he found/ntime to peruse his copy of Twelve Fail-Safe Ways to/nCharm Witches; he caught Ginny's eye and grinned at/nher before remembering his promise to Ron and/nhurriedly striking up a conversation with Monsieur/nDelacour./n/n"Out of the way, out of the way!" sang Mrs. Weasley,/ncoming through the gate with what appeared to be a/ngiant, beach-ball-sized Snitch floating in front of her./nSeconds later Harry realized that it was his birthday/ncake, which Mrs. Weasley was suspending with her/nwand, rather than risk carrying it over the uneven/nground. When the cake had finally landed in the/nmiddle of the table, Harry said, "That looks amazing,/nMrs. Weasley."/n/n"Oh, it's nothing, dear," she said fondly. Over her/nshoulder, Ron gave Harry the thumbs-up and/nmouthed, Good one./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBy seven o'clock all the guests had arrived, led into/nthe house by Fred and George, who had waited for/nthem at the end of the lane. Hagrid had honored the/noccasion by wearing his best, and horrible, hairy/nbrown suit. Although Lupin smiled as he shook/nHarry's hand, Harry thought he looked rather/nunhappy. It was all very odd; Tonks, beside him,/nlooked simply radiant./n/n"Happy birthday, Harry," she said, hugging him/ntightly./n/n"Seventeen, eh!" said Hagrid as he accepted a bucket-/nsized glass of wine from Fred. "Six years ter the day/nsince we met, Harry, d'yeh remember it?"/n/n"Vaguely," said Harry, grinning up at him. "Didn't you/nsmash down the front door, give Dudley a pig's tail,/nand tell me I was a wizard?"/n/n"I forge' the details," Hagrid chortled. "All righ', Ron,/nHermione?"/n/n"We're fine," said Hermione. "How are you?"/n/n"Ar, not bad. Bin busy, we got some newborn/nunicorns, I'll show yeh when yeh get back — " Harry/navoided Ron's and Hermione's gazes as Hagrid/nrummaged in his pocket. "Here, Harry — couldn'/nthink what ter get yeh, but then I remembered this."/nHe pulled out a small, slightly furry drawstring pouch/nwith a long string, evidently intended to be worn/naround the neck. "Mokeskin. Hide anythin' in there/nan' no one but the owner can get it out. They're rare,/nthem."/n/n"Hagrid, thanks!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" 'S'nothin'," said Hagrid with a wave of a dustbin-lid-/nsized hand. "An' there's Charlie! Always liked him —/nhey! Charlie!"/n/nCharlie approached, running his hand slightly/nruefully over his new, brutally short haircut. He was/nshorter than Ron, thickset, with a number of burns/nand scratches up his muscley arms./n/n"Hi, Hagrid, how's it going?"/n/n"Bin meanin' ter write fer ages. How's Norbert doin'?"/n/n"Norbert?" Charlie laughed. "The Norwegian/nRidgeback? We call her Norberta now."/n/n"Wha — Norbert's a girl?"/n/n"Oh yeah," said Charlie./n/n"How can you tell?" asked Hermione./n/n"They're a lot more vicious," said Charlie. He looked/nover his shoulder and dropped his voice. "Wish Dad/nwould hurry up and get here. Mum's getting edgy."/n/nThey all looked over at Mrs. Weasley. She was trying/nto talk to Madame Delacour while glancing repeatedly/nat the gate./n/n"I think we'd better start without Arthur," she called/nto the garden at large after a moment or two. "He/nmust have been held up at — oh!"/n/nThey all saw it at the same time: a streak of light that/ncame flying across the yard and onto the table, where/nit resolved itself into a bright silver weasel, which/nstood on its hind legs and spoke with Mr. Weasley's/nvoice./n/n/n/n/n/n"Minister of Magic coming with me."/n/nThe Patronus dissolved into thin air, leaving Fleur's/nfamily peering in astonishment at the place where it/nhad vanished./n/n"We shouldn't be here," said Lupin at once. "Harry —/nI'm sorry — I'll explain another time — "/n/nHe seized Tonks's wrist and pulled her away; they/nreached the fence, climbed over it, and vanished from/nsight. Mrs. Weasley looked bewildered./n/n"The Minister — but why — ? I don't understand — "/n/nBut there was no time to discuss the matter; a second/nlater, Mr. Weasley had appeared out of thin air at the/ngate, accompanied by Rufus Scrimgeour, instantly/nrecognizable by his mane of grizzled hair./n/nThe two newcomers marched across the yard toward/nthe garden and the lantern- lit table, where everybody/nsat in silence, watching them draw closer. As/nScrimgeour came within range of the lantern light,/nHarry saw that he looked much older than the last/ntime they had met, scraggy and grim./n/n"Sorry to intrude," said Scrimgeour, as he limped to a/nhalt before the table. "Especially as I can see that I/nam gate-crashing a party."/n/nHis eyes lingered for a moment on the giant Snitch/ncake./n/n"Many happy returns."/n/n"Thanks," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I require a private word with you," Scrimgeour went/non. "Also with Mr. Ronald Weasley and Miss/nHermione Granger."/n/n"Us?" said Ron, sounding surprised. "Why us?"/n/n"I shall tell you that when we are somewhere more/nprivate," said Scrimgeour. "Is there such a place?" he/ndemanded of Mr. Weasley./n/n"Yes, of course," said Mr. Weasley, who looked/nnervous. "The, er, sitting room, why don't you use/nthat?"/n/n"You can lead the way," Scrimgeour said to Ron./n"There will be no need for you to accompany us,/nArthur."/n/nHarry saw Mr. Weasley exchange a worried look with/nMrs. Weasley as he, Ron, and Hermione stood up. As/nthey led the way back to the house in silence, Harry/nknew that the other two were thinking the same as he/nwas: Scrimgeour must, somehow, have learned that/nthe three of them were planning to drop out of/nHogwarts./n/nScrimgeour did not speak as they all passed through/nthe messy kitchen and into the Burrow's sitting room./nAlthough the garden had been full of soft golden/nevening light, it was already dark in here: Harry/nflicked his wand at the oil lamps as he entered and/nthey illuminated the shabby but cozy room./nScrimgeour sat himself in the sagging armchair that/nMr. Weasley normally occupied, leaving Harry, Ron,/nand Hermione to squeeze side by side onto the sofa./nOnce they had done so, Scrimgeour spoke./n/n"I have some questions for the three of you, and I/nthink it will be best if we do it individually. If you two"/n/n/n/n/n/n— he pointed at Harry and Hermione — "can wait/nupstairs, I will start with Ronald."/n/n"We're not going anywhere," said Harry, while/nHermione nodded vigorously. "You can speak to us/ntogether, or not at all."/n/nScrimgeour gave Harry a cold, appraising look. Harry/nhad the impression that the Minister was wondering/nwhether it was worthwhile opening hostilities this/nearly./n/n"Very well then, together," he said, shrugging. He/ncleared his throat. "I am here, as I'm sure you know,/nbecause of Albus Dumbledore's will."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione looked at one another./n/n"A surprise, apparently! You were not aware then that/nDumbledore had left you anything?"/n/n"A-all of us?" said Ron. "Me and Hermione too?"/n/n"Yes, all of—"/n/nBut Harry interrupted./n/n"Dumbledore died over a month ago. Why has it taken/nthis long to give us what he left us?"/n/n"Isn't it obvious?" said Hermione, before Scrimgeour/ncould answer. "They wanted to examine whatever he's/nleft us. You had no right to do that!" she said, and her/nvoice trembled slightly./n/n"I had every right," said Scrimgeour dismissively. "The/nDecree for Justifiable Confiscation gives the Ministry/nthe power to confiscate the contents of a will — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"That law was created to stop wizards passing on/nDark artifacts," said Hermione, "and the Ministry is/nsupposed to have powerful evidence that the/ndeceased's possessions are illegal before seizing them!/nAre you telling me that you thought Dumbledore was/ntrying to pass us something cursed?"/n/n"Are you planning to follow a career in Magical Law,/nMiss Granger?" asked Scrimgeour./n/n"No, I'm not," retorted Hermione. "I'm hoping to do/nsome good in the world!"/n/nRon laughed. Scrimgeour 's eyes flickered toward him/nand away again as Harry spoke./n/n"So why have you decided to let us have our things/nnow? Can't think of a pretext to keep them?"/n/n"No, it'll be because the thirty-one days are up," said/nHermione at once. "They can't keep the objects longer/nthan that unless they can prove they're dangerous./nRight?"/n/n"Would you say you were close to Dumbledore,/nRonald?" asked Scrimgeour, ignoring Hermione. Ron/nlooked startled./n/n"Me? Not — not really ... It was always Harry who ..."/n/nRon looked around at Harry and Hermione, to see/nHermione giving him a stop-talking-now\ sort of look,/nbut the damage was done: Scrimgeour looked as/nthough he had heard exactly what he had expected,/nand wanted, to hear. He swooped like a bird of prey/nupon Ron's answer./n/n"If you were not very close to Dumbledore, how do you/naccount for the fact that he remembered you in his/n/n/n/n/n/nwill? He made exceptionally few personal bequests./nThe vast majority of his possessions — his private/nlibrary, his magical instruments, and other personal/neffects — were left to Hogwarts. Why do you think you/nwere singled out?"/n/n"I ... dunno," said Ron. "I ... when I say we weren't/nclose ... I mean, I think he liked me. ..."/n/n"You're being modest, Ron," said Hermione./n"Dumbledore was very fond of you."/n/nThis was stretching the truth to breaking point; as far/nas Harry knew, Ron and Dumbledore had never been/nalone together, and direct contact between them had/nbeen negligible. However, Scrimgeour did not seem to/nbe listening. He put his hand inside his cloak and/ndrew out a drawstring pouch much larger than the/none Hagrid had given Harry. From it, he removed a/nscroll of parchment which he unrolled and read/naloud./n/n" 'The Last Will and Testament of Albus Percival/nWulfric Brian Dumbledore' ... Yes, here we are. ... 'To/nRonald Bilius Weasley, I leave my Deluminator, in the/nhope that he will remember me when he uses it.' "/n/nScrimgeour took from the bag an object that Harry/nhad seen before: It looked something like a silver/ncigarette lighter, but it had, he knew, the power to/nsuck all light from a place, and restore it, with a/nsimple click. Scrimgeour leaned forward and passed/nthe Deluminator to Ron, who took it and turned it/nover in his fingers, looking stunned./n/n"That is a valuable object," said Scrimgeour, watching/nRon. "It may even be unique. Certainly it is of/nDumbledore's own design. Why would he have left/nyou an item so rare?"/n/n/n/n/n/nRon shook his head, looking bewildered./n/n"Dumbledore must have taught thousands of/nstudents," Scrimgeour persevered. "Yet the only ones/nhe remembered in his will are you three. Why is that?/nTo what use did he think you would put his/nDeluminator, Mr. Weasley?"/n/n"Put out lights, I s'pose," mumbled Ron. "What else/ncould I do with it?"/n/nEvidently Scrimgeour had no suggestions. After/nsquinting at Ron for a moment or two, he turned back/nto Dumbledore's will./n/n" To Miss Hermione Jean Granger, I leave my copy of/nThe Tales of Beedle the Bard, in the hope that she will/nfind it entertaining and instructive.' "/n/nScrimgeour now pulled out of the bag a small book/nthat looked as ancient as the copy of Secrets of the/nDarkest Art upstairs. Its binding was stained and/npeeling in places. Hermione took it from Scrimgeour/nwithout a word. She held the book in her lap and/ngazed at it. Harry saw that the title was in runes; he/nhad never learned to read them. As he looked, a tear/nsplashed onto the embossed symbols./n/n"Why do you think Dumbledore left you that book,/nMiss Granger?" asked Scrimgeour./n/n"He ... he knew I liked books," said Hermione in a/nthick voice, mopping her eyes with her sleeve./n/n"But why that particular book?"/n/n"I don't know. He must have thought I'd enjoy it."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Did you ever discuss codes, or any means of passing/nsecret messages, with Dumbledore?"/n/n/n/n"No, I didn't," said Hermione, still wiping her eyes on/nher sleeve. "And if the Ministry hasn't found any/nhidden codes in this book in thirty-one days, I doubt/nthat I will."/n/nShe suppressed a sob. They were wedged together so/ntightly that Ron had difficulty extracting his arm to/nput it around Hermione 's shoulders. Scrimgeour/nturned back to the will./n/n" 'To Harry James Potter,' " he read, and Harry's/ninsides contracted with a sudden excitement, " 'I leave/nthe Snitch he caught in his first Quidditch match at/nHogwarts, as a reminder of the rewards of/nperseverance and skill.' "/n/nAs Scrimgeour pulled out the tiny, walnut-sized/ngolden ball, its silver wings fluttered rather feebly,/nand Harry could not help feeling a definite sense of/nanticlimax./n/n"Why did Dumbledore leave you this Snitch?" asked/nScrimgeour./n/n"No idea," said Harry. "For the reasons you just read/nout, I suppose ... to remind me what you can get if/nyou ... persevere and whatever it was."/n/n"You think this a mere symbolic keepsake, then?"/n/n"I suppose so," said Harry. "What else could it be?"/n/n"I'm asking the questions," said Scrimgeour, shifting/nhis chair a little closer to the sofa. Dusk was really/nfalling outside now; the marquee beyond the windows/ntowered ghostly white over the hedge./n/n/n/n/n/n"I notice that your birthday cake is in the shape of a/nSnitch," Scrimgeour said to Harry. "Why is that?"/n/nHermione laughed derisively./n/n"Oh, it can't be a reference to the fact Harry's a great/nSeeker, that's way too obvious," she said. "There must/nbe a secret message from Dumbledore hidden in the/nicing!"/n/n"I don't think there's anything hidden in the icing,"/nsaid Scrimgeour, "but a Snitch would be a very good/nhiding place for a small object. You know why, I'm/nsure?"/n/nHarry shrugged. Hermione, however, answered: Harry/nthought that answering questions correctly was such/na deeply ingrained habit she could not suppress the/nurge./n/n"Because Snitches have flesh memories," she said./n/n"What?" said Harry and Ron together; both/nconsidered Hermione 's Quidditch knowledge/nnegligible./n/n"Correct," said Scrimgeour. "A Snitch is not touched/nby bare skin before it is released, not even by the/nmaker, who wears gloves. It carries an enchantment/nby which it can identify the first human to lay hands/nupon it, in case of a disputed capture. This Snitch" —/nhe held up the tiny golden ball — "will remember your/ntouch, Potter. It occurs to me that Dumbledore, who/nhad prodigious magical skill, whatever his other/nfaults, might have enchanted this Snitch so that it/nwill open only for you."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry's heart was beating rather fast. He was sure/nthat Scrimgeour was right. How could he avoid taking/nthe Snitch with his bare hand in front of the Minister?/n/n/n/n"You don't say anything," said Scrimgeour. "Perhaps/nyou already know what the Snitch contains?"/n/n"No," said Harry, still wondering how he could appear/nto touch the Snitch without really doing so. If only he/nknew Legilimency, really knew it, and could read/nHermione's mind; he could practically hear her brain/nwhirring beside him./n/n"Take it," said Scrimgeour quietly./n/nHarry met the Minister's yellow eyes and knew he had/nno option but to obey. He held out his hand, and/nScrimgeour leaned forward again and placed the/nSnitch, slowly and deliberately, into Harry's palm./n/nNothing happened. As Harry's fingers closed around/nthe Snitch, its tired wings fluttered and were still./nScrimgeour, Ron, and Hermione continued to gaze/navidly at the now partially concealed ball, as if still/nhoping it might transform in some way./n/n"That was dramatic," said Harry coolly. Both Ron and/nHermione laughed./n/n"That's all, then, is it?" asked Hermione, making to/nprise herself off the sofa./n/n"Not quite," said Scrimgeour, who looked bad-/ntempered now. "Dumbledore left you a second/nbequest, Potter."/n/n"What is it?" asked Harry, excitement rekindling./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nScrimgeour did not bother to read from the will this/ntime./n/n"The sword of Godric Gryffindor," he said./n/nHermione and Ron both stiffened. Harry looked/naround for a sign of the ruby-encrusted hilt, but/nScrimgeour did not pull the sword from the leather/npouch, which in any case looked much too small to/ncontain it./n/n"So where is it?" Harry asked suspiciously./n/n"Unfortunately," said Scrimgeour, "that sword was/nnot Dumbledore 's to give away. The sword of Godric/nGryffindor is an important historical artifact, and as/nsuch, belongs — "/n/n"It belongs to Harry!" said Hermione hotly. "It chose/nhim, he was the one who found it, it came to him out/nof the Sorting Hat — "/n/n"According to reliable historical sources, the sword/nmay present itself to any worthy Gryffindor," said/nScrimgeour. "That does not make it the exclusive/nproperty of Mr. Potter, whatever Dumbledore may/nhave decided." Scrimgeour scratched his badly/nshaven cheek, scrutinizing Harry. "Why do you think/n— ?"/n/n" — Dumbledore wanted to give me the sword?" said/nHarry, struggling to keep his temper. "Maybe he/nthought it would look nice on my wall."/n/n"This is not a joke, Potter!" growled Scrimgeour. "Was/nit because Dumbledore believed that only the sword of/nGodric Gryffindor could defeat the Heir of Slytherin?/nDid he wish to give you that sword, Potter, because he/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbelieved, as do many, that you are the one destined to/ndestroy He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named?"/n/n"Interesting theory," said Harry. "Has anyone ever/ntried sticking a sword in Voldemort? Maybe the/nMinistry should put some people onto that, instead of/nwasting their time stripping down Deluminators or/ncovering up breakouts from Azkaban. So is this what/nyou've been doing, Minister, shut up in your office,/ntrying to break open a Snitch? People are dying — I/nwas nearly one of them — Voldemort chased me/nacross three counties, he killed Mad-Eye Moody, but/nthere's been no word about any of that from the/nMinistry, has there? And you still expect us to/ncooperate with you!"/n/n"You go too far!" shouted Scrimgeour, standing up;/nHarry jumped to his feet too. Scrimgeour limped/ntoward Harry and jabbed him hard in the chest with/nthe point of his wand: It singed a hole in Harry's T-/nshirt like a lit cigarette./n/n"Oi!" said Ron, jumping up and raising his own wand,/nbut Harry said,/n/n"No! D'you want to give him an excuse to arrest us?"/n/n"Remembered you're not at school, have you?" said/nScrimgeour, breathing hard into Harry's face./n"Remembered that I am not Dumbledore, who forgave/nyour insolence and insubordination? You may wear/nthat scar like a crown, Potter, but it is not up to a/nseventeen-year-old boy to tell me how to do my job!/n/nIt's time you learned some respect!"/n/n"It's time you earned it," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe floor trembled; there was a sound of running/nfootsteps, then the door to the sitting room burst/nopen and Mr. and Mrs. Weasley ran in./n/n"We — we thought we heard — " began Mr. Weasley,/nlooking thoroughly alarmed at the sight of Harry and/nthe Minister virtually nose to nose./n/n" — raised voices," panted Mrs. Weasley./n/nScrimgeour took a couple of steps back from Harry,/nglancing at the hole he had made in Harry's T-shirt./nHe seemed to regret his loss of temper./n/n"It — it was nothing," he growled. "I ... regret your/nattitude," he said, looking Harry full in the face once/nmore. "You seem to think that the Ministry does not/ndesire what you — what Dumbledore — desired. We/nought to be working together."/n/n"I don't like your methods, Minister," said Harry./n"Remember?"/n/nFor the second time, he raised his right fist and/ndisplayed to Scrimgeour the scars that still showed/nwhite on the back of it, spelling I must not tell lies./nScrimgeour 's expression hardened. He turned away/nwithout another word and limped from the room. Mrs./nWeasley hurried after him; Harry heard her stop at/nthe back door. After a minute or so she called, "He's/ngone!"/n/n"What did he want?" Mr. Weasley asked, looking/naround at Harry, Ron, and Hermione as Mrs. Weasley/ncame hurrying back to them./n/n"To give us what Dumbledore left us," said Harry./n"They've only just released the contents of his will."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nOutside in the garden, over the dinner tables, the/nthree objects Scrimgeour had given them were passed/nfrom hand to hand. Everyone exclaimed over the/nDeluminator and The Tales of Beedle the Bard and/nlamented the fact that Scrimgeour had refused to/npass on the sword, but none of them could offer any/nsuggestion as to why Dumbledore would have left/nHarry an old Snitch. As Mr. Weasley examined the/nDeluminator for the third or fourth time, Mrs./n/nWeasley said tentatively, "Harry, dear, everyone's/nawfully hungry, we didn't like to start without you. .../nShall I serve dinner now?"/n/nThey all ate rather hurriedly and then, after a hasty/nchorus of "Happy Birthday" and much gulping of/ncake, the party broke up. Hagrid, who was invited to/nthe wedding the following day, but was far too bulky/nto sleep in the overstretched Burrow, left to set up a/ntent for himself in a neighboring field./n/n"Meet us upstairs," Harry whispered to Hermione,/nwhile they helped Mrs. Weasley restore the garden to/nits normal state. "After everyone's gone to bed."/n/nUp in the attic room, Ron examined his Deluminator,/nand Harry filled Hagrid's mokeskin purse, not with/ngold, but with those items he most prized, apparently/nworthless though some of them were: the Marauder's/nMap, the shard of Sirius's enchanted mirror, and/nR.A.B.'s locket. He pulled the strings tight and slipped/nthe purse around his neck, then sat holding the old/nSnitch and watching its wings flutter feebly. At last,/nHermione tapped on the door and tiptoed inside./n/n" Muffliato," she whispered, waving her wand in the/ndirection of the stairs./n/n"Thought you didn't approve of that spell?" said Ron./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Times change," said Hermione. "Now, show us that/nDeluminator."/n/nRon obliged at once. Holding it up in front of him, he/nclicked it. The solitary lamp they had lit went out at/nonce./n/n"The thing is," whispered Hermione through the dark,/n"we could have achieved that with Peruvian Instant/nDarkness Powder."/n/nThere was a small click, and the ball of light from the/nlamp flew back to the ceiling and illuminated them all/nonce more./n/n"Still, it's cool," said Ron, a little defensively. "And/nfrom what they said, Dumbledore invented it himself!"/n/n"I know, but surely he wouldn't have singled you out/nin his will just to help us turn out the lights!"/n/n"D'you think he knew the Ministry would confiscate/nhis will and examine everything he'd left us?" asked/nHarry./n/n"Definitely," said Hermione. "He couldn't tell us in the/nwill why he was leaving us these things, but that still/ndoesn't explain ..."/n/n"... why he couldn't have given us a hint when he was/nalive?" asked Ron./n/n"Well, exactly," said Hermione, now flicking through/nThe Tales of Beedle the Bard. "If these things are/nimportant enough to pass on right under the nose of/nthe Ministry, you'd think he'd have let us know why/n... unless he thought it was obvious?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Thought wrong, then, didn't he?" said Ron. "I always/nsaid he was mental. Brilliant and everything, but/ncracked. Leaving Harry an old Snitch — what the hell/nwas that about?"/n/n"I've no idea," said Hermione. "When Scrimgeour/nmade you take it, Harry, I was so sure that something/nwas going to happen!"/n/n"Yeah, well," said Harry, his pulse quickening as he/nraised the Snitch in his fingers. "I wasn't going to try/ntoo hard in front of Scrimgeour, was I?"/n/n"What do you mean?" asked Hermione./n/n"The Snitch I caught in my first ever Quidditch/nmatch?" said Harry. "Don't you remember?"/n/nHermione looked simply bemused. Ron, however,/ngasped, pointing frantically from Harry to the Snitch/nand back again until he found his voice./n/n"That was the one you nearly swallowed!"/n/n"Exactly," said Harry, and with his heart beating fast,/nhe pressed his mouth to the Snitch./n/nIt did not open. Frustration and bitter disappointment/nwelled up inside him: He lowered the golden sphere,/nbut then Hermione cried out./n/n"Writing! There's writing on it, quick, look!"/n/nHe nearly dropped the Snitch in surprise and/nexcitement. Hermione was quite right. Engraved upon/nthe smooth golden surface, where seconds before/nthere had been nothing, were five words written in the/nthin, slanting handwriting that Harry recognized as/nDumbledore's:/n/n/n/n/n/nI open at the close./n/nHe had barely read them when the words vanished/nagain./n/n" 'I open at the close ...' What's that supposed to/nmean?"/n/nHermione and Ron shook their heads, looking blank./n/n"I open at the close ... at the close ... I open at the/nclose ..."/n/nBut no matter how often they repeated the words,/nwith many different inflections, they were unable to/nwring any more meaning from them./n/n"And the sword," said Ron finally, when they had at/nlast abandoned their attempts to divine meaning in/nthe Snitch's inscription. "Why did he want Harry to/nhave the sword?"/n/n"And why couldn't he just have told me?" Harry said/nquietly. "It was there, it was right there on the wall of/nhis office during all our talks last year! If he wanted/nme to have it, why didn't he just give it to me then?"/n/nHe felt as though he were sitting in an examination/nwith a question he ought to have been able to answer/nin front of him, his brain slow and unresponsive. Was/nthere something he had missed in the long talks with/nDumbledore last year? Ought he to know what it all/nmeant? Had Dumbledore expected him to/nunderstand?/n/n"And as for this book," said Hermione, "The Tales of/nBeedle the Bard ... I've never even heard of them!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You've never heard of The Tales of Beedle the Bard?"/nsaid Ron incredulously. "You're kidding, right?"/n/n/n/n"No, I'm not!" said Hermione in surprise. "Do you/nknow them, then?"/n/n"Well, of course I do!"/n/nHarry looked up, diverted. The circumstance of Ron/nhaving read a book that Hermione had not was/nunprecedented. Ron, however, looked bemused by/ntheir surprise./n/n"Oh come on! All the old kids' stories are supposed to/nbe Beedle 's, aren't they? The Fountain of Fair/nFortune' ... The Wizard and the Hopping Pot' .../n'Babbitty Rabbitty and her Cackling Stump' ..."/n/n"Excuse me?" said Hermione, giggling. "What was that/nlast one?/n/n"Come off it!" said Ron, looking in disbelief from Harry/nto Hermione. "You must've heard of Babbitty Rabbitty/n/n/n/n"Ron, you know full well Harry and I were brought up/nby Muggles!" said Hermione. "We didn't hear stories/nlike that when we were little, we heard 'Snow White/nand the Seven Dwarfs' and 'Cinderella' — "/n/n"What's that, an illness?" asked Ron./n/n"So these are children's stories?" asked Hermione,/nbending again over the runes./n/n"Yeah," said Ron uncertainly, "I mean, that's just/nwhat you hear, you know, that all these old stories/ncame from Beedle. I dunno what they're like in the/noriginal versions."/n/n/n/n/n/n"But I wonder why Dumbledore thought I should read/nthem?"/n/n/n/nSomething creaked downstairs./n/n"Probably just Charlie, now Mum's asleep, sneaking/noff to regrow his hair," said Ron nervously./n/n"All the same, we should get to bed," whispered/nHermione. "It wouldn't do to oversleep tomorrow."/n/n"No," agreed Ron. "A brutal triple murder by the/nbridegroom's mother might put a bit of a damper on/nthe wedding. I'll get the lights."/n/nAnd he clicked the Deluminator once more as/nHermione left the room./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Wedding
text: /n/n/nThree o'clock on the following afternoon found Harry,/nRon, Fred, and George standing outside the great/nwhite marquee in the orchard, awaiting the arrival of/nthe wedding guests. Harry had taken a large dose of/nPolyjuice Potion and was now the double of a/nredheaded Muggle boy from the local village, Ottery/nSt. Catchpole, from whom Fred had stolen hairs using/na Summoning Charm. The plan was to introduce/nHarry as "Cousin Barny" and trust to the great/nnumber of Weasley relatives to camouflage him./n/nAll four of them were clutching seating plans, so that/nthey could help show people to the right seats. A host/nof white-robed waiters had arrived an hour earlier,/nalong with a golden-jacketed band, and all of these/nwizards were currently sitting a short distance away/nunder a tree; Harry could see a blue haze of pipe/nsmoke issuing from the spot./n/nBehind Harry, the entrance to the marquee revealed/nrows and rows of fragile golden chairs set on either/nside of a long purple carpet. The supporting poles/n/n/n/n/nwere entwined with white and gold flowers. Fred and/nGeorge had fastened an enormous bunch of golden/nballoons over the exact point where Bill and Fleur/nwould shortly become husband and wife. Outside,/nbutterflies and bees were hovering lazily over the/ngrass and hedgerow. Harry was rather uncomfortable./nThe Muggle boy whose appearance he was affecting/nwas slightly fatter than him, and his dress robes felt/nhot and tight in the full glare of a summer's day./n/n"When I get married," said Fred, tugging at the collar/nof his own robes, "I won't be bothering with any of/nthis nonsense. You can all wear what you like, and I'll/nput a full Body-Bind Curse on Mum until it's all/nover."/n/n"She wasn't too bad this morning, considering," said/nGeorge. "Cried a bit about Percy not being here, but/nwho wants him? Oh blimey, brace yourselves — here/nthey come, look."/n/nBrightly colored figures were appearing, one by one,/nout of nowhere at the distant boundary of the yard./nWithin minutes a procession had formed, which/nbegan to snake its way up through the garden toward/nthe marquee. Exotic flowers and bewitched birds/nfluttered on the witches' hats, while precious gems/nglittered from many of the wizards' cravats; a hum of/nexcited chatter grew louder and louder, drowning the/nsound of the bees as the crowd approached the tent./n/n"Excellent, I think I see a few veela cousins," said/nGeorge, craning his neck for a better look. "They'll/nneed help understanding our English customs, I'll/nlook after them. ..."/n/n"Not so fast, Your Holeyness," said Fred, and darting/npast the gaggle of middle-aged witches heading the/nprocession, he said, "Here — permettez-moi to assister/n/n/n/n/n/nvous," to a pair of pretty French girls, who giggled and/nallowed him to escort them inside. George was left to/ndeal with the middle-aged witches and Ron took/ncharge of Mr. Weasley's old Ministry colleague/nPerkins, while a rather deaf old couple fell to Harry's/nlot./n/n"Wotcher," said a familiar voice as he came out of the/nmarquee again and found Tonks and Lupin at the/nfront of the queue.
