Muggle-born, though I heard she pretended/notherwise — "/n/n"She never pretended anything of the sort! Kendra/nwas a fine woman," whispered Doge miserably, but/nAuntie Muriel ignored him./n/n" — proud and very domineering, the sort of witch who/nwould have been mortified to produce a Squib — "/n/n"Ariana was not a Squib!" wheezed Doge./n/n"So you say, Elphias, but explain, then, why she/nnever attended Hogwarts!" said Auntie Muriel. She/nturned back to Harry. "In our day, Squibs were often/nhushed up, though to take it to the extreme of/nactually imprisoning a little girl in the house and/npretending she didn't exist — "/n/n"I tell you, that's not what happened!" said Doge, but/nAuntie Muriel steamrollered on, still addressing/nHarry./n/n"Squibs were usually shipped off to Muggle schools/nand encouraged to integrate into the Muggle/ncommunity . . . much kinder than trying to find them a/nplace in the Wizarding world, where they must always/nbe second class; but naturally Kendra Dumbledore/nwouldn't have dreamed of letting her daughter go to a/nMuggle school — "/n/n"Ariana was delicate!" said Doge desperately. "Her/nhealth was always too poor to permit her — "/n/n" — to permit her to leave the house?" cackled Muriel./n"And yet she was never taken to St. Mungo's and no/nHealer was ever summoned to see her!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Really, Muriel, how you can possibly know whether/n/n/n/n"For your information, Elphias, my cousin Lancelot/nwas a Healer at St. Mungo's at the time, and he told/nmy family in strictest confidence that Ariana had/nnever been seen there. All most suspicious, Lancelot/nthought!"/n/nDoge looked to be on the verge of tears. Auntie Muriel,/nwho seemed to be enjoying herself hugely, snapped/nher fingers for more champagne. Numbly Harry/nthought of how the Dursleys had once shut him up,/nlocked him away, kept him out of sight, all for the/ncrime of being a wizard. Had Dumbledore's sister/nsuffered the same fate in reverse: imprisoned for her/nlack of magic? And had Dumbledore truly left her to/nher fate while he went off to Hogwarts, to prove/nhimself brilliant and talented?/n/n"Now, if Kendra hadn't died first," Muriel resumed,/n/n"I'd have said that it was she who finished off Ariana/n/n/n/n"How can you, Muriel?" groaned Doge. "A mother kill/nher own daughter? Think what you are saying!"/n/n"If the mother in question was capable of imprisoning/nher daughter for years on end, why not?" shrugged/nAuntie Muriel. "But as I say, it doesn't fit, because/nKendra died before Ariana — of what, nobody ever/nseemed sure — "/n/n"Oh, no doubt Ariana murdered her," said Doge with/na brave attempt at scorn. "Why not?"/n/n"Yes, Ariana might have made a desperate bid for/nfreedom and killed Kendra in the struggle," said/nAuntie Muriel thoughtfully. "Shake your head all you/n/n/n/n/n/nlike, Elphias! You were at Ariana's funeral, were you/nnot?"/n/n"Yes I was," said Doge, through trembling lips. "And a/nmore desperately sad occasion I cannot remember./nAlbus was heartbroken — "/n/n"His heart wasn't the only thing. Didn't Aberforth/nbreak Albus 's nose halfway through the service?"/n/nIf Doge had looked horrified before this, it was/nnothing to how he looked now. Muriel might have/nstabbed him. She cackled loudly and took another/nswig of champagne, which dribbled down her chin./n/n"How do you — ?" croaked Doge./n/n"My mother was friendly with old Bathilda Bagshot,"/nsaid Auntie Muriel happily. "Bathilda described the/nwhole thing to Mother while I was listening at the/ndoor. A coffin-side brawl! The way Bathilda told it,/nAberforth shouted that it was all Albus 's fault that/nAriana was dead and then punched him in the face./nAccording to Bathilda, Albus did not even defend/nhimself, and that's odd enough in itself, Albus could/nhave destroyed Aberforth in a duel with both hands/ntied behind his back."/n/nMuriel swigged yet more champagne. The recitation of/nthese old scandals seemed to elate her as much as/nthey horrified Doge. Harry did not know what to/nthink, what to believe: He wanted the truth, and yet/nall Doge did was sit there and bleat feebly that Ariana/nhad been ill. Harry could hardly believe that/nDumbledore would not have intervened if such/ncruelty was happening inside his own house, and yet/nthere was undoubtedly something odd about the/nstory./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And I'll tell you something else," Muriel said,/nhiccuping slightly as she lowered her goblet. "I think/nBathilda has spilled the beans to Rita Skeeter. All/nthose hints in Skeeter's interview about an important/nsource close to the Dumbledores — goodness knows/nshe was there all through the Ariana business, and it/nwould fit!"/n/n"Bathilda would never talk to Rita Skeeter!" whispered/nDoge./n/n"Bathilda Bagshot?" Harry said. "The author of A/nHistory of Magic?"/n/nThe name was printed on the front of one of Harry's/ntextbooks, though admittedly not one of the ones he/nhad read most attentively./n/n"Yes," said Doge, clutching at Harry's question like a/ndrowning man at a life belt. "A most gifted magical/nhistorian and an old friend of Albus's."/n/n"Quite gaga these days, I've heard," said Auntie/nMuriel cheerfully./n/n"If that is so, it is even more dishonorable for Skeeter/nto have taken advantage of her," said Doge, "and no/nreliance can be placed on anything Bathilda may have/nsaid!"/n/n"Oh, there are ways of bringing back memories, and/nI'm sure Rita Skeeter knows them all," said Auntie/nMuriel. "But even if Bathilda's completely cuckoo, I'm/nsure she'd still have old photographs, maybe even/nletters. She knew the Dumbledores for years. ... Well/nworth a trip to Godric's Hollow, I'd have thought."/n/nHarry, who had been taking a sip of butterbeer,/nchoked. Doge banged him on the back as Harry/n/n/n/n/n/ncoughed, looking at Auntie Muriel through streaming/neyes. Once he had control of his voice again, he/nasked, "Bathilda Bagshot lives in Godric's Hollow?"/n/n"Oh yes, she's been there forever! The Dumbledores/nmoved there after Percival was imprisoned, and she/nwas their neighbor."/n/n"The Dumbledores lived in Godric's Hollow?"/n/n"Yes, Barry, that's what I just said," said Auntie/nMuriel testily./n/nHarry felt drained, empty. Never once, in six years,/nhad Dumbledore told Harry that they had both lived/nand lost loved ones in Godric's Hollow. Why? Were/nLily and James buried close to Dumbledore 's mother/nand sister? Had Dumbledore visited their graves,/nperhaps walked past Lily's and James's to do so? And/nhe had never once told Harry . . . never bothered to say/n/n/n/nAnd why it was so important, Harry could not explain/neven to himself, yet he felt it had been tantamount to/na lie not to tell him that they had this place and these/nexperiences in common. He stared ahead of him,/nbarely noticing what was going on around him, and/ndid not realize that Hermione had appeared out of the/ncrowd until she drew up a chair beside him./n/n"I simply can't dance anymore," she panted, slipping/noff one of her shoes and rubbing the sole of her foot./n"Ron's gone looking to find more butterbeers. It's a bit/nodd, I've just seen Viktor storming away from Luna's/nfather, it looked like they'd been arguing — " She/ndropped her voice, staring at him. "Harry, are you/nokay?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry did not know where to begin, but it did not/nmatter. At that moment, something large and silver/ncame falling through the canopy over the dance floor./nGraceful and gleaming, the lynx landed lightly in the/nmiddle of the astonished dancers. Heads turned, as/nthose nearest it froze absurdly in mid-dance. Then/nthe Patronus's mouth opened wide and it spoke in the/nloud, deep, slow voice of Kingsley Shacklebolt./n/n"The Ministry has fallen. Scrimgeour is dead. They are/ncoming."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n9/n/n/n/n

title: A Place To Hide
text: /nEverything seemed fuzzy, slow. Harry and Hermione/njumped to their feet and drew their wands. Many/npeople were only just realizing that something strange/nhad happened; heads were still turning toward the/nsilver cat as it vanished. Silence spread outward in/ncold ripples from the place where the Patronus had/nlanded. Then somebody screamed./n/nHarry and Hermione threw themselves into the/npanicking crowd. Guests were sprinting in all/ndirections; many were Disapparating; the protective/nenchantments around the Burrow had broken./n/n"Ron!" Hermione cried. "Ron, where are you?"/n/nAs they pushed their way across the dance floor,/nHarry saw cloaked and masked figures appearing in/nthe crowd; then he saw Lupin and Tonks, their wands/nraised, and heard both of them shout, "Protego\", a/ncry that was echoed on all sides —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Ron! Ron!" Hermione called, half sobbing as she and/nHarry were buffeted by terrified guests: Harry seized/nher hand to make sure they weren't separated as a/nstreak of light whizzed over their heads, whether a/nprotective charm or something more sinister he did/nnot know —/n/nAnd then Ron was there. He caught hold of/nHermione 's free arm, and Harry felt her turn on the/nspot; sight and sound were extinguished as darkness/npressed in upon him; all he could feel was Hermione's/nhand as he was squeezed through space and time,/naway from the Burrow, away from the descending/nDeath Eaters, away, perhaps, from Voldemort/nhimself. .../n/n"Where are we?" said Ron's voice./n/nHarry opened his eyes. For a moment he thought they/nhad not left the wedding after all: They still seemed to/nbe surrounded by people./n/n"Tottenham Court Road," panted Hermione. "Walk,/njust walk, we need to find somewhere for you to/nchange."/n/nHarry did as she asked. They half walked, half ran up/nthe wide dark street thronged with late-night revelers/nand lined with closed shops, stars twinkling above/nthem. A double-decker bus rumbled by and a group/nof merry pub-goers ogled them as they passed; Harry/nand Ron were still wearing dress robes./n/n"Hermione, we haven't got anything to change into,"/nRon told her, as a young woman burst into raucous/ngiggles at the sight of him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Why didn't I make sure I had the Invisibility Cloak/nwith me?" said Harry, inwardly cursing his own/nstupidity. "All last year I kept it on me and — "/n/n"It's okay, I've got the Cloak, I've got clothes for both/nof you," said Hermione. "Just try and act naturally/nuntil — this will do."/n/nShe led them down a side street, then into the shelter/nof a shadowy alleyway./n/n"When you say you've got the Cloak, and clothes ..."/nsaid Harry, frowning at Hermione, who was carrying/nnothing except her small beaded handbag, in which/nshe was now rummaging./n/n"Yes, they're here," said Hermione, and to Harry and/nRon's utter astonishment, she pulled out a pair of/njeans, a sweatshirt, some maroon socks, and finally/nthe silvery Invisibility Cloak./n/n"How the ruddy hell — ?"/n/n"Undetectable Extension Charm," said Hermione./n"Tricky, but I think I've done it okay; anyway, I/nmanaged to fit everything we need in here." She gave/nthe fragile-looking bag a little shake and it echoed like/na cargo hold as a number of heavy objects rolled/naround inside it. "Oh, damn, that'll be the books," she/nsaid, peering into it, "and I had them all stacked by/nsubject. ... Oh well. ... Harry, you'd better take the/nInvisibility Cloak. Ron, hurry up and change. ..."/n/n"When did you do all this?" Harry asked as Ron/nstripped off his robes./n/n"I told you at the Burrow, I've had the essentials/npacked for days, you know, in case we needed to/nmake a quick getaway. I packed your rucksack this/n/n/n/n/n/nmorning, Harry, after you changed, and put it in here./n... I just had a feeling. ..."/n/n"You're amazing, you are," said Ron, handing her his/nbundled-up robes./n/n"Thank you," said Hermione, managing a small smile/nas she pushed the robes into the bag. "Please, Harry,/nget that Cloak on!"/n/nHarry threw the Invisibility Cloak around his/nshoulders and pulled it up over his head, vanishing/nfrom sight. He was only just beginning to appreciate/nwhat had happened./n/n"The others — everyone at the wedding — "/n/n"We can't worry about that now," whispered/nHermione. "It's you they're after, Harry, and we'll just/nput everyone in even more danger by going back."/n/n"She's right," said Ron, who seemed to know that/nHarry was about to argue, even if he could not see his/nface. "Most of the Order was there, they'll look after/neveryone."/n/nHarry nodded, then remembered that they could not/nsee him, and said, "Yeah." But he thought of Ginny,/nand fear bubbled like acid in his stomach./n/n"Come on, I think we ought to keep moving," said/nHermione./n/nThey moved back up the side street and onto the/nmain road again, where a group of men on the/nopposite side was singing and weaving across the/npavement./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Just as a matter of interest, why Tottenham Court/nRoad?" Ron asked Hermione./n/n/n/n"I've no idea, it just popped into my head, but I'm/nsure we're safer out in the Muggle world, it's not/nwhere they'll expect us to be."/n/n"True," said Ron, looking around, "but don't you feel a/nbit — exposed?"/n/n"Where else is there?" asked Hermione, cringing as/nthe men on the other side of the road started wolf-/nwhistling at her. "We can hardly book rooms at the/nLeaky Cauldron, can we? And Grimmauld Place is out/nif Snape can get in there. ... I suppose we could try/nmy parents' house, though I think there's a chance/nthey might check there. ... Oh, I wish they'd shut up!"/n/n"All right, darling?" the drunkest of the men on the/nother pavement was yelling. "Fancy a drink? Ditch/nginger and come and have a pint!"/n/n"Let's sit down somewhere," Hermione said hastily as/nRon opened his mouth to shout back across the road./n"Look, this will do, in here!"/n/nIt was a small and shabby all-night cafe. A light layer/nof grease lay on all the Formica- topped tables, but it/nwas at least empty. Harry slipped into a booth first/nand Ron sat next to him opposite Hermione, who had/nher back to the entrance and did not like it: She/nglanced over her shoulder so frequently she appeared/nto have a twitch. Harry did not like being stationary;/nwalking had given the illusion that they had a goal./nBeneath the Cloak he could feel the last vestiges of/nPolyjuice leaving him, his hands returning to their/nusual length and shape. He pulled his glasses out of/nhis pocket and put them on again./n/n/n/n/n/nAfter a minute or two, Ron said, "You know, we're not/nfar from the Leaky Cauldron here, it's only in Charing/nCross — "/n/n"Ron, we can't!" said Hermione at once./n/n"Not to stay there, but to find out what's going on!"/n/n"We know what's going on! Voldemort's taken over the/nMinistry, what else do we need to know?"/n/n"Okay, okay, it was just an idea!"/n/nThey relapsed into a prickly silence. The gum-chewing/nwaitress shuffled over and Hermione ordered two/ncappuccinos: As Harry was invisible, it would have/nlooked odd to order him one. A pair of burly workmen/nentered the cafe and squeezed into the next booth./nHermione dropped her voice to a whisper./n/n"I say we find a quiet place to Disapparate and head/nfor the countryside. Once we're there, we could send a/nmessage to the Order."/n/n"Can you do that talking Patronus thing, then?"/nasked Ron./n/n"I've been practicing and I think so," said Hermione./n/n"Well, as long as it doesn't get them into trouble,/nthough they might've been arrested already. God,/nthat's revolting," Ron added after one sip of the/nfoamy, grayish coffee. The waitress had heard; she/nshot Ron a nasty look as she shuffled off to take the/nnew customers' orders. The larger of the two/nworkmen, who was blond and quite huge, now that/nHarry came to look at him, waved her away. She/nstared, affronted./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Let's get going, then, I don't want to drink this/nmuck," said Ron. "Hermione, have you got Muggle/nmoney to pay for this?"/n/n"Yes, I took out all my Building Society savings before/nI came to the Burrow. I'll bet all the change is at the/nbottom," sighed Hermione, reaching for her beaded/nbag./n/nThe two workmen made identical movements, and/nHarry mirrored them without conscious thought: All/nthree of them drew their wands. Ron, a few seconds/nlate in realizing what was going on, lunged across the/ntable, pushing Hermione sideways onto her bench./n/nThe force of the Death Eaters' spells shattered the/ntiled wall where Ron's head had just been, as Harry,/nstill invisible, yelled, "Stupefyl"/n/nThe great blond Death Eater was hit in the face by a/njet of red light: He slumped sideways, unconscious./nHis companion, unable to see who had cast the spell,/nfired another at Ron: Shining black ropes flew from/nhis wand-tip and bound Ron head to foot — the/nwaitress screamed and ran for the door — Harry sent/nanother Stunning Spell at the Death Eater with the/ntwisted face who had tied up Ron, but the spell/nmissed, rebounded on the window, and hit the/nwaitress, who collapsed in front of the door./n/n"Expulsol" bellowed the Death Eater, and the table/nbehind which Harry was standing blew up: The force/nof the explosion slammed him into the wall and he felt/nhis wand leave his hand as the Cloak slipped off him./n/n"Petrificus TotalusV' screamed Hermione from out of/nsight, and the Death Eater fell forward like a statue to/nland with a crunching thud on the mess of broken/nchina, table, and coffee. Hermione crawled out from/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nunderneath the bench, shaking bits of glass ashtray/nout of her hair and trembling all over./n/n"D-diffindo," she said, pointing her wand at Ron, who/nroared in pain as she slashed open the knee of his/njeans, leaving a deep cut. "Oh, I'm so sorry, Ron, my/nhand's shaking! Diffindol"/n/nThe severed ropes fell away. Ron got to his feet,/nshaking his arms to regain feeling in them. Harry/npicked up his wand and climbed over all the debris to/nwhere the large blond Death Eater was sprawled/nacross the bench./n/n"I should've recognized him, he was there the night/nDumbledore died," he said. He turned over the darker/nDeath Eater with his foot; the man's eyes moved/nrapidly between Harry, Ron, and Hermione./n/n"That's Dolohov," said Ron. "I recognize him from the/nold wanted posters. I think the big one's Thorfinn/nRowle."/n/n"Never mind what they're called!" said Hermione a/nlittle hysterically. "How did they find us? What are we/ngoing to do?"/n/nSomehow her panic seemed to clear Harry's head./n/n"Lock the door," he told her, "and Ron, turn out the/nlights."/n/nHe looked down at the paralyzed Dolohov, thinking/nfast as the lock clicked and Ron used the/nDeluminator to plunge the cafe into darkness. Harry/ncould hear the men who had jeered at Hermione/nearlier, yelling at another girl in the distance./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What are we going to do with them?" Ron whispered/nto Harry through the dark; then, even more quietly,/n"Kill them? They'd kill us. They had a good go just/nnow."/n/nHermione shuddered and took a step backward./nHarry shook his head./n/n"We just need to wipe their memories," said Harry./n"It's better like that, it'll throw them off the scent. If/nwe killed them it'd be obvious we were here."/n/n"You're the boss," said Ron, sounding profoundly/nrelieved. "But I've never done a Memory Charm."/n/n"Nor have I," said Hermione, "but I know the theory."/n/nShe took a deep, calming breath, then pointed her/nwand at Dolohov's forehead and said, "Obliviate."/n/nAt once, Dolohov's eyes became unfocused and/ndreamy./n/n"Brilliant!" said Harry, clapping her on the back./n"Take care of the other one and the waitress while/nRon and I clear up."/n/n"Clear up?" said Ron, looking around at the partly/ndestroyed cafe. "Why?"/n/n"Don't you think they might wonder what's happened/nif they wake up and find themselves in a place that/nlooks like it's just been bombed?"/n/n"Oh right, yeah ..."/n/nRon struggled for a moment before managing to/nextract his wand from his pocket./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's no wonder I can't get it out, Hermione, you/npacked my old jeans, they're tight."/n/n"Oh, I'm so sorry," hissed Hermione, and as she/ndragged the waitress out of sight of the windows,/nHarry heard her mutter a suggestion as to where Ron/ncould stick his wand instead./n/nOnce the cafe was restored to its previous condition,/nthey heaved the Death Eaters back into their booth/nand propped them up facing each other./n/n"But how did they find us?" Hermione asked, looking/nfrom one inert man to the other. "How did they know/nwhere we were?"/n/nShe turned to Harry./n/n"You — you don't think you've still got your Trace on/nyou, do you, Harry?"/n/n"He can't have," said Ron. "The Trace breaks at/nseventeen, that's Wizarding law, you can't put it on/nan adult."/n/n"As far as you know," said Hermione. "What if the/nDeath Eaters have found a way to put it on a/nseventeen-year-old?"/n/n"But Harry hasn't been near a Death Eater in the last/ntwenty-four hours. Who's supposed to have put a/nTrace back on him?"/n/nHermione did not reply. Harry felt contaminated,/ntainted: Was that really how the Death Eaters had/nfound them?/n/n"If I can't use magic, and you can't use magic near/nme, without us giving away our position — " he began./n/n/n/n/n/n"We're not splitting up!" said Hermione firmly./n/n/n/n"We need a safe place to hide," said Ron. "Give us/ntime to think things through."/n/n"Grimmauld Place," said Harry./n/nThe other two gaped./n/n"Don't be silly, Harry, Snape can get in there!"/n/n"Ron's dad said they've put up jinxes against him —/nand even if they haven't worked," he pressed on as/nHermione began to argue, "so what? I swear, I'd like/nnothing better than to meet Snape!"/n/n"But — "/n/n"Hermione, where else is there? It's the best chance/nwe've got. Snape's only one Death Eater. If I've still/ngot the Trace on me, we'll have whole crowds of them/non us wherever else we go."/n/nShe could not argue, though she looked as if she/nwould have liked to. While she unlocked the cafe/ndoor, Ron clicked the Deluminator to release the/ncafe's light. Then, on Harry's count of three, they/nreversed the spells upon their three victims, and/nbefore the waitress or either of the Death Eaters could/ndo more than stir sleepily, Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nhad turned on the spot and vanished into the/ncompressing darkness once more./n/nSeconds later Harry's lungs expanded gratefully and/nhe opened his eyes: They were now standing in the/nmiddle of a familiar small and shabby square. Tall,/ndilapidated houses looked down on them from every/nside. Number twelve was visible to them, for they had/nbeen told of its existence by Dumbledore, its Secret-/n/n/n/n/nKeeper, and they rushed toward it, checking every few/nyards that they were not being followed or observed./nThey raced up the stone steps, and Harry tapped the/nfront door once with his wand. They heard a series of/nmetallic clicks and the clatter of a chain, then the/ndoor swung open with a creak and they hurried over/nthe threshold./n/nAs Harry closed the door behind them, the old-/nfashioned gas lamps sprang into life, casting/nflickering light along the length of the hallway. It/nlooked just as Harry remembered it: eerie,/ncobwebbed, the outlines of the house-elf heads on the/nwall throwing odd shadows up the staircase. Long/ndark curtains concealed the portrait of Sirius's/nmother. The only thing that was out of place was the/ntroll's leg umbrella stand, which was lying on its side/nas if Tonks had just knocked it over again./n/n"I think somebody's been in here," Hermione/nwhispered, pointing toward it./n/n"That could've happened as the Order left," Ron/nmurmured back./n/n"So where are these jinxes they put up against/nSnape?" Harry asked./n/n"Maybe they're only activated if he shows up?"/nsuggested Ron./n/nYet they remained close together on the doormat,/nbacks against the door, scared to move farther into/nthe house./n/n"Well, we can't stay here forever," said Harry, and he/ntook a step forward./n/n"Severus Snape?"/n/n/n/n/n/nMad-Eye Moody's voice whispered out of the/ndarkness, making all three of them jump back in/nfright. "We're not Snape!" croaked Harry, before/nsomething whooshed over him like cold air and his/ntongue curled backward on itself, making it/nimpossible to speak. Before he had time to feel inside/nhis mouth, however, his tongue had unraveled again./n/nThe other two seemed to have experienced the same/nunpleasant sensation. Ron was making retching/nnoises; Hermione stammered, "That m-must have b-/nbeen the T-Tongue-Tying Curse Mad-Eye set up for/nSnape!"/n/nGingerly Harry took another step forward. Something/nshifted in the shadows at the end of the hall, and/nbefore any of them could say another word, a figure/nhad risen up out of the carpet, tall, dust-colored, and/nterrible: Hermione screamed and so did Mrs. Black,/nher curtains flying open; the gray figure was gliding/ntoward them, faster and faster, its waist-length hair/nand beard streaming behind it, its face sunken,/nfleshless, with empty eye sockets: Horribly familiar,/ndreadfully altered, it raised a wasted arm, pointing at/nHarry./n/n"No!" Harry shouted, and though he had raised his/nwand no spell occurred to him. "No! It wasn't us! We/ndidn't kill you — "/n/nOn the word kill, the figure exploded in a great cloud/nof dust: Coughing, his eyes watering, Harry looked/naround to see Hermione crouched on the floor by the/ndoor with her arms over her head, and Ron, who was/nshaking from head to foot, patting her clumsily on the/nshoulder and saying, "It's all r-right. ... It's g-gone. ..."/n/nDust swirled around Harry like mist, catching the/nblue gaslight, as Mrs. Black continued to scream./n/n/n/n/n/n"Mudbloods, filth, stains of dishonor, taint of shame on/nthe house of my fathers — "/n/n"SHUT UP!" Harry bellowed, directing his wand at her,/nand with a bang and a burst of red sparks, the/ncurtains swung shut again, silencing her./n/n"That ... that was ..." Hermione whimpered, as Ron/nhelped her to her feet./n/n"Yeah," said Harry, "but it wasn't really him, was it?/nJust something to scare Snape."/n/nHad it worked, Harry wondered, or had Snape already/nblasted the horror-figure aside as casually as he had/nkilled the real Dumbledore? Nerves still tingling, he/nled the other two up the hall, half-expecting some new/nterror to reveal itself, but nothing moved except for a/nmouse skittering along the skirting board./n/n"Before we go any farther, I think we'd better check,"/nwhispered Hermione, and she raised her wand and/nsaid, "Homenum revelio."/n/nNothing happened./n/n"Well, you've just had a big shock," said Ron kindly./n"What was that supposed to do?"/n/n"It did what I meant it to do!" said Hermione rather/ncrossly. "That was a spell to reveal human presence,/nand there's nobody here except us!"/n/n"And old Dusty," said Ron, glancing at the patch of/ncarpet from which the corpse-figure had risen./n/n"Let's go up," said Hermione with a frightened look at/nthe same spot, and she led the way up the creaking/nstairs to the drawing room on the first floor./n/n/n/n/n/nHermione waved her wand to ignite the old gas lamps,/nthen, shivering slightly in the drafty room, she/nperched on the sofa, her arms wrapped tightly around/nher. Ron crossed to the window and moved the heavy/nvelvet curtain aside an inch./n/n"Can't see anyone out there," he reported. "And you'd/nthink, if Harry still had a Trace on him, they'd have/nfollowed us here. I know they can't get in the house,/nbut — what's up, Harry?"/n/nHarry had given a cry of pain: His scar had burned/nagain as something flashed across his mind like a/nbright light on water. He saw a large shadow and felt/na fury that was not his own pound through his body,/nviolent and brief as an electric shock./n/n"What did you see?" Ron asked, advancing on Harry./n"Did you see him at my place?"/n/n"No, I just felt anger — he's really angry — "/n/n"But that could be at the Burrow," said Ron loudly./n"What else? Didn't you see anything? Was he cursing/nsomeone?"/n/n"No, I just felt anger — I couldn't tell — "/n/nHarry felt badgered, confused, and Hermione did not/nhelp as she said in a frightened voice, "Your scar,/nagain? But what's going on? I thought that/nconnection had closed!"/n/n"It did, for a while," muttered Harry; his scar was still/npainful, which made it hard to concentrate. "I — I/nthink it's started opening again whenever he loses/ncontrol, that's how it used to — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But then you've got to close your mind!" said/nHermione shrilly. "Harry, Dumbledore didn't want you/nto use that connection, he wanted you to shut it/ndown, that's why you were supposed to use/nOcclumency! Otherwise Voldemort can plant false/nimages in your mind, remember — "/n/n"Yeah, I do remember, thanks," said Harry through/ngritted teeth; he did not need Hermione to tell him/nthat Voldemort had once used this selfsame/nconnection between them to lead him into a trap, nor/nthat it had resulted in Sirius's death. He wished that/nhe had not told them what he had seen and felt; it/nmade Voldemort more threatening, as though he were/npressing against the window of the room, and still the/npain in his scar was building and he fought it: It was/nlike resisting the urge to be sick./n/nHe turned his back on Ron and Hermione, pretending/nto examine the old tapestry of the Black family tree on/nthe wall. Then Hermione shrieked: Harry drew his/nwand again and spun around to see a silver Patronus/nsoar through the drawing room window and land/nupon the floor in front of them, where it solidified into/nthe weasel that spoke with the voice of Ron's father./n/n"Family safe, do not reply, we are being watched."/n/nThe Patronus dissolved into nothingness. Ron let out/na noise between a whimper and a groan and dropped/nonto the sofa: Hermione joined him, gripping his arm./n/n"They're all right, they're all right!" she whispered,/nand Ron half laughed and hugged her./n/n"Harry," he said over Hermione's shoulder, "I — "/n/n"It's not a problem," said Harry, sickened by the pain/nin his head. "It's your family, 'course you're worried./n/n/n/n/n/nI'd feel the same way." He thought of Ginny. "I do feel/nthe same way."/n/nThe pain in his scar was reaching a peak, burning as/nit had done in the garden of the Burrow. Faintly he/nheard Hermione say, "I don't want to be on my own./nCould we use the sleeping bags I've brought and/ncamp in here tonight?"/n/nHe heard Ron agree. He could not fight the pain much/nlonger: He had to succumb./n/n"Bathroom," he muttered, and he left the room as fast/nas he could without running./n/nHe barely made it: Bolting the door behind him with/ntrembling hands, he grasped his pounding head and/nfell to the floor, then in an explosion of agony, he felt/nthe rage that did not belong to him possess his soul,/nsaw a long room lit only by firelight, and the great/nblond Death Eater on the floor, screaming and/nwrithing, and a slighter figure standing over him,/nwand outstretched, while Harry spoke in a high, cold,/nmerciless voice./n/n"More, Rowle, or shall we end it and feed you to/nNagini? Lord Voldemort is not sure that he will forgive/nthis time. ... You called me back for this, to tell me/nthat Harry Potter has escaped again? Draco, give/nRowle another taste of our displeasure. ... Do it, or/nfeel my wrath yourself!"/n/nA log fell in the fire: Flames reared, their light darting/nacross a terrified, pointed white face — with a sense/nof emerging from deep water, Harry drew heaving/nbreaths and opened his eyes./n/nHe was spread-eagled on the cold black marble floor,/nhis nose inches from one of the silver serpent tails/n/n/n/n/n/nthat supported the large bathtub. He sat up. Malfoy's/ngaunt, petrified face seemed branded on the inside of/nhis eyes. Harry felt sickened by what he had seen, by/nthe use to which Draco was now being put by/nVoldemort./n/nThere was a sharp rap on the door, and Harry jumped/nas Hermione's voice rang out./n/n"Harry, do you want your toothbrush? I've got it/nhere."/n/n"Yeah, great, thanks," he said, fighting to keep his/nvoice casual as he stood up to let her in./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n10/n/n/n/n

title: Kreacher's Tale
text: /nHarry woke early next morning, wrapped in a sleeping/nbag on the drawing room floor. A chink of sky was/nvisible between the heavy curtains: It was the cool,/nclear blue of watered ink, somewhere between night/nand dawn, and everything was quiet except for Ron/nand Hermione's slow, deep breathing. Harry glanced/nover at the dark shapes they made on the floor beside/nhim. Ron had had a fit of gallantry and insisted that/nHermione sleep on the cushions from the sofa, so that/nher silhouette was raised above his. Her arm curved/nto the floor, her fingers inches from Ron's. Harry/nwondered whether they had fallen asleep holding/nhands. The idea made him feel strangely lonely./n/nHe looked up at the shadowy ceiling, the cobwebbed/nchandelier. Less than twenty-four hours ago, he had/nbeen standing in the sunlight at the entrance to the/nmarquee, waiting to show in wedding guests. It/nseemed a lifetime away. What was going to happen/nnow? He lay on the floor and he thought of the/nHorcruxes, of the daunting, complex mission/nDumbledore had left him. ... Dumbledore .../n/n/n/n/nThe grief that had possessed him since Dumbledore's/ndeath felt different now. The accusations he had/nheard from Muriel at the wedding seemed to have/nnested in his brain like diseased things, infecting his/nmemories of the wizard he had idolized. Could/nDumbledore have let such things happen? Had he/nbeen like Dudley, content to watch neglect and abuse/nas long as it did not affect him? Could he have turned/nhis back on a sister who was being imprisoned and/nhidden?/n/nHarry thought of Godric's Hollow, of graves/nDumbledore had never mentioned there; he thought/nof mysterious objects left without explanation in/nDumbledore's will, and resentment swelled in the/ndarkness. Why hadn't Dumbledore told him? Why/nhadn't he explained? Had Dumbledore actually cared/nabout Harry at all? Or had Harry been nothing more/nthan a tool to be polished and honed, but not trusted,/nnever confided in?/n/nHarry could not stand lying there with nothing but/nbitter thoughts for company. Desperate for something/nto do, for distraction, he slipped out of his sleeping/nbag, picked up his wand, and crept out of the room./nOn the landing he whispered, "Lumos," and started to/nclimb the stairs by wandlight./n/nOn the second landing was the bedroom in which he/nand Ron had slept last time they had been here; he/nglanced into it. The wardrobe doors stood open and/nthe bedclothes had been ripped back. Harry/nremembered the overturned troll leg downstairs./nSomebody had searched the house since the Order/nhad left. Snape? Or perhaps Mundungus, who had/npilfered plenty from this house both before and after/nSirius died? Harry's gaze wandered to the portrait/nthat sometimes contained Phineas Nigellus Black,/nSirius's great-great-grandfather, but it was empty,/n/n/n/n/nshowing nothing but a stretch of muddy backdrop./nPhineas Nigellus was evidently spending the night in/nthe headmaster's study at Hogwarts./n/nHarry continued up the stairs until he reached the/ntopmost landing, where there were only two doors./n/nThe one facing him bore a nameplate reading SIRIUS./nHarry had never entered his godfather's bedroom/nbefore. He pushed open the door, holding his wand/nhigh to cast light as widely as possible. The room was/nspacious and must once have been handsome. There/nwas a large bed with a carved wooden headboard, a/ntall window obscured by long velvet curtains, and a/nchandelier thickly coated in dust with candle stubs/nstill resting in its sockets, solid wax hanging in/nfrostlike drips. A fine film of dust covered the pictures/non the walls and the bed's headboard; a spider's web/nstretched between the chandelier and the top of the/nlarge wooden wardrobe, and as Harry moved deeper/ninto the room, he heard a scurrying of disturbed mice./n/nThe teenage Sirius had plastered the walls with so/nmany posters and pictures that little of the walls'/nsilvery-gray silk was visible. Harry could only assume/nthat Sirius's parents had been unable to remove the/nPermanent Sticking Charm that kept them on the/nwall, because he was sure they would not have/nappreciated their eldest son's taste in decoration./nSirius seemed to have gone out of his way to annoy/nhis parents. There were several large Gryffindor/nbanners, faded scarlet and gold, just to underline his/ndifference from all the rest of the Slytherin family./nThere were many pictures of Muggle motorcycles, and/nalso (Harry had to admire Sirius's nerve) several/nposters of bikini-clad Muggle girls; Harry could tell/nthat they were Muggles because they remained quite/nstationary within their pictures, faded smiles and/nglazed eyes frozen on the paper. This was in contrast/nto the only Wizarding photograph on the walls, which/n/n/n/n/nwas a picture of four Hogwarts students standing arm/nin arm, laughing at the camera./n/n/n/nWith a leap of pleasure, Harry recognized his father;/nhis untidy black hair stuck up at the back like/nHarry's, and he too wore glasses. Beside him was/nSirius, carelessly handsome, his slightly arrogant face/nso much younger and happier than Harry had ever/nseen it alive. To Sirius's right stood Pettigrew, more/nthan a head shorter, plump and watery-eyed, flushed/nwith pleasure at his inclusion in this coolest of gangs,/nwith the much-admired rebels that James and Sirius/nhad been. On James's left was Lupin, even then a/nlittle shabby-looking, but he had the same air of/ndelighted surprise at finding himself liked and/nincluded ... or was it simply because Harry knew how/nit had been, that he saw these things in the picture?/nHe tried to take it from the wall; it was his now, after/nall, Sirius had left him everything, but it would not/nbudge. Sirius had taken no chances in preventing his/nparents from redecorating his room./n/nHarry looked around at the floor. The sky outside was/ngrowing brighter: A shaft of light revealed bits of/npaper, books, and small objects scattered over the/ncarpet. Evidently Sirius's bedroom had been searched/ntoo, although its contents seemed to have been/njudged mostly, if not entirely, worthless. A few of the/nbooks had been shaken roughly enough to part/ncompany with their covers, and sundry pages littered/nthe floor./n/nHarry bent down, picked up a few of the pieces of/npaper, and examined them. He recognized one as part/nof an old edition of A History of Magic, by Bathilda/nBagshot, and another as belonging to a motorcycle/nmaintenance manual. The third was handwritten and/ncrumpled. He smoothed it out./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDear Padfoot,/n/n/n/nThank you, thank you, for Harry's birthday present! It/nwas his favorite by far. One year old and already/nzooming along on a toy broomstick, he looked so/npleased with himself, I'm enclosing a picture so you/ncan see. You know it only rises about two feet off the/nground, but he nearly killed the cat and he smashed a/nhorrible vase Petunia sent me for Christmas (no/ncomplaints there). Of course, James thought it was so/nfunny, says he's going to be a great Quidditch player,/nbut we've had to pack away all the ornaments and/nmake sure we don't take our eyes off him when he gets/ngoing./n/nWe had a very quiet birthday tea, just us and old/nBathilda, who has always been sweet to us and who/ndotes on Harry. We were so sorry you couldn't come,/nbut the Order's got to come first, and Harry's not old/nenough to know it's his birthday anyway! James is/ngetting a bit frustrated shut up here, he tries not to/nshow it but I can tell — also, Dumbledore's still got his/nInvisibility Cloak, so no chance of little excursions. If/nyou could visit, it would cheer him up so much. Wormy/nwas here last weekend, I thought he seemed down,/nbut that was probably the news about the McKinnons;/n/nI cried all evening when I heard./n/nBathilda drops in most days, she's a fascinating old/nthing with the most amazing stories about Dumbledore,/nI'm not sure he'd be pleased if he knew! I don't know/nhow much to believe, actually, because it seems/nincredible that Dumbledore/n/nHarry's extremities seemed to have gone numb. He/nstood quite still, holding the miraculous paper in his/nnerveless fingers while inside him a kind of quiet/neruption sent joy and grief thundering in equal/n/n/n/n/n/nmeasure through his veins. Lurching to the bed, he/nsat down./n/n/n/nHe read the letter again, but could not take in any/nmore meaning than he had done the first time, and/nwas reduced to staring at the handwriting itself. She/nhad made her "g"s the same way he did: He searched/nthrough the letter for every one of them, and each felt/nlike a friendly little wave glimpsed from behind a veil./nThe letter was an incredible treasure, proof that Lily/nPotter had lived, really lived, that her warm hand had/nonce moved across this parchment, tracing ink into/nthese letters, these words, words about him, Harry,/nher son./n/nImpatiently brushing away the wetness in his eyes, he/nreread the letter, this time concentrating on the/nmeaning. It was like listening to a half-remembered/nvoice./n/nThey had had a cat . . . perhaps it had perished, like/nhis parents, at Godric's Hollow ... or else fled when/nthere was nobody left to feed it. ... Sirius had bought/nhim his first broomstick. . . . His parents had known/nBathilda Bagshot; had Dumbledore introduced them?/nDumblecLore's still got his Invisibility Cloak ... There/nwas something funny there. .../n/nHarry paused, pondering his mother's words. Why/nhad Dumbledore taken James's Invisibility Cloak?/nHarry distinctly remembered his headmaster telling/nhim years before, "I don't need a cloak to become/ninvisible." Perhaps some less gifted Order member/nhad needed its assistance, and Dumbledore had acted/nas carrier? Harry passed on. .../n/nWormy was here . . . Pettigrew, the traitor, had seemed/n"down," had he? Was he aware that he was seeing/nJames and Lily alive for the last time?/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd finally Bathilda again, who told incredible stories/nabout Dumbledore. It seems incredible that/nDumbledore —/n/nThat Dumbledore what? But there were any number/nof things that would seem incredible about/nDumbledore; that he had once received bottom marks/nin a Transfiguration test, for instance, or had taken/nup goat-charming like Aberforth. .../n/nHarry got to his feet and scanned the floor: Perhaps/nthe rest of the letter was here somewhere. He seized/npapers, treating them, in his eagerness, with as little/nconsideration as the original searcher; he pulled open/ndrawers, shook out books, stood on a chair to run his/nhand over the top of the wardrobe, and crawled under/nthe bed and armchair./n/nAt last, lying facedown on the floor, he spotted what/nlooked like a torn piece of paper under the chest of/ndrawers. When he pulled it out, it proved to be most/nof the photograph Lily had described in her letter. A/nblack-haired baby was zooming in and out of the/npicture on a tiny broom, roaring with laughter, and a/npair of legs that must have belonged to James was/nchasing after him. Harry tucked the photograph into/nhis pocket with Lily's letter and continued to look for/nthe second sheet./n/nAfter another quarter of an hour, however, he was/nforced to conclude that the rest of his mother's letter/nwas gone. Had it simply been lost in the sixteen years/nthat had elapsed since it had been written, or had it/nbeen taken by whoever had searched the room? Harry/nread the first sheet again, this time looking for clues/nas to what might have made the second sheet/nvaluable. His toy broomstick could hardly be/nconsidered interesting to the Death Eaters. ... The/nonly potentially useful thing he could see here was/n/n/n/n/npossible information on Dumbledore. It seems/nincredible that Dumbledore — what?/n/n"Harry? Harry! HarryV'/n/n"I'm here!" he called. "What's happened?"/n/nThere was a clatter of footsteps outside the door, and/nHermione burst inside./n/n"We woke up and didn't know where you were!" she/nsaid breathlessly. She turned and shouted over her/nshoulder, "Ron! I've found him!"/n/nRon's annoyed voice echoed distantly from several/nfloors below./n/n"Good! Tell him from me he's a git!"/n/n"Harry, don't just disappear, please, we were terrified!/nWhy did you come up here anyway?" She gazed/naround the ransacked room. "What have you been/ndoing?"/n/n"Look what I've just found."/n/nHe held out his mother's letter. Hermione took it and/nread it while Harry watched her. When she reached/nthe end of the page she looked up at him./n/n"Oh, Harry ..."/n/n"And there's this too."/n/nHe handed her the torn photograph, and Hermione/nsmiled at the baby zooming in and out of sight on the/ntoy broom./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I've been looking for the rest of the letter," Harry/nsaid, "but it's not here."/n/nHermione glanced around./n/n"Did you make all this mess, or was some of it done/nwhen you got here?"/n/n"Someone had searched before me," said Harry./n/n"I thought so. Every room I looked into on the way up/nhad been disturbed. What were they after, do you/nthink?"/n/n"Information on the Order, if it was Snape."/n/n"But you'd think he'd already have all he needed, I/nmean, he was in the Order, wasn't he?"/n/n"Well then," said Harry, keen to discuss his theory,/n"what about information on Dumbledore? The second/npage of this letter, for instance. You know this/nBathilda my mum mentions, you know who she is?"/n/n"Who?"/n/n"Bathilda Bagshot, the author of — "/n/n"A History of Magic," said Hermione, looking/ninterested. "So your parents knew her? She was an/nincredible magical historian."/n/n"And she's still alive," said Harry, "and she lives in/nGodric's Hollow, Ron's Auntie Muriel was talking/nabout her at the wedding. She knew Dumbledore 's/nfamily too. Be pretty interesting to talk to, wouldn't/nshe?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere was a little too much understanding in the/nsmile Hermione gave him for Harry's liking. He took/nback the letter and the photograph and tucked them/ninside the pouch around his neck, so as not to have/nto look at her and give himself away./n/n"I understand why you'd love to talk to her about your/nmum and dad, and Dumbledore too," said Hermione./n"But that wouldn't really help us in our search for the/nHorcruxes, would it?" Harry did not answer, and she/nrushed on, "Harry, I know you really want to go to/nGodric's Hollow, but I'm scared, I'm scared at how/neasily those Death Eaters found us yesterday. It just/nmakes me feel more than ever that we ought to avoid/nthe place where your parents are buried, I'm sure/nthey'd be expecting you to visit it."/n/n"It's not just that," Harry said, still avoiding looking at/nher. "Muriel said stuff about Dumbledore at the/nwedding. I want to know the truth. ..."/n/nHe told Hermione everything that Muriel had told/nhim. When he had finished, Hermione said, "Of/ncourse, I can see why that's upset you, Harry — "/n/n"I'm not upset," he lied, "I'd just like to know whether/nor not it's true or — "/n/n"Harry, do you really think you'll get the truth from a/nmalicious old woman like Muriel, or from Rita/nSkeeter? How can you believe them? You knew/nDumbledore!"/n/n"I thought I did," he muttered./n/n"But you know how much truth there was in/neverything Rita wrote about you! Doge is right, how/ncan you let these people tarnish your memories of/nDumbledore?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHe looked away, trying not to betray the resentment/nhe felt. There it was again: Choose what to believe. He/nwanted the truth. Why was everybody so determined/nthat he should not get it?/n/n"Shall we go down to the kitchen?" Hermione/nsuggested after a little pause. "Find something for/nbreakfast?"/n/nHe agreed, but grudgingly, and followed her out onto/nthe landing and past the second door that led off it./nThere were deep scratch marks in the paintwork/nbelow a small sign that he had not noticed in the/ndark. He paused at the top of the stairs to read it. It/nwas a pompous little sign, neatly lettered by hand,/nthe sort of thing that Percy Weasley might have stuck/non his bedroom door:/n/nDo Not Enter/n/nWithout the Express Permission of/nRegulus Arcturus Black/n/nExcitement trickled through Harry, but he was not/nimmediately sure why. He read the sign again./nHermione was already a flight of stairs below him./n/n"Hermione," he said, and he was surprised that his/nvoice was so calm. "Come back up here."/n/n"What's the matter?"/n/n"R.A.B. I think I've found him."/n/nThere was a gasp, and then Hermione ran back up/nthe stairs./n/n"In your mum's letter? But I didn't see — "/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry shook his head, pointing at Regulus's sign. She/nread it, then clutched Harry's arm so tightly that he/nwinced./n/n"Sirius's brother?" she whispered./n/n"He was a Death Eater," said Harry, "Sirius told me/nabout him, he joined up when he was really young/nand then got cold feet and tried to leave — so they/nkilled him."/n/n"That fits!" gasped Hermione. "If he was a Death Eater/nhe had access to Voldemort, and if he became/ndisenchanted, then he would have wanted to bring/nVoldemort down!"/n/nShe released Harry, leaned over the banister, and/nscreamed, "Ron! RON! Get up here, quick!"/n/nRon appeared, panting, a minute later, his wand/nready in his hand./n/n"What's up? If it's massive spiders again I want/nbreakfast before I — "/n/nHe frowned at the sign on Regulus's door, to which/nHermione was silently pointing./n/n"What? That was Sirius's brother, wasn't it? Regulus/nArcturus ... Regulus ... R.A.B.l The locket — you don't/nreckon — ?"/n/n"Let's find out," said Harry. He pushed the door: It/nwas locked. Hermione pointed her wand at the handle/nand said, "Alohomora." There was a click, and the/ndoor swung open./n/nThey moved over the threshold together, gazing/naround. Regulus's bedroom was slightly smaller than/n/n/n/n/n/nSirius's, though it had the same sense of former/ngrandeur. Whereas Sirius had sought to advertise his/ndifference from the rest of the family, Regulus had/nstriven to emphasize the opposite. The Slytherin/ncolors of emerald and silver were everywhere, draping/nthe bed, the walls, and the windows. The Black family/ncrest was painstakingly painted over the bed, along/nwith its motto, TOU JOURS PUR. Beneath this was a/ncollection of yellow newspaper cuttings, all stuck/ntogether to make a ragged collage. Hermione crossed/nthe room to examine them./n/n"They're all about Voldemort," she said. "Regulus/nseems to have been a fan for a few years before he/njoined the Death Eaters. ..."/n/nA little puff of dust rose from the bedcovers as she sat/ndown to read the clippings. Harry, meanwhile, had/nnoticed another photograph; a Hogwarts Quidditch/nteam was smiling and waving out of the frame. He/nmoved closer and saw the snakes emblazoned on/ntheir chests: Slytherins. Regulus was instantly/nrecognizable as the boy sitting in the middle of the/nfront row: He had the same dark hair and slightly/nhaughty look of his brother, though he was smaller,/nslighter, and rather less handsome than Sirius had/nbeen./n/n"He played Seeker," said Harry./n/n"What?" said Hermione vaguely; she was still/nimmersed in Voldemort's press clippings./n/n"He's sitting in the middle of the front row, that's/nwhere the Seeker ... Never mind," said Harry, realizing/nthat nobody was listening: Ron was on his hands and/nknees, searching under the wardrobe. Harry looked/naround the room for likely hiding places and/napproached the desk. Yet again, somebody had/n/n/n/n/nsearched before them. The drawers' contents had/nbeen turned over recently, the dust disturbed, but/nthere was nothing of value there: old quills, out-of-/ndate textbooks that bore evidence of being roughly/nhandled, a recently smashed ink bottle, its sticky/nresidue covering the contents of the drawer./n/n"There's an easier way," said Hermione, as Harry/nwiped his inky fingers on his jeans. She raised her/nwand and said, "Accio Locked."/n/nNothing happened. Ron, who had been searching the/nfolds of the faded curtains, looked disappointed./n/n"Is that it, then? It's not here?"/n/n"Oh, it could still be here, but under counter-/nenchantments," said Hermione. "Charms to prevent it/nbeing summoned magically, you know."/n/n"Like Voldemort put on the stone basin in the cave,"/nsaid Harry, remembering how he had been unable to/nSummon the fake locket./n/n"How are we supposed to find it then?" asked Ron./n/n"We search manually," said Hermione./n/n"That's a good idea," said Ron, rolling his eyes, and he/nresumed his examination of the curtains./n/nThey combed every inch of the room for more than an/nhour, but were forced, finally, to conclude that the/nlocket was not there./n/nThe sun had risen now; its light dazzled them even/nthrough the grimy landing windows./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It could be somewhere else in the house, though,"/nsaid Hermione in a rallying tone as they walked back/ndownstairs: As Harry and Ron had become more/ndiscouraged, she seemed to have become more/ndetermined. "Whether he'd managed to destroy it or/nnot, he'd want to keep it hidden from Voldemort,/nwouldn't he? Remember all those awful things we had/nto get rid of when we were here last time? That clock/nthat shot bolts at everyone and those old robes that/ntried to strangle Ron; Regulus might have put them/nthere to protect the locket's hiding place, even though/nwe didn't realize it at ... at ..."/n/nHarry and Ron looked at her. She was standing with/none foot in midair, with the dumbstruck look of one/nwho had just been Obliviated; her eyes had even/ndrifted out of focus./n/n"... at the time," she finished in a whisper./n/n"Something wrong?" asked Ron./n/n"There was a locket."/n/n"What?" said Harry and Ron together./n/n"In the cabinet in the drawing room. Nobody could/nopen it. And we ... we ..."/n/nHarry felt as though a brick had slid down through/nhis chest into his stomach. He remembered: He had/neven handled the thing as they passed it around, each/ntrying in turn to prise it open. It had been tossed into/na sack of rubbish, along with the snuffbox of Wartcap/npowder and the music box that had made everyone/nsleepy. .../n/n"Kreacher nicked loads of things back from us," said/nHarry. It was the only chance, the only slender hope/n/n/n/n/n/nleft to them, and he was going to cling to it until/nforced to let go. "He had a whole stash of stuff in his/ncupboard in the kitchen. C'mon."/n/nHe ran down the stairs taking two steps at a time, the/nother two thundering along in his wake. They made/nso much noise that they woke the portrait of Sirius's/nmother as they passed through the hall./n/n"Filth). Mudbloods\ Scum)" she screamed after them as/nthey dashed down into the basement kitchen and/nslammed the door behind them./n/nHarry ran the length of the room, skidded to a halt at/nthe door of Kreacher's cupboard, and wrenched it/nopen. There was the nest of dirty old blankets in/nwhich the house-elf had once slept, but they were no/nlonger glittering with the trinkets Kreacher had/nsalvaged. The only thing there was an old copy of/nNature's Nobility: A Wizarding Genealogy. Refusing to/nbelieve his eyes, Harry snatched up the blankets and/nshook them. A dead mouse fell out and rolled/ndismally across the floor. Ron groaned as he threw/nhimself into a kitchen chair; Hermione closed her/neyes./n/n"It's not over yet," said Harry, and he raised his voice/nand called, " Kreacherl"/n/nThere was a loud crack and the house-elf that Harry/nhad so reluctantly inherited from Sirius appeared out/nof nowhere in front of the cold and empty fireplace:/ntiny, half human-sized, his pale skin hanging off him/nin folds, white hair sprouting copiously from his/nbatlike ears. He was still wearing the filthy rag in/nwhich they had first met him, and the contemptuous/nlook he bent upon Harry showed that his attitude to/nhis change of ownership had altered no more than his/noutfit./n/n/n/n/n/n"Master," croaked Kreacher in his bullfrog's voice, and/nhe bowed low, muttering to his knees, "back in my/nMistress's old house with the blood-traitor Weasley/nand the Mudblood — "/n/n"I forbid you to call anyone 'blood traitor' or/n'Mudblood,' " growled Harry. He would have found/nKreacher, with his snoutlike nose and bloodshot eyes,/na distinctly unlovable object even if the elf had not/nbetrayed Sirius to Voldemort./n/n"I've got a question for you," said Harry, his heart/nbeating rather fast as he looked down at the elf, "and/nI order you to answer it truthfully. Understand?"/n/n"Yes, Master," said Kreacher, bowing low again: Harry/nsaw his lips moving soundlessly, undoubtedly framing/nthe insults he was now forbidden to utter./n/n"Two years ago," said Harry, his heart now/nhammering against his ribs, "there was a big gold/nlocket in the drawing room upstairs. We threw it out./nDid you steal it back?"/n/nThere was a moment's silence, during which Kreacher/nstraightened up to look Harry full in the face. Then he/nsaid, "Yes."/n/n"Where is it now?" asked Harry jubilantly as Ron and/nHermione looked gleeful./n/nKreacher closed his eyes as though he could not bear/nto see their reactions to his next word./n/n"Gone."/n/n"Gone?" echoed Harry, elation flooding out of him./n"What do you mean, it's gone?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe elf shivered. He swayed./n/n/n/n"Kreacher," said Harry fiercely, "I order you — "/n/n"Mundungus Fletcher," croaked the elf, his eyes still/ntight shut. "Mundungus Fletcher stole it all: Miss/nBella's and Miss Cissy's pictures, my Mistress's/ngloves, the Order of Merlin, First Class, the goblets/nwith the family crest, and — and — "/n/nKreacher was gulping for air: His hollow chest was/nrising and falling rapidly, then his eyes flew open and/nhe uttered a bloodcurdling scream./n/n" — and the locket, Master Regulus's locket, Kreacher/ndid wrong, Kreacher failed in his orders!"/n/nHarry reacted instinctively: As Kreacher lunged for/nthe poker standing in the grate, he launched himself/nupon the elf, flattening him. Hermione's scream/nmingled with Kreacher's, but Harry bellowed louder/nthan both of them: "Kreacher, I order you to stay/nstill!"/n/nHe felt the elf freeze and released him. Kreacher lay/nflat on the cold stone floor, tears gushing from his/nsagging eyes./n/n"Harry, let him up!" Hermione whispered./n/n"So he can beat himself up with the poker?" snorted/nHarry, kneeling beside the elf. "I don't think so. Right,/nKreacher, I want the truth: How do you know/nMundungus Fletcher stole the locket?"/n/n"Kreacher saw him!" gasped the elf as tears poured/nover his snout and into his mouth full of graying/nteeth. "Kreacher saw him coming out of Kreacher's/ncupboard with his hands full of Kreacher's treasures./n/n/n/n/n/nKreacher told the sneak thief to stop, but Mundungus/nFletcher laughed and r-ran. ..."/n/n"You called the locket 'Master Regulus 's,' " said Harry./n"Why? Where did it come from? What did Regulus/nhave to do with it? Kreacher, sit up and tell me/neverything you know about that locket, and/neverything Regulus had to do with it!"/n/nThe elf sat up, curled into a ball, placed his wet face/nbetween his knees, and began to rock backward and/nforward. When he spoke, his voice was muffled but/nquite distinct in the silent, echoing kitchen./n/n"Master Sirius ran away, good riddance, for he was a/nbad boy and broke my Mistress's heart with his/nlawless ways. But Master Regulus had proper pride;/nhe knew what was due to the name of Black and the/ndignity of his pure blood. For years he talked of the/nDark Lord, who was going to bring the wizards out of/nhiding to rule the Muggles and the Muggle-borns . . ./nand when he was sixteen years old, Master Regulus/njoined the Dark Lord. So proud, so proud, so happy to/nserve .../n/n"And one day, a year after he had joined, Master/nRegulus came down to the kitchen to see Kreacher./nMaster Regulus always liked Kreacher. And Master/nRegulus said ... he said ..."/n/nThe old elf rocked faster than ever./n/n"... he said that the Dark Lord required an elf."/n/n"Voldemort needed an elf?" Harry repeated, looking/naround at Ron and Hermione, who looked just as/npuzzled as he did./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Oh yes," moaned Kreacher. "And Master Regulus had/nvolunteered Kreacher. It was an honor, said Master/nRegulus, an honor for him and for Kreacher, who/nmust be sure to do whatever the Dark Lord ordered/nhim to do ... and then to c-come home."/n/nKreacher rocked still faster, his breath coming in/nsobs./n/n"So Kreacher went to the Dark Lord. The Dark Lord/ndid not tell Kreacher what they were to do, but took/nKreacher with him to a cave beside the sea. And/nbeyond the cave there was a cavern, and in the/ncavern was a great black lake ..."/n/nThe hairs on the back of Harry's neck stood up./nKreacher's croaking voice seemed to come to him from/nacross that dark water. He saw what had happened/nas clearly as though he had been present./n/n"... There was a boat ..."/n/nOf course there had been a boat; Harry knew the/nboat, ghostly green and tiny, bewitched so as to carry/none wizard and one victim toward the island in the/ncenter. This, then, was how Voldemort had tested the/ndefenses surrounding the Horcrux: by borrowing a/ndisposable creature, a house-elf .../n/n"There was a b-basin full of potion on the island. The/nD-Dark Lord made Kreacher drink it. ..."/n/nThe elf quaked from head to foot./n/n"Kreacher drank, and as he drank, he saw terrible/nthings. ... Kreacher's insides burned. ... Kreacher/ncried for Master Regulus to save him, he cried for his/nMistress Black, but the Dark Lord only laughed. .../n/nHe made Kreacher drink all the potion. ... He dropped/n/n/n/n/na locket into the empty basin. ... He filled it with more/npotion./n/n"And then the Dark Lord sailed away, leaving/nKreacher on the island. ..."/n/nHarry could see it happening. He watched/nVoldemort's white, snakelike face vanishing into/ndarkness, those red eyes fixed pitilessly on the/nthrashing elf whose death would occur within/nminutes, whenever he succumbed to the desperate/nthirst that the burning potion caused its victim. .../n/nBut here, Harry's imagination could go no further, for/nhe could not see how Kreacher had escaped./n/n"Kreacher needed water, he crawled to the island's/nedge and he drank from the black lake ... and hands,/ndead hands, came out of the water and dragged/nKreacher under the surface. ..."/n/n"How did you get away?" Harry asked, and he was not/nsurprised to hear himself whispering./n/nKreacher raised his ugly head and looked at Harry/nwith his great, bloodshot eyes./n/n"Master Regulus told Kreacher to come back," he/nsaid./n/n"I know — but how did you escape the Inferi?"/n/nKreacher did not seem to understand./n/n"Master Regulus told Kreacher to come back," he/nrepeated./n/n"I know, but — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, it's obvious, isn't it, Harry?" said Ron. "He/nDisapparated!"/n/n"But ... you couldn't Apparate in and out of that/ncave," said Harry, "otherwise Dumbledore — "/n/n"Elf magic isn't like wizard's magic, is it?" said Ron. "I/nmean, they can Apparate and Disapparate in and out/nof Hogwarts when we can't."/n/nThere was silence as Harry digested this. How could/nVoldemort have made such a mistake? But even as he/nthought this, Hermione spoke, and her voice was icy./n/n"Of course, Voldemort would have considered the/nways of house-elves far beneath his notice, just like/nall the purebloods who treat them like animals. ... It/nwould never have occurred to him that they might/nhave magic that he didn't."/n/n"The house-elf's highest law is his Master's bidding,"/nintoned Kreacher. "Kreacher was told to come home,/nso Kreacher came home. ..."/n/n"Well, then, you did what you were told, didn't you?"/nsaid Hermione kindly. "You didn't disobey orders at/nall!"/n/nKreacher shook his head, rocking as fast as ever./n/n"So what happened when you got back?" Harry asked./n"What did Regulus say when you told him what had/nhappened?"/n/n"Master Regulus was very worried, very worried,"/ncroaked Kreacher. "Master Regulus told Kreacher to/nstay hidden and not to leave the house. And then ... it/nwas a little while later . . . Master Regulus came to find/nKreacher in his cupboard one night, and Master/n/n/n/n/nRegulus was strange, not as he usually was,/ndisturbed in his mind, Kreacher could tell . . . and he/nasked Kreacher to take him to the cave, the cave/nwhere Kreacher had gone with the Dark Lord. ..."/n/nAnd so they had set off. Harry could visualize them/nquite clearly, the frightened old elf and the thin, dark/nSeeker who had so resembled Sirius. ... Kreacher/nknew how to open the concealed entrance to the/nunderground cavern, knew how to raise the tiny boat;/nthis time it was his beloved Regulus who sailed with/nhim to the island with its basin of poison. .../n/n"And he made you drink the potion?" said Harry,/ndisgusted./n/nBut Kreacher shook his head and wept. Hermione's/nhands leapt to her mouth: She seemed to have/nunderstood something./n/n"M-Master Regulus took from his pocket a locket like/nthe one the Dark Lord had," said Kreacher, tears/npouring down either side of his snoutlike nose. "And/nhe told Kreacher to take it and, when the basin was/nempty, to switch the lockets. ..."/n/nKreacher's sobs came in great rasps now; Harry had/nto concentrate hard to understand him./n/n"And he ordered — Kreacher to leave — without him./nAnd he told Kreacher — to go home — and never to/ntell my Mistress — what he had done — but to/ndestroy — the first locket. And he drank — all the/npotion — and Kreacher swapped the lockets — and/nwatched ... as Master Regulus . . . was dragged/nbeneath the water ... and ..."/n/n"Oh, Kreacher!" wailed Hermione, who was crying./n/nShe dropped to her knees beside the elf and tried to/n/n/n/n/n/nhug him. At once he was on his feet, cringing away/nfrom her, quite obviously repulsed./n/n"The Mudblood touched Kreacher, he will not allow it,/nwhat would his Mistress say?"/n/n"I told you not to call her 'Mudblood'!" snarled Harry,/nbut the elf was already punishing himself: He fell to/nthe ground and banged his forehead on the floor./n/n"Stop him — stop him!" Hermione cried. "Oh, don't/nyou see now how sick it is, the way they've got to/nobey?"/n/n"Kreacher — stop, stop!" shouted Harry./n/nThe elf lay on the floor, panting and shivering, green/nmucus glistening around his snout, a bruise already/nblooming on his pallid forehead where he had struck/nhimself, his eyes swollen and bloodshot and/nswimming in tears. Harry had never seen anything so/npitiful./n/n"So you brought the locket home," he said/nrelentlessly, for he was determined to know the full/nstory. "And you tried to destroy it?"/n/n"Nothing Kreacher did made any mark upon it,"/nmoaned the elf. "Kreacher tried everything, everything/nhe knew, but nothing, nothing would work. ... So/nmany powerful spells upon the casing, Kreacher was/nsure the way to destroy it was to get inside it, but it/nwould not open. . . . Kreacher punished himself, he/ntried again, he punished himself, he tried again./nKreacher failed to obey orders, Kreacher could not/ndestroy the locket! And his Mistress was mad with/ngrief, because Master Regulus had disappeared, and/nKreacher could not tell her what had happened, no,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nbecause Master Regulus had f-f-forbidden him to tell/nany of the f-f-family what happened in the c-cave. ..."/n/nKreacher began to sob so hard that there were no/nmore coherent words. Tears flowed down Hermione's/ncheeks as she watched Kreacher, but she did not dare/ntouch him again. Even Ron, who was no fan of/nKreacher's, looked troubled. Harry sat back on his/nheels and shook his head, trying to clear it./n/n"I don't understand you, Kreacher," he said finally./n"Voldemort tried to kill you, Regulus died to bring/nVoldemort down, but you were still happy to betray/nSirius to Voldemort? You were happy to go to/nNarcissa and Bellatrix, and pass information to/nVoldemort through them. ..."/n/n"Harry, Kreacher doesn't think like that," said/nHermione, wiping her eyes on the back of her hand./n"He's a slave; house-elves are used to bad, even/nbrutal treatment; what Voldemort did to Kreacher/nwasn't that far out of the common way. What do/nwizard wars mean to an elf like Kreacher? He's loyal/nto people who are kind to him, and Mrs. Black must/nhave been, and Regulus certainly was, so he served/nthem willingly and parroted their beliefs. I know what/nyou're going to say," she went on as Harry began to/nprotest, "that Regulus changed his mind . . . but he/ndoesn't seem to have explained that to Kreacher, does/nhe? And I think I know why. Kreacher and Regulus 's/nfamily were all safer if they kept to the old pure-blood/nline. Regulus was trying to protect them all."/n/n"Sirius — "/n/n"Sirius was horrible to Kreacher, Harry, and it's no/ngood looking like that, you know it's true. Kreacher/nhad been alone for a long time when Sirius came to/nlive here, and he was probably starving for a bit of/n/n/n/n/n/naffection. I'm sure 'Miss Cissy' and 'Miss Bella' were/nperfectly lovely to Kreacher when he turned up, so he/ndid them a favor and told them everything they/nwanted to know. I've said all along that wizards would/npay for how they treat house-elves. Well, Voldemort/ndid ... and so did Sirius."/n/nHarry had no retort. As he watched Kreacher sobbing/non the floor, he remembered what Dumbledore had/nsaid to him, mere hours after Sirius's death: I do not/nthink Sirius ever saw Kreacher as a being with feelings/nas acute as a human's. .../n/n"Kreacher," said Harry after a while, "when you feel/nup to it, er ... please sit up."/n/nIt was several minutes before Kreacher hiccuped/nhimself into silence. Then he pushed himself into a/nsitting position again, rubbing his knuckles into his/neyes like a small child./n/n"Kreacher, I am going to ask you to do something,"/nsaid Harry. He glanced at Hermione for assistance. He/nwanted to give the order kindly, but at the same time,/nhe could not pretend that it was not an order./nHowever, the change in his tone seemed to have/ngained her approval: She smiled encouragingly./n/n"Kreacher, I want you, please, to go and find/nMundungus Fletcher. We need to find out where the/nlocket — where Master Regulus's locket is. It's really/nimportant. We want to finish the work Master/nRegulus started, we want to — er — ensure that he/ndidn't die in vain."/n/nKreacher dropped his fists and looked up at Harry./n"Find Mundungus Fletcher?" he croaked./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"And bring him here, to Grimmauld Place," said/nHarry. "Do you think you could do that for us?"/n/nAs Kreacher nodded and got to his feet, Harry had a/nsudden inspiration. He pulled out Hagrid's purse and/ntook out the fake Horcrux, the substitute locket in/nwhich Regulus had placed the note to Voldemort./n/n"Kreacher, I'd, er, like you to have this," he said,/npressing the locket into the elf's hand. "This belonged/nto Regulus and I'm sure he'd want you to have it as a/ntoken of gratitude for what you — "/n/n"Overkill, mate," said Ron as the elf took one look at/nthe locket, let out a howl of shock and misery, and/nthrew himself back onto the ground./n/nIt took them nearly half an hour to calm down/nKreacher, who was so overcome to be presented with/na Black family heirloom for his very own that he was/ntoo weak at the knees to stand properly. When finally/nhe was able to totter a few steps they all accompanied/nhim to his cupboard, watched him tuck up the locket/nsafely in his dirty blankets, and assured him that/nthey would make its protection their first priority/nwhile he was away. He then made two low bows to/nHarry and Ron, and even gave a funny little spasm in/nHermione's direction that might have been an attempt/nat a respectful salute, before Disapparating with the/nusual loud crack./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Bribe
text: /nIf Kreacher could escape a lake full of Inferi, Harry/nwas confident that the capture of Mundungus would/ntake a few hours at most, and he prowled the house/nall morning in a state of high anticipation. However,/nKreacher did not return that morning or even that/nafternoon. By nightfall, Harry felt discouraged and/nanxious, and a supper composed largely of moldy/nbread, upon which Hermione had tried a variety of/nunsuccessful Transfigurations, did nothing to help./n/nKreacher did not return the following day, nor the day/nafter that. However, two cloaked men had appeared in/nthe square outside number twelve, and they remained/nthere into the night, gazing in the direction of the/nhouse that they could not see./n/n"Death Eaters, for sure," said Ron, as he, Harry, and/nHermione watched from the drawing room windows./n"Reckon they know we're in here?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't think so," said Hermione, though she looked/nfrightened, "or they'd have sent Snape in after us,/nwouldn't they?"/n/n"D'you reckon he's been in here and had his tongue/ntied by Moody's curse?" asked Ron./n/n"Yes," said Hermione, "otherwise he'd have been able/nto tell that lot how to get in, wouldn't he? But they're/nprobably watching to see whether we turn up. They/nknow that Harry owns the house, after all."/n/n"How do they — ?" began Harry./n/n"Wizarding wills are examined by the Ministry,/nremember? They'll know Sirius left you the place."/n/nThe presence of the Death Eaters outside increased/nthe ominous mood inside number twelve. They had/nnot heard a word from anyone beyond Grimmauld/nPlace since Mr. Weasley's Patronus, and the strain/nwas starting to tell. Restless and irritable, Ron had/ndeveloped an annoying habit of playing with the/nDeluminator in his pocket: This particularly/ninfuriated Hermione, who was whiling away the wait/nfor Kreacher by studying The Tales of Beedle the Bard/nand did not appreciate the way the lights kept/nflashing on and off./n/n"Will you stop it!" she cried on the third evening of/nKreacher's absence, as all light was sucked from the/ndrawing room yet again./n/n"Sorry, sorry!" said Ron, clicking the Deluminator and/nrestoring the lights. "I don't know I'm doing it!"/n/n"Well, can't you find something useful to occupy/nyourself?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What, like reading kids' stories?"/n/n"Dumbledore left me this book, Ron — "/n/n" — and he left me the Deluminator, maybe I'm/nsupposed to use it!"/n/nUnable to stand the bickering, Harry slipped out of/nthe room unnoticed by either of them. He headed/ndownstairs toward the kitchen, which he kept visiting/nbecause he was sure that was where Kreacher was/nmost likely to reappear. Halfway down the flight of/nstairs into the hall, however, he heard a tap on the/nfront door, then metallic clicks and the grinding of the/nchain./n/nEvery nerve in his body seemed to tauten: He pulled/nout his wand, moved into the shadows beside the/ndecapitated elf heads, and waited. The door opened:/nHe saw a glimpse of the lamplit square outside, and a/ncloaked figure edged into the hall and closed the door/nbehind it. The intruder took a step forward, and/nMoody's voice asked, "Severus Snape ?" Then the dust/nfigure rose from the end of the hall and rushed him,/nraising its dead hand./n/n"It was not I who killed you, Albus," said a quiet voice./n/nThe jinx broke: The dust-figure exploded again, and it/nwas impossible to make out the newcomer through/nthe dense gray cloud it left behind./n/nHarry pointed his wand into the middle of it./n/n"Don't move!"/n/nHe had forgotten the portrait of Mrs. Black: At the/nsound of his yell, the curtains hiding her flew open/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nand she began to scream, "Mudbloods and filth/ndishonoring my house — "/n/nRon and Hermione came crashing down the stairs/nbehind Harry, wands pointing, like his, at the/nunknown man now standing with his arms raised in/nthe hall below./n/n"Hold your fire, it's me, Remus!"/n/n"Oh, thank goodness," said Hermione weakly,/npointing her wand at Mrs. Black instead; with a bang,/nthe curtains swished shut again and silence fell. Ron/ntoo lowered his wand, but Harry did not./n/n"Show yourself!" he called back./n/nLupin moved forward into the lamplight, hands still/nheld high in a gesture of surrender./n/n"I am Remus John Lupin, werewolf, sometimes known/nas Moony, one of the four creators of the Marauder's/nMap, married to Nymphadora, usually known as/nTonks, and I taught you how to produce a Patronus,/nHarry, which takes the form of a stag."/n/n"Oh, all right," said Harry, lowering his wand, "but I/nhad to check, didn't I?"/n/n"Speaking as your ex-Defense Against the Dark Arts/nteacher, I quite agree that you had to check. Ron,/nHermione, you shouldn't be quite so quick to lower/nyour defenses."/n/nThey ran down the stairs toward him. Wrapped in a/nthick black traveling cloak, he looked exhausted, but/npleased to see them./n/n"No sign of Severus, then?" he asked./n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Harry. "What's going on? Is everyone/nokay?"/n/n"Yes," said Lupin, "but we're all being watched. There/nare a couple of Death Eaters in the square outside — "/n/n"We know — "/n/n"I had to Apparate very precisely onto the top step/noutside the front door to be sure that they would not/nsee me. They can't know you're in here or I'm sure/nthey'd have more people out there; they're staking out/neverywhere that's got any connection with you, Harry./nLet's go downstairs, there's a lot to tell you, and I/nwant to know what happened after you left the/nBurrow."/n/nThey descended into the kitchen, where Hermione/npointed her wand at the grate. A fire sprang up/ninstantly: It gave the illusion of coziness to the stark/nstone walls and glistened off the long wooden table./nLupin pulled a few butterbeers from beneath his/ntraveling cloak and they sat down./n/n"I'd have been here three days ago but I needed to/nshake off the Death Eater tailing me," said Lupin. "So,/nyou came straight here after the wedding?"/n/n"No," said Harry, "only after we ran into a couple of/nDeath Eaters in a cafe on Tottenham Court Road."/n/nLupin slopped most of his butterbeer down his front./n/n" What ?"/n/nThey explained what had happened; when they had/nfinished, Lupin looked aghast./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But how did they find you so quickly? It's impossible/nto track anyone who Apparates, unless you grab hold/nof them as they disappear!"/n/n"And it doesn't seem likely they were just strolling/ndown Tottenham Court Road at the time, does it?"/nsaid Harry./n/n"We wondered," said Hermione tentatively, "whether/nHarry could still have the Trace on him?"/n/n"Impossible," said Lupin. The scars on the back of/nhis right hand seemed to be tingling again./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Magic Is Might
text: /nAs August wore on, the square of unkempt grass in/nthe middle of Grimmauld Place shriveled in the sun/nuntil it was brittle and brown. The inhabitants of/nnumber twelve were never seen by anybody in the/nsurrounding houses, and nor was number twelve/nitself. The Muggles who lived in Grimmauld Place had/nlong since accepted the amusing mistake in the/nnumbering that had caused number eleven to sit/nbeside number thirteen./n/nAnd yet the square was now attracting a trickle of/nvisitors who seemed to find the anomaly most/nintriguing. Barely a day passed without one or two/npeople arriving in Grimmauld Place with no other/npurpose, or so it seemed, than to lean against the/nrailings facing numbers eleven and thirteen, watching/nthe join between the two houses. The lurkers were/nnever the same two days running, although they all/nseemed to share a dislike for normal clothing. Most of/nthe Londoners who passed them were used to/neccentric dressers and took little notice, though/noccasionally one of them might glance back,/n/n/n/n/nwondering why anyone would wear such long cloaks/nin this heat./n/nThe watchers seemed to be gleaning little satisfaction/nfrom their vigil.
