Ron cut across her, his voice/nharsh./n/nHarry and Hermione looked at each other./n/n"I'm sorry," Ron said, moaning a little as he raised/nhimself to look at them, "but it feels like a — a jinx or/nsomething. Can't we call him You-Know-Who —/nplease?"/n/n"Dumbledore said fear of a name — " began Harry./n/n"In case you hadn't noticed, mate, calling You-Know-/nWho by his name didn't do Dumbledore much good in/nthe end," Ron snapped back. "Just — just show You-/nKnow-Who some respect, will you?"/n/n"Respect?" Harry repeated, but Hermione shot him a/nwarning look; apparently he was not to argue with/nRon while the latter was in such a weakened/ncondition./n/nHarry and Hermione half carried, half dragged Ron/nthrough the entrance of the tent. The interior was/n/n/n/n/n/nexactly as Harry remembered it: a small flat, complete/nwith bathroom and tiny kitchen. He shoved aside an/nold armchair and lowered Ron carefully onto the lower/nberth of a bunk bed. Even this very short journey had/nturned Ron whiter still, and once they had settled him/non the mattress he closed his eyes again and did not/nspeak for a while./n/n"I'll make some tea," said Hermione breathlessly,/npulling kettle and mugs from the depths of her bag/nand heading toward the kitchen./n/nHarry found the hot drink as welcome as the/nfirewhisky had been on the night that Mad-Eye had/ndied; it seemed to burn away a little of the fear/nfluttering in his chest. After a minute or two, Ron/nbroke the silence./n/n"What d'you reckon happened to the Cattermoles?"/n/n"With any luck, they'll have got away," said Hermione,/nclutching her hot mug for comfort. "As long as Mr./nCattermole had his wits about him, he'll have/ntransported Mrs. Cattermole by Side-Along- Apparition/nand they'll be fleeing the country right now with their/nchildren. That's what Harry told her to do."/n/n"Blimey, I hope they escaped," said Ron, leaning back/non his pillows. The tea seemed to be doing him good;/na little of his color had returned. "I didn't get the/nfeeling Reg Cattermole was all that quick-witted,/nthough, the way everyone was talking to me when I/nwas him. God, I hope they made it. ... If they both end/nup in Azkaban because of us ..."/n/nHarry looked over at Hermione and the question he/nhad been about to ask — about whether Mrs./nCattermole 's lack of a wand would prevent her/nApparating alongside her husband — died in his/n/n/n/n/n/nthroat. Hermione was watching Ron fret over the fate/nof the Cattermoles, and there was such tenderness in/nher expression that Harry felt almost as if he had/nsurprised her in the act of kissing him./n/n"So, have you got it?" Harry asked her, partly to/nremind her that he was there./n/n"Got — got what?" she said with a little start./n/n"What did we just go through all that for? The locket!/nWhere's the locket?"/n/n" You got it?" shouted Ron, raising himself a little/nhigher on his pillows. "No one tells me anything!/nBlimey, you could have mentioned it!"/n/n"Well, we were running for our lives from the Death/nEaters, weren't we?" said Hermione. "Here."/n/nAnd she pulled the locket out of the pocket of her/nrobes and handed it to Ron./n/nIt was as large as a chicken's egg. An ornate letter S,/ninlaid with many small green stones, glinted dully in/nthe diffused light shining through the tent's canvas/nroof./n/n"There isn't any chance someone's destroyed it since/nKreacher had it?" asked Ron hopefully. "I mean, are/nwe sure it's still a Horcrux?"/n/n"I think so," said Hermione, taking it back from him/nand looking at it closely. "There 'd be some sign of/ndamage if it had been magically destroyed."/n/nShe passed it to Harry, who turned it over in his/nfingers. The thing looked perfect, pristine. He/nremembered the mangled remains of the diary, and/n/n/n/n/n/nhow the stone in the Horcrux ring had been cracked/nopen when Dumbledore destroyed it./n/n/n/n"I reckon Kreacher's right," said Harry. "We're going to/nhave to work out how to open this thing before we can/ndestroy it."/n/nSudden awareness of what he was holding, of what/nlived behind the little golden doors, hit Harry as he/nspoke. Even after all their efforts to find it, he felt a/nviolent urge to fling the locket from him. Mastering/nhimself again, he tried to prise the locket apart with/nhis fingers, then attempted the charm Hermione had/nused to open Regulus's bedroom door. Neither/nworked. He handed the locket back to Ron and/nHermione, each of whom did their best, but were no/nmore successful at opening it than he had been./n/n"Can you feel it, though?" Ron asked in a hushed/nvoice, as he held it tight in his clenched fist./n/n"What d'you mean?"/n/nRon passed the Horcrux to Harry. After a moment or/ntwo, Harry thought he knew what Ron meant. Was it/nhis own blood pulsing through his veins that he could/nfeel, or was it something beating inside the locket, like/na tiny metal heart?/n/n"What are we going to do with it?" Hermione asked./n/n"Keep it safe till we work out how to destroy it," Harry/nreplied, and, little though he wanted to, he hung the/nchain around his own neck, dropping the locket out/nof sight beneath his robes, where it rested against his/nchest beside the pouch Hagrid had given him./n/n"I think we should take it in turns to keep watch/noutside the tent," he added to Hermione, standing up/n/n/n/n/n/nand stretching. "And we'll need to think about some/nfood as well. You stay there," he added sharply, as/nRon attempted to sit up and turned a nasty shade of/ngreen./n/nWith the Sneakoscope Hermione had given Harry for/nhis birthday set carefully upon the table in the tent,/nHarry and Hermione spent the rest of the day sharing/nthe role of lookout. However, the Sneakoscope/nremained silent and still upon its point all day, and/nwhether because of the protective enchantments and/nMuggle-repelling charms Hermione had spread/naround them, or because people rarely ventured this/nway, their patch of wood remained deserted, apart/nfrom occasional birds and squirrels. Evening brought/nno change; Harry lit his wand as he swapped places/nwith Hermione at ten o'clock, and looked out upon a/ndeserted scene, noting the bats fluttering high above/nhim across the single patch of starry sky visible from/ntheir protected clearing./n/nHe felt hungry now, and a little light-headed./n/nHermione had not packed any food in her magical/nbag, as she had assumed that they would be/nreturning to Grimmauld Place that night, so they had/nhad nothing to eat except some wild mushrooms that/nHermione had collected from amongst the nearest/ntrees and stewed in a billycan. After a couple of/nmouthfuls Ron had pushed his portion away, looking/nqueasy; Harry had only persevered so as not to hurt/nHermione 's feelings./n/nThe surrounding silence was broken by odd rustlings/nand what sounded like crackings of twigs: Harry/nthought that they were caused by animals rather than/npeople, yet he kept his wand held tight at the ready./nHis insides, already uncomfortable due to their/ninadequate helping of rubbery mushrooms, tingled/nwith unease./n/n/n/n/n/nHe had thought that he would feel elated if they/nmanaged to steal back the Horcrux, but somehow he/ndid not; all he felt as he sat looking out at the/ndarkness, of which his wand lit only a tiny part, was/nworry about what would happen next. It was as/nthough he had been hurtling toward this point for/nweeks, months, maybe even years, but now he had/ncome to an abrupt halt, run out of road./n/nThere were other Horcruxes out there somewhere, but/nhe did not have the faintest idea where they could be./nHe did not even know what all of them were./nMeanwhile he was at a loss to know how to destroy/nthe only one that they had found, the Horcrux that/ncurrently lay against the bare flesh of his chest./nCuriously, it had not taken heat from his body, but/nlay so cold against his skin it might just have/nemerged from icy water. From time to time Harry/nthought, or perhaps imagined, that he could feel the/ntiny heartbeat ticking irregularly alongside his own./n/nNameless forebodings crept upon him as he sat there/nin the dark: He tried to resist them, push them away,/nyet they came at him relentlessly. Neither can live/nwhile the other survives. Ron and Hermione, now/ntalking softly behind him in the tent, could walk away/nif they wanted to: He could not. And it seemed to/nHarry as he sat there trying to master his own fear/nand exhaustion, that the Horcrux against his chest/nwas ticking away the time he had left. ... Stupid idea,/nhe told himself, don't think that. .../n/nHis scar was starting to prickle again. He was afraid/nthat he was making it happen by having these/nthoughts, and tried to direct them into another/nchannel. He thought of poor Kreacher, who had/nexpected them home and had received Yaxley instead./nWould the elf keep silent or would he tell the Death/nEater everything he knew? Harry wanted to believe/n/n/n/n/nthat Kreacher had changed toward him in the past/nmonth, that he would be loyal now, but who knew/nwhat would happen? What if the Death Eaters/ntortured the elf? Sick images swarmed into Harry's/nhead and he tried to push these away too, for there/nwas nothing he could do for Kreacher: He and/nHermione had already decided against trying to/nsummon him; what if someone from the Ministry/ncame too? They could not count on elfish Apparition/nbeing free from the same flaw that had taken Yaxley/nto Grimmauld Place on the hem of Hermione 's sleeve./n/nHarry's scar was burning now. He thought that there/nwas so much they did not know: Lupin had been right/nabout magic they had never encountered or imagined./nWhy hadn't Dumbledore explained more? Had he/nthought that there would be time; that he would live/nfor years, for centuries perhaps, like his friend Nicolas/nFlamel? If so, he had been wrong. ... Snape had seen/nto that. ... Snape, the sleeping snake, who had struck/nat the top of the tower . . ./n/nAnd Dumbledore had fallen ... fallen .../n/n" Give it to me, Gregorovitch."/n/nHarry's voice was high, clear, and cold, his wand held/nin front of him by a long-fingered white hand. The/nman at whom he was pointing was suspended upside/ndown in midair, though there were no ropes holding/nhim; he swung there, invisibly and eerily bound, his/nlimbs wrapped about him, his terrified face, on a level/nwith Harry's, ruddy due to the blood that had rushed/nto his head. He had pure-white hair and a thick,/nbushy beard: a trussed-up Father Christmas./n/n"I have it not, I have it no more! It was, many years/nago, stolen from me!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Do not lie to Lord Voldemort, Gregorovitch. He/nknows. ... He always knows."/n/nThe hanging man's pupils were wide, dilated with/nfear, and they seemed to swell, bigger and bigger until/ntheir blackness swallowed Harry whole —/n/nAnd now Harry was hurrying along a dark corridor in/nstout little Gregorovitch 's wake as he held a lantern/naloft: Gregorovitch burst into the room at the end of/nthe passage and his lantern illuminated what looked/nlike a workshop; wood shavings and gold gleamed in/nthe swinging pool of light, and there on the window/nledge sat perched, like a giant bird, a young man with/ngolden hair. In the split second that the lantern's light/nilluminated him, Harry saw the delight upon his/nhandsome face, then the intruder shot a Stunning/nSpell from his wand and jumped neatly backward out/nof the window with a crow of laughter./n/nAnd Harry was hurtling back out of those wide,/ntunnellike pupils and Gregorovitch 's face was stricken/nwith terror./n/n"Who was the thief, Gregorovitch?" said the high cold/nvoice./n/n"I do not know, I never knew, a young man — no —/nplease — PLEASE !"/n/nA scream that went on and on and then a burst of/ngreen light —/n/n" Harryl "/n/nHe opened his eyes, panting, his forehead throbbing./nHe had passed out against the side of the tent, had/nslid sideways down the canvas, and was sprawled on/nthe ground. He looked up at Hermione, whose bushy/n/n/n/n/n/nhair obscured the tiny patch of sky visible through/nthe dark branches high above them./n/n"Dream," he said, sitting up quickly and attempting to/nmeet Hermione 's glower with a look of innocence./n"Must've dozed off, sorry."/n/n"I know it was your scar! I can tell by the look on your/nface! You were looking into Vol — "/n/n"Don't say his name!" came Ron's angry voice from/nthe depths of the tent./n/n"Fine," retorted Hermione. "You-Know-Who's mind,/nthen!"/n/n"I didn't mean it to happen!" Harry said. "It was a/ndream! Can you control what you dream about,/nHermione?"/n/n"If you just learned to apply Occlumency — "/n/nBut Harry was not interested in being told off; he/nwanted to discuss what he had just seen./n/n"He's found Gregorovitch, Hermione, and I think he's/nkilled him, but before he killed him he read/nGregorovitch 's mind and I saw — "/n/n"I think I'd better take over the watch if you're so tired/nyou're falling asleep," said Hermione coldly./n/n"I can finish the watch!"/n/n"No, you're obviously exhausted. Go and lie down."/n/nShe dropped down in the mouth of the tent, looking/nstubborn. Angry, but wishing to avoid a row, Harry/nducked back inside./n/n/n/n/n/nRon's still-pale face was poking out from the lower/nbunk; Harry climbed into the one above him, lay/ndown, and looked up at the dark canvas ceiling. After/nseveral moments, Ron spoke in a voice so low that it/nwould not carry to Hermione, huddled in the/nentrance./n/n"What's You-Know-Who doing?"/n/nHarry screwed up his eyes in the effort to remember/nevery detail, then whispered into the darkness./n/n"He found Gregorovitch. He had him tied up, he was/ntorturing him."/n/n"How's Gregorovitch supposed to make him a new/nwand if he's tied up?"/n/n"I dunno. ... It's weird, isn't it?"/n/nHarry closed his eyes, thinking of all he had seen and/nheard. The more he recalled, the less sense it made./n/n... Voldemort had said nothing about Harry's wand,/nnothing about the twin cores, nothing about/nGregorovitch making a new and more powerful wand/nto beat Harry's. .../n/n"He wanted something from Gregorovitch," Harry/nsaid, eyes still closed tight. "He asked him to hand it/nover, but Gregorovitch said it had been stolen from/nhim ... and then ... then ..."/n/nHe remembered how he, as Voldemort, had seemed to/nhurtle through Gregorovitch 's eyes, into his/nmemories. .../n/n"He read Gregorovitch 's mind, and I saw this young/nbloke perched on a windowsill, and he fired a curse at/nGregorovitch and jumped out of sight. He stole it, he/n/n/n/n/n/nstole whatever You-Know-Who's after. And I ... I think/nI've seen him somewhere. ..."/n/nHarry wished he could have another glimpse of the/nlaughing boy's face. The theft had happened many/nyears ago, according to Gregorovitch. Why did the/nyoung thief look familiar?/n/nThe noises of the surrounding woods were muffled/ninside the tent; all Harry could hear was Ron's/nbreathing. After a while, Ron whispered, "Couldn't/nyou see what the thief was holding?"/n/n"No ... it must've been something small."/n/n"Harry?"/n/nThe wooden slats of Ron's bunk creaked as he/nrepositioned himself in bed./n/n"Harry, you don't reckon You-Know-Who's after/nsomething else to turn into a Horcrux?"/n/n"I don't know," said Harry slowly. "Maybe. But/nwouldn't it be dangerous for him to make another/none? Didn't Hermione say he had pushed his soul to/nthe limit already?"/n/n"Yeah, but maybe he doesn't know that."/n/n"Yeah ... maybe," said Harry./n/nHe had been sure that Voldemort had been looking/nfor a way around the problem of the twin cores, sure/nthat Voldemort sought a solution from the old/nwandmaker . . . and yet he had killed him, apparently/nwithout asking him a single question about wandlore./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWhat was Voldemort trying to find? Why, with the/nMinistry of Magic and the Wizarding world at his feet,/nwas he far away, intent on the pursuit of an object/nthat Gregorovitch had once owned, and which had/nbeen stolen by the unknown thief?/n/nHarry could still see the blond-haired youth's face; it/nwas merry, wild; there was a Fred and George-ish air/nof triumphant trickery about him. He had soared from/nthe windowsill like a bird, and Harry had seen him/nbefore, but he could not think where. .../n/nWith Gregorovitch dead, it was the merry-faced thief/nwho was in danger now, and it was on him that/nHarry's thoughts dwelled, as Ron's snores began to/nrumble from the lower bunk and as he himself drifted/nslowly into sleep once more./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Goblin's Revenge
text: /nEarly next morning, before the other two were awake,/nHarry left the tent to search the woods around them/nfor the oldest, most gnarled, and resilient-looking tree/nhe could find. There in its shadow he buried Mad-Eye/nMoody's eye and marked the spot by gouging a small/ncross in the bark with his wand. It was not much, but/nHarry felt that Mad-Eye would have much preferred/nthis to being stuck on Dolores Umbridge's door. Then/nhe returned to the tent to wait for the others to wake,/nand discuss what they were going to do next./n/nHarry and Hermione felt that it was best not to stay/nanywhere too long, and Ron agreed, with the sole/nproviso that their next move took them within reach/nof a bacon sandwich. Hermione therefore removed the/nenchantments she had placed around the clearing,/nwhile Harry and Ron obliterated all the marks and/nimpressions on the ground that might show they had/ncamped there. Then they Disapparated to the/noutskirts of a small market town./n/n/n/n/n/n/nOnce they had pitched the tent in the shelter of a/nsmall copse of trees and surrounded it with freshly/ncast defensive enchantments, Harry ventured out/nunder the Invisibility Cloak to find sustenance. This,/nhowever, did not go as planned. He had barely/nentered the town when an unnatural chill, a/ndescending mist, and a sudden darkening of the skies/nmade him freeze where he stood./n/n"But you can make a brilliant Patronus!" protested/nRon, when Harry arrived back at the tent empty-/nhanded, out of breath, and mouthing the single word,/ndementors./n/n"I couldn't ... make one," he panted, clutching the/nstitch in his side. "Wouldn't ... come."/n/nTheir expressions of consternation and/ndisappointment made Harry feel ashamed. It had/nbeen a nightmarish experience, seeing the dementors/ngliding out of the mist in the distance and realizing,/nas the paralyzing cold choked his lungs and a distant/nscreaming filled his ears, that he was not going to be/nable to protect himself. It had taken all Harry's/nwillpower to uproot himself from the spot and run,/nleaving the eyeless dementors to glide amongst the/nMuggles who might not be able to see them, but/nwould assuredly feel the despair they cast wherever/nthey went./n/n"So we still haven't got any food."/n/n"Shut up, Ron," snapped Hermione. "Harry, what/nhappened? Why do you think you couldn't make your/nPatronus? You managed perfectly yesterday!"/n/n"I don't know."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe sat low in one of Perkins's old armchairs, feeling/nmore humiliated by the moment. He was afraid that/nsomething had gone wrong inside him. Yesterday/nseemed a long time ago: Today he might have been/nthirteen years old again, the only one who collapsed/non the Hogwarts Express./n/nRon kicked a chair leg./n/n"What?" he snarled at Hermione. "I'm starving! All I've/nhad since I bled half to death is a couple of/ntoadstools!"/n/n"You go and fight your way through the dementors,/nthen," said Harry, stung./n/n"I would, but my arm's in a sling, in case you hadn't/nnoticed!"/n/n"That's convenient."/n/n"And what's that supposed to — ?"/n/n"Of course!" cried Hermione, clapping a hand to her/nforehead and startling both of them into silence./n"Harry, give me the locket! Come on," she said/nimpatiently, clicking her fingers at him when he did/nnot react, "the Horcrux, Harry, you're still wearing it!"/n/nShe held out her hands, and Harry lifted the golden/nchain over his head. The moment it parted contact/nwith Harry's skin he felt free and oddly light. He had/nnot even realized that he was clammy or that there/nwas a heavy weight pressing on his stomach until/nboth sensations lifted./n/n"Better?" asked Hermione./n/n"Yeah, loads better!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry," she said, crouching down in front of him and/nusing the kind of voice he associated with visiting the/nvery sick, "you don't think you've been possessed, do/nyou?"/n/n"What? No!" he said defensively. "I remember/neverything we've done while I've been wearing it. I/nwouldn't know what I'd done if I'd been possessed,/nwould I? Ginny told me there were times when she/ncouldn't remember anything."/n/n"Hmm," said Hermione, looking down at the heavy/ngold locket. "Well, maybe we ought not to wear it. We/ncan just keep it in the tent."/n/n"We are not leaving that Horcrux lying around," Harry/nstated firmly. "If we lose it, if it gets stolen — "/n/n"Oh, all right, all right," said Hermione, and she/nplaced it around her own neck and tucked it out of/nsight down the front of her shirt. "But we'll take turns/nwearing it, so nobody keeps it on too long."/n/n"Great," said Ron irritably, "and now we've sorted that/nout, can we please get some food?"/n/n"Fine, but we'll go somewhere else to find it," said/nHermione with half a glance at Harry. "There's no/npoint staying where we know dementors are swooping/naround."/n/nIn the end they settled down for the night in a far-/nflung field belonging to a lonely farm, from which they/nhad managed to obtain eggs and bread./n/n"It's not stealing, is it?" asked Hermione in a troubled/nvoice, as they devoured scrambled eggs on toast. "Not/nif I left some money under the chicken coop?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRon rolled his eyes and said, with his cheeks bulging,/n/n" 'Er-my-nee, 'oo worry 'oo much. 'Elax!"/n/nAnd, indeed, it was much easier to relax when they/nwere comfortably well fed: The argument about the/ndementors was forgotten in laughter that night, and/nHarry felt cheerful, even hopeful, as he took the first/nof the three night watches./n/nThis was their first encounter with the fact that a full/nstomach meant good spirits; an empty one, bickering/nand gloom. Harry was least surprised by this,/nbecause he had suffered periods of near starvation at/nthe Dursleys'. Hermione bore up reasonably well on/nthose nights when they managed to scavenge nothing/nbut berries or stale biscuits, her temper perhaps a/nlittle shorter than usual and her silences rather dour./nRon, however, had always been used to three/ndelicious meals a day, courtesy of his mother or of the/nHogwarts house-elves, and hunger made him both/nunreasonable and irascible. Whenever lack of food/ncoincided with Ron's turn to wear the Horcrux, he/nbecame downright unpleasant./n/n"So where next?" was his constant refrain. He did not/nseem to have any ideas himself, but expected Harry/nand Hermione to come up with plans while he sat and/nbrooded over the low food supplies. Accordingly Harry/nand Hermione spent fruitless hours trying to decide/nwhere they might find the other Horcruxes, and how/nto destroy the one they had already got, their/nconversations becoming increasingly repetitive as/nthey had no new information./n/nAs Dumbledore had told Harry that he believed/nVoldemort had hidden the Horcruxes in places/nimportant to him, they kept reciting, in a sort of/ndreary litany, those locations they knew that/nVoldemort had lived or visited. The orphanage where/n/n/n/n/nhe had been born and raised; Hogwarts, where he had/nbeen educated; Borgin and Burkes, where he had/nworked after completing school; then Albania, where/nhe had spent his years of exile: These formed the/nbasis of their speculations./n/n"Yeah, let's go to Albania. Shouldn't take more than/nan afternoon to search an entire country," said Ron/nsarcastically./n/n"There can't be anything there. He'd already made five/nof his Horcruxes before he went into exile, and/nDumbledore was certain the snake is the sixth," said/nHermione. "We know the snake's not in Albania, it's/nusually with Vol — "/n/n"Didn't I ask you to stop saying that?"/n/n"Fine! The snake is usually with You-Knotu-Who —/nhappy?"/n/n"Not particularly."/n/n"I can't see him hiding anything at Borgin and/nBurkes," said Harry, who had made this point many/ntimes before, but said it again simply to break the/nnasty silence. Why hadn't Dumbledore told him?/nOr had he, in fact, told Harry, but Harry had not/nrealized it at the time?/n/n"Think!" whispered Hermione. "Think! Where would/nhe have left it?"/n/n"Not at Hogwarts," said Harry, resuming his pacing./n/n"Somewhere in Hogsmeade?" suggested Hermione./n/n"The Shrieking Shack?" said Harry. "Nobody ever goes/nin there."/n/n/n/n/n/n"But Snape knows how to get in, wouldn't that be a/nbit risky?"/n/n"Dumbledore trusted Snape," Harry reminded her./n/n"Not enough to tell him that he had swapped the/nswords," said Hermione./n/n"Yeah, you're right!" said Harry, and he felt even more/ncheered at the thought that Dumbledore had had/nsome reservations, however faint, about Snape 's/ntrustworthiness. "So, would he have hidden the sword/nwell away from Hogsmeade, then? What d'you reckon,/nRon? Ron?"/n/nHarry looked around. For one bewildered moment he/nthought that Ron had left the tent, then realized that/nRon was lying in the shadow of a lower bunk, looking/nstony./n/n"Oh, remembered me, have you?" he said./n/n"What?"/n/nRon snorted as he stared up at the underside of the/nupper bunk./n/n"You two carry on. Don't let me spoil your fun."/n/nPerplexed, Harry looked to Hermione for help, but she/nshook her head, apparently as nonplussed as he was./n/n"What's the problem?" asked Harry./n/n"Problem? There's no problem," said Ron, still/nrefusing to look at Harry. "Not according to you,/nanyway."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere were several plunks on the canvas over their/nheads. It had started to rain./n/n/n/n"Well, you've obviously got a problem," said Harry./n"Spit it out, will you?"/n/nRon swung his long legs off the bed and sat up. He/nlooked mean, unlike himself./n/n"All right, I'll spit it out. Don't expect me to skip up/nand down the tent because there's some other damn/nthing we've got to find. Just add it to the list of stuff/nyou don't know."/n/n"I don't know?" repeated Harry, "I don't know?"/n/nPlunk, plunk, plunk. The rain was falling harder and/nheavier; it pattered on the leaf-strewn bank all around/nthem and into the river chattering through the dark./nDread doused Harry's jubilation: Ron was saying/nexactly what he had suspected and feared him to be/nthinking./n/n"It's not like I'm not having the time of my life here,"/nsaid Ron, "you know, with my arm mangled and/nnothing to eat and freezing my backside off every/nnight. I just hoped, you know, after we'd been/nrunning round a few weeks, we'd have achieved/nsomething."/n/n"Ron," Hermione said, but in such a quiet voice that/nRon could pretend not to have heard it over the loud/ntattoo the rain was now beating on the tent./n/n"I thought you knew what you'd signed up for," said/nHarry./n/n"Yeah, I thought I did too."/n/n/n/n/n/n"So what part of it isn't living up to your/nexpectations?" asked Harry. Anger was coming to his/ndefense now. "Did you think we'd be staying in five-/nstar hotels? Finding a Horcrux every other day? Did/nyou think you'd be back to Mummy by Christmas?"/n/n"We thought you knew what you were doing!" shouted/nRon, standing up, and his words pierced Harry like/nscalding knives. "We thought Dumbledore had told/nyou what to do, we thought you had a real plan!"/n/n"Ron!" said Hermione, this time clearly audible over/nthe rain thundering on the tent roof, but again, he/nignored her./n/n"Well, sorry to let you down," said Harry, his voice/nquite calm even though he felt hollow, inadequate./n/n"I've been straight with you from the start, I told you/neverything Dumbledore told me. And in case you/nhaven't noticed, we've found one Horcrux — "/n/n"Yeah, and we're about as near getting rid of it as we/nare to finding the rest of them — nowhere effing near,/nin other words!"/n/n"Take off the locket, Ron," Hermione said, her voice/nunusually high. "Please take it off. You wouldn't be/ntalking like this if you hadn't been wearing it all day."/n/n"Yeah, he would," said Harry, who did not want/nexcuses made for Ron. "D'you think I haven't noticed/nthe two of you whispering behind my back? D'you/nthink I didn't guess you were thinking this stuff?"/n/n"Harry, we weren't — "/n/n"Don't lie!" Ron hurled at her. "You said it too, you/nsaid you were disappointed, you said you'd thought/nhe had a bit more to go on than — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"I didn't say it like that — Harry, I didn't!" she cried./n/n/n/nThe rain was pounding the tent, tears were pouring/ndown Hermione's face, and the excitement of a few/nminutes before had vanished as if it had never been, a/nshort-lived firework that had flared and died, leaving/neverything dark, wet, and cold. The sword of/nGryffindor was hidden they knew not where, and they/nwere three teenagers in a tent whose only/nachievement was not, yet, to be dead./n/n"So why are you still here?" Harry asked Ron./n/n"Search me," said Ron./n/n"Go home then," said Harry./n/n"Yeah, maybe I will!" shouted Ron, and he took/nseveral steps toward Harry, who did not back away./n"Didn't you hear what they said about my sister? But/nyou don't give a rat's fart, do you, it's only the/nForbidden Forest, Harry I've-Faced-Worse Potter/ndoesn't care what happens to her in here — well, I do,/nall right, giant spiders and mental stuff — "/n/n"I was only saying — she was with the others, they/nwere with Hagrid — "/n/n"Yeah, I get it, you don't care! And what about the/nrest of my family, 'the Weasleys don't need another/nkid injured,' did you hear that?"/n/n"Yeah, I — "/n/n"Not bothered what it meant, though?"/n/n"Ron!" said Hermione, forcing her way between them./n"I don't think it means anything new has happened,/nanything we don't know about; think, Ron, Bill's/n/n/n/n/n/nalready scarred, plenty of people must have seen that/nGeorge has lost an ear by now, and you're supposed/nto be on your deathbed with spattergroit, I'm sure/nthat's all he meant — "/n/n"Oh, you're sure, are you? Right then, well, I won't/nbother myself about them. It's all right for you two,/nisn't it, with your parents safely out of the way — "/n/n"My parents are dead)." Harry bellowed./n/n"And mine could be going the same way!" yelled Ron./n/n"Then GO!" roared Harry. "Go back to them, pretend/nyou've got over your spattergroit and Mummy'll be/nable to feed you up and — "/n/nRon made a sudden movement: Harry reacted, but/nbefore either wand was clear of its owner's pocket,/nHermione had raised her own./n/n"Protego\" she cried, and an invisible shield expanded/nbetween her and Harry on the one side and Ron on/nthe other; all of them were forced backward a few/nsteps by the strength of the spell, and Harry and Ron/nglared from either side of the transparent barrier as/nthough they were seeing each other clearly for the/nfirst time. Harry felt a corrosive hatred toward Ron:/nSomething had broken between them./n/n"Leave the Horcrux," Harry said./n/nRon wrenched the chain from over his head and cast/nthe locket into a nearby chair. He turned to/nHermione./n/n"What are you doing?"/n/n"What do you mean?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Are you staying, or what?"/n/n"I ..." She looked anguished. "Yes — yes, I'm staying./nRon, we said we'd go with Harry, we said we'd help — "/n/n"I get it. You choose him."/n/n"Ron, no — please — come back, come back!"/n/nShe was impeded by her own Shield Charm; by the/ntime she had removed it he had already stormed into/nthe night. Harry stood quite still and silent, listening/nto her sobbing and calling Ron's name amongst the/ntrees./n/nAfter a few minutes she returned, her sopping hair/nplastered to her face./n/n"He's g-g-gone! Disapparated!"/n/nShe threw herself into a chair, curled up, and started/nto cry./n/nHarry felt dazed. He stooped, picked up the Horcrux,/nand placed it around his own neck. He dragged/nblankets off Ron's bunk and threw them over/nHermione. Then he climbed onto his own bed and/nstared up at the dark canvas roof, listening to the/npounding of the rain./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Godric's Hollow
text: /nWhen Harry woke the following day it was several/nseconds before he remembered what had happened./nThen he hoped, childishly, that it had been a dream,/nthat Ron was still there and had never left. Yet by/nturning his head on his pillow he could see Ron's/ndeserted bunk. It was like a dead body in the way it/nseemed to draw his eyes. Harry jumped down from/nhis own bed, keeping his eyes averted from Ron's./nHermione, who was already busy in the kitchen, did/nnot wish Harry good morning, but turned her face/naway quickly as he went by./n/nHe's gone, Harry told himself. He's gone. He had to/nkeep thinking it as he washed and dressed, as though/nrepetition would dull the shock of it. He's gone and/nhe's not coming back. And that was the simple truth/nof it, Harry knew, because their protective/nenchantments meant that it would be impossible,/nonce they vacated this spot, for Ron to find them/nagain./n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe and Hermione ate breakfast in silence. Hermione 's/neyes were puffy and red; she looked as if she had not/nslept. They packed up their things, Hermione/ndawdling. Harry knew why she wanted to spin out/ntheir time on the riverbank; several times he saw her/nlook up eagerly, and he was sure she had deluded/nherself into thinking that she heard footsteps through/nthe heavy rain, but no red-haired figure appeared/nbetween the trees. Every time Harry imitated her,/nlooked around (for he could not help hoping a little,/nhimself) and saw nothing but rain-swept woods,/nanother little parcel of fury exploded inside him. He/ncould hear Ron saying, " We thought you knew what/nyou were doing \" , and he resumed packing with a/nhard knot in the pit of his stomach./n/nThe muddy river beside them was rising rapidly and/nwould soon spill over onto their bank. They had/nlingered a good hour after they would usually have/ndeparted their campsite. Finally having entirely/nrepacked the beaded bag three times, Hermione/nseemed unable to find any more reasons to delay: She/nand Harry grasped hands and Disapparated,/nreappearing on a windswept heather-covered hillside./n/nThe instant they arrived, Hermione dropped Harry's/nhand and walked away from him, finally sitting down/non a large rock, her face on her knees, shaking with/nwhat he knew were sobs. He watched her, supposing/nthat he ought to go and comfort her, but something/nkept him rooted to the spot. Everything inside him felt/ncold and tight: Again he saw the contemptuous/nexpression on Ron's face. Harry strode off through the/nheather, walking in a large circle with the distraught/nHermione at its center, casting the spells she usually/nperformed to ensure their protection./n/nThey did not discuss Ron at all over the next few/ndays. Harry was determined never to mention his/n/n/n/n/n/nname again, and Hermione seemed to know that it/nwas no use forcing the issue, although sometimes at/nnight when she thought he was sleeping, he would/nhear her crying. Meanwhile Harry had started/nbringing out the Marauder's Map and examining it by/nwandlight. He was waiting for the moment when/nRon's labeled dot would reappear in the corridors of/nHogwarts, proving that he had returned to the/ncomfortable castle, protected by his status of/npureblood. However, Ron did not appear on the map,/nand after a while Harry found himself taking it out/nsimply to stare at Ginny's name in the girls'/ndormitory, wondering whether the intensity with/nwhich he gazed at it might break into her sleep, that/nshe would somehow know he was thinking about her,/nhoping that she was all right./n/nBy day, they devoted themselves to trying to/ndetermine the possible locations of Gryffindor's/nsword, but the more they talked about the places in/nwhich Dumbledore might have hidden it, the more/ndesperate and far-fetched their speculation became./nCudgel his brains though he might, Harry could not/nremember Dumbledore ever mentioning a place in/nwhich he might hide something. There were moments/nwhen he did not know whether he was angrier with/nRon or with Dumbledore. We thought you knew what/nyou were doing. . . . We thought Dumbledore had told/nyou what to do. . . . We thought you had a real plan\/n/nHe could not hide it from himself: Ron had been right./nDumbledore had left him with virtually nothing. They/nhad discovered one Horcrux, but they had no means/nof destroying it: The others were as unattainable as/nthey had ever been. Hopelessness threatened to/nengulf him. He was staggered now to think of his own/npresumption in accepting his friends' offers to/naccompany him on this meandering, pointless/njourney. He knew nothing, he had no ideas, and he/n/n/n/n/nwas constantly, painfully on the alert for any/nindication that Hermione too was about to tell him/nthat she had had enough, that she was leaving./n/nThey were spending many evenings in near silence,/nand Hermione took to bringing out Phineas Nigellus's/nportrait and propping it up in a chair, as though he/nmight fill part of the gaping hole left by Ron's/ndeparture. Despite his previous assertion that he/nwould never visit them again, Phineas Nigellus did not/nseem able to resist the chance to find out more about/nwhat Harry was up to, and consented to reappear,/nblindfolded, every few days or so. Harry was even glad/nto see him, because he was company, albeit of a snide/nand taunting kind. They relished any news about/nwhat was happening at Hogwarts, though Phineas/nNigellus was not an ideal informer. He venerated/nSnape, the first Slytherin headmaster since he/nhimself had controlled the school, and they had to be/ncareful not to criticize or ask impertinent questions/nabout Snape, or Phineas Nigellus would instantly/nleave his painting./n/nHowever, he did let drop certain snippets. Snape/nseemed to be facing a constant, low level of mutiny/nfrom a hard core of students. Ginny had been banned/nfrom going into Hogsmeade. Snape had reinstated/nUmbridge's old decree forbidding gatherings of three/nor more students or any unofficial student societies./n/nFrom all of these things, Harry deduced that Ginny,/nand probably Neville and Luna along with her, had/nbeen doing their best to continue Dumbledore's Army./nThis scant news made Harry want to see Ginny so/nbadly it felt like a stomachache; but it also made him/nthink of Ron again, and of Dumbledore, and of/nHogwarts itself, which he missed nearly as much as/nhis ex-girlfriend. Indeed, as Phineas Nigellus talked/nabout Snape 's crackdown, Harry experienced a split/n/n/n/n/nsecond of madness when he imagined simply going/nback to school to join the destabilization of Snape's/nregime: Being fed, and having a soft bed, and other/npeople being in charge, seemed the most wonderful/nprospect in the world at that moment. But then he/nremembered that he was Undesirable Number One,/nthat there was a ten-thousand-Galleon price on his/nhead, and that to walk into Hogwarts these days was/njust as dangerous as walking into the Ministry of/nMagic. Indeed, Phineas Nigellus inadvertently/nemphasized this fact by slipping in leading questions/nabout Harry and Hermione's whereabouts. Hermione/nshoved him back inside the beaded bag every time he/ndid this, and Phineas Nigellus invariably refused to/nreappear for several days after these unceremonious/ngood-byes./n/nThe weather grew colder and colder. They did not/ndare remain in any one area too long, so rather than/nstaying in the south of England, where a hard ground/nfrost was the worst of their worries, they continued to/nmeander up and down the country, braving a/nmountainside, where sleet pounded the tent; a wide,/nflat marsh, where the tent was flooded with chill/nwater; and a tiny island in the middle of a Scottish/nloch, where snow half buried the tent in the night./n/nThey had already spotted Christmas trees twinkling/nfrom several sitting room windows before there came/nan evening when Harry resolved to suggest, again,/nwhat seemed to him the only unexplored avenue left/nto them. They had just eaten an unusually good meal:/nHermione had been to a supermarket under the/nInvisibility Cloak (scrupulously dropping the money/ninto an open till as she left), and Harry thought that/nshe might be more persuadable than usual on a/nstomach full of spaghetti Bolognese and tinned pears./nHe had also had the foresight to suggest that they/ntake a few hours' break from wearing the Horcrux,/n/n/n/n/nwhich was hanging over the end of the bunk beside/nhim./n/n/n/n"Hermione?"/n/n"Hmm?" She was curled up in one of the sagging/narmchairs with The Tales of Beedle the Bard. He could/nnot imagine how much more she could get out of the/nbook, which was not, after all, very long; but evidently/nshe was still deciphering something in it, because/nSpellman's Syllabary lay open on the arm of the chair./n/nHarry cleared his throat. He felt exactly as he had/ndone on the occasion, several years previously, when/nhe had asked Professor McGonagall whether he could/ngo into Hogsmeade, despite the fact that he had not/npersuaded the Dursleys to sign his permission slip./n/n"Hermione, I've been thinking, and — "/n/n"Harry, could you help me with something?"/n/nApparently she had not been listening to him. She/nleaned forward and held out The Tales of Beedle the/nBard./n/n"Look at that symbol," she said, pointing to the top of/na page. Above what Harry assumed was the title of/nthe story (being unable to read runes, he could not be/nsure) , there was a picture of what looked like a/ntriangular eye, its pupil crossed with a vertical line./n/n"I never took Ancient Runes, Hermione."/n/n"I know that, but it isn't a rune and it's not in the/nsyllabary, either. All along I thought it was a picture/nof an eye, but I don't think it is! It's been inked in,/nlook, somebody's drawn it there, it isn't really part of/nthe book. Think, have you ever seen it before?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"No ... No, wait a moment." Harry looked closer. "Isn't/nit the same symbol Luna's dad was wearing round his/nneck?"/n/n/n/n"Well, that's what I thought too!"/n/n"Then it's Grindelwald's mark."/n/nShe stared at him, openmouthed./n/n"What?"/n/n"Krum told me ..."/n/nHe recounted the story that Viktor Krum had told him/nat the wedding. Hermione looked astonished./n/n" Grindelwald's mark?"/n/nShe looked from Harry to the weird symbol and back/nagain. "I've never heard that Grindelwald had a mark./nThere's no mention of it in anything I've ever read/nabout him."/n/n"Well, like I say, Krum reckoned that symbol was/ncarved on a wall at Durmstrang, and Grindelwald put/nit there."/n/nShe fell back into the old armchair, frowning./n/n"That's very odd. If it's a symbol of Dark Magic, what's/nit doing in a book of children's stories?"/n/n"Yeah, it is weird," said Harry. "And you'd think/nScrimgeour would have recognized it. He was/nMinister, he ought to have been expert on Dark stuff."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I know. ... Perhaps he thought it was an eye, just like/nI did. All the other stories have little pictures over the/ntitles."/n/n/n/nShe did not speak, but continued to pore over the/nstrange mark. Harry tried again./n/n"Hermione?"/n/n"Hmm?"/n/n"I've been thinking. I — I want to go to Godric's/nHollow."/n/nShe looked up at him, but her eyes were unfocused,/nand he was sure she was still thinking about the/nmysterious mark on the book./n/n"Yes," she said. "Yes, I've been wondering that too. I/nreally think we'll have to."/n/n"Did you hear me right?" he asked./n/n"Of course I did. You want to go to Godric's Hollow. I/nagree, I think we should. I mean, I can't think of/nanywhere else it could be either. It'll be dangerous,/nbut the more I think about it, the more likely it seems/nit's there."/n/n"Er — what's there?" asked Harry./n/nAt that, she looked just as bewildered as he felt./n/n"Well, the sword, Harry! Dumbledore must have/nknown you'd want to go back there, and I mean,/nGodric's Hollow is Godric Gryffindor's birthplace — "/n/n"Really? Gryffindor came from Godric's Hollow?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, did you ever even open A History of Magic?"/n/n/n/n"Erm," he said, smiling for what felt like the first time/nin months: The muscles in his face felt oddly stiff. "I/nmight've opened it, you know, when I bought it ... just/nthe once. ..."/n/n"Well, as the village is named after him I'd have/nthought you might have made the connection," said/nHermione. She sounded much more like her old self/nthan she had done of late; Harry half expected her to/nannounce that she was off to the library. "There's a/nbit about the village in A History of Magic, wait ..."/n/nShe opened the beaded bag and rummaged for a/nwhile, finally extracting her copy of their old school/ntextbook, A History of Magic by Bathilda Bagshot,/nwhich she thumbed through until finding the page/nshe wanted./n/n" 'Upon the signature of the International Statute of/nSecrecy in 1689, wizards went into hiding for good. It/nwas natural, perhaps, that they formed their own/nsmall communities within a community. Many small/nvillages and hamlets attracted several magical/nfamilies, who banded together for mutual support and/nprotection. The villages of Tinworth in Cornwall, Upper/nFlagley in Yorkshire, and Ottery St. Catchpole on the/nsouth coast of England were notable homes to knots of/nWizarding families who lived alongside tolerant and/nsometimes Confunded Muggles. Most celebrated of/nthese half-magical dwelling places is, perhaps,/n/nGodric's Hollow, the West Country village where the/ngreat wizard Godric Gryffindor was born, and where/nBowman Wright, Wizarding smith, forged the first/nGolden Snitch. The graveyard is full of the names of/nancient magical families, and this accounts, no doubt,/nfor the stories of hauntings that have dogged the little/nchurch beside it for many centuries.'/n/n/n/n/n/n"You and your parents aren't mentioned," Hermione/nsaid, closing the book, "because Professor Bagshot/ndoesn't cover anything later than the end of the/nnineteenth century. But you see? Godric's Hollow,/nGodric Gryffindor, Gryffindor's sword; don't you think/nDumbledore would have expected you to make the/nconnection?"/n/n"Oh yeah ..."/n/nHarry did not want to admit that he had not been/nthinking about the sword at all when he suggested/nthey go to Godric's Hollow. For him, the lure of the/nvillage lay in his parents' graves, the house where he/nhad narrowly escaped death, and in the person of/nBathilda Bagshot./n/n"Remember what Muriel said?" he asked eventually./n"Who?"/n/n"You know," he hesitated: He did not want to say/nRon's name. "Ginny's great-aunt. At the wedding. The/none who said you had skinny ankles."/n/n"Oh," said Hermione. It was a sticky moment: Harry/nknew that she had sensed Ron's name in the offing./nHe rushed on:/n/n"She said Bathilda Bagshot still lives in Godric's/nHollow."/n/n"Bathilda Bagshot," murmured Hermione, running/nher index finger over Bathilda's embossed name on/nthe front cover of A History of Magic. "Well, I suppose/n/n/n/nShe gasped so dramatically that Harry's insides/nturned over; he drew his wand, looking around at the/n/n/n/n/n/nentrance, half expecting to see a hand forcing its way/nthrough the entrance flap, but there was nothing/nthere./n/n"What?" he said, half angry, half relieved. "What did/nyou do that for? I thought you'd seen a Death Eater/nunzipping the tent, at least — "/n/n"Harry, what if Bathilda' s got the sword? What if/nDumbledore entrusted it to her?"/n/nHarry considered this possibility. Bathilda would be/nan extremely old woman by now, and according to/nMuriel, she was "gaga." Was it likely that Dumbledore/nwould have hidden the sword of Gryffindor with her?/n/nIf so, Harry felt that Dumbledore had left a great deal/nto chance: Dumbledore had never revealed that he/nhad replaced the sword with a fake, nor had he so/nmuch as mentioned a friendship with Bathilda. Now,/nhowever, was not the moment to cast doubt on/nHermione's theory, not when she was so surprisingly/nwilling to fall in with Harry's dearest wish./n/n"Yeah, he might have done! So, are we going to go to/nGodric's Hollow?"/n/n"Yes, but we'll have to think it through carefully,/nHarry." She was sitting up now, and Harry could tell/nthat the prospect of having a plan again had lifted her/nmood as much as his. "We'll need to practice/nDisapparating together under the Invisibility Cloak for/na start, and perhaps Disillusionment Charms would/nbe sensible too, unless you think we should go the/nwhole hog and use Polyjuice Potion? In that case we'll/nneed to collect hair from somebody. I actually think/nwe'd better do that, Harry, the thicker our disguises/nthe better. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry let her talk, nodding and agreeing whenever/nthere was a pause, but his mind had left the/nconversation. For the first time since he had/ndiscovered that the sword in Gringotts was a fake, he/nfelt excited./n/nHe was about to go home, about to return to the place/nwhere he had had a family. It was in Godric's Hollow/nthat, but for Voldemort, he would have grown up and/nspent every school holiday. He could have invited/nfriends to his house. ... He might even have had/nbrothers and sisters. ... It would have been his/nmother who had made his seventeenth birthday cake./nThe life he had lost had hardly ever seemed so real to/nhim as at this moment, when he knew he was about/nto see the place where it had been taken from him./nAfter Hermione had gone to bed that night, Harry/nquietly extracted his rucksack from Hermione 's/nbeaded bag, and from inside it, the photograph album/nHagrid had given him so long ago. For the first time in/nmonths, he perused the old pictures of his parents,/nsmiling and waving up at him from the images, which/nwere all he had left of them now./n/nHarry would gladly have set out for Godric's Hollow/nthe following day, but Hermione had other ideas./nConvinced as she was that Voldemort would expect/nHarry to return to the scene of his parents' deaths,/nshe was determined that they would set off only after/nthey had ensured that they had the best disguises/npossible. It was therefore a full week later — once/nthey had surreptitiously obtained hairs from innocent/nMuggles who were Christmas shopping, and had/npracticed Apparating and Disapparating while/nunderneath the Invisibility Cloak together — that/nHermione agreed to make the journey./n/nThey were to Apparate to the village under cover of/ndarkness, so it was late afternoon when they finally/n/n/n/n/n/nswallowed Polyjuice Potion, Harry transforming into a/nbalding, middle-aged Muggle man, Hermione into his/nsmall and rather mousy wife. The beaded bag/ncontaining all of their possessions (apart from the/nHorcrux, which Harry was wearing around his neck)/nwas tucked into an inside pocket of Hermione 's/nbuttoned-up coat. Harry lowered the Invisibility Cloak/nover them, then they turned into the suffocating/ndarkness once again./n/nHeart beating in his throat, Harry opened his eyes./nThey were standing hand in hand in a snowy lane/nunder a dark blue sky, in which the night's first stars/nwere already glimmering feebly. Cottages stood on/neither side of the narrow road, Christmas decorations/ntwinkling in their windows. A short way ahead of/nthem, a glow of golden streetlights indicated the/ncenter of the village./n/n"All this snow!" Hermione whispered beneath the/ncloak. "Why didn't we think of snow? After all our/nprecautions, we'll leave prints! We'll just have to get/nrid of them — you go in front, I'll do it — "/n/nHarry did not want to enter the village like a/npantomime horse, trying to keep themselves/nconcealed while magically covering their traces./n/n"Let's take off the Cloak," said Harry, and when she/nlooked frightened, "Oh, come on, we don't look like us/nand there's no one around."/n/nHe stowed the Cloak under his jacket and they made/ntheir way forward unhampered, the icy air stinging/ntheir faces as they passed more cottages: Any one of/nthem might have been the one in which James and/nLily had once lived or where Bathilda lived now. Harry/ngazed at the front doors, their snow-burdened roofs,/nand their front porches, wondering whether he/n/n/n/n/nremembered any of them, knowing deep inside that it/nwas impossible, that he had been little more than a/nyear old when he had left this place forever. He was/nnot even sure whether he would be able to see the/ncottage at all; he did not know what happened when/nthe subjects of a Fidelius Charm died. Then the little/nlane along which they were walking curved to the left/nand the heart of the village, a small square, was/nrevealed to them./n/nStrung all around with colored lights, there was what/nlooked like a war memorial in the middle, partly/nobscured by a windblown Christmas tree. There were/nseveral shops, a post office, a pub, and a little church/nwhose stained-glass windows were glowing jewel-/nbright across the square./n/nThe snow here had become impacted: It was hard and/nslippery where people had trodden on it all day./nVillagers were crisscrossing in front of them, their/nfigures briefly illuminated by streetlamps. They heard/na snatch of laughter and pop music as the pub door/nopened and closed; then they heard a carol start up/ninside the little church./n/n"Harry, I think it's Christmas Eve!" said Hermione./n/n"Is it?"/n/nHe had lost track of the date; they had not seen a/nnewspaper for weeks./n/n"I'm sure it is," said Hermione, her eyes upon the/nchurch. "They ... they'll be in there, won't they? Your/nmum and dad? I can see the graveyard behind it."/n/nHarry felt a thrill of something that was beyond/nexcitement, more like fear. Now that he was so near,/nhe wondered whether he wanted to see after all./n/n/n/n/n/nPerhaps Hermione knew how he was feeling, because/nshe reached for his hand and took the lead for the/nfirst time, pulling him forward. Halfway across the/nsquare, however, she stopped dead./n/n"Harry, look!"/n/nShe was pointing at the war memorial. As they had/npassed it, it had transformed. Instead of an obelisk/ncovered in names, there was a statue of three people:/na man with untidy hair and glasses, a woman with/nlong hair and a kind, pretty face, and a baby boy/nsitting in his mother's arms. Snow lay upon all their/nheads, like fluffy white caps./n/nHarry drew closer, gazing up into his parents' faces./nHe had never imagined that there would be a statue./n/n. . . How strange it was to see himself represented in/nstone, a happy baby without a scar on his forehead./n/n/n/n"C'mon," said Harry, when he had looked his fill, and/nthey turned again toward the church. As they crossed/nthe road, he glanced over his shoulder; the statue had/nturned back into the war memorial./n/nThe singing grew louder as they approached the/nchurch. It made Harry's throat constrict, it reminded/nhim so forcefully of Hogwarts, of Peeves bellowing/nrude versions of carols from inside suits of armor, of/nthe Great Hall's twelve Christmas trees, of/nDumbledore wearing a bonnet he had won in a/ncracker, of Ron in a hand-knitted sweater. . . ./n/nThere was a kissing gate at the entrance to the/ngraveyard. Hermione pushed it open as quietly as/npossible and they edged through it. On either side of/nthe slippery path to the church doors, the snow lay/ndeep and untouched. They moved off through the/n/n/n/n/nsnow, carving deep trenches behind them as they/nwalked around the building, keeping to the shadows/nbeneath the brilliant windows./n/nBehind the church, row upon row of snowy/ntombstones protruded from a blanket of pale blue/nthat was flecked with dazzling red, gold, and green/nwherever the reflections from the stained glass hit the/nsnow. Keeping his hand closed tightly on the wand in/nhis jacket pocket, Harry moved toward the nearest/ngrave./n/n"Look at this, it's an Abbott, could be some long-lost/nrelation of Hannah's!"/n/n"Keep your voice down," Hermione begged him./n/nThey waded deeper and deeper into the graveyard,/ngouging dark tracks into the snow behind them,/nstooping to peer at the words on old headstones,/nevery now and then squinting into the surrounding/ndarkness to make absolutely sure that they were/nunaccompanied ./n/n"Harry, here!"/n/nHermione was two rows of tombstones away; he had/nto wade back to her, his heart positively banging in/nhis chest./n/n"Is it — ?"/n/n/n/n"No, but look!"/n/nShe pointed to the dark stone. Harry stooped down/nand saw, upon the frozen, lichen-spotted granite, the/nwords KENDRA DUMBLEDORE and, a short way/nbelow her dates of birth and death, AND HER/nDAUGHTER ARIANA. There was also a quotation:/n/n/n/n/nWhere your treasure is, there will your heart be also./n/n/n/nSo Rita Skeeter and Muriel had got some of their facts/nright. The Dumbledore family had indeed lived here,/nand part of it had died here./n/nSeeing the grave was worse than hearing about it./nHarry could not help thinking that he and/nDumbledore both had deep roots in this graveyard,/nand that Dumbledore ought to have told him so, yet/nhe had never thought to share the connection. They/ncould have visited the place together; for a moment/nHarry imagined coming here with Dumbledore, of/nwhat a bond that would have been, of how much it/nwould have meant to him. But it seemed that to/nDumbledore, the fact that their families lay side by/nside in the same graveyard had been an unimportant/ncoincidence, irrelevant, perhaps, to the job he wanted/nHarry to do./n/nHermione was looking at Harry, and he was glad that/nhis face was hidden in shadow. He read the words on/nthe tombstone again. Where your treasure is, there/nwill your heart be also. He did not understand what/nthese words meant. Surely Dumbledore had chosen/nthem, as the eldest member of the family once his/nmother had died./n/n"Are you sure he never mentioned — ?" Hermione/nbegan./n/n"No," said Harry curtly, then, "let's keep looking," and/nhe turned away, wishing he had not seen the stone:/n/nHe did not want his excited trepidation tainted with/nresentment./n/n"Here!" cried Hermione again a few moments later/nfrom out of the darkness. "Oh no, sorry! I thought it/nsaid Potter."/n/n/n/n/n/nShe was rubbing at a crumbling, mossy stone, gazing/ndown at it, a little frown on her face./n/n/n/n"Harry, come back a moment."/n/nHe did not want to be sidetracked again, and only/ngrudgingly made his way back through the snow/ntoward her./n/n"What?"/n/n"Look at this!"/n/nThe grave was extremely old, weathered so that Harry/ncould hardly make out the name. Hermione showed/nhim the symbol beneath it./n/n"Harry, that's the mark in the book!"/n/nHe peered at the place she indicated: The stone was/nso worn that it was hard to make out what was/nengraved there, though there did seem to be a/ntriangular mark beneath the nearly illegible name./n/n"Yeah ... it could be. ..."/n/nHermione lit her wand and pointed it at the name on/nthe headstone./n/n"It says Ig — Ignotus, I think. ..."/n/n"I'm going to keep looking for my parents, all right?"/nHarry told her, a slight edge to his voice, and he set/noff again, leaving her crouched beside the old grave./n/nEvery now and then he recognized a surname that,/nlike Abbott, he had met at Hogwarts. Sometimes there/nwere several generations of the same Wizarding family/nrepresented in the graveyard: Harry could tell from/n/n/n/n/n/nthe dates that it had either died out, or the current/nmembers had moved away from Godric's Hollow./nDeeper and deeper amongst the graves he went, and/nevery time he reached a new headstone he felt a little/nlurch of apprehension and anticipation./n/nThe darkness and the silence seemed to become, all of/na sudden, much deeper. Harry looked around,/nworried, thinking of dementors, then realized that the/ncarols had finished, that the chatter and flurry of/nchurchgoers were fading away as they made their way/nback into the square. Somebody inside the church/nhad just turned off the lights./n/nThen Hermione's voice came out of the blackness for/nthe third time, sharp and clear from a few yards/naway./n/n"Harry, they're here ... right here."/n/nAnd he knew by her tone that it was his mother and/nfather this time: He moved toward her, feeling as if/nsomething heavy were pressing on his chest, the/nsame sensation he had had right after Dumbledore/nhad died, a grief that had actually weighed on his/nheart and lungs./n/nThe headstone was only two rows behind Kendra and/nAriana's. It was made of white marble, just like/nDumbledore's tomb, and this made it easy to read, as/nit seemed to shine in the dark. Harry did not need to/nkneel or even approach very close to it to make out/nthe words engraved upon it./n/nJAMES POTTER/nBORN 27 MARCH 1960/n/nLILY POTTER/n/nBORN 30 JANUARY 1960/n/n/n/n/n/nDIED 31 OCTOBER 1981/n/n/n/nThe last enemy that shall be destroyed is death./n/nHarry read the words slowly, as though he would/nhave only one chance to take in their meaning, and/nhe read the last of them aloud./n/n" The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death'..."/n/nA horrible thought came to him, and with it a kind of/npanic. "Isn't that a Death Eater idea? Why is that/nthere?"/n/n"It doesn't mean defeating death in the way the Death/nEaters mean it, Harry," said Hermione, her voice/ngentle. "It means ... you know ... living beyond death./nLiving after death."/n/nBut they were not living, thought Harry: They were/ngone. The empty words could not disguise the fact/nthat his parents' moldering remains lay beneath snow/nand stone, indifferent, unknowing. And tears came/nbefore he could stop them, boiling hot then instantly/nfreezing on his face, and what was the point in wiping/nthem off or pretending? He let them fall, his lips/npressed hard together, looking down at the thick/nsnow hiding from his eyes the place where the last of/nLily and James lay, bones now, surely, or dust, not/nknowing or caring that their living son stood so near,/nhis heart still beating, alive because of their sacrifice/nand close to wishing, at this moment, that he was/nsleeping under the snow with them./n/nHermione had taken his hand again and was gripping/nit tightly. He could not look at her, but returned the/npressure, now taking deep, sharp gulps of the night/nair, trying to steady himself, trying to regain control./nHe should have brought something to give them, and/nhe had not thought of it, and every plant in the/n/n/n/n/ngraveyard was leafless and frozen. But Hermione/nraised her wand, moved it in a circle through the air,/nand a wreath of Christmas roses blossomed before/nthem. Harry caught it and laid it on his parents'/ngrave./n/nAs soon as he stood up he wanted to leave: He did not/nthink he could stand another moment there. He put/nhis arm around Hermione's shoulders, and she put/nhers around his waist, and they turned in silence and/nwalked away through the snow, past Dumbledore's/nmother and sister, back toward the dark church and/nthe out-of-sight kissing gate./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Bathilda's Secret
text: /n"Harry, stop."/n/n"What's wrong?"/n/nThey had only just reached the grave of the unknown/nAbbott./n/n"There's someone there. Someone watching us. I can/ntell. There, over by the bushes."/n/nThey stood quite still, holding on to each other, gazing/nat the dense black boundary of the graveyard. Harry/ncould not see anything./n/n"Are you sure?"/n/n"I saw something move, I could have sworn I did. ..."/nShe broke from him to free her wand arm./n/n"We look like Muggles," Harry pointed out./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Muggles who 've just been laying flowers on your/nparents' grave! Harry, I'm sure there's someone over/nthere!"/n/n/n/nHarry thought of A History of Magic ; the graveyard/nwas supposed to be haunted: what if — ? But then he/nheard a rustle and saw a little eddy of dislodged snow/nin the bush to which Hermione had pointed. Ghosts/ncould not move snow./n/n"It's a cat," said Harry, after a second or two, "or a/nbird. If it was a Death Eater we'd be dead by now. But/nlet's get out of here, and we can put the Cloak back/non."/n/nThey glanced back repeatedly as they made their way/nout of the graveyard. Harry, who did not feel as/nsanguine as he had pretended when reassuring/nHermione, was glad to reach the gate and the slippery/npavement. They pulled the Invisibility Cloak back over/nthemselves. The pub was fuller than before: Many/nvoices inside it were now singing the carol that they/nhad heard as they approached the church. For a/nmoment Harry considered suggesting they take refuge/ninside it, but before he could say anything Hermione/nmurmured, "Let's go this way," and pulled him down/nthe dark street leading out of the village in the/nopposite direction from which they had entered. Harry/ncould make out the point where the cottages ended/nand the lane turned into open country again. They/nwalked as quickly as they dared, past more windows/nsparkling with multicolored lights, the outlines of/nChristmas trees dark through the curtains./n/n"How are we going to find Bathilda's house?" asked/nHermione, who was shivering a little and kept/nglancing back over her shoulder. "Harry? What do you/nthink? Harry?"/n/n/n/n/n/nShe tugged at his arm, but Harry was not paying/nattention. He was looking toward the dark mass that/nstood at the very end of this row of houses. Next/nmoment he had sped up, dragging Hermione along/nwith him; she slipped a little on the ice./n/n"Harry — "/n/n"Look. ... Look at it, Hermione. ..."/n/n"I don't ... oh!"/n/nHe could see it; the Fidelius Charm must have died/nwith James and Lily. The hedge had grown wild in the/nsixteen years since Hagrid had taken Harry from the/nrubble that lay scattered amongst the waist-high/ngrass. Most of the cottage was still standing, though/nentirely covered in dark ivy and snow, but the right/nside of the top floor had been blown apart; that, Harry/nwas sure, was where the curse had backfired. He and/nHermione stood at the gate, gazing up at the wreck of/nwhat must once have been a cottage just like those/nthat flanked it./n/n"I wonder why nobody's ever rebuilt it?" whispered/nHermione./n/n"Maybe you can't rebuild it?" Harry replied. "Maybe/nit's like the injuries from Dark Magic and you can't/nrepair the damage?"/n/nHe slipped a hand from beneath the Cloak and/ngrasped the snowy and thickly rusted gate, not/nwishing to open it, but simply to hold some part of the/nhouse./n/n"You're not going to go inside? It looks unsafe, it/nmight — oh, Harry, look!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHis touch on the gate seemed to have done it. A sign/nhad risen out of the ground in front of them, up/nthrough the tangles of nettles and weeds, like some/nbizarre, fast-growing flower, and in golden letters/nupon the wood it said:/n/n/n/nOn this spot, on the night of 31 October 1 981, Lily and/nJames Potter lost their lives. Their son, Harry, remains/nthe only wizard ever to have survived the Killing Curse./nThis house, invisible to Muggles, has been left in its/nruined state as a monument to the Potters and as a/nreminder of the violence that tore apart their family./n/nAnd all around these neatly lettered words, scribbles/nhad been added by other witches and wizards who/nhad come to see the place where the Boy Who Lived/nhad escaped. Some had merely signed their names in/nEverlasting Ink; others had carved their initials into/nthe wood, still others had left messages. The most/nrecent of these, shining brightly over sixteen years'/nworth of magical graffiti, all said similar things./n/nGood luck, Harry, wherever you are./n/nIf you read this, Harry, we're all behind you!/n/nLong live Harry Potter./n/n"They shouldn't have written on the sign!" said/nHermione, indignant./n/nBut Harry beamed at her./n/n"It's brilliant. I'm glad they did. I ..."/n/nHe broke off. A heavily muffled figure was hobbling up/nthe lane toward them, silhouetted by the bright lights/n/n/n/n/n/nin the distant square. Harry thought, though it was/nhard to judge, that the figure was a woman. She was/nmoving slowly, possibly frightened of slipping on the/nsnowy ground. Her stoop, her stoutness, her shuffling/ngait all gave an impression of extreme age. They/nwatched in silence as she drew nearer. Harry was/nwaiting to see whether she would turn into any of the/ncottages she was passing, but he knew instinctively/nthat she would not. At last she came to a halt a few/nyards from them and simply stood there in the middle/nof the frozen road, facing them./n/nHe did not need Hermione's pinch to his arm. There/nwas next to no chance that this woman was a Muggle:/nShe was standing there gazing at a house that ought/nto have been completely invisible to her, if she was/nnot a witch. Even assuming that she was a witch,/nhowever, it was odd behavior to come out on a night/nthis cold, simply to look at an old ruin. By all the/nrules of normal magic, meanwhile, she ought not to/nbe able to see Hermione and him at all. Nevertheless,/nHarry had the strangest feeling that she knew that/nthey were there, and also who they were. Just as he/nhad reached this uneasy conclusion, she raised a/ngloved hand and beckoned./n/nHermione moved closer to him under the Cloak, her/narm pressed against his./n/n"How does she know?"/n/nHe shook his head. The woman beckoned again, more/nvigorously. Harry could think of many reasons not to/nobey the summons, and yet his suspicions about her/nidentity were growing stronger every moment that/nthey stood facing each other in the deserted street./n/nWas it possible that she had been waiting for them all/nthese long months? That Dumbledore had told her to/n/n/n/n/n/nwait, and that Harry would come in the end? Was it/nnot likely that it was she who had moved in the/nshadows in the graveyard and had followed them to/nthis spot? Even her ability to sense them suggested/nsome Dumbledore-ish power that he had never/nencountered before./n/nFinally Harry spoke, causing Hermione to gasp and/njump./n/n"Are you Bathilda?"/n/nThe muffled figure nodded and beckoned again./n/nBeneath the Cloak Harry and Hermione looked at/neach other. Harry raised his eyebrows; Hermione gave/na tiny, nervous nod./n/nThey stepped toward the woman and, at once, she/nturned and hobbled off back the way they had come./nLeading them past several houses, she turned in at a/ngate. They followed her up the front path through a/ngarden nearly as overgrown as the one they had just/nleft. She fumbled for a moment with a key at the front/ndoor, then opened it and stepped back to let them/npass./n/nShe smelled bad, or perhaps it was her house: Harry/nwrinkled his nose as they sidled past her and pulled/noff the Cloak. Now that he was beside her, he realized/nhow tiny she was; bowed down with age, she came/nbarely level with his chest. She closed the door behind/nthem, her knuckles blue and mottled against the/npeeling paint, then turned and peered into Harry's/nface. Her eyes were thick with cataracts and sunken/ninto folds of transparent skin, and her whole face was/ndotted with broken veins and liver spots. He/nwondered whether she could make him out at all;/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/neven if she could, it was the balding Muggle whose/nidentity he had stolen that she would see./n/nThe odor of old age, of dust, of unwashed clothes and/nstale food intensified as she unwound a moth-eaten/nblack shawl, revealing a head of scant white hair/nthrough which the scalp showed clearly./n/n"Bathilda?" Harry repeated./n/nShe nodded again. Harry became aware of the locket/nagainst his skin; the thing inside it that sometimes/nticked or beat had woken; he could feel it pulsing/nthrough the cold gold. Did it know, could it sense,/nthat the thing that would destroy it was near?/n/nBathilda shuffled past them, pushing Hermione aside/nas though she had not seen her, and vanished into/nwhat seemed to be a sitting room./n/n"Harry, I'm not sure about this," breathed Hermione./n/n"Look at the size of her; I think we could overpower/nher if we had to," said Harry. "Listen, I should have/ntold you, I knew she wasn't all there. Muriel called her/n'gaga.' "/n/n"Come!" called Bathilda from the next room./n/nHermione jumped and clutched Harry's arm./n/n"It's okay," said Harry reassuringly, and he led the/nway into the sitting room./n/nBathilda was tottering around the place lighting/ncandles, but it was still very dark, not to mention/nextremely dirty. Thick dust crunched beneath their/nfeet, and Harry's nose detected, underneath the dank/nand mildewed smell, something worse, like meat gone/n/n/n/n/nbad. He wondered when was the last time anyone had/nbeen inside Bathilda's house to check whether she/nwas coping. She seemed to have forgotten that she/ncould do magic, too, for she lit the candles clumsily/nby hand, her trailing lace cuff in constant danger of/ncatching fire./n/n"Let me do that," offered Harry, and he took the/nmatches from her. She stood watching him as he/nfinished lighting the candle stubs that stood on/nsaucers around the room, perched precariously on/nstacks of books and on side tables crammed with/ncracked and moldy cups./n/nThe last surface on which Harry spotted a candle was/na bow-fronted chest of drawers on which there stood/na large number of photographs. When the flame/ndanced into life, its reflection wavered on their dusty/nglass and silver. He saw a few tiny movements from/nthe pictures. As Bathilda fumbled with logs for the/nfire, he muttered " Tergeo ": The dust vanished from/nthe photographs, and he saw at once that half a/ndozen were missing from the largest and most ornate/nframes. He wondered whether Bathilda or somebody/nelse had removed them. Then the sight of a/nphotograph near the back of the collection caught his/neye, and he snatched it up./n/nIt was the golden-haired, merry-faced thief, the young/nman who had perched on Gregorovitch's windowsill,/nsmiling lazily up at Harry out of the silver frame. And/nit came to Harry instantly where he had seen the boy/nbefore: in The Life and Lies of Albus Dumbledore, arm/nin arm with the teenage Dumbledore, and that must/nbe where all the missing photographs were: in Rita's/nbook./n/n"Mrs. — Miss — Bagshot?" he said, and his voice/nshook slightly. "Who is this?"/n/n/n/n/n/nBathilda was standing in the middle of the room/nwatching Hermione light the fire for her./n/n"Miss Bagshot?" Harry repeated, and he advanced/nwith the picture in his hands as the flames burst into/nlife in the fireplace. Bathilda looked up at his voice,/nand the Horcrux beat faster upon his chest./n/n"Who is this person?" Harry asked her, pushing the/npicture forward./n/nShe peered at it solemnly, then up at Harry./n/n"Do you know who this is?" he repeated in a much/nslower and louder voice than usual. "This man? Do/nyou know him? What's he called?"/n/nBathilda merely looked vague. Harry felt an awful/nfrustration. How had Rita Skeeter unlocked Bathilda's/nmemories?/n/n"Who is this man?" he repeated loudly./n/n"Harry, what are you doing?" asked Hermione./n/n"This picture, Hermione, it's the thief, the thief who/nstole from Gregorovitch! Please!" he said to Bathilda./n"Who is this?"/n/nBut she only stared at him./n/n"Why did you ask us to come with you, Mrs. — Miss/n— Bagshot?" asked Hermione, raising her own voice./n"Was there something you wanted to tell us?"/n/nGiving no sign that she had heard Hermione, Bathilda/nnow shuffled a few steps closer to Harry. With a little/njerk of her head she looked back into the hall./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You want us to leave?" he asked./n/n/n/nShe repeated the gesture, this time pointing firstly at/nhim, then at herself, then at the ceiling./n/n"Oh, right ... Hermione, I think she wants me to go/nupstairs with her."/n/n"All right," said Hermione, "let's go."/n/nBut when Hermione moved, Bathilda shook her head/nwith surprising vigor, once more pointing first at/nHarry, then to herself./n/n"She wants me to go with her, alone."/n/n"Why?" asked Hermione, and her voice rang out sharp/nand clear in the candlelit room; the old lady shook her/nhead a little at the loud noise./n/n"Maybe Dumbledore told her to give the sword to me,/nand only to me?"/n/n"Do you really think she knows who you are?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry, looking down into the milky eyes/nfixed upon his own, "I think she does."/n/n"Well, okay then, but be quick, Harry."/n/n"Lead the way," Harry told Bathilda./n/nShe seemed to understand, because she shuffled/naround him toward the door. Harry glanced back at/nHermione with a reassuring smile, but he was not/nsure she had seen it; she stood hugging herself in the/nmidst of the candlelit squalor, looking toward the/nbookcase. As Harry walked out of the room, unseen/nby both Hermione and Bathilda, he slipped the silver-/n/n/n/n/n/nframed photograph of the unknown thief inside his/njacket./n/nThe stairs were steep and narrow: Harry was half/ntempted to place his hands on stout Bathilda's/nbackside to ensure that she did not topple over/nbackward on top of him, which seemed only too likely./nSlowly, wheezing a little, she climbed to the upper/nlanding, turned immediately right, and led him into a/nlow-ceilinged bedroom./n/nIt was pitch-black and smelled horrible: Harry had/njust made out a chamber pot protruding from under/nthe bed before Bathilda closed the door and even that/nwas swallowed by the darkness./n/n"Lumos," said Harry, and his wand ignited. He gave a/nstart: Bathilda had moved close to him in those few/nseconds of darkness, and he had not heard her/napproach./n/n"You are Potter?" she whispered./n/n"Yes, I am."/n/nShe nodded slowly, solemnly. Harry felt the Horcrux/nbeating fast, faster than his own heart: It was an/nunpleasant, agitating sensation./n/n"Have you got anything for me?" Harry asked, but she/nseemed distracted by his lit wand-tip./n/n"Have you got anything for me?" he repeated./n/nThen she closed her eyes and several things/nhappened at once: Harry's scar prickled painfully; the/nHorcrux twitched so that the front of his sweater/nactually moved; the dark, fetid room dissolved/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nmomentarily. He felt a leap of joy and spoke in a high,/ncold voice: Hold him)./n/nHarry swayed where he stood: The dark, foul-smelling/nroom seemed to close around him again; he did not/nknow what had just happened./n/n"Have you got anything for me?" he asked for a third/ntime, much louder./n/n"Over here," she whispered, pointing to the corner./nHarry raised his wand and saw the outline of a/ncluttered dressing table beneath the curtained/nwindow./n/nThis time she did not lead him. Harry edged between/nher and the unmade bed, his wand raised. He did not/nwant to look away from her./n/n"What is it?" he asked as he reached the dressing/ntable, which was heaped high with what looked and/nsmelled like dirty laundry./n/n"There," she said, pointing at the shapeless mass./n/nAnd in the instant that he looked away, his eyes/nraking the tangled mess for a sword hilt, a ruby, she/nmoved weirdly: He saw it out of the corner of his eye;/npanic made him turn and horror paralyzed him as he/nsaw the old body collapsing and the great snake/npouring from the place where her neck had been./n/nThe snake struck as he raised his wand: The force of/nthe bite to his forearm sent the wand spinning up/ntoward the ceiling; its light swung dizzyingly around/nthe room and was extinguished: Then a powerful blow/nfrom the tail to his midriff knocked the breath out of/nhim: He fell backward onto the dressing table, into/nthe mound of filthy clothing —/n/n/n/n/n/nHe rolled sideways, narrowly avoiding the snake's tail,/nwhich thrashed down upon the table where he had/nbeen a second earlier: Fragments of the glass surface/nrained upon him as he hit the floor.
