From below he/nheard Hermione call, "Harry?"/n/nHe could not get enough breath into his lungs to call/nback: Then a heavy smooth mass smashed him to the/nfloor and he felt it slide over him, powerful, muscular/n/n/n/n"No!" he gasped, pinned to the floor./n/n"Yes," whispered the voice. "Yesss ... hold you ... hold/nyou ..."/n/n"Accio ... Accio Wand ..."/n/nBut nothing happened and he needed his hands to try/nto force the snake from him as it coiled itself around/nhis torso, squeezing the air from him, pressing the/nHorcrux hard into his chest, a circle of ice that/nthrobbed with life, inches from his own frantic heart,/nand his brain was flooding with cold, white light, all/nthought obliterated, his own breath drowned, distant/nfootsteps, everything going. .../n/nA metal heart was banging outside his chest, and now/nhe was flying, flying with triumph in his heart,/nwithout need of broomstick or thestral. .../n/nHe was abruptly awake in the sour-smelling/ndarkness; Nagini had released him. He scrambled up/nand saw the snake outlined against the landing light:/nIt struck, and Hermione dived aside with a shriek; her/ndeflected curse hit the curtained window, which/nshattered. Frozen air filled the room as Harry ducked/nto avoid another shower of broken glass and his foot/nslipped on a pencil-like something — his wand —/n/n/n/n/nHe bent and snatched it up, but now the room was/nfull of the snake, its tail thrashing; Hermione was/nnowhere to be seen and for a moment Harry thought/nthe worst, but then there was a loud bang and a flash/nof red light, and the snake flew into the air, smacking/nHarry hard in the face as it went, coil after heavy coil/nrising up to the ceiling. Harry raised his wand, but as/nhe did so, his scar seared more painfully, more/npowerfully than it had done in years./n/n"He's coming! Hermione, he's comingl"/n/nAs he yelled the snake fell, hissing wildly. Everything/nwas chaos: It smashed shelves from the wall, and/nsplintered china flew everywhere as Harry jumped/nover the bed and seized the dark shape he knew to be/nHermione —/n/nShe shrieked with pain as he pulled her back across/nthe bed: The snake reared again, but Harry knew that/nworse than the snake was coming, was perhaps/nalready at the gate, his head was going to split open/nwith the pain from his scar —/n/nThe snake lunged as he took a running leap, dragging/nHermione with him; as it struck, Hermione screamed,/n/n" ConfringoV' and her spell flew around the room,/nexploding the wardrobe mirror and ricocheting back/nat them, bouncing from floor to ceiling; Harry felt the/nheat of it sear the back of his hand. Glass cut his/ncheek as, pulling Hermione with him, he leapt from/nbed to broken dressing table and then straight out of/nthe smashed window into nothingness, her scream/nreverberating through the night as they twisted in/nmidair. .../n/nAnd then his scar burst open and he was Voldemort/nand he was running across the fetid bedroom, his/nlong white hands clutching at the windowsill as he/n/n/n/n/n/nglimpsed the bald man and the little woman twist and/nvanish, and he screamed with rage, a scream that/nmingled with the girl's, that echoed across the dark/ngardens over the church bells ringing in Christmas/nDay. .../n/nAnd his scream was Harry's scream, his pain was/nHarry's pain ... that it could happen here, where it/nhad happened before ... here, within sight of that/nhouse where he had come so close to knowing what it/nwas to die ... to die. ... The pain was so terrible .../nripped from his body. ... But if he had no body, why/ndid his head hurt so badly; if he was dead, how could/nhe feel so unbearably, didn't pain cease with death,/ndidn't it go .../n/nThe night wet and windy, two children dressed as/npumpkins waddling across the square, and the shop/nwindows covered in paper spiders, all the tawdry/nMuggle trappings of a world in which they did not/nbelieve. ... And he was gliding along, that sense of/npurpose and power and rightness in him that he/nalways knew on these occasions. . . . Not anger . . . that/nwas for weaker souls than he ... but triumph, yes. .../nHe had waited for this, he had hoped for it. .../n/n"Nice costume, mister!"/n/nHe saw the small boy's smile falter as he ran near/nenough to see beneath the hood of the cloak, saw the/nfear cloud his painted face: Then the child turned and/nran away. ... Beneath the robe he fingered the handle/nof his wand. ... One simple movement and the child/nwould never reach his mother . . . but unnecessary,/nquite unnecessary. . . ./n/nAnd along a new and darker street he moved, and/nnow his destination was in sight at last, the Fidelius/nCharm broken, though they did not know it yet. .../n/n/n/n/n/nAnd he made less noise than the dead leaves/nslithering along the pavement as he drew level with/nthe dark hedge, and stared over it. .../n/nThey had not drawn the curtains; he saw them quite/nclearly in their little sitting room, the tall black-haired/nman in his glasses, making puffs of colored smoke/nerupt from his wand for the amusement of the small/nblack-haired boy in his blue pajamas. The child was/nlaughing and trying to catch the smoke, to grab it in/nhis small fist. .../n/nA door opened and the mother entered, saying words/nhe could not hear, her long dark-red hair falling over/nher face. Now the father scooped up the son and/nhanded him to the mother. He threw his wand down/nupon the sofa and stretched, yawning. . . ./n/nThe gate creaked a little as he pushed it open, but/nJames Potter did not hear. His white hand pulled out/nthe wand beneath his cloak and pointed it at the/ndoor, which burst open./n/nHe was over the threshold as James came sprinting/ninto the hall. It was easy, too easy, he had not even/npicked up his wand. .../n/n"Lily, take Harry and go! It's him! Go! Run! Ill hold/nhim off!"/n/nHold him off, without a wand in his hand! . . . He/nlaughed before casting the curse. . . ./n/n"Avada Kedavra!"/n/nThe green light filled the cramped hallway, it lit the/npram pushed against the wall, it made the banisters/nglare like lightning rods, and James Potter fell like a/nmarionette whose strings were cut. .../n/n/n/n/n/nHe could hear her screaming from the upper floor,/ntrapped, but as long as she was sensible, she, at/nleast, had nothing to fear. ... He climbed the steps,/nlistening with faint amusement to her attempts to/nbarricade herself in. ... She had no wand upon her/neither. ... How stupid they were, and how trusting,/nthinking that their safety lay in friends, that weapons/ncould be discarded even for moments. .../n/nHe forced the door open, cast aside the chair and/nboxes hastily piled against it with one lazy wave of his/nwand ... and there she stood, the child in her arms. At/nthe sight of him, she dropped her son into the crib/nbehind her and threw her arms wide, as if this would/nhelp, as if in shielding him from sight she hoped to be/nchosen instead. . . ./n/n"Not Harry, not Harry, please not Harry!"/n/n"Stand aside, you silly girl . . . stand aside, now. "/n/n"Not Harry, please no, take me, kill me instead — "/n/n"This is my last warning — "/n/n"Not Harry! Please . . . have mercy . . . have mercy. . . ./n/nNot Harry! Not Harry! Please — I'll do anything — "/n/n"Stand aside. Stand aside, girl!"/n/nHe could have forced her away from the crib, but it/nseemed more prudent to finish them all. .../n/nThe green light flashed around the room and she/ndropped like her husband. The child had not cried all/nthis time: He could stand, clutching the bars of his crib,/nand he looked up into the intruder's face with a kind of/nbright interest, perhaps thinking that it was his father/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwho hid beneath the cloak, making more pretty lights,/nand his mother would pop up any moment, laughing —/n/nHe pointed the wand very carefully into the boy's face:/nHe wanted to see it happen, the destruction of this one,/ninexplicable danger. The child began to cry: It had seen/nthat he was not James. He did not like it crying, he/nhad never been able to stomach the small ones/nwhining in the orphanage —/n/n"Avada Kedavra!"/n/nAnd then he broke: He was nothing, nothing but pain/nand terror, and he must hide himself, not here in the/nrubble of the ruined house, where the child was/ntrapped and screaming, but far away . . . far away. . . ./n/n"No," he moaned./n/nThe snake rustled on the filthy, cluttered floor, and he/nhad killed the boy, and yet he was the boy. . . ./n/n"No ..."/n/nAnd now he stood at the broken window of Bathilda's/nhouse, immersed in memories of his greatest loss, and/nat his feet the great snake slithered over broken china/nand glass. ... He looked down and saw something .../nsomething incredible. . . ./n/n"No ..."/n/n"Harry, it's all right, you're all right!"/n/nHe stooped down and picked up the smashed/nphotograph. There he was, the unknown thief, the/nthief he was seeking. . . ./n/n"No ... I dropped it. ... I dropped it. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, it's okay, wake up, wake up!"/n/n/n/nHe was Harry. ... Harry, not Voldemort ... and the/nthing that was rustling was not a snake. ... He opened/nhis eyes./n/n"Harry," Hermione whispered. "Do you feel all — all/nright?"/n/n"Yes," he lied./n/nHe was in the tent, lying on one of the lower bunks/nbeneath a heap of blankets. He could tell that it was/nalmost dawn by the stillness and the quality of the/ncold, flat light beyond the canvas ceiling. He was/ndrenched in sweat; he could feel it on the sheets and/nblankets./n/n"We got away."/n/n"Yes," said Hermione. "I had to use a Hover Charm to/nget you into your bunk, I couldn't lift you. You've/nbeen ... Well, you haven't been quite ..."/n/nThere were purple shadows under her brown eyes and/nhe noticed a small sponge in her hand: She had been/nwiping his face./n/n"You've been ill," she finished. "Quite ill."/n/n"How long ago did we leave?"/n/n"Hours ago. It's nearly morning."/n/n"And I've been ... what, unconscious?"/n/n"Not exactly," said Hermione uncomfortably. "You've/nbeen shouting and moaning and ... things," she/nadded in a tone that made Harry feel uneasy. What/n/n/n/n/n/nhad he done? Screamed curses like Voldemort, cried/nlike the baby in the crib?/n/n"I couldn't get the Horcrux off you," Hermione said,/nand he knew she wanted to change the subject. "It/nwas stuck, stuck to your chest. You've got a mark; I'm/nsorry, I had to use a Severing Charm to get it away./nThe snake bit you too, but I've cleaned the wound and/nput some dittany on it. ..."/n/nHe pulled the sweaty T-shirt he was wearing away/nfrom himself and looked down. There was a scarlet/noval over his heart where the locket had burned him./nHe could also see the half-healed puncture marks to/nhis forearm./n/n"Where Ve you put the Horcrux?"/n/n"In my bag. I think we should keep it off for a while."/n/nHe lay back on his pillows and looked into her/npinched gray face./n/n"We shouldn't have gone to Godric's Hollow. It's my/nfault, it's all my fault, Hermione, I'm sorry."/n/n"It's not your fault. I wanted to go too; I really thought/nDumbledore might have left the sword there for you."/n/n"Yeah, well ... we got that wrong, didn't we?"/n/n"What happened, Harry? What happened when she/ntook you upstairs? Was the snake hiding somewhere?/nDid it just come out and kill her and attack you?"/n/n"No," he said. "She was the snake ... or the snake was/nher ... all along."/n/n"W-what?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHe closed his eyes. He could still smell Bathilda's/nhouse on him: It made the whole thing horribly vivid./n/n"Bathilda must've been dead a while. The snake was/n... was inside her. You-Know-Who put it there in/nGodric's Hollow, to wait. You were right. He knew I'd/ngo back."/n/n"The snake was inside her?"/n/nHe opened his eyes again: Hermione looked revolted,/nnauseated./n/n"Lupin said there would be magic we'd never/nimagined," Harry said. "She didn't want to talk in/nfront of you, because it was Parseltongue, all/nParseltongue, and I didn't realize, but of course I/ncould understand her. Once we were up in the room,/nthe snake sent a message to You-Know-Who, I heard/nit happen inside my head, I felt him get excited, he/nsaid to keep me there ... and then ..."/n/nHe remembered the snake coming our of Bathilda's/nneck: Hermione did not need to know the details./n/n"... she changed, changed into the snake, and/nattacked."/n/nHe looked down at the puncture marks./n/n"It wasn't supposed to kill me, just keep me there till/nYou-Know-Who came."/n/nIf he had only managed to kill the snake, it would/nhave been worth it, all of it. ... Sick at heart, he sat up/nand threw back the covers./n/n"Harry, no, I'm sure you ought to rest!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're the one who needs sleep. No offense, but you/nlook terrible. I'm fine. I'll keep watch for a while./nWhere's my wand?"/n/nShe did not answer, she merely looked at him./n"Where's my wand, Hermione?"/n/nShe was biting her lip, and tears swam in her eyes./n"Harry ..."/n/n" Where's my wand?"/n/nShe reached down beside the bed and held it out to/nhim./n/nThe holly and phoenix wand was nearly severed in/ntwo. One fragile strand of phoenix feather kept both/npieces hanging together. The wood had splintered/napart completely. Harry took it into his hands as/nthough it was a living thing that had suffered a/nterrible injury. He could not think properly:/nEverything was a blur of panic and fear. Then he held/nout the wand to Hermione./n/n"Mend it. Please."/n/n"Harry, I don't think, when it's broken like this — "/n"Please, Hermione, try!"/n/n"R-Reparo."/n/nThe dangling half of the wand resealed itself. Harry/nheld it up./n/n"Lumosl"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe wand sparked feebly, then went out. Harry/npointed it at Hermione./n/n" Expelliarmusl"/n/nHermione 's wand gave a little jerk, but did not leave/nher hand. The feeble attempt at magic was too much/nfor Harry's wand, which split into two again. He/nstared at it, aghast, unable to take in what he was/nseeing . . . the wand that had survived so much . . ./n/n"Harry," Hermione whispered so quietly he could/nhardly hear her. "I'm so, so sorry. I think it was me./n/nAs we were leaving, you know, the snake was coming/nfor us, and so I cast a Blasting Curse, and it/nrebounded everywhere, and it must have — must/nhave hit — "/n/n"It was an accident," said Harry mechanically. He felt/nempty, stunned. "We'll — we'll find a way to repair it."/n/n"Harry, I don't think we're going to be able to," said/nHermione, the tears trickling down her face./n"Remember . . . remember Ron? When he broke his/nwand, crashing the car? It was never the same again,/nhe had to get a new one."/n/nHarry thought of Ollivander, kidnapped and held/nhostage by Voldemort; of Gregorovitch, who was dead./nHow was he supposed to find himself a new wand?/n/n"Well," he said, in a falsely matter-of-fact voice, "well,/nI'll just borrow yours for now, then. While I keep/nwatch."/n/nHer face glazed with tears, Hermione handed over her/nwand, and he left her sitting beside his bed, desiring/nnothing more than to get away from her./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Life And Lies Of Albus Dumbledore
text: /nThe sun was coming up: The pure, colorless vastness/nof the sky stretched over him, indifferent to him and/nhis suffering. Harry sat down in the tent entrance and/ntook a deep breath of clean air. Simply to be alive to/nwatch the sun rise over the sparkling snowy hillside/nought to have been the greatest treasure on earth, yet/nhe could not appreciate it: His senses had been/nspiked by the calamity of losing his wand. He looked/nout over a valley blanketed in snow, distant church/nbells chiming through the glittering silence./n/nWithout realizing it, he was digging his fingers into/nhis arms as if he were trying to resist physical pain./n/nHe had spilled his own blood more times than he/ncould count; he had lost all the bones in his right arm/nonce; this journey had already given him scars to his/nchest and forearm to join those on his hand and/nforehead, but never, until this moment, had he felt/nhimself to be fatally weakened, vulnerable, and/nnaked, as though the best part of his magical power/nhad been torn from him. He knew exactly what/n/n/n/nHermione would say if he expressed any of this: The/nwand is only as good as the wizard. But she was/nwrong, his case was different. She had not felt the/nwand spin like the needle of a compass and shoot/ngolden flames at his enemy. He had lost the/nprotection of the twin cores, and only now that it was/ngone did he realize how much he had been counting/nupon it./n/nHe pulled the pieces of the broken wand out of his/npocket and, without looking at them, tucked them/naway in Hagrid's pouch around his neck. The pouch/nwas now too full of broken and useless objects to take/nany more. Harry's hand brushed the old Snitch/nthrough the mokeskin and for a moment he had to/nfight the temptation to pull it out and throw it away./nImpenetrable, unhelpful, useless, like everything else/nDumbledore had left behind —/n/nAnd his fury at Dumbledore broke over him now like/nlava, scorching him inside, wiping out every other/nfeeling. Out of sheer desperation they had talked/nthemselves into believing that Godric's Hollow held/nanswers, convinced themselves that they were/nsupposed to go back, that it was all part of some/nsecret path laid out for them by Dumbledore; but/nthere was no map, no plan. Dumbledore had left them/nto grope in the darkness, to wrestle with unknown/nand undreamed-of terrors, alone and unaided:/n/nNothing was explained, nothing was given freely, they/nhad no sword, and now, Harry had no wand. And he/nhad dropped the photograph of the thief, and it would/nsurely be easy now for Voldemort to find out who he/nwas. ... Voldemort had all the information now. .../n/n"Harry?"/n/nHermione looked frightened that he might curse her/nwith her own wand. Her face streaked with tears, she/n/n/n/n/n/ncrouched down beside him, two cups of tea trembling/nin her hands and something bulky under her arm./n/n"Thanks," he said, taking one of the cups./n/n"Do you mind if I talk to you?"/n/n"No," he said because he did not want to hurt her/nfeelings./n/n"Harry, you wanted to know who that man in the/npicture was. Well ... I've got the book."/n/nTimidly she pushed it onto his lap, a pristine copy of/nThe Life and Lies of Albus Dumbledore./n/n"Where — how — ?"/n/n"It was in Bathilda's sitting room, just lying there. .../nThis note was sticking out of the top of it."/n/nHermione read the few lines of spiky, acid-green/nwriting aloud./n/n" 'Dear Batty, Thanks for your help. Here's a copy of/nthe book, hope you like it. You said everything, even if/nyou don't remember it. Rita.' I think it must have/narrived while the real Bathilda was alive, but perhaps/nshe wasn't in any fit state to read it?"/n/n"No, she probably wasn't."/n/nHarry looked down upon Dumbledore 's face and/nexperienced a surge of savage pleasure: Now he would/nknow all the things that Dumbledore had never/nthought it worth telling him, whether Dumbledore/nwanted him to or not./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're still really angry at me, aren't you?" said/nHermione; he looked up to see fresh tears leaking out/nof her eyes, and knew that his anger must have/nshown in his face./n/n"No," he said quietly. "No, Hermione, I know it was an/naccident. You were trying to get us out of there alive,/nand you were incredible. I'd be dead if you hadn't/nbeen there to help me."/n/nHe tried to return her watery smile, then turned his/nattention to the book. Its spine was stiff; it had clearly/nnever been opened before. He riffled through the/npages, looking for photographs. He came across the/none he sought almost at once, the young Dumbledore/nand his handsome companion, roaring with laughter/nat some long-forgotten joke. Harry dropped his eyes to/nthe caption./n/nAlbus Dumbledore, shortly after his mother's death,/nwith his friend Gellert Grindelwald./n/nHarry gaped at the last word for several long/nmoments. Grindelwald. His friend Grindelwald. He/nlooked sideways at Hermione, who was still/ncontemplating the name as though she could not/nbelieve her eyes. Slowly she looked up at Harry./n/n" Grindelwald?"/n/nIgnoring the remainder of the photographs, Harry/nsearched the pages around them for a recurrence of/nthat fatal name. He soon discovered it and read/ngreedily, but became lost: It was necessary to go/nfurther back to make sense of it all, and eventually he/nfound himself at the start of a chapter entitled "The/nGreater Good." Together, he and Hermione started to/nread:/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nNow approaching his eighteenth birthday,/n/nDumbledore left Hogwarts in a blaze of glory — Head/nBoy, Prefect, Winner of the Barnabus Finkley Prize for/nExceptional Spell-Casting, British Youth/nRepresentative to the Wizengamot, Gold Medal-/nWinner for Ground-Breaking Contribution to the/nInternational Alchemical Conference in Cairo./nDumbledore intended, next, to take a Grand Tour/nwith Elphias "Dogbreath" Doge, the dim-witted but/ndevoted sidekick he had picked up at school./n/nThe two young men were staying at the Leaky/nCauldron in London, preparing to depart for Greece the/nfollowing morning, when an owl arrived bearing news/nof Dumbledore' s mother's death. "Dogbreath" Doge,/nwho refused to be interviewed for this book, has given/nthe public his own sentimental version of what/nhappened next. He represents Kendra's death as a/ntragic blow, and Dumbledore's decision to give up his/nexpedition as an act of noble self-sacrifice./n/nCertainly Dumbledore returned to Godric's Hollow at/nonce, supposedly to "care" for his younger brother/nand sister. But how much care did he actually give/nthem?/n/n"He were a head case, that Aberforth," says Enid/nSmeek, whose family lived on the outskirts of Godric's/nHollow at that time. "Ran wild. 'Course, with his mum/nand dad gone you'd have felt sorry for him, only he/nkept chucking goat dung at my head. I don't think/nAlbus was fussed about him, I never saw them/ntogether, anyway."/n/nSo what was Albus doing, if not comforting his wild/nyoung brother? The answer, it seems, is ensuring the/ncontinued imprisonment of his sister. For, though her/nfirst jailer had died, there was no change in the pitiful/ncondition of Ariana Dumbledore. Her very existence/n/n/n/n/ncontinued to be known only to those few outsiders/nwho, like "Dogbreath" Doge, could be counted upon to/nbelieve in the story of her "ill health."/n/nAnother such easily satisfied friend of the family was/nBathilda Bagshot, the celebrated magical historian/nwho has lived in Godric's Hollow for many years./nKendra, of course, had rebuffed Bathilda when she/nfirst attempted to welcome the family to the village./nSeveral years later, however, the author sent an owl to/nAlbus at Hog warts, having been favorably impressed/nby his paper on trans-species transformation in/nTransfiguration Today. This initial contact led to/nacquaintance with the entire Dumbledore family . At/nthe time of Kendra's death, Bathilda was the only/nperson in Godric's Hollow who was on speaking terms/nwith Dumbledore's mother./n/nUnfortunately, the brilliance that Bathilda exhibited/nearlier in her life has now dimmed. "The fire's lit, but/nthe cauldron's empty," as Ivor Dillonsby put it to me,/nor, in Enid Smeek's slightly earthier phrase, "She's/nnutty as squirrel poo." Nevertheless, a combination of/ntried-and-tested reporting techniques enabled me to/nextract enough nuggets of hard fact to string together/nthe whole scandalous story./n/nLike the rest of the Wizarding world, Bathilda puts/nKendra's premature death down to a backfiring/ncharm, a story repeated by Albus and Aberforth in/nlater years. Bathilda also parrots the family line on/nAriana, calling her "frail" and "delicate." On one/nsubject, however, Bathilda is well worth the effort I/nput into procuring Veritaserum, for she, and she/nalone, knows the full story of the best-kept secret of/nAlbus Dumbledore's life. Now revealed for the first/ntime, it calls into question everything that his/nadmirers believed of Dumbledore: his supposed/nhatred of the Dark Arts, his opposition to the/n/n/n/n/noppression of Muggles, even his devotion to his own/nfamily./n/nThe very same summer that Dumbledore went home/nto Godric's Hollow, now an orphan and head of the/nfamily, Bathilda Bagshot agreed to accept into her/nhome her great-nephew, Gellert Grindelwald./n/nThe name of Grindelwald is justly famous: In a list of/nMost Dangerous Dark Wizards of All Time, he would/nmiss out on the top spot only because You-Know-Who/narrived, a generation later, to steal his crown. As/nGrindelwald never extended his campaign of terror to/nBritain, however, the details of his rise to power are/nnot widely known here./n/nEducated at Durmstrang, a school famous even then/nfor its unfortunate tolerance of the Dark Arts,/nGrindelwald showed himself quite as precociously/nbrilliant as Dumbledore. Rather than channel his/nabilities into the attainment of awards and prizes,/nhowever, Gellert Grindelwald devoted himself to other/npursuits. At sixteen years old, even Durmstrang felt it/ncould no longer turn a blind eye to the twisted/nexperiments of Gellert Grindelwald, and he was/nexpelled./n/nHitherto, all that has been known of Grindelwald 's/nnext movements is that he "traveled abroad for some/nmonths." It can now be revealed that Grindelwald/nchose to visit his great-aunt in Godric's Hollow, and/nthat there, intensely shocking though it will be for/nmany to hear it, he struck up a close friendship with/nnone other than Albus Dumbledore./n/n"He seemed a charming boy to me," babbles Bathilda,/n"whatever he became later. Naturally I introduced him/nto poor Albus, who was missing the company of lads/nhis own age. The boys took to each other at once."/n/n/n/n/n/nThey certainly did. Bathilda shows me a letter, kept/nby her, that Albus Dumbledore sent Gellert/nGrindelwald in the dead of night./n/n"Yes, even after they'd spent all day in discussion —/nboth such brilliant young boys, they got on like a/ncauldron on fire — I'd sometimes hear an owl tapping/nat Gellert's bedroom window, delivering a letter from/nAlbus! An idea would have struck him, and he had to/nlet Gellert know immediately!"/n/nAnd what ideas they were. Profoundly shocking/nthough Albus Dumbledore' s fans will find it, here are/nthe thoughts of their seventeen-year-old hero, as/nrelayed to his new best friend. (A copy of the original/nletter may be seen on page 463.)/n/nGellert —/n/nYour point about Wizard dominance being FOR THE/nMUGGLES' OWN GOOD — this, I think , is the crucial/npoint. Yes, we have been given power and yes, that/npower gives us the right to rule, but it also gives us/nresponsibilities over the ruled. We must stress this/npoint, it will be the foundation stone upon which we/nbuild. Where we are opposed, as we surely will be, this/nmust be the basis of all our counterarguments. We/nseize control FOR THE GREATER GOOD. And from this/nit follows that where we meet resistance, we must use/nonly the force that is necessary and no more. (This was/nyour mistake at Durmstrang! But I do not complain,/nbecause if you had not been expelled, we would never/nhave met.)/n/nAlbus/n/nAstonished and appalled though his many admirers/nwill be, this letter constitutes proof that Albus/nDumbledore once dreamed of overthrowing the Statute/n/n/n/n/n/nof Secrecy and establishing Wizard rule over Muggles./nWhat a blow for those who have always portrayed/nDumbledore as the Muggle-boms' greatest champion!/nHow hollow those speeches promoting Muggle rights/nseem in the light of this damning new evidence! How/ndespicable does Albus Dumbledore appear, busy/nplotting his rise to power when he should have been/nmourning his mother and caring for his sister!/n/nNo doubt those determined to keep Dumbledore on/nhis crumbling pedestal will bleat that he did not, after/nall, put his plans into action, that he must have/nsuffered a change of heart, that he came to his/nsenses. However, the truth seems altogether more/nshocking./n/nBarely two months into their great new friendship,/nDumbledore and Grindelwald parted, never to see each/nother again until they met for their legendary duel (for/nmore, see chapter 22). What caused this abrupt/nrupture? Had Dumbledore come to his senses? Had he/ntold Grindelwald he wanted no more part in his plans?/nAlas, no./n/n"It was poor little Ariana dying, I think, that did it,"/nsays Bathilda. "It came as an awful shock. Gellert was/nthere in the house when it happened, and he came/nback to my house all of a dither, told me he wanted to/ngo home the next day. Terribly distressed, you know./nSo I arranged a Portkey and that was the last I saw of/nhim./n/n"Albus was beside himself at Ariana's death. It was so/ndreadful for those two brothers. They had lost/neverybody except each other. No wonder tempers ran/na little high. Aberforth blamed Albus, you know, as/npeople will under these dreadful circumstances. But/nAberforth always talked a little madly, poor boy. All/nthe same, breaking Albus's nose at the funeral was/n/n/n/n/nnot decent. It would have destroyed Kendra to see her/nsons fighting like that, across her daughter's body. A/nshame Gellert could not have stayed for the funeral./n/n... He would have been a comfort to Albus, at least./n/n/n/nThis dreadful coffin- side brawl, known only to those/nfew who attended Ariana Dumbledore's funeral, raises/nseveral questions. Why exactly did Aberforth/nDumbledore blame Albus for his sister's death? Was/nit, as "Batty" pretends, a mere effusion of grief? Or/ncould there have been some more concrete reason for/nhis fury? Grindelwald, expelled from Durmstrang for/nnear-fatal attacks upon fellow students, fled the/ncountry hours after the girl's death, and Albus (out of/nshame or fear?) never saw him again, not until forced/nto do so by the pleas of the Wizarding world./n/nNeither Dumbledore nor Grindelwald ever seems to/nhave referred to this brief boyhood friendship in later/nlife. However, there can be no doubt that Dumbledore/ndelayed, for some five years of turmoil, fatalities, and/ndisappearances, his attack upon Gellert Grindelwald./nWas it lingering affection for the man or fear of/nexposure as his once best friend that caused/nDumbledore to hesitate? Was it only reluctantly that/nDumbledore set out to capture the man he was once/nso delighted he had met?/n/nAnd how did the mysterious Ariana die? Was she the/ninadvertent victim of some Dark rite? Did she stumble/nacross something she ought not to have done, as the/ntwo young men sat practicing for their attempt at/nglory and domination? Is it possible that Ariana/nDumbledore was the first person to die "for the/ngreater good"?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe chapter ended here and Harry looked up./nHermione had reached the bottom of the page before/nhim. She tugged the book out of Harry's hands,/nlooking a little alarmed by his expression, and closed/nit without looking at it, as though hiding something/nindecent./n/n"Harry — "/n/nBut he shook his head. Some inner certainty had/ncrashed down inside him; it was exactly as he had felt/nafter Ron left. He had trusted Dumbledore, believed/nhim the embodiment of goodness and wisdom. All was/nashes: How much more could he lose? Ron,/nDumbledore, the phoenix wand .../n/n"Harry." She seemed to have heard his thoughts./n"Listen to me. It — it doesn't make very nice reading/n/n/n/n"Yeah, you could say that — "/n/n" — but don't forget, Harry, this is Rita Skeeter/nwriting."/n/n"You did read that letter to Grindelwald, didn't you?"/n/n"Yes, I — I did." She hesitated, looking upset, cradling/nher tea in her cold hands. "I think that's the worst bit./nI know Bathilda thought it was all just talk, but 'For/nthe Greater Good' became Grindelwald 's slogan, his/njustification for all the atrocities he committed later./nAnd . . . from that ... it looks like Dumbledore gave him/nthe idea. They say 'For the Greater Good' was even/ncarved over the entrance to Nurmengard."/n/n"What's Nurmengard?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The prison Grindelwald had built to hold his/nopponents. He ended up in there himself, once/nDumbledore had caught him. Anyway, it's — it's an/nawful thought that Dumbledore 's ideas helped/nGrindelwald rise to power. But on the other hand,/neven Rita can't pretend that they knew each other for/nmore than a few months one summer when they were/nboth really young, and — "/n/n"I thought you'd say that," said Harry. He did not/nwant to let his anger spill out at her, but it was hard/nto keep his voice steady. "I thought you'd say They/nwere young. ' They were the same age as we are now./nAnd here we are, risking our lives to fight the Dark/nArts, and there he was, in a huddle with his new best/nfriend, plotting their rise to power over the Muggles."/n/nHis temper would not remain in check much longer:/nHe stood up and walked around, trying to work some/nof it off./n/n"I'm not trying to defend what Dumbledore wrote,"/nsaid Hermione. "All that 'right to rule' rubbish, it's/n'Magic Is Might' all over again. But Harry, his mother/nhad just died, he was stuck alone in the house — "/n/n"Alone? He wasn't alone! He had his brother and/nsister for company, his Squib sister he was keeping/nlocked up — "/n/n"I don't believe it," said Hermione. She stood up too./n"Whatever was wrong with that girl, I don't think she/nwas a Squib. The Dumbledore we knew would never,/never have allowed — "/n/n"The Dumbledore we thought we knew didn't want to/nconquer Muggles by force!" Harry shouted, his voice/nechoing across the empty hilltop, and several/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nblackbirds rose into the air, squawking and spiraling/nagainst the pearly sky./n/n"He changed, Harry, he changed! It's as simple as/nthat! Maybe he did believe these things when he was/nseventeen, but the whole of the rest of his life was/ndevoted to fighting the Dark Arts! Dumbledore was/nthe one who stopped Grindelwald, the one who always/nvoted for Muggle protection and Muggle-born rights,/nwho fought You-Know-Who from the start, and who/ndied trying to bring him down!"/n/nRita's book lay on the ground between them, so that/nthe face of Albus Dumbledore smiled dolefully at/nboth./n/n"Harry, I'm sorry, but I think the real reason you're so/nangry is that Dumbledore never told you any of this/nhimself."/n/n"Maybe I am!" Harry bellowed, and he flung his arms/nover his head, hardly knowing whether he was trying/nto hold in his anger or protect himself from the weight/nof his own disillusionment. "Look what he asked from/nme, Hermione! Risk your life, Harry! And again! And/nagain! And don't expect me to explain everything, just/ntrust me blindly, trust that I know what I'm doing,/ntrust me even though I don't trust you! Never the/nwhole truth! Never!"/n/nHis voice cracked with the strain, and they stood/nlooking at each other in the whiteness and the/nemptiness, and Harry felt they were as insignificant/nas insects beneath that wide sky./n/n"He loved you," Hermione whispered. "I know he loved/nyou."/n/n/n/nHarry dropped his arms./n/n/n/n/n/n"I don't know who he loved, Hermione, but it was/nnever me. This isn't love, the mess he's left me in. He/nshared a damn sight more of what he was really/nthinking with Gellert Grindelwald than he ever shared/nwith me."/n/nHarry picked up Hermione 's wand, which he had/ndropped in the snow, and sat back down in the/nentrance of the tent./n/n"Thanks for the tea. I'll finish the watch. You get back/nin the warm."/n/nShe hesitated, but recognized the dismissal. She/npicked up the book and then walked back past him/ninto the tent, but as she did so, she brushed the top/nof his head lightly with her hand. He closed his eyes/nat her touch, and hated himself for wishing that what/nshe said was true: that Dumbledore had really cared./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Silver Doe
text: /nIt was snowing by the time Hermione took over the/nwatch at midnight. Harry's dreams were confused and/ndisturbing: Nagini wove in and out of them, first/nthrough a gigantic, cracked ring, then through a/nwreath of Christmas roses. He woke repeatedly,/npanicky, convinced that somebody had called out to/nhim in the distance, imagining that the wind/nwhipping around the tent was footsteps or voices./n/nFinally he got up in the darkness and joined/nHermione, who was huddled in the entrance to the/ntent reading A History of Magic by the light of her/nwand. The snow was still falling thickly, and she/ngreeted with relief his suggestion of packing up early/nand moving on./n/n"Well go somewhere more sheltered," she agreed,/nshivering as she pulled on a sweatshirt over her/npajamas. "I kept thinking I could hear people moving/noutside. I even thought I saw somebody once or/ntwice."/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry paused in the act of pulling on a jumper and/nglanced at the silent, motionless Sneakoscope on the/ntable./n/n"I'm sure I imagined it," said Hermione, looking/nnervous. "The snow in the dark, it plays tricks on/nyour eyes. ... But perhaps we ought to Disapparate/nunder the Invisibility Cloak, just in case?"/n/nHalf an hour later, with the tent packed, Harry/nwearing the Horcrux, and Hermione clutching the/nbeaded bag, they Disapparated. The usual tightness/nengulfed them; Harry's feet parted company with the/nsnowy ground, then slammed hard onto what felt like/nfrozen earth covered with leaves./n/n"Where are we?" he asked, peering around at a fresh/nmass of trees as Hermione opened the beaded bag/nand began tugging out tent poles./n/n"The Forest of Dean," she said. "I came camping here/nonce with my mum and dad."/n/nHere too snow lay on the trees all around and it was/nbitterly cold, but they were at least protected from the/nwind. They spent most of the day inside the tent,/nhuddled for warmth around the useful bright blue/nflames that Hermione was so adept at producing, and/nwhich could be scooped up and carried around in a/njar. Harry felt as though he was recuperating from/nsome brief but severe illness, an impression/nreinforced by Hermione 's solicitousness. That/nafternoon fresh flakes drifted down upon them, so/nthat even their sheltered clearing had a fresh dusting/nof powdery snow./n/nAfter two nights of little sleep, Harry's senses seemed/nmore alert than usual. Their escape from Godric's/nHollow had been so narrow that Voldemort seemed/n/n/n/n/n/nsomehow closer than before, more threatening. As/ndarkness drew in again Harry refused Hermione's/noffer to keep watch and told her to go to bed./n/nHarry moved an old cushion into the tent mouth and/nsat down, wearing all the sweaters he owned but even/nso, still shivery. The darkness deepened with the/npassing hours until it was virtually impenetrable. He/nwas on the point of taking out the Marauder's Map, so/nas to watch Ginny's dot for a while, before he/nremembered that it was the Christmas holidays and/nthat she would be back at the Burrow./n/nEvery tiny movement seemed magnified in the/nvastness of the forest. Harry knew that it must be full/nof living creatures, but he wished they would all/nremain still and silent so that he could separate their/ninnocent scurryings and prowlings from noises that/nmight proclaim other, sinister movements. He/nremembered the sound of a cloak slithering over dead/nleaves many years ago, and at once thought he heard/nit again before mentally shaking himself. Their/nprotective enchantments had worked for weeks; why/nshould they break now? And yet he could not throw/noff the feeling that something was different tonight./n/nSeveral times he jerked upright, his neck aching/nbecause he had fallen asleep, slumped at an awkward/nangle against the side of the tent. The night reached/nsuch a depth of velvety blackness that he might have/nbeen suspended in limbo between Disapparition and/nApparition. He had just held up a hand in front of his/nface to see whether he could make out his fingers/nwhen it happened./n/nA bright silver light appeared right ahead of him,/nmoving through the trees. Whatever the source, it was/nmoving soundlessly. The light seemed simply to drift/ntoward him./n/n/n/n/n/nHe jumped to his feet, his voice frozen in his throat,/nand raised Hermione's wand. He screwed up his eyes/nas the light became blinding, the trees in front of it/npitch-black in silhouette, and still the thing came/ncloser. .../n/nAnd then the source of the light stepped out from/nbehind an oak. It was a silver- white doe, moon-bright/nand dazzling, picking her way over the ground, still/nsilent, and leaving no hoofprints in the fine powdering/nof snow. She stepped toward him, her beautiful head/nwith its wide, long-lashed eyes held high./n/nHarry stared at the creature, filled with wonder, not/nat her strangeness, but at her inexplicable familiarity./nHe felt that he had been waiting for her to come, but/nthat he had forgotten, until this moment, that they/nhad arranged to meet. His impulse to shout for/nHermione, which had been so strong a moment ago,/nhad gone. He knew, he would have staked his life on/nit, that she had come for him, and him alone./n/nThey gazed at each other for several long moments/nand then she turned and walked away./n/n"No," he said, and his voice was cracked with lack of/nuse. "Come back!"/n/nShe continued to step deliberately through the trees,/nand soon her brightness was striped by their thick/nblack trunks. For one trembling second he hesitated./nCaution murmured it could be a trick, a lure, a trap./nBut instinct, overwhelming instinct, told him that this/nwas not Dark Magic. He set off in pursuit./n/nSnow crunched beneath his feet, but the doe made no/nnoise as she passed through the trees, for she was/nnothing but light. Deeper and deeper into the forest/nshe led him, and Harry walked quickly, sure that/n/n/n/n/n/nwhen she stopped, she would allow him to approach/nher properly. And then she would speak and the voice/nwould tell him what he needed to know./n/nAt last, she came to a halt. She turned her beautiful/nhead toward him once more, and he broke into a run,/na question burning in him, but as he opened his lips/nto ask it, she vanished./n/nThough the darkness had swallowed her whole, her/nburnished image was still imprinted on his retinas; it/nobscured his vision, brightening when he lowered his/neyelids, disorienting him. Now fear came: Her/npresence had meant safety./n/n"Lumos\" he whispered, and the wand-tip ignited./n/nThe imprint of the doe faded away with every blink of/nhis eyes as he stood there, listening to the sounds of/nthe forest, to distant crackles of twigs, soft swishes of/nsnow. Was he about to be attacked? Had she enticed/nhim into an ambush? Was he imagining that/nsomebody stood beyond the reach of the wandlight,/nwatching him?/n/nHe held the wand higher. Nobody ran out at him, no/nflash of green light burst from behind a tree. Why,/nthen, had she led him to this spot?/n/nSomething gleamed in the light of the wand, and/nHarry spun about, but all that was there was a small,/nfrozen pool, its cracked black surface glittering as he/nraised the wand higher to examine it./n/nHe moved forward rather cautiously and looked down./nThe ice reflected his distorted shadow and the beam/nof wandlight, but deep below the thick, misty gray/ncarapace, something else glinted. A great silver cross/n/n/n/n/n/nHis heart skipped into his mouth: He dropped to his/nknees at the pool's edge and angled the wand so as to/nflood the bottom of the pool with as much light as/npossible. A glint of deep red ... It was a sword with/nglittering rubies in its hilt. ... The sword of Gryffindor/nwas lying at the bottom of the forest pool./n/nBarely breathing, he stared down at it. How was this/npossible? How could it have come to be lying in a/nforest pool, this close to the place where they were/ncamping? Had some unknown magic drawn Hermione/nto this spot, or was the doe, which he had taken to be/na Patronus, some kind of guardian of the pool? Or/nhad the sword been put into the pool after they had/narrived, precisely because they were here? In which/ncase, where was the person who had wanted to pass/nit to Harry? Again he directed the wand at the/nsurrounding trees and bushes, searching for a/nhuman outline, for the glint of an eye, but he could/nnot see anyone there. All the same, a little more fear/nleavened his exhilaration as he returned his attention/nto the sword reposing upon the bottom of the frozen/npool./n/nHe pointed the wand at the silvery shape and/nmurmured, "Accio Sword."/n/nIt did not stir. He had not expected it to. If it had been/nthat easy, the sword would have lain on the ground/nfor him to pick up, not in the depths of a frozen pool./nHe set off around the circle of ice, thinking hard/nabout the last time the sword had delivered itself to/nhim. He had been in terrible danger then, and had/nasked for help./n/n"Help," he murmured, but the sword remained upon/nthe pool bottom, indifferent, motionless./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWhat was it, Harry asked himself (walking again),/nthat Dumbledore had told him the last time he had/nretrieved the sword? Only a true Gryffindor could have/npulled that out of the hat. And what were the qualities/nthat defined a Gryffindor? A small voice inside Harry's/nhead answered him: Their daring, nerve, and chivalry/nset Gryffindors apart./n/nHarry stopped walking and let out a long sigh, his/nsmoky breath dispersing rapidly upon the frozen air./nHe knew what he had to do. If he was honest with/nhimself, he had thought it might come to this from/nthe moment he had spotted the sword through the/nice./n/nHe glanced around at the surrounding trees again,/nbut was convinced now that nobody was going to/nattack him. They had had their chance as he walked/nalone through the forest, had had plenty of/nopportunity as he examined the pool. The only reason/nto delay at this point was because the immediate/nprospect was so deeply uninviting./n/nWith fumbling fingers Harry started to remove his/nmany layers of clothing. Where "chivalry" entered into/nthis, he thought ruefully, he was not entirely sure,/nunless it counted as chivalrous that he was not/ncalling for Hermione to do it in his stead./n/nAn owl hooted somewhere as he stripped off, and he/nthought with a pang of Hedwig. He was shivering/nnow, his teeth chattering horribly, and yet he/ncontinued to strip off until at last he stood there in/nhis underwear, barefooted in the snow. He placed the/npouch containing his wand, his mother's letter, the/nshard of Sirius's mirror, and the old Snitch on top of/nhis clothes, then he pointed Hermione's wand at the/nice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Diffindo."/n/n/n/nIt cracked with a sound like a bullet in the silence:/n/nThe surface of the pool broke and chunks of dark ice/nrocked on the ruffled water. As far as Harry could/njudge, it was not deep, but to retrieve the sword he/nwould have to submerge himself completely./n/nContemplating the task ahead would not make it/neasier or the water warmer. He stepped to the pool's/nedge and placed Hermione's wand on the ground, still/nlit. Then, trying not to imagine how much colder he/nwas about to become or how violently he would soon/nbe shivering, he jumped./n/nEvery pore of his body screamed in protest: The very/nair in his lungs seemed to freeze solid as he was/nsubmerged to his shoulders in the frozen water. He/ncould hardly breathe; trembling so violently the water/nlapped over the edges of the pool, he felt for the blade/nwith his numb feet. He only wanted to dive once./n/nHarry put off the moment of total submersion from/nsecond to second, gasping and shaking, until he told/nhimself that it must be done, gathered all his courage,/nand dived./n/nThe cold was agony: It attacked him like fire. His/nbrain itself seemed to have frozen as he pushed/nthrough the dark water to the bottom and reached/nout, groping for the sword. His fingers closed around/nthe hilt; he pulled it upward./n/nThen something closed tight around his neck. He/nthought of water weeds, though nothing had brushed/nhim as he dived, and raised his empty hand to free/nhimself. It was not weed: The chain of the Horcrux/nhad tightened and was slowly constricting his/nwindpipe./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry kicked out wildly, trying to push himself back/nto the surface, but merely propelled himself into the/nrocky side of the pool. Thrashing, suffocating, he/nscrabbled at the strangling chain, his frozen fingers/nunable to loosen it, and now little lights were popping/ninside his head, and he was going to drown, there was/nnothing left, nothing he could do, and the arms that/nclosed around his chest were surely Death's. .../n/nChoking and retching, soaking and colder than he/nhad ever been in his life, he came to facedown in the/nsnow. Somewhere close by, another person was/npanting and coughing and staggering around./nHermione had come again, as she had come when the/nsnake attacked. ... Yet it did not sound like her, not/nwith those deep coughs, not judging by the weight of/nthe footsteps. .../n/nHarry had no strength to lift his head and see his/nsavior's identity. All he could do was raise a shaking/nhand to his throat and feel the place where the locket/nhad cut tightly into his flesh. It was gone: Someone/nhad cut him free. Then a panting voice spoke from/nover his head./n/n"Are — you — mental?"/n/nNothing but the shock of hearing that voice could/nhave given Harry the strength to get up. Shivering/nviolently, he staggered to his feet. There before him/nstood Ron, fully dressed but drenched to the skin, his/nhair plastered to his face, the sword of Gryffindor in/none hand and the Horcrux dangling from its broken/nchain in the other./n/n"Why the hell," panted Ron, holding up the Horcrux,/nwhich swung backward and forward on its shortened/nchain in some parody of hypnosis, "didn't you take/nthis thing off before you dived?"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry could not answer. The silver doe was nothing,/nnothing compared with Ron's reappearance; he could/nnot believe it. Shuddering with cold, he caught up the/npile of clothes still lying at the water's edge and began/nto pull them on. As he dragged sweater after sweater/nover his head, Harry stared at Ron, half expecting him/nto have disappeared every time he lost sight of him,/nand yet he had to be real: He had just dived into the/npool, he had saved Harry's life./n/n"It was y-you?" Harry said at last, his teeth/nchattering, his voice weaker than usual due to his/nnear-strangulation./n/n"Well, yeah," said Ron, looking slightly confused./n"Y-you cast that doe?"/n/n"What? No, of course not! I thought it was you doing/nit!"/n/n/n/n"My Patronus is a stag."/n/n"Oh yeah. I thought it looked different. No antlers."/n/nHarry put Hagrid's pouch back around his neck,/npulled on a final sweater, stooped to pick up/nHermione's wand, and faced Ron again./n/n"How come you're here?"/n/nApparently Ron had hoped that this point would come/nup later, if at all./n/n"Well, I've — you know — I've come back. If — " He/ncleared his throat. "You know. You still want me."/n/nThere was a pause, in which the subject of Ron's/ndeparture seemed to rise like a wall between them./n/n/n/n/n/nYet he was here. He had returned. He had just saved/nHarry's life./n/nRon looked down at his hands. He seemed/nmomentarily surprised to see the things he was/nholding./n/n"Oh yeah, I got it out," he said, rather unnecessarily,/nholding up the sword for Harry's inspection. "That's/nwhy you jumped in, right?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "But I don't understand. How did/nyou get here? How did you find us?"/n/n"Long story," said Ron. "I've been looking for you for/nhours, it's a big forest, isn't it? And I was just/nthinking I'd have to kip under a tree and wait for/nmorning when I saw that deer coming and you/nfollowing."/n/n"You didn't see anyone else?"/n/n"No," said Ron. "I — "/n/nBut he hesitated, glancing at two trees growing close/ntogether some yards away./n/n"I did think I saw something move over there, but I/nwas running to the pool at the time, because you'd/ngone in and you hadn't come up, so I wasn't going to/nmake a detour to — hey!"/n/nHarry was already hurrying to the place Ron had/nindicated. The two oaks grew close together; there/nwas a gap of only a few inches between the trunks at/neye level, an ideal place to see but not be seen. The/nground around the roots, however, was free of snow,/nand Harry could see no sign of footprints. He walked/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nback to where Ron stood waiting, still holding the/nsword and the Horcrux./n/n/n/n"Anything there?" Ron asked./n/n"No," said Harry./n/n"So how did the sword get in that pool?"/n/n"Whoever cast the Patronus must have put it there."/n/nThey both looked at the ornate silver sword, its rubied/nhilt glinting a little in the light from Hermione's wand./n/n"You reckon this is the real one?" asked Ron./n/n"One way to find out, isn't there?" said Harry./n/nThe Horcrux was still swinging from Ron's hand. The/nlocket was twitching slightly. Harry knew that the/nthing inside it was agitated again. It had sensed the/npresence of the sword and had tried to kill Harry/nrather than let him possess it. Now was not the time/nfor long discussions; now was the moment to destroy/nthe locket once and for all. Harry looked around,/nholding Hermione's wand high, and saw the place: a/nflattish rock lying in the shadow of a sycamore tree./n/n"Come here," he said, and he led the way, brushed/nsnow from the rock's surface, and held out his hand/nfor the Horcrux. When Ron offered the sword,/nhowever, Harry shook his head./n/n"No, you should do it."/n/n"Me?" said Ron, looking shocked. "Why?"/n/n"Because you got the sword out of the pool. I think it's/nsupposed to be you."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe was not being kind or generous. As certainly as he/nhad known that the doe was benign, he knew that/nRon had to be the one to wield the sword./n/nDumbledore had at least taught Harry something/nabout certain kinds of magic, of the incalculable/npower of certain acts./n/n"I'm going to open it," said Harry, "and you stab it./nStraightaway, okay? Because whatever's in there will/nput up a fight. The bit of Riddle in the diary tried to/nkill me."/n/n"How are you going to open it?" asked Ron. He looked/nterrified./n/n"I'm going to ask it to open, using Parseltongue," said/nHarry. The answer came so readily to his lips that he/nthought that he had always known it deep down:/nPerhaps it had taken his recent encounter with Nagini/nto make him realize it. He looked at the serpentine S,/ninlaid with glittering green stones: It was easy to/nvisualize it as a minuscule snake, curled upon the/ncold rock./n/n"No!" said Ron. "No, don't open it! I'm serious!"/n/n"Why not?" asked Harry. "Let's get rid of the damn/nthing, it's been months — "/n/n"I can't, Harry, I'm serious — you do it — "/n/n"But why?"/n/n"Because that thing's bad for me!" said Ron, backing/naway from the locket on the rock. "I can't handle it!/n/nI'm not making excuses, Harry, for what I was like,/nbut it affects me worse than it affected you and/nHermione, it made me think stuff — stuff I was/nthinking anyway, but it made everything worse, I/n/n/n/n/ncan't explain it, and then I'd take it off and I'd get my/nhead on straight again, and then I'd have to put the/neffing thing back on — I can't do it, Harry!"/n/nHe had backed away, the sword dragging at his side,/nshaking his head./n/n"You can do it," said Harry, "you can! You've just got/nthe sword, I know it's supposed to be you who uses it./nPlease, just get rid of it, Ron."/n/nThe sound of his name seemed to act like a stimulant./nRon swallowed, then, still breathing hard through his/nlong nose, moved back toward the rock./n/n"Tell me when," he croaked./n/n"On three," said Harry, looking back down at the/nlocket and narrowing his eyes, concentrating on the/nletter S, imagining a serpent, while the contents of the/nlocket rattled like a trapped cockroach. It would have/nbeen easy to pity it, except that the cut around/nHarry's neck still burned./n/n"One ... two ... three ... open."/n/nThe last word came as a hiss and a snarl and the/ngolden doors of the locket swung wide with a little/nclick./n/nBehind both of the glass windows within blinked a/nliving eye, dark and handsome as Tom Riddle's eyes/nhad been before he turned them scarlet and slit-/npupiled./n/n"Stab," said Harry, holding the locket steady on the/nrock./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRon raised the sword in his shaking hands: The point/ndangled over the frantically swiveling eyes, and Harry/ngripped the locket tightly, bracing himself, already/nimagining blood pouring from the empty windows./n/nThen a voice hissed from out of the Horcrux./n/n"I have seen your heart, and it is mine."/n/n"Don't listen to it!" Harry said harshly. "Stab it!"/n/n"I have seen your dreams, Ronald Weasley, and I have/nseen your fears. All you desire is possible, but all that/nyou dread is also possible. ..."/n/n"Stab!" shouted Harry; his voice echoed off the/nsurrounding trees, the sword point trembled, and Ron/ngazed down into Riddle's eyes./n/n" Least loved, always, by the mother who craved a/ndaughter . . . Least loved, now, by the girl who prefers/nyour friend . . . Second best, always, eternally/novershadowed ..."/n/n"Ron, stab it now!" Harry bellowed: He could feel the/nlocket quivering in his grip and was scared of what/nwas coming. Ron raised the sword still higher, and as/nhe did so, Riddle's eyes gleamed scarlet./n/nOut of the locket's two windows, out of the eyes, there/nbloomed, like two grotesque bubbles, the heads of/nHarry and Hermione, weirdly distorted./n/nRon yelled in shock and backed away as the figures/nblossomed out of the locket, first chests, then waists,/nthen legs, until they stood in the locket, side by side/nlike trees with a common root, swaying over Ron and/nthe real Harry, who had snatched his fingers away/nfrom the locket as it burned, suddenly, white-hot./n/n/n/n/n"Ron!" he shouted, but the Riddle-Harry was now/nspeaking with Voldemort's voice and Ron was gazing,/nmesmerized, into its face./n/n" Why return? We were better without you, happier/nwithout you, glad of your absence. . . . We laughed at/nyour stupidity, your cowardice, your presumption — "/n/n" Presumption?' echoed the Riddle-Hermione, who was/nmore beautiful and yet more terrible than the real/nHermione: She swayed, cackling, before Ron, who/nlooked horrified yet transfixed, the sword hanging/npointlessly at his side. " Who could look at you, who/nwould ever look at you, beside Harry Potter? What/nhave you ever done, compared with the Chosen One?/nWhat are you, compared with the Boy Who Lived?"/n/n"Ron, stab it, STAB IT!" Harry yelled, but Ron did not/nmove: His eyes were wide, and the Riddle-Harry and/nthe Riddle-Hermione were reflected in them, their hair/nswirling like flames, their eyes shining red, their/nvoices lifted in an evil duet./n/n" Your mother confessed," sneered Riddle-Harry, while/nRiddle-Hermione jeered, "that she would have/npreferred me as a son, would be glad to exchange ..."/n/n"Who wouldn't prefer him, what woman would take/nyou, you are nothing, nothing, nothing to him," crooned/nRiddle-Hermione, and she stretched like a snake and/nentwined herself around Riddle-Harry, wrapping him/nin a close embrace: Their lips met./n/nOn the ground in front of them, Ron's face filled with/nanguish. He raised the sword high, his arms shaking./n/n"Do it, Ron!" Harry yelled./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRon looked toward him, and Harry thought he saw a/ntrace of scarlet in his eyes./n/n"Ron — ?"/n/nThe sword flashed, plunged: Harry threw himself out/nof the way, there was a clang of metal and a long,/ndrawn-out scream. Harry whirled around, slipping in/nthe snow, wand held ready to defend himself: but/nthere was nothing to fight./n/nThe monstrous versions of himself and Hermione/nwere gone: There was only Ron, standing there with/nthe sword held slackly in his hand, looking down at/nthe shattered remains of the locket on the flat rock./n/nSlowly, Harry walked back to him, hardly knowing/nwhat to say or do. Ron was breathing heavily: His/neyes were no longer red at all, but their normal blue;/nthey were also wet./n/nHarry stooped, pretending he had not seen, and/npicked up the broken Horcrux. Ron had pierced the/nglass in both windows: Riddle's eyes were gone, and/nthe stained silk lining of the locket was smoking/nslightly. The thing that had lived in the Horcrux had/nvanished; torturing Ron had been its final act./n/nThe sword clanged as Ron dropped it. He had sunk to/nhis knees, his head in his arms. He was shaking, but/nnot, Harry realized, from cold. Harry crammed the/nbroken locket into his pocket, knelt down beside Ron,/nand placed a hand cautiously on his shoulder. He/ntook it as a good sign that Ron did not throw it off./n/n"After you left," he said in a low voice, grateful for the/nfact that Ron's face was hidden, "she cried for a week./nProbably longer, only she didn't want me to see. There/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwere loads of nights when we never even spoke to/neach other. With you gone ..."/n/nHe could not finish; it was only now that Ron was/nhere again that Harry fully realized how much his/nabsence had cost them./n/n"She's like my sister," he went on. "I love her like a/nsister and I reckon she feels the same way about me./nIt's always been like that. I thought you knew."/n/nRon did not respond, but turned his face away from/nHarry and wiped his nose noisily on his sleeve. Harry/ngot to his feet again and walked to where Ron's/nenormous rucksack lay yards away, discarded as Ron/nhad run toward the pool to save Harry from drowning./nHe hoisted it onto his own back and walked back to/nRon, who clambered to his feet as Harry approached,/neyes bloodshot but otherwise composed./n/n"I'm sorry," he said in a thick voice. "I'm sorry I left. I/nknow I was a — a — "/n/nHe looked around at the darkness, as if hoping a bad/nenough word would swoop down upon him and claim/nhim./n/n"You've sort of made up for it tonight," said Harry./n"Getting the sword. Finishing off the Horcrux. Saving/nmy life."/n/n"That makes me sound a lot cooler than I was," Ron/nmumbled./n/n"Stuff like that always sounds cooler than it really/nwas," said Harry. "I've been trying to tell you that for/nyears."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nSimultaneously they walked forward and hugged,/nHarry gripping the still-sopping back of Ron's jacket./n/n"And now," said Harry as they broke apart, "all we've/ngot to do is find the tent again."/n/nBut it was not difficult. Though the walk through the/ndark forest with the doe had seemed lengthy, with/nRon by his side the journey back seemed to take a/nsurprisingly short time. Harry could not wait to wake/nHermione, and it was with quickening excitement that/nhe entered the tent, Ron lagging a little behind him./n/nIt was gloriously warm after the pool and the forest,/nthe only illumination the bluebell flames still/nshimmering in a bowl on the floor. Hermione was fast/nasleep, curled up under her blankets, and did not/nmove until Harry had said her name several times./n/n"Hermionel"/n/nShe stirred, then sat up quickly, pushing her hair out/nof her face./n/n"What's wrong? Harry? Are you all right?"/n/n"It's okay, everything's fine. More than fine. I'm great./nThere's someone here."/n/n"What do you mean? Who — ?"/n/nShe saw Ron, who stood there holding the sword and/ndripping onto the threadbare carpet. Harry backed/ninto a shadowy corner, slipped off Ron's rucksack,/nand attempted to blend in with the canvas./n/nHermione slid out of her bunk and moved like a/nsleepwalker toward Ron, her eyes upon his pale face./nShe stopped right in front of him, her lips slightly/n/n/n/n/n/nparted, her eyes wide. Ron gave a weak, hopeful smile/nand half raised his arms./n/nHermione launched herself forward and started/npunching every inch of him that she could reach./n/n"Ouch — ow — gerroff! What the — ? Hermione —/nOW!"/n/n"You — complete — arse — Ronald — Weasley!"/n/nShe punctuated every word with a blow: Ron backed/naway, shielding his head as Hermione advanced./n/n"You — crawl — back — here — after — weeks — and/n— weeks — oh, where's my wand?"/n/nShe looked as though ready to wrestle it out of/nHarry's hands and he reacted instinctively./n/n"Protegol"/n/nThe invisible shield erupted between Ron and/nHermione: The force of it knocked her backward onto/nthe floor. Spitting hair out of her mouth, she leapt up/nagain./n/n"Hermione!" said Harry. "Calm — "/n/n"I will not calm down!" she screamed. Never before/nhad he seen her lose control like this; she looked/nquite demented. "Give me back my wand! Give it back/nto me\"/n/n"Hermione, will you please — "/n/n"Don't you tell me what to do, Harry Potter!" she/nscreeched. "Don't you dare! Give it back now! And/nYOU!"/n/n/n/n/n/nShe was pointing at Ron in dire accusation: It was/nlike a malediction, and Harry could not blame Ron for/nretreating several steps./n/n"I came running after you! I called you! I begged you/nto come back!"/n/n"I know," Ron said, "Hermione, I'm sorry, I'm really —/n/n/n/n"Oh, you're sorry!"/n/nShe laughed, a high-pitched, out-of-control sound;/nRon looked at Harry for help, but Harry merely/ngrimaced his helplessness./n/n"You come back after weeks — weeks — and you/nthink it's all going to be all right if you just say/nsorry?"/n/n"Well, what else can I say?" Ron shouted, and Harry/nwas glad that Ron was fighting back./n/n"Oh, I don't know!" yelled Hermione with awful/nsarcasm. "Rack your brains, Ron, that should only/ntake a couple of seconds — "/n/n"Hermione," interjected Harry, who considered this a/nlow blow, "he just saved my — "/n/n"I don't care!" she screamed. "I don't care what he's/ndone! Weeks and weeks, we could have been dead for/nall he knew — "/n/n"I knew you weren't dead!" bellowed Ron, drowning/nher voice for the first time, and approaching as close/nas he could with the Shield Charm between them./n"Harry's all over the Prophet, all over the radio, they're/nlooking for you everywhere, all these rumors and/n/n/n/n/nmental stories, I knew I'd hear straight off if you were/ndead, you don't know what it's been like — "/n/n/n/n"What it's been like for you?"/n/nHer voice was now so shrill only bats would be able to/nhear it soon, but she had reached a level of/nindignation that rendered her temporarily speechless,/nand Ron seized his opportunity./n/n"I wanted to come back the minute I'd Disapparated,/nbut I walked straight into a gang of Snatchers,/nHermione, and I couldn't go anywhere!"/n/n"A gang of what?" asked Harry, as Hermione threw/nherself down into a chair with her arms and legs/ncrossed so tightly it seemed unlikely that she would/nunravel them for several years./n/n"Snatchers," said Ron. "They're everywhere — gangs/ntrying to earn gold by rounding up Muggle-borns and/nblood traitors, there's a reward from the Ministry for/neveryone captured. I was on my own and I look like I/nmight be school age; they got really excited, thought I/nwas a Muggle-born in hiding. I had to talk fast to get/nout of being dragged to the Ministry."/n/n"What did you say to them?"/n/n"Told them I was Stan Shunpike. First person I could/nthink of."/n/n"And they believed that?"/n/n"They weren't the brightest. One of them was/ndefinitely part troll, the smell off him. ..."/n/nRon glanced at Hermione, clearly hopeful she might/nsoften at this small instance of humor, but her/n/n/n/n/n/nexpression remained stony above her tightly knotted/nlimbs./n/n"Anyway, they had a row about whether I was Stan or/nnot. It was a bit pathetic to be honest, but there were/nstill five of them and only one of me and they'd taken/nmy wand. Then two of them got into a fight and while/nthe others were distracted I managed to hit the one/nholding me in the stomach, grabbed his wand,/nDisarmed the bloke holding mine, and Disapparated./n/nI didn't do it so well, Splinched myself again" — Ron/nheld up his right hand to show two missing/nfingernails; Hermione raised her eyebrows coldly —/n"and I came out miles from where you were. By the/ntime I got back to that bit of riverbank where we'd/nbeen ... you'd gone."/n/n"Gosh, what a gripping story," Hermione said in the/nlofty voice she adopted when wishing to wound. "You/nmust have been simply terrified. Meanwhile we went/nto Godric's Hollow and, let's think, what happened/nthere, Harry? Oh yes, You-Know- Who's snake turned/nup, it nearly killed both of us, and then You-Know-/nWho himself arrived and missed us by about a/nsecond."/n/n"What?" Ron said, gaping from her to Harry, but/nHermione ignored him./n/n"Imagine losing fingernails, Harry! That really puts/nour sufferings into perspective, doesn't it?"/n/n"Hermione," said Harry quietly, "Ron just saved my/nlife."/n/nShe appeared not to have heard him./n/n"One thing I would like to know, though," she said,/nfixing her eyes on a spot a foot over Ron's head. "How/n/n/n/n/n/nexactly did you find us tonight? That's important./n/nOnce we know, we'll be able to make sure we're not/nvisited by anyone else we don't want to see."/n/nRon glared at her, then pulled a small silver object/nfrom his jeans pocket./n/n"This."/n/nShe had to look at Ron to see what he was showing/nthem./n/n"The Deluminator?" she asked, so surprised she/nforgot to look cold and fierce./n/n"It doesn't just turn the lights on and off," said Ron. "I/ndon't know how it works or why it happened then and/nnot any other time, because I've been wanting to come/nback ever since I left. But I was listening to the radio/nreally early on Christmas morning and I heard ... I/nheard you."/n/nHe was looking at Hermione./n/n"You heard me on the radio?" she asked/nincredulously./n/n"No, I heard you coming out of my pocket. Your/nvoice," he held up the Deluminator again, "came out/nof this."/n/n"And what exactly did I say?" asked Hermione, her/ntone somewhere between skepticism and curiosity./n/n"My name. 'Ron.' And you said ... something about a/nwand. ..."/n/nHermione turned a fiery shade of scarlet. Harry/nremembered: It had been the first time Ron's name/n/n/n/n/n/nhad been said aloud by either of them since the day/nhe had left; Hermione had mentioned it when talking/nabout repairing Harry's wand./n/n"So I took it out," Ron went on, looking at the/nDeluminator, "and it didn't seem different or/nanything, but I was sure I'd heard you. So I clicked it./nAnd the light went out in my room, but another light/nappeared right outside the window."/n/nRon raised his empty hand and pointed in front of/nhim, his eyes focused on something neither Harry nor/nHermione could see./n/n"It was a ball of light, kind of pulsing, and bluish, like/nthat light you get around a Portkey, you know?"/n/n"Yeah," said Harry and Hermione together/nautomatically./n/n"I knew this was it," said Ron. "I grabbed my stuff and/npacked it, then I put on my rucksack and went out/ninto the garden./n/n"The little ball of light was hovering there, waiting for/nme, and when I came out it bobbed along a bit and I/nfollowed it behind the shed and then it ... well, it went/ninside me."/n/n"Sorry?" said Harry, sure he had not heard correctly./n/n"It sort of floated toward me," said Ron, illustrating/nthe movement with his free index finger, "right to my/nchest, and then — it just went straight through. It/nwas here," he touched a point close to his heart, "I/ncould feel it, it was hot. And once it was inside me I/nknew what I was supposed to do, I knew it would take/nme where I needed to go. So I Disapparated and came/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nout on the side of a hill. There was snow everywhere./n/n/n/n"We were there," said Harry. "We spent two nights/nthere, and the second night I kept thinking I could/nhear someone moving around in the dark and calling/nout!"/n/n"Yeah, well, that would've been me," said Ron. "Your/nprotective spells work, anyway, because I couldn't see/nyou and I couldn't hear you. I was sure you were/naround, though, so in the end I got in my sleeping bag/nand waited for one of you to appear. I thought you'd/nhave to show yourselves when you packed up the/ntent."/n/n"No, actually," said Hermione. "We've been/nDisapparating under the Invisibility Cloak as an extra/nprecaution. And we left really early, because, as Harry/nsays, we'd heard somebody blundering around."/n/n"Well, I stayed on that hill all day," said Ron. "I kept/nhoping you'd appear. But when it started to get dark I/nknew I must have missed you, so I clicked the/nDeluminator again, the blue light came out and went/ninside me, and I Disapparated and arrived here in/nthese woods. I still couldn't see you, so I just had to/nhope one of you would show yourselves in the end —/nand Harry did. Well, I saw the doe first, obviously."/n/n"You saw the what?" said Hermione sharply./n/nThey explained what had happened, and as the story/nof the silver doe and the sword in the pool unfolded,/nHermione frowned from one to the other of them,/nconcentrating so hard she forgot to keep her limbs/nlocked together./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But it must have been a Patronus!" she said./n"Couldn't you see who was casting it? Didn't you see/nanyone? And it led you to the sword! I can't believe/nthis! Then what happened?"/n/nRon explained how he had watched Harry jump into/nthe pool and had waited for him to resurface; how he/nhad realized that something was wrong, dived in, and/nsaved Harry, then returned for the sword. He got as/nfar as the opening of the locket, then hesitated, and/nHarry cut in./n/n" — and Ron stabbed it with the sword."/n/n"And ... and it went? Just like that?" she whispered./n/n"Well, it — it screamed," said Harry with half a glance/nat Ron. "Here."/n/nHe threw the locket into her lap; gingerly she picked it/nup and examined its punctured windows./n/nDeciding that it was at last safe to do so, Harry/nremoved the Shield Charm with a wave of Hermione's/nwand and turned to Ron./n/n"Did you just say you got away from the Snatchers/nwith a spare wand?"/n/n"What?" said Ron, who had been watching Hermione/nexamining the locket. "Oh — oh yeah."/n/nHe tugged open a buckle on his rucksack and pulled/na short, dark wand out of its pocket. "Here. I figured/nit's always handy to have a backup."/n/n"You were right," said Harry, holding out his hand./n"Mine's broken."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're kidding?" Ron said, but at that moment/nHermione got to her feet, and he looked apprehensive/nagain./n/nHermione put the vanquished Horcrux into the/nbeaded bag, then climbed back into her bed and/nsettled down without another word./n/nRon passed Harry the new wand./n/n"About the best you could hope for, I think,"/nmurmured Harry./n/n"Yeah," said Ron. "Could've been worse. Remember/nthose birds she set on me?"/n/n"I still haven't ruled it out," came Hermione's muffled/nvoice from beneath her blankets, but Harry saw Ron/nsmiling slightly as he pulled his maroon pajamas out/nof his rucksack./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Xenophilius Lovegood
text: /nHarry had not expected Hermione's anger to abate/novernight, and was therefore unsurprised that she/ncommunicated mainly by dirty looks and pointed/nsilences the next morning. Ron responded by/nmaintaining an unnaturally somber demeanor in her/npresence as an outward sign of continuing remorse./n/nIn fact, when all three of them were together Harry/nfelt like the only non-mourner at a poorly attended/nfuneral. During those few moments he spent alone/nwith Harry, however (collecting water and searching/nthe undergrowth for mushrooms), Ron became/nshamelessly cheery./n/n"Someone helped us," he kept saying. "Someone sent/nthat doe. Someone's on our side. One Horcrux down,/nmate!"/n/nBolstered by the destruction of the locket, they set to/ndebating the possible locations of the other/nHorcruxes, and even though they had discussed the/nmatter so often before, Harry felt optimistic, certain/nthat more breakthroughs would succeed the first./n/n/n/n/nHermione's sulkiness could not mar his buoyant/nspirits: The sudden upswing in their fortunes, the/nappearance of the mysterious doe, the recovery of/nGryffindor's sword, and above all, Ron's return, made/nHarry so happy that it was quite difficult to maintain/na straight face./n/nLate in the afternoon he and Ron escaped Hermione's/nbaleful presence again, and under the pretense of/nscouring the bare hedges for nonexistent/nblackberries, they continued their ongoing exchange/nof news. Harry had finally managed to tell Ron the/nwhole story of his and Hermione's various/nwanderings, right up to the full story of what had/nhappened at Godric's Hollow; Ron was now filling/nHarry in on everything he had discovered about the/nwider Wizarding world during his weeks away./n/n"... and how did you find out about the Taboo?" he/nasked Harry after explaining the many desperate/nattempts of Muggle-borns to evade the Ministry./n/n"The what?"/n/n"You and Hermione have stopped saying You-Know-/nWho's name!"/n/n"Oh, yeah. Well, it's just a bad habit we've slipped/ninto," said Harry. "But I haven't got a problem calling/nhim V — "/n/n"NO!" roared Ron, causing Harry to jump into the/nhedge and Hermione (nose buried in a book at the/ntent entrance) to scowl over at them. "Sorry," said/nRon, wrenching Harry back out of the brambles, "but/nthe name's been jinxed, Harry, that's how they track/npeople! Using his name breaks protective/nenchantments, it causes some kind of magical/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndisturbance — it's how they found us in Tottenham/nCourt Road!"/n/n/n/n"Because we used his name?"/n/n"Exactly! You've got to give them credit, it makes/nsense. It was only people who were serious about/nstanding up to him, like Dumbledore, who ever dared/nuse it. Now they've put a Taboo on it, anyone who/nsays it is trackable — quick-and-easy way to find/nOrder members! They nearly got Kingsley — "/n/n"You're kidding?"/n/n"Yeah, a bunch of Death Eaters cornered him, Bill/nsaid, but he fought his way out. He's on the run now,/njust like us." Ron scratched his chin thoughtfully with/nthe end of his wand. "You don't reckon Kingsley could/nhave sent that doe?"/n/n"His Patronus is a lynx, we saw it at the wedding,/nremember?"/n/n"Oh yeah ..."/n/nThey moved farther along the hedge, away from the/ntent and Hermione./n/n"Harry ... you don't reckon it could've been/nDumbledore?"/n/n"Dumbledore what?"/n/nRon looked a little embarrassed, but said in a low/nvoice, "Dumbledore ... the doe? I mean," Ron was/nwatching Harry out of the corners of his eyes, "he had/nthe real sword last, didn't he?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry did not laugh at Ron, because he understood/ntoo well the longing behind the question. The idea/nthat Dumbledore had managed to come back to them,/nthat he was watching over them, would have been/ninexpressibly comforting. He shook his head./n/n"Dumbledore's dead," he said. "I saw it happen, I saw/nthe body. He's definitely gone. Anyway, his Patronus/nwas a phoenix, not a doe."/n/n"Patronuses can change, though, can't they?" said/nRon. "Tonks's changed, didn't it?"/n/n"Yeah, but if Dumbledore was alive, why wouldn't he/nshow himself? Why wouldn't he just hand us the/nsword?"/n/n"Search me," said Ron. "Same reason he didn't give it/nto you while he was alive? Same reason he left you an/nold Snitch and Hermione a book of kids' stories?"/n/n"Which is what?" asked Harry, turning to look Ron/nfull in the face, desperate for the answer./n/n"I dunno," said Ron. "Sometimes I've thought, when/nI've been a bit hacked off, he was having a laugh or —/nor he just wanted to make it more difficult. But I don't/nthink so, not anymore. He knew what he was doing/nwhen he gave me the Deluminator, didn't he? He —/nwell," Ron's ears turned bright red and he became/nengrossed in a tuft of grass at his feet, which he/nprodded with his toe, "he must've known I'd run out/non you."/n/n"No," Harry corrected him. "He must've known you'd/nalways want to come back."/n/nRon looked grateful, but still awkward.
