Partly to/nchange the subject, Harry said, "Speaking of/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore, have you heard what Skeeter wrote/nabout him?"/n/n"Oh yeah," said Ron at once, "people are talking about/nit quite a lot. 'Course, if things were different, it'd be/nhuge news, Dumbledore being pals with Grindelwald,/nbut now it's just something to laugh about for people/nwho didn't like Dumbledore, and a bit of a slap in the/nface for everyone who thought he was such a good/nbloke. I don't know that it's such a big deal, though./nHe was really young when they — "/n/n"Our age," said Harry, just as he had retorted to/nHermione, and something in his face seemed to/ndecide Ron against pursuing the subject./n/nA large spider sat in the middle of a frosted web in the/nbrambles. Harry took aim at it with the wand Ron had/ngiven him the previous night, which Hermione had/nsince condescended to examine, and had decided was/nmade of blackthorn./n/n"Engorgio."/n/nThe spider gave a little shiver, bouncing slightly in the/nweb. Harry tried again. This time the spider grew/nslightly larger./n/n"Stop that," said Ron sharply. "I'm sorry I said/nDumbledore was young, okay?"/n/nHarry had forgotten Ron's hatred of spiders./n/n"Sorry — Reducio."/n/nThe spider did not shrink. Harry looked down at the/nblackthorn wand. Every minor spell he had cast with/nit so far that day had seemed less powerful than those/nhe had produced with his phoenix wand. The new one/n/n/n/n/n/nfelt intrusively unfamiliar, like having somebody else's/nhand sewn to the end of his arm./n/n"You just need to practice," said Hermione, who had/napproached them noiselessly from behind and had/nstood watching anxiously as Harry tried to enlarge/nand reduce the spider. "It's all a matter of confidence,/nHarry."/n/nHe knew why she wanted it to be all right: She still/nfelt guilty about breaking his wand. He bit back the/nretort that sprang to his lips, that she could take the/nblackthorn wand if she thought it made no difference,/nand he would have hers instead. Keen for them all to/nbe friends again, however, he agreed; but when Ron/ngave Hermione a tentative smile, she stalked off and/nvanished behind her book once more./n/nAll three of them returned to the tent when darkness/nfell, and Harry took first watch. Sitting in the/nentrance, he tried to make the blackthorn wand/nlevitate small stones at his feet; but his magic still/nseemed clumsier and less powerful than it had done/nbefore. Hermione was lying on her bunk reading,/nwhile Ron, after many nervous glances up at her, had/ntaken a small wooden wireless out of his rucksack/nand started to try and tune it./n/n"There's this one program," he told Harry in a low/nvoice, "that tells the news like it really is. All the/nothers are on You- Know- Who's side and are following/nthe Ministry line, but this one ... you wait till you/nhear it, it's great. Only they can't do it every night,/nthey have to keep changing locations in case they're/nraided, and you need a password to tune in. .../n/nTrouble is, I missed the last one. ..."/n/nHe drummed lightly on the top of the radio with his/nwand, muttering random words under his breath. He/n/n/n/n/n/nthrew Hermione many covert glances, plainly fearing/nan angry outburst, but for all the notice she took of/nhim he might not have been there. For ten minutes or/nso Ron tapped and muttered, Hermione turned the/npages of her book, and Harry continued to practice/nwith the blackthorn wand./n/nFinally Hermione climbed down from her bunk. Ron/nceased his tapping at once./n/n"If it's annoying you, 111 stop!" he told Hermione/nnervously./n/nHermione did not deign to respond, but approached/nHarry./n/n"We need to talk," she said./n/nHe looked at the book still clutched in her hand. It/nwas The Life and Lies of Albus Dumbledore./n/n"What?" he said apprehensively. It flew through his/nmind that there was a chapter on him in there; he/nwas not sure he felt up to hearing Rita's version of his/nrelationship with Dumbledore. Hermione 's answer,/nhowever, was completely unexpected./n/n"I want to go and see Xenophilius Lovegood."/n/nHe stared at her./n/n"Sorry?"/n/n"Xenophilius Lovegood. Luna's father. I want to go/nand talk to him!"/n/n"Er — why?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe took a deep breath, as though bracing herself,/nand said, "It's that mark, the mark in Beedle the/nBard. Look at this!"/n/nShe thrust The Life and Lies ofAlbus Dumbledore/nunder Harry's unwilling eyes and he saw a/nphotograph of the original letter that Dumbledore had/nwritten Grindelwald, with Dumbledore 's familiar thin,/nslanting handwriting. He hated seeing absolute proof/nthat Dumbledore really had written those words, that/nthey had not been Rita's invention./n/n"The signature," said Hermione. "Look at the/nsignature, Harry!"/n/nHe obeyed. For a moment he had no idea what she/nwas talking about, but, looking more closely with the/naid of his lit wand, he saw that Dumbledore had/nreplaced the A of Albus with a tiny version of the/nsame triangular mark inscribed upon The Tales of/nBeedle the Bard./n/n"Er — what are you — ?" said Ron tentatively, but/nHermione quelled him with a look and turned back to/nHarry./n/n"It keeps cropping up, doesn't it?" she said. "I know/nViktor said it was Grindelwald 's mark, but it was/ndefinitely on that old grave in Godric's Hollow, and/nthe dates on the headstone were long before/nGrindelwald came along! And now this! Well, we can't/nask Dumbledore or Grindelwald what it means — I/ndon't even know whether Grindelwald's still alive —/nbut we can ask Mr. Lovegood. He was wearing the/nsymbol at the wedding. I'm sure this is important,/nHarry!"/n/nHarry did not answer immediately. He looked into her/nintense, eager face and then out into the surrounding/n/n/n/n/n/ndarkness, thinking. After a long pause he said,/n"Hermione, we don't need another Godric's Hollow./n/nWe talked ourselves into going there, and — "/n/n"But it keeps appearing, Harry! Dumbledore left me/nThe Tales of Beedle the Bard, how do you know we're/nnot supposed to find out about the sign?"/n/n"Here we go again!" Harry felt slightly exasperated./n/n"We keep trying to convince ourselves Dumbledore left/nus secret signs and clues — "/n/n"The Deluminator turned out to be pretty useful,"/npiped up Ron. "I think Hermione's right, I think we/nought to go and see Lovegood."/n/nHarry threw him a dark look. He was quite sure that/nRon's support of Hermione had little to do with a/ndesire to know the meaning of the triangular rune./n/n"It won't be like Godric's Hollow," Ron added,/n"Lovegood's on your side, Harry, The Quibbler's been/nfor you all along, it keeps telling everyone they've got/nto help you!"/n/n"I'm sure this is important!" said Hermione earnestly./n/n"But don't you think if it was, Dumbledore would/nhave told me about it before he died?"/n/n"Maybe ... maybe it's something you need to find out/nfor yourself," said Hermione with a faint air of/nclutching at straws./n/n"Yeah," said Ron sycophantically, "that makes sense."/n/n"No, it doesn't," snapped Hermione, "but I still think/nwe ought to talk to Mr. Lovegood. A symbol that links/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore, Grindelwald, and Godric's Hollow?/nHarry, I'm sure we ought to know about this!"/n/n/n/n"I think we should vote on it," said Ron. "Those in/nfavor of going to see Lovegood — "/n/nHis hand flew into the air before Hermione's. Her lips/nquivered suspiciously as she raised her own./n/n"Outvoted, Harry, sorry," said Ron, clapping him on/nthe back./n/n"Fine," said Harry, half amused, half irritated. "Only,/nonce we've seen Lovegood, let's try and look for some/nmore Horcruxes, shall we? Where do the Lovegoods/nlive, anyway? Do either of you know?"/n/n"Yeah, they're not far from my place," said Ron. "I/ndunno exactly where, but Mum and Dad always point/ntoward the hills whenever they mention them./nShouldn't be hard to find."/n/nWhen Hermione had returned to her bunk, Harry/nlowered his voice./n/n"You only agreed to try and get back in her good/nbooks."/n/n"All's fair in love and war," said Ron brightly, "and/nthis is a bit of both. Cheer up, it's the Christmas/nholidays, Luna 'll be home!"/n/nThey had an excellent view of the village of Ottery St./nCatchpole from the breezy hillside to which they/nDisapparated next morning. From their high vantage/npoint the village looked like a collection of toy houses/nin the great slanting shafts of sunlight stretching to/nearth in the breaks between clouds. They stood for a/nminute or two looking toward the Burrow, their hands/n/n/n/n/nshadowing their eyes, but all they could make out/nwere the high hedges and trees of the orchard, which/nafforded the crooked little house protection from/nMuggle eyes./n/n"It's weird, being this near, but not going to visit,"/nsaid Ron./n/n"Well, it's not like you haven't just seen them. You/nwere there for Christmas," said Hermione coldly./n/n"I wasn't at the Burrow!" said Ron with an/nincredulous laugh. "Do you think I was going to go/nback there and tell them all I'd walked out on you?/nYeah, Fred and George would've been great about it./nAnd Ginny, she'd have been really understanding."/n/n"But where have you been, then?" asked Hermione,/nsurprised./n/n"Bill and Fleur's new place. Shell Cottage. Bill's/nalways been decent to me. He — he wasn't impressed/nwhen he heard what I'd done, but he didn't go on/nabout it. He knew I was really sorry. None of the rest/nof the family know I was there. Bill told Mum he and/nFleur weren't going home for Christmas because they/nwanted to spend it alone. You know, first holiday after/nthey were married. I don't think Fleur minded. You/nknow how much she hates Celestina Warbeck."/n/nRon turned his back on the Burrow./n/n"Let's try up here," he said, leading the way over the/ntop of the hill./n/nThey walked for a few hours, Harry, at Hermione 's/ninsistence, hidden beneath the Invisibility Cloak. The/ncluster of low hills appeared to be uninhabited apart/nfrom one small cottage, which seemed deserted./n/n/n/n/n/n"Do you think it's theirs, and they've gone away for/nChristmas?" said Hermione, peering through the/nwindow at a neat little kitchen with geraniums on the/nwindowsill. Ron snorted./n/n"Listen, I've got a feeling you'd be able to tell who lived/nthere if you looked through the Lovegoods' window./nLet's try the next lot of hills."/n/nSo they Disapparated a few miles farther north./n/n"Aha!" shouted Ron, as the wind whipped their hair/nand clothes. Ron was pointing upward, toward the top/nof the hill on which they had appeared, where a most/nstrange-looking house rose vertically against the sky,/na great black cylinder with a ghostly moon hanging/nbehind it in the afternoon sky. "That's got to be/nLuna's house, who else would live in a place like that?/nIt looks like a giant rook!"/n/n"It's nothing like a bird," said Hermione, frowning at/nthe tower./n/n"I was talking about a chess rook," said Ron. "A castle/nto you."/n/nRon's legs were the longest and he reached the top of/nthe hill first. When Harry and Hermione caught up/nwith him, panting and clutching stitches in their/nsides, they found him grinning broadly./n/n"It's theirs," said Ron. "Look."/n/nThree hand-painted signs had been tacked to a/nbroken-down gate. The first read,/n/nTHE QUIBBLER. EDITOR: X. LOVEGOOD/n/nthe second,/n/n/n/n/n/nPICK YOUR OWN MISTLETOE/n/n/n/nthe third,/n/nKEEP OFF THE DIRIGIBLE PLUMS/n/nThe gate creaked as they opened it. The zigzagging/npath leading to the front door was overgrown with a/nvariety of odd plants, including a bush covered in the/norange radishlike fruit Luna sometimes wore as/nearrings. Harry thought he recognized a Snargaluff/nand gave the wizened stump a wide berth. Two aged/ncrab apple trees, bent with the wind, stripped of/nleaves but still heavy with berry-sized red fruits and/nbushy crowns of white-beaded mistletoe, stood/nsentinel on either side of the front door. A little owl/nwith a slightly flattened, hawklike head peered down/nat them from one of the branches./n/n"You'd better take off the Invisibility Cloak, Harry,"/nsaid Hermione. "It's you Mr. Lovegood wants to help,/nnot us."/n/nHe did as she suggested, handing her the Cloak to/nstow in the beaded bag. She then rapped three times/non the thick black door, which was studded with iron/nnails and bore a knocker shaped like an eagle./n/nBarely ten seconds passed, then the door was flung/nopen and there stood Xenophilius Lovegood, barefoot/nand wearing what appeared to be a stained nightshirt/nHis long white candyfloss hair was dirty and/nunkempt. Xenophilius had been positively dapper at/nBill and Fleur's wedding by comparison./n/n"What? What is it? Who are you? What do you want?"/nhe cried in a high-pitched, querulous voice, looking/nfirst at Hermione, then at Ron, and finally at Harry,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nupon which his mouth fell open in a perfect, comical/n/nO./n/n/n/n"Hello, Mr. Lovegood," said Harry, holding out his/nhand. "I'm Harry, Harry Potter."/n/nXenophilius did not take Harry's hand, although the/neye that was not pointing inward at his nose slid/nstraight to the scar on Harry's forehead./n/n"Would it be okay if we came in?" asked Harry./n"There's something we'd like to ask you."/n/n"I ... I'm not sure that's advisable," whispered/nXenophilius. He swallowed and cast a quick look/naround the garden. "Rather a shock ... My word ... I/n... I'm afraid I don't really think I ought to — "/n/n"It won't take long," said Harry, slightly disappointed/nby this less-than-warm welcome./n/n"I — oh, all right then. Come in, quickly. QuicklyV'/n/nThey were barely over the threshold when Xenophilius/nslammed the door shut behind them. They were/nstanding in the most peculiar kitchen Harry had ever/nseen. The room was perfectly circular, so that it felt/nlike being inside a giant pepper pot. Everything was/ncurved to fit the walls — the stove, the sink, and the/ncupboards — and all of it had been painted with/nflowers, insects, and birds in bright primary colors./nHarry thought he recognized Luna's style: The effect,/nin such an enclosed space, was slightly/noverwhelming./n/nIn the middle of the floor, a wrought-iron spiral/nstaircase led to the upper levels. There was a great/ndeal of clattering and banging coming from overhead:/nHarry wondered what Luna could be doing./n/n/n/n/n/n"You'd better come up," said Xenophilius, still looking/nextremely uncomfortable, and he led the way./n/nThe room above seemed to be a combination of living/nroom and workplace, and as such, was even more/ncluttered than the kitchen. Though much smaller and/nentirely round, the room somewhat resembled the/nRoom of Requirement on the unforgettable occasion/nthat it had transformed itself into a gigantic labyrinth/ncomprised of centuries of hidden objects. There were/npiles upon piles of books and papers on every surface./nDelicately made models of creatures Harry did not/nrecognize, all flapping wings or snapping jaws, hung/nfrom the ceiling./n/nLuna was not there: The thing that was making such/na racket was a wooden object covered in magically/nturning cogs and wheels. It looked like the bizarre/noffspring of a workbench and a set of old shelves, but/nafter a moment Harry deduced that it was an old-/nfashioned printing press, due to the fact that it was/nchurning out Quibblers./n/n"Excuse me," said Xenophilius, and he strode over to/nthe machine, seized a grubby tablecloth from beneath/nan immense number of books and papers, which all/ntumbled onto the floor, and threw it over the press,/nsomewhat muffling the loud bangs and clatters. He/nthen faced Harry./n/n"Why have you come here?"/n/nBefore Harry could speak, however, Hermione let out/na small cry of shock./n/n"Mr. Lovegood — what's that?"/n/nShe was pointing at an enormous, gray spiral horn,/nnot unlike that of a unicorn, which had been/n/n/n/n/n/nmounted on the wall, protruding several feet into the/nroom./n/n"It is the horn of a Crumple-Horned Snorkack," said/nXenophilius./n/n"No it isn't!" said Hermione./n/n"Hermione," muttered Harry, embarrassed, "now's not/nthe moment — "/n/n"But Harry, it's an Erumpent horn! It's a Class B/nTradeable Material and it's an extraordinarily/ndangerous thing to have in a house!"/n/n"How d'you know it's an Erumpent horn?" asked Ron,/nedging away from the horn as fast as he could, given/nthe extreme clutter of the room./n/n"There's a description in Fantastic Beasts and Where/nto Find Them .! Mr. Lovegood, you need to get rid of it/nstraightaway, don't you know it can explode at the/nslightest touch?"/n/n"The Crumple-Horned Snorkack," said Xenophilius/nvery clearly, a mulish look upon his face, "is a shy/nand highly magical creature, and its horn — "/n/n"Mr. Lovegood, I recognize the grooved markings/naround the base, that's an Erumpent horn and it's/nincredibly dangerous — I don't know where you got it/n/n/n/n"I bought it," said Xenophilius dogmatically, "two/nweeks ago, from a delightful young wizard who knew/nof my interest in the exquisite Snorkack. A Christmas/nsurprise for my Luna. Now," he said, turning to/nHarry, "why exactly have you come here, Mr. Potter?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"We need some help," said Harry, before Hermione/ncould start again./n/n/n/n"Ah," said Xenophilius. "Help. Hmm."/n/nHis good eye moved again to Harry's scar. He seemed/nsimultaneously terrified and mesmerized./n/n"Yes. The thing is ... helping Harry Potter ... rather/ndangerous ..."/n/n"Aren't you the one who keeps telling everyone it's/ntheir first duty to help Harry?" said Ron. "In that/nmagazine of yours?"/n/nXenophilius glanced behind him at the concealed/nprinting press, still banging and clattering beneath/nthe tablecloth./n/n"Er — yes, I have expressed that view. However — "/n/n"That's for everyone else to do, not you personally?"/nsaid Ron./n/nXenophilius did not answer. He kept swallowing, his/neyes darting between the three of them. Harry had the/nimpression that he was undergoing some painful/ninternal struggle./n/n"Where's Luna?" asked Hermione. "Let's see what she/nthinks."/n/nXenophilius gulped. He seemed to be steeling himself./nFinally he said in a shaky voice difficult to hear over/nthe noise of the printing press, "Luna is down at the/nstream, fishing for Freshwater Plimpies. She ... she/nwill like to see you. I'll go and call her and then —/nyes, very well. I shall try to help you."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe disappeared down the spiral staircase and they/nheard the front door open and close. They looked at/neach other./n/n"Cowardly old wart," said Ron. "Luna's got ten times/nhis guts."/n/n"He's probably worried about what'll happen to them/nif the Death Eaters find out I was here," said Harry./n/n"Well, I agree with Ron," said Hermione. "Awful old/nhypocrite, telling everyone else to help you and trying/nto worm out of it himself. And for heaven's sake keep/naway from that horn."/n/nHarry crossed to the window on the far side of the/nroom. He could see a stream, a thin, glittering ribbon/nlying far below them at the base of the hill. They were/nvery high up; a bird fluttered past the window as he/nstared in the direction of the Burrow, now invisible/nbeyond another line of hills. Ginny was over there/nsomewhere. They were closer to each other today than/nthey had been since Bill and Fleur's wedding, but she/ncould have no idea he was gazing toward her now,/nthinking of her. He supposed he ought to be glad of it;/nanyone he came into contact with was in danger,/nXenophilius's attitude proved that./n/nHe turned away from the window and his gaze fell/nupon another peculiar object standing upon the/ncluttered, curved sideboard: a stone bust of a/nbeautiful but austere-looking witch wearing a most/nbizarre-looking headdress. Two objects that/nresembled golden ear trumpets curved out from the/nsides. A tiny pair of glittering blue wings was stuck to/na leather strap that ran over the top of her head,/nwhile one of the orange radishes had been stuck to a/nsecond strap around her forehead./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Look at this," said Harry./n/n/n/n"Fetching," said Ron. "Surprised he didn't wear that/nto the wedding."/n/nThey heard the front door close, and a moment later/nXenophilius had climbed back up the spiral staircase/ninto the room, his thin legs now encased in/nWellington boots, bearing a tray of ill-assorted/nteacups and a steaming teapot./n/n"Ah, you have spotted my pet invention," he said,/nshoving the tray into Hermione's arms and joining/nHarry at the statue's side. "Modeled, fittingly enough,/nupon the head of the beautiful Rowena Ravenclaw./n/n'Wit beyond measure is man's greatest treasureV "/n/nHe indicated the objects like ear trumpets./n/n"These are the Wrackspurt siphons — to remove all/nsources of distraction from the thinker's immediate/narea. Here," he pointed out the tiny wings, "a billywig/npropeller, to induce an elevated frame of mind./nFinally," he pointed to the orange radish, "the/nDirigible Plum, so as to enhance the ability to accept/nthe extraordinary."/n/nXenophilius strode back to the tea tray, which/nHermione had managed to balance precariously on/none of the cluttered side tables./n/n"May I offer you all an infusion of Gurdyroots?" said/nXenophilius. "We make it ourselves." As he started to/npour out the drink, which was as deeply purple as/nbeetroot juice, he added, "Luna is down beyond/nBottom Bridge, she is most excited that you are here./nShe ought not to be too long, she has caught nearly/nenough Plimpies to make soup for all of us. Do sit/ndown and help yourselves to sugar./n/n/n/n/n/n"Now," he removed a tottering pile of papers from an/narmchair and sat down, his Wellingtoned legs/ncrossed, "how may I help you, Mr. Potter?"/n/n"Well," said Harry, glancing at Hermione, who nodded/nencouragingly, "it's about that symbol you were/nwearing around your neck at Bill and Fleur's/nwedding, Mr. Lovegood. We wondered what it meant."/n/nXenophilius raised his eyebrows./n/n"Are you referring to the sign of the Deathly Hallows?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Tale Of The Three Brothers
text: /nHarry turned to look at Ron and Hermione. Neither of/nthem seemed to have understood what Xenophilius/nhad said either./n/n"The Deathly Hallows?"/n/n"That's right," said Xenophilius. "You haven't heard of/nthem? I'm not surprised. Very, very few wizards/nbelieve. Witness that knuckle-headed young man at/nyour brother's wedding," he nodded at Ron, "who/nattacked me for sporting the symbol of a well-known/nDark wizard! Such ignorance. There is nothing Dark/nabout the Hallows — at least, not in that crude sense./nOne simply uses the symbol to reveal oneself to other/nbelievers, in the hope that they might help one with/nthe Quest."/n/nHe stirred several lumps of sugar into his Gurdyroot/ninfusion and drank some./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'm sorry," said Harry. "I still don't really/nunderstand."/n/nTo be polite, he took a sip from his cup too, and/nalmost gagged: The stuff was quite disgusting, as/nthough someone had liquidized bogey-flavored Every/nFlavor Beans./n/n"Well, you see, believers seek the Deathly Hallows,"/nsaid Xenophilius, smacking his lips in apparent/nappreciation of the Gurdyroot infusion./n/n"But what are the Deathly Hallows?" asked Hermione./n/nXenophilius set aside his empty teacup./n/n"I assume that you are all familiar with "The Tale of/nthe Three Brothers'?"/n/nHarry said, "No," but Ron and Hermione both said,/n"Yes." Xenophilius nodded gravely./n/n"Well, well, Mr. Potter, the whole thing starts with/nThe Tale of the Three Brothers' ... The printing press blocking the stairs was/nvibrating: Xenophilius was trying to shift it using a/nHover Charm. Harry did not know what Hermione/nwas waiting for./n/n"Hold tight," she whispered. "Hold tight ... any second/n/n/n/nXenophilius's paper- white face appeared over the top/nof the sideboard./n/n"Obliviate\" cried Hermione, pointing her wand first/ninto his face, then at the floor beneath them./n"Deprimo\"/n/nShe had blasted a hole in the sitting room floor. They/nfell like boulders, Harry still holding onto her hand for/ndear life; there was a scream from below, and he/nglimpsed two men trying to get out of the way as vast/nquantities of rubble and broken furniture rained all/naround them from the shattered ceiling. Hermione/ntwisted in midair and the thundering of the collapsing/nhouse rang in Harry's ears as she dragged him once/nmore into darkness./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Deathly Hallows
text: /nHarry fell, panting, onto grass and scrambled up at/nonce. They seemed to have landed in the corner of a/nfield at dusk; Hermione was already running in a/ncircle around them, waving her wand./n/n"Protego Totalum ... Salvio Hexia ..."/n/n"That treacherous old bleeder!" Ron panted, emerging/nfrom beneath the Invisibility Cloak and throwing it to/nHarry. "Hermione, you're a genius, a total genius, I/ncan't believe we got out of that!"/n/n" Cave Inimicum ... Didn't I say it was an Erumpent/nhorn, didn't I tell him? And now his house has been/nblown apart!"/n/n"Serves him right," said Ron, examining his torn jeans/nand the cuts to his legs. "What d'you reckon they'll do/nto him?"/n/n"Oh, I hope they don't kill him!" groaned Hermione./n"That's why I wanted the Death Eaters to get a/n/n/n/n/n/n/nglimpse of Harry before we left, so they knew/nXenophilius hadn't been lying!"/n/n/n/n"Why hide me, though?" asked Ron./n/n"You're supposed to be in bed with spattergroit, Ron!/nThey've kidnapped Luna because her father/nsupported Harry! What would happen to your family if/nthey knew you're with him?"/n/n"But what about your mum and dad?"/n/n"They're in Australia," said Hermione. "They should/nbe all right. They don't know anything."/n/n"You're a genius," Ron repeated, looking awed./n/n"Yeah, you are, Hermione," agreed Harry fervently. "I/ndon't know what we'd do without you."/n/nShe beamed, but became solemn at once./n/n"What about Luna?"/n/n"Well, if they're telling the truth and she's still alive —/n" began Ron./n/n"Don't say that, don't say it!" squealed Hermione./n/n"She must be alive, she must!"/n/n"Then she'll be in Azkaban, I expect," said Ron./n"Whether she survives the place, though ... Loads/ndon't. ..."/n/n"She will," said Harry. He could not bear to/ncontemplate the alternative. "She's tough, Luna,/nmuch tougher than you'd think. She's probably/nteaching all the inmates about Wrackspurts and/nNargles."/n/n/n/n/n/n"I hope you're right," said Hermione. She passed a/nhand over her eyes. "I'd feel so sorry for Xenophilius if/n/n/n/n" — if he hadn't just tried to sell us to the Death/nEaters, yeah," said Ron./n/nThey put up the tent and retreated inside it, where/nRon made them tea. After their narrow escape, the/nchilly, musty old place felt like home: safe, familiar,/nand friendly./n/n"Oh, why did we go there?" groaned Hermione after a/nfew minutes' silence. "Harry, you were right, it was/nGodric's Hollow all over again, a complete waste of/ntime! The Deathly Hallows ... such rubbish .../nalthough actually," a sudden thought seemed to have/nstruck her, "he might have made it all up, mightn't/nhe? He probably doesn't believe in the Deathly/nHallows at all, he just wanted to keep us talking until/nthe Death Eaters arrived!"/n/n"I don't think so," said Ron. "It's a damn sight harder/nmaking stuff up when you're under stress than you'd/nthink. I found that out when the Snatchers caught/nme. It was much easier pretending to be Stan,/nbecause I knew a bit about him, than inventing a/nwhole new person. Old Lovegood was under loads of/npressure, trying to make sure we stayed put. I reckon/nhe told us the truth, or what he thinks is the truth,/njust to keep us talking."/n/n"Well, I don't suppose it matters," sighed Hermione./n"Even if he was being honest, I never heard such a lot/nof nonsense in all my life."/n/n"Hang on, though," said Ron. "The Chamber of/nSecrets was supposed to be a myth, wasn't it?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But the Deathly Hallows can't exist, Ron!"/n/n/n/n"You keep saying that, but one of them can," said/nRon. "Harry's Invisibility Cloak — "/n/n" The Tale of the Three Brothers' is a story," said/nHermione firmly. "A story about how humans are/nfrightened of death. If surviving was as simple as/nhiding under the Invisibility Cloak, we'd have/neverything we need already!"/n/n"I don't know. We could do with an unbeatable wand,"/nsaid Harry, turning the blackthorn wand he so/ndisliked over in his fingers./n/n"There's no such thing, Harry!"/n/n"You said there have been loads of wands — the/nDeathstick and whatever they were called — "/n/n"All right, even if you want to kid yourself the Elder/nWand's real, what about the Resurrection Stone?" Her/nfingers sketched quotation marks around the name,/nand her tone dripped sarcasm. "No magic can raise/nthe dead, and that's that!"/n/n"When my wand connected with You-Know-Who's, it/nmade my mum and dad appear ... and Cedric ..."/n/n"But they weren't really back from the dead, were/nthey?" said Hermione. "Those kinds of — of pale/nimitations aren't the same as truly bringing someone/nback to life."/n/n"But she, the girl in the tale, didn't really come back,/ndid she? The story says that once people are dead,/nthey belong with the dead. But the second brother/nstill got to see her and talk to her, didn't he? He even/nlived with her for a while. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/nHe saw concern and something less easily definable/nin Hermione's expression. Then, as she glanced at/nRon, Harry realized that it was fear: He had scared/nher with his talk of living with dead people./n/n"So that Peverell bloke who's buried in Godric's/nHollow," he said hastily, trying to sound robustly/nsane, "you don't know anything about him, then?"/n/n"No," she replied, looking relieved at the change of/nsubject. "I looked him up after I saw the mark on his/ngrave; if he'd been anyone famous or done anything/nimportant, I'm sure he'd be in one of our books. The/nonly place I've managed to find the name 'Peverell' is/nNature's Nobility: A Wizarding Genealogy. I borrowed/nit from Kreacher," she explained as Ron raised his/neyebrows. "It lists the pure-blood families that are/nnow extinct in the male line. Apparently the Peverells/nwere one of the earliest families to vanish."/n/n" 'Extinct in the male line'?" repeated Ron./n/n"It means the name's died out," said Hermione,/n"centuries ago, in the case of the Peverells. They could/nstill have descendants, though, they'd just be called/nsomething different."/n/nAnd then it came to Harry in one shining piece, the/nmemory that had stirred at the sound of the name/n"Peverell": a filthy old man brandishing an ugly ring/nin the face of a Ministry official, and he cried aloud,/n"Marvolo Gaunt!"/n/n"Sorry?" said Ron and Hermione together./n/n"Marvolo Gaunti You -Know- Who's grandfather! In the/nPensieve! With Dumbledore! Marvolo Gaunt said he/nwas descended from the Peverells!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nRon and Hermione looked bewildered./n/n/n/n"The ring, the ring that became the Horcrux, Marvolo/nGaunt said it had the Peverell coat of arms on it! I/nsaw him waving it in the bloke from the Ministry's/nface, he nearly shoved it up his nose!"/n/n"The Peverell coat of arms?" said Hermione sharply./n"Could you see what it looked like?"/n/n"Not really," said Harry, trying to remember. "There/nwas nothing fancy on there, as far as I could see;/nmaybe a few scratches. I only ever saw it really close/nup after it had been cracked open."/n/nHarry saw Hermione 's comprehension in the sudden/nwidening of her eyes. Ron was looking from one to the/nother, astonished./n/n"Blimey ... You reckon it was this sign again? The/nsign of the Hallows?"/n/n"Why not?" said Harry excitedly. "Marvolo Gaunt was/nan ignorant old git who lived like a pig, all he cared/nabout was his ancestry. If that ring had been passed/ndown through the centuries, he might not have/nknown what it really was. There were no books in that/nhouse, and trust me, he wasn't the type to read fairy/ntales to his kids. He'd have loved to think the/nscratches on the stone were a coat of arms, because/nas far as he was concerned, having pure blood made/nyou practically royal."/n/n"Yes ... and that's all very interesting," said Hermione/ncautiously, "but Harry, if you're thinking what I think/nyou're think — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, why not? Why not?" said Harry, abandoning/ncaution. "It was a stone, wasn't it?" He looked at Ron/nfor support. "What if it was the Resurrection Stone?"/n/nRon's mouth fell open./n/n"Blimey — but would it still work if Dumbledore broke/n— ?"/n/n"Work? Work? Ron, it never worked! There's no such/nthing as a Resurrection Stone\"/n/nHermione had leapt to her feet, looking exasperated/nand angry. "Harry, you're trying to fit everything into/nthe Hallows story — "/n/n"Fit everything in?" he repeated. "Hermione, it fits of/nits own accord! I know the sign of the Deathly Hallows/nwas on that stone! Gaunt said he was descended from/nthe Peverells!"/n/n"A minute ago you told us you never saw the mark on/nthe stone properly!"/n/n"Where d'you reckon the ring is now?" Ron asked/nHarry. "What did Dumbledore do with it after he/nbroke it open?"/n/nBut Harry's imagination was racing ahead, far beyond/nRon and Hermione 's. .../n/nThree objects, or Hallows, which, if united, will make/nthe possessor master of Death . . . Master . . . Conqueror/n... Vanquisher ... The last enemy that shall be/ndestroyed is death. . . ./n/nAnd he saw himself, possessor of the Hallows, facing/nVoldemort, whose Horcruxes were no match .../n/nNeither can live while the other survives. ... Was this/n/n/n/n/n/nthe answer? Hallows versus Horcruxes? Was there a/nway, after all, to ensure that he was the one who/ntriumphed? If he were the master of the Deathly/nHallows, would he be safe?/n/n"Harry?"/n/nBut he scarcely heard Hermione: He had pulled out/nhis Invisibility Cloak and was running it through his/nfingers, the cloth supple as water, light as air. He had/nnever seen anything to equal it in his nearly seven/nyears in the Wizarding world. The Cloak was exactly/nwhat Xenophilius had described: A cloak that really/nand truly renders the wearer completely invisible, and/nendures eternally, giving constant and impenetrable/nconcealment, no matter what spells are cast at it .../n/nAnd then, with a gasp, he remembered —/n/n"Dumbledore had my Cloak the night my parents/ndied!"/n/nHis voice shook and he could feel the color in his face,/nbut he did not care./n/n"My mum told Sirius that Dumbledore borrowed the/nCloak! This is why! He wanted to examine it, because/nhe thought it was the third Hallow! Ignotus Peverell is/nburied in Godric's Hollow. ..." Harry was walking/nblindly around the tent, feeling as though great new/nvistas of truth were opening all around him. "He's my/nancestor! I'm descended from the third brother! It all/nmakes sense!"/n/nHe felt armed in certainty, in his belief in the Hallows,/nas if the mere idea of possessing them was giving him/nprotection, and he felt joyous as he turned back to/nthe other two./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry," said Hermione again, but he was busy/nundoing the pouch around his neck, his fingers/nshaking hard./n/n"Read it," he told her, pushing his mother's letter into/nher hand. "Read it! Dumbledore had the Cloak,/nHermione! Why else would he want it? He didn't need/na Cloak, he could perform a Disillusionment Charm/nso powerful that he made himself completely invisible/nwithout one!"/n/nSomething fell to the floor and rolled, glittering, under/na chair: He had dislodged the Snitch when he pulled/nout the letter. He stooped to pick it up, and then the/nnewly tapped spring of fabulous discoveries threw/nhim another gift, and shock and wonder erupted/ninside him so that he shouted out./n/n"IT'S IN HERE! He left me the ring — it's in the/nSnitch!"/n/n"You — you reckon?"/n/nHe could not understand why Ron looked taken/naback. It was so obvious, so clear to Harry:/n/nEverything fit, everything. . . . His Cloak was the third/nHallow, and when he discovered how to open the/nSnitch he would have the second, and then all he/nneeded to do was find the first Hallow, the Elder/nWand, and then —/n/nBut it was as though a curtain fell on a lit stage: All/nhis excitement, all his hope and happiness were/nextinguished at a stroke, and he stood alone in the/ndarkness, and the glorious spell was broken./n/n"That's what he's after."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe change in his voice made Ron and Hermione look/neven more scared./n/n"You-Know-Who's after the Elder Wand."/n/nHe turned his back on their strained, incredulous/nfaces. He knew it was the truth. It all made sense./nVoldemort was not seeking a new wand; he was/nseeking an old wand, a very old wand indeed. Harry/nwalked to the entrance of the tent, forgetting about/nRon and Hermione as he looked out into the night,/nthinking. .../n/nVoldemort had been raised in a Muggle orphanage./nNobody could have told him The Tales of Beedle the/nBard when he was a child, any more than Harry had/nheard them. Hardly any wizards believed in the/nDeathly Hallows. Was it likely that Voldemort knew/nabout them?/n/nHarry gazed into the darkness. ... If Voldemort had/nknown about the Deathly Hallows, surely he would/nhave sought them, done anything to possess them:/nthree objects that made the possessor master of/nDeath? If he had known about the Deathly Hallows,/nhe might not have needed Horcruxes in the first/nplace. Didn't the simple fact that he had taken a/nHallow, and turned it into a Horcrux, demonstrate/nthat he did not know this last great Wizarding secret?/n/nWhich meant that Voldemort sought the Elder Wand/nwithout realizing its full power, without/nunderstanding that it was one of three . . . for the/nwand was the Hallow that could not be hidden, whose/nexistence was best known. ... The bloody trail of the/nElder Wand is splattered across the pages of/nWizarding history . . ./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry watched the cloudy sky, curves of smoke-gray/nand silver sliding over the face of the white moon. He/nfelt lightheaded with amazement at his discoveries./n/nHe turned back into the tent. It was a shock to see/nRon and Hermione standing exactly where he had left/nthem, Hermione still holding Lily's letter, Ron at her/nside looking slightly anxious. Didn't they realize how/nfar they had traveled in the last few minutes?/n/n"This is it," Harry said, trying to bring them inside the/nglow of his own astonished certainty. "This explains/neverything. The Deathly Hallows are real, and I've got/none — maybe two — "/n/nHe held up the Snitch./n/n" — and You-Know-Who's chasing the third, but he/ndoesn't realize ... he just thinks it's a powerful wand/n/n/n/n"Harry," said Hermione, moving across to him and/nhanding him back Lily's letter, "I'm sorry, but I think/nyou've got this wrong, all wrong."/n/n"But don't you see? It all fits — "/n/n"No, it doesn't," she said. "It doesn't , Harry, you're/njust getting carried away. Please," she said as he/nstarted to speak, "please just answer me this: If the/nDeathly Hallows really existed, and Dumbledore knew/nabout them, knew that the person who possessed all/nthree of them would be master of Death — Harry, why/nwouldn't he have told you? Why?"/n/nHe had his answer ready./n/n"But you said it, Hermione! You've got to find out/nabout them for yourself! It's a Quest!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"But I only said that to try and persuade you to come/nto the Lovegoods'!" cried Hermione in exasperation. "I/ndidn't really believe it!"/n/nHarry took no notice./n/n"Dumbledore usually let me find out stuff for myself./nHe let me try my strength, take risks. This feels like/nthe kind of thing he'd do."/n/n"Harry, this isn't a game, this isn't practice! This is/nthe real thing, and Dumbledore left you very clear/ninstructions: Find and destroy the Horcruxes! That/nsymbol doesn't mean anything, forget the Deathly/nHallows, we can't afford to get sidetracked — "/n/nHarry was barely listening to her. He was turning the/nSnitch over and over in his hands, half expecting it to/nbreak open, to reveal the Resurrection Stone, to prove/nto Hermione that he was right, that the Deathly/nHallows were real./n/nShe appealed to Ron./n/n"You don't believe in this, do you?"/n/nHarry looked up. Ron hesitated./n/n"I dunno ... I mean ... bits of it sort of fit together,"/nsaid Ron awkwardly. "But when you look at the whole/nthing ..." He took a deep breath. "I think we're/nsupposed to get rid of Horcruxes, Harry. That's what/nDumbledore told us to do. Maybe ... maybe we should/nforget about this Hallows business."/n/n"Thank you, Ron," said Hermione. "I'll take first/nwatch."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd she strode past Harry and sat down in the tent/nentrance, bringing the action to a fierce full stop./n/nBut Harry hardly slept that night. The idea of the/nDeathly Hallows had taken possession of him, and he/ncould not rest while agitating thoughts whirled/nthrough his mind: the wand, the stone, and the/nCloak, if he could just possess them all. .../n/nI open at the close. ... But what was 'the close'? Why/ncouldn't he have the stone now? If only he had the/nstone, he could ask Dumbledore these questions in/nperson . . . and Harry murmured words to the Snitch/nin the darkness, trying everything, even Parseltongue,/nbut the golden ball would not open. .../n/nAnd the wand, the Elder Wand, where was that/nhidden? Where was Voldemort searching now? Harry/nwished his scar would burn and show him/nVoldemort's thoughts, because for the first time ever,/nhe and Voldemort were united in wanting the very/nsame thing. . . . Hermione would not like that idea, of/ncourse. ... But then, she did not believe .../n/nXenophilius had been right, in a way . . . Limited./nNarrow. Close-minded. The truth was that she was/nscared of the idea of the Deathly Hallows, especially of/nthe Resurrection Stone ... and Harry pressed his/nmouth again to the Snitch, kissing it, nearly/nswallowing it, but the cold metal did not yield. .../n/nIt was nearly dawn when he remembered Luna, alone/nin a cell in Azkaban, surrounded by dementors, and/nhe suddenly felt ashamed of himself. He had forgotten/nall about her in his feverish contemplation of the/nHallows. If only they could rescue her; but dementors/nin those numbers would be virtually unassailable./n/nNow he came to think about it, he had not yet tried/ncasting a Patronus with the blackthorn wand. ... He/nmust try that in the morning. . . ./n/n/n/n/n/nIf only there was a way of getting a better wand . . ./n/nAnd desire for the Elder Wand, the Deathstick,/nunbeatable, invincible, swallowed him once more. .../n/nThey packed up the tent next morning and moved on/nthrough a dreary shower of rain. The downpour/npursued them to the coast, where they pitched the/ntent that night, and persisted through the whole/nweek, through sodden landscapes that Harry found/nbleak and depressing. He could think only of the/nDeathly Hallows. It was as though a flame had been/nlit inside him that nothing, not Hermione 's flat/ndisbelief nor Ron's persistent doubts, could/nextinguish. And yet the fiercer the longing for the/nHallows burned inside him, the less joyful it made/nhim. He blamed Ron and Hermione: Their determined/nindifference was as bad as the relentless rain for/ndampening his spirits, but neither could erode his/ncertainty, which remained absolute. Harry's belief in/nand longing for the Hallows consumed him so much/nthat he felt quite isolated from the other two and their/nobsession with the Horcruxes./n/n"Obsession?" said Hermione in a low fierce voice,/nwhen Harry was careless enough to use the word one/nevening, after Hermione had told him off for his lack/nof interest in locating more Horcruxes. "We're not the/nones with an obsession, Harry! We're the ones trying/nto do what Dumbledore wanted us to do!"/n/nBut he was impervious to the veiled criticism./nDumbledore had left the sign of the Hallows for/nHermione to decipher, and he had also, Harry/nremained convinced of it, left the Resurrection Stone/nhidden in the golden Snitch. Neither can live while the/nother survives. ... master of Death ... Why didn't Ron/nand Hermione understand?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" 'The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death,' "/nHarry quoted calmly./n/n"I thought it was You-Know-Who we were supposed to/nbe fighting?" Hermione retorted, and Harry gave up/non her./n/nEven the mystery of the silver doe, which the other/ntwo insisted on discussing, seemed less important to/nHarry now, a vaguely interesting sideshow. The only/nother thing that mattered to him was that his scar/nhad begun to prickle again, although he did all he/ncould to hide this fact from the other two. He sought/nsolitude whenever it happened, but was disappointed/nby what he saw. The visions he and Voldemort were/nsharing had changed in quality; they had become/nblurred, shifting as though they were moving in and/nout of focus. Harry was just able to make out the/nindistinct features of an object that looked like a/nskull, and something like a mountain that was more/nshadow than substance. Used to images sharp as/nreality, Harry was disconcerted by the change. He was/nworried that the connection between himself and/nVoldemort had been damaged, a connection that he/nboth feared and, whatever he had told Hermione,/nprized. Somehow Harry connected these unsatisfying,/nvague images with the destruction of his wand, as if it/nwas the blackthorn wand's fault that he could no/nlonger see into Voldemort's mind as well as before./n/nAs the weeks crept on, Harry could not help but/nnotice, even through his new self-absorption, that/nRon seemed to be taking charge. Perhaps because he/nwas determined to make up for having walked out on/nthem, perhaps because Harry's descent into/nlistlessness galvanized his dormant leadership/nqualities, Ron was the one now encouraging and/nexhorting the other two into action./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Three Horcruxes left," he kept saying. "We need a/nplan of action, come on! Where haven't we looked?/nLet's go through it again. The orphanage ..."/n/nDiagon Alley, Hogwarts, the Riddle House, Borgin and/nBurkes, Albania, every place that they knew Tom/nRiddle had ever lived or worked, visited or murdered,/nRon and Hermione raked over them again, Harry/njoining in only to stop Hermione pestering him. He/nwould have been happy to sit alone in silence, trying/nto read Voldemort's thoughts, to find out more about/nthe Elder Wand, but Ron insisted on journeying to/never more unlikely places simply, Harry was aware, to/nkeep them moving./n/n"You never know," was Ron's constant refrain. "Upper/nFlagley is a Wizarding village, he might've wanted to/nlive there. Let's go and have a poke around."/n/nThese frequent forays into Wizarding territory brought/nthem within occasional sight of Snatchers./n/n"Some of them are supposed to be as bad as Death/nEaters," said Ron. "The lot that got me were a bit/npathetic, but Bill reckons some of them are really/ndangerous. They said on Potterwatch — "/n/n"On what?" said Harry./n/n" Potterwatch , didn't I tell you that's what it was/ncalled? The program I keep trying to get on the radio,/nthe only one that tells the truth about what's going/non! Nearly all the programs are following You-Know-/nWho's line, all except Potterwatch. I really want you to/nhear it, but it's tricky tuning in. ..."/n/nRon spent evening after evening using his wand to/nbeat out various rhythms on top of the wireless while/nthe dials whirled. Occasionally they would catch/n/n/n/n/n/nsnatches of advice on how to treat dragon pox, and/nonce a few bars of "A Cauldron Full of Hot Strong/nLove." While he tapped, Ron continued to try to hit on/nthe correct password, muttering strings of random/nwords under his breath./n/n"They're normally something to do with the Order," he/ntold them. "Bill had a real knack for guessing them./nI'm bound to get one in the end. ..."/n/nBut not until March did luck favor Ron at last. Harry/nwas sitting in the tent entrance, on guard duty,/nstaring idly at a clump of grape hyacinths that had/nforced their way through the chilly ground, when Ron/nshouted excitedly from inside the tent./n/n"I've got it, I've got it! Password was Altars'! Get in/nhere, Harry!"/n/nRoused for the first time in days from his/ncontemplation of the Deathly Hallows, Harry hurried/nback inside the tent to find Ron and Hermione/nkneeling on the floor beside the little radio. Hermione,/nwho had been polishing the sword of Gryffindor just/nfor something to do, was sitting open-mouthed,/nstaring at the tiny speaker, from which a most/nfamiliar voice was issuing./n/n"... apologize for our temporary absence from the/nairwaves, which was due to a number of house calls/nin our area by those charming Death Eaters."/n/n"But that's Lee Jordan!" said Hermione./n/n"I know!" beamed Ron. "Cool, eh?"/n/n"... now found ourselves another secure location," Lee/nwas saying, "and I'm pleased to tell you that two of/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nour regular contributors have joined me here this/nevening. Evening, boys!"/n/n"Hi."/n/n"Evening, River."/n/n" 'River,' that's Lee," Ron explained. "They've all got/ncode names, but you can usually tell — "/n/n"Shh!" said Hermione./n/n"But before we hear from Royal and Romulus," Lee/nwent on, "let's take a moment to report those deaths/nthat the Wizarding Wireless Network News and Daily/nProphet don't think important enough to mention. It is/nwith great regret that we inform our listeners of the/nmurders of Ted Tonks and Dirk Cresswell."/n/nHarry felt a sick, swooping in his belly. He, Ron, and/nHermione gazed at one another in horror./n/n"A goblin by the name of Gornuk was also killed. It is/nbelieved that Muggle-born Dean Thomas and a/nsecond goblin, both believed to have been traveling/nwith Tonks, Cresswell, and Gornuk, may have/nescaped. If Dean is listening, or if anyone has any/nknowledge of his whereabouts, his parents and sisters/nare desperate for news./n/n"Meanwhile, in Gaddley, a Muggle family of five has/nbeen found dead in their home. Muggle authorities/nare attributing the deaths to a gas leak, but members/nof the Order of the Phoenix inform me that it was the/nKilling Curse — more evidence, as if it were needed, of/nthe fact that Muggle slaughter is becoming little more/nthan a recreational sport under the new regime./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Finally, we regret to inform our listeners that the/nremains of Bathilda Bagshot have been discovered in/nGodric's Hollow. The evidence is that she died several/nmonths ago. The Order of the Phoenix informs us that/nher body showed unmistakable signs of injuries/ninflicted by Dark Magic./n/n"Listeners, I'd like to invite you now to join us in a/nminute's silence in memory of Ted Tonks, Dirk/nCresswell, Bathilda Bagshot, Gornuk, and the/nunnamed, but no less regretted, Muggles murdered/nby the Death Eaters."/n/nSilence fell, and Harry, Ron, and Hermione did not/nspeak. Half of Harry yearned to hear more, half of him/nwas afraid of what might come next. It was the first/ntime he had felt fully connected to the outside world/nfor a long time./n/n"Thank you," said Lee's voice. "And now we turn to/nregular contributor Royal, for an update on how the/nnew Wizarding order is affecting the Muggle world."/n/n"Thanks, River," said an unmistakable voice, deep,/nmeasured, reassuring./n/n"Kingsley!" burst out Ron./n/n"We know!" said Hermione, hushing him./n/n"Muggles remain ignorant of the source of their/nsuffering as they continue to sustain heavy/ncasualties," said Kingsley. "However, we continue to/nhear truly inspirational stories of wizards and witches/nrisking their own safety to protect Muggle friends and/nneighbors, often without the Muggles' knowledge. I'd/nlike to appeal to all our listeners to emulate their/nexample, perhaps by casting a protective charm over/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nany Muggle dwellings in your street. Many lives could/nbe saved if such simple measures are taken."/n/n"And what would you say, Royal, to those listeners/nwho reply that in these dangerous times, it should be/nWizards first'?" asked Lee./n/n"I'd say that it's one short step from Wizards first' to/n'Purebloods first,' and then to 'Death Eaters,' " replied/nKingsley. "We're all human, aren't we? Every human/nlife is worth the same, and worth saving."/n/n"Excellently put, Royal, and you've got my vote for/nMinister of Magic if ever we get out of this mess," said/nLee. "And now, over to Romulus for our popular/nfeature 'Pals of Potter. ' "/n/n"Thanks, River," said another very familiar voice; Ron/nstarted to speak, but Hermione forestalled him in a/nwhisper./n/n"We know it's Lupin\"/n/n"Romulus, do you maintain, as you have every time/nyou've appeared on our program, that Harry Potter is/nstill alive?"/n/n"I do," said Lupin firmly. "There is no doubt at all in/nmy mind that his death would be proclaimed as/nwidely as possible by the Death Eaters if it had/nhappened, because it would strike a deadly blow at/nthe morale of those resisting the new regime. The Boy/nWho Lived' remains a symbol of everything for which/nwe are fighting: the triumph of good, the power of/ninnocence, the need to keep resisting."/n/nA mixture of gratitude and shame welled up in Harry./nHad Lupin forgiven him, then, for the terrible things/nhe had said when they had last met?/n/n/n/n/n/n"And what would you say to Harry if you knew he was/nlistening, Romulus?"/n/n/n/n"I'd tell him we're all with him in spirit," said Lupin,/nthen hesitated slightly. "And I'd tell him to follow his/ninstincts, which are good and nearly always right."/n/nHarry looked at Hermione, whose eyes were full of/ntears./n/n"Nearly always right," she repeated./n/n"Oh, didn't I tell you?" said Ron in surprise. "Bill told/nme Lupin's living with Tonks again! And apparently/nshe's getting pretty big too. ..."/n/n"... and our usual update on those friends of Harry/nPotter's who are suffering for their allegiance?" Lee/nwas saying./n/n"Well, as regular listeners will know, several of the/nmore outspoken supporters of Harry Potter have now/nbeen imprisoned, including Xenophilius Lovegood,/nerstwhile editor of The Quibbler," said Lupin./n/n"At least he's still alive!" muttered Ron./n/n"We have also heard within the last few hours that/nRubeus Hagrid" — all three of them gasped, and so/nnearly missed the rest of the sentence — "well-known/ngamekeeper at Hogwarts School, has narrowly/nescaped arrest within the grounds of Hogwarts, where/nhe is rumored to have hosted a 'Support Harry Potter'/nparty in his house. However, Hagrid was not taken/ninto custody, and is, we believe, on the run."/n/n"I suppose it helps, when escaping from Death Eaters,/nif you've got a sixteen-foot-high half brother?" asked/nLee./n/n/n/n/n/n"It would tend to give you an edge," agreed Lupin/ngravely. "May I just add that while we here at/nPotterwatch applaud Hagrid's spirit, we would urge/neven the most devoted of Harry's supporters against/nfollowing Hagrid's lead. 'Support Harry Potter' parties/nare unwise in the present climate."/n/n"Indeed they are, Romulus," said Lee, "so we suggest/nthat you continue to show your devotion to the man/nwith the lightning scar by listening to PotterwatcM/nAnd now let's move to news concerning the wizard/nwho is proving just as elusive as Harry Potter. We like/nto refer to him as the Chief Death Eater, and here to/ngive his views on some of the more insane rumors/ncirculating about him, I'd like to introduce a new/ncorrespondent: Rodent."/n/n" 'Rodent'?" said yet another familiar voice, and Harry,/nRon, and Hermione cried out together:/n/n"Fred!"/n/n"No — is it George?"/n/n"It's Fred, I think," said Ron, leaning in closer, as/nwhichever twin it was said,/n/n"I'm not being 'Rodent,' no way, I told you I wanted to/nbe 'Rapier'!"/n/n"Oh, all right then. 'Rapier,' could you please give us/nyour take on the various stories we've been hearing/nabout the Chief Death Eater?"/n/n"Yes, River, I can," said Fred. "As our listeners will/nknow, unless they've taken refuge at the bottom of a/ngarden pond or somewhere similar, You-Know-Who's/nstrategy of remaining in the shadows is creating a/nnice little climate of panic. Mind you, if all the alleged/n/n/n/n/nsightings of him are genuine, we must have a good/nnineteen You-Know-Whos running around the place."/n/n/n/n"Which suits him, of course," said Kingsley. "The air/nof mystery is creating more terror than actually/nshowing himself."/n/n"Agreed," said Fred. "So, people, let's try and calm/ndown a bit. Things are bad enough without inventing/nstuff as well. For instance, this new idea that You-/nKnow-Who can kill with a single glance from his eyes./nThat's a basilisk, listeners. One simple test: Check/nwhether the thing that's glaring at you has got legs. If/nit has, it's safe to look into its eyes, although if it/nreally is You-Know-Who, that's still likely to be the/nlast thing you ever do."/n/nFor the first time in weeks and weeks, Harry was/nlaughing: He could feel the weight of tension leaving/nhim./n/n"And the rumors that he keeps being sighted abroad?"/nasked Lee./n/n"Well, who wouldn't want a nice little holiday after all/nthe hard work he's been putting in?" asked Fred./n"Point is, people, don't get lulled into a false sense of/nsecurity, thinking he's out of the country. Maybe he/nis, maybe he isn't, but the fact remains he can move/nfaster than Severus Snape confronted with shampoo/nwhen he wants to, so don't count on him being a long/nway away if you're planning on taking any risks. I/nnever thought I'd hear myself say it, but safety first!"/n/n"Thank you very much for those wise words, Rapier,"/nsaid Lee. "Listeners, that brings us to the end of/nanother Potterwatch. We don't know when it will be/npossible to broadcast again, but you can be sure we/nshall be back. Keep twiddling those dials: The next/n/n/n/n/npassword will be 'Mad-Eye.' Keep each other safe:/nKeep faith. Good night."/n/n/n/nThe radio's dial twirled and the lights behind the/ntuning panel went out. Harry, Ron, and Hermione/nwere still beaming. Hearing familiar, friendly voices/nwas an extraordinary tonic; Harry had become so/nused to their isolation he had nearly forgotten that/nother people were resisting Voldemort. It was like/nwaking from a long sleep./n/n"Good, eh?" said Ron happily./n/n"Brilliant," said Harry./n/n"It's so brave of them," sighed Hermione admiringly./n"If they were found ..."/n/n"Well, they keep on the move, don't they?" said Ron./n"Like us."/n/n"But did you hear what Fred said?" asked Harry/nexcitedly; now the broadcast was over, his thoughts/nturned again toward his all-consuming obsession./n"He's abroad! He's still looking for the Wand, I knew/nit!"/n/n/n/n"Harry — "/n/n"Come on, Hermione, why are you so determined not/nto admit it? Vol — "/n/n"HARRY, NO!"/n/n" — demort's after the Elder Wand!"/n/n"The name's Taboo!" Ron bellowed, leaping to his feet/nas a loud crack sounded outside the tent. "I told you,/nHarry, I told you, we can't say it anymore — we've got/n/n/n/n/n/nto put the protection back around us — quickly — it's/nhow they find — "/n/nBut Ron stopped talking, and Harry knew why. The/nSneakoscope on the table had lit up and begun to/nspin; they could hear voices coming nearer and/nnearer: rough, excited voices. Ron pulled the/nDeluminator out of his pocket and clicked it: Their/nlamps went out./n/n"Come out of there with your hands up!" came a/nrasping voice through the darkness. "We know you're/nin there! You've got half a dozen wands pointing at/nyou and we don't care who we curse!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Malfoy Manor
text: /nHarry looked around at the other two, now mere/noutlines in the darkness. He saw Hermione point her/nwand, not toward the outside, but into his face; there/nwas a bang, a burst of white light, and he buckled in/nagony, unable to see. He could feel his face swelling/nrapidly under his hands as heavy footfalls/nsurrounded him./n/n"Get up, vermin."/n/nUnknown hands dragged Harry roughly off the/nground. Before he could stop them, someone had/nrummaged through his pockets and removed the/nblackthorn wand. Harry clutched at his excruciatingly/npainful face, which felt unrecognizable beneath his/nfingers, tight, swollen, and puffy as though he had/nsuffered some violent allergic reaction. His eyes had/nbeen reduced to slits through which he could barely/nsee; his glasses fell off as he was bundled out of the/ntent; all he could make out were the blurred shapes of/nfour or five people wrestling Ron and Hermione/noutside too./n/n/n/n/n"Get — off — her!" Ron shouted. There was the/nunmistakable sound of knuckles hitting flesh: Ron/ngrunted in pain and Hermione screamed, "No! Leave/nhim alone, leave him alone!"/n/n"Your boyfriend's going to have worse than that done/nto him if he's on my list," said the horribly familiar,/nrasping voice. "Delicious girl ... What a treat ... I do/nenjoy the softness of the skin. ..."/n/nHarry's stomach turned over. He knew who this was:/nFenrir Grey back, the werewolf who was permitted to/nwear Death Eater robes in return for his hired/nsavagery./n/n"Search the tent!" said another voice./n/nHarry was thrown facedown onto the ground. A thud/ntold him that Ron had been cast down beside him./nThey could hear footsteps and crashes; the men were/npushing over chairs inside the tent as they searched./n/n"Now, let's see who we've got," said Greyback's/ngloating voice from overhead, and Harry was rolled/nover onto his back. A beam of wandlight fell into his/nface and Grey back laughed./n/n"I'll be needing butterbeer to wash this one down./nWhat happened to you, ugly?"/n/nHarry did not answer immediately./n/n"I said," repeated Greyback, and Harry received a/nblow to the diaphragm that made him double over in/npain, "what happened to you?"/n/n"Stung," Harry muttered. "Been stung."/n/n"Yeah, looks like it," said a second voice./n/n/n/n/n/n"What's your name?" snarled Greyback./n/n"Dudley," said Harry./n/n"And your first name?"/n/n"I — Vernon. Vernon Dudley."/n/n"Check the list, Scabior," said Greyback, and Harry/nheard him move sideways to look down at Ron,/ninstead. "And what about you, ginger?"/n/n"Stan Shunpike," said Ron./n/n"Like 'ell you are," said the man called Scabior. "We/nknow Stan Shunpike, 'e's put a bit of work our way."/n/nThere was another thud./n/n"I'b Bardy," said Ron, and Harry could tell that his/nmouth was full of blood. "Bardy Weadley."/n/n"A Weasley?" rasped Greyback. "So you're related to/nblood traitors even if you're not a Mudblood. And/nlastly, your pretty little friend ..." The relish in his/nvoice made Harry's flesh crawl./n/n"Easy, Greyback," said Scabior over the jeering of the/nothers./n/n"Oh, I'm not going to bite just yet. We'll see if she's a/nbit quicker at remembering her name than Barny./nWho are you, girly?"/n/n"Penelope Clearwater," said Hermione. She sounded/nterrified, but convincing./n/n"What's your blood status?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Half-blood," said Hermione./n/n/n/n"Easy enough to check," said Scabior. "But the 'ole lot/nof 'em look like they could still be 'ogwarts age — "/n/n"Weh lebt," said Ron./n/n"Left, 'ave you, ginger?" said Scabior. "And you/ndecided to go camping? And you thought, just for a/nlaugh, you'd use the Dark Lord's name?"/n/n"Nod a laugh," said Ron. "Aggiden."/n/n"Accident?" There was more jeering laughter./n/n"You know who used to like using the Dark Lord's/nname, Weasley?" growled Greyback. "The Order of the/nPhoenix. Mean anything to you?"/n/n"Doh."/n/n"Well, they don't show the Dark Lord proper respect,/nso the name's been Tabooed. A few Order members/nhave been tracked that way. We'll see. Bind them up/nwith the other two prisoners!"/n/nSomeone yanked Harry up by the hair, dragged him a/nshort way, pushed him down into a sitting position,/nthen started binding him back-to-back with other/npeople. Harry was still half blind, barely able to see/nanything through his puffed-up eyes. When at last/nthe man tying them had walked away, Harry/nwhispered to the other prisoners./n/n"Anyone still got a wand?"/n/n"No," said Ron and Hermione from either side of him./n/n"This is all my fault. I said the name, I'm sorry — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry?"/n/n/n/nIt was a new, but familiar, voice, and it came from/ndirectly behind Harry, from the person tied to/nHermione's left./n/n"Dean?"/n/n"It is you! If they find out who they've got — ! They're/nSnatchers, they're only looking for truants to sell for/ngold — "/n/n"Not a bad little haul for one night," Greyback was/nsaying, as a pair of hobnailed boots marched close by/nHarry and they heard more crashes from inside the/ntent. "A Mudblood, a runaway goblin, and three/ntruants. You checked their names on the list yet,/nScabior?" he roared./n/n"Yeah. There's no Vernon Dudley on 'ere, Greyback."/n/n"Interesting," said Greyback. "That's interesting."/n/nHe crouched down beside Harry, who saw, through/nthe infinitesimal gap left between his swollen eyelids,/na face covered in matted gray hair and whiskers, with/npointed brown teeth and sores at the corners of his/nmouth. Greyback smelled as he had done at the top of/nthe tower where Dumbledore had died: of dirt, sweat,/nand blood./n/n"So you aren't wanted, then, Vernon? Or are you on/nthat list under a different name? What House were/nyou in at Hogwarts?"/n/n"Slytherin," said Harry automatically./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Funny 'ow they all thinks we wants to 'ear that,"/njeered Scabior out of the shadows. "But none of 'em/ncan tell us where the common room is."/n/n"It's in the dungeons," said Harry clearly. "You enter/nthrough the wall. It's full of skulls and stuff and it's/nunder the lake, so the light's all green."/n/nThere was a short pause./n/n"Well, well, looks like we really 'ave caught a little/nSlytherin," said Scabior. "Good for you, Vernon,/n/n'cause there ain't a lot of Mudblood Slytherins. Who's/nyour father?"/n/n"He works at the Ministry," Harry lied. He knew that/nhis whole story would collapse with the smallest/ninvestigation, but on the other hand, he only had/nuntil his face regained its usual appearance before/nthe game was up in any case. "Department of Magical/nAccidents and Catastrophes."/n/n"You know what, Greyback," said Scabior. "I think/nthere is a Dudley in there."/n/nHarry could barely breathe: Could luck, sheer luck,/nget them safely out of this?/n/n"Well, well," said Greyback, and Harry could hear the/ntiniest note of trepidation in that callous voice, and/nknew that Greyback was wondering whether he had/nindeed just attacked and bound the son of a Ministry/nofficial. Harry's heart was pounding against the ropes/naround his ribs; he would not have been surprised to/nknow that Greyback could see it. "If you're telling the/ntruth, ugly, you've got nothing to fear from a trip to/nthe Ministry. I expect your father'll reward us just for/npicking you up."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"But," said Harry, his mouth bone dry, "if you just let/nus — "/n/n/n/n"Hey!" came a shout from inside the tent. "Look at/nthis, Greyback!"/n/nA dark figure came bustling toward them, and Harry/nsaw a glint of silver in the light of their wands. They/nhad found Gryffindor's sword./n/n"Ve-e-ry nice," said Greyback appreciatively, taking it/nfrom his companion. "Oh, very nice indeed. Looks/ngoblin-made, that. Where did you get something like/nthis?"/n/n"It's my father's," Harry lied, hoping against hope that/nit was too dark for Greyback to see the name etched/njust below the hilt. "We borrowed it to cut firewood — "/n/n" 'ang on a minute, Greyback! Look at this, in the/nPropheti"/n/nAs Scabior said it, Harry's scar, which was stretched/ntight across his distended forehead, burned savagely./nMore clearly than he could make out anything around/nhim, he saw a towering building, a grim fortress, jet-/nblack and forbidding; Voldemort's thoughts had/nsuddenly become razor-sharp again; he was gliding/ntoward the gigantic building with a sense of calmly/neuphoric purpose. .../n/nSo close ...So close . . ./n/nWith a huge effort of will Harry closed his mind to/nVoldemort's thoughts, pulling himself back to where/nhe sat, tied to Ron, Hermione, Dean, and Griphook in/nthe darkness, listening to Greyback and Scabior./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" ''ermione Granger,' " Scabior was saying, " 'the/nMudblood who is known to be traveling with 'arry/nPotter.' "/n/nHarry's scar burned in the silence, but he made a/nsupreme effort to keep himself present, not to slip/ninto Voldemort's mind. He heard the creak of/nGreyback's boots as he crouched down in front of/nHermione./n/n"You know what, little girly? This picture looks a hell/nof a lot like you."/n/n"It isn't! It isn't me!"/n/nHermione 's terrified squeak was as good as a/nconfession./n/n" '... known to be traveling with Harry Potter,' "/nrepeated Grey back quietly./n/nA stillness had settled over the scene. Harry's scar/nwas exquisitely painful, but he struggled with all his/nstrength against the pull of Voldemort's thoughts: It/nhad never been so important to remain in his own/nright mind./n/n"Well, this changes things, doesn't it?" whispered/nGreyback. Nobody spoke: Harry sensed the gang of/nSnatchers watching, frozen, and felt Hermione 's arm/ntrembling against his. Greyback got up and took a/ncouple of steps to where Harry sat, crouching down/nagain to stare closely at his misshapen features./n/n"What's that on your forehead, Vernon?" he asked/nsoftly, his breath foul in Harry's nostrils as he/npressed a filthy finger to the taut scar./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Don't touch it!" Harry yelled; he could not stop/nhimself; he thought he might be sick from the pain of/nit./n/n/n/n"I thought you wore glasses, Potter?" breathed/nGreyback./n/n"I found glasses!" yelped one of the Snatchers/nskulking in the background. "There was glasses in the/ntent, Greyback, wait — "/n/nAnd seconds later Harry's glasses had been rammed/nback onto his face. The Snatchers were closing in/nnow, peering at him./n/n"It is!" rasped Greyback. "We've caught Potter!"/n/nThey all took several steps backward, stunned by/nwhat they had done. Harry, still fighting to remain/npresent inside his own splitting head, could think of/nnothing to say: Fragmented visions were breaking/nacross the surface of his mind —/n/n— He was gliding around the high walls of the black/nfortress —/n/nNo, he was Harry, tied up and wandless, in grave/ndanger —/n/n— looking up, up to the topmost window, the highest/ntower —/n/nHe was Harry, and they were discussing his fate in/nlow voices —/n/n— Time to fly .../n/n"...to the Ministry?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"To hell with the Ministry," growled Greyback. "They'll/ntake the credit, and we won't get a look in. I say we/ntake him straight to You-Know-Who."/n/n"Will you summon 'im? 'ere?" said Scabior, sounding/nawed, terrified./n/n"No," snarled Greyback, "I haven't got — they say he's/nusing the Malfoys' place as a base. We'll take the boy/nthere."/n/nHarry thought he knew why Greyback was not calling/nVoldemort. The werewolf might be allowed to wear/nDeath Eater robes when they wanted to use him, but/nonly Voldemort's inner circle were branded with the/nDark Mark: Greyback had not been granted this/nhighest honor./n/nHarry's scar seared again —/n/n— and he rose into the night, flying straight up to the/nwindow at the very top of the tower —/n/n"... completely sure it's him? 'Cause if it ain't,/nGreyback, we're dead."/n/n"Who's in charge here?" roared Greyback, covering his/nmoment of inadequacy. "I say that's Potter, and him/nplus his wand, that's two hundred thousand Galleons/nright there! But if you're too gutless to come along,/nany of you, it's all for me, and with any luck, I'll get/nthe girl thrown in!"/n/n— The window was the merest slit in the black rock,/nnot big enough for a man to enter. ...A skeletal figure/nwas just visible through it, curled beneath a blanket. . . ./nDead, or sleeping ... ?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"All right!" said Scabior. "All right, we're in! And what/nabout the rest of 'em, Greyback, what'll we do with/n/n/n/n'em?/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Might as well take the lot. We've got two Mudbloods,/nthat's another ten Galleons. Give me the sword as/nwell. If they're rubies, that's another small fortune/nright there."/n/nThe prisoners were dragged to their feet. Harry could/nhear Hermione's breathing, fast and terrified./n/n"Grab hold and make it tight. I'll do Potter!" said/nGreyback, seizing a fistful of Harry's hair; Harry could/nfeel his long yellow nails scratching his scalp. "On/nthree! One — two — three — "/n/nThey Disapparated, pulling the prisoners with them./nHarry struggled, trying to throw off Greyback's hand,/nbut it was hopeless: Ron and Hermione were/nsqueezed tightly against him on either side, he could/nnot separate from the group, and as the breath was/nsqueezed out of him his scar seared more painfully/nstill —/n/n— as he forced himself through the slit of a window/nlike a snake and landed, lightly as vapor, inside the/ncell-like room —/n/nThe prisoners lurched into one another as they/nlanded in a country lane. Harry's eyes, still puffy, took/na moment to acclimatize, then he saw a pair of/nwrought-iron gates at the foot of what looked like a/nlong drive. He experienced the tiniest trickle of relief./nThe worst had not happened yet: Voldemort was not/nhere. He was, Harry knew, for he was fighting to/nresist the vision, in some strange, fortresslike place,/nat the top of a tower. How long it would take/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nVoldemort to get to this place, once he knew that/nHarry was here, was another matter. .../n/nOne of the Snatchers strode to the gates and shook/nthem./n/n"How do we get in? They're locked, Greyback, I can't/n— blimey!"/n/nHe whipped his hands away in fright. The iron was/ncontorting, twisting itself out of the abstract furls and/ncoils into a frightening face, which spoke in a/nclanging, echoing voice: "State your purpose!"/n/n"We've got Potter!" Greyback roared triumphantly./n"We've captured Harry Potter!"/n/nThe gates swung open./n/n"Come on!" said Greyback to his men, and the/nprisoners were shunted through the gates and up the/ndrive, between high hedges that muffled their/nfootsteps. Harry saw a ghostly white shape above/nhim, and realized it was an albino peacock. He/nstumbled and was dragged onto his feet by Greyback;/nnow he was staggering along sideways, tied back-to-/nback to the four other prisoners. Closing his puffy/neyes, he allowed the pain in his scar to overcome him/nfor a moment, wanting to know what Voldemort was/ndoing, whether he knew yet that Harry was caught. .../n/nThe emaciated figure stirred beneath its thin blanket/nand rolled over toward him, eyes opening in a skull of/na face. ... The frail man sat up, great sunken eyes/nfixed upon him, upon Voldemort, and then he smiled./nMost of his teeth were gone. .../n/n"So, you have come. I thought you would ... one day./nBut your journey was pointless. I never had it."/n/n/n/n/n/n" You lie]"/n/n/n/nAs Voldemort's anger throbbed inside him, Harry's/nscar threatened to burst with pain, and he wrenched/nhis mind back to his own body, fighting to remain/npresent as the prisoners were pushed over gravel./n/nLight spilled out over all of them./n/n"What is this?" said a woman's cold voice./n/n"We're here to see He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named!"/nrasped Greyback./n/n"Who are you?"/n/n"You know me!"
