Harry/nstraightened up, still holding Bellatrix's./n/n"I said, drop them!" she screeched, pressing the blade/ninto Hermione's throat: Harry saw beads of blood/nappear there./n/n"All right!" he shouted, and he dropped Bellatrix's/nwand onto the floor at his feet. Ron did the same with/nWormtail's. Both raised their hands to shoulder/nheight./n/n"Good!" she leered. "Draco, pick them up! The Dark/nLord is coming, Harry Potter! Your death approaches!"/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry knew it; his scar was bursting with the pain of/nit, and he could feel Voldemort flying through the sky/nfrom far away, over a dark and stormy sea, and soon/nhe would be close enough to Apparate to them, and/nHarry could see no way out./n/n"Now," said Bellatrix softly, as Draco hurried back to/nher with the wands, "Cissy, I think we ought to tie/nthese little heroes up again, while Greyback takes/ncare of Miss Mudblood. I am sure the Dark Lord will/nnot begrudge you the girl, Greyback, after what you/nhave done tonight."/n/nAt the last word there was a peculiar grinding noise/nfrom above. All of them looked upward in time to see/nthe crystal chandelier tremble; then, with a creak and/nan ominous jingling, it began to fall. Bellatrix was/ndirectly beneath it; dropping Hermione, she threw/nherself aside with a scream. The chandelier crashed/nto the floor in an explosion of crystal and chains,/nfalling on top of Hermione and the goblin, who still/nclutched the sword of Gryffindor. Glittering shards of/ncrystal flew in all directions: Draco doubled over, his/nhands covering his bloody face./n/nAs Ron ran to pull Hermione out of the wreckage,/nHarry took his chance: He leapt over an armchair and/nwrested the three wands from Draco's grip, pointed all/nof them at Greyback, and yelled, "Stupefyl" The/nwerewolf was lifted off his feet by the triple spell, flew/nup to the ceiling, and then smashed to the ground./n/nAs Narcissa dragged Draco out of the way of further/nharm, Bellatrix sprang to her feet, her hair flying as/nshe brandished the silver knife; but Narcissa had/ndirected her wand at the doorway./n/n"Dobby!" she screamed, and even Bellatrix froze./n/n"You! You dropped the chandelier — ?"/n/n/n/n/n/nThe tiny elf trotted into the room, his shaking finger/npointing at his old mistress./n/n"You must not hurt Harry Potter," he squeaked./n/n"Kill him, Cissy!" shrieked Bellatrix, but there was/nanother loud crack, and Narcissa's wand too flew into/nthe air and landed on the other side of the room./n/n"You dirty little monkey!" bawled Bellatrix. "How dare/nyou take a witch's wand, how dare you defy your/nmasters?"/n/n"Dobby has no master!" squealed the elf. "Dobby is a/nfree elf, and Dobby has come to save Harry Potter and/nhis friends!"/n/nHarry's scar was blinding him with pain. Dimly he/nknew that they had moments, seconds before/nVoldemort was with them./n/n"Ron, catch — and GO!" he yelled, throwing one of the/nwands to him; then he bent down to tug Griphook out/nfrom under the chandelier. Hoisting the groaning/ngoblin, who still clung to the sword, over one/nshoulder, Harry seized Dobby's hand and spun on the/nspot to Disapparate./n/nAs he turned into darkness he caught one last view of/nthe drawing room: of the pale, frozen figures of/nNarcissa and Draco, of the streak of red that was/nRon's hair, and a blur of flying silver, as Bellatrix's/nknife flew across the room at the place where he was/nvanishing —/n/nBill and Fleur's . . . Shell Cottage . . . Bill and Fleur's . . ./n/nHe had disappeared into the unknown; all he could/ndo was repeat the name of the destination and hope/n/n/n/n/n/nthat it would suffice to take him there. The pain in his/nforehead pierced him, and the weight of the goblin/nbore down upon him; he could feel the blade of/nGryffindor's sword bumping against his back; Dobby's/nhand jerked in his; he wondered whether the elf was/ntrying to take charge, to pull them in the right/ndirection, and tried, by squeezing the fingers, to/nindicate that that was fine with him. .../n/nAnd then they hit solid earth and smelled salty air./nHarry fell to his knees, relinquished Dobby's hand,/nand attempted to lower Griphook gently to the/nground./n/n"Are you all right?" he said as the goblin stirred, but/nGriphook merely whimpered./n/nHarry squinted around through the darkness. There/nseemed to be a cottage a short way away under the/nwide starry sky, and he thought he saw movement/noutside it./n/n"Dobby, is this Shell Cottage?" he whispered,/nclutching the two wands he had brought from the/nMalfoys', ready to fight if he needed to. "Have we come/nto the right place? Dobby?"/n/nHe looked around. The little elf stood feet from him./n"DOBBY!"/n/nThe elf swayed slightly, stars reflected in his wide,/nshining eyes. Together, he and Harry looked down at/nthe silver hilt of the knife protruding from the elf's/nheaving chest./n/n"Dobby — no — HELP!" Harry bellowed toward the/ncottage, toward the people moving there. "HELP!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe did not know or care whether they were wizards or/nMuggles, friends or foes; all he cared about was that a/ndark stain was spreading across Dobby's front, and/nthat he had stretched out his thin arms to Harry with/na look of supplication. Harry caught him and laid him/nsideways on the cool grass./n/n"Dobby, no, don't die, don't die — "/n/nThe elf's eyes found him, and his lips trembled with/nthe effort to form words./n/n"Harry ... Potter ..."/n/nAnd then with a little shudder the elf became quite/nstill, and his eyes were nothing more than great/nglassy orbs, sprinkled with light from the stars they/ncould not see./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Wandmaker
text: /nIt was like sinking into an old nightmare; for an/ninstant Harry knelt again beside Dumbledore's body/nat the foot of the tallest tower at Hogwarts, but in/nreality he was staring at a tiny body curled upon the/ngrass, pierced by Bellatrix's silver knife. Harry's voice/nwas still saying, "Dobby ... Dobby ..." even though he/nknew that the elf had gone where he could not call/nhim back./n/nAfter a minute or so he realized that they had, after/nall, come to the right place, for here were Bill and/nFleur, Dean and Luna, gathering around him as he/nknelt over the elf./n/n"Hermione?" he said suddenly. "Where is she?"/n/n"Ron's taken her inside," said Bill. "She'll be all right."/n/nHarry looked back down at Dobby. He stretched out a/nhand and pulled the sharp blade from the elf's body,/nthen dragged off his own jacket and covered Dobby in/nit like a blanket./n/n/n/n/nThe sea was rushing against rock somewhere nearby;/nHarry listened to it while the others talked, discussing/nmatters in which he could take no interest, making/ndecisions. Dean carried the injured Griphook into the/nhouse, Fleur hurrying with them; now Bill was/nmaking suggestions about burying the elf. Harry/nagreed without really knowing what he was saying. As/nhe did so, he gazed down at the tiny body, and his/nscar prickled and burned, and in one part of his/nmind, viewed as if from the wrong end of a long/ntelescope, he saw Voldemort punishing those they/nhad left behind at Malfoy Manor. His rage was/ndreadful and yet Harry's grief for Dobby seemed to/ndiminish it, so that it became a distant storm that/nreached Harry from across a vast, silent ocean./n/n"I want to do it properly," were the first words of/nwhich Harry was fully conscious of speaking. "Not by/nmagic. Have you got a spade?"/n/nAnd shortly afterward he had set to work, alone,/ndigging the grave in the place that Bill had shown him/nat the end of the garden, between bushes. He dug/nwith a kind of fury, relishing the manual work,/nglorying in the non-magic of it, for every drop of his/nsweat and every blister felt like a gift to the elf who/nhad saved their lives./n/nHis scar burned, but he was master of the pain; he/nfelt it, yet was apart from it. He had learned control at/nlast, learned to shut his mind to Voldemort, the very/nthing Dumbledore had wanted him to learn from/nSnape. Just as Voldemort had not been able to/npossess Harry while Harry was consumed with grief/nfor Sirius, so his thoughts could not penetrate Harry/nnow, while he mourned Dobby. Grief, it seemed, drove/nVoldemort out ... though Dumbledore, of course,/nwould have said that it was love. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nOn Harry dug, deeper and deeper into the hard, cold/nearth, subsuming his grief in sweat, denying the pain/nin his scar. In the darkness, with nothing but the/nsound of his own breath and the rushing sea to keep/nhim company, the things that had happened at the/nMalfoys' returned to him, the things he had heard/ncame back to him, and understanding blossomed in/nthe darkness. .../n/nThe steady rhythm of his arms beat time with his/nthoughts. Hallows ... Horcruxes ... Hallows .../nHorcruxes ... Yet he no longer burned with that weird,/nobsessive longing. Loss and fear had snuffed it out:/n/nHe felt as though he had been slapped awake again./n/nDeeper and deeper Harry sank into the grave, and he/nknew where Voldemort had been tonight, and whom/nhe had killed in the topmost cell of Nurmengard, and/nwhy. .../n/nAnd he thought of Wormtail, dead because of one/nsmall unconscious impulse of mercy. . . . Dumbledore/nhad foreseen that. ... How much more had he known?/n/nHarry lost track of time. He knew only that the/ndarkness had lightened a few degrees when he was/nrejoined by Ron and Dean./n/n"How's Hermione?"/n/n"Better," said Ron. "Fleur's looking after her."/n/nHarry had his retort ready for when they asked him/nwhy he had not simply created a perfect grave with/nhis wand, but he did not need it. They jumped down/ninto the hole he had made with spades of their own,/nand together they worked in silence until the hole/nseemed deep enough./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry wrapped the elf more snugly in his jacket. Ron/nsat on the edge of the grave and stripped off his shoes/nand socks, which he placed upon the elf's bare feet./nDean produced a woolen hat, which Harry placed/ncarefully upon Dobby's head, muffling his batlike/nears./n/n"We should close his eyes."/n/nHarry had not heard the others coming through the/ndarkness. Bill was wearing a traveling cloak, Fleur a/nlarge white apron, from the pocket of which protruded/na bottle of what Harry recognized to be Skele-Gro./nHermione was wrapped in a borrowed dressing gown,/npale and unsteady on her feet; Ron put an arm/naround her when she reached him. Luna, who was/nhuddled in one of Fleur's coats, crouched down and/nplaced her fingers tenderly upon each of the elf's/neyelids, sliding them over his glassy stare./n/n"There," she said softly. "Now he could be sleeping."/n/nHarry placed the elf into the grave, arranged his tiny/nlimbs so that he might have been resting, then/nclimbed out and gazed for the last time upon the little/nbody. He forced himself not to break down as he/nremembered Dumbledore's funeral, and the rows and/nrows of golden chairs, and the Minister of Magic in/nthe front row, the recitation of Dumbledore's/nachievements, the stateliness of the white marble/ntomb. He felt that Dobby deserved just as grand a/nfuneral, and yet here the elf lay between bushes in a/nroughly dug hole./n/n"I think we ought to say something," piped up Luna./n"I'll go first, shall I?"/n/nAnd as everybody looked at her, she addressed the/ndead elf at the bottom of the grave./n/n/n/n/n/n"Thank you so much, Dobby, for rescuing me from/nthat cellar. It's so unfair that you had to die, when/nyou were so good and brave. I'll always remember/nwhat you did for us. I hope you're happy now."/n/nShe turned and looked expectantly at Ron, who/ncleared his throat and said in a thick voice, "Yeah .../nthanks, Dobby."/n/n"Thanks," muttered Dean./n/nHarry swallowed./n/n"Good-bye, Dobby," he said. It was all he could/nmanage, but Luna had said it all for him. Bill raised/nhis wand, and the pile of earth beside the grave rose/nup into the air and fell neatly upon it, a small,/nreddish mound./n/n"D'you mind if I stay here a moment?" he asked the/nothers./n/nThey murmured words he did not catch; he felt gentle/npats upon his back, and then they all traipsed back/ntoward the cottage, leaving Harry alone beside the elf./n/nHe looked around: There were a number of large/nwhite stones, smoothed by the sea, marking the edge/nof the flower beds. He picked up one of the largest/nand laid it, pillowlike, over the place where Dobby 's/nhead now rested. He then felt in his pocket for a/nwand./n/nThere were two in there. He had forgotten, lost track;/nhe could not now remember whose wands these were;/nhe seemed to remember wrenching them out of/nsomeone's hand. He selected the shorter of the two,/nwhich felt friendlier in his hand, and pointed it at the/nrock./n/n/n/n/n/nSlowly, under his murmured instruction, deep cuts/nappeared upon the rock's surface. He knew that/nHermione could have done it more neatly, and/nprobably more quickly, but he wanted to mark the/nspot as he had wanted to dig the grave. When Harry/nstood up again, the stone read:/n/nHERE LIES DOBBY, A FREE ELF./n/nHe looked down at his handiwork for a few more/nseconds, then walked away, his scar still prickling a/nlittle, and his mind full of those things that had come/nto him in the grave, ideas that had taken shape in the/ndarkness, ideas both fascinating and terrible./n/nThey were all sitting in the living room when he/nentered the little hall, their attention focused upon/nBill, who was talking. The room was light-colored,/npretty, with a small fire of driftwood burning brightly/nin the fireplace. Harry did not want to drop mud upon/nthe carpet, so he stood in the doorway, listening./n/n"... lucky that Ginny's on holiday. If she'd been at/nHogwarts, they could have taken her before we/nreached her. Now we know she's safe too."/n/nHe looked around and saw Harry standing there./n/n"I've been getting them all out of the Burrow," he/nexplained. "Moved them to Muriel's. The Death Eaters/nknow Ron's with you now, they're bound to target the/nfamily — don't apologize," he added at the sight of/nHarry's expression. "It was always a matter of time,/nDad's been saying so for months. We're the biggest/nblood-traitor family there is."/n/n"How are they protected?" asked Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Fidelius Charm. Dad's Secret-Keeper. And we've/ndone it on this cottage too; I'm Secret-Keeper here./nNone of us can go to work, but that's hardly the most/nimportant thing now. Once Ollivander and Griphook/nare well enough, we'll move them to Muriel's too./nThere isn't much room here, but she's got plenty./nGriphook's legs are on the mend, Fleur's given him/nSkele-Gro; we could probably move them in an hour/n/n/n/nor —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," Harry said, and Bill looked startled. "I need both/nof them here. I need to talk to them. It's important."/n/nHe heard the authority in his own voice, the/nconviction, the sense of purpose that had come to him/nas he dug Dobby's grave. All of their faces were/nturned toward him, looking puzzled./n/n"I'm going to wash," Harry told Bill, looking down at/nhis hands, still covered in mud and Dobby's blood./n"Then 111 need to see them, straightaway."/n/nHe walked into the little kitchen, to the basin beneath/na window overlooking the sea. Dawn was breaking/nover the horizon, shell pink and faintly gold, as he/nwashed, again following the train of thought that had/ncome to him in the dark garden. .../n/nDobby would never be able to tell them who had sent/nhim to the cellar, but Harry knew what he had seen./n/nA piercing blue eye had looked out of the mirror/nfragment, and then help had come. Help will always/nbe given at Hog warts to those who ask for it/n/nHarry dried his hands, impervious to the beauty of/nthe scene outside the window and to the murmuring/nof the others in the sitting room. He looked out over/nthe ocean and felt closer, this dawn, than ever before,/ncloser to the heart of it all./n/n/n/n/n/nAnd still his scar prickled, and he knew that/nVoldemort was getting there too. Harry understood/nand yet did not understand. His instinct was telling/nhim one thing, his brain quite another. The/nDumbledore in Harry's head smiled, surveying Harry/nover the tips of his fingers, pressed together as if in/nprayer./n/nYou gave Ron the Deluminator. You understood him. . . ./nYou gave him a way back. . . ./n/nAnd you understood Wormtail too. ... You knew there/nwas a bit of regret there, somewhere. .../n/nAnd if you knew them ... What did you know about/nme, Dumbledore?/n/nAm I meant to know, but not to seek? Did you know/nhow hard I'd find that? Is that why you made it this/ndifficult? So I'd have time to work that out?/n/nHarry stood quite still, eyes glazed, watching the place/nwhere a bright gold rim of dazzling sun was rising/nover the horizon. Then he looked down at his clean/nhands and was momentarily surprised to see the/ncloth he was holding in them. He set it down and/nreturned to the hall, and as he did so, he felt his scar/npulse angrily, and there flashed across his mind, swift/nas the reflection of a dragonfly over water, the outline/nof a building he knew extremely well./n/nBill and Fleur were standing at the foot of the stairs./n/n"I need to speak to Griphook and Ollivander," Harry/nsaid./n/n"No," said Fleur. "You will 'ave to wait, 'Arry. Zey are/nboth ill, tired — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I'm sorry," he said without heat, "but it can't wait. I/nneed to talk to them now. Privately — and separately./nIt's urgent."/n/n"Harry, what the hell's going on?" asked Bill. "You/nturn up here with a dead house-elf and a half-/nconscious goblin, Hermione looks as though she's/nbeen tortured, and Ron's just refused to tell me/nanything — "/n/n"We can't tell you what we're doing," said Harry flatly./n"You're in the Order, Bill, you know Dumbledore left/nus a mission. We're not supposed to talk about it to/nanyone else."/n/nFleur made an impatient noise, but Bill did not look/nat her; he was staring at Harry. His deeply scarred/nface was hard to read. Finally Bill said, "All right. Who/ndo you want to talk to first?"/n/nHarry hesitated. He knew what hung on his decision./nThere was hardly any time left; now was the moment/nto decide: Horcruxes or Hallows?/n/n"Griphook," Harry said. "I'll speak to Griphook first."/n/nHis heart was racing as if he had been sprinting and/nhad just cleared an enormous obstacle./n/n"Up here, then," said Bill, leading the way./n/nHarry had walked up several steps before stopping/nand looking back./n/n"I need you two as well!" he called to Ron and/nHermione, who had been skulking, half concealed, in/nthe doorway of the sitting room./n/nThey both moved into the light, looking oddly relieved./n/n/n/n/n/n"How are you?" Harry asked Hermione. "You were/namazing — coming up with that story when she was/nhurting you like that — "/n/nHermione gave a weak smile as Ron gave her a one-/narmed squeeze./n/n"What are we doing now, Harry?" he asked./n/n"You'll see. Come on."/n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione followed Bill up the steep/nstairs onto a small landing. Three doors led off it./n/n"In here," said Bill, opening the door into his and/nFleur's room. It too had a view of the sea, now flecked/nwith gold in the sunrise. Harry moved to the window,/nturned his back on the spectacular view, and waited,/nhis arms folded, his scar prickling. Hermione took the/nchair beside the dressing table; Ron sat on the arm./n/nBill reappeared, carrying the little goblin, whom he/nset down carefully upon the bed. Griphook grunted/nthanks, and Bill left, closing the door upon them all./n/n"I'm sorry to take you out of bed," said Harry. "How/nare your legs?"/n/n"Painful," replied the goblin. "But mending."/n/nHe was still clutching the sword of Gryffindor, and/nwore a strange look: half truculent, half intrigued./nHarry noted the goblin's sallow skin, his long thin/nfingers, his black eyes. Fleur had removed his shoes:/nHis long feet were dirty. He was larger than a house-/nelf, but not by much. His domed head was much/nbigger than a human's./n/n"You probably don't remember — " Harry began./n/n/n/n/n/n" — that I was the goblin who showed you to your/nvault, the first time you ever visited Gringotts?" said/nGriphook. "I remember, Harry Potter. Even amongst/ngoblins, you are very famous."/n/nHarry and the goblin looked at each other, sizing each/nother up. Harry's scar was still prickling. He wanted/nto get through this interview with Griphook quickly,/nand at the same time was afraid of making a false/nmove. While he tried to decide on the best way to/napproach his request, the goblin broke the silence./n/n"You buried the elf," he said, sounding unexpectedly/nrancorous. "I watched you from the window of the/nbedroom next door."/n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/nGriphook looked at him out of the corners of his/nslanting black eyes./n/n"You are an unusual wizard, Harry Potter."/n/n"In what way?" asked Harry, rubbing his scar/nabsently./n/n"You dug the grave."/n/n"So?"/n/nGriphook did not answer. Harry rather thought he/nwas being sneered at for acting like a Muggle, but it/ndid not much matter to him whether Griphook/napproved of Dobby's grave or not. He gathered himself/nfor the attack./n/n"Griphook, I need to ask — "/n/n"You also rescued a goblin."/n/n/n/n/n/n"What?"/n/n/n/n"You brought me here. Saved me."/n/n"Well, I take it you're not sorry?" said Harry a little/nimpatiently./n/n"No, Harry Potter," said Griphook, and with one finger/nhe twisted the thin black beard upon his chin, "but/nyou are a very odd wizard."/n/n"Right," said Harry. "Well, I need some help,/n/nGriphook, and you can give it to me."/n/nThe goblin made no sign of encouragement, but/ncontinued to frown at Harry as though he had never/nseen anything like him./n/n"I need to break into a Gringotts vault."/n/nHarry had not meant to say it so baldly; the words/nwere forced from him as pain shot through his/nlightning scar and he saw, again, the outline of/nHogwarts. He closed his mind firmly. He needed to/ndeal with Griphook first. Ron and Hermione were/nstaring at Harry as though he had gone mad./n/n"Harry — " said Hermione, but she was cut off by/nGriphook./n/n"Break into a Gringotts vault?" repeated the goblin,/nwincing a little as he shifted his position upon the/nbed. "It is impossible."/n/n"No, it isn't," Ron contradicted him. "It's been done."/n/n"Yeah," said Harry. "The same day I first met you,/nGriphook. My birthday, seven years ago."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"The vault in question was empty at the time,"/nsnapped the goblin, and Harry understood that even/nthough Griphook had left Gringotts, he was offended/nat the idea of its defenses being breached. "Its/nprotection was minimal."/n/n"Well, the vault we need to get into isn't empty, and/nI'm guessing its protection will be pretty powerful,"/nsaid Harry. "It belongs to the Lestranges."/n/nHe saw Hermione and Ron look at each other,/nastonished, but there would be time enough to/nexplain after Griphook had given his answer./n/n"You have no chance," said Griphook flatly. "No/nchance at all. If you seek beneath our floors, a/ntreasure that was never yours — "/n/n"Thief you have been warned, beware — yeah, I/nknow, I remember," said Harry. "But I'm not trying to/nget myself any treasure, I'm not trying to take/nanything for personal gain. Can you believe that?"/n/nThe goblin looked slantwise at Harry, and the/nlightning scar on Harry's forehead prickled, but he/nignored it, refusing to acknowledge its pain or its/ninvitation./n/n"If there was a wizard of whom I would believe that/nthey did not seek personal gain," said Griphook/nfinally, "it would be you, Harry Potter. Goblins and/nelves are not used to the protection or the respect/nthat you have shown this night. Not from wand-/ncarriers."/n/n"Wand-carriers," repeated Harry: The phrase fell oddly/nupon his ears as his scar prickled, as Voldemort/nturned his thoughts northward, and as Harry burned/nto question Ollivander next door./n/n/n/n/n/n"The right to carry a wand," said the goblin quietly,/n"has long been contested between wizards and/ngoblins."/n/n"Well, goblins can do magic without wands," said/nRon./n/n"That is immaterial! Wizards refuse to share the/nsecrets of wand-lore with other magical beings, they/ndeny us the possibility of extending our powers!"/n/n"Well, goblins won't share any of their magic either,"/nsaid Ron. "You won't tell us how to make swords and/narmor the way you do. Goblins know how to work/nmetal in a way wizards have never — "/n/n"It doesn't matter," said Harry, noting Griphook's/nrising color. "This isn't about wizards versus goblins/nor any other sort of magical creature — "/n/nGriphook gave a nasty laugh./n/n"But it is, it is about precisely that! As the Dark Lord/nbecomes ever more powerful, your race is set still/nmore firmly above mine! Gringotts falls under/nWizarding rule, house-elves are slaughtered, and who/namongst the wand-carriers protests?"/n/n"We do!" said Hermione. She had sat up straight, her/neyes bright. "We protest! And I'm hunted quite as/nmuch as any goblin or elf, Griphook! I'm a Mudblood!"/n/n"Don't call yourself — " Ron muttered./n/n"Why shouldn't I?" said Hermione. "Mudblood, and/nproud of it! I've got no higher position under this new/norder than you have, Griphook! It was me they chose/nto torture, back at the Malfoys'!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAs she spoke, she pulled aside the neck of the/ndressing gown to reveal the thin cut Bellatrix had/nmade, scarlet against her throat./n/n"Did you know that it was Harry who set Dobby free?"/nshe asked. "Did you know that we've wanted elves to/nbe freed for years?" (Ron fidgeted uncomfortably on/nthe arm of Hermione's chair.) "You can't want You-/nKnow-Who defeated more than we do, Griphook!"/n/nThe goblin gazed at Hermione with the same curiosity/nhe had shown Harry./n/n"What do you seek within the Lestranges' vault?" he/nasked abruptly. "The sword that lies inside it is a/nfake. This is the real one." He looked from one to the/nother of them. "I think that you already know this./n/nYou asked me to lie for you back there."/n/n"But the fake sword isn't the only thing in that vault,/nis it?" asked Harry. "Perhaps you've seen the other/nthings in there?"/n/nHis heart was pounding harder than ever. He/nredoubled his efforts to ignore the pulsing of his scar./n/nThe goblin twisted his beard around his finger again./n/n"It is against our code to speak of the secrets of/nGringotts. We are the guardians of fabulous/ntreasures. We have a duty to the objects placed in our/ncare, which were, so often, wrought by our fingers."/n/nThe goblin stroked the sword, and his black eyes/nroved from Harry to Hermione to Ron and then back/nagain./n/n"So young," he said finally, "to be fighting so many."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Will you help us?" said Harry. "We haven't got a hope/nof breaking in without a goblin's help. You're our one/nchance."/n/n"I shall ... think about it," said Griphook/nmaddeningly./n/n"But — " Ron started angrily; Hermione nudged him in/nthe ribs./n/n"Thank you," said Harry./n/nThe goblin bowed his great domed head in/nacknowledgement, then flexed his short legs./n/n"I think," he said, settling himself ostentatiously upon/nBill and Fleur's bed, "that the Skele-Gro has finished/nits work. I may be able to sleep at last. Forgive me. ..."/n/n"Yeah, of course," said Harry, but before leaving the/nroom he leaned forward and took the sword of/nGryffindor from beside the goblin. Griphook did not/nprotest, but Harry thought he saw resentment in the/ngoblin's eyes as he closed the door upon him./n/n"Little git," whispered Ron. "He's enjoying keeping us/nhanging."/n/n"Harry," whispered Hermione, pulling them both away/nfrom the door, into the middle of the still-dark/nlanding, "are you saying what I think you're saying?/nAre you saying there's a Horcrux in the Lestranges'/nvault?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry. "Bellatrix was terrified when she/nthought we'd been in there, she was beside herself./nWhy? What did she think we'd seen, what else did she/nthink we might have taken? Something she was/npetrified You-Know-Who would find out about."/n/n/n/n/n/n"But I thought we were looking for places You-Know-/nWho's been, places he's done something important?"/nsaid Ron, looking baffled. "Was he ever inside the/nLestranges' vault?"/n/n"I don't know whether he was ever inside Gringotts,"/nsaid Harry. "He never had gold there when he was/nyounger, because nobody left him anything. He would/nhave seen the bank from the outside, though, the first/ntime he ever went to Diagon Alley."/n/nHarry's scar throbbed, but he ignored it; he wanted/nRon and Hermione to understand about Gringotts/nbefore they spoke to Ollivander./n/n"I think he would have envied anyone who had a key/nto a Gringotts vault. I think he'd have seen it as a real/nsymbol of belonging to the Wizarding world. And don't/nforget, he trusted Bellatrix and her husband. They/nwere his most devoted servants before he fell, and/nthey went looking for him after he vanished. He said it/nthe night he came back, I heard him."/n/nHarry rubbed his scar./n/n"I don't think he'd have told Bellatrix it was a/nHorcrux, though. He never told Lucius Malfoy the/ntruth about the diary. He probably told her it was a/ntreasured possession and asked her to place it in her/nvault. The safest place in the world for anything you/nwant to hide, Hagrid told me ... except for Hogwarts."/n/nWhen Harry had finished speaking, Ron shook his/nhead./n/n"You really understand him."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Bits of him," said Harry. "Bits ... I just wish I'd/nunderstood Dumbledore as much. But well see./n/nCome on — Ollivander now."/n/nRon and Hermione looked bewildered but impressed/nas they followed him across the little landing and/nknocked upon the door opposite Bill and Fleur's. A/nweak "Come in!" answered them./n/nThe wandmaker was lying on the twin bed farthest/nfrom the window. He had been held in the cellar for/nmore than a year, and tortured, Harry knew, on at/nleast one occasion. He was emaciated, the bones of/nhis face sticking out sharply against the yellowish/nskin. His great silver eyes seemed vast in their/nsunken sockets. The hands that lay upon the blanket/ncould have belonged to a skeleton. Harry sat down on/nthe empty bed, beside Ron and Hermione. The rising/nsun was not visible here. The room faced the cliff- top/ngarden and the freshly dug grave./n/n"Mr. Ollivander, I'm sorry to disturb you," Harry said./n/n"My dear boy." Ollivander's voice was feeble. "You/nrescued us. I thought we would die in that place. I/ncan never thank you ... never thank you ... enough."/n/n"We were glad to do it."/n/nHarry's scar throbbed. He knew, he was certain, that/nthere was hardly any time left in which to beat/nVoldemort to his goal, or else to attempt to thwart/nhim. He felt a flutter of panic ... yet he had made his/ndecision when he chose to speak to Griphook first./nFeigning a calm he did not feel, he groped in the/npouch around his neck and took out the two halves of/nhis broken wand./n/n"Mr. Ollivander, I need some help."/n/n/n/n/n/n"Anything. Anything," said the wandmaker weakly./n/n"Can you mend this? Is it possible?"/n/nOllivander held out a trembling hand, and Harry/nplaced the two barely connected halves into his palm./n/n"Holly and phoenix feather," said Ollivander in a/ntremulous voice. "Eleven inches. Nice and supple."/n/n"Yes," said Harry. "Can you — ?"/n/n"No," whispered Ollivander. "I am sorry, very sorry,/nbut a wand that has suffered this degree of damage/ncannot be repaired by any means that I know of."/n/nHarry had been braced to hear it, but it was a blow/nnevertheless. He took the wand halves back and/nreplaced them in the pouch around his neck./nOllivander stared at the place where the shattered/nwand had vanished, and did not look away until/nHarry had taken from his pocket the two wands he/nhad brought from the Malfoys'./n/n"Can you identify these?" Harry asked./n/nThe wandmaker took the first of the wands and held/nit close to his faded eyes, rolling it between his/nknobble-knuckled fingers, flexing it slightly./n/n"Walnut and dragon heartstring," he said. "Twelve-/nand-three-quarter inches. Unyielding. This wand/nbelonged to Bellatrix Lestrange."/n/n"And this one?"/n/nOllivander performed the same examination./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Hawthorn and unicorn hair. Ten inches precisely./nReasonably springy. This was the wand of Draco/nMalfoy."/n/n/n/n"Was?" repeated Harry. "Isn't it still his?"/n"Perhaps not. If you took it — "/n/n"— I did — "/n/n/n/n" — then it may be yours. Of course, the manner of/ntaking matters. Much also depends upon the wand/nitself. In general, however, where a wand has been/nwon, its allegiance will change."/n/nThere was silence in the room, except for the distant/nrushing of the sea./n/n"You talk about wands like they've got feelings," said/nHarry, "like they can think for themselves."/n/n"The wand chooses the wizard," said Ollivander. "That/nmuch has always been clear to those of us who have/nstudied wandlore."/n/n"A person can still use a wand that hasn't chosen/nthem, though?" asked Harry./n/n"Oh yes, if you are any wizard at all you will be able to/nchannel your magic through almost any instrument./nThe best results, however, must always come where/nthere is the strongest affinity between wizard and/nwand. These connections are complex. An initial/nattraction, and then a mutual quest for experience,/nthe wand learning from the wizard, the wizard from/nthe wand."/n/nThe sea gushed forward and backward; it was a/nmournful sound./n/n/n/n/n/n"I took this wand from Draco Malfoy by force," said/nHarry. "Can I use it safely?"/n/n"I think so. Subtle laws govern wand ownership, but/nthe conquered wand will usually bend its will to its/nnew master."/n/n"So I should use this one?" said Ron, pulling/nWormtail's wand out of his pocket and handing it to/nOllivander./n/n"Chestnut and dragon heartstring. Nine-and-a-/nquarter inches. Brittle. I was forced to make this/nshortly after my kidnapping, for Peter Pettigrew. Yes,/nif you won it, it is more likely to do your bidding, and/ndo it well, than another wand."/n/n"And this holds true for all wands, does it?" asked/nHarry./n/n"I think so," replied Ollivander, his protuberant eyes/nupon Harry's face. "You ask deep questions, Mr./n/nPotter. Wandlore is a complex and mysterious branch/nof magic."/n/n"So, it isn't necessary to kill the previous owner to/ntake true possession of a wand?" asked Harry./n/nOllivander swallowed./n/n"Necessary? No, I should not say that it is necessary/nto kill."/n/n"There are legends, though," said Harry, and as his/nheart rate quickened, the pain in his scar became/nmore intense; he was sure that Voldemort had/ndecided to put his idea into action. "Legends about a/nwand — or wands — that have passed from hand to/nhand by murder."/n/n/n/n/n/nOllivander turned pale. Against the snowy pillow he/nwas light gray, and his eyes were enormous,/nbloodshot, and bulging with what looked like fear./n/n"Only one wand, I think," he whispered./n/n"And You-Know-Who is interested in it, isn't he?"/nasked Harry./n/n"I — how?" croaked Ollivander, and he looked/nappealingly at Ron and Hermione for help. "How do/nyou know this?"/n/n"He wanted you to tell him how to overcome the/nconnection between our wands," said Harry./n/nOllivander looked terrified./n/n"He tortured me, you must understand that! The/nCruciatus Curse, I — I had no choice but to tell him/nwhat I knew, what I guessed!"/n/n"I understand," said Harry. "You told him about the/ntwin cores? You said he just had to borrow another/nwizard's wand?"/n/nOllivander looked horrified, transfixed, by the amount/nthat Harry knew. He nodded slowly./n/n"But it didn't work," Harry went on. "Mine still beat/nthe borrowed wand. Do you know why that is?"/n/nOllivander shook his head as slowly as he had just/nnodded./n/n"I had ... never heard of such a thing. Your wand/nperformed something unique that night. The/nconnection of the twin cores is incredibly rare, yet/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nwhy your wand should have snapped the borrowed/nwand, I do not know. ..."/n/n"We were talking about the other wand, the wand that/nchanges hands by murder. When You-Know-Who/nrealized my wand had done something strange, he/ncame back and asked about that other wand, didn't/nhe?"/n/n"How do you know this?"/n/nHarry did not answer./n/n"Yes, he asked," whispered Ollivander. "He wanted to/nknow everything I could tell him about the wand/nvariously known as the Deathstick, the Wand of/nDestiny, or the Elder Wand."/n/nHarry glanced sideways at Hermione. She looked/nflabbergasted./n/n"The Dark Lord," said Ollivander in hushed and/nfrightened tones, "had always been happy with the/nwand I made him — yew and phoenix feather,/nthirteen-and-a-half inches — until he discovered the/nconnection of the twin cores. Now he seeks another,/nmore powerful wand, as the only way to conquer/nyours."/n/n"But he'll know soon, if he doesn't already, that/nmine's broken beyond repair," said Harry quietly./n/n"No!" said Hermione, sounding frightened. "He can't/nknow that, Harry, how could he — ?"/n/n"Priori Incantatem," said Harry. "We left your wand/nand the blackthorn wand at the Malfoys', Hermione. If/nthey examine them properly, make them re-create the/nspells they've cast lately, they'll see that yours broke/n/n/n/n/n/nmine, they'll see that you tried and failed to mend it,/nand they'll realize that I've been using the blackthorn/none ever since."/n/nThe little color she had regained since their arrival/nhad drained from her face. Ron gave Harry a/nreproachful look, and said, "Let's not worry about/nthat now — "/n/nBut Mr. Ollivander intervened./n/n"The Dark Lord no longer seeks the Elder Wand only/nfor your destruction, Mr. Potter. He is determined to/npossess it because he believes it will make him truly/ninvulnerable."/n/n"And will it?"/n/n"The owner of the Elder Wand must always fear/nattack," said Ollivander, "but the idea of the Dark/nLord in possession of the Deathstick is, I must admit/n... formidable."/n/nHarry was suddenly reminded of how he had been/nunsure, when they first met, of how much he liked/nOllivander. Even now, having been tortured and/nimprisoned by Voldemort, the idea of the Dark wizard/nin possession of this wand seemed to enthrall him as/nmuch as it repulsed him./n/n"You — you really think this wand exists, then, Mr./nOllivander?" asked Hermione./n/n"Oh yes," said Ollivander. "Yes, it is perfectly possible/nto trace the wand's course through history. There are/ngaps, of course, and long ones, where it vanishes from/nview, temporarily lost or hidden; but always it/nresurfaces. It has certain identifying characteristics/nthat those who are learned in wandlore recognize./n/n/n/n/nThere are written accounts, some of them obscure,/nthat I and other wandmakers have made it our/nbusiness to study. They have the ring of authenticity."/n/n"So you — you don't think it can be a fairy tale or a/nmyth?" Hermione asked hopefully./n/n"No," said Ollivander. "Whether it needs to pass by/nmurder, I do not know. Its history is bloody, but that/nmay be simply due to the fact that it is such a/ndesirable object, and arouses such passions in/nwizards. Immensely powerful, dangerous in the wrong/nhands, and an object of incredible fascination to all of/nus who study the power of wands."/n/n"Mr. Ollivander," said Harry, "you told You-Know-Who/nthat Gregorovitch had the Elder Wand, didn't you?"/n/nOllivander turned, if possible, even paler. He looked/nghostly as he gulped./n/n"But how — how do you — ?"/n/n"Never mind how I know it," said Harry, closing his/neyes momentarily as his scar burned and he saw, for/nmere seconds, a vision of the main street in/nHogsmeade, still dark, because it was so much/nfarther north. "You told You-Know-Who that/nGregorovitch had the wand?"/n/n"It was a rumor," whispered Ollivander. "A rumor,/nyears and years ago, long before you were born! I/nbelieve Gregorovitch himself started it. You can see/nhow good it would be for business: that he was/nstudying and duplicating the qualities of the Elder/nWand!"/n/n"Yes, I can see that," said Harry. He stood up. "Mr./nOllivander, one last thing, and then we'll let you get/n/n/n/n/n/nsome rest. What do you know about the Deathly/nHallows?"/n/n/n/n"The — the what?" asked the wandmaker, looking/nutterly bewildered./n/n"The Deathly Hallows."/n/n"I'm afraid I don't know what you're talking about. Is/nthis still something to do with wands?"/n/nHarry looked into the sunken face and believed that/nOllivander was not acting. He did not know about the/nHallows./n/n"Thank you," said Harry. "Thank you very much. We'll/nleave you to get some rest now."/n/nOllivander looked stricken./n/n"He was torturing me!" he gasped. "The Cruciatus/nCurse ... you have no idea. ..."/n/n"I do," said Harry. "I really do. Please get some rest./nThank you for telling me all of this."/n/nHe led Ron and Hermione down the staircase. Harry/ncaught a glimpse of Bill, Fleur, Luna, and Dean/nsitting at the table in the kitchen, cups of tea in front/nof them. They all looked up at Harry as he appeared/nin the doorway, but he merely nodded to them and/ncontinued into the garden, Ron and Hermione behind/nhim. The reddish mound of earth that covered Dobby/nlay ahead, and Harry walked back to it, as the pain in/nhis head built more and more powerfully. It was a/nhuge effort now to close down the visions that were/nforcing themselves upon him, but he knew that he/nwould have to resist only a little longer. He would/nyield very soon, because he needed to know that his/n/n/n/n/ntheory was right. He must make only one more short/neffort, so that he could explain to Ron and Hermione./n/n"Gregorovitch had the Elder Wand a long time ago,"/nhe said. "I saw You-Know-Who trying to find him./nWhen he tracked him down, he found that/nGregorovitch didn't have it anymore: It was stolen/nfrom him by Grindelwald. How Grindelwald found out/nthat Gregorovitch had it, I don't know — but if/nGregorovitch was stupid enough to spread the rumor,/nit can't have been that difficult."/n/nVoldemort was at the gates of Hogwarts; Harry could/nsee him standing there, and see too the lamp bobbing/nin the pre-dawn, coming closer and closer./n/n"And Grindelwald used the Elder Wand to become/npowerful. And at the height of his power, when/nDumbledore knew he was the only one who could/nstop him, he dueled Grindelwald and beat him, and/nhe took the Elder Wand."/n/n"Dumbledore had the Elder Wand?" said Ron. "But/nthen — where is it now?"/n/n"At Hogwarts," said Harry, fighting to remain with/nthem in the cliff-top garden./n/n"But then, let's go!" said Ron urgently. "Harry, let's go/nand get it before he does!"/n/n"It's too late for that," said Harry. He could not help/nhimself, but clutched his head, trying to help it resist./n"He knows where it is. He's there now."/n/n"Harry!" Ron said furiously. "How long have you/nknown this — why have we been wasting time? Why/ndid you talk to Griphook first? We could have gone —/nwe could still go — "/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Harry, and he sank to his knees in the/ngrass. "Hermione's right. Dumbledore didn't want me/nto have it. He didn't want me to take it. He wanted me/nto get the Horcruxes."/n/n"The unbeatable wand, Harry!" moaned Ron./n/n"I'm not supposed to ... I'm supposed to get the/nHorcruxes. ..."/n/nAnd now everything was cool and dark: The sun was/nbarely visible over the horizon as he glided alongside/nSnape, up through the grounds toward the lake./n/n"I shall join you in the castle shortly," he said in his/nhigh, cold voice. "Leave me now."/n/nSnape bowed and set off back up the path, his black/ncloak billowing behind him. Harry walked slowly,/nwaiting for Snape 's figure to disappear. It would not/ndo for Snape, or indeed anyone else, to see where he/nwas going. But there were no lights in the castle/nwindows, and he could conceal himself ... and in a/nsecond he had cast upon himself a Disillusionment/nCharm that hid him even from his own eyes./n/nAnd he walked on, around the edge of the lake, taking/nin the outlines of the beloved castle, his first kingdom,/nhis birthright. .../n/nAnd here it was, beside the lake, reflected in the dark/nwaters. The white marble tomb, an unnecessary blot/non the familiar landscape. He felt again that rush of/ncontrolled euphoria, that heady sense of purpose in/ndestruction. He raised the old yew wand: How fitting/nthat this would be its last great act./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThe tomb split open from head to foot. The shrouded/nfigure was as long and thin as it had been in life. He/nraised the wand again./n/nThe wrappings fell open. The face was translucent,/npale, sunken, yet almost perfectly preserved. They/nhad left his spectacles on the crooked nose: He felt/namused derision. Dumbledore's hands were folded/nupon his chest, and there it lay, clutched beneath/nthem, buried with him./n/nHad the old fool imagined that marble or death would/nprotect the wand? Had he thought that the Dark Lord/nwould be scared to violate his tomb? The spiderlike/nhand swooped and pulled the wand from/nDumbledore's grasp, and as he took it, a shower of/nsparks flew from its tip, sparkling over the corpse of/nits last owner, ready to serve a new master at last./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Shell Cottage
text: /nBill and Fleur's cottage stood alone on a cliff/noverlooking the sea, its walls embedded with shells/nand whitewashed. It was a lonely and beautiful place./nWherever Harry went inside the tiny cottage or its/ngarden, he could hear the constant ebb and flow of/nthe sea, like the breathing of some great, slumbering/ncreature. He spent much of the next few days making/nexcuses to escape the crowded cottage, craving the/ncliff-top view of open sky and wide, empty sea, and/nthe feel of cold, salty wind on his face./n/nThe enormity of his decision not to race Voldemort to/nthe wand still scared Harry. He could not remember,/never before, choosing not to act. He was full of doubts,/ndoubts that Ron could not help voicing whenever they/nwere together./n/n"What if Dumbledore wanted us to work out the/nsymbol in time to get the wand?" "What if working out/nwhat the symbol meant made you 'worthy' to get the/nHallows?" "Harry, if that really is the Elder Wand,/nhow the hell are we supposed to finish off You-Know-/n/n/n/n/nWho?" Harry had no answers: There were moments/nwhen he wondered whether it had been outright/nmadness not to try to prevent Voldemort breaking/nopen the tomb. He could not even explain/nsatisfactorily why he had decided against it: Every/ntime he tried to reconstruct the internal arguments/nthat had led to his decision, they sounded feebler to/nhim./n/nThe odd thing was that Hermione's support made him/nfeel just as confused as Ron's doubts. Now forced to/naccept that the Elder Wand was real, she maintained/nthat it was an evil object, and that the way Voldemort/nhad taken possession of it was repellent, not to be/nconsidered./n/n"You could never have done that, Harry," she said/nagain and again. "You couldn't have broken into/nDumbledore's grave."/n/nBut the idea of Dumbledore's corpse frightened Harry/nmuch less than the possibility that he might have/nmisunderstood the living Dumbledore's intentions. He/nfelt that he was still groping in the dark; he had/nchosen his path but kept looking back, wondering/nwhether he had misread the signs, whether he should/nnot have taken the other way. From time to time,/nanger at Dumbledore crashed over him again,/npowerful as the waves slamming themselves against/nthe cliff beneath the cottage, anger that Dumbledore/nhad not explained before he died./n/n"But is he dead?" said Ron, three days after they had/narrived at the cottage. Harry had been staring out/nover the wall that separated the cottage garden from/nthe cliff when Ron and Hermione had found him; he/nwished they had not, having no wish to join in with/ntheir argument./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yes, he is, Ron, please don't start that again!"/n/n"Look at the facts, Hermione," said Ron, speaking/nacross Harry, who continued to gaze at the horizon./n"The silver doe. The sword. The eye Harry saw in the/nmirror — "/n/n"Harry admits he could have imagined the eye! Don't/nyou, Harry?"/n/n"I could have," said Harry without looking at her./n/n"But you don't think you did, do you?" asked Ron./n/n"No, I don't," said Harry./n/n"There you go!" said Ron quickly, before Hermione/ncould carry on. "If it wasn't Dumbledore, explain how/nDobby knew we were in the cellar, Hermione?"/n/n"I can't — but can you explain how Dumbledore sent/nhim to us if he's lying in a tomb at Hogwarts?"/n/n"I dunno, it could've been his ghost!"/n/n"Dumbledore wouldn't come back as a ghost," said/nHarry. There was little about Dumbledore he was sure/nof now, but he knew that much. "He would have gone/non."/n/n"What d'you mean, 'gone on'?" asked Ron, but before/nHarry could say any more, a voice behind them said, "/n'Arry?"/n/nFleur had come out of the cottage, her long silver hair/nflying in the breeze./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" 'Arry, Grip'ook would like to speak to you. 'E eez in/nze smallest bedroom, 'e says 'e does not want to be/nover'eard."/n/nHer dislike of the goblin sending her to deliver/nmessages was clear; she looked irritable as she/nwalked back around the house./n/nGriphook was waiting for them, as Fleur had said, in/nthe tiniest of the cottage's three bedrooms, in which/nHermione and Luna slept by night. He had drawn the/nred cotton curtains against the bright, cloudy sky,/nwhich gave the room a fiery glow at odds with the rest/nof the airy, light cottage./n/n"I have reached my decision, Harry Potter," said the/ngoblin, who was sitting cross-legged in a low chair,/ndrumming its arms with his spindly fingers. "Though/nthe goblins of Gringotts will consider it base/ntreachery, I have decided to help you — "/n/n"That's great!" said Harry, relief surging through him./n"Griphook, thank you, we're really — "/n/n" — in return," said the goblin firmly, "for payment."/n/nSlightly taken aback, Harry hesitated./n/n"How much do you want? I've got gold."/n/n"Not gold," said Griphook. "I have gold."/n/nHis black eyes glittered; there were no whites to his/neyes./n/n"I want the sword. The sword of Godric Gryffindor."/nHarry's spirits plummeted./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You can't have that," he said. "I'm sorry."/n/n"Then," said the goblin softly, "we have a problem."/n/n"We can give you something else," said Ron eagerly./n"I'll bet the Lestranges have got loads of stuff, you can/ntake your pick once we get into the vault."/n/nHe had said the wrong thing. Griphook flushed/nangrily./n/n"I am not a thief, boy! I am not trying to procure/ntreasures to which I have no right!"/n/n"The sword's ours — "/n/n"It is not," said the goblin./n/n"We're Gryffindors, and it was Godric Gryffindor's — "/n/n"And before it was Gryffindor's, whose was it?"/ndemanded the goblin, sitting up straight./n/n"No one's," said Ron. "It was made for him, wasn't it?"/n/n"No!" cried the goblin, bristling with anger as he/npointed a long finger at Ron. "Wizarding arrogance/nagain! That sword was Ragnuk the First's, taken from/nhim by Godric Gryffindor! It is a lost treasure, a/nmasterpiece of goblinwork! It belongs with the/ngoblins! The sword is the price of my hire, take it or/nleave it!"/n/nGriphook glared at them. Harry glanced at the other/ntwo, then said, "We need to discuss this, Griphook, if/nthat's all right. Could you give us a few minutes?"/n/nThe goblin nodded, looking sour./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDownstairs in the empty sitting room, Harry walked/nto the fireplace, brow furrowed, trying to think what/nto do. Behind him, Ron said, "He's having a laugh. We/ncan't let him have that sword."/n/n"It is true?" Harry asked Hermione. "Was the sword/nstolen by Gryffindor?"/n/n"I don't know," she said hopelessly. "Wizarding history/noften skates over what the wizards have done to other/nmagical races, but there's no account that I know of/nthat says Gryffindor stole the sword."/n/n"It'll be one of those goblin stories," said Ron, "about/nhow the wizards are always trying to get one over on/nthem. I suppose we should think ourselves lucky he/nhasn't asked for one of our wands."/n/n"Goblins have got good reason to dislike wizards,/n/nRon," said Hermione. "They've been treated brutally in/nthe past."/n/n"Goblins aren't exactly fluffy little bunnies, though,/nare they?" said Ron. "They've killed plenty of us./nThey've fought dirty too."/n/n"But arguing with Griphook about whose race is most/nunderhanded and violent isn't going to make him/nmore likely to help us, is it?"/n/nThere was a pause while they tried to think of a way/naround the problem. Harry looked out of the window/nat Dobby's grave. Luna was arranging sea lavender in/na jam jar beside the headstone./n/n"Okay," said Ron, and Harry turned back to face him,/n"how's this? We tell Griphook we need the sword until/nwe get inside the vault, and then he can have it./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nThere's a fake in there, isn't there? We switch them,/nand give him the fake."/n/n"Ron, he'd know the difference better than we would!"/nsaid Hermione. "He's the only one who realized there/nhad been a swap!"/n/n"Yeah, but we could scarper before he realizes — "/n/nHe quailed beneath the look Hermione was giving/nhim./n/n"That," she said quietly, "is despicable. Ask for his/nhelp, then double-cross him? And you wonder why/ngoblins don't like wizards, Ron?"/n/nRon's ears had turned red./n/n"All right, all right! It was the only thing I could think/nof! What's your solution, then?"/n/n"We need to offer him something else, something just/nas valuable."/n/n"Brilliant. I'll go and get one of our other ancient/ngoblin-made swords and you can gift wrap it."/n/nSilence fell between them again. Harry was sure that/nthe goblin would accept nothing but the sword, even/nif they had something as valuable to offer him. Yet the/nsword was their one, indispensable weapon against/nthe Horcruxes./n/nHe closed his eyes for a moment or two and listened/nto the rush of the sea. The idea that Gryffindor might/nhave stolen the sword was unpleasant to him: He had/nalways been proud to be a Gryffindor; Gryffindor had/nbeen the champion of Muggle-borns, the wizard who/nhad clashed with the pureblood-loving Slytherin. .../n/n/n/n/n"Maybe he's lying," Harry said, opening his eyes/nagain. "Griphook. Maybe Gryffindor didn't take the/nsword. How do we know the goblin version of history's/nright?"/n/n"Does it make a difference?" asked Hermione./n"Changes how I feel about it," said Harry./n/nHe took a deep breath./n/n"Well tell him he can have the sword after he's helped/nus get into that vault — but we'll be careful to avoid/ntelling him exactly when he can have it."/n/nA grin spread slowly across Ron's face. Hermione,/nhowever, looked alarmed./n/n"Harry, we can't — "/n/n"He can have it," Harry went on, "after we've used it/non all of the Horcruxes. I'll make sure he gets it then./nI'll keep my word."/n/n"But that could be years!" said Hermione./n/n"I know that, but he needn't. I won't be lying .../nreally."/n/nHarry met her eyes with a mixture of defiance and/nshame. He remembered the words that had been/nengraved over the gateway to Nurmengard: FOR THE/nGREATER GOOD. He pushed the idea away. What/nchoice did they have?/n/n"I don't like it," said Hermione./n/n"Nor do I, much," Harry admitted./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, I think it's genius," said Ron, standing up/nagain. "Let's go and tell him."/n/n/n/nBack in the smallest bedroom, Harry made the offer,/ncareful to phrase it so as not to give any definite time/nfor the handover of the sword. Hermione frowned at/nthe floor while he was speaking; he felt irritated at/nher, afraid that she might give the game away./nHowever, Griphook had eyes for nobody but Harry./n/n"I have your word, Harry Potter, that you will give me/nthe sword of Gryffindor if I help you?"/n/n"Yes," said Harry./n/n"Then shake," said the goblin, holding out his hand./n/nHarry took it and shook. He wondered whether those/nblack eyes saw any misgivings in his own. Then/nGriphook relinquished him, clapped his hands/ntogether, and said, "So. We begin!"/n/nIt was like planning to break into the Ministry all over/nagain. They settled to work in the smallest bedroom,/nwhich was kept, according to Griphook's preference,/nin semidarkness./n/n"I have visited the Lestranges' vault only once,"/nGriphook told them, "on the occasion I was told to/nplace inside it the false sword. It is one of the most/nancient chambers. The oldest Wizarding families store/ntheir treasures at the deepest level, where the vaults/nare largest and best protected. ..."/n/nThey remained shut in the cupboardlike room for/nhours at a time. Slowly the days stretched into weeks./nThere was problem after problem to overcome, not/nleast of which was that their store of Polyjuice Potion/nwas greatly depleted./n/n/n/n/n/n"There's really only enough left for one of us," said/nHermione, tilting the thick mudlike potion against the/nlamplight./n/n"That'll be enough," said Harry, who was examining/nGriphook's hand-drawn map of the deepest/npassageways./n/nThe other inhabitants of Shell Cottage could hardly/nfail to notice that something was going on now that/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione only emerged for/nmealtimes. Nobody asked questions, although Harry/noften felt Bill's eyes on the three of them at the table,/nthoughtful, concerned./n/nThe longer they spent together, the more Harry/nrealized that he did not much like the goblin./nGriphook was unexpectedly bloodthirsty, laughed at/nthe idea of pain in lesser creatures, and seemed to/nrelish the possibility that they might have to hurt/nother wizards to reach the Lestranges' vault. Harry/ncould tell that his distaste was shared by the other/ntwo, but they did not discuss it: They needed/nGriphook./n/nThe goblin ate only grudgingly with the rest of them./nEven after his legs had mended, he continued to/nrequest trays of food in his room, like the still-frail/nOllivander, until Bill (following an angry outburst/nfrom Fleur) went upstairs to tell him that the/narrangement could not continue. Thereafter Griphook/njoined them at the overcrowded table, although he/nrefused to eat the same food, insisting, instead, on/nlumps of raw meat, roots, and various fungi./n/nHarry felt responsible: It was, after all, he who had/ninsisted that the goblin remain at Shell Cottage so/nthat he could question him; his fault that the whole/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWeasley family had been driven into hiding, that Bill,/nFred, George, and Mr. Weasley could no longer work./n/n"I'm sorry," he told Fleur, one blustery April evening/nas he helped her prepare dinner. "I never meant you/nto have to deal with all of this."/n/nShe had just set some knives to work, chopping up/nsteaks for Griphook and Bill, who had preferred his/nmeat bloody ever since he had been attacked by/nGreyback. While the knives sliced away behind her,/nher somewhat irritable expression softened./n/n" 'Arry, you saved my sister's life, I do not forget."/n/nThis was not, strictly speaking, true, but Harry/ndecided against reminding her that Gabrielle had/nnever been in real danger./n/n"Anyway," Fleur went on, pointing her wand at a pot/nof sauce on the stove, which began to bubble at once,/n"Mr. Ollivander leaves for Muriel's zis evening. Zat will/nmake zings easier. Ze goblin," she scowled a little at/nthe mention of him, "can move downstairs, and you,/nRon, and Dean can take zat room."/n/n"We don't mind sleeping in the living room," said/nHarry, who knew that Griphook would think poorly of/nhaving to sleep on the sofa; keeping Griphook happy/nwas essential to their plans. "Don't worry about us."/nAnd when she tried to protest he went on, "We'll be off/nyour hands soon too, Ron, Hermione, and I. We won't/nneed to be here much longer."/n/n"But what do you mean?" she said, frowning at him,/nher wand pointing at the casserole dish now/nsuspended in midair. "Of course you must not leave,/nyou are safe 'ere!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nShe looked rather like Mrs. Weasley as she said it,/nand he was glad that the back door opened at that/nmoment. Luna and Dean entered, their hair damp/nfrom the rain outside and their arms full of driftwood./n/n"... and tiny little ears," Luna was saying, "a bit like a/nhippo's, Daddy says, only purple and hairy. And if/nyou want to call them, you have to hum; they prefer a/nwaltz, nothing too fast. ..."/n/nLooking uncomfortable, Dean shrugged at Harry as/nhe passed, following Luna into the combined dining/nand sitting room where Ron and Hermione were/nlaying the dinner table. Seizing the chance to escape/nFleur's questions, Harry grabbed two jugs of pumpkin/njuice and followed them./n/n"... and if you ever come to our house I'll be able to/nshow you the horn, Daddy wrote to me about it but I/nhaven't seen it yet, because the Death Eaters took me/nfrom the Hogwarts Express and I never got home for/nChristmas," Luna was saying, as she and Dean relaid/nthe fire./n/n"Luna, we told you," Hermione called over to her./n"That horn exploded. It came from an Erumpent, not/na Crumple-Horned Snorkack — "/n/n"No, it was definitely a Snorkack horn," said Luna/nserenely. "Daddy told me. It will probably have re-/nformed by now, they mend themselves, you know."/n/nHermione shook her head and continued laying down/nforks as Bill appeared, leading Mr. Ollivander down/nthe stairs. The wandmaker still looked exceptionally/nfrail, and he clung to Bill's arm as the latter/nsupported him, carrying a large suitcase./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n'Tm going to miss you, Mr. Ollivander," said Luna,/napproaching the old man./n/n"And I you, my dear," said Ollivander, patting her on/nthe shoulder. "You were an inexpressible comfort to/nme in that terrible place."/n/n"So, au revoir, Mr. Ollivander," said Fleur, kissing him/non both cheeks. "And I wonder whezzer you could/noblige me by delivering a package to Bill's Auntie/nMuriel? I never returned 'er tiara."/n/n"It will be an honor," said Ollivander with a little bow,/n"the very least I can do in return for your generous/nhospitality."/n/nFleur drew out a worn velvet case, which she opened/nto show the wandmaker. The tiara sat glittering and/ntwinkling in the light from the low-hanging lamp./n/n"Moonstones and diamonds," said Griphook, who had/nsidled into the room without Harry noticing. "Made by/ngoblins, I think?"/n/n"And paid for by wizards," said Bill quietly, and the/ngoblin shot him a look that was both furtive and/nchallenging./n/nA strong wind gusted against the cottage windows as/nBill and Ollivander set off into the night. The rest of/nthem squeezed in around the table; elbow to elbow/nand with barely enough room to move, they started to/neat. The fire crackled and popped in the grate beside/nthem. Fleur, Harry noticed, was merely playing with/nher food; she glanced at the window every few/nminutes; however, Bill returned before they had/nfinished their first course, his long hair tangled by the/nwind./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Everything's fine," he told Fleur. "Ollivander settled/nin, Mum and Dad say hello. Ginny sends you all her/nlove. Fred and George are driving Muriel up the wall,/nthey're still operating an Owl-Order business out of/nher back room. It cheered her up to have her tiara/nback, though. She said she thought we'd stolen it."/n/n"Ah, she eez charmante, your aunt," said Fleur/ncrossly, waving her wand and causing the dirty plates/nto rise and form a stack in midair. She caught them/nand marched out of the room./n/n"Daddy's made a tiara," piped up Luna. "Well, more of/na crown, really."/n/nRon caught Harry's eye and grinned; Harry knew that/nhe was remembering the ludicrous headdress they/nhad seen on their visit to Xenophilius./n/n"Yes, he's trying to re-create the lost diadem of/nRavenclaw. He thinks he's identified most of the main/nelements now. Adding the billywig wings really made/na difference — "/n/nThere was a bang on the front door. Everyone's head/nturned toward it. Fleur came running out of the/nkitchen, looking frightened; Bill jumped to his feet,/nhis wand pointing at the door; Harry, Ron, and/nHermione did the same. Silently Griphook slipped/nbeneath the table, out of sight./n/n"Who is it?" Bill called./n/n"It is I, Remus John Lupin!" called a voice over the/nhowling wind. Harry experienced a thrill of fear; what/nhad happened? "I am a werewolf, married to/nNymphadora Tonks, and you, the Secret-Keeper of/nShell Cottage, told me the address and bade me come/nin an emergency!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Lupin," muttered Bill, and he ran to the door and/nwrenched it open./n/nLupin fell over the threshold. He was white-faced,/nwrapped in a traveling cloak, his graying hair/nwindswept. He straightened up, looked around the/nroom, making sure of who was there, then cried/naloud, "It's a boy! We've named him Ted, after Dora's/nfather!"/n/nHermione shrieked./n/n"Wha — ? Tonks — Tonks has had the baby?"/n/n"Yes, yes, she's had the baby!" shouted Lupin. All/naround the table came cries of delight, sighs of relief:/nHermione and Fleur both squealed,/n/n"Congratulations!" and Ron said, "Blimey, a baby!" as/nif he had never heard of such a thing before./n/n"Yes — yes — a boy," said Lupin again, who seemed/ndazed by his own happiness. He strode around the/ntable and hugged Harry; the scene in the basement of/nGrimmauld Place might never have happened./n/n"You'll be godfather?" he said as he released Harry./n/n"M-me?" stammered Harry/n/n"You, yes, of course — Dora quite agrees, no one/nbetter — "/n/n"I — yeah — blimey — "/n/nHarry felt overwhelmed, astonished, delighted; now/nBill was hurrying to fetch wine, and Fleur was/npersuading Lupin to join them for a drink./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I can't stay long, I must get back," said Lupin,/nbeaming around at them all: He looked years younger/nthan Harry had ever seen him. "Thank you, thank/nyou, Bill."/n/nBill had soon filled all of their goblets, they stood and/nraised them high in a toast./n/n"To Teddy Remus Lupin," said Lupin, "a great wizard/nin the making!"/n/n" 'Oo does 'e look like?" Fleur inquired./n/n"I think he looks like Dora, but she thinks he is like/nme. Not much hair. It looked black when he was/nborn, but I swear it's turned ginger in the hour since./nProbably be blond by the time I get back. Andromeda/nsays Tonks's hair started changing color the day that/nshe was born." He drained his goblet. "Oh, go on/nthen, just one more," he added, beaming, as Bill made/nto fill it again./n/nThe wind buffeted the little cottage and the fire leapt/nand crackled, and Bill was soon opening another/nbottle of wine. Lupin's news seemed to have taken/nthem out of themselves, removed them for a while/nfrom their state of siege: Tidings of new life were/nexhilarating. Only the goblin seemed untouched by/nthe suddenly festive atmosphere, and after a while he/nslunk back to the bedroom he now occupied alone./nHarry thought he was the only one who had noticed/nthis, until he saw Bill's eyes following the goblin up/nthe stairs./n/n"No ... no ... I really must get back," said Lupin at/nlast, declining yet another goblet of wine. He got to his/nfeet and pulled his traveling cloak back around/nhimself./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Good-bye, good-bye — I'll try and bring some/npictures in a few days' time — they'll all be so glad to/nknow that I've seen you — "/n/n/n/nHe fastened his cloak and made his farewells,/nhugging the women and grasping hands with the/nmen, then, still beaming, returned into the wild night./n/n"Godfather, Harry!" said Bill as they walked into the/nkitchen together, helping clear the table. "A real/nhonor! Congratulations!"/n/nAs Harry set down the empty goblets he was carrying,/nBill pulled the door behind him closed, shutting out/nthe still-voluble voices of the others, who were/ncontinuing to celebrate even in Lupin's absence./n/n"I wanted a private word, actually, Harry. It hasn't/nbeen easy to get an opportunity with the cottage this/nfull of people."/n/nBill hesitated./n/n"Harry, you're planning something with Griphook."/n/nIt was a statement, not a question, and Harry did not/nbother to deny it. He merely looked at Bill, waiting./n/n"I know goblins," said Bill. "I've worked for Gringotts/never since I left Hogwarts. As far as there can be/nfriendship between wizards and goblins, I have goblin/nfriends — or, at least, goblins I know well, and like."/nAgain, Bill hesitated./n/n"Harry, what do you want from Griphook, and what/nhave you promised him in return?"/n/n"I can't tell you that," said Harry. "Sorry, Bill."/n/n/n/n/n/nThe kitchen door opened behind them; Fleur was/ntrying to bring through more empty goblets./n/n/n/n"Wait," Bill told her. "Just a moment."/n/nShe backed out and he closed the door again./n/n"Then I have to say this," Bill went on. "If you have/nstruck any kind of bargain with Griphook, and most/nparticularly if that bargain involves treasure, you/nmust be exceptionally careful. Goblin notions of/nownership, payment, and repayment are not the same/nas human ones."/n/nHarry felt a slight squirm of discomfort, as though a/nsmall snake had stirred inside him./n/n"What do you mean?" he asked./n/n"We are talking about a different breed of being," said/nBill. "Dealings between wizards and goblins have been/nfraught for centuries — but you'll know all that from/nHistory of Magic. There has been fault on both sides, I/nwould never claim that wizards have been innocent./nHowever, there is a belief among some goblins, and/nthose at Gringotts are perhaps most prone to it, that/nwizards cannot be trusted in matters of gold and/ntreasure, that they have no respect for goblin/nownership."/n/n"I respect — " Harry began, but Bill shook his head./n/n"You don't understand, Harry, nobody could/nunderstand unless they have lived with goblins. To a/ngoblin, the rightful and true master of any object is/nthe maker, not the purchaser. All goblin-made objects/nare, in goblin eyes, rightfully theirs."/n/n"But if it was bought — "/n/n/n/n/n/n" — then they would consider it rented by the one who/nhad paid the money. They have, however, great/ndifficulty with the idea of goblin-made objects passing/nfrom wizard to wizard. You saw Griphook's face when/nthe tiara passed under his eyes. He disapproves. I/nbelieve he thinks, as do the fiercest of his kind, that it/nought to have been returned to the goblins once the/noriginal purchaser died. They consider our habit of/nkeeping goblin-made objects, passing them from/nwizard to wizard without further payment, little more/nthan theft."/n/nHarry had an ominous feeling now; he wondered/nwhether Bill guessed more than he was letting on./n/n"All I am saying," said Bill, setting his hand on the/ndoor back into the sitting room, "is to be very careful/nwhat you promise goblins, Harry. It would be less/ndangerous to break into Gringotts than to renege on a/npromise to a goblin."/n/n"Right," said Harry as Bill opened the door, "yeah./nThanks. I'll bear that in mind."/n/nAs he followed Bill back to the others a wry thought/ncame to him, born no doubt of the wine he had/ndrunk. He seemed set on course to become just as/nreckless a godfather to Teddy Lupin as Sirius Black/nhad been to him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: Gringotts
text: /nTheir plans were made, their preparations complete;/nin the smallest bedroom a single long, coarse black/nhair (plucked from the sweater Hermione had been/nwearing at Malfoy Manor) lay curled in a small glass/nphial on the mantelpiece./n/n"And you'll be using her actual wand," said Harry,/nnodding toward the walnut wand, "so I reckon you'll/nbe pretty convincing."/n/nHermione looked frightened that the wand might sting/nor bite her as she picked it up./n/n"I hate this thing," she said in a low voice. "I really/nhate it. It feels all wrong, it doesn't work properly for/nme. ... It's like a bit of her."/n/nHarry could not help but remember how Hermione/nhad dismissed his loathing of the blackthorn wand,/ninsisting that he was imagining things when it did not/nwork as well as his own, telling him to simply/npractice. He chose not to repeat her own advice back/n/n/n/n/nto her, however; the eve of their attempted assault on/nGringotts felt like the wrong moment to antagonize/nher./n/n"It'll probably help you get in character, though," said/nRon. "Think what that wand's done!"/n/n"But that's my point!" said Hermione. "This is the/nwand that tortured Neville's mum and dad, and who/nknows how many other people? This is the wand that/nkilled Sirius!"/n/nHarry had not thought of that: He looked down at the/nwand and was visited by a brutal urge to snap it, to/nslice it in half with Gryffindor's sword, which was/npropped against the wall beside him./n/n"I miss my wand," Hermione said miserably. "I wish/nMr. Ollivander could have made me another one too."/n/nMr. Ollivander had sent Luna a new wand that/nmorning. She was out on the back lawn at that/nmoment, testing its capabilities in the late afternoon/nsun. Dean, who had lost his wand to the Snatchers,/nwas watching rather gloomily./n/nHarry looked down at the hawthorn wand that had/nonce belonged to Draco Malfoy. He had been/nsurprised, but pleased, to discover that it worked for/nhim at least as well as Hermione 's had done./nRemembering what Ollivander had told them of the/nsecret workings of wands, Harry thought he knew/nwhat Hermione 's problem was: She had not won the/nwalnut wand's allegiance by taking it personally from/nBellatrix./n/nThe door of the bedroom opened and Griphook/nentered. Harry reached instinctively for the hilt of the/nsword and drew it close to him, but regretted his/n/n/n/n/n/naction at once: He could tell that the goblin had/nnoticed. Seeking to gloss over the sticky moment, he/nsaid, "We've just been checking the last-minute stuff,/nGriphook. We've told Bill and Fleur we're leaving/ntomorrow, and we've told them not to get up to see us/noff."/n/nThey had been firm on this point, because Hermione/nwould need to transform into Bellatrix before they left,/nand the less that Bill and Fleur knew or suspected/nabout what they were about to do, the better. They/nhad also explained that they would not be returning./nAs they had lost Perkins's old tent on the night that/nthe Snatchers caught them, Bill had lent them/nanother one. It was now packed inside the beaded/nbag, which, Harry was impressed to learn, Hermione/nhad protected from the Snatchers by the simple/nexpedient of stuffing it down her sock./n/nThough he would miss Bill, Fleur, Luna, and Dean,/nnot to mention the home comforts they had enjoyed/nover the last few weeks, Harry was looking forward to/nescaping the confinement of Shell Cottage. He was/ntired of trying to make sure that they were not/noverheard, tired of being shut in the tiny, dark/nbedroom. Most of all, he longed to be rid of Griphook./nHowever, precisely how and when they were to part/nfrom the goblin without handing over Gryffindor's/nsword remained a question to which Harry had no/nanswer. It had been impossible to decide how they/nwere going to do it, because the goblin rarely left/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione alone together for more/nthan five minutes at a time: "He could give my mother/nlessons," growled Ron, as the goblin's long fingers/nkept appearing around the edges of doors. With Bill's/nwarning in mind, Harry could not help suspecting/nthat Griphook was on the watch for possible/nskulduggery. Hermione disapproved so heartily of the/nplanned double-cross that Harry had given up/n/n/n/n/nattempting to pick her brains on how best to do it;/nRon, on the rare occasions that they had been able to/nsnatch a few Griphook-free moments, had come up/nwith nothing better than "Well just have to wing it,/nmate."/n/nHarry slept badly that night. Lying awake in the early/nhours, he thought back to the way he had felt the/nnight before they had infiltrated the Ministry of Magic/nand remembered a determination, almost an/nexcitement. Now he was experiencing jolts of anxiety,/nnagging doubts: He could not shake off the fear that it/nwas all going to go wrong. He kept telling himself that/ntheir plan was good, that Griphook knew what they/nwere facing, that they were well-prepared for all the/ndifficulties they were likely to encounter, yet still he/nfelt uneasy. Once or twice he heard Ron stir and was/nsure that he too was awake, but they were sharing/nthe sitting room with Dean, so Harry did not speak./n/nIt was a relief when six o'clock arrived and they could/nslip out of their sleeping bags, dress in the/nsemidarkness, then creep out into the garden, where/nthey were to meet Hermione and Griphook. The dawn/nwas chilly, but there was little wind now that it was/nMay. Harry looked up at the stars still glimmering/npalely in the dark sky and listened to the sea washing/nbackward and forward against the cliff: He was going/nto miss the sound./n/nSmall green shoots were forcing their way up through/nthe red earth of Dobby's grave now; in a year's time/nthe mound would be covered in flowers. The white/nstone that bore the elf's name had already acquired a/nweathered look. He realized now that they could/nhardly have laid Dobby to rest in a more beautiful/nplace, but Harry ached with sadness to think of/nleaving him behind. Looking down on the grave, he/nwondered yet again how the elf had known where to/n/n/n/n/ncome to rescue them. His fingers moved/nabsentmindedly to the little pouch still strung around/nhis neck, through which he could feel the jagged/nmirror fragment in which he had been sure he had/nseen Dumbledore's eye. Then the sound of a door/nopening made him look around./n/nBellatrix Lestrange was striding across the lawn/ntoward them, accompanied by Griphook. As she/nwalked, she was tucking the small, beaded bag into/nthe inside pocket of another set of the old robes they/nhad taken from Grimmauld Place. Though Harry/nknew perfectly well that it was really Hermione, he/ncould not suppress a shiver of loathing.
