"Ginny,/nyou stay in this room, you hear me?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGinny did not seem to like the idea much, but under/nher father's unusually stern gaze, she nodded. Mr./nand Mrs. Weasley and Lupin headed off for the stairs/nas well./n/n"Where's Ron?" asked Harry. "Where's Hermione?"/n/n"They must have gone up to the Great Hall already,"/nMr. Weasley called over his shoulder./n/n"I didn't see them pass me," said Harry./n/n"They said something about a bathroom," said Ginny,/n"not long after you left."/n/n"A bathroom?"/n/nHarry strode across the room to an open door leading/noff the Room of Requirement and checked the/nbathroom beyond. It was empty./n/n"You're sure they said bath — ?"/n/nBut then his scar seared and the Room of/nRequirement vanished: He was looking through the/nhigh wrought-iron gates with winged boars on pillars/nat either side, looking through the dark grounds/ntoward the castle, which was ablaze with lights./nNagini lay draped over his shoulders. He was/npossessed of that cold, cruel sense of purpose that/npreceded murder./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Battle Of Hogwarts
text: /nThe enchanted ceiling of the Great Hall was dark and/nscattered with stars, and below it the four long House/ntables were lined with disheveled students, some in/ntraveling cloaks, others in dressing gowns. Here and/nthere shone the pearly white figures of the school/nghosts. Every eye, living and dead, was fixed upon/nProfessor McGonagall, who was speaking from the/nraised platform at the top of the Hall. Behind her/nstood the remaining teachers, including the palomino/ncentaur, Firenze, and the members of the Order of the/nPhoenix who had arrived to fight./n/n"... evacuation will be overseen by Mr. Filch and/nMadam Pomfrey. Prefects, when I give the word, you/nwill organize your House and take your charges, in an/norderly fashion, to the evacuation point."/n/nMany of the students looked petrified. However, as/nHarry skirted the walls, scanning the Gryffindor table/nfor Ron and Hermione, Ernie Macmillan stood up at/nthe Hufflepuff table and shouted, "And what if we/nwant to stay and fight?"/n/n/n/n/nThere was a smattering of applause./n/n"If you are of age, you may stay," said Professor/nMcGonagall./n/n"What about our things?" called a girl at the/nRavenclaw table. "Our trunks, our owls?"/n/n"We have no time to collect possessions," said/nProfessor McGonagall. "The important thing is to get/nyou out of here safely."/n/n"Where's Professor Snape?" shouted a girl from the/nSlytherin table./n/n"He has, to use the common phrase, done a bunk,"/nreplied Professor McGonagall, and a great cheer/nerupted from the Gryffindors, Hufflepuffs, and/nRavenclaws./n/nHarry moved up the Hall alongside the Gryffindor/ntable, still looking for Ron and Hermione. As he/npassed, faces turned in his direction, and a great deal/nof whispering broke out in his wake./n/n"We have already placed protection around the/ncastle," Professor McGonagall was saying, "but it is/nunlikely to hold for very long unless we reinforce it. I/nmust ask you, therefore, to move quickly and calmly,/nand do as your prefects — "/n/nBut her final words were drowned as a different voice/nechoed throughout the Hall. It was high, cold, and/nclear: There was no telling from where it came; it/nseemed to issue from the walls themselves. Like the/nmonster it had once commanded, it might have lain/ndormant there for centuries./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I know that you are preparing to fight." There were/nscreams amongst the students, some of whom/nclutched each other, looking around in terror for the/nsource of the sound. "Your efforts are futile. You/ncannot fight me. I do not want to kill you. I have great/nrespect for the teachers of Hogwarts. I do not want to/nspill magical blood."/n/nThere was silence in the Hall now, the kind of silence/nthat presses against the eardrums, that seems too/nhuge to be contained by walls./n/n"Give me Harry Potter," said Voldemort's voice, "and/nnone shall be harmed. Give me Harry Potter, and I/nshall leave the school untouched. Give me Harry/nPotter, and you will be rewarded./n/n"You have until midnight."/n/nThe silence swallowed them all again. Every head/nturned, every eye in the place seemed to have found/nHarry, to hold him frozen in the glare of thousands of/ninvisible beams. Then a figure rose from the Slytherin/ntable and he recognized Pansy Parkinson as she/nraised a shaking arm and screamed, "But he's there!/nPotter's there\ Someone grab him!"/n/nBefore Harry could speak, there was a massive/nmovement. The Gryffindors in front of him had risen/nand stood facing, not Harry, but the Slytherins. Then/nthe Hufflepuffs stood, and almost at the same/nmoment, the Ravenclaws, all of them with their backs/nto Harry, all of them looking toward Pansy instead,/nand Harry, awestruck and overwhelmed, saw wands/nemerging everywhere, pulled from beneath cloaks and/nfrom under sleeves./n/n"Thank you, Miss Parkinson," said Professor/nMcGonagall in a clipped voice. "You will leave the Hall/n/n/n/n/n/nfirst with Mr. Filch. If the rest of your House could/nfollow."/n/nHarry heard the grinding of benches and then the/nsound of the Slytherins trooping out on the other side/nof the Hall./n/n"Ravenclaws, follow on!" cried Professor McGonagall./n/nSlowly the four tables emptied. The Slytherin table/nwas completely deserted, but a number of older/nRavenclaws remained seated while their fellows filed/nout; even more Hufflepuffs stayed behind, and half of/nGryffindor remained in their seats, necessitating/nProfessor McGonagall's descent from the teachers'/nplatform to chivvy the underage on their way./n/n"Absolutely not, Creevey, go! And you, Peakes!"/n/nHarry hurried over to the Weasleys, all sitting/ntogether at the Gryffindor table./n/n"Where are Ron and Hermione?"/n/n"Haven't you found — ?" began Mr. Weasley, looking/nworried./n/nBut he broke off as Kingsley had stepped forward on/nthe raised platform to address those who had/nremained behind./n/n"We've only got half an hour until midnight, so we/nneed to act fast! A battle plan has been agreed/nbetween the teachers of Hogwarts and the Order of/nthe Phoenix. Professors Flitwick, Sprout, and/nMcGonagall are going to take groups of fighters up to/nthe three highest towers — Ravenclaw, Astronomy,/nand Gryffindor — where they'll have a good overview,/nexcellent positions from which to work spells./n/n/n/n/n/nMeanwhile Remus" — he indicated Lupin — "Arthur"/n— he pointed toward Mr. Weasley, sitting at the/nGryffindor table — "and I will take groups into the/ngrounds. We'll need somebody to organize defense of/nthe entrances of the passageways into the school — "/n/n"Sounds like a job for us," called Fred, indicating/nhimself and George, and Kingsley nodded his/napproval./n/n"All right, leaders up here and we'll divide up the/ntroops!"/n/n"Potter," said Professor McGonagall, hurrying up to/nhim, as students flooded the platform, jostling for/nposition, receiving instructions, " Aren't you supposed/nto be looking for something?"/n/n"What? Oh," said Harry, "oh yeah!"/n/nHe had almost forgotten about the Horcrux, almost/nforgotten that the battle was being fought so that he/ncould search for it: The inexplicable absence of Ron/nand Hermione had momentarily driven every other/nthought from his mind./n/n"Then go, Potter, go!"/n/n"Right — yeah — "/n/nHe sensed eyes following him as he ran out of the/nGreat Hall again, into the entrance hall still crowded/nwith evacuating students. He allowed himself to be/nswept up the marble staircase with them, but at the/ntop he hurried off along a deserted corridor. Fear and/npanic were clouding his thought processes. He tried/nto calm himself, to concentrate on finding the/nHorcrux, but his thoughts buzzed as frantically and/nfruitlessly as wasps trapped beneath a glass. Without/n/n/n/n/nRon and Hermione to help him he could not seem to/nmarshal his ideas. He slowed down, coming to a halt/nhalfway along an empty passage, where he sat down/nupon the plinth of a departed statue and pulled the/nMarauder's Map out of the pouch around his neck./n/nHe could not see Ron's or Hermione's names/nanywhere on it, though the density of the crowd of/ndots now making its way to the Room of Requirement/nmight, he thought, be concealing them. He put the/nmap away, pressed his hands over his face, and/nclosed his eyes, trying to concentrate. .../n/nVoldemort thought I'd go to Ravenclaw Tower./n/nThere it was: a solid fact, the place to start. Voldemort/nhad stationed Alecto Carrow in the Ravenclaw/ncommon room, and there could only be one/nexplanation: Voldemort feared that Harry already/nknew his Horcrux was connected to that House./n/nBut the only object anyone seemed to associate with/nRavenclaw was the lost diadem . . . and how could the/nHorcrux be the diadem? How was it possible that/nVoldemort, the Slytherin, had found the diadem that/nhad eluded generations of Ravenclaws? Who could/nhave told him where to look, when nobody had seen/nthe diadem in living memory?/n/nIn living memory .../n/nBeneath his fingers, Harry's eyes flew open again. He/nleapt up from the plinth and tore back the way he had/ncome, now in pursuit of his one last hope. The sound/nof hundreds of people marching toward the Room of/nRequirement grew louder and louder as he returned/nto the marble stairs. Prefects were shouting/ninstructions, trying to keep track of the students in/ntheir own Houses; there was much pushing and/nshoving; Harry saw Zacharias Smith bowling over/n/n/n/n/nfirst-years to get to the front of the queue; here and/nthere younger students were in tears, while older ones/ncalled desperately for friends or siblings. .../n/nHarry caught sight of a pearly white figure drifting/nacross the entrance hall below and yelled as loudly as/nhe could over the clamor./n/n"Nick! NICK! I need to talk to you!"/n/nHe forced his way back through the tide of students,/nfinally reaching the bottom of the stairs, where Nearly/nHeadless Nick, ghost of Gryffindor Tower, stood/nwaiting for him./n/n"Harry! My dear boy!"/n/nNick made to grasp Harry's hands with both of his/nown: Harry's felt as though they had been thrust into/nicy water./n/n"Nick, you've got to help me. Who's the ghost of/nRavenclaw Tower?"/n/nNearly Headless Nick looked surprised and a little/noffended./n/n"The Gray Lady, of course; but if it is ghostly services/nyou require — ?"/n/n"It's got to be her — d'you know where she is?"/n/n"Let's see. ..."/n/nNick's head wobbled a little on his ruff as he turned/nhither and thither, peering over the heads of the/nswarming students./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"That's her over there, Harry, the young woman with/nthe long hair."/n/nHarry looked in the direction of Nick's transparent,/npointing finger and saw a tall ghost who caught sight/nof Harry looking at her, raised her eyebrows, and/ndrifted away through a solid wall./n/nHarry ran after her. Once through the door of the/ncorridor into which she had disappeared, he saw her/nat the very end of the passage, still gliding smoothly/naway from him./n/n"Hey — wait — come back!"/n/nShe consented to pause, floating a few inches from/nthe ground. Harry supposed that she was beautiful,/nwith her waist-length hair and floor-length cloak, but/nshe also looked haughty and proud. Close to, he/nrecognized her as a ghost he had passed several times/nin the corridor, but to whom he had never spoken./n/n"You're the Gray Lady?"/n/nShe nodded but did not speak./n/n"The ghost of Ravenclaw Tower?"/n/n"That is correct."/n/nHer tone was not encouraging./n/n"Please: I need some help. I need to know anything/nyou can tell me about the lost diadem."/n/nA cold smile curved her lips./n/n"I am afraid," she said, turning to leave, "that I cannot/nhelp you."/n/n/n/n/n/n"WAIT!"/n/n/n/nHe had not meant to shout, but anger and panic were/nthreatening to overwhelm him. He glanced at his/nwatch as she hovered in front of him: It was a quarter/nto midnight./n/n"This is urgent," he said fiercely. "If that diadem's at/nHogwarts, I've got to find it, fast."/n/n"You are hardly the first student to covet the diadem,"/nshe said disdainfully. "Generations of students have/nbadgered me — "/n/n"This isn't about trying to get better marks!" Harry/nshouted at her. "It's about Voldemort — defeating/nVoldemort — or aren't you interested in that?"/n/nShe could not blush, but her transparent cheeks/nbecame more opaque, and her voice was heated as/nshe replied, "Of course I — how dare you suggest — ?"/n/n"Well, help me, then!"/n/nHer composure was slipping./n/n"It — it is not a question of — " she stammered. "My/nmother's diadem — "/n/n"Your mother's?"/n/nShe looked angry with herself./n/n"When I lived," she said stiffly, "I was Helena/nRavenclaw."/n/n"You're her daughter? But then, you must know what/nhappened to it!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"While the diadem bestows wisdom," she said with an/nobvious effort to pull herself together, "I doubt that it/nwould greatly increase your chances of defeating the/nwizard who calls himself Lord — "/n/n"Haven't I just told you, I'm not interested in wearing/nit!" Harry said fiercely. "There's no time to explain —/nbut if you care about Hogwarts, if you want to see/nVoldemort finished, you've got to tell me anything you/nknow about the diadem!"/n/nShe remained quite still, floating in midair, staring/ndown at him, and a sense of hopelessness engulfed/nHarry. Of course, if she had known anything, she/nwould have told Flitwick or Dumbledore, who had/nsurely asked her the same question. He had shaken/nhis head and made to turn away when she spoke in a/nlow voice./n/n"I stole the diadem from my mother."/n/n"You — you did what?"/n/n" I stole the diadem," repeated Helena Ravenclaw in a/nwhisper. "I sought to make myself cleverer, more/nimportant than my mother. I ran away with it."/n/nHe did not know how he had managed to gain her/nconfidence, and did not ask; he simply listened, hard,/nas she went on:/n/n"My mother, they say, never admitted that the diadem/nwas gone, but pretended that she had it still. She/nconcealed her loss, my dreadful betrayal, even from/nthe other founders of Hogwarts./n/n"Then my mother fell ill — fatally ill. In spite of my/nperfidy, she was desperate to see me one more time./nShe sent a man who had long loved me, though I/n/n/n/n/n/nspurned his advances, to find me. She knew that he/nwould not rest until he had done so."/n/n/n/nHarry waited. She drew a deep breath and threw back/nher head./n/n"He tracked me to the forest where I was hiding./n/nWhen I refused to return with him, he became violent./nThe Baron was always a hot-tempered man. Furious/nat my refusal, jealous of my freedom, he stabbed me."/n/n"The Baron? You mean — ?"/n/n"The Bloody Baron, yes," said the Gray Lady, and she/nlifted aside the cloak she wore to reveal a single dark/nwound in her white chest. "When he saw what he had/ndone, he was overcome with remorse. He took the/nweapon that had claimed my life, and used it to kill/nhimself. All these centuries later, he wears his chains/nas an act of penitence ... as he should," she added/nbitterly./n/n"And . . . and the diadem?"/n/n"It remained where I had hidden it when I heard the/nBaron blundering through the forest toward me./nConcealed inside a hollow tree./n/n"A hollow tree?" repeated Harry. "What tree? Where/nwas this?"/n/n"A forest in Albania. A lonely place I thought was far/nbeyond my mother's reach."/n/n"Albania," repeated Harry. Sense was emerging/nmiraculously from confusion, and now he understood/nwhy she was telling him what she had denied/nDumbledore and Flitwick. "You've already told/nsomeone this story, haven't you? Another student?"/n/n/n/n/nShe closed her eyes and nodded./n/n/n/n"I had ... no idea. . . . He was . . . flattering. He seemed/nto ... to understand ... to sympathize. ..."/n/nYes, Harry thought, Tom Riddle would certainly have/nunderstood Helena Ravenclaw's desire to possess/nfabulous objects to which she had little right./n/n"Well, you weren't the first person Riddle wormed/nthings out of," Harry muttered. "He could be/ncharming when he wanted. ..."/n/nSo Voldemort had managed to wheedle the location of/nthe lost diadem out of the Gray Lady. He had traveled/nto that far-flung forest and retrieved the diadem from/nits hiding place, perhaps as soon as he left Hogwarts,/nbefore he even started work at Borgin and Burkes./n/nAnd wouldn't those secluded Albanian woods have/nseemed an excellent refuge when, so much later,/nVoldemort had needed a place to lie low, undisturbed,/nfor ten long years?/n/nBut the diadem, once it became his precious Horcrux,/nhad not been left in that lowly tree. ... No, the diadem/nhad been returned secretly to its true home, and/nVoldemort must have put it there —/n/n" — the night he asked for a job!" said Harry, finishing/nhis thought./n/n"I beg your pardon?"/n/n"He hid the diadem in the castle, the night he asked/nDumbledore to let him teach!" said Harry. Saying it/nout loud enabled him to make sense of it all. "He/nmust've hidden the diadem on his way up to, or down/nfrom, Dumbledore 's office! But it was still worth trying/n/n/n/n/nto get the job — then he might've got the chance to/nnick Gryffindor's sword as well — thank you, thanks!"/n/n/n/nHarry left her floating there, looking utterly/nbewildered. As he rounded the corner back into the/nentrance hall, he checked his watch. It was five/nminutes until midnight, and though he now knew/nwhat the last Horcrux was, he was no closer to/ndiscovering where it was. .../n/nGenerations of students had failed to find the diadem;/nthat suggested that it was not in Ravenclaw Tower —/nbut if not there, where? What hiding place had Tom/nRiddle discovered inside Hogwarts Castle, that he/nbelieved would remain secret forever?/n/nLost in desperate speculation, Harry turned a corner,/nbut he had taken only a few steps down the new/ncorridor when the window to his left broke open with/na deafening, shattering crash. As he leapt aside, a/ngigantic body flew in through the window and hit the/nopposite wall. Something large and furry detached/nitself, whimpering, from the new arrival and flung/nitself at Harry./n/n"Hagrid!" Harry bellowed, fighting off Fang the/nboarhound's attentions as the enormous bearded/nfigure clambered to his feet. "What the — ?"/n/n"Harry, yer here! Yer here\"/n/nHagrid stooped down, bestowed upon Harry a cursory/nand rib-cracking hug, then ran back to the shattered/nwindow./n/n"Good boy, Grawpy!" he bellowed through the hole in/nthe window. "I'll see yer in a moment, there's a good/nlad!"/n/n/n/n/n/nBeyond Hagrid, out in the dark night, Harry saw/nbursts of light in the distance and heard a weird,/nkeening scream. He looked down at his watch: It was/nmidnight. The battle had begun./n/n"Blimey, Harry," panted Hagrid, "this is it, eh? Time/nter fight?"/n/n"Hagrid, where have you come from?"/n/n"Heard You-Know-Who from up in our cave," said/nHagrid grimly. "Voice carried, didn' it? Yeh got till/nmidnight ter gimme Potter.' Knew yeh mus' be here,/nknew what mus' be happenin'. Get down, Fang. So we/ncome ter join in, me an' Grawpy an' Fang. Smashed/nour way through the boundary by the forest, Grawpy/nwas carryin' us, Fang an' me. Told him ter let me/ndown at the castle, so he shoved me through the/nwindow, bless him. Not exac'ly what I meant, bu' —/nwhere's Ron an' Hermione?"/n/n"That," said Harry, "is a really good question. Come/non."/n/nThey hurried together along the corridor, Fang/nlolloping beside them. Harry could hear movement/nthrough the corridors all around: running footsteps,/nshouts; through the windows, he could see more/nflashes of light in the dark grounds./n/n"Where're we goin'?" puffed Hagrid, pounding along at/nHarry's heels, making the floorboards quake./n/n"I dunno exactly," said Harry, making another/nrandom turn, "but Ron and Hermione must be/naround here somewhere. ..."/n/nThe first casualties of the battle were already strewn/nacross the passage ahead: The two stone gargoyles/n/n/n/n/n/nthat usually guarded the entrance to the staffroom/nhad been smashed apart by a jinx that had sailed/nthrough another broken window. Their remains/nstirred feebly on the floor, and as Harry leapt over one/nof their disembodied heads, it moaned faintly, "Oh,/ndon't mind me ... I'll just lie here and crumble. ..."/n/nIts ugly stone face made Harry think suddenly of the/nmarble bust of Rowena Ravenclaw at Xenophilius's/nhouse, wearing that mad headdress — and then of/nthe statue in Ravenclaw Tower, with the stone diadem/nupon her white curls. .../n/nAnd as he reached the end of the passage, the/nmemory of a third stone effigy came back to him: that/nof an ugly old warlock, onto whose head Harry/nhimself had placed a wig and a battered old tiara. The/nshock shot through Harry with the heat of firewhisky,/nand he nearly stumbled./n/nHe knew, at last, where the Horcrux sat waiting for/nhim. .../n/nTom Riddle, who confided in no one and operated/nalone, might have been arrogant enough to assume/nthat he, and only he, had penetrated the deepest/nmysteries of Hogwarts Castle. Of course, Dumbledore/nand Flitwick, those model pupils, had never set foot in/nthat particular place, but he, Harry, had strayed off/nthe beaten track in his time at school — here at last/nwas a secret he and Voldemort knew, that/nDumbledore had never discovered —/n/nHe was roused by Professor Sprout, who was/nthundering past followed by Neville and half a dozen/nothers, all of them wearing earmuffs and carrying/nwhat appeared to be large potted plants./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Mandrakes!" Neville bellowed at Harry over his/nshoulder as he ran. "Going to lob them over the walls/n— they won't like this!"/n/nHarry knew now where to go: He sped off, with Hagrid/nand Fang galloping behind him. They passed portrait/nafter portrait, and the painted figures raced alongside/nthem, wizards and witches in ruffs and breeches, in/narmor and cloaks, cramming themselves into each/nothers' canvases, screaming news from other parts of/nthe castle. As they reached the end of this corridor,/nthe whole castle shook, and Harry knew, as a gigantic/nvase blew off its plinth with explosive force, that it/nwas in the grip of enchantments more sinister than/nthose of the teachers and the Order./n/n"It's all righ', Fang — it's all righ'!" yelled Hagrid, but/nthe great boarhound had taken flight as slivers of/nchina flew like shrapnel through the air, and Hagrid/npounded off after the terrified dog, leaving Harry/nalone./n/nHe forged on through the trembling passages, his/nwand at the ready, and for the length of one corridor/nthe little painted knight, Sir Cadogan, rushed from/npainting to painting beside him, clanking along in his/narmor, screaming encouragement, his fat little pony/ncantering behind him./n/n"Braggarts and rogues, dogs and scoundrels, drive/nthem out, Harry Potter, see them off!"/n/nHarry hurtled around a corner and found Fred and a/nsmall knot of students, including Lee Jordan and/nHannah Abbott, standing beside another empty/nplinth, whose statue had concealed a secret/npassageway. Their wands were drawn and they were/nlistening at the concealed hole./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Nice night for it!" Fred shouted as the castle quaked/nagain, and Harry sprinted by, elated and terrified in/nequal measure. Along yet another corridor he dashed,/nand then there were owls everywhere, and Mrs. Norris/nwas hissing and trying to bat them with her paws, no/ndoubt to return them to their proper place. .../n/n"Potter!"/n/nAberforth Dumbledore stood blocking the corridor/nahead, his wand held ready./n/n"I've had hundreds of kids thundering through my/npub, Potter!"/n/n"I know, we're evacuating," Harry said, "Voldemort's/n/n/n/n" — attacking because they haven't handed you over,/nyeah," said Aberforth, "I'm not deaf, the whole of/nHogsmeade heard him. And it never occurred to any/nof you to keep a few Slytherins hostage? There are/nkids of Death Eaters you've just sent to safety./nWouldn't it have been a bit smarter to keep 'em here?"/n/n"It wouldn't stop Voldemort," said Harry, "and your/nbrother would never have done it."/n/nAberforth grunted and tore away in the opposite/ndirection./n/nYour brother would never have done it. ... Well, it was/nthe truth, Harry thought as he ran on again;/nDumbledore, who had defended Snape for so long,/nwould never have held students ransom. .../n/nAnd then he skidded around a final corner and with a/nyell of mingled relief and fury he saw them: Ron and/nHermione, both with their arms full of large, curved,/n/n/n/n/n/ndirty yellow objects, Ron with a broomstick under his/narm./n/n"Where the hell have you been?" Harry shouted./n/n"Chamber of Secrets," said Ron./n/n"Chamber — what?" said Harry, coming to an/nunsteady halt before them./n/n"It was Ron, all Ron's idea!" said Hermione/nbreathlessly. "Wasn't it absolutely brilliant? There we/nwere, after you left, and I said to Ron, even if we find/nthe other one, how are we going to get rid of it? We/nstill hadn't got rid of the cup! And then he thought of/nit! The basilisk!"/n/n"What the — ?"/n/n"Something to get rid of Horcruxes," said Ron simply./n/nHarry's eyes dropped to the objects clutched in Ron/nand Hermione's arms: great curved fangs, torn, he/nnow realized, from the skull of a dead basilisk./n/n"But how did you get in there?" he asked, staring/nfrom the fangs to Ron. "You need to speak/nParseltongue!"/n/n"He did!" whispered Hermione. "Show him, Ron!"/n/nRon made a horrible strangled hissing noise./n/n"It's what you did to open the locket," he told Harry/napologetically. "I had to have a few goes to get it right,/nbut," he shrugged modestly, "we got there in the end."/n/n"He was amazing." said Hermione. "Amazing!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"So ..." Harry was struggling to keep up. "So ..."/n/n/n/n"So we're another Horcrux down," said Ron, and from/nunder his jacket he pulled the mangled remains of/nHufflepuff's cup. "Hermione stabbed it. Thought she/nshould. She hasn't had the pleasure yet."/n/n"Genius!" yelled Harry./n/n"It was nothing," said Ron, though he looked/ndelighted with himself. "So what's new with you?"/n/nAs he said it, there was an explosion from overhead:/nAll three of them looked up as dust fell from the/nceiling and they heard a distant scream./n/n"I know what the diadem looks like, and I know where/nit is," said Harry, talking fast. "He hid it exactly where/nI hid my old Potions book, where everyone's been/nhiding stuff for centuries. He thought he was the only/none to find it. Come on."/n/nAs the walls trembled again, he led the other two back/nthrough the concealed entrance and down the/nstaircase into the Room of Requirement. It was empty/nexcept for three women: Ginny, Tonks, and an elderly/nwitch wearing a moth-eaten hat, whom Harry/nrecognized immediately as Neville's grandmother./n/n"Ah, Potter," she said crisply as if she had been/nwaiting for him. "You can tell us what's going on."/n/n"Is everyone okay?" said Ginny and Tonks together./n/n" 'S far as we know," said Harry. "Are there still people/nin the passage to the Hog's Head?"/n/nHe knew that the room would not be able to/ntransform while there were still users inside it./n/n/n/n/n/n"I was the last to come through," said Mrs./nLongbottom. "I sealed it, I think it unwise to leave it/nopen now Aberforth has left his pub. Have you seen/nmy grandson?"/n/n"He's fighting," said Harry./n/n"Naturally," said the old lady proudly. "Excuse me, I/nmust go and assist him."/n/nWith surprising speed she trotted off toward the stone/nsteps./n/nHarry looked at Tonks./n/n"I thought you were supposed to be with Teddy at/nyour mother's?"/n/n"I couldn't stand not knowing — " Tonks looked/nanguished. "She'll look after him — have you seen/nRemus?"/n/n"He was planning to lead a group of fighters into the/ngrounds — "/n/nWithout another word, Tonks sped off./n/n"Ginny," said Harry, "I'm sorry, but we need you to/nleave too. Just for a bit. Then you can come back in."/n/nGinny looked simply delighted to leave her sanctuary./n/n"And then you can come back in!" he shouted after/nher as she ran up the steps after Tonks. " You've got to/ncome back ini"/n/n"Hang on a moment!" said Ron sharply. "We've/nforgotten someone!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Who?" asked Hermione./n/n/n/n"The house-elves, they'll all be down in the kitchen,/nwon't they?"/n/n"You mean we ought to get them fighting?" asked/nHarry./n/n"No," said Ron seriously, "I mean we should tell them/nto get out. We don't want any more Dobbies, do we?/nWe can't order them to die for us — "/n/nThere was a clatter as the basilisk fangs cascaded out/nof Hermione 's arms. Running at Ron, she flung them/naround his neck and kissed him full on the mouth./nRon threw away the fangs and broomstick he was/nholding and responded with such enthusiasm that he/nlifted Hermione off her feet./n/n"Is this the moment?" Harry asked weakly, and when/nnothing happened except that Ron and Hermione/ngripped each other still more firmly and swayed on/nthe spot, he raised his voice. "01! There's a war going/non here!"/n/nRon and Hermione broke apart, their arms still/naround each other./n/n"I know, mate," said Ron, who looked as though he/nhad recently been hit on the back of the head with a/nBludger, "so it's now or never, isn't it?"/n/n"Never mind that, what about the Horcrux?" Harry/nshouted. "D'you think you could just — just hold it in/nuntil we've got the diadem?"/n/n"Yeah — right — sorry — " said Ron, and he and/nHermione set about gathering up fangs, both pink in/nthe face./n/n/n/n/n/nIt was clear, as the three of them stepped back into/nthe corridor upstairs, that in the minutes that they/nhad spent in the Room of Requirement the situation/nwithin the castle had deteriorated severely: The walls/nand ceiling were shaking worse than ever; dust filled/nthe air, and through the nearest window, Harry saw/nbursts of green and red light so close to the foot of the/ncastle that he knew the Death Eaters must be very/nnear to entering the place. Looking down, Harry saw/nGrawp the giant meandering past, swinging what/nlooked like a stone gargoyle torn from the roof and/nroaring his displeasure./n/n"Let's hope he steps on some of them!" said Ron as/nmore screams echoed from close by./n/n"As long as it's not any of our lot!" said a voice: Harry/nturned and saw Ginny and Tonks, both with their/nwands drawn at the next window, which was missing/nseveral panes. Even as he watched, Ginny sent a well-/naimed jinx into a crowd of fighters below./n/n"Good girl!" roared a figure running through the dust/ntoward them, and Harry saw Aberforth again, his gray/nhair flying as he led a small group of students past./n"They look like they might be breaching the north/nbattlements, they've brought giants of their own!"/n/n"Have you seen Remus?" Tonks called after him./n/n"He was dueling Dolohov," shouted Aberforth,/n/n"haven't seen him since!/n/n"Tonks," said Ginny, "Tonks, I'm sure he's okay — "/nBut Tonks had run off into the dust after Aberforth./nGinny turned, helpless, to Harry, Ron, and Hermione./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"They'll be all right," said Harry, though he knew they/nwere empty words. "Ginny, we'll be back in a moment,/njust keep out of the way, keep safe — come on!" he/nsaid to Ron and Hermione, and they ran back to the/nstretch of wall beyond which the Room of/nRequirement was waiting to do the bidding of the next/nentrant./n/nI need the place where everything is hidden, Harry/nbegged of it inside his head, and the door materialized/non their third run past./n/nThe furor of the battle died the moment they crossed/nthe threshold and closed the door behind them: All/nwas silent. They were in a place the size of a cathedral/nwith the appearance of a city, its towering walls built/nof objects hidden by thousands of long-gone students./n/n"And he never realized anyone could get in?" said/nRon, his voice echoing in the silence./n/n"He thought he was the only one," said Harry. "Too/nbad for him I've had to hide stuff in my time ... this/nway," he added, "I think it's down here. ..."/n/nHe passed the stuffed troll and the Vanishing Cabinet/nDraco Malfoy had mended last year with such/ndisastrous consequences, then hesitated, looking up/nand down aisles of junk; he could not remember/nwhere to go next. .../n/n" Accio Diadem)." cried Hermione in desperation, but/nnothing flew through the air toward them. It seemed/nthat, like the vault at Gringotts, the room would not/nyield its hidden objects that easily./n/n"Let's split up," Harry told the other two. "Look for a/nstone bust of an old man wearing a wig and a tiara!/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nIt's standing on a cupboard and it's definitely/nsomewhere near here. ..."/n/n/n/nThey sped off up adjacent aisles; Harry could hear the/nothers' footsteps echoing through the towering piles of/njunk, of bottles, hats, crates, chairs, books, weapons,/nbroomsticks, bats. .../n/n"Somewhere near here," Harry muttered to himself./n"Somewhere ... somewhere ..."/n/nDeeper and deeper into the labyrinth he went, looking/nfor objects he recognized from his one previous trip/ninto the room. His breath was loud in his ears, and/nthen his very soul seemed to shiver: There it was,/nright ahead, the blistered old cupboard in which he/nhad hidden his old Potions book, and on top of it, the/npockmarked stone warlock wearing a dusty old wig/nand what looked like an ancient, discolored tiara./n/nHe had already stretched out his hand, though he/nremained ten feet away, when a voice behind him/nsaid, "Hold it, Potter."/n/nHe skidded to a halt and turned around. Crabbe and/nGoyle were standing behind him, shoulder to/nshoulder, wands pointing right at Harry. Through the/nsmall space between their leering faces he saw Draco/nMalfoy./n/n"That's my wand you're holding, Potter," said Malfoy,/npointing his own through the gap between Crabbe/nand Goyle./n/n"Not anymore," panted Harry, tightening his grip on/nthe hawthorn wand. "Winners, keepers, Malfoy. Who's/nlent you theirs?"/n/n"My mother," said Draco./n/n/n/n/n/nHarry laughed, though there was nothing very/nhumorous about the situation. He could not hear Ron/nor Hermione anymore. They seemed to have run out/nof earshot, searching for the diadem./n/n"So how come you three aren't with Voldemort?"/nasked Harry./n/n"We're gonna be rewarded," said Crabbe: His voice/nwas surprisingly soft for such an enormous person;/nHarry had hardly ever heard him speak before./n/nCrabbe was smiling like a small child promised a/nlarge bag of sweets. "We 'ung back, Potter. We decided/nnot to go. Decided to bring you to 'im."/n/n"Good plan," said Harry in mock admiration. He could/nnot believe that he was this close, and was going to be/nthwarted by Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle. He began/nedging slowly backward toward the place where the/nHorcrux sat lopsided upon the bust. If he could just/nget his hands on it before the fight broke out . . ./n/n"So how did you get in here?" he asked, trying to/ndistract them./n/n"I virtually lived in the Room of Hidden Things all last/nyear," said Malfoy, his voice brittle. "I know how to get/nin."/n/n/n/n"We was hiding in the corridor outside," grunted/nGoyle. "We can do Diss-lusion Charms now! And/nthen," his face split into a gormless grin, "you turned/nup right in front of us and said you was looking for a/ndie-dum! What's a die-dum?"/n/n"Harry?" Ron's voice echoed suddenly from the other/nside of the wall to Harry's right. "Are you talking to/nsomeone?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWith a whiplike movement, Crabbe pointed his wand/nat the fifty-foot mountain of old furniture, of broken/ntrunks, of old books and robes and unidentifiable/njunk, and shouted, "DescendoV'/n/nThe wall began to totter, then the top third crumbled/ninto the aisle next door where Ron stood./n/n"Ron!" Harry bellowed, as somewhere out of sight/nHermione screamed, and Harry heard innumerable/nobjects crashing to the floor on the other side of the/ndestabilized wall: He pointed his wand at the rampart,/ncried, "Finite!" and it steadied./n/n"No!" shouted Malfoy, staying Crabbe's arm as the/nlatter made to repeat his spell. "If you wreck the room/nyou might bury this diadem thing!"/n/n"What's that matter?" said Crabbe, tugging himself/nfree. "It's Potter the Dark Lord wants, who cares/nabout a die-dum?"/n/n"Potter came in here to get it," said Malfoy with ill-/ndisguised impatience at the slow-wittedness of his/ncolleagues, "so that must mean — "/n/n" 'Must mean?" Crabbe turned on Malfoy with/nundisguised ferocity. "Who cares what you think? I/ndon't take your orders no more, Draco. You an' your/ndad are finished."/n/n"Harry?" shouted Ron again, from the other side of/nthe junk wall. "What's going on?"/n/n"Harry?" mimicked Crabbe. "What's going — no,/n/nPotter! Cruciol"/n/nHarry had lunged for the tiara; Crabbe's curse missed/nhim but hit the stone bust, which flew into the air;/n/n/n/n/n/nthe diadem soared upward and then dropped out of/nsight in the mass of objects on which the bust had/nrested./n/n"STOP!" Malfoy shouted at Crabbe, his voice echoing/nthrough the enormous room. "The Dark Lord wants/nhim alive — "/n/n"So? I'm not killing him, am I?" yelled Crabbe,/nthrowing off Malfoy's restraining arm. "But if I can, I/nwill, the Dark Lord wants him dead anyway, what's/nthediff— ?"/n/nA jet of scarlet light shot past Harry by inches:/nHermione had run around the corner behind him and/nsent a Stunning Spell straight at Crabbe 's head. It/nonly missed because Malfoy pulled him out of the/nway./n/n"It's that Mudblood! Avada Kedavral"/n/nHarry saw Hermione dive aside, and his fury that/nCrabbe had aimed to kill wiped all else from his mind./nHe shot a Stunning Spell at Crabbe, who lurched out/nof the way, knocking Malfoy's wand out of his hand; it/nrolled out of sight beneath a mountain of broken/nfurniture and boxes./n/n"Don't kill him! DONT KILL HIM!" Malfoy yelled at/nCrabbe and Goyle, who were both aiming at Harry:/nTheir split second's hesitation was all Harry needed./n/n" Expelliarmusl"/n/nGoyle 's wand flew out of his hand and disappeared/ninto the bulwark of objects beside him; Goyle leapt/nfoolishly on the spot, trying to retrieve it; Malfoy/njumped out of range of Hermione 's second Stunning/nSpell, and Ron, appearing suddenly at the end of the/n/n/n/n/naisle, shot a full Body-Bind Curse at Crabbe, which/nnarrowly missed./n/nCrabbe wheeled around and screamed, "Avada/nKedavraY' again. Ron leapt out of sight to avoid the jet/nof green light. The wandless Malfoy cowered behind a/nthree-legged wardrobe as Hermione charged toward/nthem, hitting Goyle with a Stunning Spell as she/ncame./n/n"It's somewhere here!" Harry yelled at her, pointing at/nthe pile of junk into which the old tiara had fallen./n"Look for it while I go and help R — "/n/n"HARRY!" she screamed./n/nA roaring, billowing noise behind him gave him a/nmoment's warning. He turned and saw both Ron and/nCrabbe running as hard as they could up the aisle/ntoward them./n/n"Like it hot, scum?" roared Crabbe as he ran./n/nBut he seemed to have no control over what he had/ndone. Flames of abnormal size were pursuing them,/nlicking up the sides of the junk bulwarks, which were/ncrumbling to soot at their touch./n/n"Aguamenti\" Harry bawled, but the jet of water that/nsoared from the tip of his wand evaporated in the air./n/n"RUN!"/n/nMalfoy grabbed the Stunned Goyle and dragged him/nalong; Crabbe outstripped all of them, now looking/nterrified; Harry, Ron, and Hermione pelted along in/nhis wake, and the fire pursued them. It was not/nnormal fire; Crabbe had used a curse of which Harry/nhad no knowledge: As they turned a corner the flames/n/n/n/n/nchased them as though they were alive, sentient,/nintent upon killing them. Now the fire was mutating,/nforming a gigantic pack of fiery beasts: Flaming/nserpents, chimaeras, and dragons rose and fell and/nrose again, and the detritus of centuries on which/nthey were feeding was thrown up in the air into their/nfanged mouths, tossed high on clawed feet, before/nbeing consumed by the inferno./n/nMalfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle had vanished from view:/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione stopped dead; the fiery/nmonsters were circling them, drawing closer and/ncloser, claws and horns and tails lashed, and the heat/nwas solid as a wall around them./n/n"What can we do?" Hermione screamed over the/ndeafening roars of the fire. "What can we do?"/n/n"Here!"/n/nHarry seized a pair of heavy-looking broomsticks from/nthe nearest pile of junk and threw one to Ron, who/npulled Hermione onto it behind him. Harry swung his/nleg over the second broom and, with hard kicks to the/nground, they soared up into the air, missing by feet/nthe horned beak of a flaming raptor that snapped its/njaws at them. The smoke and heat were becoming/noverwhelming: Below them the cursed fire was/nconsuming the contraband of generations of hunted/nstudents, the guilty outcomes of a thousand banned/nexperiments, the secrets of the countless souls who/nhad sought refuge in the room. Harry could not see a/ntrace of Malfoy, Crabbe, or Goyle anywhere: He/nswooped as low as he dared over the marauding/nmonsters of flame to try to find them, but there was/nnothing but fire: What a terrible way to die. ... He had/nnever wanted this. .../n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry, let's get out, let's get out!" bellowed Ron,/nthough it was impossible to see where the door was/nthrough the black smoke./n/nAnd then Harry heard a thin, piteous human scream/nfrom amidst the terrible commotion, the thunder of/ndevouring flame./n/n"It's — too — dangerous — !" Ron yelled, but Harry/nwheeled in the air. His glasses giving his eyes some/nsmall protection from the smoke, he raked the/nfirestorm below, seeking a sign of life, a limb or a face/nthat was not yet charred like wood. .../n/nAnd he saw them: Malfoy with his arms around the/nunconscious Goyle, the pair of them perched on a/nfragile tower of charred desks, and Harry dived./n/nMalfoy saw him coming and raised one arm, but even/nas Harry grasped it he knew at once that it was no/ngood: Goyle was too heavy and Malfoy 's hand, covered/nin sweat, slid instantly out of Harry's —/n/n"IF WE DIE FOR THEM, I'LL KILL YOU, HARRY!"/nroared Ron's voice, and, as a great flaming chimaera/nbore down upon them, he and Hermione dragged/nGoyle onto their broom and rose, rolling and pitching,/ninto the air once more as Malfoy clambered up behind/nHarry./n/n"The door, get to the door, the door!" screamed Malfoy/nin Harry's ear, and Harry sped up, following Ron,/nHermione, and Goyle through the billowing black/nsmoke, hardly able to breathe: and all around them/nthe last few objects unburned by the devouring flames/nwere flung into the air, as the creatures of the cursed/nfire cast them high in celebration: cups and shields, a/nsparkling necklace, and an old, discolored tiara —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n" What are you doing, what are you doing, the door's/nthat way\" screamed Malfoy, but Harry made a/nhairpin swerve and dived. The diadem seemed to fall/nin slow motion, turning and glittering as it dropped/ntoward the maw of a yawning serpent, and then he/nhad it, caught it around his wrist —/n/nHarry swerved again as the serpent lunged at him; he/nsoared upward and straight toward the place where,/nhe prayed, the door stood open: Ron, Hermione, and/nGoyle had vanished; Malfoy was screaming and/nholding Harry so tightly it hurt. Then, through the/nsmoke, Harry saw a rectangular patch on the wall/nand steered the broom at it, and moments later clean/nair filled his lungs and they collided with the wall in/nthe corridor beyond./n/nMalfoy fell off the broom and lay facedown, gasping,/ncoughing, and retching. Harry rolled over and sat up:/nThe door to the Room of Requirement had vanished,/nand Ron and Hermione sat panting on the floor beside/nGoyle, who was still unconscious./n/n"C-Crabbe," choked Malfoy as soon as he could/nspeak. "C-Crabbe ..."/n/n"He's dead," said Ron harshly./n/nThere was silence, apart from panting and coughing./nThen a number of huge bangs shook the castle, and a/ngreat cavalcade of transparent figures galloped past/non horses, their heads screaming with bloodlust/nunder their arms. Harry staggered to his feet when/nthe Headless Hunt had passed and looked around:/n/nThe battle was still going on all around him. He could/nhear more screams than those of the retreating/nghosts. Panic flared within him./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Where's Ginny?" he said sharply. "She was here. She/nwas supposed to be going back into the Room of/nRequirement."/n/n"Blimey, d'you reckon it'll still work after that fire?"/nasked Ron, but he too got to his feet, rubbing his/nchest and looking left and right. "Shall we split up/nand look — ?"/n/n"No," said Hermione, getting to her feet too. Malfoy/nand Goyle remained slumped hopelessly on the/ncorridor floor; neither of them had wands. "Let's stick/ntogether. I say we go — Harry, what's that on your/narm?"/n/n"What? Oh yeah — "/n/nHe pulled the diadem from his wrist and held it up. It/nwas still hot, blackened with soot, but as he looked at/nit closely he was just able to make out the tiny words/netched upon it: WIT BEYOND MEASURE IS MAN'S/nGREATEST TREASURE./n/nA bloodlike substance, dark and tarry, seemed to be/nleaking from the diadem. Suddenly Harry felt the/nthing vibrate violently, then break apart in his hands,/nand as it did so, he thought he heard the faintest,/nmost distant scream of pain, echoing not from the/ngrounds or the castle, but from the thing that had/njust fragmented in his fingers./n/n"It must have been Fiendfyre!" whimpered Hermione,/nher eyes on the broken pieces./n/n"Sorry?"/n/n"Fiendfyre — cursed fire — it's one of the substances/nthat destroy Horcruxes, but I would never, ever have/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/ndared use it, it's so dangerous — how did Crabbe/nknow how to — ?"/n/n"Must've learned from the Carrows," said Harry/ngrimly./n/n"Shame he wasn't concentrating when they/nmentioned how to stop it, really," said Ron, whose/nhair, like Hermione's, was singed, and whose face was/nblackened. "If he hadn't tried to kill us all, I'd be quite/nsorry he was dead."/n/n"But don't you realize?" whispered Hermione. "This/nmeans, if we can just get the snake — "/n/nBut she broke off as yells and shouts and the/nunmistakable noises of dueling filled the corridor./nHarry looked around and his heart seemed to fail:/nDeath Eaters had penetrated Hogwarts. Fred and/nPercy had just backed into view, both of them dueling/nmasked and hooded men./n/nHarry, Ron, and Hermione ran forward to help: Jets of/nlight flew in every direction and the man dueling/nPercy backed off, fast: Then his hood slipped and they/nsaw a high forehead and streaked hair —/n/n"Hello, Minister!" bellowed Percy, sending a neat jinx/nstraight at Thicknesse, who dropped his wand and/nclawed at the front of his robes, apparently in awful/ndiscomfort. "Did I mention I'm resigning?"/n/n"You're joking, Perce!" shouted Fred as the Death/nEater he was battling collapsed under the weight of/nthree separate Stunning Spells. Thicknesse had fallen/nto the ground with tiny spikes erupting all over him;/nhe seemed to be turning into some form of sea urchin./nFred looked at Percy with glee./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You actually are joking, Perce. ... I don't think I've/nheard you joke since you were — "/n/nThe air exploded. They had been grouped together,/nHarry, Ron, Hermione, Fred, and Percy, the two/nDeath Eaters at their feet, one Stunned, the other/nTransfigured; and in that fragment of a moment,/nwhen danger seemed temporarily at bay, the world/nwas rent apart. Harry felt himself flying through the/nair, and all he could do was hold as tightly as possible/nto that thin stick of wood that was his one and only/nweapon, and shield his head in his arms: He heard/nthe screams and yells of his companions without a/nhope of knowing what had happened to them —/n/nAnd then the world resolved itself into pain and/nsemidarkness: He was half buried in the wreckage of/na corridor that had been subjected to a terrible/nattack. Cold air told him that the side of the castle/nhad been blown away, and hot stickiness on his/ncheek told him that he was bleeding copiously. Then/nhe heard a terrible cry that pulled at his insides, that/nexpressed agony of a kind neither flame nor curse/ncould cause, and he stood up, swaying, more/nfrightened than he had been that day, more/nfrightened, perhaps, than he had been in his life. .../n/nAnd Hermione was struggling to her feet in the/nwreckage, and three redheaded men were grouped on/nthe ground where the wall had blasted apart. Harry/ngrabbed Hermione 's hand as they staggered and/nstumbled over stone and wood./n/n"No — no — no!" someone was shouting. "No! Fred!/nNo!"/n/nAnd Percy was shaking his brother, and Ron was/nkneeling beside them, and Fred's eyes stared without/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nseeing, the ghost of his last laugh still etched upon/nhis face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Elder Wand
text: /nThe world had ended, so why had the battle not/nceased, the castle fallen silent in horror, and every/ncombatant laid down their arms? Harry's mind was in/nfree fall, spinning out of control, unable to grasp the/nimpossibility, because Fred Weasley could not be/ndead, the evidence of all his senses must be lying —/n/nAnd then a body fell past the hole blown into the side/nof the school, and curses flew in at them from the/ndarkness, hitting the wall behind their heads./n/n"Get down!" Harry shouted, as more curses flew/nthrough the night: He and Ron had both grabbed/nHermione and pulled her to the floor, but Percy lay/nacross Fred's body, shielding it from further harm,/nand when Harry shouted, "Percy, come on, we've got/nto move!" he shook his head./n/n"Percy!" Harry saw tear tracks streaking the grime/ncoating Ron's face as he seized his elder brother's/nshoulders and pulled, but Percy would not budge./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Percy, you can't do anything for him! We're going to/n/n/n/nHermione screamed, and Harry, turning, did not need/nto ask why. A monstrous spider the size of a small car/nwas trying to climb through the huge hole in the wall:/nOne of Aragog's descendants had joined the fight./n/nRon and Harry shouted together; their spells collided/nand the monster was blown backward, its legs jerking/nhorribly, and vanished into the darkness./n/n"It brought friends!" Harry called to the others,/nglancing over the edge of the castle through the hole/nin the wall the curses had blasted: More giant spiders/nwere climbing the side of the building, liberated from/nthe Forbidden Forest, into which the Death Eaters/nmust have penetrated. Harry fired Stunning Spells/ndown upon them, knocking the lead monster into its/nfellows, so that they rolled back down the building/nand out of sight. Then more curses came soaring over/nHarry's head, so close he felt the force of them blow/nhis hair./n/n"Let's move, NOW!"/n/nPushing Hermione ahead of him with Ron, Harry/nstooped to seize Fred's body under the armpits. Percy,/nrealizing what Harry was trying to do, stopped/nclinging to the body and helped; together, crouching/nlow to avoid the curses flying at them from the/ngrounds, they hauled Fred out of the way./n/n"Here," said Harry, and they placed him in a niche/nwhere a suit of armor had stood earlier. He could not/nbear to look at Fred a second longer than he had to,/nand after making sure that the body was well hidden,/nhe took off after Ron and Hermione. Malfoy and Goyle/nhad vanished, but at the end of the corridor, which/n/n/n/n/nwas now full of dust and falling masonry, glass long/ngone from the windows, he saw many people running/nbackward and forward, whether friends or foes he/ncould not tell. It/ndid nothing to Snape, who for a split second seemed/nto think he had been reprieved: But then Voldemort's/nintention became clear. The snake's cage was rolling/nthrough the air, and before Snape could do anything/nmore than yell, it had encased him, head and/nshoulders, and Voldemort spoke in Parseltongue./n/n"Kill."/n/nThere was a terrible scream. Harry saw Snape 's face/nlosing the little color it had left; it whitened as his/nblack eyes widened, as the snake's fangs pierced his/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nneck, as he failed to push the enchanted cage off/nhimself, as his knees gave way and he fell to the floor./n/n"I regret it," said Voldemort coldly./n/nHe turned away; there was no sadness in him, no/nremorse. It was time to leave this shack and take/ncharge, with a wand that would now do his full/nbidding. He pointed it at the starry cage holding the/nsnake, which drifted upward, off Snape, who fell/nsideways onto the floor, blood gushing from the/nwounds in his neck. Voldemort swept from the room/nwithout a backward glance, and the great serpent/nfloated after him in its huge protective sphere./n/nBack in the tunnel and his own mind, Harry opened/nhis eyes: He had drawn blood biting down on his/nknuckles in the effort not to shout out. Now he was/nlooking through the tiny crack between crate and/nwall, watching a foot in a black boot trembling on the/nfloor./n/n"Harry!" breathed Hermione behind him, but he had/nalready pointed his wand at the crate blocking his/nview. It lifted an inch into the air and drifted sideways/nsilently. As quietly as he could, he pulled himself up/ninto the room./n/nHe did not know why he was doing it, why he was/napproaching the dying man: He did not know what he/nfelt as he saw Snape's white face, and the fingers/ntrying to staunch the bloody wound at his neck./n/nHarry took off the Invisibility Cloak and looked down/nupon the man he hated, whose widening black eyes/nfound Harry as he tried to speak. Harry bent over/nhim, and Snape seized the front of his robes and/npulled him close./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nA terrible rasping, gurgling noise issued from Snape's/nthroat./n/n"Take ... it. ... Take ... it. ..."/n/nSomething more than blood was leaking from Snape./nSilvery blue, neither gas nor liquid, it gushed from his/nmouth and his ears and his eyes, and Harry knew/nwhat it was, but did not know what to do —/n/nA flask, conjured from thin air, was thrust into his/nshaking hands by Hermione. Harry lifted the silvery/nsubstance into it with his wand. When the flask was/nfull to the brim, and Snape looked as though there/nwas no blood left in him, his grip on Harry's robes/nslackened./n/n"Look ... at ... me. ..." he whispered./n/nThe green eyes found the black, but after a second,/nsomething in the depths of the dark pair seemed to/nvanish, leaving them fixed, blank, and empty. The/nhand holding Harry thudded to the floor, and Snape/nmoved no more./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Prince's Tale
text: /nHarry remained kneeling at Snape's side, simply/nstaring down at him, until quite suddenly a high, cold/nvoice spoke so close to them that Harry jumped to his/nfeet, the flask gripped tightly in his hands, thinking/nthat Voldemort had reentered the room./n/nVoldemort 's voice reverberated from the walls and/nfloor, and Harry realized that he was talking to/nHogwarts and to all the surrounding area, that the/nresidents of Hogsmeade and all those still fighting in/nthe castle would hear him as clearly as if he stood/nbeside them, his breath on the back of their necks, a/ndeathblow away./n/n"You have fought," said the high, cold voice,/n/n"valiantly. Lord Voldemort knows how to value/nbravery./n/n"Yet you have sustained heavy losses. If you continue/nto resist me, you will all die, one by one. I do not wish/nthis to happen. Every drop of magical blood spilled is/na loss and a waste./n/n/n/n/n"Lord Voldemort is merciful. I command my forces to/nretreat immediately./n/n/n/n"You have one hour. Dispose of your dead with/ndignity. Treat your injured./n/n"I speak now, Harry Potter, directly to you. You have/npermitted your friends to die for you rather than face/nme yourself. I shall wait for one hour in the Forbidden/nForest. If, at the end of that hour, you have not come/nto me, have not given yourself up, then battle/nrecommences. This time, I shall enter the fray myself,/nHarry Potter, and I shall find you, and I shall punish/nevery last man, woman, and child who has tried to/nconceal you from me. One hour."/n/nBoth Ron and Hermione shook their heads frantically,/nlooking at Harry./n/n"Don't listen to him," said Ron./n/n"It'll be all right," said Hermione wildly. "Let's — let's/nget back to the castle, if he's gone to the forest we'll/nneed to think of a new plan — "/n/nShe glanced at Snape's body, then hurried back to/nthe tunnel entrance. Ron followed her. Harry gathered/nup the Invisibility Cloak, then looked down at Snape./nHe did not know what to feel, except shock at the way/nSnape had been killed, and the reason for which it/nhad been done. .../n/nThey crawled back through the tunnel, none of them/ntalking, and Harry wondered whether Ron and/nHermione could still hear Voldemort ringing in their/nheads, as he could./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nYou have permitted your friends to die for you rather/nthan face me yourself I shall wait for one hour in the/nForbidden Forest. . . . One hour. . . ./n/nSmall bundles seemed to litter the lawn at the front of/nthe castle. It could only be an hour or so from dawn,/nyet it was pitch-black. The three of them hurried/ntoward the stone steps. A lone clog, the size of a small/nboat, lay abandoned in front of them. There was no/nother sign of Grawp or of his attacker./n/nThe castle was unnaturally silent. There were no/nflashes of light now, no bangs or screams or shouts./nThe flagstones of the deserted entrance hall were/nstained with blood. Emeralds were still scattered all/nover the floor, along with pieces of marble and/nsplintered wood. Part of the banisters had been blown/naway./n/n"Where is everyone?" whispered Hermione./n/nRon led the way to the Great Hall. Harry stopped in/nthe doorway./n/nThe House tables were gone and the room was/ncrowded. The survivors stood in groups, their arms/naround each other's necks. The injured were being/ntreated upon the raised platform by Madam Pomfrey/nand a group of helpers. Firenze was amongst the/ninjured; his flank poured blood and he shook where/nhe lay, unable to stand./n/nThe dead lay in a row in the middle of the Hall. Harry/ncould not see Fred's body, because his family/nsurrounded him. George was kneeling at his head;/nMrs. Weasley was lying across Fred's chest, her body/nshaking, Mr. Weasley stroking her hair while tears/ncascaded down his cheeks./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nWithout a word to Harry, Ron and Hermione walked/naway. Harry saw Hermione approach Ginny, whose/nface was swollen and blotchy, and hug her. Ron/njoined Bill, Fleur, and Percy, who flung an arm/naround Ron's shoulders. As Ginny and Hermione/nmoved closer to the rest of the family, Harry had a/nclear view of the bodies lying next to Fred: Remus and/nTonks, pale and still and peaceful-looking, apparently/nasleep beneath the dark, enchanted ceiling./n/nThe Great Hall seemed to fly away, become smaller,/nshrink, as Harry reeled backward from the doorway./nHe could not draw breath. He could not bear to look/nat any of the other bodies, to see who else had died/nfor him. He could not bear to join the Weasleys, could/nnot look into their eyes, when if he had given himself/nup in the first place, Fred might never have died. .../n/nHe turned away and ran up the marble staircase./nLupin, Tonks ... He yearned not to feel. ... He wished/nhe could rip out his heart, his innards, everything/nthat was screaming inside him. .../n/nThe castle was completely empty; even the ghosts/nseemed to have joined the mass mourning in the/nGreat Hall. Harry ran without stopping, clutching the/ncrystal flask of Snape's last thoughts, and he did not/nslow down until he reached the stone gargoyle/nguarding the headmaster's office./n/n"Password?"/n/n"Dumbledore!" said Harry without thinking, because/nit was he whom he yearned to see, and to his surprise/nthe gargoyle slid aside, revealing the spiral staircase/nbehind./n/nBut when Harry burst into the circular office he found/na change. The portraits that hung all around the/n/n/n/n/n/nwalls were empty. Not a single headmaster or/nheadmistress remained to see him; all, it seemed, had/nflitted away, charging through the paintings that lined/nthe castle, so that they could have a clear view of/nwhat was going on./n/nHarry glanced hopelessly at Dumbledore's deserted/nframe, which hung directly behind the headmaster's/nchair, then turned his back on it. The stone Pensieve/nlay in the cabinet where it had always been: Harry/nheaved it onto the desk and poured Snape's memories/ninto the wide basin with its runic markings around/nthe edge. To escape into someone else's head would/nbe a blessed relief. ... Nothing that even Snape had/nleft him could be worse than his own thoughts. The/nmemories swirled, silver white and strange, and/nwithout hesitating, with a feeling of reckless/nabandonment, as though this would assuage his/ntorturing grief, Harry dived./n/nHe fell headlong into sunlight, and his feet found/nwarm ground. When he straightened up, he saw that/nhe was in a nearly deserted playground. A single huge/nchimney dominated the distant skyline. Two girls/nwere swinging backward and forward, and a skinny/nboy was watching them from behind a clump of/nbushes. His black hair was overlong and his clothes/nwere so mismatched that it looked deliberate: too/nshort jeans, a shabby, overlarge coat that might have/nbelonged to a grown man, an odd smocklike shirt./n/nHarry moved closer to the boy. Snape looked no more/nthan nine or ten years old, sallow, small, stringy./nThere was undisguised greed in his thin face as he/nwatched the younger of the two girls swinging higher/nand higher than her sister./n/n"Lily, don't do it!" shrieked the elder of the two./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut the girl had let go of the swing at the very height/nof its arc and flown into the air, quite literally flown,/nlaunched herself skyward with a great shout of/nlaughter, and instead of crumpling on the playground/nasphalt, she soared like a trapeze artist through the/nair, staying up far too long, landing far too lightly./n/n"Mummy told you not to!"/n/nPetunia stopped her swing by dragging the heels of/nher sandals on the ground, making a crunching,/ngrinding sound, then leapt up, hands on hips./n/n"Mummy said you weren't allowed, Lily!"/n/n"But I'm fine," said Lily, still giggling. "Tuney, look at/nthis. Watch what I can do."/n/nPetunia glanced around. The playground was/ndeserted apart from themselves and, though the girls/ndid not know it, Snape. Lily had picked up a fallen/nflower from the bush behind which Snape lurked./nPetunia advanced, evidently torn between curiosity/nand disapproval. Lily waited until Petunia was near/nenough to have a clear view, then held out her palm./nThe flower sat there, opening and closing its petals,/nlike some bizarre, many-lipped oyster./n/n"Stop it!" shrieked Petunia./n/n"It's not hurting you," said Lily, but she closed her/nhand on the blossom and threw it back to the ground./n/n"It's not right," said Petunia, but her eyes had/nfollowed the flower's flight to the ground and lingered/nupon it. "How do you do it?" she added, and there/nwas definite longing in her voice./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"It's obvious, isn't it?" Snape could no longer contain/nhimself, but had jumped out from behind the bushes./nPetunia shrieked and ran backward toward the/nswings, but Lily, though clearly startled, remained/nwhere she was. Snape seemed to regret his/nappearance. A dull flush of color mounted the sallow/ncheeks as he looked at Lily./n/n"What's obvious?" asked Lily./n/nSnape had an air of nervous excitement. With a/nglance at the distant Petunia, now hovering beside the/nswings, he lowered his voice and said, "I know what/nyou are."/n/n"What do you mean?"/n/n"You're ... you're a witch," whispered Snape./n/nShe looked affronted./n/n" That's not a very nice thing to say to somebody!"/n/nShe turned, nose in the air, and marched off toward/nher sister./n/n"No!" said Snape. He was highly colored now, and/nHarry wondered why he did not take off the/nridiculously large coat, unless it was because he did/nnot want to reveal the smock beneath it. He flapped/nafter the girls, looking ludicrously batlike, like his/nolder self./n/nThe sisters considered him, united in disapproval,/nboth holding on to one of the swing poles as though it/nwas the safe place in tag./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You are," said Snape to Lily. "You are a witch. I've/nbeen watching you for a while. But there's nothing/nwrong with that. My mum's one, and I'm a wizard."/n/nPetunia's laugh was like cold water./n/n"Wizard!" she shrieked, her courage returned now/nthat she had recovered from the shock of his/nunexpected appearance. "I know who you are. You're/nthat Snape boy! They live down Spinner's End by the/nriver," she told Lily, and it was evident from her tone/nthat she considered the address a poor/nrecommendation. "Why have you been spying on us?"/n/n"Haven't been spying," said Snape, hot and/nuncomfortable and dirty-haired in the bright sunlight./n"Wouldn't spy on you, anyway," he added spitefully,/n/n" you're a Muggle."/n/nThough Petunia evidently did not understand the/nword, she could hardly mistake the tone./n/n"Lily, come on, we're leaving!" she said shrilly. Lily/nobeyed her sister at once, glaring at Snape as she left./nHe stood watching them as they marched through the/nplayground gate, and Harry, the only one left to/nobserve him, recognized Snape 's bitter/ndisappointment, and understood that Snape had been/nplanning this moment for a while, and that it had all/ngone wrong. . . ./n/nThe scene dissolved, and before Harry knew it, re-/nformed around him. He was now in a small thicket of/ntrees. He could see a sunlit river glittering through/ntheir trunks. The shadows cast by the trees made a/nbasin of cool green shade. Two children sat facing/neach other, cross-legged on the ground. Snape had/nremoved his coat now; his odd smock looked less/npeculiar in the half light./n/n/n/n/n/n"... and the Ministry can punish you if you do magic/noutside school, you get letters."/n/n"But I have done magic outside school!"/n/n"We're all right. We haven't got wands yet. They let/nyou off when you're a kid and you can't help it. But/nonce you're eleven," he nodded importantly, "and they/nstart training you, then you've got to go careful."/n/nThere was a little silence. Lily had picked up a fallen/ntwig and twirled it in the air, and Harry knew that she/nwas imagining sparks trailing from it. Then she/ndropped the twig, leaned in toward the boy, and said,/n"It is real, isn't it? It's not a joke? Petunia says you're/nlying to me. Petunia says there isn't a Hogwarts. It is/nreal, isn't it?"/n/n"It's real for us," said Snape. "Not for her. But we'll get/nthe letter, you and me."/n/n"Really?" whispered Lily./n/n"Definitely," said Snape, and even with his poorly cut/nhair and his odd clothes, he struck an oddly/nimpressive figure sprawled in front of her, brimful of/nconfidence in his destiny./n/n"And will it really come by owl?" Lily whispered./n/n"Normally," said Snape. "But you're Muggle-born, so/nsomeone from the school will have to come and/nexplain to your parents."/n/n"Does it make a difference, being Muggle-born?"/n/nSnape hesitated. His black eyes, eager in the greenish/ngloom, moved over the pale face, the dark red hair./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," he said. "It doesn't make any difference."/n/n"Good," said Lily, relaxing: It was clear that she had/nbeen worrying./n/n"You've got loads of magic," said Snape. "I saw that./nAll the time I was watching you ..."/n/nHis voice trailed away; she was not listening, but had/nstretched out on the leafy ground and was looking up/nat the canopy of leaves overhead. He watched her as/ngreedily as he had watched her in the playground./n/n"How are things at your house?" Lily asked./n/nA little crease appeared between his eyes./n/n"Fine," he said./n/n"They're not arguing anymore?"/n/n"Oh yes, they're arguing," said Snape. He picked up a/nfistful of leaves and began tearing them apart,/napparently unaware of what he was doing. "But it/nwon't be that long and I'll be gone."/n/n"Doesn't your dad like magic?"/n/n"He doesn't like anything, much," said Snape./n/n"Severus?"/n/nA little smile twisted Snape 's mouth when she said/nhis name./n/n"Yeah?"/n/n"Tell me about the dementors again."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"What d'you want to know about them for?"/n/n"If I use magic outside school — "/n/n"They wouldn't give you to the dementors for that!/nDementors are for people who do really bad stuff./nThey guard the wizard prison, Azkaban. You're not/ngoing to end up in Azkaban, you're too — "/n/nHe turned red again and shredded more leaves. Then/na small rustling noise behind Harry made him turn:/nPetunia, hiding behind a tree, had lost her footing./n/n"Tuney!" said Lily, surprise and welcome in her voice,/nbut Snape had jumped to his feet./n/n"Who's spying now?" he shouted. "What d'you want?"/n/nPetunia was breathless, alarmed at being caught./nHarry could see her struggling for something hurtful/nto say./n/n"What is that you're wearing, anyway?" she said,/npointing at Snape's chest. "Your mum's blouse?"/n/nThere was a crack: A branch over Petunia's head had/nfallen. Lily screamed: The branch caught Petunia on/nthe shoulder, and she staggered backward and burst/ninto tears./n/n"Tuney!"/n/nBut Petunia was running away. Lily rounded on/nSnape./n/n"Did you make that happen?"/n/n"No." He looked both defiant and scared./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You did!" She was backing away from him. "You did)./nYou hurt her!"/n/n/n/n"No — no I didn't!"/n/nBut the lie did not convince Lily: After one last/nburning look, she ran from the little thicket, off after/nher sister, and Snape looked miserable and confused./n/n/n/nAnd the scene re-formed. Harry looked around: He/nwas on platform nine and three-quarters, and Snape/nstood beside him, slightly hunched, next to a thin,/nsallow-faced, sour-looking woman who greatly/nresembled him. Snape was staring at a family of four/na short distance away. The two girls stood a little/napart from their parents. Lily seemed to be pleading/nwith her sister; Harry moved closer to listen./n/n"... I'm sorry, Tuney, I'm sorry! Listen — " She caught/nher sister's hand and held tight to it, even though/nPetunia tried to pull it away. "Maybe once I'm there —/nno, listen, Tuney! Maybe once I'm there, I'll be able to/ngo to Professor Dumbledore and persuade him to/nchange his mind!"/n/n"I don't — want — to — go!" said Petunia, and she/ndragged her hand back out of her sister's grasp. "You/nthink I want to go to some stupid castle and learn to/nbe a — a — "/n/nHer pale eyes roved over the platform, over the cats/nmewling in their owners' arms, over the owls/nfluttering and hooting at each other in cages, over the/nstudents, some already in their long black robes,/nloading trunks onto the scarlet steam engine or else/ngreeting one another with glad cries after a summer/napart./n/n/n/n/n/n" — you think I want to be a — a freak?"/n/nLily's eyes filled with tears as Petunia succeeded in/ntugging her hand away./n/n"I'm not a freak," said Lily. "That's a horrible thing to/nsay."/n/n"That's where you're going," said Petunia with relish./n"A special school for freaks. You and that Snape boy/n... weirdos, that's what you two are. It's good you're/nbeing separated from normal people. It's for our/nsafety."/n/nLily glanced toward her parents, who were looking/naround the platform with an air of wholehearted/nenjoyment, drinking in the scene. Then she looked/nback at her sister, and her voice was low and fierce./n/n"You didn't think it was such a freak's school when/nyou wrote to the headmaster and begged him to take/nyou."/n/nPetunia turned scarlet./n/n"Beg? I didn't beg!"/n/n"I saw his reply. It was very kind."/n/n"You shouldn't have read — " whispered Petunia, "that/nwas my private — how could you — ?"/n/nLily gave herself away by half-glancing toward where/nSnape stood nearby. Petunia gasped./n/n"That boy found it! You and that boy have been/nsneaking in my room!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"No — not sneaking — " Now Lily was on the/ndefensive. "Severus saw the envelope, and he couldn't/nbelieve a Muggle could have contacted Hogwarts,/nthat's all! He says there must be wizards working/nundercover in the postal service who take care of — "/n/n"Apparently wizards poke their noses in everywhere!"/nsaid Petunia, now as pale as she had been flushed./n/n" Freak)." she spat at her sister, and she flounced off to/nwhere her parents stood. .../n/nThe scene dissolved again. Snape was hurrying along/nthe corridor of the Hogwarts Express as it clattered/nthrough the countryside. He had already changed into/nhis school robes, had perhaps taken the first/nopportunity to take off his dreadful Muggle clothes. At/nlast he stopped, outside a compartment in which a/ngroup of rowdy boys were talking. Hunched in a/ncorner seat beside the window was Lily, her face/npressed against the windowpane./n/nSnape slid open the compartment door and sat down/nopposite Lily. She glanced at him and then looked/nback out of the window. She had been crying./n/n"I don't want to talk to you," she said in a constricted/nvoice./n/n"Why not?"/n/n"Tuney h-hates me. Because we saw that letter from/nDumbledore."/n/n"So what?"/n/nShe threw him a look of deep dislike./n/n"So she's my sister!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"She's only a — " He caught himself quickly; Lily, too/nbusy trying to wipe her eyes without being noticed,/ndid not hear him./n/n"But we're going!" he said, unable to suppress the/nexhilaration in his voice. "This is it! We're off to/nHogwarts!"/n/nShe nodded, mopping her eyes, but in spite of herself,/nshe half smiled./n/n"You'd better be in Slytherin," said Snape, encouraged/nthat she had brightened a little./n/n"Slytherin?"/n/nOne of the boys sharing the compartment, who had/nshown no interest at all in Lily or Snape until that/npoint, looked around at the word, and Harry, whose/nattention had been focused entirely on the two beside/nthe window, saw his father: slight, black-haired like/nSnape, but with that indefinable air of having been/nwell-cared-for, even adored, that Snape so/nconspicuously lacked./n/n"Who wants to be in Slytherin? I think I'd leave,/nwouldn't you?" James asked the boy lounging on the/nseats opposite him, and with a jolt, Harry realized/nthat it was Sirius. Sirius did not smile./n/n"My whole family have been in Slytherin," he said./n/n"Blimey," said James, "and I thought you seemed all/nright!"/n/nSirius grinned./n/n"Maybe I'll break the tradition. Where are you/nheading, if you've got the choice?"/n/n/n/n/n/nJames lifted an invisible sword./n/n/n/n" 'Gryffindor, where dwell the brave at heart!' Like my/ndad."/n/nSnape made a small, disparaging noise. James turned/non him./n/n"Got a problem with that?"/n/n"No," said Snape, though his slight sneer said/notherwise. "If you'd rather be brawny than brainy — "/n/n"Where 're you hoping to go, seeing as you're neither?"/ninterjected Sirius./n/nJames roared with laughter. Lily sat up, rather/nflushed, and looked from James to Sirius in dislike./n/n"Come on, Severus, let's find another compartment."/n/n"Oooooo ..."/n/nJames and Sirius imitated her lofty voice; James tried/nto trip Snape as he passed./n/n"See ya, Snivellus!" a voice called, as the/ncompartment door slammed. .../n/nAnd the scene dissolved once more. .../n/nHarry was standing right behind Snape as they faced/nthe candlelit House tables, lined with rapt faces. Then/nProfessor McGonagall said, "Evans, Lily!"/n/nHe watched his mother walk forward on trembling/nlegs and sit down upon the rickety stool. Professor/nMcGonagall dropped the Sorting Hat onto her head,/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nand barely a second after it had touched the dark red/nhair, the hat cried, " Gryffindoii"/n/n/n/nHarry heard Snape let out a tiny groan. Lily took off/nthe hat, handed it back to Professor McGonagall, then/nhurried toward the cheering Gryffindors, but as she/nwent she glanced back at Snape, and there was a sad/nlittle smile on her face. Harry saw Sirius move up the/nbench to make room for her. She took one look at/nhim, seemed to recognize him from the train, folded/nher arms, and firmly turned her back on him./n/nThe roll call continued. Harry watched Lupin,/nPettigrew, and his father join Lily and Sirius at the/nGryffindor table. At last, when only a dozen students/nremained to be sorted, Professor McGonagall called/nSnape./n/nHarry walked with him to the stool, watched him/nplace the hat upon his head. "Slytherinl" cried the/nSorting Hat./n/nAnd Severus Snape moved off to the other side of the/nHall, away from Lily, to where the Slytherins were/ncheering him, to where Lucius Malfoy, a prefect badge/ngleaming upon his chest, patted Snape on the back as/nhe sat down beside him. .../n/nAnd the scene changed. .../n/nLily and Snape were walking across the castle/ncourtyard, evidently arguing. Harry hurried to catch/nup with them, to listen in. As he reached them, he/nrealized how much taller they both were: A few years/nseemed to have passed since their Sorting./n/n"... thought we were supposed to be friends?" Snape/nwas saying. "Best friends?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"We are, Sev, but I don't like some of the people you're/nhanging round with! I'm sorry, but I detest Avery and/nMulciber! Mulciber\ What do you see in him, Sev, he's/ncreepy!
