"He/nwill know what to do with it. And Severus, be very/ncareful, they may not take kindly to your appearance/nafter George Weasley's mishap — "/n/nSnape turned at the door./n/n"Don't worry, Dumbledore," he said coolly. "I have a/nplan. ..."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nAnd Snape left the room. Harry rose up out of the/nPensieve, and moments later he lay on the carpeted/nfloor in exactly the same room: Snape might just have/nclosed the door./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Forest Again
text: /nFinally, the truth. Lying with his face pressed into the/ndusty carpet of the office where he had once thought/nhe was learning the secrets of victory, Harry/nunderstood at last that he was not supposed to/nsurvive. His job was to walk calmly into Death's/nwelcoming arms. Along the way, he was to dispose of/nVoldemort's remaining links to life, so that when at/nlast he flung himself across Voldemort's path, and did/nnot raise a wand to defend himself, the end would be/nclean, and the job that ought to have been done in/nGodric's Hollow would be finished: Neither would live,/nneither could survive./n/nHe felt his heart pounding fiercely in his chest. How/nstrange that in his dread of death, it pumped all the/nharder, valiantly keeping him alive. But it would have/nto stop, and soon. Its beats were numbered. How/nmany would there be time for, as he rose and walked/nthrough the castle for the last time, out into the/ngrounds and into the forest?/n/n/n/n/n/n/nTerror washed over him as he lay on the floor, with/nthat funeral drum pounding inside him. Would it hurt/nto die? All those times he had thought that it was/nabout to happen and escaped, he had never really/nthought of the thing itself: His will to live had always/nbeen so much stronger than his fear of death. Yet it/ndid not occur to him now to try to escape, to outrun/nVoldemort. It was over, he knew it, and all that was/nleft was the thing itself: dying./n/nIf he could only have died on that summer's night/nwhen he had left number four, Privet Drive, for the/nlast time, when the noble phoenix-feather wand had/nsaved him! If he could only have died like Hedwig, so/nquickly he would not have known it had happened!/n/nOr if he could have launched himself in front of a/nwand to save someone he loved. ... He envied even his/nparents' deaths now. This cold-blooded walk to his/nown destruction would require a different kind of/nbravery. He felt his fingers trembling slightly and/nmade an effort to control them, although no one could/nsee him; the portraits on the walls were all empty./n/nSlowly, very slowly, he sat up, and as he did so he felt/nmore alive and more aware of his own living body/nthan ever before. Why had he never appreciated what/na miracle he was, brain and nerve and bounding/nheart? It would all be gone ... or at least, he would be/ngone from it. His breath came slow and deep, and his/nmouth and throat were completely dry, but so were/nhis eyes./n/nDumbledore's betrayal was almost nothing. Of course/nthere had been a bigger plan; Harry had simply been/ntoo foolish to see it, he realized that now. He had/nnever questioned his own assumption that/nDumbledore wanted him alive. Now he saw that his/nlife span had always been determined by how long it/ntook to eliminate all the Horcruxes. Dumbledore had/n/n/n/n/npassed the job of destroying them to him, and/nobediently he had continued to chip away at the/nbonds tying not only Voldemort, but himself, to life!/nHow neat, how elegant, not to waste any more lives,/nbut to give the dangerous task to the boy who had/nalready been marked for slaughter, and whose death/nwould not be a calamity, but another blow against/nVoldemort./n/nAnd Dumbledore had known that Harry would not/nduck out, that he would keep going to the end, even/nthough it was his end, because he had taken trouble/nto get to know him, hadn't he? Dumbledore knew, as/nVoldemort knew, that Harry would not let anyone else/ndie for him now that he had discovered it was in his/npower to stop it. The images of Fred, Lupin, and/nTonks lying dead in the Great Hall forced their way/nback into his mind's eye, and for a moment he could/nhardly breathe: Death was impatient. .../n/nBut Dumbledore had overestimated him. He had/nfailed: The snake survived. One Horcrux remained to/nbind Voldemort to the earth, even after Harry had/nbeen killed. True, that would mean an easier job for/nsomebody. He wondered who would do it. ... Ron and/nHermione would know what needed to be done, of/ncourse. ... That would have been why Dumbledore/nwanted him to confide in two others ... so that if he/nfulfilled his true destiny a little early, they could carry/non. .../n/nLike rain on a cold window, these thoughts pattered/nagainst the hard surface of the incontrovertible truth,/nwhich was that he must die. I must die. It must end./n/nRon and Hermione seemed a long way away, in a far-/noff country; he felt as though he had parted from/nthem long ago. There would be no good-byes and no/nexplanations, he was determined of that. This was a/n/n/n/n/n/njourney they could not take together, and the/nattempts they would make to stop him would waste/nvaluable time. He looked down at the battered gold/nwatch he had received on his seventeenth birthday./nNearly half of the hour allotted by Voldemort for his/nsurrender had elapsed./n/nHe stood up. His heart was leaping against his ribs/nlike a frantic bird. Perhaps it knew it had little time/nleft, perhaps it was determined to fulfill a lifetime's/nbeats before the end. He did not look back as he/nclosed the office door./n/nThe castle was empty. He felt ghostly striding through/nit alone, as if he had already died. The portrait people/nwere still missing from their frames; the whole place/nwas eerily still, as if all its remaining lifeblood were/nconcentrated in the Great Hall where the dead and/nthe mourners were crammed./n/nHarry pulled the Invisibility Cloak over himself and/ndescended through the floors, at last walking down/nthe marble staircase into the entrance hall. Perhaps/nsome tiny part of him hoped to be sensed, to be seen,/nto be stopped, but the Cloak was, as ever,/nimpenetrable, perfect, and he reached the front doors/neasily./n/nThen Neville nearly walked into him. He was one half/nof a pair that was carrying a body in from the/ngrounds. Harry glanced down and felt another dull/nblow to his stomach: Colin Creevey, though underage,/nmust have sneaked back just as Malfoy, Crabbe, and/nGoyle had done. He was tiny in death./n/n"You know what? I can manage him alone, Neville,"/nsaid Oliver Wood, and he heaved Colin over his/nshoulder in a fireman's lift and carried him into the/nGreat Hall./n/n/n/n/n/nNeville leaned against the door frame for a moment/nand wiped his forehead with the back of his hand. He/nlooked like an old man. Then he set off down the/nsteps again into the darkness to recover more bodies./n/nHarry took one glance back at the entrance of the/nGreat Hall. People were moving around, trying to/ncomfort each other, drinking, kneeling beside the/ndead, but he could not see any of the people he loved,/nno hint of Hermione, Ron, Ginny, or any of the other/nWeasleys, no Luna. He felt he would have given all the/ntime remaining to him for just one last look at them;/nbut then, would he ever have the strength to stop/nlooking? It was better like this./n/nHe moved down the steps and out into the darkness./n/nIt was nearly four in the morning, and the deathly/nstillness of the grounds felt as though they were/nholding their breath, waiting to see whether he could/ndo what he must./n/nHarry moved toward Neville, who was bending over/nanother body./n/n"Neville."/n/n"Blimey, Harry, you nearly gave me heart failure!"/n/nHarry had pulled off the Cloak: The idea had come to/nhim out of nowhere, born out of a desire to make/nabsolutely sure./n/n"Where are you going, alone?" Neville asked/nsuspiciously./n/n"It's all part of the plan," said Harry. "There's/nsomething I've got to do. Listen — Neville — "/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Harry!" Neville looked suddenly scared. "Harry,/nyou're not thinking of handing yourself over?"/n/n/n/n"No," Harry lied easily. " 'Course not ... this is/nsomething else. But I might be out of sight for a while./nYou know Voldemort's snake, Neville? He's got a huge/nsnake. ... Calls it Nagini ..."/n/n"I've heard, yeah. ... What about it?"/n/n"It's got to be killed. Ron and Hermione know that,/nbut just in case they — "/n/nThe awfulness of that possibility smothered him for a/nmoment, made it impossible to keep talking. But he/npulled himself together again: This was crucial, he/nmust be like Dumbledore, keep a cool head, make/nsure there were backups, others to carry on./nDumbledore had died knowing that three people still/nknew about the Horcruxes; now Neville would take/nHarry's place: There would still be three in the secret./n/n"Just in case they're — busy — and you get the/nchance — "/n/n"Kill the snake?"/n/n"Kill the snake," Harry repeated./n/n"All right, Harry. You're okay, are you?"/n/n"I'm fine. Thanks, Neville."/n/nBut Neville seized his wrist as Harry made to move/non./n/n"We're all going to keep fighting, Harry. You know/nthat?"/n/n/n/n/n/n"Yeah, I — "/n/n/n/nThe suffocating feeling extinguished the end of the/nsentence; he could not go on. Neville did not seem to/nfind it strange. He patted Harry on the shoulder,/nreleased him, and walked away to look for more/nbodies./n/nHarry swung the Cloak back over himself and walked/non. Someone else was moving not far away, stooping/nover another prone figure on the ground. He was feet/naway from her when he realized it was Ginny./n/nHe stopped in his tracks. She was crouching over a/ngirl who was whispering for her mother./n/n"It's all right," Ginny was saying. "It's okay. We're/ngoing to get you inside."/n/n"But I want to go home," whispered the girl. "I don't/nwant to fight anymore!"/n/n"I know," said Ginny, and her voice broke. "It's going/nto be all right."/n/nRipples of cold undulated over Harry's skin. He/nwanted to shout out to the night, he wanted Ginny to/nknow that he was there, he wanted her to know where/nhe was going. He wanted to be stopped, to be dragged/nback, to be sent back home. .../n/nBut he was home. Hogwarts was the first and best/nhome he had known. He and Voldemort and Snape,/nthe abandoned boys, had all found home here. .../n/nGinny was kneeling beside the injured girl now,/nholding her hand. With a huge effort Harry forced/nhimself on. He thought he saw Ginny look around as/nhe passed, and wondered whether she had sensed/n/n/n/n/n/nsomeone walking nearby, but he did not speak, and/nhe did not look back./n/nHagrid's hut loomed out of the darkness. There were/nno lights, no sound of Fang scrabbling at the door,/nhis bark booming in welcome. All those visits to/nHagrid, and the gleam of the copper kettle on the fire,/nand rock cakes and giant grubs, and his great/nbearded face, and Ron vomiting slugs, and Hermione/nhelping him save Norbert .../n/nHe moved on, and now he reached the edge of the/nforest, and he stopped./n/nA swarm of dementors was gliding amongst the trees;/nhe could feel their chill, and he was not sure he would/nbe able to pass safely through it. He had no strength/nleft for a Patronus. He could no longer control his own/ntrembling. It was not, after all, so easy to die. Every/nsecond he breathed, the smell of the grass, the cool/nair on his face, was so precious: To think that people/nhad years and years, time to waste, so much time it/ndragged, and he was clinging to each second. At the/nsame time he thought that he would not be able to go/non, and knew that he must. The long game was/nended, the Snitch had been caught, it was time to/nleave the air. .../n/nThe Snitch. His nerveless fingers fumbled for a/nmoment with the pouch at his neck and he pulled it/nout./n/nI open at the close./n/nBreathing fast and hard, he stared down at it. Now/nthat he wanted time to move as slowly as possible, it/nseemed to have sped up, and understanding was/ncoming so fast it seemed to have bypassed thought./nThis was the close. This was the moment./n/n/n/n/n/nHe pressed the golden metal to his lips and/nwhispered, "I am about to die."/n/nThe metal shell broke open. He lowered his shaking/nhand, raised Draco's wand beneath the Cloak, and/nmurmured, "Lumos."/n/nThe black stone with its jagged crack running down/nthe center sat in the two halves of the Snitch. The/nResurrection Stone had cracked down the vertical line/nrepresenting the Elder Wand. The triangle and circle/nrepresenting the Cloak and the stone were still/ndiscernible./n/nAnd again Harry understood without having to think./nIt did not matter about bringing them back, for he/nwas about to join them. He was not really fetching/nthem: They were fetching him./n/nHe closed his eyes and turned the stone over in his/nhand three times./n/nHe knew it had happened, because he heard slight/nmovements around him that suggested frail bodies/nshifting their footing on the earthy, twig- strewn/nground that marked the outer edge of the forest. He/nopened his eyes and looked around./n/nThey were neither ghost nor truly flesh, he could see/nthat. They resembled most closely the Riddle that had/nescaped from the diary so long ago, and he had been/nmemory made nearly solid. Less substantial than/nliving bodies, but much more than ghosts, they/nmoved toward him, and on each face, there was the/nsame loving smile./n/nJames was exactly the same height as Harry. He was/nwearing the clothes in which he had died, and his/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhair was untidy and ruffled, and his glasses were a/nlittle lopsided, like Mr. Weasley's./n/nSirius was tall and handsome, and younger by far/nthan Harry had seen him in life. He loped with an/neasy grace, his hands in his pockets and a grin on his/nface./n/nLupin was younger too, and much less shabby, and/nhis hair was thicker and darker. He looked happy to/nbe back in this familiar place, scene of so many/nadolescent wanderings./n/nLily's smile was widest of all. She pushed her long/nhair back as she drew close to him, and her green/neyes, so like his, searched his face hungrily, as/nthough she would never be able to look at him/nenough./n/n"You've been so brave."/n/nHe could not speak. His eyes feasted on her, and he/nthought that he would like to stand and look at her/nforever, and that would be enough./n/n"You are nearly there," said James. "Very close. We/nare ... so proud of you."/n/n"Does it hurt?"/n/nThe childish question had fallen from Harry's lips/nbefore he could stop it./n/n"Dying? Not at all," said Sirius. "Quicker and easier/nthan falling asleep."/n/n"And he will want it to be quick. He wants it over,"/nsaid Lupin./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I didn't want you to die," Harry said. These words/ncame without his volition. "Any of you. I'm sorry — "/n/n/n/nHe addressed Lupin more than any of them,/nbeseeching him./n/n" — right after you'd had your son ... Remus, I'm sorry/n/n/n/n"I am sorry too," said Lupin. "Sorry I will never know/nhim . . . but he will know why I died and I hope he will/nunderstand. I was trying to make a world in which he/ncould live a happier life."/n/nA chilly breeze that seemed to emanate from the heart/nof the forest lifted the hair at Harry's brow. He knew/nthat they would not tell him to go, that it would have/nto be his decision./n/n"You'll stay with me?"/n/n"Until the very end," said James./n/n"They won't be able to see you?" asked Harry./n/n"We are part of you," said Sirius. "Invisible to anyone/nelse."/n/nHarry looked at his mother./n/n"Stay close to me," he said quietly./n/nAnd he set off. The dementors' chill did not overcome/nhim; he passed through it with his companions, and/nthey acted like Patronuses to him, and together they/nmarched through the old trees that grew closely/ntogether, their branches tangled, their roots gnarled/nand twisted underfoot. Harry clutched the Cloak/ntightly around him in the darkness, traveling deeper/n/n/n/n/nand deeper into the forest, with no idea where exactly/nVoldemort was, but sure that he would find him./nBeside him, making scarcely a sound, walked James,/nSirius, Lupin, and Lily, and their presence was his/ncourage, and the reason he was able to keep putting/none foot in front of the other./n/nHis body and mind felt oddly disconnected now, his/nlimbs working without conscious instruction, as if he/nwere passenger, not driver, in the body he was about/nto leave. The dead who walked beside him through/nthe forest were much more real to him now than the/nliving back at the castle: Ron, Hermione, Ginny, and/nall the others were the ones who felt like ghosts as he/nstumbled and slipped toward the end of his life,/ntoward Voldemort. .../n/nA thud and a whisper: Some other living creature had/nstirred close by. Harry stopped under the Cloak,/npeering around, listening, and his mother and father,/nLupin and Sirius stopped too./n/n"Someone there," came a rough whisper close at/nhand. "He's got an Invisibility Cloak. Could it be — ?"/n/nTwo figures emerged from behind a nearby tree: Their/nwands flared, and Harry saw Yaxley and Dolohov/npeering into the darkness, directly at the place Harry,/nhis mother and father and Sirius and Lupin stood./nApparently they could not see anything./n/n"Definitely heard something," said Yaxley. "Animal,/nd'you reckon?"/n/n"That head case Hagrid kept a whole bunch of stuff in/nhere," said Dolohov, glancing over his shoulder./n/nYaxley looked down at his watch./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Time's nearly up. Potter's had his hour. He's not/ncoming."/n/n"And he was sure he'd come! He won't be happy."/n/n"Better go back," said Yaxley. "Find out what the plan/nis now."/n/nHe and Dolohov turned and walked deeper into the/nforest. Harry followed them, knowing that they would/nlead him exactly where he wanted to go. He glanced/nsideways, and his mother smiled at him, and his/nfather nodded encouragement./n/nThey had traveled on mere minutes when Harry saw/nlight ahead, and Yaxley and Dolohov stepped out into/na clearing that Harry knew had been the place where/nthe monstrous Aragog had once lived. The remnants/nof his vast web were there still, but the swarm of/ndescendants he had spawned had been driven out by/nthe Death Eaters, to fight for their cause./n/nA fire burned in the middle of the clearing, and its/nflickering light fell over a crowd of completely silent,/nwatchful Death Eaters. Some of them were still/nmasked and hooded; others showed their faces. Two/ngiants sat on the outskirts of the group, casting/nmassive shadows over the scene, their faces cruel,/nrough-hewn like rock. Harry saw Fenrir, skulking,/nchewing his long nails; the great blond Rowle was/ndabbing at his bleeding lip. He saw Lucius Malfoy,/nwho looked defeated and terrified, and Narcissa,/nwhose eyes were sunken and full of apprehension./n/nEvery eye was fixed upon Voldemort, who stood with/nhis head bowed, and his white hands folded over the/nElder Wand in front of him. He might have been/npraying, or else counting silently in his mind, and/nHarry, standing still on the edge of the scene, thought/n/n/n/n/nabsurdly of a child counting in a game of hide-and-/nseek. Behind his head, still swirling and coiling, the/ngreat snake Nagini floated in her glittering, charmed/ncage, like a monstrous halo./n/nWhen Dolohov and Yaxley rejoined the circle,/nVoldemort looked up./n/n"No sign of him, my Lord," said Dolohov./n/nVoldemort 's expression did not change. The red eyes/nseemed to burn in the firelight. Slowly he drew the/nElder Wand between his long fingers./n/n"My Lord — "/n/nBellatrix had spoken: She sat closest to Voldemort,/ndisheveled, her face a little bloody but otherwise/nunharmed./n/nVoldemort raised his hand to silence her, and she did/nnot speak another word, but eyed him in worshipful/nfascination./n/n"I thought he would come," said Voldemort in his/nhigh, clear voice, his eyes on the leaping flames. "I/nexpected him to come."/n/nNobody spoke. They seemed as scared as Harry,/nwhose heart was now throwing itself against his ribs/nas though determined to escape the body he was/nabout to cast aside. His hands were sweating as he/npulled off the Invisibility Cloak and stuffed it beneath/nhis robes, with his wand. He did not want to be/ntempted to fight./n/n"I was, it seems ... mistaken," said Voldemort./n/n"You weren't."/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry said it as loudly as he could, with all the force/nhe could muster: He did not want to sound afraid./n/nThe Resurrection Stone slipped from between his/nnumb fingers, and out of the corner of his eyes he/nsaw his parents, Sirius, and Lupin vanish as he/nstepped forward into the firelight. At that moment he/nfelt that nobody mattered but Voldemort. It was just/nthe two of them./n/nThe illusion was gone as soon as it had come. The/ngiants roared as the Death Eaters rose together, and/nthere were many cries, gasps, even laughter./nVoldemort had frozen where he stood, but his red/neyes had found Harry, and he stared as Harry moved/ntoward him, with nothing but the fire between them./n/nThen a voice yelled: "HARRY! NO!"/n/nHe turned: Hagrid was bound and trussed, tied to a/ntree nearby. His massive body shook the branches/noverhead as he struggled, desperate./n/n"NO! NO! HARRY, WHAT'RE YEH — ?"/n/n"QUIET!" shouted Rowle, and with a flick of his wand/nHagrid was silenced./n/nBellatrix, who had leapt to her feet, was looking/neagerly from Voldemort to Harry, her breast heaving./nThe only things that moved were the flames and the/nsnake, coiling and uncoiling in the glittering cage/nbehind Voldemort's head./n/nHarry could feel his wand against his chest, but he/nmade no attempt to draw it. He knew that the snake/nwas too well protected, knew that if he managed to/npoint the wand at Nagini, fifty curses would hit him/nfirst. And still, Voldemort and Harry looked at each/nother, and now Voldemort tilted his head a little to/n/n/n/n/nthe side, considering the boy standing before him,/nand a singularly mirthless smile curled the lipless/nmouth./n/n"Harry Potter," he said very softly. His voice might/nhave been part of the spitting fire. "The Boy Who/nLived."/n/nNone of the Death Eaters moved. They were waiting:/nEverything was waiting. Hagrid was struggling, and/nBellatrix was panting, and Harry thought inexplicably/nof Ginny, and her blazing look, and the feel of her lips/non his —/n/nVoldemort had raised his wand. His head was still/ntilted to one side, like a curious child, wondering what/nwould happen if he proceeded. Harry looked back into/nthe red eyes, and wanted it to happen now, quickly,/nwhile he could still stand, before he lost control,/nbefore he betrayed fear —/n/nHe saw the mouth move and a flash of green light,/nand everything was gone./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: King's Cross
text: /nHe lay facedown, listening to the silence. He was/nperfectly alone. Nobody was watching. Nobody else/nwas there. He was not perfectly sure that he was/nthere himself./n/nA long time later, or maybe no time at all, it came to/nhim that he must exist, must be more than/ndisembodied thought, because he was lying, definitely/nlying, on some surface. Therefore he had a sense of/ntouch, and the thing against which he lay existed too./n/nAlmost as soon as he had reached this conclusion,/nHarry became conscious that he was naked./nConvinced as he was of his total solitude, this did not/nconcern him, but it did intrigue him slightly. He/nwondered whether, as he could feel, he would be able/nto see. In opening them, he discovered that he had/neyes./n/nHe lay in a bright mist, though it was not like mist he/nhad ever experienced before. His surroundings were/nnot hidden by cloudy vapor; rather the cloudy vapor/n/n/n/n/nhad not yet formed into surroundings. The floor on/nwhich he lay seemed to be white, neither warm nor/ncold, but simply there, a flat, blank something on/nwhich to be./n/nHe sat up. His body appeared unscathed. He touched/nhis face. He was not wearing glasses anymore./n/nThen a noise reached him through the unformed/nnothingness that surrounded him: the small soft/nthumpings of something that flapped, flailed, and/nstruggled. It was a pitiful noise, yet also slightly/nindecent. He had the uncomfortable feeling that he/nwas eavesdropping on something furtive, shameful./n/nFor the first time, he wished he were clothed./n/nBarely had the wish formed in his head than robes/nappeared a short distance away. He took them and/npulled them on: They were soft, clean, and warm. It/nwas extraordinary how they had appeared, just like/nthat, the moment he had wanted them. .../n/nHe stood up, looking around. Was he in some great/nRoom of Requirement? The longer he looked, the more/nthere was to see. A great domed glass roof glittered/nhigh above him in sunlight. Perhaps it was a palace./nAll was hushed and still, except for those odd/nthumping and whimpering noises coming from/nsomewhere close by in the mist. .../n/nHarry turned slowly on the spot, and his/nsurroundings seemed to invent themselves before his/neyes. A wide-open space, bright and clean, a hall/nlarger by far than the Great Hall, with that clear,/ndomed glass ceiling. It was quite empty. He was the/nonly person there, except for —/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe recoiled. He had spotted the thing that was/nmaking the noises. It had the form of a small, naked/nchild, curled on the ground, its skin raw and rough,/nflayed-looking, and it lay shuddering under a seat/nwhere it had been left, unwanted, stuffed out of sight,/nstruggling for breath./n/nHe was afraid of it. Small and fragile and wounded/nthough it was, he did not want to approach it./nNevertheless he drew slowly nearer, ready to jump/nback at any moment. Soon he stood near enough to/ntouch it, yet he could not bring himself to do it. He/nfelt like a coward. He ought to comfort it, but it/nrepulsed him./n/n"You cannot help."/n/nHe spun around. Albus Dumbledore was walking/ntoward him, sprightly and upright, wearing sweeping/nrobes of midnight blue./n/n"Harry." He spread his arms wide, and his hands were/nboth whole and white and undamaged. "You/nwonderful boy. You brave, brave man. Let us walk."/n/nStunned, Harry followed as Dumbledore strode away/nfrom where the flayed child lay whimpering, leading/nhim to two seats that Harry had not previously/nnoticed, set some distance away under that high,/nsparkling ceiling. Dumbledore sat down in one of/nthem, and Harry fell into the other, staring at his old/nheadmaster's face. Dumbledore 's long silver hair and/nbeard, the piercingly blue eyes behind half-moon/nspectacles, the crooked nose: Everything was as he/nhad remembered it. And yet.../n/n"But you're dead," said Harry./n/n"Oh yes," said Dumbledore matter-of-factly./n/n/n/n/n/n"Then ... I'm dead too?"/n/n/n/n"Ah," said Dumbledore, smiling still more broadly./n"That is the question, isn't it? On the whole, dear boy,/nI think not."/n/nThey looked at each other, the old man still beaming./n"Not?" repeated Harry./n/n"Not," said Dumbledore./n/n"But ..." I meant to/nlet him kill me!"/n/n"And that," said Dumbledore, "will, I think, have/nmade all the difference."/n/nHappiness seemed to radiate from Dumbledore like/nlight, like fire: Harry had never seen the man so/nutterly, so palpably content./n/n"Explain," said Harry./n/n"But you already know," said Dumbledore. He/ntwiddled his thumbs together./n/n"I let him kill me," said Harry. "Didn't I?"/n/n"You did," said Dumbledore, nodding. "Go on!"/n/n"So the part of his soul that was in me ..."/n/nDumbledore nodded still more enthusiastically,/nurging Harry onward, a broad smile of encouragement/non his face./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"... has it gone?"/n/n/n/n"Oh yes!" said Dumbledore. "Yes, he destroyed it./n/nYour soul is whole, and completely your own, Harry."/n/n"But then ..."/n/nHarry glanced over his shoulder to where the small,/nmaimed creature trembled under the chair./n/n"What is that, Professor?"/n/n"Something that is beyond either of our help," said/nDumbledore./n/n"But if Voldemort used the Killing Curse," Harry/nstarted again, "and nobody died for me this time —/nhow can I be alive?"/n/n"I think you know," said Dumbledore. If it was indeed a palace in which they/nsat, it was an odd one, with chairs set in little rows/nand bits of railing here and there, and still, he and/nDumbledore and the stunted creature under the chair/nwere the only beings there. Then the answer rose to/nhis lips easily, without effort./n/n"He took my blood," said Harry./n/n"Precisely!" said Dumbledore. "He took your blood and/nrebuilt his living body with it! Your blood in his veins,/nHarry, Lily's protection inside both of you! He tethered/nyou to life while he lives!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I live . . . while he lives? But I thought ... I thought it/nwas the other way round! I thought we both had to/ndie? Or is it the same thing?"/n/nHe was distracted by the whimpering and thumping/nof the agonized creature behind them and glanced/nback at it yet again./n/n"Are you sure we can't do anything?"/n/n"There is no help possible."/n/n"Then explain ... more," said Harry, and Dumbledore/nsmiled./n/n"You were the seventh Horcrux, Harry, the Horcrux/nhe never meant to make. He had rendered his soul so/nunstable that it broke apart when he committed those/nacts of unspeakable evil, the murder of your parents,/nthe attempted killing of a child. But what escaped/nfrom that room was even less than he knew. He left/nmore than his body behind. He left part of himself/nlatched to you, the would-be victim who had survived./n/n"And his knowledge remained woefully incomplete,/nHarry! That which Voldemort does not value, he takes/nno trouble to comprehend. Of house-elves and/nchildren's tales, of love, loyalty, and innocence,/nVoldemort knows and understands nothing. Nothing./nThat they all have a power beyond his own, a power/nbeyond the reach of any magic, is a truth he has/nnever grasped./n/n"He took your blood believing it would strengthen/nhim. He took into his body a tiny part of the/nenchantment your mother laid upon you when she/ndied for you. His body keeps her sacrifice alive, and/nwhile that enchantment survives, so do you and so/ndoes Voldemort's one last hope for himself."/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore smiled at Harry, and Harry stared at/nhim./n/n/n/n"And you knew this? You knew — all along?"/n/n"I guessed. But my guesses have usually been good,"/nsaid Dumbledore happily, and they sat in silence for/nwhat seemed like a long time, while the creature/nbehind them continued to whimper and tremble./n/n"There's more," said Harry. "There's more to it. Why/ndid my wand break the wand he borrowed?"/n/n"As to that, I cannot be sure."/n/n"Have a guess, then," said Harry, and Dumbledore/nlaughed./n/n"What you must understand, Harry, is that you and/nLord Voldemort have journeyed together into realms/nof magic hitherto unknown and untested. But here is/nwhat I think happened, and it is unprecedented, and/nno wandmaker could, I think, ever have predicted it/nor explained it to Voldemort./n/n"Without meaning to, as you now know, Lord/nVoldemort doubled the bond between you when he/nreturned to a human form. But then,/nif he had been able to understand, he could not be/nLord Voldemort, and might never have murdered at/nall./n/n"Having ensured this two-fold connection, having/nwrapped your destinies together more securely than/n/n/n/n/n/never two wizards were joined in history, Voldemort/nproceeded to attack you with a wand that shared a/ncore with yours. And now something very strange/nhappened, as we know. The cores reacted in a way/nthat Lord Voldemort, who never knew that your wand/nwas twin of his, had never expected./n/n"He was more afraid than you were that night, Harry./nYou had accepted, even embraced, the possibility of/ndeath, something Lord Voldemort has never been able/nto do. Your/nwand now contained the power of your enormous/ncourage and of Voldemort's own deadly skill: What/nchance did that poor stick of Lucius Malfoy's stand?"/n/n"But if my wand was so powerful, how come/nHermione was able to break it?" asked Harry./n/n"My dear boy, its remarkable effects were directed/nonly at Voldemort, who had tampered so ill-advisedly/nwith the deepest laws of magic. Only toward him was/nthat wand abnormally powerful. Otherwise it was a/nwand like any other ... though a good one, I am sure,"/nDumbledore finished kindly./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHarry sat in thought for a long time, or perhaps/nseconds. It was very hard to be sure of things like/ntime, here./n/n"He killed me with your wand."/n/n"He failed to kill you with my wand," Dumbledore/ncorrected Harry. "I think we can agree that you are/nnot dead — though, of course," he added, as if fearing/nhe had been discourteous, "I do not minimize your/nsufferings, which I am sure were severe."/n/n"I feel great at the moment, though," said Harry,/nlooking down at his clean, unblemished hands./n"Where are we, exactly?"/n/n"Well, I was going to ask you that," said Dumbledore,/nlooking around. "Where would you say that we are?"/n/nUntil Dumbledore had asked, Harry had not known./nNow, however, he found that he had an answer ready/nto give./n/n"It looks," he said slowly, "like King's Cross station./nExcept a lot cleaner and empty, and there are no/ntrains as far as I can see."/n/n"King's Cross station!" Dumbledore was chuckling/nimmoderately. "Good gracious, really?"/n/n"Well, where do you think we are?" asked Harry, a/nlittle defensively./n/n"My dear boy, I have no idea. This is, as they say,/nyour party."/n/nHarry had no idea what this meant; Dumbledore was/nbeing infuriating. He glared at him, then remembered/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/na much more pressing question than that of their/ncurrent location./n/n"The Deathly Hallows," he said, and he was glad to/nsee that the words wiped the smile from/nDumbledore's face./n/n"Ah, yes," he said. He even looked a little worried./n"Well?"/n/nFor the first time since Harry had met Dumbledore,/nhe looked less than an old man, much less. He looked/nfleetingly like a small boy caught in wrongdoing./n/n"Can you forgive me?" he said. "Can you forgive me/nfor not trusting you? For not telling you? Harry, I only/nfeared that you would fail as I had failed. I only/ndreaded that you would make my mistakes. I crave/nyour pardon, Harry. I have known, for some time now,/nthat you are the better man."/n/n"What are you talking about?" asked Harry, startled/nby Dumbledore's tone, by the sudden tears in his/neyes./n/n"The Hallows, the Hallows," murmured Dumbledore./n"A desperate man's dream!"/n/n"But they're real!"/n/n"Real, and dangerous, and a lure for fools," said/nDumbledore. "And I was such a fool. But you know,/ndon't you? I have no secrets from you anymore. You/nknow."/n/n"What do I know?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore turned his whole body to face Harry, and/ntears still sparkled in the brilliantly blue eyes./n/n/n/n"Master of death, Harry, master of Death! Was I/nbetter, ultimately, than Voldemort?"/n/n"Of course you were," said Harry. "Of course — how/ncan you ask that? You never killed if you could avoid/nit!"/n/n/n/n"True, true," said Dumbledore, and he was like a/nchild seeking reassurance. "Yet I too sought a way to/nconquer death, Harry."/n/n"Not the way he did," said Harry. After all his anger at/nDumbledore, how odd it was to sit here, beneath the/nhigh, vaulted ceiling, and defend Dumbledore from/nhimself. "Hallows, not Horcruxes."/n/n"Hallows," murmured Dumbledore, "not Horcruxes./nPrecisely."/n/nThere was a pause. The creature behind them/nwhimpered, but Harry no longer looked around./n/n"Grindelwald was looking for them too?" he asked./n/nDumbledore closed his eyes for a moment and/nnodded./n/n"It was the thing, above all, that drew us together," he/nsaid quietly. "Two clever, arrogant boys with a shared/nobsession. He wanted to come to Godric's Hollow, as I/nam sure you have guessed, because of the grave of/nIgnotus Peverell. He wanted to explore the place the/nthird brother had died."/n/n"So it's true?" asked Harry. "All of it? The Peverell/nbrothers — "/n/n/n/n/n/n" — were the three brothers of the tale," said/nDumbledore, nodding. "Oh yes, I think so. Whether/nthey met Death on a lonely road ... I think it more/nlikely that the Peverell brothers were simply gifted,/ndangerous wizards who succeeded in creating those/npowerful objects. The story of them being Death's own/nHallows seems to me the sort of legend that might/nhave sprung up around such creations./n/n"The Cloak, as you know now, traveled down through/nthe ages, father to son, mother to daughter, right/ndown to Ignotus's last living descendant, who was/nborn, as Ignotus was, in the village of Godric's/nHollow."/n/nDumbledore smiled at Harry./n/n"Me?"/n/n"You. You have guessed, I know, why the Cloak was/nin my possession on the night your parents died./nJames had showed it to me just a few days/npreviously. It explained much of his undetected/nwrong-doing at school! I could hardly believe what I/nwas seeing. I asked to borrow it, to examine it. I had/nlong since given up my dream of uniting the Hallows,/nbut I could not resist, could not help taking a closer/nlook. ... It was a Cloak the likes of which I had never/nseen, immensely old, perfect in every respect . . . and/nthen your father died, and I had two Hallows at last,/nall to myself!"/n/nHis tone was unbearably bitter./n/n"The Cloak wouldn't have helped them survive,/nthough," Harry said quickly. "Voldemort knew where/nmy mum and dad were. The Cloak couldn't have/nmade them curse-proof."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"True," sighed Dumbledore. "True."/n/n/n/nHarry waited, but Dumbledore did not speak, so he/nprompted him./n/n"So you'd given up looking for the Hallows when you/nsaw the Cloak?"/n/n"Oh yes," said Dumbledore faintly. It seemed that he/nforced himself to meet Harry's eyes. "You know what/nhappened. You know. You cannot despise me more/nthan I despise myself."/n/n"But I don't despise you — "/n/n"Then you should," said Dumbledore. He drew a deep/nbreath. "You know the secret of my sister's ill health,/nwhat those Muggles did, what she became. You know/nhow my poor father sought revenge, and paid the/nprice, died in Azkaban. You know how my mother/ngave up her own life to care for Ariana./n/n"I resented it, Harry."/n/nDumbledore stated it baldly, coldly. He was looking/nnow over the top of Harry's head, into the distance./n/n"I was gifted, I was brilliant. I wanted to escape. I/nwanted to shine. I wanted glory./n/n"Do not misunderstand me," he said, and pain/ncrossed the face so that he looked ancient again. "I/nloved them. I loved my parents, I loved my brother/nand my sister, but I was selfish, Harry, more selfish/nthan you, who are a remarkably selfless person, could/npossibly imagine./n/n"So that, when my mother died, and I was left the/nresponsibility of a damaged sister and a wayward/n/n/n/n/n/nbrother, I returned to my village in anger and/nbitterness. Trapped and wasted, I thought! And then,/nof course, he came. ..."/n/nDumbledore looked directly into Harry's eyes again./n/n"Grindelwald. You cannot imagine how his ideas/ncaught me, Harry, inflamed me. Muggles forced into/nsubservience. We wizards triumphant. Grindelwald/nand I, the glorious young leaders of the revolution./n/n"Oh, I had a few scruples. I assuaged my conscience/nwith empty words. It would all be for the greater good,/nand any harm done would be repaid a hundredfold in/nbenefits for wizards. Did I know, in my heart of/nhearts, what Gellert Grindelwald was? I think I did,/nbut I closed my eyes. If the plans we were making/ncame to fruition, all my dreams would come true./n/n"And at the heart of our schemes, the Deathly/nHallows! How they fascinated him, how they/nfascinated both of us! The unbeatable wand, the/nweapon that would lead us to power! The/nResurrection Stone — to him, though I pretended not/nto know it, it meant an army of Inferi! To me, I/nconfess, it meant the return of my parents, and the/nlifting of all responsibility from my shoulders./n/n"And the Cloak ... somehow, we never discussed the/nCloak much, Harry. Both of us could conceal/nourselves well enough without the Cloak, the true/nmagic of which, of course, is that it can be used to/nprotect and shield others as well as its owner. I/nthought that, if we ever found it, it might be useful in/nhiding Ariana, but our interest in the Cloak was/nmainly that it completed the trio, for the legend said/nthat the man who united all three objects would then/nbe truly master of death, which we took to mean/n'invincible.'/n/n/n/n/n/n"Invincible masters of death, Grindelwald and/nDumbledore! Two months of insanity, of cruel/ndreams, and neglect of the only two members of my/nfamily left to me./n/n"And then ... you know what happened. Reality/nreturned in the form of my rough, unlettered, and/ninfinitely more admirable brother. I did not want to/nhear the truths he shouted at me. I did not want to/nhear that I could not set forth to seek Hallows with a/nfragile and unstable sister in tow./n/n"The argument became a fight. Grindelwald lost/ncontrol. That which I had always sensed in him,/nthough I pretended not to, now sprang into terrible/nbeing. And Ariana . . . after all my mother's care and/ncaution ... lay dead upon the floor."/n/nDumbledore gave a little gasp and began to cry in/nearnest. Harry reached out and was glad to find that/nhe could touch him: He gripped his arm tightly and/nDumbledore gradually regained control./n/n"Well, Grindelwald fled, as anyone but I could have/npredicted. He vanished, with his plans for seizing/npower, and his schemes for Muggle torture, and his/ndreams of the Deathly Hallows, dreams in which I/nhad encouraged him and helped him. He ran, while I/nwas left to bury my sister, and learn to live with my/nguilt and my terrible grief, the price of my shame./n/n"Years passed. There were rumors about him. They/nsaid he had procured a wand of immense power. I,/nmeanwhile, was offered the post of Minister of Magic,/nnot once, but several times. Naturally, I refused. I had/nlearned that I was not to be trusted with power."/n/n"But you'd have been better, much better, than Fudge/nor Scrimgeour!" burst out Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n"Would I?" asked Dumbledore heavily. "I am not so/nsure. I had proven, as a very young man, that power/nwas my weakness and my temptation. It is a curious/nthing, Harry, but perhaps those who are best suited/nto power are those who have never sought it. Those/nwho, like you, have leadership thrust upon them, and/ntake up the mantle because they must, and find to/ntheir own surprise that they wear it well./n/n"I was safer at Hogwarts. I think I was a good teacher/n/n/n/n"You were the best — "/n/n" — you are very kind, Harry. But while I busied/nmyself with the training of young wizards,/n/nGrindelwald was raising an army. They say he feared/nme, and perhaps he did, but less, I think, than I/nfeared him./n/n"Oh, not death," said Dumbledore, in answer to/nHarry's questioning look. "Not what he could do to me/nmagically. I knew that we were evenly matched,/nperhaps that I was a shade more skillful. It was the/ntruth I feared. You see, I never knew which of us, in/nthat last, horrific fight, had actually cast the curse/nthat killed my sister. You may call me cowardly: You/nwould be right. Harry, I dreaded beyond all things the/nknowledge that it had been I who brought about her/ndeath, not merely through my arrogance and/nstupidity, but that I actually struck the blow that/nsnuffed out her life./n/n"I think he knew it, I think he knew what frightened/nme. I delayed meeting him until finally, it would have/nbeen too shameful to resist any longer. People were/ndying and he seemed unstoppable, and I had to do/nwhat I could./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"Well, you know what happened next. I won the duel./n/nI won the wand."/n/nAnother silence. Harry did not ask whether/nDumbledore had ever found out who struck Ariana/ndead. He did not want to know, and even less did he/nwant Dumbledore to have to tell him. At last he knew/nwhat Dumbledore would have seen when he looked in/nthe Mirror of Erised, and why Dumbledore had been/nso understanding of the fascination it had exercised/nover Harry./n/nThey sat in silence for a long time, and the/nwhimperings of the creature behind them barely/ndisturbed Harry anymore./n/nAt last he said, "Grindelwald tried to stop Voldemort/ngoing after the wand. He lied, you know, pretended he/nhad never had it."/n/nDumbledore nodded, looking down at his lap, tears/nstill glittering on the crooked nose./n/n"They say he showed remorse in later years, alone in/nhis cell at Nurmengard. I hope that it is true. I would/nlike to think he did feel the horror and shame of what/nhe had done. Perhaps that lie to Voldemort was his/nattempt to make amends ... to prevent Voldemort/nfrom taking the Hallow ..."/n/n"... or maybe from breaking into your tomb?"/nsuggested Harry, and Dumbledore dabbed his eyes./n/nAfter another short pause Harry said, "You tried to/nuse the Resurrection Stone."/n/nDumbledore nodded./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"When I discovered it, after all those years, buried in/nthe abandoned home of the Gaunts — the Hallow I/nhad craved most of all, though in my youth I had/nwanted it for very different reasons — I lost my head,/nHarry. I quite forgot that it was now a Horcrux, that/nthe ring was sure to carry a curse. I picked it up, and/nI put it on, and for a second I imagined that I was/nabout to see Ariana, and my mother, and my father,/nand to tell them how very, very sorry I was. .../n/n"I was such a fool, Harry. After all those years I had/nlearned nothing. I was unworthy to unite the Deathly/nHallows, I had proved it time and again, and here was/nfinal proof."/n/n"Why?" said Harry. "It was natural! You wanted to see/nthem again. What's wrong with that?"/n/n"Maybe a man in a million could unite the Hallows,/nHarry. I was fit only to possess the meanest of them,/nthe least extraordinary. I was fit to own the Elder/nWand, and not to boast of it, and not to kill with it. I/nwas permitted to tame and to use it, because I took it,/nnot for gain, but to save others from it./n/n"But the Cloak, I took out of vain curiosity, and so it/ncould never have worked for me as it works for you,/nits true owner. The stone I would have used in an/nattempt to drag back those who are at peace, rather/nthan to enable my self-sacrifice, as you did. You are/nthe worthy possessor of the Hallows."/n/nDumbledore patted Harry's hand, and Harry looked/nup at the old man and smiled; he could not help/nhimself. How could he remain angry with Dumbledore/nnow?/n/n"Why did you have to make it so difficult?"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nDumbledore's smile was tremulous./n/n/n/n"I am afraid I counted on Miss Granger to slow you/nup, Harry. I was afraid that your hot head might/ndominate your good heart. I was scared that, if/npresented outright with the facts about those/ntempting objects, you might seize the Hallows as I/ndid, at the wrong time, for the wrong reasons. If you/nlaid hands on them, I wanted you to possess them/nsafely. You are the true master of death, because the/ntrue master does not seek to run away from Death./n/nHe accepts that he must die, and understands that/nthere are far, far worse things in the living world than/ndying."/n/n"And Voldemort never knew about the Hallows?"/n/n"I do not think so, because he did not recognize the/nResurrection Stone he turned into a Horcrux. But/neven if he had known about them, Harry, I doubt that/nhe would have been interested in any except the first./nHe would not think that he needed the Cloak, and as/nfor the stone, whom would he want to bring back/nfrom the dead? He fears the dead. He does not love."/n/n"But you expected him to go after the wand?"/n/n"I have been sure that he would try, ever since your/nwand beat Voldemort's in the graveyard of Little/nHangleton. At first, he was afraid that you had/nconquered him by superior skill. Once he had/nkidnapped Ollivander, however, he discovered the/nexistence of the twin cores. He thought that explained/neverything. Yet the borrowed wand did no better/nagainst yours! So Voldemort, instead of asking/nhimself what quality it was in you that had made your/nwand so strong, what gift you possessed that he did/nnot, naturally set out to find the one wand that, they/nsaid, would beat any other. For him, the Elder Wand/n/n/n/n/nhas become an obsession to rival his obsession with/nyou. He believes that the Elder Wand removes his last/nweakness and makes him truly invincible. Poor/nSeverus ..."/n/n"If you planned your death with Snape, you meant/nhim to end up with the Elder Wand, didn't you?"/n/n"I admit that was my intention," said Dumbledore,/n"but it did not work as I intended, did it?"/n/n"No," said Harry. "That bit didn't work out."/n/nThe creature behind them jerked and moaned, and/nHarry and Dumbledore sat without talking for the/nlongest time yet. The realization of what would/nhappen next settled gradually over Harry in the long/nminutes, like softly falling snow./n/n"I've got to go back, haven't I?"/n/n"That is up to you."/n/n"I've got a choice?"/n/n"Oh yes." Dumbledore smiled at him. "We are in/nKing's Cross, you say? I think that if you decided not/nto go back, you would be able to ... let's say ... board/na train."/n/n"And where would it take me?"/n/n"On," said Dumbledore simply./n/nSilence again./n/n"Voldemort's got the Elder Wand."/n/n"True. Voldemort has the Elder Wand."/n/n/n/n/n/n"But you want me to go back?"/n/n"I think," said Dumbledore, "that if you choose to/nreturn, there is a chance that he may be finished for/ngood. I cannot promise it. But I know this, Harry, that/nyou have less to fear from returning here than he/ndoes."/n/nHarry glanced again at the raw-looking thing that/ntrembled and choked in the shadow beneath the/ndistant chair./n/n"Do not pity the dead, Harry. Pity the living, and,/nabove all, those who live without love. By returning,/nyou may ensure that fewer souls are maimed, fewer/nfamilies are torn apart. If that seems to you a worthy/ngoal, then we say good-bye for the present."/n/nHarry nodded and sighed. Leaving this place would/nnot be nearly as hard as walking into the forest had/nbeen, but it was warm and light and peaceful here,/nand he knew that he was heading back to pain and/nthe fear of more loss. He stood up, and Dumbledore/ndid the same, and they looked for a long moment into/neach other's faces./n/n"Tell me one last thing," said Harry. "Is this real? Or/nhas this been happening inside my head?"/n/nDumbledore beamed at him, and his voice sounded/nloud and strong in Harry's ears even though the/nbright mist was descending again, obscuring his/nfigure./n/n"Of course it is happening inside your head, Harry,/nbut why on earth should that mean that it is not/nreal?" */n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n

title: The Flaw In The Plan
text: /nHe was lying facedown on the ground again. The/nsmell of the forest filled his nostrils. He could feel the/ncold hard ground beneath his cheek, and the hinge of/nhis glasses, which had been knocked sideways by the/nfall, cutting into his temple. Every inch of him ached,/nand the place where the Killing Curse had hit him felt/nlike the bruise of an iron-clad punch. You/nshould have realized," he said as he saw Voldemort's/nnostrils flare, "he asked you to spare her life, didn't/nhe?"/n/n"He desired her, that was all," sneered Voldemort,/n/n"but when she had gone, he agreed that there were/nother women, and of purer blood, worthier of him — "/n/n"Of course he told you that," said Harry, "but he was/nDumbledore's spy from the moment you threatened/nher, and he's been working against you ever since!/nDumbledore was already dying when Snape finished/nhim!"/n/n"It matters not!" shrieked Voldemort, who had/nfollowed every word with rapt attention, but now let/nout a cackle of mad laughter. "It matters not whether/nSnape was mine or Dumbledore's, or what petty/nobstacles they tried to put in my path! I crushed them/n/n/n/n/nas I crushed your mother, Snape 's supposed great/nlove\ Oh, but it all makes sense, Potter, and in ways/nthat you do not understand!/n/n"Dumbledore was trying to keep the Elder Wand from/nme! He intended that Snape should be the true/nmaster of the wand! But I got there ahead of you, little/nboy — I reached the wand before you could get your/nhands on it, I understood the truth before you caught/nup. I killed Severus Snape three hours ago, and the/nElder Wand, the Deathstick, the Wand of Destiny is/ntruly mine! Dumbledore 's last plan went wrong, Harry/nPotter!"/n/n"Yeah, it did," said Harry. "You're right. But before/nyou try to kill me, I'd advise you to think about what/nyou've done. ... Think, and try for some remorse,/nRiddle. ..."/n/n"What is this?"/n/nOf all the things that Harry had said to him, beyond/nany revelation or taunt, nothing had shocked/nVoldemort like this. Harry saw his pupils contract to/nthin slits, saw the skin around his eyes whiten./n/n"It's your one last chance," said Harry, "it's all you've/ngot left. ... I've seen what you'll be otherwise. ... Be a/nman ... try ... Try for some remorse. ..."/n/n"You dare — ?" said Voldemort again./n/n"Yes, I dare," said Harry, "because Dumbledore's last/nplan hasn't backfired on me at all. It's backfired on/nyou, Riddle."/n/nVoldemort's hand was trembling on the Elder Wand,/nand Harry gripped Draco's very tightly. The moment,/nhe knew, was seconds away./n/n/n/n/n/n"That wand still isn't working properly for you/nbecause you murdered the wrong person. Severus/nSnape was never the true master of the Elder Wand./nHe never defeated Dumbledore."/n/n"He killed — "/n/n"Aren't you listening? Snape never beat Dumbledorel/nDumbledore's death was planned between them!/nDumbledore intended to die undefeated, the wand's/nlast true master! If all had gone as planned, the/nwand's power would have died with him, because it/nhad never been won from him!"/n/n"But then, Potter, Dumbledore as good as gave me the/nwand!" Voldemort's voice shook with malicious/npleasure. "I stole the wand from its last master's/ntomb! I removed it against its last master's wishes! Its/npower is mine!"/n/n"You still don't get it, Riddle, do you? Possessing the/nwand isn't enough! Holding it, using it, doesn't make/nit really yours. Didn't you listen to Ollivander? The/nwand chooses the wizard. ... The Elder Wand/nrecognized a new master before Dumbledore died,/nsomeone who never even laid a hand on it. The new/nmaster removed the wand from Dumbledore against/nhis will, never realizing exactly what he had done, or/nthat the world's most dangerous wand had given him/nits allegiance. ..."/n/nVoldemort's chest rose and fell rapidly, and Harry/ncould feel the curse coming, feel it building inside the/nwand pointed at his face./n/n"The true master of the Elder Wand was Draco/nMalfoy."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBlank shock showed in Voldemort's face for a/nmoment, but then it was gone./n/n"But what does it matter?" he said softly. "Even if you/nare right, Potter, it makes no difference to you and/nme. You no longer have the phoenix wand: We duel/non skill alone ... and after I have killed you, I can/nattend to Draco Malfoy. ..."/n/n"But you're too late," said Harry. "You've missed your/nchance. I got there first. I overpowered Draco weeks/nago. I took this wand from him."/n/nHarry twitched the hawthorn wand, and he felt the/neyes of everyone in the Hall upon it./n/n"So it all comes down to this, doesn't it?" whispered/nHarry. "Does the wand in your hand know its last/nmaster was Disarmed? Because if it does ... I am the/ntrue master of the Elder Wand."/n/nA red-gold glow burst suddenly across the enchanted/nsky above them as an edge of dazzling sun appeared/nover the sill of the nearest window. The light hit both/nof their faces at the same time, so that Voldemort's/nwas suddenly a flaming blur. Harry heard the high/nvoice shriek as he too yelled his best hope to the/nheavens, pointing Draco's wand:/n/n"Avada KedavraV'/n/n" Expelliarmus\ "/n/nThe bang was like a cannon blast, and the golden/nflames that erupted between them, at the dead center/nof the circle they had been treading, marked the point/nwhere the spells collided. Harry saw Voldemort's/ngreen jet meet his own spell, saw the Elder Wand fly/nhigh, dark against the sunrise, spinning across the/n/n/n/n/nenchanted ceiling like the head of Nagini, spinning/nthrough the air toward the master it would not kill,/nwho had come to take full possession of it at last. And/nHarry, with the unerring skill of the Seeker, caught/nthe wand in his free hand as Voldemort fell backward,/narms splayed, the slit pupils of the scarlet eyes rolling/nupward. Tom Riddle hit the floor with a mundane/nfinality, his body feeble and shrunken, the white/nhands empty, the snakelike face vacant and/nunknowing. Voldemort was dead, killed by his own/nrebounding curse, and Harry stood with two wands in/nhis hand, staring down at his enemy's shell./n/nOne shivering second of silence, the shock of the/nmoment suspended: and then the tumult broke/naround Harry as the screams and the cheers and the/nroars of the watchers rent the air. The fierce new sun/ndazzled the windows as they thundered toward him,/nand the first to reach him were Ron and Hermione,/nand it was their arms that were wrapped around him,/ntheir incomprehensible shouts that deafened him./nThen Ginny, Neville, and Luna were there, and then/nall the Weasleys and Hagrid, and Kingsley and/nMcGonagall and Flitwick and Sprout, and Harry could/nnot hear a word that anyone was shouting, nor tell/nwhose hands were seizing him, pulling him, trying to/nhug some part of him, hundreds of them pressing in,/nall of them determined to touch the Boy Who Lived,/nthe reason it was over at last —/n/nThe sun rose steadily over Hogwarts, and the Great/nHall blazed with life and light. Harry was an/nindispensable part of the mingled outpourings of/njubilation and mourning, of grief and celebration./n/nThey wanted him there with them, their leader and/nsymbol, their savior and their guide, and that he had/nnot slept, that he craved the company of only a few of/nthem, seemed to occur to no one. He must speak to/nthe bereaved, clasp their hands, witness their tears,/n/n/n/n/nreceive their thanks, hear the news now creeping in/nfrom every quarter as the morning drew on; that the/nImperiused up and down the country had come back/nto themselves, that Death Eaters were fleeing or else/nbeing captured, that the innocent of Azkaban were/nbeing released at that very moment, and that Kingsley/nShacklebolt had been named temporary Minister of/nMagic. .../n/nThey moved Voldemort's body and laid it in a/nchamber off the Hall, away from the bodies of Fred,/nTonks, Lupin, Colin Creevey, and fifty others who had/ndied fighting him. McGonagall had replaced the/nHouse tables, but nobody was sitting according to/nHouse anymore: All were jumbled together, teachers/nand pupils, ghosts and parents, centaurs and house-/nelves, and Firenze lay recovering in a corner, and/nGrawp peered in through a smashed window, and/npeople were throwing food into his laughing mouth./nAfter a while, exhausted and drained, Harry found/nhimself sitting on a bench beside Luna./n/n"I'd want some peace and quiet, if it were me," she/nsaid./n/n"I'd love some," he replied./n/n"I'll distract them all," she said. "Use your Cloak."/n/nAnd before he could say a word she had cried, "Oooh,/nlook, a Blibbering Humdinger!" and pointed out of the/nwindow. Everyone who heard looked around, and/nHarry slid the Cloak up over himself, and got to his/nfeet./n/nNow he could move through the Hall without/ninterference. He spotted Ginny two tables away; she/nwas sitting with her head on her mother's shoulder:/nThere would be time to talk later, hours and days and/n/n/n/n/n/nmaybe years in which to talk. He saw Neville, the/nsword of Gryffindor lying beside his plate as he ate,/nsurrounded by a knot of fervent admirers. Along the/naisle between the tables he walked, and he spotted/nthe three Malfoys, huddled together as though unsure/nwhether or not they were supposed to be there, but/nnobody was paying them any attention. Everywhere/nhe looked he saw families reunited, and finally, he/nsaw the two whose company he craved most./n/n"It's me," he muttered, crouching down between/nthem. "Will you come with me?"/n/nThey stood up at once, and together he, Ron, and/nHermione left the Great Hall. Great chunks were/nmissing from the marble staircase, part of the/nbalustrade gone, and rubble and bloodstains/noccurred every few steps as they climbed./n/nSomewhere in the distance they could hear Peeves/nzooming through the corridors singing a victory song/nof his own composition:/n/nWe did it, we bashed them, wee Potter's the one,/n/nAnd Voldy's gone moldy, so now let's have fun!/n/n"Really gives a feeling for the scope and tragedy of the/nthing, doesn't it?" said Ron, pushing open a door to/nlet Harry and Hermione through./n/nHappiness would come, Harry thought, but at the/nmoment it was muffled by exhaustion, and the pain of/nlosing Fred and Lupin and Tonks pierced him like a/nphysical wound every few steps. Most of all he felt the/nmost stupendous relief, and a longing to sleep. But/nfirst he owed an explanation to Ron and Hermione,/nwho had stuck with him for so long, and who/ndeserved the truth. Painstakingly he recounted what/n/n/n/n/nhe had seen in the Pensieve and what had happened/nin the forest, and they had not even begun to express/nall their shock and amazement when at last they/narrived at the place to which they had been walking,/nthough none of them had mentioned their/ndestination./n/nSince he had last seen it, the gargoyle guarding the/nentrance to the headmaster's study had been knocked/naside; it stood lopsided, looking a little punch-drunk,/nand Harry wondered whether it would be able to/ndistinguish passwords anymore./n/n"Can we go up?" he asked the gargoyle./n/n"Feel free," groaned the statue./n/nThey clambered over him and onto the spiral stone/nstaircase that moved slowly upward like an escalator./nHarry pushed open the door at the top./n/nHe had one, brief glimpse of the stone Pensieve on the/ndesk where he had left it, and then an earsplitting/nnoise made him cry out, thinking of curses and/nreturning Death Eaters and the rebirth of Voldemort/n/n/n/nBut it was applause. All around the walls, the/nheadmasters and headmistresses of Hogwarts were/ngiving him a standing ovation; they waved their hats/nand in some cases their wigs, they reached through/ntheir frames to grip each other's hands; they danced/nup and down on the chairs in which they had been/npainted; Dilys Derwent sobbed unashamedly; Dexter/nFortescue was waving his ear-trumpet; and Phineas/nNigellus called, in his high, reedy voice, "And let it be/nnoted that Slytherin House played its part! Let our/ncontribution not be forgotten!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBut Harry had eyes only for the man who stood in the/nlargest portrait directly behind the headmaster's/nchair. Tears were sliding down from behind the half-/nmoon spectacles into the long silver beard, and the/npride and the gratitude emanating from him filled/nHarry with the same balm as phoenix song./n/nAt last, Harry held up his hands, and the portraits fell/nrespectfully silent, beaming and mopping their eyes/nand waiting eagerly for him to speak. He directed his/nwords at Dumbledore, however, and chose them with/nenormous care. Exhausted and bleary-eyed though he/nwas, he must make one last effort, seeking one last/npiece of advice./n/n"The thing that was hidden in the Snitch," he began,/n/n"I dropped it in the forest. I don't know exactly where,/nbut I'm not going to go looking for it again. Do you/nagree?"/n/n"My dear boy, I do," said Dumbledore, while his fellow/npictures looked confused and curious. "A wise and/ncourageous decision, but no less than I would have/nexpected of you. Does anyone else know where it fell?"/n/n"No one," said Harry, and Dumbledore nodded his/nsatisfaction./n/n"I'm going to keep Ignotus's present, though," said/nHarry, and Dumbledore beamed./n/n"But of course, Harry, it is yours forever, until you/npass it on!"/n/n"And then there's this."/n/nHarry held up the Elder Wand, and Ron and/nHermione looked at it with a reverence that, even in/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nhis befuddled and sleep-deprived state, Harry did not/nlike to see./n/n"I don't want it," said Harry./n/n"What?" said Ron loudly. "Are you mental?"/n/n"I know it's powerful," said Harry wearily. "But I was/nhappier with mine. So ..."/n/nHe rummaged in the pouch hung around his neck,/nand pulled out the two halves of holly still just/nconnected by the finest thread of phoenix feather./nHermione had said that they could not be repaired,/nthat the damage was too severe. All he knew was that/nif this did not work, nothing would./n/nHe laid the broken wand upon the headmaster's desk,/ntouched it with the very tip of the Elder Wand, and/nsaid, "Reparo."/n/nAs his wand resealed, red sparks flew out of its end./nHarry knew that he had succeeded. He picked up the/nholly and phoenix wand and felt a sudden warmth in/nhis fingers, as though wand and hand were rejoicing/nat their reunion./n/n"I'm putting the Elder Wand," he told Dumbledore,/nwho was watching him with enormous affection and/nadmiration, "back where it came from. It can stay/nthere. If I die a natural death like Ignotus, its power/nwill be broken, won't it? The previous master will/nnever have been defeated. That'll be the end of it."/n/nDumbledore nodded. They smiled at each other./n/n"Are you sure?" said Ron. There was the faintest trace/nof longing in his voice as he looked at the Elder Wand./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I think Harry's right," said Hermione quietly./n/n"That wand's more trouble than it's worth," said/nHarry. "And quite honestly," he turned away from the/npainted portraits, thinking now only of the four-poster/nbed lying waiting for him in Gryffindor Tower, and/nwondering whether Kreacher might bring him a/nsandwich there, "I've had enough trouble for a/nlifetime."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nayue/n/n/n/n

title: Nineteen Years Later
text: /nAutumn seemed to arrive suddenly that year. The/nmorning of the first of September was crisp and/ngolden as an apple, and as the little family bobbed/nacross the rumbling road toward the great sooty/nstation, the fumes of car exhausts and the breath of/npedestrians sparkled like cobwebs in the cold air. Two/nlarge cages rattled on top of the laden trolleys the/nparents were pushing; the owls inside them hooted/nindignantly, and the redheaded girl trailed tearfully/nbehind her brothers, clutching her father's arm./n/n"It won't be long, and you'll be going too," Harry told/nher./n/n"Two years," sniffed Lily. "I want to go now\"/n/nThe commuters stared curiously at the owls as the/nfamily wove its way toward the barrier between/nplatforms nine and ten. Albus's voice drifted back to/nHarry over the surrounding clamor; his sons had/nresumed the argument they had started in the car./n/n/n/n/n/n/n"I won'ti I won't be in Slytherin!"/n/n"James, give it a rest!" said Ginny./n/n"I only said he might be," said James, grinning at his/nyounger brother. "There's nothing wrong with that. He/nmight be in Slyth — "/n/nBut James caught his mother's eye and fell silent./n/nThe five Potters approached the barrier. With a/nslightly cocky look over his shoulder at his younger/nbrother, James took the trolley from his mother and/nbroke into a run. A moment later, he had vanished./n/n"You'll write to me, won't you?" Albus asked his/nparents immediately, capitalizing on the momentary/nabsence of his brother./n/n"Every day, if you want us to," said Ginny./n/n"Not every day," said Albus quickly. "James says most/npeople only get letters from home about once a/nmonth."/n/n"We wrote to James three times a week last year,"/nsaid Ginny./n/n"And you don't want to believe everything he tells you/nabout Hogwarts," Harry put in. "He likes a laugh,/nyour brother."/n/nSide by side, they pushed the second trolley forward,/ngathering speed. As they reached the barrier, Albus/nwinced, but no collision came. Instead, the family/nemerged onto platform nine and three-quarters,/nwhich was obscured by thick white steam that was/npouring from the scarlet Hogwarts Express. Indistinct/nfigures were swarming through the mist, into which/nJames had already disappeared./n/n/n/n/n/n"Where are they?" asked Albus anxiously, peering at/nthe hazy forms they passed as they made their way/ndown the platform./n/n"Well find them," said Ginny reassuringly./n/nBut the vapor was dense, and it was difficult to make/nout anybody's faces. Detached from their owners,/nvoices sounded unnaturally loud. Harry thought he/nheard Percy discoursing loudly on broomstick/nregulations, and was quite glad of the excuse not to/nstop and say hello. .../n/n"I think that's them, Al," said Ginny suddenly./n/nA group of four people emerged from the mist,/nstanding alongside the very last carriage. Their faces/nonly came into focus when Harry, Ginny, Lily, and/nAlbus had drawn right up to them./n/n"Hi," said Albus, sounding immensely relieved./n/nRose, who was already wearing her brand-new/nHogwarts robes, beamed at him./n/n"Parked all right, then?" Ron asked Harry. "I did./nHermione didn't believe I could pass a Muggle driving/ntest, did you? She thought I'd have to Confund the/nexaminer."/n/n"No, I didn't," said Hermione, "I had complete faith in/nyou."/n/n"As a matter of fact, I did Confund him," Ron/nwhispered to Harry, as together they lifted Albus 's/ntrunk and owl onto the train. "I only forgot to look in/nthe wing mirror, and let's face it, I can use a/nSupersensory Charm for that."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nBack on the platform, they found Lily and Hugo,/nRose's younger brother, having an animated/ndiscussion about which House they would be sorted/ninto when they finally went to Hogwarts./n/n"If you're not in Gryffindor, we'll disinherit you," said/nRon, "but no pressure."/n/n"Ron\"/n/nLily and Hugo laughed, but Albus and Rose looked/nsolemn./n/n"He doesn't mean it," said Hermione and Ginny, but/nRon was no longer paying attention. Catching Harry's/neye, he nodded covertly to a point some fifty yards/naway. The steam had thinned for a moment, and/nthree people stood in sharp relief against the shifting/nmist./n/n"Look who it is."/n/nDraco Malfoy was standing there with his wife and/nson, a dark coat buttoned up to his throat. His hair/nwas receding somewhat, which emphasized the/npointed chin. The new boy resembled Draco as much/nas Albus resembled Harry. Draco caught sight of/nHarry, Ron, Hermione, and Ginny staring at him,/nnodded curtly, and turned away again./n/n"So that's little Scorpius," said Ron under his breath./n"Make sure you beat him in every test, Rosie. Thank/nGod you inherited your mother's brains."/n/n"Ron, for heaven's sake," said Hermione, half stern,/nhalf amused. "Don't try to turn them against each/nother before they've even started school!"/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/n"You're right, sorry," said Ron, but unable to help/nhimself, he added, "Don't get too friendly with him,/nthough, Rosie. Granddad Weasley would never forgive/nyou if you married a pureblood."/n/n"Hey!"/n/nJames had reappeared; he had divested himself of his/ntrunk, owl, and trolley, and was evidently bursting/nwith news./n/n"Teddy's back there," he said breathlessly, pointing/nback over his shoulder into the billowing clouds of/nsteam. "Just seen him! And guess what he's doing?/nSnogging Victoire\"/n/nHe gazed up at the adults, evidently disappointed by/nthe lack of reaction./n/n"Our Teddy! Teddy Lupin\ Snogging our Victoire! Our/ncousin! And I asked Teddy what he was doing — "/n/n"You interrupted them?" said Ginny. "You are so like/nRon — "/n/n" — and he said he'd come to see her off! And then he/ntold me to go away. He's snogging her!" James added/nas though worried he had not made himself clear./n/n"Oh, it would be lovely if they got married!" whispered/nLily ecstatically. "Teddy would really be part of the/nfamily then!"/n/n"He already comes round for dinner about four times/na week," said Harry. "Why don't we just invite him to/nlive with us and have done with it?"/n/n"Yeah!" said James enthusiastically. "I don't mind/nsharing with A1 — Teddy could have my room!"/n/n/n/n/n/n"No," said Harry firmly, "you and A1 will share a room/nonly when I want the house demolished."/n/nHe checked the battered old watch that had once/nbeen Fabian Prewett's./n/n"It's nearly eleven, you'd better get on board."/n/n"Don't forget to give Neville our love!" Ginny told/nJames as she hugged him./n/n"Mum! I can't give a professor love\"/n/n"But you know Neville — "/n/nJames rolled his eyes./n/n"Outside, yeah, but at school he's Professor/nLongbottom, isn't he? I can't walk into Herbology and/ngive him love. ..."/n/nShaking his head at his mother's foolishness, he/nvented his feelings by aiming a kick at Albus./n/n"See you later, Al. Watch out for the thestrals."/n/n"I thought they were invisible? You said they were/ninvisible !"/n/nBut James merely laughed, permitted his mother to/nkiss him, gave his father a fleeting hug, then leapt/nonto the rapidly filling train. They saw him wave, then/nsprint away up the corridor to find his friends./n/n"Thestrals are nothing to worry about," Harry told/nAlbus. "They're gentle things, there's nothing scary/nabout them. Anyway, you won't be going up to school/nin the carriages, you'll be going in the boats."/n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nGinny kissed Albus good-bye./n/n"See you at Christmas."/n/n"Bye, Al," said Harry as his son hugged him. "Don't/nforget Hagrid's invited you to tea next Friday. Don't/nmess with Peeves. Don't duel anyone till you've/nlearned how. And don't let James wind you up."/n/n"What if I'm in Slytherin?"/n/nThe whisper was for his father alone, and Harry knew/nthat only the moment of departure could have forced/nAlbus to reveal how great and sincere that fear was./n/nHarry crouched down so that Albus 's face was slightly/nabove his own. Alone of Harry's three children, Albus/nhad inherited Lily's eyes./n/n"Albus Severus," Harry said quietly, so that nobody/nbut Ginny could hear, and she was tactful enough to/npretend to be waving to Rose, who was now on the/ntrain, "you were named for two headmasters of/nHogwarts. One of them was a Slytherin and he was/nprobably the bravest man I ever knew."/n/n"But just say — "/n/n" — then Slytherin House will have gained an excellent/nstudent, won't it? It doesn't matter to us, Al. But if it/nmatters to you, you'll be able to choose Gryffindor/nover Slytherin. The Sorting Hat takes your choice into/naccount."/n/n"Really?"/n/n"It did for me," said Harry./n/n/n/n/n/n/n/nHe had never told any of his children that before, and/nhe saw the wonder in Albus's face when he said it./n/nBut now the doors were slamming all along the/nscarlet train, and the blurred outlines of parents were/nswarming forward for final kisses, last-minute/nreminders. Albus jumped into the carriage and Ginny/nclosed the door behind him. Students were hanging/nfrom the windows nearest them. A great number of/nfaces, both on the train and off, seemed to be turned/ntoward Harry./n/n"Why are they all staring?" demanded Albus as he/nand Rose craned around to look at the other/nstudents./n/n"Don't let it worry you," said Ron. "It's me. I'm/nextremely famous."/n/nAlbus, Rose, Hugo, and Lily laughed. The train began/nto move, and Harry walked alongside it, watching his/nson's thin face, already ablaze with excitement. Harry/nkept smiling and waving, even though it was like a/nlittle bereavement, watching his son glide away from/nhim. .../n/nThe last trace of steam evaporated in the autumn air./nThe train rounded a corner. Harry's hand was still/nraised in farewell./n/n"He'll be all right," murmured Ginny./n/nAs Harry looked at her, he lowered his hand/nabsentmindedly and touched the lightning scar on his/nforehead./n/n"I know he will."/n/nThe scar had not pained Harry for nineteen years. All/nwas well./n/n/n/n/n/n
